Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice ($\mathrm{DC}$). Let a common-space IVP
interface and bounded time-scheme family be given as in
[[def-common-space-linear-scheme-interface]]. If
the scheme is consistent on its dense invariant subspace, then it is
convergent on every finite time interval if and only if it is stable there,
with stability, consistency, and convergence all measured in the same norm
of $X$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Let $D$ be the finite-support sequences. By [F4], $D$ is dense in $X$; it is invariant under $U(t)$ because $U(t)$ multiplies coordinates and does not add support. The heat IVP and its finite-time bound are supplied by [F3].

Since $m=\nu+1$, $\tau_m=m^{-2}>0$ and $\tau_m\to0$ as $\nu\to\infty$. Let $P_m$ be truncation to coordinates $0,\ldots,m-1$ and $R_m$ inclusion. Their norms are at most $1$ by the coordinate supremum estimates and at least $1$ by testing $e_0$, so both have norm $1$ by [F7]. Also $P_mR_m=I_{G_m}$ and $\ker P_m$ is invariant under $U(\tau_m)$ because $U$ is diagonal. The finite maximum $L_m:=\max_{0\le j<m}|1-\tau_mj^2|$ bounds every diagonal multiplier, so $\|Q_mg\|_\infty\le L_m\|g\|_\infty$ and $Q_m$ is bounded. Thus [F2] defines the common-space step $S_m$.

For $j<m$, $0\le1-j^2/m^2\le1$; on coordinates $j\ge m$ the lift uses the multipliers $\exp(-j^2/m^2)\in(0,1]$ from [F3]. Hence every coordinate multiplier of $S_m$ lies in $[0,1]$. Therefore $\|S_mx\|_\infty\le \|x\|_\infty$ for every $x\in c_0$, and [F7] gives $\|S_m\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1$. The bound $\|S_m^n x\|_\infty\le\|x\|_\infty$ holds at $n=0$; if it holds at $n$, applying the contraction estimate to $S_m^nx$ proves it at $n+1$. Induction [F8] gives it for every $n$, and then [F7] gives $\|S_m^n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1$. The family is stable on every finite time interval.

Fix $v\in D$, supported in coordinates $0,\ldots,N$. For $m>N$, direct evaluation and $0<\exp(-r\tau_mj^2)\le1$ give $\max_{\substack{r\in\mathbb N\\r\tau_m\le T}}\frac{\|(S_m-U(\tau_m))U(r\tau_m)v\|_\infty}{\tau_m}\le\|v\|_\infty\max_{0\le j\le N}\frac{|1-\tau_mj^2-\exp(-\tau_mj^2)|}{\tau_m}.$ For $j=0$ the quotient is zero. Multiplication by the fixed $\|v\|_\infty$ preserves this limit. The bound is independent of $r$, so the family is consistent on $D$.
By [F6] and the explicit DC assumption [A1], this consistent stable family converges to the heat semigroup in the common supremum norm, uniformly over grid times in each bounded time interval.

linear IVP interface** consists of a Banach space $X$ over $\mathbb K$ and a
strongly continuous semigroup $U(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$, $t\ge0$, as defined in

each $T>0$ there is $M_T<\infty$ such that
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|U(t)\|\le M_T.$$
The solution with initial value $x\in X$ is $u(t)=U(t)x$. This definition
records the solution operators and their continuous dependence in the same
norm; it makes no claim about a generator domain.

A **consistency subspace** is a dense linear subspace $D\subseteq X$ satisfying
$U(t)D\subseteq D$ for every $t\ge0$. Here dense means
$\overline D^{\,X}=X$, and invariant means the displayed inclusion. It need
not be the domain of a differential generator.

A **common-space time-scheme family** is a sequence of positive time steps
$(\tau_\nu)_{\nu\in\mathbb N}$ with $\tau_\nu\to0$ and bounded linear maps
$S_\nu:X\to X$ in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. Write
$S_\nu^0=I_X$ and recursively set $S_\nu^{n+1}=S_\nu S_\nu^n$ for
$n\in\mathbb N$. All scheme and solution errors below
use the norm of this same space $X$; write $\|\cdot\|$ for that norm and
$\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ for the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm]].

The family is **consistent on $D$** when for every $x\in D$ and $T>0$,
$$\lim_{\nu\to\infty}\max_{\substack{r\in\mathbb N\\r\tau_\nu\le T}}\frac{\|(S_\nu-U(\tau_\nu))U(r\tau_\nu)x\|}{\tau_\nu}=0.$$
The maximum is over a nonempty finite set because it includes $r=0$. This is
the local defect divided by one time step, uniformly over the exact orbit on
the finite time interval.

The family is **stable on finite time intervals** when for every $T>0$ there
is $C_T<\infty$ such that
$$\|S_\nu^n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C_T\quad\text{whenever }\nu,n\in\mathbb N\text{ and }n\tau_\nu\le T.$$
It is **convergent on finite time intervals** when for every $x\in X$ and
$T>0$,
$$\lim_{\nu\to\infty}\max_{\substack{n\in\mathbb N\\n\tau_\nu\le T}}\|S_\nu^n x-U(n\tau_\nu)x\|=0.$$
The maximum convention includes time zero. This locally uniform-in-grid-time
convergence is the hypothesis used for the reverse implication in the
equivalence theorem below.

derivations.claim: Let $D$ be the finite-support sequences. It is dense by [F4] and invariant under the diagonal semigroup [F3]. Since $m=\nu+1$, $\tau_m=m^{-1}>0$ and $\tau_m\to0$. Then $P_mR_m=I$ and $\ker P_m$ is invariant under diagonal $U(\tau_m)$. The finite maximum $L_m:=\max_{0\le j<m}|1-\tau_mj^2|$ gives $\|Q_mg\|_\infty\le L_m\|g\|_\infty$, so $Q_m$ is bounded. For $m>N$, every supported coordinate is updated by $1-\tau_mj^2$; since $0<\exp(-r\tau_mj^2)\le1$, we have $\max_{\substack{r\in\mathbb N\\r\tau_m\le T}}\frac{\|(S_m-U(\tau_m))U(r\tau_m)v\|_\infty}{\tau_m}\le\|v\|_\infty\max_{0\le j\le N}\frac{|1-\tau_mj^2-\exp(-\tau_mj^2)|}{\tau_m}.$ For $j=0$ the quotient vanishes. On the highest grid mode $e_{m-1}$, the one-step multiplier is $1-\frac{(m-1)^2}{m}=3-m-\frac1m.$ For $m\ge4$ its magnitude is $m-3+1/m$, which tends to infinity. No uniform finite-time power bound can hold, so the family is unstable.

case and modulus $|a+ib|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ in the complex case. A scalar
sequence here is a function $x:\mathbb N\to\mathbb K$, including index zero. Let

$$\ell^\infty=\{x=(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}:\text{there is }C\ge0\text{ with }|x_n|\le C\text{ for all }n\},\qquad c_0=\{x\in\ell^\infty:x_n\to0\},$$

both equipped with $\|x\|_\infty=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}|x_n|$.  Thus $c_0$ is
a specified linear subspace of the bounded-sequence space $\ell^\infty$.

has a finite supremum by [[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]. This proves that
the displayed norm exists, rather than presuming existence in the definition
of boundedness. Its uniqueness requires no choice of supremum witnesses.

Here $x_n\to0$ means that for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there is

Addition and scalar multiplication are coordinatewise. The scalar triangle
inequality makes bounded sequences and null sequences linear spaces and gives
the triangle inequality for the displayed supremum norm. Absolute homogeneity
follows coordinatewise, and a zero supremum forces every coordinate to vanish.

For either scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, the space
$c_0(\mathbb K)$ with the supremum norm is a Banach space.  No choice
principle is used.

Let $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$. Use coordinates indexed by $\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}$. Define $\ell^1(\mathbb K)=\{a:\sum_{n=0}^\infty|a_n|<\infty\}$, with coordinatewise operations and norm $\|a\|_1=\sum_n|a_n|$. Let $P_N$ retain coordinates $0,\ldots,N$ and set all others to zero. Then $$\|x-P_Nx\|_\infty\longrightarrow0\quad(x\in c_0(\mathbb K)),\qquad\|a-P_Na\|_1\longrightarrow0\quad(a\in\ell^1(\mathbb K)).$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

derivations.claim: Let $D$ be the finite-support sequences. By [F4], $X$ is Banach; the identity maps $U(t)=I_X$ form a strongly continuous semigroup with finite-time bound $M_T=1$. By [F5], $D$ is dense and it is invariant under $U$. The positive steps $\tau_m=1/m$ tend to zero, so this is common-space scheme data.

The positive coordinate weights make the displayed maximum a norm: homogeneity and definiteness hold coordinatewise, and the triangle inequality follows by applying the scalar triangle inequality in every coordinate before taking the maximum. The truncation satisfies $\|P_mx\|_{G_m}\le m\|x\|_\infty$, and inclusion satisfies $\|R_mg\|_\infty\le\|g\|_{G_m}$, so both are bounded. Also $P_mR_m=I_{G_m}$ and $\ker P_m$ is invariant under $U=I$. For $g=\sum_{j<m}g_je_j$, the zeroth output coordinate is $g_0+mg_{m-1}$, coordinates $1$ through $m-2$ if present remain $g_j$, and coordinate $m-1$ becomes $0$. Since $|g_0|\le\|g\|_{G_m}$, $m|g_{m-1}|\le\|g\|_{G_m}$, and $|g_j|\le\|g\|_{G_m}$ for $1\le j\le m-2$, it follows that $\|Q_mg\|_{G_m}\le2\|g\|_{G_m}$, including $m=2$. Thus $Q_m$ is bounded and the grid lift [F2] is defined. Also $Q_m^2=Q_m$: it fixes each $e_j$ for $j<m-1$, and $Q_m^2e_{m-1}=Q_m(me_0)=me_0=Q_me_{m-1}$. By induction [F7], $Q_m^n=Q_m$ for every $n\ge1$: the base $n=1$ is immediate, and $Q_m^n=Q_m$ implies $Q_m^{n+1}=Q_mQ_m=Q_m^2=Q_m$. Meanwhile $Q_m^0=I$. By [F6], $\|Q_m^n\|_{G_m\to G_m}\le2$ for every $n\ge0$, so the grid updates are stable in their mesh norms.

Fix $v\in D$ and choose $N\in\mathbb N$ such that $v_j=0$ for every $j>N$ (take $N=0$ for the zero sequence). For $m\ge N+2$, one has $P_mv=v$, the high coordinate $v_{m-1}=0$ since $m-1>N$, and $Q_mv=v$. Since $U=I$, the lift gives $S_mv=v$. Thus the local defect is zero on every $v\in D$ for all sufficiently large $m$, which proves consistency.

For $e_{m-1}$, the lift gives $S_me_{m-1}=m e_0$. Its common-space norm is therefore $m$, while $\|e_{m-1}\|_\infty=1$. Testing this unit vector in [F6] gives $\|S_m\|_{X\to X}\ge m$. For every $T>0$, all sufficiently large $m$ have $\tau_m\le T$, so the common-space family is not stable.

The same vector satisfies $\|e_{m-1}\|_{G_m}=m$ but $\|R_me_{m-1}\|_\infty=1$; thus no positive uniform lower comparison constant $a$ exists. Also $\|P_m\|_{X\to G_m}\ge m$ by testing the unit vector $e_{m-1}$ in [F6]. The hypotheses needed in [F3] fail, exactly where the grid norm ceases to control the reconstructed common-space norm and the restriction norm. The grid stability calculation therefore cannot certify common-space stability.

$W\subseteq V$ be a normed subspace over that same field: use [[def-normed-subspace]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-normed-subspace]] for $\mathbb C$. If $W$ admits an ordered basis of finite

derivations.claim: Every $y\in K$ has a representation whose positive-coefficient vectors are linearly independent. Start with any nonnegative coefficient list and discard its zero coefficients. If its remaining vectors are dependent, take a nonzero relation $\sum_j c_j a_j=0$ and change its sign so some $c_j>0$. For the current positive coefficients $t_j$, put $s=\min_{c_j>0}t_j/c_j$. Replacing each $t_j$ by $t_j-sc_j$ preserves the represented vector, leaves every coefficient nonnegative, and makes at least one positive coefficient zero. Repeating at most $m$ times leaves an independent positive support.

Fix an independent index set $J$ and let $A_J$ have columns $a_j$, $j\in J$. Its Gram matrix $G_J=A_J^TA_J$ is invertible: for every nonzero $v$, $v^TG_Jv=\|A_Jv\|_2^2>0$ by independence. On the closed subspace $S_J=\operatorname{span}\{a_j:j\in J\}$, the map $R_J(y)=G_J^{-1}A_J^Ty$ is continuous and satisfies $A_JR_J(y)=y$. Hence $A_J(\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{|J|})= S_J\cap R_J^{-1}(\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{|J|})$ is closed: $S_J$ is closed by [F1], the nonnegative orthant is closed, and $R_J$ is continuous. For $J=\varnothing$ this cone is $\{0\}$, also closed.

By step 1.1, $K$ is the union of the cones in step 1.2 over independent subsets $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}$. There are only finitely many such subsets, so this union is closed. Each component is a convex cone, and directly taking nonnegative combinations shows $K$ is convex.

Let $f:U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ on an open set. For every natural $r$, the locus
$$U_{\ge r}:=\{x\in U:\operatorname{rank}Df(x)\ge r\}$$
is open. Thus $x\mapsto\operatorname{rank}Df(x)$ is lower semicontinuous. In particular the submersion locus, the immersion locus, and every locus on which the derivative has the largest possible rank are open.

Let $f:U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^k$, $k\ge1$, and let $c$ be a regular value. Near each point, a regular level set is a $C^k$ graph over $\ker Df(a)$ of dimension $m-n$.

More precisely, for $a\in f^{-1}(c)$ put $K=\ker Df(a)$ and $E=K^\perp$, so $\mathbb R^m=K\oplus E$. There are neighbourhoods $P\subseteq K$ of $0$ and $Q\subseteq E$ of $0$ and a $C^k$ map $g:P\to Q$ with $g(0)=0$ and $Dg(0)=0$ such that, near $a$,
$$f^{-1}(c)=\{a+u+g(u):u\in P\}.$$
The empty fibre satisfies the regular-value convention vacuously, and when $m=n$ the local graph has zero-dimensional domain and is the isolated point $a$.

For a $C^2$ scalar field near $a$,

$$f(a+h)=f(a)+\nabla f(a)\cdot h+\frac12\langle H_f(a)h,h\rangle+o(\|h\|^2).$$

derivations.claim: If $q=0$, then $H$ is the unique map into $\mathbb R^0$ and the level is all of $U$. The curve $\gamma(t)=x+td+\tfrac12t^2z$ has the required value and first two derivatives.

Now suppose $q>0$ and take the graph in [F1]. Put $v=D^2\psi(0)[d,d]$. Since $H(x+td+\psi(td))=H(x)$ for small $t$, [F2] and $\psi(td)=\tfrac12t^2v+o(t^2)$ give $DH(x)d=0$ and $DH(x)v+D^2H(x)[d,d]=0$.

The compatibility equation for $z$ and step 1.2 imply $e=z-v\in\ker DH(x)$. Define $u(t)=td+\tfrac12t^2e$ and $\gamma(t)=x+u(t)+\psi(u(t))$. This curve stays on $H=H(x)$ by [F1]. Using [F2] and $D\psi(0)=0$ gives $\gamma(t)=x+td+\tfrac12t^2(e+v)+o(t^2) =x+td+\tfrac12t^2z+o(t^2)$, so its first two derivatives at $0$ are $d$ and $z$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $x\in\mathbb R^n$. Then there is a unique $p\in C$ such that $\|x-p\|_2\le\|x-z\|_2$ for every $z\in C$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, let $x\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $p\in C$. Then $p$ is the nearest point of $C$ to $x$ if and only if

derivations.claim: If $r=0$, then $\mathbb R^r=\{0\}$ and $b=0$. Alternative 1 holds with $x=0\in\mathbb R^n$, while alternative 2 is impossible because the only $y\in\mathbb R^0$ is $0$ and $b^Ty=0$. This handles the zero-dimensional ambient case. Now assume $r\ge1$. Let $C=\{\sum_{j=1}^n x_j A_j:x_j\ge0\}$, where $A_j$ are the columns of $A$. This is a nonempty convex cone and is closed by [F1]. If $b\in C$, its nonnegative coefficients give alternative 1. If $b\notin C$, let $p$ be its nearest point in $C$ by [F2] and put $z=b-p\ne0$.

Applying [F3] with $c=0$ and $c=2p$ gives both $\langle z,p\rangle\ge0$ and $\langle z,p\rangle\le0$, hence $\langle z,p\rangle=0$. Applying [F3] to arbitrary $c\in C$ then gives $\langle z,c\rangle\le0$. In particular $A_j^Tz\le0$ for every column, and $\langle z,b\rangle=\langle z,p+z\rangle=\|z\|_2^2>0$. Thus $y=-z$ satisfies $A^Ty\ge0$ and $b^Ty=-\|z\|_2^2<0$, which is alternative 2.
The alternatives cannot both hold: if $Ax=b$ with $x\ge0$ and $A^Ty\ge0$, then $b^Ty=x^TA^Ty\ge0$, contradicting $b^Ty<0$. Step 1.1 produces one alternative in every case, so exactly one holds.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be $C^2$. Let $p,m\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed; when the target
dimension is positive, let $h:U\to\mathbb R^p$ and
$g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):U\to\mathbb R^m$ be componentwise $C^2$, and when it
is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The smooth inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},
$$
and
$$
\mathcal L_C(x)=\{d:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\}.
$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with
$Dg_i(x)w<0$ for every active $i$; the latter condition is vacuous if
$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition
just stated. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is the stationarity,
feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity system below.

For $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, the Lagrangian and KKT
system are
$$
L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x),
$$
$$
h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\le0,\quad \lambda\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \nabla_xL(x,\nu,\lambda)=0.
$$
The critical cone for a KKT tuple is
$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap
\{d:\nabla f(x)^Td=0\}$. These definitions use the differentiability and
gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $f:U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ on an open set. For every natural $r$, the locus
$$U_{\ge r}:=\{x\in U:\operatorname{rank}Df(x)\ge r\}$$
is open. Thus $x\mapsto\operatorname{rank}Df(x)$ is lower semicontinuous. In particular the submersion locus, the immersion locus, and every locus on which the derivative has the largest possible rank are open.

Let $f:U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^k$, $k\ge1$, and let $c$ be a regular value. Near each point, a regular level set is a $C^k$ graph over $\ker Df(a)$ of dimension $m-n$.

More precisely, for $a\in f^{-1}(c)$ put $K=\ker Df(a)$ and $E=K^\perp$, so $\mathbb R^m=K\oplus E$. There are neighbourhoods $P\subseteq K$ of $0$ and $Q\subseteq E$ of $0$ and a $C^k$ map $g:P\to Q$ with $g(0)=0$ and $Dg(0)=0$ such that, near $a$,
$$f^{-1}(c)=\{a+u+g(u):u\in P\}.$$
The empty fibre satisfies the regular-value convention vacuously, and when $m=n$ the local graph has zero-dimensional domain and is the isolated point $a$.

For a $C^2$ scalar field near $a$,

$$f(a+h)=f(a)+\nabla f(a)\cdot h+\frac12\langle H_f(a)h,h\rangle+o(\|h\|^2).$$

derivations.claim: Take $d\in T_C(x)$ and use its defining feasible sequence $x+t_kd_k$, where $t_k\downarrow0$ and $d_k\to d$. For $h(x)=0$, Taylor expansion gives $0=h(x+t_kd_k)=t_kDh(x)d+o(t_k)$, hence $Dh(x)d=0$. For active $i$, feasibility gives $0\ge g_i(x+t_kd_k)=t_kDg_i(x)d+o(t_k)$, hence $Dg_i(x)d\le0$. Therefore $d\in\mathcal L_C(x)$.

Now take $d\in\mathcal L_C(x)$. Let $w$ be the MFCQ direction; if no inequality is active set $w=0$. Both $d$ and $w$ lie in $\ker Dh(x)$. When there are equality constraints, [F2] supplies a local graph $x+u+\psi(u)$ over this kernel; with no equalities use $\psi=0$. For $t>0$ small, define $u(t)=td+t^{3/2}w$ and $x(t)=x+u(t)+\psi(u(t))$. Then $h(x(t))=0$ and [F3] yields $x(t)-x=td+t^{3/2}w+O(t^2)$, so $(x(t)-x)/t\to d$.

If $i$ is active, Taylor expansion gives $g_i(x(t))=tDg_i(x)d+t^{3/2}Dg_i(x)w+O(t^2)+o(t^2)$. When $Dg_i(x)d<0$, its order-$t$ term makes this negative for all sufficiently small $t>0$. When $Dg_i(x)d=0$, MFCQ gives $Dg_i(x)w<0$, and its order-$t^{3/2}$ term dominates the remainder of order $t^2$. Inactive inequalities remain strict by continuity. Since there are finitely many inequalities, one positive $\tau$ works for all of them and every $0<t<\tau$. Thus $x(t)$ is feasible for such $t$.
Taking $t_k=\tau/2^{k+1}$ gives feasible points with $t_k\downarrow0$ and $(x(t_k)-x)/t_k\to d$, so $d\in T_C(x)$. This proves $\mathcal L_C(x)\subseteq T_C(x)$; step 1.1 gives the reverse inclusion.

is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The smooth inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},
$$
and
$$
\mathcal L_C(x)=\{d:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\}.
$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with
$Dg_i(x)w<0$ for every active $i$; the latter condition is vacuous if
$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition
just stated. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is the stationarity,
feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity system below.

For $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, the Lagrangian and KKT

$$
L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x),
$$
$$
h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\le0,\quad \lambda\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \nabla_xL(x,\nu,\lambda)=0.
$$

$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap
\{d:\nabla f(x)^Td=0\}$. These definitions use the differentiability and
gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

derivations.claim: For $d\in\mathcal L_C(x)$, the equality term in stationarity vanishes, and inactive multipliers vanish by complementarity. Therefore $\nabla f(x)^Td=-\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_iDg_i(x)d$. Every summand on the right is nonnegative because $\lambda_i\ge0$ and $Dg_i(x)d\le0$.

The sum in step 1.1 is zero exactly when each term with $\lambda_i>0$ is zero; because each such term is nonnegative, this is equivalent to $Dg_i(x)d=0$ for every positively weighted active index. That is the claimed equivalence and critical-cone description.

A subset is convex when it contains the segment joining each pair of its
points ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). A function
$F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is proper if it never equals
$-\infty$ and is finite at at least one point. Its domain is
$\operatorname{dom}F=\{x:F(x)<+\infty\}$. Its epigraph is
$\operatorname{epi}F=\{(x,t):F(x)\le t\}$. It is closed convex when its
epigraph is a closed convex set. For a nonempty convex set $S$,
$\operatorname{aff}S$ is its smallest containing affine subspace and
$\operatorname{ri}S$ is its interior relative to $\operatorname{aff}S$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $m,p\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed, let
$f_0,g_1,\ldots,g_m$ be proper closed convex functions on $\mathbb R^n$,
let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$ have full row rank, and let
$b\in\mathbb R^p$. Full row rank means that the rows are linearly
independent, vacuously when $p=0$. The common domain is
$D=\operatorname{dom}f_0\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}g_i$. The primal
problem is to minimize $f_0(x)$ over $x\in D$ satisfying $Ax=b$ and
$g_i(x)\le0$. An inequality is trivial if $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $x\in D$;
trivial inequalities may be removed without changing the feasible set.
Unless stated otherwise, the inequalities below are the remaining,
nontrivial ones. The primal value is
$$
p^*=\inf\{f_0(x):x\in D,\ Ax=b,\ g_i(x)\le0\text{ for all }i\}.
$$

For $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+$ and $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, the extended
Lagrangian is
$$
L(x,\lambda,\nu)=\begin{cases}f_0(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)+\nu^T(Ax-b),&x\in D,\\+\infty,&x\notin D.\end{cases}
$$
The dual function and dual value are
$$
q(\lambda,\nu)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}L(x,\lambda,\nu),\qquad d^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0,\ \nu\in\mathbb R^p}q(\lambda,\nu).
$$
The dual supremum is attained when some admissible $(\lambda,\nu)$ has
$q(\lambda,\nu)=d^*$; the optimal duality gap is $p^*-d^*$ when both values
are finite.

Slater's condition means that there is
$x_s\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_0)\cap
\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g_i)$ with $Ax_s=b$ and
$g_i(x_s)<0$ for every remaining inequality. Relative interior is used in
the affine hull of each domain, so the domain need not have ambient interior.

derivations.claim: Since $x$ is feasible, $Ax-b=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$. Since $\lambda_i\ge0$, this gives $L(x,\lambda,\nu)=f_0(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x)\le f_0(x)$. The infimum defining $q$ is no larger than this particular Lagrangian value, so $q(\lambda,\nu)\le f_0(x)$.

The bound in step 1.1 holds for every primal feasible $x$ and every dual feasible pair. Taking the infimum over primal feasible $x$ and the supremum over dual feasible pairs gives $d^*\le p^*$ when the primal set is nonempty.

$$\langle x-p,z-p\rangle\le0\qquad(z\in C).$$

unit sphere
$$S=\{v\in V:\|v\|=1\}.$$
Then $S$ is sequentially compact: every sequence $(v_k)$ in $S$ has a
subsequence $(v_{k_j})$ converging in the norm metric of $V$ to some $v\in S$.

Consequently, if $(M,g)$ is a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold, $p\in M$
and
$$S_pM=\{v\in T_pM:|v|_g=1\},$$
then $S_pM$ is sequentially compact: every sequence of unit tangent vectors at
$p$ has a subsequence converging in the norm metric of $T_pM$ to a unit tangent
vector at $p$.

two-point sphere (dimension one) are included.

derivations.claim: Let $W=\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}p)$. Since $0$ belongs to the domain, $W$ is a linear subspace; relative interior gives a ball about $0$ in $W$ contained in $\operatorname{dom}p$. If $W=\{0\}$, take $\ell=0$. Otherwise identify $W$ with a Euclidean coordinate space. The restriction of $p$ to that open ball is finite and convex, so [F1] makes it continuous at $0$.

In $W\times\mathbb R$, let $E=\{(z,t):p(z)\le t\}$ and let $\overline E$ be its closure. The set $E$ is convex, $(0,p(0))\in E$, and $\overline E$ is nonempty, closed and convex. Continuity from step 1.1 shows that $(0,p(0)-\epsilon)\notin\overline E$ for every $\epsilon>0$: choose $\delta>0$ so $p(z)>p(0)-\epsilon/3$ whenever $\|z\|<\delta$, while a sufficiently small open ball about $(0,p(0)-\epsilon)$ has $\|z\|<\delta$ and $t<p(0)-2\epsilon/3$, so it misses $E$. Thus $(0,p(0))$ is a boundary point of $\overline E$.

For each positive integer $k$, project $z_k=(0,p(0)-1/k)$ onto $\overline E$, obtaining $y_k$. Since $(0,p(0))\in\overline E$, the projection distance is at most $1/k$, so $y_k\to(0,p(0))$. The unit vectors $a_k=(y_k-z_k)/\|y_k-z_k\|_2$ have a convergent subsequence by [F3], with unit limit $a=(s,\alpha)\in W\times\mathbb R$. For each $y\in\overline E$, [F2] gives $\langle a_k,y-y_k\rangle\ge0$; passing along that subsequence gives $\langle a,y-(0,p(0))\rangle\ge0$.

The epigraph contains every upward vertical ray, so the support inequality forces $\alpha\ge0$. If $\alpha=0$, points $(z,p(z))\in E$ for all sufficiently small $z$ and $-z$ in the ball from step 1.1 force both $\langle s,z\rangle\ge0$ and $\langle s,-z\rangle\ge0$. Hence $s=0$, contradicting $\|a\|_2=1$. Therefore $\alpha>0$. Setting $\ell(z)=-\langle s,z\rangle/\alpha$, the support inequality at $(z,p(z))$ yields $p(z)\ge p(0)+\ell(z)$ for $z$ in the domain; outside the domain the inequality is automatic because $p(z)=+\infty$.

abla f(x_*)^Td\ge0$ for every $d\in\mathcal L_C(x_*)$. Form a matrix $B$ with columns $
abla h_j(x_*),-
abla h_j(x_*)$ for each equality and $-
abla g_i(x_*)$ for each active inequality, and set $c=
abla f(x_*)$. If alternative 1 of [F2] failed, alternative 2 would give $B^Td\ge0$ and $c^Td<0$. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. Then $f$ is convex if and only if

$$f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Equivalently, $\nabla f(x)$ is a subgradient at every $x$ ([[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

Use the program and dimensions of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]. For any $x\in U$,
$\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, define coordinatewise
$[v]_i^+=\max\{v_i,0\}$ and the scaled residual
$$
r_{\mathrm{KKT}}(x,\nu,\lambda)=\|\nabla f(x)+Dh(x)^T\nu+Dg(x)^T\lambda\|_2+\|h(x)\|_2+\|[g(x)]^+\|_2+\|[-\lambda]^+\|_2+\|\lambda\circ g(x)\|_2.
$$
The symbol $\circ$ denotes coordinatewise multiplication. The norm is the
Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and the norm of the
zero-dimensional vector is $0$.

For a convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $x\in C$, its (outward) normal
cone is
$$
N_C(x)=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }y\in C\}.
$$
This definition applies in particular when $C$ is closed and convex.

abla g_i(x_*)^Td\le g_i(y)\le0$. Hence $

abla f(x_*)^Td\ge f(x_*)$. Since $y$ was arbitrary, $x_*$ is globally minimizing. Step 1.1 also gives $\langle-
abla f(x_*),y-x_*angle\le0$ for every feasible $y$, which is exactly $-
abla f(x_*)\in N_C(x_*)$ by [F2].

Let $(x,\nu,\lambda)$ satisfy the KKT conditions for the program of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]. For every
$d\in\mathcal L_C(x)$,
$$
\nabla f(x)^Td=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Dg_i(x)d=0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\text{ with }\lambda_i>0.
$$
Thus the critical cone is the linearized cone with equality imposed on each
positively weighted active inequality.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with closed sets as in
[[def-metric-topology]] and the finite intersection property as in
[[def-finite-intersection-property]]. For a family $\mathcal{A}$ of subsets of
$X$ write

$$\bigcap \mathcal{A} \;:=\; \{\, x \in X : x \in F \text{ for every } F \in \mathcal{A} \,\},$$

so that $\bigcap \emptyset = X$, matching the convention for the empty finite
intersection in [[def-finite-intersection-property]].

Then $(X,d)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]) **if and only if** every
family $\mathcal{A}$ of closed subsets of $X$ with the finite intersection
property satisfies $\bigcap \mathcal{A} \ne \emptyset$.

No choice principle is used in either direction: complementation is a canonical
bijection, so no member of a family ever has to be selected.

A subset is convex when it contains the segment joining each pair of its
points ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). A function
$F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is proper if it never equals
$-\infty$ and is finite at at least one point. Its domain is
$\operatorname{dom}F=\{x:F(x)<+\infty\}$. Its epigraph is
$\operatorname{epi}F=\{(x,t):F(x)\le t\}$. It is closed convex when its
epigraph is a closed convex set. For a nonempty convex set $S$,
$\operatorname{aff}S$ is its smallest containing affine subspace and
$\operatorname{ri}S$ is its interior relative to $\operatorname{aff}S$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $m,p\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed, let
$f_0,g_1,\ldots,g_m$ be proper closed convex functions on $\mathbb R^n$,
let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$ have full row rank, and let
$b\in\mathbb R^p$. Full row rank means that the rows are linearly
independent, vacuously when $p=0$. The common domain is
$D=\operatorname{dom}f_0\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}g_i$. The primal
problem is to minimize $f_0(x)$ over $x\in D$ satisfying $Ax=b$ and
$g_i(x)\le0$. An inequality is trivial if $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $x\in D$;
trivial inequalities may be removed without changing the feasible set.
Unless stated otherwise, the inequalities below are the remaining,
nontrivial ones. The primal value is
$$
p^*=\inf\{f_0(x):x\in D,\ Ax=b,\ g_i(x)\le0\text{ for all }i\}.
$$

For $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+$ and $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, the extended
Lagrangian is
$$
L(x,\lambda,\nu)=\begin{cases}f_0(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)+\nu^T(Ax-b),&x\in D,\\+\infty,&x\notin D.\end{cases}
$$
The dual function and dual value are
$$
q(\lambda,\nu)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}L(x,\lambda,\nu),\qquad d^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0,\ \nu\in\mathbb R^p}q(\lambda,\nu).
$$
The dual supremum is attained when some admissible $(\lambda,\nu)$ has
$q(\lambda,\nu)=d^*$; the optimal duality gap is $p^*-d^*$ when both values
are finite.

Slater's condition means that there is
$x_s\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_0)\cap
\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g_i)$ with $Ax_s=b$ and
$g_i(x_s)<0$ for every remaining inequality. Relative interior is used in
the affine hull of each domain, so the domain need not have ambient interior.

For the convex program and Lagrangian dual of
[[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]], every primal feasible
$x$ and every dual feasible $(\lambda,\nu)$ satisfy
$$q(\lambda,\nu)\le f_0(x).$$
Consequently, when the primal feasible set is nonempty, $d^*\le p^*$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and let
$p:V\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be convex, never $-\infty$, and finite somewhere.
If $0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}p)$ and $p(0)\in\mathbb R$, then
there is a linear functional $\ell:V\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$p(z)\ge p(0)+\ell(z)\qquad(z\in V).$$

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be convex. Then $f$ is locally Lipschitz on $U$: every $a\in U$ has a neighbourhood on which one finite constant bounds $|f(x)-f(y)|$ by $\|x-y\|_2$.

derivations.claim: For perturbations $u\in\mathbb R^m$ and $v\in\mathbb R^p$, define $ P(u,v)=\inf\{f_0(x):x\in D,\ g_i(x)\le u_i\ (1\le i\le m),\ Ax-b=v\}. $ This value function is convex. Indeed, for two perturbations with finite values, choose feasible points with objective within $\epsilon$ of their respective infima. A convex combination of those points lies in $D$, its inequalities and equality residual are bounded by the same convex combination of perturbations, and convexity of $f_0$ bounds its objective. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves the convex inequality. If one perturbation value is $-\infty$, arbitrarily low feasible objective values and the same convex-combination argument give value $-\infty$ at each strict convex combination with another feasible perturbation.

Let $S=\operatorname{aff}D$ and $Y=A(S)-b$. Since the Slater point $x_s$ lies in every relative-interior domain, $x_s$ has a relative neighborhood in $S$ contained in $D$. Each $g_i$ is finite and convex on its domain and continuous near $x_s$ in its affine hull by [F4]; after intersecting finitely many neighborhoods, there are a relative neighborhood $U_s\subseteq D$ of $x_s$ and $\eta>0$ with $g_i(y)<-\eta$ on $U_s$ for every $i$ (take any $\eta>0$ if $m=0$). The affine map $y\mapsto Ay-b$ from $S$ onto $Y$ has a linear right inverse on its direction space: choose preimages of a finite basis of $Y$. Consequently, its image of $U_s$ contains a relative neighborhood $W$ of $0$ in $Y$. For every $v\in W$, choose the corresponding $y\in U_s$; for every $u\in\prod_i(-\eta,\infty)$, that $y$ satisfies $g_i(y)<u_i$ and $Ay-b=v$. Thus $P(u,v)<+\infty$ on a relative neighborhood of $0$ in $Z=\mathbb R^m\times Y$.

The value $P(0,0)=p^*$ is finite. The convexity from step 1.1 and the neighborhood from step 1.2 imply that $P$ never equals $-\infty$: if $P(z)=-\infty$ for some perturbation $z$, choose a small $\theta>0$ so $-\theta z/(1-\theta)$ lies in that neighborhood. Convexity would give $P(0)\le\theta P(z)+(1-\theta)P(-\theta z/(1-\theta))=-\infty$, contrary to finiteness. Hence $P$ is proper and $0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}P)$ relative to $Z$. By [F3] there is a linear functional $\ell(u,v)=a^Tu+c(v)$ on $Z$ such that $P(u,v)\ge p^*+a^Tu+c(v)$.

Relaxing one inequality right-hand side cannot increase the infimum, so $P(te_i,0)\le P(0,0)=p^*$ for small $t>0$. The support inequality in step 2.1 gives $P(te_i,0)\ge p^*+t a_i$, hence $a_i\le0$. Define $\lambda_*=-a\ge0$ and extend $c$ from the finite-dimensional subspace $Y$ to a linear functional on $\mathbb R^p$ by extending a basis; write the negative of this extension as $
u_*^T$. For any $x\in D$, the perturbation $(g(x),Ax-b)$ is feasible using $x$ itself, so $ f_0(x)\ge P(g(x),Ax-b)\ge p^*+a^Tg(x)+c(Ax-b). $ Thus $L(x,\lambda_*,
u_*)\ge p^*$ for all $x$, and $q(\lambda_*,
u_*)\ge p^*$.

At the primal minimizer, weak duality [F2] and feasibility give $ p^*\le q(\lambda_*,
u_*)\le L(x_*,\lambda_*,
u_*)= p^*+\sum_i\lambda_{*,i}g_i(x_*)\le p^*. $ Every inequality is therefore equality. Since every summand $\lambda_{*,i}g_i(x_*)$ is nonpositive, their sum being zero forces each one to be zero. Thus $q(\lambda_*,
u_*)=p^*=d^*$, the dual supremum is attained, and complementarity holds.

is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The smooth inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},
$$
and
$$
\mathcal L_C(x)=\{d:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\}.
$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with
$Dg_i(x)w<0$ for every active $i$; the latter condition is vacuous if
$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition
just stated. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is the stationarity,
feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity system below.

For $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, the Lagrangian and KKT
system are
$$
L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x),

$$

$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap
\{d:\nabla f(x)^Td=0\}$. These definitions use the differentiability and
gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]], if $x_*$ is a local
minimizer and MFCQ holds at $x_*$, then there exist
$\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+$ such that
$(x_*,\nu,\lambda)$ satisfies the KKT system.

u,\lambda)$ and $(\widehat
u,\widehat\lambda)$ are two KKT pairs at $x$. Complementarity and strict negativity of each inactive $g_i(x)$ force both corresponding multipliers to be $0$. u=\widehat
u$ and $\lambda=\widehat\lambda$.

$$

For $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+$ and $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, the extended
Lagrangian is
$$
L(x,\lambda,\nu)=\begin{cases}f_0(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)+\nu^T(Ax-b),&x\in D,\\+\infty,&x\notin D.\end{cases}
$$
The dual function and dual value are
$$
q(\lambda,\nu)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}L(x,\lambda,\nu),\qquad d^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0,\ \nu\in\mathbb R^p}q(\lambda,\nu).
$$
The dual supremum is attained when some admissible $(\lambda,\nu)$ has
$q(\lambda,\nu)=d^*$; the optimal duality gap is $p^*-d^*$ when both values
are finite.

Slater's condition means that there is
$x_s\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_0)\cap
\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g_i)$ with $Ax_s=b$ and
$g_i(x_s)<0$ for every remaining inequality. Relative interior is used in
the affine hull of each domain, so the domain need not have ambient interior.

For the convex program and Lagrangian dual of
[[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]], every primal feasible
$x$ and every dual feasible $(\lambda,\nu)$ satisfy
$$q(\lambda,\nu)\le f_0(x).$$
Consequently, when the primal feasible set is nonempty, $d^*\le p^*$.

Consider the finite-dimensional convex program of
[[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]]. Assume its equality
matrix has independent rows, Slater's condition holds, and the finite primal
value $p^*\in\mathbb R$ is attained at $x_*$. Then there are
$\lambda_*\ge0$ and $\nu_*$ such that
$$q(\lambda_*,\nu_*)=d^*=p^*.$$
Moreover, every inequality multiplier satisfies
$\lambda_{*,i}g_i(x_*)=0$. The Slater and attainment hypotheses do not assert
that a primal minimizer is unique.

derivations.claim: The epigraph of $\phi$ is exactly $E=\{(x,y,t):y\ge0,\ t\ge0,\ x^2\le yt\}$. For $y>0$ this is the inequality $t\ge x^2/y$; when $y=0$ it forces $x=0$ and $t\ge0$; for $y<0$ it is empty. Thus $E$ is closed, being defined by continuous non-strict inequalities. It is convex: if $|x_j|\le\sqrt{y_jt_j}$ for $j=1,2$, then for $0\le\theta\le1$, $ |\theta x_1+(1-\theta)x_2| \le\theta\sqrt{y_1t_1}+(1-\theta)\sqrt{y_2t_2} \le\sqrt{(\theta y_1+(1-\theta)y_2) (\theta t_1+(1-\theta)t_2)} $ by Cauchy–Schwarz. Therefore $\phi$ is closed convex. The objective is continuous and has second derivative $e^{-x}>0$ in $x$, so it is closed convex and proper as well.

On its domain $\phi\ge0$. If $y>0$, $\phi(x,y)\le0$ forces $x=0$; if $y=0$, finiteness already forces $x=0$. Hence the feasible set is $\{(0,y):y\ge0\}$ and $f_0=1$ throughout it, so $p^*=1$ and the primal minimum is attained, for example at $(0,0)$. No point has $\phi(x,y)<0$, so Slater fails.

For $\lambda\ge0$, every point in the Lagrangian domain has $e^{-x}+\lambda\phi(x,y)\ge0$, so $q(\lambda)\ge0$. At $\lambda=0$, taking $x\to+\infty$ gives $q(0)=0$. For $\lambda>0$, take $(x_k,y_k)=(k,k^3)$; then $e^{-x_k}+\lambda\phi(x_k,y_k)=e^{-k}+\lambda/k\to0$, so again $q(\lambda)=0$. Therefore $d^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}q(\lambda)=0$ and the positive duality gap is $p^*-d^*=1$. This does not contradict [F2], because its Slater hypothesis fails.

The calculation gives a closed convex primal problem with attained finite optimum and a strict gap; the missing strict-feasibility condition is exactly the boundary that blocks the Slater theorem's certificate.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be $C^2$. Let $p,m\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed; when the target
dimension is positive, let $h:U\to\mathbb R^p$ and
$g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):U\to\mathbb R^m$ be componentwise $C^2$, and when it
is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The smooth inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},
$$
and
$$
\mathcal L_C(x)=\{d:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\}.
$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with
$Dg_i(x)w<0$ for every active $i$; the latter condition is vacuous if
$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition
just stated. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is the stationarity,
feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity system below.

For $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, the Lagrangian and KKT
system are
$$
L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x),
$$
$$
h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\le0,\quad \lambda\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \nabla_xL(x,\nu,\lambda)=0.
$$
The critical cone for a KKT tuple is
$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap
\{d:\nabla f(x)^Td=0\}$. These definitions use the differentiability and
gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

For the $C^2$ program of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]], LICQ at a feasible
point $x$ implies MFCQ there. If $x$ is a local minimizer, its KKT
multipliers exist and are unique.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex, and suppose the objective
$f:U\to\mathbb R$ and inequalities $g_i:U\to\mathbb R$ are differentiable
and convex. Let the equalities be $Ax=b$. If a feasible tuple
$(x_*,\nu,\lambda)$ satisfies the KKT conditions with $\lambda\ge0$, then

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.
citations.use_explanation: The ODE solution supplies graph-domain membership and y'=f(s,y(s)).

citations.quote: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.
citations.use_explanation: Continuous partials give the total derivative matrix used in the path chain rule.

citations.quote: If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a\in U$, then some $C,\delta>0$ satisfy $\|f(a+h)-f(a)\|_2\le C\|h\|_2$ whenever $\|h\|_2<\delta$ and $a+h\in U$. In particular $f$ is continuous at $a$.
citations.use_explanation: Total differentiability gives continuity of f and hence continuity of the solution derivative and composition.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: By [F2]–[F3], $f$ is continuous on $V$. Since $y'=f(s,y(s))$, the derivative of $y$ is continuous on $I$; hence $y$ is continuously differentiable and the path $q(s):=(s,y(s))$ has derivative $q'(s)=(1,f(s,y(s)))$.

For each $i$, the component map $f_i$ is totally differentiable, so [F4] applied to $g_i=f_i\circ q$ gives the displayed derivative formula. The bounds give $|g_i'(s)|\le M_{t,i}+\sum_{j=1}^dM_{ij}F_j=B_i$ for every $s\in(a,b)$. Continuity of $g_i$ on $[a,b]$ follows from continuity of $f$ and $y$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and consider a first-order IVP and solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **one-step method** is a family of maps $\Psi_h(t,v)$, defined for admitted times $t$, positive step sizes $h$, and states $v$, whose value is the method's approximation at time $t+h$ from the single input state $v$ at time $t$. It does not use earlier numerical states.

If $y$ is an exact solution on an interval containing $[t,t+h]$, the **local defect** is

$$\delta_h(t;y):=\Psi_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h).$$

Let $K\subseteq D$ be a fixed compact time-state set. The method has **uniform local order $p$ on $K$ along $y$** if there are constants $C\ge0$ and $h_0>0$, independent of the admitted starting time $t$ and step $0<h\le h_0$, such that

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le C h^{p+1}$$

whenever the exact solution graph on $[t,t+h]$ and the associated method time-state inputs, stages, and outputs under consideration lie in $K$. Here $p$ is a positive integer and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

The method has **one-step Lipschitz stability on $K$** with constant $L\ge0$ if

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$

for every admitted step size $h$, admitted time $t$, and input states $u,v$ with $(t,u),(t,v)\in K$. This is a bound on the change in one step; it is separate from absolute or linear stability regions and does not itself assert a global error estimate.

Let $d\ge1$, let $V\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $f:V\to\mathbb R^d$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and let $y:I\to\mathbb R^d$ solve $y'=f(t,y)$ on an open interval $I$. Fix $a<b$ with $[a,b]\subset I$ such that $(s,y(s))\in V$ for every $s\in[a,b]$. Suppose finite constants $F_j,M_{t,i},M_{ij}\ge0$ satisfy for all $s\in[a,b]$

$$|f_j(s,y(s))|\le F_j,\qquad |\partial_t f_i(s,y(s))|\le M_{t,i},\qquad |\partial_{z_j}f_i(s,y(s))|\le M_{ij}\qquad(1\le i,j\le d).$$

Define $g_i(s):=f_i(s,y(s))$ and $B_i:=M_{t,i}+\sum_{j=1}^dM_{ij}F_j$. Then $g_i$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and

$$g_i'(s)=\partial_t f_i(s,y(s))+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{z_j}f_i(s,y(s))f_j(s,y(s)),\qquad |g_i'(s)|\le B_i.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: By [F3]–[F4], $f$ is totally differentiable and continuous on $V$, with state derivative matrix $D_yf$. On each open convex fiber $V_t$, the derivative bound and [F5]–[F6] make $f(t,\cdot)$ $L$-Lipschitz. Thus the hypotheses of [F7] hold and the IVP has a unique maximal solution; the given solution agrees with it throughout $[0,T]$.

Fix any $t\in[0,T)$ and $h>0$ with $t+h\le T$ satisfying the stated compact-set condition, and fix a component $i$. Define $g_i(s):=f_i(t+s,y(t+s))$ for $0\le s\le h$. The exact path segment lies in $K\subset V$, so [F8] gives $|g_i'(s)|\le B_i$ on $(0,h)$.
For each $s\in(0,h]$, [F10] applied to $g_i$ on $[0,s]$ yields $|g_i(s)-g_i(0)|\le B_i s$; at $s=0$ the same inequality is equality.

Apply [F9] to the IVP restarted at $(t,y(t))$; then $y_i(t+h)-y_i(t)=\int_0^h g_i(s)\,ds$. Euler's output from the exact state is $y_i(t)+hg_i(0)$, so $\delta_{h,i}(t;y)=\int_0^h(g_i(0)-g_i(s))\,ds$. Using [step 2.1] gives $|\delta_{h,i}(t;y)|\le\int_0^h B_i s\,ds=B_i h^2/2$. Squaring the component bounds, summing, and using [F11] gives the asserted Euclidean norm estimate. Its constant is independent of $t$ and $h$, proving uniform local order one under [F1].

For any admitted $t\in[0,T]$, $h>0$, and $u,v\in V_t$, [F3] identifies the derivative of $z\mapsto f(t,z)$ with $D_yf(t,z)$; [F5]–[F6] give $\|f(t,u)-f(t,v)\|_2\le L\|u-v\|_2$. Therefore [F12] gives $\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le\|u-v\|_2+h\|f(t,u)-f(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$, which is the one-step stability bound in [F1] for inputs in $K$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and consider a first-order IVP and solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **one-step method** is a family of maps $\Psi_h(t,v)$, defined for admitted times $t$, positive step sizes $h$, and states $v$, whose value is the method's approximation at time $t+h$ from the single input state $v$ at time $t$. It does not use earlier numerical states.

If $y$ is an exact solution on an interval containing $[t,t+h]$, the **local defect** is

$$\delta_h(t;y):=\Psi_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h).$$

Let $K\subseteq D$ be a fixed compact time-state set. The method has **uniform local order $p$ on $K$ along $y$** if there are constants $C\ge0$ and $h_0>0$, independent of the admitted starting time $t$ and step $0<h\le h_0$, such that

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le C h^{p+1}$$

whenever the exact solution graph on $[t,t+h]$ and the associated method time-state inputs, stages, and outputs under consideration lie in $K$. Here $p$ is a positive integer and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

The method has **one-step Lipschitz stability on $K$** with constant $L\ge0$ if

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$

for every admitted step size $h$, admitted time $t$, and input states $u,v$ with $(t,u),(t,v)\in K$. This is a bound on the change in one step; it is separate from absolute or linear stability regions and does not itself assert a global error estimate.

derivations.claim: For $t<0$, $y(t)=-t^2/2$ and $y'(t)=-t=|t|$; for $t>0$, $y(t)=t^2/2$ and $y'(t)=t=|t|$. At $t=0$, $\lim_{s\to0}(y(s)-y(0))/s=\lim_{s\to0}|s|/2=0=|0|$. Hence $y$ is the exact solution through $y(0)=0$.

At $t_h=-h/2$, the exact value is $y(t_h)=-h^2/8$ and the explicit midpoint stage time is $0$, where $f(0,z)=0$ for every stage value $z$. Thus $M_h(t_h,y(t_h))=y(t_h)=-h^2/8$, while $y(t_h+h)=y(h/2)=h^2/8$.

Therefore $\delta_h(t_h;y)=-h^2/4$. The exact segment has $|t|\le h/2\le1/2$ and $|y(t)|\le1/8$; the input and output states are $-h^2/8$, and the midpoint stage state is $h^2/8$, all in $[-1,1]$. Their time coordinates also lie in $[-1,1]$, so the definition applies on the fixed compact set $K$. If a uniform order-two bound held, $h^2/4\le Ch^3$ for every $0<h\le1$, forcing $C\ge1/(4h)$ as $h\downarrow0$, which is impossible.

For an arbitrary $t\in\mathbb R$ and $h>0$, the method increment from the exact state is $h|t+h/2|$. If $[t,t+h]$ lies on either side of $0$, then $y$ is quadratic there and this increment equals $y(t+h)-y(t)$, so the defect is zero. If $t<0<t+h$, put $r=-t/h\in(0,1)$. Using $y(t)=-t^2/2$ and $y(t+h)=(t+h)^2/2$ gives $\delta_h(t;y)=-h^2r^2$ for $0<r\le1/2$ and $\delta_h(t;y)=-h^2(1-r)^2$ for $1/2\le r<1$. Thus every crossing step has $|\delta_h(t;y)|\le h^2/4$, and the same bound holds for every step. In particular, it holds uniformly for all admitted starts and steps in $K$; together with step 3.1, the uniform local order is exactly one.

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $V\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be an open time-state domain whose fibers $V_t:=\{z:(t,z)\in V\}$ are open and convex. Let $K\subset V$ be compact. Let $f:V\to\mathbb R^d$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and suppose $y$ is a solution of $y'=f(t,y)$, $y(0)=y_0$, on an open interval containing $[0,T]$, with graph on $[0,T]$ contained in $K$. For each local defect under consideration, require the Euler input and output time-state pairs to lie in $K$; the exact solution segment already lies in $K$.

For $1\le i,j\le d$, assume finite constants $F_j,M_{t,i},M_{ij},L\ge0$ satisfy throughout $V$

$$|f_j(t,z)|\le F_j,\qquad |\partial_t f_i(t,z)|\le M_{t,i},\qquad |\partial_{z_j}f_i(t,z)|\le M_{ij},\qquad \|D_yf(t,z)w\|_2\le L\|w\|_2\quad(w\in\mathbb R^d).$$

Here $D_yf$ is the matrix with entries $\partial_{z_j}f_i$, and the last inequality defines the operator bound used below. The forward Euler map is $\Psi_h(t,v)=v+h f(t,v)$. Then, with $B_i:=M_{t,i}+\sum_{j=1}^dM_{ij}F_j$, for every $t\in[0,T)$ and $h>0$ with $t+h\le T$ whose Euler input and output pairs lie in $K$, its local defect satisfies

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le \frac{h^2}{2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^d B_i^2\right)^{1/2},$$

so it has uniform local order one on $K$ along $y|_{[0,T]}$, with $h_0=T$. For every $t\in[0,T]$, every admitted $h>0$, and every $u,v\in V_t$,

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2.$$

This is a local defect and one-step stability result. It does not assert a global error estimate or an order for any other named method.

derivations.claim: Fix $T>0$, let $R:=e^T(1+T)+1$, and take $V=(-1,T+1)\times(-R,R)$ and $K=[0,T]\times[-R+1,R-1]$. These are an open domain with convex state fibers and a compact subset $K\subset V$. For $f(t,z)=z$, the bounds in [F2] hold throughout $V$ with $F_1=R$, $M_{t,1}=0$, $M_{11}=1$, and $L=1$. The function $y(t)=e^t$ solves the IVP, its graph on $[0,T]$ lies in $K$, and for every $0<h\le T-t$ the Euler output state $e^t(1+h)$ lies between $0$ and $e^T(1+T)=R-1$, so its input and output pairs lie in $K$. Starting from $e^t$, Euler returns $e^t(1+h)$ and the exact endpoint is $e^{t+h}=e^te^h$. Therefore [F1] gives $\delta_h(t;y)=e^t(1+h-e^h)$.
Apply [F3] to $s\mapsto e^s$ at $0$ with increment $h$: there is $\theta_h\in(0,h)$ with $e^h=1+h+\tfrac12 e^{\theta_h}h^2$. Thus $|\delta_h(t;y)|=\tfrac12 e^{t+\theta_h}h^2$.

Since $0<\theta_h<h$, for $0\le t\le T-h$ we have $\tfrac12h^2\le |\delta_h(t;y)|\le \tfrac12e^T h^2$. The lower and upper bounds establish uniform $\Theta(h^2)$ error, hence order exactly one under [F1].
For any scalar inputs $u,v$, $|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)|=|(1+h)(u-v)|=(1+h)|u-v|$. This verifies the stated stability factor; it also agrees with [F2] for $f(t,z)=z$ and $L=1$.

citations.quote: Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Since $\phi'(t)=-t\phi(t)$, for $t\ge x>0$ we have $\phi(t)\le t\phi(t)/x$. Integrating and using $\int_x^\infty t\phi(t)\,dt=\phi(x)$, obtained by integrating $-\phi'$, gives $\bar\Phi(x)\le\phi(x)/x$.

Integration by parts on $[x,R]$, followed by $R\to\infty$, gives $ \bar\Phi(x)=\frac{\phi(x)}x-\int_x^\infty\frac{\phi(t)}{t^2}\,dt. $ The remainder is at most $\bar\Phi(x)/x^2$, hence $\bar\Phi(x)(1+x^{-2})\ge\phi(x)/x$, which is the stated lower bound.

Dividing the two bounds by $\phi(x)/x>0$ traps the ratio $\bar\Phi(x)/(\phi(x)/x)$ between $x^2/(x^2+1)$ and $1$, so it tends to $1$. Taking logarithms gives $\log\bar\Phi(x)=-x^2/2-\log x-\tfrac12\log(2\pi)+o(1)$; division by $-x^2/2$ yields the asserted logarithmic limit.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be a real IID sequence. If $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$ and $\mu=\mathbb E[Y_1]$, then $\mathbb E[\bar Y_n]=\mu$ for every $n\ge1$. If also $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)$, then $\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_n)=\sigma^2/n$ for every $n\ge1$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$
