Let $(P_\lambda,A_\lambda)_{\lambda\in\Lambda}$ be a family of probability measures and measurable events with $p_\lambda=P_\lambda(A_\lambda)>0$ and $p_\lambda\to0$ along the stated rare-event limit. An estimator $\widehat p_\lambda$ is **unbiased with finite variance** when $\mathbb E[\widehat p_\lambda]=p_\lambda$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p_\lambda)<\infty$. Its **relative error** is
$
\operatorname{RE}(\widehat p_\lambda)=\frac{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p_\lambda)}}{p_\lambda}.
$
It has **bounded relative error** if these relative errors remain bounded for all sufficiently rare indices. It is **logarithmically efficient** if $\widehat p_\lambda\ge0$, its second moment is finite and positive, and
$
\lim_{\lambda}\frac{\log\mathbb E[\widehat p_\lambda^2]}{\log(p_\lambda^2)}=1.
$
Logarithmic efficiency is a weaker asymptotic property than bounded relative error; the definitions impose no implication between an algorithm's efficiency and its proposal-fitting success.

For a specified cost model, let $W_\lambda$ be the expected work of one estimator replication. Record both its variance and its **variance-work product** $W_\lambda\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p_\lambda)$; for relative precision, record $W_\lambda\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p_\lambda)/p_\lambda^2$. These quantities depend on the cost model. Comparing algorithms requires the same declared work convention.

For a single event $A$ under a probability measure $P$, put $p=P(A)>0$. If $P$ has density $f$ with respect to $\mu$, the **zero-variance event proposal** is the probability density
$
q^*(x)=\frac{\mathbf 1_A(x)f(x)}{p}.
$
It is a formal benchmark because its normalizing constant is the unknown event probability $p$. Ordinary importance-sampling estimators and their weighted-second-moment condition are defined in [[alg-importance-sampling]] and [[thm-ordinary-importance-sampling-finite-variance-under-weighted-second-moment]].

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space. An **unnormalized target density** is a measurable function $\tilde p:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$Z_p:=\int_{\mathsf X}\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
The target probability measure is $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$. A **proposal density** is a measurable $q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\int q\,d\mu=1$; write $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. The input integrand $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, and the input sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ is IID with law $Q$, in the sense of [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. The normalizing constant $Z_p$ is known for this algorithm.

**Admissible conditions for an unbiased estimate:** $n\ge1$, $q>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{x:f(x)\tilde p(x)\ne0\}$, and the random variable
$$Y:=\begin{cases}f(X_1)\tilde p(X_1)/(Z_pq(X_1)),&q(X_1)>0,\\0,&q(X_1)=0\end{cases}$$
is integrable under $Q$. The support condition makes the value on $q=0$ immaterial to the target integral.

**Well-defined weights:** The reciprocal map $r(s)=1/s$ for $s>0$ and $r(s)=0$ for $s\le0$ is Borel. Its composition with $q$, multiplied by the measurable inputs, makes the piecewise weight and weighted integrand measurable ([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]], [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]).

**Procedure and output:** For each supplied draw $X_i$, set $Y_i=f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i))$ when $q(X_i)>0$ and set $Y_i=0$ otherwise. Return
$$\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i.$$
Separate variance and central limit claims require the corresponding weighted second-moment hypothesis.

derivations.claim: The density $q^*$ is nonnegative and $\int q^*\,d\mu=P(A)/p=1$, so it defines a proposal probability measure $Q^*$ supported on $\{x\in A:f(x)>0\}$ up to a $Q^*$-null set.

For $Q^*$-almost every $X$, we have $X\in A$ and $f(X)>0$. Substitution of $q^*(X)=f(X)/p$ into [F2] gives $Z=p$ almost surely. Every term in the IID sample average is therefore the same constant $p$; its expectation is $p$ and its variance is zero.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $\phi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$ be the standard-normal density and $\bar\Phi(x)=\int_x^\infty\phi(t)\,dt$. For every $x>0$,
$
\frac{x}{x^2+1}\phi(x)\le \bar\Phi(x)\le\frac{\phi(x)}{x}.
$
Consequently $\bar\Phi(x)\sim\phi(x)/x$ and $\log\bar\Phi(x)\sim -x^2/2$ as $x\to\infty$.

These quantities depend on the cost model. Comparing algorithms requires the same declared work convention.

$
q^*(x)=\frac{\mathbf 1_A(x)f(x)}{p}.
$
It is a formal benchmark because its normalizing constant is the unknown event probability $p$. Ordinary importance-sampling estimators and their weighted-second-moment condition are defined in [[alg-importance-sampling]] and [[thm-ordinary-importance-sampling-finite-variance-under-weighted-second-moment]].

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $\tilde p\ge0$ and $q\ge0$ be measurable densities with $Z_p=\int\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$ and $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and set $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$ and $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. Let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $\int|f|\tilde p\,d\mu<\infty$. Suppose $q>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{f\tilde p\ne0\}$ and $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are IID with law $Q$. For the ordinary importance sampling estimator in [[alg-importance-sampling]],
$$\mathbb E_Q[\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}]=\int f\,d\pi.$$

Use the hypotheses and notation of [[thm-ordinary-importance-sampling-is-unbiased]]. Define
$$Y_i:=\begin{cases}f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i)),&q(X_i)>0,\\0,&q(X_i)=0\end{cases},\qquad \theta:=\int f\,d\pi,\qquad \sigma^2:=\operatorname{Var}_Q(Y_1).$$
If $\mathbb E_Q[Y_1^2]<\infty$, then $\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}$ has finite variance and
$$\operatorname{Var}_Q(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}})=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}=\frac1n\left(\frac1{Z_p^2}\int_{\{q>0\}}\frac{f(x)^2\tilde p(x)^2}{q(x)}\,d\mu(x)-\theta^2\right).$$
This finite-sample conclusion is choice-free. For the central limit conclusion, let $(X_i)_{i\ge1}$ be an IID sequence with law $Q$, and apply the estimator to its first $n$ draws for each $n\ge1$. If, in addition, AC holds, then
$$\sqrt n\bigl(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}-\theta\bigr)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2).$$
No finite variance or normal-limit claim is made when the weighted second moment is infinite.

Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be a real IID sequence. If $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$ and $\mu=\mathbb E[Y_1]$, then $\mathbb E[\bar Y_n]=\mu$ for every $n\ge1$. If also $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)$, then $\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_n)=\sigma^2/n$ for every $n\ge1$.

derivations.claim: For every $x\in\mathbb R$, the density ratio is $\phi(x)/\phi(x-a)=\exp(-ax+a^2/2)$. The proposal has positive density on $A_a$, and $0\le Z_a\le e^{-a^2/2}$ on $A_a$, so the event-support and integrability hypotheses of [F4] hold. Hence $\mathbb E_{Q_a}Z_a=p_a$.

Direct integration gives $ \mathbb E_{Q_a}Z_a^2=\int_a^\infty e^{-2ax+a^2}\phi(x-a)\,dx. $ With $y=x-a$, the integrand becomes $e^{-2ay-a^2}\phi(y)=e^{a^2}\phi(y+2a)$; the integral is $e^{a^2}\bar\Phi(2a)$, which is finite for every $a>0$.

For the average of $n\ge1$ IID contributions, [F6] gives
$$
\mathbb E[\widehat p_{a,n}^2]=p_a^2+\frac{\mathbb E[Z_a^2]-p_a^2}{n},\qquad
p_a^2\le\mathbb E[\widehat p_{a,n}^2]\le p_a^2+\mathbb E[Z_a^2].
$$
By [F2], $\log p_a^2=-a^2+o(a^2)$ and $\log\mathbb E[Z_a^2]=a^2+\log\bar\Phi(2a)=-a^2+o(a^2)$. Therefore also $\log(p_a^2+\mathbb E[Z_a^2])=-a^2+o(a^2)$. The two bounds squeeze $\log\mathbb E[\widehat p_{a,n}^2]=-a^2+o(a^2)$, while $2\log p_a=-a^2+o(a^2)$. By [F3], the logarithmic-efficiency ratio tends to $1$.

Mills' equivalent in [F2] yields $ \frac{\mathbb E Z_a^2}{p_a^2}\sim \frac{e^{a^2}\phi(2a)/(2a)}{(\phi(a)/a)^2} =\sqrt{\pi/2}\,a. $ Using [F4] and [F5], $\operatorname{RE}(\widehat p_{a,1})^2=\mathbb E Z_a^2/p_a^2-1\sim\sqrt{\pi/2}\,a$; taking square roots gives the stated divergence.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $A\in\mathcal X$, and let the target probability measure $P$ have a pointwise finite measurable density $f:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with respect to $\mu$, so $P(B)=\int_B f\,d\mu$. Let $\{q_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ be pointwise finite probability densities with respect to $\mu$, and write $Q_\theta(dx)=q_\theta(x)\mu(dx)$, where $\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite nonempty set equipped with lexicographic order. For each $\theta\in\Theta$, supply an exact admissibility checker $\mathcal C(A,f,q_\theta)$ that returns `admissible` if and only if $P|_A\ll Q_\theta$ and the contribution
$$
w_\theta(x)=\begin{cases}\mathbf1_A(x)f(x)/q_\theta(x),&q_\theta(x)>0,\\0,&q_\theta(x)=0\end{cases}
$$
is integrable under $Q_\theta$, where $P|_A(B):=P(B\cap A)$ for measurable $B$. Supply an initial parameter $\theta_0\in\Theta$, a pilot size $m\ge1$, and a production size $n\ge1$.

1. Draw an IID pilot $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m\sim q_{\theta_0}$.
2. If no $Y_j$ lies in $A$, return `pilot-no-hit`.
3. For every $\theta\in\Theta$, compute
$
s_\theta(y)=\begin{cases}\log q_\theta(y),&y\in A,\\0,&y\notin A,\end{cases}
\qquad S(\theta)=\sum_{j=1}^m s_\theta(Y_j),
$
with $\log 0=-\infty$. Pointwise finiteness rules out $+\infty$, and the piecewise score avoids the undefined product $0\cdot(-\infty)$. If all scores equal $-\infty$, return `no-finite-maximizer`. Otherwise choose the lexicographically least maximizer $\widehat\theta$ among the finite scores and freeze it.
4. Evaluate $\mathcal C(A,f,q_{\widehat\theta})$. If it returns inadmissible, return `inadmissible-production-proposal`. Otherwise draw an IID production sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim q_{\widehat\theta}$, independent of the pilot conditional on $\widehat\theta$, and return the ordinary importance-sampling estimate
$
\widehat p_{\rm CE}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n w_{\widehat\theta}(X_i)
$
using the piecewise-defined contribution $w_{\widehat\theta}$ above.

The finite candidate set makes the score comparisons and tie rule deterministic. The supplied exact checker is an input oracle; the procedure does not infer support or integrability from a pilot fit. If its check fails, no production estimate or unbiasedness or finite-variance claim is returned.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $\tilde p\ge0$ and $q\ge0$ be measurable densities with $Z_p=\int\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$ and $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and set $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$ and $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. Let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $\int|f|\tilde p\,d\mu<\infty$. Suppose $q>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{f\tilde p\ne0\}$ and $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are IID with law $Q$. For the ordinary importance sampling estimator in [[alg-importance-sampling]],
$$\mathbb E_Q[\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}]=\int f\,d\pi.$$

derivations.claim: The pilot outcome space need not be finite. For each $\theta\in\Theta$, the score $S(\theta)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable, and $\Theta$ is finite. Therefore the success event, the exact-checker acceptance event, and the lexicographically least maximizing selector $\widehat\theta$ on success are $\mathcal G$-measurable. Partition $H$ into the finitely many events $H_\theta=H\cap\{\widehat\theta=\theta\}$. Conditional independence of the production sample from the pilot given $\widehat\theta$, as specified in [F1], means that on each $H_\theta$ its conditional law given $\mathcal G$ is IID $Q_\theta$.

On each $H_\theta$, the checker gives the support and integrability hypotheses for [F2]. That theorem gives conditional expectation $P(A)$ for each production contribution given $\mathcal G$, and linearity gives the same conditional expectation for their average. Since the finitely many $H_\theta$ partition $H$ and $\widetilde p_{\rm CE}=0$ off $H$, this proves $\mathbb E[\widetilde p_{\rm CE}\mid\mathcal G]=\mathbf1_H P(A)$ almost surely.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space as in [[def-probability-measure]]. A finite nested event sequence of length $L\ge1$ is a sequence of measurable sets
$
\Omega=A_0\supseteq A_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq A_L=A
$
such that $P(A_\ell)>0$ for $0\le\ell\le L$. Its **conditional level probabilities** and **level laws** are
$
p_\ell=\frac{P(A_\ell)}{P(A_{\ell-1})}\in(0,1],\qquad
\pi_\ell(B)=\frac{P(B\cap A_\ell)}{P(A_\ell)}
\quad (B\in\mathcal F).
$
The target probability is $p=P(A_L)$. Independence across levels means that the complete sample arrays used at distinct levels are mutually independent; correct marginal laws alone do not imply this condition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ be a standard Borel space, $M$ a probability kernel on it, and $T,R\in\mathcal E$ disjoint target and return sets. Write $S=E\setminus(T\cup R)$ and let $C=\{\mathtt{hit},\mathtt{return},\partial\}$ have the discrete sigma-algebra; $\partial$ is the cemetery outcome meaning the budget expired before either set was reached.

For budget $m=0$, define
$
\kappa_0(x,\cdot)=
\begin{cases}
\delta_{\mathtt{hit}},&x\in T,\\
\delta_{\mathtt{return}},&x\in R,\\
\delta_{\partial},&x\in S.
\end{cases}
$
For $m\ge0$, define the finite-budget stopped-status kernel recursively by
$
\kappa_{m+1}(x,\cdot)=
\begin{cases}
\delta_{\mathtt{hit}},&x\in T,\\
\delta_{\mathtt{return}},&x\in R,\\
\displaystyle\int_E\kappa_m(y,\cdot)\,M(x,dy),&x\in S.
\end{cases}
$
Thus a target hit at the initial state counts at budget zero; each additional budget unit permits one more transition. The **exact-hitting status kernel**, when used, is the limit law of these statuses and treats nontermination as $\partial$; it is an exact sampler for $P_x(\tau_T<\tau_R)$ only when the requested event is the finite first hit represented by that limit. The budgeted kernel is distinct from an exact-hitting oracle.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\in\mathbb N_0$. For each $0\le k\le T$, let $(\mathsf X_k,\mathcal X_k)$ be a standard Borel space. Let $\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X_0$, and for $1\le k\le T$ let $M_k:\mathsf X_{k-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf X_k$ be a probability kernel. A **potential** at time $k$ is a finite-valued nonnegative measurable function $G_k:\mathsf X_k\to[0,\infty)$. Write $\mathsf X_{0:t}=\prod_{k=0}^t\mathsf X_k$ with its finite-product sigma-algebra.

For each $0\le t\le T$, let $P_t^M$ be the finite path law with ordered kernel integral $\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{k=1}^tM_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$, supplied by Ionescu–Tulcea ([[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]]). The **unnormalized Feynman–Kac path measure** is
$$\gamma_t(A)=\int_{\mathsf X_{0:t}}\mathbf 1_A(x_{0:t})\prod_{k=0}^tG_k(x_k)\,P_t^M(dx_{0:t}),\qquad A\in\bigotimes_{k=0}^t\mathcal X_k.$$
Its **normalizer** is $Z_t=\gamma_t(\mathsf X_{0:t})=\gamma_t(1)\in[0,\infty]$. Only when $0<Z_t<\infty$ define the normalized path target $\pi_t^{\mathrm{FK}}=\gamma_t/Z_t$. The sequence $(\gamma_t)$ with its kernels and potentials is the Feynman–Kac flow.

State-space filtering kernels are conditional-law versions as in [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. A Feynman–Kac path target is not by itself an assertion that a pointwise conditional version has been selected at observation-null histories.

derivations.claim: For $m=0$, the three status probabilities are the indicators of the disjoint partition $T,R,S$; they are measurable and sum to one. Thus $\kappa_0$ is a probability kernel.

At $m=0$ the hit status occurs exactly when $X_0\in T$. For $m+1$, points in $T$ or $R$ stop immediately, while from $S$ the first $M$-transition is followed by the budget-$m$ rule. The finite-prefix law [F3] and induction therefore identify $\kappa_m(x,\{\mathtt{hit}\})$ with $P_x(\tau_T<\tau_R,\tau_T\le m)$; integrating against $\mu$ gives $p_m$.

Suppose $\kappa_m$ is a probability kernel. For each $c\in C$, the function $y\mapsto\kappa_m(y,\{c\})$ is measurable. By [F2], its $M(x,\cdot)$-integral is measurable in $x$. On $T$ and $R$ the next status is the corresponding point mass; on $S$ the three integrals sum to $\int 1\,M(x,dy)=1$. Hence $\kappa_{m+1}$ is a probability kernel, and induction proves the first claim.

In the one-step Feynman–Kac model, the product of potentials is $\mathbf1_{\{\mathtt{hit}\}}$; [F4] therefore gives normalizer $\int\mathbf1_{\{\mathtt{hit}\}}\,d(\mu\kappa_m)=p_m$. The success events by budgets $m$ increase to $\{\tau_T<\tau_R\}$; countable additivity gives the limit identity.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

$

derivations.claim: By [F4], $p_m=P_\mu(\tau_T<\tau_R,\tau_T\le m)$. The events increase to $\{\tau_T<\tau_R\}$, and the omitted part at budget $m$ is $\{\tau_T<\tau_R,\tau_T>m\}\subseteq\{\tau_T\wedge\tau_R>m\}$. Countable additivity [F3] gives the displayed difference and tail bound.

Replace the transition kernels one at a time and telescope the difference of the two normalizers. For the term replacing $M_j$, the earlier kernels and potentials define a finite measure of mass at most one, because the initial law is a probability and every potential lies in $[0,1]$. The remaining kernel-potential composition is a measurable function $g_j$ with $0\le g_j\le1$, measurable by [F5] and kernel composition. By the layer-cake identity $g_j(y)=\int_0^1\mathbf1_{\{g_j(y)>t\}}\,dt$, the total-variation definition bounds $|M_jg_j(x)-\widetilde M_jg_j(x)|\le\epsilon_j$ for every $x$. Integrating against that finite measure bounds the telescoping term by $\epsilon_j$; summing yields $\sum_j\epsilon_j$.

If $A_h\subseteq A$, then $P(A)-P(A_h)=P(A\setminus A_h)$ by finite additivity on disjoint measurable sets. A bound on this value requires an additional estimate for the missed-crossing event; continuity of a path alone does not supply a uniform grid-rate without quantitative regularity.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space as in [[def-probability-measure]]. A finite nested event sequence of length $L\ge1$ is a sequence of measurable sets
$
\Omega=A_0\supseteq A_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq A_L=A
$
such that $P(A_\ell)>0$ for $0\le\ell\le L$. Its **conditional level probabilities** and **level laws** are
$
p_\ell=\frac{P(A_\ell)}{P(A_{\ell-1})}\in(0,1],\qquad
\pi_\ell(B)=\frac{P(B\cap A_\ell)}{P(A_\ell)}
\quad (B\in\mathcal F).
$
The target probability is $p=P(A_L)$. Independence across levels means that the complete sample arrays used at distinct levels are mutually independent; correct marginal laws alone do not imply this condition.

For the nested event levels of [[def-nested-rare-event-levels]],
$
P(A_L)=\prod_{\ell=1}^L p_\ell.
$

Input the nested levels and exact conditional samplers for $\pi_{\ell-1}$ from [[def-nested-rare-event-levels]], a particle count $N\ge1$, and a declared per-draw work cost $c_\ell>0$ for each level. If any conditional sampler is unavailable, return conditional-sampler-unavailable.

For each level $\ell=1,\ldots,L$, independently of every other level, draw $X_{\ell,1},\ldots,X_{\ell,N}$ IID from $\pi_{\ell-1}$. Set
$
\widehat p_\ell=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf1_{A_\ell}(X_{\ell,i}),
\qquad
\widehat p=\prod_{\ell=1}^L\widehat p_\ell.
$
Return $\widehat p$, the level counts, total draw work $W=N\sum_{\ell=1}^Lc_\ell$, and status success if all level counts are positive or zero-level-estimate otherwise. The zero estimate is not a proof that $P(A_L)=0$.

The procedure is an ideal independent-level baseline. It does not assert that a branching or Markov mutation method produces independent exact conditional draws.

Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be a real IID sequence. If $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$ and $\mu=\mathbb E[Y_1]$, then $\mathbb E[\bar Y_n]=\mu$ for every $n\ge1$. If also $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)$, then $\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_n)=\sigma^2/n$ for every $n\ge1$.

derivations.claim: Under $\pi_{\ell-1}$, the indicator $\mathbf1_{A_\ell}$ is Bernoulli with success probability $P(A_\ell)/P(A_{\ell-1})=p_\ell$. Thus [F4] gives $\mathbb E\widehat p_\ell=p_\ell$ and $\mathbb E\widehat p_\ell^2=p_\ell^2+p_\ell(1-p_\ell)/N$ at each level.

The level arrays are independent by [F3], so $\mathbb E\widehat p=\prod_\ell p_\ell=p$ by [F2], and $\mathbb E\widehat p^2=\prod_\ell[p_\ell^2+p_\ell(1-p_\ell)/N]$. Subtracting $p^2=\prod_\ell p_\ell^2$ gives the displayed variance and, after division by $p^2>0$, the relative-variance formula. The work equality is the $LN$ declared draws weighted by their level costs in [F3].

Put $a_\ell=p_\ell^2$ and $v_\ell=p_\ell(1-p_\ell)/N$. Then $0\le a_\ell\le1$ and $0\le v_\ell\le1/(4N)$. By step 2.1 and finite product expansion,
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p)=\prod_{\ell=1}^L(a_\ell+v_\ell)-\prod_{\ell=1}^La_\ell
=\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,L\}}\left(\prod_{\ell\in S}v_\ell\right)\left(\prod_{j\notin S}a_j\right)
\le\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,L\}}\left(\frac1{4N}\right)^{|S|}
=\left(1+\frac1{4N}\right)^L-1.
$$

For fixed $L$, expansion of the finite binomial gives $(1+1/(4N))^L-1\le \frac{L}{4N}(1+1/(4N))^{L-1}=O(L/N)$. The relative formula in step 2.1 still contains $(1-p_\ell)/(Np_\ell)$, so this absolute bound does not give a rarity-uniform relative bound.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space as in [[def-probability-measure]]. A finite nested event sequence of length $L\ge1$ is a sequence of measurable sets
$
\Omega=A_0\supseteq A_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq A_L=A
$
such that $P(A_\ell)>0$ for $0\le\ell\le L$. Its **conditional level probabilities** and **level laws** are
$
p_\ell=\frac{P(A_\ell)}{P(A_{\ell-1})}\in(0,1],\qquad
\pi_\ell(B)=\frac{P(B\cap A_\ell)}{P(A_\ell)}
\quad (B\in\mathcal F).
$
The target probability is $p=P(A_L)$. Independence across levels means that the complete sample arrays used at distinct levels are mutually independent; correct marginal laws alone do not imply this condition.

Input the nested levels of [[def-nested-rare-event-levels]] on a standard Borel state space $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$, a particle count $N\ge1$, and probability kernels $K_\ell$ for $1\le\ell<L$. Each mutation kernel must satisfy
$
K_\ell(x,A_\ell)=1\quad(x\in A_\ell),\qquad \pi_\ell K_\ell=\pi_\ell.
$
If a required kernel is unavailable or violates its declared conditions, return mutation-kernel-unavailable.

Apply the canonical full-resampling sequential importance-resampling procedure of [[alg-sequential-importance-resampling]] to the following finite Feynman–Kac model: initial law $P$, initial potential $G_0\equiv1$, identity transition $M_1$, event potential $G_1=\mathbf1_{A_1}$, and, for $2\le\ell\le L$, transition $M_\ell=K_{\ell-1}$ and potential $G_\ell=\mathbf1_{A_\ell}$. Use multinomial full resampling at every selection and proposal kernels equal to the target transitions, so each Radon–Nikodym correction is one.

Return the SIR normalizer estimate $\widehat p$ and the full particle output. If any incremental average event weight is zero, report status zero-particle-prefix and $\widehat p=0$, as in the canonical SIR procedure. This status does not assert that the target probability is zero. The exact conditional level sampler is not inferred from the existence of an invariant kernel; kernel accessibility is an input requirement.

Let $\nu$ be a probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$, $M$ a probability kernel on $E$, $G,f:E\to[0,1]$ measurable, $z\in[0,1]$, and $N\ge1$. Draw $Y_1,\ldots,Y_N$ IID from the probability law $\nu M$. Put $a=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^NG(Y_i)$. If $a>0$, set
$
\eta^N=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^NG(Y_i)\delta_{Y_i}}{Na};
$
if $a=0$, let $\eta^N$ be any probability measure. Define the one-step unnormalized estimate $\Gamma^N(f)=za\,\eta^N(f)$. Then
$
\mathbb E[\Gamma^N(f)]=z\,\nu M(Gf),
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\Gamma^N(f))\le\frac{z^2}{4N}.
$
The estimate is the normalizer update $za$ multiplied by the weighted empirical mean of $f$. The zero-weight fallback does not affect $\Gamma^N$.

Use the full-resampling SIR model in [[alg-fixed-level-sir-splitting]] with $N\ge1$, positive level probabilities, and each $K_\ell$ supported on $A_\ell$ and invariant for $\pi_\ell=P(\,\cdot\mid A_\ell)$. Then every prefix Feynman–Kac normalizer is $Z_\ell=P(A_\ell)$, and the product normalizer estimate $\widehat p$ is unbiased:
$
\mathbb E[\widehat p]=P(A_L).
$
This conclusion asserts no finite-$N$ variance bound, accuracy guarantee, or uniform-in-rarity efficiency.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\in\mathbb N_0$. For each $0\le k\le T$, let $(\mathsf X_k,\mathcal X_k)$ be a standard Borel space. Let $\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X_0$, and for $1\le k\le T$ let $M_k:\mathsf X_{k-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf X_k$ be a probability kernel. A **potential** at time $k$ is a finite-valued nonnegative measurable function $G_k:\mathsf X_k\to[0,\infty)$. Write $\mathsf X_{0:t}=\prod_{k=0}^t\mathsf X_k$ with its finite-product sigma-algebra.

For each $0\le t\le T$, let $P_t^M$ be the finite path law with ordered kernel integral $\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{k=1}^tM_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$, supplied by Ionescu–Tulcea ([[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]]). The **unnormalized Feynman–Kac path measure** is
$$\gamma_t(A)=\int_{\mathsf X_{0:t}}\mathbf 1_A(x_{0:t})\prod_{k=0}^tG_k(x_k)\,P_t^M(dx_{0:t}),\qquad A\in\bigotimes_{k=0}^t\mathcal X_k.$$
Its **normalizer** is $Z_t=\gamma_t(\mathsf X_{0:t})=\gamma_t(1)\in[0,\infty]$. Only when $0<Z_t<\infty$ define the normalized path target $\pi_t^{\mathrm{FK}}=\gamma_t/Z_t$. The sequence $(\gamma_t)$ with its kernels and potentials is the Feynman–Kac flow.

State-space filtering kernels are conditional-law versions as in [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. A Feynman–Kac path target is not by itself an assertion that a pointwise conditional version has been selected at observation-null histories.

Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be a real IID sequence. If $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$ and $\mu=\mathbb E[Y_1]$, then $\mathbb E[\bar Y_n]=\mu$ for every $n\ge1$. If also $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)$, then $\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_n)=\sigma^2/n$ for every $n\ge1$.
Assume AC. For real $X\in L^2(P)$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid\mathcal G)]+\operatorname{Var}(E[X\mid\mathcal G])$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: By [F4], the estimate is unbiased for $Z_L=P(A_L)$, so its mean-square error equals its variance.

Set $Q_L\equiv1$, and recursively $Q_{p-1}=M_p(G_pQ_p)$ for $p=L,\ldots,1$. Since $M_p$ is a probability kernel and $0\le G_p\le1$, backward induction gives $0\le Q_p\le1$. By [F5], $Z_L=P(A_L)=\int Q_0\,dP$.

Let $\Gamma_p^N=\widehat Z_p\eta_p^N$ be the unnormalized weighted empirical measure after level $p$, and put $U_p=\Gamma_p^N(Q_p)$. Conditional on the particle history through level $p-1$, [F2] gives IID proposals from $\eta_{p-1}^NM_p$; applying [F3] with $z=\widehat Z_{p-1}$, $\nu=\eta_{p-1}^N$, and $f=Q_p$ yields $ \mathbb E[U_p\mid\mathcal F_{p-1}] =\widehat Z_{p-1}\eta_{p-1}^N(M_p(G_pQ_p)) =U_{p-1}, \quad \operatorname{Var}(U_p\mid\mathcal F_{p-1}) \le\frac{\widehat Z_{p-1}^{\,2}}{4N} \le\frac1{4N}. $ Here the final inequality holds because $\widehat Z_{p-1}$ is a product of averages of potentials in $[0,1]$.

The initial particles are IID from $P$, so $U_0=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^NQ_0(X_0^i)$. Since $Q_0^2\le Q_0$, [F8] gives $\operatorname{Var}(Q_0(X_0))\le\mathbb E Q_0-(\mathbb E Q_0)^2\le1/4$; [F6] then gives $\operatorname{Var}(U_0)\le1/(4N)$. Iterating [F7] with the conditional mean identity from step 2.1 gives $ \operatorname{Var}(U_L) =\operatorname{Var}(U_0)+\sum_{p=1}^L \mathbb E[\operatorname{Var}(U_p\mid\mathcal F_{p-1})] \le\frac{L+1}{4N}. $

Since $Q_L\equiv1$, $U_L=\Gamma_L^N(1)=\widehat Z_L=\widehat p$. Step 1.1 and step 3.1 prove both assertions. The constant does not involve $P(A_L)$, so no lower bound on the event probability is needed for this absolute error bound.

$
\widehat p_\ell=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf1_{A_\ell}(X_{\ell,i}),
\qquad
\widehat p=\prod_{\ell=1}^L\widehat p_\ell.
$
Return $\widehat p$, the level counts, total draw work $W=N\sum_{\ell=1}^Lc_\ell$, and status success if all level counts are positive or zero-level-estimate otherwise. The zero estimate is not a proof that $P(A_L)=0$.

Run [[alg-independent-fixed-level-splitting]] on the nested levels of [[def-nested-rare-event-levels]] with $N\ge1$ draws per level. Then
$
\mathbb E[\widehat p]=p,\qquad
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p)}{p^2}
=\prod_{\ell=1}^L\left(1+\frac{1-p_\ell}{Np_\ell}\right)-1,
\qquad
W=N\sum_{\ell=1}^L c_\ell.
$
In absolute error,
$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p)\le\left(1+\frac1{4N}\right)^L-1.
$
For fixed $L$, the right side is $O(L/N)$, uniformly in the rarity of $p$; the relative-variance formula has factors $1/p_\ell$ and gives no uniform relative-efficiency claim.

The two designs use the product estimator specified in [F1]. With two levels and $N=2$, [F2] gives relative variance $ \left(1+\frac{1/4}{2(3/4)}\right)\left(1+\frac{2/3}{2(1/3)}\right)-1 =\frac76\cdot2-1=\frac43. $ The work is $2\cdot2=4$.

In the augmented chain, the conditional probabilities are $3/4,1,1,1/3$, and $N=1,L=4$. The two unit-probability factors in [F2] equal one, while the other factors are $4/3$ and $3$; the relative variance is $4-1=3$, with work $1\cdot4=4$.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $A\in\mathcal X$, and let the target probability measure $P$ have a pointwise finite measurable density $f:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with respect to $\mu$, so $P(B)=\int_B f\,d\mu$. Let $\{q_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ be pointwise finite probability densities with respect to $\mu$, and write $Q_\theta(dx)=q_\theta(x)\mu(dx)$, where $\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite nonempty set equipped with lexicographic order. For each $\theta\in\Theta$, supply an exact admissibility checker $\mathcal C(A,f,q_\theta)$ that returns `admissible` if and only if $P|_A\ll Q_\theta$ and the contribution
$$
w_\theta(x)=\begin{cases}\mathbf1_A(x)f(x)/q_\theta(x),&q_\theta(x)>0,\\0,&q_\theta(x)=0\end{cases}
$$
is integrable under $Q_\theta$, where $P|_A(B):=P(B\cap A)$ for measurable $B$. Supply an initial parameter $\theta_0\in\Theta$, a pilot size $m\ge1$, and a production size $n\ge1$.

1. Draw an IID pilot $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m\sim q_{\theta_0}$.
2. If no $Y_j$ lies in $A$, return `pilot-no-hit`.
3. For every $\theta\in\Theta$, compute
$
s_\theta(y)=\begin{cases}\log q_\theta(y),&y\in A,\\0,&y\notin A,\end{cases}
\qquad S(\theta)=\sum_{j=1}^m s_\theta(Y_j),
$
with $\log 0=-\infty$. Pointwise finiteness rules out $+\infty$, and the piecewise score avoids the undefined product $0\cdot(-\infty)$. If all scores equal $-\infty$, return `no-finite-maximizer`. Otherwise choose the lexicographically least maximizer $\widehat\theta$ among the finite scores and freeze it.
4. Evaluate $\mathcal C(A,f,q_{\widehat\theta})$. If it returns inadmissible, return `inadmissible-production-proposal`. Otherwise draw an IID production sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim q_{\widehat\theta}$, independent of the pilot conditional on $\widehat\theta$, and return the ordinary importance-sampling estimate
$
\widehat p_{\rm CE}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n w_{\widehat\theta}(X_i)
$
using the piecewise-defined contribution $w_{\widehat\theta}$ above.

The finite candidate set makes the score comparisons and tie rule deterministic. The supplied exact checker is an input oracle; the procedure does not infer support or integrability from a pilot fit. If its check fails, no production estimate or unbiasedness or finite-variance claim is returned.

Use [[alg-cross-entropy-pilot-production]]. Let $\mathcal G=\sigma(Y_1,\ldots,Y_m)$ and let $H\in\mathcal G$ be the event that the pilot succeeds and the algorithm's exact admissibility checker accepts the selected parameter $\widehat\theta$. On $H$, the checker guarantees $P|_A\ll Q_{\widehat\theta}$ and integrability under $Q_{\widehat\theta}$ of the piecewise contribution $w_{\widehat\theta}$ defined in the algorithm. Define $\widetilde p_{\rm CE}$ to equal the returned production estimate on $H$ and zero off $H$. Then
$$
\mathbb E[\widetilde p_{\rm CE}\mid\mathcal G]=\mathbf1_H P(A)\quad\text{almost surely}.
$$
In particular, the production estimate is conditionally unbiased almost surely on the successful, admissible pilot event. This gives no probability-of-success, proposal-optimization, finite-variance, logarithmic-efficiency, or total-work guarantee.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space as in [[def-probability-measure]]. A finite nested event sequence of length $L\ge1$ is a sequence of measurable sets
$
\Omega=A_0\supseteq A_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq A_L=A
$
such that $P(A_\ell)>0$ for $0\le\ell\le L$. Its **conditional level probabilities** and **level laws** are
$
p_\ell=\frac{P(A_\ell)}{P(A_{\ell-1})}\in(0,1],\qquad
\pi_\ell(B)=\frac{P(B\cap A_\ell)}{P(A_\ell)}
\quad (B\in\mathcal F).
$
The target probability is $p=P(A_L)$. Independence across levels means that the complete sample arrays used at distinct levels are mutually independent; correct marginal laws alone do not imply this condition.

Input the nested levels and exact conditional samplers for $\pi_{\ell-1}$ from [[def-nested-rare-event-levels]], a particle count $N\ge1$, and a declared per-draw work cost $c_\ell>0$ for each level. If any conditional sampler is unavailable, return conditional-sampler-unavailable.

For each level $\ell=1,\ldots,L$, independently of every other level, draw $X_{\ell,1},\ldots,X_{\ell,N}$ IID from $\pi_{\ell-1}$. Set
$
\widehat p_\ell=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf1_{A_\ell}(X_{\ell,i}),
\qquad
\widehat p=\prod_{\ell=1}^L\widehat p_\ell.
$
Return $\widehat p$, the level counts, total draw work $W=N\sum_{\ell=1}^Lc_\ell$, and status success if all level counts are positive or zero-level-estimate otherwise. The zero estimate is not a proof that $P(A_L)=0$.

The procedure is an ideal independent-level baseline. It does not assert that a branching or Markov mutation method produces independent exact conditional draws.

Run [[alg-independent-fixed-level-splitting]] on the nested levels of [[def-nested-rare-event-levels]] with $N\ge1$ draws per level. Then
$
\mathbb E[\widehat p]=p,\qquad
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p)}{p^2}
=\prod_{\ell=1}^L\left(1+\frac{1-p_\ell}{Np_\ell}\right)-1,
\qquad
W=N\sum_{\ell=1}^L c_\ell.
$
In absolute error,
$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p)\le\left(1+\frac1{4N}\right)^L-1.
$
For fixed $L$, the right side is $O(L/N)$, uniformly in the rarity of $p$; the relative-variance formula has factors $1/p_\ell$ and gives no uniform relative-efficiency claim.

derivations.claim: Let $U,V$ be independent Bernoulli$(1/2)$. Construct the level-one sample by $X_1=1+V$ if $U=1$, and $X_1=3+V$ if $U=0$; then $X_1\sim P$. Construct $X_2=1$ if $U=1$, and $X_2=2$ if $U=0$; then $X_2\sim P(\cdot\mid A_1)$.

The correct marginal success probabilities are $P(X_1\in A_1)=1/2$ and $P(X_2\in A_2)=1/2$. But the two indicators both equal $U$, so their product has expectation $1/2$, while $P(A_2)=1/4$. Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ be a standard Borel space, $M$ a probability kernel on it, and $T,R\in\mathcal E$ disjoint target and return sets. Write $S=E\setminus(T\cup R)$ and let $C=\{\mathtt{hit},\mathtt{return},\partial\}$ have the discrete sigma-algebra; $\partial$ is the cemetery outcome meaning the budget expired before either set was reached.

For budget $m=0$, define
$
\kappa_0(x,\cdot)=
\begin{cases}
\delta_{\mathtt{hit}},&x\in T,\\
\delta_{\mathtt{return}},&x\in R,\\
\delta_{\partial},&x\in S.
\end{cases}
$
For $m\ge0$, define the finite-budget stopped-status kernel recursively by
$
\kappa_{m+1}(x,\cdot)=
\begin{cases}
\delta_{\mathtt{hit}},&x\in T,\\
\delta_{\mathtt{return}},&x\in R,\\
\displaystyle\int_E\kappa_m(y,\cdot)\,M(x,dy),&x\in S.
\end{cases}
$
Thus a target hit at the initial state counts at budget zero; each additional budget unit permits one more transition. The **exact-hitting status kernel**, when used, is the limit law of these statuses and treats nontermination as $\partial$; it is an exact sampler for $P_x(\tau_T<\tau_R)$ only when the requested event is the finite first hit represented by that limit. The budgeted kernel is distinct from an exact-hitting oracle.

Under the hypotheses of [[def-finite-budget-stopped-event-kernel]], every $\kappa_m$ is a measurable probability kernel from $E$ to $C$. For an initial probability law $\mu$, let
$
p_m=\int_E\kappa_m(x,\{\mathtt{hit}\})\,\mu(dx).
$
Then $p_m=P_\mu(\tau_T<\tau_R,\ \tau_T\le m)$. In the one-step Feynman–Kac model with initial law $\mu$, transition $\kappa_m$, initial potential $1$, and terminal potential $\mathbf1_{\{\mathtt{hit}\}}$, the normalizer is exactly $p_m$. The limit $\lim_{m\to\infty}p_m=P_\mu(\tau_T<\tau_R)$ is the exact-hitting normalizer; an exact simulator with finite expected work requires a separate termination-cost bound.

Assume AC. In the stopped-event setup of [[def-finite-budget-stopped-event-kernel]], with $(E,\mathcal E)$ standard Borel and initial probability law $\mu$, let $p=P_\mu(\tau_T<\tau_R)$ and let $p_m$ be the finite-budget normalizer of [[lem-finite-budget-stopped-normalizer]]. Then
$
0\le p-p_m=P_\mu(\tau_T<\tau_R,\tau_T>m)\le P_\mu(\tau_T\wedge\tau_R>m).
$
Thus the finite-budget stopped normalizer estimates the truncated event; a rate for its bias requires a tail bound for the stopping time. Separately, assume AC and let both finite-horizon Feynman–Kac models have the same finite horizon $H\in\mathbb N_0$, the same standard Borel state spaces $(\mathsf X_j,\mathcal X_j)$ for $0\le j\le H$, the same initial law $\mu_0$, and the same potentials $G_j:\mathsf X_j\to[0,1]$ for $0\le j\le H$. Let their transition kernels be $M_j,\widetilde M_j:\mathsf X_{j-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf X_j$ for $1\le j\le H$, and suppose
$$
\sup_x\|M_j(x,\cdot)-\widetilde M_j(x,\cdot)\|_{\rm TV}\le\epsilon_j,\qquad \epsilon_j\ge0,
$$
where $\|\nu-\nu'\|_{\rm TV}=\sup_B|\nu(B)-\nu'(B)|$. If $Z_H^M$ and $Z_H^{\widetilde M}$ are the normalizers in the common Feynman–Kac setup of [[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]], then $|Z_H^M-Z_H^{\widetilde M}|\le\sum_{j=1}^H\epsilon_j$. If a grid-detected crossing event $A_h$ is contained in a continuous-time target event $A$, its probability bias is exactly $P(A\setminus A_h)$; no grid-error rate follows without a separate path regularity or crossing-probability bound.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space. An **unnormalized target density** is a measurable function $\tilde p:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$Z_p:=\int_{\mathsf X}\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
The target probability measure is $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$. A **proposal density** is a measurable $q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\int q\,d\mu=1$; write $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. The input integrand $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, and the input sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ is IID with law $Q$, in the sense of [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. The normalizing constant $Z_p$ is known for this algorithm.

**Admissible conditions for an unbiased estimate:** $n\ge1$, $q>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{x:f(x)\tilde p(x)\ne0\}$, and the random variable
$$Y:=\begin{cases}f(X_1)\tilde p(X_1)/(Z_pq(X_1)),&q(X_1)>0,\\0,&q(X_1)=0\end{cases}$$
is integrable under $Q$. The support condition makes the value on $q=0$ immaterial to the target integral.

**Well-defined weights:** The reciprocal map $r(s)=1/s$ for $s>0$ and $r(s)=0$ for $s\le0$ is Borel. Its composition with $q$, multiplied by the measurable inputs, makes the piecewise weight and weighted integrand measurable ([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]], [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]).

**Procedure and output:** For each supplied draw $X_i$, set $Y_i=f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i))$ when $q(X_i)>0$ and set $Y_i=0$ otherwise. Return
$$\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i.$$
Separate variance and central limit claims require the corresponding weighted second-moment hypothesis.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $\tilde p\ge0$ and $q\ge0$ be measurable densities with $Z_p=\int\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$ and $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and set $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$ and $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. Let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $\int|f|\tilde p\,d\mu<\infty$. Suppose $q>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{f\tilde p\ne0\}$ and $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are IID with law $Q$. For the ordinary importance sampling estimator in [[alg-importance-sampling]],
$$\mathbb E_Q[\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}]=\int f\,d\pi.$$

Use the hypotheses and notation of [[thm-ordinary-importance-sampling-is-unbiased]]. Define
$$Y_i:=\begin{cases}f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i)),&q(X_i)>0,\\0,&q(X_i)=0\end{cases},\qquad \theta:=\int f\,d\pi,\qquad \sigma^2:=\operatorname{Var}_Q(Y_1).$$
If $\mathbb E_Q[Y_1^2]<\infty$, then $\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}$ has finite variance and
$$\operatorname{Var}_Q(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}})=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}=\frac1n\left(\frac1{Z_p^2}\int_{\{q>0\}}\frac{f(x)^2\tilde p(x)^2}{q(x)}\,d\mu(x)-\theta^2\right).$$
This finite-sample conclusion is choice-free. For the central limit conclusion, let $(X_i)_{i\ge1}$ be an IID sequence with law $Q$, and apply the estimator to its first $n$ draws for each $n\ge1$. If, in addition, AC holds, then
$$\sqrt n\bigl(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}-\theta\bigr)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2).$$
No finite variance or normal-limit claim is made when the weighted second moment is infinite.

Let $(P_\lambda,A_\lambda)_{\lambda\in\Lambda}$ be a family of probability measures and measurable events with $p_\lambda=P_\lambda(A_\lambda)>0$ and $p_\lambda\to0$ along the stated rare-event limit. An estimator $\widehat p_\lambda$ is **unbiased with finite variance** when $\mathbb E[\widehat p_\lambda]=p_\lambda$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p_\lambda)<\infty$. Its **relative error** is
$
\operatorname{RE}(\widehat p_\lambda)=\frac{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p_\lambda)}}{p_\lambda}.
$
It has **bounded relative error** if these relative errors remain bounded for all sufficiently rare indices. It is **logarithmically efficient** if $\widehat p_\lambda\ge0$, its second moment is finite and positive, and
$
\lim_{\lambda}\frac{\log\mathbb E[\widehat p_\lambda^2]}{\log(p_\lambda^2)}=1.
$
Logarithmic efficiency is a weaker asymptotic property than bounded relative error; the definitions impose no implication between an algorithm's efficiency and its proposal-fitting success.

For a specified cost model, let $W_\lambda$ be the expected work of one estimator replication. Record both its variance and its **variance-work product** $W_\lambda\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p_\lambda)$; for relative precision, record $W_\lambda\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p_\lambda)/p_\lambda^2$. These quantities depend on the cost model. Comparing algorithms requires the same declared work convention.

For a single event $A$ under a probability measure $P$, put $p=P(A)>0$. If $P$ has density $f$ with respect to $\mu$, the **zero-variance event proposal** is the probability density
$
q^*(x)=\frac{\mathbf 1_A(x)f(x)}{p}.
$
It is a formal benchmark because its normalizing constant is the unknown event probability $p$. Ordinary importance-sampling estimators and their weighted-second-moment condition are defined in [[alg-importance-sampling]] and [[thm-ordinary-importance-sampling-finite-variance-under-weighted-second-moment]].

derivations.claim: Both constants are finite and positive because the defining series converge for exponents $2$ and $3$, and $Q(k)>0$ for every $k$; hence $P\ll Q$. The likelihood ratio is $P(k)/Q(k)=(c_2/c_3)k$.
By [F1], $ \mathbb E_Q Z=\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\frac{c_3}{k^3}\frac{c_2}{c_3}k =c_2\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}k^{-2}=P(A_m)\in(0,\infty), $ so [F2] confirms unbiasedness.

The second moment is $ \mathbb E_Q Z^2=\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\frac{c_3}{k^3}\left(\frac{c_2}{c_3}k\right)^2 =\frac{c_2^2}{c_3}\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\frac1k=\infty $ by divergence of the harmonic tail. Thus the weighted second-moment hypothesis in [F3] is absent and this unbiased estimator has infinite variance; [F4] therefore rules out describing its second-moment efficiency as finite.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

This status does not assert that the target probability is zero. The exact conditional level sampler is not inferred from the existence of an invariant kernel; kernel accessibility is an input requirement.

Let $\nu$ be a probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$, $M$ a probability kernel on $E$, $G,f:E\to[0,1]$ measurable, $z\in[0,1]$, and $N\ge1$. Draw $Y_1,\ldots,Y_N$ IID from the probability law $\nu M$. Put $a=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^NG(Y_i)$. If $a>0$, set
$
\eta^N=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^NG(Y_i)\delta_{Y_i}}{Na};
$
if $a=0$, let $\eta^N$ be any probability measure. Define the one-step unnormalized estimate $\Gamma^N(f)=za\,\eta^N(f)$. Then
$
\mathbb E[\Gamma^N(f)]=z\,\nu M(Gf),
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\Gamma^N(f))\le\frac{z^2}{4N}.
$
The estimate is the normalizer update $za$ multiplied by the weighted empirical mean of $f$. The zero-weight fallback does not affect $\Gamma^N$.

Use the full-resampling fixed-level SIR model of [[alg-fixed-level-sir-splitting]] on nested levels $A_0\supseteq\cdots\supseteq A_L$, with $N\ge1$ particles and positive finite prefixes $Z_p=P(A_p)>0$. Its event potentials satisfy $0\le G_p\le1$. Then
$
\mathbb E[\widehat p]=P(A_L),\qquad
\mathbb E[(\widehat p-P(A_L))^2]
=\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p)
\le\frac{L+1}{4N}.
$
The bound is an absolute mean-square error bound for fixed $L$; it is not a relative-efficiency claim.

Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be a real IID sequence. If $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$ and $\mu=\mathbb E[Y_1]$, then $\mathbb E[\bar Y_n]=\mu$ for every $n\ge1$. If also $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)$, then $\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_n)=\sigma^2/n$ for every $n\ge1$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$
Assume AC. For real $X\in L^2(P)$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid\mathcal G)]+\operatorname{Var}(E[X\mid\mathcal G])$.

Use the full-resampling SIR model in [[alg-fixed-level-sir-splitting]] with $N\ge1$, positive level probabilities, and each $K_\ell$ supported on $A_\ell$ and invariant for $\pi_\ell=P(\,\cdot\mid A_\ell)$. Then every prefix Feynman–Kac normalizer is $Z_\ell=P(A_\ell)$, and the product normalizer estimate $\widehat p$ is unbiased:
$
\mathbb E[\widehat p]=P(A_L).
$
This conclusion asserts no finite-$N$ variance bound, accuracy guarantee, or uniform-in-rarity efficiency.

derivations.claim: Write $\alpha_p=1+(B_p-1)/N$. The initial particles are IID from $P$, $\widehat Z_0=1$ and $G_0=1$, so $U_0=N^{-1}\sum_iq_0(X_0^i)$ has mean $Z$ and second moment $Z^2+[P(q_0^2)-Z^2]/N\le\alpha_0Z^2$. All $U_p$ lie in $[0,1]$ by [F2], so all following conditional second moments exist.

Conditional on the particle history $\mathcal F_{p-1}$, put $z=\widehat Z_{p-1}$, $a=\eta_{p-1}^NM_p(G_pq_p)$ and $b=\eta_{p-1}^NM_p[(G_pq_p)^2]$. By [F1] and [F3], $\mathbb E[U_p^2\mid\mathcal F_{p-1}]=z^2[a^2+(b-a^2)/N]$. On $z>0$, the hypothesis $b\le B_pa^2$ bounds this by $\alpha_p z^2a^2=\alpha_pU_{p-1}^2$, using $q_{p-1}=M_p(G_pq_p)$. If $a=0$ this same calculation gives zero, without division by $a$. If $z=0$, the zero-normalizer branch makes $U_p=U_{p-1}=0$, so the inequality also holds without a hypothesis on the fallback empirical law.

Taking expectations in step 1.2 and iterating over $p=1,\ldots,L$ yields $\mathbb EU_L^2\le\prod_{p=1}^L\alpha_p\,\mathbb EU_0^2\le Z^2\prod_{p=0}^L\alpha_p$. Since $q_L=1$, $U_L=\widehat Z_L$. Its mean is $Z$ by [F4], so subtracting $Z^2$ proves the claimed MSE bound. If $B_0=1$ then $\alpha_0=1$; if every remaining $B_p\le B$, each remaining factor is at most $1+(B-1)/N$, giving the specialization.

Assume AC and the Brownian filtered-space conventions in [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite integers, let $W=(W^1,\ldots,W^m)$ be the driving standard Brownian motion, and consider the autonomous It\^o SDE
$$dX_t=b(X_t)\,dt+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(X_t)\,dW^j_t,$$
where $b:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and $\sigma_j:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$. For a differentiable vector-valued function $f$, $Df(x)$ is its Jacobian and $L_i f(x):=Df(x)\sigma_i(x)$; this definition is applied componentwise when $f$ is matrix-valued.

On a deterministic grid $t_n=nh$, define $\Delta W_n^j=W^j_{t_{n+1}}-W^j_{t_n}$ and the iterated It\^o integral
$$I_{ij,n}:=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}(W^i_s-W^i_{t_n})\,dW^j_s,\qquad 1\le i,j\le m.$$
The integrand is predictable and square-integrable, so this is the $L^2$ It\^o integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]]; its finite energy is $\mathbb E\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}(W^i_s-W^i_{t_n})^2ds=h^2/2$ by [[thm-ito-isometry-and-linearity-in-predictable-l2]].

The general Milstein Taylor update is
$$Y_{n+1}=Y_n+b(Y_n)h+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(Y_n)\Delta W_n^j+\sum_{i,j=1}^m L_i\sigma_j(Y_n)I_{ij,n}.$$
The diffusion fields have **commutative noise** when $L_i\sigma_j(x)=L_j\sigma_i(x)$ for every $x$ and every $i,j$. Under that condition, the equivalent update using only Brownian increments is
$$Y_{n+1}=Y_n+b(Y_n)h+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(Y_n)\Delta W_n^j+\frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^m L_i\sigma_j(Y_n)\bigl(\Delta W_n^i\Delta W_n^j-\delta_{ij}h\bigr).$$
For scalar noise ($d=m=1$), this reads
$$Y_{n+1}=Y_n+b(Y_n)h+\sigma(Y_n)\Delta W_n+\frac12\sigma(Y_n)\sigma'(Y_n)\bigl((\Delta W_n)^2-h\bigr).$$

For every $1\le i,j\le m$, define the Brownian area component $A_{ij,n}:=(I_{ij,n}-I_{ji,n})/2$ and the symmetric part $S_{ij,n}:=(I_{ij,n}+I_{ji,n})/2$. In particular, $A_{ii,n}=0$ and $S_{ii,n}=I_{ii,n}$. Then $A_{ji,n}=-A_{ij,n}$, $S_{ji,n}=S_{ij,n}$, and reindexing the sums gives
$$\sum_{i,j}L_i\sigma_j I_{ij,n}=\frac12\sum_{i,j}(L_i\sigma_j+L_j\sigma_i)S_{ij,n}+\frac12\sum_{i,j}(L_i\sigma_j-L_j\sigma_i)A_{ij,n}.$$
The second sum vanishes under commutative noise; otherwise the general update includes the area components. A noncommuting Milstein implementation must sample or approximate the needed areas and account for their approximation error and computational cost; this definition makes no claim that an exact area sample is free or that a particular area sampler has a specified error rate.

For this pair, $C_b^k(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^q)$ means that every component and every partial derivative of orders at most $k$ exists, is continuous, and is bounded. This notation is componentwise for vector and matrix valued functions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]: $B$ is a standard Brownian
motion on a filtered probability space, adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$,
with $B_t-B_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ of law $N(0,t-s)$ for $0\le s<t$.
For this localized-calculus definition the filtration satisfies the usual
conditions, as required by
[[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]].

1. **Real continuous Brownian Ito process.** A real progressively measurable process
   $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **continuous Brownian Ito process** when there are
   * a finite real $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $X_0$,
   * a real progressively measurable process $b=(b_s)_{s\ge0}$
     [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]] with
     $\int_0^t|b_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every finite $t\ge0$, and
   * a real predictable process $\sigma=(\sigma_s)_{s\ge0}$, locally
     square-integrable in the sense that $\int_0^t\sigma_s^2\,ds<\infty$
     almost surely for every finite $t$
     [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]],

   such that, up to equality at all times on a measurable probability-one event,
   $$X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s,\qquad t\ge0,$$
   where the first integral is the pathwise Lebesgue integral of $s\mapsto
   b_s(\omega)$ and the second is the localized Ito integral
   $\sigma\cdot B$ of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. One writes
   $\displaystyle dX_t=b_t\,dt+\sigma_t\,dB_t$ for the display, and $b$ is
   called the **drift** and $\sigma$ the **diffusion coefficient** of this
   representation.

2. **Multidimensional Brownian-driven process.** Let $d\ge1$ and $m\ge1$ be
   finite integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional
   Brownian motion [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] that is adapted to
   $(\mathcal F_t)$ and whose vector increment $B_t-B_s$ is independent of
   $\mathcal F_s$ for $0\le s<t$, let $X_0$ be a finite
   $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vector, let $b$ be an
   $\mathbb R^d$-valued progressively measurable process with
   $\int_0^t|b^i_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i$ and finite $t$, and let
   $\sigma=(\sigma^{ik})$ be an $\mathbb R^{d\times m}$-valued predictable
   process, each entry predictable
   [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]], with
   $\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i,k$ and finite $t$.
   Then
   $$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
   defines an $\mathbb R^d$-valued **continuous Brownian Ito process** driven by
   $B$, using the progressive integral versions of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. Other progressive representatives agreeing on one measurable full event at every time represent the same process. No claim is made that an arbitrary null-path modification remains adapted.

The following well-definedness clauses are part of the definition and are used
throughout.

3. **The drift integral is a genuine pathwise integral.** Progressive
   measurability gives measurable sections and makes the positive and negative
   integrals $\mathcal F_t$-measurable by the parameter-integral part of Tonelli
   [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], applied to Lebesgue measure on $[0,t]$ and the probability measure on $\mathcal F_t$.
   On the event where both extended integrals are finite, their difference is
   the drift integral; set it to zero otherwise. This is an adapted measurable
   convention, is finite everywhere, and on one probability-one event is
   absolutely continuous on every finite interval (take the countable
   intersection over integer horizons). It is progressive: the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto\int_0^tb_s(\omega)\,ds$, with the preceding finite-value
   convention, is measurable on every $[0,T]\times\Omega$ by parameter
   integration, and is adapted. Thus the definition uses the standard
   almost-sure drift and local-energy classes under the usual conditions.

4. **The stochastic integral exists, is unique and is continuous.** By
   [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]] and
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]] the localized integral $\sigma\cdot B$ is a
   well-defined adapted process with continuous paths, unique up to
   indistinguishability, and each of its finite-energy pieces is a
   square-integrable martingale. The displayed integral representative is progressive; $X$ is adapted by its required progressive measurability and has
   continuous paths, $X_t$ is finite almost surely for each $t$, and
   $M^i_t:=\sum_k\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s$ is a continuous local
   martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ in the sense of
   [[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]] for every $i$, with the common energy localizers described in clause 6.

5. **The coefficients are not part of the process.** A continuous Brownian Ito
   process may admit several representations $X=X_0+b\cdot\mathrm{Leb}
   +\sigma\cdot B$ with different pointwise representatives $(b,\sigma)$ (for example, altering a coefficient only at the single time zero), even for the same Brownian
   motion and filtration; this does not assert nonuniqueness of their equivalence classes modulo $\mathrm dt\otimes P$; conversely, two processes with the same displayed
   integral representation and the same $X_0$ are indistinguishable. Every
   statement on this page that mentions a decomposition uses only properties
   common to all representations of the given process. The separate
   quadratic-covariation definition that follows this item on its owning page
   is formulated from $X$ itself and not from $(b,\sigma)$; no
   quadratic-covariation definition is made inside this item.

6. **The class is closed under stopping and under linear combinations.**
   If $\tau$ is a stopping time, the literal stopped process $X^\tau$ is
   progressive. Indeed on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto(t\wedge\tau(\omega),\omega)$ is measurable into
   $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F_T$: the truncated time $\tau\wedge T$
   is $\mathcal F_T$-measurable, minimum is continuous, and rectangle inverse
   images give the assertion. Compose with the progressive restriction of $X$.
   Its drift is $b1_{[0,\tau]}$ and its diffusion is
   $\sigma1_{[0,\tau]}$; these retain almost-sure integrability and the required
   progressive/predictable measurability. The drift identity is pathwise.
   For the stochastic identity, apply the finite-energy stopping identity of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]], clause 4, on the canonical energy intervals
   of $\sigma$. The truncated integrand has finite energy on these same
   intervals. Comparing its canonical intervals with them at their pairwise
   minima by clause 4 identifies the localized integrals there. Countably
   many full-event agreements and exhaustion then give the identity at all
   times on one full event. Thus stopping closure uses localization, not a
   direct application of clause 4 to a possibly infinite-energy integrand.
   For finitely many coefficients, use the common continuous energy
   $E_t=\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2ds$ and times
   $\kappa_n=\inf\{t:E_t\ge n\}\wedge n$, $n\ge1$.
   The same continuous-energy test as in the local-integrability definition
   makes these stopping times increasing to infinity almost surely, and bounds
   every stopped coefficient's expected energy by $n$. The preceding
   pairwise-minimum comparison shows that every integral stopped there is its
   finite-energy integral. Finite sums of these square-integrable martingales
   are martingales: finite sums preserve adaptation and integrability, and summing the integral test over any $A\in\mathcal F_s$ proves the conditional-expectation identity; hence their sums
   are local martingales with this common sequence. For fixed real constants,
   finite linear combinations of processes driven by the same vector Brownian
   motion have the combined coefficients. Their integrability follows from
   the triangle inequality and $(\sum_{j=1}^r u_j)^2\le r\sum_j u_j^2$.

7. **No pathwise integral against Brownian motion is defined.** The display
   defines the stochastic integral only as the localized limit of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]; no integral $\int_0^tH_s(\omega)\,dB_s(\omega)$
   along the individual path is asserted, and the page's examples show that
   the pathwise Riemann--Stieltjes route is unavailable.

No choice beyond the declared AC of the ambient interfaces enters the
construction: the coefficients $b,\sigma$ and the process are given data, and
the canonically localized integral is constructed in
[[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. The Axiom of Choice is declared because the
conditional-expectation and $L^2$ interfaces used downstream assume it, and
the countable-choice obligations inherited from those interfaces are declared
as dependencies of this item.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to $f(x)=x_i x_j$ on $[t_n,t_n+h]$. It gives $W^i_{t_n+h}W^j_{t_n+h}-W^i_{t_n}W^j_{t_n}=\int_{t_n}^{t_n+h}W_s^i\,dW_s^j+\int_{t_n}^{t_n+h}W_s^j\,dW_s^i+\delta_{ij}h$. Expand each integrand as its value at $t_n$ plus its Brownian increment; the two constant terms cancel from the two sides, leaving $\Delta W_n^i\Delta W_n^j=I_{ij,n}+I_{ji,n}+\delta_{ij}h$.

Under commutativity, pair the summand with indices $(i,j)$ with the summand $(j,i)$. The coefficients agree by [L1], so the sum equals $\frac12\sum_{i,j}L_i\sigma_j(Y_n)(I_{ij,n}+I_{ji,n})$. Substituting step 1.1 gives the displayed Brownian-increment formula. The argument includes $i=j$, where the summand is one half of $L_i\sigma_i(Y_n)((\Delta W_n^i)^2-h)$.

routine_steps.claim: Setting $i=j=1$ in step 1.1 yields $I_n=((\Delta W_n)^2-h)/2$. By [F2], $\Delta W_n$ is independent of $\mathcal F_{t_n}$ and has law $N(0,h)$. Scaling the density in [F3] and integrating by parts give $\mathbb E[\Delta W_n\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]=0$, $\mathbb E[(\Delta W_n)^2\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]=h$, $\mathbb E[(\Delta W_n)^3\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]=0$, and $\mathbb E[(\Delta W_n)^4\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]=3h^2$.

Substituting the four conditional moments from step 1.2 into $I_n=((\Delta W_n)^2-h)/2$ gives $\mathbb E[I_n\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]=(h-h)/2=0$, $\mathbb E[I_n^2\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]=(3h^2-2h^2+h^2)/4=h^2/2$, and $\mathbb E[\Delta W_n I_n\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]=(0-h\cdot0)/2=0$. Each equality is an equality of conditional-expectation versions by the event-integral definition [F4].
