citations.quote:
Assume AC and the Brownian filtered-space conventions in [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite integers, let $W=(W^1,\ldots,W^m)$ be the driving standard Brownian motion, and consider the autonomous It\^o SDE
$$dX_t=b(X_t)\,dt+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(X_t)\,dW^j_t,$$
where $b:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and $\sigma_j:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$. For a differentiable vector-valued function $f$, $Df(x)$ is its Jacobian and $L_i f(x):=Df(x)\sigma_i(x)$; this definition is applied componentwise when $f$ is matrix-valued.

On a deterministic grid $t_n=nh$, define $\Delta W_n^j=W^j_{t_{n+1}}-W^j_{t_n}$ and the iterated It\^o integral
$$I_{ij,n}:=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}(W^i_s-W^i_{t_n})\,dW^j_s,\qquad 1\le i,j\le m.$$
The integrand is predictable and square-integrable, so this is the $L^2$ It\^o integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]]; its finite energy is $\mathbb E\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}(W^i_s-W^i_{t_n})^2ds=h^2/2$ by [[thm-ito-isometry-and-linearity-in-predictable-l2]].

The general Milstein Taylor update is
$$Y_{n+1}=Y_n+b(Y_n)h+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(Y_n)\Delta W_n^j+\sum_{i,j=1}^m L_i\sigma_j(Y_n)I_{ij,n}.$$
The diffusion fields have **commutative noise** when $L_i\sigma_j(x)=L_j\sigma_i(x)$ for every $x$ and every $i,j$. Under that condition, the equivalent update using only Brownian increments is
$$Y_{n+1}=Y_n+b(Y_n)h+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(Y_n)\Delta W_n^j+\frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^m L_i\sigma_j(Y_n)\bigl(\Delta W_n^i\Delta W_n^j-\delta_{ij}h\bigr).$$
For scalar noise ($d=m=1$), this reads
$$Y_{n+1}=Y_n+b(Y_n)h+\sigma(Y_n)\Delta W_n+\frac12\sigma(Y_n)\sigma'(Y_n)\bigl((\Delta W_n)^2-h\bigr).$$

For every $1\le i,j\le m$, define the Brownian area component $A_{ij,n}:=(I_{ij,n}-I_{ji,n})/2$ and the symmetric part $S_{ij,n}:=(I_{ij,n}+I_{ji,n})/2$. In particular, $A_{ii,n}=0$ and $S_{ii,n}=I_{ii,n}$. Then $A_{ji,n}=-A_{ij,n}$, $S_{ji,n}=S_{ij,n}$, and reindexing the sums gives
$$\sum_{i,j}L_i\sigma_j I_{ij,n}=\frac12\sum_{i,j}(L_i\sigma_j+L_j\sigma_i)S_{ij,n}+\frac12\sum_{i,j}(L_i\sigma_j-L_j\sigma_i)A_{ij,n}.$$
The second sum vanishes under commutative noise; otherwise the general update includes the area components. A noncommuting Milstein implementation must sample or approximate the needed areas and account for their approximation error and computational cost; this definition makes no claim that an exact area sample is free or that a particular area sampler has a specified error rate.

For this pair, $C_b^k(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^q)$ means that every component and every partial derivative of orders at most $k$ exists, is continuous, and is bounded. This notation is componentwise for vector and matrix valued functions.

Let the finite-dimensional Brownian It\^o setting and the integrals $I_{ij,n}$ be as in [[def-milstein-scheme-and-iterated-integrals]]. For every grid interval of length $h>0$,
$$I_{ij,n}+I_{ji,n}=\Delta W_n^i\Delta W_n^j-\delta_{ij}h.$$
In the scalar case, writing $I_n=I_{11,n}$ and $\Delta W_n=\Delta W_n^1$, this gives
$$I_n=\frac12\bigl((\Delta W_n)^2-h\bigr),\quad \mathbb E[I_n\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]=0,\quad \mathbb E[I_n^2\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]=\frac{h^2}{2},\quad \mathbb E[\Delta W_n I_n\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]=0.$$
Consequently, under the commutativity condition in the Definition, the double-integral term in the general Milstein Taylor increment equals
$$\sum_{i,j}L_i\sigma_j(Y_n)I_{ij,n}=\frac12\sum_{i,j}L_i\sigma_j(Y_n)\bigl(\Delta W_n^i\Delta W_n^j-\delta_{ij}h\bigr).$$

Let $X$ solve the finite-dimensional autonomous SDE in [[def-milstein-scheme-and-iterated-integrals]] with $b,\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m\in C_b^3(\mathbb R^d)$, using the $C_b^3$ convention in that Definition. Let $0<h\le1$ and let $[t,t+h]$ be a deterministic interval. Define $L_0f:=Df\,b+\frac12\sum_{k=1}^mD^2f[\sigma_k,\sigma_k]$ and $L_if:=Df\,\sigma_i$ for $i\ge1$. Then there is a remainder $R_{t,h}\in L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ such that
$$X_{t+h}=X_t+b(X_t)h+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(X_t)\Delta W^j+\sum_{i,j=1}^mL_i\sigma_j(X_t)I_{ij}+R_{t,h},$$
where $\Delta W^j=W^j_{t+h}-W^j_t$ and $I_{ij}=\int_t^{t+h}(W_s^i-W_t^i)dW_s^j$. Moreover, for the conditioning sigma algebra $\mathcal F_t$ there is a conditional-expectation version $r_{t,h}=\mathbb E[R_{t,h}\mid\mathcal F_t]$ with
$$|r_{t,h}|\le Ch^2,\qquad \mathbb E[|R_{t,h}|^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\le Ch^3\quad\text{almost surely},$$
where $C$ depends only on $d,m$ and the coefficient bounds, not on $t,h$ or $X_t$.

Let $N\ge1$, $0<h\le1$, and $Nh\le T$. Let $(\mathcal F_n)_{n=0}^N$ be a filtration as in [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]. For every $n$, let $e_n,u_n,r_n$ be square-integrable $\mathbb R^d$-valued, $\mathcal F_n$-measurable random vectors; let $M_{n+1},Q_{n+1}$ be square-integrable and $\mathcal F_{n+1}$-measurable. Say $Z$ is orthogonal to $\mathcal F_n$ if $\mathbb E\langle H,Z\rangle=0$ for every square-integrable $\mathcal F_n$-measurable vector $H$. Suppose
$$e_0=0,\quad e_{n+1}=e_n+hu_n+r_n+M_{n+1}+Q_{n+1},$$
$$|u_n|\le L|e_n|,\qquad |r_n|\le C_0h^2,$$
and $M_{n+1},Q_{n+1}$ are orthogonal to $\mathcal F_n$, with
$$\mathbb E|M_{n+1}|^2\le C_1h\,\mathbb E|e_n|^2,\qquad \mathbb E|Q_{n+1}|^2\le C_1h^3.$$
Then $\mathbb E|e_N|^2\le C_T h^2$, where $C_T$ depends only on $T,L,C_0,C_1$ and not on $h$ or $N$. This is a local-to-global estimate for an order-one grid RMS error when the drift error is Lipschitz and the centered one-step defect has second moment $O(h^3)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]: $B$ is a standard Brownian
motion on a filtered probability space, adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$,
with $B_t-B_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ of law $N(0,t-s)$ for $0\le s<t$.
For this localized-calculus definition the filtration satisfies the usual
conditions, as required by
[[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]].

1. **Real continuous Brownian Ito process.** A real progressively measurable process
   $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **continuous Brownian Ito process** when there are
   * a finite real $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $X_0$,
   * a real progressively measurable process $b=(b_s)_{s\ge0}$
     [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]] with
     $\int_0^t|b_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every finite $t\ge0$, and
   * a real predictable process $\sigma=(\sigma_s)_{s\ge0}$, locally
     square-integrable in the sense that $\int_0^t\sigma_s^2\,ds<\infty$
     almost surely for every finite $t$
     [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]],

   such that, up to equality at all times on a measurable probability-one event,
   $$X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s,\qquad t\ge0,$$
   where the first integral is the pathwise Lebesgue integral of $s\mapsto
   b_s(\omega)$ and the second is the localized Ito integral
   $\sigma\cdot B$ of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. One writes
   $\displaystyle dX_t=b_t\,dt+\sigma_t\,dB_t$ for the display, and $b$ is
   called the **drift** and $\sigma$ the **diffusion coefficient** of this
   representation.

2. **Multidimensional Brownian-driven process.** Let $d\ge1$ and $m\ge1$ be
   finite integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional
   Brownian motion [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] that is adapted to
   $(\mathcal F_t)$ and whose vector increment $B_t-B_s$ is independent of
   $\mathcal F_s$ for $0\le s<t$, let $X_0$ be a finite
   $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vector, let $b$ be an
   $\mathbb R^d$-valued progressively measurable process with
   $\int_0^t|b^i_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i$ and finite $t$, and let
   $\sigma=(\sigma^{ik})$ be an $\mathbb R^{d\times m}$-valued predictable
   process, each entry predictable
   [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]], with
   $\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i,k$ and finite $t$.
   Then
   $$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
   defines an $\mathbb R^d$-valued **continuous Brownian Ito process** driven by
   $B$, using the progressive integral versions of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. Other progressive representatives agreeing on one measurable full event at every time represent the same process. No claim is made that an arbitrary null-path modification remains adapted.

The following well-definedness clauses are part of the definition and are used
throughout.

3. **The drift integral is a genuine pathwise integral.** Progressive
   measurability gives measurable sections and makes the positive and negative
   integrals $\mathcal F_t$-measurable by the parameter-integral part of Tonelli
   [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], applied to Lebesgue measure on $[0,t]$ and the probability measure on $\mathcal F_t$.
   On the event where both extended integrals are finite, their difference is
   the drift integral; set it to zero otherwise. This is an adapted measurable
   convention, is finite everywhere, and on one probability-one event is
   absolutely continuous on every finite interval (take the countable
   intersection over integer horizons). It is progressive: the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto\int_0^tb_s(\omega)\,ds$, with the preceding finite-value
   convention, is measurable on every $[0,T]\times\Omega$ by parameter
   integration, and is adapted. Thus the definition uses the standard
   almost-sure drift and local-energy classes under the usual conditions.

4. **The stochastic integral exists, is unique and is continuous.** By
   [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]] and
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]] the localized integral $\sigma\cdot B$ is a
   well-defined adapted process with continuous paths, unique up to
   indistinguishability, and each of its finite-energy pieces is a
   square-integrable martingale. The displayed integral representative is progressive; $X$ is adapted by its required progressive measurability and has
   continuous paths, $X_t$ is finite almost surely for each $t$, and
   $M^i_t:=\sum_k\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s$ is a continuous local
   martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ in the sense of
   [[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]] for every $i$, with the common energy localizers described in clause 6.

5. **The coefficients are not part of the process.** A continuous Brownian Ito
   process may admit several representations $X=X_0+b\cdot\mathrm{Leb}
   +\sigma\cdot B$ with different pointwise representatives $(b,\sigma)$ (for example, altering a coefficient only at the single time zero), even for the same Brownian
   motion and filtration; this does not assert nonuniqueness of their equivalence classes modulo $\mathrm dt\otimes P$; conversely, two processes with the same displayed
   integral representation and the same $X_0$ are indistinguishable. Every
   statement on this page that mentions a decomposition uses only properties
   common to all representations of the given process. The separate
   quadratic-covariation definition that follows this item on its owning page
   is formulated from $X$ itself and not from $(b,\sigma)$; no
   quadratic-covariation definition is made inside this item.

6. **The class is closed under stopping and under linear combinations.**
   If $\tau$ is a stopping time, the literal stopped process $X^\tau$ is
   progressive. Indeed on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto(t\wedge\tau(\omega),\omega)$ is measurable into
   $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F_T$: the truncated time $\tau\wedge T$
   is $\mathcal F_T$-measurable, minimum is continuous, and rectangle inverse
   images give the assertion. Compose with the progressive restriction of $X$.
   Its drift is $b1_{[0,\tau]}$ and its diffusion is
   $\sigma1_{[0,\tau]}$; these retain almost-sure integrability and the required
   progressive/predictable measurability. The drift identity is pathwise.
   For the stochastic identity, apply the finite-energy stopping identity of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]], clause 4, on the canonical energy intervals
   of $\sigma$. The truncated integrand has finite energy on these same
   intervals. Comparing its canonical intervals with them at their pairwise
   minima by clause 4 identifies the localized integrals there. Countably
   many full-event agreements and exhaustion then give the identity at all
   times on one full event. Thus stopping closure uses localization, not a
   direct application of clause 4 to a possibly infinite-energy integrand.
   For finitely many coefficients, use the common continuous energy
   $E_t=\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2ds$ and times
   $\kappa_n=\inf\{t:E_t\ge n\}\wedge n$, $n\ge1$.
   The same continuous-energy test as in the local-integrability definition
   makes these stopping times increasing to infinity almost surely, and bounds
   every stopped coefficient's expected energy by $n$. The preceding
   pairwise-minimum comparison shows that every integral stopped there is its
   finite-energy integral. Finite sums of these square-integrable martingales
   are martingales: finite sums preserve adaptation and integrability, and summing the integral test over any $A\in\mathcal F_s$ proves the conditional-expectation identity; hence their sums
   are local martingales with this common sequence. For fixed real constants,
   finite linear combinations of processes driven by the same vector Brownian
   motion have the combined coefficients. Their integrability follows from
   the triangle inequality and $(\sum_{j=1}^r u_j)^2\le r\sum_j u_j^2$.

7. **No pathwise integral against Brownian motion is defined.** The display
   defines the stochastic integral only as the localized limit of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]; no integral $\int_0^tH_s(\omega)\,dB_s(\omega)$
   along the individual path is asserted, and the page's examples show that
   the pathwise Riemann--Stieltjes route is unavailable.

No choice beyond the declared AC of the ambient interfaces enters the
construction: the coefficients $b,\sigma$ and the process are given data, and
the canonically localized integral is constructed in
[[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. The Axiom of Choice is declared because the
conditional-expectation and $L^2$ interfaces used downstream assume it, and
the countable-choice obligations inherited from those interfaces are declared
as dependencies of this item.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim:
Subtract the exact update from [L1]. With $u_n=b(Y_n)-b(X_{t_n})$, set
$$M_{n+1}=\sum_j(\sigma_j(Y_n)-\sigma_j(X_{t_n}))\Delta W_n^j+\frac12\sum_{i,j}(L_i\sigma_j(Y_n)-L_i\sigma_j(X_{t_n}))(\Delta W_n^i\Delta W_n^j-\delta_{ij}h).$$
Then $e_{n+1}=e_n+hu_n+M_{n+1}-R_{n+1}$. The increments after $t_n$ are independent of $\mathcal F_{t_n}$ by [F1]; their first moments vanish, and each centered quadratic factor has mean zero. Hence $M_{n+1}$ is orthogonal to every square-integrable $\mathcal F_{t_n}$-measurable vector.

The derivatives of $b$ are bounded, so $|u_n|\le C|e_n|$. Also each $L_i\sigma_j$ is globally Lipschitz: its derivative is a sum of products of first and second derivatives of the diffusion fields, all bounded by [L1]. The linear Gaussian term in $M_{n+1}$ has conditional second moment at most $Ch|e_n|^2$. For the quadratic term, $\mathbb E[(\Delta W_i\Delta W_j-\delta_{ij}h)^2\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]\le2h^2$ by independent centered normal coordinates; the finite sum and the Lipschitz bound therefore give second moment at most $Ch^2|e_n|^2\le Ch|e_n|^2$. Thus $\mathbb E|M_{n+1}|^2\le Ch\,\mathbb E|e_n|^2$.

Initially $e_0=0$. For each $n\le N$, apply [L4] to the recurrence restricted to the first $n$ steps; its constants are the same because $nh\le T$. Thus $\max_{0\le n\le N}\mathbb E|e_n|^2\le C_T h^2$, and taking square roots gives the stated grid root-mean-square order one. When $m=1$, the only commutativity equation is $L_1\sigma_1=L_1\sigma_1$; if all diffusion fields vanish, the stochastic terms and their bounds vanish and the same proof reduces to the deterministic recurrence. The argument uses AC only through [A1].

routine_steps.claim: Define $e_n=Y_n-X_{t_n}$. Apply [L3] to the exact solution on $[t_n,t_{n+1}]$. Using [L2] and commutativity, the exact Taylor increment has the same product form as the update [L1], except that its coefficients are evaluated at $X_{t_n}$ and it includes the remainder $R_{n+1}$.

Let $r_n=\mathbb E[R_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]$ and $Q_{n+1}=-(R_{n+1}-r_n)$. By [L3], $|r_n|\le Ch^2$, $\mathbb E|R_{n+1}|^2\le Ch^3$, and hence $\mathbb E|Q_{n+1}|^2\le2\mathbb E|R_{n+1}|^2+2\mathbb E|r_n|^2\le Ch^3$ because $h\le1$. The defining event-integral property of conditional expectation makes $Q_{n+1}$ orthogonal to every square-integrable $\mathcal F_{t_n}$-measurable vector. Therefore the recurrence in step 1.2 has the form required by [L4], with local mean $-r_n$ and centered terms $M_{n+1},Q_{n+1}$.

Assume AC and the Brownian filtered-space conventions in [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Consider the scalar additive-noise It\^o SDE
$$dX_t=b(X_t)\,dt+\sigma\,dW_t,$$
where $\sigma\in\mathbb R$ is constant. Given a step size $h>0$, a grid value $Y_n$, and the Brownian increment $\Delta W_n=W_{t_{n+1}}-W_{t_n}$, the explicit stochastic Heun update is the two-stage rule
$$Z_n=Y_n+b(Y_n)h+\sigma\Delta W_n,\qquad Y_{n+1}=Y_n+\frac h2\bigl(b(Y_n)+b(Z_n)\bigr)+\sigma\Delta W_n.$$
The predictor $Z_n$ uses the same increment as the corrector. One step evaluates $b$ at $Y_n$ and $Z_n$ and uses one Gaussian increment. The weak order-two guarantee authored in this pair is only for this constant-diffusion scheme; the displayed update omits terms required for the corresponding multiplicative-noise guarantee.

In this definition and its consumers, $C_b^k(\mathbb R;\mathbb R)$ means that the function and all its derivatives through order $k$ are continuous and bounded.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

derivations.claim:
Taylor-expand $u(t+h,x+D)$ in its spatial argument through degree five. The sixth-derivative bound and step 1.1 yield
$$\mathbb E u(t+h,x+D)=u+u_x\mathbb ED+\frac12u_{xx}\mathbb ED^2+\frac16u_{xxx}\mathbb ED^3+\frac1{24}u_{xxxx}\mathbb ED^4+\frac1{120}u_{xxxxx}\mathbb ED^5+O(h^3),$$
where the displayed derivatives are evaluated at $(t+h,x)$. Substituting the moment formulas, the coefficients through order $h^2$ are $hLu$ and $\frac12h^2L^2u$, because
$$L^2u=\left(BB_1+\frac12\sigma^2B_2\right)u_x+(B^2+\sigma^2B_1)u_{xx}+B\sigma^2u_{xxx}+\frac14\sigma^4u_{xxxx}.$$
Thus $\mathbb E u(t+h,x+D)=u(t+h,x)+hLu(t+h,x)+\frac12h^2L^2u(t+h,x)+O(h^3)$.

Since $u_t=-Lu$ and $L$ is independent of $t$, differentiating the backward equation gives $u_{tt}=L^2u$. Taylor's formula in time at fixed $x$, with bounded $u_{ttt}$, therefore gives
$$u(t,x)=u(t+h,x)+hLu(t+h,x)+\frac12h^2L^2u(t+h,x)+O(h^3).$$
The coefficient and derivative bounds in the Statement make the constants in the preceding expansions uniform in $t,x,h$.
The expansions in steps 2.1 and 3.1 have identical terms through order $h^2$; subtracting them leaves a remainder bounded by $Ch^3$, which is the asserted one-step weak defect.

routine_steps.claim:
Put $B=b(x)$, $B_j=b^{(j)}(x)$, $\delta=Bh+\sigma w$, and $D=\sigma w+Bh+\frac h2(b(x+\delta)-B)$. Taylor's formula through degree three gives $b(x+\delta)=B+B_1\delta+\frac12B_2\delta^2+\frac16B_3\delta^3+\rho_4$, with $|\rho_4|\le\|b^{(4)}\|_\infty|\delta|^4/24$. From [F1], $\mathbb Ew=0$, $\mathbb Ew^2=h$, $\mathbb Ew^3=0$, $\mathbb Ew^4=3h^2$, $\mathbb Ew^5=0$, and $\mathbb E|w|^6=15h^3$. Substituting $\delta=Bh+\sigma w$ and collecting terms of order at most $h^2$ gives
$$\begin{aligned}\mathbb ED&=Bh+\left(\frac12BB_1+\frac14\sigma^2B_2\right)h^2+O(h^3),\\\mathbb ED^2&=\sigma^2h+(B^2+\sigma^2B_1)h^2+O(h^3),\\\mathbb ED^3&=3B\sigma^2h^2+O(h^3),\\\mathbb ED^4&=3\sigma^4h^2+O(h^3),\qquad \mathbb ED^5=O(h^3).\end{aligned}$$
For the second moment, the $h^2$ terms are $(Bh)^2$ and $2(\sigma w)(\frac12B_1\sigma hw)$; for the third they are $3(\sigma w)^2(Bh)$; for the fourth it is $\mathbb E(\sigma w)^4$. All other terms either contain an odd Gaussian moment or have expected magnitude $O(h^3)$ by $\mathbb E|\delta|^4=O(h^2)$ and the displayed remainder bound. Since $b$ is bounded, $|D|\le |\sigma||w|+h\|b\|_\infty$, so $\mathbb E|D|^6\le Ch^3$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]: $B$ is a standard Brownian
motion on a filtered probability space, adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$,
with $B_t-B_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ of law $N(0,t-s)$ for $0\le s<t$.
For this localized-calculus definition the filtration satisfies the usual
conditions, as required by
[[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]].

1. **Real continuous Brownian Ito process.** A real progressively measurable process
   $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **continuous Brownian Ito process** when there are
   * a finite real $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $X_0$,
   * a real progressively measurable process $b=(b_s)_{s\ge0}$
     [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]] with
     $\int_0^t|b_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every finite $t\ge0$, and
   * a real predictable process $\sigma=(\sigma_s)_{s\ge0}$, locally
     square-integrable in the sense that $\int_0^t\sigma_s^2\,ds<\infty$
     almost surely for every finite $t$
     [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]],

   such that, up to equality at all times on a measurable probability-one event,
   $$X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s,\qquad t\ge0,$$
   where the first integral is the pathwise Lebesgue integral of $s\mapsto
   b_s(\omega)$ and the second is the localized Ito integral
   $\sigma\cdot B$ of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. One writes
   $\displaystyle dX_t=b_t\,dt+\sigma_t\,dB_t$ for the display, and $b$ is
   called the **drift** and $\sigma$ the **diffusion coefficient** of this
   representation.

2. **Multidimensional Brownian-driven process.** Let $d\ge1$ and $m\ge1$ be
   finite integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional
   Brownian motion [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] that is adapted to
   $(\mathcal F_t)$ and whose vector increment $B_t-B_s$ is independent of
   $\mathcal F_s$ for $0\le s<t$, let $X_0$ be a finite
   $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vector, let $b$ be an
   $\mathbb R^d$-valued progressively measurable process with
   $\int_0^t|b^i_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i$ and finite $t$, and let
   $\sigma=(\sigma^{ik})$ be an $\mathbb R^{d\times m}$-valued predictable
   process, each entry predictable
   [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]], with
   $\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i,k$ and finite $t$.
   Then
   $$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
   defines an $\mathbb R^d$-valued **continuous Brownian Ito process** driven by
   $B$, using the progressive integral versions of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. Other progressive representatives agreeing on one measurable full event at every time represent the same process. No claim is made that an arbitrary null-path modification remains adapted.

The following well-definedness clauses are part of the definition and are used
throughout.

3. **The drift integral is a genuine pathwise integral.** Progressive
   measurability gives measurable sections and makes the positive and negative
   integrals $\mathcal F_t$-measurable by the parameter-integral part of Tonelli
   [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], applied to Lebesgue measure on $[0,t]$ and the probability measure on $\mathcal F_t$.
   On the event where both extended integrals are finite, their difference is
   the drift integral; set it to zero otherwise. This is an adapted measurable
   convention, is finite everywhere, and on one probability-one event is
   absolutely continuous on every finite interval (take the countable
   intersection over integer horizons). It is progressive: the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto\int_0^tb_s(\omega)\,ds$, with the preceding finite-value
   convention, is measurable on every $[0,T]\times\Omega$ by parameter
   integration, and is adapted. Thus the definition uses the standard
   almost-sure drift and local-energy classes under the usual conditions.

4. **The stochastic integral exists, is unique and is continuous.** By
   [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]] and
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]] the localized integral $\sigma\cdot B$ is a
   well-defined adapted process with continuous paths, unique up to
   indistinguishability, and each of its finite-energy pieces is a
   square-integrable martingale. The displayed integral representative is progressive; $X$ is adapted by its required progressive measurability and has
   continuous paths, $X_t$ is finite almost surely for each $t$, and
   $M^i_t:=\sum_k\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s$ is a continuous local
   martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ in the sense of
   [[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]] for every $i$, with the common energy localizers described in clause 6.

5. **The coefficients are not part of the process.** A continuous Brownian Ito
   process may admit several representations $X=X_0+b\cdot\mathrm{Leb}
   +\sigma\cdot B$ with different pointwise representatives $(b,\sigma)$ (for example, altering a coefficient only at the single time zero), even for the same Brownian
   motion and filtration; this does not assert nonuniqueness of their equivalence classes modulo $\mathrm dt\otimes P$; conversely, two processes with the same displayed
   integral representation and the same $X_0$ are indistinguishable. Every
   statement on this page that mentions a decomposition uses only properties
   common to all representations of the given process. The separate
   quadratic-covariation definition that follows this item on its owning page
   is formulated from $X$ itself and not from $(b,\sigma)$; no
   quadratic-covariation definition is made inside this item.

6. **The class is closed under stopping and under linear combinations.**
   If $\tau$ is a stopping time, the literal stopped process $X^\tau$ is
   progressive. Indeed on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto(t\wedge\tau(\omega),\omega)$ is measurable into
   $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F_T$: the truncated time $\tau\wedge T$
   is $\mathcal F_T$-measurable, minimum is continuous, and rectangle inverse
   images give the assertion. Compose with the progressive restriction of $X$.
   Its drift is $b1_{[0,\tau]}$ and its diffusion is
   $\sigma1_{[0,\tau]}$; these retain almost-sure integrability and the required
   progressive/predictable measurability. The drift identity is pathwise.
   For the stochastic identity, apply the finite-energy stopping identity of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]], clause 4, on the canonical energy intervals
   of $\sigma$. The truncated integrand has finite energy on these same
   intervals. Comparing its canonical intervals with them at their pairwise
   minima by clause 4 identifies the localized integrals there. Countably
   many full-event agreements and exhaustion then give the identity at all
   times on one full event. Thus stopping closure uses localization, not a
   direct application of clause 4 to a possibly infinite-energy integrand.
   For finitely many coefficients, use the common continuous energy
   $E_t=\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2ds$ and times
   $\kappa_n=\inf\{t:E_t\ge n\}\wedge n$, $n\ge1$.
   The same continuous-energy test as in the local-integrability definition
   makes these stopping times increasing to infinity almost surely, and bounds
   every stopped coefficient's expected energy by $n$. The preceding
   pairwise-minimum comparison shows that every integral stopped there is its
   finite-energy integral. Finite sums of these square-integrable martingales
   are martingales: finite sums preserve adaptation and integrability, and summing the integral test over any $A\in\mathcal F_s$ proves the conditional-expectation identity; hence their sums
   are local martingales with this common sequence. For fixed real constants,
   finite linear combinations of processes driven by the same vector Brownian
   motion have the combined coefficients. Their integrability follows from
   the triangle inequality and $(\sum_{j=1}^r u_j)^2\le r\sum_j u_j^2$.

7. **No pathwise integral against Brownian motion is defined.** The display
   defines the stochastic integral only as the localized limit of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]; no integral $\int_0^tH_s(\omega)\,dB_s(\omega)$
   along the individual path is asserted, and the page's examples show that
   the pathwise Riemann--Stieltjes route is unavailable.

No choice beyond the declared AC of the ambient interfaces enters the
construction: the coefficients $b,\sigma$ and the process are given data, and
the canonically localized integral is constructed in
[[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. The Axiom of Choice is declared because the
conditional-expectation and $L^2$ interfaces used downstream assume it, and
the countable-choice obligations inherited from those interfaces are declared
as dependencies of this item.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and the Brownian filtered-space conventions in [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite integers, let $W=(W^1,\ldots,W^m)$ be the driving standard Brownian motion, and consider the autonomous It\^o SDE
$$dX_t=b(X_t)\,dt+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(X_t)\,dW^j_t,$$
where $b:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and $\sigma_j:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$. For a differentiable vector-valued function $f$, $Df(x)$ is its Jacobian and $L_i f(x):=Df(x)\sigma_i(x)$; this definition is applied componentwise when $f$ is matrix-valued.

On a deterministic grid $t_n=nh$, define $\Delta W_n^j=W^j_{t_{n+1}}-W^j_{t_n}$ and the iterated It\^o integral
$$I_{ij,n}:=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}(W^i_s-W^i_{t_n})\,dW^j_s,\qquad 1\le i,j\le m.$$
The integrand is predictable and square-integrable, so this is the $L^2$ It\^o integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]]; its finite energy is $\mathbb E\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}(W^i_s-W^i_{t_n})^2ds=h^2/2$ by [[thm-ito-isometry-and-linearity-in-predictable-l2]].

The general Milstein Taylor update is
$$Y_{n+1}=Y_n+b(Y_n)h+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(Y_n)\Delta W_n^j+\sum_{i,j=1}^m L_i\sigma_j(Y_n)I_{ij,n}.$$
The diffusion fields have **commutative noise** when $L_i\sigma_j(x)=L_j\sigma_i(x)$ for every $x$ and every $i,j$. Under that condition, the equivalent update using only Brownian increments is
$$Y_{n+1}=Y_n+b(Y_n)h+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(Y_n)\Delta W_n^j+\frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^m L_i\sigma_j(Y_n)\bigl(\Delta W_n^i\Delta W_n^j-\delta_{ij}h\bigr).$$
For scalar noise ($d=m=1$), this reads
$$Y_{n+1}=Y_n+b(Y_n)h+\sigma(Y_n)\Delta W_n+\frac12\sigma(Y_n)\sigma'(Y_n)\bigl((\Delta W_n)^2-h\bigr).$$

For every $1\le i,j\le m$, define the Brownian area component $A_{ij,n}:=(I_{ij,n}-I_{ji,n})/2$ and the symmetric part $S_{ij,n}:=(I_{ij,n}+I_{ji,n})/2$. In particular, $A_{ii,n}=0$ and $S_{ii,n}=I_{ii,n}$. Then $A_{ji,n}=-A_{ij,n}$, $S_{ji,n}=S_{ij,n}$, and reindexing the sums gives
$$\sum_{i,j}L_i\sigma_j I_{ij,n}=\frac12\sum_{i,j}(L_i\sigma_j+L_j\sigma_i)S_{ij,n}+\frac12\sum_{i,j}(L_i\sigma_j-L_j\sigma_i)A_{ij,n}.$$
The second sum vanishes under commutative noise; otherwise the general update includes the area components. A noncommuting Milstein implementation must sample or approximate the needed areas and account for their approximation error and computational cost; this definition makes no claim that an exact area sample is free or that a particular area sampler has a specified error rate.

For this pair, $C_b^k(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^q)$ means that every component and every partial derivative of orders at most $k$ exists, is continuous, and is bounded. This notation is componentwise for vector and matrix valued functions.

Assume AC. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, let $W$ be an $m$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to a filtration satisfying [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], and let $X$ solve
$$dX_t=b(X_t)dt+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(X_t)dW_t^j,\qquad X_0\in L^2(\mathbb R^d).$$
Assume $b,\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m\in C_b^3(\mathbb R^d)$ as defined in [[def-milstein-scheme-and-iterated-integrals]]. Put $L_i f=Df\,\sigma_i$ and assume commutative noise $L_i\sigma_j=L_j\sigma_i$ for all $i,j$. On the uniform grid $t_n=nh$, $h=T/N\le1$, initialize $Y_0=X_0$ and use the product-increment Milstein update in the Definition. Then there is a constant $C_T$, independent of $N$, such that
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\mathbb E|Y_n-X_{t_n}|^2\le C_T h^2.$$
Thus the grid root-mean-square error is $O(h)$ on $[0,T]$. For $m=1$ the commutativity condition is automatic and the scheme is the scalar Milstein update. No claim is made for a noncommuting-noise scheme without an area sampler satisfying a separately proved approximation bound.

Fix a refinement factor $M\in\mathbb N$ with $M\ge2$, a base scale $T>0$, and a finite level $L\in\mathbb N\cup\{0\}$. The geometric mesh widths are $h_\ell=T M^{-\ell}$ for $0\le\ell\le L$. Let $P$ be a real random variable with $\mathbb E|P|<\infty$, and for each $\ell$ let $P_\ell$ be a real random variable with $\mathbb E[P_\ell^2]<\infty$.

At level $0$, set $\Delta_0=P_0$. At each level $\ell\ge1$, choose a joint law for a pair $(P_\ell^{\mathrm f},P_{\ell-1}^{\mathrm c})$ whose marginals are the laws of $P_\ell$ and $P_{\ell-1}$, respectively. Such a joint law is a coupling of the two levels. Define the correction $\Delta_\ell=P_\ell^{\mathrm f}-P_{\ell-1}^{\mathrm c}$. This construction gives $\mathbb E\Delta_\ell=\mathbb E P_\ell-\mathbb E P_{\ell-1}$.

For each level choose a positive integer $N_\ell$ and take $\Delta_{\ell,1},\ldots,\Delta_{\ell,N_\ell}$ to be independent copies of $\Delta_\ell$. Require the complete sample blocks from distinct levels to be independent. Write $\bar\Delta_\ell=N_\ell^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N_\ell}\Delta_{\ell,i}$. The finite-level multilevel Monte Carlo estimator is
$$\widehat\mu_{L,\mathbf N}=\sum_{\ell=0}^L\bar\Delta_\ell.$$
All corrections have finite second moments because each level approximation does. The shared randomness inside one fine/coarse pair is what can reduce the correction variance; the estimator still uses independent sample blocks across levels.

Let $M\ge2$ be an integer, $T>0$, and $h_\ell=T M^{-\ell}$. Let $P$ be an integrable real target. Suppose we are given an infinite compatible hierarchy: for every $\ell\ge0$ a square-integrable level approximation $P_\ell$, and for every $\ell\ge1$ a fixed coupling of the laws of $P_\ell$ and $P_{\ell-1}$. Define $\Delta_0=P_0$ and, under each coupling, $\Delta_\ell=P_\ell^{\mathrm f}-P_{\ell-1}^{\mathrm c}$. For each finite $L$, use the first $L+1$ levels and their couplings, with independent sample blocks across levels, as in [[def-mlmc-hierarchy-and-coupled-corrections]]. Suppose there are constants $C_b,C_v,C_c>0$ and exponents $\alpha\ge\frac12$ and $\beta>0$ such that, for every $\ell\ge0$,
$$|\mathbb E P_\ell-\mathbb E P|\le C_b h_\ell^\alpha,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\Delta_\ell)\le C_v h_\ell^\beta,$$
and the work for one level-$\ell$ correction sample is at most $C_c h_\ell^{-1}$. For every sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$, there are a finite level $L$ and positive integer sample counts $N_0,\ldots,N_L$ for which the estimator of [[def-mlmc-hierarchy-and-coupled-corrections]] satisfies
$$\mathbb E\left[(\widehat\mu_{L,\mathbf N}-\mathbb E P)^2\right]\le\epsilon^2$$
and its total work has the following upper bounds, with constants independent of $\epsilon$:
$$\begin{cases} O(\epsilon^{-2}),&\beta>1,\\ O\!\left(\epsilon^{-2}(\log\epsilon^{-1})^2\right),&\beta=1,\\ O\!\left(\epsilon^{-2-(1-\beta)/\alpha}\right),&0<\beta<1. \end{cases}$$
This is an upper bound under the three rate assumptions; it does not assert a matching lower bound or that the rates hold for a particular discretization.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For all sufficiently fine levels, [L2] gives $\|Y_\ell(T)-X_T\|_2\le C h_\ell$, where $\|Z\|_2=(\mathbb E|Z|^2)^{1/2}$. There are only finitely many coarser dyadic levels; each has finitely many steps and finite second moments because the coefficients and derivatives are bounded. Enlarging $C$ therefore makes the same error bound valid for every level. The same argument gives $\mathbb E|\psi(Y_\ell(T))|^2<\infty$, since $|\psi(x)|\le |\psi(0)|+\operatorname{Lip}(\psi)|x|$.

The fine and coarse approximations in $\Delta_\ell$ use the same Brownian path and hence the same exact terminal value $X_T$. By [F3], $\|U+V\|_2\le\|U\|_2+\|V\|_2$; with $h_{\ell-1}=2h_\ell$ this gives
$$\|Y_\ell^f(T)-Y_{\ell-1}^c(T)\|_2\le\|Y_\ell^f(T)-X_T\|_2+\|Y_{\ell-1}^c(T)-X_T\|_2\le C(h_\ell+h_{\ell-1})\le C'h_\ell.$$
For each $\ell\ge1$, the Lipschitz property yields $\operatorname{Var}(\Delta_\ell)\le\mathbb E|\Delta_\ell|^2\le\operatorname{Lip}(\psi)^2\mathbb E|Y_\ell^f(T)-Y_{\ell-1}^c(T)|^2\le C_vh_\ell^2$. At level zero, $\Delta_0=P_0$ by [F1] and has finite variance by step 1.1; increasing $C_v$ to also dominate $\operatorname{Var}(P_0)/h_0^2$ makes the same envelope hold there.

Again by the Lipschitz property and [F3],
$$|\mathbb E P_\ell-\mathbb E\psi(X_T)|\le\mathbb E|\psi(Y_\ell(T))-\psi(X_T)|\le\operatorname{Lip}(\psi)\|Y_\ell(T)-X_T\|_2\le C_bh_\ell.$$
The finite-level second-moment statement in step 1.1 verifies the square-integrability premise of [F1].

A level-$\ell$ fine path has $T/h_\ell=2^\ell$ steps and its coarse companion has $2^{\ell-1}$ steps. Each commutative Milstein step uses a fixed finite number of coefficient/derivative evaluations and Gaussian vector samples for fixed $d,m$; [L1] requires no Lévy-area sampler. Thus one correction sample has work at most $C(2^\ell+2^{\ell-1})\le C_ch_\ell^{-1}$, including the finitely many coarse initial levels after increasing $C_c$.

routine_steps.claim: The estimates in steps 1.2, 2.1, and 2.2 verify [F2] with $\alpha=1$ and $\beta=2$. Since $2>1$ and $1\ge1/2$, applying [F2] proves the stated $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ MLMC work bound. The local variance argument uses only the strong order-one result [L2] for nested commutative-Milstein paths; AC is inherited as stated in [A1].

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

Hence the one-step increment variance is $h/2+h^2/8$, and the derivative correction is a separate nonzero fluctuation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]: $B$ is a standard Brownian
motion on a filtered probability space, adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$,
with $B_t-B_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ of law $N(0,t-s)$ for $0\le s<t$.
For this localized-calculus definition the filtration satisfies the usual
conditions, as required by
[[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]].

1. **Real continuous Brownian Ito process.** A real progressively measurable process
   $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **continuous Brownian Ito process** when there are
   * a finite real $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $X_0$,
   * a real progressively measurable process $b=(b_s)_{s\ge0}$
     [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]] with
     $\int_0^t|b_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every finite $t\ge0$, and
   * a real predictable process $\sigma=(\sigma_s)_{s\ge0}$, locally
     square-integrable in the sense that $\int_0^t\sigma_s^2\,ds<\infty$
     almost surely for every finite $t$
     [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]],

   such that, up to equality at all times on a measurable probability-one event,
   $$X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s,\qquad t\ge0,$$
   where the first integral is the pathwise Lebesgue integral of $s\mapsto
   b_s(\omega)$ and the second is the localized Ito integral
   $\sigma\cdot B$ of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. One writes
   $\displaystyle dX_t=b_t\,dt+\sigma_t\,dB_t$ for the display, and $b$ is
   called the **drift** and $\sigma$ the **diffusion coefficient** of this
   representation.

2. **Multidimensional Brownian-driven process.** Let $d\ge1$ and $m\ge1$ be
   finite integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional
   Brownian motion [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] that is adapted to
   $(\mathcal F_t)$ and whose vector increment $B_t-B_s$ is independent of
   $\mathcal F_s$ for $0\le s<t$, let $X_0$ be a finite
   $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vector, let $b$ be an
   $\mathbb R^d$-valued progressively measurable process with
   $\int_0^t|b^i_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i$ and finite $t$, and let
   $\sigma=(\sigma^{ik})$ be an $\mathbb R^{d\times m}$-valued predictable
   process, each entry predictable
   [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]], with
   $\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i,k$ and finite $t$.
   Then
   $$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
   defines an $\mathbb R^d$-valued **continuous Brownian Ito process** driven by
   $B$, using the progressive integral versions of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. Other progressive representatives agreeing on one measurable full event at every time represent the same process. No claim is made that an arbitrary null-path modification remains adapted.

The following well-definedness clauses are part of the definition and are used
throughout.

3. **The drift integral is a genuine pathwise integral.** Progressive
   measurability gives measurable sections and makes the positive and negative
   integrals $\mathcal F_t$-measurable by the parameter-integral part of Tonelli
   [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], applied to Lebesgue measure on $[0,t]$ and the probability measure on $\mathcal F_t$.
   On the event where both extended integrals are finite, their difference is
   the drift integral; set it to zero otherwise. This is an adapted measurable
   convention, is finite everywhere, and on one probability-one event is
   absolutely continuous on every finite interval (take the countable
   intersection over integer horizons). It is progressive: the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto\int_0^tb_s(\omega)\,ds$, with the preceding finite-value
   convention, is measurable on every $[0,T]\times\Omega$ by parameter
   integration, and is adapted. Thus the definition uses the standard
   almost-sure drift and local-energy classes under the usual conditions.

4. **The stochastic integral exists, is unique and is continuous.** By
   [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]] and
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]] the localized integral $\sigma\cdot B$ is a
   well-defined adapted process with continuous paths, unique up to
   indistinguishability, and each of its finite-energy pieces is a
   square-integrable martingale. The displayed integral representative is progressive; $X$ is adapted by its required progressive measurability and has
   continuous paths, $X_t$ is finite almost surely for each $t$, and
   $M^i_t:=\sum_k\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s$ is a continuous local
   martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ in the sense of
   [[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]] for every $i$, with the common energy localizers described in clause 6.

5. **The coefficients are not part of the process.** A continuous Brownian Ito
   process may admit several representations $X=X_0+b\cdot\mathrm{Leb}
   +\sigma\cdot B$ with different pointwise representatives $(b,\sigma)$ (for example, altering a coefficient only at the single time zero), even for the same Brownian
   motion and filtration; this does not assert nonuniqueness of their equivalence classes modulo $\mathrm dt\otimes P$; conversely, two processes with the same displayed
   integral representation and the same $X_0$ are indistinguishable. Every
   statement on this page that mentions a decomposition uses only properties
   common to all representations of the given process. The separate
   quadratic-covariation definition that follows this item on its owning page
   is formulated from $X$ itself and not from $(b,\sigma)$; no
   quadratic-covariation definition is made inside this item.

6. **The class is closed under stopping and under linear combinations.**
   If $\tau$ is a stopping time, the literal stopped process $X^\tau$ is
   progressive. Indeed on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto(t\wedge\tau(\omega),\omega)$ is measurable into
   $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F_T$: the truncated time $\tau\wedge T$
   is $\mathcal F_T$-measurable, minimum is continuous, and rectangle inverse
   images give the assertion. Compose with the progressive restriction of $X$.
   Its drift is $b1_{[0,\tau]}$ and its diffusion is
   $\sigma1_{[0,\tau]}$; these retain almost-sure integrability and the required
   progressive/predictable measurability. The drift identity is pathwise.
   For the stochastic identity, apply the finite-energy stopping identity of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]], clause 4, on the canonical energy intervals
   of $\sigma$. The truncated integrand has finite energy on these same
   intervals. Comparing its canonical intervals with them at their pairwise
   minima by clause 4 identifies the localized integrals there. Countably
   many full-event agreements and exhaustion then give the identity at all
   times on one full event. Thus stopping closure uses localization, not a
   direct application of clause 4 to a possibly infinite-energy integrand.
   For finitely many coefficients, use the common continuous energy
   $E_t=\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2ds$ and times
   $\kappa_n=\inf\{t:E_t\ge n\}\wedge n$, $n\ge1$.
   The same continuous-energy test as in the local-integrability definition
   makes these stopping times increasing to infinity almost surely, and bounds
   every stopped coefficient's expected energy by $n$. The preceding
   pairwise-minimum comparison shows that every integral stopped there is its
   finite-energy integral. Finite sums of these square-integrable martingales
   are martingales: finite sums preserve adaptation and integrability, and summing the integral test over any $A\in\mathcal F_s$ proves the conditional-expectation identity; hence their sums
   are local martingales with this common sequence. For fixed real constants,
   finite linear combinations of processes driven by the same vector Brownian
   motion have the combined coefficients. Their integrability follows from
   the triangle inequality and $(\sum_{j=1}^r u_j)^2\le r\sum_j u_j^2$.

7. **No pathwise integral against Brownian motion is defined.** The display
   defines the stochastic integral only as the localized limit of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]; no integral $\int_0^tH_s(\omega)\,dB_s(\omega)$
   along the individual path is asserted, and the page's examples show that
   the pathwise Riemann--Stieltjes route is unavailable.

construction: the coefficients $b,\sigma$ and the process are given data, and
the canonically localized integral is constructed in
[[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. The Axiom of Choice is declared because the
conditional-expectation and $L^2$ interfaces used downstream assume it, and
the countable-choice obligations inherited from those interfaces are declared
as dependencies of this item.

Let the finite-dimensional Brownian It\^o setting and the integrals $I_{ij,n}$ be as in [[def-milstein-scheme-and-iterated-integrals]]. For every grid interval of length $h>0$,
$$I_{ij,n}+I_{ji,n}=\Delta W_n^i\Delta W_n^j-\delta_{ij}h.$$
In the scalar case, writing $I_n=I_{11,n}$ and $\Delta W_n=\Delta W_n^1$, this gives
$$I_n=\frac12\bigl((\Delta W_n)^2-h\bigr),\quad \mathbb E[I_n\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]=0,\quad \mathbb E[I_n^2\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]=\frac{h^2}{2},\quad \mathbb E[\Delta W_n I_n\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]=0.$$
Consequently, under the commutativity condition in the Definition, the double-integral term in the general Milstein Taylor increment equals
$$\sum_{i,j}L_i\sigma_j(Y_n)I_{ij,n}=\frac12\sum_{i,j}L_i\sigma_j(Y_n)\bigl(\Delta W_n^i\Delta W_n^j-\delta_{ij}h\bigr).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$. For predictable
$H,K$ with finite energy $E\int_0^TH^2ds,E\int_0^TK^2ds<\infty$ the integrals
$\int_0^TH\,dB$ of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] satisfy
$$\int_0^T(H+K)\,dB=\int_0^TH\,dB+\int_0^TK\,dB,\qquad \int_0^T(aH)\,dB=a\int_0^TH\,dB\quad(a\in\mathbb R),$$
and the identities are equalities of $L^2(P)$-classes (almost sure
equalities). Moreover the map $H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is an isometry,
$$E\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)^2=E\int_0^TH^2ds=\|H\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)},$$
it takes values in the mean-zero subspace of $L^2(P)$, and the bilinear cross
identity
$$E\Bigl[\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_0^TK\,dB\Bigr)\Bigr]=E\int_0^TH_sK_s\,ds$$
holds for all such $H,K$. In particular the image of the map is a closed
subspace of $L^2(P)$ isometric to the predictable $L^2$ space of $H$'s, and
$H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is injective up to the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Assume AC. Real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ embeds isometrically as a closed subspace of real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. For $X\in L^2(P)$, $U=E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is its orthogonal projection onto this subspace. It uniquely minimizes $E[(X-Z)^2]$ over $Z\in L^2(\mathcal G)$ as an almost-sure class.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The Jacobian of $\sigma_2$ sends $(1,0)$ to $(0,1)$, so $L_1\sigma_2=(0,1)$; the Jacobian of the constant field $\sigma_1$ is zero, so $L_2\sigma_1=(0,0)$. Thus commutativity fails. Starting from $X_0=(0,0)$, the first coordinate is $W_t^1$ and the second is $\int_0^tW_s^1dW_s^2$. The general Milstein Taylor update [F2] therefore has second-coordinate increment $I_{12}$ on the first step.

By [L1], the endpoints determine $I_{12}+I_{21}=UV$, where $U=\Delta W^1$ and $V=\Delta W^2$. Let $\pi_n=\{0=s_0<\cdots<s_{q_n}=h\}$ be deterministic partitions with mesh $|\pi_n|\to0$, and put $S_n=\sum_{k=0}^{q_n-1}W^1_{s_k}(W^2_{s_{k+1}}-W^2_{s_k})$. The It\^o isometry [F3] gives $\mathbb E|S_n-I_{12}|^2=\sum_k\int_{s_k}^{s_{k+1}}(s-s_k)ds\le h|\pi_n|/2\to0$.

For $0<s<h$, write $A=W_s^1$ and $U-A=W_h^1-W_s^1$; their joint density is $p_s(a)p_{h-s}(u-a)$, where $p_r$ is the $N(0,r)$ density. Dividing by the marginal density $p_h(u)$ and completing the square gives $\mathbb E[A\mid U=u]=(s/h)u$. At $s=0$ and $s=h$ the same formula follows from $A=0$ and $A=U$, respectively. For $\ell_k=s_{k+1}-s_k$, the pair $B_k=W^2_{s_{k+1}}-W^2_{s_k}$ and $V-B_k$ has density $p_{\ell_k}(b)p_{h-\ell_k}(v-b)$ when $\ell_k<h$; completing the square gives $\mathbb E[B_k\mid V=v]=(\ell_k/h)v$, and if $\ell_k=h$ then $B_k=V$ gives the same result. Independence of the two Brownian coordinate processes [F1] makes the joint density of $(A,U,B_k,V)$ the product of these two pair densities. Dividing by $p_h(u)p_h(v)$ shows that the conditional density of $(A,B_k)$ given $(U,V)=(u,v)$ factors, so $\mathbb E[AB_k\mid U,V]=(s/h)U(\ell_k/h)V$. Therefore
$$\mathbb E[S_n\mid\sigma(U,V)]=\frac{UV}{h^2}\sum_k s_k(s_{k+1}-s_k)\longrightarrow\frac{UV}{2},$$
because the sum is a left Riemann sum for $\int_0^h s\,ds=h^2/2$. By [F7], step 1.2 implies $S_n\to I_{12}$ in $L^1$; conditional expectation is $L^1$-contractive by [F6], so [F5] gives $\mathbb E[I_{12}\mid\sigma(U,V)]=UV/2$.

The isometry [F3] gives $\mathbb E I_{12}^2=\int_0^h\mathbb E(W_s^1)^2ds=h^2/2$. Also $U,V$ are independent with second moments $h$, so step 2.1 gives $J:=\mathbb E[I_{12}\mid\sigma(U,V)]=UV/2$ and $\mathbb E J^2=\mathbb E[U^2V^2]/4=h^2/4$. By [F8], $\mathbb E[(I_{12}-J)J]=0$; expanding the square therefore gives $\mathbb E|I_{12}-J|^2=\mathbb E I_{12}^2-\mathbb E J^2=h^2/4>0$. If $I_{12}$ were a measurable function of $(U,V)$, the conditional-expectation identity [F5] would give $I_{12}=J$ almost surely, contradicting this positive residual. Thus the endpoint increments do not determine the required area sample, and any approximation has a separate error and cost.

$$f_\lambda(t)=\begin{cases}\lambda e^{-\lambda t},&t>0,\\0,&t\le0\end{cases}$$
defines a probability law on $\mathbb R$ with survival
$S(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$ for $t\ge0$. For $k,\eta>0$, the density
$$f_{k,\eta}(t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{\eta}(t/\eta)^{k-1}e^{-(t/\eta)^k},&t>0,\\0,&t\le0\end{cases}$$
defines a probability law with survival $S(t)=e^{-(t/\eta)^k}$ for $t\ge0$.

$\dfrac{k}{\eta}(t/\eta)^{k-1}$ for $t>0$.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of

citations.use_explanation: [F2] Independence of the generated sigma-algebras gives the product formula for every measurable rectangle in a finite product of real lines. Iterating the sigma-finite product-measure theorem gives the finite product law of the marginals. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

A family $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ of sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$ is
**independent** when it is independent as a family of event classes in the
sense of [[def-independent-families-of-event-classes]].

A family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ of events is **independent** when the singleton event
classes $\bigl(\{A_i\}\bigr)_{i\in I}$ are independent. Equivalently, for every
finite choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}$,

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_{i_k}\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_{i_k}).$$

For two events this reduces to the familiar identity
$\mathbb P(A\cap B)=\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

derivations.claim: If $r_0=0$, nonnegativity of the finite sum implies every $r_j=0$, so the set of active clocks is empty and no finite candidate time is defined.

Suppose $r_0>0$. For $t\ge0$, independence in [F2] and the unit exponential survival in [F1] give $\mathbb P(T_*>t)=\prod_{j:r_j>0}\mathbb P(E_j>r_jt)=\prod_{j:r_j>0}e^{-r_jt}=e^{-r_0t}.$ Thus $T_*$ has the unique law $\operatorname{Exp}(r_0)$ specified in [F1].

For a channel $j$ with $r_j>0$, the scaled clock $E_j/r_j$ has density $r_j e^{-r_jt}$ on $t>0$ by change of variables in [F1]. Independence [F2] therefore gives the joint density that channel $j$ rings first at time $t$ as $r_j e^{-r_jt}\prod_{k\ne j:r_k>0}e^{-r_kt}=r_j e^{-r_0t}.$ Integrating over $t>0$ yields $\mathbb P(J_*=j)=r_j/r_0$, and this joint density factors as $r_0e^{-r_0t}(r_j/r_0)$, proving independence of $T_*$ and $J_*$.

For distinct active $i,j$, the independent scaled clocks have continuous densities, so their equality has probability zero: conditioning on $E_i/r_i$ leaves the independent variable $E_j/r_j$ with zero probability at each singleton. A finite union over pairs shows the minimum is unique almost surely. Together with steps 1.2 and 2.1 this proves all assertions.

Fix positive integers $d$ and $R$. A **reaction propensity system** consists of a state set $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ that is finite or countable, increments $\nu_j\in\mathbb Z^d$ for $1\le j\le R$, and propensities $a_j:E\to[0,\infty)$. Here “countable” means finite or countably infinite, as in [[def-countable]]. The total propensity
$$\lambda(x):=\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)$$
is finite for every $x\in E$, and $a_j(x)>0$ implies $x+\nu_j\in E$. Here $\mathbb N$ and $\mathbb Z$ have the meanings in [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-integers]], and addition in $\mathbb Z^d$ is coordinatewise.

A **reaction event** of channel $j$ at state $x$ records the marked transition $x\mapsto x+\nu_j$. The counting process $N_j(t)$ records the number of channel-$j$ events by time $t$. A zero increment $\nu_j=0$ is allowed: it records a reaction event without changing the state.

For a time-homogeneous system, the **reaction generator operator** on bounded functions $f:E\to\mathbb R$ is
$$(Qf)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0} a_j(x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
When $E$ is finite, $\Lambda:=\max_{x\in E}\lambda(x)<\infty$. If no active reaction has zero increment, the corresponding matrix has off-diagonal entries $q_{xy}=\sum_{j:x+\nu_j=y}a_j(x)$ and diagonal $q_{xx}=-\lambda(x)$. With zero-increment events, the operator formula remains valid and the matrix diagonal is instead minus the sum of state-changing rates; the zero-increment channels remain part of the marked event process.

For a finite horizon $T$, a **time-dependent propensity system** replaces $a_j(x)$ by functions $a_j:[0,T]\times E\to[0,\infty)$ whose sections $t\mapsto a_j(t,x)$ are measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B([0,T])$ of the usual topology on $[0,T]$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Require finite total rate $\lambda(t,x):=\sum_j a_j(t,x)$. Its time-dependent generator operator is
$$(Q_t f)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(t,x)>0} a_j(t,x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
This definition specifies a stochastic model. It does not assert that a physical chemical system follows that model.
citations.use_explanation: [F1] A reaction system has finitely many channels, finite total rate at each state, admissible poststates, and generator operator $Qf(x)=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0}a_j(x)(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x))$ for bounded $f$; for the stated $V$, the theorem uses that same finite sum as a local expression. ([[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]])

citations.quote:
Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.
citations.use_explanation: [F4] Expectation is integration against the probability measure, is linear on integrable variables, and preserves almost-sure order. ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]], [[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]])

citations.quote:
Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.
citations.use_explanation: [A1] Countable Choice is used only in the stated exponential and probability-product existence interfaces. ([[def-countable-choice]])

citations.quote:
Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.
citations.use_explanation: [A2] Dependent Choice is used only in the countable-product probability-space construction. ([[def-dependent-choice]])

derivations.claim: Fix $n\ge\max\{1,V(x_0)\}$ and set $K_n=\{x\in E:V(x)\le n\}$. This is finite by properness. The set $D_n=\{x+\nu_j:x\in K_n,\ a_j(x)>0,\ 1\le j\le R\}\setminus K_n$ of one-reaction exit states is finite, and $F_n=K_n\cup D_n$ is finite. The rate bound $M_n:=\max_{x\in K_n}\lambda(x)$ is therefore finite. For fixed ordered channel labels $j_1,\ldots,j_m$, the density of event times $0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T$ before the first exit is the product of the successive channel rates and exponential no-event factors. Summing over channel labels bounds this density by $M_n^m$, since at each event the sum of active channel rates is at most $M_n$. The ordered simplex has volume $T^m/m!$, so the probability of at least $m$ events before exit by $T$ is at most $(M_nT)^m/m!$, which tends to zero. Thus infinitely many jumps cannot occur in finite time while the process remains in $K_n$.

Stop the process at $\tau_n:=\inf\{t\ge0:X_t\notin K_n\}$. The stopped path takes values in the finite set $F_n$ and is frozen after exit. Let $C_n=\max_{y\in F_n}V(y)$. Conditional on the reaction history through time $s$, partition on the finite vector of last-used stream indices; on each part [F3] gives independence of all unused coordinates. If $s$ falls within a holding interval, the residual exponential wait has the same law because $e^{-\lambda(w+u)}/e^{-\lambda w}=e^{-\lambda u}$. Thus for $x=X_s\in K_n$, the density of one channel-$j$ event at elapsed time $u$ and no earlier event is $a_j(x)e^{-\lambda(x)u}$. The probability of at least two events within $h$ is at most $(M_nh)^2/2$ by integrating the summed first-two-event density, bounded by $M_n^2$, over the ordered two-time simplex. Since $V\le C_n$ on $F_n$, the first-event term differs from $h(QV)(x)$ by at most $C_nM_n^2h^2/2$, using $|1-e^{-z}|\le z$ for $z\ge0$; the multiple-event remainder is bounded by $2C_n(M_nh)^2/2$. Thus, uniformly over $x\in K_n$, $\mathbb E[V(X_{(s+h)\wedge\tau_n})-V(X_{s\wedge\tau_n})\mid\mathcal F_s]=h\,1_{\{s<\tau_n\}}(QV)(X_s)+O(h^2).$ Summing this identity on a uniform partition of $[0,t]$ and letting the mesh tend to zero gives $\mathbb E[V(X_{t\wedge\tau_n})]=V(x_0)+\mathbb E\int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}(QV)(X_s)\,ds.$ The error sum is $O(th)$; the Riemann sums converge because the stopped path has finitely many jumps by step 1.1 and $QV$ is bounded on $K_n$.

Set $g_n(t)=\mathbb E[V(X_{t\wedge\tau_n})]$. From step 2.1, $QV\le cV$, and $V\ge1$, we obtain $g_n(t)\le V(x_0)+c\int_0^t g_n(s)\,ds.$ Here $g_n$ is bounded on each finite interval because $X_{t\wedge\tau_n}\in F_n$. Iterating the integral inequality $m$ times bounds it by $V(x_0)\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}(ct)^k/k!+C_n(ct)^m/m!$; the last term tends to zero and the sum tends to $V(x_0)e^{ct}$. Hence $g_n(t)\le V(x_0)e^{ct}$.
On $\{\tau_n\le T\}$ the exit state satisfies $V(X_{\tau_n})>n$, so $n\,\mathbb P(\tau_n\le T)\le g_n(T)\le V(x_0)e^{cT}$.

Fix any finite $T>0$. If $\tau_\infty\le T$ but $\tau_n>T$ for some integer $n\ge\max\{1,V(x_0)\}$, infinitely many events occur in finite time while the process remains in $K_n$, an event of probability zero by step 1.1. A countable union over such $n$ is still null, so outside it explosion by $T$ forces $\tau_n\le T$ for every sufficiently large integer $n$. Step 4.1 gives $\mathbb P(\tau_\infty\le T)\le V(x_0)e^{cT}/n$ for arbitrarily large $n$, hence this probability is zero. Taking integer $T\ge1$ proves $\mathbb P(\tau_\infty=\infty)=1$. The argument uses Countable Choice and Dependent Choice only as declared in [A1] and [A2]; it uses no Axiom of Choice.
