Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $\Omega=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ carry the countable product probability measure of fair bits. For any finite family of pairwise disjoint infinite coordinate sequences $j_{s,1},j_{s,2},\ldots$, define
$$B_{s,k}(\omega)=\omega_{j_{s,k}},\qquad U_s(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}B_{s,k}(\omega)2^{-k}.$$
Then each $U_s$ has the uniform Borel law on $[0,1]$, and the family $(U_s)$ is independent. No other choice principle is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(U,V)$ have product Lebesgue probability law on $(0,1)^2$, and set
$$R=\sqrt{-2\log U},\quad \Theta=2\pi V,\quad Z=(R\cos\Theta,R\sin\Theta).$$
Then $Z$ has the Borel density
$$g(x,y)=\frac1{2\pi}e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2}=\phi(x)\phi(y),\qquad \phi(t)=\frac{e^{-t^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}.$$
In particular, its coordinates are independent with density $\phi$. Also $\mathbb P(R>r)=e^{-r^2/2}$ for $r\ge0$ and $\mathbb E R^2=2$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by

For each attempt, read a fresh non-overlapping block of $k$ bits and interpret it as a uniform integer $R\in\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. If $R\ge n$, reject the block and start another attempt. derivations.claim: By minimality of $k$, $n\le N<2n$ for $n>1$. [F1] gives acceptance probability $a=n/N>1/2$ and rejection probability $r=1-a<1/2$. On one accepted block, the $n$ possible accepted integers have equal probability $1/N$, with $m$ of them returning $1$ and $n-m$ returning $0$.

By independence of attempts, the probability that the first accepted block occurs at attempt $j$ and returns $1$ is $r^{j-1}m/N$, while the probability that it occurs at attempt $j$ is $r^{j-1}n/N$. Summing over $1\le j\le M_{\max}$ gives success probability $1-r^{M_{\max}}$ and returned-one probability $(m/n)(1-r^{M_{\max}})$; dividing yields conditional success probability $m/n$. The no-acceptance event has probability $r^{M_{\max}}<2^{-M_{\max}}$.

With no cap, $r^M\to0$, so the probability of never accepting is zero. Let $J$ be the first accepted attempt, setting $J=\infty$ on the null nontermination event. For each $M$, $J\wedge M=\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}\mathbf1_{\{J>j\}}$; these truncations increase to $J$, and independence gives $\mathbb P(J>j)=r^j$. By [F3] and the geometric identity [F4] with $0\le r<1/2$, $\mathbb E J=\sum_{j\ge0}r^j=(1-r)^{-1}=N/n<2$. Taking $M\to\infty$ in step 2.1 gives output-one probability $m/n$ and hence the exact Bernoulli$(m/n)$ law. Each attempt consumes $k$ bits, so the expected bit cost is $kN/n<2k$. statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Initially $F(\ell)\le u\le F(r)$ by the algorithm's bracket test. If $F(m)\le u$, replacing $\ell$ by $m$ preserves both inequalities by monotonicity; if $F(m)>u$, replacing $r$ by $m$ preserves them. After $N$ steps, $r-\ell=(b-a)2^{-N}$, so the modulus certificate gives $F(r)-F(\ell)\le\varepsilon$. Since $\widehat x\in[\ell,r]$, monotonicity puts both $F(\widehat x)$ and $u$ in this range, proving $|F(\widehat x)-u|\le\varepsilon$. For a continuous $F$, uniform continuity [F3] supplies a positive distance tolerance; since $(b-a)2^{-N}\to0$ by [F4], some finite $N$ meets it. A successful run evaluates the two endpoints once and one midpoint per update, hence uses $N+2$ CDF evaluations; the budget explicitly includes these endpoints.

For fixed depth $N$, the grid consists of the $2^N$ cells in the partition of $[a,b]$; their left endpoints are $a+j(b-a)2^{-N}$ for $0\le j<2^N$. At each bisection, the tested midpoint separates the remaining candidate left endpoints into lower and upper halves, and the rule keeps the upper half exactly when $\widetilde F(m)\le u$. Induction on the $N$ updates shows that the final $\ell$ is the greatest such left endpoint and $r$ is the next grid point. As $u$ increases, the predicate set can only grow, so the selected cell midpoint $g(u)$ is nondecreasing.

Since $Q(u)\in[a,b]$, [A4] implies $|F(\widehat x)-F(Q(u))|\ge m|\widehat x-Q(u)|$. By [F1], $Q(u)\le Q(u)$ implies $u\le F(Q(u))$. For every $y<Q(u)$, the reverse implication in [F1] gives $F(y)<u$; taking $y\uparrow Q(u)$ and using [A3] gives $F(Q(u))\le u$. Thus $F(Q(u))=u$, and step 1.1 yields $m|\widehat x-Q(u)|\le\varepsilon$.

Fix $x$ and set $E=\{u\in[0,1]:g(u)\le x\}$ and $t=\sup(E\cup\{0\})$. Monotonicity makes $E$ an initial interval. If $u<t$, then $u\in E$, so $\widetilde F(x)\ge\widetilde F(g(u))\ge u-\varepsilon$. If $u>t$, then $u\notin E$, so $g(u)>x$ and $\widetilde F(x)\le\widetilde F(g(u))\le u+\varepsilon$. Taking one-sided limits gives $|\widetilde F(x)-t|\le\varepsilon$; if $t=0$ or $1$, the missing side follows from $0\le\widetilde F(x)\le1$. The set $E$ is either an initial closed or open interval, or empty/all; its $q$-bit midpoint-grid probability differs from $t$ by at most $\delta_q$, using the strict or non-strict CDF bound in [F2]. Thus $d_K(\mathcal L(g(U_q)),\widetilde F)\le\delta_q+\varepsilon$.
The uniform CDF error implies $d_K(\widetilde F,F)\le\eta$. The triangle inequality for the supremum norm of CDF differences and step 2.2 give the stated $\delta_q+\varepsilon+\eta$ bound.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice as in [[thm-independent-fair-bit-streams-produce-uniforms]]. Let $U=\sum_{j\ge1}B_j2^{-j}$ be the uniform variable from an independent fair-bit stream. For $b\ge1$, put
$$K_b=\sum_{j=1}^b B_j2^{b-j},\qquad U_b=(K_b+1/2)2^{-b},\qquad \delta_b=2^{-b-1}.$$
Then $K_b$ is uniform on $\{0,\ldots,2^b-1\}$, $|U-U_b|\le\delta_b$ pointwise, the 1-Wasserstein and Kolmogorov distances between their laws are at most $\delta_b$, and their total-variation distance is exactly $1$. We use $W_1(\mu,
u)=\inf\mathbb E|X-Y|$ over couplings, $d_K(\mu,
u)=\sup_x|F_\mu(x)-F_
u(x)|$, and $d_{m TV}(\mu,
u)=\sup_A|\mu(A)-
u(A)|$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(U,V)$ have product Lebesgue probability law on $(0,1)^2$, and set
$$R=\sqrt{-2\log U},\quad \Theta=2\pi V,\quad Z=(R\cos\Theta,R\sin\Theta).$$
Then $Z$ has the Borel density
$$g(x,y)=\frac1{2\pi}e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2}=\phi(x)\phi(y),\qquad \phi(t)=\frac{e^{-t^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}.$$
In particular, its coordinates are independent with density $\phi$. Also $\mathbb P(R>r)=e^{-r^2/2}$ for $r\ge0$ and $\mathbb E R^2=2$.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Input an integer bit budget $b\ge1$, two disjoint ideal fair-bit subsequences as in
[[thm-independent-fair-bit-streams-produce-uniforms]], and a fixed deterministic
configuration consisting of finite dyadic format parameters, positive integer
series truncation indices $N\ge1$ and nonnegative integer total split budgets
$B\ge0$ for the log/root interval evaluators, positive dyadic log/root width
targets, and phase parameters $0<\tau\le1/4$, integer exponent limits
$e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$, integer precisions $2\le p_0\le p_{\max}$,
and a positive integer elementary-series cap $J\ge1$. Every call uses
these fixed parameters; a failed call returns `inconclusive` with its supplier
status. No success at a requested width is promised for arbitrary fixed budgets.
The midpoint convention is [[thm-midpoint-bit-stream-coupling-and-error]], and
the exact reference transform is [[lem-box-muller-product-density-and-radius-moment]].

1. Take the first $b$ bits from each subsequence and form the exact dyadics
   $u_j=(K_j+1/2)2^{-b}$. Enclose $u_1$ by directed dyadic endpoints in the
   selected format. If this is non-finite or its lower endpoint is not
   positive, return `inconclusive`; underflow may not turn a log argument
   into an accepted interval containing zero.

2. Apply [[alg-budgeted-validated-range-evaluation]] to the logarithm DAG on
   that interval with the configured finite parameters and log width target.
   On `certified(L,X)`, write $L=[L_-,L_+]$ and set
   $\widehat\ell=L_-$, $\eta_\ell=L_+-L_-$. The natural logarithm equals
   the integral logarithm by [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]], so
   $L_-\le\log u_1<0$. Compute the exact dyadic $q=-2\widehat\ell\ge0$.

3. Enclose $q$ by directed endpoints in the configured format; reject
   non-finite endpoints or a negative lower endpoint. Apply the same budgeted
   procedure to its square-root DAG with the root width target. On a
   certified interval $S=[S_-,S_+]$, set $\widehat r=S_-$ and
   $\eta_s=S_+-S_-$. The range guarantee of
   [[thm-budgeted-range-evaluation-terminates-and-is-sound]] gives
   $|\widehat\ell-\log u_1|\le\eta_\ell$ and
   $|\widehat r-\sqrt q|\le\eta_s$. Width differences and the products in
   these instructions are exact dyadic arithmetic.

4. Call [[alg-na-certified-unit-circle-phase]] on the exact rational
   $q_{\rm phase}=2u_2$ and configured phase parameters. On its certified
   return $(\widehat w,\epsilon)$, set
   $\widehat t=(\Re\widehat w,\Im\widehat w)$ and $\eta_t=\epsilon$.
   By [[thm-na-certified-unit-circle-phase-enclosure]],
   $\|\widehat t-(\cos(2\pi u_2),\sin(2\pi u_2))\|_2\le\eta_t$,
   including pi, angle, truncation and directed-endpoint errors. This is the
   existing phase routine, with its existing canonical-pi bridge.

5. Return the exact dyadic vector $\widehat Z=\widehat r\,\widehat t$ and
   the dyadic certificates $\eta_\ell,\eta_s,\eta_t$. If any preceding
   supplier call has a non-finite status, propagate it as `inconclusive`.
   Final vector multiplication is exact dyadic multiplication; rounding it
   further requires a separate added error certificate.

The output is the dyadic vector together with the reported evaluator certificates.
Its arithmetic suppliers provide neither an IID source nor exact normal output.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

derivations.claim: The all-input-success hypothesis makes the computed output a deterministic function of the two finite bit blocks on the original probability space; no conditioning changes their law. Couple each ideal uniform input $U_j$ to its midpoint $U_{j,b}$ using the same bits. On the event $G=\{U_1\ge\delta+\delta_b\}$, both $U_1$ and $U_{1,b}$ are at least $\delta$. The mean-value theorem and logarithm derivative [F6] give $|\log U_1-\log U_{1,b}|\le\delta_b/\delta$. For $x\ge y\ge0$, [F7] and $(\sqrt x-\sqrt y)(\sqrt x+\sqrt y)=x-y$ give $(\sqrt x-\sqrt y)^2\le x-y$; interchanging $x,y$ proves $|\sqrt x-\sqrt y|\le\sqrt{|x-y|}$. Thus the radial change before evaluator error is at most $\sqrt{2\delta_b/\delta}$. The angular unit vector changes by at most $2\pi|U_2-U_{2,b}|\le2\pi\delta_b$, and the midpoint radius is at most $R_\delta$. Thus the exact transform difference on $G$ is at most $\sqrt{2\delta_b/\delta}+2\pi R_\delta\delta_b$.

Put $r_b=\sqrt{-2\log U_{1,b}}$ and $t_b=(\cos(2\pi U_{2,b}),\sin(2\pi U_{2,b}))$. The certified log interval $[L_-,L_+]$ contains $\log U_{1,b}$, so $q=-2L_-\ge0$ and $|q-r_b^2|=2|L_--\log U_{1,b}|\le2\eta_\ell$. The certified root interval contains $\sqrt q$ and has width at most $\eta_s$, hence $|\widehat r-\sqrt q|\le\eta_s$. The square-root inequality from step 1.1 yields $|\widehat r-r_b|\le\eta_s+\sqrt{2\eta_\ell}=\eta_r$. The phase certificate gives $\|\widehat t-t_b\|_2\le\eta_t$, so $\|\widehat t\|_2\le1+\eta_t$. Therefore the evaluator perturbation satisfies $\|\widehat r\,\widehat t-r_b t_b\|_2\le|\widehat r-r_b|\|\widehat t\|_2+r_b\|\widehat t-t_b\|_2\le\eta_r(1+\eta_t)+R_\delta\eta_t$, using [F4] and $\|t_b\|_2=1$. Combining with step 1.1 gives $\|Z-\widehat Z\|_2\le e$ on $G$.

Since $U_1$ is uniform by [F1], $\mathbb P(G^c)=p$. For every bounded-Lipschitz test function the difference on $G$ is at most $e$, and on $G^c$ it is at most $2$. Taking expectations and then the supremum gives $d_{\rm BL}(\mathcal L(Z),\mathcal L(\widehat Z))\le e+2p$.

By [F2], $\mathbb E\|Z\|_2^2=2$, so [F3] gives $\mathbb E[\|Z\|_2\mathbf1_{G^c}]\le\sqrt{2p}$. The smallest midpoint is $2^{-b-1}$, hence every exact midpoint radius is at most $R_b$; [F4] gives $\|\widehat Z\|_2\le(R_b+\eta_r)(1+\eta_t)$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, $x\in U\cap\mathbb R$, and $h>0$ with $x+ih\in U$. For a holomorphic $f:U\to\mathbb C$ that is real-valued on some real interval $I\subseteq U\cap\mathbb R$ containing $x$, the **complex-step estimate** is

$$C_hf(x):=\frac{\operatorname{Im}f(x+ih)}{h}.$$

For an inexact complex evaluation $\widehat f(x+ih)$, define its imaginary-component error by $\delta_{\rm im}:=|\operatorname{Im}\widehat f(x+ih)-\operatorname{Im}f(x+ih)|$. The inexact estimate is $\widehat C_hf(x):=\operatorname{Im}\widehat f(x+ih)/h$; its evaluation-error contribution is controlled by $\delta_{\rm im}/h$. No claim is made that arbitrary code representing a real function has a holomorphic extension.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb C$. The function $f$ is **complex differentiable at $a$** if the limit

$$ \lim_{\substack{h\to0\\ h\ne0,\ a+h\in U}}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} $$

exists in the metric of [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. Its value is the **complex derivative** of $f$ at $a$, denoted $f'(a)$. The increments are nonzero and remain in the domain; because $U$ is open, all sufficiently small increments are allowed.

The function $f$ is **holomorphic on $U$** when it is complex differentiable at every point of $U$. A function holomorphic on all of $\mathbb C$ is **entire**. The word analytic is reserved for the local power-series notion.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and write $f=u+iv:U\to\mathbb C$. The following are equivalent:

1. $f$ is complex differentiable at $a$.
2. Under $\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$, the map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and $Df(a)$ is multiplication by a complex number.
3. The map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and $\partial_{\bar z}f(a)=0$.
4. The map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations

$$ u_x(a)=v_y(a),\qquad u_y(a)=-v_x(a). $$

When these conditions hold,

$$ f'(a)=u_x(a)+iv_x(a)=v_y(a)-iu_y(a)=\partial_zf(a). $$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open and let $f=u+iv:U\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic. Under the coordinate identification $\mathbb C=\mathbb R^2$, the map $(u,v):U\to\mathbb R^2$ is real analytic in the sense of [[def-real-analytic-map-on-the-plane]] and is of class $C^k$ for every natural $k$, hence smooth.

Let $f$ be holomorphic on $D(a,R)$, let $0<r<R$, and let $\gamma(t)=a+r\exp(it)$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$. Define $f^{(0)}=f$ and, whenever it exists, $f^{(n+1)}=(f^{(n)})'$. Then every $f^{(n)}$ exists on $D(a,r)$ and, for every $z\in D(a,r)$ and $n\in\mathbb N$,

$$f^{(n)}(z)=\frac{n!}{2\pi i}\int_\gamma\frac{f(\zeta)}{(\zeta-z)^{n+1}}\,d\zeta.$$

In particular, every holomorphic function has complex derivatives of all orders locally.
Let $f=u+iv$ be holomorphic on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb C$, and suppose $u,v\in C^2(U)$. Then the complex derivative $f':U\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic.

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-taylor-schlomilch-roche-remainder]], there are points $\xi_L,\xi_C$ between $a$ and $x$ such that
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_L)}{\iota((n+1)!)}(x-a)^{n+1}$$
and
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_C)}{\iota(n!)}(x-\xi_C)^n(x-a).$$

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $f$ have derivatives through order $n$ at $a$, and let $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical embedding. The **Taylor polynomial of degree at most $n$ about $a$** is
$$T_{n,a}f(x):=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\frac{f^{(j)}(a)}{\iota(j!)}(x-a)^j.$$
The **Taylor remainder** is $R_{n,a}f(x):=f(x)-T_{n,a}f(x)$.

The factorials are natural numbers as in [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]] and enter real arithmetic only through $\iota$ ([[def-canonical-natural]]); they are nonzero ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]]). The sum and powers are those of [[def-finite-sum]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]], and [[def-integer-power]]. For $n=0$, $T_{0,a}f$ is the constant $f(a)$.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

derivations.claim: Put $g(t):=\operatorname{Im}f(x+it)$ for $0\le t\le h$. By [F4], its coordinate functions are smooth. By [F3], $g'(t)=v_y(x,t)=u_x(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}f'(x+it)$. If $q=p+ir$ is holomorphic, [F3] gives $\partial_y p=-\partial_xr=-\operatorname{Im}q'$ and $\partial_y r=\partial_xp=\operatorname{Re}q'$. Applying [F5] to $f$ and then to $f'$ makes $f'$ and $f''$ holomorphic, so these identities give $g''(t)=-\operatorname{Im}f''(x+it)$ and $g'''(t)=-\operatorname{Re}f'''(x+it)$.

At real arguments near $x$, $f$ is real by hypothesis, so its real-direction difference quotients show that $f'$ is real there; applying the same argument to the holomorphic function $f'$ shows that $f''$ is real there. Thus $g(0)=0$, $g'(0)=f'(x)$, and $g''(0)=-\operatorname{Im}f''(x)=0$. By step 1.1, $|g'''(t)|\le M_3$ on $[0,h]$.

Apply [F6] to $g$ from $0$ to $h$. For some $\xi\in(0,h)$, $g(h)=h f'(x)+g'''(\xi)h^3/6$. Since $h>0$, [F8] gives $|g(h)/h-f'(x)|=|g'''(\xi)|h^2/6\le M_3h^2/6$. By [F1] and [F7], $g(h)/h=C_hf(x)$, proving the exact complex-step error bound.
By [F1] and [F8], $|\widehat C_hf(x)-C_hf(x)|\le\delta_{\rm im}/h$. [F9] and step 3.1 give the inexact bound.

Apply [F2] with $n=2$ to $y=x+h$ and $y=x-h$. Subtracting the two expansions cancels the equal even-order terms and gives $D_h^0f(x)-f'(x)=h^2(f'''(\xi_+)+f'''(\xi_-))/12$ for intermediate points $\xi_+\in(x,x+h)$ and $\xi_-\in(x-h,x)$. Let $m,n\ge1$, $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $x\in U$, $F:U\to\mathbb R^m$, $f:U\to\mathbb R$, and let $v\in\mathbb R^n$. Use the Jacobian $JF(x)$ and gradient $\nabla f(x)$ of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], the Hessian $H_f(x)$ of [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]], and the published Euclidean vector norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ of [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]. The Jacobian-vector products below require $JF(x)$ to exist, and the Hessian-vector products require $H_f(x)$ to exist. Each gradient-difference Hessian-vector estimate also requires $\nabla f$ to exist at every point in its stencil. The exact products are $JF(x)v$ and $H_f(x)v$, respectively.

For $h>0$ with the required points in $U$, define the forward and central Jacobian-vector estimates

$$J_h^+(F,x,v):=\frac{F(x+hv)-F(x)}h,\qquad J_h^0(F,x,v):=\frac{F(x+hv)-F(x-hv)}{2h},$$

and the gradient-difference Hessian-vector estimates

$$H_h^+(f,x,v):=\frac{\nabla f(x+hv)-\nabla f(x)}h,\qquad H_h^0(f,x,v):=\frac{\nabla f(x+hv)-\nabla f(x-hv)}{2h}.$$

For each requested vector value $z(y)$, write an inexact evaluation as $\widehat z(y)=z(y)+e$. When an error bound is specified, it is per call: $\|e\|_2\le\delta$ for that call's $\delta\ge0$. Errors may be dependent or random; a stated bound on a random error is understood to hold almost surely. Define the inexact estimates by substitution:

$$\widehat J_h^+(F,x,v):=\frac{\widehat F(x+hv)-\widehat F(x)}h,\qquad \widehat J_h^0(F,x,v):=\frac{\widehat F(x+hv)-\widehat F(x-hv)}{2h},$$

$$\widehat H_h^+(f,x,v):=\frac{\widehat{\nabla f}(x+hv)-\widehat{\nabla f}(x)}h,\qquad \widehat H_h^0(f,x,v):=\frac{\widehat{\nabla f}(x+hv)-\widehat{\nabla f}(x-hv)}{2h}.$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, $f\in C^k(U)$, and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval such that $a+th\in U$ for every $t\in I$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-canonical-natural]]. For $g(t)=f(a+th)$ and every $0\le r\le k$,

$$g^{(r)}(t)=\sum_{|\alpha|=r}\frac{\iota(r!)}{\iota(\alpha!)}D^\alpha f(a+th)h^\alpha\qquad(t\in I).$$
Let $k\ge2$. If $f\in C^k(U)$ for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, then every iterated derivative of $f$ of order $k$ is unchanged by any permutation of its coordinate differentiations.

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-taylor-schlomilch-roche-remainder]], there are points $\xi_L,\xi_C$ between $a$ and $x$ such that
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_L)}{\iota((n+1)!)}(x-a)^{n+1}$$
and
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_C)}{\iota(n!)}(x-\xi_C)^n(x-a).$$

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $f$ have derivatives through order $n$ at $a$, and let $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical embedding. The **Taylor polynomial of degree at most $n$ about $a$** is
$$T_{n,a}f(x):=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\frac{f^{(j)}(a)}{\iota(j!)}(x-a)^j.$$
The **Taylor remainder** is $R_{n,a}f(x):=f(x)-T_{n,a}f(x)$.

The factorials are natural numbers as in [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]] and enter real arithmetic only through $\iota$ ([[def-canonical-natural]]); they are nonzero ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]]). The sum and powers are those of [[def-finite-sum]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]], and [[def-integer-power]]. For $n=0$, $T_{0,a}f$ is the constant $f(a)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be the function space of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], with $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$.

### The $p$-norm, for a rational exponent $p \ge 1$

Let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_p \;:=\; \Bigl(\sum_{k<n} |x_k|^{p}\Bigr)^{1/p},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]), the sum is the finite
sum of [[def-finite-sum]], and both powers are the **rational** powers of
[[def-rational-power]].

**Every power written here is defined.** Each base $|x_k|$ is a nonnegative real
and $p > 0$, so $|x_k|^{p}$ is given by [[def-rational-power]] for $|x_k| > 0$
and by its supplementary clause $0^{p} = 0$ for $|x_k| = 0$; the sum of these
nonnegative terms is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), and
$1/p$ is a positive rational, so the outer power is defined for the same two
reasons. The value does not depend on which representative of $p$ or of $1/p$ is
used ([[lem-rational-power-well-defined]]).

**The exponent is rational in this definition.**
[[def-rational-power]] supplies the nonnegative-base powers used here, and
[[thm-minkowski-finite]] supplies the corresponding triangle inequality for
rational $p \ge 1$. This item makes no claim with $p$ ranging over a real
interval; its rational domain is unchanged.

### The maximum norm

For $n \ge 1$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_\infty \;:=\; \max\{\, |x_k| \;:\; k < n \,\},$$

the maximum of a nonempty finite set of reals, which exists and is one of its
elements ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is required and propagates.** At $n = 0$ the set
$\{|x_k| : k<n\}$ is empty and has no maximum ([[def-max-min]]). This is the same
restriction the published [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] carries, for the same reason, and
**every statement on this page that mentions $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ inherits
it**. The $p$-norms for rational $p \ge 1$ carry no such restriction: at $n = 0$
each is the empty sum raised to a positive rational power, hence $0$.

### The three cases the rest of the page uses

- $\lVert x\rVert_1 = \sum_{k<n}|x_k|$, since $t^{1} = t$ for $t \ge 0$
  ([[lem-rational-power-laws]], and $0^{1} = 0$ by the supplementary clause).
- $\lVert x\rVert_2 = \bigl(\sum_{k<n}|x_k|^{2}\bigr)^{1/2} = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}x_k^{2}}$,
  which is exactly the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: the
  exponent $2$ agrees with the integer power, so $|x_k|^{2} = x_k^{2}$
  ([[lem-of-abs-value]]), and $t^{1/2}$ is the unique nonnegative square root of
  $t$, which is $\sqrt{t}$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[thm-of-square-roots]]).
  **The two notations denote the same function and no second Euclidean norm is
  introduced.**
- $\lVert x\rVert_\infty$ as above, for $n \ge 1$.

That each of these is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], and
that the metrics they induce are exactly the published $d_1$, $d_2$ and
$d_\infty$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], is
[[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]; it is proved there
and is not assumed here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$, with the norms
of [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]. Then:

1. $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.
3. **The dictionary.** For $n \ge 1$ and all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert x-y\rVert_1 = d_1(x,y), \qquad \lVert x-y\rVert_2 = d_2(x,y), \qquad \lVert x-y\rVert_\infty = d_\infty(x,y),$$
   where $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are the metrics of the published
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]. So the metric induced by each of these three norms
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]) **is** the correspondingly named published
   metric, not merely one equivalent to it.

**Consequence, used repeatedly below and stated once here.** By clause 3 at
$p = 2$, the metric space $(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ of the published metric-spaces
page and the metric space underlying the normed space
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, \lVert\cdot\rVert_2)$ of this page are the same object. Hence
completeness ([[thm-euclidean-space-complete]] clause 2), Heine-Borel
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]] clause 2) and the compactness equivalences
([[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]]) are statements about this page's normed
space, **with their hypothesis $n \ge 1$ inherited unchanged and not weakened**.
Nothing below cites any of those three theorems for $n = 0$.

**Why this lemma exists.** Without it the library would hold a norm-induced
metric on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and a separately published metric on the same set with
no recorded relation, and every later citation would have to guess which was
meant. The proof of clause 3 is a comparison of two written expressions; the
value is that the comparison is made and recorded.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $X,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space.
Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].$$
Moreover, covariance is symmetric and bilinear on finite linear combinations.
On finite full-power-set probability spaces these formulas reduce to the
published finite identities.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.

Let $m,n\ge1$, $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $F:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be differentiable at $x\in U$, and $J:=JF(x)$ be its Jacobian as defined in [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. A **structural row pattern** is a list of sets $S_i\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, one for each row $0\le i<m$, such that $J_{ij}=0$ whenever $j\notin S_i$. It is a safe pattern only when every actual nonzero lies in the declared support.

The **column-interference graph** has vertices $0,\ldots,n-1$ and an edge between distinct columns $j,k$ exactly when some row support $S_i$ contains both. A **proper coloring** is a map $\chi:\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\to C$ to a set of color labels such that adjacent columns have different labels. For a color $c\in C$, its seed vector $s^c\in\mathbb R^n$ has coordinate $s^c_j=1$ when $\chi(j)=c$ and $0$ otherwise. The compressed product is $Js^c$.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $(M,+,0)$ be a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]), let $S$ be a finite set with $n:=|S|$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]), and let $a:S\to M$. Choose a bijection $\phi:n\to S$ and define

$$\sum_{s\in S}a_s:=a_{\phi(0)}+a_{\phi(1)}+\cdots+a_{\phi(n-1)},$$

where the right side is the finite monoid product of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] written additively. In particular, the sum over the empty set is $0$.

This value is independent of the enumeration. If $\psi:n\to S$ is another bijection, then $\phi^{-1}\circ\psi$ is a permutation of $n$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and generalised commutativity gives

$$\sum_{k<n}a_{\psi(k)}=\sum_{k<n}a_{\phi(k)}$$

([[thm-generalised-associativity]]). Thus the displayed notation names one element of $M$ and does not select a preferred enumeration.

When $M$ is the additive monoid of $\mathbb R$ or of $\mathbb N$, this definition agrees with [[def-sum-over-a-finite-index-set]]: both enumerate $S$, apply the same finite recursion with identity $0$, and are independent of the enumeration.

A **semigroup** is a pair $(S,*)$ consisting of a set $S$ and an associative
binary operation $*$ on $S$ ([[def-binary-operation]]).

A **monoid** is a triple $(M,*,e)$ in which $(M,*)$ is a semigroup and $e \in M$
is a two-sided identity for $*$ ([[def-identity-element]]), that is,

$$e * x \;=\; x \;=\; x * e \qquad \text{for every } x \in M .$$

By [[lem-identity-unique]] a binary operation has at most one two-sided identity,
so $e$ is determined by $(M,*)$ and may be called **the identity of $M$**; it is
written $e$, or $e_M$ when several monoids are in play, and $1$ or $0$ in
multiplicative or additive notation. For that reason a monoid is often written
simply as $(M,*)$, or as $M$.

A semigroup or monoid is **commutative** (for monoids also called **abelian**)
when its operation is commutative.

A subset $N \subseteq M$ is a **submonoid** when $e \in N$ and $N$ is closed under
$*$; the restricted operation then makes $(N,*,e)$ a monoid, associativity being
inherited ([[def-binary-operation]]).

If two distinct columns of $S_i$ had color $c$, the graph definition in [F1] would make them adjacent, contradicting proper coloring. Thus at most one summand in step 1.1 is nonzero. If the specified $j\in S_i$ has color $c$, it is that sole summand and equals $J_{ij}$ because $s^c_j=1$; if no such column exists, every summand is zero and the row product is $0$ by [F4]. Entries outside the safe pattern are zero by [F1].

To verify the collision caveat, let $F(z_0,z_1)=z_0+2z_1$ and $G(z_0,z_1)=3z_0$, and evaluate both Jacobians at $(0,0)$. By [F2], their one-row Jacobians are $(1,2)$ and $(3,0)$, both supported in $S_0=\{0,1\}$. Assign columns $0$ and $1$ the same color, whose seed is $(1,1)^T$ by [F1]. Both compressed products equal $3$ by [F3], so this color collision cannot determine the entries.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open, $x\in I$, and $h>0$. For the forward bound assume $[x,x+h]\subset I$, $f\in C^2$ on a neighborhood of that interval, and $|f''(y)|\le M_2$ there. For the central bound assume $[x-h,x+h]\subset I$, $f\in C^3$ on a neighborhood of that interval, and $|f'''(y)|\le M_3$ there. Then

$$|D_h^+f(x)-f'(x)|\le \frac{M_2h}{2},\qquad |D_h^0f(x)-f'(x)|\le \frac{M_3h^2}{6}.$$

If each function evaluation has absolute error at most $\delta\ge0$ as in [[def-finite-difference-stencils-and-evaluation-error-model]], then

$$|\widehat D_h^+f(x)-f'(x)|\le \frac{M_2h}{2}+\frac{2\delta}{h},\qquad |\widehat D_h^0f(x)-f'(x)|\le \frac{M_3h^2}{6}+\frac{2\delta}{h}.$$

For the central stencil the evaluation contribution is in fact at most $\delta/h$; the displayed $2\delta/h$ is a uniform conservative bound for both stencils.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct
analogue, and its place is taken by the factorisation of $b^n - a^n$ and the
resulting Lipschitz estimate ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

Set $r:=h/h_0$ and $a:=M_3h_0^2/6>0$. From $h_0^3=6\delta/M_3$, $E_0(h)=a(r^2+2/r)$ and $E_0(h_0)=3a$. The difference is $a(r^2+2/r-3)=a(r-1)^2(r+2)/r\ge0$, with equality only at $r=1$. Thus $h_0$ uniquely minimizes the unconstrained bound, and the minimum is $3a=M_3h_0^2/2$.

If $0<r_1<r_2\le1$, then $(r_1+r_1^{-1})-(r_2+r_2^{-1})=(r_2-r_1)(1/(r_1r_2)-1)>0$, since $r_1r_2<1$. Hence $E_+$ strictly decreases up to $h_+$; the global bound from step 1.1 gives the cap minimizer $\min\{h_+,H\}$.

If $0<r_1<r_2\le1$, then $(r_1^2+2/r_1)-(r_2^2+2/r_2)=(r_2-r_1)(2/(r_1r_2)-(r_1+r_2))>0$, since $r_1r_2<1$ and $r_1+r_2<2$. Hence the central bound strictly decreases up to $h_0$, so the cap minimizer is $\min\{h_0,H\}$.

For a color $c\in C$, its seed vector $s^c\in\mathbb R^n$ has coordinate $s^c_j=1$ when $\chi(j)=c$ and $0$ otherwise. The compressed product is $Js^c$.

Let the objects and notation be those of [[def-structural-column-coloring-for-sparse-jacobian-recovery]], and suppose $\chi$ is a proper coloring of the graph of a safe structural row pattern. For every row $0\le i<m$, every color $c$, and every column $j\in S_i$ with $\chi(j)=c$,

$$J_{ij}=(Js^c)_i.$$

Entries with $j\notin S_i$ are zero by the safe-pattern hypothesis. Thus all entries are recovered from one compressed product per color. A color collision in a row does not give a general recovery guarantee: two distinct Jacobians supported on that colliding row can have the same compressed product.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, $x\in U\cap\mathbb R$, and $h>0$ with $x+ih\in U$. For a holomorphic $f:U\to\mathbb C$ that is real-valued on some real interval $I\subseteq U\cap\mathbb R$ containing $x$, the **complex-step estimate** is

$$C_hf(x):=\frac{\operatorname{Im}f(x+ih)}{h}.$$

For an inexact complex evaluation $\widehat f(x+ih)$, define its imaginary-component error by $\delta_{\rm im}:=|\operatorname{Im}\widehat f(x+ih)-\operatorname{Im}f(x+ih)|$. The inexact estimate is $\widehat C_hf(x):=\operatorname{Im}\widehat f(x+ih)/h$; its evaluation-error contribution is controlled by $\delta_{\rm im}/h$. No claim is made that arbitrary code representing a real function has a holomorphic extension.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $x\in U\cap\mathbb R$, and suppose $f:U\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, real-valued on a real interval $I\subseteq U\cap\mathbb R$ around $x$, and $\{x+it:0\le t\le h\}\subset U$ for $h>0$. Suppose $|\operatorname{Re}f'''(x+it)|\le M_3$ for $0\le t\le h$, with $M_3\ge0$. Then

$$|C_hf(x)-f'(x)|\le \frac{M_3h^2}{6}.$$

If the evaluated imaginary component has error at most $\delta_{\rm im}$, then

$$|\widehat C_hf(x)-f'(x)|\le \frac{M_3h^2}{6}+\frac{\delta_{\rm im}}h.$$

Holomorphy and real-axis reality are essential to the formula: real differentiability of the restriction alone is insufficient.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $m,n\ge1$, $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $F:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be differentiable at $x\in U$, and $J:=JF(x)$ be its Jacobian as defined in [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. A **structural row pattern** is a list of sets $S_i\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, one for each row $0\le i<m$, such that $J_{ij}=0$ whenever $j\notin S_i$. It is a safe pattern only when every actual nonzero lies in the declared support.

The **column-interference graph** has vertices $0,\ldots,n-1$ and an edge between distinct columns $j,k$ exactly when some row support $S_i$ contains both. A **proper coloring** is a map $\chi:\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\to C$ to a set of color labels such that adjacent columns have different labels. For a color $c\in C$, its seed vector $s^c\in\mathbb R^n$ has coordinate $s^c_j=1$ when $\chi(j)=c$ and $0$ otherwise. The compressed product is $Js^c$.

Let the objects and notation be those of [[def-structural-column-coloring-for-sparse-jacobian-recovery]], and suppose $\chi$ is a proper coloring of the graph of a safe structural row pattern. For every row $0\le i<m$, every color $c$, and every column $j\in S_i$ with $\chi(j)=c$,

$$J_{ij}=(Js^c)_i.$$

Entries with $j\notin S_i$ are zero by the safe-pattern hypothesis. Thus all entries are recovered from one compressed product per color. A color collision in a row does not give a general recovery guarantee: two distinct Jacobians supported on that colliding row can have the same compressed product.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open, $x\in I$, and $h>0$. When $x+h\in I$, the **forward difference** of $f:I\to\mathbb R$ is

$$D_h^+f(x):=\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}.$$

When $x-h,x+h\in I$, the **central difference** is

$$D_h^0f(x):=\frac{f(x+h)-f(x-h)}{2h}.$$

An evaluation with absolute error bound $\delta\ge0$ is a value $\widehat f(y)=f(y)+e_y$ with $|e_y|\le\delta$ at each requested point $y$. The corresponding inexact quotients are obtained by replacing each $f(y)$ in the displayed stencil by $\widehat f(y)$. The bound is absolute and applies separately to each call; no correlation or relative-error assumption is included.

Let $H>0$. Consider the conservative error bounds from [[thm-forward-and-central-difference-truncation-and-evaluation-error-bounds]] on a permitted step interval $(0,H]$, where every stencil with $h\le H$ stays inside the domain. If $M_2>0$ and $\delta>0$, the forward bound

$$E_+(h)=M_2h/2+2\delta/h$$

has the unique unconstrained minimizer $h_+=\sqrt{4\delta/M_2}$ and minimum $2\sqrt{M_2\delta}$. On $(0,H]$ the minimizer is $\min\{h_+,H\}$. If $M_3>0$ and $\delta>0$, the central conservative bound

$$E_0(h)=M_3h^2/6+2\delta/h$$

has the unique unconstrained minimizer $h_0=\sqrt[3]{6\delta/M_3}$ and minimum $M_3h_0^2/2$; on $(0,H]$ the minimizer is $\min\{h_0,H\}$. These optimize the displayed error bounds, not the unknown actual error.

If $\delta=0$ and the corresponding truncation constant is positive, the bound has infimum $0$ as $h\downarrow0$ and no minimizer for $h>0$. If the corresponding truncation constant is $0$ and $\delta>0$, the bound decreases with $h$, so its capped minimum is at $H$. If $\delta$ and the corresponding truncation constant are both zero, every permitted step is optimal.

Fix an input dimension $n\ge0$, finitely many operation nodes $1,\ldots,T$, and a designated output node $o$, either an input coordinate or an operation, whose value space is $\mathbb R$. Input coordinate $i$ has value $x_i$ and value space $\mathbb R$ with its standard Euclidean inner product. Operation node $j$ has an ordered list of parent slots $p_{j,1},\ldots,p_{j,r_j}$; each slot points to an input or an operation with index less than $j$. Repeated parent slots are allowed and count separately. The graph is a finite straight-line program because every operation reads only earlier values and there are no data-dependent loops.

For each operation $j$, choose a dimension $d_j\ge0$, set $E_j=\mathbb R^{d_j}$ with its standard Euclidean inner product, take an open set $U_j\subseteq E_{p_{j,1}}\times\cdots\times E_{p_{j,r_j}}$ with the product inner product, and choose a primitive map $\phi_j:U_j\to E_j$. A smooth primitive is $C^1$: it is totally differentiable and its derivative matrix is continuous. For Hessian-vector products require the primitive to be $C^2$, meaning $C^1$ with a continuously differentiable derivative map. Derivatives are represented in these coordinates, and every transpose is the Euclidean transpose for the stated inner products; the gradient of a scalar output is the Euclidean gradient. The real-arithmetic primal recursion is $z_j=\phi_j(z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,z_{p_{j,r_j}})$ whenever the parent tuple lies in $U_j$. Its admissible input domain is the set of $x\in\mathbb R^n$ for which every operation in this recursion is defined. The graph's scalar output function $f$ is the value at $o$: it is $x_i$ when $o$ is input coordinate $i$, and $z_j$ when $o$ is operation node $j$.

The **primal tape** is the finite ordered record of input and node values, parent-slot indices, primitive identities, and (when applicable) selected branch labels. A deterministic replay starts from the identical checkpoint state and applies the identical primitive maps in the identical order, so it reproduces the same real-arithmetic values and local derivative inputs. Opaque solver calls are not primitive operations unless their complete deterministic map and derivative rule are explicitly supplied.

A piecewise-$C^1$ primitive is specified by finitely many open branch regions and a $C^1$ formula on each region; its primal boundary value, if any, is specified separately. If the current parent tuple lies strictly inside exactly one declared branch, the program uses that branch and its derivative. At a branch boundary or ambiguous branch selection, forward or reverse AD returns NONDIFFERENTIABLE; it does not silently choose a subgradient or generalized derivative. If no primal value is specified at a boundary, that input is outside the program's domain. All correctness theorems below apply on a fixed strict branch. The same convention applies to piecewise-$C^2$ primitives for Hessian-vector products.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is
**continuously differentiable**, or of class $C^1$, when it is totally
differentiable at every point of $U$ and the entries of its derivative matrix
are continuous functions on $U$.

For an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $a\in U$, a **local inverse of $f$ at
$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a\in U$, then some $C,\delta>0$ satisfy $\|f(a+h)-f(a)\|_2\le C\|h\|_2$ whenever $\|h\|_2<\delta$ and $a+h\in U$. In particular $f$ is continuous at $a$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: Begin with the open input domain $\mathbb R^n$, whose coordinate maps are continuous and $C^1$. Suppose the values through node $j-1$ are defined and continuous on an open set $\Omega_{j-1}$. The parent tuple $g_j(x)=(z_{p_{j,1}}(x),\ldots,z_{p_{j,r_j}}(x))$ is continuous there. Thus $\Omega_j:=\{x\in\Omega_{j-1}:g_j(x)\in U_j\}$ is open in $\Omega_{j-1}$, hence open in $\mathbb R^n$, because $U_j$ is open. This proves by finite induction that the full admissible domain is open.

For each operation $j$, assume its parent-node maps are $C^1$ on $\Omega_j$. Their tuple $g_j$ is $C^1$ componentwise. Since $z_j=\phi_j\circ g_j$, [F4] gives $Dz_j(x)=D\phi_j(g_j(x))Dg_j(x)$. Both matrix factors vary continuously because $\phi_j$ and the parent maps are $C^1$; hence $Dz_j$ is continuous and $z_j$ is $C^1$ by [F2]. Thus every operation value is $C^1$; the scalar output is $C^1$ whether it is one of these operation values or an input coordinate projection.

The input is a finite sequence of deterministic $C^1$ transitions $F_1,\ldots,F_T$ between open subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, with starting state $x_0$. Every transition is evaluated on one fixed strict branch and has its exact local reverse rule. The last transition has scalar output and may be the terminal objective, so its scalar cotangent is $1$; for an empty sequence the terminal value is the starting state. A transition tape stores the local values needed by its exact reverse rule. A deterministic replay applies the same transition maps, in the same order, to the identical checkpoint state and therefore reproduces the same values and local derivative inputs. The procedure returns the terminal output and cotangent at $x_0$; an invalid domain evaluation returns DOMAIN_ERROR, and a branch boundary returns NONDIFFERENTIABLE. A checkpoint schedule is permitted only when its saved states and all deterministic replays lie in these declared domains.

**Uniform-block mode.** For $T=0$, return $x_0$ and the supplied cotangent without work. For $T\ge1$, require an integer slot budget $m\ge1$, set $q=\lceil T/m\rceil$, and during one forward pass save $x_{jq}$ for $j=0,\ldots,\lceil T/q\rceil-1$ (all indices are below $T$). This uses at most $m$ saved states. Partition the steps into blocks $[a,b]$ with $a=jq$ and $b=\min(a+q,T)$. Process the blocks from last to first. Within one block, for $\ell=b,b-1,\ldots,a+1$, restore $x_a$, replay $F_{a+1},\ldots,F_{\ell-1}$ without recording, evaluate $F_\ell$ once while recording its local tape, apply its reverse rule to the current cotangent, and discard the one-step tape and replay workspace. Retain only the checkpoint states, the live state/cotangent, and the ordinary one-step reverse tape. Do not infer any optimality property of this schedule.

**Binomial mode.** Define $C(d,0)=C(0,t)=1$, and $C(d,t)=C(d-1,t)+C(d,t-1)$ for integers $d,t\ge1$. The recursive procedure REVERSE$(a,N,d,t,x_a,\bar x_{a+N})$ requires integer indices $0\le a\le a+N\le T$, nonnegative integer budgets $d,t$, the capacity condition $N\le C(d,t)$, and a known starting state $x_a$. If $N=0$, return the pair $(x_a,\bar x_a)$, the known terminal state and unchanged cotangent. If $N=1$, evaluate and record the unique transition, apply its local reverse rule, and return its output and input cotangents. If $N\ge2$, then $d,t\ge1$. Put $L=\min(N-1,C(d,t-1))$, $R=N-L$; replay the first $L$ transitions from $x_a$ without recording and save the resulting midpoint state $x_{a+L}$. Call REVERSE$(a+L,R,d-1,t,x_{a+L},\bar x_{a+N})$ on the right block. Release the midpoint checkpoint, restore the caller's supplied $x_a$, and call REVERSE$(a,L,d,t-1,x_a,\bar x_{a+L})$ on the left block, where $\bar x_{a+L}$ is the cotangent returned by the right call. Return the right call's terminal value and the left call's cotangent at $x_a$. The top-level call uses $a=0,N=T$, with the specified terminal cotangent. A recursive call with $N>1$ and $d=0$ or $t=0$ is a schedule failure; the capacity condition makes that branch unreachable.

The parameter $d$ bounds the number of simultaneously saved state snapshots. The parameter $t$ bounds, for each transition, the number of additional unrecorded forward evaluations beyond its one recorded evaluation. Both are finite integer inputs. This mode gives a binomial capacity bound; it does not promise a numerical error estimate or an optimal schedule for arbitrary nonuniform primitive costs. For the storage count in the paired theorem, $R_s$ bounds scalar storage for one full primal state. The binomial recursion may reuse one mutable cotangent workspace: each call consumes its terminal cotangent and returns the cotangent at its start, reusing the same buffer through both children. Let $G$ bound the largest one-step tape and local reverse scratch, the constant number of live cotangent/work vectors, and the scalar call-frame records; it excludes the $d$ saved primal states and one live primal state.

derivations.claim: In uniform mode, for any block start $x_a$, deterministic replay reproduces the original $x_{a+1},\ldots,x_b$: the first replayed transition starts from the identical $x_a$, and induction applies each same map $F_j$ to the same preceding state. Thus the recorded local tape at step $\ell$ has the same primitive inputs as the original forward trajectory, so its reverse rule is the same one used by the full tape. Processing blocks and then their steps in decreasing order is exactly reverse transition order; [F2] gives the same terminal and initial cotangents.

A block of length $r$ has replay prefix lengths $r-1,r-2,\ldots,0$ before its $r$ recorded local evaluations. Therefore its additional unrecorded evaluations total $\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}j=r(r-1)/2$. The number of blocks is $s=\lceil T/q\rceil\le m$, each $r_\ell\le q$, so the sum is at most $m q(q-1)/2$. The checkpoint indices are $0,q,\ldots,(s-1)q<T$; $T/q\le m$, so $s=\lceil T/q\rceil\le m$. Only those states, one live state, and one local tape are retained.

In binomial mode the recurrence and boundary values give $C(d,t)=\binom{d+t}{d}$: the binomial coefficients have the same boundary values and Pascal recurrence, so induction on $d+t$ identifies them. For $d,t\ge1$, write $A=C(d,t-1)$, $B=C(d-1,t)$, so $C(d,t)=A+B$. If $N\ge2$, $L=\min(N-1,A)$ satisfies $1\le L<N$; if $L=N-1$, then $R=1\le B$, and otherwise $L=A$ and $R=N-A\le B$. Thus both recursive capacities hold and both child lengths are strictly less than $N$; the recursion terminates at $N=1$ or $N=0$.

Induct on $N$. For $N=0$, the empty interval has terminal state $x_{a+N}=x_a$ and unchanged cotangent, exactly the returned pair. For $N=1$, the single evaluation returns its exact output state and its local reverse rule returns the exact input cotangent. For $N\ge2$, midpoint replay produces the exact $x_{a+L}$ by [F3]. By induction the right child returns terminal state $x_{a+N}$ and the exact cotangent at that midpoint; the left child returns terminal state $x_{a+L}$ and, after the earlier transitions, the exact cotangent at $x_a$. The parent returns the right child's terminal state and the left child's starting cotangent, so both outputs are correct. Every interval is split into disjoint left and right steps and each base step is recorded and reversed once. Therefore the terminal value and initial cotangent agree with the ordinary reverse sweep.

During a right child, the saved midpoint occupies one slot and its child uses at most $d-1$ further snapshots; after that child returns, the midpoint is released and the left child uses at most $d$. Thus peak snapshot count is at most $d$. A step in a right child has at most $t$ replays by induction. A step in the left child is replayed once at the current split and then has at most $t-1$ replays in the left child, hence at most $t$ total. Each step also has one recorded forward and one reverse call, giving work $\widehat W+\overline W+tW$. Each recursive child decreases $d+t$ by one, so at most $d+t+1$ call frames are active; each frame stores a fixed number of scalar indices and flags. The algorithm reuses its cotangent buffer and has only the bounded one-step tape and local scratch included in $G$. $$D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad D_yF(a,b)v:=DF(a,b)(0,v),$$

is invertible.  Put similarly $D_xF(a,b)u:=DF(a,b)(u,0)$.  Then there are open
neighbourhoods $P$ of $a$ and $Q$ of $b$, and a unique $C^1$ map

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

After shrinking $P,Q$ if necessary, $D_yF(x,\varphi(x))$ is invertible and

Input a $C^2$ graph, admissible $x$, and direction $v$. First run the forward tangent recurrence to compute every $\dot z_j=Dz_j(x)v$. Initialize every operation and input cotangent and tangent-cotangent accumulator to zero. Seed the output by setting its cotangent/tangent-cotangent pair to $(1,0)$: if $o$ is an operation, set $(\bar z_o,\dot{\bar z}_o)=(1,0)$; if $o$ is input coordinate $i$, set $(\bar x_i,\dot{\bar x}_i)=(1,0)$. In reverse topological order, for each node $j$ and parent slot $k$, let $A_{j,k}=D_k\phi_j(z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,z_{p_{j,r_j}})$, compute
$$c_{j,k}=A_{j,k}^{T}\bar z_j,\qquad \dot c_{j,k}=A_{j,k}^{T}\dot{\bar z}_j+\bigl(DA_{j,k}(z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,z_{p_{j,r_j}})[\dot z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,\dot z_{p_{j,r_j}}]\bigr)^{T}\bar z_j,$$
and add $c_{j,k}$ and $\dot c_{j,k}$ to the parent's cotangent and tangent-cotangent accumulators. Use $(\bar x_i,\dot{\bar x}_i)$ for input coordinate $i$ and $(\bar z_\ell,\dot{\bar z}_\ell)$ for operation node $\ell$. If the same parent occurs in multiple slots, add every slot contribution.
Return the input tangent of the gradient, $(\dot{\bar x}_1,\ldots,\dot{\bar x}_n)$. Repeated parent slots receive separate additions. Outside the admissible domain return DOMAIN_ERROR; at a branch boundary return NONDIFFERENTIABLE. The transpose is the real Euclidean transpose, not a complex adjoint.

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

derivations.claim: By [F4], the input reverse accumulator is the function $x\mapsto\operatorname{grad} f(x)$. Since $f$ is $C^2$ by [F2] under the primitive hypotheses in [F1], its directional derivative at $x$ exists. By [F3], the forward recurrence supplies every primitive-input direction $\dot z_{pa}=Dz_{pa}(x)v$.

At a node $j$, the exact reverse contribution to parent slot $i$ is $A^T\bar z_j$. Since each primitive is $C^2$, $A$ is $C^1$; the finite reverse recurrence is therefore differentiable, as it consists of sums and bounded bilinear matrix-vector products of $C^1$ maps. Differentiate this matrix-vector product along $x+tv$. The product rule [F6] gives $A^T\dot{\bar z}_j+(DA[\dot z_{pa}])^T\bar z_j$, exactly the second recurrence in [F5]. Reverse topological induction therefore shows that every $\dot{\bar z}_i$ equals the directional derivative of the corresponding exact reverse accumulator. If the scalar output is an input coordinate, its seeded gradient is the constant coordinate vector and the initialized tangent-cotangent remains zero, as this recurrence also gives.
At the inputs, step 2.1 identifies the returned vector with $D(\operatorname{grad} f)(x)v$, which by definition is $H_f(x)v$.

derivations.claim: Starting with output cotangent $1$, the exact reverse recurrence at a node sums one local derivative-transpose contribution from each outgoing parent-slot edge. By induction in reverse topological order, its expansion at input block $i$ has one ordered derivative product for every path from $i$ to the output: the length-zero path at the output node has product $1$ (including when the output itself is an input), and extending a path by one edge multiplies its product by that edge's local derivative. Fix a path $\pi=(e_1,\ldots,e_s)$. Insert one factor at a time to write
$$\widetilde A_{e_s}\cdots\widetilde A_{e_1}-A_{e_s}\cdots A_{e_1}=\sum_{\ell=1}^s\widetilde A_{e_s}\cdots\widetilde A_{e_{\ell+1}}(\widetilde A_{e_\ell}-A_{e_\ell})A_{e_{\ell-1}}\cdots A_{e_1}.$$
This identity follows by cancellation of consecutive products in the telescoping sum.

Submultiplicativity of the induced operator norm and [A1] bound the $\ell$th summand by $\eta_{e_\ell}\prod_{r<\ell}\|A_{e_r}\|\prod_{r>\ell}(\|A_{e_r}\|+\eta_{e_r})$. Summing these bounds over $\ell$ controls the error on this path.

The perturbed and exact gradients are finite sums over the same paths by step 1.1. The triangle inequality therefore bounds their difference by the sum of the pathwise errors from step 2.1, which is exactly the displayed bound.

Let $R:\Theta\times Z\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$, where $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $Z\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ are open. Suppose $R(\theta_0,z_0)=0$ and the state Jacobian $R_z(\theta_0,z_0)$ is invertible. The Euclidean implicit function theorem gives a local $C^1$ solution branch $z=\phi(\theta)$, and
$$D\phi(\theta_0)=-R_z(\theta_0,z_0)^{-1}R_\theta(\theta_0,z_0).$$
For a scalar $C^1$ objective $J(\theta,z)$, its derivative along that branch is
$$D(J(\theta,\phi(\theta)))|_{\theta_0}=J_\theta-J_zR_z^{-1}R_\theta.$$
Equivalently, if $\lambda$ solves $R_z^T\lambda=J_z^T$, this derivative is $J_\theta-\lambda^TR_\theta$. These formulas concern the exact local solution branch; differentiating a stopped iteration is a separate finite-map derivative.

For the real mathematical solve primitive $\phi(A,b)=A^{-1}b$, let $A,B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $b,\widehat x\in\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$, and suppose certified exact-residual bounds satisfy
$$\|I-AB\|_2\le d<1,\qquad \|b-A\widehat x\|_2\le\rho,\qquad \|B\|_2\le M,\qquad K=\frac{M}{1-d}.$$
Then $A$ is invertible; writing $x=A^{-1}b$, the fixed linear derivative approximations $\widetilde J_bh=Bh$ and $\widetilde J_AH=-BH\widehat x$ obey
$$\|\widetilde J_b-J_b\|\le\eta_b=Kd,\qquad \|\widetilde J_A-J_A\|\le\eta_A=Kd\|\widehat x\|_2+K^2\rho.$$
Use Euclidean vector norms and Frobenius matrix-input norm. For any stored matrix $B$ and stored cotangent $c\in\mathbb R^n$, the exact adjoints are $B^Tc$ and $-(B^Tc)\widehat x^T$. Let $u$ be the unit roundoff in [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]], and assume $nu<1$. For each $j=1,\ldots,n$, compute $\widehat\lambda_j$ by the sequential real dot rule: $p_i=\operatorname{fl}(B_{ij}c_i)$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$, $s_1=p_1$, and $s_i=\operatorname{fl}(s_{i-1}+p_i)$ for $i=2,\ldots,n$, with each product and addition rounded separately; set $\widehat\lambda_j=s_n$. Form the matrix cotangent as the componentwise rounded outer product $-\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\lambda\widehat x^T)$. Assume every operation succeeds in the operationwise model [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]]: each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite. Put $\gamma_n=nu/(1-nu)$ and $t=\gamma_n\|B\|_F$. The resulting cotangent errors are bounded by $(\eta_b+t)\|c\|_2$ and $[\eta_A+(t+u(M+t))\|\widehat x\|_2]\|c\|_2$, respectively. These are derivative approximations to the mathematical solve map, not derivatives of the rounded program.

The fixed $B$ may be assembled from stored basis-vector solves using a triangular, Cholesky or QR backend; its defect must be certified rather than inferred from a factor residual. Replay must preserve the same $\widehat x,B$ and strict graph branch. Reverse accumulation additions are excluded.

derivations.claim: The system gives $u_2=1$ and $u_1+\theta u_2=2$, hence $u(\theta)=(2-\theta,1)^T$ and $J(\theta)=3-\theta$. Therefore $J'(0)=-1$.

The objective has no explicit $\theta$ dependence, so $J_\theta=0$; the adjoint formula gives $J_\theta-\lambda^TR_\theta=-(1,1)\cdot(1,0)=-1$.
The adjoint result agrees with the direct derivative in step 1.1, verifying this nonsingular linear-solve instance.

In any arithmetic satisfying the operationwise model and representing $0,1,2,3$, with these small operations in range, at $\theta=0$ the primal and basis solves give $\widehat x=(2,1)^T$ and $B=I$ exactly. Their inverse defect and primal residual are zero. The certified solve-Jacobian result [[lem-certified-linear-solve-jacobian-and-pullback-error]] therefore gives zero fixed-map discrepancy; the actual dot and product operations here are also exact, and return derivative $-1$.

Input a graph from [[def-finite-straight-line-computational-program]] and an admissible point $x$. Evaluate and store all primal values in topological order. Initialize every operation cotangent and every input cotangent to zero. Seed the scalar output by setting its cotangent to $1$: if $o$ is an operation, set $\bar z_o=1$; if $o$ is input coordinate $i$, set $\bar x_i=1$. For $j=T,T-1,\ldots,1$, and for every parent slot $k=1,\ldots,r_j$, compute the contribution
$$c_{j,k}=D_k\phi_j(z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,z_{p_{j,r_j}})^T\bar z_j$$
and add it to the cotangent accumulator of that parent: use $\bar x_i$ if the parent is input coordinate $i$, and $\bar z_\ell$ if it is operation node $\ell$. If the same parent node occurs in multiple slots, add every slot contribution. Return the scalar output $f(x)$ and the input cotangents $(\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_n)$ as the Euclidean gradient. A point outside the admissible domain returns DOMAIN_ERROR; a branch boundary or ambiguous active branch returns NONDIFFERENTIABLE and no gradient. The procedure differentiates the real-arithmetic graph; it makes no floating-point error claim.

For a finite $C^1$ program with one scalar output $f$, on a fixed strict branch and at every admissible $x$, the reverse-mode algorithm returns $Df(x)^T1$, the gradient of $f$. More precisely, at any operation node $i$, if its value is temporarily treated as an independent variable and all later operations are recomputed from it, then the accumulated cotangent at $i$ is the derivative of the scalar output with respect to that independent node value.
