Fix an input dimension $n\ge0$, finitely many operation nodes $1,\ldots,T$, and a designated output node $o$, either an input coordinate or an operation, whose value space is $\mathbb R$. Input coordinate $i$ has value $x_i$ and value space $\mathbb R$ with its standard Euclidean inner product. Operation node $j$ has an ordered list of parent slots $p_{j,1},\ldots,p_{j,r_j}$; each slot points to an input or an operation with index less than $j$. Repeated parent slots are allowed and count separately. The graph is a finite straight-line program because every operation reads only earlier values and there are no data-dependent loops.

For each operation $j$, choose a dimension $d_j\ge0$, set $E_j=\mathbb R^{d_j}$ with its standard Euclidean inner product, take an open set $U_j\subseteq E_{p_{j,1}}\times\cdots\times E_{p_{j,r_j}}$ with the product inner product, and choose a primitive map $\phi_j:U_j\to E_j$. A smooth primitive is $C^1$: it is totally differentiable and its derivative matrix is continuous. For Hessian-vector products require the primitive to be $C^2$, meaning $C^1$ with a continuously differentiable derivative map. Derivatives are represented in these coordinates, and every transpose is the Euclidean transpose for the stated inner products; the gradient of a scalar output is the Euclidean gradient. The real-arithmetic primal recursion is $z_j=\phi_j(z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,z_{p_{j,r_j}})$ whenever the parent tuple lies in $U_j$. Its admissible input domain is the set of $x\in\mathbb R^n$ for which every operation in this recursion is defined. The graph's scalar output function $f$ is the value at $o$: it is $x_i$ when $o$ is input coordinate $i$, and $z_j$ when $o$ is operation node $j$.

The **primal tape** is the finite ordered record of input and node values, parent-slot indices, primitive identities, and (when applicable) selected branch labels. A deterministic replay starts from the identical checkpoint state and applies the identical primitive maps in the identical order, so it reproduces the same real-arithmetic values and local derivative inputs. Opaque solver calls are not primitive operations unless their complete deterministic map and derivative rule are explicitly supplied.

If the current parent tuple lies strictly inside exactly one declared branch, the program uses that branch and its derivative. At a branch boundary or ambiguous branch selection, forward or reverse AD returns NONDIFFERENTIABLE; it does not silently choose a subgradient or generalized derivative. If no primal value is specified at a boundary, that input is outside the program's domain. All correctness theorems below apply on a fixed strict branch. The same convention applies to piecewise-$C^2$ primitives for Hessian-vector products.

Let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be the output of a finite $C^1$ program on a fixed strict branch. For every admissible $x\in\Omega$ and direction $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the forward-mode algorithm returns $Df(x)v$.

For a finite $C^1$ program with one scalar output $f$, on a fixed strict branch and at every admissible $x$, the reverse-mode algorithm returns $Df(x)^T1$, the gradient of $f$. More precisely, at any operation node $i$, if its value is temporarily treated as an independent variable and all later operations are recomputed from it, then the accumulated cotangent at $i$ is the derivative of the scalar output with respect to that independent node value.

derivations.claim: The primal values are $z_1=1+2=3$, $z_2=3\cdot3=9$, $z_3=1\cdot2=2$, and $f=z_2+z_3=11$.

The forward value $11$ and both derivative calculations agree with the stated output and gradient.

Suppose $R(\theta_0,z_0)=0$ and the state Jacobian $R_z(\theta_0,z_0)$ is invertible. The Euclidean implicit function theorem gives a local $C^1$ solution branch $z=\phi(\theta)$, and
$$D\phi(\theta_0)=-R_z(\theta_0,z_0)^{-1}R_\theta(\theta_0,z_0).$$
For a scalar $C^1$ objective $J(\theta,z)$, its derivative along that branch is
$$D(J(\theta,\phi(\theta)))|_{\theta_0}=J_\theta-J_zR_z^{-1}R_\theta.$$
Equivalently, if $\lambda$ solves $R_z^T\lambda=J_z^T$, this derivative is $J_\theta-\lambda^TR_\theta$. These formulas concern the exact local solution branch; differentiating a stopped iteration is a separate finite-map derivative.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $x\in\mathbb F^n$, $y\in\mathbb F^m$ have stored real or complex entries, with $m,n\ge1$. Use the operationwise arithmetic model, successful sequential dot products, and $0<u<1$ with $(\max(m,n)-1)u<1$. Define
$$g_k=\frac{1+6u}{1-(k-1)u}-1,\qquad F=\|A\|_F,\quad X=\|x\|_2,\quad Y=\|y\|_2.$$
For $\widehat v=\operatorname{fl}(Ax)$ and $\widehat w=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-y)$, put $V=g_nFX$ and $W=V+u(\|\widehat v\|_2+Y)$. Then
$$\|\widehat w-(Ax-y)\|_2\le W.$$
For a stored real $\lambda>0$, also compute $\widehat z=\operatorname{fl}(A^*\widehat w)$, $\widehat l=\operatorname{fl}(\lambda x)$ and $\widehat r=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat z+\widehat l)$, rounding scalar multiplication componentwise. The exact intended normal residual $r=A^*(Ax-y)+\lambda x$ satisfies
$$\|\widehat r-r\|_2\le\rho:=FW+g_mF\|\widehat w\|_2+u\lambda X+u(\|\widehat z\|_2+\|\widehat l\|_2).$$
Norms in these certificates mean exact norms or certified upper bounds. Uncontrolled rounding of the certificate itself is not authorized. The linear bound applies columnwise to certify $\|I-AB\|_2\le\|I-AB\|_F$ from stored basis-solve columns $B$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be as in [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]]. Here fl is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, on each real exact result that is zero or normal; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range x, fl(sqrt(x)) is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression ab+c; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

**A floating-point system.** A floating-point system consists of a nonempty
finite set $\mathbb F\subseteq\mathbb R$ of representable numbers with
$0\in\mathbb F$ and $-\mathbb F=\mathbb F$, a positive real
$N_{\max}\in\mathbb F$ (the largest normal magnitude), a positive real
$N_{\min}\in\mathbb F$ (the smallest normal magnitude), with
$N_{\min}\le N_{\max}$, and a rounding map
$\operatorname{fl}$ defined on $0$ and on the real numbers $t$ with
$N_{\min}\le|t|\le N_{\max}$, taking values in $\mathbb F$ and satisfying
$\operatorname{fl}(0)=0$.

**Unit roundoff.** A real $u>0$ is a **unit roundoff** for the system when
every real $t$ with $N_{\min}\le|t|\le N_{\max}$ satisfies

$$\operatorname{fl}(t)=t(1+\delta)\qquad\text{for some }\delta\text{ with }|\delta|\le u,$$

with $|\cdot|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). The model quantifies all
subsequent error analysis through the single constant $u$ and says nothing
about the internal bit representation beyond the bound $|\delta|\le u$.

**The standard relative model.** For each operation
$\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$ and all $x,y\in\mathbb F$ such that $x\circ y$ is
zero or is a real number in the normal range
($N_{\min}\le|x\circ y|\le N_{\max}$; for $\div$ this includes $y\ne 0$), the
computed result is

$$\operatorname{fl}(x\circ y)=(x\circ y)(1+\delta)\qquad\text{for some }\delta\text{ with }|\delta|\le u.$$

When $x\circ y=0$, this identity is the exact-zero rule
$\operatorname{fl}(0)=0$ and one may take $\delta=0$.

**The exclusions are part of the model, and are stated explicitly.**

- **Overflow** is excluded: when $|x\circ y|>N_{\max}$ the result is not a real
  number of the form $(x\circ y)(1+\delta)$ with $|\delta|\le u$.
- **Underflow** is excluded: when $0<|x\circ y|<N_{\min}$ the result falls into
  the subnormal or lost range and need not satisfy the relative bound.
- **Invalid operations** are excluded: when $x\circ y$ is not a real number
  (for example $0/0$), there is no real $\delta$ for the displayed identity.

Every item on this page that uses the model therefore carries the hypotheses
that the relevant operations lie in the normal range, and statements about
overflow, underflow or invalid operations are made only where the exclusion is
mentioned.

Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $n\ge 1$, let $u\ge 0$, let
$\delta_0,\dots,\delta_{n-1}\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $|\delta_i|\le u$ for every
$i<n$, and suppose $n u<1$. Then

$$\prod_{i<n}(1+\delta_i)=1+\theta_n\qquad\text{with}\qquad|\theta_n|\le\gamma_n:=\frac{n u}{1-n u}.$$

derivations.claim: For every $z$, $\|ABz\|\ge(1-d)\|z\|$. Thus [F3] makes $AB$, hence both square factors, invertible and gives $\|(AB)^{-1}\|\le1/(1-d)$. Since $A^{-1}=B(AB)^{-1}$, $\|A^{-1}\|\le K$. The identity $B-A^{-1}=A^{-1}(AB-I)$ gives $\|B-A^{-1}\|\le Kd$, while $\widehat x-x=A^{-1}(A\widehat x-b)$ gives $\|\widehat x-x\|\le K\rho$. The residuals in these identities are exact; [F2] explains how to certify them from rounded evaluations.

Apply [F1] at the exact point $(A,b)$. For the matrix edge, $BH\widehat x-A^{-1}Hx=(B-A^{-1})H\widehat x+A^{-1}H(\widehat x-x)$. Since $\|H\|_2\le\|H\|_F$, step 1.1 gives $\eta_A$; the vector edge gives $\eta_b$. Taking Euclidean/Frobenius adjoints yields the stated pullbacks with the same norm discrepancies. This explicitly accounts for the perturbed primal evaluation point through $\rho$.

Fix an output coordinate $j$ of $\widehat\lambda$ and put $q_i=B_{ij}c_i$. By success in [F4] and the relative bound in [F5], $p_i=q_i(1+\alpha_i)$ with $|\alpha_i|\le u$; exact-zero products have $\alpha_i=0$. For each addition $i=2,\ldots,n$, write $s_i=(s_{i-1}+p_i)(1+\beta_i)$ with $|\beta_i|\le u$, taking $\beta_i=0$ when the exact sum is zero. Expanding gives $\widehat\lambda_j=s_n=\sum_{i=1}^n q_i(1+\alpha_i)\prod_{k=\max(2,i)}^n(1+\beta_k)$, with an empty product interpreted as $1$. Each coefficient has at most $n$ factors: for $i=1$ it has one product factor and $n-1$ addition factors, while for $i\ge2$ it has one product factor and $n-i+1$ addition factors. Thus [F6], $nu<1$, and monotonicity of $ku/(1-ku)$ imply that each coefficient differs from $1$ by at most $\gamma_n$. Hence $|\widehat\lambda_j-(B^Tc)_j|\le\gamma_n\sum_i|B_{ij}||c_i|$. Stacking these bounds and applying $\||B|^T|c|\|_2\le\|B\|_F\|c\|_2$ gives $\|\widehat\lambda-B^Tc\|_2\le t\|c\|_2$ and then $\|\widehat\lambda\|_2\le(M+t)\|c\|_2$. Each rounded outer-product entry has error at most $u|\widehat\lambda_i\widehat x_j|$, so its Frobenius error is at most $u(M+t)\|\widehat x\|_2\|c\|_2$. Combining these bounds with step 1.2 gives the stated vector and matrix cotangent estimates.

For each realized nonzero $c$, any cotangent error vector $z$ is the action on $c$ of the linear map $zc^T/\|c\|^2$, whose induced norm is $\|z\|/\|c\|$; vectorize the matrix cotangent for the matrix edge. When $c=0$, successful operations return exact zero. Thus the realized rounded pullbacks admit local linear-map perturbations with the displayed bounds, without asserting global linearity of rounding. The graph perturbation theorem may propagate these realized maps with exact accumulation.

Fix a relative open cover $\mathcal U$ of $[a,b]$. Let $S$ be the set of
$x\in[a,b]$ for which $[a,x]$ has a finite subcover. A member containing $a$
contains a relative neighborhood $[a,a+\delta)$ for some $\delta>0$; choosing
$\eta=\min(\delta/2,(b-a)/2)$ shows $a+\eta\in S$. Thus $S$ is nonempty and
bounded above by $b$. By [A1], $c=\sup S$ exists.

If $c<b$, a cover member containing $c$ contains
$(c-\delta,c+\delta)\cap[a,b]$ for some $\delta>0$. Let
$\eta=\min(\delta/2,(b-c)/2)>0$. Since $c$ is the supremum, choose $x\in S$
with $x>c-\eta$. A finite cover of $[a,x]$ together with the member covering
$c$ covers $[a,c+\eta]$. This places $c+\eta$ in $S$, contradicting that
$c$ is an upper bound. Hence $c=b$.

If $b\in S$, the required finite subcover already exists. Otherwise a
cover member containing $b$ contains $(b-\delta,b]$ for some $\delta>0$.
Because $b=\sup S$, choose $x\in S$ with $x>b-\delta$. A finite cover of
$[a,x]$ and that member cover all of $[a,b]$.

derivations.claim:
If $x=0$, $y=0$ is a root. If $x>0$, let
$S=\{q\ge0:q^2\le x\}$. It contains $0$. If $q>x+1$, then
$q^2>(x+1)^2>x$, so $x+1$ bounds $S$ above. By [A1], $y=\sup S$ exists
and $y\ge0$.

Suppose $y^2<x$. Put $\epsilon=\min(1,(x-y^2)/(2y+1))>0$. Then
$2y\epsilon+\epsilon^2\le(2y+1)\epsilon\le x-y^2$, so
$(y+\epsilon)^2\le x$. Thus $y+\epsilon\in S$, contradicting that $y$ is
an upper bound. If $y^2>x$, put $\epsilon=(y^2-x)/(4y)$. Since
$0<y^2-x\le y^2$, $0<\epsilon\le y/4$, and
$(y-\epsilon)^2=y^2-2y\epsilon+\epsilon^2>x$. Every $q\in S$ therefore
satisfies $q<y-\epsilon$, contradicting that $y$ is the least upper bound.
Hence $y^2=x$.

An exact dyadic rational is a number $m2^q$ with integers $m,q$.
Fix integers $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$. Put
$\eta=2^{e_{\min}-p+1}$ and
$N_{\max}=(2^p-1)2^{e_{\max}-p+1}$. The finite representable set $\mathbb F$
consists of zero, both signs of every normal number $k2^{e-p+1}$ with
$e_{\min}\le e\le e_{\max}$ and $2^{p-1}\le k<2^p$, and both signs of every
subnormal number $k\eta$ with $1\le k<2^{p-1}$. The smallest positive
subnormal is $\eta$, the smallest positive normal is $2^{e_{\min}}$, and the
largest finite magnitude is $N_{\max}$. The extended endpoint set also contains
$-\infty$ and $+\infty$ as enclosure sentinels; they are not finite machine
numbers.

For a real $x$ with $|x|\le N_{\max}$, define $\operatorname{rd}(x)$ as the
greatest member of $\mathbb F$ not exceeding $x$, and $\operatorname{ru}(x)$ as
the least member of $\mathbb F$ not less than $x$. Define
$\rho(x)=\operatorname{ru}(x)-\operatorname{rd}(x)$. For nonzero $x$ in the
subnormal range, define the absolute-error bound $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=\eta$;
for $2^e\le |x|<2^{e+1}$ in the normal range, define
$\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=2^{e-p+2}$. At finite overflow, a directed result is
the corresponding infinite sentinel and its error bound is $+\infty$; the
status is `overflow`. The rounding procedure reports `finite`, `subnormal`, or
`overflow`, so no relative-error assumption is implicit.

An exact rational intermediate may be converted by comparing integer
numerators and denominators after clearing powers of two. A directed interval
endpoint is the resulting greatest lower or least upper member of $\mathbb F$.

derivations.claim:
If $x$ is representable, both directed roundings equal $x$. Otherwise
there are consecutive representables $a<b$ with $a<x<b$: finiteness of
$\mathbb F$ and the definitions of greatest lower and least upper values give
these neighbors. Hence $\operatorname{rd}(x)=a\le x\le b=\operatorname{ru}(x)$.

If $0\le x<2^{e_{\min}}$, both neighboring nonnegative representables
are in the subnormal lattice with step $\eta$, so $x-a<\eta$ and $b-x<\eta$.
If $2^e\le x<2^{e+1}$ is normal, consecutive representables within the bin
are spaced by $2^{e-p+1}$. A bracket reaching the upper bin endpoint has no
larger gap; in all cases each endpoint error is at most the stated, more
conservative $2^{e-p+2}$. Symmetry of $\mathbb F$ gives the same bounds for
negative $x$.

For $x>N_{\max}$, $N_{\max}<x<+infty$, and for $x<-N_{\max}$,
$-\infty<x<-N_{\max}$; the prescribed extended endpoints therefore bracket
$x$. The status and infinite absolute-error bound explicitly record that no
finite error estimate is available outside the finite range.

A **Dedekind-complete ordered field** is a commutative field $\mathbb R$ with
identity $1>0$, a total order compatible with addition and multiplication, and
the least-upper-bound axiom: every nonempty subset of $\mathbb R$ that is
bounded above has a least upper bound in $\mathbb R$. Throughout this batch,
all real variables, intervals, limits, derivatives and integrals are taken in
such a field. The integers and rationals are interpreted in their usual
embedded copies. For $x\in\mathbb R$, define $|x|=x$ when $x\ge0$ and
$|x|=-x$ when $x<0$.

A **real interval** is a closed set $[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ with finite dyadic
endpoints $a\le b$. Its width is $b-a$, midpoint is $(a+b)/2$, and its
midpoint-radius form is $m+[-r,r]$ with $m=(a+b)/2$ and $r=(b-a)/2$. The empty
set is the status `empty`; the whole real line is `entire`. `overflow`,
`domain-error`, `split-domain`, and `inconclusive` are computation statuses,
not finite intervals.

A **complex rectangle** is $X+iY=\{x+iy:x\in X,\ y\in Y\}$ for real intervals
$X,Y$. Complex addition and multiplication use
$(x+iy)+(u+iv)=(x+u)+i(y+v)$ and
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$. For $z=x+iy$, its complex modulus is
$|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and for $z\ne0$ its reciprocal is
$1/z=(x-iy)/(x^2+y^2)$. A
**complex ball** $B(c,r)$ is
$\{z\in\mathbb C:|z-c|\le r\}$ with dyadic complex center $c$ and dyadic
$r\ge0$. For any two represented sets $S,T$, the inclusion order is
$S\sqsubseteq T$ iff $S\subseteq T$.

The width of a complex rectangle with coordinate widths $w_X,w_Y$ is its
Euclidean diameter $\sqrt{w_X^2+w_Y^2}$; the width of a ball $B(c,r)$ is its
diameter $2r$. Width comparisons against a dyadic tolerance can be decided by
exact rational comparisons after squaring the nonnegative quantities.

The **range** of a real or complex function $f$ on a set $S$ is
$f(S)=\{f(x):x\in S\cap\operatorname{dom}(f)\}$. A finite expression DAG is a
finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes, constant nodes, and operation
nodes; constants are exact dyadics or are supplied with certified enclosing
intervals. Sharing a node means the exact same intermediate value is reused.

In a Dedekind-complete ordered field, every $x\ge0$ has a unique $y\ge0$ with
$y^2=x$.

derivations.claim:
By [L1], $-|x|\le x\le|x|$ and $-|y|\le y\le|y|$. Adding gives
$-(|x|+|y|)\le x+y\le|x|+|y|$, hence $|x+y|\le|x|+|y|$. The product
identity follows by considering the four sign choices for $x$ and $y$ in the
piecewise definition [L1].

For $z=x+iy$ and $w=u+iv$, expansion gives
$$
|zw|^2=(xu-yv)^2+(xv+yu)^2=(x^2+y^2)(u^2+v^2)=|z|^2|w|^2.
$$
Both moduli are nonnegative by [L2], so uniqueness of nonnegative square
roots [L3] gives $|zw|=|z||w|$. Also, if $0\le a\le b$ and
$r=\sqrt a$, $s=\sqrt b$, then $r,s\ge0$. If $r>s$, then
$a-b=r^2-s^2=(r-s)(r+s)>0$, a contradiction. Thus the square-root map is
increasing on nonnegative inputs.

The identity
$$
(x^2+y^2)(u^2+v^2)-(xu+yv)^2=(xv-yu)^2\ge0.
$$
Thus $(xu+yv)^2\le|z|^2|w|^2$. The increasing property proved in step 1.2 gives
$|xu+yv|\le|z||w|$, hence $xu+yv\le|z||w|$.
Thus $|z+w|^2=|z|^2+|w|^2+2(xu+yv)\le(|z|+|w|)^2$; applying the same
increasing property gives $|z+w|\le|z|+|w|$. By the reciprocal formula in [L2],
$w(1/w)=(u+iv)(u-iv)/(u^2+v^2)=1$. Step 1.2 gives
$|w||1/w|=|1|=1$. Here $|w|>0$: otherwise $x^2+y^2=0$ forces $x=y=0$
because each square is nonnegative, contrary to $w\ne0$. Hence
$|1/w|=1/|w|$, and another application of step 1.2 yields
$|z/w|=|z|/|w|$.

Input: a nonnegative exact dyadic rational $x$ and integer request $n\ge1$.
Output: an exact dyadic lower and upper bound for $\sqrt{x}$; no finite
storage format is needed by this procedure.

1. If $x=0$, return $[0,0]$.
2. Otherwise determine the unique integer $j$ with $2^j\le x<2^{j+1}$ from the
   exact dyadic representation, put $m=\lfloor j/2\rfloor$ and
   $\delta=2^{m-n}$.
3. Set integer indices $L=0$ and $U=2^{n+1}$. While $U-L>1$, put
   $Q=\lfloor(L+U)/2\rfloor$. If $(Q\delta)^2\le x$, replace $L$ by $Q$;
   otherwise replace $U$ by $Q$.
4. Return the exact dyadic pair $[L\delta,U\delta]$. A caller that stores
   these endpoints in a selected finite format must separately round the
   lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up, propagating the resulting
   `subnormal` or `overflow` status.

All comparisons and multiplications in the loop are exact integer/dyadic
operations. The loop has at most $n+1$ iterations.

For finite $x$ with $|x|\le N_{\max}$, the directed roundings defined in
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]] satisfy
$\operatorname{rd}(x)\le x\le\operatorname{ru}(x)$ and each endpoint error is
at most the stated $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)$ (with zero error when $x$ is
representable). For $x>N_{\max}$ the pair $(N_{\max},+\infty)$ encloses $x$;
for $x<-N_{\max}$ the pair $(-\infty,-N_{\max})$ encloses $x$. Overflow has
error bound $+\infty$ and cannot be reported as a finite-error result.

In a Dedekind-complete ordered field, every $x\ge0$ has a unique $y\ge0$ with
$y^2=x$.

derivations.claim:
For $x>0$, the initial lower candidate is $0$ and its square is at most
$x$. The initial upper candidate is $2^{n+1}\delta=2^{m+1}$; if $j=2m$ its
square is $2^{j+2}>x$, and if $j=2m+1$ its square is $2^{j+1}>x$. Thus initially
$(L\delta)^2\le x<(U\delta)^2$.

At each iteration, $Q$ lies strictly between the integer endpoints. The
exact comparison sets $L=Q$ only when $(Q\delta)^2\le x$, preserving the left
inequality; otherwise it sets $U=Q$, preserving the strict right inequality.
The square function is strictly increasing on nonnegative reals by [L3], so
the invariant implies $L\delta\le\sqrt{x}<U\delta$. The integer gap is
halved until it equals one;
the returned width is then $\delta$.

For $x=0$ the returned point interval is exact. For $x>0$, the
algorithm returns the exact dyadic pair from step 1.2. If a caller stores
these endpoints in a finite format, outward rounding preserves both
inequalities by [L2], so the stored result still contains $\sqrt{x}$.

On a fixed exponent bin, step 1.2 gives endpoints
$\delta\lfloor\sqrt{x}/\delta\rfloor$ and
$\delta(\lfloor\sqrt{x}/\delta\rfloor+1)$, both nondecreasing in $x$. At
the transition from exponent $2m$ to $2m+1$, $\delta$ is unchanged. At the
transition from exponent $2m+1$ to $2m+2$, the square-root threshold is
$2^{m+1}$ and the grid spacing doubles from $\delta$ to $2\delta$. Just below
the threshold the lower and upper endpoints are at most $2^{m+1}$; at or
above it they are at least $2^{m+1}$. Thus both exact endpoint functions are
nondecreasing across each transition. At $x=0$ both are zero. The directed
rounding maps are nondecreasing by their greatest-lower/least-upper
definitions, so storage preserves this order.

A **Dedekind-complete ordered field** is a commutative field $\mathbb R$ with
identity $1>0$, a total order compatible with addition and multiplication, and
the least-upper-bound axiom: every nonempty subset of $\mathbb R$ that is
bounded above has a least upper bound in $\mathbb R$. Throughout this batch,
all real variables, intervals, limits, derivatives and integrals are taken in
such a field. The integers and rationals are interpreted in their usual
embedded copies. For $x\in\mathbb R$, define $|x|=x$ when $x\ge0$ and
$|x|=-x$ when $x<0$.

For real $x,y$, $|xy|=|x||y|$ and $|x+y|\le|x|+|y|$. For complex
$z,w$, $|zw|=|z||w|$, $|z+w|\le|z|+|w|$, and if $w\ne0$ then
$|z/w|=|z|/|w|$.

derivations.claim:
Put $A_0=\sum_{n\ge0}|a_n|$ and $B_0=\sum_{n\ge0}|b_n|$. For every
$N$, the finite triangle inequality and [L1] give
$$
\sum_{n=0}^N|c_n|
\le\sum_{j+\ell\le N}|a_j||b_\ell|
\le\left(\sum_{j=0}^N|a_j|\right)
  \left(\sum_{\ell=0}^N|b_\ell|\right)
\le A_0B_0.
$$
These partial sums are increasing and bounded, so [F1] gives their
supremum $S$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, some partial sum exceeds
$S-\varepsilon$, since otherwise $S-\varepsilon$ would be an upper bound;
monotonicity then puts every later partial sum between $S-\varepsilon$ and
$S$. Hence $\sum c_n$ converges absolutely.

Let $A_N=\sum_{j=0}^N a_j$, $B_N=\sum_{\ell=0}^N b_\ell$, and
$C_N=\sum_{n=0}^N c_n=\sum_{j+\ell\le N}a_jb_\ell$. The difference
$A_NB_N-C_N$ is the sum over pairs $0\le j,\ell\le N$ with $j+\ell>N$.
For each such pair, $j>N/2$ or $\ell>N/2$, so by [L1]
$$
|A_NB_N-C_N|
\le B_0\sum_{j>N/2}|a_j|+A_0\sum_{\ell>N/2}|b_\ell|\longrightarrow0.
$$
Absolute convergence makes both tails tend to zero. The convergent sequence
$A_N$ is bounded: beyond some index $|A_N-A|<1$, and the finitely many
earlier values have a finite maximum absolute value. Therefore
$$
|A_NB_N-AB|\le |A_N||B_N-B|+|B||A_N-A|\longrightarrow0.
$$
Together with $|A_NB_N-C_N|\to0$, this gives $C_N\to AB$. Thus the sum
of the Cauchy product is $AB$, proving the claim.

For $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, continuity at $x\in[a,b]$ means that for every
$\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that
$|f(t)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $t\in[a,b]$ and $|t-x|<\delta$.
Differentiability at an interior point $c$ means that the two-sided limit
$$
f'(c)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h}
$$
exists in the real field; differentiability on $(a,b)$ means this holds at
every interior point. For higher derivatives, define recursively
$f^{(j+1)}=(f^{(j)})'$ on the points where the derivative exists. The class
$C^{n+1}$ on an open interval means that these derivatives through order
$n+1$ exist and are continuous there.

For real $x,y$, $|xy|=|x||y|$ and $|x+y|\le|x|+|y|$. For complex
$z,w$, $|zw|=|z||w|$, $|z+w|\le|z|+|w|$, and if $w\ne0$ then
$|z/w|=|z|/|w|$.

derivations.claim:
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, write
$f(c+h)-f(c)=h q(h)$, where $q(h)\to f'(c)$. Then $q$ is bounded for
sufficiently small $h$, so $|f(c+h)-f(c)|\le|h||q(h)|\to0$. Thus $f$ is
continuous at $c$.

The sum difference quotient is the sum of the two difference quotients,
so it tends to $f'(c)+g'(c)$. For the product, use
$$
\frac{f(c+h)g(c+h)-f(c)g(c)}h
=f(c+h)\frac{g(c+h)-g(c)}h+g(c)\frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}h.
$$
By step 1.1, $f(c+h)\to f(c)$; taking limits gives the product rule.

By step 1.1, $g$ is continuous at $c$. Since $g(c)\ne0$, $g(c+h)\ne0$
for sufficiently small $h$. Algebra gives
$$
\frac{f(c+h)/g(c+h)-f(c)/g(c)}h
=\frac{g(c)(f(c+h)-f(c))/h-f(c)(g(c+h)-g(c))/h}
       {g(c+h)g(c)}.
$$
The denominator tends to $g(c)^2\ne0$ and the numerator tends to
$g(c)f'(c)-f(c)g'(c)$, proving the quotient rule.

Put $y=f(c)$ and $\Delta(h)=f(c+h)-y$. Step 1.1 gives
$\Delta(h)\to0$, and [F1] gives $\Delta(h)/h\to f'(c)$. Differentiability
of $g$ at $y$ means
$g(y+u)-g(y)=g'(y)u+u\epsilon(u)$ for $u\ne0$, where
$\epsilon(u)\to0$; set $\epsilon(0)=0$. Then
$$
\frac{g(f(c+h))-g(f(c))}h
=g'(y)\frac{\Delta(h)}h+\epsilon(\Delta(h))\frac{\Delta(h)}h.
$$
The first term tends to $g'(y)f'(c)$; the second tends to zero because
$\epsilon(\Delta(h))\to0$ and $\Delta(h)/h$ is bounded. This proves the
chain rule, including increments with $\Delta(h)=0$.

The case $m=1$ is the derivative of the identity function, whose
quotient is exactly $1$. Suppose $(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$. Since
$x^{m+1}=x\cdot x^m$, the product rule in step 1.2 gives
$(x^{m+1})'=x^m+x(mx^{m-1})=(m+1)x^m$. Induction proves the power rule for
all $m\ge1$.

derivations.claim:
Let $0\le q<1$. For every integer $m\ge0$,
$(1-q)\sum_{k=0}^m q^k=1-q^{m+1}$. If $q=0$, its powers after the zeroth
are zero. If $0<q<1$, then $1/q=1+d$ for $d>0$, and induction gives
$(1+d)^m\ge1+md$. By [L1], $1+md$ is unbounded, so
$0\le q^m\le1/(1+md)\to0$. Thus the geometric partial sums converge to
$1/(1-q)$, with tail $q^{m+1}/(1-q)$.

For $R=0$ the factorial series is $1$. For $R>0$, choose $N$ with
$q=R/(N+2)<1$ by [L1]. If $u_n=R^n/n!$, then for $n\ge N+1$,
$u_{n+1}/u_n=R/(n+1)\le q$. Every finite tail after $N$ is therefore at
most $u_{N+1}\sum_{j\ge0}q^j=u_{N+1}/(1-q)$ by step 1.1. The positive
partial sums are increasing and bounded, so [F1] gives their supremum $S$.
For every $\varepsilon>0$, some partial sum exceeds $S-\varepsilon$, since
otherwise $S-\varepsilon$ would be an upper bound; monotonicity then puts all
later partial sums between $S-\varepsilon$ and $S$. The finite-tail
geometric bound passes to this limit and proves the stated estimate.

For $|x|\le R$, [L2] gives $|x^n/n!|\le R^n/n!$. Thus the exponential
series is uniformly Cauchy by the tail bound in step 1.2. The sine and cosine
series are subseries of this same nonnegative majorant, so their absolute
tails are uniform as well. For the formal derivative series, the exponential
terms are bounded by $R^{n-1}/(n-1)!$; sine derivatives are bounded by
$R^{2k}/(2k)!$, and nonconstant cosine derivatives by
$R^{2k-1}/(2k-1)!$. Each is a subseries of a factorial series from step 1.2.
The same tail comparison proves absolute and uniform convergence of all
stated series.

For $0\le r<1$, the absolute terms of
$\sum_{k\ge0}x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$ are bounded by $r^{2k+1}$ and the derivative
terms by $r^{2k}$. Their tails converge uniformly by step 1.1 applied to
$q=r^2$; multiplication by the fixed factor $r$ or $2$ does not affect
convergence. This proves the assertions for the odd power series and its
formal derivative series.

derivations.claim:
If $a=b$, the singleton range consists only of $f(a)$, so the conclusion
holds. Suppose $a<b$. For each natural $n\ge1$, put
$U_n=\{x\in[a,b]: |f(x)|<n\}$. These sets cover $[a,b]$ by [L2]. Each is
relatively open: at any $x\in U_n$, the margin $n-|f(x)|>0$ and [L3] gives a
neighborhood where $|f(t)-f(x)|$ is smaller than that margin; [L4] then gives
$|f(t)|<n$. By [L1] a finite
subcollection covers; taking its largest index shows $|f|$ is bounded.
Consequently $M=\sup f([a,b])$ exists by [A1].

If $M$ is not attained, for every $n\ge1$ define
$V_n=\{x\in[a,b]: f(x)<M-1/n\}$. For each $x$, $M-f(x)>0$; by [L2] choose
$n$ with $1/n<M-f(x)$, so the $V_n$ cover. Each $V_n$ is relatively open by
[L3] and the positive margin $M-1/n-f(x)$. A finite subcover and its largest
index $N$ imply $f(x)<M-1/N$ for all $x$, making $M-1/N$ an upper bound for
$f([a,b])$. This contradicts that $M$ is the least upper bound. Thus the
maximum is attained.

The function $-f$ is continuous because
$|(-f(t))-(-f(x))|=|f(t)-f(x)|$. Applying steps 1.1–1.2 to $-f$, its attained
maximum is the attained minimum of $f$.

Fix $c$ with $|c|<R_0$ and choose $R$ with $|c|<R<R_0$. For
$0<|h|<R-|c|$, the identity
$$
(c+h)^n-c^n=h\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(c+h)^{n-1-j}c^j
$$
for $n\ge1$ and [L1] yield
$|((c+h)^n-c^n)/h|\le nR^{n-1}$. Thus the tail of the difference-quotient
series beyond degree $N$ is at most
$\sum_{n>N}n|a_n|R^{n-1}$, uniformly for these $h$. The tail of the proposed
derivative series at $c$ has the same bound.

For fixed $N$, the difference quotient of the polynomial
$\sum_{n=0}^N a_nx^n$ tends to $\sum_{n=1}^Nna_nc^{n-1}$ as $h\to0$ by the
binomial identity. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ so both tails bounded
above are below $\varepsilon/3$, then choose $h$ small enough that the finite
polynomial quotient differs from its derivative by less than $\varepsilon/3$.
The full difference quotient therefore differs from
$\sum_{n\ge1}na_nc^{n-1}$ by less than $\varepsilon$, proving the derivative
formula.

For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$; the denominator interval is strictly positive because at
least one coordinate interval excludes zero. Division multiplies by this
reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

endpoint formulas. For multiplication, fixing one variable makes the product

root is monotone on $[0,\infty)$. Thus the exact ranges lie in the displayed

exact lower endpoint and each upper endpoint is no smaller than the exact

interval omits zero, so its squared interval has positive lower endpoint;
component interval operations then enclose the exact reciprocal and quotient.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, the coordinate projection intervals in [L1] contain
each real and imaginary component. By [L5]–[L6], $|i\Im z|=|\Im z|$;
the complex triangle inequality [L4] therefore gives

derivations.claim:
For a partition $P$, the maxima and minima in its sums exist by [L2]. If
$Q$ refines $P$, each old subinterval is divided into finitely many pieces;
the minimum on each piece is at least the old minimum and the maximum is at
most the old maximum. Since the piece lengths sum to the old length,
$L(g,P)\le L(g,Q)\le U(g,Q)\le U(g,P)$.

The range of $g$ has a minimum $m$ and maximum $M$ by [L2]. Thus all
lower and upper sums lie between $m(b-a)$ and $M(b-a)$, and the partition
set is nonempty. Define $I_-:=\sup_P L(g,P)$ and $I_+:=\inf_P U(g,P)$;
both exist by [F1], applying it to negatives for the infimum. For any
partitions $P,Q$, their union is a common
refinement, so step 1.1 gives
$L(g,P)\le L(g,P\cup Q)\le U(g,P\cup Q)\le U(g,Q)$. Taking the supremum
and infimum yields $I_-\le I_+$.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. For each $x\in[a,b]$, continuity [F2] gives
$\delta_x>0$ such that $|g(t)-g(x)|<\varepsilon/2$ when
$t\in[a,b]$ and $|t-x|<\delta_x$. The relative neighborhoods
$(x-\delta_x/2,x+\delta_x/2)\cap[a,b]$ cover $[a,b]$. Choose a finite
subcover with centers $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ by [L1], and put
$\delta=\min_i\delta_{x_i}/2>0$. If $u,v\in[a,b]$, $|u-v|<\delta$, and
$u$ belongs to the neighborhood centered at $x_i$, then both $u$ and $v$ are
within $\delta_{x_i}$ of $x_i$. By [L4],
$|g(u)-g(v)|\le|g(u)-g(x_i)|+|g(v)-g(x_i)|<\varepsilon$.
Thus $g$ is uniformly continuous.

Apply step 2.1 with tolerance $\varepsilon/(2(b-a))$ and choose an equal
partition with mesh smaller than its uniform-continuity radius, using [L3].
On each piece the oscillation $\max g-\min g$ is less than that tolerance,
because both extrema are attained by [L2]. Hence
$U(g,P)-L(g,P)<\varepsilon/2$. Since $I_-\ge L(g,P)$ and
$I_+\le U(g,P)$, we have $0\le I_+-I_-<\varepsilon$. This holds for every
$\varepsilon>0$, so $I_-=I_+$. Their common value defines the integral in
the statement.

Fix $c$ with $a<c<b$. Refining any partition by inserting $c$ cannot
increase its upper sum by step 1.1, so the infimum of upper sums over all
partitions equals the infimum over partitions containing $c$. Each such
upper sum is the sum of an upper sum on $[a,c]$ and one on $[c,b]$. Every
pair of partitions of these two intervals combines to a partition containing
$c$; therefore the infimum of the combined sums is the sum of the two separate
infima (choose each sum within $\varepsilon/2$ of its infimum for the reverse
inequality). The common upper/lower values from step 2.2 give
$\int_a^b g=\int_a^c g+\int_c^b g$. Endpoint cases follow from
$\int_a^a g=0$. Reversal is the definition, so the integral is oriented and
additive.

The constant function with value $d$ has every upper and lower sum equal
to $d(b-a)$, so its integral is $d(b-a)$. More generally, if constants
$m,M$ satisfy $m\le g(t)\le M$ on $[a,b]$, every lower sum is at least
$m(b-a)$ and every upper sum is at most $M(b-a)$; hence
$m(b-a)\le\int_a^b g\le M(b-a)$. If $m_0$ and $M_0$ are the attained
minimum and maximum of $g$, then
$C:=\max(|m_0|,|M_0|)=\max_{t\in[a,b]}|g(t)|$, since every value lies
between $m_0$ and $M_0$. Applying the comparison with $m=-C,M=C$ gives
$|\int_a^b g|\le C(b-a)$; reversal gives the bound with $|b-a|$ for either
orientation.

If continuous $g\le h$ on $[a,b]$, then on each partition interval the
minimum of $g$ is at most the minimum of $h$. Thus $L(g,P)\le L(h,P)$ for
every partition $P$; taking suprema of the lower sums gives
$\int_a^b g\le\int_a^b h$.

Let $g$ be continuous on an open interval $J$, fix $x_0\in J$, and put
$G(x)=\int_{x_0}^x g(t)\,dt$. The compact-segment results above define each
integral. By additivity from step 3.1 and the constant-integral calculation
in step 3.2, for $h\ne0$ sufficiently small,
$$
\frac{G(x+h)-G(x)}h
=\frac1h\int_x^{x+h}g(t)\,dt.
$$
For any $\eta>0$, continuity at $x$ gives $\delta>0$ such that
$g(x)-\eta<g(t)<g(x)+\eta$ whenever $|t-x|<\delta$. If $0<h<\delta$,
step 3.1 and the comparison in step 3.2 place this quotient between
$g(x)-\eta$ and $g(x)+\eta$. If $-\delta<h<0$, reverse the integral by
step 3.1, apply the same comparison on $[x+h,x]$, and divide by the
negative $h$; the inequalities again place the quotient between those same
constants. The extrema of $g$ on each such segment exist by [L2], and the
largest deviation from $g(x)$ is attained at one of them. Hence its limit is
$g(x)$, so $G'(x)=g(x)$.

Let $g:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $a<b$, in a Dedekind-complete
ordered field. For a partition $P=(a=x_0<\cdots<x_m=b)$ put
$$
U(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^m \left(\max_{t\in[x_{i-1},x_i]}g(t)\right)(x_i-x_{i-1}),\qquad
L(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^m \left(\min_{t\in[x_{i-1},x_i]}g(t)\right)(x_i-x_{i-1}).
$$
The supremum of the lower sums equals the infimum of the upper sums. Define
$\int_a^b g$ to be this common value, set $\int_a^a g=0$, and set
$\int_b^a g=-\int_a^b g$. This oriented Riemann integral is additive over
intervals. Refining a partition increases its lower sum and decreases its
upper sum, and any two partitions have a common refinement. It satisfies
$$
\left|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt\right|
\le |b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|.
$$
If $a<b$ and constants $m,M$ satisfy $m\le g(t)\le M$ on $[a,b]$, then
$m(b-a)\le\int_a^b g\le M(b-a)$; reversing the endpoints reverses these
inequalities. The integral is monotone in its integrand: if continuous
$g\le h$ on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b g\le\int_a^b h$.
If $g$ is continuous on an open interval $J$ and $x_0\in J$, then
$G(x)=\int_{x_0}^x g(t)\,dt$ is defined for $x\in J$ and $G'(x)=g(x)$.

the separate maxima, while its minimum is at least the sum of the separate
minima. Thus $U(f+g,P)\le U(f,P)+U(g,P)$ and
$L(f+g,P)\ge L(f,P)+L(g,P)$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose partitions whose
upper sums for $f,g$ are within $\varepsilon/2$ above their infima, and refine
both to a common partition $P$. By [L1], refinement cannot increase those
upper sums, so
$\int_a^b(f+g)\le U(f+g,P)<\int_a^b f+\int_a^b g+\varepsilon$.
Similarly choose lower sums within $\varepsilon/2$ below their suprema and
refine to a common partition; [L1] gives
$\int_a^b(f+g)\ge L(f+g,P)>\int_a^b f+\int_a^b g-\varepsilon$.
Since this holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, the integral is additive in the
integrand.

If $\alpha>0$, maxima and minima of $\alpha f$ on every partition
piece are $\alpha$ times those of $f$, so both Darboux sums scale by
$\alpha$ and their infimum/supremum do as well. If $\alpha=0$, every sum is
zero. If $\alpha<0$, multiplication reverses order, giving
$U(\alpha f,P)=\alpha L(f,P)$ and
$L(\alpha f,P)=\alpha U(f,P)$; taking the infimum and supremum, which
reverse under multiplication by negative $\alpha$, again gives
$\int_a^b\alpha f=\alpha\int_a^b f$. Combine this homogeneity with step 1.1
to obtain the displayed formula. For reversed endpoints use
$\int_b^a=-\int_a^b$; for $a=b$ use the zero-length definition.

For $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, continuity at $x\in[a,b]$ means that for every
$\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that
$|f(t)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $t\in[a,b]$ and $|t-x|<\delta$.
Differentiability at an interior point $c$ means that the two-sided limit
$$
f'(c)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h}
$$
exists in the real field; differentiability on $(a,b)$ means this holds at
every interior point. For higher derivatives, define recursively
$f^{(j+1)}=(f^{(j)})'$ on the points where the derivative exists. The class
$C^{n+1}$ on an open interval means that these derivatives through order
$n+1$ exist and are continuous there.

Let $g:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $a<b$, in a Dedekind-complete
ordered field. For a partition $P=(a=x_0<\cdots<x_m=b)$ put
$$
U(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^m \left(\max_{t\in[x_{i-1},x_i]}g(t)\right)(x_i-x_{i-1}),\qquad
L(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^m \left(\min_{t\in[x_{i-1},x_i]}g(t)\right)(x_i-x_{i-1}).
$$
The supremum of the lower sums equals the infimum of the upper sums. Define
$\int_a^b g$ to be this common value, set $\int_a^a g=0$, and set
$\int_b^a g=-\int_a^b g$. This oriented Riemann integral is additive over
intervals. Refining a partition increases its lower sum and decreases its
upper sum, and any two partitions have a common refinement. It satisfies
$$
\left|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt\right|
\le |b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|.
$$
If $a<b$ and constants $m,M$ satisfy $m\le g(t)\le M$ on $[a,b]$, then
$m(b-a)\le\int_a^b g\le M(b-a)$; reversing the endpoints reverses these
inequalities. The integral is monotone in its integrand: if continuous
$g\le h$ on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b g\le\int_a^b h$.
If $g$ is continuous on an open interval $J$ and $x_0\in J$, then
$G(x)=\int_{x_0}^x g(t)\,dt$ is defined for $x\in J$ and $G'(x)=g(x)$.

Let $f,g$ be continuous on $[a,b]$, $a<b$, and let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R$.
Then $\alpha f+\beta g$ is continuous and
$$
\int_a^b(\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t))\,dt
=\alpha\int_a^b f(t)\,dt+\beta\int_a^b g(t)\,dt.
$$
The same identity holds for the oriented integral when $b<a$, and for the
zero-length interval both sides are zero.

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
$(a,b)$, with $a<b$. Then there is $c\in(a,b)$ such that
$$
f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a).
$$

derivations.claim:
Assume first $a<b$ and let $H(x)=\int_a^x f'(t)\,dt$. By [L1],
$H'(x)=f'(x)$ on an open
interval containing $[a,b]$, and $H(a)=0$. By [L3], $H$ is continuous there.
Thus $q=f-H$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and
$q'=0$. Applying [L4] gives $q(b)-q(a)=0$, so
$f(b)-H(b)=f(a)$. Rearranging proves the first identity.

For $a=b$ the first identity is $0=0$; reversing endpoints proves it
for $a>b$.

Assume $a<b$. By [L3], $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$. These terms are continuous: for continuous
$u,v$,
$$
|u(t)v(t)-u(t_0)v(t_0)|
\le |u(t)|\,|v(t)-v(t_0)|+|v(t_0)|\,|u(t)-u(t_0)|,
$$
and continuity of $u$ bounds $|u(t)|$ near $t_0$. Thus $fg$ is continuously
differentiable. Apply step 1.1 to $fg$ and then [L2]:
$$
f(b)g(b)-f(a)g(a)=\int_a^b(f'g+fg')
=\int_a^b f'g+\int_a^b fg'.
$$
Rearranging gives the second identity. For $a=b$ both sides are zero, and
for $a>b$ reverse endpoints using [L1].

Every integral below is the oriented Riemann integral constructed from upper
and lower Darboux sums in
[[lem-continuous-functions-riemann-integrable]]. It exists for each displayed
continuous integrand on the finite interval between its endpoints, is additive
in intervals, reverses sign when the endpoints are reversed, is monotone in
the integrand, and satisfies
$|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt|\le|b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|$.
These properties also
give constant comparison bounds and the average-value difference quotient
used to differentiate the integral-defined functions.

The exponential is $\exp(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}x^k/k!$ for $x\in\mathbb R$.
The sine and cosine are the everywhere-convergent power series
$\sin x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$ and
$\cos x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k}/(2k)!$. Define
$\arctan x=\int_0^x dt/(1+t^2)$ and set $\pi=4\arctan1$. The natural
logarithm $\ln$ is defined on $(0,\infty)$ by $\ln x=\int_1^x dt/t$.

The square root is the unique nonnegative real $y$ with $y^2=x$ for $x\ge0$;
existence and uniqueness follow from
[[lem-nonnegative-square-root-exists-and-unique]]. The tangent is
$\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ on the set where $\cos x\ne0$.

For complex $z=x+iy$, the modulus $|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is defined in
[[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]]. The complex exponential is
$\exp(x+iy)=\exp(x)(\cos y+i\sin y)$. The principal complex logarithm is
$\operatorname{Log}(z)=\ln|z|+i\operatorname{Arg}(z)$ on
$\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$. For $z=x+iy$ in this domain, define
$$
\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\\
\pi/2,&x=0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi/2,&x=0,\ y<0,\\
\pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0.
\end{cases}
$$
The excluded negative real axis is the remaining case $x<0,y=0$; zero is
also excluded.

These are point functions. An interval extension must separately enclose their
exact ranges, test the stated domains, and return a non-finite status when its
finite budget cannot certify a reduction or endpoint.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
$(a,b)$, with $a<b$. Then there is $c\in(a,b)$ such that
$$
f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a).
$$

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

Let $R_0>0$ and let $(a_n)_{n\ge0}$ be real coefficients such that for every
$0<R<R_0$ both $\sum_{n\ge0}|a_n|R^n$ and
$\sum_{n\ge1}n|a_n|R^{n-1}$ converge. Then
$F(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n$ is differentiable for $|x|<R_0$, with
$F'(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}na_nx^{n-1}$.

For real $x,y$, $|xy|=|x||y|$ and $|x+y|\le|x|+|y|$. For complex
$z,w$, $|zw|=|z||w|$, $|z+w|\le|z|+|w|$, and if $w\ne0$ then
$|z/w|=|z|/|w|$.

For every real $R\ge0$, the factorial series
$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}R^n/n!$ converges. If $N\ge0$ and
$q=R/(N+2)<1$, its tail after index $N$ satisfies
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}\frac{R^n}{n!}
\le \frac{R^{N+1}}{(N+1)!(1-q)}.
$$
Consequently the series defining $\exp x$, $\sin x$, $\cos x$ and each of
their formal derivative series converge absolutely and uniformly on every
bounded interval $|x|\le R$. For $0\le r<1$, the geometric series and the
odd power series $\sum_{k\ge0}x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$, with their formal derivative
series, converge absolutely and uniformly on $|x|\le r$.

derivations.claim:
For $k\ge N+1$, consecutive absolute exponential terms have ratio
$|u|/(k+1)\le q:=|u|/(N+2)<1$. Their tail is bounded by the first omitted
term times $1+q+q^2+\cdots=1/(1-q)$, giving $R_E$. The defining power
series lies between its partial sum plus or minus this absolute tail. For
$N\ge1$, the partial sum is at least $1-|u|\ge1/2$ by alternating-series
grouping when $u<0$ and by positivity when $u\ge0$; also
$R_E\le(1/2)^2/(2(1-1/6))=3/20<1/2$. Thus the lower bound is positive.

For $y\in[1,2]$, $v=(y-1)/(y+1)\in[0,1/3]$. Set
$G(v)=2\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}v^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$. Its derivative series is
absolutely convergent for $|v|<1$ by [L6], so [L4] gives
$G'(v)=2/(1-v^2)$. By [L3], $H(y)=G(v(y))$ has derivative
$4/((y+1)^2(1-v^2))=1/y$. The integral definition [L1] has derivative
$1/y$, since its difference quotient is the average of the continuous
integrand $1/t$ near $y$; also $H(1)=\ln1=0$. For $y>1$, apply [L2] to
$H-\ln$ on $[1,y]$; its derivative is zero, so
$H(y)-\ln y=H(1)-\ln1=0$. Equality at $y=1$ holds by the integral
definition. Hence $H(y)=\ln y$ on $[1,2]$.

For each $k\ge N+1$, the absolute logarithm-series term is at most
$2|v|^{2N+3}|v|^{2(k-N-1)}/(2N+3)$. Summing this geometric majorant gives
$2|v|^{2N+3}/((2N+3)(1-v^2))$. Removing the first $N+1$ terms of $H$
leaves exactly this bounded tail.

Fix $y>0$ and let $h(x)=\ln(xy)-\ln x$ for $x>0$. From [L1], the
integral difference quotient gives $(\ln x)'=1/x$. The chain rule [L3]
therefore gives $h'(x)=y/(xy)-1/x=0$. Applying [L2] on the positive segment
between $1$ and any $x>0$ shows $h(x)=h(1)=\ln y$, so
$\ln(xy)=\ln x+\ln y$. Repeated use gives the identity for positive integer
powers of $2$; applying it to $2\cdot(1/2)=1$ gives
$\ln(1/2)=-\ln2$, hence the same identity for negative integer powers and
$j=0$. Thus $\ln(2^j y)=j\ln2+\ln y$ for every integer $j$.

For $|t|\le1/2$, the power series
$P(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^kt^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$ has radius $1$ by [L6],
and [L4] gives $P'(t)=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^kt^{2k}=1/(1+t^2)$ by the
geometric series.
The integral definition [L1] has the same derivative by the average-value
difference quotient and the same value $0$ at $t=0$. If $t>0$, [L2] applied
to $P-\arctan$ on $[0,t]$ gives equality; if $t<0$, apply [L2] on $[t,0]$;
at $t=0$ both are zero. Thus $P(t)=\arctan t$ on the stated interval.

For every omitted term index $k\ge N+1$, its magnitude is at most
$|t|^{2N+3}|t|^{2(k-N-1)}/(2N+3)$. Summing gives the displayed geometric
tail, so $A_N(t)$ plus or minus that tail encloses $\arctan t$.

derivations.claim:
Fix $x\ne c$ and set
$A=(f(x)-P_n(x))/(x-c)^{n+1}$ and
$g(t)=f(t)-P_n(t)-A(t-c)^{n+1}$ on the interval between $c$ and $x$.
Then $g(c)=g(x)=0$ and $g^{(j)}(c)=0$ for each $1\le j\le n$, because the
Taylor polynomial matches those derivatives at $c$ by [L2] and the last term
has a zero of order $n+1$.

By [L1] applied to $g$ on the interval with endpoints $c,x$, there is a
point $z_1$ strictly between them with $g'(z_1)=0$. If $n\ge1$, also
$g'(c)=0$, so [L1] applied to $g'$ between $c$ and $z_1$ gives
$z_2$ between them with $g''(z_2)=0$. Inductively, for each $j\le n$ the
zeros $g^{(j)}(c)=0$ and $g^{(j)}(z_j)=0$ give a point $z_{j+1}$ between them
with $g^{(j+1)}(z_{j+1})=0$. The last point is the required $\xi$; when
$n=0$, take $\xi=z_1$.

Since $P_n^{(n+1)}=0$ and the $(n+1)$st derivative of
$A(t-c)^{n+1}$ is $A(n+1)!$, the equation $g^{(n+1)}(\xi)=0$ gives
$A=f^{(n+1)}(\xi)/(n+1)!$ by [L2]. Substituting the definition of $A$
proves the formula. At $x=c$, $P_n(c)=f(c)$ directly.

derivations.claim:
For fixed $f,c,x$, define
$I_m=\frac1{m!}\int_c^x f^{(m+1)}(t)(x-t)^m\,dt$ for $0\le m\le n$.
For $m=0$, [L1] gives $I_0=f(x)-f(c)$. For $m\ge1$, apply integration by
parts [L1] to $u(t)=f^{(m)}(t)$ and $v(t)=(x-t)^m/m!$. Since
$v(x)=0$, $v(c)=(x-c)^m/m!$, and
$v'(t)=-(x-t)^{m-1}/(m-1)!$, it gives
$$
I_m=I_{m-1}-\frac{f^{(m)}(c)(x-c)^m}{m!}.
$$
Induction from $I_0$ yields
$I_n=f(x)-\sum_{j=0}^n f^{(j)}(c)(x-c)^j/j!=f(x)-P_n(x)$.
The oriented integration-by-parts identity makes the same recurrence valid
when $x<c$; if $x=c$, both sides are zero.

Let $d=|x-c|$ and
$\psi(t)=f^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n/n!$. This is continuous. The triangle
inequality in [L3], applied in both directions, gives
$\bigl||\psi(s)|-|\psi(t)|\bigr|\le|\psi(s)-\psi(t)|$, so $|\psi|$ is
continuous too and both functions are integrable.
By [L2] and [L4], the integral is monotone in the integrand, so
$$
\left|\int_c^x\psi(t)\,dt\right|
\le\int_{\min(c,x)}^{\max(c,x)}|\psi(t)|\,dt
\le\frac{M}{n!}\int_{\min(c,x)}^{\max(c,x)}|x-t|^n\,dt.
$$
The first inequality follows by integrating $-|\psi|\le\psi\le|\psi|$
on the forward interval and using $\int(-|\psi|)=-\int|\psi|$; orientation
does not change the absolute value. The last power integral is
$d^{n+1}/(n+1)$ by [L1], using its polynomial antiderivative on the segment
to either side of $x$. Thus the bound is $Md^{n+1}/(n+1)!$. Combining this
with step 1.1 proves the result.

citations.quote:
Every integral below is the oriented Riemann integral constructed from upper
and lower Darboux sums in
[[lem-continuous-functions-riemann-integrable]]. It exists for each displayed
continuous integrand on the finite interval between its endpoints, is additive
in intervals, reverses sign when the endpoints are reversed, is monotone in
the integrand, and satisfies
$|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt|\le|b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|$.
These properties also
give constant comparison bounds and the average-value difference quotient
used to differentiate the integral-defined functions.

The exponential is $\exp(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}x^k/k!$ for $x\in\mathbb R$.
The sine and cosine are the everywhere-convergent power series
$\sin x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$ and
$\cos x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k}/(2k)!$. Define
$\arctan x=\int_0^x dt/(1+t^2)$ and set $\pi=4\arctan1$. The natural
logarithm $\ln$ is defined on $(0,\infty)$ by $\ln x=\int_1^x dt/t$.

The square root is the unique nonnegative real $y$ with $y^2=x$ for $x\ge0$;
existence and uniqueness follow from
[[lem-nonnegative-square-root-exists-and-unique]]. The tangent is
$\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ on the set where $\cos x\ne0$.

For complex $z=x+iy$, the modulus $|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is defined in
[[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]]. The complex exponential is
$\exp(x+iy)=\exp(x)(\cos y+i\sin y)$. The principal complex logarithm is
$\operatorname{Log}(z)=\ln|z|+i\operatorname{Arg}(z)$ on
$\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$. For $z=x+iy$ in this domain, define
$$
\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\\
\pi/2,&x=0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi/2,&x=0,\ y<0,\\
\pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0.
\end{cases}
$$
The excluded negative real axis is the remaining case $x<0,y=0$; zero is
also excluded.

These are point functions. An interval extension must separately enclose their
exact ranges, test the stated domains, and return a non-finite status when its
finite budget cannot certify a reduction or endpoint.

For $|u|\le1/2$ and integer $N\ge1$, set
$E_N(u)=\sum_{k=0}^N u^k/k!$ and
$R_E=|u|^{N+1}/((N+1)!(1-|u|/(N+2)))$. Then
$\exp(u)\in[E_N(u)-R_E,E_N(u)+R_E]$, and the lower endpoint is positive.
For $y\in[1,2]$, put $v=(y-1)/(y+1)$ and
$L_N(v)=2\sum_{k=0}^N v^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$. Then
$$
\left|\ln y-L_N(v)\right|\le
\frac{2|v|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)(1-v^2)}.
$$
For every integer $j$ and $y>0$, the natural logarithm also satisfies
$\ln(2^j y)=j\ln2+\ln y$.
For $|t|\le1/2$, set $A_N(t)=\sum_{k=0}^N(-1)^kt^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$. Then
$$
\left|\arctan t-A_N(t)\right|\le
\frac{|t|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)(1-t^2)}.
$$

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
$(a,b)$, with $a<b$. Then there is $c\in(a,b)$ such that
$$
f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a).
$$

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

Let $R_0>0$ and let $(a_n)_{n\ge0}$ be real coefficients such that for every
$0<R<R_0$ both $\sum_{n\ge0}|a_n|R^n$ and
$\sum_{n\ge1}n|a_n|R^{n-1}$ converge. Then
$F(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n$ is differentiable for $|x|<R_0$, with
$F'(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}na_nx^{n-1}$.
In a Dedekind-complete ordered field, the natural numbers are unbounded above.

For real $x,y$, $|xy|=|x||y|$ and $|x+y|\le|x|+|y|$. For complex
$z,w$, $|zw|=|z||w|$, $|z+w|\le|z|+|w|$, and if $w\ne0$ then
$|z/w|=|z|/|w|$.

For every real $R\ge0$, the factorial series
$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}R^n/n!$ converges. If $N\ge0$ and
$q=R/(N+2)<1$, its tail after index $N$ satisfies
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}\frac{R^n}{n!}
\le \frac{R^{N+1}}{(N+1)!(1-q)}.
$$
Consequently the series defining $\exp x$, $\sin x$, $\cos x$ and each of
their formal derivative series converge absolutely and uniformly on every
bounded interval $|x|\le R$. For $0\le r<1$, the geometric series and the
odd power series $\sum_{k\ge0}x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$, with their formal derivative
series, converge absolutely and uniformly on $|x|\le r$.

Let $\sum_{n\ge0}a_n=A$ and $\sum_{n\ge0}b_n=B$ be absolutely convergent
real series. Define
$$
c_n=\sum_{j=0}^n a_jb_{n-j}.
$$
Then $\sum_{n\ge0}c_n$ converges absolutely and has sum $AB$. Thus the
product of the two series can be grouped by total degree without changing
its sum.

derivations.claim:
On each bounded square, the factorial series and their tails converge
uniformly by [L8]. Their Cauchy products are absolutely convergent and can be
grouped by total degree by [L9]. For sine, the coefficient of $x^r y^s$
in $\sin(x+y)$ vanishes when $r+s$ is even and otherwise equals
$(-1)^{(r+s-1)/2}/(r!s!)$, by the binomial theorem; the same coefficient
appears in $\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y$. For cosine, the coefficient in
$\cos(x+y)$ vanishes when $r+s$ is odd and otherwise equals
$(-1)^{(r+s)/2}/(r!s!)$, matching $\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y$. Thus both
addition identities hold.

On every bounded interval, [L8] gives absolute convergence of the
factorial coefficient series and their derivative series. Applying [L5] to the
two power series gives $\sin'=\cos$ and $\cos'=-\sin$. By the product rule
in [L4], the derivative of $\sin^2x+\cos^2x$ is zero; [L3] and its value
$1$ at zero give $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$.

Write $A(t)=\arctan t$, $S(t)=\sin A(t)$ and $C(t)=\cos A(t)$. From
[L1], the difference quotient for $A$ is the average of the continuous
integrand $1/(1+u^2)$ over the interval from $t$ to $t+h$, so
$A'(t)=1/(1+t^2)$. By the preceding sine and cosine identity and the chain
and product rules [L4],
$g(t)=S(t)-tC(t)$ satisfies $g'(t)=t g(t)/(1+t^2)$ and $g(0)=0$. The
quotient rule [L4] gives $(g(t)^2/(1+t^2))'=0$. By [L3], this quotient is
constant on every interval between $0$ and $t$, hence zero; therefore
$g(t)=0$. Now $C(t)^2=1/(1+t^2)$ by the preceding sine and cosine identity,
and
$C'(t)=-tC(t)/(1+t^2)$. Put $q(t)=\sqrt{1+t^2}$. Since $q(t)\ge0$ and
$q(t)^2\ge1$, it follows that $q(t)\ge1$: otherwise
$(1-q(t))(1+q(t))>0$ would imply $q(t)^2<1$. The same holds at $t+h$.
For $h$ near zero, rationalization gives
$$
|q(t+h)-q(t)|
=\frac{|h|\,|2t+h|}{q(t+h)+q(t)}
\le\frac{|h|(2|t|+|h|)}2\longrightarrow0.
$$
Thus $q$ is continuous, and the rationalized difference quotient
$(q(t+h)-q(t))/h=(2t+h)/(q(t+h)+q(t))$ tends to $t/q(t)$; hence
$q'(t)=t/q(t)$. The product rule [L4] gives $(q(t)C(t))'=0$, so [L3]
implies $q(t)C(t)$ is constant on every segment between $0$ and $t$. Its
value at zero is $1$, hence $C(t)=1/q(t)>0$.
For $t>0$ and $0\le u\le t$, the integrand satisfies
$1/(1+u^2)\ge1/(1+t^2)$. Constant comparison for the integral [L1] gives
$A(t)\ge t/(1+t^2)>0$. Also $A'(t)=1/(1+t^2)$, so
$H(t)=A(t)+A(1/t)$ has derivative
$$
H'(t)=\frac1{1+t^2}-\frac1{t^2}\frac1{1+1/t^2}=0.
$$
By [L3], $H$ is constant on the positive segment between $1$ and $t$;
$H(1)=2A(1)$. Therefore $A(t)=2A(1)-A(1/t)$ for every $t>0$, and the
positivity just proved shows $0<A(t)<2A(1)$. Similarly, the derivative of
$A(-t)+A(t)$ is zero and its value at zero is zero, so [L3] gives
$A(-t)=-A(t)$ for every real $t$. Since $\pi/2=2A(1)$, these bounds yield
$A(t)\in(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ for all real $t$ and $\tan A(t)=t$. At $t=1$,
$S(1)=C(1)>0$ and step 1.2 gives both equal $1/\sqrt2$; the addition
identities yield $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ and $\cos(\pi/2)=0$.

For $u,v\ge0$ with $uv<1$, define
$H(v)=A(u)+A(v)-A((u+v)/(1-uv))$. Differentiating with the inverse-tangent
derivative formula and the chain rule [L4], the derivative of the last term is
$$
\frac{(1+u^2)/(1-uv)^2}{1+((u+v)/(1-uv))^2}=\frac1{1+v^2},
$$
which is also $A'(v)$. Thus $H'(v)=0$ and $H(0)=0$; [L3] gives
$A(u)+A(v)=A((u+v)/(1-uv))$. Set $\alpha=A(1/5)$ and $\beta=A(1/239)$.
This identity gives $2\alpha=A(5/12)$, then $4\alpha=A(120/119)$, and also
$\beta+A(1)=A(120/119)$. Hence $4\alpha=\beta+A(1)$ and
$16\alpha-4\beta=4A(1)=\pi$.

Since $1/5$ and $1/239$ lie in $[0,1/2]$, [L2] gives rational intervals
for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with the displayed tail widths. Multiplying those
intervals by $16$ and $4$ and using the exact identity in step 2.1 gives a
certified rational interval for $\pi$; increasing the truncation count
decreases both tail bounds.

Put $q=2x/\pi$. By [L6], choose an integer $n>|q|+1$. Among the finite
ordered list $-n,-n+1,\ldots,n$, take its greatest member $k_0\le q$; then
$k_0\le q<k_0+1$. At least one of $k_0,k_0+1$ is within $1/2$ of $q$; call
it $k$. Since $0<1/(1+u^2)\le1$ on $[0,1]$, integral comparison [L1] and
step 1.3 give $0<A(1)\le1$, hence $\pi/4=A(1)\le1$. Therefore the residual
$r=x-k\pi/2$ satisfies $|r|\le\pi/4\le1$. Repeated application of the
addition identities in step 1.1 and the values proved in step 1.3 gives the
quarter-period sign and swap formulas.

Fix any $|r|\le1$ and $N\ge0$. The sine terms after degree $2N+1$ have first
omitted magnitude $|r|^{2N+3}/(2N+3)!$ and each later ratio is at most
$|r|^2/((2N+4)(2N+5))<1$. Summing this geometric majorant gives $T_s$. The
cosine terms after degree $2N$ have first omitted magnitude
$|r|^{2N+2}/(2N+2)!$ and ratio at most $|r|^2/((2N+3)(2N+4))<1$, giving
$T_c$.

Let $f$ be a real function that is $n+1$ times continuously differentiable on
an open interval containing the finite real interval $X=[a,b]$. Here
$n\ge0$ is an integer, and continuous differentiability means that the
derivatives through order $n+1$ exist there and are continuous. Let $c\in X$
be a dyadic point. Put
$$
P_n(t)=\sum_{j=0}^n\frac{f^{(j)}(c)}{j!}(t-c)^j.
$$
Supply dyadic intervals $C_j$ containing $f^{(j)}(c)/j!$ for $0\le j\le n$
and a dyadic interval $D$ containing $f^{(n+1)}(X)$. Put
$M=\max(|\inf D|,|\sup D|)$ and
$R=\max(|a-c|,|b-c|)$. The **centered Taylor-model enclosure** is
$$
\mathcal T_n(f,X,c,(C_j)_{j=0}^n,D)
=\sum_{j=0}^n C_j(X-c)^j+
\left[-\frac{M R^{n+1}}{(n+1)!},\frac{M R^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}\right],
$$
where products, powers, sums, and the final sum are evaluated by
outward-rounded interval operations. The first term carries input variation
through the polynomial; the symmetric second interval is the explicit
derivative-based remainder. If a required coefficient or derivative
enclosure is unavailable, no Taylor-model certificate is returned.

Let $n\ge0$, let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an
open interval containing the segment between $c$ and $x$, and put
$$
P_n(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n\frac{f^{(j)}(c)}{j!}(x-c)^j.
$$
Then
$$
f(x)-P_n(x)=\frac1{n!}\int_c^x f^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n\,dt.
$$
If $M\ge0$ and $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ between $c$ and $x$, then
$$
|f(x)-P_n(x)|\le\frac{M|x-c|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}.
$$
The formula and bound include $x=c$ and oriented endpoints.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

derivations.claim:
Fix $x\in X$. If $x=c$, the polynomial already equals $f(c)$ and the
remainder is zero. Otherwise the segment from $c$ to $x$ lies in $X$, so [L1]
places $f^{(n+1)}$ there in $D$ and gives $|f^{(n+1)}|\le M$; also
$|x-c|\le R$. The Taylor integral remainder bound [L2] is therefore at most
$M R^{n+1}/(n+1)!$.

For every $x\in X$, [L1] puts each exact coefficient of $P_n(x)$ inside
the corresponding $C_j$, so the polynomial interval evaluation contains
$P_n(x)$ by [L3]. The remainder from step 1.1 lies in the symmetric interval
used in $\mathcal T_n$. Thus $f(x)$ lies in the exact sum, and outward
evaluation preserves that inclusion by [L3]. Since $x$ was arbitrary, the
whole range $f(X)$ is enclosed.
