Input: a finite, well-formed, typed expression DAG with one or more designated
output nodes; finite real interval or complex rectangle assignments for its
input nodes; exact dyadic constants or constants supplied with certified
enclosing intervals/rectangles; a finite dyadic format $(p,e_{\min},e_{\max})$
with $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$; and an integer truncation index
$N\ge1$. Input interval endpoints and supplied constant enclosures use this
format. All constants, including every Machin enclosure of $\pi$, use the
same fixed $N$ and format throughout a call. Real nodes support input and
constant nodes and the operations $+,-,\times,\div,\sqrt{\phantom{x}},
\exp,\ln,\arctan,\sin,\cos,\tan$. Complex nodes support input and constant
nodes and $+,-,\times,\div,\exp,\operatorname{Log}$. Each operation has
homogeneous real or complex inputs of its stated type; no implicit conversion
between real and complex nodes is performed. Unsupported node types, arities,
or type combinations return `inconclusive` with the offending node.

Output: a finite interval/rectangle enclosure for every designated output
node, or one of `empty`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `split-domain`, `overflow`,
or `inconclusive` with the node and unresolved domain piece. If any supplied
input is `empty`, return `empty`. No value from a system `libm` routine is
treated as a certified endpoint. Each DAG node is evaluated once; shared nodes
reuse their interval/rectangle enclosure and do not preserve correlations
between distinct paths.

1. Check that node identifiers are unique, all references resolve, every
designated output is a node, and the supported node types and arities above
hold. Use each supplied input enclosure as its node value. For an exact real
dyadic constant $c$, use $[\operatorname{rd}(c),\operatorname{ru}(c)]$ in the
selected format. For an exact complex dyadic constant, do this to each
coordinate. A finite subnormal endpoint remains a valid endpoint; if a
coordinate conversion overflows, return `overflow` with that constant node.
Use a supplied certified constant enclosure as given. Construct a topological
order by repeatedly removing a node whose
predecessors have already been removed, breaking ties by lexicographically
smallest node identifier. If no such node exists before all nodes are ordered,
return `inconclusive` with a node in the cycle. Evaluate nodes in this order
and store each finite enclosure for its successors. Arithmetic nodes use
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]; if an operation returns
a non-finite status, propagate it immediately with its node and unresolved
piece. For $\sqrt{X}$ require $X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and for $\ln X$ require
$X\subseteq(0,\infty)$; otherwise return `domain-error` rather than silently
discarding points.

2. For a real exponential node, set $s=\max(0,e_{\max}+2)$ using the format
in [[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. Since
$N_{\max}<2^{e_{\max}+1}$, exact comparison gives $N_{\max}/2^s<1/2$. For
its input interval $X$, evaluate the degree-$N$ exponential polynomial on
$U=X/2^s$ by interval arithmetic and add the symmetric tail from
[[lem-range-reduced-exp-log-and-arctan-series-enclosures]], using
$\max_{u\in U}|u|$. Square the resulting interval $s$ times. If its lower
endpoint is not positive or an endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or
`overflow` with the node and input interval.

For a real logarithm node, first require $X\subseteq(0,\infty)$. List all
integers $j$ for which $X_j=X\cap[2^j,2^{j+1}]$ is nonempty; exact endpoint
comparisons find this finite list because $X$ has positive finite endpoints.
On each piece set $Y=2^{-j}X_j\subseteq[1,2]$ and $V=(Y-1)/(Y+1)$, evaluate
the positive logarithm series on $V$ with its tail determined by $\max|V|$,
and form $j\ln2+\ln Y$ by outward arithmetic. Compute the fixed enclosure for
$\ln2$ once by the same series and tail at $y=2$, hence $v=1/3$, and reuse it
in every bin. If any piece cannot be evaluated finitely, propagate its status
and that piece. Otherwise take the interval hull of all piece enclosures as
the node enclosure.

3. Partition a real arctangent input at the fixed breakpoints
$-3,-1/2,1/2,3$ into nonempty closed pieces, allowing shared endpoints.
On pieces in $[-1/2,1/2]$, evaluate its alternating power series. For positive
pieces in $[1/2,1]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4-\arctan((1-t)/(1+t))$; in $[1,3]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4+\arctan((t-1)/(t+1))$; for $t>3$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/2-\arctan(1/t)$. Evaluate negative pieces by odd symmetry.
Enclose $\pi$ using Machin's identity and the alternating series at $1/5$ and
$1/239$, forming rational partial sums and tail endpoints exactly before
final outward conversion. If every piece is finite, take the interval hull of
all piece enclosures. If any branch test or piece is unresolved, return its
non-finite status with that piece and do not use a partial hull.

4. For each sine or cosine node, first compute one outward Machin interval
$P_N$ for $\pi$ using the same $N$ and format, combining the rational series
endpoints exactly before final outward conversion. If $P_N$ is non-finite or
its lower endpoint is not positive, return `inconclusive`. For finite input
$X=[a,b]$, put $M_X=\max(|a|,|b|)$, $p_-:=\inf(P_N)>0$, and
$K=\lceil2M_X/p_-\rceil+1$, with the ceiling computed by exact rational
comparisons. If the width of $X$ is at least $2\sup(P_N)$, return
$[-1,1]$. Otherwise examine the finite candidate list $k=-K,\ldots,K$ for
the canonical cells $[k\pi/2-\pi/4,k\pi/2+\pi/4]$. For each candidate form
the exact rational interval enclosure
$C_k=kP_N/2+[-1/4,1/4]P_N$ of its canonical cell. For $k>K$, the exact
left endpoint $(2k-1)\pi/4$ of cell $k$ is at least
$(2k-1)p_-/4>M_X$; for $k<-K$, its exact right endpoint
$-(2|k|-1)\pi/4$ is at most $-(2|k|-1)p_-/4<-M_X$. Thus no omitted exact
cell can intersect $X$. Include each candidate whose $C_k$ intersects $X$;
exclude only candidates whose intersection is empty by exact comparison. Let
$X_k$ be the exact interval hull of $X\cap C_k$, without rounding these
endpoints, and form the residual enclosure $R_k=X_k-kP_N/2$. Certify
$R_k\subseteq[-1,1]$, evaluate the sine polynomial through degree $2N+1$ or
the cosine polynomial through degree $2N$, and add the corresponding explicit
geometric tail from [[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]]
by exact rational interval arithmetic. Map each enclosure by the appropriate
quarter-period sign or coordinate swap and intersect it with $[-1,1]$.
Round the final endpoints outward and take the hull over every included cell.
If no candidate is included, a cell cannot be certified in the reduced
interval, or any candidate endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or
`overflow` with the cell; never omit that piece from a finite hull.

For tangent, partition the input into the canonical pieces used for sine and
cosine. Divide the sine enclosure by the cosine enclosure only when the latter
excludes zero. If a piece contains a certified cosine zero, return
`split-domain` with that piece; if the enclosure includes zero but no pole is
certified, return `inconclusive`. Take the interval hull of tangent enclosures
only when every piece is finite.

5. For complex exponential on $X+iY$, evaluate real $\exp(X)$, $\cos(Y)$,
and $\sin(Y)$ and combine their enclosures by rectangle operations. For
principal $\operatorname{Log}$, first require a rectangle excluding zero and
every point of the negative real branch cut; otherwise return `domain-error`.
Compute an outward Machin interval $P_N$ for $\pi$ using this call's $N$ and
format; if it is non-finite or its lower endpoint is not positive, return
`inconclusive`.
Split each coordinate interval into its nonempty strictly negative and
strictly positive portions, plus the singleton $\{0\}$ when it contains zero.
Use the closures of the strictly signed portions as interval enclosures; form
their Cartesian products for the quadrant pieces, and handle products with an
axis singleton separately. Omit empty pieces. These finitely many pieces
cover the rectangle, with quadrant closures allowed to overlap their axis
pieces. On a quadrant where the denominator interval excludes zero, use
$$
\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\ y>0,\\
-\arctan((-y)/x),&x>0,\ y<0,\\
\pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0.
\end{cases}
$$
Write this call's fixed interval as $P_N=[p_-,p_+]$ and form the exact
dyadic sector intervals
$$
S_{\rm I}=[0,p_+/2],\qquad S_{\rm II}=[p_-/2,p_+],\qquad
S_{\rm III}=[-p_+,-p_-/2],\qquad S_{\rm IV}=[-p_+/2,0].
$$
For every ratio-based quadrant piece, obtain its finite real arctangent
enclosure by the real rules above; propagate any non-finite result. Form the
full argument interval $A$ in the displayed quadrant formula by exact
rational endpoint arithmetic, using this same $P_N$ for each occurrence of
$\pi$. Before final outward conversion or hull formation, replace $A$ by
$J=A\cap S_q$, where $q$ is that piece's quadrant. Compute the intersection
by exact endpoint maxima and minima. If it is empty, return `inconclusive`
with the piece and status `empty-argument-intersection`; do not omit the
piece. If the denominator interval has a zero endpoint, use $J=S_q$
instead of a ratio formula.

For an interval $J=[a,b]$ produced by either branch, apply the same final
conversion $H(J)=[\operatorname{rd}(a),\operatorname{ru}(b)]$ in the selected
format. Perform this conversion after intersection for a ratio branch and
after selecting $S_q$ for a coarse branch. Finite subnormal endpoints are
accepted; an overflow returns `overflow` with the piece. On the positive
imaginary axis use $H(P_N/2)$, on the negative imaginary axis use
$H(-P_N/2)$, and on the positive real axis use $H([0,0])$. The initial domain
check excludes the origin and negative real axis, so these are all remaining
axis cases.

On each piece enclose $\ln\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}$ using the real operations and
evaluator, and combine it with the converted argument interval into a
rectangle. If every piece is finite, take the coordinatewise hull of all
piece rectangles. If any piece, conversion or branch is unresolved, return
its status and piece without forming a partial hull.

6. Each displayed series uses indices $0,\ldots,N$, hence at most $N+1$
terms; the exponential step performs exactly $s$ interval squarings. The
logarithm bin list, arctangent partition, and sine/cosine candidate list are
finite and fixed by the input interval and call parameters. All successful
piece enclosures at a node are combined by their interval or rectangle hull;
failure of any required piece returns its status rather than a hull of only
the remaining pieces. No adaptive subdivision or precision refinement is
hidden inside this evaluator.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

For $|u|\le1/2$ and integer $N\ge1$, set
$E_N(u)=\sum_{k=0}^N u^k/k!$ and
$R_E=|u|^{N+1}/((N+1)!(1-|u|/(N+2)))$. Then
$\exp(u)\in[E_N(u)-R_E,E_N(u)+R_E]$, and the lower endpoint is positive.
For $y\in[1,2]$, put $v=(y-1)/(y+1)$ and
$L_N(v)=2\sum_{k=0}^N v^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$. Then
$$
\left|\ln y-L_N(v)\right|\le
\frac{2|v|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)(1-v^2)}.
$$
For every integer $j$ and $y>0$, the natural logarithm also satisfies
$\ln(2^j y)=j\ln2+\ln y$.
For $|t|\le1/2$, set $A_N(t)=\sum_{k=0}^N(-1)^kt^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$. Then
$$
\left|\arctan t-A_N(t)\right|\le
\frac{|t|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)(1-t^2)}.
$$

The power-series sine and cosine satisfy the addition identities and
$\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$. For $A(t)=\arctan t$ from
[[def-real-elementary-functions-and-domains]],
$$
\sin(A(t))=t\cos(A(t)),\qquad \cos(A(t))>0,
$$
so $A(t)$ is the inverse tangent with values in $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ when
$\pi=4A(1)$. It is odd; for $u,v\ge0$ with $uv<1$,
$A(u)+A(v)=A((u+v)/(1-uv))$; and for $t>0$,
$A(t)=\pi/2-A(1/t)$. In particular $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ and
$\cos(\pi/2)=0$. Also,
$$
\pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239).
$$
For every real $x$ there is an integer $k$ and $r=x-k\pi/2$ with
$|r|\le\pi/4$; the sine and cosine of $x$ are obtained from those of $r$ by
the quarter-period identities. For every real $r$ with $|r|\le1$ and every
$N\ge0$, truncating sine
through degree $2N+1$ and cosine through degree $2N$ gives absolute tail bounds
$$
T_s=\frac{|r|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)!(1-|r|^2/((2N+4)(2N+5)))}
$$
and
$$
T_c=\frac{|r|^{2N+2}}{(2N+2)!(1-|r|^2/((2N+3)(2N+4)))}.
$$

Let $\sum_{n\ge0}a_n=A$ and $\sum_{n\ge0}b_n=B$ be absolutely convergent
real series. Define
$$
c_n=\sum_{j=0}^n a_jb_{n-j}.
$$
Then $\sum_{n\ge0}c_n$ converges absolutely and has sum $AB$. Thus the
product of the two series can be grouped by total degree without changing
its sum.

derivations.claim:
For an exponential input interval, the fixed scale puts every scaled point
in $[-1/2,1/2]$. The point bound [L3] with $|u|$ replaced by the interval's
largest absolute endpoint gives a uniform tail enclosure. The truncated
polynomial interval-evaluates every point by [L2]. The tail radius increases
with the largest absolute input, and each repeated interval square preserves
inclusion by [L2]. To justify the scaling identity, put $d=2^s$. Repeated
applications of [L6] to the absolutely convergent series for $\exp u$ show
that the coefficient of $u^k$ in $(\exp u)^d$ is
$$
\sum_{n_1+\cdots+n_d=k}\frac1{n_1!\cdots n_d!}
=\frac{d^k}{k!},
$$
where the equality is the multinomial theorem. Thus $(\exp u)^d=\exp(du)$;
set $u=x/d$. Each interval squaring preserves the resulting enclosure by
[L2].

On each positive logarithm bin, every $y$ maps to
$v=(y-1)/(y+1)\in[0,1/3]$. The interval series and uniform tail from [L3]
contain $\ln y$; [L3] also proves the exact logarithm scaling identity used by
the algorithm. Each interval transform and sum preserves inclusion by [L2].
The fixed bin partition ensures that enlarging the input only enlarges the
intersection with each bin, so its interval-series enclosure and the final
hull also enlarge. The arctangent transformations follow from [L5]; on each
fixed branch the rational interval maps and fixed series are isotone, and the
tail radius is nondecreasing in the largest absolute transformed endpoint.

The outward cell interval built from $P_N$ contains each exact canonical
cell, since $\pi\in P_N$; thus its intersection hull $X_k$ contains every
input point assigned to that cell, and $X_k-kP_N/2$ contains the exact
residual $r=x-k\pi/2$. The algorithm certifies this residual inside the
Taylor range. By [L4], exact sine and cosine values are the stated signed
swaps of $\sin r$ and $\cos r$. The polynomial interval
evaluation contains each truncated value by [L2], and adding the symmetric
tail interval from [L4] contains the omitted remainder. Taking the hull over
all intersected cells therefore contains the full range. If the interval
width is at least $2\pi$, [L4] gives the safe range $[-1,1]$. For nested
inputs, each fixed canonical cell intersection enlarges and its fixed-term
interval evaluation is isotone by [L2]; the hull is therefore nested on the reduced branch. Exact rational interval
polynomial and tail operations are inclusion-isotone, and the final directed
endpoint conversions are nondecreasing. Intersecting with $[-1,1]$ preserves
containment and nesting, and ensures that the wide-input $[-1,1]$ return
contains every narrower finite result.

Tangent is defined only where cosine is nonzero. On a piece whose cosine
enclosure excludes zero, division is sound by [L2] and contains every
$\sin x/\cos x$. If cosine may vanish, the algorithm returns a split or
non-finite status, so no unsound finite value is reported. The same argument
applies to square root using the bisection supplier in [L2].

Evaluate the finite expression DAG in topological order. Every primitive
node encloses its exact value by steps 1.1–2.2; induction over the finite
node order then encloses every exact intermediate and every requested output
range. Each primitive's canonical partition and fixed truncation are nested
on common finite branches, so the same induction preserves inclusion for
nested inputs evaluated with the same format and truncation index.

citations.quote:
Every integral below is the oriented Riemann integral constructed from upper
and lower Darboux sums in
[[lem-continuous-functions-riemann-integrable]]. It exists for each displayed
continuous integrand on the finite interval between its endpoints, is additive
in intervals, reverses sign when the endpoints are reversed, is monotone in
the integrand, and satisfies
$|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt|\le|b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|$.
These properties also
give constant comparison bounds and the average-value difference quotient
used to differentiate the integral-defined functions.

The exponential is $\exp(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}x^k/k!$ for $x\in\mathbb R$.
The sine and cosine are the everywhere-convergent power series
$\sin x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$ and
$\cos x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k}/(2k)!$. Define
$\arctan x=\int_0^x dt/(1+t^2)$ and set $\pi=4\arctan1$. The natural
logarithm $\ln$ is defined on $(0,\infty)$ by $\ln x=\int_1^x dt/t$.

The square root is the unique nonnegative real $y$ with $y^2=x$ for $x\ge0$;
existence and uniqueness follow from
[[lem-nonnegative-square-root-exists-and-unique]]. The tangent is
$\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ on the set where $\cos x\ne0$.

For complex $z=x+iy$, the modulus $|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is defined in
[[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]]. The complex exponential is
$\exp(x+iy)=\exp(x)(\cos y+i\sin y)$. The principal complex logarithm is
$\operatorname{Log}(z)=\ln|z|+i\operatorname{Arg}(z)$ on
$\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$. For $z=x+iy$ in this domain, define
$$
\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\\
\pi/2,&x=0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi/2,&x=0,\ y<0,\\
\pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0.
\end{cases}
$$
The excluded negative real axis is the remaining case $x<0,y=0$; zero is
also excluded.

These are point functions. An interval extension must separately enclose their
exact ranges, test the stated domains, and return a non-finite status when its
finite budget cannot certify a reduction or endpoint.

Every finite interval returned for a requested real output node by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] on an input interval in the
domain of $\exp$, $\ln$, $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$, $\arctan$, $\sin$, $\cos$, or
$\tan$ contains the exact range of the corresponding function on that
interval. For the same typed DAG and designated real output node, if all
input intervals are nested coordinatewise, all constant enclosures are fixed,
and both calls use the same finite dyadic format and truncation index $N$,
then, whenever both calls return finite enclosures, the canonical branch-cell
and fixed-term construction makes the smaller domain's computed enclosure a
subset of the larger one's.
An unresolved fixed branch, pole, invalid domain or overflow returns its
stated non-finite status and carries no finite success claim.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

The power-series sine and cosine satisfy the addition identities and
$\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$. For $A(t)=\arctan t$ from
[[def-real-elementary-functions-and-domains]],
$$
\sin(A(t))=t\cos(A(t)),\qquad \cos(A(t))>0,
$$
so $A(t)$ is the inverse tangent with values in $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ when
$\pi=4A(1)$. It is odd; for $u,v\ge0$ with $uv<1$,
$A(u)+A(v)=A((u+v)/(1-uv))$; and for $t>0$,
$A(t)=\pi/2-A(1/t)$. In particular $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ and
$\cos(\pi/2)=0$. Also,
$$
\pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239).
$$
For every real $x$ there is an integer $k$ and $r=x-k\pi/2$ with
$|r|\le\pi/4$; the sine and cosine of $x$ are obtained from those of $r$ by
the quarter-period identities. For every real $r$ with $|r|\le1$ and every
$N\ge0$, truncating sine
through degree $2N+1$ and cosine through degree $2N$ gives absolute tail bounds
$$
T_s=\frac{|r|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)!(1-|r|^2/((2N+4)(2N+5)))}
$$
and
$$
T_c=\frac{|r|^{2N+2}}{(2N+2)!(1-|r|^2/((2N+3)(2N+4)))}.
$$

derivations.claim: Let $Z=X+iY$ be a rectangle. By [L1], its exact exponential has real and imaginary parts $\exp(X)\cos(Y)$ and $\exp(X)\sin(Y)$. The real enclosures in [L2] contain these three ranges, and rectangle multiplication and addition preserve their exact component images by [L3]. Therefore the resulting rectangle contains $\exp(Z)$.

For a principal-log branch, subdivide $Z$ into rectangles of fixed signs of the real and imaginary coordinates, with separate pieces on the coordinate axes. In a nonzero quadrant, $|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is enclosed by [L2]–[L3], hence $\ln|z|$ is enclosed by [L2]. The quotient is enclosed by [L3] and arctangent by [L2]. In quadrant I use $\arctan(y/x)$; in quadrant IV use $-\arctan((-y)/x)$; in quadrant II use $\pi-\arctan(y/(-x))$; and in quadrant III use $-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x))$. From [L4] and $\sin^2(A(t))+\cos^2(A(t))=1$, positivity of $\cos(A(t))$ gives $\cos(A(t))=1/\sqrt{1+t^2}$ and $\sin(A(t))=t/\sqrt{1+t^2}$ for $t>0$. Substituting $t=y/x$ in quadrant I gives $(\cos\operatorname{Arg}z,\sin\operatorname{Arg}z)=(x/|z|,y/|z|)$. In quadrant IV, evenness/oddness from [L1] gives the same coordinate identity with $y<0$. The addition identities shift the angle in quadrant II by $\pi-A(t)$, reversing only the cosine sign, and in quadrant III by $-\pi+A(t)$, reversing both signs; substitution of the positive coordinate ratios again gives $(x/|z|,y/|z|)$. The range of $A$ in [L4] places these angles in the respective subintervals of $(-\pi,\pi)$, so they are the principal arguments. On the admissible closure of quadrant I the argument lies in $[0,\pi/2]$; on quadrants II, III and IV it lies respectively in $[\pi/2,\pi]$, $[-\pi,-\pi/2]$ and $[-\pi/2,0]$. Since $p_-\le\pi\le p_+$ and $p_->0$, these sets are contained respectively in the algorithm's fixed sectors $S_{\rm I},S_{\rm II},S_{\rm III},S_{\rm IV}$. A finite raw ratio-based argument interval contains each exact argument by [L2]–[L3], so intersecting it with its sector retains every exact argument. Each nonempty quadrant piece has an actual point and hence an argument in that intersection; an empty intersection cannot be used for a success claim and is explicitly rejected. When the denominator reaches zero, the sector alone is a sound enclosure. The common final outward conversion $H$ preserves these containments; an overflow gives no finite claim. On the positive real axis the exact argument is zero, and on the positive and negative imaginary axes it is respectively $\pi/2$ and $-\pi/2$. Thus $H([0,0])$, $H(P_N/2)$ and $H(-P_N/2)$ enclose the axis values. The initial domain test excludes the origin and negative real axis. The strict-sign pieces, their closures and these axis pieces therefore cover every admissible point. The radial enclosure established above and the converted argument enclosure jointly contain its principal logarithm; taking the coordinatewise hull over every finite piece contains the full image. Any failed piece prevents a finite hull return.

Fix the DAG, designated output, constant enclosures, format and $N$ in the Statement, so both calls use the same $P_N$, sectors and conversion $H$. Every nonempty strict-sign piece of a smaller input rectangle, after closure, is contained in the corresponding piece of the larger rectangle. Every axis piece likewise has a corresponding containing axis piece, with the same argument interval. The radial expression $\ln\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}$ preserves inclusion on these nested pieces by [L2]–[L3]. For a quadrant whose denominator excludes zero in both calls, outward quotients and the fixed real arctangent evaluator give nested finite raw argument intervals $A\subseteq A'$ by [L2]–[L3]. Exact translations by the same $P_N$ and sign changes in the quadrant formulas preserve this inclusion. Intersection with the same sector gives $A\cap S_q\subseteq A'\cap S_q$. The greatest-lower and least-upper rounding definitions make $H$ inclusion-preserving, hence the converted argument intervals are nested as well. If enlargement changes a ratio branch to a zero-denominator coarse branch, the smaller preconversion interval is $A\cap S_q\subseteq S_q$, and therefore $H(A\cap S_q)\subseteq H(S_q)$. If both branches are coarse they use the same $H(S_q)$. The reverse change under enlargement is impossible: a containing denominator interval cannot exclude zero when the smaller one contains it. These cases exhaust quadrant branch transitions. Axis pieces remain present under enlargement and use the identical converted axis intervals, so their corresponding rectangles are nested too. Taking coordinatewise hulls preserves the inclusions for all corresponding pieces, including any additional pieces in the larger call. Complex exponential preserves inclusion through its fixed real component evaluations and rectangle operations in step 1.1. Together with [L2]–[L3], these primitive results give soundness and inclusion for the same finite typed DAG by induction in its prescribed topological order; fixed input-independent constants start the induction, and every designated output inherits it. A rectangle meeting zero or the negative real branch cut at a Log node returns `domain-error`; a failed piece, empty argument intersection or failed conversion returns its specified non-finite status. Such a branch gives no finite enclosure or nesting claim.

Input: a finite, well-formed, typed expression DAG with exactly one designated
output node, an interval/rectangle assignment box $X$ for its input nodes, a
dyadic requested width $\varepsilon>0$, finite-format parameters
$(p,e_{\min},e_{\max})$ with $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$, series
truncation index $N\ge1$, and integer total box-split budget $B\ge0$.
The supported node types, input assignments, exact dyadic constants and
supplied certified constant enclosures satisfy the admissibility conditions
of [[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]]. In particular, every input
endpoint and every endpoint of a supplied constant enclosure belongs to the
selected finite representable set $\mathbb F$. Truth of a supplied constant's
certified inclusion is a mathematical input promise, not something inferred
from its endpoints. Exact dyadic constants need not themselves be
representable; their conversion and any overflow remain the evaluator's task.

Use the following exact membership procedure for each supplied finite
endpoint and for every proposed split midpoint. Put
$\eta=2^{e_{\min}-p+1}$. Compare the value with zero, then enumerate both
signs of $k\eta$ for $k=1,\ldots,2^{p-1}-1$, and both signs of
$k2^{e-p+1}$ for $e=e_{\min},\ldots,e_{\max}$ and
$k=2^{p-1},\ldots,2^p-1$, stopping at a match. If the finite enumeration
ends without a match, report `not-in-format`. Every comparison is an exact
dyadic equality test. This is the representable set of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]], including zero
and subnormals. Before initializing the queue, check the integer/format
conditions and the finite input and supplied-constant endpoint memberships;
malformed data or a failed membership returns `inconclusive` with the
identifying input status, without an evaluator call. An empty input returns
`empty` as in the elementary evaluator.

Keep the DAG, designated output, constant enclosures, format and $N$ fixed.
Set a shared counter $R:=B$ and a queue containing $X$. Process the queue in
first-in, first-out order. For each box $Q$, evaluate the DAG by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] with the same format and $N$,
requesting only the designated output node's enclosure. The hull of no
completed leaves is recorded as `empty`.

- If evaluation returns a non-finite status, return that status and the exact
  unresolved box $Q$; it is not a tolerance certificate.
- If it returns a finite enclosure $I$ with width at most $\varepsilon$, save
  $I$ as a completed leaf enclosure.
- If it returns a finite enclosure wider than $\varepsilon$ and $R=0$, return
  `inconclusive` with the completed-leaf hull, $Q$, and the unmet width test.
- If it returns a finite enclosure wider than $\varepsilon$ and $R>0$, select
  a widest nondegenerate input coordinate (breaking ties by the first
  coordinate in the input order). If there is no such coordinate, return
  `inconclusive` with the completed-leaf hull, the unresolved parent $Q$,
  the remaining queue, and status `no-splittable-coordinate` with the unmet
  width test. Otherwise compute its midpoint $m$ by exact dyadic arithmetic
  and apply the membership procedure above in the actual selected format.
  If it reports `not-in-format`, return `inconclusive` with the completed-leaf
  hull, the unresolved parent $Q$, the remaining queue, and status
  `midpoint-not-in-format`, identifying the coordinate and exact midpoint.
  Do not enqueue either child or call the evaluator on it in this case.
  If $m\in\mathbb F$, split that coordinate into the two closed halves at
  $m$, decrement $R$ by one, and append both children to the queue.

When the queue is empty, take the hull $J$ of all completed leaf enclosures.
Return `certified(J,X)` only if $\operatorname{width}(J)\le\varepsilon$;
otherwise return `inconclusive(J,X)` and state that the global width test
failed. Each split covers its parent because the two closed halves overlap at
the midpoint and their union is the parent coordinate interval. The shared
counter makes $B$ a total split limit across the full computation.

Every finite interval returned for a requested real output node by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] on an input interval in the
domain of $\exp$, $\ln$, $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$, $\arctan$, $\sin$, $\cos$, or
$\tan$ contains the exact range of the corresponding function on that
interval. For the same typed DAG and designated real output node, if all
input intervals are nested coordinatewise, all constant enclosures are fixed,
and both calls use the same finite dyadic format and truncation index $N$,
then, whenever both calls return finite enclosures, the canonical branch-cell
and fixed-term construction makes the smaller domain's computed enclosure a
subset of the larger one's.
An unresolved fixed branch, pole, invalid domain or overflow returns its
stated non-finite status and carries no finite success claim.

For any finite complex rectangle on which the principal branch is defined,
every finite output for a requested complex node of
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] for $\exp$ or
$\operatorname{Log}$ contains the exact image. For the same typed DAG and
designated complex output node, nested input rectangles on the same admissible
branch, fixed constant enclosures, and the same finite dyadic format and
truncation index give nested finite enclosures whenever both calls return
finite results. Rectangles meeting zero, the negative real
branch cut, or an unresolved quadrant return the declared domain or
inconclusive status.

derivations.claim: The initial admission checks terminate: the format's subnormal index range, exponent range and significand ranges are finite, and each equality comparison of exact dyadics is decided by clearing powers of two and comparing integers. Their enumeration is exactly the selected representable set, so a passing endpoint test establishes membership, including for zero and subnormals. Invalid initial data stop before an evaluator call. For admitted data, every endpoint of the initial box belongs to that format. Inductively, a split enqueues children only after the exact midpoint passes the same membership test; all other endpoints are inherited from the parent. The DAG, output, constants, format and $N$ are unchanged. Hence every queued box satisfies the elementary evaluator's input conditions. Each such call terminates through its finite DAG, finite series, finite bisection and finite bin/cell/quadrant lists, or returns a specified failure. The membership guard also terminates and can stop immediately with `inconclusive`. There are at most $B$ admitted splits and therefore at most $2B+1$ processed boxes. Thus the entire procedure terminates, including every guard-stop branch.

Before a box is processed, the completed leaf boxes together with the queued boxes cover $X$. Removing a current box preserves this cover when that box is counted as the current unresolved parent. Completing it transfers it to the completed leaves; an admitted split replaces it by two closed children whose union is the parent by [L1]. A failed midpoint test retains the parent as unresolved and therefore discards no part of the cover. This proves the coverage invariant by induction. By step 1.1, each completed leaf was evaluated on admissible input, so its finite enclosure contains its exact range by [L2] or [L3]. If the queue empties without an early return, all covering leaves are completed; their enclosure hull therefore contains the exact range on all of $X$. On an early return, the completed-leaf hull is not asserted to cover the unresolved parent or remaining queue.

A `certified` return occurs only after the queue is empty without an admission, evaluator, split-guard or budget stop, and after the completed-leaf hull passes the final global width test. Step 2.1 then proves enclosure of the whole range, and the exact width comparison proves the requested tolerance. A failed midpoint membership instead returns `inconclusive` with the completed-leaf hull, unresolved parent, remaining queue and actual guard status; that partial hull is not a full-domain certificate. The other non-finite, exhausted-budget, unsplittable-coordinate and failed global-width branches likewise make no tolerance-success claim. Thus the finite guard preserves the stated certified-range, coverage and failure conclusions.

For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$; the denominator interval is strictly positive because at
least one coordinate interval excludes zero. Division multiplies by this
reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

derivations.claim:
For any $M>0$, choose a real $t>M+1$, set $x=1$ and $y=1/t$. Then
$x\in[1,2]$, $y\in(0,1]\subset Y$, and $x/y=t>M$. Replacing $y$ by $-1/t$
gives a quotient $-t<-M$. Thus the quotient set is unbounded in both
directions.

A finite interval has finite lower and upper endpoints, so choose $M$ larger
than their absolute values in step 1.1; the resulting exact quotient lies
outside that interval, contradicting the required inclusion [L2]. The branch
in [L1] avoids that contradiction by declining a finite hull.

For $|u|\le1/2$ and integer $N\ge1$, set
$E_N(u)=\sum_{k=0}^N u^k/k!$ and
$R_E=|u|^{N+1}/((N+1)!(1-|u|/(N+2)))$. Then
$\exp(u)\in[E_N(u)-R_E,E_N(u)+R_E]$, and the lower endpoint is positive.
For $y\in[1,2]$, put $v=(y-1)/(y+1)$ and
$L_N(v)=2\sum_{k=0}^N v^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$. Then
$$
\left|\ln y-L_N(v)\right|\le
\frac{2|v|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)(1-v^2)}.
$$
For every integer $j$ and $y>0$, the natural logarithm also satisfies
$\ln(2^j y)=j\ln2+\ln y$.
For $|t|\le1/2$, set $A_N(t)=\sum_{k=0}^N(-1)^kt^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$. Then
$$
\left|\arctan t-A_N(t)\right|\le
\frac{|t|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)(1-t^2)}.
$$

The power-series sine and cosine satisfy the addition identities and
$\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$. For $A(t)=\arctan t$ from
[[def-real-elementary-functions-and-domains]],
$$
\sin(A(t))=t\cos(A(t)),\qquad \cos(A(t))>0,
$$
so $A(t)$ is the inverse tangent with values in $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ when
$\pi=4A(1)$. It is odd; for $u,v\ge0$ with $uv<1$,
$A(u)+A(v)=A((u+v)/(1-uv))$; and for $t>0$,
$A(t)=\pi/2-A(1/t)$. In particular $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ and
$\cos(\pi/2)=0$. Also,
$$
\pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239).
$$
For every real $x$ there is an integer $k$ and $r=x-k\pi/2$ with
$|r|\le\pi/4$; the sine and cosine of $x$ are obtained from those of $r$ by
the quarter-period identities. For every real $r$ with $|r|\le1$ and every
$N\ge0$, truncating sine
through degree $2N+1$ and cosine through degree $2N$ gives absolute tail bounds
$$
T_s=\frac{|r|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)!(1-|r|^2/((2N+4)(2N+5)))}
$$
and
$$
T_c=\frac{|r|^{2N+2}}{(2N+2)!(1-|r|^2/((2N+3)(2N+4)))}.
$$

For every finite input DAG and finite total split budget $B$, the algorithm
[[alg-budgeted-validated-range-evaluation]] terminates. If it returns
`certified(I,X)`, then $I$ contains the exact function range on all of $X$ and
has width at most the requested $\varepsilon$. If it returns `empty`,
`entire`, `inconclusive`, domain error, split-domain, or overflow, it makes no
unconditional tolerance-success claim.

Let $g:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $a<b$, in a Dedekind-complete
ordered field. For a partition $P=(a=x_0<\cdots<x_m=b)$ put
$$
U(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^m \left(\max_{t\in[x_{i-1},x_i]}g(t)\right)(x_i-x_{i-1}),\qquad
L(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^m \left(\min_{t\in[x_{i-1},x_i]}g(t)\right)(x_i-x_{i-1}).
$$
The supremum of the lower sums equals the infimum of the upper sums. Define
$\int_a^b g$ to be this common value, set $\int_a^a g=0$, and set
$\int_b^a g=-\int_a^b g$. This oriented Riemann integral is additive over
intervals. Refining a partition increases its lower sum and decreases its
upper sum, and any two partitions have a common refinement. It satisfies
$$
\left|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt\right|
\le |b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|.
$$
If $a<b$ and constants $m,M$ satisfy $m\le g(t)\le M$ on $[a,b]$, then
$m(b-a)\le\int_a^b g\le M(b-a)$; reversing the endpoints reverses these
inequalities. The integral is monotone in its integrand: if continuous
$g\le h$ on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b g\le\int_a^b h$.
If $g$ is continuous on an open interval $J$ and $x_0\in J$, then
$G(x)=\int_{x_0}^x g(t)\,dt$ is defined for $x\in J$ and $G'(x)=g(x)$.

derivations.claim: Apply [L1] at $1/5$ and $1/239$ with $N=12$. The arctangent interval widths are at most twice the displayed tails; multiplying by $16$ and $4$ gives the two rational terms in the bound. By [L4], the integral gives $13/20\le\arctan1\le9/10<1$: its integrand is at least $4/5$ on $[0,1/2]$ and at least $1/2$ on $[1/2,1]$, while it is at most $1$ on the first half and at most $4/5$ on the second. Thus $13/5\le\pi\le18/5<4$. Before rounding, the Machin interval has width less than $2\cdot10^{-19}+10^{-30}$ by the tail estimates below, so its exact endpoints lie in $[5/2,37/10]$ using $13/5\le\pi\le18/5$. The directed conversions stay in that interval and therefore each add at most $2^{-126}$ to the width. For the first tail, $32(1/5)^{27}/(27(1-1/25))=800/(648\cdot5^{27})<2\cdot10^{-19}$, using $4000\cdot10^{18}<648\cdot5^{27}$. The second tail is less than $239^{-27}<16^{-27}=2^{-108}<10^{-30}$. Therefore exact rational comparison gives $W:=\operatorname{width}(P)<10^{-18}$ and $\pi\in P$.

Each $x\in X$ has form $x=2p$ with $p\in P$, so $|x-2\pi|=2|p-\pi|\le2W<2\cdot10^{-18}<\inf(P)/4\le\pi/4$; $\inf(P)\ge5/2$ by step 1.1. Thus $X$ lies inside the canonical $k=4$ cell. If $P=[p_-,p_+]$, the actual cell formula $C_k=kP/2+[-1/4,1/4]P$ gives $\sup C_3=7p_+/4$ and $\inf C_5=5p_-/2-p_+/4=9p_-/4-W/4$. Since $p_->2$ and $W<10^{-18}$, both $p_->7W$ and $p_->9W$ hold. Consequently $2p_- -\sup C_3=(p_--7W)/4>0$ and $\inf C_5-2p_+=(p_--9W)/4>0$. Thus $X=2P$ meets neither neighboring enclosure. All farther cells are separated as well by monotonicity of their endpoints in the integer cell index, while $C_4$ contains $X$. Hence the only included candidate is $k=4$. The interval residual computed by the evaluator is $R=X-4(P/2)=[-2W,2W]$, which contains each exact reduced argument and lies inside the certified Taylor range.

Put $r_0=2W<2\cdot10^{-18}$. Bound each odd Taylor term on $R=[-r_0,r_0]$ by the symmetric exact rational interval $[-r_0^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!,r_0^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!]$, sum these intervals exactly, and add the geometric tail before outward conversion. The polynomial interval has total width at most $2\sum_{k=0}^{12}r_0^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!\le2r_0/(1-r_0^2)<6\cdot10^{-18}$, since $r_0^2<1/3$ gives $(1-r_0^2)^{-1}<3/2$. Let $N\ge1$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. The **unnormalised (engineering) discrete Fourier transform** of $f$ is the function $X(f):\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ defined by

$$X_k(f):=\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}f([x]_N)\,e^{-2\pi ikx/N},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$

the sum being the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] over the representatives $[0]_N,\dots,[N-1]_N$ of the classes of $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[def-integers-modulo-n]]), with $e^z$ the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]]. Comparing with [[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]],

$$X_k(f)=\sqrt N\,(\mathcal F_Nf)(k),\qquad (\mathcal F_Nf)(k)=N^{-1/2}X_k(f),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$

where $\sqrt N=N^{1/2}$ is the rational power of [[def-rational-power]] and the two conversions are inverse to each other by $N^{1/2}N^{-1/2}=1$ ([[lem-rational-power-laws]]). So the two transforms determine each other, and the only difference between them is the constant $\sqrt N$.

**The transform is defined on classes and is $N$-periodic.** If $[x]_N=[x']_N$ then $x'=x+mN$ for some integer $m$ and $e^{-2\pi ikx'/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ikm}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$, so the summands depend only on classes; and $e^{-2\pi i(k+N)x/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ix}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$ for every integer $x$, both identities following from the addition law and $\exp(2\pi i\,\cdot)=1$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]). Hence $X(f)$ factors through $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ and $X_k(f)$ depends on $k$ only through its class.

**Inverse formulas.** The inversion theorem in its unitary form is the identity $f(x)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)e^{2\pi ikx/N}$ of [[thm-finite-fourier-inversion]]; substituting $(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)=N^{-1/2}X_k(f)$ and collecting $N^{-1/2}N^{-1/2}=N^{-1}$ ([[lem-rational-power-laws]]) gives the engineering form

$$f(x)=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X_k(f)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},\qquad x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z.$$

This is the convention in which the radix-two algorithm computes its output. The unitary transform is recovered by the single rescaling $N^{-1/2}=2^{-m/2}$ at length $N=2^m$. The correctness and complexity theorems refer to this unnormalised output; the convolution lemma is stated in the unitary convention.

Let $N\ge1$ and let $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ be the complex vector space of all functions $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ ([[def-function-space]], [[def-vector-space]]). For $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ define the **unitary discrete Fourier transform** $\mathcal F_Nf:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ by

$$(\mathcal F_Nf)(k):=N^{-1/2}\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}f([x]_N)\,e^{-2\pi ikx/N},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$

where $[x]_N$ is the class of the integer $x$ in $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[def-integers-modulo-n]], [[lem-congruence-is-an-equivalence-relation]]), $e^z=\exp z$ is the complex exponential ([[def-complex-exponential]]), and $N^{-1/2}$ is the rational power of the positive real $N$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]), read in $\mathbb C$ through the embedded copy of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]).

**The summands depend only on classes, and the transform is periodic in $k$.** Each summand $f([x]_N)e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$ is a complex number determined by the class $[x]_N$ and the integer $k$, and the classes $[0]_N,\dots,[N-1]_N$ are pairwise distinct and exhaust $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-standard-representatives-modulo-n]]); so the display is the finite sum, over the finite group, of the family $x\mapsto f(x)N^{-1/2}e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$, and reindexing by any other representative list leaves it unchanged ([[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], part 1). Reindexing by the transition $x\mapsto x+N$ uses $e^{-2\pi ik(x+N)/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ik}$ and $e^{-2\pi ik}=1$ for every integer $k$, because $-2\pi k\in2\pi\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]). For periodicity in $k$, the same two facts give $e^{-2\pi i(k+N)x/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ix}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$ for every integer $x$, so $(\mathcal F_Nf)(k+N)=(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]). Consequently $\mathcal F_Nf$ factors through the quotient $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ and is a well-defined function on $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, and $\mathcal F_N$ is a map $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}\to\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$.

**Form in terms of characters.** Define $\chi_k([m]):=\exp(2\pi ikm/N)$ for $k,m\in\mathbb Z$. The assignment is well defined on classes because replacing $m$ by $m+N$ multiplies the exponential by $e^{2\pi ik}=1$ ([[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]); it is multiplicative, $\chi_k(x+y)=\chi_k(x)\chi_k(y)$, by the addition law ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]]); and it takes values of modulus $1$, since $|\exp(i\theta)|=1$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]). Thus the $\chi_k$ are characters of the finite group $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ (homomorphisms into the unit circle; no continuity is required on a discrete group), and the definition reads

$$(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z/N}f(x)\,\chi_{-k}(x),$$

with the positive-sign transform obtained by replacing $k$ with $-k$. This fixes the negative-sign, $N^{-1/2}$-normalised convention of the whole page: the forward transform carries the minus sign in the exponent and the factor $N^{-1/2}$, and the inverse transform of the inversion theorem carries the plus sign with the same factor. A different, unnormalised convention is introduced later on this page for the algorithmic part; the two are related by a single explicit rescaling recorded there.

**Linearity, recorded for later use.** For $a,b\in\mathbb C$ and $f,g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ one has $\mathcal F_N(af+bg)=a\,\mathcal F_Nf+b\,\mathcal F_Ng$: the identity holds at each $k$ by distributivity in $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]) and the elementary laws of finite sums over a fixed finite index set, which follow from the recursion clauses of [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] by induction on an enumeration. Nothing else about $\mathcal F_N$ — unitarity, invertibility, the convolution law — is asserted here; those are proved in the items that follow.

Let $N\ge1$ and let $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ be the complex vector space of functions on the finite group $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[def-function-space]]). For $f,g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ the **cyclic convolution** of $f$ and $g$, unnormalised, is the function $f*g:\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ defined for $x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ by

$$(f*g)(x):=\sum_{y\in\mathbb Z/N}f(y)\,g(x-y),$$

where $x-y$ is the group operation of $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-integers-modulo-n-basic-algebra]]) and the sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $\mathbb C$ over the finite index set $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). No factor $1/N$ or $1/\sqrt N$ is inserted, and this unnormalised convention is the one used throughout the page.

**Well-definedness.** The standard-representatives bijection gives $|\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z|=N$ ([[thm-standard-representatives-modulo-n]]). For fixed $x$, $f(y)$ and $g(x-y)$ are values at classes, so the finite sum of the complex family $y\mapsto f(y)g(x-y)$ is a single complex number ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). Thus $x\mapsto(f*g)(x)$ is a well-defined function $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$.

**The operation is commutative.** Fix $x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ and let $h:\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ be $h(y):=x-y$; then $h(h(y))=x-(x-y)=y$, so $h$ is its own two-sided inverse and hence a bijection ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]], [[thm-integers-modulo-n-basic-algebra]]). Reindexing the finite sum along a bijection ([[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], part 1) with the substitution $z:=x-y$ gives

$$(f*g)(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathbb Z/N}f(y)\,g(x-y)=\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z/N}f(x-z)\,g(z)=\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z/N}g(z)\,f(x-z)=(g*f)(x),$$

the middle equality being commutativity of multiplication in $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Hence $f*g=g*f$.

Attached to the finite set $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ is its counting set function, which gives weight $1$ to each point ([[def-counting-measure]]); the displayed sum is the convolution of $f$ and $g$ against that weight on the finite group. This cyclic convolution is a different operation from the linear convolution of finite sequences of coefficients, which agrees with it only after the sequences are padded with enough zeros; the companion page exhibits the wrap that occurs without such padding, and the transform law proved later on this page computes the cyclic, not the linear, convolution.

Let $N\ge1$ and $f,g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Then for every $k\in\mathbb Z$

$$(\mathcal F_N(f*g))(k)=\sqrt N\,(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)(\mathcal F_Ng)(k),$$

where $*$ is the unnormalised cyclic convolution of [[def-cyclic-convolution-on-z-mod-n]] and $\sqrt N=N^{1/2}$ is the rational power of [[def-rational-power]]. The factor $\sqrt N$ is the price of leaving the convolution unnormalised; it is not an artefact of the proof, and the same factor appears for every pair $(f,g)$.

Let $N\ge1$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$

$$f(x)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},$$

the right-hand side being independent of the chosen integer representative of the class $x$. Consequently $\mathcal F_N$ is bijective with inverse the positive-sign transform

$$(\mathcal G_Ng)(x):=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}g(k)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},\qquad g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N},\ x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z,$$

and there is no convergence, regularity or support hypothesis anywhere.

Fix an integer $n$. Congruence modulo $n$ is an equivalence relation on
$\mathbb Z$ by [[lem-congruence-is-an-equivalence-relation]]. The
**congruence class of $a$ modulo $n$** is

$$[a]_n:=\{\,b\in\mathbb Z:b\equiv a\pmod n\,\},$$

and the **integers modulo $n$** form the quotient set

$$\mathbb Z/n:=\{\,[a]_n:a\in\mathbb Z\,\}.$$

This is the quotient-set construction of [[def-equivalence-relation]]. By
[[lem-equivalence-classes-partition]], two classes are equal exactly when their
representatives are congruent:

$$[a]_n=[b]_n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\equiv b\pmod n.$$

At $n=0$ each class is a singleton because congruence modulo $0$ is equality.
At $n=1$ there is one class, namely $\mathbb Z$ itself.

For every $n\in\mathbb N$, with addition and multiplication as in
[[def-addition-and-multiplication-modulo-n]]:

1. $(\mathbb Z/n,+,[0]_n)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), with
   $-[a]_n=[-a]_n$;
2. $(\mathbb Z/n,\cdot,[1]_n)$ is a commutative monoid
   ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]);
3. multiplication distributes over addition on both sides.

The assertions include $n=0$ and $n=1$. At $n=1$, the two distinguished
identities coincide because $[0]_1=[1]_1$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Every class in $\mathbb Z/n$
([[def-integers-modulo-n]]) contains exactly one integer $r$ with
$0\le r<n$. Consequently the map

$$r\longmapsto[r]_n\qquad(0\le r<n)$$

is a bijection from the von Neumann natural $n$ to $\mathbb Z/n$, and
$|\mathbb Z/n|=n$. This includes $n=1$, where the only representative is $0$.
For $n=0$, the map $a\mapsto[a]_0$ is a bijection $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/0$.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a, b > 0$ and let $r, s \in \mathbb{Q}$, with
rational powers as in [[def-rational-power]]. Then:

1. $a^{r} > 0$.
2. $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$.
3. $(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$; in particular $\big(ab\big)^{1/N} = a^{1/N} b^{1/N}$ for every natural $N \ge 1$.
4. $a^{-r} = \big(a^{r}\big)^{-1} = 1/a^{r}$.
5. $\big(a^{r}\big)^{s} = a^{rs}$.

Claims 2 and 3 persist in the supplementary case of [[def-rational-power]]: for
$a, b \ge 0$ and rationals $r, s > 0$ ([[def-rat-order]]) one still has
$(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$ and $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$. The two identities degenerate
differently, and it is worth saying how. In the product identity, a zero base on
either side makes both sides $0$. In the addition identity only the base $a$
occurs, so it degenerates only when $a = 0$, and then both sides are $0$; when
$a > 0$ that identity holds with no hypothesis on $b$ at all.

derivations.claim: If two integers $t,t'$ in $[-(N-1),N-1]$ have the same class modulo $M$, then $M$ divides $t-t'$. But $|t-t'|\le2N-2<M$; the only multiple of $M$ in this range is zero, so $t=t'$. Thus the definition of $b$ assigns at most one value to each residue. For each $0\le k<N$ and $0\le j<N$, the difference $k-j$ lies in $[-(N-1),N-1]$, so the cyclic-convolution sum reduces exactly to $c_k=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\alpha_jx_j\beta_{k-j}$.

For every such $j,k$, $-j^2+(k-j)^2-k^2=-2kj$, hence $\alpha_j\beta_{k-j}\gamma_k=e^{-2\pi ijk/N}$. Summing this identity against $x_j$ and using [F1] gives $\gamma_kc_k=X_k$ and therefore $(\mathcal F_Nx)(k)=N^{-1/2}\gamma_kc_k$.

Applying [F2] to $a,b$ gives $\mathcal F_Mc=\sqrt M((\mathcal F_Ma)\odot(\mathcal F_Mb))$. Applying the inverse in [F3] and dividing by $\sqrt M$ is legitimate since $M>0$; this proves the displayed FFT convolution representation of $c$.

Reindexing by the transition $x\mapsto x+N$ uses $e^{-2\pi ik(x+N)/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ik}$ and $e^{-2\pi ik}=1$ for every integer $k$, because $-2\pi k\in2\pi\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]). For periodicity in $k$, the same two facts give $e^{-2\pi i(k+N)x/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ix}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$ for every integer $x$, so $(\mathcal F_Nf)(k+N)=(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]). Consequently $\mathcal F_Nf$ factors through the quotient $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ and is a well-defined function on $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, and $\mathcal F_N$ is a map $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}\to\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$.

**Form in terms of characters.** Define $\chi_k([m]):=\exp(2\pi ikm/N)$ for $k,m\in\mathbb Z$. The assignment is well defined on classes because replacing $m$ by $m+N$ multiplies the exponential by $e^{2\pi ik}=1$ ([[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]); it is multiplicative, $\chi_k(x+y)=\chi_k(x)\chi_k(y)$, by the addition law ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]]); and it takes values of modulus $1$, since $|\exp(i\theta)|=1$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]). Thus the $\chi_k$ are characters of the finite group $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ (homomorphisms into the unit circle; no continuity is required on a discrete group), and the definition reads

$$(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z/N}f(x)\,\chi_{-k}(x),$$

with the positive-sign transform obtained by replacing $k$ with $-k$. This fixes the negative-sign, $N^{-1/2}$-normalised convention of the whole page: the forward transform carries the minus sign in the exponent and the factor $N^{-1/2}$, and the inverse transform of the inversion theorem carries the plus sign with the same factor. A different, unnormalised convention is introduced later on this page for the algorithmic part; the two are related by a single explicit rescaling recorded there.

**Linearity, recorded for later use.** For $a,b\in\mathbb C$ and $f,g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ one has $\mathcal F_N(af+bg)=a\,\mathcal F_Nf+b\,\mathcal F_Ng$: the identity holds at each $k$ by distributivity in $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]) and the elementary laws of finite sums over a fixed finite index set, which follow from the recursion clauses of [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] by induction on an enumeration. Nothing else about $\mathcal F_N$ — unitarity, invertibility, the convolution law — is asserted here; those are proved in the items that follow.

For every $n\in\mathbb N$, with addition and multiplication as in
[[def-addition-and-multiplication-modulo-n]]:

1. $(\mathbb Z/n,+,[0]_n)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), with
   $-[a]_n=[-a]_n$;
2. $(\mathbb Z/n,\cdot,[1]_n)$ is a commutative monoid
   ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]);
3. multiplication distributes over addition on both sides.

The assertions include $n=0$ and $n=1$. At $n=1$, the two distinguished
identities coincide because $[0]_1=[1]_1$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Every class in $\mathbb Z/n$
([[def-integers-modulo-n]]) contains exactly one integer $r$ with
$0\le r<n$. Consequently the map

$$r\longmapsto[r]_n\qquad(0\le r<n)$$

is a bijection from the von Neumann natural $n$ to $\mathbb Z/n$, and
$|\mathbb Z/n|=n$. This includes $n=1$, where the only representative is $0$.
For $n=0$, the map $a\mapsto[a]_0$ is a bijection $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/0$.

Let $(M,+,0)$ be a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]), let $S$ be a finite set with $n:=|S|$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]), and let $a:S\to M$. Choose a bijection $\phi:n\to S$ and define

$$\sum_{s\in S}a_s:=a_{\phi(0)}+a_{\phi(1)}+\cdots+a_{\phi(n-1)},$$

where the right side is the finite monoid product of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] written additively. In particular, the sum over the empty set is $0$.

This value is independent of the enumeration. If $\psi:n\to S$ is another bijection, then $\phi^{-1}\circ\psi$ is a permutation of $n$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and generalised commutativity gives

$$\sum_{k<n}a_{\psi(k)}=\sum_{k<n}a_{\phi(k)}$$

([[thm-generalised-associativity]]). Thus the displayed notation names one element of $M$ and does not select a preferred enumeration.

When $M$ is the additive monoid of $\mathbb R$ or of $\mathbb N$, this definition agrees with [[def-sum-over-a-finite-index-set]]: both enumerate $S$, apply the same finite recursion with identity $0$, and are independent of the enumeration.

Let $(M,+,0)$ be a commutative monoid and let all index sets below be finite.

1. If $h:T\to S$ is a bijection and $a:S\to M$, then $\sum_{t\in T}a_{h(t)}=\sum_{s\in S}a_s$.
2. If $S$ and $T$ are disjoint and $a:S\cup T\to M$, then $\sum_{u\in S\cup T}a_u=\sum_{s\in S}a_s+\sum_{t\in T}a_t$.
3. If $a:S\times T\to M$, then
   $$\sum_{(s,t)\in S\times T}a_{s,t}=\sum_{s\in S}\left(\sum_{t\in T}a_{s,t}\right)=\sum_{t\in T}\left(\sum_{s\in S}a_{s,t}\right).$$

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

$$\ker(\exp)=2\pi i\mathbb Z,$$
and $\exp z=\exp w$ exactly when $z-w\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]].

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a, b > 0$ and let $r, s \in \mathbb{Q}$, with
rational powers as in [[def-rational-power]]. Then:

1. $a^{r} > 0$.
2. $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$.
3. $(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$; in particular $\big(ab\big)^{1/N} = a^{1/N} b^{1/N}$ for every natural $N \ge 1$.
4. $a^{-r} = \big(a^{r}\big)^{-1} = 1/a^{r}$.
5. $\big(a^{r}\big)^{s} = a^{rs}$.

Claims 2 and 3 persist in the supplementary case of [[def-rational-power]]: for
$a, b \ge 0$ and rationals $r, s > 0$ ([[def-rat-order]]) one still has
$(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$ and $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$. The two identities degenerate
differently, and it is worth saying how. In the product identity, a zero base on
either side makes both sides $0$. In the addition identity only the base $a$
occurs, so it degenerates only when $a = 0$, and then both sides are $0$; when
$a > 0$ that identity holds with no hypothesis on $b$ at all.

derivations.claim: By [F2], the pair $(u,v)$ with $j=u+rv$ runs exactly once through the $N$ input indices, and $(k_1,k_2)$ with $k=k_2+sk_1$ runs exactly once through the $N$ output indices. Therefore the definition [F1] gives $(\mathcal F_Nx)(k_2+sk_1)=(rs)^{-1/2}\sum_{u=0}^{r-1}\sum_{v=0}^{s-1}x_{u+rv}e^{-2\pi i(u+rv)(k_2+sk_1)/(rs)}$.

Expanding the exponent gives $(u+rv)(k_2+sk_1)/(rs)=uk_2/(rs)+uk_1/r+vk_2/s+vk_1$. Since $vk_1$ is an integer, its exponential factor is $1$ by [F4]. Also $(rs)^{-1/2}=r^{-1/2}s^{-1/2}$ by [F4]. Regrouping the finite sums in [F3] now yields $(rs)^{-1/2}\sum_{u=0}^{r-1}e^{-2\pi iuk_2/N}e^{-2\pi iuk_1/r}\sum_{v=0}^{s-1}x_{u+rv}e^{-2\pi ivk_2/s}$.

The inner sum in step 2.1 is $s^{1/2}(\mathcal F_sx^{(u)})(k_2)$ by [F1]. The remaining coefficient and sum are exactly $r^{-1/2}\sum_{u=0}^{r-1}y^{(k_2)}_u e^{-2\pi iuk_1/r}=(\mathcal F_ry^{(k_2)})(k_1)$, again by [F1] and the definition of $y^{(k_2)}$. This is the claimed identity.

Let $N\ge1$ and let $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ be the complex vector space of functions on the finite group $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[def-function-space]]). For $f,g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ the **cyclic convolution** of $f$ and $g$, unnormalised, is the function $f*g:\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ defined for $x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ by

$$(f*g)(x):=\sum_{y\in\mathbb Z/N}f(y)\,g(x-y),$$

where $x-y$ is the group operation of $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-integers-modulo-n-basic-algebra]]) and the sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $\mathbb C$ over the finite index set $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). No factor $1/N$ or $1/\sqrt N$ is inserted, and this unnormalised convention is the one used throughout the page.

**Well-definedness.** The standard-representatives bijection gives $|\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z|=N$ ([[thm-standard-representatives-modulo-n]]). For fixed $x$, $f(y)$ and $g(x-y)$ are values at classes, so the finite sum of the complex family $y\mapsto f(y)g(x-y)$ is a single complex number ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). Thus $x\mapsto(f*g)(x)$ is a well-defined function $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$.

**The operation is commutative.** Fix $x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ and let $h:\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ be $h(y):=x-y$; then $h(h(y))=x-(x-y)=y$, so $h$ is its own two-sided inverse and hence a bijection ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]], [[thm-integers-modulo-n-basic-algebra]]). Reindexing the finite sum along a bijection ([[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], part 1) with the substitution $z:=x-y$ gives

$$(f*g)(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathbb Z/N}f(y)\,g(x-y)=\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z/N}f(x-z)\,g(z)=\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z/N}g(z)\,f(x-z)=(g*f)(x),$$

the middle equality being commutativity of multiplication in $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Hence $f*g=g*f$.

Attached to the finite set $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ is its counting set function, which gives weight $1$ to each point ([[def-counting-measure]]); the displayed sum is the convolution of $f$ and $g$ against that weight on the finite group. This cyclic convolution is a different operation from the linear convolution of finite sequences of coefficients, which agrees with it only after the sequences are padded with enough zeros; the companion page exhibits the wrap that occurs without such padding, and the transform law proved later on this page computes the cyclic, not the linear, convolution.

Let $(M,+,0)$ be a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]), let $S$ be a finite set with $n:=|S|$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]), and let $a:S\to M$. Choose a bijection $\phi:n\to S$ and define

$$\sum_{s\in S}a_s:=a_{\phi(0)}+a_{\phi(1)}+\cdots+a_{\phi(n-1)},$$

where the right side is the finite monoid product of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] written additively. In particular, the sum over the empty set is $0$.

This value is independent of the enumeration. If $\psi:n\to S$ is another bijection, then $\phi^{-1}\circ\psi$ is a permutation of $n$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and generalised commutativity gives

$$\sum_{k<n}a_{\psi(k)}=\sum_{k<n}a_{\phi(k)}$$

([[thm-generalised-associativity]]). Thus the displayed notation names one element of $M$ and does not select a preferred enumeration.

When $M$ is the additive monoid of $\mathbb R$ or of $\mathbb N$, this definition agrees with [[def-sum-over-a-finite-index-set]]: both enumerate $S$, apply the same finite recursion with identity $0$, and are independent of the enumeration.

For every $n\in\mathbb N$, with addition and multiplication as in
[[def-addition-and-multiplication-modulo-n]]:

1. $(\mathbb Z/n,+,[0]_n)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), with
   $-[a]_n=[-a]_n$;
2. $(\mathbb Z/n,\cdot,[1]_n)$ is a commutative monoid
   ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]);
3. multiplication distributes over addition on both sides.

The assertions include $n=0$ and $n=1$. At $n=1$, the two distinguished
identities coincide because $[0]_1=[1]_1$.

derivations.claim: A nonzero summand in [F1] has $0\le j<n$ and its second index is a residue in $\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$. If $k<n+m-1$ and $j>k$, then $k-j<0$ and $M+k-j\ge M-(n-1)\ge m$, so $[k-j]_M$ lies outside the support of $b$ and the summand is zero. If $j\le k$, then $k-j\ge0$; whenever $k-j\ge m$ the summand is again zero, and otherwise the cyclic representative equals the ordinary index $k-j$. Therefore the nonzero terms of [F1] are exactly the linear-convolution terms.

Every index sum $j+q$ with $a_jb_q\ne0$ satisfies $0\le j+q\le n+m-2<M$. Hence no such sum wraps modulo $M$. For $k\ge n+m-1$, no supported pair has sum congruent to $k$ modulo $M$: a sum is at most $n+m-2$, and its difference from $k$ has magnitude less than $M$ for the output indices $0\le k<M$. Thus all cyclic terms vanish there. This proves the asserted zero tail and completes the claim.
