Let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be as in [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]]. Here fl is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, on each real exact result that is zero or normal; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range x, fl(sqrt(x)) is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression ab+c; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

**A floating-point system.** A floating-point system consists of a nonempty
finite set $\mathbb F\subseteq\mathbb R$ of representable numbers with
$0\in\mathbb F$ and $-\mathbb F=\mathbb F$, a positive real
$N_{\max}\in\mathbb F$ (the largest normal magnitude), a positive real
$N_{\min}\in\mathbb F$ (the smallest normal magnitude), with
$N_{\min}\le N_{\max}$, and a rounding map
$\operatorname{fl}$ defined on $0$ and on the real numbers $t$ with
$N_{\min}\le|t|\le N_{\max}$, taking values in $\mathbb F$ and satisfying
$\operatorname{fl}(0)=0$.

**Unit roundoff.** A real $u>0$ is a **unit roundoff** for the system when
every real $t$ with $N_{\min}\le|t|\le N_{\max}$ satisfies

$$\operatorname{fl}(t)=t(1+\delta)\qquad\text{for some }\delta\text{ with }|\delta|\le u,$$

with $|\cdot|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). The model quantifies all
subsequent error analysis through the single constant $u$ and says nothing
about the internal bit representation beyond the bound $|\delta|\le u$.

**The standard relative model.** For each operation
$\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$ and all $x,y\in\mathbb F$ such that $x\circ y$ is
zero or is a real number in the normal range
($N_{\min}\le|x\circ y|\le N_{\max}$; for $\div$ this includes $y\ne 0$), the
computed result is

$$\operatorname{fl}(x\circ y)=(x\circ y)(1+\delta)\qquad\text{for some }\delta\text{ with }|\delta|\le u.$$

When $x\circ y=0$, this identity is the exact-zero rule
$\operatorname{fl}(0)=0$ and one may take $\delta=0$.

**The exclusions are part of the model, and are stated explicitly.**

- **Overflow** is excluded: when $|x\circ y|>N_{\max}$ the result is not a real
  number of the form $(x\circ y)(1+\delta)$ with $|\delta|\le u$.
- **Underflow** is excluded: when $0<|x\circ y|<N_{\min}$ the result falls into
  the subnormal or lost range and need not satisfy the relative bound.
- **Invalid operations** are excluded: when $x\circ y$ is not a real number
  (for example $0/0$), there is no real $\delta$ for the displayed identity.

Every item on this page that uses the model therefore carries the hypotheses
that the relevant operations lie in the normal range, and statements about
overflow, underflow or invalid operations are made only where the exclusion is
mentioned.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: Write $p_1=\operatorname{fl}(z_rw_r)$ and $p_2=\operatorname{fl}(z_iw_i)$. By [F1], $|p_1-z_rw_r|\le u|z_rw_r|$ and $|p_2-z_iw_i|\le u|z_iw_i|$. Rounding their difference adds error at most $u|p_1-p_2|\le u(1+u)(|z_rw_r|+|z_iw_i|)$. Therefore the real-part error is at most $(2u+u^2)(|z_rw_r|+|z_iw_i|)$. The same calculation for the imaginary part gives $(2u+u^2)(|z_rw_i|+|z_iw_r|)$.

Applying [F2] to both component sums shows that each component error is at most $(2u+u^2)|z||w|$. The complex modulus of the two-component error is consequently at most $\sqrt2(2u+u^2)|z||w|$. Since $u\le1/16$, $\sqrt2(2+u)u\le\sqrt2(33/16)u<3u$, proving the stated bound.

For $N\ge1$ and $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1})\in\mathbb R^N$, the **DCT-II** is the vector $X\in\mathbb R^N$ with $X_k=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}x_j\cos(\pi(j+1/2)k/N)$ for $0\le k<N$. Its even extension $E_Nx\in\mathbb R^{2N}$ is $(E_Nx)_j=x_j$ and $(E_Nx)_{2N-1-j}=x_j$ for $0\le j<N$.

For $N\ge1$ and $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\in\mathbb R^N$, the **DST-I** is the vector $Y\in\mathbb R^N$ with $Y_k=\sum_{j=1}^{N}x_j\sin(\pi jk/(N+1))$ for $1\le k\le N$. Its odd extension $O_Nx\in\mathbb R^{2(N+1)}$ has $(O_Nx)_0=(O_Nx)_{N+1}=0$, $(O_Nx)_j=x_j$, and $(O_Nx)_{2(N+1)-j}=-x_j$ for $1\le j\le N$.

These definitions fix the transform type, index range, extension symmetry, and endpoint normalization. Their orthogonality, inverse formulas, and relation to the unitary DFT are proved in separate results.

Let $N\ge1$ and let $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ be the complex vector space of all functions $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ ([[def-function-space]], [[def-vector-space]]). For $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ define the **unitary discrete Fourier transform** $\mathcal F_Nf:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ by

$$(\mathcal F_Nf)(k):=N^{-1/2}\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}f([x]_N)\,e^{-2\pi ikx/N},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$

where $[x]_N$ is the class of the integer $x$ in $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[def-integers-modulo-n]], [[lem-congruence-is-an-equivalence-relation]]), $e^z=\exp z$ is the complex exponential ([[def-complex-exponential]]), and $N^{-1/2}$ is the rational power of the positive real $N$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]), read in $\mathbb C$ through the embedded copy of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]).

derivations.claim: For $1\le r<2N$, put $\theta=\pi r/N$ and $S_r=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\cos(\theta(j+1/2))$. If $r$ is even, its numerator is zero. If $r$ is odd, $e^{iN\theta}=-1$ and $1-e^{i\theta}=-2ie^{i\theta/2}\sin(\theta/2)$ by [F3]. Here $0<\theta/2<\pi$, so [F5] also implies $\sin(\theta/2)\ne0$; the quotient is purely imaginary. In either case its real part is zero, hence $S_r=0$; also $S_0=N$.

derivations.claim: For $1\le r\le2N$, let $T_r=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\cos(\pi rj/(N+1))$. Put $z=e^{\pi i r/(N+1)}$. Since $0<\pi r/(N+1)<2\pi$, [F5] gives $z\ne1$; also $z^{2(N+1)}=1$, so the geometric sum over $j=0,\ldots,2(N+1)-1$ is zero. Pair the terms with indices $j$ and $2(N+1)-j$ for $1\le j\le N$; they are conjugates, while the unpaired terms are $1$ and $(-1)^r$. Taking real parts gives $1+(-1)^r+2T_r=0$. Hence $T_r=-1$ for even $r$ and $T_r=0$ for odd $r$; also define $T_0=N$.

Applying [F4] to each product $S_{kj}S_{\ell j}$ gives $(S^TS)_{k\ell}=\tfrac12(T_{|k-\ell|}-T_{k+\ell})$. If $k=\ell$, then the first term is $T_0=N$ and the second is $T_{2k}=-1$, giving $(N+1)/2$. If $k\ne\ell$, then $|k-\ell|$ and $k+\ell$ have the same parity and both are between $1$ and $2N$; their $T$ values from step 1.1 agree, giving zero. Therefore $S^TS=((N+1)/2)I_N$.

Since $S$ is symmetric and $(N+1)/2>0$, step 2.1 gives $S^{-1}=2(N+1)^{-1}S$, proving the inverse formula. For the odd extension, pair its positions $j$ and $2(N+1)-j$: their DFT terms are $x_j e^{-\pi i jk/(N+1)}-x_j e^{\pi i jk/(N+1)}=-2ix_j\sin(\pi jk/(N+1))$ by [F3]. Summing and applying [F2] gives the claimed DFT relation.

Let $\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ be the set of formal real polynomials of
[[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]]. Associate to every
$P\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ an eventually zero coefficient sequence $(p_k)$:
use its displayed finite coefficient list and extend it by zeros when $P\ne0$,
and put $p_k=0$ for every $k$ when $P=0$. Do the same for $Q$, with coefficients
$(q_k)$. Define $P+Q$ coefficientwise and define $PQ$ by the convolution
coefficients
$$ (P+Q)_k=p_k+q_k,\qquad (PQ)_k=\sum_{j=0}^{k}p_jq_{k-j}. $$
using the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. In either construction, discard
trailing zero coefficients; if every coefficient is zero, the result is the zero
polynomial. Scalar multiplication and subtraction are the corresponding
coefficientwise operations. Thus these formulas define operations on the formal
coefficient-list objects, independently of evaluation.

Write $1=(1)$ and $X=(0,1)$, and define
$$ \Phi(P,Q):=(Q,2XQ-P)\qquad(P,Q\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}). $$
Apply [[thm-recursion]] to the set
$\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}\times\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$, first with initial value
$(1,X)$ and then with initial value $(1,2X)$, always using the function $\Phi$.
This gives unique pair sequences $H^T,H^U$. Define $T_n$ and $U_n$ to be the
first coordinates of $H^T_n$ and $H^U_n$, respectively. Since the first
coordinate of $\Phi(P,Q)$ is $Q$, the second coordinate of $H^T_n$ is
$T_{n+1}$ and the second coordinate of $H^U_n$ is $U_{n+1}$. Consequently
$$ T_0=1,\quad T_1=X,\quad T_{n+2}=2XT_{n+1}-T_n, $$
$$ U_0=1,\quad U_1=2X,\quad U_{n+2}=2XU_{n+1}-U_n $$
for every $n\in\mathbb N$. These unique sequences are the **Chebyshev
polynomials of the first and second kinds**.

For every $n\in\mathbb N$ and real $\theta$,
$$T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos(n\theta),\qquad U_n(\cos\theta)\sin\theta=\sin((n+1)\theta).$$ In particular, for $n\ge1$ and $0\le j\le n$, $T_n(\cos(j\pi/n))=(-1)^j$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-induction-principle]].

Every integral below is the oriented Riemann integral constructed from upper
and lower Darboux sums in
[[lem-continuous-functions-riemann-integrable]]. It exists for each displayed
continuous integrand on the finite interval between its endpoints, is additive
in intervals, reverses sign when the endpoints are reversed, is monotone in
the integrand, and satisfies
$|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt|\le|b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|$.
These properties also
give constant comparison bounds and the average-value difference quotient
used to differentiate the integral-defined functions.

The exponential is $\exp(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}x^k/k!$ for $x\in\mathbb R$.
The sine and cosine are the everywhere-convergent power series
$\sin x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$ and
$\cos x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k}/(2k)!$. Define
$\arctan x=\int_0^x dt/(1+t^2)$ and set $\pi=4\arctan1$. The natural
logarithm $\ln$ is defined on $(0,\infty)$ by $\ln x=\int_1^x dt/t$.

The square root is the unique nonnegative real $y$ with $y^2=x$ for $x\ge0$;
existence and uniqueness follow from
[[lem-nonnegative-square-root-exists-and-unique]]. The tangent is
$\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ on the set where $\cos x\ne0$.

For complex $z=x+iy$, the modulus $|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is defined in
[[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]]. The complex exponential is
$\exp(x+iy)=\exp(x)(\cos y+i\sin y)$. The principal complex logarithm is
$\operatorname{Log}(z)=\ln|z|+i\operatorname{Arg}(z)$ on
$\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$. For $z=x+iy$ in this domain, define
$$
\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\\
\pi/2,&x=0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi/2,&x=0,\ y<0,\\
\pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0.
\end{cases}
$$
The excluded negative real axis is the remaining case $x<0,y=0$; zero is
also excluded.

These are point functions. An interval extension must separately enclose their
exact ranges, test the stated domains, and return a non-finite status when its
finite budget cannot certify a reduction or endpoint.

For every $x\in\mathbb R$,

$$\frac{d}{dx}\arctan x=\frac1{1+x^2},\qquad \arctan x=\int_0^x\frac{dt}{1+t^2}.$$

For $|x|<1$,

$$\arctan x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n x^{2n+1}}{2n+1}.$$

At the endpoint, the ordinarily convergent alternating series satisfies

$$\frac\pi4=1-\frac13+\frac15-\frac17+\cdots.$$

If the real series $\sum_{n\ge0}a_n$ converges ordinarily to $s$, then it is Abel summable to $s$:

$$\lim_{x\uparrow1}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_nx^n=s.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

Let $\gamma$ be the unique smallest positive zero of cosine supplied by [[thm-cosine-has-a-smallest-positive-zero]]. Define
$$\pi:=2\gamma.$$

Thus $\pi>0$ and $\pi/2=\gamma$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and the integral identity in [F2], the interval-evaluator arctangent and the principal arctangent have the same value at $1$.

Let $a_n=(-1)^n/(2n+1)$. The endpoint statement in [F2] says $\sum_{n\ge0}a_n=\pi/4$; [F3] gives $\lim_{x\uparrow1}\sum_{n\ge0}a_n(x^2)^n=\pi/4$. Multiplication by $x$ and the interior power-series identity in [F2] show $\lim_{x\uparrow1}\arctan x=\pi/4$, where [F5] fixes this as the canonical Fourier constant.

The principal arctangent is differentiable at $1$ by [F2], hence continuous there by [F4]. Therefore step 1.2 gives $\arctan(1)=\pi/4$. Step 1.1 and [F1] now give $4\arctan(1)=\pi$, proving that the interval evaluator and the Fourier formulas use the same constant.

Every finite interval returned for a requested real output node by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] on an input interval in the
domain of $\exp$, $\ln$, $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$, $\arctan$, $\sin$, $\cos$, or
$\tan$ contains the exact range of the corresponding function on that
interval. For the same typed DAG and designated real output node, if all
input intervals are nested coordinatewise, all constant enclosures are fixed,
and both calls use the same finite dyadic format and truncation index $N$,
then, whenever both calls return finite enclosures, the canonical branch-cell
and fixed-term construction makes the smaller domain's computed enclosure a
subset of the larger one's.
An unresolved fixed branch, pole, invalid domain or overflow returns its
stated non-finite status and carries no finite success claim.

A **real interval** is a closed set $[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ with finite dyadic
endpoints $a\le b$. Its width is $b-a$, midpoint is $(a+b)/2$, and its
midpoint-radius form is $m+[-r,r]$ with $m=(a+b)/2$ and $r=(b-a)/2$. The empty
set is the status `empty`; the whole real line is `entire`. `overflow`,
`domain-error`, `split-domain`, and `inconclusive` are computation statuses,
not finite intervals.

A **complex rectangle** is $X+iY=\{x+iy:x\in X,\ y\in Y\}$ for real intervals
$X,Y$. Complex addition and multiplication use
$(x+iy)+(u+iv)=(x+u)+i(y+v)$ and
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$. For $z=x+iy$, its complex modulus is
$|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and for $z\ne0$ its reciprocal is
$1/z=(x-iy)/(x^2+y^2)$. A
**complex ball** $B(c,r)$ is
$\{z\in\mathbb C:|z-c|\le r\}$ with dyadic complex center $c$ and dyadic
$r\ge0$. For any two represented sets $S,T$, the inclusion order is
$S\sqsubseteq T$ iff $S\subseteq T$.

The width of a complex rectangle with coordinate widths $w_X,w_Y$ is its
Euclidean diameter $\sqrt{w_X^2+w_Y^2}$; the width of a ball $B(c,r)$ is its
diameter $2r$. Width comparisons against a dyadic tolerance can be decided by
exact rational comparisons after squaring the nonnegative quantities.

The **range** of a real or complex function $f$ on a set $S$ is
$f(S)=\{f(x):x\in S\cap\operatorname{dom}(f)\}$. A finite expression DAG is a
finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes, constant nodes, and operation
nodes; constants are exact dyadics or are supplied with certified enclosing
intervals. Sharing a node means the exact same intermediate value is reused.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

The value $4\arctan(1)$ stipulated for $\pi$ by [[def-real-elementary-functions-and-domains]] equals the canonical circle constant $\pi$ used in the finite Fourier conventions, including [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]]. Thus the Machin enclosure of $\pi$ used by the interval evaluator encloses the same constant as the DFT and Bluestein formulas.

Input an exact rational $q$, a target $0<\tau\le1/4$, integer dyadic exponent limits $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$, an initial precision $p_0\ge2$, a finite precision cap $p_{\max}\ge p_0$, and a finite elementary-series cap $J\ge1$. The target value is $w=e^{\pi iq}=\cos(\pi q)+i\sin(\pi q)$ by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], for the canonical Fourier $\pi$ identified with the interval evaluator's constant by [[thm-na-interval-pi-matches-canonical-fourier-pi]]. For precision $p=p_0,p_0+1,\ldots,p_{\max}$, build the finite expression DAG for $\cos(\pi q)$ and $\sin(\pi q)$, with rational constants enclosed by directed dyadic rounding, and call [[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] using the dyadic format $(p,e_{\min},e_{\max})$ and truncation index $J$; its fixed finite-cell rules govern range reduction. If either result is non-finite, continue at the next precision unless the precision cap is reached, in which case return `inconclusive` with the supplier status. If the results are finite intervals $C=[c_-,c_+]$ and $S=[s_-,s_+]$, set $\widehat w=c_-+is_-$ and compute an upward-rounded dyadic $\epsilon\ge(c_+-c_-)+(s_+-s_-)$. If $\epsilon\le\tau$, return `certified(\widehat w,\epsilon)`; otherwise continue or return `inconclusive` at the cap. A non-finite endpoint or overflow returns its explicit failure status. The routine makes no finite-error claim on a failure branch.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

derivations.claim: By [F1], the real coordinate of $w=e^{\pi iq}$ lies in $[c_-,c_+]$ and its imaginary coordinate lies in $[s_-,s_+]$. Since $\widehat w=c_-+is_-$ by [F2], the coordinate differences satisfy $|\Re(w-\widehat w)|\le c_+-c_-$ and $|\Im(w-\widehat w)|\le s_+-s_-$.
Applying [F3] to these two coordinate differences gives $|w-\widehat w|\le(c_+-c_-)+(s_+-s_-)\le\epsilon$. The algorithm returns only when $\epsilon\le\tau$, proving the claim.

Let $N\ge1$ and let $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ be the complex vector space of all functions $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$, with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication ([[def-function-space]], [[def-vector-space]]). For $f,g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ define

$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z/N}f(x)\,\overline{g(x)},$$

the sum being the finite sum over the finite index set $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ in the additive commutative monoid of $\mathbb C$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). Enumerating the group by its standard representatives gives the equivalent formula

$$\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}f([x]_N)\,\overline{g([x]_N)},$$

where $\overline{\phantom{z}}$ is complex conjugation ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). **The two displays agree.** By [[thm-standard-representatives-modulo-n]] the map $x\mapsto[x]_N$ is a bijection from the von Neumann natural $N=\{0,\dots,N-1\}$ onto $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, and the summand $f(x)\overline{g(x)}$ depends only on the class $x$; a finite commutative-monoid sum is unchanged by reindexing along a bijection ([[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], part 1), so the second display is a rewrite of the first. No representative of a class is ever selected: every application of $f$ or of $g$ is an evaluation at a class.

**The pairing is an inner product** in the sense of [[def-inner-product-space]] and [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], with the linear-first convention fixed there. Linearity in the first argument, $\langle af_1+bf_2,g\rangle=a\langle f_1,g\rangle+b\langle f_2,g\rangle$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C$, follows from the field laws of $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]) together with the two elementary laws of a finite sum over a fixed finite index set, $\sum_x(u_x+v_x)=\sum_xu_x+\sum_xv_x$ and $\sum_x c\,u_x=c\sum_xu_x$; each of these laws is proved from the recursion clauses of [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] by induction on an enumeration of the index set. Conjugate symmetry, $\langle f,g\rangle=\overline{\langle g,f\rangle}$, follows from the same two laws together with the fact that complex conjugation is an involutive field automorphism, hence $\overline{g(x)\overline{f(x)}}=\overline{g(x)}\,f(x)$ and conjugation commutes with finite sums ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

**Positive definiteness.** Taking $g=f$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=\sum_x|f(x)|^2$ by $z\overline z=|z|^2$ ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]), a sum of nonnegative real numbers, so $\langle f,f\rangle\ge0$. For the vanishing clause, reindex by the standard representatives to identify this group sum of the real family $x\mapsto|f(x)|^2$ with the sequential real sum $\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}|f([x]_N)|^2$ ([[def-finite-sum]], [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]]); by claim 4 of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] a finite sum of nonnegative reals vanishes only if every term vanishes, and $|f([x]_N)|^2=0$ happens exactly when $f([x]_N)=0$ ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Since every class of $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ is $[x]_N$ for some $0\le x<N$, this forces $f=0$.

This is the pairing induced by the counting set function on the finite set $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, which weights a finite set by its cardinality and therefore gives weight $1$ to each point ([[def-counting-measure]]). No factor $1/N$ is inserted anywhere in the definition; a normalisation constant is carried by the transform, not by the pairing.

Let $u\le1/16$. For $z,w\in\mathbb C$, compute $\operatorname{fl}_{\mathbb C}(zw)$ from the four real products, one real subtraction, and one real addition specified in [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]]. If every nonzero intermediate is normal and no operation overflows, then

$$
|\operatorname{fl}_{\mathbb C}(zw)-zw|\le3u|z||w|.
$$

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].
Whenever [[alg-na-certified-unit-circle-phase]] returns `certified(\widehat w,\epsilon)` on rational input $q$, its output satisfies $|\widehat w-e^{\pi iq}|\le\epsilon\le\tau$.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

**A floating-point system.** A floating-point system consists of a nonempty
finite set $\mathbb F\subseteq\mathbb R$ of representable numbers with
$0\in\mathbb F$ and $-\mathbb F=\mathbb F$, a positive real
$N_{\max}\in\mathbb F$ (the largest normal magnitude), a positive real
$N_{\min}\in\mathbb F$ (the smallest normal magnitude), with
$N_{\min}\le N_{\max}$, and a rounding map
$\operatorname{fl}$ defined on $0$ and on the real numbers $t$ with
$N_{\min}\le|t|\le N_{\max}$, taking values in $\mathbb F$ and satisfying
$\operatorname{fl}(0)=0$.

**Unit roundoff.** A real $u>0$ is a **unit roundoff** for the system when
every real $t$ with $N_{\min}\le|t|\le N_{\max}$ satisfies

$$\operatorname{fl}(t)=t(1+\delta)\qquad\text{for some }\delta\text{ with }|\delta|\le u,$$

with $|\cdot|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). The model quantifies all
subsequent error analysis through the single constant $u$ and says nothing
about the internal bit representation beyond the bound $|\delta|\le u$.

**The standard relative model.** For each operation
$\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$ and all $x,y\in\mathbb F$ such that $x\circ y$ is
zero or is a real number in the normal range
($N_{\min}\le|x\circ y|\le N_{\max}$; for $\div$ this includes $y\ne 0$), the
computed result is

$$\operatorname{fl}(x\circ y)=(x\circ y)(1+\delta)\qquad\text{for some }\delta\text{ with }|\delta|\le u.$$

When $x\circ y=0$, this identity is the exact-zero rule
$\operatorname{fl}(0)=0$ and one may take $\delta=0$.

**The exclusions are part of the model, and are stated explicitly.**

- **Overflow** is excluded: when $|x\circ y|>N_{\max}$ the result is not a real
  number of the form $(x\circ y)(1+\delta)$ with $|\delta|\le u$.
- **Underflow** is excluded: when $0<|x\circ y|<N_{\min}$ the result falls into
  the subnormal or lost range and need not satisfy the relative bound.
- **Invalid operations** are excluded: when $x\circ y$ is not a real number
  (for example $0/0$), there is no real $\delta$ for the displayed identity.

Every item on this page that uses the model therefore carries the hypotheses
that the relevant operations lie in the normal range, and statements about
overflow, underflow or invalid operations are made only where the exclusion is
mentioned.

Let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be as in [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]]. Here fl is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, on each real exact result that is zero or normal; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range x, fl(sqrt(x)) is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression ab+c; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: Let $t=\operatorname{fl}_{\mathbb C}(\widehat wb)$. By [F1] and [F2], $|t-wb|\le3u|\widehat w||b|+\epsilon|b|\le(15u/4+\epsilon)|b|$. Thus $|t|\le(1+15u/4+\epsilon)|b|\le95|b|/64$.

For $q_\pm=\operatorname{fl}_{\mathbb C}(a\pm t)$, [F3] gives $|q_\pm-(a\pm t)|\le u(|a|+|t|)$ by [F4]. If $c=1/\sqrt2$ and $\widehat c=\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt{1/2})$, then correct rounding gives $|\widehat c-c|\le uc$. The componentwise rounded scaling therefore satisfies $|\operatorname{fl}_{\mathbb C}(\widehat c q_\pm)-cq_\pm|\le(2u+u^2)c|q_\pm|$, and $|q_\pm|\le(1+u)(|a|+|t|)$.

Combining steps 1.1–1.2 and using $\sqrt2c=1$, the two-output error norm is at most $(15u/4+\epsilon)|b|+\alpha(|a|+95|b|/64)$, where $\alpha=u+(2u+u^2)(1+u)=3u+3u^2+u^3\le817u/256$. Since $15/4+(817/256)(95/64)<9$, this is at most $(817u/256)|a|+(9u+\epsilon)|b|$.

By [F4], $\sqrt{(817/256)^2+9^2}<10$, so $(817u/256)|a|+9u|b|\le10u\sqrt{|a|^2+|b|^2}$; [F5] identifies the square-root factor as $\|(a,b)\|_2$. Also $\epsilon|b|\le\epsilon\sqrt{|a|^2+|b|^2}$. Adding the bounds proves the claim.

Let $M\ge1$, $N=2M$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Define the even and odd parts $e,o\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/M}$ by

$$e(r):=f(2r),\qquad o(r):=f(2r+1),\qquad r\in\mathbb Z/M\mathbb Z,$$

where $2r$ and $2r+1$ denote the classes in $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ of the corresponding integers; the maps $r\mapsto2r$ and $r\mapsto2r+1$ from $\mathbb Z/M\mathbb Z$ to $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ are well defined and injective with disjoint images, which together exhaust $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$. Let $X(f)$, $X(e)$, $X(o)$ be the unnormalised transforms of [[def-unnormalised-engineering-dft-and-conversion]], the latter two extended periodically to $\mathbb Z$. Then for every $k\in\mathbb Z$

$$X_k(f)=X_k(e)+e^{-2\pi ik/N}X_k(o),\qquad X_{k+M}(f)=X_k(e)-e^{-2\pi ik/N}X_k(o).$$

Thus an $N$-point transform is computed from the two $M$-point transforms of its even and odd parts together with the twiddle factors $e^{-2\pi ik/N}$; this is the radix-two (decimation-in-time) step of the fast Fourier transform, and it holds for every input class list, with no hypothesis beyond $N=2M$.

Let $N\ge1$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. The **unnormalised (engineering) discrete Fourier transform** of $f$ is the function $X(f):\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ defined by

$$X_k(f):=\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}f([x]_N)\,e^{-2\pi ikx/N},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$

the sum being the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] over the representatives $[0]_N,\dots,[N-1]_N$ of the classes of $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[def-integers-modulo-n]]), with $e^z$ the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]]. Comparing with [[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]],

$$X_k(f)=\sqrt N\,(\mathcal F_Nf)(k),\qquad (\mathcal F_Nf)(k)=N^{-1/2}X_k(f),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$

where $\sqrt N=N^{1/2}$ is the rational power of [[def-rational-power]] and the two conversions are inverse to each other by $N^{1/2}N^{-1/2}=1$ ([[lem-rational-power-laws]]). So the two transforms determine each other, and the only difference between them is the constant $\sqrt N$.

**The transform is defined on classes and is $N$-periodic.** If $[x]_N=[x']_N$ then $x'=x+mN$ for some integer $m$ and $e^{-2\pi ikx'/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ikm}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$, so the summands depend only on classes; and $e^{-2\pi i(k+N)x/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ix}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$ for every integer $x$, both identities following from the addition law and $\exp(2\pi i\,\cdot)=1$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]). Hence $X(f)$ factors through $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ and $X_k(f)$ depends on $k$ only through its class.

**Inverse formulas.** The inversion theorem in its unitary form is the identity $f(x)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)e^{2\pi ikx/N}$ of [[thm-finite-fourier-inversion]]; substituting $(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)=N^{-1/2}X_k(f)$ and collecting $N^{-1/2}N^{-1/2}=N^{-1}$ ([[lem-rational-power-laws]]) gives the engineering form

$$f(x)=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X_k(f)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},\qquad x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z.$$

This is the convention in which the radix-two algorithm computes its output. The unitary transform is recovered by the single rescaling $N^{-1/2}=2^{-m/2}$ at length $N=2^m$. The correctness and complexity theorems refer to this unnormalised output; the convolution lemma is stated in the unitary convention.

Let $N\ge1$ and let $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ be the complex vector space of all functions $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ ([[def-function-space]], [[def-vector-space]]). For $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ define the **unitary discrete Fourier transform** $\mathcal F_Nf:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ by

$$(\mathcal F_Nf)(k):=N^{-1/2}\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}f([x]_N)\,e^{-2\pi ikx/N},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$

where $[x]_N$ is the class of the integer $x$ in $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[def-integers-modulo-n]], [[lem-congruence-is-an-equivalence-relation]]), $e^z=\exp z$ is the complex exponential ([[def-complex-exponential]]), and $N^{-1/2}$ is the rational power of the positive real $N$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]), read in $\mathbb C$ through the embedded copy of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]).

**The summands depend only on classes, and the transform is periodic in $k$.** Each summand $f([x]_N)e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$ is a complex number determined by the class $[x]_N$ and the integer $k$, and the classes $[0]_N,\dots,[N-1]_N$ are pairwise distinct and exhaust $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-standard-representatives-modulo-n]]); so the display is the finite sum, over the finite group, of the family $x\mapsto f(x)N^{-1/2}e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$, and reindexing by any other representative list leaves it unchanged ([[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], part 1). Reindexing by the transition $x\mapsto x+N$ uses $e^{-2\pi ik(x+N)/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ik}$ and $e^{-2\pi ik}=1$ for every integer $k$, because $-2\pi k\in2\pi\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]). For periodicity in $k$, the same two facts give $e^{-2\pi i(k+N)x/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ix}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$ for every integer $x$, so $(\mathcal F_Nf)(k+N)=(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]). Consequently $\mathcal F_Nf$ factors through the quotient $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ and is a well-defined function on $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, and $\mathcal F_N$ is a map $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}\to\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$.

**Form in terms of characters.** Define $\chi_k([m]):=\exp(2\pi ikm/N)$ for $k,m\in\mathbb Z$. The assignment is well defined on classes because replacing $m$ by $m+N$ multiplies the exponential by $e^{2\pi ik}=1$ ([[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]); it is multiplicative, $\chi_k(x+y)=\chi_k(x)\chi_k(y)$, by the addition law ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]]); and it takes values of modulus $1$, since $|\exp(i\theta)|=1$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]). Thus the $\chi_k$ are characters of the finite group $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ (homomorphisms into the unit circle; no continuity is required on a discrete group), and the definition reads

$$(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z/N}f(x)\,\chi_{-k}(x),$$

with the positive-sign transform obtained by replacing $k$ with $-k$. This fixes the negative-sign, $N^{-1/2}$-normalised convention of the whole page: the forward transform carries the minus sign in the exponent and the factor $N^{-1/2}$, and the inverse transform of the inversion theorem carries the plus sign with the same factor. A different, unnormalised convention is introduced later on this page for the algorithmic part; the two are related by a single explicit rescaling recorded there.

**Linearity, recorded for later use.** For $a,b\in\mathbb C$ and $f,g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ one has $\mathcal F_N(af+bg)=a\,\mathcal F_Nf+b\,\mathcal F_Ng$: the identity holds at each $k$ by distributivity in $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]) and the elementary laws of finite sums over a fixed finite index set, which follow from the recursion clauses of [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] by induction on an enumeration. Nothing else about $\mathcal F_N$ — unitarity, invertibility, the convolution law — is asserted here; those are proved in the items that follow.

Let $m\in\mathbb N$ and $N=2^{m}$. The **radix-two fast Fourier transform** $\operatorname{FFT}_m:\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}\to\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ is defined by recursion on $m$ as follows. At $m=0$ the group is $\mathbb Z/1\mathbb Z$ and $\operatorname{FFT}_0:=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/1}}$. For $m\ge1$, given $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/2^{m}}$ with even and odd parts $e,o\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/2^{m-1}}$ ([[lem-radix-two-even-odd-dft-factorisation]]), and given $E:=\operatorname{FFT}_{m-1}(e)$ and $O:=\operatorname{FFT}_{m-1}(o)$, extend $E$ and $O$ from $\mathbb Z/2^{m-1}\mathbb Z$ to $\mathbb Z$ by $2^{m-1}$-periodicity and set

$$\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k):=E(k)+e^{-2\pi ik/2^{m}}O(k),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.$$

Then $\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k+2^{m})=\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k)$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z$, because $E$ and $O$ are $2^{m-1}$-periodic and $e^{-2\pi i(k+2^{m})/2^{m}}=e^{-2\pi ik/2^{m}}e^{-2\pi i}=e^{-2\pi ik/2^{m}}$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]); hence $\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)$ factors through $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/2^{m}\mathbb Z$ and $\operatorname{FFT}_m$ is a well-defined map $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/2^{m}}\to\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/2^{m}}$.

**The recursion is legitimate.** Put $\mathcal F_m:=\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/2^m}$ for each $m\in\mathbb N$, and use the tagged state set $A:=\{(m,g):m\in\mathbb N,\ g:\mathcal F_m\to\mathcal F_m\}$. For a state $(m,g)\in A$ and $f\in\mathcal F_{m+1}$, let $e,o\in\mathcal F_m$ be the even and odd parts supplied by [[lem-radix-two-even-odd-dft-factorisation]], and define $g^+(f)\in\mathcal F_{m+1}$ by $g^+(f)([k]_{2^{m+1}}):=g(e)([k]_{2^m})+e^{-2\pi ik/2^{m+1}}g(o)([k]_{2^m})$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$. This is well defined on $[k]_{2^{m+1}}$: replacing $k$ by $k+2^{m+1}$ leaves the recursive values unchanged modulo $2^m$ and multiplies the twiddle by $e^{-2\pi i}=1$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]). Thus $g^+$ is a total map $\mathcal F_{m+1}\to\mathcal F_{m+1}$, and $T:A\to A$ defined by $T(m,g):=(m+1,g^+)$ is a total step function. Starting from $a:=(0,\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal F_0})$, the recursion theorem [[thm-recursion]] gives a unique $H:\mathbb N\to A$ with $H(0)=a$ and $H(m+1)=T(H(m))$. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]], [[def-natural-numbers]]) the first coordinate of $H(m)$ is $m$; writing $H(m)=(m,\operatorname{FFT}_m)$ gives $\operatorname{FFT}_m:\mathcal F_m\to\mathcal F_m$ and exactly the base and combine clauses above. Termination is immediate from recursion on $m$: each recursive call uses level $m-1$, and the base case $m=0$ returns the input. The exponent arithmetic uses $2^{m+1}=2\cdot2^m$ and, for the rescaling below, $2^{-m/2}=(2^m)^{-1/2}$ ([[lem-power-laws]], [[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]).

**What the algorithm computes.** Correctness is proved separately later on this page: $\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k)=X_k(f)$ for every input, where $X$ is the unnormalised transform of [[def-unnormalised-engineering-dft-and-conversion]]; the unitary transform of this page is recovered from the output by the single rescaling $2^{-m/2}$ at length $N=2^{m}$. The operation count is likewise the subject of a later item. At level $m$ the recursion forms the even and odd parts of a length-$2^{m}$ list and performs one combine per output value, reading $E$ and $O$ at their classes and multiplying by the twiddle factors $e^{-2\pi ik/2^{m}}$.

Let $m\in\mathbb N$, $N=2^{m}$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Then

$$\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k)=X_k(f)\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z,$$

where $X$ is the unnormalised $N$-point discrete Fourier transform of [[def-unnormalised-engineering-dft-and-conversion]]. Equivalently $\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)=2^{m/2}\,\mathcal F_Nf$ for the unitary transform of [[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]]; consequently the algorithm returns the unitary transform after the single rescaling $2^{-m/2}$, and it does so for every input of length $2^{m}$. Correctness is separate from speed: the operation count is the subject of a different theorem, and no floating-point or stability claim is made here.

Let $u\le1/16$, let $|w|=1$, and let $|\widehat w-w|\le\epsilon\le1/4$. For $a,b\in\mathbb C$, perform the successful butterfly of [[alg-na-computed-unitary-radix-two-fft]] using $\widehat w$. If each exact nonzero real intermediate is normal and every operation succeeds under the operationwise model, then its computed pair $(\widehat y_+,widehat y_-)$ satisfies

$$
\left\|(\widehat y_+,\widehat y_-)-2^{-1/2}(a+wb,a-wb)\right\|_2\le(10u+\epsilon)\left\|(a,b)\right\|_2.
$$

Let $N\ge1$ and $f,g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Then

$$\langle\mathcal F_Nf,\mathcal F_Ng\rangle=\langle f,g\rangle,$$

where both pairings are the counting inner products of [[def-counting-inner-product-on-complex-functions-on-z-mod-n]]. In particular

$$\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}|(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)|^2=\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}|f(x)|^2,$$

so $\mathcal F_N$ preserves the counting inner product; invertibility of $\mathcal F_N$ is not asserted here.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let $N\ge1$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$

$$f(x)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},$$

the right-hand side being independent of the chosen integer representative of the class $x$. Consequently $\mathcal F_N$ is bijective with inverse the positive-sign transform

$$(\mathcal G_Ng)(x):=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}g(k)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},\qquad g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N},\ x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z,$$

and there is no convergence, regularity or support hypothesis anywhere.

Every integral below is the oriented Riemann integral constructed from upper
and lower Darboux sums in
[[lem-continuous-functions-riemann-integrable]]. It exists for each displayed
continuous integrand on the finite interval between its endpoints, is additive
in intervals, reverses sign when the endpoints are reversed, is monotone in
the integrand, and satisfies
$|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt|\le|b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|$.
These properties also
give constant comparison bounds and the average-value difference quotient
used to differentiate the integral-defined functions.

The exponential is $\exp(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}x^k/k!$ for $x\in\mathbb R$.
The sine and cosine are the everywhere-convergent power series
$\sin x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$ and
$\cos x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k}/(2k)!$. Define
$\arctan x=\int_0^x dt/(1+t^2)$ and set $\pi=4\arctan1$. The natural
logarithm $\ln$ is defined on $(0,\infty)$ by $\ln x=\int_1^x dt/t$.

The square root is the unique nonnegative real $y$ with $y^2=x$ for $x\ge0$;
existence and uniqueness follow from
[[lem-nonnegative-square-root-exists-and-unique]]. The tangent is
$\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ on the set where $\cos x\ne0$.

For complex $z=x+iy$, the modulus $|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is defined in
[[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]]. The complex exponential is
$\exp(x+iy)=\exp(x)(\cos y+i\sin y)$. The principal complex logarithm is
$\operatorname{Log}(z)=\ln|z|+i\operatorname{Arg}(z)$ on
$\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$. For $z=x+iy$ in this domain, define
$$
\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\\
\pi/2,&x=0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi/2,&x=0,\ y<0,\\
\pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0.
\end{cases}
$$
The excluded negative real axis is the remaining case $x<0,y=0$; zero is
also excluded.

These are point functions. An interval extension must separately enclose their
exact ranges, test the stated domains, and return a non-finite status when its
finite budget cannot certify a reduction or endpoint.

Let $N\ge1$ and let $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ be the complex vector space of all functions $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$, with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication ([[def-function-space]], [[def-vector-space]]). For $f,g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ define

$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z/N}f(x)\,\overline{g(x)},$$

the sum being the finite sum over the finite index set $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ in the additive commutative monoid of $\mathbb C$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). Enumerating the group by its standard representatives gives the equivalent formula

$$\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}f([x]_N)\,\overline{g([x]_N)},$$

where $\overline{\phantom{z}}$ is complex conjugation ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). **The two displays agree.** By [[thm-standard-representatives-modulo-n]] the map $x\mapsto[x]_N$ is a bijection from the von Neumann natural $N=\{0,\dots,N-1\}$ onto $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, and the summand $f(x)\overline{g(x)}$ depends only on the class $x$; a finite commutative-monoid sum is unchanged by reindexing along a bijection ([[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], part 1), so the second display is a rewrite of the first. No representative of a class is ever selected: every application of $f$ or of $g$ is an evaluation at a class.

**The pairing is an inner product** in the sense of [[def-inner-product-space]] and [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], with the linear-first convention fixed there. Linearity in the first argument, $\langle af_1+bf_2,g\rangle=a\langle f_1,g\rangle+b\langle f_2,g\rangle$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C$, follows from the field laws of $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]) together with the two elementary laws of a finite sum over a fixed finite index set, $\sum_x(u_x+v_x)=\sum_xu_x+\sum_xv_x$ and $\sum_x c\,u_x=c\sum_xu_x$; each of these laws is proved from the recursion clauses of [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] by induction on an enumeration of the index set. Conjugate symmetry, $\langle f,g\rangle=\overline{\langle g,f\rangle}$, follows from the same two laws together with the fact that complex conjugation is an involutive field automorphism, hence $\overline{g(x)\overline{f(x)}}=\overline{g(x)}\,f(x)$ and conjugation commutes with finite sums ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

**Positive definiteness.** Taking $g=f$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=\sum_x|f(x)|^2$ by $z\overline z=|z|^2$ ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]), a sum of nonnegative real numbers, so $\langle f,f\rangle\ge0$. For the vanishing clause, reindex by the standard representatives to identify this group sum of the real family $x\mapsto|f(x)|^2$ with the sequential real sum $\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}|f([x]_N)|^2$ ([[def-finite-sum]], [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]]); by claim 4 of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] a finite sum of nonnegative reals vanishes only if every term vanishes, and $|f([x]_N)|^2=0$ happens exactly when $f([x]_N)=0$ ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Since every class of $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ is $[x]_N$ for some $0\le x<N$, this forces $f=0$.

This is the pairing induced by the counting set function on the finite set $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, which weights a finite set by its cardinality and therefore gives weight $1$ to each point ([[def-counting-measure]]). No factor $1/N$ is inserted anywhere in the definition; a normalisation constant is carried by the transform, not by the pairing.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a, b > 0$ and let $r, s \in \mathbb{Q}$, with
rational powers as in [[def-rational-power]]. Then:

1. $a^{r} > 0$.
2. $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$.
3. $(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$; in particular $\big(ab\big)^{1/N} = a^{1/N} b^{1/N}$ for every natural $N \ge 1$.
4. $a^{-r} = \big(a^{r}\big)^{-1} = 1/a^{r}$.
5. $\big(a^{r}\big)^{s} = a^{rs}$.

Claims 2 and 3 persist in the supplementary case of [[def-rational-power]]: for
$a, b \ge 0$ and rationals $r, s > 0$ ([[def-rat-order]]) one still has
$(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$ and $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$. The two identities degenerate
differently, and it is worth saying how. In the product identity, a zero base on
either side makes both sides $0$. In the addition identity only the base $a$
occurs, so it degenerates only when $a = 0$, and then both sides are $0$; when
$a > 0$ that identity holds with no hypothesis on $b$ at all.

derivations.claim: For $m=0$, $N=1$ and the algorithm returns the input exactly, so the error is $0=(1+\eta)^0-1$. For $m\ge1$, [F1] gives the exact unnormalised top outputs $X_k(e)+wX_k(o)$ and $X_k(e)-wX_k(o)$, with $w=e^{-2\pi ik/N}$. The child unitary outputs are $E_k=X_k(e)/\sqrt{N/2}$ and $O_k=X_k(o)/\sqrt{N/2}$; dividing the parent unnormalised outputs by $\sqrt N=\sqrt2\sqrt{N/2}$ gives exactly $U_w(E_k,O_k)=2^{-1/2}(E_k+wO_k,E_k-wO_k)$. By [F7], $|w|=1$ and the scaling identity holds, so the columns of $U_w$ have squared norm $1$ and inner product $2^{-1}(w-w)=0$; hence $U_w$ preserves the pair norm.

Suppose the recursive transform of length $N/2$ has error bound $\rho_{m-1}=(1+\eta)^{m-1}-1$. By [F3] and [F6], stacking the exact even and odd transforms has norm $\|x\|_2$; stacking their computed errors has norm at most $\rho_{m-1}\|x\|_2$, since the even and odd input coordinates partition $x$. Hence the stacked computed suboutputs have norm at most $(1+\rho_{m-1})\|x\|_2$. For each $k$, [F2] bounds the top butterfly error by $\eta$ times the norm of its computed input pair. Squaring these bounds and summing over $k$ shows that the total top-stage error norm is at most $\eta(1+\rho_{m-1})\|x\|_2$. The prior subtransform errors contribute at most $\rho_{m-1}\|x\|_2$ through the direct sum of exact norm-preserving blocks in step 1.1. Therefore the total error is at most $[\rho_{m-1}+\eta(1+\rho_{m-1})]\|x\|_2=((1+\eta)^m-1)\|x\|_2$. Induction proves the forward bound for every $m$.

By [F4], the inverse implementation is conjugation before and after the forward routine and conjugation preserves every coordinate modulus. Applying step 2.1 to $\overline{x}$ gives the same error norm for the inverse direction.

If $m\eta\le1$, then $1+\eta\le e^\eta$ by the power series [F5], so $(1+\eta)^m\le e^{m\eta}$. For $0\le t\le1$, $e^t-1=\sum_{j\ge1}t^j/j!\le t\sum_{j\ge1}1/j!<2t$. Thus $((1+\eta)^m-1)\le2m\eta$. If $\epsilon_{\rm tw}=O(u)$, this is $O(mu)=O(u\log_2N)$, with the smallness condition already imposed.

Input $N\ge1$, $x\in\mathbb C^N$, a phase tolerance $0<\tau\le1/4$, integer dyadic exponent limits $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$, an initial phase precision $p_0\ge2$, a finite precision cap $p_{\max}\ge p_0$, a finite elementary-series cap $J\ge1$, and a maximum radix-two recursion depth $d_{\max}\ge0$. At precision $p$, phase endpoints use the dyadic format with precision $p$ and exponent limits $e_{\min},e_{\max}$. The output convention is the **unnormalised** DFT $X_k=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}x_je^{-2\pi ijk/N}$ ([[def-unnormalised-engineering-dft-and-conversion]]); the procedure returns an approximate vector or the first `inconclusive`/`range-failure` status.

1. For $N=1$, return $x_0$.
2. If $N=2^m$ with $m\ge1$, call [[alg-na-computed-unitary-radix-two-fft]] in `forward` mode with controls $(\tau,e_{\min},e_{\max},p_0,p_{\max},J,d_{\max})$ and multiply each output by the computed scalar $\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt N)$. A failed subcall or scale operation returns its status.
3. If $N$ is composite and not a power of two, find its least divisor $r$ with $1<r<N$ by trial division and put $s=N/r$. For $u=0,\ldots,r-1$, recursively call this procedure with the same controls on the strided vector $(x_{u+rv})_{v=0}^{s-1}$ to obtain an approximate unnormalised length-$s$ DFT $U_u$. For each $0\le k_2<s$ and $0\le u<r$, call [[alg-na-certified-unit-circle-phase]] on $(q,\tau,e_{\min},e_{\max},p_0,p_{\max},J)$ with $q=-2uk_2/N$ to obtain the twiddle enclosure, then multiply its returned phase by $U_u(k_2)$ using $\operatorname{fl}_{\mathbb C}$. Apply this procedure recursively, with the same controls, to the resulting vector indexed by $u$ at length $r$. Store its output $k_1$ at index $k_2+sk_1$. Propagate any failed phase or arithmetic status.
4. If $N$ is prime, set $M$ to the least power of two with $M\ge2N-1$. For each $0\le j<N$, call [[alg-na-certified-unit-circle-phase]] on $(q,\tau,e_{\min},e_{\max},p_0,p_{\max},J)$ with $q=-j^2/N$ to obtain $\widehat\alpha_j$, and set $a_j=\operatorname{fl}_{\mathbb C}(\widehat\alpha_jx_j)$; set the remaining entries of $a\in\mathbb C^M$ to zero. For each $-(N-1)\le t\le N-1$, obtain $\widehat\beta_t$ by the same call with $q=t^2/N$ and set $b_{[t]_M}=\widehat\beta_t$, setting other entries of $b$ to zero. Compute the cyclic convolution with [[alg-na-computed-fft-cyclic-and-linear-convolution]] in `cyclic` mode using controls $(\tau,e_{\min},e_{\max},p_0,p_{\max},J,d_{\max})$. For each $0\le k<N$, obtain $\widehat\gamma_k$ by the same phase call with $q=-k^2/N$ and set $\widehat X_k=\operatorname{fl}_{\mathbb C}(\widehat\gamma_k\widehat c_k)$. Return the first $N$ entries or the first failure status.

The divisor search and phase-enclosure work have separate integer/interval budgets and are not counted as complex arithmetic operations in the operation-count theorem. The exact factorization lemmas and the chirp-phase error theorem state what is guaranteed; this procedure by itself makes no general mixed-radix stability claim.

Let $N\ge1$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. The **unnormalised (engineering) discrete Fourier transform** of $f$ is the function $X(f):\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ defined by

$$X_k(f):=\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}f([x]_N)\,e^{-2\pi ikx/N},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$

the sum being the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] over the representatives $[0]_N,\dots,[N-1]_N$ of the classes of $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[def-integers-modulo-n]]), with $e^z$ the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]]. Comparing with [[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]],

$$X_k(f)=\sqrt N\,(\mathcal F_Nf)(k),\qquad (\mathcal F_Nf)(k)=N^{-1/2}X_k(f),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$

where $\sqrt N=N^{1/2}$ is the rational power of [[def-rational-power]] and the two conversions are inverse to each other by $N^{1/2}N^{-1/2}=1$ ([[lem-rational-power-laws]]). So the two transforms determine each other, and the only difference between them is the constant $\sqrt N$.

**The transform is defined on classes and is $N$-periodic.** If $[x]_N=[x']_N$ then $x'=x+mN$ for some integer $m$ and $e^{-2\pi ikx'/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ikm}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$, so the summands depend only on classes; and $e^{-2\pi i(k+N)x/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ix}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$ for every integer $x$, both identities following from the addition law and $\exp(2\pi i\,\cdot)=1$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]). Hence $X(f)$ factors through $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ and $X_k(f)$ depends on $k$ only through its class.

**Inverse formulas.** The inversion theorem in its unitary form is the identity $f(x)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)e^{2\pi ikx/N}$ of [[thm-finite-fourier-inversion]]; substituting $(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)=N^{-1/2}X_k(f)$ and collecting $N^{-1/2}N^{-1/2}=N^{-1}$ ([[lem-rational-power-laws]]) gives the engineering form

$$f(x)=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X_k(f)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},\qquad x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z.$$

This is the convention in which the radix-two algorithm computes its output. The unitary transform is recovered by the single rescaling $N^{-1/2}=2^{-m/2}$ at length $N=2^m$. The correctness and complexity theorems refer to this unnormalised output; the convolution lemma is stated in the unitary convention.

Let $r,s\ge2$, $N=rs$, and $x=(x_j)_{j=0}^{N-1}\in\mathbb C^N$. For $0\le u<r$ define $x^{(u)}_v=x_{u+rv}$ for $0\le v<s$. For $0\le k_2<s$ set $y^{(k_2)}_u=e^{-2\pi iuk_2/N}(\mathcal F_sx^{(u)})(k_2)$ for $0\le u<r$. Then for $0\le k_1<r$ and $0\le k_2<s$,

$$
(\mathcal F_Nx)(k_2+sk_1)=(\mathcal F_ry^{(k_2)})(k_1).
$$

Here every $\mathcal F_q$ is the negative-sign unitary DFT with normalization $q^{-1/2}$ from [[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]]. Thus the inner transforms are the $r$ length-$s$ transforms of strided input subsequences; the twiddle multiplication is explicit; and the outer transforms are the $s$ length-$r$ transforms. No coprimality of $r$ and $s$ is assumed.

Let $N\ge1$, $M\ge2N-1$, and $x\in\mathbb C^N$. Put $\alpha_j=e^{-\pi i j^2/N}$ for $0\le j<N$, $\beta_t=e^{\pi i t^2/N}$ for $-(N-1)\le t\le N-1$, and $\gamma_k=e^{-\pi i k^2/N}$ for $0\le k<N$. Embed $a_j=\alpha_jx_j$ for $0\le j<N$ and $a_j=0$ otherwise in $\mathbb C^M$. Embed $b_{[t]_M}=\beta_t$ for $-(N-1)\le t\le N-1$ and set its other entries to zero; this is well-defined because these $2N-1$ integers have distinct classes modulo $M$. Let $c=a*_M b$ be the unnormalised cyclic convolution on $\mathbb Z/M\mathbb Z$. Then, for $0\le k<N$,

$$
(\mathcal F_Nx)(k)=N^{-1/2}\gamma_k\,c_k,
$$

where $\gamma_k=e^{-\pi i k^2/N}$. Moreover $c=\sqrt M\,\mathcal F_M^{-1}((\mathcal F_Ma)\odot(\mathcal F_Mb))$, where $\odot$ is coordinatewise multiplication. The identity is exact for every $N$; padding to a radix-two $M$ is an implementation choice, not a mathematical restriction.

Let $T_m$ be the number of complex-number multiplications and additions performed by the recursion of [[def-recursive-radix-two-fast-fourier-transform]] on an input of length $N=2^{m}$, counted as the operations of the two recursive subproblems of length $2^{m-1}$ plus, at the top level, the $2^{m}$ twiddle multiplications $e^{-2\pi ik/2^{m}}O(k)$ and the $2^{m}$ additions $E(k)+\cdot$ needed to form all $2^{m}$ output values, and with no other operations counted. Then $T_0=0$, $T_m\le2T_{m-1}+2\cdot2^{m}$ for $m\ge1$, and

$$T_m\le2m\,2^{m}=2N\log_2N\qquad(m\ge0).$$

In particular there is the explicit constant $C=2$ with $T_m\le C\,m\,2^{m}$ for every $m$, so at length $N=2^{m}$ the algorithm uses at most $2N\log_2N$ complex arithmetic operations, whereas independent direct evaluation of all $N$ coefficients uses $N(N-1)$ additions and $N^{2}$ multiplications. The count is of arithmetic operations only: integer index arithmetic, twiddle evaluation, memory access and bit complexity are not counted, and no numerical-stability claim is made.

Input two finite complex sequences $a,b$, a mode `cyclic` or `linear`, and phase/FFT controls: a twiddle tolerance $0<\tau\le1/4$, integer dyadic exponent limits $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$, an initial phase precision $p_0\ge2$, a finite precision cap $p_{\max}\ge p_0$, a finite elementary-series cap $J\ge1$, and a maximum radix-two recursion depth $d_{\max}\ge0$. At precision $p$, phase endpoints use the dyadic format with precision $p$ and exponent limits $e_{\min},e_{\max}$. In cyclic mode the inputs must have the same length $M=2^q$ with integer $q\ge0$; the requested exact operation is cyclic convolution on $\mathbb Z/M\mathbb Z$. In linear mode, with lengths $n,m\ge1$, set $L=n+m-1$, choose the least power of two $M\ge L$, and append zeros to both inputs to length $M$; the requested output is the first $L$ entries of their cyclic convolution. If a dimension, control constraint, power-of-two condition, or range check fails, return its status.

For either mode, call [[alg-na-computed-unitary-radix-two-fft]] on each length-$M$ input with direction `forward` and the same $(\tau,e_{\min},e_{\max},p_0,p_{\max},J,d_{\max})$ controls. Multiply corresponding transform entries as $\operatorname{fl}_{\mathbb C}(\widehat A_k\widehat B_k)$ using the six-real-operation complex product of [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]]. Call the same FFT routine on this product vector with direction `inverse` and the same controls, and multiply each output component by the computed real scalar $\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt M)$ using componentwise rounded real scaling. Return the length-$M$ cyclic result, or its first $L$ entries in linear mode, only if every phase, recursion-budget, and arithmetic operation succeeds; otherwise return the first `inconclusive` or `range-failure` status and index. The exact convolution identity and numerical-error claim are separate results.

Let $N\ge1$ and $f,g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Then for every $k\in\mathbb Z$

$$(\mathcal F_N(f*g))(k)=\sqrt N\,(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)(\mathcal F_Ng)(k),$$

where $*$ is the unnormalised cyclic convolution of [[def-cyclic-convolution-on-z-mod-n]] and $\sqrt N=N^{1/2}$ is the rational power of [[def-rational-power]]. The factor $\sqrt N$ is the price of leaving the convolution unnormalised; it is not an artefact of the proof, and the same factor appears for every pair $(f,g)$.

Let $N\ge1$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$

$$f(x)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},$$

the right-hand side being independent of the chosen integer representative of the class $x$. Consequently $\mathcal F_N$ is bijective with inverse the positive-sign transform

$$(\mathcal G_Ng)(x):=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}g(k)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},\qquad g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N},\ x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z,$$

and there is no convergence, regularity or support hypothesis anywhere.

Let $N\ge1$ and let $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ be the complex vector space of functions on the finite group $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[def-function-space]]). For $f,g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ the **cyclic convolution** of $f$ and $g$, unnormalised, is the function $f*g:\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ defined for $x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ by

$$(f*g)(x):=\sum_{y\in\mathbb Z/N}f(y)\,g(x-y),$$

where $x-y$ is the group operation of $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-integers-modulo-n-basic-algebra]]) and the sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $\mathbb C$ over the finite index set $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). No factor $1/N$ or $1/\sqrt N$ is inserted, and this unnormalised convention is the one used throughout the page.

**Well-definedness.** The standard-representatives bijection gives $|\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z|=N$ ([[thm-standard-representatives-modulo-n]]). For fixed $x$, $f(y)$ and $g(x-y)$ are values at classes, so the finite sum of the complex family $y\mapsto f(y)g(x-y)$ is a single complex number ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). Thus $x\mapsto(f*g)(x)$ is a well-defined function $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$.

**The operation is commutative.** Fix $x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ and let $h:\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ be $h(y):=x-y$; then $h(h(y))=x-(x-y)=y$, so $h$ is its own two-sided inverse and hence a bijection ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]], [[thm-integers-modulo-n-basic-algebra]]). Reindexing the finite sum along a bijection ([[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], part 1) with the substitution $z:=x-y$ gives

$$(f*g)(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathbb Z/N}f(y)\,g(x-y)=\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z/N}f(x-z)\,g(z)=\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z/N}g(z)\,f(x-z)=(g*f)(x),$$

the middle equality being commutativity of multiplication in $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Hence $f*g=g*f$.

Attached to the finite set $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ is its counting set function, which gives weight $1$ to each point ([[def-counting-measure]]); the displayed sum is the convolution of $f$ and $g$ against that weight on the finite group. This cyclic convolution is a different operation from the linear convolution of finite sequences of coefficients, which agrees with it only after the sequences are padded with enough zeros; the companion page exhibits the wrap that occurs without such padding, and the transform law proved later on this page computes the cyclic, not the linear, convolution.

Let $m\in\mathbb N$, $N=2^{m}$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Then

$$\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k)=X_k(f)\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z,$$

where $X$ is the unnormalised $N$-point discrete Fourier transform of [[def-unnormalised-engineering-dft-and-conversion]]. Equivalently $\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)=2^{m/2}\,\mathcal F_Nf$ for the unitary transform of [[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]]; consequently the algorithm returns the unitary transform after the single rescaling $2^{-m/2}$, and it does so for every input of length $2^{m}$. Correctness is separate from speed: the operation count is the subject of a different theorem, and no floating-point or stability claim is made here.

Let $N\ge1$ and let $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ be the complex vector space of all functions $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ ([[def-function-space]], [[def-vector-space]]). For $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ define the **unitary discrete Fourier transform** $\mathcal F_Nf:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ by

$$(\mathcal F_Nf)(k):=N^{-1/2}\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}f([x]_N)\,e^{-2\pi ikx/N},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$

where $[x]_N$ is the class of the integer $x$ in $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[def-integers-modulo-n]], [[lem-congruence-is-an-equivalence-relation]]), $e^z=\exp z$ is the complex exponential ([[def-complex-exponential]]), and $N^{-1/2}$ is the rational power of the positive real $N$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]), read in $\mathbb C$ through the embedded copy of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]).

**The summands depend only on classes, and the transform is periodic in $k$.** Each summand $f([x]_N)e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$ is a complex number determined by the class $[x]_N$ and the integer $k$, and the classes $[0]_N,\dots,[N-1]_N$ are pairwise distinct and exhaust $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-standard-representatives-modulo-n]]); so the display is the finite sum, over the finite group, of the family $x\mapsto f(x)N^{-1/2}e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$, and reindexing by any other representative list leaves it unchanged ([[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], part 1). Reindexing by the transition $x\mapsto x+N$ uses $e^{-2\pi ik(x+N)/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ik}$ and $e^{-2\pi ik}=1$ for every integer $k$, because $-2\pi k\in2\pi\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]). For periodicity in $k$, the same two facts give $e^{-2\pi i(k+N)x/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ix}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$ for every integer $x$, so $(\mathcal F_Nf)(k+N)=(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]). Consequently $\mathcal F_Nf$ factors through the quotient $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ and is a well-defined function on $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, and $\mathcal F_N$ is a map $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}\to\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$.

**Form in terms of characters.** Define $\chi_k([m]):=\exp(2\pi ikm/N)$ for $k,m\in\mathbb Z$. The assignment is well defined on classes because replacing $m$ by $m+N$ multiplies the exponential by $e^{2\pi ik}=1$ ([[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]); it is multiplicative, $\chi_k(x+y)=\chi_k(x)\chi_k(y)$, by the addition law ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]]); and it takes values of modulus $1$, since $|\exp(i\theta)|=1$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]). Thus the $\chi_k$ are characters of the finite group $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ (homomorphisms into the unit circle; no continuity is required on a discrete group), and the definition reads

$$(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z/N}f(x)\,\chi_{-k}(x),$$

with the positive-sign transform obtained by replacing $k$ with $-k$. This fixes the negative-sign, $N^{-1/2}$-normalised convention of the whole page: the forward transform carries the minus sign in the exponent and the factor $N^{-1/2}$, and the inverse transform of the inversion theorem carries the plus sign with the same factor. A different, unnormalised convention is introduced later on this page for the algorithmic part; the two are related by a single explicit rescaling recorded there.

**Linearity, recorded for later use.** For $a,b\in\mathbb C$ and $f,g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ one has $\mathcal F_N(af+bg)=a\,\mathcal F_Nf+b\,\mathcal F_Ng$: the identity holds at each $k$ by distributivity in $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]) and the elementary laws of finite sums over a fixed finite index set, which follow from the recursion clauses of [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] by induction on an enumeration. Nothing else about $\mathcal F_N$ — unitarity, invertibility, the convolution law — is asserted here; those are proved in the items that follow.

Let $N\ge1$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. The **unnormalised (engineering) discrete Fourier transform** of $f$ is the function $X(f):\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ defined by
