Input an integer $k\ge1$ and dimension $d\in\{2,3\}$. The coordinate vertices are $\{0,\ldots,k-1\}^d$. Identify them with the zero-based matrix indices $0,\ldots,k^d-1$ by the lexicographic bijection $q(i_1,\ldots,i_d)=\sum_{a=1}^d i_a k^{d-a}$. The grid graph has an edge between two coordinate vertices exactly when they differ by $1$ in one coordinate and agree in all others. Use the graph and ordering conventions of [[def-symmetric-structural-elimination-graph-and-ordering]] on these indices. Thus $d=2$ gives the five-point graph and $d=3$ the seven-point graph.

Order a rectangular coordinate subbox recursively as follows. For each coordinate whose side length is at least $2$, choose its lower median coordinate, namely the coordinate with $\lfloor(m-1)/2\rfloor$ positions below it in a side of length $m$. Let $S$ be the union of the coordinate hyperplanes at those selected medians. Delete $S$, obtaining at most $2^d$ nonempty rectangular child boxes. Recursively order the child boxes in lexicographic order of their lower corners, then append the vertices of $S$ in lexicographic order. If no coordinate has side length at least $2$, append the remaining vertex as a terminal separator. Apply this rule first to the whole grid. The resulting order is the **coordinate nested-dissection ordering**.

The recursion uses only the graph geometry. It makes no fill or complexity claim for arbitrary graphs.

Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and use the coordinate grid and recursive ordering of [[alg-nested-dissection-ordering-on-regular-grids]]. For a recursion box $B$, let $S_B$ be its median separator; for the terminal one-vertex box take $S_B=B$. Let $\partial^+B$ be the set of grid vertices outside $B$ adjacent to some vertex of $B$. If $v\in S_B$, then every later filled neighbor of $v$ lies in $S_B\cup\partial^+B$. If every side of $B$ has length at most $s$, then
$$
|\{v\}\cup N^+_\pi(v)|\le |S_B|+|\partial^+B|\le 3d\,s^{d-1}.
$$

Use the zero-based graph and ordering of [[def-symmetric-structural-elimination-graph-and-ordering]]. For distinct remaining vertices $x,y\in V_k$, the pair $\{x,y\}$ is an edge of $G_k$ if and only if the original graph $G_0$ contains a finite walk from $x$ to $y$ all of whose internal vertices belong to $\{v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}\}$. A walk may repeat vertices; its internal vertices are the entries other than its two endpoints.

Assume exact arithmetic, a Hermitian positive-definite $A$, and a successful ordered factorization using [[alg-multifrontal-cholesky-and-sparse-triangular-solves]]. The fronts and contribution arrays give the same Cholesky factor as scalar elimination in ordering $\pi$. With $d_r=\ell_r+1=|F_r|$, the arithmetic work for assembly and scalar front updates is
$$O\!\left(\sum_{r=1}^n d_r^2\right),$$
the symbolic factor allocation has exactly $\sum_{r=1}^n d_r$ positions, and each forward/back substitution solve uses $O(\sum_r d_r)$ scalar operations. These are arithmetic and factor-storage counts; they are not wall-clock or total workspace bounds.

derivations.claim: If a box side has length $m\ge2$, the median rule leaves each child side with length at most $\lceil m/2\rceil$; a side of length $1$ stays $1$. Iterating gives side lengths at depth $r$ at most $s_r=\lceil k/2^r\rceil$. There are at most $2^{dr}$ boxes at that depth because each box has at most $2^d$ children. By depth $R=\lceil\log_2 k\rceil$, every side has length $1$, so all remaining boxes are terminal. For $0\le r\le R$, $k/2^r\ge1/2$, hence $s_r\le2k/2^r$.

If $k=1$, the grid and its ordering contain one terminal pivot and its factor column contains only the diagonal. Hence $d_v=1$ for its unique vertex, and [F3] gives $O(1)$ work and exactly one stored factor entry.

Let $G'$ be the structural graph of $A$ and let $G$ be the full nearest-neighbor grid on the same vertices. They use the same coordinate ordering. If a pair is an edge in a filled graph of $G'$, [F3] supplies a witness walk in $G'$ with internal vertices eliminated earlier; since $G'$ is a subgraph of $G$, the same walk witnesses that edge in the corresponding filled graph of $G$. Thus every later filled neighbor in $G'$ is also one in $G$, and each subgraph column size is at most the full-grid column size. Fix a box at depth $r$. Its separator has at most $d s_r^{d-1}$ vertices by the union bound over its at most $d$ median hyperplanes; the terminal singleton satisfies the same bound. By [F2], each such pivot has full-grid column size at most $3d s_r^{d-1}$, so the same bound holds for $A$.

The factorization work contributed by one depth-$r$ box is therefore at most a constant depending only on $d$ times $s_r^{d-1}s_r^{2(d-1)}=s_r^{3(d-1)}$, using [F4]. Summing over at most $2^{dr}$ boxes at each depth and using $s_r\le2k/2^r$ gives [step 2.1, F4, algebra]
$$
O\!\left(k^{3(d-1)}\sum_{r=0}^{R}2^{-r(2d-3)}\right).
$$
For $d=2$, the geometric ratio is $2^{-1}$, so this is $O(k^3)$. For $d=3$, the ratio is $2^{-3}$, so it is $O(k^6)$.

The storage contributed by one depth-$r$ box is at most a constant times $s_r^{d-1}s_r^{d-1}=s_r^{2(d-1)}$, again by [F2] and [F4]. Summing over boxes and using $s_r\le2k/2^r$ gives [step 2.1, F2, F4, algebra]
$$
O\!\left(k^{2(d-1)}\sum_{r=0}^{R}2^{-r(d-2)}\right).
$$
For $d=2$, there are $O(\log k)$ equal-order terms, giving $O(k^2\log k)$. For $d=3$, the series is bounded by $\sum_{r\ge0}2^{-r}=2$, giving $O(k^4)$.

When $d=2$, $n=k^2$ gives $k^3=n^{3/2}$ and $k^2\log k=O(n\log n)$ for $k\ge2$. When $d=3$, $n=k^3$ gives $k^6=n^2$ and $k^4=n^{4/3}$. Thus steps 1.2, 3.1 and 3.2 give the displayed rates and the $k=1$ case. The proof used the coordinate-box and grid-boundary counts in [F1]–[F2] together with the fill containment proved in step 2.1, so it does not imply a bound for arbitrary graphs.

Let $F$ be a field, let $n\in\mathbb N$ (including $0$), and let $A\in M_{n\times n}(F)$ satisfy
$A_{ij}=A_{ji}$ for every $i,j<n$ (that is, $A$ is symmetric). Its
**structural graph** is
the simple undirected graph $G_0=(V,E_0)$ with vertex set
$V=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ and edge set

$$E_0:=\bigl\{\{i,j\}:0\le i<j<n,\ A_{ij}\ne0\bigr\}.$$

An **elimination ordering** is a listing $v_0,\ldots,v_{n-1}$ in which every
vertex of $V$ occurs exactly once. Define the current vertex set by
$V_k=\{v_\ell:k\le\ell<n\}$, starting with the structural graph $G_0$. At
step $k$, the **later neighbors** of $v_k$ are

$$N_k(v_k):=\{u\in V_k\setminus\{v_k\}:\{u,v_k\}\in E_k\}.$$

The filled graph $G_{k+1}=(V_{k+1},E_{k+1})$ is obtained by deleting $v_k$ and
its incident edges, retaining all edges between remaining vertices, and adding
every edge between two distinct vertices of $N_k(v_k)$. An edge added at step
$k$ that was not already in $E_k$ is a **fill edge**. Repeating this rule
defines the symbolic elimination pattern for the ordering; it is defined from
the initial graph and ordering alone, without numerical pivot values.

If $N_k(v_k)$ is nonempty, the **parent** of $v_k$ is the later neighbor
$v_\ell$ with least position $\ell>k$ in the ordering. If $N_k(v_k)$ is
empty, $v_k$ is a root. Each non-root has a unique parent, and positions strictly increase along parent edges, so there is no directed cycle. If the underlying undirected graph had a cycle, its least-position vertex would be a child of both adjacent later vertices, contradicting uniqueness. Thus the parent relation is an elimination forest.

derivations.claim:
Write a vector as $x=(x_0,y_1,\ldots,y_m)$. The quadratic form is $x^TAx=x_0^2+\sum_i y_i^2+2t x_0\sum_i y_i$. Since $m\sum_i y_i^2-(\sum_i y_i)^2=\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2\ge0$, we have $|\sum_i y_i|\le\sqrt m\,\|y\|_2$. Therefore [given, algebra]
$$2t|x_0|\left|\sum_i y_i\right|\le 2t\sqrt m\,|x_0|\|y\|_2\le t\sqrt m(x_0^2+\|y\|_2^2)=\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2.$$
It follows that $x^TAx\ge\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2>0$ for $x\ne0$, so $A$ is positive definite.

In leaf-first order, each leaf has exactly one later neighbor, the center. By [F1] no pair of distinct remaining neighbors exists, so eliminating that leaf adds no edge. This holds for every leaf; eliminating the last center also adds no edge.

In center-first order, the center's later-neighbor set is all $m$ leaves. By [F1], the graph update inserts every pair of distinct leaves, so it has $\binom m2$ leaf-to-leaf fill edges not in the original star.

The pivot at the center is $1$. Its Schur complement on the leaves is $I_m-t^2\mathbf1\mathbf1^T$, whose off-diagonal entries are $-t^2\ne0$. Thus the symbolic fill edges from step 1.3 are also numerical nonzeros for this matrix, while step 1.2 gives no fill in the other order.
Steps 1.2 and 2.1 exhibit respectively $0$ and $\binom m2$ fill edges for two orderings of the same positive-definite sparse matrix.

Input an integer $k\ge1$ and dimension $d\in\{2,3\}$. The coordinate vertices are $\{0,\ldots,k-1\}^d$. Identify them with the zero-based matrix indices $0,\ldots,k^d-1$ by the lexicographic bijection $q(i_1,\ldots,i_d)=\sum_{a=1}^d i_a k^{d-a}$. The grid graph has an edge between two coordinate vertices exactly when they differ by $1$ in one coordinate and agree in all others. Use the graph and ordering conventions of [[def-symmetric-structural-elimination-graph-and-ordering]] on these indices. Thus $d=2$ gives the five-point graph and $d=3$ the seven-point graph.

Order a rectangular coordinate subbox recursively as follows. For each coordinate whose side length is at least $2$, choose its lower median coordinate, namely the coordinate with $\lfloor(m-1)/2\rfloor$ positions below it in a side of length $m$. Let $S$ be the union of the coordinate hyperplanes at those selected medians. Delete $S$, obtaining at most $2^d$ nonempty rectangular child boxes. Recursively order the child boxes in lexicographic order of their lower corners, then append the vertices of $S$ in lexicographic order. If no coordinate has side length at least $2$, append the remaining vertex as a terminal separator. Apply this rule first to the whole grid. The resulting order is the **coordinate nested-dissection ordering**.

The recursion uses only the graph geometry. It makes no fill or complexity claim for arbitrary graphs.

Let $d\in\{2,3\}$, $k\ge2$, and $n=k^d$. Identify the coordinate grid $\{0,\ldots,k-1\}^d$ with the zero-based matrix indices by the lexicographic bijection in [[alg-nested-dissection-ordering-on-regular-grids]]. Let $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive definite, with structural graph a subgraph of the $d$-dimensional nearest-neighbor grid. Under the coordinate nested-dissection ordering, exact scalar multifrontal Cholesky has
$$
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
d&\text{arithmetic work}&\text{symbolic factor storage}\\
2&O(n^{3/2})&O(n\log n)\\
3&O(n^2)&O(n^{4/3}).
\end{array}
$$
The storage is the number of allocated factor entries, including structural zeros, and excludes temporary contribution arrays. The bounds use the stated grid geometry; they assert no general-graph bound. For $k=1$, there is one pivot and both work and factor storage are $O(1)$.

derivations.claim:
For every grid vertex $v$, let $b(v)=4-\deg_{G_k}(v)$ be its number of missing boundary neighbors. Expanding squares gives [given, algebra]
$$x^TA_kx=\sum_{\{v,w\}\in E(G_k)}(x_v-x_w)^2+\sum_{v\in G_k}b(v)x_v^2.$$
The right side is nonnegative. If it is zero, every adjacent pair has equal coordinates and every boundary vertex with $b(v)>0$ has value zero. The grid is connected and has a boundary vertex, so all coordinates are equal to zero. Hence $A_k$ is positive definite.

By [F1], the order is the coordinate nested-dissection order on the five-point grid. The matrix is symmetric positive definite by step 1.1 and its off-diagonal pattern is exactly $G_k$. For $k\ge2$, applying [F2] with $n=k^2$ gives work $O((k^2)^{3/2})=O(k^3)$ and factor storage $O(k^2\log(k^2))=O(k^2\log k)$. For $k=1$, the matrix and factor each have one entry.
Step 1.1 verifies the matrix hypothesis and step 2.1 gives the nested-dissection cost specialization.

Divide complex values by a nonzero real denominator by separately dividing their real and imaginary components, using the model's real operations; no complex division is used. Any invalid operation, nonfinite output or nonzero exact intermediate outside the normal range returns `range-failure`. Hermitian counterparts, sign changes and conjugation are exact copies.

For a complex value $z=x+iy$, $|z|$ denotes its exact mathematical modulus $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$; this convention does not add a modulus operation to the floating-point model. Moduli in guard specifications and error bounds have this meaning, while the algorithm obtains only the rigorous bounds produced by the rounded scaled-norm procedure below.

The pivot controller uses exact real-RAM arithmetic on the stored real components and the supplied exact $u,\theta$, separately from the rounded numerical kernel. Its allowed operations are real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a certified nonzero real denominator, fixed nonnegative integer powers, and comparisons. Each field operation or comparison consumes one unit of the nonnegative integer controller budget; a fixed power is expanded into its stated finite chain of multiplications. Before any controller operation, if no unit remains, return `pivot-inconclusive`. Exact sign/absolute-value and maximum decisions use comparisons and conditional sign changes. For binary/rational stored values and rational $u,\theta$, exact rational arithmetic implements this controller with finite integers; no bit-complexity bound is claimed. There is no optional unspecified certifier or sign oracle. For complex modulus guards, a successful two-component scaled norm first scales by the larger absolute real component, then rounds both divisions, squares, sum, positive square root and rescaling. Its returned $h$ gives bounds $h/(1+u)^4\le|z|\le h/(1-u)^4$; zero is exact. Maxima use the corresponding lower/upper bounds and an empty maximum is zero. Evaluate modulus guards once per distinct stored complex value in row-major order, using only the displayed rounded scaled norm; its finite floating operations carry their own range status. No exact square root or additional modulus operation is used by the controller. Evaluate each displayed rational bound left to right, entrywise in row-major order; evaluate column maxima in increasing row order, then the at-most-two-term matrix-vector bounds in increasing column order, and finally the acceptance comparisons in row order. Compute each of $(1-u)^4,(1+u)^4,(1+u)^5$ by left-associated repeated multiplication. These prescribed finite expression trees and finite input loops fix the guard procedure and its budget count. If acceptance is not established, evaluate the stated lower-bound failure comparisons; if neither conclusion follows, return `pivot-inconclusive` without refinement.

For $k=1$, write $D=[d]$, $d$ real. If $d=0$ return `pivot-failure`. Certify $\max_i|B_{i1}|\le|d|/\theta$ using the guard bounds. A rigorous lower maximum exceeding $|d|/\theta$ returns `pivot-failure`; an unresolved comparison returns `pivot-inconclusive`. Set $\widehat M_{i1}$ by rounded real-component divisions of $B_{i1}$ by $d$.

For $k=2$, write $D=\begin{pmatrix}a&z\\\overline z&c\end{pmatrix}$ with real $a,c$, and set $s=\max(|a|,|c|,|\operatorname{Re}z|,|\operatorname{Im}z|)$. If $s=0$ return `pivot-failure`. Compute the four real entries of $\widehat E=\operatorname{fl}(D/s)$ and the conjugate counterpart by copying. In order compute
$$p=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat a\widehat c),\quad q_1=\operatorname{fl}((\operatorname{Re}\widehat z)^2),\quad q_2=\operatorname{fl}((\operatorname{Im}\widehat z)^2),\quad q=\operatorname{fl}(q_1+q_2),\quad \widehat d=\operatorname{fl}(p-q).$$
Put $\epsilon_d=3((1+u)^5-1)$ and $\widehat J=\operatorname{adj}(\widehat E)=\begin{pmatrix}\widehat c&-\widehat z\\-\overline{\widehat z}&\widehat a\end{pmatrix}$ by copies. Unless $|\widehat d|>\epsilon_d$ is certified, return `pivot-inconclusive`. For each entry obtain rigorous modulus bounds $j^-_{ij}\le|\widehat J_{ij}|\le j^+_{ij}$ and set
$$U_{ij}=\frac{j^+_{ij}}{s(1-u)(|\widehat d|-\epsilon_d)},\qquad V_{ij}=\frac{j^-_{ij}}{s(1+u)(|\widehat d|+\epsilon_d)}.$$
Let $c_j^-,c_j^+$ bound $\max_i|B_{ij}|$. Accept only if $U c^+\le\theta^{-1}(1,1)^T$ componentwise. If any coordinate of $V c^-$ exceeds $\theta^{-1}$ return `pivot-failure`; otherwise an unresolved test returns `pivot-inconclusive`. On acceptance compute $\widehat B_s=\operatorname{fl}(B/s)$, $K=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat B_s\widehat J)$ by sequential two-term complex dots, then $\widehat M=\operatorname{fl}(K/\widehat d)$ by real-component divisions. No explicit reciprocal $1/s$ is formed.

For either block size, compute each allocated lower-triangle entry of $\widehat Z=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat M B^*)$ by sequential $k$-term dots. Compute $\operatorname{fl}(C-\widehat Z)$ there, retain only its real component on the diagonal, and obtain upper entries by exact conjugation. Return `success` with stored $D,\widehat M,\widehat S$ and the pivot certificates. An empty trailing block returns empty $\widehat M,\widehat S$. Additional sparsity drops must be recorded separately as additive perturbations.

$$g_k=\frac{1+6u}{1-(k-1)u}-1,\qquad F=\|A\|_F,\quad X=\|x\|_2,\quad Y=\|y\|_2.$$
For $\widehat v=\operatorname{fl}(Ax)$ and $\widehat w=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-y)$, put $V=g_nFX$ and $W=V+u(\|\widehat v\|_2+Y)$. Then
$$\|\widehat w-(Ax-y)\|_2\le W.$$
For a stored real $\lambda>0$, also compute $\widehat z=\operatorname{fl}(A^*\widehat w)$, $\widehat l=\operatorname{fl}(\lambda x)$ and $\widehat r=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat z+\widehat l)$, rounding scalar multiplication componentwise. The exact intended normal residual $r=A^*(Ax-y)+\lambda x$ satisfies
$$\|\widehat r-r\|_2\le\rho:=FW+g_mF\|\widehat w\|_2+u\lambda X+u(\|\widehat z\|_2+\|\widehat l\|_2).$$
Norms in these certificates mean exact norms or certified upper bounds. Uncontrolled rounding of the certificate itself is not authorized. The linear bound applies columnwise to certify $\|I-AB\|_2\le\|I-AB\|_F$ from stored basis-solve columns $B$.

product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest

derivations.claim: For two-by-two $D$, put $E=D/s$ and $J=\operatorname{adj}(E)$. Each real component of $E$ has magnitude at most one. Expansion of the determinant computation multiplies each of its three quadratic terms by at most five factors $1+\delta_i$, $|\delta_i|\le u$, including scaling. For $0<u<1$, the coefficient deviation is at most $(1+u)^5-1$, since the lower deviation $1-(1-u)^5$ is no greater. Also $|E_{11}E_{22}|+(\operatorname{Re}E_{12})^2+(\operatorname{Im}E_{12})^2\le3$. Thus $|\widehat d-\det E|\le\epsilon_d$. Acceptance gives $\det E\ne0$. The entrywise scaling bound $|J-\widehat J|\le u|J|$ implies $|J|\le|\widehat J|/(1-u)$ and $|J|\ge|\widehat J|/(1+u)$. The algorithm's $U,V$ therefore bound $|D^{-1}|$ above and below. The modulus guard follows by expanding its scaled sum, square root and rescaling, giving relative factors between $(1-u)^4$ and $(1+u)^4$. The resulting maximum/product interval tests prove exact acceptance or definite threshold failure; unresolved cases are explicitly inconclusive. Scalar pivots satisfy the same scalar threshold argument.

Define $R=\widehat J/(s\widehat d)$ for analysis only. Scaling gives $\|\widehat J-J\|_F\le u\|J\|_F\le\sqrt2u\|J\|_2$. The inverse formula gives $\|D^{-1}\|_2=\|J\|_2/(s|\det E|)$, and step 1.1 gives $|\det E|/|\widehat d|\le1+\mu$. Subtract the two inverse expressions to obtain $\|R-D^{-1}\|_2\le\nu\|D^{-1}\|_2$ and $\|R\|_2\le(1+\nu)\|D^{-1}\|_2$. This retains the actual scaled-determinant sensitivity.

The computed $B/s$ has Frobenius error at most $u\|B\|_F/s$. By [F2], its product with $\widehat J$ adds at most $g_2(1+u)\|B\|_F\|\widehat J\|_F/s$. Since $\|\widehat J\|_F\le\sqrt2\|\widehat J\|_2$, the product discrepancy relative to $B\widehat J/s$ is at most $(\sqrt2g_2(1+u)+u)\|B\|_F\|\widehat J\|_2/s$. Final real-component division adds the factor $1+u$ to that error and at most $u\|BR\|_F$. Thus $\|\widehat M-BR\|_F\le\chi\|B\|_F\|R\|_2$. Step 1.2 proves the stated $e_M$ and $\|\widehat M\|_F\le(1+\omega_2)\|B\|_F\|D^{-1}\|_2$. For a scalar pivot the direct real-component divisions instead give these bounds with $\omega_1=u$.

The update dot bound [F2] gives $\|\widehat Z-\widehat MB^*\|_F\le g_k\|\widehat M\|_F\|B\|_F$. Replacing $\widehat M$ by $M$ adds at most $e_M\|B\|_2$. Final subtraction adds at most $u(\|C\|_F+\|\widehat Z\|_F)$. Combining these with step 2.1 gives raw Schur error at most $u\|C\|_F+q_k\|B\|_F^2\|D^{-1}\|_2$. The exact Schur complement is Hermitian. Copying one chosen computed triangle doubles at most the squared Frobenius error; projecting the diagonal to its real part decreases error. Thus $\|\Delta\|_2\le\beta$. Finally $\|C\|_F\le\sqrt t\|C\|_2$ and $\|B\|_F^2\le k\|B\|_2^2$, proving the stated $\eta_{k,t}$ bound. Empty trailing arrays have zero residual.

Put $H=\widehat M-M$. Direct block multiplication gives the displayed full residual, because $N=HD$ and $\widehat MD\widehat M^*-MB^*=HB^*+\widehat MN^*$. The Hermitian off-diagonal matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&N^*\\N&0\end{pmatrix}$ has norm $\|N\|_2$: its square is block diagonal with $N^*N,NN^*$, or equivalently use the defining singular-value maximum. Also $\|N\|_2\le e_M\|D\|_2$. Triangle inequality and step 2.2 therefore give $\|F\|_2\le f$. Every coefficient is an explicit finite function under successful certification, and tends to zero linearly for a fixed nonsingular normalized pivot as $u\to0$.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let
$\lVert\cdot\rVert$ be a declared norm on the matrix space
$M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and let
$\tau\ge 0$ be a declared tolerance. The **numerical rank of $A$ at
tolerance $\tau$** is

$$\operatorname{rank}_{\tau}(A)\;:=\;\min\Bigl\{\,\operatorname{rank}B\;:\;B\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F),\ \lVert A-B\rVert\le\tau\,\Bigr\}.$$

The minimum exists: it is a minimum of a nonempty subset of the finite set
$\{0,1,\dots,\min(m,n)\}$, the value $\operatorname{rank}A$ being attained at
$B=A$.

**Scale.** The tolerance may be declared absolutely, as a real number
$\tau\ge 0$, or relative to a scale, as $\tau=\tau_0\lVert A\rVert$ for a
declared factor $\tau_0\ge 0$. Both enter the definition through the single
threshold $\tau$; the scale only fixes which threshold is meant, and every
statement about $\operatorname{rank}_{\tau}$ is a statement about that one
threshold.

**Why the exact-rank discontinuity forces the parameter.** Exact rank is
locally constant at the full-rank matrices but discontinuous at every
nonmaximal-rank matrix
([[thm-exact-rank-is-locally-constant-at-full-rank-and-discontinuous-at-nonmaximal-rank-matrices]]);
an exact rank read from noisy data is therefore unstable. Numerical rank
replaces exact rank by the smallest exact rank attainable within the declared
norm tolerance $\tau$: it is, by construction, constant on every open ball of
radius below the relevant gaps, and it counts as rank exactly those directions
that perturbation of size at most $\tau$ cannot erase.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, let

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

be a singular value decomposition with $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0$, and fix an
integer $k$ with $0\le k<\dim V$. Define

$$T_kv:=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(k,r)} s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j.$$

Then $\operatorname{rank}T_k\le k$, one has

$$\lVert T-T_k\rVert=s_{k+1}$$

with the convention $s_{k+1}=0$ when $k\ge r$, and every linear map
$A:V\to W$ with $\operatorname{rank}A\le k$ satisfies

$$\lVert T-A\rVert\ge s_{k+1}.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. Then $\operatorname{rank} T$ equals the number of positive
singular values of $T$.

Save the input as $C_0=C$ and initialize $U=I_M$, $V=I_p$, and empty ordered lists of stored local left and right transformations. For $k=1,\ldots,p$, in this order:

1. Let $x=C_{k:M,k}$. If $x=0$, use the identity left transformation. Otherwise choose $\phi=x_1/|x_1|$ when $x_1\ne0$ and $\phi=1$ when $x_1=0$, set $\alpha=-\phi\|x\|_2$, $v=x-\alpha e_1$, and $h=v/\|v\|_2$. Use the Householder reflector $H=I-2hh^*$ on rows $k:M$. Update $C\leftarrow H^*C$ on those rows and append this local transformation to the left list. In exact arithmetic update $U\leftarrow U\operatorname{diag}(I_{k-1},H)$. In finite precision update columns $k:M$ of the dense accumulator $U$ by right application of the same stored local reflector data, using the separate-block branch of [[alg-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-updates]] and making no target-zero write to $U$.

A finite-precision implementation uses the same branches, tests finiteness after each operation, and returns `range-failure` if a required quantity is nonfinite.

1. If $A$ is not full column rank, return `rank-deficient-input`. Otherwise initialize a column permutation $\Pi$ and the full column-pivoted QR factorization $A\Pi=QR$, where $Q\in\mathbb F^{m\times m}$ is unitary and $R\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ is upper trapezoidal, using the greedy residual-norm pivot convention. Partition $R=\begin{bmatrix}R_{11}&R_{12}\\0&R_{22}\end{bmatrix}$ after the first $k$ rows and columns. Do not return the reduced QR form. The selected first $k$ columns then have a nonsingular leading block. For $k=0$, return this full factorization with `success`.
2. For $k>0$, refactor the current fixed column order in the full QR form, without further pivoting whenever needed, using unitary Householder or Givens transformations. If the selected leading block is singular, return `singular-selected-block`.
3. Form $X=R_{11}^{-1}R_{12}$. For $1\le i\le k$ let $\omega_i=\|e_i^*R_{11}^{-1}\|_2$; for $1\le j\le n-k$ let $\gamma_j=\|R_{22}(:,j)\|_2$. Define the swap score $s_{ij}=\bigl(|X_{ij}|^2+(\omega_i\gamma_j)^2\bigr)^{1/2}$.
4. If $\max_{i,j}|X_{ij}|>f$, choose the lexicographically first pair attaining the largest $|X_{ij}|$. Otherwise, if $\max_{i,j}s_{ij}>f$, choose the lexicographically first pair attaining the largest score. If neither inequality holds, return `success` and the factors, permutation, $X$, and maximum score. The first branch retains the usual coefficient-triggered swap; the second controls the trailing residual needed for the strong spectral comparison.
5. When a violating pair was chosen, if the swap count is already $S$, return `swap-budget-exhausted` with the current partial factors. Otherwise interchange the chosen selected and trailing columns, restore triangular form with Givens rotations, increment the swap count, and return to step 2. Thus a cap $S\ge\binom nk-1$ is sufficient in exact arithmetic whenever the input is full column rank.

Write the diagonal as $d_i$ and superdiagonal as $e_i$, and set $e_0=0$.

The zero entries split the active blocks. If every active block has size one, stop with `converged`. Otherwise process the active blocks in increasing order of $\ell$, skipping singleton blocks. Let $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$.

1. Every Householder reflector $H_v=I-2vv^*$ is orthogonal or unitary.
2. For every nonzero $z\in \mathbb F^m$, there is a Householder reflector $H$
   such that $Hz=\alpha e_1$ with $|\alpha|=\|z\|_2$.
3. For every pair $(a,b)\in \mathbb F^2$ not both zero, there is a real or

   $$G\binom{a}{b}=\binom{\alpha}{0}$$

derivations.claim: The first right rotation acts on the leading adjacent column pair of the active block and creates at most the first subdiagonal bulge. Each left rotation annihilates the current subdiagonal entry; because it mixes only two adjacent rows, it can create at most the next second-superdiagonal bulge. The following right rotation mixes only the adjacent columns supporting that bulge, annihilates it, and creates at most the next subdiagonal bulge. Induction along the block therefore keeps one bulge at a time and removes it at the next alternating rotation. The zero coupling at a deflated block endpoint prevents a bulge from leaving the block, so the final matrix is upper bidiagonal.

Every right operation multiplies on the right by a unitary Givens factor and every left operation multiplies on the left by the adjoint of a unitary Givens factor. Their products therefore give unitary $U_s,V_s$ and the final matrix is exactly $U_s^*BV_s$.

Left and right unitary factors preserve singular values, since $(U_s^*(B+E_D)V_s)^*(U_s^*(B+E_D)V_s)=V_s^*(B+E_D)^*(B+E_D)V_s$ is unitarily similar to $(B+E_D)^*(B+E_D)$. Deflation occurs before the sweep rotations, and setting each listed superdiagonal entry to zero adds exactly its negative there; hence the matrix entering the unitary sweep is $B+E_D$. With no deflation $E_D=0$, so step 1.2 gives equal singular values for $B_+$ and $B$.

Input a real or complex matrix $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ with $m\ge n$, a target $k$ with $0\le k<n$, a factor $f\ge1$, and a finite swap cap $S\in\mathbb N\cup\{0\}$. The exact-arithmetic version is specified below. A finite-precision implementation uses the same branches, tests finiteness after each operation, and returns `range-failure` if a required quantity is nonfinite.

1. If $A$ is not full column rank, return `rank-deficient-input`. Otherwise initialize a column permutation $\Pi$ and the full column-pivoted QR factorization $A\Pi=QR$, where $Q\in\mathbb F^{m\times m}$ is unitary and $R\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ is upper trapezoidal, using the greedy residual-norm pivot convention. Partition $R=\begin{bmatrix}R_{11}&R_{12}\\0&R_{22}\end{bmatrix}$ after the first $k$ rows and columns. Do not return the reduced QR form. The selected first $k$ columns then have a nonsingular leading block. For $k=0$, return this full factorization with `success`.
2. For $k>0$, refactor the current fixed column order in the full QR form, without further pivoting whenever needed, using unitary Householder or Givens transformations. If the selected leading block is singular, return `singular-selected-block`.
3. Form $X=R_{11}^{-1}R_{12}$. For $1\le i\le k$ let $\omega_i=\|e_i^*R_{11}^{-1}\|_2$; for $1\le j\le n-k$ let $\gamma_j=\|R_{22}(:,j)\|_2$. Define the swap score $s_{ij}=\bigl(|X_{ij}|^2+(\omega_i\gamma_j)^2\bigr)^{1/2}$.
4. If $\max_{i,j}|X_{ij}|>f$, choose the lexicographically first pair attaining the largest $|X_{ij}|$. Otherwise, if $\max_{i,j}s_{ij}>f$, choose the lexicographically first pair attaining the largest score. If neither inequality holds, return `success` and the factors, permutation, $X$, and maximum score. The first branch retains the usual coefficient-triggered swap; the second controls the trailing residual needed for the strong spectral comparison.
5. When a violating pair was chosen, if the swap count is already $S$, return `swap-budget-exhausted` with the current partial factors. Otherwise interchange the chosen selected and trailing columns, restore triangular form with Givens rotations, increment the swap count, and return to step 2. Thus a cap $S\ge\binom nk-1$ is sufficient in exact arithmetic whenever the input is full column rank.

The statuses are `success`, `rank-deficient-input`, `singular-selected-block`, `swap-budget-exhausted`, and `range-failure`. In particular, ordinary column-pivoted QR is only the initialization: the procedure does not assert that its output alone satisfies the strong bounds. Both exact and finite-precision outputs use the full factor shape; exact-arithmetic success satisfies the singular-value comparison theorem. A finite-precision `success` is a candidate until the following certificate is verified. Retain the ordered local transformation data representing an exact unitary product $W$ separately from the rounded dense $Q$. Let $\widehat R$ denote the returned upper trapezoidal matrix. A certificate consists of a nonsingular $\widehat R_{11}$, rigorous upper bounds $b_{ij}$ on the exact real numbers $\bigl(|(\widehat R_{11}^{-1}\widehat R_{12})_{ij}|^2+\|e_i^*\widehat R_{11}^{-1}\|_2^2\|\widehat R_{22}(:,j)\|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}$, and $\varepsilon\ge0$ with $\|A\Pi-W\widehat R\|_2\le\varepsilon$. All $b_{ij}\le f$ are required. For $k=0$ there are no score or inverse conditions. The bounds must account for arithmetic and input representation; ordinary rounded score and residual evaluations do not constitute this certificate. Exact arithmetic on represented data or validated outward enclosures may establish it. If certification is unavailable or a bound exceeds its threshold, report `uncertified` for the certificate, retaining the algorithm status and all candidate outputs. A verified certificate gives the residual-adjusted comparisons for the returned blocks even if swaps were stopped by the budget.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ have full column rank, $m\ge n$, and let $A\Pi=QR$ be a full QR factorization, with $Q\in\mathbb F^{m\times m}$ unitary and $R\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ upper trapezoidal. Partition $R=\begin{bmatrix}R_{11}&R_{12}\\0&R_{22}\end{bmatrix}$ after the first $k$ rows and columns, where $R_{11}\in\mathbb F^{k\times k}$ is nonsingular and $1\le k<n$. Write $X=R_{11}^{-1}R_{12}$, $\omega_i=\|e_i^*R_{11}^{-1}\|_2$, and $\gamma_j=\|R_{22}(:,j)\|_2$. Let $J$ be the selected set of $k$ columns and define its volume by $\operatorname{vol}(A(:,J))=\det(A(:,J)^*A(:,J))^{1/2}$. Replacing selected column $i$ by trailing column $j$ changes this volume by the factor
$$\frac{\operatorname{vol}(A(:,(J\setminus\{i\})\cup\{j\}))}{\operatorname{vol}(A(:,J))}=\bigl(|X_{ij}|^2+(\omega_i\gamma_j)^2\bigr)^{1/2}.$$

derivations.claim: If $k=0$, the algorithm's first branch returns `success` without a swap. Assume $1\le k<n$. Every accepted swap has score strictly greater than $f\ge1$. By [F2] it multiplies the selected volume by a factor strictly greater than one. Thus the selected volume strictly increases at each swap, so no selected subset can recur because its volume is determined by the fixed input matrix and subset.

For $1\le k<n$, there are exactly $\binom nk$ possible selected $k$-column subsets. The initial subset has positive volume by full column rank, and by step 1.1 no subset can recur after a strict increase. If $\binom nk-1$ swaps have occurred, all $\binom nk$ subsets have therefore been visited; a remaining violation would prescribe another swap to an already visited subset, contradicting step 1.1. Thus a cap at least $\binom nk-1$ cannot be reached with a violation remaining, and the algorithm returns success.

For $k=0$ the coefficient assertion is vacuous. For $1\le k<n$, success gives $s_{ij}\le f$ for all pairs. Since $|X_{ij}|\le s_{ij}$ by the score definition, $\max_{i,j}|X_{ij}|\le f$. If a smaller cap is reached while a violation remains, the algorithm returns `swap-budget-exhausted`; if no violation remains first, it returns success.

Each Givens factor is chosen using [[def-real-and-complex-givens-transformations]] and its annihilation guarantee in [[thm-householder-reflectors-and-givens-transformations-are-unitary-and-annihilate-targeted-entries]].

After each processed block, increment $s$ by one. Once all current active blocks have been processed, start a new pass. If any operation, norm or pivot is invalid or nonfinite, or a nonzero exact intermediate is outside the normal range, return `range-failure` with the partial $B$, accumulators, transformation lists, deflation record, and available residual reports. On `budget-exhausted`, return the current $B$, diagonal candidates, accumulators, transformation lists, deflation record, triplet residuals, and orthogonality residuals. On `converged`, return $B_{final}$ (diagonal), the candidate singular values obtained by the scaled two-component modulus evaluation of its diagonal entries (real absolute value is exact), both dense accumulators, both transformation lists, the deflation record, and triplet/orthogonality residuals; also return its tall embedding $\overline B_{final}=\begin{bmatrix}B_{final}\\0_{M-p,p}\end{bmatrix}$. In finite precision form each dense product by row-by-column multiplication, with six-real-operation complex products and sequential componentwise rounded additions under the operationwise model; return `range-failure` if any required intermediate is invalid, nonfinite, or outside the normal range. Their exact theoretical factors are the products represented by the ordered local transformation lists together with the bidiagonal-reduction lists. If $m\ge n$, set $\widehat U=U_C$ and $\widehat V=V_C$; for each nonzero diagonal entry $d_i$ of $B_{final}$, multiply column $i$ of $\widehat U$ by $d_i/|d_i|$ in exact arithmetic, using componentwise division by the successful scaled modulus readout in finite precision. If $m<n$, set $\widehat U=V_C$ and $\widehat V=U_C$; in this wide orientation multiply column $i$ of $\widehat V$ by $d_i/|d_i|$ instead. This phase placement makes the exact singular-value factorization nonnegative in both orientations and keeps the left/right vector dimensions correct. Sort the candidate values in nonincreasing order, breaking ties by their original diagonal index, and permute the corresponding columns of the returned triplet vectors in the same way; leave $B_{final}$ and the transformation lists in their algorithmic order. For every candidate triplet $(\widehat\sigma_i,\widehat u_i,\widehat v_i)$, report $\|A\widehat v_i-\widehat\sigma_i\widehat u_i\|_2$ and $\|A^*\widehat u_i-\widehat\sigma_i\widehat v_i\|_2$. Matrix residuals use the Frobenius norm defined in [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]. Any additional sparsity cleanup is recorded separately in the deflation record with its discarded-entry perturbation.

For $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, the exact-arithmetic algorithm [[alg-householder-bidiagonalization]] returns unitary $U,V$ and an upper bidiagonal $B\in\mathbb F^{p\times p}$, $p=\min(m,n)$, such that if $m\ge n$ then $U^*AV=\begin{bmatrix}B\\0\end{bmatrix}$, and if $m<n$ then $U^*A^*V=\begin{bmatrix}B\\0\end{bmatrix}$.

Consider one exact-arithmetic sweep of [[alg-implicit-shifted-bidiagonal-qr-with-deflation]] on an unreduced upper bidiagonal block, with no nonzero deflation. If its right rotations have product $V_s$ and its left rotations have product $U_s$, the restored bidiagonal block is $B_+=U_s^*BV_s$. Consequently $B_+$ and $B$ have the same singular values. If a set $D$ of superdiagonal entries is deflated, then the transformed output instead equals the corresponding unitary transform of $B+E_D$, where $E_D$ has those entries negated and all other entries zero.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Use [[alg-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-updates]] successfully, with $0<u<1$ and $(r-1)u<1$ for every Householder dimension $r$. For a nonzero Householder column define
$$e=(1+u)^{r+3}-1,\quad a_\phi=\frac{1+u}{(1-u)^4}-1,\quad a_\alpha=(1+a_\phi)(1+e)(1+u)-1,\quad d_v=a_\alpha+u(2+a_\alpha),$$
$$a_\tau=\frac{1+u}{(1-u)^{2r}}-1,\quad g=\frac{1+6u}{1-(r-1)u}-1,\quad c_U=2\bigl((1+a_\tau)(1+u)(1+6u)(1+g)-1\bigr),$$
$$\eta_H(r)=\max\{a_\alpha+8d_v,(1+u)c_U+3u\}.$$
For a Givens step define
$$a_2=\frac{1+u}{(1-u)^2}-1,\quad q=\max\left\{\left(\frac{1+u}{1-u}\right)^3-1,\frac{(1+a_2)(1+6u)(1+u)}{(1-u)^3}-1\right\},$$
$$\epsilon=\sqrt2(7u+6u^2)(1+q),\quad v=q+\epsilon,\quad \eta_G=2v+u+2q.$$
Each complete left update, including its target zero write, has an exact unitary representative $W$ and perturbation $E$ with
$$W(C+E)=C_+,\qquad \|E\|_F\le\eta\|C\|_F,$$
where $\eta=\eta_H(r)$ or $\eta_G$. Identity branches have $E=0$. The corresponding right relation follows by conjugate transposition. For a Givens application without an annihilation overwrite use the smaller coefficient $v$; for a Householder separate-block application use $(1+u)c_U+3u$. All coefficients are explicit and $O(ru)$ or $O(u)$ for fixed dimensions.

derivations.claim: Iterating the norm inequality from [A1] gives $\|C_j\|_F\le(1+\eta_j)\|C_{j-1}\|_F+\delta_j$. Induction from $C_0$ yields $\|C_j\|_F\le\left(\prod_{r=1}^j(1+\eta_r)\right)\|C_0\|_F+\sum_{r=1}^j\delta_r\prod_{s=r+1}^j(1+\eta_s)$: the base case $j=0$ is equality, and the one-step inequality multiplies every prior term by $1+\eta_j$ and adds $\delta_j$.

The original-input perturbation is the sum of each $E_j$ and each $D_j$ transported by products of later unitary factors. Unitary left/right multiplication preserves Frobenius norm, so $\|E\|_F\le\sum_{j=1}^J\eta_j\|C_{j-1}\|_F+\sum_{j=1}^J\delta_j$. Substitute step 1.1. For the $C_0$ terms, $\sum_j\eta_j\prod_{r<j}(1+\eta_r)=\prod_r(1+\eta_r)-1$. For a fixed $\delta_i$, its contribution is $\delta_i\left(1+\sum_{j>i}\eta_j\prod_{i<r<j}(1+\eta_r)\right)=\delta_i\prod_{r>i}(1+\eta_r)$. These identities give the stated bound.

The same coordinate unwinding gives $C_J= L^*(C_0+E)R$ for products $L,R$ of the unitary update factors, hence $C_0+E=L C_JR^*$. Step 2.1 gives its error bound; setting every $\delta_j=0$ gives the no-deflation case.

product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ have singular value decomposition
$A=U\Sigma V^*$, and let $\tau\ge0$ be a declared threshold. The
**truncated singular-value pseudoinverse at threshold $\tau$** is

$$ A_\tau^+ := V\Sigma_\tau^+U^*, $$

where $\Sigma_\tau^+\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is the transposed-shape
diagonal matrix whose $i$th diagonal entry is $\sigma_i^{-1}$ when
$\sigma_i>\tau$ and is $0$ when $\sigma_i\le\tau$; every off-diagonal entry is
$0$.

The threshold is part of the definition, exactly as in
[[def-numerical-rank-relative-to-a-norm-scale-and-tolerance]]: changing
$\tau$ changes which singular directions are retained.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and let $b\in\mathbb F^m$. Then $A^+b$ is
a least-squares solution of $Ax=b$, and among all least-squares solutions it
is the unique one of minimum Euclidean norm.

product spaces, let

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

be a singular value decomposition with $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0$, and fix an
integer $k$ with $0\le k<\dim V$. Define

$$T_kv:=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(k,r)} s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j.$$

Then $\operatorname{rank}T_k\le k$, one has

$$\lVert T-T_k\rVert=s_{k+1}$$

with the convention $s_{k+1}=0$ when $k\ge r$, and every linear map
$A:V\to W$ with $\operatorname{rank}A\le k$ satisfies

$$\lVert T-A\rVert\ge s_{k+1}.$$

$$\operatorname{rank}_\tau(A)=\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}:\sigma_i(A)>\tau\}.$$

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. A matrix $B\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is a
**Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse** of $A$ when

$$ABA=A,\qquad BAB=B,$$

and the two square products are self-adjoint:

$$ (AB)^*=AB,\qquad (BA)^*=BA. $$

When such a matrix exists and is unique, it is denoted by $A^+$.

The four displayed relations are the **Penrose equations**. They are written in
the matrix product and adjoint conventions of
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] and
[[thm-matrix-of-the-adjoint-is-the-conjugate-transpose]].

For every matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or
$\mathbb C$, there exists a unique matrix $A^+\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$
satisfying the four Penrose equations of
[[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

derivations.claim: Let $I=\{i\le p:\sigma_i>\tau\}$. By [F1]–[F2], $A_\tau=\sum_{i\in I}\sigma_i u_i v_i^*$ and $A_\tau^+=\sum_{i\in I}\sigma_i^{-1}v_i u_i^*$. Orthonormality gives $A_\tau A_\tau^+=\sum_{i\in I}u_i u_i^*$ and $A_\tau^+A_\tau=\sum_{i\in I}v_i v_i^*$, which are self-adjoint. Using $u_i^*u_j=v_i^*v_j=\delta_{ij}$ in those sums verifies the two Penrose product equations. Together with self-adjointness, these are the four equations; by [F6], $A_\tau^+$ is the unique Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse of $A_\tau$. The calculation includes $I=\varnothing$, when both matrices and sums are zero.
By [F5], $q$ is the spectral numerical rank retained by the strict threshold. The SVD truncation and [F4] give $\|A-A_\tau\|_2=\sigma_{q+1}\le\tau$; when $q=p$, the tail is zero.
Apply [F3] to $M=A_\tau$. Its unique minimum-norm least-squares solution is $A_\tau^+b=x_\tau$, proving the truncated-model claim.
By [F7], $\|(A-A_\tau)x_\tau\|_2\le\|A-A_\tau\|_2\|x_\tau\|_2$; [F8] gives $\|Ax_\tau-b\|_2\le\|A_\tau x_\tau-b\|_2+\|(A-A_\tau)x_\tau\|_2$. Combining with step 1.2 proves the stated residual bound.

Steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 2.2, and 3.1 prove all stated claims and the limitation.

If two finite lists differ coordinatewise by at most $\epsilon$, their ordered lists do too: otherwise at the violating rank the count of entries above or below the corresponding threshold contradicts the coordinatewise bounds. Apply this to the diagonal magnitudes and combine with step 2.1. For exact readout $\widehat\sigma_i=s_i$ the first bound follows already from step 2.1; for rounded readout the additional modulus allowance gives the stated extension. Real sign removal is exact.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ with $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$
and $m\ge n$.

A **full QR factorisation** of $A$ is a factorisation

$$A=QR,$$where $Q\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ is orthogonal or unitary and $R\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ is upper trapezoidal. A **reduced QR factorisation** is a factorisation$$A=\widehat Q\widehat R,$$where $\widehat Q\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ has orthonormal columns ($\widehat Q^*\widehat Q=I_n$) and $\widehat R\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ is upper triangular. A **column-pivoted QR factorisation** is a factorisation$$A\Pi=\widehat Q R,$$

where $\Pi$ is a permutation matrix acting on columns, $\widehat Q$ has
orthonormal columns, and $R$ is upper trapezoidal or upper triangular according
to whether the full or reduced form is used. Computationally, one obtains these
factorisations by successive Householder reflectors or Givens transformations
that zero entries below the diagonal, with the pivoted version choosing the next
column after a permutation.

Input a real or complex matrix $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ with $m\ge n$, a target $k$ with $0\le k<n$, a factor $f\ge1$, and a finite swap cap $S\in\mathbb N\cup\{0\}$. The exact-arithmetic version is specified below. A finite-precision implementation uses the same branches, tests finiteness after each operation, and returns `range-failure` if a required quantity is nonfinite.

1. If $A$ is not full column rank, return `rank-deficient-input`. Otherwise initialize a column permutation $\Pi$ and the full column-pivoted QR factorization $A\Pi=QR$, where $Q\in\mathbb F^{m\times m}$ is unitary and $R\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ is upper trapezoidal, using the greedy residual-norm pivot convention. Partition $R=\begin{bmatrix}R_{11}&R_{12}\\0&R_{22}\end{bmatrix}$ after the first $k$ rows and columns. Do not return the reduced QR form. The selected first $k$ columns then have a nonsingular leading block. For $k=0$, return this full factorization with `success`.
2. For $k>0$, refactor the current fixed column order in the full QR form, without further pivoting whenever needed, using unitary Householder or Givens transformations. If the selected leading block is singular, return `singular-selected-block`.
3. Form $X=R_{11}^{-1}R_{12}$. For $1\le i\le k$ let $\omega_i=\|e_i^*R_{11}^{-1}\|_2$; for $1\le j\le n-k$ let $\gamma_j=\|R_{22}(:,j)\|_2$. Define the swap score $s_{ij}=\bigl(|X_{ij}|^2+(\omega_i\gamma_j)^2\bigr)^{1/2}$.
4. If $\max_{i,j}|X_{ij}|>f$, choose the lexicographically first pair attaining the largest $|X_{ij}|$. Otherwise, if $\max_{i,j}s_{ij}>f$, choose the lexicographically first pair attaining the largest score. If neither inequality holds, return `success` and the factors, permutation, $X$, and maximum score. The first branch retains the usual coefficient-triggered swap; the second controls the trailing residual needed for the strong spectral comparison.
5. When a violating pair was chosen, if the swap count is already $S$, return `swap-budget-exhausted` with the current partial factors. Otherwise interchange the chosen selected and trailing columns, restore triangular form with Givens rotations, increment the swap count, and return to step 2. Thus a cap $S\ge\binom nk-1$ is sufficient in exact arithmetic whenever the input is full column rank.

The statuses are `success`, `rank-deficient-input`, `singular-selected-block`, `swap-budget-exhausted`, and `range-failure`. In particular, ordinary column-pivoted QR is only the initialization: the procedure does not assert that its output alone satisfies the strong bounds. Both exact and finite-precision outputs use the full factor shape; exact-arithmetic success satisfies the singular-value comparison theorem. A finite-precision `success` is a candidate until the following certificate is verified. Retain the ordered local transformation data representing an exact unitary product $W$ separately from the rounded dense $Q$. Let $\widehat R$ denote the returned upper trapezoidal matrix. A certificate consists of a nonsingular $\widehat R_{11}$, rigorous upper bounds $b_{ij}$ on the exact real numbers $\bigl(|(\widehat R_{11}^{-1}\widehat R_{12})_{ij}|^2+\|e_i^*\widehat R_{11}^{-1}\|_2^2\|\widehat R_{22}(:,j)\|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}$, and $\varepsilon\ge0$ with $\|A\Pi-W\widehat R\|_2\le\varepsilon$. All $b_{ij}\le f$ are required. For $k=0$ there are no score or inverse conditions. The bounds must account for arithmetic and input representation; ordinary rounded score and residual evaluations do not constitute this certificate. Exact arithmetic on represented data or validated outward enclosures may establish it. If certification is unavailable or a bound exceeds its threshold, report `uncertified` for the certificate, retaining the algorithm status and all candidate outputs. A verified certificate gives the residual-adjusted comparisons for the returned blocks even if swaps were stopped by the budget.

Let $n\ge1$, and let $B,\widetilde B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$ be upper bidiagonal, $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with $0\le\epsilon<1$. Suppose each corresponding nonzero diagonal or superdiagonal entry is multiplied by a scalar whose modulus lies in $[1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon]$, and every zero entry remains zero. Put $q=(1+\epsilon)/(1-\epsilon)$. Then $B$ and $\widetilde B$ have the same number of zero singular values, and for each positive singular value in descending order,
$$q^{-2n}\sigma_i(B)\le\sigma_i(\widetilde B)\le q^{2n}\sigma_i(B).$$

This is a relative perturbation theorem. A computed bidiagonal SVD inherits it only when a separate backward-error analysis verifies this componentwise relative assumption; an absolute normwise perturbation estimate by itself is not that verification.

equivalently, simultaneously for every $i$,

$$x_i^{(k+1)}=\frac{b_i-\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}x_j^{(k)}}{a_{ii}}.$$

derivations.claim: By [A1], every $a_{ii}\ne0$. Thus $D$ and the lower-triangular matrix $D-L$ have nonzero diagonal, so the solves in [F1] and [F2] are uniquely defined by [L2].
By [F1]–[F2] and [L3], the iteration matrices are $G_J=D^{-1}(L+U)$ and $G_G=(D-L)^{-1}U$.

For each row $i$, set $q_i=\sum_{j\ne i}|a_{ij}|/|a_{ii}|$ and $q_J=\max_i q_i<1$. Since $L_{ij}=-a_{ij}$ below the diagonal and $U_{ij}=-a_{ij}$ above it, $\sum_j|(G_J)_{ij}|=q_i$. Hence for any eigenpair $G_Jz=\lambda z$ with $z\ne0$, choose $i$ with $|z_i|=\max_j|z_j|$; the row equation gives $|\lambda||z_i|\le q_i|z_i|\le q_J|z_i|$, so $|\lambda|<1$ and $\rho(G_J)<1$.

Let $G_Gz=\lambda z$ with $z\ne0$, and choose $i$ with $|z_i|=\max_j|z_j|=:R$. The equation $Uz=\lambda(D-L)z$ in row $i$ is $\sum_{j>i}U_{ij}z_j=\lambda(a_{ii}z_i-\sum_{j<i}L_{ij}z_j)$, so $|\lambda|\,|a_{ii}z_i-\sum_{j<i}L_{ij}z_j| \le\sum_{j>i}|U_{ij}||z_j|$. By the reverse triangle inequality and [A1], the left factor is at least $|\lambda|(|a_{ii}|-\sum_{j<i}|a_{ij}|)R$, while the right side is at most $\sum_{j>i}|a_{ij}|R$. Therefore $|\lambda|\le\max_i\frac{\sum_{j>i}|a_{ij}|}{|a_{ii}|-\sum_{j<i}|a_{ij}|}<1$; the denominators are positive and each strict inequality follows from [A1]. Thus $\rho(G_G)<1$.
The bounds in steps 3.1 and 3.2 and [L4] imply that both methods converge to the unique solution of $Ax=b$ for every $b$ and every initial vector.

derivations.claim: If $n>1$ and $a_{ii}=0$, [A1] forces every off-diagonal entry in row $i$ to vanish, contradicting strong connectivity. If $n=1$, the strict-row hypothesis forces $|a_{11}|>0$. Hence every diagonal entry is nonzero, and the Jacobi and lower-triangular Gauss–Seidel solves are defined by [L5].

Define $C_{ii}=0$ and $C_{ij}=|a_{ij}|/|a_{ii}|$ for $i\ne j$. Its row sums are at most $1$, one is strictly below $1$, and its positive-entry graph is the graph in [A1]. By [L2], choose $v>0$ with $Cv<v$, and set $q_J=\max_i (Cv)_i/v_i<1$.

By [F1], $|G_J|=C$ entrywise. For $\|z\|_v:=\max_i |z_i|/v_i$, nonnegativity gives $|G_Jz|\le C|z|\le\|z\|_v Cv\le q_J\|z\|_v v$. Thus every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $G_J$ satisfies $|\lambda|\le q_J<1$, so $\rho(G_J)<1$.

Set $B_L=|D|^{-1}|L|$ and $B_U=|D|^{-1}|U|$. Then $C=B_L+B_U$, $B_L$ is strictly lower triangular, and $(I-B_L)^{-1}=\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}B_L^r\ge I$. Thus $H:=(I-B_L)^{-1}B_U=\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}B_L^rB_U\ge0$. Since $(I-B_L)v-B_Uv=(I-C)v>0$, multiplying by $(I-B_L)^{-1}\ge I$ gives $Hv<v$. Consequently $q_G:=\max_i(Hv)_i/v_i<1$.

Because $D-L=D(I-D^{-1}L)$ and $D^{-1}L$ is strictly lower triangular, $(D-L)^{-1}U=\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}(D^{-1}L)^rD^{-1}U$. Entrywise absolute values obey $|XY|\le|X||Y|$, so $|G_G|\le H$. The same weighted-vector estimate as in step 3.1 yields $\|G_Gz\|_v\le q_G\|z\|_v$; hence $\rho(G_G)<1$.
By [L3]–[L4], the two spectral-radius bounds imply convergence to the unique solution of $Ax=b$ for every right-hand side and every initial vector.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$

Let $T$ be an endomorphism of an $n$-dimensional vector space over $F$. If

$$\chi_T(x)=\prod_{i<n}(x-\lambda_i)$$

in $F[x]$, then $\det(T)=\prod_{i<n}\lambda_i$. Thus the determinant is the product of the eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F1], $M_\omega$ is lower triangular with diagonal $a_{ii}/\omega\ne0$, hence invertible by [L5]. Also $A=M_\omega-N_\omega$ by [L1], so [L2] applies with iteration matrix $G_\omega$. The matrix $N_\omega$ is upper triangular with diagonal entries $(\omega^{-1}-1)a_{ii}$. Thus [L6]–[L7] give $\det(M_\omega)=\omega^{-n}\prod_i a_{ii}$ and $\det(N_\omega)=(\omega^{-1}-1)^n\prod_i a_{ii}$. From $M_\omega G_\omega=N_\omega$ and multiplicativity, $\det(G_\omega)=\det(N_\omega)/\det(M_\omega)=(1-\omega)^n$.

For sufficiency, suppose $A$ is positive definite and $0<\omega<2$. Then $Q:=M_\omega+M_\omega^*-A=(2/\omega-1)D$ is positive definite. For an eigenpair $G_\omega v=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$, one has $\lambda\ne1$ since $Av=(1-\lambda)M_\omega v$ and $A$ is invertible. Put $a=v^*Av>0$. Then $v^*M_\omega v=a/(1-\lambda)$, so $v^*Qv=a\left(2\operatorname{Re}\frac{1}{1-\lambda}-1\right) =a\frac{1-|\lambda|^2}{|1-\lambda|^2}>0$. Therefore $|\lambda|<1$ for every eigenvalue and $\rho(G_\omega)<1$.

If SOR converges for every right-hand side and start, [L3] gives $\rho(G_\omega)<1$. By [L8]–[L9], $|\det(G_\omega)|=\prod_{j=1}^n|\lambda_j|\le\rho(G_\omega)^n<1$. Step 1.1 therefore gives $|1-\omega|<1$, which for real $\omega$ is equivalent to $0<\omega<2$.

Assume now that SOR converges for every right-hand side and start. Then $\rho(G_\omega)<1$ by [L3], so $1$ is not an eigenvalue of $G_\omega$ and $I-G_\omega$ is invertible. By [L2], $A=M_\omega(I-G_\omega)$ is invertible. For $b=0$, its unique solution is $x_*=0$. For arbitrary $e^{(0)}:=x^{(0)}$, set $e^{(k)}:=x^{(k)}-x_*=x^{(k)}$ and $\delta_k=e^{(k+1)}-e^{(k)}$. The homogeneous SOR recurrence gives $M_\omega e^{(k+1)}=N_\omega e^{(k)}$, hence $Ae^{(k)}+M_\omega\delta_k=0$. Expanding the Hermitian quadratic form gives $(e^{(k)})^*Ae^{(k)}-(e^{(k+1)})^*Ae^{(k+1)} =\delta_k^*(M_\omega+M_\omega^*-A)\delta_k =(2/\omega-1)\delta_k^*D\delta_k$. The last equality follows from [L1] and [F1].

By step 2.1, $c:=2/\omega-1>0$. Summing the identity in step 2.2 from $k=0$ to $N-1$ and taking $N\to\infty$ (the error tends to $0$ by the assumed convergence) gives $(e^{(0)})^*Ae^{(0)}=c\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\delta_k^*D\delta_k$. Moreover $\delta_0\ne0$: otherwise step 2.2 implies $Ae^{(0)}=0$, contrary to invertibility of $A$. Since $D$ has positive diagonal, the first summand is strictly positive and all others are nonnegative. Thus $(e^{(0)})^*Ae^{(0)}>0$ for every nonzero $e^{(0)}$, so [L4] gives that $A$ is positive definite.
By [L3], $\rho(G_\omega)<1$ implies convergence to the unique solution for every right-hand side and every initial vector. Steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove the reverse implication.

Input $n\ge1$, $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $b,x^{(0)}\in\mathbb C^n$, and an
iteration budget $m\in\mathbb N_0$. Check dimensions; on a mismatch return
`invalid-input`. Form $D,L,U$ by
[[def-diagonal-lower-upper-splitting-convention]]. If some diagonal entry of
$A$ is zero, return `pivot-failure(i)` for the least such index $i$.

Otherwise set $M=D$ and $N=L+U$, so $A=M-N$. For each
$k=0,\ldots,m-1$, compute the diagonal solve

$$D x^{(k+1)}=(L+U)x^{(k)}+b,$$

equivalently, simultaneously for every $i$,

$$x_i^{(k+1)}=\frac{b_i-\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}x_j^{(k)}}{a_{ii}}.$$

Return `completed` with $x^{(m)}$. The solve is the unique diagonal instance of
[[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]] when the pivot
check succeeds; [[thm-forward-and-back-substitution-are-correct-unique-and-quadratic-cost]]
gives its well-definedness. A zero budget returns $x^{(0)}$. The procedure
reports no convergence or accuracy certificate.

Let $n\ge1$ and $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ satisfy strict row diagonal
dominance:

$$|a_{ii}|>\sum_{j\ne i}|a_{ij}|\qquad(i=1,\ldots,n).$$

Then the Jacobi and fixed-order Gauss–Seidel iterations defined by
[[alg-jacobi-stationary-iteration]] and
[[alg-gauss-seidel-stationary-iteration]] converge in exact arithmetic to the
unique solution of $Ax=b$ for every $b,x^{(0)}\in\mathbb R^n$.

Input $n\ge1$, $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $b,x^{(0)}\in\mathbb C^n$, a real
relaxation parameter $\omega$, and an iteration budget $m\in\mathbb N_0$.
Check dimensions; on a mismatch return `invalid-input`. If $\omega=0$, return
`invalid-relaxation`. Form $D,L,U$ by
[[def-diagonal-lower-upper-splitting-convention]]. If some diagonal entry of
$A$ is zero, return `pivot-failure(i)` for the least such index $i$.

Otherwise set

$$M_\omega=\omega^{-1}D-L,\qquad N_\omega=(\omega^{-1}-1)D+U,$$

so $A=M_\omega-N_\omega$. For each $k=0,\ldots,m-1$, solve

$$M_\omega x^{(k+1)}=N_\omega x^{(k)}+b$$

by forward substitution in increasing index order. The lower-triangular
coefficient matrix has diagonal entries $a_{ii}/\omega$, which are nonzero
after the checks. Return `completed` with $x^{(m)}$. The solve is unique by
[[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]] and
[[thm-forward-and-back-substitution-are-correct-unique-and-quadratic-cost]].
A zero budget returns $x^{(0)}$. This procedure is defined for every real
$\omega\ne0$; it reports no convergence or accuracy certificate.

Let $n\ge1$, $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ be Hermitian with strictly positive
diagonal, and let $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$. Write
$A=D-L-L^*$ by [[def-diagonal-lower-upper-splitting-convention]], and define

$$M_\omega=\omega^{-1}D-L,\qquad N_\omega=(\omega^{-1}-1)D+L^*,\qquad G_\omega=M_\omega^{-1}N_\omega.$$

The SOR iteration is $x^{(k+1)}=G_\omega x^{(k)}+M_\omega^{-1}b$. It converges
to the unique solution of $Ax=b$ for every $b,x^{(0)}\in\mathbb C^n$ if and
only if $A$ is positive definite (meaning $x^*Ax>0$ for every nonzero $x$)
and $0<\omega<2$.

Let $n\ge 1$ and $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$; over $\mathbb R$ the same definition uses transpose
instead of conjugate transpose.

The matrix $A$ is **Hermitian positive definite** if $A=A^*$ and

$$x^*Ax>0$$for every nonzero vector $x\in \mathbb C^n$. A **Cholesky factorisation with positive diagonal** of $A$ is a factorisation$$A=LL^*,$$

where $L$ is lower triangular and every diagonal entry of $L$ is a positive real
number.

The Hermitian terminology matches
[[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]], and the
triangular terminology matches
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]].

Here $D=2I$, $L_{21}=1$, and $U=L^*$. By [F1], $M_\omega=\begin{pmatrix}4/3&0\\-1&4/3\end{pmatrix}$ and $N_\omega=\begin{pmatrix}-2/3&1\\0&-2/3\end{pmatrix}$, hence $G_\omega=M_\omega^{-1}N_\omega= \begin{pmatrix}-1/2&3/4\\-3/8&1/16\end{pmatrix}$. The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

derivations.claim: Define $h(u)=\sin u-u\cos u$. By [F1], [F2], and [F5], $h$ is differentiable and hence continuous, with $h'(u)=u\sin u\geq0$ on $(0,\pi/2)$ by [F4]. For $u>0$, the mean value theorem on $[0,u]$ gives $h(u)\geq h(0)=0$; at $u=0$ equality is immediate.

For $0<u<\pi/2$, define $r(u)=\sin u/u$. By the quotient rule, the identity derivative in [F5], and step 1.1, $r'(u)=(u\cos u-\sin u)/u^2=-h(u)/u^2\leq0$. The function $r$ is continuous on $[u,\pi/2]$ by [F5], so the mean value theorem gives $r(u)\geq r(\pi/2)=2/\pi$ by [F3] and [F4]; at $u=\pi/2$ equality holds. Multiplying by $u$ and checking $u=0$ proves the first inequality.

If $u\ne v$, sine is continuous on the closed interval between them and differentiable inside by [F1] and [F5]. The mean value theorem gives $|\sin u-\sin v|=|\cos c|\,|u-v|\leq|u-v|$ for some interior $c$, by [F3] and [F4]. If $u=v$, both sides are zero.

Let $C[-1,1]$ be the real continuous functions on $[-1,1]$, with
$\|f\|_\infty:=\sup_{x\in[-1,1]}|f(x)|$. Let $\mathcal P_n$ be the
restrictions to $[-1,1]$ of real polynomials of degree at most $n$, including
the zero polynomial. Interval notation is that of [[def-interval]]. Continuity and polynomial degree have the conventions of
[[def-continuity-real]] and
[[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]].

For each $n\in\mathbb N$ (with naturals in real expressions interpreted by
their canonical real images), the first-kind Chebyshev root angles and nodes are
$$\theta_j^{R,n}=\frac{(2j+1)\pi}{2n+2},\qquad x_j^{R,n}=\cos\theta_j^{R,n},\qquad 0\leq j\leq n.$$
They are the roots of $T_{n+1}$ by
[[thm-chebyshev-multiple-angle-identities]]. For $n\geq1$, the
Chebyshev–Lobatto angles and nodes are
$$\theta_j^{L,n}=\frac{j\pi}{n},\qquad x_j^{L,n}=\cos\theta_j^{L,n},\qquad 0\leq j\leq n.$$
They include both endpoints and are the extrema of $T_n$ by the same
identity. At $n=0$, define the Lobatto node to be $x_0^{L,0}=0$. The
cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$, so each listed family has
distinct nodes; the root family at $n=0$ also consists of $0$.

For either family $\sigma\in\{R,L\}$, write its nodes as
$x_0,\ldots,x_n$ and define
$$\ell_{j,n}^{\sigma}(x)= \prod_{\substack{0\leq k\leq n\\k\ne j}} \frac{x-x_k}{x_j-x_k},\qquad I_n^\sigma f=\sum_{j=0}^n f(x_j)\ell_{j,n}^{\sigma}.$$
These are the cardinal formula and interpolation sum of
[[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] specialized to this node family.
The displayed cosine arrays decrease, whereas that supplier orders nodes
increasingly: use $z_i=x_{n-i}$ and data $y_i=f(z_i)$. Its cardinal
function with index $n-j$ is exactly the displayed $\ell_{j,n}^\sigma$,
by reindexing the finite product, and its interpolation sum is $I_n^\sigma$.
The empty product at $n=0$ is $1$, so the same identification holds for the
single node. Distinctness makes every denominator nonzero;
[[lem-cardinal-basis-degree-and-values]] supplies the degree and cardinal
values. The finite sum is linear in the data and maps $C[-1,1]$ into
$\mathcal P_n$. Its operator norm is
$$\Lambda_n^\sigma:= \sup\{\|I_n^\sigma g\|_\infty:g\in C[-1,1],\ \|g\|_\infty\leq1\}.$$
If $\ell_{j,n}^\sigma(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n a_{jk}x^k$, then
$|\ell_{j,n}^\sigma(x)|\leq\sum_{k=0}^n|a_{jk}|$ for $|x|\leq1$; hence
$\|I_n^\sigma g\|_\infty\leq\sum_{j,k}|a_{jk}|<\infty$ whenever
$\|g\|_\infty\leq1$. Define the best degree-$n$ uniform
approximation error by
$$E_n(f):=\inf_{p\in\mathcal P_n}\|f-p\|_\infty .$$

These quantities are real and well-defined. Polynomial functions are
continuous, and sums and scalar multiples of continuous functions remain
continuous by [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]. The interval
$[-1,1]\subset\mathbb R$ is nonempty, closed, and bounded, so
[[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]] implies
that for every such continuous function $h$ there are finite minimum and
maximum values $m_h,M_h$. Since $m_h\leq h(x)\leq M_h$, one has
$|h(x)|\leq\max(|m_h|,|M_h|)$, so each supremum norm above is finite. The set defining $\Lambda_n^\sigma$ contains
the zero function and is bounded above by the displayed finite coefficient
sum. The set defining $E_n(f)$ contains the zero polynomial and is bounded
below by zero. Completeness of $\mathbb R$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]])
therefore gives the stated finite supremum and infimum. Also, $n+1$ has
positive real image by [[def-canonical-natural]] and
[[lem-of-naturals-positive]], and $n$ has positive real image when $n\geq1$;
thus the root-angle denominator and the Lobatto denominator in its stated
range are nonzero.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Then $I_n y$ from [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] is the unique real polynomial of degree at most $n$ satisfying $p(x_i)=y_i$ for every $i=0,\ldots,n$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Each cardinal function $\ell_j$ of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] is the evaluation of a formal polynomial of degree $n$. The node function $\omega_n$ is the evaluation of a monic formal polynomial of degree $n+1$, and $\omega_n(x)\ne0$ whenever $x$ differs from every node. The function $I_n y$ is the evaluation of a formal polynomial of degree at most $n$. At every pair $i,j\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, $\ell_j(x_i)=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise.

derivations.claim: Put $z_i=x_{n-i}$, so $z_0<\cdots<z_n$ by [F1]. Under this reverse indexing, the supplier cardinal function at index $n-j$ is $\ell_j$ by the specialization in [F1]. Applying [F3] gives its degree and cardinal values, including the one-node empty-product case $n=0$.

Prescribe data $y_i=1$ at $i=n-j$ and $0$ otherwise on the increasingly ordered nodes $z_i$ from step 1.1. The polynomial $\ell_j$ has these data by step 1.1. The supplier uniqueness theorem [F2] makes it the unique degree-at-most-$n$ polynomial with the required cardinal values.
Put $L(x)=\sum_j|\ell_{j,n}^\sigma(x)|$. For every $g$ with $\|g\|_\infty\leq1$, the defining sum gives $|I_n^\sigma g(x)|\leq L(x)$, hence $\Lambda_n^\sigma\leq\sup_xL(x)$.

Prescribe $y_i=p(z_i)$ on the ordered nodes in step 1.1. By [F1] and [F3], their cardinal sum is $I_n^\sigma p$ and has degree at most $n$. The polynomial $p$ itself interpolates those data, so the supplier uniqueness theorem [F2] gives $I_n^\sigma p=p$.

Fix $x$. Prescribe $\operatorname{sgn}(\ell_{j,n}^\sigma(x))$ at each node, with $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0$, sort nodes increasingly, interpolate these values linearly, and extend constantly to the interval endpoints. The resulting continuous $g_x$ has norm at most $1$ and $I_n^\sigma g_x(x)=L(x)$, so $\Lambda_n^\sigma\geq\|I_n^\sigma g_x\|_\infty\geq L(x)$. Taking the supremum in $x$ and using step 1.3 proves equality. For $n=0$ the same construction is constant on the one-node interval.

[[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]]. Associate to every
$P\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ an eventually zero coefficient sequence $(p_k)$:
use its displayed finite coefficient list and extend it by zeros when $P\ne0$,
and put $p_k=0$ for every $k$ when $P=0$. Do the same for $Q$, with coefficients
$(q_k)$. Define $P+Q$ coefficientwise and define $PQ$ by the convolution
coefficients
$$ (P+Q)_k=p_k+q_k,\qquad (PQ)_k=\sum_{j=0}^{k}p_jq_{k-j}. $$
using the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. In either construction, discard
trailing zero coefficients; if every coefficient is zero, the result is the zero
polynomial. Scalar multiplication and subtraction are the corresponding
coefficientwise operations. Thus these formulas define operations on the formal
coefficient-list objects, independently of evaluation.

Write $1=(1)$ and $X=(0,1)$, and define
$$ \Phi(P,Q):=(Q,2XQ-P)\qquad(P,Q\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}). $$
Apply [[thm-recursion]] to the set
$\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}\times\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$, first with initial value
$(1,X)$ and then with initial value $(1,2X)$, always using the function $\Phi$.
This gives unique pair sequences $H^T,H^U$. Define $T_n$ and $U_n$ to be the
first coordinates of $H^T_n$ and $H^U_n$, respectively. Since the first
coordinate of $\Phi(P,Q)$ is $Q$, the second coordinate of $H^T_n$ is

$$ T_0=1,\quad T_1=X,\quad T_{n+2}=2XT_{n+1}-T_n, $$

polynomials of the first and second kinds**.
