countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $\Omega=\varnothing$, then $v=0$ and the conclusion is immediate. Assume henceforth $\Omega\ne\varnothing$. Extend $v$ by zero to $\widetilde v$ on $\mathbb R^d$ and define $g_i$ to be its cellwise derivative on mesh cells and zero outside $\overline\Omega$. On each cell apply the simplex Green formula to $v\varphi e_i$ for an arbitrary $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$. Fact [F1] gives the cell identity. Interior facet terms cancel by [F2]; boundary facet terms vanish by the zero-boundary clause of [F2]. Summing the finitely many cell identities gives $$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\widetilde v\,\partial_i\varphi =-\int_{\mathbb R^d}g_i\varphi.$$ Both functions are in $L^p$, so [F7] gives $\widetilde v\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^d)$ with gradient $g$.

Put $d_\Omega(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^d\setminus\Omega)$, which is $1$-Lipschitz. Choose a smooth scalar step $\theta$ with $\theta(s)=0$ for $s\le1$, $\theta(s)=1$ for $s\ge2$, and $0\le\theta\le1$. For $\epsilon>0$ set $\zeta_\epsilon(x)=\theta(d_\Omega(x)/\epsilon)$ and convolve it with a nonnegative smooth mollifier of integral one supported in the ball of radius $\epsilon/4$, obtaining $\eta_\epsilon$. Then $\eta_\epsilon$ is smooth, supported in $\Omega$, equals zero where $d_\Omega\le3\epsilon/4$, equals one where $d_\Omega\ge9\epsilon/4$, and $\|\nabla\eta_\epsilon\|_\infty\le\|\theta'\|_\infty/\epsilon$. Since $\Omega$ is bounded, its support is compact in $\Omega$.

Let $M$ be the maximum of the cellwise suprema of $|\nabla v|$. Across every interior facet the polynomial traces agree; on every boundary facet they agree with zero. For a point $x$ in the mesh skeleton, its minimal mesh face is the unique mesh face whose relative interior contains $x$; the local star of that face means the union of the cells containing it. The incident simplicial cones in this star cut a small sphere about the face into a finite face-to-face triangulation of the local directions in $\Omega$. Within each connected component, top-dimensional pieces are connected by facet adjacency: perturb a path in that open component to avoid the finite union of codimension-two faces. At an interior point the direction set is the whole connected sphere, so matching traces make all incident polynomial values agree. At a boundary point every component has a boundary direction; following facet adjacencies reaches a boundary facet, where the polynomial value is zero, so all cell limits in that component are zero. Thus the cellwise continuous representatives and the exterior zero fit continuously on the whole finite polyhedral partition. Restrict this continuous function to any line segment. The segment is divided by the finitely many cell facets into finitely many intervals; on each cell interval its derivative along the segment has magnitude at most $M$, and on exterior intervals it is zero. Continuity at the interval endpoints then gives $|\widetilde v(x)-\widetilde v(y)|\le M|x-y|$ for all $x,y$. Thus $|v(x)|\le M\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^d\setminus\Omega)$.

The difference $v-\eta_\epsilon v$ and its weak gradient are supported in $E_\epsilon=\{x\in\Omega:d_\Omega(x)<9\epsilon/4\}$. On this layer, step 2.1 gives $|v|\le(9/4)M\epsilon$, and step 1.2 gives $|v\nabla\eta_\epsilon|\le(9/4)M\|\theta'\|_\infty$. Also $|\nabla v|\le M$. The sets $E_{1/n}$ decrease to the empty set and $|E_1|\le|\Omega|<\infty$, so [F5] gives $|E_{1/n}|\to0$. These bounds show $\|v-\eta_{1/n}v\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\to0$ for finite $p$.

Each $\eta_{1/n}v$ has compact support in $\Omega$. By [F5] extend it by zero to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^d)$ and approximate there by $\phi_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$. Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ equal to one near the compact support of $\eta_{1/n}v$. Then $\chi\phi_j\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and, by the weak product rule, $\chi\phi_j\to\eta_{1/n}v$ in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$. A diagonal choice with step 3.1 proves $v\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ by [F3].
A bounded set is bounded in some direction, so apply [F4] to the membership just proved. Its slab width is finite and gives the displayed Poincare inequality.

   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$

   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim: First take $u$ smooth. For $x,y\in\widehat S_d$, convexity keeps $z_t=tx+(1-t)y$ in the simplex. The segment identity and $|x-y|\le h:=\operatorname{diam}(\widehat S_d)$ give $$|u(x)-u(y)|^p\le h^p\int_0^1|\nabla u(tx+(1-t)y)|^p\,dt,$$ by [F2] and Jensen on the unit interval. Jensen again gives $$|u(x)-u_{\widehat S_d}|^p\le|\widehat S_d|^{-1} \int_{\widehat S_d}|u(x)-u(y)|^p\,dy.$$

Integrate the last bound over $x$. For $t\ge1/2$, fix $y$ and use $x\mapsto tx+(1-t)y$; its Jacobian is $t^d$, and its image is contained in the simplex, so its integral is at most $2^d\int_{\widehat S_d}|\nabla u|^p$. For $t\le1/2$, fix $x$ and use $y\mapsto tx+(1-t)y$, whose inverse Jacobian is at most $2^d$, giving the same bound. Tonelli [F3] therefore yields $$\|u-u_{\widehat S_d}\|_p^p\le2^dh^p\|\nabla u\|_p^p.$$ Taking $p$th roots proves the estimate for smooth $u$.

For arbitrary $u\in W^{1,p}$ choose smooth $u_j\to u$ in $W^{1,p}$ by [F1]. Holder on the finite-measure simplex gives $\int u_j\to\int u$, so $(u_j)_{\widehat S_d}\to u_{\widehat S_d}$; also $\|u_j-u\|_p\to0$ and $\|\nabla u_j\|_p\to\|\nabla u\|_p$. Passing to the limit in the smooth inequality of step 2.1 proves the statement.

derivations.claim: The monomials $x^\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\le r-1$ form a basis of $\mathbb P_{r-1}$. Thus if $N$ is the number of these multi-indices, then $N=\dim\mathbb P_{r-1}$. Define the linear moment map $M:\mathbb P_{r-1}\to\mathbb R^N$ by $M(q)_\alpha=|\widehat S_d|^{-1}\int_{\widehat S_d}D^\alpha q$. If every component is zero, take the largest degree $m$ of a nonzero homogeneous part of $q$. For each $|\alpha|=m$, $D^\alpha q$ is the constant $\alpha!$ times the coefficient of $x^\alpha$ in that highest homogeneous part; its zero mean forces that coefficient to vanish. This contradicts the choice of $m$. Repeating downward shows $q=0$, so $M$ is injective and, since its domain and codomain have the same finite dimension, bijective.

The vector of means of $D^\alpha v$, $|\alpha|\le r-1$, is defined because each derivative is in $L^p$ on the finite-measure simplex and therefore in $L^1$ by [F4]. By bijectivity in step 1.1 there is a unique $q\in\mathbb P_{r-1}$ with those moments. For $w=v-q$, each derivative $D^\alpha w$, $|\alpha|\le r-1$, has zero mean; and every derivative of $q$ of order at least $r$ is zero.

Apply [F1] to every mean-zero derivative of order $r-1$ in step 2.1; its $L^p$ norm is bounded by the $L^p$ norms of derivatives of order $r$ of $v$, since $D^r q=0$. Apply [F1] successively to derivatives of orders $r-2,r-3,\ldots,0$, each of which also has zero mean; at each stage its norm is bounded by the next derivative order already controlled. Thus all derivatives of $w$ of order at most $r$ are bounded by $C|v|_{W^{r,p}}$. If $s\le r$, retaining only orders through $s$ proves the first clause.

If $s>r$, the same argument controls all derivative orders at most $r-1$ by $C|v|_{W^{r,p}}$. For each $r\le|\beta|\le s$, $D^\beta w=D^\beta v$ because $D^\beta q=0$. Adding the finitely many derivative bounds through order $s$ gives $\|w\|_{W^{s,p}}\le C\sum_{j=r}^s|v|_{W^{j,p}}$, proving the second clause.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded open
reference cell, let $q\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. A **reference finite element** is a
triple $(\widehat K,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ where $\widehat P$ is an
$N$-dimensional subspace of $[C(\overline{\widehat K};\mathbb K)]^q$ for
$N\in\mathbb N_0$ and
$\widehat\Sigma=(\widehat\sigma_1,\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N)$ is a list of
linear functionals on $\widehat P$ for which
$$J_{\widehat\Sigma}:\widehat P\to\mathbb K^N,\qquad J_{\widehat\Sigma}(p):=(\widehat\sigma_1(p),\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N(p)),$$
is bijective. The functionals are the **degrees of freedom** and the triple
is **unisolvent**. Its **shape functions** are the unique dual basis
$\widehat\phi_1,\ldots,\widehat\phi_N\in\widehat P$ satisfying
$\widehat\sigma_i(\widehat\phi_j)=\delta_{ij}$.

If $X$ is a vector space of functions on $\widehat K$ containing
$\widehat P$ and each $\widehat\sigma_i$ has a well-defined bounded linear
extension to $X$, the associated **reference interpolation operator** is
$$\widehat I:X\to\widehat P,\qquad \widehat I v:=\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat\sigma_i(v)\widehat\phi_i.$$
The definition of a reference finite element does not assert that any
particular list of functionals is unisolvent or bounded on a given Sobolev
space; those are separate proof obligations. For $N=0$, $\widehat P=\{0\}$,
$\mathbb K^0=\{0\}$, the empty list gives the unique bijection between these
zero spaces, and the shape-function list is empty. The corresponding
interpolation formula is the empty sum, hence the zero map into $\{0\}$.

Let $(\widehat K,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ be a reference finite element
with $N=\dim\widehat P$, dual shape functions $\widehat\phi_i$, and bounded
extensions of its degrees of freedom to a function space $X$ containing
$\widehat P$. Then the operator
$$\widehat I v:=\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat\sigma_i(v)\widehat\phi_i$$
is the unique linear map $X\to\widehat P$ satisfying
$\widehat\sigma_i(\widehat I v)=\widehat\sigma_i(v)$ for every $i$, and
$\widehat I p=p$ for every $p\in\widehat P$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
$\widehat S_d$ be the reference simplex, let $\widehat P$ be a finite
dimensional $\mathbb K$-space of polynomial functions on it, let
$\widehat F$ be any facet, and let integer $m\ge0$. For $1\le p,q\le\infty$ there is a finite
constant $C$ such that
$$|v|_{W^{m,p}(\widehat S_d)}+\|v\|_{L^p(\widehat F)}\le C\|v\|_{L^q(\widehat S_d)}\qquad(v\in\widehat P).$$
For every pair of integers $0\le m\le\ell$, there is also a finite
constant $C$ such that
$$|v|_{W^{\ell,p}(\widehat S_d)} \le C|v|_{W^{m,q}(\widehat S_d)}\qquad(v\in\widehat P).$$
For finitely many facets, one constant works for all of them. In particular,
every linear degree-of-freedom functional on $\widehat P$ is bounded with
respect to the $L^q(\widehat S_d)$ norm.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1\le p<\infty$, integer $r\ge1$,
integer $s\ge0$, and real-valued $v\in W^{\max(r,s),p}(\widehat S_d)$.
There is a polynomial $q\in\mathbb P_{r-1}(\widehat S_d)$, chosen by
matching all means $\int_{\widehat S_d}D^\alpha q=
\int_{\widehat S_d}D^\alpha v$ for $|\alpha|\le r-1$, such that:

- if $0\le s\le r$, then
  $\|v-q\|_{W^{s,p}(\widehat S_d)}\le C|v|_{W^{r,p}(\widehat S_d)}$;
- if $s>r$, then
  $\|v-q\|_{W^{s,p}(\widehat S_d)}\le
  C\sum_{j=r}^{s}|v|_{W^{j,p}(\widehat S_d)}$.

The second clause assumes $v\in W^{s,p}$; constants depend only on
$d,p,r,s$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ be an affine bijection from a bounded open
set $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ to $K$, where $A$ is invertible, and let
$1\le p\le\infty$. For every integer $r\ge0$ and scalar
$v\in W^{r,p}(K)$, the pullback $\widehat v:=v\circ F$ belongs to
$W^{r,p}(\widehat K)$. For $r\ge1$ its first weak derivatives satisfy
$$D_{\widehat x_j}\widehat v=\sum_{i=1}^d A_{ij}(D_{x_i}v)\circ F,$$
and higher derivatives are obtained by applying this constant-matrix rule
repeatedly. In particular, for each $0\le m\le r$,
$$|\widehat v|_{W^{m,p}(\widehat K)}\le C(d,m)\|A\|^m|\det A|^{-1/p}|v|_{W^{m,p}(K)},$$
where $|\det A|^{-1/p}:=1$ for $p=\infty$. The reverse estimate holds
with $A^{-1}$ and $|\det A|^{1/p}$ in place of $A$ and
$|\det A|^{-1/p}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex
$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $N\in\mathbb N_0$, choose
$x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\overline{\widehat S_d}$, and let
$\ell\ge1$ be an integer. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $\ell>d/p$, then each
point evaluation has a unique continuous-representative value and
$$|u(x_j)|\le C\|u\|_{W^{\ell,p}(\widehat S_d)}.$$
If $p=\infty$, the same conclusion holds for every $\ell\ge1$.
Consequently any finite set of Lagrange nodal evaluations is bounded on
the stated Sobolev space and defines a well-defined degree-of-freedom
functional there. No boundedness at $\ell=d/p$ is asserted.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

derivations.claim: On the reference cell, write $\widehat Iw$ as the finite sum of its degree-of-freedom values times the dual shape functions. The assumed boundedness of each functional and [F2] bound $|\widehat Iw|_{W^{m,p}}\le C\|w\|_{W^{\ell,p}}$. For any reproduced $q$, linearity gives $$\widehat v-\widehat I\widehat v =(\widehat v-q)-\widehat I(\widehat v-q),$$ so $$|\widehat v-\widehat I\widehat v|_{W^{m,p}} \le|\widehat v-q|_{W^{m,p}}+C\|\widehat v-q\|_{W^{\ell,p}}.$$ For the automatic Lagrange application, under the additional Axiom of Choice, $d\ge2$, and $\ell>d/p$, [F6] verifies nodal-functional boundedness. For the generic estimate, boundedness is the explicit hypothesis, so this additional choice assumption is not used.

If $\ell\le r\le k+1$ and $\widehat v$ is real-valued, choose the
Bramble–Hilbert polynomial $q\in\mathbb P_{r-1}\subseteq\mathbb P_k$ from
[F3]. If $\widehat v$ is complex-valued, apply the first clause of [F3] to
$\operatorname{Re}\widehat v$ and $\operatorname{Im}\widehat v$ separately,
obtaining $q_R,q_I\in\mathbb P_{r-1}$, and set $q=q_R+iq_I$. In either
case $q$ is reproduced by $\widehat I$. Since $m\le r$ and $\ell\le r$,
[F3] bounds both terms in step 1.1 for the real case; for the complex case,
[F8] combines the two real estimates and changes only the constant. Thus
$|\widehat v-\widehat I\widehat v|_{W^{m,p}}\le
C|\widehat v|_{W^{r,p}}$.

If $\ell>k+1$ and $\widehat v$ is real-valued, choose the
Bramble–Hilbert polynomial $q\in\mathbb P_k$ from [F3]. If $\widehat v$ is
complex-valued, apply the second clause of [F3] with $r=k+1$, $s=\ell$ to
its real and imaginary parts, obtaining $q_R,q_I\in\mathbb P_k$, and set
$q=q_R+iq_I$. In either case $q$ is reproduced by $\widehat I$. Then [F3]
bounds the $W^{\ell,p}$ norm of $\widehat v-q$ by
$C\sum_{n=k+1}^{\ell}|\widehat v|_{W^{n,p}}$; because $m\le k+1<\ell$,
the same controls its $W^{m,p}$ norm. For complex $\widehat v$, [F8]
combines the component estimates with at most a fixed change in $C$. Step 1.1 gives $$|\widehat v-\widehat I\widehat v|_{W^{m,p}} \le
C\sum_{n=k+1}^{\ell}|\widehat v|_{W^{n,p}}.$$

For $\widehat v=v\circ F_K$, use [F4] to transform the physical error to the reference cell and the reference derivatives of $v$ back to the physical cell. The product of the two determinant factors cancels; the remaining matrix factors are bounded by $C\|A_K^{-1}\|^m\|A_K\|^r\le C h_K^{r-m}$ by [F5]. This gives the first physical estimate from step 2.1.

In the second case, apply the same transformation separately to each order $n$ in step 2.2. Its matrix factor is bounded by $C\|A_K^{-1}\|^m\|A_K\|^n\le C h_K^{n-m}$ by [F5]; summing over $k+1\le n\le\ell$ gives the second physical estimate. The constants in [F2]–[F7] are uniform over the fixed reference element and the shape-regular family, proving uniformity.

derivations.claim: For $\widehat v\in H(\operatorname{div},\widehat S_d)$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(K)$, put $\widehat\phi=\phi\circ F$. Then [F1] and the determinant substitution give $$\int_K(\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{div}}\widehat v)\cdot\nabla\phi\,dx =\int_{\widehat S_d}\widehat v\cdot\nabla\widehat\phi\,d\widehat x =-\int_{\widehat S_d}(\widehat{\operatorname{div}}\widehat v)\widehat\phi\,d\widehat x.$$ The final expression equals $-\int_K[(\det A)^{-1}\widehat{\operatorname{div}}\widehat v\circ F^{-1}]\phi\,dx$. This is the distributional divergence identity.

For smooth $\widehat v$, differentiate $v=A^{-T}\widehat v\circ F^{-1}$ componentwise. In three dimensions, write $C=A^{-1}$. For any $z\in\mathbb R^3$ and indices $m,\ell$, the scalar triple product gives $$z\cdot((C^Te_m)\times(C^Te_\ell)) =\det[z,C^Te_m,C^Te_\ell] =\det(C)\det[C^{-T}z,e_m,e_\ell] =\det(C)\,z\cdot(C^{-1}(e_m\times e_\ell)).$$ Since this holds for every $z$, comparing components yields $\epsilon_{ijk}C_{mj}C_{\ell k}=(\det A)^{-1}A_{ir}\epsilon_{rm\ell}$. The chain rule then gives $\operatorname{curl}_xv=(\det A)^{-1}A(\operatorname{curl}_{\widehat x}\widehat v)\circ F^{-1}$. In two dimensions write $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ and $\Delta=ad-bc>0$. Then $v_1=(d\widehat v_1-c\widehat v_2)/\Delta$, $v_2=(-b\widehat v_1+a\widehat v_2)/\Delta$, $\partial_{x_1}=(d\partial_{\widehat x_1}-c\partial_{\widehat x_2})/\Delta$, and $\partial_{x_2}=(-b\partial_{\widehat x_1}+a\partial_{\widehat x_2})/\Delta$. Substituting these four expressions and cancelling the two mixed terms gives $\partial_{x_1}v_2-\partial_{x_2}v_1 =(\det A)^{-1}(\partial_{\widehat x_1}\widehat v_2- \partial_{\widehat x_2}\widehat v_1)\circ F^{-1}$.

The physical field and candidate divergence in step 1.1 lie in $L^2(K)$: affine change of variables makes their squared norms finite constant multiples of the reference squared norms, and multiplication by the fixed matrix $A/(\det A)$ preserves finiteness. The test identity in step 1.1 therefore gives membership in $H(\operatorname{div},K)$ and the asserted divergence formula.

For $d=3$, take $\psi\in C_c^\infty(K;\mathbb R^3)$ and set $\widehat\psi=A^T(\psi\circ F)$. The component calculation in step 1.2 gives $\operatorname{curl}_{\widehat x}\widehat\psi= \det(A)A^{-1}(\operatorname{curl}_x\psi)\circ F$. Change variables and use the weak curl identity on the reference cell: $$\int_Kv\cdot\operatorname{curl}\psi\,dx =\int_{\widehat S_d}\widehat v\cdot\operatorname{curl}\widehat\psi\,d\widehat x =\int_{\widehat S_d}(\widehat{\operatorname{curl}}\widehat v)\cdot\widehat\psi\,d\widehat x =\int_K[(\det A)^{-1}A(\widehat{\operatorname{curl}}\widehat v)\circ F^{-1}]\cdot\psi\,dx.$$ For $d=2$, take $\phi\in C_c^\infty(K)$ and set $\widehat\phi=\phi\circ F$. The determinant identity $\det(A)\det(A^{-T}\widehat v,A^{-T}\nabla\widehat\phi) =\det(\widehat v,\nabla\widehat\phi)$ transforms the weak scalar-curl pairing into $\int_{\widehat S_d}(\widehat v_1\partial_2\widehat\phi- \widehat v_2\partial_1\widehat\phi)$, which by the weak reference curl identity equals $\int_{\widehat S_d}(\widehat{\operatorname{curl}}\widehat v)\widehat\phi$ and hence the pairing with the asserted physical scalar curl. In both dimensions the mapped field and candidate curl lie in $L^2$ by the fixed-matrix and determinant bounds. Thus the weak definition gives the claimed $H(\operatorname{curl})$ mapping.

Along an edge this equality is the line-form identity $v\cdot dx=\widehat v\cdot d\widehat x$. On a facet, integration against a pulled-back tangent vector and scalar weight gives $$\int_Fv\cdot(A\widehat\tau)(\widehat q\circ F^{-1})\,dS =\int_{\widehat F}(\widehat v\cdot\widehat\tau)\widehat qJ_F\,d\widehat S,$$ where $J_F$ is the affine facet surface Jacobian. The normal-flux moment with scalar weight $\widehat q$ equals $\int_{\widehat F}(\widehat v\cdot\widehat n)\widehat q\,d\widehat S$. The signs are those of the selected outward facet orientation; reversing it reverses the signed normal moment.

For $\widehat u\in W^{1,2}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)$, apply [F5] to $F^{-1}$. For each $i$,
$D_{x_i}(\widehat u\circ F^{-1})=\sum_j(A^{-1})_{ji}(D_{\widehat x_j}\widehat u)\circ F^{-1}.$
In vector notation this is
$\nabla_x(\widehat u\circ F^{-1})=A^{-T}(\widehat\nabla\widehat u)\circ F^{-1}=\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{curl}}(\widehat\nabla\widehat u),$
which proves the scalar-gradient identity.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d=2$ or $3$ and let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ map a reference
simplex to an affine cell with $\det A>0$. The contravariant Piola map
$\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{div}}\widehat v=(\det A)^{-1}A\widehat v\circ F^{-1}$
maps $H(\operatorname{div},\widehat S_d)$ into $H(\operatorname{div},K)$ and
$$\operatorname{div}(\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{div}}\widehat v) =(\det A)^{-1}(\widehat{\operatorname{div}}\widehat v)\circ F^{-1}.$$
The covariant Piola map
$\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{curl}}\widehat v=A^{-T}\widehat v\circ F^{-1}$
maps $H(\operatorname{curl},\widehat S_d)$ into $H(\operatorname{curl},K)$;
in $d=2$ its scalar curl is
$(\det A)^{-1}(\widehat{\operatorname{curl}}\widehat v)\circ F^{-1}$,
and in $d=3$ its vector curl is
$(\det A)^{-1}A(\widehat{\operatorname{curl}}\widehat v)\circ F^{-1}$.
For every $\widehat u\in W^{1,2}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)$, the scalar
pullback $u=\widehat u\circ F^{-1}$ belongs to $W^{1,2}(K;\mathbb R)$ and
its gradient satisfies
$$\nabla u=\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{curl}}(\widehat\nabla\widehat u).$$
For smooth fields, contravariant normal fluxes satisfy
$v\cdot n\,dS=\widehat v\cdot\widehat n\,d\widehat S$; covariant tangential
pullbacks satisfy $v(F(\widehat x))\cdot A\widehat\tau=
\widehat v(\widehat x)\cdot\widehat\tau$ for every reference tangent
$\widehat\tau$. Thus edge line integrals and normal-flux moments are
preserved, and face tangential moments transform with this pullback and
the induced facet surface Jacobian. These formulas record the chosen
orientation; reversing a facet orientation reverses its signed moment.

Let $(\widehat K,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ be a reference finite element
with $N=\dim\widehat P$, dual shape functions $\widehat\phi_i$, and bounded
extensions of its degrees of freedom to a function space $X$ containing
$\widehat P$. Then the operator
$$\widehat I v:=\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat\sigma_i(v)\widehat\phi_i$$
is the unique linear map $X\to\widehat P$ satisfying
$\widehat\sigma_i(\widehat I v)=\widehat\sigma_i(v)$ for every $i$, and
$\widehat I p=p$ for every $p\in\widehat P$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge2$. For every integer $k\ge0$ and
$1\le p\le\infty$, there is a bounded linear operator
$$E_{k,p}:W^{k,p}(\widehat S_d)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^d)$$
whose restriction to $\widehat S_d$ is the input class. Consequently
$\widehat S_d$ is a $W^{k,p}$-extension domain in the sense of
[[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]]. The operator may
be chosen with support in one fixed bounded set.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded open
reference cell, let $q\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. A **reference finite element** is a
triple $(\widehat K,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ where $\widehat P$ is an
$N$-dimensional subspace of $[C(\overline{\widehat K};\mathbb K)]^q$ for
$N\in\mathbb N_0$ and
$\widehat\Sigma=(\widehat\sigma_1,\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N)$ is a list of
linear functionals on $\widehat P$ for which
$$J_{\widehat\Sigma}:\widehat P\to\mathbb K^N,\qquad J_{\widehat\Sigma}(p):=(\widehat\sigma_1(p),\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N(p)),$$
is bijective. The functionals are the **degrees of freedom** and the triple
is **unisolvent**. Its **shape functions** are the unique dual basis
$\widehat\phi_1,\ldots,\widehat\phi_N\in\widehat P$ satisfying
$\widehat\sigma_i(\widehat\phi_j)=\delta_{ij}$.

If $X$ is a vector space of functions on $\widehat K$ containing
$\widehat P$ and each $\widehat\sigma_i$ has a well-defined bounded linear
extension to $X$, the associated **reference interpolation operator** is
$$\widehat I:X\to\widehat P,\qquad \widehat I v:=\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat\sigma_i(v)\widehat\phi_i.$$
The definition of a reference finite element does not assert that any
particular list of functionals is unisolvent or bounded on a given Sobolev
space; those are separate proof obligations. For $N=0$, $\widehat P=\{0\}$,
$\mathbb K^0=\{0\}$, the empty list gives the unique bijection between these
zero spaces, and the shape-function list is empty. The corresponding
interpolation formula is the empty sum, hence the zero map into $\{0\}$.

derivations.claim: Suppose $p<\infty$ and $\ell>d/p$. Then $\ell p>d$, so apply [F2] with $k=\ell$, $n=d$, and extension domain [F1]. It gives a continuous representative on the closed simplex and a bound for its supremum by $C\|u\|_{W^{\ell,p}}$. Two continuous representatives of the same almost-everywhere class agree everywhere: if their difference were nonzero at a point of the closed simplex, continuity on the closure and the fact that the simplex is the closure of its interior would give a nonempty interior ball on which the difference stays nonzero, contradicting almost-everywhere equality. Thus every $u(x_j)$ is uniquely defined and obeys the displayed bound.

If $p=\infty$, choose any finite $q>d$. Since the simplex has finite volume, [F4] gives $\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^q}\le|\widehat S_d|^{1/q}\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty}$ for $|\alpha|\le1$, so $W^{\ell,\infty}\subset W^{1,q}$ continuously. The same simplex extension result [F1] and embedding [F2], now with $k=1$ and $q>d$, give a unique continuous representative and the required bound by $\|u\|_{W^{\ell,\infty}}$. In either branch, [F5] identifies each evaluation with a bounded linear degree of freedom; finitely many nodes have a common bound by taking the maximum of their constants.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

derivations.claim: The first matrix is $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$, with determinant $6>0$. Applying it to the three vertices gives $(0,0),(2,0),(0,3)$. This is a right triangle with legs $2$ and $3$, so its area is $\frac12\cdot2\cdot3=3$.

The second matrix is $B=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$, with determinant $6>0$. Applying it to the square's vertices gives $(0,0),(2,0),(1,3),(3,3)$, whose opposite edges are parallel because they are translates of the two column vectors $(2,0)$ and $(1,3)$. Hence the image is a parallelogram with base length $2$ and altitude $3$, so its area is $2\cdot3=6$. It is an affine image of a square, not a simplicial cell.

derivations.claim: For an equilateral triangle with side $a=1/n$, its altitude is $\sqrt3a/2$, so its area is $\sqrt3a^2/4$ and its incenter lies one third of the altitude from each side; hence $\rho=\sqrt3a/6$. Its diameter is $h=a$, so $h/\rho=2\sqrt3$, independently of $n$. By [F1] this family is shape regular.

For $0<\epsilon\le1$, the sliver triangle's incenter joined to its three vertices partitions it into three triangles with common altitude $\rho_\epsilon$, so its area is $\rho_\epsilon$ times half its perimeter. Its side lengths are $1,\epsilon,\sqrt{1+\epsilon^2}$, its longest side is $h_\epsilon=\sqrt{1+\epsilon^2}$ and its area is $\epsilon/2$. Its perimeter is $1+\epsilon+\sqrt{1+\epsilon^2}$, so $$\rho_\epsilon= \frac{\epsilon}{1+\epsilon+\sqrt{1+\epsilon^2}}.$$ The numerator of $h_\epsilon/\rho_\epsilon$ tends to $1$, while its denominator is of order $\epsilon$; hence the ratio tends to infinity. The second triangle in each strip is congruent, so every cell has the same ratio. Thus no uniform shape-regularity constant exists for this fixed-square mesh family.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded open
reference cell, let $q\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. A **reference finite element** is a
triple $(\widehat K,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ where $\widehat P$ is an
$N$-dimensional subspace of $[C(\overline{\widehat K};\mathbb K)]^q$ for
$N\in\mathbb N_0$ and
$\widehat\Sigma=(\widehat\sigma_1,\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N)$ is a list of
linear functionals on $\widehat P$ for which
$$J_{\widehat\Sigma}:\widehat P\to\mathbb K^N,\qquad J_{\widehat\Sigma}(p):=(\widehat\sigma_1(p),\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N(p)),$$
is bijective. The functionals are the **degrees of freedom** and the triple
is **unisolvent**. Its **shape functions** are the unique dual basis
$\widehat\phi_1,\ldots,\widehat\phi_N\in\widehat P$ satisfying
$\widehat\sigma_i(\widehat\phi_j)=\delta_{ij}$.

If $X$ is a vector space of functions on $\widehat K$ containing
$\widehat P$ and each $\widehat\sigma_i$ has a well-defined bounded linear
extension to $X$, the associated **reference interpolation operator** is
$$\widehat I:X\to\widehat P,\qquad \widehat I v:=\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat\sigma_i(v)\widehat\phi_i.$$
The definition of a reference finite element does not assert that any
particular list of functionals is unisolvent or bounded on a given Sobolev
space; those are separate proof obligations. For $N=0$, $\widehat P=\{0\}$,
$\mathbb K^0=\{0\}$, the empty list gives the unique bijection between these
zero spaces, and the shape-function list is empty. The corresponding
interpolation formula is the empty sum, hence the zero map into $\{0\}$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Choose $R>0$ with $\overline{B(c,R)}\subset\widehat S_2$, and choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(B(c,R))$ equal to one on $B(c,R/2)$. For $0<\epsilon<R/4$, put $L_\epsilon=\log(R/\epsilon)$ and $$u_\epsilon(x)=\chi(x)\, \frac{\log\!\left(R/\sqrt{|x-c|^2+\epsilon^2}\right)}{L_\epsilon}.$$ This is smooth and compactly supported in the simplex, and $u_\epsilon(c)=1$.

In polar coordinates about $c$, $r\ge0$ and the stated range $0<\epsilon<R/4$ gives $r^2+\epsilon^2\ge\epsilon^2>0$ and the radial derivative has no zero denominator. The undivided logarithm has uniformly bounded squared $L^2$ integral on $B(c,R)$: its absolute value is bounded by $\log(R/r)+C$ for $0<r<R$ and small $\epsilon$, and $\int_0^R r(\log(R/r)+C)^2dr<\infty$. Its radial derivative has magnitude $r/(r^2+\epsilon^2)$, so $$\int_0^R\frac{r^3}{(r^2+\epsilon^2)^2}\,dr \le C+\log(R/\epsilon)=C+L_\epsilon,$$ by splitting at $r=\epsilon$. After division by $L_\epsilon$, these estimates show the $L^2$ norm and the gradient contribution from $\chi\nabla\log(R/\sqrt{r^2+\epsilon^2})$ tend to zero. The term $\nabla\chi$ is supported where $R/2\le r<R$, on which the logarithm is uniformly bounded; its divided $L^2$ norm also tends to zero. Therefore $\|u_\epsilon\|_{W^{1,2}(\widehat S_2)}\to0$.

If point evaluation at $c$ were bounded, some finite $C$ would satisfy $|u(c)|\le C\|u\|_{W^{1,2}}$ for every smooth $u$. By [F2] this is the boundedness condition for the candidate nodal functional. Applying it to $u_\epsilon$ gives $1\le C\|u_\epsilon\|_{W^{1,2}}\to0$, a contradiction. Hence evaluation is unbounded at the critical exponent.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a matching simplicial mesh as in
[[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Set $C_{-1}(\mathcal T;\mathbb Z)=0$.
For $0\le k\le d$, let
$C_k(\mathcal T;\mathbb Z)$ be the free abelian group generated by ordered
$k$-faces $[v_0,\ldots,v_k]$, with the orientation relation
$$[v_{\pi(0)},\ldots,v_{\pi(k)}]=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)[v_0,\ldots,v_k]$$
for every permutation $\pi$. Define $\partial_0:C_0\to C_{-1}$ to be the
zero map. For $1\le k\le d$, define the **simplicial boundary**
homomorphism $\partial_k:C_k\to C_{k-1}$ on a generator by
$$\partial_k[v_0,\ldots,v_k]:=\sum_{j=0}^k(-1)^j [v_0,\ldots,\widehat v_j,\ldots,v_k].$$
This is the oriented incidence convention; no geometric
integration is part of the definition. The identity
$\partial_{k-1}\partial_k=0$ is proved directly from this alternating
formula in the following lemma.

Orient every top-dimensional cell of a matching simplicial mesh by the
ambient orientation of $\mathbb R^d$, and orient each facet by the induced
boundary convention of [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. In the sum
of the oriented boundaries of all top-dimensional cells, every interior
facet occurs twice with opposite signs; every boundary facet occurs once.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to the first triangle and the ordered triangle $[v_0,v_2,v_3]$ to obtain $$\partial[v_0,v_1,v_2]=[v_1,v_2]-[v_0,v_2]+[v_0,v_1],$$ $$\partial[v_0,v_2,v_3]=[v_2,v_3]-[v_0,v_3]+[v_0,v_2].$$ The edge $[v_0,v_2]$ appears with coefficient $-1$ in the first boundary and $+1$ in the second.

Adding the two formulas cancels the shared diagonal and leaves $[v_0,v_1]+[v_1,v_2]+[v_2,v_3]-[v_0,v_3]$, which is the oriented outer boundary since $-[v_0,v_3]=[v_3,v_0]$. This explicit calculation agrees with the general cancellation rule [F2].

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space. Vectors $x,y\in V$ are
**orthogonal**, written $x\perp y$, when

$$\langle x,y\rangle=0 .$$

For a subset $S\subseteq V$ the **orthogonal complement** of $S$ is

$$S^\perp:=\{\,v\in V : \langle v,s\rangle=0 \text{ for every } s\in S\,\}.$$

**Orthogonality is symmetric.** If $\langle x,y\rangle=0$, then
$\langle y,x\rangle=\overline{\langle x,y\rangle}=0$, so $x\perp y$ exactly
when $y\perp x$; in particular the condition defining $S^\perp$ is symmetric in
its two arguments.

**$S^\perp$ is a linear subspace.** Let $s\in S$ and scalars $a,b$; then
$\langle 0,s\rangle=0$, and if $u,v\in S^\perp$ then
$\langle au+bv,s\rangle=a\langle u,s\rangle+b\langle v,s\rangle=0$ by linearity
in the first argument, so $au+bv\in S^\perp$. Thus $S^\perp$ is a linear
subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]) for every subset $S$, whether or not
$S$ is a subspace. Moreover $0\in S^\perp$ always, and $v\in V$ lies in
$\{0\}^\perp$ for every $v$, so $\{0\}^\perp=V$.

**Monotonicity.** If $S\subseteq T\subseteq V$, then every vector orthogonal to
all of $T$ is orthogonal to all of $S$, so $T^\perp\subseteq S^\perp$.

**Nontriviality of orthogonality.** By positive definiteness
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2=0$ exactly for $v=0$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]),
so a vector orthogonal to itself is zero, and $\{0\}^\perp=V$, $V^\perp=\{0\}$.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space with induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. Then $\|v\|\ge0$ with $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\,\|v\|$ for every scalar $\lambda$, and $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$; hence $\|\cdot\|$ is a norm on $V$, read over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]].

derivations.claim: Uniqueness in [F2] gives linearity of $A^*$: for scalars $a,b$ and $y_1,y_2\in Y$, conjugate-linearity of the second slot shows that $aA^*y_1+bA^*y_2$ satisfies the defining identity for $ay_1+by_2$, so it equals $A^*(ay_1+by_2)$. For $w=A^*y$, [F2], [F4] and [F7] give $\|w\|^2=\langle Aw,y\rangle\le|\langle Aw,y\rangle|\le\|A\|\|w\|\|y\|$. Dividing when $w\ne0$, and treating $w=0$ directly, proves $\|A^*y\|\le\|A\|\|y\|$. Thus $A^*$ is bounded, and composition and addition make $B_\lambda$ linear and bounded with $\|B_\lambda x\|\le(\|A\|^2+\lambda)\|x\|$. The adjoint identity and conjugate symmetry [F6] give $\langle B_\lambda x,z\rangle=\langle Ax,Az\rangle+\lambda\langle x,z\rangle=\langle x,B_\lambda z\rangle$ for all $x,z\in X$. In particular, $\langle B_\lambda x,x\rangle=\|Ax\|^2+\lambda\|x\|^2\ge\lambda\|x\|^2$.

By [F4], $\|B_\lambda x\|\,\|x\|\ge |\langle B_\lambda x,x\rangle|=\langle B_\lambda x,x\rangle\ge \lambda\|x\|^2$. Thus $\|B_\lambda x\|\ge\lambda\|x\|$ for $x\ne0$; the same inequality is trivial for $x=0$. Hence $B_\lambda$ is injective. If $B_\lambda x_n$ converges, this inequality applied to $x_n-x_m$ makes $(x_n)$ Cauchy; completeness of $X$ and boundedness of $B_\lambda$ show its limit lies in $\operatorname{ran}B_\lambda$. Therefore the range is closed.

If $z\in(\operatorname{ran}B_\lambda)^\perp$, [F8] gives $\langle z,B_\lambda x\rangle=0$ for every $x\in X$. By conjugate symmetry [F6] this is $\langle B_\lambda x,z\rangle=0$, and the symmetry identity from step 1.1 gives $\langle x,B_\lambda z\rangle=0$ for every $x\in X$. Taking $x=B_\lambda z$ and using positive definiteness [F6] yields $B_\lambda z=0$; injectivity from step 2.1 then gives $z=0$. Thus the closed range has zero orthogonal complement.

By [F5] and the Countable Choice assumption [A1], a closed subspace with zero orthogonal complement is all of $X$; so $B_\lambda$ is surjective as well as injective. For $y=B_\lambda x$, step 2.1 gives $\|B_\lambda^{-1}y\|=\|x\|\le\|y\|/\lambda$, proving $\|B_\lambda^{-1}\|\le1/\lambda$.

product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and

$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ have singular value decomposition
$A=U\Sigma V^*$, and let $\tau\ge0$ be a declared threshold. The
**truncated singular-value pseudoinverse at threshold $\tau$** is

$$ A_\tau^+ := V\Sigma_\tau^+U^*, $$

where $\Sigma_\tau^+\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is the transposed-shape
diagonal matrix whose $i$th diagonal entry is $\sigma_i^{-1}$ when
$\sigma_i>\tau$ and is $0$ when $\sigma_i\le\tau$; every off-diagonal entry is
$0$.

The threshold is part of the definition, exactly as in
[[def-numerical-rank-relative-to-a-norm-scale-and-tolerance]]: changing
$\tau$ changes which singular directions are retained.

Then $\|v\|\ge0$ with $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\,\|v\|$ for every scalar $\lambda$, and $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$; hence $\|\cdot\|$ is a norm on $V$, read over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]].

If $I_\tau$ is empty, [F2] makes $A_\tau^+=0$. Otherwise orthonormality of the retained $v_i$ and [F1] give $\|A_\tau^+e\|^2=\sum_{i\in I_\tau} |\langle e,u_i\rangle|^2/\sigma_i^2\le (\max_{i\in I_\tau}\sigma_i^{-1})^2\sum_{i\in I_\tau}|\langle e,u_i\rangle|^2$. so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space with induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. Then $\|v\|\ge0$ with $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\,\|v\|$ for every scalar $\lambda$, and $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$; hence $\|\cdot\|$ is a norm on $V$, read over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]].

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

derivations.claim: Let $x=R_\lambda g$. Under [A1], [F2] gives the Hilbert adjoint used in the definition of $R_\lambda$. By [F1], $(A^*A+\lambda I_X)x=A^*g$. Pairing with $x$ and using [F2] gives $\langle A^*Ax,x\rangle_X=\langle Ax,Ax\rangle_Y=\|Ax\|^2$ and $\langle A^*g,x\rangle_X=\langle g,Ax\rangle_Y$ by [F2]–[F4]. Hence $\|Ax\|^2+\lambda\|x\|^2=\langle g,Ax\rangle_Y$.

The left side of step 1.1 is real and nonnegative. By [F5], with $s=\|Ax\|$ and $t=\|g\|$, step 1.1 gives $\lambda\|x\|^2=\langle g,Ax\rangle-s^2\le |\langle g,Ax\rangle|-s^2\le ts-s^2$. Completing the square gives $ts-s^2=\frac{t^2}{4}-(s-t/2)^2\le t^2/4$. Since $\lambda>0$, taking nonnegative square roots yields $\|R_\lambda g\|=\|x\|\le\|g\|/(2\sqrt\lambda)$.
The pointwise inequality of step 2.1 holds for every $g\in Y$. Taking the supremum over the unit ball in [F6] gives $\|R_\lambda\|\le1/(2\sqrt\lambda)$.

boundaries.reason: The Statement is pointwise for a vector $g$; zero data is handled in step 2.1.

boundaries.evidence: With $g=0$, step 1.1 forces $x=0$ and the estimate in step 2.1 is equality at zero.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real or complex
Hilbert spaces and let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded, with Hilbert adjoint $A^*$. For
$\lambda>0$, define

$$B_\lambda:=A^*A+\lambda I_X.$$

Then $B_\lambda:X\to X$ is bijective and

$$\|B_\lambda^{-1}\|\le\frac1\lambda.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:X\to Y$ be bounded, with Hilbert adjoint $A^*$. For $\lambda>0$, put
$R_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*$, which is well-defined by
[[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]]. Then for every $g\in Y$,

$$\|R_\lambda g\|\le\frac{\|g\|}{2\sqrt\lambda},\qquad \|R_\lambda\|\le\frac1{2\sqrt\lambda}.$$

The proof uses the normal equation and the Hilbert-space inner product; it
does not use a compact-operator convergence rate or a source condition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, let $b\in\mathbb F^m$, and let
$\lambda\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\lambda>0$. The **Tikhonov regularised
least-squares objective** is the map

$$ J_\lambda(x):=\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|x\|_2^2 \qquad(x\in\mathbb F^n), $$

where $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm induced by the standard inner product
([[def-inner-product-norm]]).

The parameter $\lambda$ is part of the problem data. The second term penalises
large norms of $x$, so the regularised problem is not the same optimisation
problem as the unregularised least-squares problem.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, let $b\in\mathbb F^m$, and let
$\lambda\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\lambda>0$. Then
the Tikhonov objective

$$J_\lambda(x)=\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|x\|_2^2$$

is strictly convex and has the unique minimiser

$$x_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I)^{-1}A^*b.$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$. The metric used here is $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$, supplied over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]].

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space with induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. Then $\|v\|\ge0$ with $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\,\|v\|$ for every scalar $\lambda$, and $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$; hence $\|\cdot\|$ is a norm on $V$, read over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]].

Let stored $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ and $y\in\mathbb F^m$ be real or complex, $m,n\ge1$, and let stored real $\lambda>0$. Let $x_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I)^{-1}A^*y$. Compute $\alpha=\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt\lambda)>0$ under the successful normal-range square-root model, and solve the stored augmented problem $\min_x\|[A;\alpha I]x-[y;0]\|_2$ by scaled Householder QR and rounded substitution. For complex inputs use the realification described below, so the backend uses only real triangular divisions. Every operation must succeed; failed pivots, invalid operations and out-of-range nonzero intermediates return range-failure.

For any returned $\widehat x$, evaluate $\widehat r$ and its certified allowance $\rho$ by [[lem-rounded-linear-and-normal-residual-certificates]] for the intended residual $r=(A^*A+\lambda I)\widehat x-A^*y$. Then
$$\|\widehat x-x_\lambda\|_2\le\frac{\|\widehat r\|_2+\rho}{\lambda}.$$
This bounds returned-output roundoff relative to the exact direct-solve target $x_{\rm stop}=x_\lambda$. It also certifies the solve term in any larger analytic error chain, irrespective of the backend. The representation of $\sqrt\lambda$ contributes no hidden change of target: $|\alpha^2-\lambda|\le(2u+u^2)\lambda$. If residual evaluation instead uses exact $\alpha^2$, add $|\alpha^2-\lambda|\|\widehat x\|_2$ to its allowance; rounding a computed $\alpha^2$ needs its own scalar error as well.

The backend's nearby least-squares conclusion holds under the completed QR/solve hypotheses and nonsingularity condition. In real dimension, write $C=[A;\alpha I]$ and $\epsilon_Q=\beta_Q\|C\|_F$. A sufficient check is $\epsilon_Q<\alpha$ and $\|\Delta R\|_F<\alpha-\epsilon_Q$. An explicit certified nonsingularity check may replace this sufficient margin.

For a Hilbert-space discrete operator, supply isometries $U:\mathbb F^n\to X$ and $V:\mathbb F^m\to Y$ with $A_h=VAU^*$, and return $U\widehat x$. With coefficient datum $y_c=V^*y_\delta$, the exact normal solution lies in $\operatorname{ran}U$ and the coefficient residual lifts isometrically, so the same certificate applies to $r_h$; likewise use $V^*y_{h,\delta}$ for $r_{h,h}$. If a stored coefficient datum $\widehat y_c$ differs from $V^*y$ by at most $\epsilon_y$, add $\|A\|_2\epsilon_y$ to the residual allowance. If the returned output also has an orthogonal component $z\perp\operatorname{ran}U$ of norm at most $\epsilon_\perp$, add $\lambda\epsilon_\perp$. Finite rank alone does not supply these coordinate or output certificates.

derivations.claim: By [F7], $A$ is bounded, and [F8] supplies the Hilbert-space hypotheses. By [F1], both shifted normal operators are invertible, so the displayed $R_\lambda$ and $R_{\lambda,h}$ are defined. Multiplying their definitions by their normal operators gives $(A^*A+\lambda I)R_\lambda=A^*$ and $(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I)R_{\lambda,h}=A_h^*$.

Adding and subtracting the intermediate vectors $R_\lambda y$, $R_\lambda y_\delta$, and $R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta$ cancels the intervening terms and proves the stated four-term identity. Since $y_\delta=y+e$, [F2] gives $\|R_\lambda y-R_\lambda y_\delta\|=\|R_\lambda e\| \le\delta/(2\sqrt\lambda)$.

Adding and subtracting $x_{\mathrm{stop}}$ gives the optional stopping/roundoff identity. The normal equation for $R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta$ and the definition of $r_{\mathrm{stop}}$ imply $(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I)(x_{\mathrm{stop}}-R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta) =r_{\mathrm{stop}}$. By [F1], the stopping term is at most $\|r_{\mathrm{stop}}\|/\lambda$; the other term is exactly the stated roundoff difference.

In the refined datum case, $y_\delta-y_{h,\delta}=(Ax^\dagger+e)-(A_hx^\dagger+e)=d_h$. Inserting $R_\lambda y_{h,\delta}$ and $R_{\lambda,h}y_{h,\delta}$ into the chain therefore gives the displayed five-term identity by cancellation.

Let $z=R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta$. The normal equation in step 1.1 gives $(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I)(\widetilde x-z)=r_h$. By [F1], $\|\widetilde x-z\|\le\|r_h\|/\lambda$. The triangle inequality [F9] applied to the four-term identity, using step 1.2 for its noise term, proves the stated total error bound.

Applying [F2] to $d_h$ bounds its pre-inversion contribution by $\|R_\lambda d_h\|\le\|d_h\|/(2\sqrt\lambda)$. Applying [F1] to $r_{h,h}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I)(\widetilde x_h-R_{\lambda,h}y_{h,\delta})$ gives the stated refined solve-residual bound. Under the residual-evaluation hypothesis, the triangle inequality [F9] gives $\|r_{h,h}\|\le\|\widehat r_{h,h}\|+\rho_{h,h}$.

By [F4], an assumed operator-norm bound $\|R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h}\|\le\eta_{\lambda,h}$ gives $\|(R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h})y_\delta\| \le\eta_{\lambda,h}\|y_\delta\|$. Also, the triangle inequality [F9] gives $\|r_h\|\le\|\widehat r_h\|+\|r_h-\widehat r_h\| \le\|\widehat r_h\|+\rho_h$ under the stated residual-evaluation hypothesis. These are conditional estimates, not automatic stability claims.

In the finite-matrix case with $A_h=A$ and the exact regularized output $\widetilde x=R_\lambda y_\delta$, [F5]–[F6] identify $R_\lambda$ with the canonical Tikhonov minimizer. The baseline identity from step 1.2 then reduces to the displayed finite-matrix bias/noise formula.

For stored finite data, or for supplied isometric coordinates $A_h=VMU^*$ and returned output $U\widehat x$, apply [F10] to the coefficient matrix $M$ (the matrix case uses identity embeddings) and datum $g=y_\delta$ or $g=y_{h,\delta}$. The exact normal residual lifts isometrically to $r_h$ or $r_{h,h}$, with any certified coordinate-data and orthogonal-output allowances from [F10]. Hence steps 2.2 and 3.1 apply. For the exact direct augmented solve, $x_{\mathrm{stop}}=R_{\lambda,h}g$, and [F10] bounds the returned-output term by $(\|\widehat r\|+\rho)/\lambda$. The analytic identity and its independent bias, noise and discretization terms are unchanged.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces, let
$A:X\to Y$ be compact (hence bounded), and let $A_h:X\to Y$ be a bounded
discrete operator whose range is a finite-dimensional subspace of $Y$. For
$\lambda>0$,
define

$$R_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*,\qquad R_{\lambda,h}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A_h^*.$$

These maps are well-defined by [[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]]. Let $x^\dagger\in X$, $y=Ax^\dagger$, $y_\delta=y+e$ with $\|e\|\le\delta$ and $\delta\ge0$, and let $\widetilde x\in X$. Define the exact discrete normal-equation residual

$$r_h=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)\widetilde x-A_h^*y_\delta.$$

Then the following chain is exact:

$$x^\dagger-\widetilde x=(x^\dagger-R_\lambda y) +(R_\lambda y-R_\lambda y_\delta) +(R_\lambda y_\delta-R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta) +(R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta-\widetilde x).$$

Its norm satisfies

$$\|x^\dagger-\widetilde x\|\le \|x^\dagger-R_\lambda y\|+\frac{\delta}{2\sqrt\lambda} +\|(R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h})y_\delta\|+\frac{\|r_h\|}{\lambda}.$$

The first term is regularization bias, the second is data noise, the third is the regularized-operator discretization difference, and the fourth is the solve residual. The third term receives a numerical bound only when an operator-perturbation bound is supplied: if $\|R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h}\|\le\eta_{\lambda,h}$, it is at most $\eta_{\lambda,h}\|y_\delta\|$. If residual evaluation returns $\widehat r_h$ with a certified $\|r_h-\widehat r_h\|\le\rho_h$, the last term is at most $(\|\widehat r_h\|+\rho_h)/\lambda$. If an algorithm has a specified exact-arithmetic stopping output $x_{\mathrm{stop}}$ and returns a computed output $\widetilde x$, the last difference can further split as

$$R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta-\widetilde x= (R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta-x_{\mathrm{stop}}) +(x_{\mathrm{stop}}-\widetilde x).$$

Writing $r_{\mathrm{stop}}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)x_{\mathrm{stop}} -A_h^*y_\delta$, the first term is at most $\|r_{\mathrm{stop}}\|/\lambda$; the second is the separate returned-output roundoff term. Any bound on that roundoff or on residual-evaluation error requires its own arithmetic hypotheses. For a discretized datum $y_{h,\delta}=A_hx^\dagger+e$ formed before inversion, put $d_h=(A-A_h)x^\dagger=y_\delta-y_{h,\delta}$. Let $\widetilde x_h\in X$ be a computed discrete output. The corresponding exact refinement is

$$x^\dagger-\widetilde x_h=(x^\dagger-R_\lambda y) +(R_\lambda y-R_\lambda y_\delta) +R_\lambda d_h+(R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h})y_{h,\delta} +(R_{\lambda,h}y_{h,\delta}-\widetilde x_h),$$

so the forward residual discarded by quadrature or collocation is counted before inversion as $R_\lambda d_h$, with $\|R_\lambda d_h\|\le\|d_h\|/(2\sqrt\lambda)$. The separate operator discretization and solve terms remain. For this refined chain, define $r_{h,h}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)\widetilde x_h-A_h^*y_{h,\delta}$; then $\|R_{\lambda,h}y_{h,\delta}-\widetilde x_h\|\le\|r_{h,h}\|/\lambda$. If its evaluation returns $\widehat r_{h,h}$ with a certified $\|r_{h,h}-\widehat r_{h,h}\|\le\rho_{h,h}$, the last term is at most $(\|\widehat r_{h,h}\|+\rho_{h,h})/\lambda$. No rate for $d_h$, no operator perturbation estimate, and no floating-point residual bound is implicit. When $X,Y$ are finite-dimensional and $b=Ax^\dagger+e$, the same identity is the canonical Tikhonov bias/noise formula

$$x^\dagger-A^\#_\lambda b=(I-A^\#_\lambda A)x^\dagger-A^\#_\lambda e, \qquad A^\#_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I)^{-1}A^*.$$

Here $\lambda$ is the coefficient of $\|x\|^2$ in
$\|Ax-b\|^2+\lambda\|x\|^2$.

For stored finite matrices, [[lem-computed-augmented-tikhonov-solve-residual-and-output-error]] supplies the concrete augmented-QR or independently certified-residual application: take its $\rho$ as $\rho_h$ with datum $y_\delta$, or as $\rho_{h,h}$ with datum $y_{h,\delta}$. It bounds returned-output roundoff for the exact direct-solve target and retains explicit real/complex realization, square-root representation, successful-operation and nonsingularity conditions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p$ be a real number with
$0<p<\infty$. Write $\mathcal M(X,\mu)$ for the measurable functions
$f:X\to\mathbb R$. For $f\in\mathcal M(X,\mu)$ define the extended-valued
$p$-functional

$$\|f\|_p:=\begin{cases}\left(\int |f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p},&\displaystyle\int |f|^p\,d\mu<\infty,\\+\infty,&\displaystyle\int |f|^p\,d\mu=+\infty.\end{cases}$$

The finite power uses [[def-real-power]], while the second clause avoids
applying real powers to the extended value $+\infty$. The integral is the
nonnegative Lebesgue integral of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

The class

$$\mathcal L^p(\mu):=\{f\in\mathcal M(X,\mu): \|f\|_p<\infty\}$$

is the measurable-function space used on this page before passing to
almost-everywhere equivalence classes.

For $1\le p<\infty$, the pointwise operations make $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ a real
vector space by
[[thm-calligraphic-l-p-and-l-infinity-are-vector-spaces-for-p-at-least-one]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
