$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces, let
$A:X\to Y$ be compact (hence bounded), and let $A_h:X\to Y$ be a bounded
discrete operator whose range is a finite-dimensional subspace of $Y$. For
$\lambda>0$,
define

$$R_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*,\qquad R_{\lambda,h}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A_h^*.$$

These maps are well-defined by [[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]]. Let $x^\dagger\in X$, $y=Ax^\dagger$, $y_\delta=y+e$ with $\|e\|\le\delta$ and $\delta\ge0$, and let $\widetilde x\in X$. Define the exact discrete normal-equation residual

$$r_h=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)\widetilde x-A_h^*y_\delta.$$

Then the following chain is exact:

$$x^\dagger-\widetilde x=(x^\dagger-R_\lambda y) +(R_\lambda y-R_\lambda y_\delta) +(R_\lambda y_\delta-R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta) +(R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta-\widetilde x).$$

Its norm satisfies

$$\|x^\dagger-\widetilde x\|\le \|x^\dagger-R_\lambda y\|+\frac{\delta}{2\sqrt\lambda} +\|(R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h})y_\delta\|+\frac{\|r_h\|}{\lambda}.$$

The first term is regularization bias, the second is data noise, the third is the regularized-operator discretization difference, and the fourth is the solve residual. The third term receives a numerical bound only when an operator-perturbation bound is supplied: if $\|R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h}\|\le\eta_{\lambda,h}$, it is at most $\eta_{\lambda,h}\|y_\delta\|$. If residual evaluation returns $\widehat r_h$ with a certified $\|r_h-\widehat r_h\|\le\rho_h$, the last term is at most $(\|\widehat r_h\|+\rho_h)/\lambda$. If an algorithm has a specified exact-arithmetic stopping output $x_{\mathrm{stop}}$ and returns a computed output $\widetilde x$, the last difference can further split as

$$R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta-\widetilde x= (R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta-x_{\mathrm{stop}}) +(x_{\mathrm{stop}}-\widetilde x).$$

Writing $r_{\mathrm{stop}}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)x_{\mathrm{stop}} -A_h^*y_\delta$, the first term is at most $\|r_{\mathrm{stop}}\|/\lambda$; the second is the separate returned-output roundoff term. Any bound on that roundoff or on residual-evaluation error requires its own arithmetic hypotheses. For a discretized datum $y_{h,\delta}=A_hx^\dagger+e$ formed before inversion, put $d_h=(A-A_h)x^\dagger=y_\delta-y_{h,\delta}$. Let $\widetilde x_h\in X$ be a computed discrete output. The corresponding exact refinement is

$$x^\dagger-\widetilde x_h=(x^\dagger-R_\lambda y) +(R_\lambda y-R_\lambda y_\delta) +R_\lambda d_h+(R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h})y_{h,\delta} +(R_{\lambda,h}y_{h,\delta}-\widetilde x_h),$$

so the forward residual discarded by quadrature or collocation is counted before inversion as $R_\lambda d_h$, with $\|R_\lambda d_h\|\le\|d_h\|/(2\sqrt\lambda)$. The separate operator discretization and solve terms remain. For this refined chain, define $r_{h,h}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)\widetilde x_h-A_h^*y_{h,\delta}$; then $\|R_{\lambda,h}y_{h,\delta}-\widetilde x_h\|\le\|r_{h,h}\|/\lambda$. If its evaluation returns $\widehat r_{h,h}$ with a certified $\|r_{h,h}-\widehat r_{h,h}\|\le\rho_{h,h}$, the last term is at most $(\|\widehat r_{h,h}\|+\rho_{h,h})/\lambda$. No rate for $d_h$, no operator perturbation estimate, and no floating-point residual bound is implicit. When $X,Y$ are finite-dimensional and $b=Ax^\dagger+e$, the same identity is the canonical Tikhonov bias/noise formula

$$x^\dagger-A^\#_\lambda b=(I-A^\#_\lambda A)x^\dagger-A^\#_\lambda e, \qquad A^\#_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I)^{-1}A^*.$$

Here $\lambda$ is the coefficient of $\|x\|^2$ in
$\|Ax-b\|^2+\lambda\|x\|^2$.

For stored finite matrices, [[lem-computed-augmented-tikhonov-solve-residual-and-output-error]] supplies the concrete augmented-QR or independently certified-residual application: take its $\rho$ as $\rho_h$ with datum $y_\delta$, or as $\rho_{h,h}$ with datum $y_{h,\delta}$. It bounds returned-output roundoff for the exact direct-solve target and retains explicit real/complex realization, square-root representation, successful-operation and nonsingularity conditions.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $x\in\mathbb F^n$, $y\in\mathbb F^m$ have stored real or complex entries, with $m,n\ge1$. Use the operationwise arithmetic model, successful sequential dot products, and $0<u<1$ with $(\max(m,n)-1)u<1$. Define
$$g_k=\frac{1+6u}{1-(k-1)u}-1,\qquad F=\|A\|_F,\quad X=\|x\|_2,\quad Y=\|y\|_2.$$
For $\widehat v=\operatorname{fl}(Ax)$ and $\widehat w=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-y)$, put $V=g_nFX$ and $W=V+u(\|\widehat v\|_2+Y)$. Then
$$\|\widehat w-(Ax-y)\|_2\le W.$$
For a stored real $\lambda>0$, also compute $\widehat z=\operatorname{fl}(A^*\widehat w)$, $\widehat l=\operatorname{fl}(\lambda x)$ and $\widehat r=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat z+\widehat l)$, rounding scalar multiplication componentwise. The exact intended normal residual $r=A^*(Ax-y)+\lambda x$ satisfies
$$\|\widehat r-r\|_2\le\rho:=FW+g_mF\|\widehat w\|_2+u\lambda X+u(\|\widehat z\|_2+\|\widehat l\|_2).$$
Norms in these certificates mean exact norms or certified upper bounds. Uncontrolled rounding of the certificate itself is not authorized. The linear bound applies columnwise to certify $\|I-AB\|_2\le\|I-AB\|_F$ from stored basis-solve columns $B$.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $m\ge n\ge1$, have full column rank. Successful scaled Householder QR gives the exactly orthonormal reduced representative $\widehat Q$ and computed triangular $\widehat R$ with
$$A+\Delta_Q=\widehat Q\widehat R,\qquad \|\Delta_Q\|_F\le\beta_Q\|A\|_F,\qquad \beta_Q=(1+\kappa_m)^n-1,$$
where $\kappa_m$ is the proved local-step coefficient. Apply the stored reflectors to $b$ by rounded rank-one updates and let $\widehat y$ be the first $n$ coordinates. Set $\beta_b=\beta_Q$. Alternatively, if an explicitly supplied exactly orthonormal $\widehat Q$ has entries admissible as arithmetic inputs and $\widehat y=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat Q^Tb)$ uses sequential rounded dots, set $\beta_b=\sqrt n\,\gamma_m$. Solve $\widehat R\widehat x=\widehat y$ by successful rounded back substitution. Suppose $mu<1$ and $\gamma_{n+3}<1/8$. There exist $\delta b$ and upper triangular $\Delta R$ with
$$(\widehat R+\Delta R)\widehat x=\widehat Q^T(b+\delta b),\qquad \|\delta b\|_2\le\beta_b\|b\|_2,\qquad \|\Delta R\|_F\le\gamma_{n+3}\|\widehat R\|_F.$$
If $\widehat R+\Delta R$ is nonsingular, $\widehat x$ is the unique least-squares solution for $\widetilde A=\widehat Q(\widehat R+\Delta R)$ and $\widetilde b=b+\delta b$. The relative matrix perturbation is at most $\beta_Q+\gamma_{n+3}(1+\beta_Q)$; the right-hand perturbation is at most $\beta_b$. For fixed $m,n$, both perturbation coefficients are $O(u)$. If additionally $\beta_Q\le19\gamma_{n+3}/(1+\gamma_{n+3})$ and $\beta_b\le20\gamma_{n+3}$, both relative data perturbation bounds are at most $20\gamma_{n+3}$. These two coefficient comparisons are additional checks; they do not follow from $mu<1$ and $\gamma_{n+3}<1/8$ alone. Success and nonsingularity are explicit hypotheses.

Let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be as in [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]]. Here fl is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, on each real exact result that is zero or normal; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range x, fl(sqrt(x)) is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression ab+c; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, let $b\in\mathbb F^m$, and let
$\lambda\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\lambda>0$. Then
the Tikhonov objective

$$J_\lambda(x)=\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|x\|_2^2$$

is strictly convex and has the unique minimiser

$$x_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I)^{-1}A^*b.$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

If $C+\Delta_Q=\widehat Q\widehat R$, then $\|\widehat Rz\|=\|(C+\Delta_Q)z\|\ge(\alpha-\epsilon_Q)\|z\|$. Under the sufficient margin, the further triangular perturbation preserves a positive lower bound. Thus the nonsingularity premise in [F2] holds under the stated check. The theorem still explicitly requires successful arithmetic; exact full rank alone does not ensure rounded success.

By [F3], $\alpha=\sqrt\lambda(1+\delta)$, $|\delta|\le u$, whence $|\alpha^2-\lambda|\le(2u+u^2)\lambda$. For any $z$, Cauchy-Schwarz gives $\|(A^*A+\lambda I)z\|\|z\|\ge\langle(A^*A+\lambda I)z,z\rangle=\|Az\|^2+\lambda\|z\|^2\ge\lambda\|z\|^2$. The normal equation [F4] therefore implies $\|\widehat x-x_\lambda\|\le\|r\|/\lambda\le(\|\widehat r\|+\rho)/\lambda$ by [F1]. Replacing the coefficient in a residual by $\alpha^2$ changes that exact residual by $(\alpha^2-\lambda)\widehat x$, giving the stated additional allowance.

For complex inputs identify $z=z_R+iz_I$ with $(z_R,z_I)\in\mathbb R^{2n}$. The real matrix $A_R=\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Re}A&-\operatorname{Im}A\\\operatorname{Im}A&\operatorname{Re}A\end{pmatrix}$ represents exactly the same linear map, preserves vector norms, and satisfies $\|A_R\|_2=\|A\|_2$, $\|A_R\|_F=\sqrt2\|A\|_F$ by direct component sums. Apply [F2] to $[A_R;\alpha I_{2n}]$ and datum $((\operatorname{Re}y,\operatorname{Im}y),0)$; this is exactly the original complex objective. Mapping its output back needs only component pairing, so introduces no arithmetic error or unmodeled complex division.

In exact arithmetic with the intended $\sqrt\lambda$, full-rank augmented QR returns the unique minimizer in [F4], hence $x_{\rm stop}=x_\lambda$. Step 1.2 bounds the returned computed output's difference from that target, including square-root representation and all solve error through its certified residual. For an iterative stopping target different from $x_\lambda$, retain separate stopping and output terms rather than calling their sum pure roundoff.

In the supplied Hilbert representation, $U^*U=I$, $V^*V=I$, and $A_h^*=UA^*V^*$. The subspaces $\operatorname{ran}U$ and its orthogonal complement are invariant under $A_h^*A_h+\lambda I$; on the complement that operator is $\lambda I$ and its right-hand side $A_h^*y$ has zero component. Thus the exact normal solution is $Ux_\lambda$, with coefficient datum $V^*y$. Direct substitution gives $r_h=U((A^*A+\lambda I)\widehat x-A^*V^*y)$, and isometry preserves its norm. For every coefficient vector $e$, put $w=A^*e$. Then $\|w\|_2^2=\langle Aw,e\rangle\le|\langle Aw,e\rangle|\le\|A\|_2\|w\|_2\|e\|_2$ by [F5]–[F6]; dividing for $w\ne0$ (and checking $w=0$ directly) gives $\|A^*e\|_2\le\|A\|_2\|e\|_2$. Let $m,n$ be nonnegative integers, $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $b\in\mathbb R^m$, and $c\in\mathbb R^n$. The standard-form minimization linear program with data $(A,b,c)$ is
$$\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}.$$
Its feasible set is $P(A,b)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x_j\ge0\text{ for every }j\}$, and a feasible $x$ is optimal if $c^{\mathsf T}x\le c^{\mathsf T}z$ for every $z\in P(A,b)$. The notation $x\ge0$ is componentwise. The revised-simplex basis algorithms on this page require a full-row-rank matrix, meaning $\operatorname{rank}(A)=m$; a rank-deficient raw system must first be reduced by exact row operations, with inconsistent rows reported as infeasible. For $m=0$, the empty system has its usual zero-dimensional interpretation.

A vector $q\in\mathbb R^m$ satisfying $A^{\mathsf T}q\ge0$ and $b^{\mathsf T}q<0$ is called a **Farkas infeasibility certificate** for this sign convention. Indeed, any feasible $x\ge0$ would give $b^{\mathsf T}q=x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}q\ge0$.

A vector $q\in\mathbb R^m$ satisfying $A^{\mathsf T}q\ge0$ and $b^{\mathsf T}q<0$ is called a **Farkas infeasibility certificate** for this sign convention. Indeed, any feasible $x\ge0$ would give $b^{\mathsf T}q=x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}q\ge0$.

Use the standard-form problem of [[def-revised-simplex-standard-form-linear-program]]. Assume $A$ has full row rank $m$. An ordered basis is a list $B=(B_1,\ldots,B_m)$ of distinct column indices for which the square matrix $A_B=[a_{B_1}\ \cdots\ a_{B_m}]$ is invertible. Write $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\{B_1,\ldots,B_m\}$ and $c_B=(c_{B_1},\ldots,c_{B_m})^{\mathsf T}$. The basic vector $x(B)$ is defined by $x_B(B)=A_B^{-1}b$ and $x_j(B)=0$ for $j\in N$; the basis is primal feasible, and $x(B)$ is a basic feasible solution, exactly when $A_B^{-1}b\ge0$.

The basis multiplier is $y(B)=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B$. For every column $j$, its reduced cost is $\bar c_j=c_j-a_j^{\mathsf T}y(B)$. In particular, $\bar c_{B_i}=0$ for each basic index. The basis is dual feasible when $\bar c_j\ge0$ for every $j\in N$. When $m=0$, take the empty basis and the empty multiplier; these formulas remain meaningful.

A primal-feasible basis is **degenerate** if some basic coordinate is zero. A simplex pivot is **degenerate** if its ratio-test step length is zero.

derivations.claim: If the support columns indexed by $S(x)$ are dependent, choose a nonzero vector $d$ supported on $S(x)$ with $Ad=0$. Since each $x_j>0$ on this finite support, choose $\varepsilon>0$ smaller than $x_j/|d_j|$ for every nonzero $d_j$. Then $x+\varepsilon d$ and $x-\varepsilon d$ are distinct nonnegative solutions of $Az=b$, and their midpoint is $x$; hence $x$ is not extreme.

Suppose the support columns are independent and $x=tu+(1-t)v$ for feasible $u,v$ and $0<t<1$. For $j\notin S(x)$, nonnegativity and $x_j=0$ force $u_j=v_j=0$. Thus $u-v$ is supported on $S(x)$ and $A(u-v)=0$; independence forces $u=v$, and the convex-combination identity then gives $u=v=x$. This proves extremality under its stated definition.

If the support columns of a feasible point are dependent, take $d$ as in step 1.1 and choose its sign so some $d_j<0$. With $t=\min_{d_j<0}x_j/(-d_j)>0$, the point $x+td$ remains feasible, remains nonnegative, and has strictly fewer positive coordinates. Repeating this support reduction at most $n$ times gives a feasible point whose support columns are independent.

Because $A$ has rank $m$, its columns span $\mathbb R^m$. Extend the independent support columns from step 2.1 to $m$ independent columns of $A$ by repeatedly taking the least-index column outside their current span; assigning zero to each added coordinate makes the reduced point the basic vector of that basis. It is therefore a basic feasible solution. When $m=0$, support reduction gives the zero vector and the empty list is the required basis.

A basic feasible solution has support contained in an independent basis, so its support columns are independent and step 1.2 makes it extreme. Conversely, an extreme feasible point has independent support by step 1.1 and extends to a basis by step 3.1. Thus the three stated conditions are equivalent, and step 3.1 proves existence whenever $P(A,b)$ is nonempty.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be $C^2$. Let $p,m\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed; when the target
dimension is positive, let $h:U\to\mathbb R^p$ and
$g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):U\to\mathbb R^m$ be componentwise $C^2$, and when it
is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The smooth inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},
$$
and
$$
\mathcal L_C(x)=\{d:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\}.
$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with
$Dg_i(x)w<0$ for every active $i$; the latter condition is vacuous if
$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition
just stated. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is the stationarity,
feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity system below.

For $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, the Lagrangian and KKT
system are
$$
L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x),
$$
$$
h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\le0,\quad \lambda\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \nabla_xL(x,\nu,\lambda)=0.
$$
The critical cone for a KKT tuple is
$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap
\{d:\nabla f(x)^Td=0\}$. These definitions use the differentiability and
gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex, and suppose the objective
$f:U\to\mathbb R$ and inequalities $g_i:U\to\mathbb R$ are differentiable
and convex. Let the equalities be $Ax=b$. If a feasible tuple
$(x_*,\nu,\lambda)$ satisfies the KKT conditions with $\lambda\ge0$, then
$x_*$ is a global minimizer over the feasible set $C$. Moreover,
$-\nabla f(x_*)\in N_C(x_*)$, where the normal cone has the convention of
[[def-kkt-residual-and-normal-cone]].

derivations.claim: Define $r_j=1$, $r_B=-d$, and all other nonbasic components of $r$ to be zero. Since $A_Bd=a_j$, we have $Ar=a_j-A_Bd=0$; also $c^{\mathsf T}r=c_j-c_B^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-1}a_j=\bar c_j$.

If every $d_i\le0$, then $r\ge0$, so $x+\lambda r$ is feasible for every $\lambda\ge0$. Its cost is $c^{\mathsf T}x+\lambda\bar c_j$, which tends to $-\infty$ as $\lambda\to\infty$; this proves the ray branch.

If some $d_i>0$, set $\theta=\min_{d_i>0}x_{B_i}/d_i$. Each ratio is nonnegative, the finite nonempty index set has a minimum, and $x_B-\theta d\ge0$: rows with $d_i>0$ satisfy the ratio bound, while rows with $d_i\le0$ do not decrease. The entering component is $\theta\ge0$, so $x+\theta r$ is feasible.

For any minimizing row $i$, replacing column $B_i$ by $a_j$ gives a basis: in coordinates of $A_B$, the replacement column is $d$, whose $i$th entry is positive, so expansion along that column gives a nonzero determinant. The unique basic vector of the new basis is $x+\theta r$, because that vector satisfies the constraints and has zero on the remaining nonbasic variables.

The objective change is $c^{\mathsf T}(x+\theta r)-c^{\mathsf T}x=\theta c^{\mathsf T}r=\theta\bar c_j$. Since $\theta\ge0$ and $\bar c_j<0$, it is nonpositive and is zero exactly when $\theta=0$, the degenerate-pivot case.

If $n=0$, the feasible set contains only the empty vector, so its feasible basic vector is optimal. Suppose $n\ge1$. Set $U=\mathbb R^n$, $f(z)=c^{\mathsf T}z$, $h(z)=Az-b$, $g_j(z)=-z_j$, $
u=-y(B)$, and $\lambda=c-A^{\mathsf T}y(B)$. The open convex domain is $U=\mathbb R^n$, and the affine functions are differentiable and convex. The vector $\lambda$ is the reduced-cost vector, including zero basic coordinates by [F2], so it is nonnegative; $x$ is feasible by hypothesis. For each $j$, either $j$ is nonbasic and $x_j=0$, or $j$ is basic and $\lambda_j=0$, so $\lambda_jg_j(x)=0$. Since $Dg=-I$, the stationarity expression is $
abla f(x)+A^{\mathsf T}
u+Dg(x)^{\mathsf T}\lambda=c-A^{\mathsf T}y(B)-\lambda=0$. These are precisely the KKT conditions of [F3], and [F4] proves that $x$ globally minimizes $c^{\mathsf T}z$ over $P(A,b)$.

Let $F$ be a field, and let $m,n,s\in\mathbb N$, where $\mathbb N$ includes
$0$. A **compressed sparse row (CSR) record** for an $m$ by $n$ matrix over
$F$ consists of integer arrays $r=(r_0,\ldots,r_m)$ and
$c=(c_0,\ldots,c_{s-1})$, and a value array $v=(v_0,\ldots,v_{s-1})\in F^s$,
satisfying

$$r_0=0,\qquad 0=r_0\le r_1\le\cdots\le r_m=s,\qquad 0\le c_t<n\quad(0\le t<s).$$

For each row $i<m$, its **stored entries** are the indices
$t$ with $r_i\le t<r_{i+1}$. The row is empty exactly when
$r_i=r_{i+1}$. Repeated column indices within one row and stored values
$v_t=0_F$ are permitted; each such entry remains a separate stored entry.

The represented matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ is defined entrywise by

$$A_{ij}:=\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}v_t\qquad(0\le i<m,\ 0\le j<n),$$

where $\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}$ is $1_F$ when $c_t=j$ and $0_F$ otherwise, and an
empty sum is $0_F$. Repeated entries in column $j$ are therefore added. The
number $s$ is the **stored-entry count**; it is not in general the number of
nonzero entries of $A$.

A CSR record is **canonical** when no row repeats a column and no stored value
is zero. In that case every nonzero matrix entry is stored exactly once and
$s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)$, where $\operatorname{nnz}(A)$ denotes the number of
nonzero entries of $A$. If $m=0$, the endpoint conditions force $s=0$ and the
row-pointer array has its single entry $r_0=0$. If $n=0$, the column-index
condition forces $s=0$ as well.

derivations.claim: The intervals $[r_i,r_{i+1})$ are disjoint and, because $r_0=0$ and $r_m=s$, their union is $[0,s)$. Thus each stored index has exactly one row $i(t)$, including the empty-stream case $s=0$. After processing the first $k$ stored indices, the accumulator satisfies $w_j=\sum_{0\le t<k,\ c_t=j}v_ty_{i(t)}$: this holds at $k=0$, and the next update adds exactly its one summand to component $c_k$.

At $k=s$, for each column $j$ the CSR reconstruction in [F2] gives $(A^{\mathsf T}y)_j=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}A_{ij}y_i=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}\mathbf1_{c_t=j}v_ty_i=\sum_{0\le t<s,\ c_t=j}v_ty_{i(t)}=w_j$. The finite row intervals partition the stored indices, so the reindexing counts every stored term once; real multiplication distributes over finite sums. By [F1], $c-w$ is the reduced-cost vector when $y=y(B)$.

Each of the $s$ updates performs one multiplication and one addition, and initialization and final subtraction each touch exactly $n$ coordinates. The count follows the stated loop, so duplicate indices and zero-valued entries still contribute one multiplication and one addition each; no timing, bandwidth, or factorization conclusion follows.

Input a standard-form problem as in [[def-revised-simplex-standard-form-linear-program]], whose stored matrix, right-hand side, and cost entries are finite binary floating-point values, together with finite stored candidate vectors $\hat x\in\mathbb R^n$ and $\hat y\in\mathbb R^m$. A finite binary value is interpreted as its exact dyadic rational (an integer times an integer power of $2$). If a dimension is wrong or any value is NaN or infinite, return `invalid-input`. Otherwise use exact integer/rational arithmetic to compute $r_p=A\hat x-b$, $r_d=c-A^{\mathsf T}\hat y$, $g=c^{\mathsf T}\hat x-b^{\mathsf T}\hat y$, $\rho_p=\|r_p\|_\infty$, and $\rho_d=\|r_d\|_\infty$, where $\|z\|_\infty=\max_i|z_i|$ and the empty-vector value is zero. Return these exact values and $|g|$ as the exact primal-dual objective difference for the stored data. Return `verified-optimal-for-stored-data` exactly when $\hat x\ge0$, $r_p=0$, $r_d\ge0$, and $g=0$. The exact arithmetic is a verification procedure for a candidate produced by a floating-point solver; it does not define a basis factorization or bound uncertainty in data before they were stored. If a statement about pre-rounded data is required, separate certified input intervals must be supplied and propagated. The procedure makes no operation-count or runtime claim.

Let $m,n$ be nonnegative integers, $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $b\in\mathbb R^m$, and $c\in\mathbb R^n$. The standard-form minimization linear program with data $(A,b,c)$ is

Its feasible set is $P(A,b)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x_j\ge0\text{ for every }j\}$, and a feasible $x$ is optimal if $c^{\mathsf T}x\le c^{\mathsf T}z$ for every $z\in P(A,b)$. The leaving basic column $a_{B_i}$ has $q^{\mathsf T}a_{B_i}=1$, hence its new reduced cost is $-\alpha\ge0$.

The augmented matrix $[DA\ I]$ has full row rank because it contains the identity columns; $x=0,u=Db$ is feasible for the Phase I problem and has objective $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Db\ge0$.

By [F2] the Phase I primal algorithm terminates at an optimum or an unbounded ray. Its objective is $\sum_i u_i\ge0$ at every feasible point, so a negative-cost ray is impossible; it terminates at a minimum with nonnegative reduced costs.

Suppose the minimum $w^*>0$. Any feasible original $x$ would give a Phase I feasible point $(x,u=0)$ of objective zero, contradicting minimality. Let $y$ be the terminal basis multiplier for the Phase I objective $(0,\mathbf1)$. Nonnegative reduced costs on the original columns, using [F3], give $(DA)^{\mathsf T}y\le0$, and the basic-vector identity gives $(Db)^{\mathsf T}y=w^*>0$.

Suppose instead that $w^*=0$. Since every artificial variable is nonnegative and their sum is zero, each artificial variable has value zero, and the original coordinates satisfy $DAx=Db$. If an artificial variable is basic at tableau row $k$ and some original nonbasic column has a nonzero coefficient in row $k$ of $B^{-1}DA$, pivot that column in. The pivot is nonzero, and the entering variable and leaving artificial variable both have value zero, so the represented feasible point is unchanged and one artificial basic variable is removed.

Input a standard-form problem as in [[def-revised-simplex-standard-form-linear-program]], whose stored matrix, right-hand side, and cost entries are finite binary floating-point values, together with finite stored candidate vectors $\hat x\in\mathbb R^n$ and $\hat y\in\mathbb R^m$. A finite binary value is interpreted as its exact dyadic rational (an integer times an integer power of $2$). If a dimension is wrong or any value is NaN or infinite, return `invalid-input`. Otherwise use exact integer/rational arithmetic to compute $r_p=A\hat x-b$, $r_d=c-A^{\mathsf T}\hat y$, $g=c^{\mathsf T}\hat x-b^{\mathsf T}\hat y$, $\rho_p=\|r_p\|_\infty$, and $\rho_d=\|r_d\|_\infty$, where $\|z\|_\infty=\max_i|z_i|$ and the empty-vector value is zero. Return these exact values and $|g|$ as the exact primal-dual objective difference for the stored data. Return `verified-optimal-for-stored-data` exactly when $\hat x\ge0$, $r_p=0$, $r_d\ge0$, and $g=0$. In every other finite-input case return `candidate-only` with the residuals and gap; a nonzero or small residual is never rounded to zero and does not certify infeasibility.

The exact arithmetic is a verification procedure for a candidate produced by a floating-point solver; it does not define a basis factorization or bound uncertainty in data before they were stored. If a statement about pre-rounded data is required, separate certified input intervals must be supplied and propagated. The procedure makes no operation-count or runtime claim.

For a standard-form problem and finite candidate vectors $x,y$, let $r_p=Ax-b$, $r_d=c-A^{\mathsf T}y$, and $g=c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y$, as computed exactly by [[alg-revised-simplex-residual-audit]]. Then
$$g=x^{\mathsf T}r_d+y^{\mathsf T}r_p,$$
and consequently
$$|g|\le \|x\|_1\|r_d\|_\infty+\|y\|_1\|r_p\|_\infty.$$
Here $\|z\|_1=\sum_i|z_i|$ and $\|z\|_\infty=\max_i|z_i|$, with both norms equal to zero on the empty vector. This bounds the primal-dual objective difference for the stored data; when either vector is infeasible it does not bound distance to an optimal value. If $Ax=b$, $x\ge0$, $c-A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0$, and $g=0$, then $x$ is optimal.

The basic vector $x(B)$ is defined by $x_B(B)=A_B^{-1}b$ and $x_j(B)=0$ for $j\in N$; the basis is primal feasible, and $x(B)$ is a basic feasible solution, exactly when $A_B^{-1}b\ge0$.

The basis multiplier is $y(B)=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B$. For every column $j$, its reduced cost is $\bar c_j=c_j-a_j^{\mathsf T}y(B)$. In particular, $\bar c_{B_i}=0$ for each basic index. The basis is dual feasible when $\bar c_j\ge0$ for every $j\in N$. When $m=0$, take the empty basis and the empty multiplier; these formulas remain meaningful.

A primal-feasible basis is **degenerate** if some basic coordinate is zero. A simplex pivot is **degenerate** if its ratio-test step length is zero.

Let $B$ be a primal-feasible basis for the standard-form problem of [[def-revised-simplex-standard-form-linear-program]] and [[def-revised-simplex-basis-dictionary]], and let $j$ be a nonbasic index with reduced cost $\bar c_j<0$. Put $d=A_B^{-1}a_j$. If $d_i\le0$ for every basic row $i$, then $r_j=1$, $r_B=-d$, and $r_k=0$ for the other nonbasic indices define a feasible ray with $Ar=0$ and $c^{\mathsf T}r=\bar c_j<0$; the LP is unbounded below. If some $d_i>0$, the step $\theta=\min_{d_i>0}(x_{B_i}/d_i)$ is finite and nonnegative, every minimizing row gives a valid pivot, the new basic vector is feasible, and the objective change is $\theta\bar c_j\le0$, strictly negative exactly when $\theta>0$. Finally, if all nonbasic reduced costs are nonnegative at a primal-feasible basis, its basic vector is optimal.

Let $B$ be a basis of the minimization problem for which all nonbasic reduced costs are nonnegative. At an iteration of [[alg-revised-dual-simplex-with-finite-budget]], a pivot chosen from a row $i$ with $x_{B_i}<0$ and a column $j$ with $d_{ij}=(A_B^{-1}a_j)_i<0$ minimizing $\bar c_j/(-d_{ij})$ preserves dual feasibility. If there is no nonbasic $j$ with $d_{ij}<0$, then $q=A_B^{-\mathsf T}e_i$ satisfies $A^{\mathsf T}q\ge0$ and $b^{\mathsf T}q<0$, so $q$ is a Farkas infeasibility certificate as defined in [[def-revised-simplex-standard-form-linear-program]] and the primal problem is infeasible. If the current basis is both primal and dual feasible, it is optimal. A finite pivot-budget exhaustion is inconclusive and does not assert infeasibility or convergence.

derivations.claim: With $B=(2)$, $A_B=1$, $x_2=1$, and $y=c_2=2$. Thus $\bar c_1=1-2=-1$, so $x_1$ is a valid entering variable.

For the changed right-hand side $b=-1$ and basis $B=(1)$, $x_1=-1$ while $y=1$ and $\bar c_2=1\ge0$, so the basis is dual feasible and primal infeasible. Its only nonbasic coefficient is $d_{12}=A_B^{-1}a_2=1\ge0$.
The direction coefficient is $d=A_B^{-1}a_1=1$ and the ratio is $x_2/d=1$. The pivot yields $x_1=1,x_2=0$ and changes cost by $1\cdot(-1)=-1$, from $2$ to $1$.
At the new basis $B=(1)$, $y=c_1=1$ and $\bar c_2=2-1=1\ge0$. The vector is feasible, so [F2] proves it is optimal; the primal and dual objective values are both $1$.

There is no eligible negative coefficient. The certificate from [F3] is $q=1$, for which $A^{\mathsf T}q=(1,1)\ge0$ and $b^{\mathsf T}q=-1<0$. Thus the modified system has no nonnegative feasible vector.

Input the exact standard-form data of [[def-revised-simplex-standard-form-linear-program]] with full-row-rank $A$ and a primal-feasible basis $B$ as in [[def-revised-simplex-basis-dictionary]]. Use exact arithmetic. At each iteration compute $x_B=A_B^{-1}b$, $y=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B$, and all nonbasic reduced costs $\bar c_j=c_j-a_j^{\mathsf T}y$.

1. If every nonbasic $\bar c_j\ge0$, return `optimal` with $x(B)$ and $y$.
2. Otherwise choose the least index $j\notin B$ with $\bar c_j<0$ and solve $A_Bd=a_j$.
3. If no component $d_i$ is positive, return `unbounded` with the ray whose $j$th component is $1$, whose basic components are $-d$, and whose other nonbasic components are $0$.
4. Otherwise compute $\theta=\min_{d_i>0}x_{B_i}/d_i$. Among minimizing rows, leave the basic variable of least index. Replace its basis column by $a_j$ and repeat.

The algorithm assumes an exact initial feasible basis. It makes no iteration bound polynomial in $m$ or $n$.

Let $B$ be a primal-feasible basis for the standard-form problem of [[def-revised-simplex-standard-form-linear-program]] and [[def-revised-simplex-basis-dictionary]], and let $j$ be a nonbasic index with reduced cost $\bar c_j<0$. Put $d=A_B^{-1}a_j$. If $d_i\le0$ for every basic row $i$, then $r_j=1$, $r_B=-d$, and $r_k=0$ for the other nonbasic indices define a feasible ray with $Ar=0$ and $c^{\mathsf T}r=\bar c_j<0$; the LP is unbounded below. If some $d_i>0$, the step $\theta=\min_{d_i>0}(x_{B_i}/d_i)$ is finite and nonnegative, every minimizing row gives a valid pivot, the new basic vector is feasible, and the objective change is $\theta\bar c_j\le0$, strictly negative exactly when $\theta>0$. Finally, if all nonbasic reduced costs are nonnegative at a primal-feasible basis, its basic vector is optimal.

For exact arithmetic and a finite standard-form LP with full-row-rank $A$, the primal algorithm of [[alg-revised-primal-simplex-bland-rule]], started from any primal-feasible basis, terminates after finitely many pivots at an optimal basis or returns a feasible ray of strictly negative cost. If the feasible set is nonempty and the objective is bounded below, an optimal basis exists and is returned. The number of pivots is at most the number of possible bases, hence at most $\binom{n}{m}$; this is a finiteness bound, not a polynomial-time claim. Every pivot may be degenerate, so the objective need not decrease strictly at each step.

derivations.claim: Initially $B=(5,6,7)$, $x_B=(0,0,1)$, and the only negative reduced cost is $\bar c_1=-10$. For entering $x_1$, $d=(1/2,1/2,1)$ gives ratios $(0,0,1)$ for $(x_5,x_6,x_7)$, so the least-index leaving tie is $x_5$ and $\theta=0$. The next basis is $(1,6,7)$.

At $B=(1,6,7)$ the negative reduced costs are $\bar c_2=-53$ and $\bar c_3=-41$. Both rules choose $x_2$. Its direction is $d=(-11,4,11)$; the eligible ratios for $(x_6,x_7)$ are $(0,1/11)$, so $x_6$ leaves at $\theta=0$ and the basis becomes $(1,2,7)$.

At $B=(1,2,7)$ the negative reduced cost is $\bar c_3=-29/2$. Its direction is $d=(1/2,1/2,-1/2)$, so the eligible ratios for $(x_1,x_2)$ are $(0,0)$; the least-index leaving variable is $x_1$, giving $\theta=0$ and basis $(3,2,7)$.

At $B=(3,2,7)$ the negative reduced costs are $\bar c_4=-18$ and $\bar c_5=-15$, so both rules choose $x_4$. Its direction is $d=(-8,2,0)$; the only eligible ratio is $0$ for $x_2$, which leaves and gives basis $(3,4,7)$.

At $B=(3,4,7)$ the only negative reduced cost is $\bar c_5=-21/2$. Its direction is $d=(1/2,1/4,0)$; the eligible ratios for $(x_3,x_4)$ are $(0,0)$, so $x_3$ leaves at $\theta=0$ and the basis becomes $(5,4,7)$. Thus the first five pivots agree under both rules.

At $B=(5,4,7)$, $\bar c_1=-22$ and $\bar c_6=-24$. The most-negative rule chooses $x_6$, whose direction $d=(-9,1,0)$ has only the eligible ratio $0$ for $x_4$. The pivot leaves $x_4$ and returns to $(5,6,7)$ with the same basic vector and objective $0$; repeating the deterministic choices cycles.

At the same basis $(5,4,7)$, Bland chooses $x_1$ because $1<6$. Its direction is $d=(-4,1/2,1)$; the eligible ratios for $(x_4,x_7)$ are $(0,1)$, so $x_4$ leaves and the next basis is $(5,1,7)$, still with $\theta=0$.

At $B=(5,1,7)$ the only negative reduced cost is $\bar c_3=-1$. Its direction is $d=(-2,-1,1)$, so only $x_7$ is eligible and its ratio is $1$. The pivot gives basis $(5,1,3)$ and basic values $(2,1,1)$, hence $x_1=x_3=1$ and the other original variables are zero.

At this final basis the objective is $-10+9=-1$ and the remaining reduced costs for $(x_2,x_4,x_6,x_7)$ are $(30,42,18,1)$, all nonnegative. The basic vector is feasible, so [F2] proves it optimal; [F3] also confirms finite termination. Input any exact equality system $Ax=b$ with $x\ge0$, including a rank-deficient raw system. Let $D$ be diagonal with $D_{ii}=-1$ when $b_i<0$ and $D_{ii}=1$ otherwise; set $\widetilde A=DA$ and $\widetilde b=Db\ge0$. Add artificial variables $u\in\mathbb R^m$ and solve the Phase I problem $\min\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}u$ subject to $\widetilde A x+u=\widetilde b$, $x,u\ge0$, starting at $x=0,u=\widetilde b$ with artificial basis $I_m$. Use the exact primal algorithm of [[alg-revised-primal-simplex-bland-rule]] and its finite-termination result [[thm-revised-simplex-bland-rule-finite-termination]].

At a terminal optimum, if $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}u>0$, return `infeasible` and the basis multiplier $y$ for the Phase I objective. If the optimum is zero, set every artificial variable to zero and remove artificial basic variables as follows. For a zero-valued artificial basic variable, inspect its row in $B^{-1}\widetilde A$. If some original nonbasic column has a nonzero coefficient there, pivot the least-index such column into the basis; the pivot may have either sign because the leaving basic value is zero. If no such coefficient exists, and the transformed right-hand-side entry is zero, delete that redundant equation and its zero artificial basic variable. Repeat until all remaining basic columns are original; return the row-reduced equivalent system and its original feasible basis. A zero row with nonzero transformed right-hand side returns `inconsistent-row`. All tests are exact; a finite-precision near-zero objective is not treated as zero.

For any exact system $Ax=b$, $x\ge0$, the Phase I procedure of [[alg-revised-simplex-phase-one]] terminates. Its minimum artificial-variable sum is zero if and only if the original system is feasible. If the minimum is positive, its returned vector yields a Farkas infeasibility certificate, as defined in [[def-revised-simplex-standard-form-linear-program]], with $A^{\mathsf T}q\ge0$ and $b^{\mathsf T}q<0$. If the minimum is zero, the extraction procedure returns an equivalent full-row-rank reduced system with a basic feasible solution using only original columns; zero-valued artificial basic variables are either pivoted out or their redundant equations are removed.

derivations.claim: The third right-hand side is negative, so $D=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-1)$ gives $\widetilde A=DA=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\1&1&-1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\widetilde b=Db=(1,1,3)^{\mathsf T}$. The Phase I point $x=(1,1,0)$, $u=(0,0,1)$ satisfies $\widetilde A x+u=\widetilde b$ and has objective $1$.

The Phase I dual vector $y=(-1,-1,1)$ satisfies $\widetilde A^{\mathsf T}y=(0,0,-1)^{\mathsf T}\le0$ and $\widetilde b^{\mathsf T}y=1$. For any Phase I feasible $(x,u)$, its objective $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}u$ is at least $\widetilde b^{\mathsf T}y=1$ by multiplying the constraints by $y$ and using $\widetilde A^{\mathsf T}y\le0$, $u\ge0$, and $y\le\mathbf1$. Thus the displayed feasible point attains the Phase I optimum $1>0$.

The original Farkas vector is $q=-D^{\mathsf T}y=(1,1,1)$. Direct calculation gives $A^{\mathsf T}q=(0,0,1)^{\mathsf T}\ge0$ and $b^{\mathsf T}q=1+1-3=-1<0$. Hence no $x\ge0$ can satisfy $Ax=b$, as also follows from [F2].

Input finite stored binary data for the standard-form LP of [[def-revised-simplex-basis-dictionary]], with full-row-rank $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, a candidate ordered basis $B$ of $m$ distinct in-range indices, and a nonnegative integer budget $K$ of basis evaluations. Stored values represent their exact dyadic rationals. Invalid dimensions, nonfinite inputs or repeated/out-of-range basis indices return `invalid-input`. Nonsingularity of $C=A_B$ must be established as part of an admitted basis input; a numerical rank threshold is not such an establishment. A basis whose validity is unavailable returns `basis-validity-inconclusive`.

A caller may request a primal or dual simplex transition after an audit, or only an audit. It may supply a finite sequence of transition records, one for each requested basis replacement, from [[alg-revised-primal-simplex-bland-rule]] or [[alg-revised-dual-simplex-with-finite-budget]]. A transition record has fields `mode` (primal or dual), `basis_before` (the ordered current basis, with its validity witness), `leaving_position` $i$, and `entering_index` $j$; it is checked rather than trusted as already verified. The initial basis and each record's `basis_before` must carry the validity witness described here. After a replacement, its checked nonzero pivot coefficient establishes the new basis; the next record supplies a fresh witness if it uses exact inverse or enclosure checks.

An admitted basis input includes either an exact rational inverse witness $G$ with $CG=GC=I_m$, checked exactly, or a rational matrix $H$ and rational $q$ with $0\le q<1$ and $\|I_m-HC\|_\infty\le q$, also checked exactly. The second certificate proves that $C$ is nonsingular; if a rational $M\ge\|H\|_\infty/(1-q)$ is supplied, it also proves $\|C^{-1}\|_\infty\le M$. For $m=0$, the empty inverse witness satisfies the identities. If neither validity certificate is verified, return `basis-validity-inconclusive` before factorization. A numerical rank threshold is never a validity certificate.

With an exact inverse witness, check a transition by exact rational arithmetic: compute $x_B=Gb$, $y=G^{\mathsf T}c_B$, $d_k=Ga_k$ for every nonbasic $k$, and $\bar c_k=c_k-a_k^{\mathsf T}y$. A primal record is admissible exactly when $x_B\ge0$, $j$ is the least-index nonbasic column with $\bar c_j<0$, some $d_{rj}>0$, and $i$ minimizes $x_{B_r}/d_{rj}$ over rows with $d_{rj}>0$, with ties resolved by least basic-variable index. A dual record is admissible exactly when every nonbasic $\bar c_k\ge0$, $B_i$ is the least-index basic variable with $x_{B_i}<0$, $d_{ij}<0$, and $j$ minimizes $\bar c_k/(-d_{ik})$ over nonbasic $k$ with $d_{ik}<0$, with ties resolved by least variable index. In either case, the checked nonzero pivot coefficient proves the replacement basis nonsingular.

Certified rational enclosures may instead establish a transition. For each current $D=C$ and $D=C^{\mathsf T}$, provide rational $H_D,q_D,M_D$ with $0\le q_D<1$, $\|I_m-H_DD\|_\infty\le q_D$, and $M_D\ge\|H_D\|_\infty/(1-q_D)$; verify these inequalities exactly. For each solve $Dz=r$, combine its returned candidate $\widehat z$ and a rational upper bound $\eta$ for its Step 3 residual bound to enclose each exact coordinate of $D^{-1}r$ in $[\widehat z_\ell-M_D\eta,\widehat z_\ell+M_D\eta]$. Propagate the rational intervals through reduced costs and ratios by outward exact interval arithmetic. Admit the record only when the intervals prove every required sign and comparison, including the least-index rules; an equality used to resolve a tie must be proved exactly. If a needed sign, ratio comparison, basis match, or tie is not established, return `pivot-inconclusive` with the current basis and its last completed audit, without changing the basis.

For $m\ge1$, use the operationwise arithmetic of [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]], with $0<u<1$, $mu<1$, $(m+3)u<1$, and $\gamma_{m+3}<1/8$. All nonzero exact intermediates must be normal. Norms and certificate expressions below are evaluated exactly or by certified upward bounds; failure to obtain a finite valid bound is a numerical failure. Process the following loop:

1. Maintain an attempt counter $t$, initially $0$. If $t=K$, return `budget-exhausted` with the current basis, the last completed audit if any, and the basis to which that audit belongs. Otherwise set $t\leftarrow t+1$ before starting this basis evaluation. Every budget, numerical-failure, basis-validity-inconclusive, or pivot-inconclusive return includes the current basis and identifies the basis associated with any retained audit; state explicitly when no audit exists.
2. Separately for $D=C=A_B$ and $D=C^{\mathsf T}$, copy the current stored entries into a working matrix $W$. For $k=1,\ldots,m$, set $r=m-k+1$, take the active column $x=W_{k:m,k}$ and trailing block $T=W_{k:m,k+1:m}$, and call [[alg-scaled-householder-reflector-formation-and-application]] once on $(x,T)$. On success, save its reflector data and replace the active block $W_{k:m,k:m}$ by its returned output, which writes the new diagonal entry and exact zeros below it; leave earlier rows and columns unchanged. If $x=0$, save an identity marker and leave the trailing block unchanged. Stop with `numerical-failure` at the first failed call, recording the factorization, column $k$, and failure stage. The final $W$ is the computed upper-triangular factor $\widehat R_D$.

   To apply these stored reflectors to any right-hand side $s$, start with $z=s$ and visit $k=1,\ldots,m$ in that same order. Skip an identity marker. Otherwise, on the active suffix $z_{k:m}$ compute the sequential rounded dot $d=\operatorname{fl}(v_k^{\mathsf T}z_{k:m})$, then $p=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau_k v_k)$, $u=\operatorname{fl}(p\,d)$ componentwise, and $z_{k:m}=\operatorname{fl}(z_{k:m}-u)$ componentwise, using the operation order of [[alg-scaled-householder-reflector-formation-and-application]] without a column overwrite. Stop at the first failure and record the right-hand side, reflector index, and failure stage. For $Dz=s$, apply this replay to obtain the transformed right-hand side and solve $\widehat R_D\widehat z=z$ by descending substitution: for $i=m,\ldots,1$, sequentially compute $t_i=\operatorname{fl}(\sum_{j=i+1}^m(\widehat R_D)_{ij}\widehat z_j)$, $h_i=\operatorname{fl}(z_i-t_i)$, and $\widehat z_i=\operatorname{fl}(h_i/(\widehat R_D)_{ii})$. A zero diagonal or any failed operation returns `numerical-failure` with the solve and row index. Reuse the $C$ factorization for $\widehat x_B$ and every nonbasic direction $\widehat d_j$; reuse the $C^{\mathsf T}$ factorization for $\widehat y$. Never substitute a rounded dense orthogonal product for the exact orthogonal representative in the proof. After every admitted basis replacement discard both factorizations and recompute; no rank-one factorization-update implementation is claimed.
3. Independently certify each returned solve for its actual current matrix $D=C$ or $C^{\mathsf T}$ and right-hand side $r$. Compute $\widehat v=\operatorname{fl}(D\widehat z)$ and $\widehat w=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-r)$ by the sequential products/subtraction of [[lem-rounded-linear-and-normal-residual-certificates]]. Put
$$g_m=\frac{1+6u}{1-(m-1)u}-1,\qquad W=g_m\|D\|_F\|\widehat z\|_2+u(\|\widehat v\|_2+\|r\|_2).$$
With the local coefficient $\kappa_m$ of [[lem-scaled-householder-step-meets-local-backward-error-premise]], put
$$\beta=(1+\kappa_m)^m-1,\qquad \beta_D=\beta+\gamma_{m+3}(1+\beta),$$
and report the valid upper bound
$$\eta(D,r,\widehat z)=\min\{\|\widehat w\|_2+W,\ \beta_D\|D\|_F\|\widehat z\|_2+\beta\|r\|_2\}.$$
A finite concrete certificate option uses exact rational arithmetic on the stored dyadic entries and a rational upper bound for $u$ satisfying all displayed admissibility inequalities. Use $\|v\|_2\le\sum_i|v_i|$ and $\|D\|_F\le\sum_{i,j}|D_{ij}|$ as rational upper bounds for every norm in the two nonnegative expressions. For the local coefficient, substitute $\bar e_m=(1+u)^{m+3}-1$ for $e_m=(1+u)^{m/2+3}-1$ in the source formula: put $\bar d_m=\bar e_m+u(2+\bar e_m)$, $a_m=(1+u)/(1-u)^m-1$, $g_m^{\rm QR}=mu/(1-mu)$, $c_m=2((1+a_m)(1+u)^2(1+g_m^{\rm QR})-1)$, and $\bar\kappa_m=\max\{\bar e_m+8\bar d_m,(1+u)c_m+3u\}$. These are rational upper bounds because $m+3\ge m/2+3$ and all constituent nonnegative formulas increase in their arguments. Then $\bar\beta=(1+\bar\kappa_m)^m-1$ and $\bar\beta_D=\bar\beta+\gamma_{m+3}(1+\bar\beta)$ are rational upper bounds for the QR coefficients. Compute both candidate bounds by finite exact rational sums/products/powers and take their minimum as the returned $\eta$. This implements the certificate without a norm oracle; other finite certified upper-bound procedures are allowed. Any factorization, substitution, dot, subtraction, range or certificate failure returns `numerical-failure`, with its stage and the last completed audit; it returns no certificate for the failed solve.
4. Embed $\widehat x_B$ in $\widehat x\in\mathbb R^n$ with zero nonbasic entries, and call [[alg-revised-simplex-residual-audit]] on these actual stored $\widehat x,\widehat y$. Retain its exact $r_p=A\widehat x-b$, $r_d=c-A^{\mathsf T}\widehat y$, objective difference $g$, and audit status together with all solve residual bounds. `basis-solves-residual-certified` means only that the returned bounds certify those linear equations; any requested thresholds must also be checked before declaring them met. `verified-optimal-for-stored-data` is issued only by the exact audit's primal/sign/zero-gap checks. Other completed candidates remain `candidate-only`; small residuals or a failed/ambiguous pivot never certify infeasibility.
5. Return if audit-only mode or the caller has no further transition. Otherwise compare the next record with the current basis and apply the exact or enclosure admission predicate above. A failed or unresolved predicate returns `pivot-inconclusive` or `basis-validity-inconclusive`, retaining the current basis and last completed audit. On admission, replace position $i$ by $j$, discard both factorizations, and continue at Step 1. Exact driver invariants remain those of the existing driver, not consequences of successful floating solves.

For $m=0$, skip QR and substitution: the basis and multiplier are empty, every direction is the empty vector, and their basis-equation residuals and solve bounds $\eta$ are zero. Evaluate the existing exact audit with $\widehat x=0$; no basis replacement is possible. The budget and invalid-input branches remain in force.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $m\ge n\ge1$, have full column rank. Successful scaled Householder QR gives the exactly orthonormal reduced representative $\widehat Q$ and computed triangular $\widehat R$ with
$$A+\Delta_Q=\widehat Q\widehat R,\qquad \|\Delta_Q\|_F\le\beta_Q\|A\|_F,\qquad \beta_Q=(1+\kappa_m)^n-1,$$
where $\kappa_m$ is the proved local-step coefficient. Apply the stored reflectors to $b$ by rounded rank-one updates and let $\widehat y$ be the first $n$ coordinates. Set $\beta_b=\beta_Q$. Alternatively, if an explicitly supplied exactly orthonormal $\widehat Q$ has entries admissible as arithmetic inputs and $\widehat y=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat Q^Tb)$ uses sequential rounded dots, set $\beta_b=\sqrt n\,\gamma_m$. Solve $\widehat R\widehat x=\widehat y$ by successful rounded back substitution. Suppose $mu<1$ and $\gamma_{n+3}<1/8$. There exist $\delta b$ and upper triangular $\Delta R$ with
$$(\widehat R+\Delta R)\widehat x=\widehat Q^T(b+\delta b),\qquad \|\delta b\|_2\le\beta_b\|b\|_2,\qquad \|\Delta R\|_F\le\gamma_{n+3}\|\widehat R\|_F.$$
If $\widehat R+\Delta R$ is nonsingular, $\widehat x$ is the unique least-squares solution for $\widetilde A=\widehat Q(\widehat R+\Delta R)$ and $\widetilde b=b+\delta b$. The relative matrix perturbation is at most $\beta_Q+\gamma_{n+3}(1+\beta_Q)$; the right-hand perturbation is at most $\beta_b$. For fixed $m,n$, both perturbation coefficients are $O(u)$. If additionally $\beta_Q\le19\gamma_{n+3}/(1+\gamma_{n+3})$ and $\beta_b\le20\gamma_{n+3}$, both relative data perturbation bounds are at most $20\gamma_{n+3}$. These two coefficient comparisons are additional checks; they do not follow from $mu<1$ and $\gamma_{n+3}<1/8$ alone. Success and nonsingularity are explicit hypotheses.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $x\in\mathbb F^n$, $y\in\mathbb F^m$ have stored real or complex entries, with $m,n\ge1$. Use the operationwise arithmetic model, successful sequential dot products, and $0<u<1$ with $(\max(m,n)-1)u<1$. Define
$$g_k=\frac{1+6u}{1-(k-1)u}-1,\qquad F=\|A\|_F,\quad X=\|x\|_2,\quad Y=\|y\|_2.$$
For $\widehat v=\operatorname{fl}(Ax)$ and $\widehat w=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-y)$, put $V=g_nFX$ and $W=V+u(\|\widehat v\|_2+Y)$. Then
$$\|\widehat w-(Ax-y)\|_2\le W.$$
For a stored real $\lambda>0$, also compute $\widehat z=\operatorname{fl}(A^*\widehat w)$, $\widehat l=\operatorname{fl}(\lambda x)$ and $\widehat r=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat z+\widehat l)$, rounding scalar multiplication componentwise. The exact intended normal residual $r=A^*(Ax-y)+\lambda x$ satisfies
$$\|\widehat r-r\|_2\le\rho:=FW+g_mF\|\widehat w\|_2+u\lambda X+u(\|\widehat z\|_2+\|\widehat l\|_2).$$
Norms in these certificates mean exact norms or certified upper bounds. Uncontrolled rounding of the certificate itself is not authorized. The linear bound applies columnwise to certify $\|I-AB\|_2\le\|I-AB\|_F$ from stored basis-solve columns $B$.

For a standard-form problem and finite candidate vectors $x,y$, let $r_p=Ax-b$, $r_d=c-A^{\mathsf T}y$, and $g=c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y$, as computed exactly by [[alg-revised-simplex-residual-audit]]. Then
$$g=x^{\mathsf T}r_d+y^{\mathsf T}r_p,$$
and consequently
$$|g|\le \|x\|_1\|r_d\|_\infty+\|y\|_1\|r_p\|_\infty.$$
Here $\|z\|_1=\sum_i|z_i|$ and $\|z\|_\infty=\max_i|z_i|$, with both norms equal to zero on the empty vector. This bounds the primal-dual objective difference for the stored data; when either vector is infeasible it does not bound distance to an optimal value. If $Ax=b$, $x\ge0$, $c-A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0$, and $g=0$, then $x$ is optimal.

derivations.claim: If $m=0$, the empty solve residuals are zero and only the finite audit and budget branches remain. If $m\ge1$, nonsingularity makes each square $D$ full column rank. Apply [F2] under [A1]; since the exact representative is square, $\widehat Q\widehat Q^{\mathsf T}=I$. Multiplication of its triangular equation therefore gives $(D+\Delta_D)\widehat z=r+\delta r$, where $\Delta_D=\Delta_Q+\widehat Q\Delta_R$. No nonsingularity of $\widehat R+\Delta_R$ or exact orthogonality of a rounded dense output is used.

Orthogonality and [F2] imply $\|\widehat R\|_F=\|D+\Delta_Q\|_F\le(1+\beta)\|D\|_F$. Hence $\|\Delta_D\|_F\le[\beta+\gamma_{m+3}(1+\beta)]\|D\|_F=\beta_D\|D\|_F$. Rearranging step1.1 yields $\|D\widehat z-r\|_2\le\|\delta r\|_2+\|\Delta_D\|_F\|\widehat z\|_2\le\beta\|r\|_2+\beta_D\|D\|_F\|\widehat z\|_2$.

The triangle inequality and [F3] give the independent upper bound $\|D\widehat z-r\|_2\le\|\widehat w\|_2+W$. Both quantities in the reported minimum are upper bounds, so their minimum is an upper bound. Applying this to each current primal, transpose-multiplier and direction solve proves all residual conclusions. The same conclusion holds when the algorithm uses rational or other certified upper bounds, since both evaluated candidates remain upper bounds. Finally $D(\widehat z-z_*)=D\widehat z-r$, so the defining induced-norm inequality gives $\|\widehat z-z_*\|_2\le\|D^{-1}\|_2\|D\widehat z-r\|_2\le\|D^{-1}\|_2\eta$. This is conditional on the actual inverse norm, not an assertion that the procedure computes it.

By [F1], the completed audit uses the actual stored candidate vectors and original stored LP data. Apply [F4] to obtain the displayed identity, norm bound and exactly conditional optimality statement. Since [F1] labels no other branch verified-optimal and rejects unestablished transitions, no small residual, unresolved sign/ratio comparison or numerical failure is converted into a pivot, optimality or infeasibility certificate.

Each canonical factorization, vector application, substitution and residual loop has finite dimensions; each elementary call either completes or returns its first failure by [F1]. Verifying a transition record uses only finitely many exact rational matrix products or certified interval operations over the finite basis and column sets; unresolved comparisons return inconclusive. The dyadic audit uses finitely many exact integer/rational operations. Before each attempt the counter increases, and [F1] allows at most $K$ attempts and no unbounded internal transition search. Every admitted basis replacement discards old factors before computing new certificates. Consequently the procedure terminates with only the stated current-basis outputs or failure/inconclusive status, proving the remaining claims.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function. Recall that a metric takes nonnegative real values
([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]).

- $f$ is **Lipschitz** with **constant** $L$, where $L \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $L \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; L \, d_X(x,x') \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X .$$
  $f$ is *Lipschitz* if it is Lipschitz with some such constant.
- Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $0 < \alpha \le 1$ ([[def-rat-order]]). $f$ is
  **$\alpha$-Hölder** with **constant** $C$, where $C \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $C \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; C \, d_X(x,x')^{\alpha} \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X ,$$
  the power being the rational power of a nonnegative base
  ([[def-rational-power]]). $f$ is *$\alpha$-Hölder* if it is so with some such
  constant, and *Hölder* if it is $\alpha$-Hölder for some rational
  $\alpha \in (0,1]$.
- $f$ is a **contraction** with constant $q$ if it is Lipschitz with constant $q$
  and $0 \le q < 1$. The number $q$ is then called a **contraction constant** for
  $f$.

**The power $d_X(x,x')^{\alpha}$ is defined at every pair, including $x = x'$.**
The base $d_X(x,x')$ is a nonnegative real, and [[def-rational-power]] defines
$a^{\alpha}$ for every $a > 0$ and, by its supplementary clause, sets
$0^{\alpha} = 0$ for every rational $\alpha > 0$. Since $\alpha > 0$ is required
here, the displayed inequality at $x = x'$ reads $0 \le C \cdot 0$, which holds;
so no separate clause and no restriction to $x \ne x'$ is needed. Note that this
does not by itself explain the strict inequality $\alpha>0$: if one extended the
formula to $\alpha=0$ using the convention $0^0=1$ of [[def-integer-power]], the
equal-point inequality would still be the automatic $0\le C$. Globally, however,
that extension would reduce to the bounded-diameter condition
$d_Y(f(x),f(x'))\le C$, outside the standard Hölder range adopted here.

**Why the exponent is rational on this page and why it is at most $1$.** At this
point in the reading order only rational powers are available
([[def-rational-power]]), so $\alpha$ ranges over the rationals. The upper
bound $\alpha \le 1$ is the standard convention, and it is where the notion is
useful: the classical theory reserves the name for $\alpha \in (0,1]$, and
nothing in this library uses an exponent outside that range. No claim is made
here about what an exponent $\alpha > 1$ would do.

**Constants are not unique and are not part of the data.** If $f$ is Lipschitz
with constant $L$ it is Lipschitz with every constant $L' \ge L$, and likewise
for Hölder constants; the adjectives above are existential statements. A
*contraction*, by contrast, requires a constant strictly below $1$, and that is a
real restriction: exhibiting the constant is part of exhibiting a contraction, and
a map that shrinks every distance without admitting one uniform constant is not a
contraction here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse ([[def-field]]). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
[[thm-of-archimedean]] on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

derivations.claim: Put $d=y-x$. If $d=0$ the inequality is equality. Otherwise define $\phi(s)=f(x+sd)$ on $[0,1]$. By [F2] and continuity of $\nabla f$, $\phi$ is continuous on $[0,1]$, differentiable on $(0,1)$, and $\phi'(s)=\langle\nabla f(x+sd),d\rangle$.

For an arbitrary natural $N\ge1$, partition $[0,1]$ at $j/N$. Applying [F1] on each subinterval gives $\xi_j\in(j/N,(j+1)/N)$ with $\phi((j+1)/N)-\phi(j/N)=\phi'(\xi_j)/N$. Telescoping and subtracting $\phi'(0)$ yields $$f(y)-f(x)-\langle\nabla f(x),d\rangle=\frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(\phi'(\xi_j)-\phi'(0))\le\frac{L\|d\|_2^2}{N^2}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(j+1)=\frac{L}{2}(1+1/N)\|d\|_2^2,$$ because [F3] and [F4] give $|\phi'(s)-\phi'(0)|\le Ls\|d\|_2^2$ and $\xi_j<(j+1)/N$. To evaluate the finite sum for every natural $N$, its value is $N(N+1)/2$: at $N=0$ both sides are zero, and the recursion [F6] adds $N+1$ when $N$ is increased by one, giving $(N+1)(N+2)/2$. [F7] proves this identity by induction. Only finitely many mean-value points are used for each fixed $N$.

The left side of the bound in step 1.2 is independent of $N$. Suppose it exceeded $L\|d\|_2^2/2$ by $\delta>0$. For $L\|d\|_2^2>0$, [F5] lets us choose $N$ with $1/N<2\delta/(L\|d\|_2^2)$, making the right side in step 1.2 strictly smaller than the left side, a contradiction. If $L\|d\|_2^2=0$, step 1.2 already gives the desired bound.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. Its effective domain is $\operatorname{dom}g=\{x:g(x)<+\infty\}$. The function is **proper** if $\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing$; it is **convex** if
$$g((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\le(1-\theta)g(x)+\theta g(y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n,\ 0\le\theta\le1),$$
using the endpoint convention $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ of [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functionals-on-a-banach-space]]. It is **closed** (equivalently, lower semicontinuous in the extended-real convex-analysis convention used here) if its epigraph
$$\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:g(x)\le s\}$$
is closed in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. The proximal-gradient items on this page assume $g$ is proper, closed and convex.

This page's closed-epigraph convention is explicit: it does not silently use an equivalence between sequential lower semicontinuity and topological closedness that would require an additional choice principle in the library's generic sequential convention. In finite dimensions this is the standard closed proper convex input to proximal algorithms.
Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $x\in\mathbb R^n$. Then there is a unique $p\in C$ such that $\|x-p\|_2\le\|x-z\|_2$ for every $z\in C$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, let $x\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $p\in C$. Then $p$ is the nearest point of $C$ to $x$ if and only if

$$\langle x-p,z-p\rangle\le0\qquad(z\in C).$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $\bigl(x^{(j)}\bigr)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$
be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose range
$\{\, x^{(j)} : j \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is a bounded subset of
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Then there are a strictly increasing $i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
([[def-sequence]], [[lem-index-map-grows]]) and a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$
with

$$x^{(i_j)} \longrightarrow p \quad \text{in } (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$$

([[def-metric-convergence]]). By [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] the same
statement holds with $d_2$ replaced by the metric of any norm on
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$, boundedness and convergence both being unchanged by that
replacement ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).

**This is assembled from published theorems and is not proved again by
bisection.** The bisection is in [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], published at order 120;
what is added here is the passage from compactness to sequential compactness and
the reading of the conclusion in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

**Choice cost: none.** [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no
choice principle, and "compact implies sequentially compact" is a theorem of ZF
([[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]]). The five-way equivalence
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] is **not** used, precisely because it is
stated under countable choice and dependent choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) and
would overcharge this corollary; the arrow-by-arrow account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

derivations.claim: Let $d$ be the dimension of the direction space of $\operatorname{aff}D$. If $d=0$, then $D$ is a singleton $\{x_0\}$ and the constant affine function $g(x_0)$ is a minorant. If $d>0$, choose $d+1$ affinely independent points of $D$ spanning $\operatorname{aff}D$ and let $x_0$ be their barycenter. Their simplex lies in $D$ by convexity, and its barycenter has all positive barycentric coordinates, so a relative neighborhood of $x_0$ in $\operatorname{aff}D$ lies in $D$. Thus $x_0$ is a relative-interior point of $D$.

Put $p=(x_0,g(x_0))\in E_g$ and $q_j=(x_0,g(x_0)-1/j)$ for integers $j\ge1$. Each $q_j$ lies outside $E_g$ and tends to $p$. Let $p_j$ be its unique nearest point in $E_g$, supplied by [F1]. Since $p\in E_g$, $\|q_j-p_j\|_2\le1/j$, and consequently $p_j\to p$.

Normalize $u_j=(q_j-p_j)/\|q_j-p_j\|_2$, which is defined because $q_j\notin E_g$ and $E_g$ is closed. The vectors $u_j$ have norm one, so [F3] gives a subsequence converging to a unit vector $u=(a,c)$. Both $q_j$ and $p_j$ have horizontal coordinate in $\operatorname{aff}D$, so the horizontal component $a$ lies in the direction space of $\operatorname{aff}D$. For every fixed $z\in E_g$, [F2] gives $\langle u_j,z-p_j\rangle\le0$; passage to the subsequence limit gives $\langle u,z-p\rangle\le0$.

The upward vertical ray $p+(0,s)$ lies in $E_g$ for all $s\ge0$, so step 2.1 forces $c\le0$. If $c=0$, relative interior from step 1.1 lets each direction $h$ in the affine-hull direction space be tested at $x_0+\varepsilon h$ and $x_0-\varepsilon h$ for sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$. Applying step 2.1 to the corresponding epigraph points gives $\langle a,h\rangle=0$ for every such $h$. Since $a$ lies in that direction space, $a=0$, contradicting $\|u\|_2=1$. Hence $c<0$.

For any $x\in D$, apply step 2.1 to $(x,g(x))\in E_g$ to get $\langle a,x-x_0\rangle+c(g(x)-g(x_0))\le0$. Dividing by $c<0$ reverses the inequality and yields $g(x)\ge g(x_0)+\langle -a/c,x-x_0\rangle$. Set $a_0=-a/c$ and $b_0=g(x_0)-\langle a_0,x_0\rangle$. This is the desired affine bound on $D$, and outside $D$ the value is $+\infty$, so the bound holds on all of $\mathbb R^n$.
