In finite dimensions this is the standard closed proper convex input to proximal algorithms.

Let $X$ be a real vector space and $K\subseteq X$. The set $K$ is **convex** if $\lambda u+(1-\lambda)v\in K$ for all $u,v\in K$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$. Fix a nonempty convex $K$ and an extended-real functional $I:K\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ ([[def-proper-coercive-and-weakly-lower-semicontinuous-functional]]), with the sums and positive-weight products of [[def-extended-reals]]. For convex combinations only, additionally define $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$; this is a local convention, since that product is left undefined in the general extended-real arithmetic. Then $I$ is **convex** if
$$I\big(\lambda u+(1-\lambda)v\big)\le\lambda I(u)+(1-\lambda)I(v),\qquad u,v\in K,\ \lambda\in[0,1],$$
and **strictly convex** if the inequality is strict whenever $u\ne v$, $I(u),I(v)<+\infty$ and $\lambda\in(0,1)$. A convex functional has convex sublevel sets: for every $t\in\mathbb R$ the set $\{u\in K:I(u)\le t\}$ is convex. Only real coefficients are used: on a complex vector space these notions are read on the underlying real structure.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

derivations.claim: Since $\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing$, choose $x_0$ with $g(x_0)<+\infty$. The value $f(x_0)$ is real, so $F(x_0)<+\infty$ and $F$ is proper.

For $x,y$ with finite $F$ and $0\le\theta\le1$, both $g(x),g(y)$ are finite. Applying convexity separately to $f$ and $g$ and adding gives $F((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\le(1-\theta)F(x)+\theta F(y)$; if either value of $F$ is $+\infty$, the extended-real convexity inequality is automatic. Thus $F$ is convex.

For $r\in\mathbb R$, let $\Phi(x,s)=(x,s-f(x))$. It is continuous: the first coordinates are unchanged, while continuity of $f$ makes the last coordinate $s-f(x)$ continuous. The identity $\operatorname{epi}F=\Phi^{-1}(\operatorname{epi}g)$ follows by rearranging $f(x)+g(x)\le s$, including points where $g(x)=+\infty$. If a point lies outside $\operatorname{epi}F$, its image lies outside the closed set $\operatorname{epi}g$, so an open ball about that image misses $\operatorname{epi}g$; continuity of $\Phi$ supplies a neighborhood of the original point mapped into that ball. Hence the complement of $\operatorname{epi}F$ is open and $F$ is closed.

citations.quote:
For any set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, its extended-real indicator is
$$\iota_C(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}$$

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. Its effective domain is $\operatorname{dom}g=\{x:g(x)<+\infty\}$. The function is **proper** if $\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing$; it is **convex** if
$$g((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\le(1-\theta)g(x)+\theta g(y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n,\ 0\le\theta\le1),$$
using the endpoint convention $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ of [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functionals-on-a-banach-space]]. It is **closed** (equivalently, lower semicontinuous in the extended-real convex-analysis convention used here) if its epigraph
$$\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:g(x)\le s\}$$
is closed in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. The proximal-gradient items on this page assume $g$ is proper, closed and convex.

This page's closed-epigraph convention is explicit: it does not silently use an equivalence between sequential lower semicontinuity and topological closedness that would require an additional choice principle in the library's generic sequential convention. In finite dimensions this is the standard closed proper convex input to proximal algorithms.
Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $x\in\mathbb R^n$. Then there is a unique $p\in C$ such that $\|x-p\|_2\le\|x-z\|_2$ for every $z\in C$.

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex, and let $t>0$. For $v\in\mathbb R^n$, define the set-valued proximal mapping
$$\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)=\left\{u\in\mathbb R^n:g(u)+\frac{\|u-v\|_2^2}{2t}\le g(w)+\frac{\|w-v\|_2^2}{2t}\text{ for every }w\in\mathbb R^n\right\}.$$
The existence and uniqueness theorem on this page proves that this set is a singleton for every admissible $g,t,v$; its unique member is also denoted $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: Since $C$ is nonempty, some $x\in C$ has $\iota_C(x)=0<+\infty$, so the indicator is proper. If $x,y\in C$, convexity of $C$ puts every convex combination in $C$, where the indicator is zero; if either endpoint is outside $C$, the convexity inequality is automatic for an interior coefficient, and at endpoints it is equality. Thus $\iota_C$ is convex.

Its epigraph is exactly $C\times[0,+\infty)$: for $x\in C$ the inequality $0\le s$ is required, and for $x\notin C$ no real $s$ satisfies $+\infty\le s$. This product is closed because both factors are closed, so $\iota_C$ is closed.

If $n=0$, then $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ by [F6], and nonempty $C\subseteq\mathbb R^0$ is $\{0\}$. The proximal objective has this sole point as its unique minimizer, and it is also the unique nearest point in $C$ to $v=0$. Hence the claim holds for $n=0$.

Now assume $n\ge1$. The proximal objective is finite exactly on $C$, where it equals $\|u-v\|_2^2/(2t)$. Since $2t>0$, minimizing it over all $\mathbb R^n$ is equivalent to minimizing distance from $v$ over $C$. By [F4] the latter has a unique minimizer, which is therefore exactly the singleton in [F5].

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. Its effective domain is $\operatorname{dom}g=\{x:g(x)<+\infty\}$. The function is **proper** if $\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing$; it is **convex** if
$$g((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\le(1-\theta)g(x)+\theta g(y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n,\ 0\le\theta\le1),$$
using the endpoint convention $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ of [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functionals-on-a-banach-space]]. It is **closed** (equivalently, lower semicontinuous in the extended-real convex-analysis convention used here) if its epigraph
$$\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:g(x)\le s\}$$
is closed in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. The proximal-gradient items on this page assume $g$ is proper, closed and convex.

This page's closed-epigraph convention is explicit: it does not silently use an equivalence between sequential lower semicontinuity and topological closedness that would require an additional choice principle in the library's generic sequential convention. In finite dimensions this is the standard closed proper convex input to proximal algorithms.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. Then there are $a\in\mathbb R^n$ and $b\in\mathbb R$ such that
$$g(x)\ge\langle a,x\rangle+b\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^n).$$

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and convex, and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex under the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. Then $F=f+g$ is proper, closed and convex in the same convention.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and compact. Every lower semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded below and attains a minimum. Dually, every upper semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded above and attains a maximum.

Let $n\ge1$, let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and let $f:A\to\mathbb R$.

- Upper semicontinuity is equivalent to relative openness of every strict sublevel set $\{f<\alpha\}$ and to relative closedness of every weak superlevel set $\{f\ge\alpha\}$.
- Lower semicontinuity is equivalent to relative openness of every strict superlevel set and to relative closedness of every weak sublevel set.

Relative openness and closedness refer to the subspace topology on $A$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]], [[def-metric-topology]]).

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex in the convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}g$ and $\eta\ge0$, define
$$\partial_\eta g(x)=\{p\in\mathbb R^n:g(z)\ge g(x)+\langle p,z-x\rangle-\eta\text{ for every }z\in\mathbb R^n\}.$$
Write $\partial g(x)=\partial_0g(x)$. If $x\notin\operatorname{dom}g$, set $\partial_\eta g(x)=\varnothing$. When $g$ is finite-valued on a convex domain, $\partial g(x)$ agrees with [[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]].

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex, and let $t>0$. For $v\in\mathbb R^n$, define the set-valued proximal mapping
$$\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)=\left\{u\in\mathbb R^n:g(u)+\frac{\|u-v\|_2^2}{2t}\le g(w)+\frac{\|w-v\|_2^2}{2t}\text{ for every }w\in\mathbb R^n\right\}.$$
The existence and uniqueness theorem on this page proves that this set is a singleton for every admissible $g,t,v$; its unique member is also denoted $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: If $n=0$, [F10] gives $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$. Properness [F1] forces $g(0)$ to be finite. Every input $v$, candidate $u$, competitor $z$ and subgradient vector $p$ is $0$. The objective in [F8] has only the candidate $0$, so $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(0)=\{0\}$. The inequality in [F7] is $g(0)\ge g(0)+0$, so $\partial g(0)=\{0\}$ and $(v-u)/t=0\in\partial g(0)$; both directions of the resolvent equivalence hold. Firm nonexpansiveness and nonexpansiveness both reduce to $0\le0$. This proves every conclusion for $n=0$ without compactness or an affine-minorant argument. For the remainder assume $n\ge1$.

Define $H(x)=g(x)+\|x-v\|_2^2/(2t)$. The quadratic is finite and continuous, and the identity $$\|(1-\theta)x+\theta y-v\|_2^2=(1-\theta)\|x-v\|_2^2+\theta\|y-v\|_2^2-\theta(1-\theta)\|x-y\|_2^2$$ shows it is convex. Thus [F3] makes $H$ proper, closed and convex. Choose $x_0\in\operatorname{dom}g$ and put $c=H(x_0)$. Then $S=\{x:H(x)\le c\}$ is nonempty and closed: it is the inverse image of $\operatorname{epi}H$ under the continuous map $x\mapsto(x,c)$.

By [F2], completing the square gives $$H(x)\ge b+\langle a,x\rangle+\frac{\|x-v\|_2^2}{2t}=b+\langle a,v\rangle-\frac t2\|a\|_2^2+\frac1{2t}\|x-(v-ta)\|_2^2.$$ Thus $H(x)\le c$ forces $x$ into a fixed-radius ball, so $S$ is bounded and hence compact by [F4]. The restriction $H|_S$ is real-valued; each weak sublevel set is the intersection of $S$ with the inverse image of $\operatorname{epi}H$ under $x\mapsto(x,r)$ for its level $r$, hence closed in $S$. By [F6] it is lower semicontinuous, so [F5] gives a minimizer on $S$. Every point outside $S$ has value greater than $c$, while the minimum on $S$ is at most $c$, so this minimizer is global.

The quadratic satisfies $\|\frac{x+y}{2}-v\|_2^2=\frac12\|x-v\|_2^2+\frac12\|y-v\|_2^2-\frac14\|x-y\|_2^2$. If two distinct points minimized $H$, convexity of $g$ and this identity would make their midpoint have strictly smaller value, a contradiction. Hence the global minimizer is unique, proving the singleton claim.

Suppose $u$ minimizes $H$ and fix $z\in\operatorname{dom}g$. For $0<\alpha<1$, convexity gives $g(u+\alpha(z-u))\le(1-\alpha)g(u)+\alpha g(z)$. Minimality and expansion of the quadratic therefore imply $$0\le H(u+\alpha(z-u))-H(u)\le\alpha\left(g(z)-g(u)+\frac{\langle u-v,z-u\rangle}{t}\right)+\frac{\alpha^2}{2t}\|z-u\|_2^2.$$ Divide by $\alpha$ and let $\alpha\downarrow0$; the parenthesized term is nonnegative. The same subgradient inequality is automatic for $z\notin\operatorname{dom}g$, so $(v-u)/t\in\partial g(u)$.

Conversely, if $(v-u)/t\in\partial g(u)$, then for every finite-valued $g(z)$ the subgradient inequality and $$\|z-v\|_2^2-\|u-v\|_2^2=\|z-u\|_2^2+2\langle u-v,z-u\rangle$$ give $H(z)-H(u)\ge\|z-u\|_2^2/(2t)\ge0$. Infinite-valued competitors cannot lower $H$, so $u$ is the unique minimizer from step 2.2. This proves the reverse implication.

Let $u_i=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v_i)$ and $p_i=(v_i-u_i)/t$. From step 3.1, $p_i\in\partial g(u_i)$. Applying the two subgradient inequalities with $(u_1,u_2)$ and $(u_2,u_1)$ and adding yields $\langle p_1-p_2,u_1-u_2\rangle\ge0$. Substitution and multiplication by $t>0$ give $\|u_1-u_2\|_2^2\le\langle u_1-u_2,v_1-v_2\rangle$. By [F9] the right side is at most $\|u_1-u_2\|_2\|v_1-v_2\|_2$; if $u_1=u_2$ nonexpansiveness is immediate, and otherwise division gives it.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be the function space of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], with $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$.

### The $p$-norm, for a rational exponent $p \ge 1$

Let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_p \;:=\; \Bigl(\sum_{k<n} |x_k|^{p}\Bigr)^{1/p},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]), the sum is the finite
sum of [[def-finite-sum]], and both powers are the **rational** powers of
[[def-rational-power]].

**Every power written here is defined.** Each base $|x_k|$ is a nonnegative real
and $p > 0$, so $|x_k|^{p}$ is given by [[def-rational-power]] for $|x_k| > 0$
and by its supplementary clause $0^{p} = 0$ for $|x_k| = 0$; the sum of these
nonnegative terms is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), and
$1/p$ is a positive rational, so the outer power is defined for the same two
reasons. The value does not depend on which representative of $p$ or of $1/p$ is
used ([[lem-rational-power-well-defined]]).

**The exponent is rational in this definition.**
[[def-rational-power]] supplies the nonnegative-base powers used here, and
[[thm-minkowski-finite]] supplies the corresponding triangle inequality for
rational $p \ge 1$. This item makes no claim with $p$ ranging over a real
interval; its rational domain is unchanged.

### The maximum norm

For $n \ge 1$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_\infty \;:=\; \max\{\, |x_k| \;:\; k < n \,\},$$

the maximum of a nonempty finite set of reals, which exists and is one of its
elements ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is required and propagates.** At $n = 0$ the set
$\{|x_k| : k<n\}$ is empty and has no maximum ([[def-max-min]]). This is the same
restriction the published [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] carries, for the same reason, and
**every statement on this page that mentions $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ inherits
it**. The $p$-norms for rational $p \ge 1$ carry no such restriction: at $n = 0$
each is the empty sum raised to a positive rational power, hence $0$.

### The three cases the rest of the page uses

- $\lVert x\rVert_1 = \sum_{k<n}|x_k|$, since $t^{1} = t$ for $t \ge 0$
  ([[lem-rational-power-laws]], and $0^{1} = 0$ by the supplementary clause).
- $\lVert x\rVert_2 = \bigl(\sum_{k<n}|x_k|^{2}\bigr)^{1/2} = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}x_k^{2}}$,
  which is exactly the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: the
  exponent $2$ agrees with the integer power, so $|x_k|^{2} = x_k^{2}$
  ([[lem-of-abs-value]]), and $t^{1/2}$ is the unique nonnegative square root of
  $t$, which is $\sqrt{t}$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[thm-of-square-roots]]).
  **The two notations denote the same function and no second Euclidean norm is
  introduced.**
- $\lVert x\rVert_\infty$ as above, for $n \ge 1$.

That each of these is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], and
that the metrics they induce are exactly the published $d_1$, $d_2$ and
$d_\infty$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], is
[[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]; it is proved there
and is not assumed here.

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex, and let $t>0$. For $v\in\mathbb R^n$, define the set-valued proximal mapping
$$\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)=\left\{u\in\mathbb R^n:g(u)+\frac{\|u-v\|_2^2}{2t}\le g(w)+\frac{\|w-v\|_2^2}{2t}\text{ for every }w\in\mathbb R^n\right\}.$$
The existence and uniqueness theorem on this page proves that this set is a singleton for every admissible $g,t,v$; its unique member is also denoted $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$.

For $\tau>0$ and $z\in\mathbb R$, define the **soft-thresholding map**
$$S_\tau(z)=\begin{cases}z-\tau,&z>\tau,\\0,&-\tau\le z\le\tau,\\z+\tau,&z<-\tau.\end{cases}$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$, with the norms
of [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]. Then:

1. $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.
3. **The dictionary.** For $n \ge 1$ and all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert x-y\rVert_1 = d_1(x,y), \qquad \lVert x-y\rVert_2 = d_2(x,y), \qquad \lVert x-y\rVert_\infty = d_\infty(x,y),$$
   where $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are the metrics of the published
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]. So the metric induced by each of these three norms
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]) **is** the correspondingly named published
   metric, not merely one equivalent to it.

**Consequence, used repeatedly below and stated once here.** By clause 3 at
$p = 2$, the metric space $(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ of the published metric-spaces
page and the metric space underlying the normed space
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, \lVert\cdot\rVert_2)$ of this page are the same object. Hence
completeness ([[thm-euclidean-space-complete]] clause 2), Heine-Borel
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]] clause 2) and the compactness equivalences
([[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]]) are statements about this page's normed
space, **with their hypothesis $n \ge 1$ inherited unchanged and not weakened**.
Nothing below cites any of those three theorems for $n = 0$.

**Why this lemma exists.** Without it the library would hold a norm-induced
metric on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and a separately published metric on the same set with
no recorded relation, and every later citation would have to guess which was
meant. The proof of clause 3 is a comparison of two written expressions; the
value is that the comparison is made and recorded.

**Clause 1 is about an arbitrary norm; clauses 2 to 4 are about
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with $n \ge 1$.**

1. **Finite and reverse triangle inequalities.** Let $V$ be a vector space over
   $\mathbb{R}$ and $N$ a norm on it ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For every
   $p \in \mathbb{N}$ and every list $u : p \to V$
   ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]),
   $$N\Bigl(\sum_{j<p} u_j\Bigr) \;\le\; \sum_{j<p} N(u_j),$$
   and for all $u, w \in V$,
   $$\bigl|N(u) - N(w)\bigr| \;\le\; N(u - w).$$

Now let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ carry the norms of
[[def-p-norms-on-rn]] and write $\iota$ for the canonical natural
([[def-canonical-natural]]).

2. **Every norm is dominated by the $1$-norm.** Let $N$ be a norm on
   $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and put $C := \max\{\, N(e_k) : k<n \,\}$, a maximum over a
   nonempty finite set of reals ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]],
   [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). Then $C \ge 0$ and
   $$N(x) \;\le\; C\,\lVert x\rVert_1 \qquad \text{for every } x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}.$$
3. **The comparison chain.** For every $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert x\rVert_\infty \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2 \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_1 \;\le\; \iota(n)\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty , \qquad \lVert x\rVert_1 \;\le\; \sqrt{\iota(n)}\;\lVert x\rVert_2 .$$
   In particular $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1$, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and
   $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ are pairwise equivalent norms on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   with the constants displayed ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).
4. **Every norm is Lipschitz for the Euclidean metric.** With $N$ and $C$ as in
   clause 2, $N : (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2) \to (\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ is
   Lipschitz with constant $C\sqrt{\iota(n)}$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]],
   [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), hence uniformly continuous and
   continuous ([[thm-metric-regularity-hierarchy]], [[def-metric-continuity]]).

**Where $n \ge 1$ enters.** Clauses 2 and 4 need the maximum defining $C$ to
exist, and clause 3 mentions $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$; at $n = 0$ each is a
maximum over the empty index set and does not exist, exactly as in
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] and [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]. Clause 1 carries no hypothesis
on the dimension and no hypothesis on the space.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. Its effective domain is $\operatorname{dom}g=\{x:g(x)<+\infty\}$. The function is **proper** if $\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing$; it is **convex** if
$$g((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\le(1-\theta)g(x)+\theta g(y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n,\ 0\le\theta\le1),$$
using the endpoint convention $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ of [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functionals-on-a-banach-space]]. It is **closed** (equivalently, lower semicontinuous in the extended-real convex-analysis convention used here) if its epigraph
$$\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:g(x)\le s\}$$
is closed in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. The proximal-gradient items on this page assume $g$ is proper, closed and convex.

This page's closed-epigraph convention is explicit: it does not silently use an equivalence between sequential lower semicontinuity and topological closedness that would require an additional choice principle in the library's generic sequential convention. In finite dimensions this is the standard closed proper convex input to proximal algorithms.

derivations.claim: Set $h(u)=\lambda\|u\|_1$. It is finite everywhere and $h(0)=0$, so its effective domain is nonempty. By [F4] and $\lambda>0$, the norm triangle and homogeneity inequalities give $$h((1-\theta)u+\theta w)\le(1-\theta)h(u)+\theta h(w)\qquad(0\le\theta\le1),$$ so $h$ is convex. It is continuous by [F5]. To see its epigraph is closed, take any $(u,s)$ with $s<h(u)$, set $\varepsilon=(h(u)-s)/3$, and choose $\delta_0>0$ so $\|u'-u\|_2<\delta_0$ implies $|h(u')-h(u)|<\varepsilon$. If $\|(u'-u,s'-s)\|_2<\min\{\delta_0,\varepsilon\}$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, then $s'<s+\varepsilon<h(u)-\varepsilon<h(u')$, so this neighborhood misses the epigraph. Thus the complement is open and the epigraph is closed. By [F6], $h$ is proper, closed and convex, as required by the proximal definition.

By [F1], the objective in [F2] is the sum over coordinates of $\phi_i(u_i)=\lambda|u_i|+(u_i-v_i)^2/(2t)$. It is enough to find the unique minimizer of each scalar function: the sum is minimized exactly when every coordinate is at its scalar minimum, and the positive quadratic term makes each scalar function strictly convex.

Fix a scalar $s=v_i$. On $u\ge0$, completing the square shows the minimum is at $u=\max\{s-t\lambda,0\}$; on $u\le0$ it is at $u=\min\{s+t\lambda,0\}$. If $s>t\lambda$, the first candidate is $s-t\lambda>0$ and has value strictly below the common boundary value at $0$, while the second candidate is $0$. If $s<-t\lambda$, the symmetric argument gives the unique minimizer $s+t\lambda<0$. If $-t\lambda\le s\le t\lambda$, both half-line minima are $0$. Thus the unique scalar minimizer is $S_{t\lambda}(s)$ in all three cases.
Applying step 2.2 to each of the finitely many coordinates gives the unique vector minimizer $(S_{t\lambda}(v_i))_{i=1}^n$, which is the proximal point by [F2].

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For every $t>0$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the set $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$ is a singleton. Its unique element $u$ satisfies the resolvent equivalence
$$u=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (v-u)/t\in\partial g(u).$$
For any $v_1,v_2$ and $u_i=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v_i)$,
$$\|u_1-u_2\|_2^2\le\langle u_1-u_2,v_1-v_2\rangle.$$
In particular the proximal map is nonexpansive.

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex in the convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}g$ and $\eta\ge0$, define
$$\partial_\eta g(x)=\{p\in\mathbb R^n:g(z)\ge g(x)+\langle p,z-x\rangle-\eta\text{ for every }z\in\mathbb R^n\}.$$
Write $\partial g(x)=\partial_0g(x)$. If $x\notin\operatorname{dom}g$, set $\partial_\eta g(x)=\varnothing$. When $g$ is finite-valued on a convex domain, $\partial g(x)$ agrees with [[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]].

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex, and let $t>0$. For $v\in\mathbb R^n$, define the set-valued proximal mapping
$$\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)=\left\{u\in\mathbb R^n:g(u)+\frac{\|u-v\|_2^2}{2t}\le g(w)+\frac{\|w-v\|_2^2}{2t}\text{ for every }w\in\mathbb R^n\right\}.$$
The existence and uniqueness theorem on this page proves that this set is a singleton for every admissible $g,t,v$; its unique member is also denoted $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$.

abla f(y)\in\partial g(x^+)$. For finite $g(z)$, [F2] gives $$g(z)-g(x^+)\ge\langle L(y-x^+)-
abla f(y),z-x^+angle.$$ Add $\langle

If $g(z)=+\infty$, the right side is $+\infty$ and the inequality holds automatically, so the finite-$g(z)$ calculation proves the statement for every $z$.

Let $g$ be proper, closed and convex, let $L>0$, let $f$ be differentiable at $y$, and set $x^+=\operatorname{prox}_{g/L}(y-
abla f(y)/L)$. For every $z\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$g(x^+)+\langle
abla f(y),x^+-yangle+ rac{L}{2}\|x^+-y\|_2^2+ rac{L}{2}\|x^+-z\|_2^2\le g(z)+\langle
abla f(y),z-yangle+ rac{L}{2}\|z-y\|_2^2.$$

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable and suppose $\nabla f$ is Lipschitz with constant $L\ge0$ in the Euclidean norm. Then
$$f(y)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|y-x\|_2^2\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. Then $f$ is convex if and only if

$$f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Equivalently, $\nabla f(x)$ is a subgradient at every $x$ ([[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and convex, and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex under the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. Then $F=f+g$ is proper, closed and convex in the same convention.

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For every $t>0$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the set $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$ is a singleton. Its unique element $u$ satisfies the resolvent equivalence
$$u=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (v-u)/t\in\partial g(u).$$
For any $v_1,v_2$ and $u_i=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v_i)$,
$$\|u_1-u_2\|_2^2\le\langle u_1-u_2,v_1-v_2\rangle.$$
In particular the proximal map is nonexpansive.

derivations.claim: Write $d=x^+-y$. If $g(z)=+\infty$, then $F(z)=+\infty$ and the asserted inequality holds because [F5] makes its right side finite. Otherwise $F(z)$ and $F(x^+)$ are real, so ordinary subtraction is valid. By [F2] and [F3], $$F(z)-F(x^+)\ge g(z)-g(x^+)+\langle\nabla f(y),z-x^+\rangle-\frac{L}{2}\|d\|_2^2.$$ The three-point inequality [F1], after rearrangement, gives $$g(z)-g(x^+)+\langle\nabla f(y),z-x^+\rangle\ge\frac{L}{2}\|d\|_2^2+\frac{L}{2}\bigl(\|x^+-z\|_2^2-\|z-y\|_2^2\bigr).$$ Substitution yields $$F(z)-F(x^+)\ge\frac{L}{2}\bigl(\|x^+-z\|_2^2-\|z-y\|_2^2\bigr).$$

Since $z-y=(z-x^+)+d$, the difference of squares in step 1.1 is $$\|x^+-z\|_2^2-\|z-y\|_2^2=-2\langle z-x^+,d\rangle-\|d\|_2^2=2\langle y-z,d\rangle+\|d\|_2^2.$$ Multiplying by $L/2$ gives the finite-gap inequality; adding the finite value $F(x^+)$ yields the displayed statement.

citations.quote: Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed and convex. Its indicator $\iota_C$ is proper, closed and convex in the convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For every $t>0$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, $\operatorname{prox}_{t\iota_C}(v)$ is the singleton consisting of the unique nearest point in $C$ to $v$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, let $x\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $p\in C$. Then $p$ is the nearest point of $C$ to $x$ if and only if

$$\langle x-p,z-p\rangle\le0\qquad(z\in C).$$

Use the program and dimensions of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]. For any $x\in U$,
$\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, define coordinatewise
$[v]_i^+=\max\{v_i,0\}$ and the scaled residual
$$
r_{\mathrm{KKT}}(x,\nu,\lambda)=\|\nabla f(x)+Dh(x)^T\nu+Dg(x)^T\lambda\|_2+\|h(x)\|_2+\|[g(x)]^+\|_2+\|[-\lambda]^+\|_2+\|\lambda\circ g(x)\|_2.
$$
The symbol $\circ$ denotes coordinatewise multiplication. The norm is the
Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and the norm of the
zero-dimensional vector is $0$.

For a convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $x\in C$, its (outward) normal
cone is
$$
N_C(x)=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }y\in C\}.
$$
This definition applies in particular when $C$ is closed and convex.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex, and suppose the objective
$f:U\to\mathbb R$ and inequalities $g_i:U\to\mathbb R$ are differentiable
and convex. Let the equalities be $Ax=b$. If a feasible tuple
$(x_*,\nu,\lambda)$ satisfies the KKT conditions with $\lambda\ge0$, then
$x_*$ is a global minimizer over the feasible set $C$. Moreover,
$-\nabla f(x_*)\in N_C(x_*)$, where the normal cone has the convention of
[[def-kkt-residual-and-normal-cone]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Now assume $n\ge1$. Fix $x\in C$ and put $v=x-
abla f(x)/L$. By [F1], $T_L^C(x)=P_C(v)$. If $G_L^C(x)=0$, then $x=P_C(v)$, so [F2] gives $\langle-

abla f(x)\in N_C(x)$ by [F3].

The feasible tuple meets the hypotheses of [F4], which gives global minimality and $-\nabla f(x_*)\in N_C(x_*)$; step 1.3 then gives the fixed point. Assume $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is convex and continuously differentiable with $L$-Lipschitz gradient, $L>0$, and $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is proper, closed and convex. For a finite iteration budget $N\ge1$, initial point $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and exact evaluations of $T_L$ from [[def-proximal-gradient-mapping]], the proximal-gradient mode returns
$$x_k=T_L(x_{k-1}),\qquad k=1,\ldots,N.$$

The FISTA mode sets $t_1=1$, $y_1=x_0$, and for $k=1,\ldots,N$ computes
$$x_k=T_L(y_k),\qquad t_{k+1}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4t_k^2}}2,\qquad y_{k+1}=x_k+\frac{t_k-1}{t_{k+1}}(x_k-x_{k-1}).$$
It returns $x_N$. A fixed-period restart with period $m\in\mathbb N$, $m\ge1$, runs this FISTA recurrence for at most $m$ updates per block and, after each full block, resets $t_1=1$, $y_1$ to the block's last iterate, and the previous iterate to that same point. A final shorter block stops at the budget. Each call uses the exact proximal point; no inexact call is covered by this algorithm definition. The finite budget makes the output a finite iterate even when no convergence or monotonicity of consecutive accelerated objective values is asserted.

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be convex and continuously differentiable with $L$-Lipschitz gradient, $L>0$, and let $g$ be proper, closed and convex. Put $F=f+g$ and $x^+=T_L(y)$. For every $z\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$F(z)\ge F(x^+)+\frac{L}{2}\|x^+-y\|_2^2+L\langle y-z,x^+-y\rangle.$$

derivations.claim: The recurrence [F1] gives $t_k\ge1$ for every $k$: it starts at $1$ and $t_{k+1}\ge t_k+1/2$. Thus $z_k=(1-1/t_k)x_{k-1}+(1/t_k)x_*$ is a convex combination (and $z_1=x_*$). The same recurrence gives $t_k(y_k-z_k)=u_{k-1}$, where at $k=1$ this reads $y_1-x_*=u_0$. Also $u_k=t_k(x_k-z_k)=u_{k-1}+t_k(x_k-y_k)$.

For $k\ge2$, convexity gives $F(z_k)\le(1-1/t_k)F(x_{k-1})+(1/t_k)F(x_*)$. Apply [F2] with $y=y_k$, $z=z_k$, and $x_k=T_L(y_k)$. The upper bound for $F(z_k)-F(x_k)$ and its lower bound from [F2], multiplied by $2t_k^2/L$, imply $$\frac{2t_k^2}{L}(F(x_k)-F(x_*))\le\frac{2t_k(t_k-1)}{L}(F(x_{k-1})-F(x_*))-t_k^2\|x_k-y_k\|_2^2-2t_k^2\langle y_k-z_k,x_k-y_k\rangle.$$ Using [F1] to replace $t_k(t_k-1)$ by $t_{k-1}^2$, and the two vector identities of step 1.1 to replace the last two terms by $\|u_{k-1}\|_2^2-\|u_k\|_2^2$, gives the claimed recurrence for $k\ge2$. At $k=1$, $z_1=x_*$ and [F2] directly gives $F(x_1)-F(x_*)\le(L/2)(\|x_0-x_*\|_2^2-\|x_1-x_*\|_2^2)$; since $t_1=1$ and $u_1=x_1-x_*$, this is the claimed base case without using $F(x_0)$.

Let $F=f+g$ satisfy the exact FISTA hypotheses of [[alg-proximal-gradient-and-fista]], and suppose $x_*$ minimizes $F$. Use its iterates $x_k,y_k,t_k$ and set $t_0=0$, $u_0=x_0-x_*$, and
$$u_k=t_kx_k-(t_k-1)x_{k-1}-x_*\qquad(k\ge1).$$
Then for every $k\ge1$,
$$\frac{2t_k^2}{L}\bigl(F(x_k)-F(x_*)\bigr)+\|u_k\|_2^2\le\frac{2t_{k-1}^2}{L}\bigl(F(x_{k-1})-F(x_*)\bigr)+\|u_{k-1}\|_2^2,$$
where the $k=1$ right-hand objective term is interpreted as zero.

Assume $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is convex and continuously differentiable with $L$-Lipschitz gradient, $L>0$, and $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is proper, closed and convex. For a finite iteration budget $N\ge1$, initial point $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and exact evaluations of $T_L$ from [[def-proximal-gradient-mapping]], the proximal-gradient mode returns
$$x_k=T_L(x_{k-1}),\qquad k=1,\ldots,N.$$

The FISTA mode sets $t_1=1$, $y_1=x_0$, and for $k=1,\ldots,N$ computes
$$x_k=T_L(y_k),\qquad t_{k+1}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4t_k^2}}2,\qquad y_{k+1}=x_k+\frac{t_k-1}{t_{k+1}}(x_k-x_{k-1}).$$
It returns $x_N$. A fixed-period restart with period $m\in\mathbb N$, $m\ge1$, runs this FISTA recurrence for at most $m$ updates per block and, after each full block, resets $t_1=1$, $y_1$ to the block's last iterate, and the previous iterate to that same point. A final shorter block stops at the budget. Each call uses the exact proximal point; no inexact call is covered by this algorithm definition. The finite budget makes the output a finite iterate even when no convergence or monotonicity of consecutive accelerated objective values is asserted.

derivations.claim: Summing the energy recurrence of [F1] from $1$ to $k$ cancels all intermediate potentials. The $k=1$ base term is $\|u_0\|_2^2=\|x_0-x_*\|_2^2$, and every later objective coefficient is nonnegative; dropping $\|u_k\|_2^2$ gives $$F(x_k)-F(x_*)\le\frac{L\|x_0-x_*\|_2^2}{2t_k^2}.$$ The gap is nonnegative because $x_*$ minimizes $F$.

Since $\sqrt{1+4t_k^2}\ge2t_k$, [F2] gives $t_{k+1}\ge t_k+1/2$. Starting from $t_1=1$, induction yields $t_k\ge(k+1)/2$. Substitution into step 1.1 gives the stated bound. Finite objective values for the iterates follow from [F3].

where $\partial_{\eta}g$ is defined in [[def-extended-real-epsilon-subdifferential]]. In proximal-gradient mode $y_k=x_{k-1}$; in FISTA mode use the same momentum update as the exact recurrence. Let $f$ be convex, continuously differentiable and have $L$-Lipschitz gradient, $L>0$, and let $g$ be proper, closed and convex. Given $y$, suppose $x^+$ and $\eta\ge0$ satisfy
$$L(y-x^+)-\nabla f(y)\in\partial_\eta g(x^+).$$
With $F=f+g$, for every $z\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$F(z)\ge F(x^+)+\frac{L}{2}\|x^+-y\|_2^2+L\langle y-z,x^+-y\rangle-\eta.$$

derivations.claim: The recurrence [F1] gives $t_k\ge1$ for every $k$, so $z_k=(1-1/t_k)x_{k-1}+(1/t_k)x_*$ is a convex combination. It also gives $t_k(y_k-z_k)=u_{k-1}$ and $u_k=u_{k-1}+t_k(x_k-y_k)$, including $k=1$ with $z_1=x_*$.

For $k\ge2$, convexity gives $F(z_k)\le(1-1/t_k)F(x_{k-1})+(1/t_k)F(x_*)$. Apply [F2] at $y_k,z_k$; the same multiplication and norm expansion as in step 1.1 yield $$\frac{2t_k^2}{L}(F(x_k)-F(x_*))\le\frac{2t_k(t_k-1)}{L}(F(x_{k-1})-F(x_*))+\|u_{k-1}\|_2^2-\|u_k\|_2^2+\frac{2t_k^2}{L}\eta_k.$$ Use $t_k(t_k-1)=t_{k-1}^2$ to obtain the stated recurrence. For $k=1$, [F2] with $z=x_*$ gives the same base inequality directly, and $t_1=1$ leaves the previous objective term zero.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $y_k=x_{k-1}$ at each proximal-gradient call. Put $d_k=x_k-x_{k-1}$. The norm identity and [F2] give $$F(x_k)-F(x_*)\le\frac{L}{2}\bigl(\|x_{k-1}-x_*\|_2^2-\|x_k-x_*\|_2^2\bigr)+\eta_k.$$ Summing from $1$ to $N$ telescopes the squared distances and yields $\sum_{k=1}^N(F(x_k)-F(x_*))\le L\|x_0-x_*\|_2^2/2+\sum_{k=1}^N\eta_k$. The minimum of $N$ real numbers is at most their average, proving the finite-$N$ bound.

Each gap is nonnegative because $x_*$ minimizes $F$. If the error series is summable, step 1.1 bounds the partial sums of the nonnegative gaps uniformly by $L\|x_0-x_*\|_2^2/2+\sum_{k\ge1}\eta_k$. A nonnegative sequence with bounded partial sums has terms tending to zero: otherwise some $\varepsilon>0$ would be exceeded infinitely often and the partial sums would be unbounded.

Let $F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be a proper convex extended-real function ([[def-extended-reals]]). For $\mu>0$, say that $F$ is **$\mu$-strongly convex** if for every $x,y\in\operatorname{dom}F$ and $0<\theta<1$,
$$F((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\le(1-\theta)F(x)+\theta F(y)-\frac\mu2\theta(1-\theta)\|x-y\|_2^2.$$
This definition permits $F$ to be extended-real-valued outside its effective domain. The endpoint cases are identities and are not included in the strict range for $\theta$.

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For every $t>0$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the set $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$ is a singleton. Its unique element $u$ satisfies the resolvent equivalence
$$u=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (v-u)/t\in\partial g(u).$$
For any $v_1,v_2$ and $u_i=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v_i)$,
$$\|u_1-u_2\|_2^2\le\langle u_1-u_2,v_1-v_2\rangle.$$
In particular the proximal map is nonexpansive.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. Then $f$ is convex if and only if

$$f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Equivalently, $\nabla f(x)$ is a subgradient at every $x$ ([[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be convex and continuously differentiable with $L$-Lipschitz gradient, $L>0$, and let $g$ be proper, closed and convex. Put $F=f+g$ and $x^+=T_L(y)$. For every $z\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$F(z)\ge F(x^+)+\frac{L}{2}\|x^+-y\|_2^2+L\langle y-z,x^+-y\rangle.$$

Under the exact FISTA hypotheses of [[alg-proximal-gradient-and-fista]], suppose $F=f+g$ has a minimizer $x_*$. For every $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$ and $k\ge1$,
$$0\le F(x_k)-F(x_*)\le\frac{2L\|x_0-x_*\|_2^2}{(k+1)^2}.$$

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex in the convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}g$ and $\eta\ge0$, define
$$\partial_\eta g(x)=\{p\in\mathbb R^n:g(z)\ge g(x)+\langle p,z-x\rangle-\eta\text{ for every }z\in\mathbb R^n\}.$$
Write $\partial g(x)=\partial_0g(x)$. If $x\notin\operatorname{dom}g$, set $\partial_\eta g(x)=\varnothing$. When $g$ is finite-valued on a convex domain, $\partial g(x)$ agrees with [[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: If $r\in\partial F(x)$ and $z\in\operatorname{dom}F$, [F6] gives the subgradient lower bound at $(1-\theta)x+\theta z$, while [F1] gives the strong-convexity upper bound there. Combine them, divide by $\theta>0$, and let $\theta\downarrow0$. This gives $$F(z)\ge F(x)+\langle r,z-x\rangle+\frac\mu2\|z-x\|_2^2.$$ Taking $z=x_*$ and maximizing the right-hand upper bound $\langle r,x-x_*\rangle-(\mu/2)\|x-x_*\|^2$ by completing the square yields $F(x)-F(x_*)\le\|r\|_2^2/(2\mu)$.

Strong convexity and minimality imply $F(w)-F(x_*)\ge(\mu/2)\|w-x_*\|_2^2$ for every finite $w$: apply [F1] to $(x_*,w)$, use $F(x_*)\le F((1-\theta)x_*+\theta w)$, divide by $\theta$, and let $\theta\downarrow0$.

For an exact step $x^+=T_L(x)$, [F2] gives $p=L(x-x^+)-\nabla f(x)\in\partial g(x^+)$. Adding the gradient inequality [F3] shows $r=p+\nabla f(x^+)\in\partial F(x^+)$ by [F6]. If $d=x^+-x$, [F7] and Lipschitz continuity give $\|r\|_2\le L\|d\|_2+L\|d\|_2=2L\|d\|_2$. Step 1.1 therefore yields $F(x^+)-F(x_*)\le(2L^2/\mu)\|d\|_2^2$.

By [F4], $F(x)-F(x^+)\ge(L/2)\|d\|_2^2$. Combining with step 2.1 gives $F(x)-F(x_*)\ge(1+\mu/(4L))(F(x^+)-F(x_*))$. Apply this at every proximal-gradient step and induct to obtain the stated factor $q^k$.

Apply [F5] to one FISTA block starting at a restart point $w$. Step 1.2 gives $\|w-x_*\|_2^2\le2(F(w)-F(x_*))/\mu$, so the block-end gap is at most $4L(F(w)-F(x_*))/(\mu(m+1)^2)$. Since $m+1\ge\sqrt{8L/\mu}$, this factor is at most $1/2$. Each completed restart starts the next block at its last iterate; induction over blocks proves the stated restart-point bound.

The existence and uniqueness theorem on this page proves that this set is a singleton for every admissible $g,t,v$; its unique member is also denoted $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$.

$$\operatorname{prox}_{t\lambda\|\cdot\|_1}(v)=\big(S_{t\lambda}(v_i)\big)_{i=1}^n,$$
where $S_\tau$ is the soft-thresholding map of [[def-soft-thresholding-function]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For every $t>0$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the set $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$ is a singleton. Its unique element $u$ satisfies the resolvent equivalence
$$u=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (v-u)/t\in\partial g(u).$$
For any $v_1,v_2$ and $u_i=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v_i)$,
$$\|u_1-u_2\|_2^2\le\langle u_1-u_2,v_1-v_2\rangle.$$
In particular the proximal map is nonexpansive.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. Its effective domain is $\operatorname{dom}g=\{x:g(x)<+\infty\}$. The function is **proper** if $\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing$; it is **convex** if
$$g((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\le(1-\theta)g(x)+\theta g(y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n,\ 0\le\theta\le1),$$
using the endpoint convention $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ of [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functionals-on-a-banach-space]]. It is **closed** (equivalently, lower semicontinuous in the extended-real convex-analysis convention used here) if its epigraph
$$\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:g(x)\le s\}$$
is closed in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. The proximal-gradient items on this page assume $g$ is proper, closed and convex.

This page's closed-epigraph convention is explicit: it does not silently use an equivalence between sequential lower semicontinuity and topological closedness that would require an additional choice principle in the library's generic sequential convention. In finite dimensions this is the standard closed proper convex input to proximal algorithms.

Let $X$ be a real vector space and $K\subseteq X$. The set $K$ is **convex** if $\lambda u+(1-\lambda)v\in K$ for all $u,v\in K$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$. Fix a nonempty convex $K$ and an extended-real functional $I:K\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ ([[def-proper-coercive-and-weakly-lower-semicontinuous-functional]]), with the sums and positive-weight products of [[def-extended-reals]]. For convex combinations only, additionally define $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$; this is a local convention, since that product is left undefined in the general extended-real arithmetic. Then $I$ is **convex** if
$$I\big(\lambda u+(1-\lambda)v\big)\le\lambda I(u)+(1-\lambda)I(v),\qquad u,v\in K,\ \lambda\in[0,1],$$
and **strictly convex** if the inequality is strict whenever $u\ne v$, $I(u),I(v)<+\infty$ and $\lambda\in(0,1)$. A convex functional has convex sublevel sets: for every $t\in\mathbb R$ the set $\{u\in K:I(u)\le t\}$ is convex. Only real coefficients are used: on a complex vector space these notions are read on the underlying real structure.

derivations.claim: The function $g$ is finite everywhere, hence proper. Its epigraph is the intersection of the two closed halfspaces $\lambda(u_2-u_1)\le s$ and $-\lambda(u_2-u_1)\le s$, so it is closed. The triangle inequality for absolute value gives convexity under [F5]. Write a candidate $u$ uniquely as $u=(a-b,a+b)$, so $a$ is its mean and $b$ its half-difference. Direct expansion gives $\|u-v\|_2^2=2(a-m)^2+2(b-d)^2$ and $g(u)=2\lambda|b|$. Hence the objective is $$\frac{(a-m)^2}{t}+\frac{(b-d)^2}{t}+2\lambda|b|.$$ The first term is uniquely minimized at $a=m$; the remaining terms depend only on $b$.

The $b$-dependent objective is $2\lambda|b|+(b-d)^2/t$, which under the scalar/one-coordinate identification is the proximal objective for the proper, closed, convex function $2\lambda|\cdot|$ with parameter $t/2$. By [F2], its unique minimizer is $S_{(t/2)(2\lambda)}(d)=S_{t\lambda}(d)$. This and $a=m$ give the displayed vector. derivations.claim: Under the scalar/one-coordinate identification [F2], $f(x)=x^2/4$ is convex and continuously differentiable, since $$f((1-\alpha)x+\alpha z)=(1-\alpha)f(x)+\alpha f(z)-\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}4(x-z)^2\qquad(0\le\alpha\le1).$$ Also $f'(x)=x/2$, so its gradient is $1/2$-Lipschitz and $L=1$ is valid. The FISTA mode sets $t_1=1$, $y_1=x_0$, and for $k=1,\ldots,N$ computes
$$x_k=T_L(y_k),\qquad t_{k+1}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4t_k^2}}2,\qquad y_{k+1}=x_k+\frac{t_k-1}{t_{k+1}}(x_k-x_{k-1}).$$
It returns $x_N$. A fixed-period restart with period $m\in\mathbb N$, $m\ge1$, runs this FISTA recurrence for at most $m$ updates per block and, after each full block, resets $t_1=1$, $y_1$ to the block's last iterate, and the previous iterate to that same point. A final shorter block stops at the budget. Each call uses the exact proximal point; no inexact call is covered by this algorithm definition. The finite budget makes the output a finite iterate even when no convergence or monotonicity of consecutive accelerated objective values is asserted.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed and convex. Its indicator $\iota_C$ is proper, closed and convex in the convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For every $t>0$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, $\operatorname{prox}_{t\iota_C}(v)$ is the singleton consisting of the unique nearest point in $C$ to $v$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $p,m\in\mathbb N$ (zero allowed), and take $A\in\mathbb R^{p	imes n}$, $b\in\mathbb R^p$, $G\in\mathbb R^{m	imes n}$, and $d\in\mathbb R^m$. Let $C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ Gx\le d\}$ be nonempty and let $f:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R$ be convex and continuously differentiable with $L$-Lipschitz gradient, $L>0$. For $x\in C$, the projected-gradient mapping of [[def-proximal-gradient-mapping]] satisfies
$$G_L^C(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad-
abla f(x)\in N_C(x),$$
where $N_C$ has the outward convention of [[def-kkt-residual-and-normal-cone]]. If a feasible tuple $(x_*,
u,\lambda)$ satisfies $\lambda\ge0$, $
abla f(x_*)+A^T
u+G^T\lambda=0$, and $\lambda_i((Gx_*-d)_i)=0$ for every inequality, then $x_*$ is such a fixed point and is a global minimizer over $C$. The converse to this KKT-multiplier implication is not asserted.

derivations.claim: The function is a continuously differentiable convex quadratic, with $$f((1-\alpha)x+\alpha z)=(1-\alpha)f(x)+\alpha f(z)-\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}2\|x-z\|_2^2\qquad(0\le\alpha\le1).$$ Its gradient is $\nabla f(x)=(x_1+2,x_2)$, whose Lipschitz constant is $1$, hence $L=2$ is valid. At $x_0$, the unprojected point is $x_0-\nabla f(x_0)/2=(-1,0)$; coordinatewise projection onto $C$ gives $x_1=(0,0)$. Repeating the same computation shows the iterate remains there.

For every $z\in C$, $\langle(-2,0),z-(0,0)\rangle=-2z_1\le0$, hence $(-2,0)\in N_C(0)$ by the outward-cone definition. Equivalently, write $C$ as $-x_i\le0$ with $G=-I,d=0$; at $x_*=0$, $\lambda=(2,0)\ge0$ has zero complementarity and $\nabla f(0)+G^T\lambda=(2,0)-(2,0)=0$. By [F3], this KKT tuple certifies global minimality and the projected-gradient fixed point.
