citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real process
$B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the increments
   $B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}}$ are mutually independent and have laws
   $N(0,t_j-t_{j-1})$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every
   $\omega\in A$.

By
[[lem-brownian-gaussian-covariance-is-equivalent-to-independent-stationary-normal-increments]],
the first two clauses are equivalent to saying that $B$ is a centered Gaussian
process with covariance $\min(s,t)$. Clause 3 is additional: it cannot be
recovered from finite-dimensional distributions alone.

No filtration is part of this definition. In particular, no completed or
right-continuous filtration and no Markov or martingale assertion is silently
imposed. Modifications and indistinguishability retain the distinct meanings in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. The cases
$n=0$, $t_1=0$, and zero-length increments are respectively vacuous or already
covered by $B_0=0$; the increment list itself is strictly increasing.

Choice is declared because the normal-law and Gaussian/increment-equivalence
interfaces construct and identify normal laws under AC. The continuity clause
selects no path and makes no additional use of choice.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

For real $a,b,t$, $\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)$. For a finite mutually independent family $(X_j)_{j=1}^n$ of real random variables, $\varphi_{\sum_jX_j}(t)=\prod_j\varphi_{X_j}(t)$. The empty sum has characteristic function one.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, and let $p_t$ and $P_t$ be the Brownian transition
kernel and operators of [[def-brownian-transition-semigroup]].

1. **Expectation form.** If $B$ is a standard Brownian motion
   [[def-brownian-motion]], then for every $t\ge0$, every $x\in\mathbb R$ and
   every bounded Borel $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$,
   $$P_tf(x)=E\bigl[f(x+B_t)\bigr].$$
2. **Semigroup identity.** For all $s,t\ge0$, $P_sP_t=P_{s+t}$ as operators on
   bounded Borel functions.
3. **Kernel identity.** For all $s,t>0$ and all $x,z\in\mathbb R$,
   $$\int_{\mathbb R}p_s(x,y)\,p_t(y,z)\,dy=p_{s+t}(x,z).$$
   Conversely, the kernel identity for all $x,z$ implies the semigroup identity
   for all bounded Borel $f$.
4. **Probability kernels.** $P_t1=1$ for every $t\ge0$, so each $P_t$ is a
   probability kernel operator and $\|P_tf\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty$.

Put $C=C([0,\infty),\mathbb R)$, give $C$ the uniform-on-compacts topology,
and write $\pi_t(f)=f(t)$. Then
$$\mathcal B(C)=\sigma(\pi_t:t\ge0)=\sigma(\pi_q:q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,\infty)).$$
Here each expression on the right denotes the smallest sigma-algebra on $C$
making every displayed coordinate map measurable. No choice principle is used.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Write $\beta_s=W_s-(s/h)W_h$. For any finite times $s_1,\ldots,s_k\in[0,h]$, [F1] makes $(\beta_{s_1},\ldots,\beta_{s_k},W_h)$ jointly Gaussian. Direct covariance calculation gives $\operatorname{Cov}(\beta_{s_i},W_h)=s_i-(s_i/h)h=0$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(\beta_s,\beta_t)=\min(s,t)-st/h$. Hence [F2] makes every finite vector of bridge residual coordinates independent of $W_h$. The countable generating coordinates in [F4] then make the entire continuous residual path independent of $W_h$. Therefore conditioning on $W_h=y-x$ gives exactly the explicit bridge process from the definition, for each $y$.

If $t=0$, the restricted bridge path is the constant initial value $x$ and the density ratio is $p_h(y-x)/p_h(y-x)=1$. Now take $0<t<h$ and fix $0=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_k=t$. By independent increments and [F3], the joint density of $X_{s_1},\ldots,X_{s_k},X_h$ at $z_1,\ldots,z_k,y$ is $p_{s_1}(z_1-x)\prod_{i=2}^kp_{s_i-s_{i-1}}(z_i-z_{i-1}) p_{h-t}(y-z_k).$ Dividing by the strictly positive endpoint density $p_h(y-x)$ gives the conditional bridge density for these coordinates. By step 1.1 this is the finite-dimensional law of the bridge in the definition. The same expression is the Brownian path density on $[0,t]$ multiplied by $p_{h-t}(y-X_t)/p_h(y-x)$ when the coordinate at time $t$ is included; integrating out that last coordinate uses the convolution identity [F3].

Thus the restriction-density identity holds for every finite cylinder event on $[0,t]$. The density is nonnegative and integrates to one by [F3]. The class of path events for which the identity holds is a lambda-system containing the generating cylinder pi-system of [F4]; Dynkin's pi-lambda theorem therefore extends the identity to all Borel path events on $[0,t]$. This proves the restriction assertion.

By step 1.1, the joint law of the residual bridge path and endpoint $W_h$ is the product of the bridge residual law and the $N(0,h)$ endpoint density. Applying the measurable map $(\beta,z)\mapsto(x+(s/h)z+\beta_s)_{0\le s\le h}$ and translating $z=y-x$ gives the stated full-path disintegration. The endpoint density is continuous and positive for every $y$ since $h>0$. The degenerate cases $t=0$ and a one-coordinate cylinder follow from the same formulas; $t=h$ is excluded from the restriction statement. AC is used only through [A1].

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $B$ be a standard Brownian motion
[[def-brownian-motion]]. All path operations below use a fixed
everywhere-continuous, zero-start representative: choose a measurable
probability-one event on which the paths are continuous and $B_0=0$, and
replace $B$ by the zero path off this event, as in
[[def-wiener-measure-on-continuous-path-space]]. Retain the notation $B$ for
this representative and use its own raw natural filtration and usual
augmentation. This preserves every finite-dimensional law; all maxima and
hitting times below refer to this representative, without transferring
stopping times between the raw filtrations of different versions.
Let $a>0$ and $T>0$, and put
$$M_T:=\sup_{0\le s\le T}B_s,\qquad \tau_a:=\inf\{s\ge0:B_s=a\} .$$
Then:

1. The path reflected at $\tau_a$ has Wiener law: for each $T>0$ the process
   $(B_u)_{0\le u\le T}$ and its reflection $\widetilde B_u:=B_u$ for
   $u\le\tau_a\wedge T$, $\widetilde B_u:=2a-B_u$ for
   $\tau_a\wedge T<u\le T$, have the same law on the cylinder sigma-algebra
   $\sigma(\pi_u:u\in[0,T])$ of $\mathbb R^{[0,T]}$.
2. For every $b\le a$,
   $$P(M_T\ge a,\ B_T\le b)=P(B_T\ge2a-b),$$
   and in particular $P(M_T\ge a)=2P(B_T\ge a)$.

Assume AC. Let $h>0$, $x,y\in\mathbb R$, and let $W$ be a standard scalar
Brownian motion on $[0,h]$. The **scalar Brownian bridge from $x$ to $y$ over
duration $h$** is the continuous Gaussian process
$$B^{x,y,h}_t=x+\frac{t}{h}(y-x)+W_t-\frac{t}{h}W_h, \qquad 0\le t\le h.$$
It starts at $x$ and ends at $y$. Its law does not depend on which Brownian
motion is used. The endpoint-conditional and restriction-density properties are established
separately on the A page.

Assume AC, let $h>0$ and $x,y\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mu_{x,y}^h$ be the
law on $C([0,h])$ of the bridge in
[[def-scalar-brownian-bridge-from-x-to-y]]. If $X_s=x+W_s$ is Brownian motion
started at $x$, then for every Borel path event $A\subseteq C([0,h])$ and
Borel set $D\subseteq\mathbb R$,
$$\mathbb P\{X\in A,\ X_h\in D\}= \int_D p_h(y-x)\,\mu_{x,y}^h(A)\,dy,$$
where $p_t(z)=(2\pi t)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/(2t)}$. In particular this specifies
the endpoint-conditioned bridge law for every endpoint $y$. For every
$0\le t<h$, the restriction of $\mu_{x,y}^h$ to path events up to time $t$
has density
$$\frac{p_{h-t}(y-X_t)}{p_h(y-x)}$$
relative to Brownian motion $X$ started at $x$ on $[0,t]$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, and let $p_t$ and $P_t$ be the Brownian transition
kernel and operators of [[def-brownian-transition-semigroup]].

1. **Expectation form.** If $B$ is a standard Brownian motion
   [[def-brownian-motion]], then for every $t\ge0$, every $x\in\mathbb R$ and
   every bounded Borel $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$,
   $$P_tf(x)=E\bigl[f(x+B_t)\bigr].$$
2. **Semigroup identity.** For all $s,t\ge0$, $P_sP_t=P_{s+t}$ as operators on
   bounded Borel functions.
3. **Kernel identity.** For all $s,t>0$ and all $x,z\in\mathbb R$,
   $$\int_{\mathbb R}p_s(x,y)\,p_t(y,z)\,dy=p_{s+t}(x,z).$$
   Conversely, the kernel identity for all $x,z$ implies the semigroup identity
   for all bounded Borel $f$.
4. **Probability kernels.** $P_t1=1$ for every $t\ge0$, so each $P_t$ is a
   probability kernel operator and $\|P_tf\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: First assume $x,y>c$, put $a=x-c>0$, $z=x-y$, and let $W^z$ denote the canonical bridge from $0$ to $z$ over duration $h$. The bridge event in the Statement has the law of $\{\sup_{s\le h}W^{z}_s\ge a\}$: subtracting the bridge path from $x$ negates its centered Gaussian residual and has terminal value $z$. Since $z=a-(y-c)<a$, the restriction and endpoint-disintegration statement [F2] applies to this endpoint.

Write $q(z)=\mathbb P\{\sup_{s\le h}W^z_s\ge a\}$. From [F1], for $u<v<a$, $\mathbb P\{\sup_{s\le h}W_s\ge a,\ u<W_h\le v\} =\int_u^vp_h(2a-r)dr.$ Indeed, subtract the reflection identities at $v$ and $u$ and change variables in the Gaussian endpoint integral [F3]. The full endpoint disintegration [F2] then identifies $q(r)p_h(r)=p_h(2a-r)$ for Lebesgue-almost every $r<a$.

The function $q$ is continuous on $(-\infty,a)$. Under the explicit bridge representation, changing endpoint from $r$ to $r'$ changes the path uniformly by at most $|r-r'|$. Thus the crossing indicators converge almost surely as $r'\to r$ unless the bridge maximum equals $a$. For fixed $r<a$, if that maximum equals $a$, it is attained before $h$; hence for some $t_k=h(1-1/k)<h$ the bridge maximum on $[0,t_k]$ equals $a$. By the restriction density in [F2], this event has probability zero because the Brownian maximum on $[0,t_k]$ has a continuous distribution by the reflection identity [F1] and the continuous Gaussian density [F3]. The countable union over $k\ge2$ is null. Dominated convergence proves continuity of $q$.

Both $q(r)p_h(r)$ and $p_h(2a-r)$ are continuous on $r<a$. Step 1.2 shows they agree almost everywhere there; if their difference were nonzero at one point, continuity would make it nonzero on an interval of positive Lebesgue measure, a contradiction. Hence $q(z)=\frac{p_h(2a-z)}{p_h(z)}$ for the specified endpoint $z<a$. Since $2a-z=(x-c)+(y-c)$ and $z=(x-c)-(y-c)$, the Gaussian density ratio is $\exp\left(-\frac{((x-c)+(y-c))^2-((x-c)-(y-c))^2}{2h}\right) =\exp\left(-\frac{2(x-c)(y-c)}h\right).$

If $x=c$ or $y=c$, the bridge begins or ends at the barrier, so the event in the Statement is certain and the right side is $e^0=1$. These boundary cases complete the claim for $x,y\ge c$. The strict case used $z<a$, which follows exactly from $y>c$; no formula is asserted when an endpoint lies below the barrier. AC is used only through [A1].

citations.quote: Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice as in the finite-dimensional Gaussian and Brownian
interfaces. Let a node represent an interval $[u,u+h]$, where $h>0$, and let
$\Delta W\in\mathbb R^m$ be its already sampled parent increment. Draw a fresh
vector $Z\sim N_m(0,(h/4)I_m)$ independently of the parent and of every
innovation used at another node. Store the two child increments
$$\Delta W_L=\tfrac12\Delta W+Z,\qquad \Delta W_R=\tfrac12\Delta W-Z.$$

For a finite ordered list of $q\in\mathbb N_0$ split requests, each naming an
existing leaf, apply the rule once to each requested leaf and retain every
parent. Process a rejected trial's left child before its right child; if a
child is later refined, draw a new independent innovation for it. Each request
replaces one leaf by two children, so the result is a finite rooted tree with
the sampled increments, interval lengths, and left-to-right order. Never
discard a sampled parent and redraw a replacement for the same interval. The
procedure assigns increments at dyadic tree nodes; it does not by itself
define values at nondyadic times or prove that the node-selection rule is
predictable. In an adaptive run, a finite work budget supplies a finite list
of requests.

The independence assertion for the two children is unconditional before the
parent is revealed. Conditional on a fixed parent, their sum is fixed and their
conditional covariance is $-(h/4)I_m$; they are not conditionally independent.
The exact fixed-depth Brownian increment law is proved separately on the A page.

derivations.claim: Put $I=[-c,c]$ and $p=\mathbb P\{G_1\in I\}>0$. For each Borel $A$, the event that the first accepted draw lies in $A$ is the disjoint union over $k\ge0$ of the events that the first $k$ draws lie outside $I$ and draw $k+1$ lies in $A\cap I$. Independence therefore gives $\mathbb P\{R\in A\}=\sum_{k=0}^\infty(1-p)^k \mathbb P\{G_1\in A\cap I\}=\frac{\mathbb P\{G_1\in A\cap I\}}p.$ This is exactly the stated truncated-normal law.

The law is symmetric, so $\mathbb ER=0$. Both $I$ and its complement have positive probability. On $I$, $G_1^2\le c^2$ with strict inequality on a positive-probability subset; on $I^c$, $G_1^2>c^2$. Hence $\mathbb E[G_1^2\mid G_1\in I]<c^2< \mathbb E[G_1^2\mid G_1\notin I].$ The unconditional variance $h=\mathbb EG_1^2$ is the strict weighted average of these two conditional second moments. Therefore $\operatorname{Var}(R)=\mathbb E[G_1^2\mid G_1\in I]<h$.

The resampled increment is thus not $N(0,h)$, whereas bridge refinement in [F2] preserves the already sampled parent increment by exact sum consistency. This example concerns endpoint-dependent rejection; it does not contradict the predictable-grid error theorem, whose step lengths are fixed from current information.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and use the finite-dimensional Brownian-motion
convention of [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]. Let the state dimension
$d$ and noise dimension $m$ be positive finite integers, and fix $T>0$ and
$N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$. Set $h=T/N>0$ and $t_k=kh$ for
$0\le k\le N$. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel.
Write $|\cdot|$ for the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|_F$ for the Frobenius
norm. Suppose finite constants $L,K$ satisfy, for every $s,t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|^2+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F^2\le K^2(1+|x|^2),$$
and
$$|b(t,x)-b(s,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(s,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|)|t-s|^{1/2}.$$
Let $W$ be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion on a filtered
probability space, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and law
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ whenever $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X_0$ be
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of future Brownian increments, and
$\mathbb E|X_0|^2<\infty$.

The **Euler–Maruyama algorithm** takes these data as input and returns
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$:

1. Set $Y_0=X_0$.
2. For $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, form $\Delta W_k=W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}$ and set
   $$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)\Delta W_k.$$

The output is the grid approximation for the coefficient pair $(b,\sigma)$.
The companion step-process and interpolation definition uses this same grid
and endpoint convention.

Assume AC. Fix $m\ge1$, $h>0$, and a finite tree depth $r\ge0$. Take a root
increment $D_\varnothing\sim N_m(0,hI_m)$. At each internal node $v$ of
length $\ell_v=h/2^{|v|}$, use the split in
[[alg-dyadic-brownian-bridge-increment-tree]] with a fresh
$Z_v\sim N_m(0,(\ell_v/4)I_m)$ independent of the root and of all other
innovations. Then the $2^r$ increments at depth $r$ are mutually independent
and each has law $N_m(0,(h/2^r)I_m)$. At every internal node its increment is

conditional on a fixed parent, the two children have covariance
$-(\ell_v/4)I_m$ and are not independent.

Applying [F1] on the first fine half-step gives $Y_{1/2}=(1+h/2)y_0+\Delta W_1$. The second half-step gives $Y_f=(1+h/2)Y_{1/2}+\Delta W_2$, so substitution yields the displayed fine formula.

Substitute [F2] into $Y_f$ and subtract $Y_c$ from step 1.1: $Y_f-Y_c=\bigl((1+h/2)^2-(1+h)\bigr)y_0+ \bigl((1+h/2)(\Delta W/2+Z)+(\Delta W/2-Z)-\Delta W\bigr) =\frac{h^2}{4}y_0+\frac h4\Delta W+\frac h2Z.$ For $y_0=0$, independence and the variances in [F2] give $\operatorname{Var}(Y_f-Y_c)=(h/4)^2h+(h/2)^2(h/4)=h^3/8$. The case $h=0$ is excluded; for every $h>0$ the fine difference has strictly positive variance at $y_0=0$. A nonzero initial value changes the mean by $h^2y_0/4$ but not that variance. For a finite parameter $\lambda\ge0$, the **Poisson count law**
$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The
normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a Poisson point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,
then
$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$
and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

derivations.claim: If $A\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\alpha)$ and $B\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\beta)$ are independent, then for $\alpha,\beta>0$ and $n\in\mathbb N_0$ their convolution is $$\mathbb P(A+B=n)=e^{-(\alpha+\beta)} \sum_{k=0}^n\frac{\alpha^k\beta^{n-k}}{k!(n-k)!} =e^{-(\alpha+\beta)}\frac{(\alpha+\beta)^n}{n!},$$ by the binomial theorem. If either parameter is zero, the corresponding count is identically zero by [F1], and the same conclusion follows. Thus an independent sum has Poisson law with the sum of its parameters.

citations.quote:
Fix positive integers $d$ and $R$. A **reaction propensity system** consists of a state set $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ that is finite or countable, increments $\nu_j\in\mathbb Z^d$ for $1\le j\le R$, and propensities $a_j:E\to[0,\infty)$. Here “countable” means finite or countably infinite, as in [[def-countable]]. The total propensity
$$\lambda(x):=\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)$$
is finite for every $x\in E$, and $a_j(x)>0$ implies $x+\nu_j\in E$. Here $\mathbb N$ and $\mathbb Z$ have the meanings in [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-integers]], and addition in $\mathbb Z^d$ is coordinatewise.

A **reaction event** of channel $j$ at state $x$ records the marked transition $x\mapsto x+\nu_j$. The counting process $N_j(t)$ records the number of channel-$j$ events by time $t$. A zero increment $\nu_j=0$ is allowed: it records a reaction event without changing the state.

For a time-homogeneous system, the **reaction generator operator** on bounded functions $f:E\to\mathbb R$ is
$$(Qf)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0} a_j(x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
When $E$ is finite, $\Lambda:=\max_{x\in E}\lambda(x)<\infty$. If no active reaction has zero increment, the corresponding matrix has off-diagonal entries $q_{xy}=\sum_{j:x+\nu_j=y}a_j(x)$ and diagonal $q_{xx}=-\lambda(x)$. With zero-increment events, the operator formula remains valid and the matrix diagonal is instead minus the sum of state-changing rates; the zero-increment channels remain part of the marked event process.

For a finite horizon $T$, a **time-dependent propensity system** replaces $a_j(x)$ by functions $a_j:[0,T]\times E\to[0,\infty)$ whose sections $t\mapsto a_j(t,x)$ are measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B([0,T])$ of the usual topology on $[0,T]$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Require finite total rate $\lambda(t,x):=\sum_j a_j(t,x)$. Its time-dependent generator operator is
$$(Q_t f)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(t,x)>0} a_j(t,x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
This definition specifies a stochastic model. It does not assert that a physical chemical system follows that model.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $R\ge1$, let $r_1,\ldots,r_R\ge0$, and set $r_0=\sum_{j=1}^R r_j$. On a common probability space let $E_1,\ldots,E_R$ be independent random variables, each with the unit exponential law $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$, whose survival at $t\ge0$ is $e^{-t}$. If $r_0>0$, define
$$T_*:=\min_{j:r_j>0}\frac{E_j}{r_j},\qquad J_*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{j:r_j>0}\frac{E_j}{r_j}.$$
Then ties have probability zero, $T_*\sim\operatorname{Exp}(r_0)$, $J_*$ is independent of $T_*$, and
$$\mathbb P(J_*=j)=\frac{r_j}{r_0}.$$
If $r_0=0$, every $r_j=0$ and no finite reaction clock is active.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, and let $E$ be finite with a reaction system from [[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]]. Supply the independent random streams required by [[alg-gillespie-direct-method-for-reaction-networks]] and [[alg-next-reaction-random-time-change-method]]. Define the reference marked process recursively: at state $x$, if $\lambda(x)>0$, its next reaction time has law $\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda(x))$ and its channel is independent of that time with probabilities $a_j(x)/\lambda(x)$; if $\lambda(x)=0$, it remains at $x$. Then both algorithms have the law of this reference process on every finite horizon. The process has generator operator
$$(Qf)(x)=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0}a_j(x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr),$$
absorbing states are handled exactly, and for $\Lambda=\max_{x\in E}\lambda(x)$ the expected total reaction count on $[0,T]$ is at most $\Lambda T$. A zero-increment channel is still a marked reaction event, but it contributes zero to the state generator.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Uniformly over $x\in D\cup F$, the no-event probability in a time interval of length $\delta$ is $e^{-\lambda(x)\delta}$, where $\lambda(x)=0$ on $F$ and $\lambda(x)\le A$ on $D$. Its difference from $1-\lambda(x)\delta$ is at most $A^2\delta^2/2$. For a channel $j$ from $x\in D$, the probability that it fires once at time $r\in(0,\delta)$ and no later event occurs is $$\int_0^\delta a_j(x)e^{-\lambda(x)r} e^{-\lambda(x+\nu_j)(\delta-r)}\,dr.$$ Both rates in the exponent are at most $A$, so its difference from $a_j(x)\delta$ is at most $a_j(x)A\delta^2$. Summing over channels gives at most $\lambda(x)A\delta^2\le A^2\delta^2$. After the first event, the conditional probability of another before $\delta$ is at most $A(\delta-r)$; integrating against the first-event rate, at most $A$, shows that the probability of at least two events is at most $A^2\delta^2/2$. These estimates are uniform on the finite state set.

Since $D\cup F$ is finite and $\partial_t v$ is continuous, uniformly in $s$ and $x$, $$v(s+\delta,x)=v(s,x)+\delta\partial_s v(s,x)+o(\delta).$$ The zero-event probability is $1-\lambda(x)\delta+O(\delta^2)$; the single-channel probabilities are $a_j(x)\delta+O(\delta^2)$ by step 1.1; and the multiple-event probability is $O(\delta^2)$. In the zero-event case, the contribution is $v(s,x)+\delta(\partial_s v(s,x)-\lambda(x)v(s,x))+o(\delta)$. The one-event channel contributions are $\delta\sum_j a_j(x)v(s,x+
u_j)+o(\delta)$, because the time change in $v(s+\delta,x+
u_j)$ is multiplied by an $O(\delta)$ event probability. The multiple-event contribution is $O(\delta^2)$. Adding the cases, the order-$\delta$ terms are $$\delta\partial_s v(s,x)+\delta\sum_j a_j(x)(v(s,x+
u_j)-v(s,x)),$$ with a uniform $o(\delta)$ remainder. This is $\delta(\partial_s v(s,x)+Qv(s,\cdot)(x))+o(\delta)$; for $x\in F$ the chain is fixed and $Q=0$. Multiple-event payoffs contribute $O(\delta^2)$ because $v$ is bounded on the finite set.

Sum the conditional identity in step 2.1 over a deterministic partition of $[0,t]$ and take expectations. The uniform $o(\delta)$ remainders sum to $o(1)$. By [F3] the chain has finitely many jumps almost surely on $[0,t]$; therefore $s\mapsto\partial_s v(s,X_s)+Qv(s,\cdot)(X_s)$ is bounded and piecewise continuous, so its Riemann sums converge pathwise. Boundedness and dominated convergence let expectations pass to the integral. The left side telescopes to $\mathbb E[v(t,X_t)]-\mathbb E[v(0,X_0)]$, proving the identity.

For a finite parameter $\lambda\ge0$, the **Poisson count law**
$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The
normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a Poisson point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,
then
$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$
and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

**Inputs.** A finite-channel reaction propensity system
[[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]], an initial state
$x_0\in E$, a deterministic grid $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N=T$ with finite $N$,
and a draw budget $B\in\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$. Write
$h_n=t_{n+1}-t_n$. At each step the count vector has the product law whose
$j$th marginal is $\operatorname{Pois}(a_j(x_n)h_n)$, as defined in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]]. The budget counts scalar Poisson draws.

**Procedure.** Set $x=x_0$, grid index $n=0$, Poisson-draw counter $d=0$, and
status **horizon**.

1. If $n=N$, return the completed path with status **horizon**. If $x\notin E$,
   set status **invalid-state**, hold $x$ fixed to $T$, and return. If
   $\lambda(x)=0$, hold $x$ fixed to $T$ and return status
   **absorbed**.
2. If fewer than $R$ draws remain in budget $B$ (that is, $B-d<R$), return the path prefix with
   status **budget-exhausted**; it does not define a terminal sample at $T$.
3. Draw conditionally independent $K_{j,n}\sim\operatorname{Pois}(a_j(x)h_n)$,
   $1\le j\le R$, and set $y=x+\sum_{j=1}^R K_{j,n}\nu_j$. Increase
   $d\leftarrow d+R$.
4. Advance time to $t_{n+1}$. If $y\notin E$, set $x=y$, set status
   **invalid-state**, and keep $y$ fixed through all remaining grid times. If
   $y\in E$, set $x\leftarrow y$, increment $n\leftarrow n+1$, and continue.

The run has at most $N$ iterations. Each valid step uses exactly $R$ scalar
Poisson draws, $R$ propensity evaluations, and one finite stoichiometric
update. Under the unit-operation convention that each scalar draw,
propensity evaluation, and stoichiometric update costs one unit, its work is
$O(RN)$; the cost internal to a particular random-number generator is
excluded. Under the same convention, an event-count SSA implementation does
one exponential draw and one channel selection per simulated event, so its
work on a realized path is $O(M_T)$, where $M_T$ is that path's event count
before $T$. This compares operation counts only; it does not compare
parameter-dependent random-number costs. The method is approximate; its
Poisson leap can leave the physical state set, and no error guarantee is
asserted here for unbounded rates or the budget-exhausted prefix.

proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a Poisson point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,
then
$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$
and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, and let $E$ be finite with a reaction system from [[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]]. Supply the independent random streams required by [[alg-gillespie-direct-method-for-reaction-networks]] and [[alg-next-reaction-random-time-change-method]]. Define the reference marked process recursively: at state $x$, if $\lambda(x)>0$, its next reaction time has law $\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda(x))$ and its channel is independent of that time with probabilities $a_j(x)/\lambda(x)$; if $\lambda(x)=0$, it remains at $x$. Then both algorithms have the law of this reference process on every finite horizon. The process has generator operator
$$(Qf)(x)=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0}a_j(x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr),$$
absorbing states are handled exactly, and for $\Lambda=\max_{x\in E}\lambda(x)$ the expected total reaction count on $[0,T]$ is at most $\Lambda T$. A zero-increment channel is still a marked reaction event, but it contributes zero to the state generator.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: For the Poisson leap, the probability of zero total counts is $e^{-\lambda(x)h}$. The probability that exactly channel $j$ fires once is $a_j(x)h e^{-\lambda(x)h}$, so its difference from $a_j(x)h$ is at most $a_j(x)\lambda(x)h^2$. Summing these errors over $j$ gives at most $\lambda(x)^2h^2\le A^2h^2$. If $N=\sum_jK_j$, independence and [F5] give $$\mathbb E[N(N-1)\mid x] =\sum_j(a_j(x)h)^2+2\sum_{i<j}a_i(x)a_j(x)h^2 =(\lambda(x)h)^2,$$ hence $\mathbb P(N\ge2\mid x)\le(\lambda(x)h)^2/2\le A^2h^2/2$. The zero-count probability differs from $1-\lambda(x)h$ by at most $A^2h^2/2$. A single allowed channel event remains in $E$ by [F1], so only the $N\ge2$ part can trigger the invalid-state branch. The zero-count, total single-count, and multiple-count contributions are bounded respectively by $GA^2h^2/2$, $GA^2h^2$, and $GA^2h^2/2$. Thus $|(K_hg)(x)-g(x)-h(Qg)(x)|\le2GA^2h^2$.

For the exact chain, the no-event probability is $e^{-\lambda(x)h}$, which differs from $1-\lambda(x)h$ by at most $A^2h^2/2$. The probability of one channel-$j$ event and no later event is $$\int_0^h a_j(x)e^{-\lambda(x)s} e^{-\lambda(x+\nu_j)(h-s)}\,ds.$$ Its difference from $a_j(x)h$ is at most $a_j(x)Ah^2$, since all total rates on $E$ are at most $A$; summing over $j$ gives at most $\lambda(x)Ah^2\le A^2h^2$. The probability of two or more events is at most $A^2h^2/2$: conditional on a first event at time $s$, a later event has probability at most $A(h-s)$, and integration against the first-event rate bounded by $A$ gives the bound. The no-event, total single-event, and multiple-event contributions are bounded respectively by $GA^2h^2/2$, $GA^2h^2$, and $GA^2h^2/2$. Therefore $|(Q_hg)(x)-g(x)-h(Qg)(x)|\le2GA^2h^2$.

Subtract the two first-order expansions from steps 1.1 and 1.2 and use the triangle inequality. This gives $|(K_hg)(x)-(Q_hg)(x)|\le4GA^2h^2$ for every $x\in E$. Outside $E$ both kernels hold the state fixed, so the same bound holds there. Taking the supremum proves the final inequality.

Fix finitely many stoichiometric vectors $\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_R\in\mathbb Z^d$,
an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, nonnegative propensity functions
$a_j:U\to[0,\infty)$, and a volume parameter $V\ge1$. At a density state
$x\in U$ for which every positive-rate destination $x+\nu_j/V$ lies in $U$,
the density-scaled jump model has jump $\nu_j/V$ at rate $Va_j(x)$. For a
twice differentiable test function $\phi$ defined at those destinations, its
generator is
$$\mathcal L_V\phi(x)=V\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0} a_j(x)\bigl(\phi(x+\nu_j/V)-\phi(x)\bigr).$$

Put $b(x)=\sum_j\nu_j a_j(x)$ and
$C(x)=\sum_j a_j(x)\nu_j\nu_j^{\mathsf T}$. The associated
**chemical Langevin diffusion generator** is
$$\mathcal G_V\phi(x)=b(x)\cdot\nabla\phi(x) +\frac{1}{2V}\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)\, \nu_j^{\mathsf T}D^2\phi(x)\nu_j.$$
A Markov diffusion with this generator is called the chemical Langevin
model here. The definition does not assert existence, uniqueness, positivity,
or approximation accuracy for either process. In an SDE representation the
drift is $b$ and the covariance matrix per unit time is $C/V$.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $D$ and $F$ be disjoint
finite sets of states, and let a finite-channel reaction chain move from a
state $x\in D$ by channel $j$ to $x+\nu_j\in D\cup F$ at rate $a_j(x)$.
Assume its total rate is at most $A<\infty$ on $D$, and make every state in
$F$ absorbing. Let $v:[0,T]\times(D\cup F)\to\mathbb R$ have a continuously
differentiable time section for each state, with $\partial_t v$ continuous
in time. Define
$$Qf(x)=\sum_j a_j(x)(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x))\quad(x\in D),\qquad Qf(x)=0\quad(x\in F).$$
Then, for the stopped chain $X$ and $0\le t\le T$,
$$\mathbb E[v(t,X_t)] = \mathbb E[v(0,X_0)] + \mathbb E\int_0^t(\partial_s v(s,X_s)+Qv(s,\cdot)(X_s))\,ds.$$
In particular, $D$ may be the finite set of lattice states inside a compact
stopping region, and $F$ the finite set of one-jump exit destinations.

Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. derivations.claim:
Fix an interior lattice state $x$ and a time $s$. For channel $j$, apply one-variable Taylor's theorem to $r\mapsto u(s,x+r
u_j/V)$ on $[0,1]$. Its third-order remainder has absolute value at most $M\|
u_j\|^3/(6V^3)$. Multiplying by $Va_j(x)$ and summing over channels gives $$\mathcal L_Vu(s,x)= \sum_j a_j(x)
u_j\cdot
abla u(s,x) + rac1{2V}\sum_j a_j(x)
u_j^{\mathsf T}D^2u(s,x)
u_j+R_V(s,x),$$ where $$|R_V(s,x)|\le  rac{M}{6V^2}\sum_jA_j\|
u_j\|^3.$$ The first two terms are exactly $\mathcal G_Vu(s,x)$ by [F1].

Set $\Psi_V(x)=V(x-x_0)$, $D_V=\Psi_V(D)$, and let $F_V$ be the images under $\Psi_V$ of the one-jump exit destinations from $D$. These are disjoint finite subsets of $\mathbb Z^d$. The transported stopped chain $\widetilde X=\Psi_V(\bar X)$ moves from $y\in D_V$ by channel increment $\nu_j$ at rate $Va_j(x_0+y/V)$ and is fixed on $F_V$. For $\widetilde u(s,y)=u(s,x_0+y/V)$, its time derivative is unchanged and its reaction generator on $D_V$ equals $\mathcal L_Vu(s,x_0+y/V)$. Apply [F2] to this integer-lattice chain and $\widetilde u$. Before $\tau_X$, the integrand is $\partial_su+\mathcal L_Vu=(\mathcal L_V-\mathcal G_V)u$ by the backward equation [A3]. After exit, $\bar X$ is fixed at an exit destination where $u(s,\bar X_s)=g(\bar X_s)$ is independent of $s$, so both its time derivative and stopped generator vanish. At time $T$, $u(T,\bar X_T)=g(\bar X_T)$, and at time $0$, $u(0,x_0)=\mathbb E g(\bar Z_T)$. Therefore $$\mathbb E g(\bar X_T)-\mathbb E g(\bar Z_T) =\mathbb E\int_0^{T\wedge\tau_X} (\mathcal L_V-\mathcal G_V)u(s,X^V_s)\,ds.$$

Bound the integrand in step 1.2 by step 1.1 and use $T\wedge\tau_X\le T$. This proves the stopped-process estimate. Under [A4], the stopped and original terminal payoffs agree unless their respective process exits by time $T$; on that event their difference is at most $2G$. The triangle inequality for the two expectations adds at most $2G\mathbb P(\tau_X\le T)+2G\mathbb P(\tau_Z\le T)$, which proves the unstopped bound.

citations.quote:
Fix positive integers $d$ and $R$. A **reaction propensity system** consists of a state set $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ that is finite or countable, increments $\nu_j\in\mathbb Z^d$ for $1\le j\le R$, and propensities $a_j:E\to[0,\infty)$. Here “countable” means finite or countably infinite, as in [[def-countable]]. The total propensity
$$\lambda(x):=\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)$$
is finite for every $x\in E$, and $a_j(x)>0$ implies $x+\nu_j\in E$. Here $\mathbb N$ and $\mathbb Z$ have the meanings in [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-integers]], and addition in $\mathbb Z^d$ is coordinatewise.

A **reaction event** of channel $j$ at state $x$ records the marked transition $x\mapsto x+\nu_j$. The counting process $N_j(t)$ records the number of channel-$j$ events by time $t$. A zero increment $\nu_j=0$ is allowed: it records a reaction event without changing the state.

For a time-homogeneous system, the **reaction generator operator** on bounded functions $f:E\to\mathbb R$ is
$$(Qf)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0} a_j(x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
When $E$ is finite, $\Lambda:=\max_{x\in E}\lambda(x)<\infty$. If no active reaction has zero increment, the corresponding matrix has off-diagonal entries $q_{xy}=\sum_{j:x+\nu_j=y}a_j(x)$ and diagonal $q_{xx}=-\lambda(x)$. With zero-increment events, the operator formula remains valid and the matrix diagonal is instead minus the sum of state-changing rates; the zero-increment channels remain part of the marked event process.

For a finite horizon $T$, a **time-dependent propensity system** replaces $a_j(x)$ by functions $a_j:[0,T]\times E\to[0,\infty)$ whose sections $t\mapsto a_j(t,x)$ are measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B([0,T])$ of the usual topology on $[0,T]$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Require finite total rate $\lambda(t,x):=\sum_j a_j(t,x)$. Its time-dependent generator operator is
$$(Q_t f)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(t,x)>0} a_j(t,x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
This definition specifies a stochastic model. It does not assert that a physical chemical system follows that model.

Fix a state $x\in E$ and step $h\ge0$ in
[[alg-explicit-poisson-tau-leaping]]. Let
$\Delta Y=\sum_{j=1}^R\nu_jK_j$, where conditionally independent
$K_j\sim\operatorname{Pois}(a_j(x)h)$. Then
$$\mathbb E[\Delta Y\mid x]=h\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)\nu_j,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(\Delta Y\mid x)=h\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)\nu_j\nu_j^{\mathsf T},$$
and
$$\mathbb E[\|\Delta Y\|^2\mid x] =h\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)\|\nu_j\|^2 +h^2\left\|\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)\nu_j\right\|^2.$$

**Inputs.** A finite-channel reaction propensity system
[[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]], an initial state
$x_0\in E$, a deterministic grid $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N=T$ with finite $N$,
and a draw budget $B\in\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$. Write
$h_n=t_{n+1}-t_n$. At each step the count vector has the product law whose
$j$th marginal is $\operatorname{Pois}(a_j(x_n)h_n)$, as defined in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]]. The budget counts scalar Poisson draws.

**Procedure.** Set $x=x_0$, grid index $n=0$, Poisson-draw counter $d=0$, and
status **horizon**.

1. If $n=N$, return the completed path with status **horizon**. If $x\notin E$,
   set status **invalid-state**, hold $x$ fixed to $T$, and return. If
   $\lambda(x)=0$, hold $x$ fixed to $T$ and return status
   **absorbed**.
2. If fewer than $R$ draws remain in budget $B$ (that is, $B-d<R$), return the path prefix with
   status **budget-exhausted**; it does not define a terminal sample at $T$.
3. Draw conditionally independent $K_{j,n}\sim\operatorname{Pois}(a_j(x)h_n)$,
   $1\le j\le R$, and set $y=x+\sum_{j=1}^R K_{j,n}\nu_j$. Increase
   $d\leftarrow d+R$.
4. Advance time to $t_{n+1}$. If $y\notin E$, set $x=y$, set status
   **invalid-state**, and keep $y$ fixed through all remaining grid times. If
   $y\in E$, set $x\leftarrow y$, increment $n\leftarrow n+1$, and continue.

The run has at most $N$ iterations. Each valid step uses exactly $R$ scalar
Poisson draws, $R$ propensity evaluations, and one finite stoichiometric
update. Under the unit-operation convention that each scalar draw,
propensity evaluation, and stoichiometric update costs one unit, its work is
$O(RN)$; the cost internal to a particular random-number generator is
excluded. Under the same convention, an event-count SSA implementation does
one exponential draw and one channel selection per simulated event, so its
work on a realized path is $O(M_T)$, where $M_T$ is that path's event count
before $T$. This compares operation counts only; it does not compare
parameter-dependent random-number costs. The method is approximate; its
Poisson leap can leave the physical state set, and no error guarantee is
asserted here for unbounded rates or the budget-exhausted prefix.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,
then
$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$
and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

Let $h\ge0$ and let $\lambda_1,\lambda_2\ge0$. Let $C,R_1,R_2$ be
independent counts with laws
$$C\sim\operatorname{Pois}(h\min(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)),\quad R_1\sim\operatorname{Pois}(h(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)^+),\quad R_2\sim\operatorname{Pois}(h(\lambda_2-\lambda_1)^+),$$
and set $K_1=C+R_1$, $K_2=C+R_2$. Then $K_i\sim\operatorname{Pois}(h\lambda_i)$,
$$\mathbb E(K_1-K_2)=h(\lambda_1-\lambda_2),\qquad \operatorname{Var}(K_1-K_2)=h|\lambda_1-\lambda_2|,$$
and
$$\operatorname{Cov}(K_1,K_2)=h\min(\lambda_1,\lambda_2).$$

derivations.claim: For lattice states $x,z$, write $e=x-z$ and $\delta_j=a_j(x)-a_j(z)$. Bounded rates and the integer lattice's minimum nonzero distance one imply $|\delta_j|\le L\|e\|$ for a constant $L$; this also holds when one state is outside $E$, where the extended rate is zero. In one half interval, shared counts cancel from the increment difference $\eta$. The independent residual Poisson counts and [F5] give $$m:=\mathbb E[\eta\mid x,z]=h\sum_j\nu_j\delta_j,\qquad \mathbb E[\|\eta-m\|^2\mid x,z]=h\sum_j|\delta_j|\|\nu_j\|^2.$$ Thus $\|m\|\le Ch\|e\|$ and the centered second moment is at most $Ch\|e\|$. If $e=0$, then $\eta=0$. Otherwise $\|e\|\ge1$, so $h\|e\|\le h\|e\|^2$. For $h\le1$ this proves $$\mathbb E[\|\eta\|^2\mid x,z]\le Ch\|e\|^2.$$

Let $R$ be the fine-path increment on the first half interval from $x$. By [F3], [F4], and the triangle inequality, $$\mathbb E\|R\|\le\sum_j\|\nu_j\|\,h a_j(x)\le Ch.$$ By [F2] and bounded propensities, $\mathbb E\|R\|^2\le Ch$ for $h\le1$. If $x'=x+R$, then $$\mathbb E\|x'-z\|\le\|e\|+Ch,\qquad \mathbb E\|x'-z\|^2\le C(\|e\|^2+h).$$ For the second inequality, expand $\|e+R\|^2$ and use $\|\mathbb ER\|\le Ch$ and $\mathbb E\|R\|^2\le Ch$; the cross term is bounded by $Ch\|e\|\le Ch\|e\|^2$ when $e\ne0$, and is zero when $e=0$.

Write the two half-interval differences as $\eta_i=m_i+\xi_i$, where $m_i$ is the conditional mean and $\xi_i$ is centered given the starting states of that half interval. Step 1.1 gives $$\|m_1\|\le Ch\|e\|,\qquad \mathbb E\|\xi_1\|^2\le Ch\|e\|^2.$$ The second half starts at $x'$ and $z$, so $\|m_2\|\le Ch\|x'-z\|$. Steps 1.1 and 1.2 therefore give $$\mathbb E\|m_2\|^2\le Ch^2(\|e\|^2+h),\qquad \mathbb E\|\xi_2\|^2\le Ch(\|e\|+h)\le Ch\|e\|^2+Ch^2.$$ For the latter inequality, use $\mathbb E\|x'-z\|\le\|e\|+Ch$ and $\|e\|\le\|e\|^2$ when $e\ne0$. Fresh second-half residual counts are conditionally centered, hence $\mathbb E[\xi_1\cdot\xi_2]=0$.

The endpoint error is $e'=e+m_1+\xi_1+m_2+\xi_2$. First, $$\mathbb E\|e+\eta_1\|^2 =\|e+m_1\|^2+\mathbb E\|\xi_1\|^2 \le(1+Ch)\|e\|^2.$$ At the start of the second half, $e+m_1+\xi_1+m_2$ is measurable and $\mathbb E[\xi_2\mid x',z]=0$, so its expected inner product with $\xi_2$ is zero. The remaining cross terms satisfy $$2|\mathbb E(\xi_1\cdot m_2)| \le2(\mathbb E\|\xi_1\|^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E\|m_2\|^2)^{1/2} \le Ch^{3/2}\|e\|\sqrt{\|e\|^2+h}\le Ch\|e\|^2,$$ with value zero if $e=0$, and $$2|\mathbb E((e+m_1)\cdot m_2)| \le h\|e+m_1\|^2+h^{-1}\mathbb E\|m_2\|^2 \le Ch\|e\|^2+Ch^2.$$ The additional terms satisfy $\mathbb E\|m_2\|^2\le Ch\|e\|^2+Ch^2$ and $\mathbb E\|\xi_2\|^2\le Ch\|e\|^2+Ch^2$ by step 2.1. Combining these exact expansion terms proves $$\mathbb E[\|e'\|^2\mid e]\le(1+Ch)\|e\|^2+Ch^2.$$

Let $u_n=\mathbb E\|e_n\|^2$ at coarse endpoints. Since $u_0=0$, step 3.1 gives $u_{n+1}\le(1+Ch)u_n+Ch^2$. There are $N=T/(2h)$ coarse intervals, so iteration yields $$u_N\le Ch^2\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}(1+Ch)^r \le Ch^2N e^{ChN}\le C_T h.$$

If $e_N
e0$, its integer coordinates imply $\|e_N\|^2\ge1$, hence $\mathbb P(e_N
e0)\le\mathbb E\|e_N\|^2\le C_T h$. The payoff difference is zero when $e_N=0$ and is at most $2G$ in absolute value otherwise. Its variance is at most its second moment, hence at most $4G^2\mathbb P(e_N

citations.quote:
Fix positive integers $d$ and $R$. A **reaction propensity system** consists of a state set $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ that is finite or countable, increments $\nu_j\in\mathbb Z^d$ for $1\le j\le R$, and propensities $a_j:E\to[0,\infty)$. Here “countable” means finite or countably infinite, as in [[def-countable]]. The total propensity
$$\lambda(x):=\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)$$
is finite for every $x\in E$, and $a_j(x)>0$ implies $x+\nu_j\in E$. Here $\mathbb N$ and $\mathbb Z$ have the meanings in [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-integers]], and addition in $\mathbb Z^d$ is coordinatewise.

A **reaction event** of channel $j$ at state $x$ records the marked transition $x\mapsto x+\nu_j$. The counting process $N_j(t)$ records the number of channel-$j$ events by time $t$. A zero increment $\nu_j=0$ is allowed: it records a reaction event without changing the state.

For a time-homogeneous system, the **reaction generator operator** on bounded functions $f:E\to\mathbb R$ is
$$(Qf)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0} a_j(x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
When $E$ is finite, $\Lambda:=\max_{x\in E}\lambda(x)<\infty$. If no active reaction has zero increment, the corresponding matrix has off-diagonal entries $q_{xy}=\sum_{j:x+\nu_j=y}a_j(x)$ and diagonal $q_{xx}=-\lambda(x)$. With zero-increment events, the operator formula remains valid and the matrix diagonal is instead minus the sum of state-changing rates; the zero-increment channels remain part of the marked event process.

For a finite horizon $T$, a **time-dependent propensity system** replaces $a_j(x)$ by functions $a_j:[0,T]\times E\to[0,\infty)$ whose sections $t\mapsto a_j(t,x)$ are measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B([0,T])$ of the usual topology on $[0,T]$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Require finite total rate $\lambda(t,x):=\sum_j a_j(t,x)$. Its time-dependent generator operator is
$$(Q_t f)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(t,x)>0} a_j(t,x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
This definition specifies a stochastic model. It does not assert that a physical chemical system follows that model.

**Inputs.** A finite-channel reaction propensity system
[[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]], an initial state
$x_0\in E$, a deterministic grid $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N=T$ with finite $N$,
and a draw budget $B\in\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$. Write
$h_n=t_{n+1}-t_n$. At each step the count vector has the product law whose
$j$th marginal is $\operatorname{Pois}(a_j(x_n)h_n)$, as defined in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]]. The budget counts scalar Poisson draws.

**Procedure.** Set $x=x_0$, grid index $n=0$, Poisson-draw counter $d=0$, and
status **horizon**.

1. If $n=N$, return the completed path with status **horizon**. If $x\notin E$,
   set status **invalid-state**, hold $x$ fixed to $T$, and return. If
   $\lambda(x)=0$, hold $x$ fixed to $T$ and return status
   **absorbed**.
2. If fewer than $R$ draws remain in budget $B$ (that is, $B-d<R$), return the path prefix with
   status **budget-exhausted**; it does not define a terminal sample at $T$.
3. Draw conditionally independent $K_{j,n}\sim\operatorname{Pois}(a_j(x)h_n)$,
   $1\le j\le R$, and set $y=x+\sum_{j=1}^R K_{j,n}\nu_j$. Increase
   $d\leftarrow d+R$.
4. Advance time to $t_{n+1}$. If $y\notin E$, set $x=y$, set status
   **invalid-state**, and keep $y$ fixed through all remaining grid times. If
   $y\in E$, set $x\leftarrow y$, increment $n\leftarrow n+1$, and continue.

The run has at most $N$ iterations. Each valid step uses exactly $R$ scalar
Poisson draws, $R$ propensity evaluations, and one finite stoichiometric
update. Under the unit-operation convention that each scalar draw,
propensity evaluation, and stoichiometric update costs one unit, its work is
$O(RN)$; the cost internal to a particular random-number generator is
excluded. Under the same convention, an event-count SSA implementation does
one exponential draw and one channel selection per simulated event, so its
work on a realized path is $O(M_T)$, where $M_T$ is that path's event count
before $T$. This compares operation counts only; it does not compare
parameter-dependent random-number costs. The method is approximate; its
Poisson leap can leave the physical state set, and no error guarantee is
asserted here for unbounded rates or the budget-exhausted prefix.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $E$ be finite, let
$A=\max_{x\in E}\sum_j a_j(x)$, and assume
$a_j(x)=0$ whenever $x+\nu_j\notin E$. Extend every state outside $E$ as
absorbing, as in [[alg-explicit-poisson-tau-leaping]]. For $h\ge0$, let
$Q_h$ be the exact reaction-chain transition kernel and $K_h$ the Poisson
tau-leap transition kernel. If $g:\mathbb Z^d\to\mathbb R$ is bounded, then
$$\left|(K_hg)(x)-g(x)-h(Qg)(x)\right| \le2A^2h^2\|g\|_\infty,$$
$$\left|(Q_hg)(x)-g(x)-h(Qg)(x)\right| \le2A^2h^2\|g\|_\infty,$$
and hence
$$\|K_hg-Q_hg\|_\infty\le4A^2h^2\|g\|_\infty.$$
The bounds include the multi-reaction leap probability that can trigger the
invalid-state branch.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,
then
$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$
and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, and let $E$ be finite with a reaction system from [[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]]. Supply the independent random streams required by [[alg-gillespie-direct-method-for-reaction-networks]] and [[alg-next-reaction-random-time-change-method]]. Define the reference marked process recursively: at state $x$, if $\lambda(x)>0$, its next reaction time has law $\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda(x))$ and its channel is independent of that time with probabilities $a_j(x)/\lambda(x)$; if $\lambda(x)=0$, it remains at $x$. Then both algorithms have the law of this reference process on every finite horizon. The process has generator operator
$$(Qf)(x)=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0}a_j(x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr),$$
absorbing states are handled exactly, and for $\Lambda=\max_{x\in E}\lambda(x)$ the expected total reaction count on $[0,T]$ is at most $\Lambda T$. A zero-increment channel is still a marked reaction event, but it contributes zero to the state generator.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Both $K_h$ and $Q_h$ are Markov kernels: they preserve nonnegative functions and constants, so each is a contraction in the supremum norm. Outside $E$, both hold the state fixed by the stated extension.

The finite algebraic identity $$K_h^N-Q_h^N=\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}K_h^{N-1-r}(K_h-Q_h)Q_h^r$$ follows by cancellation of consecutive terms. Apply it to $g$, use the contraction from step 1.1 and the one-step bound [F3] to obtain $$\|(K_h^N-Q_h^N)g\|_\infty \le N\,4A^2h^2\|g\|_\infty=4A^2T h\|g\|_\infty.$$ Evaluating at $x_0$ proves the weak-order bound.

While the leap state is in $E$, any single channel count produces a state in $E$ by [F1]. Therefore an invalid endpoint requires at least two total channel firings in that step. If $M_n=\sum_jK_{j,n}$, independence [F2] and the factorial moment [F4] give $$\mathbb E[M_n(M_n-1)\mid Y_n] =\sum_j(a_j(Y_n)h)^2+2\sum_{i<j}a_i(Y_n)a_j(Y_n)h^2 =(\lambda(Y_n)h)^2\le(Ah)^2.$$ Since $\mathbf 1_{\{M_n\ge2\}}\le M_n(M_n-1)/2$, the conditional invalid-step probability is at most $A^2h^2/2$. A union bound over $N=T/h$ steps gives $\mathbb P(\text{invalid by }T)\le A^2T h/2$.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let
$E\subseteq\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^d$ be finite, let
$A=\max_{x\in E}\sum_j a_j(x)<\infty$ for the system
[[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]], and assume
$a_j(x)=0$ whenever $x+\nu_j\notin E$. Extend the exact chain by making every
state outside $E$ absorbing, and let $K_h$ be the tau-leap kernel in
[[alg-explicit-poisson-tau-leaping]] with the same absorbing-invalid-state
convention. For $T=Nh$ with $N\in\mathbb N$, an initial state $x_0\in E$, and
a bounded payoff $g:\mathbb Z^d\to\mathbb R$, the leap satisfies
$$\left|\mathbb E_{x_0}g(Y_N)-\mathbb E_{x_0}g(X_T)\right| \le4A^2T h\,\|g\|_\infty.$$
Its probability of ever entering an invalid state by $T$ is at most
$\tfrac12A^2T h$. This separately bounds the absorbing invalid-state branch;
the result makes no claim for unbounded rates.

Assume the finite-state reaction system of
[[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]] has propensities
bounded on $E$ and extended by zero to states outside $E$. Let
$h_\ell=T2^{-\ell}$ for $\ell\ge1$, and couple a fine step $h=h_\ell$ to a
coarse step $2h$ as follows. On each of the two half intervals, with fine
state $x$ and coarse state $z$, use for channel $j$ a shared
$\operatorname{Pois}(h\min(a_j(x),a_j(z)))$ count and independent residual
counts of means $h(a_j(x)-a_j(z))^+$ and $h(a_j(z)-a_j(x))^+$ for the fine
and coarse paths, as in
[[lem-shared-minimum-poisson-count-coupling]]. Use independent copies across
channels and fresh copies on the two half intervals. Update the fine state after each half interval, and keep
the coarse propensities frozen at its state at the start of the coarse
interval. Then, for every bounded $g:\mathbb Z^d\to\mathbb R$,
$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(g(Y_{h_\ell}(T))-g(Y_{h_{\ell-1}}(T))\right) \le C h_\ell,$$
where $C$ depends on $T$, the finite network, and $\|g\|_\infty$, but not
on $\ell$. This is a variance bound for the stated coupled Poisson leap;
independent levels are not covered.

Fix a refinement factor $M\in\mathbb N$ with $M\ge2$, a base scale $T>0$, and a finite level $L\in\mathbb N\cup\{0\}$. The geometric mesh widths are $h_\ell=T M^{-\ell}$ for $0\le\ell\le L$. Let $P$ be a real random variable with $\mathbb E|P|<\infty$, and for each $\ell$ let $P_\ell$ be a real random variable with $\mathbb E[P_\ell^2]<\infty$.

At level $0$, set $\Delta_0=P_0$. At each level $\ell\ge1$, choose a joint law for a pair $(P_\ell^{\mathrm f},P_{\ell-1}^{\mathrm c})$ whose marginals are the laws of $P_\ell$ and $P_{\ell-1}$, respectively. Such a joint law is a coupling of the two levels. Define the correction $\Delta_\ell=P_\ell^{\mathrm f}-P_{\ell-1}^{\mathrm c}$. This construction gives $\mathbb E\Delta_\ell=\mathbb E P_\ell-\mathbb E P_{\ell-1}$.

For each level choose a positive integer $N_\ell$ and take $\Delta_{\ell,1},\ldots,\Delta_{\ell,N_\ell}$ to be independent copies of $\Delta_\ell$. Require the complete sample blocks from distinct levels to be independent. Write $\bar\Delta_\ell=N_\ell^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N_\ell}\Delta_{\ell,i}$. The finite-level multilevel Monte Carlo estimator is
$$\widehat\mu_{L,\mathbf N}=\sum_{\ell=0}^L\bar\Delta_\ell.$$
All corrections have finite second moments because each level approximation does. The shared randomness inside one fine/coarse pair is what can reduce the correction variance; the estimator still uses independent sample blocks across levels.

Use the finite hierarchy and estimator of [[def-mlmc-hierarchy-and-coupled-corrections]]. Put $V_\ell=\operatorname{Var}(\Delta_\ell)$. Then
$$\mathbb E\widehat\mu_{L,\mathbf N}=\mathbb E P_L,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_{L,\mathbf N})=\sum_{\ell=0}^L\frac{V_\ell}{N_\ell},$$
and the mean square error for the target $\mathbb E P$ is exactly
$$\mathbb E\left[(\widehat\mu_{L,\mathbf N}-\mathbb E P)^2\right] =\sum_{\ell=0}^L\frac{V_\ell}{N_\ell}+(\mathbb E P_L-\mathbb E P)^2.$$

Let $M\ge2$ be an integer, $T>0$, and $h_\ell=T M^{-\ell}$. Let $P$ be an integrable real target. Suppose we are given an infinite compatible hierarchy: for every $\ell\ge0$ a square-integrable level approximation $P_\ell$, and for every $\ell\ge1$ a fixed coupling of the laws of $P_\ell$ and $P_{\ell-1}$. Define $\Delta_0=P_0$ and, under each coupling, $\Delta_\ell=P_\ell^{\mathrm f}-P_{\ell-1}^{\mathrm c}$. For each finite $L$, use the first $L+1$ levels and their couplings, with independent sample blocks across levels, as in [[def-mlmc-hierarchy-and-coupled-corrections]]. Suppose there are constants $C_b,C_v,C_c>0$ and exponents $\alpha\ge\frac12$ and $\beta>0$ such that, for every $\ell\ge0$,
$$|\mathbb E P_\ell-\mathbb E P|\le C_b h_\ell^\alpha,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\Delta_\ell)\le C_v h_\ell^\beta,$$
and the work for one level-$\ell$ correction sample is at most $C_c h_\ell^{-1}$. For every sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$, there are a finite level $L$ and positive integer sample counts $N_0,\ldots,N_L$ for which the estimator of [[def-mlmc-hierarchy-and-coupled-corrections]] satisfies
$$\mathbb E\left[(\widehat\mu_{L,\mathbf N}-\mathbb E P)^2\right]\le\epsilon^2$$
and its total work has the following upper bounds, with constants independent of $\epsilon$:
$$\begin{cases} O(\epsilon^{-2}),&\beta>1,\\ O\!\left(\epsilon^{-2}(\log\epsilon^{-1})^2\right),&\beta=1,\\ O\!\left(\epsilon^{-2-(1-\beta)/\alpha}\right),&0<\beta<1. \end{cases}$$
This is an upper bound under the three rate assumptions; it does not assert a matching lower bound or that the rates hold for a particular discretization.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

For a finite parameter $\lambda\ge0$, the **Poisson count law**
$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The
normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a Poisson point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,
then
$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$
and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

Let $h\ge0$ and let $\lambda_1,\lambda_2\ge0$. Let $C,R_1,R_2$ be
independent counts with laws
$$C\sim\operatorname{Pois}(h\min(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)),\quad R_1\sim\operatorname{Pois}(h(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)^+),\quad R_2\sim\operatorname{Pois}(h(\lambda_2-\lambda_1)^+),$$
and set $K_1=C+R_1$, $K_2=C+R_2$. Then $K_i\sim\operatorname{Pois}(h\lambda_i)$,
$$\mathbb E(K_1-K_2)=h(\lambda_1-\lambda_2),\qquad \operatorname{Var}(K_1-K_2)=h|\lambda_1-\lambda_2|,$$
and
$$\operatorname{Cov}(K_1,K_2)=h\min(\lambda_1,\lambda_2).$$
