citations.quote:
This algorithm takes an autonomous vector field $f$ on an open state domain $V\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, an admitted initial state $y$, a step $h>0$, an integer stage count $s\ge1$, and an evaluator that returns either $f(u)$ or an evaluation-failure status. In the exact mathematical model the evaluator returns $f(u)$ at every $u\in V$; the failure status records only an unavailable numerical evaluation. Define stage abscissae $c_j=j^2/s^2$ for $0\le j\le s$. Set $Y_0=y$. Before each query check that its stage state belongs to $V$; if it does not, return domain-failure with that stage index. If the evaluator reports failure, return evaluation-failure with that stage index. Query at $Y_0$ and, on success, set $Y_1=Y_0+(h/s^2)f(Y_0)$. For $j=2,\ldots,s$, query at $Y_{j-1}$ and, on success, set
$$Y_j=2Y_{j-1}-Y_{j-2}+\frac{2h}{s^2}f(Y_{j-1}).$$
If the final state $Y_s$ is outside $V$, return output-domain-failure; otherwise return success with state $Y_s$.

For a nonautonomous equation $y'=f(t,y)$, apply the same algorithm to the autonomous augmented field $\widetilde f(t,y)=(1,f(t,y))$ on the time-state domain, starting at the augmented state $(t,y)$. Its time component follows the same recurrence and equals $t+c_jh$ at stage $j$, with $c_s=1$, so the returned augmented state has time coordinate $t+h$. This is the first-order undamped RKC method; its scalar linear stability polynomial is established separately.

The stability analysis uses $T_s$ and $U_s$ from [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]]; this item defines the executable recurrence and does not itself assert an order or stability theorem.

Input a finite-dimensional real vector space $V$, a linear endomorphism $A:V\to V$, an initial vector $y\in V$, a step $h>0$, and an integer stage count $s\ge2$. Each application of $A$ is the exact value of this total linear map, so this mathematical procedure has no application-failure branch. Define
$$w_1=\frac{3}{s^2-1},\qquad b_s=\frac{s^2-1}{3s^2},\qquad a_s=1-b_s.$$
Set $V_0=y$ and $V_1=V_0+w_1hA(V_0)$. For $j=2,\ldots,s$, compute
$$V_j=2V_{j-1}+2w_1hA(V_{j-1})-V_{j-2}.$$
Return $a_sV_0+b_sV_s$. Each stage uses one application of $A$; no implicit system is solved. The output is the one-step update for the autonomous linear equation $y'=Ay$. Here $T_s$ denotes the Chebyshev polynomial defined by [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]]; the equivalent polynomial in $hA$ and its certified real stability interval are proved separately.

Let $\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ be the set of formal real polynomials of
[[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]]. Associate to every
$P\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ an eventually zero coefficient sequence $(p_k)$:
use its displayed finite coefficient list and extend it by zeros when $P\ne0$,
and put $p_k=0$ for every $k$ when $P=0$. Do the same for $Q$, with coefficients
$(q_k)$. Define $P+Q$ coefficientwise and define $PQ$ by the convolution
coefficients
$$ (P+Q)_k=p_k+q_k,\qquad (PQ)_k=\sum_{j=0}^{k}p_jq_{k-j}. $$
using the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. In either construction, discard
trailing zero coefficients; if every coefficient is zero, the result is the zero
polynomial. Scalar multiplication and subtraction are the corresponding
coefficientwise operations. Thus these formulas define operations on the formal
coefficient-list objects, independently of evaluation.

Write $1=(1)$ and $X=(0,1)$, and define
$$ \Phi(P,Q):=(Q,2XQ-P)\qquad(P,Q\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}). $$
Apply [[thm-recursion]] to the set
$\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}\times\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$, first with initial value
$(1,X)$ and then with initial value $(1,2X)$, always using the function $\Phi$.
This gives unique pair sequences $H^T,H^U$. Define $T_n$ and $U_n$ to be the
first coordinates of $H^T_n$ and $H^U_n$, respectively. Since the first
coordinate of $\Phi(P,Q)$ is $Q$, the second coordinate of $H^T_n$ is
$T_{n+1}$ and the second coordinate of $H^U_n$ is $U_{n+1}$. Consequently
$$ T_0=1,\quad T_1=X,\quad T_{n+2}=2XT_{n+1}-T_n, $$
$$ U_0=1,\quad U_1=2X,\quad U_{n+2}=2XU_{n+1}-U_n $$
for every $n\in\mathbb N$. These unique sequences are the **Chebyshev
polynomials of the first and second kinds**.

Let $T_n$ and $U_n$ be the real evaluation functions of the Chebyshev polynomials defined by [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]]. For every natural $n$,

$$|T_n(x)|\le 1,\qquad |U_n(x)|\le n+1\quad(-1\le x\le1),$$

and for $n\ge1$, $|T_n(x)|>1$ whenever $|x|>1$. Also,

$$T_n(1)=1,\quad T_n(-1)=(-1)^n,\quad U_n(1)=n+1,\quad U_n(-1)=(-1)^n(n+1).$$

For every natural $n\ge1$, $T_n$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $2^{n-1}$, while $U_n$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $2^n$. This degree and leading-coefficient assertion is exactly the content of [[lem-chebyshev-degree-leading-coefficients-and-extreme-values]]; that item does not assert an extremum bound.

The evaluation functions are twice differentiable at $1$, with

$$T_n'(1)=n^2,\qquad T_n''(1)=\frac{n^2(n^2-1)}{3}.$$

Here each natural number in a real formula denotes its canonical real image ([[def-canonical-natural]]), and powers use [[def-integer-power]].

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism and let $p(x)=\sum_{k\geq0}a_kx^k\in F[x]$. Define

$$p(T):=\sum_{k\geq0}a_kT^k\in\mathcal L(V,V),$$

where $T^0:=I_V$ and $T^{k+1}:=T\circ T^k$. The sum is finite because the coefficient sequence of $p$ has finite support. In particular, the zero polynomial evaluates to the zero endomorphism and the constant polynomial $1$ evaluates to $I_V$.

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: Put $e_j=\widehat Y_j-Y_j$, where $Y_j$ is the unperturbed recurrence with the same $A,h,y$. The first two updates give $e_0=0$ and $e_1=\delta_1$, and subtraction of the recurrences gives $e_j=2Xe_{j-1}-e_{j-2}+\delta_j$ for $j\ge2$.

By [F5], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of $A$. Under either spectral interval premise, the eigenvalues of $X$ lie in $[-1,1]$. Thus [F4] and [F6] imply $\|U_k(X)v\|_2\le(k+1)\|v\|_2$ for every vector $v$: expand in that eigenbasis and bound each squared coordinate.

Define $U_k(X)$ by polynomial evaluation [F6]. Induction using [F3] and step 1.1 gives $e_s=\sum_{j=1}^s U_{s-j}(X)\delta_j.$ For $s=1$ this is $U_0(X)\delta_1=\delta_1$. At a successor stage, the coefficient of the most recent old perturbation is $2X=U_1(X)$; for every earlier perturbation, multiplying by $2X$ and subtracting its prior coefficient uses $2XU_k(X)-U_{k-1}(X)=U_{k+1}(X)$. The new perturbation has coefficient $U_0(X)=I$. This proves the formula by induction.

Apply the triangle inequality [F7] to step 2.1 and then step 1.2: $\|e_s\|_2\le\sum_{j=1}^s(s-j+1)\|\delta_j\|_2\le\varepsilon\sum_{k=0}^{s-1}(k+1)=\frac{s(s+1)}2\varepsilon.$ For linear RKC2 the returned perturbation is $b_se_s$; since $0<b_s<1$, its norm is at most the same bound. Adding a separate output perturbation uses the triangle inequality once more.

Input an initial pair $(t,y)$, a step $h>0$, an open time-state domain $D$, and a right-hand-side evaluator for $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$. Before each query, check that its time-state pair is in $D$; return domain-failure with that stage index if it is not. If the evaluator reports failure, return evaluation-failure with that stage index. Execute:

1. Query $f(t,y)$. On success set $Y_1=y+h f(t,y)$.
2. Query $f(t+h,Y_1)$. On success set $Y_2=\frac34y+\frac14\bigl(Y_1+h f(t+h,Y_1)\bigr)$.
3. Query $f(t+h/2,Y_2)$. On success set $y^+=\frac13y+\frac23\bigl(Y_2+h f(t+h/2,Y_2)\bigr)$.
4. If $(t+h,y^+)\notin D$, return output-domain-failure; otherwise return success with $(t+h,y^+)$.

The equivalent tableau has $c=(0,1,1/2)$, $b=(1/6,1/6,2/3)$, and rows of $A$ equal to $(0,0,0)$, $(1,0,0)$, and $(1/4,1/4,0)$. The procedure uses only explicit function evaluations; it has no implicit stage solve. If a numerical evaluator can fail even at a domain point, its failure is returned unchanged with the corresponding stage index. The exact mathematical method assumes all queried values exist.

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be an open time-state domain, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be the right-hand side of a first-order initial-value problem in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. An explicit $s$-stage Runge–Kutta tableau consists of a positive integer $s$, real coefficients $a_{ij}$, $b_i$, and $c_i$ with $a_{ij}=0$ whenever $j\ge i$, and
$$c_i=\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}\qquad(1\le i\le s).$$
The finite row sum is empty, hence $c_1=0$.

For a step size $h>0$ from an admitted base pair $(t,y)\in D$, compute in order
$$Y_i=y+h\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}K_j,\qquad t_i=t+c_i h,\qquad K_i=f(t_i,Y_i)\quad(i=1,\ldots,s).$$
The strict lower-triangular condition makes each stage depend only on already computed slopes; no implicit stage equation is solved. If every stage is defined, the candidate output is
$$y^+=y+h\sum_{i=1}^s b_iK_i.$$

The procedure accepts an exact right-hand-side evaluation oracle that returns either the value $f(t_i,Y_i)$ or an evaluation-failure status. Before each query it checks $(t_i,Y_i)\in D$. It returns domain-failure with the first failing stage if that check fails, evaluation-failure with the stage index if the oracle fails, and domain-failure at output if $(t+h,y^+)\notin D$. Otherwise it returns success with $(t+h,y^+)$. In the exact mathematical model the oracle returns $f$ at every point of $D$; the failure branch records only an unavailable numerical evaluation. On success this is a one-step map in the sense of [[def-one-step-ode-method-local-defect-order-and-stability]].

derivations.claim: Rewriting the recurrences in [F1] as explicit RK stages gives rows of $A$ equal to $(0,0,0)$, $(1,0,0)$, and $(1/4,1/4,0)$, with $c=(0,1,1/2)$ and $b=(1/6,1/6,2/3)$. Thus $\sum b_i=1$, $\sum b_ic_i=1/2$, $\sum b_ic_i^2=1/3$, and $\sum b_i(Ac)_i=1/6$.

In the autonomous case $Y_1=E_h(y)\in C$. Since $Y_1\in C$, [A2] gives $E_h(Y_1)\in C$; [A1] and [F2] then give $Y_2=\frac34y+\frac14E_h(Y_1)\in C$. Applying [A2] to $Y_2$ gives $E_h(Y_2)\in C$, and [A1] gives $y^+=\frac13y+\frac23E_h(Y_2)\in C$.
The order equations in step 1.1 are exactly the order-one through order-three hypotheses of [F4], so the stated tube assumptions imply uniform local order at least three.

Convexity in [A1] gives $\Phi(Y_1)\le\Phi(y)$, $\Phi(Y_2)\le\frac34\Phi(y)+\frac14\Phi(E_h(Y_1))\le\Phi(y)$, and $\Phi(y^+)\le\frac13\Phi(y)+\frac23\Phi(E_h(Y_2))\le\Phi(y)$. Each last inequality uses [A2] at the relevant stage.

For a nonautonomous field the three formulas in [F1] use exactly $E_{t,h}$ at $y$, $E_{t+h,h}$ at $Y_1$, and $E_{t+h/2,h}$ at $Y_2$. Applying [A2] at those three start times and repeating the convex-combination calculations in steps 1.2–2.2 proves invariance and nonincrease.

citations.quote:
Input a first-order right-hand side $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ on an open time-state domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$, an admitted pair $(t,y)\in D$, a step $h>0$, an integer stage count $s\ge2$, and a right-hand-side evaluator that returns either $f(\tau,u)$ or an evaluation-failure status at each queried $(\tau,u)\in D$. In the exact mathematical model the evaluator returns $f$ at every point of $D$; the failure status records only an unavailable numerical evaluation. Set
$$w_1=\frac{3}{s^2-1},\qquad b_0=b_1=b_2=\frac14,\qquad b_j=\frac{j^2-1}{3j^2}\ (3\le j\le s),\qquad a_j=1-b_j\ (0\le j\le s).$$
For the stages define $c_0=0$, $c_1=b_1w_1$, and $c_j=b_jw_1j^2$ for $2\le j\le s$. Put $Y_0=y$. Before each query check that its time-state input belongs to the declared domain; if not, return domain-failure with that stage index. If the right-hand-side evaluator reports failure, return evaluation-failure with that stage index. Query $k_0=f(t,Y_0)$ and on success set $Y_1=Y_0+b_1w_1h k_0$. For each $j=2,\ldots,s$, define
$$\mu_j=\frac{2b_j}{b_{j-1}},\qquad \nu_j=-\frac{b_j}{b_{j-2}},\qquad m_j=\frac{2b_jw_1}{b_{j-1}},\qquad g_j=-a_{j-1}m_j,$$
query $k_{j-1}=f(t+c_{j-1}h,Y_{j-1})$, and on success set
$$Y_j=(1-\mu_j-\nu_j)y+\mu_jY_{j-1}+\nu_jY_{j-2}+m_jh k_{j-1}+g_jh k_0.$$
If $(t+h,Y_s)$ is outside the declared domain, return output-domain-failure; otherwise return success with $(t+h,Y_s)$. All stages use only the initial state and already computed values, so the procedure contains no implicit solve.

For an autonomous field, omit the time argument. The abscissae above are the exact time coordinates obtained by applying the recurrence to the augmented equation $t'=1$; in particular $c_s=1$. Order, stability, and stage-amplification claims are separate proved items.

The coefficient $b_2$ agrees with the displayed formula at $j=2$; it is listed among the base values to make the recurrence unambiguous. The Chebyshev identities used to derive these coefficients are supplied by [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]].

On the scalar test equation $y'=\lambda y$, write $z=h\lambda$ and let $R(z)$ be the factor by which a successful method step multiplies $y$.

For first-order RKC with $s\ge1$ stages,
$$R_{1,s}(z)=T_s(1+z/s^2).$$
It has degree $s$, satisfies $R_{1,s}(0)=R'_{1,s}(0)=1$, and its real absolute stability set $\{z\in\mathbb R:|R_{1,s}(z)|\le1\}$ is exactly $[-2s^2,0]$.

For second-order RKC with $s\ge2$ stages, both the linear algorithm and the scalar-linear specialization of the nonlinear algorithm have
$$R_{2,s}(z)=a_s+b_sT_s(1+w_1z),\qquad w_1=\frac{3}{s^2-1},\quad b_s=\frac{s^2-1}{3s^2},\quad a_s=1-b_s.$$
This polynomial has degree $s$ and satisfies $R_{2,s}(0)=R'_{2,s}(0)=R''_{2,s}(0)=1$. It is absolutely stable on the real interval $[-2(s^2-1)/3,0]$; this is a certified interval and is not claimed to be the maximal real stability set.

Let $d\ge1$, let $A$ be a self-adjoint endomorphism of $\mathbb R^d$ with its Euclidean inner product, and assume $\langle Av,v\rangle\le0$ for every $v$. Let $\rho=\max_i(-\lambda_i)$, where $\lambda_i$ are the eigenvalues of $A$. If $h\rho\le2s^2$, first-order RKC is nonexpansive in the Euclidean norm; if $h\rho\le2(s^2-1)/3$, linear second-order RKC is nonexpansive. The same linear contraction statement holds for the nonlinear RKC method when applied to $f(y)=Ay$. No corresponding claim is made for nonnormal matrices.

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and consider a first-order IVP and solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **one-step method** is a family of maps $\Psi_h(t,v)$, defined for admitted times $t$, positive step sizes $h$, and states $v$, whose value is the method's approximation at time $t+h$ from the single input state $v$ at time $t$. It does not use earlier numerical states.

If $y$ is an exact solution on an interval containing $[t,t+h]$, the **local defect** is

$$\delta_h(t;y):=\Psi_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h).$$

Let $K\subseteq D$ be a fixed compact time-state set. The method has **uniform local order $p$ on $K$ along $y$** if there are constants $C\ge0$ and $h_0>0$, independent of the admitted starting time $t$ and step $0<h\le h_0$, such that

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le C h^{p+1}$$

whenever the exact solution graph on $[t,t+h]$ and the associated method time-state inputs, stages, and outputs under consideration lie in $K$. Here $p$ is a positive integer and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

The method has **one-step Lipschitz stability on $K$** with constant $L\ge0$ if

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$

for every admitted step size $h$, admitted time $t$, and input states $u,v$ with $(t,u),(t,v)\in K$. This is a bound on the change in one step; it is separate from absolute or linear stability regions and does not itself assert a global error estimate.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $d,N,p\ge1$, $T>0$, $h=T/N$, and $t_n=nh$. Let $y:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ solve an initial-value problem in an open time-state domain $D$. Use the Euclidean norm $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], whose triangle inequality is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]. Let $\mathcal T\subset D$ be a common compact time-state tube with positive margin in $D$, and write $\mathcal T_t:=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:(t,v)\in\mathcal T\}$. Suppose a one-step map $\Psi_{h,n}$ is defined on $\mathcal T_{t_n}$, produces $y_{n+1}=\Psi_{h,n}(y_n)$, and the entire exact path, all numerical grid states, and every method stage lie in $\mathcal T$. If constants $C,C_0,L\ge0$, independent of $N$ and $n$, satisfy
$$\|y_0-y(0)\|_2\le C_0h^p,\qquad \|\Psi_{h,n}(y(t_n))-y(t_{n+1})\|_2\le Ch^{p+1},$$
and
$$\|\Psi_{h,n}(u)-\Psi_{h,n}(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$
for every $u,v\in\mathcal T_{t_n}$ and $0\le n<N$, then, for $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, for $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $F^{n}$ be the
function space on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, with the
pointwise operations ([[def-function-space]], [[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). For $i < n$ define the **standard unit vector**
$e_i \in F^{n}$ by

$$e_i(i) = 1_F, \qquad e_i(j) = 0_F \ \text{ for } j < n \text{ with } j \ne i .$$

Then:

1. **Finite sums in a function space are pointwise.** For every set $X$, every
   $p \in \mathbb{N}$, every list $u : p \to F^{X}$ and every $j \in X$,
   $$\Bigl(\sum_{k<p} u_k\Bigr)(j) \;=\; \sum_{k<p} u_k(j),$$
   the right-hand sum being taken in $(F,+,0_F)$. (Stated here for an arbitrary
   $X$ because the companion page needs it at $X = \mathbb{N}$.)
2. $e : n \to F^{n}$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$ ([[def-linear-basis]]); in
   particular $e$ is injective and its image $e[n] = \{\, e_i : i < n \,\}$ is a
   basis of $F^{n}$ with $e[n] \approx n$ ([[def-equinumerous]]);
3. for every $\lambda : n \to F$ and every $j < n$,
   $\bigl(\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i e_i\bigr)(j) = \lambda_j$; equivalently the
   coordinate list of $x \in F^{n}$ with respect to the ordered basis $e$
   ([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) is
   $i \mapsto x(i)$;
4. $F^{n}$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ with $\dim_F F^{n} = n$
   ([[def-dimension]]);
5. at $n = 0$ this reads: $F^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
   so $F^{0}$ is the zero space, the empty list is its ordered basis,
   $\varnothing$ is its basis and $\dim_F F^{0} = 0$.

Every index runs from $0$, so the coordinates of an element of $F^{n}$ are
$x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ and no statement above is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

The following are the explicit Runge–Kutta tableaus in the convention of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]].

Forward Euler has $s=1$, $A=(0)$, $b=(1)$, and $c=(0)$.

Explicit midpoint has $s=2$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\[2pt]1/2&0\end{pmatrix}$, $b=(0,1)$, and $c=(0,1/2)$.

The classical four-stage Runge–Kutta method has $s=4$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0&0\\[2pt]1/2&0&0&0\\[2pt]0&1/2&0&0\\[2pt]0&0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $b=(1/6,1/3,1/3,1/6)$, and $c=(0,1/2,1/2,1)$.

Each displayed $c_i$ is the row sum required in the definition of an explicit tableau. These tableaus specify the stage equations; their order and scalar stability functions are proved separately.

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be an open time-state domain, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be the right-hand side of a first-order initial-value problem in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. An explicit $s$-stage Runge–Kutta tableau consists of a positive integer $s$, real coefficients $a_{ij}$, $b_i$, and $c_i$ with $a_{ij}=0$ whenever $j\ge i$, and
$$c_i=\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}\qquad(1\le i\le s).$$
The finite row sum is empty, hence $c_1=0$.

For a step size $h>0$ from an admitted base pair $(t,y)\in D$, compute in order
$$Y_i=y+h\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}K_j,\qquad t_i=t+c_i h,\qquad K_i=f(t_i,Y_i)\quad(i=1,\ldots,s).$$
The strict lower-triangular condition makes each stage depend only on already computed slopes; no implicit stage equation is solved. If every stage is defined, the candidate output is
$$y^+=y+h\sum_{i=1}^s b_iK_i.$$

The procedure accepts an exact right-hand-side evaluation oracle that returns either the value $f(t_i,Y_i)$ or an evaluation-failure status. Before each query it checks $(t_i,Y_i)\in D$. It returns domain-failure with the first failing stage if that check fails, evaluation-failure with the stage index if the oracle fails, and domain-failure at output if $(t+h,y^+)\notin D$. Otherwise it returns success with $(t+h,y^+)$. In the exact mathematical model the oracle returns $f$ at every point of $D$; the failure branch records only an unavailable numerical evaluation. On success this is a one-step map in the sense of [[def-one-step-ode-method-local-defect-order-and-stability]].

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and consider a first-order IVP and solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **one-step method** is a family of maps $\Psi_h(t,v)$, defined for admitted times $t$, positive step sizes $h$, and states $v$, whose value is the method's approximation at time $t+h$ from the single input state $v$ at time $t$. It does not use earlier numerical states.

If $y$ is an exact solution on an interval containing $[t,t+h]$, the **local defect** is

$$\delta_h(t;y):=\Psi_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h).$$

Let $K\subseteq D$ be a fixed compact time-state set. The method has **uniform local order $p$ on $K$ along $y$** if there are constants $C\ge0$ and $h_0>0$, independent of the admitted starting time $t$ and step $0<h\le h_0$, such that

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le C h^{p+1}$$

whenever the exact solution graph on $[t,t+h]$ and the associated method time-state inputs, stages, and outputs under consideration lie in $K$. Here $p$ is a positive integer and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

The method has **one-step Lipschitz stability on $K$** with constant $L\ge0$ if

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$

for every admitted step size $h$, admitted time $t$, and input states $u,v$ with $(t,u),(t,v)\in K$. This is a bound on the change in one step; it is separate from absolute or linear stability regions and does not itself assert a global error estimate.

derivations.claim: On the first midpoint stage, $k_1=f(-h/2,0)=0$, so the second-stage state remains $0$. Its time is $-h/2+h/2=0$, where the definition of $f$ gives $k_2=f(0,0)=0$. Thus the method output is $0$.

The displayed piecewise function satisfies $y(0)=0$ and $y'(t)=f(t,y(t))$ for $t<0$ and $t>0$. At $t=0$ its two one-sided derivatives are both $0=f(0,y(0))$, so it is an exact solution there as well. Its value at $h/2$ is $h^2/8$, hence the local defect is $0-h^2/8=-h^2/8$.

If one constant $C$ gave the uniform order-two estimate in [F3], these admitted exact-start steps would satisfy $h^2/8\le Ch^3$, hence $1/(8h)\le C$ for every $h>0$. The left side is unbounded as $h\downarrow0$, so no such uniform constant exists. The field is continuous but not differentiable in time at $0$, identifying the missing smoothness condition.

The following are the explicit Runge–Kutta tableaus in the convention of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]].

Forward Euler has $s=1$, $A=(0)$, $b=(1)$, and $c=(0)$.

Explicit midpoint has $s=2$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\[2pt]1/2&0\end{pmatrix}$, $b=(0,1)$, and $c=(0,1/2)$.

The classical four-stage Runge–Kutta method has $s=4$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0&0\\[2pt]1/2&0&0&0\\[2pt]0&1/2&0&0\\[2pt]0&0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $b=(1/6,1/3,1/3,1/6)$, and $c=(0,1/2,1/2,1)$.

Each displayed $c_i$ is the row sum required in the definition of an explicit tableau. These tableaus specify the stage equations; their order and scalar stability functions are proved separately.

Under the smoothness and compact-tube hypotheses of [[prop-explicit-rk-order-conditions-through-four]], the forward Euler, explicit midpoint, and classical four-stage tableaus of [[def-euler-midpoint-rk4-tableaus]] have uniform local orders at least one, two, and four, respectively.

For the scalar test equation $y'=\lambda y$, set $z=h\lambda$. The corresponding stability functions, defined by $y^+=R(z)y$, are
$$R_{\mathrm E}(z)=1+z,\qquad R_{\mathrm M}(z)=1+z+\frac{z^2}{2},\qquad R_{\mathrm{RK4}}(z)=1+z+\frac{z^2}{2}+\frac{z^3}{6}+\frac{z^4}{24}.$$
The absolute stability region of a listed method is $\{z\in\mathbb C:|R(z)|\le1\}$. On the negative real axis, the Euler and midpoint regions are exactly $[-2,0]$. No maximal real interval is asserted here for RK4.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

derivations.claim: By [F4]–[F5], $y(t)=\exp(-t)$ solves $y'=-y$ with $y(0)=1$. For one step, the tableaus [F1] and factors [F2] give $R$; put $d_h:=R-e^{-h}$. Taylor's theorem [F3] applied to $e^{-h}$ gives, for $p=1,2,4$ in the respective methods, $d_h=c_0h^{p+1}+O(h^{p+2}),\qquad c_0=-\tfrac12,\tfrac16,\tfrac1{120}.$ The first omitted exponential terms after the Euler, midpoint, and RK4 polynomials in [F2] are respectively $+h^2/2$, $-h^3/6$, and $-h^5/120$; subtracting them from those polynomials gives the listed defect coefficients.

For each method and sufficiently small $h$, set $q_h:=R e^h=1+e^h d_h$, using $e^{-h}e^h=e^0=1$ from [F6]. Thus $|q_h-1|\le C h^{p+1}$ for a constant independent of $N$. For $m\le N=1/h$, factoring $q_h^m-1$ gives $|q_h^m-1|\le m|q_h-1|\max(1,|q_h|)^{m-1}\le C h^p e^C.$ The last bound follows from $|q_h|\le1+C h^{p+1}\le e^{C h^{p+1}}$ by [F5], so the factor of powers is at most $e^{CNh^{p+1}}\le e^C$.

Repeated use of [F6] gives $(e^{-h})^N=e^{-Nh}=e^{-1}$ and $e^{-h(N-1)}=e^{-1+h}$. Since $R=q_he^{-h}$, the finite-factor identity yields $R^N-e^{-1}=(R-e^{-h})\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}R^{N-1-k}e^{-kh} =d_h e^{-h(N-1)}\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}q_h^m.$ By step 2.1 each summand is $1+O(h^p)$ uniformly in $m$, and $e^{-1+h}=e^{-1}(1+O(h))$ by [F3]–[F4]. Thus the sum factor is $Ne^{-1}(1+O(h))$.

Substituting the expansion from step 1.1 and $N=1/h$ into step 3.1 gives $R^N-e^{-1}=c_0e^{-1}h^p(1+O(h)).$ Because $c_0\ne0$, taking absolute values gives the three positive constants and slopes in the Example.

This algorithm takes an autonomous vector field $f$ on an open state domain $V\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, an admitted initial state $y$, a step $h>0$, an integer stage count $s\ge1$, and an evaluator that returns either $f(u)$ or an evaluation-failure status. In the exact mathematical model the evaluator returns $f(u)$ at every $u\in V$; the failure status records only an unavailable numerical evaluation. Define stage abscissae $c_j=j^2/s^2$ for $0\le j\le s$. Set $Y_0=y$. Before each query check that its stage state belongs to $V$; if it does not, return domain-failure with that stage index. If the evaluator reports failure, return evaluation-failure with that stage index. Query at $Y_0$ and, on success, set $Y_1=Y_0+(h/s^2)f(Y_0)$. For $j=2,\ldots,s$, query at $Y_{j-1}$ and, on success, set
$$Y_j=2Y_{j-1}-Y_{j-2}+\frac{2h}{s^2}f(Y_{j-1}).$$
If the final state $Y_s$ is outside $V$, return output-domain-failure; otherwise return success with state $Y_s$.

For a nonautonomous equation $y'=f(t,y)$, apply the same algorithm to the autonomous augmented field $\widetilde f(t,y)=(1,f(t,y))$ on the time-state domain, starting at the augmented state $(t,y)$. Its time component follows the same recurrence and equals $t+c_jh$ at stage $j$, with $c_s=1$, so the returned augmented state has time coordinate $t+h$. This is the first-order undamped RKC method; its scalar linear stability polynomial is established separately.

For first-order RKC with $s\ge1$ stages,

It has degree $s$, satisfies $R_{1,s}(0)=R'_{1,s}(0)=1$, and its real absolute stability set $\{z\in\mathbb R:|R_{1,s}(z)|\le1\}$ is exactly $[-2s^2,0]$.

This algorithm takes an autonomous vector field $f$ on an open state domain $V\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, an admitted initial state $y$, a step $h>0$, an integer stage count $s\ge1$, and an evaluator that returns either $f(u)$ or an evaluation-failure status. In the exact mathematical model the evaluator returns $f(u)$ at every $u\in V$; the failure status records only an unavailable numerical evaluation. Define stage abscissae $c_j=j^2/s^2$ for $0\le j\le s$. Set $Y_0=y$. Before each query check that its stage state belongs to $V$; if it does not, return domain-failure with that stage index. If the evaluator reports failure, return evaluation-failure with that stage index. Query at $Y_0$ and, on success, set $Y_1=Y_0+(h/s^2)f(Y_0)$. For $j=2,\ldots,s$, query at $Y_{j-1}$ and, on success, set
$$Y_j=2Y_{j-1}-Y_{j-2}+\frac{2h}{s^2}f(Y_{j-1}).$$
If the final state $Y_s$ is outside $V$, return output-domain-failure; otherwise return success with state $Y_s$.

For a nonautonomous equation $y'=f(t,y)$, apply the same algorithm to the autonomous augmented field $\widetilde f(t,y)=(1,f(t,y))$ on the time-state domain, starting at the augmented state $(t,y)$. Its time component follows the same recurrence and equals $t+c_jh$ at stage $j$, with $c_s=1$, so the returned augmented state has time coordinate $t+h$. This is the first-order undamped RKC method; its scalar linear stability polynomial is established separately.

The stability analysis uses $T_s$ and $U_s$ from [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]]; this item defines the executable recurrence and does not itself assert an order or stability theorem.

On the scalar test equation $y'=\lambda y$, write $z=h\lambda$ and let $R(z)$ be the factor by which a successful method step multiplies $y$.

$$R_{1,s}(z)=T_s(1+z/s^2).$$
It has degree $s$, satisfies $R_{1,s}(0)=R'_{1,s}(0)=1$, and its real absolute stability set $\{z\in\mathbb R:|R_{1,s}(z)|\le1\}$ is exactly $[-2s^2,0]$.

For second-order RKC with $s\ge2$ stages, both the linear algorithm and the scalar-linear specialization of the nonlinear algorithm have
$$R_{2,s}(z)=a_s+b_sT_s(1+w_1z),\qquad w_1=\frac{3}{s^2-1},\quad b_s=\frac{s^2-1}{3s^2},\quad a_s=1-b_s.$$
This polynomial has degree $s$ and satisfies $R_{2,s}(0)=R'_{2,s}(0)=R''_{2,s}(0)=1$. It is absolutely stable on the real interval $[-2(s^2-1)/3,0]$; this is a certified interval and is not claimed to be the maximal real stability set.

Let $d\ge1$, let $A$ be a self-adjoint endomorphism of $\mathbb R^d$ with its Euclidean inner product, and assume $\langle Av,v\rangle\le0$ for every $v$. Let $\rho=\max_i(-\lambda_i)$, where $\lambda_i$ are the eigenvalues of $A$. If $h\rho\le2s^2$, first-order RKC is nonexpansive in the Euclidean norm; if $h\rho\le2(s^2-1)/3$, linear second-order RKC is nonexpansive. The same linear contraction statement holds for the nonlinear RKC method when applied to $f(y)=Ay$. No corresponding claim is made for nonnormal matrices.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: The matrix is nonnormal: $AA^{\mathsf T}=\begin{pmatrix}17&-4\\-4&1\end{pmatrix}$ while $A^{\mathsf T}A=\begin{pmatrix}1&-4\\-4&17\end{pmatrix}$. Its two eigenvalues are $-1$, so those of $hA$ are both $-1/2\in[-2,0]$ and the scalar stability factor is $1/2$.

The one-stage update is $I+hA=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&2\\0&1/2\end{pmatrix}.$ It sends $e_2=(0,1)$ to $(2,1/2)$, whose Euclidean norm is $\sqrt{17}/2>1=\|e_2\|_2$. Therefore eigenvalue-wise scalar stability does not imply a matrix norm bound here; the self-adjoint hypothesis in [F2] cannot be omitted.

Let $k\ge1$, $d\ge1$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be the right-hand side of a first-order initial-value problem on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$, using the convention of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **constant-step $k$-step linear multistep method** has real coefficients $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_k,\beta_0,\ldots,\beta_k$ with $\alpha_k\ne0$ and advances values by

$$\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_jY_{n+j}=h\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_j f(t_{n+j},Y_{n+j}),\qquad t_{n+j}=t_n+jh,\quad h>0.$$

Multiplying all coefficients by the same nonzero scalar leaves the method unchanged; one may normalize $\alpha_k=1$. Its **characteristic polynomials** are

$$\rho(\zeta)=\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_j\zeta^j,\qquad \sigma(\zeta)=\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_j\zeta^j.$$

For an exact solution $y$ with $p+1$ continuous derivatives, the **unscaled local residual** at $t_n$ is

$$\tau_n(h;y)=\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_jy(t_n+jh)-h\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_jy'(t_n+jh).$$

The method has **order at least $p$**, where $p\ge1$ is an integer, if this residual is $O(h^{p+1})$ uniformly for admitted starting times in every fixed compact interval on which the indicated derivatives are bounded. It is **consistent** if it has order at least one. Equivalently, with the above coefficient convention, consistency is $\rho(1)=0$ and $\rho'(1)=\sigma(1)$.

The **root condition** is that every complex root of $\rho$ has modulus at most one and every root of modulus one has algebraic multiplicity one. The method is **zero-stable** if for each $T>0$ there is a constant $M_T$ independent of $N$ such that every solution of the homogeneous recurrence $\sum_j\alpha_jY_{n+j}=0$ on the uniform grid $h=T/N$ satisfies

$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|Y_n\|_\infty\le M_T\max_{0\le j<k}\|Y_j\|_\infty.$$

Here $\|x\|_\infty=\max_{1\le i\le d}|x_i|$ for $x\in\mathbb R^d$. The root-condition equivalence for zero-stability is established separately.

Let $K$ be a field, let $d\ge1$, and let $C$ be the row-shift companion matrix associated with

$$\chi(t)=t^d+c_1t^{d-1}+\cdots+c_d.$$

Then the matrix characteristic polynomial is exactly

$$\chi_C(t)=\det(tI_d-C)=t^d+c_1t^{d-1}+\cdots+c_d.$$

Let $a$ satisfy an order-$d$ recurrence from zero over a field, let $C$ be its row-shift companion matrix, and put $v_n=(a_n,\ldots,a_{n+d-1})^{\mathsf T}$. Then

$$v_{n+1}=Cv_n\qquad\text{and}\qquad v_n=C^nv_0$$

for every $n\ge0$.

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Every nonconstant complex polynomial has a complex root. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[lem-complex-polynomial-growth-and-minimum-modulus]], [[lem-dalembert-minimum-modulus-descent]].

A field $F$ is **algebraically closed** when every nonconstant polynomial $p\in F[x]$ has a root in $F$: there is $\lambda\in F$ such that $p(\lambda)=0$.

This definition concerns roots in the field itself. It does not assert here that any particular field, including $\mathbb C$, is algebraically closed.
Every endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field has a Jordan canonical form over that field, including the endomorphism of the zero space.

A **Jordan basis over $F$** for an endomorphism $T:V\to V$ is an ordered basis obtained by concatenating Jordan strings for $T$, all with eigenvalues in $F$ ([[def-jordan-block-and-jordan-string]]). The matrix of $T$ in such a basis is block diagonal with blocks $J_m(\lambda)$ and is called a **Jordan canonical form of $T$ over $F$**.

The adjective “canonical” records the block multiset, not a prescribed order of blocks: permuting the strings usually changes the literal block diagonal matrix. On the zero space the empty basis and empty block matrix form the Jordan basis and Jordan form.

For $m\ge1$ and $\lambda\in F$, the **Jordan block** $J_m(\lambda)$ is the $m\times m$ matrix with $\lambda$ on the diagonal, $1$ on the superdiagonal, and $0$ elsewhere.

Let $T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. A **Jordan string of length $m$ for $T$ at $\lambda$** is an ordered list $(v_1,\ldots,v_m)$ satisfying

A **constant-step $k$-step linear multistep method** has real coefficients $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_k,\beta_0,\ldots,\beta_k$ with $\alpha_k\ne0$ and advances values by

$$\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_jY_{n+j}=h\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_j f(t_{n+j},Y_{n+j}),\qquad t_{n+j}=t_n+jh,\quad h>0.$$

Multiplying all coefficients by the same nonzero scalar leaves the method unchanged; one may normalize $\alpha_k=1$. Its **characteristic polynomials** are

$$\rho(\zeta)=\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_j\zeta^j,\qquad \sigma(\zeta)=\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_j\zeta^j.$$

For an exact solution $y$ with $p+1$ continuous derivatives, the **unscaled local residual** at $t_n$ is

$$\tau_n(h;y)=\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_jy(t_n+jh)-h\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_jy'(t_n+jh).$$

The method has **order at least $p$**, where $p\ge1$ is an integer, if this residual is $O(h^{p+1})$ uniformly for admitted starting times in every fixed compact interval on which the indicated derivatives are bounded. It is **consistent** if it has order at least one. Equivalently, with the above coefficient convention, consistency is $\rho(1)=0$ and $\rho'(1)=\sigma(1)$.

The **root condition** is that every complex root of $\rho$ has modulus at most one and every root of modulus one has algebraic multiplicity one. The method is **zero-stable** if for each $T>0$ there is a constant $M_T$ independent of $N$ such that every solution of the homogeneous recurrence $\sum_j\alpha_jY_{n+j}=0$ on the uniform grid $h=T/N$ satisfies

$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|Y_n\|_\infty\le M_T\max_{0\le j<k}\|Y_j\|_\infty.$$

Here $\|x\|_\infty=\max_{1\le i\le d}|x_i|$ for $x\in\mathbb R^d$. The root-condition equivalence for zero-stability is established separately.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $t_n$ and expand each $y(t_n+jh)$ through degree $p$ and each $y'(t_n+jh)$ through degree $p-1$ by [F2], on the interval containing the finitely many nodes. Bounded derivatives on the compact interval make the remainders uniform over $n$ and $j$.

Substituting those expansions into [F1] and collecting the coefficient of $y^{(m)}(t_n)h^m/m!$ gives $\tau_n(h;y)=\sum_{m=0}^{p}\mu_m\frac{h^m}{m!}y^{(m)}(t_n)+O(h^{p+1})$. The derivative term contributes $m\sum_j\beta_jj^{m-1}$ when $m\ge1$ and contributes nothing for $m=0$.

Conversely, suppose the method has order at least $p$. Induct on $m=0,\ldots,p$, testing the residual on the polynomial solution $y(t)=t^m$ of $y'=mt^{m-1}$ (with $y=1$, $y'=0$ when $m=0$). Input a vector field $f(t,y)$, a finite grid $t_0,\ldots,t_N$, starting states $Y_0,Y_1\in\mathbb R^d$ (so $N\ge1$), and for each later step a prescribed closed ball $B_{n+1}\subset\mathbb R^d$ that specifies the admissible implicit branch. Before any evaluation, if either starting state has dimension different from $d$, return `invalid-input`; otherwise, if any time increment is nonpositive, return `invalid-grid`. Set $h_n=t_{n+1}-t_n$ and $r_n=h_n/h_{n-1}$ for $1\le n<N$.

For $n=1,\ldots,N-1$, form the equation

$$\frac{(1+2r_n)Z-(1+r_n)^2Y_n+r_n^2Y_{n-1}}{h_n(1+r_n)}=f(t_{n+1},Z).$$

If this equation has exactly one root $Z$ in $B_{n+1}$, set $Y_{n+1}=Z$ and continue. If it has no root there, return `no-root` with the computed prefix; if it has more than one root there, return `ambiguous-branch` with the computed prefix. If an evaluation of $f$ is undefined, return `evaluation-failure` with the prefix. On reaching $N$, return `completed` and $(Y_0,\ldots,Y_N)$. The procedure is defined for arbitrary positive adjacent step ratios; no convergence or accuracy property is part of this algorithm.

The coefficients are those obtained from the quadratic interpolation derivative in [[lem-variable-step-bdf2-interpolation-and-local-defect]]. A separate theorem gives the uniform ratio hypotheses needed for second-order convergence; they are not part of this algorithm.

Let $h_{n-1},h_n>0$, $r_n=h_n/h_{n-1}$, and let $y$ be an exact solution with three continuous derivatives near $t_{n-1},t_n,t_{n+1}$, where $h_j=t_{j+1}-t_j$. The derivative at $t_{n+1}$ of the quadratic interpolant through $(t_{n+1},y_{n+1})$, $(t_n,y_n)$, and $(t_{n-1},y_{n-1})$ is

$$\frac{(1+2r_n)y_{n+1}-(1+r_n)^2y_n+r_n^2y_{n-1}}{h_n(1+r_n)}.$$

Equating this derivative to $f(t_{n+1},Y_{n+1})$ defines the variable-step BDF2 formula

$$\frac{(1+2r_n)Y_{n+1}-(1+r_n)^2Y_n+r_n^2Y_{n-1}}{h_n(1+r_n)}=f(t_{n+1},Y_{n+1}).$$

For an exact vector solution $y'=f(t,y)$ whose third derivative is bounded, the unscaled residual

$$\tau_n=(1+2r_n)y(t_{n+1})-(1+r_n)^2y(t_n)+r_n^2y(t_{n-1})-h_n(1+r_n)y'(t_{n+1})$$

has norm $\|\tau_n\|_\infty=O(h_n^3)$ uniformly whenever $r_n$ stays in a fixed compact subinterval of $(0,\infty)$; the formula and remainder hold componentwise.

For the homogeneous vector-valued variable-step BDF2 recurrence obtained from [[alg-variable-step-bdf2-with-selected-implicit-branch]] by setting $f=0$, let $\Delta_n=Y_n-Y_{n-1}\in\mathbb R^d$. For every $r_n=h_n/h_{n-1}>0$,

$$\Delta_{n+1}=q(r_n)\Delta_n,\qquad q(r)=\frac{r^2}{1+2r}.$$

The multiplier satisfies $q(r)\le1$ exactly when $0<r\le1+\sqrt2$. In particular, if $0<r_n\le r_*<1+\sqrt2$ for every step, then $q(r_n)\le q_*:=r_*^2/(1+2r_*)<1$ uniformly.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

derivations.claim: Put $e_n=Y_n-y(t_n)$ and $d_n=e_n-e_{n-1}$. Subtracting the exact residual in [F2] from the numerical equation in [F1], then using the BDF2 coefficients, gives $(1+2r_n)d_{n+1}-r_n^2d_n=h_n(1+r_n)\bigl(f(t_{n+1},Y_{n+1})-f(t_{n+1},y(t_{n+1}))\bigr)-\tau_n$.

Divide by $1+2r_n$ and use [F3], [A1], $\|e_{n+1}\|_\infty\le \|e_n\|_\infty+\|d_{n+1}\|_\infty$, $(1+r_n)/(1+2r_n)\le1$, and $1+2r_n\ge1$. This gives $\|d_{n+1}\|_\infty\le q_*\|d_n\|_\infty+Lh_n(\|e_n\|_\infty+\|d_{n+1}\|_\infty)+Ch_n^3$. Move the last increment term left; since $Lh_n\le1/2$, $(1-Lh_n)^{-1}\le1+2Lh_n$ and $(1-Lh_n)^{-1}\le2$. Using $\|\tau_n\|_\infty\le Ch_n^3$ from [F2] yields $\|d_{n+1}\|_\infty\le(q_*+2Lq_*h_n)\|d_n\|_\infty+2Lh_n\|e_n\|_\infty+2C h_n^3$.

Choose $A>\max\{1,q_*/(1-q_*)\}$, so $(1+A)q_*<A$, and set $E_n=\|e_n\|_\infty+A\|d_n\|_\infty$. For sufficiently small $H$, $(1+A)(q_*+2Lq_*H)\le A$. Using $e_{n+1}=e_n+d_{n+1}$ in step 2.1 gives a coefficient at most $1+2L(1+A)h_n$ on $\|e_n\|_\infty$ and at most $A$ on $\|d_n\|_\infty$; hence $E_{n+1}\le(1+C_1h_n)E_n+C_2h_n^3$ for constants independent of the grid.

The starter hypothesis gives $E_1=O(H^2)$. Iterate step 3.1 only while the preceding pair is in the local neighborhood of [A2]. The coefficients $C_1=2L(1+A)$ and $C_2$ in step 3.1 can be taken nonnegative. For every subproduct, [F4] gives $\prod_{j=r}^{s}(1+C_1h_j)\le\prod_{j=r}^{s}\exp(C_1h_j)=\exp(C_1\sum_{j=r}^{s}h_j)\le e^{C_1T}$: the unused time $T-\sum_{j=r}^{s}h_j$ is nonnegative, and [F4] gives $\exp(C_1(T-\sum_{j=r}^{s}h_j))\ge1$, which with the addition law proves the last comparison. Expanding the finite recurrence by induction therefore gives $E_n\le e^{C_1T}(E_1+C_2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}h_j^3)$; here $\sum_jh_j^3\le H^2\sum_jh_j\le TH^2$. These bounds give $\max_nE_n\le C H^2$ up to any first exit, with $C$ independent of the grid. Since $A\ge1$, $\|e_n\|_\infty\le E_n$ and $\|e_{n-1}\|_\infty\le\|e_n\|_\infty+\|d_n\|_\infty\le(1+1/A)E_n$. For sufficiently small $H$, this bound is strictly below $\eta$, so no first exit occurs. At each step [A2] therefore supplies the selected root in $K$, and induction continues through $N$. Finally $\|e_n\|_\infty\le E_n$ proves the claimed maximum error.

Input an integer $k\ge1$, a finite grid $t_0,\ldots,t_N$ with $N\ge k$, starting states $Y_0,\ldots,Y_{k-1}\in\mathbb R^d$, and a vector field $f:U\to\mathbb R^d$ on its evaluation domain $U$. Before evaluating $f$, if any starting state has dimension different from $d$, return `invalid-input`; otherwise, if the grid is not strictly increasing, return `invalid-grid`. Evaluate and store $F_j=f(t_j,Y_j)$ for $j=0,\ldots,k-1$; an undefined evaluation outside $U$ returns `evaluation-failure` with the valid prefix.

For $n=k-1,\ldots,N-1$, construct the predictor weights $b_j^n$ and corrector weights $\widehat b_j^n$ from the actual nodes as in [[lem-variable-step-adams-lagrange-weights]], then do the following:

1. Predict $Y_{n+1}^P=Y_n+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}b_j^nF_{n-j}$.
2. Evaluate $F_{n+1}^P=f(t_{n+1},Y_{n+1}^P)$. If undefined, return `evaluation-failure` with phase `predictor`.
3. Correct once by setting $Y_{n+1}=Y_n+\widehat b_0^nF_{n+1}^P+\sum_{j=1}^{k}\widehat b_j^nF_{n+1-j}$.
4. Evaluate and store $F_{n+1}=f(t_{n+1},Y_{n+1})$ for the next predictor. If undefined, return `evaluation-failure` with phase `post-corrector` and the computed $Y_{n+1}$.

After all steps return `completed` with the states. This is one predictor and one corrector pass; it does not solve the fully implicit Adams corrector equation and asserts no convergence, stability, or error bound.

Let $k\ge1$ and let $t_{n+1}>t_n>\cdots>t_{n-k+1}$ be distinct time nodes. For $j=0,\ldots,k-1$, let

$$L_j^{P}(s)=\prod_{\substack{0\le\ell<k\\\ell\ne j}}\frac{s-t_{n-\ell}}{t_{n-j}-t_{n-\ell}},\qquad b_j^n=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}L_j^P(s)\,ds.$$

These coefficients give the explicit Adams predictor

$$Y_{n+1}^P=Y_n+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}b_j^nf(t_{n-j},Y_{n-j})$$

obtained by integrating the degree-$(k-1)$ interpolant through the known derivative values $f(t_{n-j},Y_{n-j})$.

For the corrector, let $\widehat L_j(s)$, $j=0,\ldots,k$, be the Lagrange basis on the $k+1$ distinct nodes $t_{n+1},t_n,\ldots,t_{n+1-k}$ and define $\widehat b_j^n=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}\widehat L_j(s)\,ds$. These are the coefficients of the integrated degree-$k$ interpolant, with $j=0$ the endpoint derivative at $t_{n+1}$. The fully implicit corrector is

$$Y_{n+1}=Y_n+\sum_{j=0}^{k}\widehat b_j^nf(t_{n+1-j},Y_{n+1-j}),$$

where the $j=0$ term uses the unknown new endpoint value.

derivations.claim: Set $z=h\lambda$ and $Y_n=1$. By [F1] and [L1], the Euler predictor is $P=1+z$. The PECE correction is $Y_{n+1}=1+\frac z2(1+P)=1+z+z^2/2$; the final evaluation in PECE stores $\lambda Y_{n+1}$ and does not alter this value.
The fully implicit trapezoidal corrector instead solves $Y_{n+1}=1+\frac z2(1+Y_{n+1})$, so $(1-z/2)Y_{n+1}=1+z/2$ and its multiplier is $(1+z/2)/(1-z/2)$ when $z\ne2$.

At $z=-3$, the multipliers are $5/2$ and $-1/5$, respectively. Define scalar test stability at $z$ by the condition that the multiplier's modulus is at most one. Hence PECE is unstable there and the fully implicit Adams method is stable there, so their stability differs.

Let $L_x,L_y>0$, let $N_x,N_y$ be integers at least $2$, and set $h_x=L_x/N_x$ and $h_y=L_y/N_y$. The rectangular grid nodes are $(x_i,y_j)=(ih_x,jh_y)$ for $0\le i\le N_x$ and $0\le j\le N_y$. The interior index set is $I_h=\{(i,j):1\le i<N_x,\ 1\le j<N_y\}$, and its boundary is the set of grid nodes with $i\in\{0,N_x\}$ or $j\in\{0,N_y\}$. A grid function is a real-valued function on all grid nodes; $X_{h,0}$ is the vector space of grid functions that vanish on the boundary.

For grid functions $v,w$, define the weighted interior inner product and norm by
$$
\langle v,w\rangle_h=h_xh_y\sum_{i=1}^{N_x-1}\sum_{j=1}^{N_y-1}v_{ij}w_{ij},\qquad \|v\|_h=\langle v,v\rangle_h^{1/2}.
$$
The edge differences are $D_xv_{i+1/2,j}=(v_{i+1,j}-v_{ij})/h_x$ for $0\le i<N_x$, $1\le j<N_y$, and $D_yv_{i,j+1/2}=(v_{i,j+1}-v_{ij})/h_y$ for $1\le i<N_x$, $0\le j<N_y$. For a scalar coefficient $a$ sampled at face midpoints, write $a_{i+1/2,j}=a(x_i+h_x/2,y_j)$ and $a_{i,j+1/2}=a(x_i,y_j+h_y/2)$.

The positive divergence-form Dirichlet operator on interior nodes is
$$
(A_h^av)_{ij}=-\frac{a_{i+1/2,j}D_xv_{i+1/2,j}-a_{i-1/2,j}D_xv_{i-1/2,j}}{h_x}-\frac{a_{i,j+1/2}D_yv_{i,j+1/2}-a_{i,j-1/2}D_yv_{i,j-1/2}}{h_y}.
$$
For $a\equiv1$, this is the five-point Dirichlet Laplacian $-D_x^+D_x^- -D_y^+D_y^-$. The associated edge energy is
$$
E_h^a(v,w)=h_xh_y\left(\sum_{j=1}^{N_y-1}\sum_{i=0}^{N_x-1}a_{i+1/2,j}D_xv_{i+1/2,j}D_xw_{i+1/2,j}+\sum_{i=1}^{N_x-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N_y-1}a_{i,j+1/2}D_yv_{i,j+1/2}D_yw_{i,j+1/2}\right).
$$
The homogeneous scheme solves $A_h^av=f_h$ in $I_h$ with $v=0$ on the boundary. For Dirichlet data $g$, it solves the same interior equations with $v=g$ at boundary nodes. This definition specifies the rectangular Dirichlet stencil; it does not specify a Neumann or nonrectangular boundary closure.

On the grid of [[def-rectangular-grid-and-dirichlet-flux-stencil]], put $q^x_{i+1/2,j}=a_{i+1/2,j}D_xv_{i+1/2,j}$ and $q^y_{i,j+1/2}=a_{i,j+1/2}D_yv_{i,j+1/2}$. For any grid functions $v,w$,
$$
\langle A_h^av,w\rangle_h=E_h^a(v,w)-h_y\sum_{j=1}^{N_y-1}\left(q^x_{N_x-1/2,j}w_{N_x,j}-q^x_{1/2,j}w_{0,j}\right)-h_x\sum_{i=1}^{N_x-1}\left(q^y_{i,N_y-1/2}w_{i,N_y}-q^y_{i,1/2}w_{i,0}\right).

$$

If all horizontal and vertical face values satisfy $a_{i+1/2,j},a_{i,j+1/2}\ge a_0>0$, then the homogeneous Dirichlet matrix $A_h^a$ is invertible and
$$
\|(A_h^a)^{-1}\|_{\ell_h^2\to\ell_h^2}\le \frac{L_x^2}{a_0},

Fix a dimension $d\ge1$, side lengths $L_j>0$, integers $N_j\ge2$, directional diffusivities $\kappa_j>0$, and spacings $h_j=L_j/N_j$. For a finite periodic rectangular grid let
$$

$$
and define the positive centered heat operator, with indices reduced modulo $N_j$, by
$$(A_h^{\rm per}v)_i=\sum_{j=1}^d\kappa_j\frac{2v_i-v_{i+e_j}-v_{i-e_j}}{h_j^2}.$$

For a two-dimensional Dirichlet rectangle, use the nodes and weighted interior inner product of [[def-rectangular-grid-and-dirichlet-flux-stencil]]. At an interior node $(i,j)$ define
$$(A_h^{B}V)_{ij}=\kappa_x\frac{2V_{ij}-V_{i+1,j}-V_{i-1,j}}{h_x^2}+\kappa_y\frac{2V_{ij}-V_{i,j+1}-V_{i,j-1}}{h_y^2},$$
where values on boundary neighbours are the prescribed Dirichlet row $B$. Write $A_h^0$ for the square matrix on interior values when the boundary is zero. For any boundary vector $B$, let $c_h(B)$ be the result of applying this stencil to the grid vector that equals $B$ on the boundary and $0$ at interior nodes. Then $A_h^B V=A_h^0V+c_h(B)$ on interior nodes.

Let $T>0$, an integer $M\ge1$, $\Delta t=T/M$, $t_n=n\Delta t$, and $\theta\in[0,1]$. Given interior initial data $U^0$, interior source samples $F^n$, and, in the Dirichlet case, boundary rows $B^n$ for $0\le n\le M$ whose time-zero row agrees with the initial grid data, the periodic update is
$$
\frac{U^{n+1}-U^n}{\Delta t}+A_h^{\rm per}\bigl((1-\theta)U^n+\theta U^{n+1}\bigr)=(1-\theta)F^n+\theta F^{n+1},\quad 0\le n<M.
$$
The Dirichlet update, with the boundary values imposed at every time level, is
$$
\frac{U^{n+1}-U^n}{\Delta t}+A_h^0\bigl((1-\theta)U^n+\theta U^{n+1}\bigr)=(1-\theta)\bigl(F^n-c_h(B^n)\bigr)+\theta\bigl(F^{n+1}-c_h(B^{n+1})\bigr),\quad 0\le n<M.

For a homogeneous-source update with periodic rows or zero Dirichlet boundary values, let $Q_h$ be its one-step linear map when that step is well defined, and give it the operator norm induced by $\|\cdot\|_h$. The family is **grid-norm power stable on $[0,T]$** if there is $C_T<\infty$, independent of the grid and time step, such that $\|Q_h^n\|_{h\to h}\le C_T$ whenever $n\Delta t\le T$. $$

citations.quote: Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)$ linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), and let $a:H\times H\to\mathbb K$ be sesquilinear in the sense of [[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]]: linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second. The form $a$ is **bounded** with bound $M\ge0$ when $$|a(u,v)|\le M\|u\|\,\|v\|\qquad\text{for all }u,v\in H,$$ and **coercive** with constant $\alpha>0$ when $$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2\qquad\text{for all }u\in H .$$ It is **symmetric** (Hermitian) when $a(u,v)=\overline{a(v,u)}$ for all $u,v$, over $\mathbb C$ this is equivalent to $a(u,u)\in\mathbb R$ for every $u$. Indeed, writing $q(u)=a(u,u)$, sesquilinearity gives $4a(u,v)=q(u+v)-q(u-v)+i q(u+iv)-i q(u-iv)$, and real diagonal values make this identity conjugate-symmetric. Over $\mathbb R$, symmetry means $a(u,v)=a(v,u)$; real diagonal values alone do not imply symmetry. The **adjoint form** is $a^*(u,v):=\overline{a(v,u)}$, and $(a^*)^*=a$. **Real bilinear convention.** When $H$ is a real Hilbert space the same definitions apply with $a$ bilinear and coercive in the form $a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2$; the conjugation in the second slot is then the identity. More generally, a real bilinear form may satisfy the boundedness and coercivity conditions without being symmetric; symmetry is an additional property, not part of either condition. When $H=\{0\}$ every form is bounded with bound $0$ and coercive with every $\alpha>0$; this degenerate case is kept but is never load-bearing. All constants below are named and never silently improved. No choice principle is used in this definition.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Define the adjoint form by $a^\dagger(z,v):=\overline{a(v,z)}$. The sesquilinearity of $a$ shows that $a^\dagger$ is linear in $z$ and conjugate-linear in $v$. Also $|a^\dagger(z,v)|=|a(v,z)|\le M\|z\|_V\|v\|_V$, and $\operatorname{Re}a^\dagger(z,z)=\operatorname{Re}a(z,z)\ge\alpha\|z\|_V^2$.
Set $G^\dagger(v):=\overline{G(v)}$. Since $G$ is linear, $G^\dagger$ is conjugate-linear, and $|G^\dagger(v)|=|G(v)|\le\|G\|_{V^*}\|v\|_V$; hence $\|G^\dagger\|_{V^*}=\|G\|_{V^*}$.

Apply [F2] to $a^\dagger$ and $G^\dagger$. It gives a unique $z\in V$ with $a^\dagger(z,v)=G^\dagger(v)$ and $\alpha\|z\|_V\le\|G^\dagger\|_{V^*}$. Conjugating the equation gives $a(v,z)=G(v)$ for every $v$, and the norm equality in step 1.2 gives the claimed estimate and uniqueness.
