Let $k,m,n\ge1$ and $p\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n+p}$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^k$. Suppose $F(a,b,\lambda_0)=0$ and $D_yF(a,b,\lambda_0)$ is invertible. Then there are neighbourhoods and a unique $C^k$ map $\varphi$ solving $F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)=0$. More precisely, on suitable open neighbourhoods $P$ of $(a,\lambda_0)$ and $Q$ of $b$,

$$F(x,y,\lambda)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x,\lambda),$$

and

$$D\varphi(x,\lambda)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)^{-1}D_{(x,\lambda)}F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda).$$

When no parameter block is present, this is the ordinary $C^k$ implicit function theorem.

Let $k\ge1$ and let $A(\lambda)\in\mathbb C^{d\times d}$ be a $C^k$ matrix path. Let $\zeta_0$ be a simple eigenvalue of $A(0)$, and choose compatible left and right eigenvectors $p_0,q_0$ with $p_0^*q_0=1$. Then there are unique local $C^k$ functions $\zeta(\lambda),q(\lambda)$ such that
$$A(\lambda)q(\lambda)=\zeta(\lambda)q(\lambda),\qquad p_0^*q(\lambda)=1,\qquad \zeta(0)=\zeta_0,\quad q(0)=q_0.$$
There is also a unique local $C^k$ left eigenvector $p(\lambda)$ with
$$A(\lambda)^*p(\lambda)=\overline{\zeta(\lambda)}p(\lambda),\qquad p(\lambda)^*q(\lambda)=1,\qquad p(0)=p_0.$$
Moreover, $\zeta'(0)=p_0^*A'(0)q_0$.

Let $f(x,\lambda)$ be $C^5$ near $(0,0)$ in $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R$, and suppose $f(0,\lambda)=0$ for all sufficiently small $\lambda$. Assume $A=D_xf(0,0)$ has a simple pair $\pm i\omega$, $\omega>0$, and every other eigenvalue has nonzero real part. Choose $q\ne0$ with $Aq=i\omega q$ and set $E_c=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{\operatorname{Re}q,\operatorname{Im}q\}$. Let $E_s$ and $E_u$ be the real sums of generalized eigenspaces with eigenvalues of negative and positive real part, respectively, and set $E_h=E_s\oplus E_u$. For the extended system $\dot\lambda=0$, there are neighborhoods $U\subset E_c$ and $J\subset\mathbb R$ of zero and a $C^5$ map $h:U\times J\to E_h$ whose graph $x=z+h(z,\lambda)$ is tangent to $E_c\times\mathbb R$ at the origin and contains every sufficiently small periodic trajectory that remains in the chosen neighborhood.

Write $A_\lambda=D_xf(0,\lambda)$. Since $f$ is $C^5$, this matrix path is $C^4$; let $\zeta(\lambda)$ be its $C^4$ simple eigenvalue branch from [[lem-hopf-smooth-eigenpair-branch]]. For each small $\lambda$, the graph tangent plane $\operatorname{range}D_z(z+h)(0,\lambda)$ is the invariant plane spanned by the right eigenvectors for $\zeta(\lambda)$ and $\overline{\zeta(\lambda)}$.

Write $P_c,P_h$ for the spectral projections of $A$ and define

$$f_c(z,h,\lambda):=P_cf(z+h,\lambda),\qquad f_h(z,h,\lambda):=P_hf(z+h,\lambda).$$

The graph satisfies the actual invariance equation

$$D_zh(z,\lambda)f_c(z,h(z,\lambda),\lambda)=f_h(z,h(z,\lambda),\lambda),\qquad h(0,\lambda)=0,\quad D_zh(0,0)=0.$$

On a smaller neighborhood it also satisfies $h(z,\lambda)=O(\|z\|^2+|\lambda|\|z\|)$. No Axiom of Choice is used.

Assume $f$ is $C^5$ near $(0,0)$ and its Hopf data satisfy [[def-hopf-normal-form-data]]. Since $A=D_xf(0,0)$ has no zero eigenvalue, let $\xi(\lambda)$ be the unique local $C^5$ equilibrium branch with $\xi(0)=0$ supplied by the parameterized implicit-function theorem, and set $A_\lambda:=D_xf(\xi(\lambda),\lambda)$. This matrix path is $C^4$. Let $\zeta(\lambda)=\beta(\lambda)+i\omega(\lambda)$ be its $C^4$ simple critical eigenvalue branch, with $\beta(0)=0$, $\omega(0)=\omega_0$, and $\beta'(0)\ne0$. After translating by $\xi(\lambda)$, restricting to the parameterized center manifold of [[lem-local-center-manifold-for-a-simple-hopf-point]], and making a near-identity complex coordinate change, the reduced equation has the form

$$\dot z=(\beta+i\omega(\beta))z+\frac12G_{21}z|z|^2+R(z,\bar z,\beta),\qquad R=O(|z|^4+|\beta||z|^3).$$

Thus its radial cubic coefficient at $\beta=0$ is $\operatorname{Re}(G_{21})/2=\omega_0\ell_1$, where $\ell_1$ is the first Lyapunov coefficient defined in [[def-hopf-normal-form-data]]. The remainder and its first derivative satisfy the corresponding bounds $D_zR=O(|z|^3+|\beta||z|^2)$.

Let $A_n,A\in\mathbb C^{d\times d}$ with $A_n\to A$ entrywise. Let $U_1,\ldots,U_s$ be pairwise disjoint open disks whose boundaries contain no eigenvalue of $A$ and which together contain every eigenvalue of $A$. Then, for all sufficiently large $n$, each $U_j$ contains exactly the same number of eigenvalues of $A_n$, counted with algebraic multiplicity, as of $A$.

Let U⊂R^n be open and Y:U→R^n be C¹. There is a unique maximal flow Φ on an open domain
D⊂R×U containing {0}×U, and Φ is jointly C¹. Its time slices are local C¹
diffeomorphisms with inverse Φ_{−t}; $\partial_t\Phi=Y(\Phi)$ and $D_p\Phi$ is the
unique solution V of $V′=DY(\Phi)V$, V(0)=I. Each regular point has a C¹ flow box. If Y
is C², Φ and those flow boxes are C²; the second state variation W satisfies
$W′=DY(\Phi)W+D²Y(\Phi)[Ve_i,Ve_j]$, W(0)=0. Individual trajectories of a C¹ field are
C² in time. A trajectory remaining in a compact K⊂⊂U cannot have a finite maximal
endpoint. These Euclidean conclusions use no full AC or DC.

For an autonomous vector field $\dot x=f(x)$, a nonconstant solution $x_*(t)$ with least positive period $T$ has periodic orbit $\Gamma=\{x_*(t):0\le t<T\}$. Its variational fundamental matrix $Y(t)$ solves

$$\dot Y(t)=D f(x_*(t))Y(t),\qquad Y(0)=I.$$

The matrix $Y(T)$ is the **monodromy matrix**; its eigenvalues, counted with algebraic multiplicity, are the **Floquet multipliers**. The multiplier $1$ in the direction $\dot x_*(0)$ is called the **phase multiplier**.

A **local Poincare section** at $x_*(0)$ is a smooth codimension-one surface through that point whose tangent space does not contain $f(x_*(0))$. The local return map sends a nearby point on the section to its next intersection after one turn around $\Gamma$. Its derivative at $x_*(0)$ is the Poincare derivative.

The orbit is **orbitally asymptotically stable** if it is Lyapunov stable as a set and the distance from every sufficiently nearby trajectory to $\Gamma$ tends to zero as time tends to $+\infty$. It is **orbitally unstable** if it is not Lyapunov stable as a set.

Let $f$ be a $C^1$ autonomous vector field on an open subset of $\mathbb R^d$. Let $x_*(t)$ be a nonconstant periodic solution of least period $T$, let $\Gamma=\{x_*(t):0\le t<T\}$, and let $\Sigma$ be a local smooth Poincare section through $a=x_*(0)$ transverse to $f(a)$. Assume locally $\Sigma=\{y:\rho(y)=0\}$ for a smooth $\rho$ with $D\rho(a)f(a)\ne0$, and take a relatively compact section patch $W$ with $\overline W\cap\Gamma=\{a\}$. If the derivative of the local return map $P$ at $a$ has no eigenvalue on the unit circle, then $\Gamma$ is orbitally asymptotically stable when all eigenvalues of $DP(a)$ have modulus less than one, and is orbitally unstable when at least one has modulus greater than one.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

derivations.claim: Because $\pm i\omega_0$ and every other eigenvalue of $A_0$ are nonzero, $A_0$ is invertible. First set $y=x-x_0$ and $\widehat f(y,\lambda)=f(x_0+y,\lambda)$, so $\widehat f(0,0)=0$. The data in [[def-hopf-normal-form-data]] are those of this field: $A=A_0$, $B=D_x^2f(x_0,0)$, $C=D_x^3f(x_0,0)$, and $p,q$ are eigenvectors of this same $A_0$ with both declared normalizations. Apply [F1] to obtain the unique nearby equilibrium $\xi(\lambda)$ of the original field. In the parameter-dependent translated state $v=x-\xi(\lambda)$, the field is $f(v+\xi(\lambda),\lambda)$ and vanishes at $v=0$ for each fixed parameter; its critical spatial jets agree with the preceding data, since $\xi(0)=x_0$ and $\dot\lambda=0$. Apply [F2] to obtain $\zeta(\lambda)$ with $\beta'(0)\ne0$, and apply [F1] to $\operatorname{Re}\zeta(\lambda)-\widehat\beta=0$ in solved variable $\lambda$. This makes $\widehat\beta$ a valid local parameter, which we relabel $\beta$.

By [F3], every sufficiently small periodic orbit is on the parameterized center graph. Restricting to a fixed parameter and using [F4], its reduced dynamics have $\dot r=r(\beta+\omega_0\ell_1r^2)+O(r^4+|\beta|r^3)$ and $\dot\theta=\omega_0+O(|\beta|+r^2)$, with the first-derivative bounds supplied by [F4]. In particular $\dot\theta>0$ after shrinking the neighborhood.

Reparameterize by the strictly increasing angle from step 1.2 and write $dr/d\theta=\rho(r,\theta,\beta):=\dot r/\dot\theta$. The bounds in [F4] give uniformly in $\theta$ that $\rho=(r/\omega_0)(\beta+\omega_0\ell_1r^2)+O(\beta^2r+|\beta|r^3+r^4)$ and $\partial_r\rho=(\beta+3\omega_0\ell_1r^2)/\omega_0+O(\beta^2+|\beta|r^2+r^3)$. On $r>0$ the radial field is jointly $C^1$ in $(\theta,r,\beta)$ by the finite-regularity coordinate construction in [F4]. Applying [F6] to $(\theta,r,\beta)'=(1,\rho(\theta,r,\beta),0)$ gives the required common local solution and first variations, with finite composition over $[0,2\pi]$. For small $r_0>0$ and $|\beta|$, while $r\in[r_0/2,2r_0]$ the bound $|\rho/r|\le C(|\beta|+4r_0^2)$ makes the change in $\log r$ over $[0,2\pi]$ smaller than $\log2$. Thus no first exit from that interval occurs; compact continuation in [F6] supplies the full angular interval and positivity, and $\partial_\theta\log r=\rho/r=O(|\beta|+r^2)$; integrating over the bounded interval $[0,2\pi]$ gives $r(\theta;r_0)=r_0+O(|\beta|r_0+r_0^3)$. Substituting this bound into $P_\beta(r_0)-r_0=\int_0^{2\pi}\rho(r(\theta;r_0),\theta,\beta)\,d\theta$ gives $P_\beta(r_0)-r_0=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}r_0(\beta+\omega_0\ell_1r_0^2)+O(\beta^2r_0+|\beta|r_0^3+r_0^4)$. The variational derivative $Q=\partial r/\partial r_0$ solves $\partial_\theta Q=(\partial_r\rho)Q$, $Q(0)=1$, so $Q(2\pi)=\exp(\int_0^{2\pi}\partial_r\rho\,d\theta)$. The same bound on $r(\theta;r_0)$ in the derivative expansion yields $P_\beta'(r_0)=1+\frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}(\beta+3\omega_0\ell_1r_0^2)+O(\beta^2+|\beta|r_0^2+r_0^3)$. The factor $r_0$ is the persistent equilibrium.

For $r>0$, divide step 2.1 by $(2\pi/\omega_0)r$ and call the result $H(r,\beta)$. Then $H(r,\beta)=\beta+\omega_0\ell_1r^2+O(\beta^2+|\beta|r^2+r^3)$. Differentiating this quotient using both expansions in step 2.1 gives $\partial_rH(r,\beta)=2\omega_0\ell_1r+O(\beta^2/r+|\beta|r+r^2)$. If $\beta\ell_1>0$, then $|\beta+\omega_0\ell_1r^2|=|\beta|+\omega_0|\ell_1|r^2$; the error is bounded by $C(\beta^2+|\beta|r^2+r^3)$, which is at most an arbitrarily small multiple of $|\beta|+r^2$ after shrinking $r,|\beta|$. Thus there is no positive root. If $\beta=0$, then $H(r,0)=\omega_0\ell_1r^2+O(r^3)$, whose leading term dominates for all sufficiently small $r>0$, so there is no nonconstant periodic orbit at the threshold either. If $\beta\ell_1<0$, choose $0<c_-<1/\sqrt{\omega_0|\ell_1|}<c_+$. At $r=c_-\sqrt{|\beta|}$ and $r=c_+\sqrt{|\beta|}$ the leading terms have opposite signs and the error is $O(|\beta|^{3/2})$, so [F9] gives a root between them. Every root lies between fixed such multiples of $\sqrt{|\beta|}$: below a sufficiently small multiple, $|\beta|$ dominates the error; above a sufficiently large multiple, $\omega_0|\ell_1|r^2$ dominates both $|\beta|$ and the error. On this annulus, $\beta^2/r+|\beta|r+r^2=o(r)$ uniformly as $\beta\to0$, so $\partial_rH$ has the sign of $\ell_1$ and the root is unique. Since this derivative is nonzero, [F1] with $k=1$ makes the radius a $C^1$ function of $\beta$ on the punctured existence side, using the joint $C^1$ return map from [F6].

Every sufficiently small periodic trajectory lies on the center graph by [F3], and [F4] gives $\dot\theta>0$, so it meets the ray $\theta=0$ and returns after some positive integer number of turns. Reparameterize the radial equation by $\theta$; $dr/d\theta=\dot r/\dot\theta$ is a $C^1$ scalar nonautonomous ODE on $r>0$, so two solutions cannot cross by uniqueness from the augmented $C^1$ flow [F6]. Therefore the one-turn radius map is strictly increasing. If a periodic trajectory met the section in a $k$-cycle with $P_\beta^k(r)=r$, strict increase forces $P_\beta(r)=r$; indeed $P_\beta(r)>r$ would imply $P_\beta^k(r)>r$, and $P_\beta(r)<r$ would imply $P_\beta^k(r)<r$. Thus the unique positive fixed point from step 3.1 describes the unique local periodic orbit up to phase, and none exists on the opposite side.

At the root, step 3.1 gives $r^2=-\beta/(\omega_0\ell_1)+O(|\beta|^{3/2})$. The angular speed in step 1.2 is $\omega_0+O(|\beta|+r^2)$, so the return period is $2\pi/\omega_0+O(|\beta|)$. Differentiating the return map at this fixed radius yields $P_\beta'(r)=1+\frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}(\beta+3\omega_0\ell_1r^2)+O(|\beta|^{3/2})=1-\frac{4\pi}{\omega_0}\beta+O(|\beta|^{3/2})$. Thus this nontrivial radial multiplier is inside the unit circle for $\beta>0$ and outside it for $\beta<0$, when $\beta$ is sufficiently small.

The full monodromy matrix along the periodic orbit converges to $e^{(2\pi/\omega_0)A_0}$. Indeed its variational coefficient $D_xf(x(t),\lambda)$ converges uniformly to $A_0$; subtracting the two fundamental-matrix integral equations and iterating the resulting bound gives uniform convergence on the bounded period interval. The limiting matrix has the critical multiplier $1$ of algebraic multiplicity two, and all remaining multipliers $e^{2\pi\nu_j/\omega_0}$ have modulus different from one. By [F5], exactly two multipliers remain near $1$ and the others converge with multiplicity to the hyperbolic multipliers. One of the two is exactly $1$ because $\dot x_*(t)$ solves the variational equation and is periodic; the other is the radial multiplier of step 4.2. For a section $\Sigma$ transverse to $v=\dot x_*(0)$, differentiating $P(y)=\phi_{\tau(y)}(y)$ gives $DP=\pi M|_{T\Sigma}$, where $M$ is the monodromy matrix and $\pi$ is projection along $v$ onto $T\Sigma$. Thus $DP$ represents the induced map on the quotient by $\operatorname{span}\{v\}$, so its eigenvalues are exactly the non-phase Floquet multipliers.

An admissible input is a finite proof-carrying record for one equilibrium of a $C^5$ vector field $f(x,\lambda)$. The record names its critical parameter $\lambda_0$ and exact represented equilibrium $x_*$ (or its isolating data). All origin-based Hopf data mean those of $\widehat f(y,\mu)=f(x_*+y,\lambda_0+\mu)$ at $(0,0)$, using [[def-hopf-normal-form-data]]; for an isolated root this is the exact root established by its witness, not the center of its isolating ball. It contains:

- an exact equilibrium, or a root-isolation record satisfying all hypotheses and inequalities of [[thm-augmented-residual-contraction-certificate]];
- a Jacobian $A=D_xf$ and its derivative along the locally isolated equilibrium branch, with proof-carrying rational rectangle enclosures for the critical eigenvalue and left and right eigenvectors; exact witnesses verify $Aq=i\omega q$, $A^*p=-i\omega p$, $q^*q=p^*q=1$, and a root-count certificate proves that each critical eigenvalue has algebraic multiplicity one;
- rational rectangle enclosures with checked inclusion witnesses for every noncritical eigenvalue, the parameter derivative of $A$, the multilinear data $B,C$ in [[def-hopf-normal-form-data]], and the entries of $A^{-1}$ and $(2i\omega I-A)^{-1}$; inverse witnesses verify the corresponding matrix products are the identity;
- a multiplicity-cover record giving certified root counts in pairwise disjoint rectangles, with total multiplicity $d$ and the two critical roots counted once each, so the noncritical rectangles account for every remaining root of the characteristic polynomial.

A rational interval is a closed interval $[a,b]$ with exact rational endpoints $a\le b$; a rational rectangle is a product of two such intervals, interpreted as a subset of $\mathbb C$. Every witness is a finite, exactly checkable proof tied to the same vector field, parameter, certified equilibrium or equilibrium branch, and named derivative or spectral value. It must establish the stated inclusion, identity, or root count by exact identities and outward rational interval calculations; rounded floating-point output is not a witness. The multiplicity-cover record proves that its rectangle counts sum to $d$ and that the rectangles cover the roots of the characteristic polynomial with their stated algebraic multiplicities. Missing, unsupported, or unproved witnesses make the result inconclusive; malformed intervals or contradictory fields make the input invalid.

The procedure outputs one of: **certified-local-hopf** with the branch side; **inconclusive** with the first failed strict hypothesis or missing witness; or **invalid-input** for malformed rational intervals or inconsistent record fields.

Procedure:

1. Check that every interval has exact rational endpoints in increasing order and that every rectangle is a product of two such intervals. If not, return **invalid-input**.
2. Check that the equilibrium witness is for the stated vector field and parameter. An exact point must satisfy $f(x,\lambda)=0$ exactly. Otherwise check the supplied root-isolation record against every hypothesis and inequality in [[thm-augmented-residual-contraction-certificate]]; if a witness is absent or an inequality is unproved, return **inconclusive**. Check that the Jacobian and all jet, parameter-derivative, and inverse witnesses are tied to this same certified root: they must prove $A=D_xf$, $B=D_x^2f$, $C=D_x^3f$, the stated derivative $A'=\frac{d}{d\lambda}D_xf(\xi(\lambda),\lambda)$ along the unique local equilibrium branch, and the claimed inverse matrix products. A contradictory field value returns **invalid-input**; missing or insufficient proof returns **inconclusive**.
3. Check the eigenpair equations, normalizations, simplicity root counts, positive lower bound for $\omega$, and multiplicity cover. The critical witnesses must prove exactly one simple root at each of $\pm i\omega$, and the noncritical real-part rectangles must each exclude zero. If any condition is unproved, return **inconclusive**.
4. Evaluate the outward rational interval expressions for $\beta'=\operatorname{Re}(p^*A'q)$ and $\ell_1$ using the enclosures in steps 2–3. The inclusion witnesses must prove each interval operation contains its exact value. If either interval intersects zero, return **inconclusive**.
5. If all checks pass, return **certified-local-hopf**. Here $\beta'(0)$ means the derivative in $\mu=\lambda-\lambda_0$ of the critical eigenvalue's real part along the translated equilibrium branch. The branch side in the original parameter is the sign condition $\beta'(0)\ell_1(\lambda-\lambda_0)<0$, with the signs determined by the two strict intervals.

For a linear map $A$ between Euclidean spaces, write
$\|A\|_{\rm op}:=\sup_{\|u\|_2=1}\|Au\|_2$. Let $m\ge1$, let
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let
$G:V\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$. Let $y\in V$, $R>0$, and suppose the closed
ball $\overline B_2(y,R)$ lies in $V$. Assume that for some $L\ge0$,
$$\|DG(u)-DG(v)\|_{\rm op}\le L\|u-v\|_2\qquad(u,v\in\overline B_2(y,R)).$$
Let $\widehat g\in\mathbb R^m$ and $\widehat A\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$
come with certified bounds
$$\|\widehat g-G(y)\|_2\le\epsilon_g,\qquad \|\widehat A-DG(y)\|_{\rm op}\le\epsilon_J,$$
where $\epsilon_g,\epsilon_J\ge0$. Suppose $\widehat A$ is invertible and
$\|\widehat A^{-1}\|_{\rm op}\le\widehat\beta$, with
$\widehat\beta\epsilon_J<1$. Define
$$\beta:=\frac{\widehat\beta}{1-\widehat\beta\epsilon_J},\qquad \rho:=\|\widehat g\|_2+\epsilon_g,\qquad q:=\beta L R.$$
If $q<1$ and $\beta\rho\le(1-q)R$, then $G$ has exactly one zero $y^*$
in $\overline B_2(y,R)$ and
$$\|y^*-y\|_2\le\frac{\beta\rho}{1-q}.$$

Let $f(x,\lambda)$ be a real $C^3$ vector field on an open subset of $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R$, and suppose $f(0,0)=0$. Put $A=D_xf(0,0)$. Assume $A$ has a simple pair of eigenvalues $i\omega$ and $-i\omega$, where $\omega>0$, and no other eigenvalue on the imaginary axis. Let $A_{\mathbb C}$ be the complexification of $A$. Choose $q,p\in\mathbb C^d$ with

$$Aq=i\omega q,\qquad A^*p=-i\omega p,\qquad q^*q=1,\qquad p^*q=1.$$

Here $u^*v=\bar u^{\,T}v$ is the standard Hermitian product. To obtain both normalizations, start with nonzero compatible eigenvectors $q_0,p_0$ and put $q=q_0/\sqrt{q_0^*q_0}$. Simplicity gives $a:=p_0^*q\ne0$ by [[prop-simple-eigenvalues-admit-left-right-normalization]]. Set $p=p_0/\overline a$; then $q^*q=1$ and $p^*q=a/a=1$, while both eigenvector equations are preserved. Write $B=D_x^2f(0,0)$ and $C=D_x^3f(0,0)$ for the symmetric real multilinear derivatives, extended complex multilinearly. Since zero and $2i\omega$ are not eigenvalues of $A$, define

$$G_{21}:=p^*\!\left(C(q,q,\bar q)-2B\!\left(q,A^{-1}B(q,\bar q)\right)+B\!\left(\bar q,(2i\omega I-A)^{-1}B(q,q)\right)\right)$$

and define the first Lyapunov coefficient in this normalization by

$$\ell_1:=\frac{\operatorname{Re}G_{21}}{2\omega}.$$

If $q$ is rescaled to $cq$ and the unit-norm condition is dropped while $p^*q=1$ is preserved, then $\ell_1$ rescales by $|c|^2$; under the declared condition $q^*q=1$, the remaining phase freedom leaves $\ell_1$ unchanged. Its sign is the local cubic radial sign. The definition alone is not a bifurcation theorem.

For an equilibrium at arbitrary $(x_*,\lambda_0)$, apply this definition to the translated field $\widehat f(y,\mu)=f(x_*+y,\lambda_0+\mu)$ at $(y,\mu)=(0,0)$. Thus $A=D_xf(x_*,\lambda_0)$, $B=D_x^2f(x_*,\lambda_0)$ and $C=D_x^3f(x_*,\lambda_0)$, and $p,q,\omega$ refer to that same $A$. Translation preserves these spatial derivatives and their Euclidean normalization. If the equilibrium is continued as $\xi(\lambda)$, the further state change $y=x-\xi(\lambda)$ at each fixed parameter gives $\dot y=f(y+\xi(\lambda),\lambda)$; because $\dot\lambda=0$, no extra time-derivative term appears. An admissible input is a finite proof-carrying record for one equilibrium of a $C^5$ vector field $f(x,\lambda)$. The record names its critical parameter $\lambda_0$ and exact represented equilibrium $x_*$ (or its isolating data). All origin-based Hopf data mean those of $\widehat f(y,\mu)=f(x_*+y,\lambda_0+\mu)$ at $(0,0)$, using [[def-hopf-normal-form-data]]; for an isolated root this is the exact root established by its witness, not the center of its isolating ball. It contains:

- an exact equilibrium, or a root-isolation record satisfying all hypotheses and inequalities of [[thm-augmented-residual-contraction-certificate]];
- a Jacobian $A=D_xf$ and its derivative along the locally isolated equilibrium branch, with proof-carrying rational rectangle enclosures for the critical eigenvalue and left and right eigenvectors; exact witnesses verify $Aq=i\omega q$, $A^*p=-i\omega p$, $q^*q=p^*q=1$, and a root-count certificate proves that each critical eigenvalue has algebraic multiplicity one;
- rational rectangle enclosures with checked inclusion witnesses for every noncritical eigenvalue, the parameter derivative of $A$, the multilinear data $B,C$ in [[def-hopf-normal-form-data]], and the entries of $A^{-1}$ and $(2i\omega I-A)^{-1}$; inverse witnesses verify the corresponding matrix products are the identity;
- a multiplicity-cover record giving certified root counts in pairwise disjoint rectangles, with total multiplicity $d$ and the two critical roots counted once each, so the noncritical rectangles account for every remaining root of the characteristic polynomial.

A rational interval is a closed interval $[a,b]$ with exact rational endpoints $a\le b$; a rational rectangle is a product of two such intervals, interpreted as a subset of $\mathbb C$. Every witness is a finite, exactly checkable proof tied to the same vector field, parameter, certified equilibrium or equilibrium branch, and named derivative or spectral value. It must establish the stated inclusion, identity, or root count by exact identities and outward rational interval calculations; rounded floating-point output is not a witness. The multiplicity-cover record proves that its rectangle counts sum to $d$ and that the rectangles cover the roots of the characteristic polynomial with their stated algebraic multiplicities. Missing, unsupported, or unproved witnesses make the result inconclusive; malformed intervals or contradictory fields make the input invalid.

The procedure outputs one of: **certified-local-hopf** with the branch side; **inconclusive** with the first failed strict hypothesis or missing witness; or **invalid-input** for malformed rational intervals or inconsistent record fields.

Procedure:

1. Check that every interval has exact rational endpoints in increasing order and that every rectangle is a product of two such intervals. If not, return **invalid-input**.
2. Check that the equilibrium witness is for the stated vector field and parameter. An exact point must satisfy $f(x,\lambda)=0$ exactly. Otherwise check the supplied root-isolation record against every hypothesis and inequality in [[thm-augmented-residual-contraction-certificate]]; if a witness is absent or an inequality is unproved, return **inconclusive**. The critical witnesses must prove exactly one simple root at each of $\pm i\omega$, and the noncritical real-part rectangles must each exclude zero. Let $F(x,\lambda)$ be a real $C^5$ scalar function near $(0,0)$, with equilibria defined by $F(x,\lambda)=0$.

1. A **fold** occurs if $F(0,0)=F_x(0,0)=0$ and $F_\lambda(0,0)F_{xx}(0,0)\ne0$. Its local equilibrium set is a unique curve $\lambda=\phi(x)$ with
$$\phi'(0)=0,\qquad \phi''(0)=-\frac{F_{xx}(0,0)}{F_\lambda(0,0)}\ne0.$$
For $\lambda$ sufficiently close to zero, there are exactly two nearby equilibria on the side where $\lambda\phi''(0)>0$, one at $\lambda=0$, and none on the opposite side.

2. A **transcritical bifurcation** occurs if $F(0,\lambda)=0$ for all small $\lambda$, $F_x(0,0)=0$, and $F_{x\lambda}(0,0)F_{xx}(0,0)\ne0$. The local equilibria are exactly the trivial branch $x=0$ and a second branch $x=\psi(\lambda)$ with
$$\psi(0)=0,\qquad \psi'(0)=-\frac{2F_{x\lambda}(0,0)}{F_{xx}(0,0)}\ne0.$$
The two branches cross transversely.

3. A **pitchfork bifurcation** occurs if $F(-x,\lambda)=-F(x,\lambda)$ for all nearby $(x,\lambda)$, $F_x(0,0)=F_{xx}(0,0)=0$, and $F_{x\lambda}(0,0)F_{xxx}(0,0)\ne0$. The trivial equilibrium $x=0$ persists. A pair of nontrivial equilibria $x=\pm r(\lambda)$ exists on exactly the side where $\lambda\phi''(0)>0$, with
$$\phi''(0)=-\frac{F_{xxx}(0,0)}{3F_{x\lambda}(0,0)}\ne0,$$
and there are no nontrivial equilibria on the opposite side.

Let $k,m,n\ge1$ and $p\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n+p}$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^k$. Suppose $F(a,b,\lambda_0)=0$ and $D_yF(a,b,\lambda_0)$ is invertible. Then there are neighbourhoods and a unique $C^k$ map $\varphi$ solving $F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)=0$. More precisely, on suitable open neighbourhoods $P$ of $(a,\lambda_0)$ and $Q$ of $b$,

$$F(x,y,\lambda)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x,\lambda),$$

and

$$D\varphi(x,\lambda)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)^{-1}D_{(x,\lambda)}F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda).$$

When no parameter block is present, this is the ordinary $C^k$ implicit function theorem.

At $\mu=0$, $x_*=-\varepsilon^{1/3}$ is an equilibrium and $F_x(x_*,0,\varepsilon)=3\varepsilon^{2/3}>0$. By [F2] it continues as a unique smooth simple equilibrium branch near $(x_*,0)$; the equilibrium at the origin has disappeared.

Let $\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ be the set of formal real polynomials of
[[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]]. Associate to every
$P\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ an eventually zero coefficient sequence $(p_k)$:
use its displayed finite coefficient list and extend it by zeros when $P\ne0$,
and put $p_k=0$ for every $k$ when $P=0$. Do the same for $Q$, with coefficients
$(q_k)$. Define $P+Q$ coefficientwise and define $PQ$ by the convolution
coefficients
$$ (P+Q)_k=p_k+q_k,\qquad (PQ)_k=\sum_{j=0}^{k}p_jq_{k-j}. $$
using the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. In either construction, discard
trailing zero coefficients; if every coefficient is zero, the result is the zero
polynomial. Scalar multiplication and subtraction are the corresponding
coefficientwise operations. Thus these formulas define operations on the formal
coefficient-list objects, independently of evaluation.

Write $1=(1)$ and $X=(0,1)$, and define
$$ \Phi(P,Q):=(Q,2XQ-P)\qquad(P,Q\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}). $$
Apply [[thm-recursion]] to the set
$\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}\times\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$, first with initial value
$(1,X)$ and then with initial value $(1,2X)$, always using the function $\Phi$.
This gives unique pair sequences $H^T,H^U$. Define $T_n$ and $U_n$ to be the
first coordinates of $H^T_n$ and $H^U_n$, respectively. Since the first
coordinate of $\Phi(P,Q)$ is $Q$, the second coordinate of $H^T_n$ is
$T_{n+1}$ and the second coordinate of $H^U_n$ is $U_{n+1}$. Consequently
$$ T_0=1,\quad T_1=X,\quad T_{n+2}=2XT_{n+1}-T_n, $$
$$ U_0=1,\quad U_1=2X,\quad U_{n+2}=2XU_{n+1}-U_n $$
for every $n\in\mathbb N$. These unique sequences are the **Chebyshev
polynomials of the first and second kinds**.

A **formal real polynomial** is either the zero polynomial $0$, or a finite coefficient list $(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$ with $a_n\ne0$; we write the latter as $p(X)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kX^k$. The list, rather than the function it induces, is the polynomial object. Its **evaluation** at $x\in\mathbb R$ is the real number $p(x):=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kx^k$.

For nonzero $p=(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$, define $\deg p:=n$ and $\operatorname{lc}(p):=a_n$. The zero polynomial has no degree and no leading coefficient. A nonzero polynomial is **monic** when $\operatorname{lc}(p)=1$. Thus degree and leading coefficient are defined from the displayed finite list, without asserting that distinct formal polynomials define distinct functions. The conventions for finite sums and integer powers used in the evaluation are recorded in [[def-finite-sum]], [[def-integer-power]].

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

derivations.claim: Define $P(k)$ to assert that $T_k$ has no nonzero coefficient above $k$ and $T_{k+1}$ has none above $k+1$. At $k=0$, this holds because $T_0=1$ and $T_1=X$ by [F1].

Assume $P(k)$. By [F1], the coefficient of $XT_{k+1}$ at index $q$ is the coefficient of $T_{k+1}$ at index $q-1$ (zero when $q=0$), so it vanishes for $q>k+2$. The coefficient of $T_k$ vanishes for those indices as well; hence $T_{k+2}=2XT_{k+1}-T_k$ has no coefficient above $k+2$. Together with the second assertion of $P(k)$, this is $P(k+1)$.
By [F3], steps 1.1 and 1.2 prove $P(k)$ for every natural $k$. Its first clause gives the support bound for every $n$ in [A1].

Define polynomials $B_m\in\mathbb R[X]$ recursively. Put $B_0(X)=1$. If $m\ge1$ and $B_{m-1}(X)=\sum_{q=0}^{m-1}\beta_{m-1,q}X^q$, set
$$B_m(X):=m\sum_{q=0}^{m-1}\beta_{m-1,q}\left(\frac{X^{q+1}}{q+1}-\frac{1}{(q+1)(q+2)}\right).$$
Natural numbers in real denominators mean their canonical real images from [[def-canonical-natural]]; these images are positive by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and therefore invertible in $\mathbb R$ by [[thm-reals-field]]. Every sum is finite. Write $B_m:=B_m(0)$ for the Bernoulli number of index $m$.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

Let $\phi:[c,d]\to[a,b]$ be a monotone surjection, differentiable on $[c,d]$ in the one-sided endpoint sense, with Riemann-integrable derivative. For every bounded $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$,
$$f\text{ is Riemann integrable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(f\circ\phi)|\phi'|\text{ is Riemann integrable},$$
and, when these conditions hold,
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=\int_c^d f(\phi(t))|\phi'(t)|\,dt.$$
Flat subintervals of $\phi$ are allowed.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

derivations.claim: For the nonnegative integer index $m$ of [A1], the case $m=1$ gives $B_1(x)=x-\tfrac12$ by [F1]. For every $m\ge1$, [F1]–[F2] give $B'_m(x)=m\sum_{q=0}^{m-1}\beta_{m-1,q}x^q=mB_{m-1}(x)$. Integrating each monomial in [F1] over $[0,1]$, the integral of $x^{q+1}/(q+1)$ is $1/((q+1)(q+2))$, which cancels the subtracted constant term; hence $\int_0^1B_m=0$.
The reflection formula holds at $m=0$ because $B_0(x)=1$ by [F1], so $B_0(1-x)=B_0(x)=(-1)^0B_0(x)$.
For $m\ge2$, [F3] and step 1.1 applied to $B_{m-1}$ give $B_m(1)-B_m(0)=m\int_0^1B_{m-1}=0$. Thus the endpoints agree for every such $m$.

Let $m\ge1$ and assume $B_{m-1}(1-x)=(-1)^{m-1}B_{m-1}(x)$ for all $x$. By [F2], [F4], and step 1.1, the derivative of $D_m(x):=(-1)^mB_m(1-x)-B_m(x)$ is $D'_m(x)=(-1)^{m+1}mB_{m-1}(1-x)-mB_{m-1}(x)=0$, using the induction hypothesis. Hence $D_m$ is constant by [F3]; its integral on $[0,1]$ is zero because step 1.1 gives $\int_0^1B_m=0$ and [F6] gives $\int_0^1B_m(1-x)\,dx=\int_0^1B_m(x)\,dx$. A constant with zero integral on an interval of length one is zero, so reflection holds at $m$.
The base case in step 1.2 and the induction step in step 2.2 prove the reflection identity for every nonnegative integer $m$ in [A1] by [F7].

For the index $m$ in [A1], if it is odd and at least $3$, step 3.1 gives $B_m(1)=-B_m(0)$ while step 2.1 gives $B_m(1)=B_m(0)$; therefore $B_m(0)=0$. Finally each $B_m$ is a polynomial and hence continuous, so [F5] bounds it on the compact interval $[0,1]$.

$$ \Phi(P,Q):=(Q,2XQ-P)\qquad(P,Q\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}). $$
Apply [[thm-recursion]] to the set
$\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}\times\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$, first with initial value
$(1,X)$ and then with initial value $(1,2X)$, always using the function $\Phi$.
This gives unique pair sequences $H^T,H^U$. Define $T_n$ and $U_n$ to be the
first coordinates of $H^T_n$ and $H^U_n$, respectively. Since the first
coordinate of $\Phi(P,Q)$ is $Q$, the second coordinate of $H^T_n$ is
$T_{n+1}$ and the second coordinate of $H^U_n$ is $U_{n+1}$. Consequently
$$ T_0=1,\quad T_1=X,\quad T_{n+2}=2XT_{n+1}-T_n, $$
$$ U_0=1,\quad U_1=2X,\quad U_{n+2}=2XU_{n+1}-U_n $$
for every $n\in\mathbb N$. These unique sequences are the **Chebyshev
polynomials of the first and second kinds**.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

derivations.claim: Fix the integer $k$ in [A1]. The map $\theta\mapsto\cos\theta$ is a decreasing differentiable bijection from $[0,\pi]$ to $[-1,1]$ with derivative $-\sin\theta$; [F2]–[F4] verify the change-of-variable hypotheses. Therefore [F1]–[F4] give $\mu_k=\int_0^\pi T_k(\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\theta=\int_0^\pi\cos(k\theta)\sin\theta\,d\theta.$

For the nonnegative integer $k$ in [A1], the case $k=0$ gives $\mu_0=\int_0^\pi\sin\theta\,d\theta=2$ by step 1.1. For $k\ge1$, [F5] gives $\sin\theta\cos(k\theta)=\frac12(\sin((k+1)\theta)-\sin((k-1)\theta))$. [F6]–[F7] evaluate each nonzero-frequency sine integral; the $m=0$ term is identically zero.

If $k$ is odd, both positive integers among $k-1$ and $k+1$ are even, so [F6]–[F7] and step 2.1 give $\mu_k=0$. If $k\ge2$ is even, both $k-1$ and $k+1$ are odd, so they give $\mu_k=1/(k+1)-1/(k-1)=2/(1-k^2)$. Together with the $k=0$ case, this proves the formula.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and let $y=(y_0,\ldots,y_n)\in\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Write $\iota(q)$ for the canonical real image of each natural index $q$ ([[def-canonical-natural]]). Since $\iota(n)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]], division by $\iota(n)$ is defined in $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-reals-field]]). The type-I discrete cosine transform, in the Lobatto convention used here, is the vector $X=(X_0,\ldots,X_n)$ defined by
$$X_k:=y_0+(-1)^k y_n+2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}y_j\cos\!\left(\frac{\iota(j)\iota(k)\pi}{\iota(n)}\right),\qquad 0\le k\le n.$$
Here $(-1)^k$ is the natural power of the real number $-1$ from [[def-integer-power]], and the sum is the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]], empty when $n=1$. The data $y_j$ are ordered from the right endpoint toward the left endpoint at nodes $\cos(\iota(j)\pi/\iota(n))$. This definition fixes the unnormalised DCT-I convention; the transform is not defined at $n=0$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For all real $u,v$,
$$\sin(u-v)=\sin u\cos v-\cos u\sin v,\qquad \cos(u-v)=\cos u\cos v+\sin u\sin v.$$ The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

derivations.claim: For the $n$ in [A1], and any natural frequency $m$ with $1\le m<2n$, put $\alpha:=\iota(m)\pi/\iota(n)$ and $C_m:=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\cos(\iota(j)\alpha)$. Positivity of canonical naturals gives $\iota(n)>0$, and $1\le m<2n$ gives $0<\alpha/2<\pi$; hence $\sin(\alpha/2)>0$ by [F4]. The half-weighted endpoints are the DCT-I convention fixed by [F1]. By [F2], $2\sin(\alpha/2)C_m=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\bigl(\sin((\iota(j)+\tfrac12)\alpha)-\sin((\iota(j)-\tfrac12)\alpha)\bigr)=\sin((\iota(n)-\tfrac12)\alpha)+\sin(\alpha/2)=2\sin(\iota(n)\alpha/2)\cos((\iota(n)-1)\alpha/2).$ Since $\sin(\alpha/2)>0$, this gives $C_m=\sin(\iota(m)\pi/2)\cos((\iota(n)-1)\iota(m)\pi/(2\iota(n)))/\sin(\iota(m)\pi/(2\iota(n)))$.

If $m$ is even, the numerator factor $\sin(\iota(m)\pi/2)$ is $0$ by [F3], so $C_m=0$ for $1\le m<2n$. If $m$ is odd, write $(\iota(n)-1)\iota(m)\pi/(2\iota(n))=\iota(m)\pi/2-\iota(m)\pi/(2\iota(n))$; the addition formulas and $\cos(\iota(m)\pi/2)=0$ give $\cos((\iota(n)-1)\iota(m)\pi/(2\iota(n)))=\sin(\iota(m)\pi/2)\sin(\iota(m)\pi/(2\iota(n)))$, hence $C_m=1$. For $m=0$ and $m=2n$, direct evaluation gives $C_m=n$.

Define $D_m:=\frac12+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\cos(\iota(j)\iota(m)\pi/\iota(n))+\frac12(-1)^m$. Since $C_m=1+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\cos(\iota(j)\iota(m)\pi/\iota(n))$, step 1.2 gives $D_m=0$ for $1\le m<2n$ and $D_0=D_{2n}=n$.

For $k,\ell$ in [A1], [F2] makes each product in $S_{k\ell}$ one half the sum of the cosine terms with natural frequency indices $|k-\ell|$ and $k+\ell$, so $S_{k\ell}=\frac12(D_{|k-\ell|}+D_{k+\ell})$. If $k\ne\ell$, then $1\le|k-\ell|<2n$ and $1\le k+\ell<2n$ except the impossible distinct-endpoint case $k+\ell=2n$, so both terms vanish by step 2.1. If $k=\ell=0$ or $k=\ell=n$, both indices are $0$ or $2n$, giving $S_{k\ell}=n$. If $k=\ell$ is interior, the indices are $0$ and $2k$ with $1\le2k<2n$, giving $S_{k\ell}=n/2$. These cases prove the statement.

Let $a<b$, let $x_1,\ldots,x_s\in[a,b]$ be a finite indexed list (repetitions are allowed), and let $w_1,\ldots,w_s\in\mathbb R$. For every Riemann-integrable $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, define the quadrature value and residual by
$$Q(f):=\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_i f(x_i),\qquad L(f):=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-Q(f).$$
For a natural $r\ge1$, say that $Q$ is exact through degree $r-1$ if $L(p)=0$ for every formal real polynomial $p$ of degree at most $r-1$ ([[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]]). Here $r-1$ is the natural predecessor specified by [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. For any natural $q$, the factorial $q!$ in a real-valued formula denotes its canonical real image $\iota(q!)$ from [[def-canonical-natural]]. This denominator is nonzero: $q!\ne0$ by [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], every nonzero natural is a successor by [[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]] and therefore is at least $1$ in the natural order [[def-nat-order]], and its canonical real image is positive by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]], hence invertible by [[thm-reals-field]]. For $t\in[a,b]$ define
$$g_{r,t}(x):=\begin{cases}\dfrac{(x-t)^{r-1}}{\iota((r-1)!)},&x>t,\\0,&x\le t,\end{cases}\qquad K_r(t):=L(g_{r,t}).$$
The power is the natural power of [[def-integer-power]]. For $r\ge2$, $g_{r,t}$ is polynomial and continuous on each side of $t$ by [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]; the polynomial branch extends to $t$ with value $0$ because $r-1\ge1$, agreeing with the zero branch. Thus it is continuous on $[a,b]$ and Riemann-integrable by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. For $r=1$ it is the indicator of $(t,b]$; if $t=b$ it is zero, and if $t<b$, for each $\varepsilon>0$ choose $s\in(t,b)$ with $s-t<\varepsilon$ and use the partition with breakpoints $a,t,s,b$ after deleting repeated endpoints. The indicator is constant on all panels except $[t,s]$, where its oscillation is $1$, so its upper-minus-lower sum is at most $s-t<\varepsilon$; [[thm-riemann-criterion]] makes it integrable. At $r=1$ the denominator is $\iota(0!)=1$. Once $K_1$ is shown integrable, changing its values at the finitely many quadrature nodes does not change its integral by [[lem-changing-a-function-at-finitely-many-points]].

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $Q=\prod_{j<n}[a_j,b_j]\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, where $n\ge1$ and every $a_j<b_j$. If $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, then for every permutation of the coordinates the corresponding repeated Riemann integral exists and equals $\int_Qf$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $E \subseteq [a,b]$ be finite
([[def-countable]], [[def-equinumerous]]), and let $g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$
satisfy

$$g(x) \;=\; f(x) \qquad \text{for every } x \in [a,b] \setminus E .$$

Then $g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and

$$\int_a^b g \;=\; \int_a^b f .$$

In particular the values of an integrand at the endpoints of the interval, and at
any finite set of points, are irrelevant to both questions.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $|f|$, $f^{2}$ and $fg$ are integrable on $[a,b]$
   ([[def-abs-value]], [[def-integer-power]]);
2. $\max(f,g)$ and $\min(f,g)$, defined pointwise
   ([[def-max-min]]), are integrable on $[a,b]$;
3. the **triangle inequality for the integral**:
   $$\Bigl|\int_a^b f\Bigr| \;\le\; \int_a^b |f| .$$

**Claim 3 is stated with $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** For $u > v$
the right-hand side is $-\int_v^u |f| \le 0$ while the left-hand side is $\ge 0$,
so the inequality as written is false there. The form valid for *every* pair
$u,v$ on which $f$ is integrable ([[def-oriented-integral]]) is

$$\Bigl|\int_u^v f\Bigr| \;\le\; \Bigl|\int_u^v |f|\,\Bigr| ,$$

and that is the form the estimates below on this page use whenever the limits
are not known to be in increasing order.

**The converse of claim 1 fails.** Integrability of $|f|$ does not give
integrability of $f$; the witness is on the companion page.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

derivations.claim: We first establish Taylor's integral remainder by induction on the natural order $q$ ([[thm-induction-principle]]). For $r=1$, [F3] gives $f(x)=f(a)+\int_a^xf'(t)\,dt$. If the remainder formula holds at order $q\ge1$, put $u(t):=(x-t)^q/q!$. The product rule and FTC give $\int_a^xu'(t)f^{(q)}(t)\,dt=[u(t)f^{(q)}(t)]_a^x-\int_a^xu(t)f^{(q+1)}(t)\,dt$, and $u'(t)=-(x-t)^{q-1}/(q-1)!$. Rearranging yields $\int_a^x\frac{(x-t)^{q-1}}{(q-1)!}f^{(q)}(t)\,dt=\frac{(x-a)^q}{q!}f^{(q)}(a)+\int_a^x\frac{(x-t)^q}{q!}f^{(q+1)}(t)\,dt.$ Thus induction yields $f(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}f^{(j)}(a)(x-a)^j/j!+\int_a^x(x-t)^{r-1}f^{(r)}(t)/(r-1)!\,dt$.

Extend the last integral to $[a,b]$ by setting its kernel to zero when $t\ge x$. With $P_{r-1}(x):=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}f^{(j)}(a)(x-a)^j/j!$, the result is $f(x)=P_{r-1}(x)+\int_a^bg_{r,t}(x)f^{(r)}(t)\,dt$. Since $Q$ is exact on $\mathcal P_{r-1}$, $L(P_{r-1})=0$.

Suppose first that $r\ge2$. The function $(x,t)\mapsto g_{r,t}(x)f^{(r)}(t)$ is continuous on $[a,b]^2$ because $r-1\ge1$ and $f^{(r)}$ is continuous. By [F5]–[F7], applying the integral part of $L$ to step 2.1 and interchanging the two rectangle integrals gives $\int_a^b(\int_a^bg_{r,t}(x)\,dx)f^{(r)}(t)\,dt$. Each finite evaluation term of $Q$ commutes with the $t$-integral by [F6]. Therefore $L(f)=\int_a^bL(g_{r,t})f^{(r)}(t)\,dt=\int_a^bK_r(t)f^{(r)}(t)\,dt$. The function $(x,t)\mapsto g_{r,t}(x)$ is uniformly continuous on the compact square by [F8], so its $x$-integral and its finite weighted evaluations vary continuously with $t$; hence $K_r$ is continuous and integrable.

If $r=1$, exactness on constants gives $\sum_iw_i=b-a$. For $t$ outside the finite node set, [F1] gives $K_1(t)=(b-t)-\sum_{x_i>t}w_i$. It is bounded and affine between consecutive nodes. Extend each affine piece continuously to its closed subinterval; the resulting pieces are integrable by [F7] and add to an integrable piecewise function by [F6]. The kernel differs from that function at only finitely many nodes, so it is integrable and has the same integral by [F9]. Since $f'$ is continuous, [F10] makes $K_1f'$ integrable; changing the kernel values at the finite node set does not change that product integral by [F9]. By [F3]–[F4] and integration by parts, $\int_a^b(b-t)f'(t)\,dt=\int_a^bf(t)\,dt-(b-a)f(a)$, while $\sum_iw_i\int_a^{x_i}f'(t)\,dt=Q(f)-(b-a)f(a)$. Subtracting gives $\int_a^bK_1(t)f'(t)\,dt=L(f)$.

By [F2] and [F11], $f^{(r)}$ is bounded on $[a,b]$, so $\|f^{(r)}\|_\infty<\infty$. In either case, the kernel is integrable and $|K_r|$ is integrable by [F10]. Apply monotonicity in [F10] to $-|K_r|\|f^{(r)}\|_\infty\le K_r f^{(r)}\le |K_r|\|f^{(r)}\|_\infty$, and use the representation in step 3.1 or 3.2. This gives the asserted bound.
