**Inputs.** A dimension $d\ge1$; $P\ge2$ spheres with centers $q_i$, velocities
$v_i$, masses $m_i>0$, radii $r_i>0$ and fixed restitution coefficients
$e_{ij}\in[0,1]$; an initial state and horizon $T>0$; a positive time-bracket
tolerance $\epsilon_{\rm time}$, a separate positive guard-residual tolerance
$\epsilon_{\rm guard}$, an event-separation bound $\delta>0$, a certified
finite event-count bound $N_{\rm evt}\in\mathbb N$, an event budget
$B\in\mathbb N$, and a finite-budget
certificate provider. The exact smooth-mode reference dynamics are
$$q_i'=v_i,\qquad v_i'=F_i(t,q,v),$$
where $F=(F_1,\ldots,F_P)$ is a specified $C^1$ force field on an open
neighborhood of an admitted compact tube. The exact reference initial state is
nonpenetrating: $\gamma_{ij}(0):=\|q_i(0)-q_j(0)\|_2-r_i-r_j\ge0$ for every
pair. A completed provider must certify that the exact reference states remain
nonpenetrating on each smooth segment and after every exact reset; a failed or
undecidable nonpenetration check returns `unresolved`. Throughout each certified
incoming/outgoing tube every pair distance is at least a stated $\sigma>0$.
The provider supplies finite relative-velocity bounds $V$ and state/field bounds
wherever they are used below.

The provider is an explicit admissible input, not an automatically constructed
oracle for arbitrary $C^1$ fields. It must supply the following valid data,
with any failed or undecidable certificate test returning `unresolved`.

1. From the last reported reset, a continuous accumulated dense reconstruction
   $U$ and a certified uniform error $\eta_{\rm loc}$ relative to the exact
   smooth-mode solution launched from that reported state. It also supplies
   a bound $E$ on the discrepancy from the reference hybrid trajectory at
   the same aligned segment-start time, initially $E=0$. On a common mode
   prefix of duration $H$, supply a state-Lipschitz constant $L$ and the common
   solution/tube hypotheses of [[lem-ode-flow-lipschitz-on-a-tube]], and use
   $\eta_{\rm ref}=\eta_{\rm loc}+e^{LH}E$. A finite cover of certified
   convex mode tubes may be used with its propagated bounds. A Jacobian bound
   on a nonconvex compact set alone is not a substitute for these hypotheses.

2. For every pair $i<j$, exact-reference guard enclosures for
   $\gamma_{ij}(t)=\|q_i(t)-q_j(t)\|_2-r_i-r_j$, and a certificate covering
   the whole interval since the last processed event that proves
   $\gamma_{ij}\ge0$ throughout and accounts for every possible zero. Every
   zero is either the just-processed segment-start root for that pair (which may
   be ignored once) or a candidate root bracket satisfying item 3; any other
   possible zero, including a grazing or zero-speed zero, or any possible
   negative guard value returns `unresolved`. At the initial simulation time, a
   zero must be processed as an enabled incoming root or the result is
   `unresolved`. Thus a no-event result requires certified nonpenetration and
   exclusion of every unlisted zero over the whole interval, not merely
   exclusion of incoming roots. A sufficient explicit sampling assumption may
   replace a range cover only when its stated variation/domain assumptions
   justify the same exclusion. Endpoint signs or an unsuccessful sign scan
   alone do not certify absence. Dense-guard enclosures must include the
   state-error inflation $\sqrt2\eta_{\rm ref}$ as well as guard-evaluation
   and rounding error; the bound follows from
   [[lem-sphere-contact-guard-normal-and-reset-lipschitz-bounds]].

3. For each candidate event, a bracket $[a,b]$ containing exactly one root
   $\tau$ of the exact reference guard, with
   $b-a\le\epsilon_{\rm time}$ and $b-a<\delta/3$. On the entire bracket,
   certify the incoming inequality
   $\dot\gamma_{ij}(t)\le-\nu<0$, not just a derivative value at its root.
   Supply disjoint ordering certificates identifying the unique earliest
   event among all pairs. A grazing/uncertain derivative, ambiguous overlap
   or simultaneous multi-contact is unresolved; lexicographic inspection
   does not settle physical simultaneous impacts.

4. At $\widehat\tau=b$, a certified bound
   $\epsilon_{\rm obs}\ge|\gamma_{ij}(\widehat\tau,U(\widehat\tau))|$
   with $\epsilon_{\rm obs}\le\epsilon_{\rm guard}$. The provider includes
   all evaluation errors in this bound. The actual lag is nonnegative and
   bounded by
   $$\Delta:=\min\left\{b-a,\frac{\sqrt2\eta_{\rm ref}+\epsilon_{\rm obs}}{\nu}\right\}$$
   by [[lem-transverse-hybrid-event-time-error]]. Require certified bounds
   $M^-,M^+$ for the incoming/outgoing fields through this lag, and reset
   domain/tube checks. For the selected pair use the state-reset bound $L_R$
   from [[lem-sphere-contact-guard-normal-and-reset-lipschitz-bounds]], with
   a velocity bound valid for both compared reset inputs. This reset has no
   explicit time dependence. If the reset formula is evaluated inexactly, the
   computed full-state output $\widehat R(U(b))$ must come with a separate
   $\epsilon_R\ge0$ satisfying
   $\|\widehat R(U(b))-R(U(b))\|_2\le\epsilon_R$, where the norm is on the
   full state $(q,v)$; for an exact reset set $\epsilon_R=0$.

5. A certificate that the matched isolated exact events have separation at
   least $\delta$ and count at most $N_{\rm evt}$. Specify whether a horizon
   endpoint impact is included in that count or the endpoint is reported as
   a pre-impact state. Process an initial enabled root at most once. Missing
   endpoint/count/separation bookkeeping is unresolved. In particular $e=0$
   does not establish another isolated transverse event after the reset.

**Procedure.** Request these certificates for every unordered pair on each
smooth segment, inspecting the pair list in increasing lexicographic order.
If the provider certifies no further zero except the permitted just-processed
segment-start root, with nonpenetration and no unlisted zero through the chosen
horizon endpoint, return that segment, its accumulated error bound and its
certificates. Otherwise
select the certified unique earliest pair and use its upper bracket endpoint
$\widehat\tau=b$. Evaluate the binary impulse formula of
[[thm-frictionless-sphere-binary-impact-impulse-laws]] as the smooth reset
extension at $U(b)$; keep positions fixed and update only the selected two
velocities. The impulse theorem's exact contact/momentum/restitution/energy
laws concern the reference exact incoming contact. A reported approximate
state is not asserted to be exactly at contact; its reset error is recorded.

By [[lem-reset-error-after-a-mistimed-hybrid-event]], set the next aligned
reset-state error bound to
$$E\leftarrow L_R\eta_{\rm ref}+(L_RM^-+M^+)\Delta+\epsilon_R.$$
The outgoing $M^+\Delta$ term accounts for the reference trajectory's flow
from its earlier true reset to the reported time. Restart the smooth integrator
at $b$ with the reported reset state, discard the previous local reconstruction,
and start the next accumulated dense-error ledger. These recurrences compare
only matched smooth-mode prefixes and post-reset states at aligned times; they
make no same-clock state-error assertion between an exact jump and its later
reported jump.

Stop at $T$ or after $B$ accepted events. If another event is required after
the budget, return `unresolved` with the certified partial trajectory. A
completed run requires $B\ge N_{\rm evt}$ or a certified no-further-event result
before the budget is exhausted. Any missing enclosure, margin, ordering,
separation/count or restart certificate, failed reset domain, or depleted
provider budget returns `unresolved` without an event-absence claim.

The search enumerates $P(P-1)/2$ pairs per smooth segment. Root-solve guard
evaluations, dense reintegration and restart-error calculation are charged
separately from one inspection per pair. No neighbor-search acceleration,
frictional solver, or simultaneous-contact solver is specified.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

derivations.claim: For each lower index $i=1,\ldots,P-1$, the loop tests exactly $P-i$ higher indices. Every unordered pair has a unique smaller index, so these sets of tests are disjoint and include every pair once. The count is therefore $\sum_{i=1}^{P-1}(P-i)$.

Reindexing by $r=P-i$ gives $\sum_{r=1}^{P-1}r$. This sum is $P(P-1)/2$: it is $0$ for $P=0$ and $P=1$, and increasing $P$ to $P+1$ adds exactly $P$, which changes $P(P-1)/2$ to $P(P+1)/2$; induction gives the formula. For every $P\ge2$, it is at most $P^2/2$, proving the stated $O(P^2)$ bound.

Use the program and dimensions of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]. For any $x\in U$,
$\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, define coordinatewise
$[v]_i^+=\max\{v_i,0\}$ and the scaled residual
$$
r_{\mathrm{KKT}}(x,\nu,\lambda)=\|\nabla f(x)+Dh(x)^T\nu+Dg(x)^T\lambda\|_2+\|h(x)\|_2+\|[g(x)]^+\|_2+\|[-\lambda]^+\|_2+\|\lambda\circ g(x)\|_2.
$$
The symbol $\circ$ denotes coordinatewise multiplication. The norm is the
Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and the norm of the
zero-dimensional vector is $0$.

For a convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $x\in C$, its (outward) normal
cone is
$$
N_C(x)=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }y\in C\}.
$$
This definition applies in particular when $C$ is closed and convex.

Let $d\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $P_C(y)$ be the unique nearest point in $C$ to $y$, whose existence and uniqueness are [[thm-nearest-point-in-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]]. For $x\in C$, set
$$N_C(x)=\{n\in\mathbb R^d:\langle n,z-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }z\in C\};$$
for $x\notin C$, set $N_C(x)=\varnothing$. On $C$ this is the outward normal cone of [[def-kkt-residual-and-normal-cone]]. The projection variational inequality of [[lem-projection-onto-a-closed-convex-set-has-the-variational-inequality]] says $P_C(y)=p$ exactly when $p\in C$ and $y-p\in N_C(p)$.

For $T>0$, a solution of the projected contact dynamics with forcing $f:[0,T]\times C\to\mathbb R^d$ and initial state $x_0\in C$ is an absolutely continuous map $x:[0,T]\to C$ satisfying
$$f(t,x(t))-\dot x(t)\in N_C(x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in[0,T].$$
Equivalently, $\dot x(t)+N_C(x(t))\ni f(t,x(t))$. For an integer $N\ge1$, put $h=T/N$, $t_k=kh$, and define the exact explicit projection Euler nodes by
$$x_{k+1}=P_C\bigl(x_k+h f(t_k,x_k)\bigr),\qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1,$$
starting from $x_0$. Its affine interpolant joins consecutive nodes linearly on each interval $[t_k,t_{k+1}]$.

For any set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, its extended-real indicator is
$$\iota_C(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}$$

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex in the convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}g$ and $\eta\ge0$, define
$$\partial_\eta g(x)=\{p\in\mathbb R^n:g(z)\ge g(x)+\langle p,z-x\rangle-\eta\text{ for every }z\in\mathbb R^n\}.$$
Write $\partial g(x)=\partial_0g(x)$. If $x\notin\operatorname{dom}g$, set $\partial_\eta g(x)=\varnothing$. When $g$ is finite-valued on a convex domain, $\partial g(x)$ agrees with [[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]].

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For every $t>0$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the set $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$ is a singleton. Its unique element $u$ satisfies the resolvent equivalence
$$u=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (v-u)/t\in\partial g(u).$$
For any $v_1,v_2$ and $u_i=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v_i)$,
$$\|u_1-u_2\|_2^2\le\langle u_1-u_2,v_1-v_2\rangle.$$
In particular the proximal map is nonexpansive.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed and convex. Its indicator $\iota_C$ is proper, closed and convex in the convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For every $t>0$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, $\operatorname{prox}_{t\iota_C}(v)$ is the singleton consisting of the unique nearest point in $C$ to $v$.

derivations.claim: Let $n\in N_C(x)$ and $m\in N_C(y)$. Testing the definition in [F1] with $z=y$ and $z=x$ gives $\langle n,y-x\rangle\le0$ and $\langle m,x-y\rangle\le0$. Adding and changing signs yields $\langle n-m,x-y\rangle\ge0$. Thus $N_C$ is monotone.

At $x\in C$, [F2]–[F3] show $p\in\partial\iota_C(x)$ exactly when $\langle p,z-x\rangle\le0$ for every $z\in C$; inequalities for $z\notin C$ are automatic because $\iota_C(z)=+\infty$. At $x\notin C$, both $\partial\iota_C(x)$ and $N_C(x)$ are empty. Hence $\partial\iota_C=N_C$.

Given any $y\in\mathbb R^d$, put $p=P_C(y)=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau\iota_C}(y)$ by [F5]. By [F4] and step 1.2, $(y-p)/\tau\in N_C(p)$, so $y-p\in\tau N_C(p)$. If also $y-q\in\tau N_C(q)$, monotonicity [step 1.1] gives $0\le\langle(y-p-y+q)/\tau,p-q\rangle=-\|p-q\|_2^2/\tau$, hence $p=q$. Therefore the resolvent exists uniquely at every $y$ and equals $P_C$.

Suppose $(x,v)$ is monotonically related to the graph of $N_C$, so $\langle v-n,x-y\rangle\ge0$ for every $n\in N_C(y)$. Apply step 2.1 to $x+\tau v$ to obtain $p$ and $n=(x+\tau v-p)/\tau\in N_C(p)$. Then $x-p=\tau(n-v)$, and the relation gives $0\le\langle v-n,x-p\rangle=-\tau\|v-n\|_2^2$. Thus $v=n$ and $x=p$, so $(x,v)$ already lies in the graph. Every monotone extension adds no point; $N_C$ is maximal monotone.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $d\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $P_C(y)$ be the unique nearest point in $C$ to $y$, whose existence and uniqueness are [[thm-nearest-point-in-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]]. For $x\in C$, set
$$N_C(x)=\{n\in\mathbb R^d:\langle n,z-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }z\in C\};$$
for $x\notin C$, set $N_C(x)=\varnothing$. On $C$ this is the outward normal cone of [[def-kkt-residual-and-normal-cone]]. The projection variational inequality of [[lem-projection-onto-a-closed-convex-set-has-the-variational-inequality]] says $P_C(y)=p$ exactly when $p\in C$ and $y-p\in N_C(p)$.

For $T>0$, a solution of the projected contact dynamics with forcing $f:[0,T]\times C\to\mathbb R^d$ and initial state $x_0\in C$ is an absolutely continuous map $x:[0,T]\to C$ satisfying
$$f(t,x(t))-\dot x(t)\in N_C(x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in[0,T].$$
Equivalently, $\dot x(t)+N_C(x(t))\ni f(t,x(t))$. For an integer $N\ge1$, put $h=T/N$, $t_k=kh$, and define the exact explicit projection Euler nodes by
$$x_{k+1}=P_C\bigl(x_k+h f(t_k,x_k)\bigr),\qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1,$$
starting from $x_0$. Its affine interpolant joins consecutive nodes linearly on each interval $[t_k,t_{k+1}]$.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $N_C$ have the convention of [[def-projected-contact-dynamics-and-euler-step]]. An operator $A:\mathbb R^d\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^d$ is **monotone** if $\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\ge0$ for all $u\in A(x)$ and $v\in A(y)$; it is **maximal monotone** if its graph has no proper monotone graph extension. Then $N_C$ is maximal monotone. For every $\tau>0$ and $y\in\mathbb R^d$, there is a unique $p$ with $y-p\in\tau N_C(p)$, and that point is $P_C(y)$. Equivalently, $(I+\tau N_C)^{-1}=P_C$.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.
If $F,G\in AC[a,b]$, then $FG\in AC[a,b]$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: Let $x,y$ be the two solutions and define $n_x=f(t,x)-\dot x$ and $n_y=f(t,y)-\dot y$ at almost every time where both inclusions hold. By [F1] these belong to $N_C(x)$ and $N_C(y)$; [F2] gives $\langle n_x-n_y,x-y\rangle\ge0$.

The function $u(t)=\|x(t)-y(t)\|_2^2$ is absolutely continuous by [F4]. At almost every $t$, [F1] and step 1.1 give $$u'(t)=2\langle \dot x-\dot y,x-y\rangle=2\langle f(t,x)-f(t,y),x-y\rangle-2\langle n_x-n_y,x-y\rangle\le2L u(t),$$ using the Lipschitz hypothesis and [F5]. Since $u(0)=0$, [F4] integrates this differential inequality to $u(t)\le\int_0^t2Lu(s)\,ds$. Applying [F3] gives $u(t)=0$ for every $t$, so $x=y$. This argument uses no choices beyond the two axioms already required by [F4].

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $d\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $P_C(y)$ be the unique nearest point in $C$ to $y$, whose existence and uniqueness are [[thm-nearest-point-in-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]]. For $x\in C$, set
$$N_C(x)=\{n\in\mathbb R^d:\langle n,z-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }z\in C\};$$
for $x\notin C$, set $N_C(x)=\varnothing$. On $C$ this is the outward normal cone of [[def-kkt-residual-and-normal-cone]]. The projection variational inequality of [[lem-projection-onto-a-closed-convex-set-has-the-variational-inequality]] says $P_C(y)=p$ exactly when $p\in C$ and $y-p\in N_C(p)$.

For $T>0$, a solution of the projected contact dynamics with forcing $f:[0,T]\times C\to\mathbb R^d$ and initial state $x_0\in C$ is an absolutely continuous map $x:[0,T]\to C$ satisfying
$$f(t,x(t))-\dot x(t)\in N_C(x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in[0,T].$$
Equivalently, $\dot x(t)+N_C(x(t))\ni f(t,x(t))$. For an integer $N\ge1$, put $h=T/N$, $t_k=kh$, and define the exact explicit projection Euler nodes by
$$x_{k+1}=P_C\bigl(x_k+h f(t_k,x_k)\bigr),\qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1,$$
starting from $x_0$. Its affine interpolant joins consecutive nodes linearly on each interval $[t_k,t_{k+1}]$.

Let $d\in\mathbb N$, including $d=0$. Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $P_C(y)$ denote the unique nearest point in $C$ to $y$. Then
$$\|P_C(u)-P_C(v)\|_2\le\|u-v\|_2\qquad(u,v\in\mathbb R^d).$$

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, compact, and closed. Let $M\ge0$. If $u_j:[0,T]\to C$ satisfies
$$\|u_j(t)-u_j(s)\|_2\le M|t-s|\qquad(j\ge1,\ s,t\in[0,T]),$$
then some subsequence converges uniformly to a map $u:[0,T]\to C$ with the same Lipschitz bound.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $T>0$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $f:[0,T]\times C\to\mathbb R^d$ satisfy $\|f(t,x)-f(t,y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$ for all $t,x,y$, with $L\ge0$. Any two absolutely continuous solutions of the projected dynamics of [[def-projected-contact-dynamics-and-euler-step]] with the same initial state agree on $[0,T]$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$.

1. If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f'$ extends
   continuously to $[a,b]$, then $f$ is Lipschitz.
2. Every Lipschitz $f$ is absolutely continuous.
3. Every absolutely continuous $f$ is continuous and has bounded variation.

Thus, with $C^1$ understood in the endpoint-extension sense of claim 1,
$C^1\subseteq\mathrm{Lipschitz}\subseteq AC\subseteq C\cap BV$ on a compact
interval.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Every real-valued function of bounded variation on a compact interval is
differentiable almost everywhere.
If $F,G\in AC[a,b]$, then $FG\in AC[a,b]$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{C}$ be a measurable function
([[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]]). We say that $f$ is
**locally integrable** on $\mathbb{R}^n$ if for every Euclidean ball
$B(x,r)$ with $r>0$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) one has
$$\int_{B(x,r)} |f(y)|\,d\lambda(y)<\infty,$$
so the restriction of $f$ to each ball is integrable in the sense of
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]].

The set of such functions is denoted by $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^n)$.
When convenient, the same notation is also used for the corresponding
almost-everywhere equivalence classes.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then
$$\lim_{r\to0^+}A_rf(x)=f(x)$$
for Lebesgue-almost every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the
plane of pairs of naturals is countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

The bijection is exhibited, not merely asserted to exist. Define $2^m$ by
recursion on $m$ ([[thm-recursion]]) by $2^0 = 1$ and $2^{\sigma(m)} = 2^m + 2^m$,
and set

$$J(m,n) = 2^m \cdot \sigma(n + n), \qquad \text{that is} \qquad J(m,n) = 2^m(2n+1).$$

Then $J$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ onto
$\mathbb{N} \setminus \{0\}$, and $\sigma$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{N}$ onto
$\mathbb{N} \setminus \{0\}$, so $\sigma^{-1} \circ J$ is a bijection
$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. What makes $J$ bijective is the
decomposition of a nonzero natural into a power of two times an odd number,
existence and uniqueness both.

Let $(N,0,\sigma)$ be a Peano system ([[def-peano-system]]), in particular the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). For any set $A$, any element $a \in A$, and any function $f : A \to A$, there is a unique function $g : N \to A$ such that $g(0) = a$ and $g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n))$ for all $n \in N$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of subsets of $\mathbb{R}$, each of
measure zero ([[def-measure-zero-and-content-zero]]). Then

$$\bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} A_n \quad \text{has measure zero.}$$

By the padding convention of [[def-measure-zero-and-content-zero]] and
[[def-countable]] the same conclusion covers the union of an at most countable
family of null sets, a finite family being extended by copies of $\varnothing$.

**The hypothesis $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is spent at exactly one step, step 2.1
below**, where one covering sequence is selected for every $A_n$ at once. Each
$A_n$ has many such covers and nullity provides no rule for singling one out.
Nothing else in the proof selects anything: the diagonal enumeration and the
estimate are formulas.

derivations.claim: Since $d\ge1$, [F5] shows that compact $C$ is closed and bounded. Along with the stated nonemptiness and convexity, this verifies the set hypotheses in [F1] and the projection suppliers before they are used. Boundedness gives a finite diameter bound $D$ for $C$. Put $M=\|f(0,x_0)\|_2+L(T+D)$; the Lipschitz hypothesis gives $\|f(t,x)\|_2\le M$ on $[0,T]\times C$. For each exact Euler step, $P_C(x_k)=x_k$, so [F2] gives $\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|_2\le h\|f(t_k,x_k)\|_2\le hM$. Convexity keeps the affine interpolant in $C$, and its slope on each step has norm at most $M$.

On each open mesh cell $[t_k,t_{k+1})$, write $X_h$ for the affine interpolant, $\bar X_h=x_{k+1}$, $F_h=f(t_k,x_k)$, and $n_h=F_h-\dot X_h=(x_k+hF_h-x_{k+1})/h$. By the projection variational inequality in [F1], $n_h\in N_C(\bar X_h)$. Consequently, for every fixed $z\in C$, $$\langle\dot X_h-F_h,z-\bar X_h\rangle\ge0.$$

Apply [F3] to the sequence of interpolants for $N=1,2,\ldots$. Along a subsequence $N_j\to\infty$, they converge uniformly to a map $x:[0,T]\to C$ with $x(0)=x_0$ and Lipschitz constant $M$. By [F6], $x$ is absolutely continuous and differentiable almost everywhere; at each differentiability point, the Lipschitz inequality implies $\|\dot x(t)\|_2\le M$.

Fix $0\le a<b\le T$ and a fixed $z\in C$. We have $\|\bar X_h-X_h\|_2\le Mh$ and $\|\dot X_h-F_h\|_2\le2M$, so replacing $\bar X_h$ by $X_h$ in the integral of step 1.2 changes it by at most $2M^2h(b-a)$. The term with $\dot X_h$ is the endpoint difference of $\Phi_z(X_h)$, where $\Phi_z(w)=\langle w,z\rangle-\tfrac12\|w\|_2^2$. Uniform convergence gives its limit as the endpoint difference of $\Phi_z(x)$; [F7] identifies that difference with $\int_a^b\langle\dot x,z-x\rangle$. Also $$\|F_h(t)-f(t,x(t))\|_2\le L\bigl(h+Mh+\|X_h-x\|_\infty\bigr)$$ on each mesh cell, so $F_h\to f(t,x(t))$ uniformly along the selected subsequence. Passing to the limit in the integrated inequality yields $$\int_a^b g_z(t)\,dt\ge0,\qquad g_z(t):=\langle\dot x(t)-f(t,x(t)),z-x(t)\rangle.$$

The function $g_z$ is Lebesgue-integrable: [F7] gives a measurable $L^1$ version of $\dot x$; define it to be $0$ where the derivative is undefined. Boundedness of $f,x,z$ makes the other factors integrable. Extend this representative of $g_z$ by zero outside $[0,T]$ to obtain a locally integrable function on $\mathbb R$. Since every interval integral in step 3.1 is nonnegative, $G_z(t)=\int_0^t g_z(s)\,ds$ is nondecreasing. At almost every interior $t$, [F8] gives $$\lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac1{2r}\int_{t-r}^{t+r}g_z(s)\,ds=g_z(t).$$ For every sufficiently small $r>0$, the average on the left is $(G_z(t+r)-G_z(t-r))/(2r)\ge0$ because $G_z$ is nondecreasing. Taking the limit yields $g_z(t)\ge0$ almost everywhere for each fixed $z\in C$.

Fix a bijection $\rho:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Q$ from [F9]. Define $\pi_1(n_1)=n_1$ and, recursively, $\pi_{k+1}(n_1,\ldots,n_{k+1})=J(\pi_k(n_1,\ldots,n_k),n_{k+1})$. Since $J$ is a bijection, induction using [F10] shows that each $\pi_k:\mathbb N^k\to\mathbb N$ is a bijection. In particular, decoding $n$ by $\pi_d^{-1}$ and applying $\rho$ coordinatewise gives a surjection $s:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Q^d$. Thus $D_0=\{P_C(s(n)):n\in\mathbb N\}$ is countable.
It is dense in $C$: for $z\in C$ and $\eta>0$, choose in each of the finitely many coordinates a rational $q_j$ strictly between $z_j-\eta/(2d)$ and $z_j+\eta/(2d)$, using the interval-density conclusion of [F10]. For $q=(q_1,\ldots,q_d)$, [F10] gives
$$\|q-z\|_2^2=\sum_{j<d}|q_j-z_j|^2<d\left(\frac{\eta}{2d}\right)^2\le\frac{\eta^2}{4},$$
so $\|q-z\|_2<\eta/2$. Since $P_C(z)=z$, nonexpansiveness [F2] gives $\|P_C(q)-z\|_2=\|P_C(q)-P_C(z)\|_2\le\|q-z\|_2<\eta$.
For each $n$, put $z_n=P_C(s(n))\in D_0$. Step 4.1 gives a null exceptional set where $g_{z_n}<0$. Countable Choice [A1] and [F11] make their union, together with the null set where $\dot x$ does not exist, null. Outside it, $g_z(t)\ge0$ for every $z\in D_0$. For each such $t$, the expression $g_z(t)$ is continuous in $z$; if it were negative at some $z\in C$, it would be negative on a neighborhood of $z$ meeting the dense set $D_0$, a contradiction. Hence the inequality holds for every $z\in C$, so $f(t,x(t))-\dot x(t)\in N_C(x(t))$ almost everywhere by [F1]. This proves existence of a solution along the selected subsequence.

The uniqueness lemma [F4], under the same choice assumptions through its FTC supplier, shows that every uniformly convergent subsequence limit of the Euler interpolants is this same solution $x$. If the full sequence did not converge uniformly to $x$, some subsequence would stay at uniform distance at least $\delta>0$; [F3] would give a further uniformly convergent subsequence, whose limit is a solution by steps 1.2–5.1 and hence equals $x$, a contradiction. Therefore the entire sequence converges uniformly to $x$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $d\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, compact, and convex, let $T>0$, and let $x_0\in C$. Suppose $f:[0,T]\times C\to\mathbb R^d$ is Lipschitz in the explicit sense
$$\|f(t,x)-f(s,y)\|_2\le L\bigl(|t-s|+\|x-y\|_2\bigr)$$
for some $L\ge0$ and all $s,t,x,y$. Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Then the projected inclusion
$$x(0)=x_0,\qquad f(t,x(t))-\dot x(t)\in N_C(x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in[0,T]$$
has a unique absolutely continuous solution $x:[0,T]\to C$. For each integer $N\ge1$, define $h=T/N$, $t_k=kh$, and the exact projection Euler nodes by
$$x_{k+1}=P_C\bigl(x_k+h f(t_k,x_k)\bigr),\qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1.$$
Their affine interpolants converge uniformly to $x$ as $N\to\infty$. Countable Choice is used for the almost-everywhere statements and null-set unions; Dependent Choice enters through the absolutely-continuous FTC supplier used in the integrated proof. The monotonicity estimate for uniqueness makes no additional choices.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $N_C$ have the convention of [[def-projected-contact-dynamics-and-euler-step]]. An operator $A:\mathbb R^d\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^d$ is **monotone** if $\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\ge0$ for all $u\in A(x)$ and $v\in A(y)$; it is **maximal monotone** if its graph has no proper monotone graph extension. Then $N_C$ is maximal monotone. For every $\tau>0$ and $y\in\mathbb R^d$, there is a unique $p$ with $y-p\in\tau N_C(p)$, and that point is $P_C(y)$. Equivalently, $(I+\tau N_C)^{-1}=P_C$.

Let $d\in\mathbb N$, including $d=0$. Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $P_C(y)$ denote the unique nearest point in $C$ to $y$. Then
$$\|P_C(u)-P_C(v)\|_2\le\|u-v\|_2\qquad(u,v\in\mathbb R^d).$$

Let $d\in\mathbb N$, including $d=0$. Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, closed, and convex. If $y\in\mathbb R^d$, $\varepsilon\ge0$, and $p\in C$ satisfy
$$\sup_{z\in C}\langle y-p,z-p\rangle\le\varepsilon^2,$$
then $\|p-P_C(y)\|_2\le\varepsilon$.

Input a nonempty compact, closed, and convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, an exact force evaluator $f:[0,T]\times C\to\mathbb R^d$, $T>0$, integer step count $N\ge1$, initial state $x_0\in C$, tolerances $\varepsilon_k\ge0$, and finite solver budgets $B_k\in\mathbb N$ for $k=0,\ldots,N-1$. The explicit closedness condition matches [[def-projected-contact-dynamics-and-euler-step]]. Set $h=T/N$ and $t_k=kh$. At step $k$, form
$$y_k=x_k+h f(t_k,x_k).$$
Ask the projection solver for $p_{k+1}\in C$ and a certificate that
$$\sup_{z\in C}\langle y_k-p_{k+1},z-p_{k+1}\rangle\le\varepsilon_k^2.$$
If the solver does not return a feasible candidate and a valid certificate within budget $B_k$, stop and return `unresolved` with the valid prefix $x_0,\ldots,x_k$. Otherwise set $x_{k+1}=p_{k+1}$ and continue. After all $N$ steps, return `complete`, the nodes, their affine interpolant, and the per-step tolerances. The definition assumes exact force evaluations and exact verification of the displayed residual; arithmetic and force-evaluation errors are not included. With $\varepsilon_k=0$, a successful step satisfies the exact projection-Euler recurrence by [[lem-projected-euler-projection-residual-certificate]].

The algorithm makes at most $N$ solver calls and uses the stated per-call budgets. Failure to certify a projection is reported; no convergence or accuracy is inferred from a solver's unverified stopping tolerance.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$.

1. If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f'$ extends
   continuously to $[a,b]$, then $f$ is Lipschitz.
2. Every Lipschitz $f$ is absolutely continuous.
3. Every absolutely continuous $f$ is continuous and has bounded variation.

Thus, with $C^1$ understood in the endpoint-extension sense of claim 1,
$C^1\subseteq\mathrm{Lipschitz}\subseteq AC\subseteq C\cap BV$ on a compact
interval.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Every real-valued function of bounded variation on a compact interval is
differentiable almost everywhere.
If $F,G\in AC[a,b]$, then $FG\in AC[a,b]$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $P_C(y)$ be the unique nearest point in $C$ to $y$, whose existence and uniqueness are [[thm-nearest-point-in-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]]. For $x\in C$, set
$$N_C(x)=\{n\in\mathbb R^d:\langle n,z-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }z\in C\};$$
for $x\notin C$, set $N_C(x)=\varnothing$. On $C$ this is the outward normal cone of [[def-kkt-residual-and-normal-cone]]. The projection variational inequality of [[lem-projection-onto-a-closed-convex-set-has-the-variational-inequality]] says $P_C(y)=p$ exactly when $p\in C$ and $y-p\in N_C(p)$.

For $T>0$, a solution of the projected contact dynamics with forcing $f:[0,T]\times C\to\mathbb R^d$ and initial state $x_0\in C$ is an absolutely continuous map $x:[0,T]\to C$ satisfying
$$f(t,x(t))-\dot x(t)\in N_C(x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in[0,T].$$
Equivalently, $\dot x(t)+N_C(x(t))\ni f(t,x(t))$. For an integer $N\ge1$, put $h=T/N$, $t_k=kh$, and define the exact explicit projection Euler nodes by
$$x_{k+1}=P_C\bigl(x_k+h f(t_k,x_k)\bigr),\qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1,$$
starting from $x_0$. Its affine interpolant joins consecutive nodes linearly on each interval $[t_k,t_{k+1}]$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

derivations.claim: By [F12], compactness makes $C$ closed, so the projection and normal-cone hypotheses in [F11] and [F3] apply to the stated set. Let $X_h$ be the exact affine Euler interpolant, $\bar X_h(t)=x_{k+1}$ on $[t_k,t_{k+1})$, $F_h(t)=f(t_k,x_k)$, and $n_h=F_h-\dot X_h$. The projection variational inequality in [F11] gives $n_h(t)\in N_C(\bar X_h(t))$. Nonexpansiveness [F3] gives $\|\dot X_h\|_2\le M$ and $\|\bar X_h-X_h\|_2\le hM$, so $\|n_h\|_2\le2M$. For the exact solution put $n(t)=f(t,x(t))-\dot x(t)\in N_C(x(t))$. At almost every differentiability point, $x(t+s)\in C$ on both sides of $t$; the normal inequality with $z=x(t+s)$, divided by positive and negative $s$ and passed to the limit, gives $\langle n(t),\dot x(t)\rangle=0$. Hence $\|\dot x(t)\|_2^2=\langle f(t,x(t)),\dot x(t)\rangle$, so Cauchy–Schwarz [F8] gives $\|\dot x(t)\|_2\le M$ and $\|n(t)\|_2\le2M$.

By [F4] and [F5], each inexact node is within $\varepsilon_k$ of the exact projection of its own unprojected input. Comparing it with the exact node and using [F3] and the state-Lipschitz bound gives $$\|\widetilde x_{k+1}-x_{k+1}\|_2\le(1+hL)\|\widetilde x_k-x_k\|_2+\varepsilon_k.$$ Iteration from the common initial point yields $\max_k\|\widetilde x_k-x_k\|_2\le(1+hL)^N\sum_k\varepsilon_k$. By [F9], $(1+hL)^N\le e^{NhL}=e^{LT}$.

Put $e_h=X_h-x$ and $E_h=\|e_h\|_2^2$. By [F6]–[F7], $E_h$ is absolutely continuous and $E_h'=2\langle\dot X_h-\dot x,e_h\rangle$ almost everywhere. Monotonicity [F2] at $\bar X_h$ and $x$ gives $\langle n_h-n,\bar X_h-x\rangle\ge0$. Since $\|\bar X_h-X_h\|_2\le hM$ and $\|n_h-n\|_2\le4M$, differentiation yields $$\tfrac12E_h'\le L E_h+Lh(1+M)\sqrt{E_h}+4M^2h.$$ Indeed, $\|F_h-f(t,x)\|_2\le L(h+\|x_k-x(t)\|_2)\le L(\|e_h\|_2+h(1+M))$ using the within-step displacement bound; [F8] bounds its inner product with $e_h$.

Since $(\sqrt{E_h}-Lh(1+M))^2\ge0$, we have $Lh(1+M)\sqrt{E_h}\le\tfrac12E_h+\tfrac12L^2(1+M)^2h^2$. Thus $$E_h'\le(2L+1)E_h+8M^2h+L^2(1+M)^2h^2\le(2L+1)E_h+C_0h,$$ since $h\le T$. Integrating the inequality and using $E_h(0)=0$ gives $E_h(t)\le C_0hT+(2L+1)\int_0^tE_h(s)\,ds$. By [F10], $\sup_t E_h(t)\le C_0hT e^{(2L+1)T}$, hence $\sup_t\|X_h(t)-x(t)\|_2\le C\sqrt h$.

On each mesh cell, $\widetilde X_h-X_h$ is the affine interpolation of its endpoint errors, so its norm is at most the larger endpoint norm. The triangle inequality with step 3.1 gives $$\sup_t\|\widetilde X_h(t)-x(t)\|_2\le C\sqrt h+e^{LT}\sum_k\varepsilon_k,$$ which is the claimed estimate. If $\varepsilon_k=0$ all $k$, or if their sum is $O(\sqrt h)$ along a refining mesh, the stated $O(\sqrt h)$ rate follows.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

derivations.claim: Let $C=\{-1,1\}\subset\mathbb R$. It is nonempty. If $y\notin C$, put $\delta=\min(|y-1|,|y+1|)>0$. For any $z$ with $|z-y|<\delta/2$, [F3] gives $|z-1|\ge|y-1|-|z-y|>\delta/2>0$ and $|z+1|>0$, so this ball misses $C$. Thus $\mathbb R\setminus C$ is open and $C$ is closed by [F2].

For input $y=0$, both points of $C$ have distance $1$ by [F1], and these are all the points in $C$. Hence the nearest-point set is exactly $\{-1,1\}$, which is not a singleton. The claimed unique projection fails for this nonconvex closed set.

Let two spheres of radii $r_1,r_2>0$ and masses $m_1,m_2>0$ have centers $q_1,q_2\in\mathbb R^d$ at contact, so $\|q_1-q_2\|_2=r_1+r_2$. Let $n=(q_1-q_2)/(r_1+r_2)$ be the unit normal pointing from center $2$ to center $1$. Suppose the pre-impact relative normal velocity is $v_n=\langle v_1^- - v_2^-,n\rangle<0$. For prescribed restitution $e\in[0,1]$, put
$$\alpha=\frac1{m_1}+\frac1{m_2},\qquad J=-\frac{(1+e)v_n}{\alpha},\qquad v_1^+=v_1^-+\frac{J}{m_1}n,\quad v_2^+=v_2^- -\frac{J}{m_2}n.$$
Then $J>0$, total linear momentum is conserved, the post-impact relative normal velocity is $-e v_n$, each tangential velocity is unchanged, and
$$K^+-K^-=-\frac{(1-e^2)v_n^2}{2(1/m_1+1/m_2)}\le0,$$
where $K^\pm=\tfrac12m_1\|v_1^\pm\|_2^2+\tfrac12m_2\|v_2^\pm\|_2^2$. This is a single frictionless binary impulse law; it asserts no existence or uniqueness for simultaneous or frictional multi-contact.

derivations.claim: The inverse reduced mass is $1/m_1+1/m_2=1/2+1/3=5/6$, and $v_n=\langle -n-n,n\rangle=-2$. Thus $J=-(3/2)(-2)/(5/6)=18/5$. The post-impact velocities are $v_1^+=-n+(9/5)n=(4/5)n$ and $v_2^+=n-(6/5)n=(-1/5)n$.

Total momentum is $2(-n)+3n=n$ before impact and $2(4n/5)+3(-n/5)=n$ after. The relative normal speed after impact is $4/5-(-1/5)=1=-e v_n$. The kinetic energies are $K^-=1+3/2=5/2$ and $K^+=16/25+3/50=7/10$, so $K^+-K^-=-9/5$, matching $-(3/4)\cdot4/(2\cdot5/6)=-9/5$ from [F1].

Input a gap $q\ge0$, velocity $v\in\mathbb R$, constant acceleration $a\in\mathbb R$, step horizon $h>0$, mass $m>0$, restitution $e\in[0,1]$, and a finite root-search budget $B\in\mathbb N$. Define the free-flight gap and velocity by $g(s)=q+sv+\tfrac12as^2$ and $w(s)=v+as$ for $0\le s\le h$. Return one of `impact`, `free-flight`, or `unresolved` as follows.

1. If $q=0$ and $v<0$, set the incoming-root list to $\{0\}$ and the event time to $s=0$.
2. Otherwise, if $q=v=a=0$, set the incoming-root list to the empty set: then $g\equiv0$ and $w\equiv0$, so there is no root with incoming velocity. In every other case find all distinct roots $s\in(0,h]$ of $g(s)=0$ for which $w(s)<0$, in increasing order. The root search must certify that this list is complete within budget $B$. If it cannot, return `unresolved`.
3. If the list is nonempty, take its first root, set $v^-=w(s)$ and $J=-m(1+e)v^-$, and return `impact` with event time $s$, contact gap $0$, impulse $J$, and post-impact velocity $v^+=-e v^-$.
4. If there is no incoming root, certify $g(r)\ge0$ for every $r\in[0,h]$. If this fails or cannot be certified within $B$, return `unresolved`; otherwise return `free-flight` with endpoint $(g(h),w(h))$ and impulse $0$.

The procedure stops after this first event and returns at the event time. It does not integrate the post-impact mode, sustained contact, or repeated impacts. When $g\not\equiv0$, its exact algebraic branch needs to classify at most the two roots of a nonzero polynomial of degree at most two; when $g\equiv0$, it takes the explicit no-incoming-root branch above. A numerical root solver must report a certificate or `unresolved` when its budget is exhausted.

For any resolved output of [[alg-one-dimensional-first-impact-with-restitution]], let $q_*$ be the reported gap (zero at an impact, the free-flight endpoint gap otherwise), let $J$ be the reported impulse, and let $v_*$ be the reported endpoint velocity. Then $q_*\ge0$, $J\ge0$, and $q_*J=0$. On a free-flight branch, $J=0$ and $m v_*=m v+mah$. On an impact branch at time $s$, with incoming velocity $v^-=v+as$, the post-impact velocity satisfies $m v^+=m v^-+J$ and
$$\frac12m(v^+)^2-\frac12m(v^-)^2=-\frac12m(1-e^2)(v^-)^2\le0.$$
When $a=0$, the full resolved step has nonincreasing kinetic energy. For $a\ne0$, the displayed energy statement concerns only the instantaneous impact jump; work during free flight is not covered by it.

derivations.claim: The free-flight gap is $g(s)=1-2s$, whose unique root on $(0,1]$ is $s=1/2$ with $v^-=-2<0$. Hence the step returns an impact at contact for both restitution values.

If $e=0$, then $J=4$ and $v^+=0$; if $e=1$, then $J=8$ and $v^+=2$. In both cases $q_*J=0$ and $J\ge0$. The pre-impact kinetic energy is $\tfrac12(2)(-2)^2=4$; the post-impact energies are $0$ and $4$, respectively. The momentum identities are $2(-2)+4=0$ and $2(-2)+8=4=2(2)$. These equal the inelastic and elastic endpoints of [F2].

Let $d\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $P_C(y)$ be the unique nearest point in $C$ to $y$, whose existence and uniqueness are [[thm-nearest-point-in-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]]. For $x\in C$, set
$$N_C(x)=\{n\in\mathbb R^d:\langle n,z-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }z\in C\};$$
for $x\notin C$, set $N_C(x)=\varnothing$. On $C$ this is the outward normal cone of [[def-kkt-residual-and-normal-cone]]. The projection variational inequality of [[lem-projection-onto-a-closed-convex-set-has-the-variational-inequality]] says $P_C(y)=p$ exactly when $p\in C$ and $y-p\in N_C(p)$.

For $T>0$, a solution of the projected contact dynamics with forcing $f:[0,T]\times C\to\mathbb R^d$ and initial state $x_0\in C$ is an absolutely continuous map $x:[0,T]\to C$ satisfying
$$f(t,x(t))-\dot x(t)\in N_C(x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in[0,T].$$
Equivalently, $\dot x(t)+N_C(x(t))\ni f(t,x(t))$. For an integer $N\ge1$, put $h=T/N$, $t_k=kh$, and define the exact explicit projection Euler nodes by
$$x_{k+1}=P_C\bigl(x_k+h f(t_k,x_k)\bigr),\qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1,$$
starting from $x_0$. Its affine interpolant joins consecutive nodes linearly on each interval $[t_k,t_{k+1}]$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

derivations.claim: For $C=[0,\infty)$, $N_C(0)=(-\infty,0]$ because $\langle n,z\rangle=nz\le0$ for every $z\ge0$. Thus $x(t)=0$ solves the projected inclusion: $f-\dot x=-1\in N_C(0)$. For $y_\kappa(t)=-(1-e^{-\kappa t})/\kappa$, [F2] gives $y_\kappa'=-e^{-\kappa t}=-1-\kappa y_\kappa$; [F3]–[F4] give $0<e^{-\kappa t}<1$ for $t>0$, so $y_\kappa(t)<0$ and the penalty equation holds. Also $0\le1-e^{-\kappa t}\le1$, so $\sup_{0\le t\le2h}|y_\kappa(t)|\le1/\kappa$ and the exact penalty paths converge uniformly to the constrained path as $\kappa\to\infty$.

Explicit Euler gives $y_1=-h$, since the penalty is zero at $y_0=0$. At $y_1=-h$, the next value is $y_2=-h+h(-1+\kappa h)=\kappa h^2-2h$. For fixed $h>0$, $y_2\to+\infty$ as $\kappa\to\infty$, despite the continuous penalty solutions converging uniformly to zero. Therefore the timestep must be controlled as stiffness grows; this example makes no general penalty-to-rigid-impact limit claim.
