Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, let $U_0$ be unitary, and set $H_0=U_0^*AU_0$. For $j=1,\ldots,m$, suppose

$$H_j=P_j^*(H_{j-1}+E_j+D_j)P_j,$$

where each $P_j$ is unitary, $E_j$ is a local arithmetic perturbation, and $D_j$ is a local deflation perturbation. Then for $U_m=U_0P_1\cdots P_m$ there is a matrix $\Delta$ such that

$$H_m=U_m^*(A+\Delta)U_m,\qquad \|\Delta\|_F\le\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(\|E_j\|_F+\|D_j\|_F\bigr).$$

The assertion also holds over $\mathbb R$ with orthogonal factors.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

derivations.claim: If $m=0$, take $Q=Z=I_n$ and $\Delta_A=\Delta_B=0$; the equations and bound hold. For $m\ge1$, form the $3n\times3n$ block matrix $M_j=\begin{pmatrix}0&A_j&B_j\\0&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $P_j=\operatorname{diag}(Q_j,Z_j,Z_j)$. Put the local $E_j^A,E_j^B$ in the first block row of $\mathcal E_j$ and the local $D_j^A,D_j^B$ in the first block row of $\mathcal D_j$, with all other blocks zero. Then [F2] and the stated updates give $M_j=P_j^*(M_{j-1}+\mathcal E_j+\mathcal D_j)P_j$. Each $P_j$ is unitary/orthogonal because its diagonal blocks are unitary/orthogonal.

For $m\ge1$, apply [F1] to the augmented sequence. Its accumulated perturbation has only the two first-row, off-diagonal blocks, because conjugation by each block diagonal $P_j$ preserves those block positions. Call them $\Delta_A,\Delta_B$. the **B-norm** by
$$\|x\|_B:=\|L^*x\|_2=\sqrt{x^*Bx},$$
and the **B-dual residual norm** by
$$\|r\|_{B^{-1}}:=\|L^{-1}r\|_2 =\sqrt{r^*B^{-1}r}.$$
The B-orthogonality condition is $x^*By=0$; since $B=B^*$ it is equivalent
to $\langle x,y\rangle_B=0$.

restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and

self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of

derivations.claim: By [F2], $L$ is lower triangular with positive diagonal. [F3] gives $\det L\ne0$, and [F4] therefore makes $L$ invertible. Hence $C=L^{-1}AL^{-*}$ is defined. Taking adjoints and using $A=A^*$ gives $C^*=L^{-1}AL^{-*}=C$.

Regard $C$ as a real or complex endomorphism with the Euclidean inner product. In the real case [F5] applies; in the complex case $C=C^*$ implies $C$ is normal, so [F6] applies. Thus there are orthonormal $y_i$ and real $\lambda_i$ with $Cy_i=\lambda_i y_i$.

Set $x_i=L^{-*}y_i$. Then $Ax_i=AL^{-*}y_i=L Cy_i=\lambda_iLy_i=\lambda_iBx_i,$ and $x_i^*Bx_j=y_i^*L^{-1}LL^*L^{-*}y_j=y_i^*y_j=\delta_{ij}.$ The invertible change of variables $L^{-*}$ sends the basis $(y_i)$ to a basis $(x_i)$.

For every $\lambda\in\mathbb C$, $A-\lambda B=L(C-\lambda I)L^*$, so $\det(A-\lambda B)=\det(L)\det(C-\lambda I)\det(L^*).$ The diagonalisation from step 2.1 expresses $C=UDU^*$ with $D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)$ and $U$ unitary. By [F7], $\det(C-\lambda I)=\det(U)\det(D-\lambda I)\det(U^*)$ and $\det(U)\det(U^*)=\det(UU^*)=\det I=1$. Applying [F3] to the diagonal matrix gives $\det(C-\lambda I)=\prod_i(\lambda_i-\lambda)$. Also $\det(L)$ and $\det(L^*)$ are nonzero by step 1.1, so the finite roots of $\det(A-\lambda B)$ are exactly the real $\lambda_i$. Finally $\det(B)=\det(L)\det(L^*)\ne0$, so $[1:0]$ is not a homogeneous root.

Input $A,B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, with
$\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. All transformations here are exact.
Let $Q=Z=I_n$.

For a target pair $(a,b)$, define the left factor $L(a,b)$ deterministically. Use $I_2$ if $a=b=0$. Otherwise put $r=(|a|^2+|b|^2)^{1/2}$ and $L=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-\overline s&c\end{pmatrix}$. Over $\mathbb R$, take $c=a/r$, $s=b/r$. Over $\mathbb C$, if $a=0$ take $c=0$, $s=\overline b/|b|$; otherwise take $\phi=a/|a|$, $c=|a|/r$, $s=\phi\overline b/r$. Thus $L(a,b)(a,b)^T=(\gamma,0)^T$ with $|\gamma|=r$. Set $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and define the right factor
$$R(a,b)=J L(\overline b,\overline a)^*J.$$
Then $(a,b)R(a,b)=(0,\eta)$ with $|\eta|=r$; the zero pair again uses identity. These factors are real orthogonal over $\mathbb R$ or unitary over $\mathbb C$, as direct multiplication shows in [[thm-householder-reflectors-and-givens-transformations-are-unitary-and-annihilate-targeted-entries]]; the right identity follows by taking adjoints of the left annihilation of $(\overline b,\overline a)^T$ and reversing the coordinates. Use their identity embeddings on the two rows or columns specified by each step below.
1. Triangularise $B$ by left rotations. For $j=1,\ldots,n$ and, in descending
order, $i=n,n-1,\ldots,j+1$, set
$$L=L(B_{i-1,j},B_{i,j}),\quad A\leftarrow LA,\quad B\leftarrow LB, \quad Q\leftarrow QL^*.$$

2. Reduce $A$ to upper Hessenberg form while restoring triangularity of $B$.
For $j=1,\ldots,n-2$ and, in descending order, $i=n,n-1,\ldots,j+2$, set
$$L=L(A_{i-1,j},A_{i,j}),\quad A\leftarrow LA,\quad B\leftarrow LB, \quad Q\leftarrow QL^*,$$
then set
$$R=R(B_{i,i-1},B_{i,i}),\quad A\leftarrow AR,\quad B\leftarrow BR, \quad Z\leftarrow ZR.$$

Return $Q,Z,H=A,T=B$, where $H$ is upper Hessenberg and $T$ is upper
triangular in the senses of
[[def-upper-hessenberg-and-real-symmetric-tridiagonal-matrices]] and
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]. The outputs are represented by the exact products of
the recorded Givens factors; no dense rounded factor is asserted unitary.

Let $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$.

1. Every Householder reflector $H_v=I-2vv^*$ is orthogonal or unitary.
2. For every nonzero $z\in \mathbb F^m$, there is a Householder reflector $H$
   such that $Hz=\alpha e_1$ with $|\alpha|=\|z\|_2$.
3. For every pair $(a,b)\in \mathbb F^2$ not both zero, there is a real or
   complex Givens transformation $G$ such that
   $$G\binom{a}{b}=\binom{\alpha}{0}$$
   with $|\alpha|=(|a|^2+|b|^2)^{1/2}$.

derivations.claim: The triangularisation loops range over finitely many pairs $(i,j)$. For fixed $j$, descending $i$ zeros $B_{i,j}$ without changing already cleared entries below it. The rotations act on rows with indices at least $j$, whose entries in columns less than $j$ are zero by upper triangularity; hence they do not create below-diagonal entries in earlier columns. After all columns, $B$ is upper triangular.

For $j=1$ there are no earlier Hessenberg columns, so the base condition is vacuous. For general $j$, assume every earlier column already has the Hessenberg pattern. Descend through $i$; the left factor zeros $A_{i,j}$. Since $B$ was upper triangular, this left factor can create below-diagonal fill only at $B_{i,i-1}$; the paired right factor zeros that entry. It creates no further below-diagonal entries in $B$, because rows below $i$ are zero in columns $i-1,i$. The right factor does not touch column $j$ because $i-1\ge j+1$, and the left factors preserve all earlier Hessenberg columns, whose entries in rows $i-1,i$ are already zero. Thus after the loop, column $j$ of $A$ is zero below row $j+1$.

Induction over $j=1,\ldots,n-2$ proves that the final $A$ is upper Hessenberg and $B$ remains upper triangular. Each left update $A\leftarrow LA$ is matched by $Q\leftarrow QL^*$, and each right update $A\leftarrow AR$ is matched by $Z\leftarrow ZR$; direct substitution preserves $A_{\rm current}=Q^*A_{\rm input}Z$ and $B_{\rm current}=Q^*B_{\rm input}Z$. The finite loops terminate, proving the claim.

Let $A=A^*$ and let $B=B^*$ be positive definite in
$\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, where $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
If $B=LL^*$ is its Cholesky factorisation, then
$$C=L^{-1}AL^{-*}$$
is self-adjoint and has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues
$\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$. The vectors
$$x_i=L^{-*}y_i\quad (i=1,\ldots,n)$$
form a basis satisfying $Ax_i=\lambda_iBx_i$ and
$x_i^*Bx_j=\delta_{ij}$. The generalized eigenvalues of $(A,B)$ are exactly
$[\lambda_i:1]$; none is infinite.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$A,B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$. The **matrix pencil** determined by $(A,B)$ is
$A-\lambda B$. Its determinant polynomial is
$f(\lambda)=\det(A-\lambda B)$, with real coefficients viewed as complex
coefficients when $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. The pencil is **regular** if $f$ is
not the zero polynomial; otherwise it is **singular**.

For $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$ not both zero, put
$$p(\alpha,\beta)=\det(\beta A-\alpha B).$$
A **homogeneous generalized eigenvalue pair** is an equivalence class of such
pairs satisfying $p(\alpha,\beta)=0$, where $(\alpha,\beta)$ and
$(c\alpha,c\beta)$ represent the same pair for every $c\in\mathbb C\setminus
\{0\}$. If $\beta\ne0$, the associated finite generalized eigenvalue is
$\lambda=\alpha/\beta$; if $\beta=0$, the pair is an infinite generalized
eigenvalue. The pair $(0,0)$ is never an eigenvalue pair.
Write $\sigma(A,B)$ for the set of finite ratios $\alpha/\beta$ among these
homogeneous eigenvalue pairs.

The QZ results on this page assume a regular pencil. They make no assertion
about Kronecker structure or eigenvalues of a singular pencil.

derivations.claim: Let $y=L^*x$ and $C=L^{-1}AL^{-*}$. Since $L^{-1}Bx=L^*x=y$, the transformed residual is $L^{-1}r=L^{-1}(Ax-\mu Bx)=(C-\mu I)y.$ By [F1], $\|y\|_2=\|x\|_B$ and $\|L^{-1}r\|_2=\|r\|_{B^{-1}}$.

Let $u_1,\ldots,u_n$ be the orthonormal eigenbasis of $C$ from [F2], with real eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$. By [F3], these are exactly the finite generalized eigenvalues in $\sigma(A,B)$. Write $y=\sum_i c_i u_i$. Then $\|(C-\mu I)y\|_2^2 =\sum_i |c_i|^2|\lambda_i-\mu|^2 \ge \operatorname{dist}(\mu,\{\lambda_i\})^2\sum_i|c_i|^2 =\operatorname{dist}(\mu,\sigma(A,B))^2\|y\|_2^2.$ Taking square roots and applying step 1.1 proves the bound.

citations.quote:
Every regular finite square pencil $(A,B)$ over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ has
at least one homogeneous generalized eigenvalue pair $[\alpha:\beta]$ over
$\mathbb C$.

If $(A,B)$ is a regular pencil and $x\in\mathbb C^n$ satisfies $Ax=0$ and
$Bx=0$, then $x=0$.

Let $n_1,n_2\ge1$, $n=n_1+n_2$, and let $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be
block upper triangular with the same two-block partition of sizes $n_1,n_2$,
with diagonal blocks $A_{11},A_{22}$ and
$B_{11},B_{22}$. For every $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$,
$$\det(\beta A-\alpha B) =\det(\beta A_{11}-\alpha B_{11})\det(\beta A_{22}-\alpha B_{22}).$$

Let $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$.

1. Every Householder reflector $H_v=I-2vv^*$ is orthogonal or unitary.
2. For every nonzero $z\in \mathbb F^m$, there is a Householder reflector $H$
   such that $Hz=\alpha e_1$ with $|\alpha|=\|z\|_2$.
3. For every pair $(a,b)\in \mathbb F^2$ not both zero, there is a real or
   complex Givens transformation $G$ such that
   $$G\binom{a}{b}=\binom{\alpha}{0}$$
   with $|\alpha|=(|a|^2+|b|^2)^{1/2}$.

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $T:V\to V$ be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space over
a field $F$. Then $T$ is invertible if and only if $\det(T)\neq0$.
Let $D$ be an integral domain. A nonzero polynomial $f\in D[x]$ of degree $n$ has at most $n$ distinct roots in $D$.

Let $(A,B)$ be a regular pencil of order $n$. A **complex generalized Schur
form** is a factorisation
$$Q^*AZ=S,\qquad Q^*BZ=T,$$
where $Q,Z\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ are unitary in the sense of
[[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]], and $S,T$ are
upper triangular as in
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]. For its
$i$th one-by-one diagonal block, $[s_{ii}:t_{ii}]$ is the
**diagonal homogeneous pair**.

For real $A,B$, a **real generalized Schur form** has
$$Q^TAZ=S,\qquad Q^TBZ=T,$$
where $Q,Z$ are orthogonal, $S$ is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks
of size one or two, and $T$ is upper triangular. Each one-by-one diagonal
block has a nonzero real homogeneous pair. For a two-by-two diagonal block
$(S_{kk},T_{kk})$, the **diagonal homogeneous roots** are the zeros of
$\det(\beta S_{kk}-\alpha T_{kk})$ in $[\alpha:\beta]$; such a block has a
nonreal conjugate pair of finite roots. A singular pencil is outside this
definition.

If $M\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and $\det M=0$, then there is a nonzero vector $v\in\mathbb F^n$ with
$Mv=0$.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

derivations.claim: We prove the statement by induction on $n$, with the empty trailing pencil allowed after a final block is removed. For $n=1$, regularity says the scalar pair $(A,B)$ is not $(0,0)$, and $Q=Z=[1]$ gives the required form. Now let $n>1$ and assume the result for smaller regular pencils.

Choose a homogeneous eigenvalue pair $[\alpha: eta]$ by [F1]. Its homogeneous determinant is zero, so [F10] gives a nonzero vector $v$ in the kernel over $\mathbb C$. For real input and a real projective root, rescale $[\alpha: eta]$ to real coordinates and apply [F10] over $\mathbb R$. If $ eta
e0$, put $\lambda=\alpha/ eta$; then $Av=\lambda Bv$. If $Bv=0$, this also gives $Av=0$, contrary to [F2], so $Bv
e0$. If $ eta=0$, then $Bv=0$ and [F2] gives $Av
e0$.

If the input field is complex, or if the selected root for real input is real, use a one-dimensional block. Set $q=Bv$ in the finite case and $q=Av$ in the infinite case. Both vectors are nonzero by step 1.2. By [F4], choose unitary/orthogonal alignments $Lq=\gamma e_1$ and $Rv=\eta e_1$ and set $Q=L^*$, $Z=R^*$. Then $Q^*q=\gamma e_1$ and $Z^*v=\eta e_1$, so $Q^*AZ$ and $Q^*BZ$ have zeros below their first entries in the first column. The leading diagonal pair is nonzero: in the finite case its $B$ entry is nonzero, and in the infinite case its $A$ entry is nonzero.

If the input is real and the selected root is nonreal, then $ eta
e0$; write $\lambda=\alpha/ eta=a+ib$ with $b
e0$ and write the vector from step 1.2 as $v=x+iy$ in $\ker(A-\lambda B)$. The real vectors $x,y$ are linearly independent. If they were dependent, $v$ would be a nonzero complex multiple of a nonzero real vector $w$, so $(A-\lambda B)w=0$. If $Bw=0$, then $Aw=0$, contradicting [F2]. If $Bw
e0$, a coordinate with $(Bw)_i
e0$ gives $\lambda=(Aw)_i/(Bw)_i\in\mathbb R$, contradicting $b
e0$. Put $X=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{x,y\}$ and $Y=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{Bx,By\}$. Separating real and imaginary parts gives $Ax=aBx-bBy$ and $Ay=bBx+aBy$, so $A(X)\subseteq Y$. If $\dim Y<2$, then for each $\mu\in\mathbb C$ the map $(A-\mu B):X_{\mathbb C}	o Y_{\mathbb C}$ has a nonzero kernel because its domain has dimension two and its range has dimension at most one. Hence $A-\mu B$ is not invertible, so [F7] gives $\det(A-\mu B)=0$ for every $\mu$, contradicting regularity and [F8]. Thus $\dim Y=2$.

Apply [F5] to obtain orthonormal bases $z_1,z_2$ of $X$ and $q_1,q_2$ of $Y$, choosing $q_1,q_2$ by Gram–Schmidt on $Bz_1,Bz_2$. The restriction $B|_X:X\to Y$ sends a basis to the independent pair $Bz_1,Bz_2$ and is therefore an isomorphism. Its matrix in these bases is $B_{11}=Q_1^TBZ_1$, so $B_{11}$ is invertible and [F7] gives $\det(B_{11})\ne0$; the Gram–Schmidt choice makes this matrix upper triangular. Extend these bases by orthonormal bases of $Y^\perp$ and $X^\perp$ using [F6]. In these full bases, the first two columns of both transformed matrices are supported in the first two rows. Let $P$ be the invertible change-of-basis matrix from $(x,y)$ to $(z_1,z_2)$. The equations in step 2.2 give $A[z_1\ z_2]=B[z_1\ z_2]C$, where $C=P^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}P$. Thus the leading blocks satisfy $A_{11}=B_{11}C$, and $C$ is similar to $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}$. Consequently $\det(A_{11}-\mu B_{11}) =\det(B_{11})\det(C-\mu I) =\det(B_{11})\bigl((a-\mu)^2+b^2\bigr)$ is a nonzero polynomial with roots $a\pm ib$.

In either the one-dimensional case of step 2.1 or the two-dimensional case of step 3.1, the transformed pair has a nonzero leading block determinant polynomial $g$. The transformed full pencil is regular: by [F8] choose $\mu$ with $\det(A-\mu B)\ne0$; the unitary or orthogonal changes of basis preserve invertibility. By [F7], the transformed determinant at this $\mu$ is also nonzero, so the transformed full determinant polynomial is nonzero. If there is no trailing block, the transformed pencil is just its leading block and this already proves regularity. If the trailing block is nonempty, both block sizes are positive, so [F3] factors the full determinant polynomial as $g$ times the trailing determinant. A product of two nonzero complex polynomials is nonzero because their leading nonzero coefficients have nonzero product. Since $g$ and the full determinant are nonzero, the trailing determinant is nonzero, so the trailing pencil is regular.

If the trailing block is nonempty, apply the induction hypothesis to it and extend its left and right transformations by identity matrices on the leading block. If it is empty, no further transformation is needed. This produces the stated upper triangular complex form or real block upper triangular form with upper triangular second factor.

The left and right basis changes are invertible, so [F7] shows that they preserve singularity of every homogeneous pencil matrix. If there is one diagonal block, its determinant is the full determinant. With at least two blocks, split off the first diagonal block and apply [F3] repeatedly; every split has positive block sizes. The resulting product is the nonzero determinant polynomial of the regular transformed pencil, so each factor is nonzero by the leading-coefficient argument in step 4.1. Thus a homogeneous pair is a root of the full determinant exactly when it is a root of at least one diagonal block determinant. The basis changes preserve this root set, which proves the claim.

Input a regular pencil $(A,B)$ with $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$,
$n\ge1$, a nonnegative integer sweep budget $N$, and a finite stored real tolerance
$\tau\ge0$. Real input data are embedded in $\mathbb C$. Scalar updates of the
stored matrices use the operationwise model of
[[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]].
Use the canonical stored Givens generator and application order of
[[alg-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-updates]], with the common-pair
orientations and explicit coefficients $v,h,\eta$ of
[[lem-qz-two-sided-local-computed-update-bound]]. Generate each rotation ONCE
and apply its same stored coefficients to BOTH matrices. Retain the exact
normalized unitary representatives as product records, never as purported
stored dense unitary matrices. Left rotations annihilate a column's second
entry; right rotations annihilating a row's first entry use the coordinate
reversal/adjoint construction of that lemma. After each genuine matrix target
application write only its intended target to exact zero and include that
write in the local coefficient $\eta$. An external-vector application has
coefficient $v$ and no matrix-target overwrite. Local roundoff certification
requires $0<u<1$; otherwise retain diagnostics with `certificate-inconclusive`. Record each elementary
rotation separately. If the source cannot produce its admissible factor,
return `range-failure` or `certificate-inconclusive` with diagnostics.

1. Execute the finite index loops of
[[alg-generalized-hessenberg-triangular-reduction]] with these COMPUTED common
rotations: triangularize $B$ with left targets $B_{i,j}$; then reduce $A$ with
left targets $A_{i,j}$ followed by right targets $B_{i,i-1}$. Every application
updates both whole arrays. The exact initializer and
[[prop-generalized-hessenberg-triangular-reduction-preserves-form-and-equivalence]]
supply the index schedule and support induction, not exact rounded
reconstruction. Retain each local factor and residual defined against its
exact representative. Include structural target writes in that local
arithmetic residual. Record all OTHER explicit zero writes separately: their
post-action perturbations are pulled back by the local factor adjoints before
entering the pre-action $D_j^A,D_j^B$ ledger. A pure tolerance write is an
identity-factor stage. Never count a structural write twice.

Initialize the sweep counter to zero. Process active blocks in increasing first
index, splitting them at exact zero subdiagonals of $H$. In each deflation
pass execute step 2, then repeat step 3 for the smallest available non-isolated
zero diagonal of $T$ until none remains or a status exits. Test step 5 before
starting a sweep: if the target is absent and the counter equals $N$, return
`budget-exhausted`. Otherwise increment the counter, execute step 4 on all
remaining active blocks, and repeat the deflation pass. In particular $N=0$
permits initialization/deflation but no step-4 sweep.

2. On each active block $H_{a:b,a:b},T_{a:b,a:b}$, apply the following deflation
tests before a sweep. For $i=a,\ldots,b-1$, set $H_{i+1,i}$ to zero when
$$|H_{i+1,i}|\le\tau\bigl(|H_{i,i}|+|H_{i+1,i+1}|\bigr),$$
and record its old value in $D^A$. For $k=a,\ldots,b$, set $T_{k,k}$ to zero when
$$|T_{k,k}|\le\tau\bigl(|T_{k-1,k}|+|T_{k,k+1}|\bigr),$$
using zero for a missing boundary term, and record the old value in $D^B$.
Evaluate each displayed modulus by the canonical rounded scaled two-component
norm; evaluate its additions and tolerance product with the declared rounded
real operations, then compare the stored finite values exactly. Excluded
operations return `range-failure`. The tests mean these rounded comparisons,
not an assertion about exact moduli at the threshold. Save the actual old
entries, so their deflation perturbations remain exact regardless of the test.
A one-by-one diagonal pair at $k$ is isolated when $H_{k,k-1}=0$ and
$H_{k+1,k}=0$, omitting a boundary entry when $k=a$ or $k=b$. If it has
$T_{k,k}=0$ and $H_{k,k}\ne0$, report an infinite candidate for the computed pencil and deflate it
from the active block. If the isolated diagonal pair is $(0,0)$, return
`singular-pencil-suspected` without assigning an eigenvalue.

3. To move a non-isolated zero $T_{k,k}$ to the top of its active block, for
$j=k-1,k-2,\ldots,a$ apply a right Givens factor on columns $j,j+1$ that
zeros $T_{j,j}$, then, when $j+2\le b$, a left Givens factor on rows
$j+1,j+2$ that zeros the resulting bulge $H_{j+2,j}$. Finally, when $a<b$,
apply a left Givens factor on rows $a,a+1$ to zero $H_{a+1,a}$. Record all rounded update residuals and target writes. If this isolates $(H_{a,a},T_{a,a})=(h,0)$ with $h\ne0$, report
the infinite candidate and remove the first row/column from the active block.
If the isolated pair is $(0,0)$, return `singular-pencil-suspected`; if isolation
fails, return `certificate-inconclusive`. Each successful isolation removes
one index, so at most $n$ such removals occur.

4. For each remaining active block with more than one row in the current
sweep, choose the homogeneous shift $[\alpha:\beta]=[H_{b,b}:T_{b,b}]$ if this pair is nonzero and
$T_{b,b}\ne0$; if $T_{b,b}=0$, use $[0:1]$. Form
$$x=(\beta H_{a:b,a:b}-\alpha T_{a:b,a:b})e_1.$$
Compute the first two components of $x$ using the declared rounded complex
products/subtractions and generate a left Givens factor from that stored
external vector. Apply it to both matrices without a matrix-target overwrite.
Its rounding changes the selected factor, not its application certificate. Apply a right Givens factor to columns $1,2$ to restore triangularity
of $T$. For $j=2,\ldots,b-a$, alternate a left Givens factor on rows $j,j+1$
to zero the current Hessenberg bulge and a right Givens factor on columns
$j,j+1$ to zero the resulting subdiagonal entry of $T$. Update and retain the
products $Q,Z$; record every local residual including its structural target
write. Indices $1,2,j,j+1$ here are relative to the active block; apply the
embedded transformations to the entire pair, retaining the transformed off-block data. All divisions by a generalized eigenvalue ratio are avoided.

5. After each infinite isolation and before every successful return, scan all
isolated diagonal pairs. Any $(0,0)$ pair returns `singular-pencil-suspected`
without an eigenvalue. Stop with `qz-computed` only when $H$ is upper triangular
and every diagonal pair is nonzero. Otherwise stop after $N$ sweeps with
`budget-exhausted`. Range failures return `range-failure` with partial factors;
unavailable local certificates return `certificate-inconclusive`. Neither a
rounded diagnostic nor a tolerance-induced infinite candidate asserts an exact
infinite eigenvalue of the original pencil.

For local-accumulation bounds use $\ell_j=\eta$ for matrix-target actions and
$\ell_j=v$ for external-vector/raw actions, plus the separately saved actual
tolerance perturbations. For an independent residual certificate execute the
factor-action/column procedure of
[[lem-qz-two-sided-local-computed-update-bound]]: use stored raw kernels without
zero overwrites, propagate their $v$ allowances, use
[[lem-rounded-linear-and-normal-residual-certificates]] only on STORED matvec
inputs, and include the final subtraction allowance. Exact normalized factor
entries are not silently treated as stored inputs. Evaluate each certificate
using the finite exact real-controller expression trees/loops in the local
lemma and component absolute sums as norm upper bounds. Controller operations
are separate from rounded update arithmetic; for rational/binary stored data
and rational $u$ this is exact rational computation. No opaque certification
oracle is used. Failure of this residual route's dimension/range hypotheses
makes that route inconclusive and does not invalidate a valid independent
local-accumulation bound. Always retain available diagnostics.

The output is $(Q,S,T,Z,\text{status})$, the exact factor products when
available, the raw residuals $R_A=Q^*AZ-S$ and $R_B=Q^*BZ-T$, and the recorded
local arithmetic and deflation perturbations. The procedure asserts no
unconditional convergence or small-roundoff bound.

For every input of [[alg-generalized-hessenberg-triangular-reduction]], the
algorithm terminates and returns orthogonal/unitary $Q,Z$, an upper Hessenberg
matrix $H$, and an upper triangular matrix $T$ such that
$$H=Q^*AZ,\qquad T=Q^*BZ.$$

Let $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$.

1. Every Householder reflector $H_v=I-2vv^*$ is orthogonal or unitary.
2. For every nonzero $z\in \mathbb F^m$, there is a Householder reflector $H$
   such that $Hz=\alpha e_1$ with $|\alpha|=\|z\|_2$.
3. For every pair $(a,b)\in \mathbb F^2$ not both zero, there is a real or
   complex Givens transformation $G$ such that
   $$G\binom{a}{b}=\binom{\alpha}{0}$$
   with $|\alpha|=(|a|^2+|b|^2)^{1/2}$.

Let $n\ge1$, $m\ge0$, $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and
$A,B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$. Put $A_0=A$, $B_0=B$. For
$j=1,\ldots,m$, suppose exact unitary/orthogonal factors $Q_j,Z_j$ and local
arithmetic/deflation perturbations satisfy
$$A_j=Q_j^*(A_{j-1}+E_j^A+D_j^A)Z_j,$$
$$B_j=Q_j^*(B_{j-1}+E_j^B+D_j^B)Z_j.$$
Then with $Q=Q_1\cdots Q_m$ and $Z=Z_1\cdots Z_m$ (empty products are $I_n$)
there are perturbations
$\Delta_A,\Delta_B$ such that
$$A_m=Q^*(A+\Delta_A)Z,\qquad B_m=Q^*(B+\Delta_B)Z,$$
and
$$\sqrt{\|\Delta_A\|_F^2+\|\Delta_B\|_F^2} \le\sum_{j=1}^m\left( \sqrt{\|E_j^A\|_F^2+\|E_j^B\|_F^2} +\sqrt{\|D_j^A\|_F^2+\|D_j^B\|_F^2}\right).$$

Use the successful real/complex Givens arithmetic of
[[alg-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-updates]], with $0<u<1$.
For a matrix pair write $P(C,D)=(\|C\|_F^2+\|D\|_F^2)^{1/2}$ and put
$$a_2=\frac{1+u}{(1-u)^2}-1,\qquad q=\max\left\{\left(\frac{1+u}{1-u}\right)^3-1,\frac{(1+a_2)(1+6u)(1+u)}{(1-u)^3}-1\right\},$$
$$v=q+2(7u+6u^2)(1+q),\qquad h=u+2q+v,\qquad \eta=v+h.$$
Generate a single stored block $T_0=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-\overline s&c\end{pmatrix}$ from the selected target and use its same coefficients on BOTH matrices. Retain its exact unitary representative $U=T_0/\sqrt{c^2+|s|^2}$ as a factor record. Use the exact identity in the source's zero branch.

A raw common left or right action, without a target overwrite, has pair discrepancy at most $vP(C,D)$ from its exact representative. For an actual matrix target, overwrite only its intended annihilated entry with exact zero; this write has norm at most $h$ times the target pair norm. The complete action therefore satisfies
$$C_+=Q_0^*(C+E^C)Z_0,\qquad D_+=Q_0^*(D+E^D)Z_0,\qquad P(E^C,E^D)\le\ell P(C,D),$$
where $\ell=\eta$ for a target action and $\ell=v$ for a raw action; the unused factor is identity. Zero branches have zero discrepancy. A left action annihilates the second coordinate of a column. To annihilate the FIRST coordinate of a row $r=(a,b)$, let $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, generate $U$ from $(rJ)^*=(\overline b,\overline a)^T$, and use the right factor $JU^*J$, applying its stored adjoint/permuted coefficients. For a second-coordinate right target omit $J$. An external shift-vector action has no matrix-target overwrite. Grouped left/right coefficients $\ell_L,\ell_R$ compose to $\ell_L+\ell_R+\ell_L\ell_R$.

Post-action zero writes are pulled back by the exact local factor adjoints before they enter a pre-action perturbation ledger. Structural writes may be included in $E$ with $\eta$, or separately recorded with raw coefficient $v$ and write allowance $h$, never both. Tolerance deflations remain separate exact perturbations, without an $O(u)$ assertion.

There is also a concrete residual certificate for represented products $Q=Q_1\cdots Q_m$, $Z=Z_1\cdots Z_m$. Apply stored raw right-factor kernels to $e_k$ in reverse order to approximate $Ze_k$; apply stored raw adjoint left-factor kernels in order $Q_1^*,\ldots,Q_m^*$ to approximate $Q^*$ action. Omit all structural overwrites in these vector actions. For a stored current vector $y$ and discrepancy allowance $e$, propagate
$$e_{\rm next}=e+v\|y\|_2.$$
With $\widehat z\approx Ze_k$ and allowance $e_z$, compute $\widehat a=\operatorname{fl}(A\widehat z)$ by sequential stored-input dot products. When $(n-1)u<1$, its allowance relative to $AZe_k$ is
$$e_a=g_n\|A\|_F\|\widehat z\|_2+\|A\|_F e_z,\qquad g_n=\frac{1+6u}{1-(n-1)u}-1.$$
Propagate through the $Q^*$ kernels, obtaining $\widehat w,e_w$, then form $\widehat r_k=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat w-S_{:k})$ with allowance
$$e_k=e_w+u(\|\widehat w\|_2+\|S_{:k}\|_2).$$
Thus $\|Q^*AZ-S\|_F\le\sum_{k=1}^n(\|\widehat r_k\|_2+e_k)$; repeat with $B,T$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$A,B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$. The **matrix pencil** determined by $(A,B)$ is
$A-\lambda B$. Its determinant polynomial is
$f(\lambda)=\det(A-\lambda B)$, with real coefficients viewed as complex
coefficients when $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. The pencil is **regular** if $f$ is
not the zero polynomial; otherwise it is **singular**.

For $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$ not both zero, put
$$p(\alpha,\beta)=\det(\beta A-\alpha B).$$
A **homogeneous generalized eigenvalue pair** is an equivalence class of such
pairs satisfying $p(\alpha,\beta)=0$, where $(\alpha,\beta)$ and
$(c\alpha,c\beta)$ represent the same pair for every $c\in\mathbb C\setminus
\{0\}$. If $\beta\ne0$, the associated finite generalized eigenvalue is
$\lambda=\alpha/\beta$; if $\beta=0$, the pair is an infinite generalized
eigenvalue. The pair $(0,0)$ is never an eigenvalue pair.
Write $\sigma(A,B)$ for the set of finite ratios $\alpha/\beta$ among these
homogeneous eigenvalue pairs.

The QZ results on this page assume a regular pencil. They make no assertion
about Kronecker structure or eigenvalues of a singular pencil.

routine_steps.claim: The matrix $M$ is positive definite because $u^TMu=2u_1^2+u_2^2>0$ for $u\ne0$. Also $u^TKu=2u_1^2+2(u_1-u_2)^2+u_2^2>0$ for $u\ne0$. Compute $w$ by sequential summation of all $2r$ rounded real component squares of $v$, and $\widehat\tau=\operatorname{fl}(2/w)$. Compute $d=\operatorname{fl}(v^*B)$, $p=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau v)$, $Z=\operatorname{fl}(pd)$, and $\widehat B=\operatorname{fl}(B-Z)$. Return $C_+=[\widehat\alpha e_1\;\widehat B]$, writing exact zeros below the target diagonal, and store $v,\widehat\tau$. Its theoretical representative is $H(v)=I-2vv^*/(v^*v)$. For a separate block application omit the column overwrite. For a right step apply these instructions to the conjugate-transposed block and transpose back.

For a Givens target pair $(a,b)$, use the identity when $b=0$, including $(0,0)$. Otherwise choose $\lambda$ as the largest absolute real/imaginary component of $(a,b)$, round $z=a/\lambda$ and $w=b/\lambda$ componentwise, and compute $h$ as the norm of their four already scaled components. If $z\ne0$, compute $n_z$ as the norm of its two components, $\widehat\phi=\operatorname{fl}(z/n_z)$, $c=\operatorname{fl}(n_z/h)$ and $s=\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\phi\overline w)/h)$. If $z=0$, set $c=0$ and $s=\operatorname{fl}(\overline w/h)$. Store $T=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-\overline s&c\end{pmatrix}$ and apply it to the chosen two rows using two complex products and one rounded componentwise addition for each output entry. For an actual target column, set its intended annihilated entry to exact zero after the update. The initial shift-vector rotation is formed from the shift vector but applied to the matrix without zeroing an unrelated matrix entry. Right applications use the conjugate-transposed form. Its exact unitary representative is $Q=T/\sqrt{c^2+|s|^2}$; this normalization defines a mathematical representative and is not an additional rounded operation.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

derivations.claim: By the definition of column stacking, $\|\operatorname{vec}(X)\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{i=1}^{m}|x_{ij}|^2=\|X\|_F^2$ by [F1]. Both sides are nonnegative, so taking square roots proves the isometry claim.
The $j$th block of $(I_n\otimes A)\operatorname{vec}(X)$ is $Ax_j$, which is the $j$th column of $AX$. Hence $\operatorname{vec}(AX)=(I_n\otimes A)\operatorname{vec}(X)$.

The $j$th column of $XB$ is $\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}b_{\ell j}x_\ell$. The $j$th block of $(B^T\otimes I_m)\operatorname{vec}(X)$ is the same sum because its $(j,\ell)$ block is $b_{\ell j}I_m$. Thus $\operatorname{vec}(XB)=(B^T\otimes I_m)\operatorname{vec}(X)$.
Adding the identities in steps 1.2 and 1.3 gives the displayed Sylvester-map representation, completing both claims.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\geq 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$, with rows and columns indexed by
$0,\ldots,n-1$ ([[def-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]).

For $0\leq i,j<n$, the **deleted-row-and-column matrix** $A^{(i,j)}$ is
obtained by deleting row $i$ and column $j$. The **minor** and **cofactor** at
$(i,j)$ are

$$M_{ij}(A):=\det(A^{(i,j)}),\qquad C_{ij}(A):=\varepsilon_{ij}M_{ij}(A),$$

where the sign is taken in $R$ by parity: $\varepsilon_{ij}:=1_R$ when $i+j$ is
even and $\varepsilon_{ij}:=-1_R$ when $i+j$ is odd. Writing this as
$(-1)^{i+j}$ is the usual abbreviation; it is the ring element $-1_R$ raised to
a natural-number power in $R$, not a real power. When $n=1$,
$A^{(0,0)}$ is the unique $0\times0$ matrix and its determinant is defined
locally to be $1$. For $n>1$, the determinant is the published matrix
determinant ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

The **cofactor matrix** is
$\operatorname{cof}(A):=(C_{ij}(A))$, and the **adjugate** is

$$\operatorname{adj}(A):=\operatorname{cof}(A)^{\mathsf T},$$

using the published transpose operation
([[def-ring-matrix-product-identity-and-transpose]]).

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $n\ge1$, and $A\in F^{n\times n}$. The matrix $A$ is **Hurwitz** if, when its eigenvalues are considered over $\mathbb C$, every eigenvalue has strictly negative real part. For $Q,X\in F^{n\times n}$ with $Q=Q^*$, the **continuous Lyapunov equation** with coefficient $A$ and forcing $Q$ is

$$
AX+XA^*+Q=0.
$$

Here $^*$ is transpose for real matrices and conjugate transpose for complex matrices. The notations $Q\succeq0$ and $Q\succ0$ mean that $Q$ is non-negative or positive as a self-adjoint operator in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]: respectively $v^*Qv\ge0$ for all $v$, or $v^*Qv>0$ for every nonzero $v$.

Differentiate $e^{(t-s)D}e^{sT}$ with respect to $s$ and integrate from $0$ to $t$. Since $T-D=N$, this gives $e^{tT}=e^{tD}+\int_0^t e^{(t-s)D}N e^{sT}\,ds$. Iterating this identity produces ordered-integral terms with $k$ factors $N$ and diagonal exponentials between them. The remainder after $n$ iterations contains $n$ strictly upper-triangular factors, with diagonal factors between them and an upper-triangular exponential at the end; every nonzero matrix-entry path would have to increase its index at least $n$ times in an $n\times n$ matrix, so this remainder is zero.

The ordered simplex for $k$ integration variables has volume $t^k/k!$. By [F6], each $k$th term has norm at most $e^{-\alpha t}\|N\|_2^k t^k/k!$. Summing the terms $0\le k<n$ proves the bound for $e^{tT}$; [F5] and step 2.1 transfer it to $e^{tA}$.

$$M=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\0&D\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{or}\quad M=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\C&D\end{pmatrix},$$

one has $\chi_M(x)=\chi_A(x)\chi_D(x)$, including $r=0$ or $s=0$.

Let $F$ be a field and let $A\in M_n(F)$. If $n\geq1$, regard $xI_n-A$ as a matrix over the commutative polynomial ring $F[x]$. The **characteristic polynomial of $A$** is

$$\chi_A(x):=\det(xI_n-A)\in F[x].$$

For $n=0$, define the characteristic polynomial of the unique $0\times0$ matrix to be the constant polynomial $1$. This agrees with the empty-product convention and makes the characteristic polynomial monic of degree $0$ in the zero-sized case.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

Let $T:V\to V$ be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space over
a field $F$. Then $T$ is invertible if and only if $\det(T)\neq0$.

If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$
The field $\mathbb C$ is algebraically closed.

Set $Y=U^*XV$ and $D=U^*CV$; multiplying $AX+XB=C$ on the left by $U^*$ and right by $V$ gives $TY+YS=D$, and this change of variables is invertible.

By [F1], the vectorized map for $Y\mapsto TY+YS$ is $K=I_n\otimes T+S^T\otimes I_m$. Viewed in $m$-entry column blocks, $K$ is block lower triangular because $S^T$ is lower triangular; its $j$th diagonal block is $K_j=T+s_{jj}I_m$, which is upper triangular with diagonal entries $t_{ii}+s_{jj}$. Recursively applying [F5] to the first diagonal block and the remaining block gives $\chi_K(x)=\prod_{j=1}^n\chi_{K_j}(x)$. At $x=0$, [F6] and [F7] give $(-1)^{mn}\det K=\prod_{j=1}^n((-1)^m\det K_j)$, so $\det K=\prod_{j=1}^n\det K_j$. By [F8], $K$ is invertible exactly when every $K_j$ is invertible. Each $K_j$ is triangular, so [F9] and [F8] show it is invertible exactly when every diagonal entry $t_{ii}+s_{jj}$ is nonzero.

Since $A=UTU^*$ and $B=VSV^*$ with $U,V$ unitary, $A-\lambda I=U(T-\lambda I)U^*$ and $B-\lambda I=V(S-\lambda I)V^*$; these factors are invertible exactly when the corresponding middle factor is, so $\sigma(A)=\sigma(T)$ and $\sigma(B)=\sigma(S)$. By [F9], $\det(T-\lambda I)=\prod_i(t_{ii}-\lambda)$ and $\det(S-\lambda I)=\prod_j(s_{jj}-\lambda)$; [F8] therefore gives $\sigma(A)=\{t_{ii}}$ and $\sigma(B)=\{s_{jj}\}$. Applying the complex criterion from step 2.1 to this same real matrix viewed over $\mathbb C$ therefore gives the same spectral condition for invertibility over $\mathbb R$.

A square finite-dimensional linear map is bijective exactly when every right-hand side has one solution. By [F3] and [F4], its smallest singular value is positive exactly when it is invertible. This proves all equivalences.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $A\in F^{n\times n}$ be Hurwitz, let $B\in F^{n\times r}$, and let $p_1,\ldots,p_k\in\mathbb C$ be a finite shift list. The target equation is $AX+XA^*+BB^*=0$. Inputs also include the shift list and exact linear-solve operations. For real $A,B$, nonreal shifts must occur in consecutive complex-conjugate pairs; the procedure may use complex arithmetic for these paired shifts.

Before starting matrix updates, validate the real-data shift pairing by scanning the shift list once: at a real shift advance the scan index by one; at a nonreal shift require the next list entry to equal its complex conjugate, then advance the scan index by two. A missing or unequal partner returns `unpaired-complex-shift`. For complex data no pairing restriction is imposed. This validation scan consumes pairs; the update loop below still processes every individual shift in order.

Initialize $R_0=B$, let $Z_0$ have zero columns, and set $X_0=0$. For $j=1,\ldots,k$:

1. If $\operatorname{Re}p_j\ge0$, return `invalid-shift`. If $A+p_jI$ is singular, return `singular-shift`.
2. Set $c_j=-2\operatorname{Re}p_j>0$ and solve
   $$
   V_j=(A+p_jI)^{-1}R_{j-1}.
   $$
3. Set
   $$
   Z_j=[Z_{j-1},\sqrt{c_j}V_j],\qquad X_j=Z_jZ_j^*=X_{j-1}+c_jV_jV_j^*,\qquad R_j=R_{j-1}+c_jV_j.
   $$

Return `completed` with the low-rank factor $Z_k$, approximation $X_k$, and residual factor $R_k$. A finite shift list may stop before convergence; this procedure does not select shifts or assert unconditional convergence.

Using $c=-(p+\overline p)$ and [F1], expand the new Lyapunov residual as $AX_j+X_jA^*+BB^*=AX_{j-1}+X_{j-1}A^*+BB^*+c((AV)V^*+V(V^*A^*))$. Substituting step 1.2 and [A1] yields $RR^*+c(RV^*+VR^*)+c^2VV^*$.
The expression in step 2.1 factors as $(R+cV)(R+cV)^*=R_jR_j^*$ by [F1]. Together with base step 1.1, the induction step in 1.2–2.1 proves the identity for every completed iterate.

Let $A\in F^{n\times n}$ be Hurwitz and let $Q=Q^*\in F^{n\times n}$. Then the improper matrix integral

$$
X=\int_0^\infty e^{tA}Qe^{tA^*}\,dt
$$

converges and is the unique solution of $AX+XA^*+Q=0$. If $Q\succeq0$, then $X\succeq0$. If $Q\succ0$, then $X\succ0$. For $Q\succeq0$, $X\succ0$ if and only if there is no nonzero $v$ for which $e^{tA^*}v\in\ker Q^{1/2}$ for every $t\ge0$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces. In orthonormal bases $\mathcal E=(e_j)$ of $V$ and $\mathcal F=(f_i)$ of $W$,

$$[T^*]_{\mathcal E\leftarrow\mathcal F}=\overline{[T]_{\mathcal F\leftarrow\mathcal E}}^{\mathsf T}.$$

Over $\mathbb R$ this is the transpose. The statement includes zero-sized bases.

For every $n\ge1$, every commutative ring $R$, and every $A\in M_n(R)$,
$$\det(A^{\mathsf T})=\det(A).$$

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

derivations.claim: From [F1], $R_j=\left(I-2\operatorname{Re}(p_j)(A+p_jI)^{-1}\right)R_{j-1}=(A-\overline{p_j}I)(A+p_jI)^{-1}R_{j-1}$, since $-2\operatorname{Re}(p_j)=-(p_j+\overline{p_j})$. All factors are rational functions of $A$ and commute, so iterating gives $R_j=\rho_j(A)B$.

In the standard orthonormal basis, [F7] represents $A^*$ by $\overline A^{\mathsf T}$. For $z\in\mathbb C$, [F8] and [F10] give $\det(zI-A^*)=\det((zI-\overline A)^{\mathsf T})=\det(zI-\overline A)$, and [F9] applied to the Leibniz formula gives $\det(zI-\overline A)=\overline{\det(\overline z I-A)}$. Hence $\sigma(A^*)=\overline{\sigma(A)}$, so both $A$ and $A^*$ have spectrum in the open left half-plane; therefore $\sigma(A)\cap(-\sigma(A^*))=\varnothing$. By [F3], $\operatorname{sep}(A,-A^*)>0$. Subtracting the equation for $X_j$ in [F2] from the exact equation in [F5] gives $\mathcal S_{A,A^*}(X-X_j)=-R_jR_j^*$.
Applying the operator bound in [A1] to each column of $B$ and summing squared column norms gives $\|R_j\|_F\le\eta_j\|B\|_F$.

Apply [F4] to step 1.2. If $R_j=U\Sigma V^*$ is an SVD, then $R_jR_j^*=U\Sigma^2U^*$, so unitary invariance and [F6] give $\|R_jR_j^*\|_F^2=\sum_i s_i(R_j)^4\le(\sum_i s_i(R_j)^2)^2=\|R_j\|_F^4$. Therefore $\|X-X_j\|_F\le\|R_jR_j^*\|_F/\operatorname{sep}(A,-A^*)\le\eta_j^2\|B\|_F^2/\operatorname{sep}(A,-A^*)$. Since $\eta_j\to0$ and the separation is positive, the right side tends to zero.

Input a real or complex square matrix $A\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$ with $n\ge1$, a finite nonnegative deflation tolerance $\tau$, a nonnegative integer sweep budget $N$, a positive integer stagnation period $h$, finite tables of finite exceptional shifts, optional exact rational/dyadic encodings of its stored real values, and optionally a terminating exact evaluator of [[def-exact-real-2x2-discriminant-sign-predicate]]. A formation `breakdown` is propagated with the operation index and partial factors. Every scalar operation is evaluated in the operationwise model of [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]]. Any invalid, overflow, or underflow operation returns range-failure with the operation index and partial factors.

For each stored reflector with active indices $S=(s_1,\ldots,s_m)$, vector $v\in\mathbb F^m$, and real computed coefficient $\widehat\tau$, the real or complex formation routine first performs the stated finite left application. Then perform the right application in this fixed order: for each matrix row $i=1,\ldots,n$, compute $d_i=\operatorname{fl}(\sum_{a=1}^m H^L_{i,s_a}v_a)$ by left-to-right rounded products and additions; for $a=1,\ldots,m$, compute $c_a=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau\overline{v_a})$, $g_{ia}=\operatorname{fl}(d_ic_a)$, and $H^R_{i,s_a}=\operatorname{fl}(H^L_{i,s_a}-g_{ia})$. Each complex product uses the six real operations of the arithmetic model. The exact factor appended to $Q$ is $P(v)=I-2vv^*/(v^*v)$; the computed right update uses $\widehat\tau$ as displayed and is not asserted equal to multiplication by $P(v)$. For a matrix-target column, the formation routine's explicit zero writes are retained. In the initial polynomial-vector step there is no matrix-target column: use the entire active row panel for the left update and then apply the right update to the active columns. Record deflation writes separately, including a pure deflation with no following reflector as an identity-transform stage; a local error certificate must account for all other rounding and target-column writes.

1. Reduce $A$ to upper Hessenberg form with Householder similarities. For $k=1,\ldots,\max(n-2,0)$ in increasing order, use active indices $S=\{k+1,\ldots,n\}$, target $x=H_{S,k}$, and trailing left panel $B=H_{S,\{k+1,\ldots,n\}}$ with columns in increasing order. In the real branch use [[alg-scaled-householder-reflector-formation-and-application]] for the finite left application and overwrite; in the complex branch use [[alg-complex-scaled-householder-reflector-step]]. Complete each similarity by the right application above on columns $S$. If the resulting matrix fails the exact upper-Hessenberg zero-pattern check, return bulge-chase-invariant-failure with the partial factors. Store the exact unitary reflector factors as a product representation $Q_0$.
2. At each sweep, test every active first-subdiagonal entry by
   $$|h_{i,i-1}|\le\tau\bigl(|h_{i-1,i-1}|+|h_{i,i}|\bigr).$$
   For a complex entry $z=a+ib$, evaluate $|z|$ by $s=\max(|a|,|b|)$ and $s\sqrt{(a/s)^2+(b/s)^2}$ when $z\ne0$, with divisions, squares, sum, square root and final scaling rounded in the stated order; use $|0|=0$. Return range-failure if this evaluation fails. Compute the diagonal-magnitude sum first, then multiply by $\tau$ in the operationwise model; compare the resulting finite values exactly. When the test holds, set that entry to zero, record its original value as a deflation perturbation, and split the active block. The equality case deflates. Do not use the Hermitian-tridiagonal Wilkinson shift rule for a general Hessenberg matrix.
3. Check for the target Schur block structure after initialization and after each sweep. A complex active block of size at least two uses a single shift, normally its bottom-right entry. A real active block of size at least two uses the real quadratic $p(z)=z^2-sz+t$ with trailing block $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$; compute $s=\operatorname{fl}(a+d)$ and $t=\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(ad)-\operatorname{fl}(bc))$ in that order, returning range-failure if an operation fails. Maintain a counter for each active block, reset it after any deflation in that block, and after $h$ consecutive sweeps without deflation consume that block's next declared exceptional shift or real quadratic. If the required table entry is absent, return stagnation-exhausted.
4. Apply the corresponding implicit bulge chase from [[alg-exact-francis-hessenberg-qr-step]]. For the initial single-shift vector compute $x_1=\operatorname{fl}(h_{11}-\mu)$ and $x_i=h_{i1}$ for $i>1$. For the initial real double-shift vector, compute $u=He_1$, then $w=Hu$ by left-to-right rounded matrix-vector products, then $x=\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(w-su)+te_1)$ componentwise. Compute only the first $r+1$ components from the Hessenberg support pattern; on range failure return the operation index and partial factors. For a chase at column $j$, use active indices $S=I_j$, target $x=H_{S,j}$, and trailing left panel $B=H_{S,\{j+1,\ldots,n\}}$ with columns in increasing order. Call the real or complex formation routine, write the target tail zeros exactly, complete the two-sided update by the right-kernel order above on columns $S$, and append the exact reflector representation to $Q$. In the initial polynomial-vector step there is no matrix-target column; use the full active row panel for the left update and then apply the right update to its active columns. If the exact routine or its finite-precision realization returns bulge-chase-invariant-failure, return that status with the partial matrix and factors. Use [[lem-two-sided-scaled-householder-similarity-error]] to store the proved two-sided coefficient $\alpha_{m_j}=a_{m_j}+b_{m_j}+a_{m_j}b_{m_j}$, with $a$ the target-overwrite coefficient or separate-block coefficient as actually used and $b$ the right separate-block coefficient. This gives $\|E_j\|_F\le\alpha_{m_j}\|\widehat H_{j-1}\|_F$ when its $m_ju<1$ and range hypotheses hold. Apply the same certificate to every Hessenberg-initialization similarity. If any step lacks that certificate, retain the residual diagnostic and set the backward-error-certificate status to inconclusive.
5. Stop with Schur-computed when every complex block has size one, or every real block has size one or is a $2\times2$ block with negative characteristic-polynomial discriminant. Use the supplied evaluator, or the finite integer recipe in [[lem-exact-rational-two-by-two-discriminant-sign]] when exact rational/dyadic encodings are available, for each real block's $\operatorname{discSign}$ as defined in [[def-exact-real-2x2-discriminant-sign-predicate]]. If no exact sign is available, return schur-type-undecided and do not claim Schur-computed. If the target check fails when the sweep count reaches $N$, return budget-exhausted; in particular, with $N=0$ return Schur-computed only when the initialized matrix already has the target block structure. Return the partial matrix and factors on every failure or nonconvergence status.

Let $\widehat T$ be the final returned matrix. The output includes the product representation $Q$, residual matrix $R=Q^*AQ-\widehat T$ and its Frobenius norm as diagnostics, the exact orthogonality bound $0$ for that reflector product, the recorded deflation entries, and either the accumulated backward-error bound when all local certificates exist or certificate status inconclusive. Bound expressions and any claimed upper bounds are evaluated exactly or with rigorous outward allowances; uncorrected rounded residual norms are diagnostics only. A rounded dense matrix formed from $Q$ has its own orthogonality residual and is not asserted exactly unitary. The residual diagnostic does not itself give a forward eigenvalue bound. The procedure asserts no unconditional convergence of any shift schedule.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $n\ge0$ and $A\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, and let $Q^*$ denote transpose over $\mathbb R$ and conjugate transpose over $\mathbb C$. A **complex Schur pair** for $A$ is a pair $(Q,T)$ with $Q^*Q=I$ and $A=QTQ^*$, where $T$ is upper triangular.

For real $A$, a **real Schur pair** is a pair $(Q,T)$ with $Q^TQ=I$ and $A=QTQ^T$, where $T$ is block upper triangular and every diagonal block is either a real $1\times1$ block or a real $2\times2$ block with negative characteristic-polynomial discriminant. Such a $2\times2$ block has one nonreal conjugate eigenvalue pair. The definition does not assert that a finite shift strategy reaches such a pair.

For $B=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{2\times2}$, its characteristic-polynomial discriminant means the exact real number $\Delta(B)=(a+d)^2-4(ad-bc)$. “Negative discriminant” means the exact comparison $\Delta(B)<0$.

For $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $A\in F^{m\times m}$, $B\in F^{n\times n}$ with $m,n\ge1$, define the Sylvester operator $\mathcal S_{A,B}:F^{m\times n}\to F^{m\times n}$ by

$$\mathcal S_{A,B}(X)=AX+XB.$$

Equip $F^{m\times n}$ with the Frobenius norm of [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]. The column-vectorization isometry of [[lem-sylvester-vectorization-isometry-and-kronecker-identity]] identifies this norm with the Euclidean norm on $F^{mn}$. Define

$$\operatorname{sep}(A,-B):=\sigma_{\min}(\mathcal S_{A,B})=\min_{\|X\|_F=1}\|AX+XB\|_F.$$

Here $\sigma_{\min}$ denotes the smallest singular value of the finite-dimensional linear map under these inner products. The finite-dimensional singular value decomposition [[thm-singular-value-decomposition]] ensures this minimum is well-defined. The argument $-B$ is part of the conventional label: the operator being measured is $X\mapsto AX+XB$.

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $q\ge1$, and $M\in F^{q\times q}$. Define

$$\delta(M)=\begin{cases}0,&\|M\|_F=0,\\[2pt]\dfrac{|\det M|}{\|M\|_F^{q-1}},&\|M\|_F>0.\end{cases}$$

With the empty product convention when $q=1$, $0\le\delta(M)\le\sigma_{\min}(M)$.

$$
M\operatorname{adj}(M)=\det(M)I_q.
$$

Consequently, when $\det(M)\ne0$, $M^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(M)/\det(M)$; when $\det(M)=0$, $M$ is singular.

Suppose the stored entries of $B=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ have supplied exact rational encodings $a=p_a/q_a$, $b=p_b/q_b$, $c=p_c/q_c$, $d=p_d/q_d$, with integer numerators and positive integer denominators. Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $m,n\ge1$, $A\in F^{m\times m}$, $B\in F^{n\times n}$ and $C\in F^{m\times n}$. Inputs also include a pivot threshold $\tau\ge0$, Schur controls for each matrix, a fixed constant $c_0>0$, and finite sweep budgets $N_A\le c_0m$, $N_B\le c_0n$. The local transforms, certificate checks and block substitution use exact scalar arithmetic and comparisons. The delegated Schur calls retain their specified rounded arithmetic, admissible input representations, range conditions and statuses; their returned factors remain candidates until the exact checks below succeed.

The default real-block sign controller is the fixed exact real-arithmetic expression tree $s=(a-d)^2+4bc$, followed by its sign comparisons, for [[def-exact-real-2x2-discriminant-sign-predicate]]. This uses five exact arithmetic operations and at most two sign comparisons in the declared exact local arithmetic model. For rational/dyadic encoded stored values, [[lem-exact-rational-two-by-two-discriminant-sign]] gives the finite exact integer realization; a fixed-format decoder, when used, is included in the control cost. These exact controller operations are separate from the rounded Schur matrix updates. No bit-complexity bound for integer/rational arithmetic is claimed.

Choose either bounded-controller mode, the default, or arbitrary-terminating-controller mode. In bounded mode supply a nonnegative integer per-call budget $K$. Custom sign or decoding routines are finite instruction programs over exact scalar real/integer arithmetic, comparisons, register operations and branches; no opaque callback is a unit instruction. The interpreter charges one unit per executed instruction, including decoding, the built-in tree and any custom-result verification within the same per-call $K$ budget; it checks instruction/operation validity when encountered and returns undecided on exhaustion or invalid execution. An undecided sign is propagated as the Schur type-undecided status and then outer `schur-failure`. The fixed built-in sign tree or integer recipe has a fixed finite instruction count independent of matrix dimension. Any custom reported sign must agree with the built-in exact discriminant tree before acceptance. In arbitrary-terminating mode custom programs must terminate on every supplied input; record their total executed controller work as $C_{\rm aux}$. This richer mode retains finite termination but has the additional work in its cost bound. In the cubic-cost branch $K$ and representation-control instruction costs are fixed independently of matrix dimension. Programs are executed by instruction lookup without an up-front scan of unused code.

1. Run [[alg-finite-budget-francis-schur-reduction]] on $A$ and $B$ with their supplied controls and budgets. If either call does not return `Schur-computed`, return `schur-failure` with the underlying status.

2. Treat the returned factors as candidates and verify the exact certificates. In the complex branch check $U^*U=I$, $A=UTU^*$, and upper triangularity of $T$; in the real branch check $U^TU=I$, $A=UTU^T$, and the real block upper-triangular form of [[def-real-and-complex-schur-forms]]. Perform the corresponding checks for $B=VSV^*$. If any check fails, return `schur-certificate-failure`.

3. Set $D=U^*CV$. Use the column-vectorization and Kronecker convention of [[lem-sylvester-vectorization-isometry-and-kronecker-identity]]. Partition $T$ into diagonal blocks $T_{ii}$ and $S$ into diagonal blocks $S_{jj}$ as in the exact real or complex Schur form. Traverse $j$ from left to right and, for each $j$, traverse $i$ from bottom to top. Form

$$
F_{ij}=D_{ij}-\sum_{k>i}T_{ik}Y_{kj}-\sum_{\ell<j}Y_{i\ell}S_{\ell j}.
$$

The terms on the right have already been computed in this traversal order. Define $\Phi_{ij}(Z)=T_{ii}Z+ZS_{jj}$ and its matrix representation $M_{ij}=I_{s_j}\otimes T_{ii}+S_{jj}^T\otimes I_{r_i}$ on column-vectorized blocks, where $r_i,s_j\in\{1,2\}$ are the block sizes. Let $q=r_is_j\le4$ and compute $\delta(M_{ij})$ from [[lem-small-block-determinant-separation-lower-bound]]. If $\det(M_{ij})=0$, return `singular-pivot`; if $\det(M_{ij})\ne0$ and $\delta(M_{ij})\le\tau$, return `pivot-separation-failure` because the requested pivot bound is not certified. Otherwise use the cofactor adjugate formula of [[lem-adjugate-inverse-formula-over-a-field]] to set $\operatorname{vec}(Y_{ij})=\operatorname{adj}(M_{ij})\operatorname{vec}(F_{ij})/\det(M_{ij})$ and store $Y_{ij}$. The local dimension is at most four in the real block case and one in the complex triangular case.

4. After all blocks are solved, return `success` and $X=UYV^*$, together with the exact residual $C-(AX+XB)$. No computed Schur candidate is accepted as an exact factorization unless step 2 verifies its defining equalities.

For $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $A\in F^{m\times m}$, $B\in F^{n\times n}$ with $m,n\ge1$, define the Sylvester operator $\mathcal S_{A,B}:F^{m\times n}\to F^{m\times n}$ by

$$\mathcal S_{A,B}(X)=AX+XB.$$

Equip $F^{m\times n}$ with the Frobenius norm of [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]. The column-vectorization isometry of [[lem-sylvester-vectorization-isometry-and-kronecker-identity]] identifies this norm with the Euclidean norm on $F^{mn}$. Define

$$\operatorname{sep}(A,-B):=\sigma_{\min}(\mathcal S_{A,B})=\min_{\|X\|_F=1}\|AX+XB\|_F.$$

Here $\sigma_{\min}$ denotes the smallest singular value of the finite-dimensional linear map under these inner products. The finite-dimensional singular value decomposition [[thm-singular-value-decomposition]] ensures this minimum is well-defined. The argument $-B$ is part of the conventional label: the operator being measured is $X\mapsto AX+XB$.

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $m,n\ge1$, $A\in F^{m\times m}$ and $B\in F^{n\times n}$. Spectra of real matrices are taken over $\mathbb C$. The map $\mathcal S_{A,B}$ of [[def-sylvester-operator-and-separation-number]] is invertible if and only if

$$
\sigma(A)\cap(-\sigma(B))=\varnothing.
$$

Equivalently, for every $C\in F^{m\times n}$, the equation $AX+XB=C$ has a unique solution if and only if this spectral condition holds. The same condition is equivalent to $\operatorname{sep}(A,-B)>0$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $A=UTU^*$, $B=VSV^*$, and $D=U^*CV$ hold exactly. Multiplying $AX+XB$ on the left by $U^*$ and on the right by $V$ gives $TY+YS$.

In the $(i,j)$ block, $TY+YS$ equals $T_{ii}Y_{ij}+Y_{ij}S_{jj}+\sum_{k>i}T_{ik}Y_{kj}+\sum_{\ell<j}Y_{i\ell}S_{\ell j}$. The successful local solve from [F1] makes this block equal $D_{ij}$, so every block of $TY+YS$ equals the corresponding block of $D$.
Therefore $TY+YS=D=U^*CV$. Multiplying by $U$ on the left and $V^*$ on the right yields $A(UYV^*)+(UYV^*)B=C$. By [F2], this is $\mathcal S_{A,B}(X)=C$ for the returned $X=UYV^*$.
Under the stated spectral-disjointness condition, [F3] gives uniqueness for this right-hand side; hence the returned exact solution is the unique one.

Input a real or complex square matrix $A\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$ with $n\ge1$, a finite nonnegative deflation tolerance $\tau$, a nonnegative integer sweep budget $N$, a positive integer stagnation period $h$, finite tables of finite exceptional shifts, optional exact rational/dyadic encodings of its stored real values, optionally a terminating exact evaluator of [[def-exact-real-2x2-discriminant-sign-predicate]], and optionally a terminating outward evaluator for nonnegative expressions and Frobenius norms. The outward evaluator's `upadd`, `upmul`, and `upsqrt` calls return finite nonnegative represented upper bounds for the exact sum, product, and square root, while `upnormF(X)` returns a finite represented upper bound for $\|X\|_F$; any call may instead return `unavailable`. In the declared scalar-cost model, each `upadd`, `upmul`, and `upsqrt` call has unit cost and `upnormF(X)` makes one pass over the entries of $X$ with a fixed number of such calls per real component. The evaluator acts only on certificate bookkeeping. A formation `breakdown` is propagated with the operation index and partial factors. Every scalar operation in the main procedure is evaluated in the operationwise model of [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]]. Any invalid, overflow, or underflow operation in the main procedure returns range-failure with the operation index and partial factors.

Before every real or complex formation in steps 1 and 4, test the target vector componentwise for exact zero, including an external initial polynomial vector. If it is zero, mark the stage `identity`, copy all affected matrix entries unchanged, skip formation and both left and right updates, append the embedded identity $P_j=I$ to the product representation, and record $E_j=0$ and arithmetic coefficient $\alpha_j=\bar\alpha_j=0$. Do not evaluate $P(v)$ or a stored-vector norm in this branch. For a matrix target its column is already zero, so its target zero writes change nothing; for an external vector no matrix column is overwritten. Continue with the invariant checks, sweep counters and stopping tests specified below. Record and process every deflation write separately exactly as specified below; this branch does not discard a deflation perturbation. These identity instructions take precedence over the formation/update instructions in steps 1 and 4.

For each nonidentity stored reflector with active indices $S=(s_1,\ldots,s_m)$, nonzero vector $v\in\mathbb F^m$, and real computed coefficient $\widehat\tau$, the real or complex formation routine first performs the stated finite left application. Then perform the right application in this fixed order: for each matrix row $i=1,\ldots,n$, compute $d_i=\operatorname{fl}(\sum_{a=1}^m H^L_{i,s_a}v_a)$ by left-to-right rounded products and additions; for $a=1,\ldots,m$, compute $c_a=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau\overline{v_a})$, $g_{ia}=\operatorname{fl}(d_ic_a)$, and $H^R_{i,s_a}=\operatorname{fl}(H^L_{i,s_a}-g_{ia})$. Each complex product uses the six real operations of the arithmetic model. The exact factor appended to $Q$ is $P(v)=I-2vv^*/(v^*v)$; the computed right update uses $\widehat\tau$ as displayed and is not asserted equal to multiplication by $P(v)$. For a matrix-target column, the formation routine's explicit zero writes are retained. In the initial polynomial-vector step there is no matrix-target column: use the entire active row panel for the left update and then apply the right update to the active columns. Record deflation writes separately, including a pure deflation with no following reflector as an identity-transform stage; a local error certificate must account for all other rounding and target-column writes.

1. Reduce $A$ to upper Hessenberg form with Householder similarities. In the real branch use [[alg-scaled-householder-reflector-formation-and-application]] for the finite left application and overwrite; in the complex branch use [[alg-complex-scaled-householder-reflector-step]]. Complete each similarity by the right application above on columns $S$. If the resulting matrix fails the exact upper-Hessenberg zero-pattern check, return bulge-chase-invariant-failure with the partial factors. Store the exact unitary reflector factors as a product representation $Q_0$.
2. At each sweep, test every active first-subdiagonal entry by
   $$|h_{i,i-1}|\le\tau\bigl(|h_{i-1,i-1}|+|h_{i,i}|\bigr).$$
   For a complex entry $z=a+ib$, evaluate $|z|$ by $s=\max(|a|,|b|)$ and $s\sqrt{(a/s)^2+(b/s)^2}$ when $z\ne0$, with divisions, squares, sum, square root and final scaling rounded in the stated order; use $|0|=0$. derivations.claim: Hessenberg reduction uses at most $\max(n-2,0)$ reflector steps. For $n\ge3$, forming one reflector costs $O(n)$ scalar operations, and applying its two-sided similarity to the remaining dense submatrix costs $O(n^2)$; summing over at most $n$ steps gives $O(n^3)$. For $n=1,2$, there are no such steps.

For an active block of size $r\ge2$, a Francis sweep has at most $\max(r-2,0)+1$ initial/chase reflectors of length two or three. Each acts on a bounded number of rows and columns across at most $n$ entries. The active block sizes sum to at most $n$, so a full sweep and its non-controller deflation/status work cost $O(n^2)$; for $n=1$ there is no active sweep. The linear sweep budgets therefore give $O(n^3)$ matrix work for the two Schur calls. The same bound covers materializing the recorded factor products: initialization contributes $O(n^3)$ and each bounded-support chase factor updates only a bounded number of dense-factor columns, at cost $O(n)$.

Each exact Schur-certificate matrix product, the transform $U^*CV$, and the final transform $UYV^*$ cost $O(n^3)$. The block substitution has at most $n^2$ block pairs; each pair sums at most $O(n)$ earlier blocks of bounded size and solves a system of dimension at most four, so all substitution work is $O(n^3)$.

Each sweep checks at most $O(n)$ active blocks, and initialization and final checks add at most $O(n)$ such calls. With $O(n)$ sweeps there are at most $O(n^2)$ sign/representation-controller calls. A bounded call executes at most $K$ instructions, giving $O(Kn^2)$ work; the fixed built-in exact polynomial tree and rational/dyadic recipe are constant-size special cases. In arbitrary-terminating mode their actual total work is precisely the additional $C_{\rm aux}$.

The backward-error accumulator starts with one outward Frobenius norm of the input, costing $O(n^2)$ by the declared entrywise evaluator model. Each similarity uses a fixed number of scalar upper-bound calls once its local coefficient is evaluated. The explicit real/complex coefficient formulas require $O(m)$ scalar operations on active dimension $m$: their dimension-dependent powers can be formed by repeated multiplication and a square root for a half-integer exponent. Thus the at most $n$ initialization coefficients cost $O(n^2)$ in total, while each length-two/three chase coefficient costs $O(1)$. There are $O(n^2)$ chase similarities over the linear number of sweeps. Each recorded one-entry deflation has Frobenius norm equal to the modulus of its signed stored value, evaluated from that one-entry list with $O(1)$ scalar work; at most $O(n)$ such writes occur per sweep, hence $O(n^2)$ in total. Each stage then makes a fixed number of recurrence calls. Unavailable coefficient/evaluator results only stop certificate bookkeeping. Consequently this entire ancillary accumulation costs $O(n^2)$ and fits inside the cubic matrix-work bound, including failure branches.

The reductions, sweeps, exact certificates, transforms, block sums and fixed-size solves contribute $O(n^3)$, and step 1.4 supplies the complete control contribution. Adding them gives $O(n^3+Kn^2)$ and the fixed-$K$ cubic consequence, or $O(n^3+C_{\rm aux})$ for the richer terminating route. No bound on integer bit length or bit-operation cost is used.
