Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $n\ge1$, and $A\in F^{n\times n}$. The matrix $A$ is **Hurwitz** if, when its eigenvalues are considered over $\mathbb C$, every eigenvalue has strictly negative real part. For $Q,X\in F^{n\times n}$ with $Q=Q^*$, the **continuous Lyapunov equation** with coefficient $A$ and forcing $Q$ is

$$
AX+XA^*+Q=0.
$$

Here $^*$ is transpose for real matrices and conjugate transpose for complex matrices. The notations $Q\succeq0$ and $Q\succ0$ mean that $Q$ is non-negative or positive as a self-adjoint operator in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]: respectively $v^*Qv\ge0$ for all $v$, or $v^*Qv>0$ for every nonzero $v$.
citations.use_explanation: [[def-hurwitz-matrix-and-continuous-lyapunov-equation]]: [[def-hurwitz-matrix-and-continuous-lyapunov-equation]]: $A$ is Hurwitz when all its eigenvalues have negative real part, and the balance is $AX+XA^T+Q=0$.

citations.quote:
Let $A\in F^{n\times n}$ be Hurwitz and let $Q=Q^*\in F^{n\times n}$. Then the improper matrix integral

$$
X=\int_0^\infty e^{tA}Qe^{tA^*}\,dt
$$

converges and is the unique solution of $AX+XA^*+Q=0$. If $Q\succeq0$, then $X\succeq0$. If $Q\succ0$, then $X\succ0$. For $Q\succeq0$, $X\succ0$ if and only if there is no nonzero $v$ for which $e^{tA^*}v\in\ker Q^{1/2}$ for every $t\ge0$.
citations.use_explanation: [[thm-continuous-lyapunov-integral-and-positivity]]: [[thm-continuous-lyapunov-integral-and-positivity]]: For Hurwitz $A$, the Lyapunov equation has a unique solution, and the integral solution is positive definite under the stated conditions.

derivations.claim: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $-1$ and $-2$, so $A$ is Hurwitz by [F1]. Direct multiplication gives $BB^T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $AX+XA^T=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}=-BB^T$. Thus the displayed $X$ solves the balance.
For real $(u,v)$, $\begin{pmatrix}u&v\end{pmatrix}X\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix}=\frac12(u+\frac23v)^2+\frac1{36}v^2$, which is positive unless $u=v=0$. Hence $X\succ0$.
Since $A$ is Hurwitz, [F2] gives uniqueness of the solution, so this positive matrix is the unique stable Lyapunov covariance-balance solution.

For $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $A\in F^{m\times m}$, $B\in F^{n\times n}$ with $m,n\ge1$, define the Sylvester operator $\mathcal S_{A,B}:F^{m\times n}\to F^{m\times n}$ by

$$\mathcal S_{A,B}(X)=AX+XB.$$

Equip $F^{m\times n}$ with the Frobenius norm of [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]. The column-vectorization isometry of [[lem-sylvester-vectorization-isometry-and-kronecker-identity]] identifies this norm with the Euclidean norm on $F^{mn}$. Define

$$\operatorname{sep}(A,-B):=\sigma_{\min}(\mathcal S_{A,B})=\min_{\|X\|_F=1}\|AX+XB\|_F.$$

Here $\sigma_{\min}$ denotes the smallest singular value of the finite-dimensional linear map under these inner products. The finite-dimensional singular value decomposition [[thm-singular-value-decomposition]] ensures this minimum is well-defined. The argument $-B$ is part of the conventional label: the operator being measured is $X\mapsto AX+XB$.

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $m,n\ge1$, $A\in F^{m\times m}$ and $B\in F^{n\times n}$. Spectra of real matrices are taken over $\mathbb C$. The map $\mathcal S_{A,B}$ of [[def-sylvester-operator-and-separation-number]] is invertible if and only if

$$
\sigma(A)\cap(-\sigma(B))=\varnothing.
$$

Equivalently, for every $C\in F^{m\times n}$, the equation $AX+XB=C$ has a unique solution if and only if this spectral condition holds. The same condition is equivalent to $\operatorname{sep}(A,-B)>0$.
citations.use_explanation: [[thm-sylvester-unique-solvability-spectral-separation]]: [[thm-sylvester-unique-solvability-spectral-separation]]: Unique solvability holds exactly when $\sigma(A)\cap(-\sigma(B))=\varnothing$.

Let $X$ be the unique solution of $AX+XB=C$, and let $\widehat X\in F^{m\times n}$ be any approximation. Define its equation residual by $R=C-(A\widehat X+\widehat X B)$. If $\operatorname{sep}(A,-B)>0$, then

$$
\|X-\widehat X\|_F\le\frac{\|R\|_F}{\operatorname{sep}(A,-B)}.
$$
citations.use_explanation: [[thm-sylvester-residual-to-forward-error-bound]]: [[thm-sylvester-residual-to-forward-error-bound]]: $\|X-\widehat X\|_F\le\|C-(A\widehat X+\widehat X B)\|_F/\operatorname{sep}(A,-B)$ when the solution is unique.

derivations.claim: The eigenvalue sums are $\varepsilon,1,1+\varepsilon,2$, all nonzero, so [F2] gives a unique solution. In the Frobenius-orthonormal matrix-unit basis, $\mathcal S_{A,B}(E_{ij})=(a_{ii}+b_{jj})E_{ij}$; its singular values are therefore the four absolute eigenvalue sums, and [F1] gives $\operatorname{sep}(A,-B)=\varepsilon$.
The $(i,j)$ equation is $(a_{ii}+b_{jj})x_{ij}=c_{ij}$. Since $C=E_{11}$, the only nonzero entry is $x_{11}=1/\varepsilon$, hence $X=\varepsilon^{-1}E_{11}$ and $\|X\|_F=1/\varepsilon=10^6$.

If the right-hand side is perturbed by $\delta E_{11}$, the solution changes by $\delta/\varepsilon E_{11}$, whose Frobenius norm is $|\delta|/\varepsilon$. This attains the separation factor in [F3], verifying the stated sensitivity exactly.

The local transforms, certificate checks and block substitution use exact scalar arithmetic and comparisons. The delegated Schur calls retain their specified rounded arithmetic, admissible input representations, range conditions and statuses; their returned factors remain candidates until the exact checks below succeed.

The default real-block sign controller is the fixed exact real-arithmetic expression tree $s=(a-d)^2+4bc$, followed by its sign comparisons, for [[def-exact-real-2x2-discriminant-sign-predicate]]. This uses five exact arithmetic operations and at most two sign comparisons in the declared exact local arithmetic model. For rational/dyadic encoded stored values, [[lem-exact-rational-two-by-two-discriminant-sign]] gives the finite exact integer realization; a fixed-format decoder, when used, is included in the control cost. These exact controller operations are separate from the rounded Schur matrix updates. No bit-complexity bound for integer/rational arithmetic is claimed.

Choose either bounded-controller mode, the default, or arbitrary-terminating-controller mode. In bounded mode supply a nonnegative integer per-call budget $K$. Custom sign or decoding routines are finite instruction programs over exact scalar real/integer arithmetic, comparisons, register operations and branches; no opaque callback is a unit instruction. The interpreter charges one unit per executed instruction, including decoding, the built-in tree and any custom-result verification within the same per-call $K$ budget; it checks instruction/operation validity when encountered and returns undecided on exhaustion or invalid execution. An undecided sign is propagated as the Schur type-undecided status and then outer `schur-failure`. The fixed built-in sign tree or integer recipe has a fixed finite instruction count independent of matrix dimension. Any custom reported sign must agree with the built-in exact discriminant tree before acceptance. In arbitrary-terminating mode custom programs must terminate on every supplied input; record their total executed controller work as $C_{\rm aux}$. This richer mode retains finite termination but has the additional work in its cost bound. In the cubic-cost branch $K$ and representation-control instruction costs are fixed independently of matrix dimension. Programs are executed by instruction lookup without an up-front scan of unused code.

1. Run [[alg-finite-budget-francis-schur-reduction]] on $A$ and $B$ with their supplied controls and budgets. If either call does not return `Schur-computed`, return `schur-failure` with the underlying status.

2. Treat the returned factors as candidates and verify the exact certificates. In the complex branch check $U^*U=I$, $A=UTU^*$, and upper triangularity of $T$; in the real branch check $U^TU=I$, $A=UTU^T$, and the real block upper-triangular form of [[def-real-and-complex-schur-forms]]. 3. Set $D=U^*CV$. Use the column-vectorization and Kronecker convention of [[lem-sylvester-vectorization-isometry-and-kronecker-identity]]. Partition $T$ into diagonal blocks $T_{ii}$ and $S$ into diagonal blocks $S_{jj}$ as in the exact real or complex Schur form. Traverse $j$ from left to right and, for each $j$, traverse $i$ from bottom to top. Form

$$
F_{ij}=D_{ij}-\sum_{k>i}T_{ik}Y_{kj}-\sum_{\ell<j}Y_{i\ell}S_{\ell j}.
$$

The terms on the right have already been computed in this traversal order. Define $\Phi_{ij}(Z)=T_{ii}Z+ZS_{jj}$ and its matrix representation $M_{ij}=I_{s_j}\otimes T_{ii}+S_{jj}^T\otimes I_{r_i}$ on column-vectorized blocks, where $r_i,s_j\in\{1,2\}$ are the block sizes. If $\det(M_{ij})=0$, return `singular-pivot`; if $\det(M_{ij})\ne0$ and $\delta(M_{ij})\le\tau$, return `pivot-separation-failure` because the requested pivot bound is not certified. Inputs also include the shift list and exact linear-solve operations. For real $A,B$, nonreal shifts must occur in consecutive complex-conjugate pairs; the procedure may use complex arithmetic for these paired shifts.

Before starting matrix updates, validate the real-data shift pairing by scanning the shift list once: at a real shift advance the scan index by one; at a nonreal shift require the next list entry to equal its complex conjugate, then advance the scan index by two. A missing or unequal partner returns `unpaired-complex-shift`. For complex data no pairing restriction is imposed. This validation scan consumes pairs; the update loop below still processes every individual shift in order.

Initialize $R_0=B$, let $Z_0$ have zero columns, and set $X_0=0$. For $j=1,\ldots,k$:

1. If $\operatorname{Re}p_j\ge0$, return `invalid-shift`. If $A+p_jI$ is singular, return `singular-shift`.
2. Set $c_j=-2\operatorname{Re}p_j>0$ and solve
   $$
   V_j=(A+p_jI)^{-1}R_{j-1}.
   $$
3. Set
   $$
   Z_j=[Z_{j-1},\sqrt{c_j}V_j],\qquad X_j=Z_jZ_j^*=X_{j-1}+c_jV_jV_j^*,\qquad R_j=R_{j-1}+c_jV_j.
   $$

A **field** is a set $F$ equipped with two binary operations $+$ (addition) and
$\cdot$ (multiplication) and two distinguished elements $0 \ne 1$ of $F$,
satisfying:

- **(A)** $(F, +)$ is an abelian group with identity $0$: addition is
  associative and commutative, $x + 0 = x$ for all $x$, and every $x$ has an
  additive inverse $-x$ with $x + (-x) = 0$.
- **(M)** Multiplication is associative and commutative **on all of $F$**, and
  $x \cdot 1 = x$ for every $x \in F$; moreover $(F \setminus \{0\}, \cdot)$ is an
  abelian group with identity $1$, so every $x \ne 0$ has a multiplicative inverse
  $x^{-1}$ with $x \cdot x^{-1} = 1$.
- **(D)** Multiplication distributes over addition: $x \cdot (y + z) = x\cdot y + x\cdot z$.

We write $x - y := x + (-y)$ and $x/y := x \cdot y^{-1}$ (for $y \ne 0$), and
abbreviate $x \cdot y$ as $xy$.

An **ordered field** is a field $F$ ([[def-field]]) together with a subset
$P \subseteq F$, the set of **positive** elements (the *positive cone*),
satisfying:

- **(O1) Trichotomy.** For each $x \in F$, exactly one of the following holds:
  $x \in P$, or $x = 0$, or $-x \in P$.
- **(O2) Closure.** If $x, y \in P$ then $x + y \in P$ and $x \cdot y \in P$.

We write $x > 0$ for $x \in P$ (read "$x$ is positive"), and define the order by

$$a < b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; b - a \in P, \qquad a \le b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; a < b \text{ or } a = b.$$

Thus $a > b$ means $b < a$, and $a \ge b$ means $b \le a$. An element $x$ with
$-x \in P$ (equivalently $x < 0$) is called **negative**.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

record as in [[def-csr-matrix-with-stored-entry-semantics]], representing

$(i,j)$ refers to CSR row $i-1$ and column index $j-1$. This row/column order
is fixed before the procedure begins; vector component label $i$ refers to
coordinate $i-1$. The procedure performs no pivoting or reordering. All field

Let $P=\{(i,j):a_{ij}\ne0\}$. Scan each row once to check the canonical and
increasing-index conditions and to record whether its diagonal position occurs.
If the input fails either pattern condition, return `invalid-pattern`. If a row
has no diagonal position, return `missing-diagonal(i)` for the least such $i$.

Copy the value in each input slot to a work array $W$, and regard the unit
diagonal of $L$ as implicit. Process rows $i=1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order.
For each $k<i$ with $(i,k)\in P$, in increasing $k$ order, do the following:

1. If $W_{kk}=0$, return `zero-pivot(k)`.
2. Set $W_{ik}\gets W_{ik}/W_{kk}$; this value is the stored factor $L_{ik}$.
3. Let $R$ be the increasing list of one-based matrix column labels $j>k$
   represented by row $i$'s CSR segment, and let $C$ be the corresponding
   increasing list represented by row $k$'s CSR segment. Set each pointer to
   the first entry of its list, or to
   that list's end marker when it is empty. While both pointers are within
   their lists, compare their current indices. If they are equal, call their
   common value $j$ and update
   $$W_{ij}\gets W_{ij}-W_{ik}W_{kj}$$
   and advance both pointers once. If the current index in $R$ is smaller,
   advance only its pointer once; if the current index in $C$ is smaller,
   advance only its pointer once, making no arithmetic update in either
   unequal-index branch. Stop when either pointer passes the end of its list.
   Do not skip a matching slot when a current work value is zero.

After all such $k$ have been processed in row $i$, if $W_{ii}=0$, return
`zero-pivot(i)`. Otherwise the upper row entries $U_{ij}$ are the current
$W_{ij}$ for $(i,j)\in P$ and $j\ge i$. Continue to the next row.

strict-lower entries $L_{ik}=W_{ik}$ for $(i,k)\in P$) and the upper factor
$U$ (stored entries $U_{ij}=W_{ij}$ for $(i,j)\in P$, $j\ge i$). Both factors
use only positions in $P$; the diagonal of $L$ is implicit, and all other
unstored off-diagonal entries are zero. The numeric values remain stored at
their structural slots if an update makes a value zero.

follows. For $i=1,\ldots,n$ in order, initialize $y_i:=r_i$ and, for each
$k<i$ with $(i,k)\in P$ in increasing order, update
$y_i:=y_i-L_{ik}y_k$. Then for $i=n,n-1,\ldots,1$, initialize $x_i:=y_i$;

traversed only over stored strict-triangular slots. The pivot checks ensure
every denominator in this application is nonzero. This procedure defines setup
and application only; it asserts no factorization identity $A=LU$, Krylov
convergence, conditioning improvement, or accuracy guarantee.

Let $F$ be a field, and let $m,n,s\in\mathbb N$, where $\mathbb N$ includes
$0$. A **compressed sparse row (CSR) record** for an $m$ by $n$ matrix over
$F$ consists of integer arrays $r=(r_0,\ldots,r_m)$ and
$c=(c_0,\ldots,c_{s-1})$, and a value array $v=(v_0,\ldots,v_{s-1})\in F^s$,
satisfying

$$r_0=0,\qquad 0=r_0\le r_1\le\cdots\le r_m=s,\qquad 0\le c_t<n\quad(0\le t<s).$$

For each row $i<m$, its **stored entries** are the indices
$t$ with $r_i\le t<r_{i+1}$. The row is empty exactly when
$r_i=r_{i+1}$. Repeated column indices within one row and stored values
$v_t=0_F$ are permitted; each such entry remains a separate stored entry.

The represented matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ is defined entrywise by

$$A_{ij}:=\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}v_t\qquad(0\le i<m,\ 0\le j<n),$$

where $\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}$ is $1_F$ when $c_t=j$ and $0_F$ otherwise, and an
empty sum is $0_F$. Repeated entries in column $j$ are therefore added. The
number $s$ is the **stored-entry count**; it is not in general the number of
nonzero entries of $A$.

A CSR record is **canonical** when no row repeats a column and no stored value
is zero. In that case every nonzero matrix entry is stored exactly once and
$s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)$, where $\operatorname{nnz}(A)$ denotes the number of
nonzero entries of $A$. If $m=0$, the endpoint conditions force $s=0$ and the
row-pointer array has its single entry $r_0=0$. If $n=0$, the column-index
condition forces $s=0$ as well.

Validation visits the $n$ row intervals and $s$ stored entries once; the factorization loops over at most $n$ rows, finitely many pattern entries, and finite row-list merges. Every division is preceded by a nonzero-pivot check, and [A1] makes each such division defined. Thus the procedure either returns one of its specified failure statuses or completes with `ok`.

If the procedure returns `ok`, each processed pivot is nonzero by its check, so the returned $U$ has nonzero diagonal. The definition sets $L$ to be unit lower triangular and retains only upper entries in $U$.

Initially the work values occupy exactly the input slots $P$. Each multiplier is written only at a strict-lower slot in $P_L$, and each update is performed only when both matching row positions are in $P$. No update allocates a new position. Induction over the finite row and pivot loops therefore gives stored patterns $P_L$ and $P_U$ for $L$ and $U$, respectively.

The forward recurrence in [F3] applied to unit-lower $L$ and the backward recurrence in [F4] applied to $U$ are well-defined because $L_{ii}=1$ and every $U_{ii}\ne0$. By [F5] and [F6] they produce the unique successive triangular-solve outputs specified by the algorithm.

The sets $P_L$ and $P_U$ are disjoint and partition $P$: every $(i,j)\in P$ has exactly one of $i>j$ or $i\le j$. Hence $\ell+q=|P|=s$. Since the unit diagonal of $L$ is implicit, this is exactly the factor numeric-slot count.

On success, the outer lower-pattern loop processes every one of the $\ell$ positions once and performs one division there. For a fixed $(i,k)\in P_L$, the update loop visits exactly the indices in $R_{ik}\cap C_k$; each visit performs one multiplication and one subtraction. Summing these counts gives exactly $\ell$ divisions and $I$ multiplications and subtractions.

Both lists in each intersection are strictly increasing. A two-pointer merge advances at least one pointer at every comparison and stops when one list ends, so it makes at most the sum of the two list lengths, $|R_{ik}|+|C_k|$, comparisons. Summing over $P_L$ gives the bound $J$; validation visits each row interval and stored entry once.

The forward recurrence in [F3] performs one multiplication and subtraction for each stored strict-lower slot, hence $\ell$ of each and no diagonal divisions. The backward recurrence in [F4] performs one multiplication and subtraction for each stored strict-upper slot, hence $u$ of each, and one division for each of its $n$ rows. Since $\ell+u=\ell+q-n=s-n$, the stated application counts follow.

Let $F$ be a field, and let $m,n,s\in\mathbb N$, where $\mathbb N$ includes
$0$. A **compressed sparse row (CSR) record** for an $m$ by $n$ matrix over
$F$ consists of integer arrays $r=(r_0,\ldots,r_m)$ and
$c=(c_0,\ldots,c_{s-1})$, and a value array $v=(v_0,\ldots,v_{s-1})\in F^s$,
satisfying

$$r_0=0,\qquad 0=r_0\le r_1\le\cdots\le r_m=s,\qquad 0\le c_t<n\quad(0\le t<s).$$

For each row $i<m$, its **stored entries** are the indices
$t$ with $r_i\le t<r_{i+1}$. The row is empty exactly when
$r_i=r_{i+1}$. Repeated column indices within one row and stored values
$v_t=0_F$ are permitted; each such entry remains a separate stored entry.

The represented matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ is defined entrywise by

$$A_{ij}:=\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}v_t\qquad(0\le i<m,\ 0\le j<n),$$

where $\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}$ is $1_F$ when $c_t=j$ and $0_F$ otherwise, and an
empty sum is $0_F$. Repeated entries in column $j$ are therefore added. The
number $s$ is the **stored-entry count**; it is not in general the number of
nonzero entries of $A$.

A CSR record is **canonical** when no row repeats a column and no stored value
is zero. In that case every nonzero matrix entry is stored exactly once and
$s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)$, where $\operatorname{nnz}(A)$ denotes the number of
nonzero entries of $A$. If $m=0$, the endpoint conditions force $s=0$ and the
row-pointer array has its single entry $r_0=0$. If $n=0$, the column-index
condition forces $s=0$ as well.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

derivations.claim: Take $$A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&0\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$ By [F4], this is a matrix over a field. Its canonical sorted CSR pattern is $P=\{(1,1),(1,2),(2,2),(3,1),(3,3)\}$, with all diagonal entries equal to $1$. Thus the input satisfies the algorithm's domain and has no missing diagonal.

The first row gives $U_{11}=U_{12}=1$. Row 2 has no strict-lower position and gives $U_{22}=1$. In row 3 the only strict-lower position is $(3,1)$, so $L_{31}=1$. The update from this multiplier can reach only a column $j>1$ present in both row 3 and row 1; no such column exists. Hence $L_{32}$ is not stored, $U_{33}=1$, and the procedure returns `ok` with $$L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad U=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
By [F3], $(LU)_{32}=L_{31}U_{12}+L_{32}U_{22}+L_{33}U_{32}=1$, whereas $A_{32}=0$. Therefore $LU$ has a nonzero outside the input pattern, so the refuted statement is false.

Let $n,m\in\mathbb N$ with $n,m\ge1$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), let
$A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]), and let $b,x_0\in\mathbb C^n$.
The complex scalars form a field ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]).
As additional input, take maps $\mathcal P_1,\ldots,\mathcal P_m:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$.
The maps may vary with $j$; no linearity or fixedness is assumed. In the usual
matrix case, $\mathcal P_j(v)=M_j^{-1}v$ for an invertible $M_j$
([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]).
Equip each coordinate space $\mathbb C^q$ used below with the standard
Hermitian inner product
$$\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{a<q}z_a\overline{w_a}$$
and its induced Euclidean norm $\|z\|_2=\sqrt{\langle z,z\rangle}$
([[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]], [[def-inner-product-norm]]).
All arithmetic and orthogonalization are exact. Iteration and auxiliary
Hessenberg labels below start at $1$; coordinates of $A$ and ambient vectors
retain the library's zero-based convention.

The algorithm uses and stores each actual $z_j$ and makes no fixed-matrix
assumption.

Set $r_0=b-Ax_0$ and $\beta=\|r_0\|_2$. If $\beta=0$, return
`initial-solution($x_0$)`. Otherwise set $v_1=r_0/\beta$. For
$j=1,\ldots,m$, perform:

1. Obtain $z_j=\mathcal P_j(v_j)$ and set $w:=Az_j$.
2. For $i=1,\ldots,j$ in order, set
   $$h_{ij}:=\langle w,v_i\rangle,\qquad w:=w-h_{ij}v_i.$$
3. Set $h_{j+1,j}:=\|w\|_2$. If $h_{j+1,j}=0$, return
   `breakdown($j,x_{j-1}$)` with the last fully formed iterate (for $j=1$ it
   is $x_0$); do not normalize or claim a new iterate at this step.
4. If $h_{j+1,j}>0$, set $v_{j+1}:=w/h_{j+1,j}$. Let $e_0\in\mathbb C^{j+1}$
   be the standard unit vector at coordinate $0$ (coordinate $0$ is $1$ and
   all other coordinates are $0$; [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The
   iteration labels $h_{ik}$ remain one-based, while matrix slots are
   zero-based: put $Z_j\in M_{n\times j}(\mathbb C)$ with
   $(Z_j)_{a,k-1}=(z_k)_a$ for $0\le a<n$, $1\le k\le j$, and let
   $\bar H_j\in M_{(j+1)\times j}(\mathbb C)$ satisfy
   $(\bar H_j)_{i-1,k-1}=h_{ik}$ for $1\le k\le j$, $1\le i\le k+1$, and
   $(\bar H_j)_{a,b}=0$ when $a>b+1$. Choose any
   $$y_j\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb C^j}\|\beta e_0-\bar H_jy\|_2$$
   and set $x_j:=x_0+Z_jy_j$.

If all $m$ steps complete without breakdown, return
`budget-complete($m,x_m,Z_m$)`. The finite-dimensional least-squares minimizer
exists because each coordinate space $\mathbb C^q$ is finite-dimensional by
[[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], and the least-squares theorem
[[thm-least-squares-solutions-and-normal-equation]] applies; the output
relation permits any minimizer. The algorithm has no
convergence test: `budget-complete` and `breakdown` assert neither convergence
nor that a breakdown iterate solves $Ax=b$. The residual-minimization property
over the actual span of the $z_j$ is proved separately in
[[thm-flexible-gmres-residual-minimization-on-actual-preconditioned-span]].
Every division is by a positive real norm: the initial $\beta=0$ case returns
before normalizing $r_0$, and each later $h_{j+1,j}=0$ case returns before
normalizing $w$.

   `breakdown($j,x_{j-1}$)` with the last fully formed iterate (for $j=1$ it
   is $x_0$); do not normalize or claim a new iterate at this step.
4. If $h_{j+1,j}>0$, set $v_{j+1}:=w/h_{j+1,j}$. Let $e_0\in\mathbb C^{j+1}$
   be the standard unit vector at coordinate $0$ (coordinate $0$ is $1$ and
   all other coordinates are $0$; [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The
   iteration labels $h_{ik}$ remain one-based, while matrix slots are
   zero-based: put $Z_j\in M_{n\times j}(\mathbb C)$ with
   $(Z_j)_{a,k-1}=(z_k)_a$ for $0\le a<n$, $1\le k\le j$, and let
   $\bar H_j\in M_{(j+1)\times j}(\mathbb C)$ satisfy
   $(\bar H_j)_{i-1,k-1}=h_{ik}$ for $1\le k\le j$, $1\le i\le k+1$, and
   $(\bar H_j)_{a,b}=0$ when $a>b+1$. Choose any
   $$y_j\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb C^j}\|\beta e_0-\bar H_jy\|_2$$
   and set $x_j:=x_0+Z_jy_j$.

If all $m$ steps complete without breakdown, return
`budget-complete($m,x_m,Z_m$)`. The finite-dimensional least-squares minimizer
exists because each coordinate space $\mathbb C^q$ is finite-dimensional by
[[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], and the least-squares theorem
[[thm-least-squares-solutions-and-normal-equation]] applies; the output
relation permits any minimizer. The algorithm has no
convergence test: `budget-complete` and `breakdown` assert neither convergence
nor that a breakdown iterate solves $Ax=b$. The residual-minimization property
over the actual span of the $z_j$ is proved separately in
[[thm-flexible-gmres-residual-minimization-on-actual-preconditioned-span]].
Every division is by a positive real norm: the initial $\beta=0$ case returns
before normalizing $r_0$, and each later $h_{j+1,j}=0$ case returns before
normalizing $w$.

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces and let $b\in W$. A vector $x\in V$ minimises $\lVert Tx-b\rVert$ if and only if

$$T^*(Tx-b)=0,$$

equivalently $T^*Tx=T^*b$. Minimisers exist, and if $x_0$ is one minimiser, then the full set of minimisers is $x_0+\ker T$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

### Finite sums of vectors

By axiom (V1) the triple $(V, +, 0_V)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), hence
in particular a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]). So the finite
products of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] are available in it, and we write them
**additively**: for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a finite list $u : n \to V$, that is a
function on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]),

$$\sum_{i<n} u_i \;:=\; \prod_{i<n} u_i \quad \text{computed in } (V,+,0_V),$$

so that $\sum_{i<0} u_i = 0_V$ and $\sum_{i<\sigma(n)} u_i = \bigl(\sum_{i<n} u_i\bigr) + u_n$,
and the value depends only on $u_0, \dots, u_{n-1}$.

### Linear combinations

A **linear combination in $V$** is a vector of the form

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

where $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ is a finite list of scalars and
$v : n \to V$ is a finite list of vectors; the sum is the finite sum just
described, of the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. For $S \subseteq V$, a vector
$w \in V$ is a **linear combination of elements of $S$** when there are
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ and $v : n \to S$ with
$w = \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$.

**The empty case is a real case.** $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]), and at $n = 0$ the sum is the empty sum, which is
$0_V$. So $0_V$ is a linear combination of elements of every subset of $V$,
including $S = \varnothing$. The lists are indexed from $0$, so a linear
combination of length $n$ is $\lambda_0 v_0 + \dots + \lambda_{n-1}v_{n-1}$; no
statement here is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

### The span

Let $S \subseteq V$. The set of linear subspaces of $V$ containing $S$ is
nonempty, since $V$ itself is one, so its intersection is a linear subspace of
$V$ by [[lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces]]. That intersection is the **span
of $S$**,

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;:=\; \bigcap \{\, W \;:\; W \text{ is a linear subspace of } V \text{ and } S \subseteq W \,\} .$$

It contains $S$, being an intersection of sets each of which contains $S$, and it
is contained in every linear subspace of $V$ that contains $S$. So it is the
**smallest** linear subspace of $V$ containing $S$, and those two properties
determine it uniquely: if $W$ and $W'$ both contain $S$ and are each contained in
every linear subspace containing $S$, then each is contained in the other. This
is what licenses the definite article.

A subset $S \subseteq V$ **spans** $V$, or is a **spanning set** of $V$, when
$\operatorname{span}(S) = V$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq V$. Write

$$L(S) \;:=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i \;:\; n \in \mathbb{N},\ \lambda : n \to F,\ v : n \to S \,\Bigr\}$$

for the set of linear combinations of elements of $S$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]). Then

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;=\; L(S).$$

In particular $\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$, and for every
$S \subseteq V$ the span of $S$ contains $0_V$ as the empty linear combination.

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $F^{n}$ be the
function space on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, with the
pointwise operations ([[def-function-space]], [[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). For $i < n$ define the **standard unit vector**
$e_i \in F^{n}$ by

$$e_i(i) = 1_F, \qquad e_i(j) = 0_F \ \text{ for } j < n \text{ with } j \ne i .$$

Then:

1. **Finite sums in a function space are pointwise.** For every set $X$, every
   $p \in \mathbb{N}$, every list $u : p \to F^{X}$ and every $j \in X$,
   $$\Bigl(\sum_{k<p} u_k\Bigr)(j) \;=\; \sum_{k<p} u_k(j),$$
   the right-hand sum being taken in $(F,+,0_F)$. (Stated here for an arbitrary
   $X$ because the companion page needs it at $X = \mathbb{N}$.)
2. $e : n \to F^{n}$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$ ([[def-linear-basis]]); in
   particular $e$ is injective and its image $e[n] = \{\, e_i : i < n \,\}$ is a
   basis of $F^{n}$ with $e[n] \approx n$ ([[def-equinumerous]]);
3. for every $\lambda : n \to F$ and every $j < n$,
   $\bigl(\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i e_i\bigr)(j) = \lambda_j$; equivalently the
   coordinate list of $x \in F^{n}$ with respect to the ordered basis $e$
   ([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) is
   $i \mapsto x(i)$;
4. $F^{n}$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ with $\dim_F F^{n} = n$
   ([[def-dimension]]);
5. at $n = 0$ this reads: $F^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
   so $F^{0}$ is the zero space, the empty list is its ordered basis,
   $\varnothing$ is its basis and $\dim_F F^{0} = 0$.

Every index runs from $0$, so the coordinates of an element of $F^{n}$ are
$x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ and no statement above is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

derivations.claim: Since this run reaches the first step, [F1] gives $r_0\ne0$ and $\beta=\sqrt{\langle r_0,r_0\rangle}>0$. Since $\beta$ is real, $\langle r_0/\beta,r_0/\beta\rangle=\beta^{-2}\langle r_0,r_0\rangle=1$, so $v_1$ has norm $1$. Inductively suppose $v_1,\ldots,v_j$ are orthonormal. At the $i$th Gram–Schmidt substep, the current vector $w$ is orthogonal to $v_k$ for $k<i$. The update $w':=w-h_{ij}v_i$, with $h_{ij}=\langle w,v_i\rangle$, satisfies $\langle w',v_i\rangle=h_{ij}-h_{ij}\langle v_i,v_i\rangle=0$ and $\langle w',v_k\rangle=\langle w,v_k\rangle-h_{ij}\langle v_i,v_k\rangle=0$ for each $k<i$. These equalities use linearity in the first argument and orthonormality [F4]. After all $i=1,\ldots,j$, the final $w$ is orthogonal to every current basis vector. Nonbreakdown gives $h_{j+1,j}=\|w\|_2>0$; the same inner-product calculation gives $\langle v_{j+1},v_{j+1}\rangle=h_{j+1,j}^{-2}\langle w,w\rangle=1$, and its orthogonality follows from that of $w$. Induction proves orthonormality through $v_{m+1}$.

The finite matrix $\bar H_m$ defines a linear map $\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb C^{m+1}$ between finite-dimensional inner-product spaces by [F6], [F10], and [F11]. By [F7], least-squares minimizers exist and any two differ by an element of $\ker\bar H_m$. This kernel is zero: if $\bar H_my=0$, its zero-based last row $a=m$ gives $h_{m+1,m}y_{m-1}=0$, hence $y_{m-1}=0$. For each one-based row label $r=m,m-1,\ldots,2$ in descending order, matrix row $r-1$ has coefficient $h_{r,r-1}$ in column $r-2$; its other possibly nonzero terms use coordinates $y_{k-1}$ with $k\ge r$, already shown zero. Thus $h_{r,r-1}y_{r-2}=0$. Since $h_{r,r-1}=h_{(r-1)+1,r-1}>0$ by no breakdown, we obtain $y_{r-2}=0$. Thus every zero-based coordinate vanishes, $\bar H_m$ is injective, and its least-squares minimizer is unique.

At the end of column $j$, the successive subtractions give $Az_j=\sum_{i=1}^j h_{ij}v_i+w$. Since $w=h_{j+1,j}v_{j+1}$, this is $Az_j=\sum_{i=1}^{j+1}h_{ij}v_i$. Assembling these column identities for $j=1,\ldots,m$ yields $AZ_m=V_{m+1}\bar H_m$.

The initial residual is $r_0=b-Ax_0=\beta v_1$. The vector $e_0$ has value $1$ in coordinate $0$ and $0$ in every other coordinate by [F11], so $V_{m+1}\beta e_0=\beta v_1$. For any $y\in\mathbb C^m$, linearity and step 1.3 give $b-A(x_0+Z_my)=r_0-AZ_my=V_{m+1}(\beta e_0-\bar H_my)$.

For every $c\in\mathbb C^{m+1}$, orthonormality from step 1.1 and the coordinate inner product [F4] give $\|V_{m+1}c\|_2^2=\langle V_{m+1}c,V_{m+1}c\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}\sum_{k=1}^{m+1}c_{i-1}\overline{c_{k-1}}\langle v_i,v_k\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}|c_{i-1}|^2=\|c\|_2^2$. Taking the nonnegative square roots defined by [F5] proves norm preservation. Apply it to $c=\beta e_0-\bar H_my$ in step 2.1 to obtain the asserted norm identity.

Put $S=\{z_1,\ldots,z_m\}$. By [F9], every $u\in\operatorname{span}(S)$ is a finite combination $u=\sum_{a<q}c_a z_{j_a}$ for some $q\in\mathbb N$, where $a$ is a zero-based list coordinate and each $j_a\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ is a one-based column label. For each one-based column label $k=1,\ldots,m$, define the zero-based coordinate $y_{k-1}$ of $y\in\mathbb C^m$ to be $\sum_{a<q,\ j_a=k}c_a$, taking this empty sum to be zero. The finite sum laws and distributivity give $u=\sum_{k=1}^m y_{k-1}z_k=Z_my$ by the column convention in the algorithm. Conversely, each $Z_my$ is the finite linear combination $\sum_{k=1}^m y_{k-1}z_k$, so it lies in $\operatorname{span}(S)$ by [F8] and [F9]. Thus the two sets agree. By step 3.1, for every vector in this affine set its true residual norm equals $\|\beta e_0-\bar H_my\|_2$. Therefore the unique least-squares minimizer from step 1.2 gives $x_m=x_0+Z_my_m$ with minimum true residual over the whole affine span.

boundaries.reason: The theorem assumes n>=1 and m>=1, so the empty-coordinate case is outside its statement.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 uses the nonzero initial-residual branch; the algorithm returns the initial solution when the residual is zero.
For m=1, steps 1.2, 1.3, 2.1, 3.1, and 4.1 give the unique small minimizer and the one-column residual relation.
Step 1.2 proves injectivity from the nonzero subdiagonal even when A itself is singular; no nonsingularity of A is assumed.

boundaries.reason: There is no interval or endpoint parameter.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.2 proves the least-squares minimizer is unique on every nonbreakdown run, so no choice principle is used.

boundaries.reason: The statement is a direct residual-minimization theorem, not a biconditional.
The statement is a direct residual-minimization theorem, not a biconditional.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt: For $i=1,\ldots,j$ in order, set $$h_{ij}:=\langle w,v_i\rangle,\qquad w:=w-h_{ij}v_i.$$
supplier_interfaces.use: Provides the exact modified Gram–Schmidt column recurrence used to prove the Arnoldi relation.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt: Minimisers exist, and if $x_0$ is one minimiser, then the full set of minimisers is $x_0+\ker T$.
supplier_interfaces.use: Supplies existence of the finite-dimensional least-squares minimizer; uniqueness follows from the locally proved zero kernel.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt: $$e_i(i) = 1_F, \qquad e_i(j) = 0_F \ \text{ for } j < n \text{ with } j \ne i .$$
supplier_interfaces.use: Identifies e_0 as the first coordinate vector in the residual relation.

citations.quote:
Let $a<b$, put $L=b-a$ and $m=(a+b)/2$, and let $f\in C^4([a,b])$. Define
the one-block Simpson value and its kernel by

$$S(f;a,b):=\frac{L}{6}\bigl(f(a)+4f(m)+f(b)\bigr),\qquad K_{a,b}(x):=\begin{cases}\frac{(x-a)^3(3(x-a)-2L)}{72},&a\le x\le m,\\\frac{(b-x)^3(3(b-x)-2L)}{72},&m\le x\le b.\end{cases}$$

Then

$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-S(f;a,b)=\int_a^bK_{a,b}(x)f^{(4)}(x)\,dx,$$

and $K_{a,b}\le0$ with
$\int_a^b|K_{a,b}(x)|\,dx=L^5/2880$. The value $S(f;a,b)$ is the one-block
specialization of [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]].

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$. Then the closed bounded interval
$[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]]) is compact ([[def-open-cover-r]]): every family of
open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ whose union contains $[a,b]$ has a finite subfamily
whose union already contains $[a,b]$.

The proof is by repeated bisection. Supposing some open cover admits no finite
subcover, one halves the interval, keeps a half that still admits none, and
iterates; the halves shrink to a point, which the cover does reach, and a single
member of the cover then swallows a whole late-stage half. **The halving rule is
canonical**, taking the left half whenever the left half works, so the recursion
uses [[thm-recursion]] and no choice principle.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$m \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } x \in [a,b],$$

with $m, M$ real. Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]), so its Darboux sums
and integrals are defined ([[def-darboux-sums]], [[def-darboux-integral]]), and
for **every** partition $P$ of $[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]])

$$m(b-a) \;\le\; L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) \;\le\; M(b-a) .$$

In particular, taking $f$ to be the constant function with value $c$:

$$\int_a^b c \;=\; c\,(b-a) ,$$

the constant function being integrable, with $L(f,P) = U(f,P) = c(b-a)$ for
every partition $P$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

Input $a<b$, an absolute indicator tolerance $\tau>0$, a remaining depth
$D\in\mathbb N$ and a positive panel-call budget $P\in\mathbb N$, and a
deterministic evaluation routine $\operatorname{Eval}$ that returns a finite
real value at a requested node or reports failure. It reports failure when a
required node cannot be evaluated, including when its midpoint is
unrepresentable in the evaluator's arithmetic. Apply the exact-real Simpson
formulas of [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]] to the returned values;
floating-point rounding accuracy is not asserted.

Define the recursive call $A(u,v,d,p,t)$ for $u<v$, $d\ge0$, $p\ge1$ and
$t>0$ as follows.

1. Compute $m=(u+v)/2$ and the five values of $\operatorname{Eval}$ at
   $u,(3u+v)/4,m,(u+3v)/4,v$. On failure, return `failure` with no estimate.
2. Compute $S_0=Q_S(f;u,v,2)$ and $S_1=Q_S(f;u,v,4)$ from the two nested
   grids of [[def-adaptive-simpson-refinement-indicator]], and put
   $\eta=\eta_2(f;u,v)=|S_1-S_0|/15$.
3. If $\eta\le t$, return (`accepted`, estimate $S_1$, indicator $\eta$).
4. If $\eta>t$ and either $d=0$ or $p<3$, return (`cap-reached`, estimate
   $S_1$, indicator $\eta$).
5. Otherwise put $p_L=\lfloor(p-1)/2\rfloor$ and
   $p_R=\lceil(p-1)/2\rceil$. Recursively call
   $A(u,m,d-1,p_L,t/2)$ and $A(m,v,d-1,p_R,t/2)$. If either returns failure,
   return failure. Otherwise return the sum of their estimates and indicators,
   with status `cap-reached` if either child has that status and `accepted`
   otherwise.

The public call is $A(a,b,D,P,\tau)$. The budget counts recursive panel calls;
each call uses at most five point evaluations. `accepted` means that the
returned leaf indicators sum to at most $\tau$. Neither that status nor the
indicator is a certified true-error statement. A cap result is an estimate
with explicit `cap-reached` status, not a successful tolerance claim.

derivations.claim: If $d=0$ or $p<3$, the call cannot split by [F1]. It requests at most five values and either returns failure immediately on a failed evaluation or returns its finite refined value and indicator as an accepted or cap-reached leaf. The leaf estimate is its refined Simpson value and its indicator is nonnegative by [F2]; if accepted, its indicator is at most $t$.

For strong induction on positive $p$, assume [IH] the claims hold for every smaller positive panel budget. If $d>0$ and $p$ is at least $3$, [F1] gives two positive child budgets, each smaller than $p$, whose sum is $p-1$. The induction hypothesis applies to both recursive calls, so they terminate and together use at most $p-1$ panel calls; adding the parent gives at most $p$. Each call uses at most five requests, so the total is at most $5p$.

If the call does not split, its output is a single leaf and step 1.1 gives the leaf-sum representation and, when accepted, its indicator is at most $t$. If it splits, the child panels partition the parent and [F1] adds their estimates and nonnegative indicators, so the induction hypothesis gives the leaf-sum representation. The parent is accepted in this branch only when both child results are accepted; their indicator totals are each at most $t/2$ by induction, hence their sum is at most $t$. By [F1], a cap result is either returned at a rejected terminal leaf or propagated from a child; because the tree is finite by step 2.1, following such propagation reaches a rejected leaf whose depth or panel-call cap prevents another split. No implication to true error is in [F1] or [F2].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Input real endpoints $a,b$, an integer $n$, and an evaluation function $f$.
If $a\ge b$ or $n<2$, return invalid-grid without evaluating $f$. For the
remaining inputs require $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ to be evaluable at every
point of $[a,b]$. If $n$ is odd, the procedure returns
invalid-Simpson-panel-count. If $n$ is even, put
$h=(b-a)/n$ and $x_j=a+jh$ for $0\le j\le n$; return

$$Q_S(f;a,b,n):=\frac h3\sum_{j<n/2}\bigl(f(x_{2j})+4f(x_{2j+1})+f(x_{2j+2})\bigr).$$

The sum is a finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Each two-panel block
$[x_{2j},x_{2j+2}]$ uses its endpoints and midpoint. Expanding the block sum
gives weights $1,4,2,\ldots,4,1$. The even condition
$n\ge2$ makes the number of blocks a positive integer. The formula is an exact-real
procedure; floating point evaluation and summation error are separate from
its quadrature error.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$m \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } x \in [a,b],$$

with $m, M$ real. Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]), so its Darboux sums
and integrals are defined ([[def-darboux-sums]], [[def-darboux-integral]]), and
for **every** partition $P$ of $[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]])

$$m(b-a) \;\le\; L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) \;\le\; M(b-a) .$$

In particular, taking $f$ to be the constant function with value $c$:

$$\int_a^b c \;=\; c\,(b-a) ,$$

the constant function being integrable, with $L(f,P) = U(f,P) = c(b-a)$ for
every partition $P$.

citations.quote:
Input $a<b$, an absolute indicator tolerance $\tau>0$, a remaining depth
$D\in\mathbb N$ and a positive panel-call budget $P\in\mathbb N$, and a
deterministic evaluation routine $\operatorname{Eval}$ that returns a finite
real value at a requested node or reports failure. It reports failure when a
required node cannot be evaluated, including when its midpoint is
unrepresentable in the evaluator's arithmetic. Apply the exact-real Simpson
formulas of [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]] to the returned values;
floating-point rounding accuracy is not asserted.

Define the recursive call $A(u,v,d,p,t)$ for $u<v$, $d\ge0$, $p\ge1$ and
$t>0$ as follows.

1. Compute $m=(u+v)/2$ and the five values of $\operatorname{Eval}$ at
   $u,(3u+v)/4,m,(u+3v)/4,v$. On failure, return `failure` with no estimate.
2. Compute $S_0=Q_S(f;u,v,2)$ and $S_1=Q_S(f;u,v,4)$ from the two nested
   grids of [[def-adaptive-simpson-refinement-indicator]], and put
   $\eta=\eta_2(f;u,v)=|S_1-S_0|/15$.
3. If $\eta\le t$, return (`accepted`, estimate $S_1$, indicator $\eta$).
4. If $\eta>t$ and either $d=0$ or $p<3$, return (`cap-reached`, estimate
   $S_1$, indicator $\eta$).
5. Otherwise put $p_L=\lfloor(p-1)/2\rfloor$ and
   $p_R=\lceil(p-1)/2\rceil$. Recursively call
   $A(u,m,d-1,p_L,t/2)$ and $A(m,v,d-1,p_R,t/2)$. If either returns failure,
   return failure. Otherwise return the sum of their estimates and indicators,
   with status `cap-reached` if either child has that status and `accepted`
   otherwise.

The public call is $A(a,b,D,P,\tau)$. The budget counts recursive panel calls;
each call uses at most five point evaluations. `accepted` means that the
returned leaf indicators sum to at most $\tau$. Neither that status nor the
indicator is a certified true-error statement. A cap result is an estimate
with explicit `cap-reached` status, not a successful tolerance claim.

Let $a<b$, let $n\ge2$ be even, and let $f$ be real-valued at the nodes of
the uniform grids with $n$ and $2n$ subintervals. The **coarse Simpson value**
is $S_0=Q_S(f;a,b,n)$ and the **refined value** is
$S_1=Q_S(f;a,b,2n)$, using [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]]. The signed
**refinement indicator** is $(S_1-S_0)/15$ and its magnitude is
$$\eta_n(f;a,b):=\frac{|S_1-S_0|}{15}.$$

For the local two-panel case $n=2$, $S_1$ is also the sum of the two
one-block Simpson values on the halves of $[a,b]$.

This definition alone is not a bound on the true error.

Input real endpoints $a,b$, an integer $n$, and an evaluation function $f$.
If $a\ge b$ or $n<2$, return invalid-grid without evaluating $f$. For the
remaining inputs require $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ to be evaluable at every
point of $[a,b]$. If $n$ is odd, the procedure returns
invalid-Simpson-panel-count. If $n$ is even, put
$h=(b-a)/n$ and $x_j=a+jh$ for $0\le j\le n$; return

$$Q_S(f;a,b,n):=\frac h3\sum_{j<n/2}\bigl(f(x_{2j})+4f(x_{2j+1})+f(x_{2j+2})\bigr).$$

The sum is a finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Each two-panel block
$[x_{2j},x_{2j+2}]$ uses its endpoints and midpoint. Expanding the block sum
gives weights $1,4,2,\ldots,4,1$. The even condition
$n\ge2$ makes the number of blocks a positive integer. The formula is an exact-real
procedure; floating point evaluation and summation error are separate from
its quadrature error.

derivations.claim: The endpoint values are $f(0)=f(1)=1/2501$, the midpoint value is $f(1/2)=1$, and the quarter-point values are $f(1/4)=f(3/4)=1/626$. The composite rule [F3] gives $S_0=2/3+1/7503$ and $S_1=(1/12)(2+8/626+2/2501)$.
The indicator rejects the root, and $D=0$ prevents subdivision. By [F1], the procedure returns the refined estimate with `cap-reached` status; it makes no tolerance-success claim.

Input real endpoints $a,b$, an integer $n$, and an evaluation function $f$.
If $a\ge b$ or $n<2$, return invalid-grid without evaluating $f$. For the
remaining inputs require $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ to be evaluable at every
point of $[a,b]$. If $n$ is odd, the procedure returns
invalid-Simpson-panel-count. If $n$ is even, put
$h=(b-a)/n$ and $x_j=a+jh$ for $0\le j\le n$; return

$$Q_S(f;a,b,n):=\frac h3\sum_{j<n/2}\bigl(f(x_{2j})+4f(x_{2j+1})+f(x_{2j+2})\bigr).$$

The sum is a finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Each two-panel block
$[x_{2j},x_{2j+2}]$ uses its endpoints and midpoint. Expanding the block sum
gives weights $1,4,2,\ldots,4,1$. The even condition
$n\ge2$ makes the number of blocks a positive integer. The formula is an exact-real
procedure; floating point evaluation and summation error are separate from
its quadrature error.

Let $a<b$, let $n\ge2$ be even, and let $f$ be real-valued at the nodes of
the uniform grids with $n$ and $2n$ subintervals. The **coarse Simpson value**
is $S_0=Q_S(f;a,b,n)$ and the **refined value** is
$S_1=Q_S(f;a,b,2n)$, using [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]]. The signed
**refinement indicator** is $(S_1-S_0)/15$ and its magnitude is
$$\eta_n(f;a,b):=\frac{|S_1-S_0|}{15}.$$

For the local two-panel case $n=2$, $S_1$ is also the sum of the two
one-block Simpson values on the halves of $[a,b]$.

This definition alone is not a bound on the true error.

Let $a<b$, $f\in C^4([a,b])$, $n_k=2^k$ for $k\ge1$,
$h_k=(b-a)/n_k$, $Q_k=Q_S(f;a,b,n_k)$, and
$c=-(1/180)\int_a^b f^{(4)}(x)\,dx$. Let $I=\int_a^b f$. Then the
refinement indicator
$$\eta_k=\frac{|Q_{k+1}-Q_k|}{15}$$
satisfies $\eta_k=|c|h_k^4/16+o(h_k^4)$. If $c\ne0$, then
$\eta_k/|I-Q_{k+1}|\to1$. The Richardson-corrected value
$R_{k+1}=Q_{k+1}+(Q_{k+1}-Q_k)/15$ satisfies
$I-R_{k+1}=o(h_k^4)$. When $c=0$, these statements give no relative
error estimate for $\eta_k$; at no finite level does $\eta_k$ alone certify
the true error.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

derivations.claim: By [F4] and [F5], $f^{(4)}(x)=360x^2-120$ and this derivative is continuous. An antiderivative is $120x^3-120x$, so [F6]–[F7] give $\int_0^1 f^{(4)}(x)\,dx=0$. Hence $f\in C^4([0,1])$ by [F8], and the leading coefficient in [F3] is zero.

By [F4]–[F5], $x^7/7-x^5$ has derivative $f$ and $f$ is continuous, so [F6]–[F7] give the exact integral $1/7-1=-6/7$. Also $f(0)=0$, $f(1/2)=-19/64$, and $f(1)=-4$; substitution in [F1] gives $Q_{n=2}=-83/96$. The quarter-point values are $f(1/4)=-79/4096$ and $f(3/4)=-5751/4096$, so [F1] also gives $Q_{n=4}=\frac1{12}\left(4\left(-\frac{79}{4096}\right)+2\left(-\frac{19}{64}\right)+4\left(-\frac{5751}{4096}\right)-4\right)=-\frac{5267}{6144}.$ Thus the refined error is $-6/7-Q_{n=4}=5/43008$, and the coarse error is $-6/7-Q_{n=2}=5/672$.

From [F2], $\eta=|Q_{n=4}-Q_{n=2}|/15=1/2048$. Hence $\eta/(5/43008)=21/5$. The nonzero refined error and zero leading coefficient show why the asymptotic /15 relation supplies no relative finite-level guarantee in the cancelled case.
