For an ODE $y'=f(t,y)$ on states in $\mathbb R^d$ with $d\ge1$, two explicit Runge–Kutta weight vectors $b=(b_i)_{i=1}^s$ and $\widehat b=(\widehat b_i)_{i=1}^s$ are an **embedded pair** when they use the same explicit stage recursion
$$K_i=f\!\left(t_n+c_i h,\ y_n+h\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}K_j\right),\qquad 1\le i\le s,$$
but produce two one-step values
$$Y=y_n+h\sum_{i=1}^s b_iK_i,\qquad \widehat Y=y_n+h\sum_{i=1}^s\widehat b_iK_i.$$
The two methods are the **high** and **low** members when their local orders are respectively at least $p+1$ and $p$, for an integer $p\ge1$. Their **embedded difference estimator** is the nonnegative scalar
$$E_n(h):=\|\widehat Y-Y\|_2,$$
with the Euclidean norm. This definition asserts only how the estimator is computed; its reliability as a bound for either local defect is a separate claim and is not part of the definition.

The stage recursion and the local defect sign convention are those of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]] and [[def-one-step-ode-method-local-defect-order-and-stability]].

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct
analogue, and its place is taken by the factorisation of $b^n - a^n$ and the
resulting Lipschitz estimate ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

citations.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

For $y'=f(t,y)$, take the shared explicit stages
$$K_1=f(t_n,y_n),\qquad K_2=f(t_n+h,y_n+hK_1).$$
The Euler member is $Y_E=y_n+hK_1$ and the Heun explicit trapezoidal member is $Y_H=y_n+\frac h2(K_1+K_2)$. Their embedded difference is $Y_H-Y_E=\frac h2(K_2-K_1)$. The local orders are proved separately. In [[def-embedded-runge-kutta-pair-and-error-estimator]] notation, the common tableau has $c=(0,1)$, $A_{21}=1$, high weights $(1/2,1/2)$ and low weights $(1,0)$.

derivations.claim: Subtracting the two defect identities cancels the common exact value: $\widehat Y-Y=D_p-D_{p+1}=a h^{p+1}+O(h^{p+2})$. Thus there is a vector remainder $r(h)=O(h^{p+2})$ with $\widehat Y-Y=h^{p+1}(a+h r_1(h))$, where $r_1$ is bounded for all sufficiently small positive $h$.

By [F2], $|E(h)/h^{p+1}-\|a\|_2|\le h\|r_1(h)\|_2\to0$. If $a\ne0$, the same argument gives $\|D_p(h)\|_2/h^{p+1}\to\|a\|_2>0$; dividing the two positive limits proves $E(h)/\|D_p(h)\|_2\to1$. If $a=0$, the expansions give only $D_p=O(h^{p+2})$ and $E=O(h^{p+2})$, with no lower bound. To verify that the ratio-one conclusion can fail for an actual embedded Runge–Kutta pair, use the Heun–Euler pair [F3] on $y\prime=t^2$, $y(0)=0$: $K_1=0$, $K_2=h^2$, $Y_E=0$, $Y_H=h^3/2$, and the exact endpoint is $h^3/3$. Thus $D_1=-h^3/3$, the estimator is $h^3/2$, and their norm ratio is $3/2$, while the $h^2$ coefficient is zero. Conversely, for the zero field with zero initial state, both outputs and the estimator vanish identically, so no positive lower bound for the estimator follows either.

A **real interval** is a closed set $[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ with finite dyadic
endpoints $a\le b$. Its width is $b-a$, midpoint is $(a+b)/2$, and its
midpoint-radius form is $m+[-r,r]$ with $m=(a+b)/2$ and $r=(b-a)/2$. The empty
set is the status `empty`; the whole real line is `entire`. `overflow`,
`domain-error`, `split-domain`, and `inconclusive` are computation statuses,
not finite intervals.

A **complex rectangle** is $X+iY=\{x+iy:x\in X,\ y\in Y\}$ for real intervals
$X,Y$. Complex addition and multiplication use
$(x+iy)+(u+iv)=(x+u)+i(y+v)$ and
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$. For $z=x+iy$, its complex modulus is
$|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and for $z\ne0$ its reciprocal is
$1/z=(x-iy)/(x^2+y^2)$. A
**complex ball** $B(c,r)$ is
$\{z\in\mathbb C:|z-c|\le r\}$ with dyadic complex center $c$ and dyadic
$r\ge0$. For any two represented sets $S,T$, the inclusion order is
$S\sqsubseteq T$ iff $S\subseteq T$.

The width of a complex rectangle with coordinate widths $w_X,w_Y$ is its
Euclidean diameter $\sqrt{w_X^2+w_Y^2}$; the width of a ball $B(c,r)$ is its
diameter $2r$. Width comparisons against a dyadic tolerance can be decided by
exact rational comparisons after squaring the nonnegative quantities.

The **range** of a real or complex function $f$ on a set $S$ is
$f(S)=\{f(x):x\in S\cap\operatorname{dom}(f)\}$. A finite expression DAG is a
finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes, constant nodes, and operation
nodes; constants are exact dyadics or are supplied with certified enclosing
intervals. Sharing a node means the exact same intermediate value is reused.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$; the denominator interval is strictly positive because at
least one coordinate interval excludes zero. Division multiplies by this
reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

Let $d,N,p\ge1$, $T>0$, $h=T/N$, and $t_n=nh$. Let $y:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ solve an initial-value problem in an open time-state domain $D$. Use the Euclidean norm $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], whose triangle inequality is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]. Let $\mathcal T\subset D$ be a common compact time-state tube with positive margin in $D$, and write $\mathcal T_t:=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:(t,v)\in\mathcal T\}$. Suppose a one-step map $\Psi_{h,n}$ is defined on $\mathcal T_{t_n}$, produces $y_{n+1}=\Psi_{h,n}(y_n)$, and the entire exact path, all numerical grid states, and every method stage lie in $\mathcal T$. If constants $C,C_0,L\ge0$, independent of $N$ and $n$, satisfy
$$\|y_0-y(0)\|_2\le C_0h^p,\qquad \|\Psi_{h,n}(y(t_n))-y(t_{n+1})\|_2\le Ch^{p+1},$$
and
$$\|\Psi_{h,n}(u)-\Psi_{h,n}(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$
for every $u,v\in\mathcal T_{t_n}$ and $0\le n<N$, then, for $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, for $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Inputs are an IVP in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], $y'=f(t,y)$ on an open domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ with initial data $(t_0,y_0)\in D$ and requested interval $[t_0,T]$, where $t_0\le T$ and $d\ge1$; an initial proposal $0<h_{\rm init}\le h_{\max}$; an embedded pair with low order $p\ge1$ as in [[def-embedded-runge-kutta-pair-and-error-estimator]]; tolerances $\mathrm{atol}>0$ and $\mathrm{rtol}\ge0$; safety $0<\sigma<1$; scale bounds $0<\gamma_{\min}\le1\le\gamma_{\max}$; step bounds $0<h_{\min}\le h_{\max}$; and a positive integer attempt budget $N$.

**Output.** Return a record consisting of one of `success`, `failure`, `minimum-step-rejected`, or `attempt-budget-exhausted`, together with the accepted mesh $\mathcal A=((t_0,y_0),\ldots,(t_m,y_m))$. The mesh always contains the initial pair and every accepted endpoint; on `success`, $t_m=T$ and $y_m$ is the returned endpoint approximation. On any other status, $\mathcal A$ is the accepted prefix and $y_m$ is the last accepted approximation.

**Procedure.** Initialize $t:=t_0$, $y:=y_0$, $\mathcal A:=((t_0,y_0))$, and proposal $h_{\rm prop}:=h_{\rm init}$. If $t_0=T$, return `success` with $\mathcal A$. For each attempt index $k=1,\ldots,N$, perform exactly the following steps:

1. Set $h:=\min(h_{\rm prop},h_{\max},T-t)$. The last term permits a final clipped step shorter than $h_{\min}$. If $h\le0$ before reaching $T$, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$.
2. Evaluate the shared stages in tableau order, checking before each evaluation that its time-state input lies in $D$. If a stage input is outside $D$, its evaluation is undefined, or its value is nonfinite, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$. Compute both pair outputs; if either output or any arithmetic needed to compute them is undefined, fails, or is nonfinite in the rounded realization, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$.
3. Define $s_i:=\mathrm{atol}+\mathrm{rtol}\max(|(y)_i|,|(Y)_i|)$ and $Q:=\max_i |(\widehat Y-Y)_i|/s_i$, where $Y$ is the high-order value and $\widehat Y$ the low-order value. If any scale or $Q$ operation fails or is nonfinite in the rounded realization, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$. If $Q\le1$, first check $(t+h,Y)\in D$; if not, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$. Otherwise accept: set $t:=t+h$, $y:=Y$, and append $(t,y)$ to $\mathcal A$. If $Q>1$, reject and retain $t,y,\mathcal A$.
4. If the attempt was accepted and $t=T$, return `success` with $\mathcal A$. Otherwise, if it was rejected and $h\le h_{\min}$, return `minimum-step-rejected` with $\mathcal A$. These terminal checks precede the budget check, so a final accepted step that reaches $T$ succeeds and a rejection at the minimum step reports that safeguard.
5. If $k=N$, return `attempt-budget-exhausted` with $\mathcal A$. Otherwise compute
$$g=\begin{cases}\gamma_{\max},&Q=0,\\ \min(\gamma_{\max},\max(\gamma_{\min},\sigma /\sqrt[p+1]{Q})),&Q>0.\end{cases}$$
Set $h_{\rm prop}:=\min(h_{\max},\max(h_{\min},gh))$ and continue to attempt $k+1$. A failed or nonfinite rounded computation of $g$ or $h_{\rm prop}$ returns `failure` with $\mathcal A$.

Inputs are an IVP in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], $y'=f(t,y)$ on an open domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ with initial data $(t_0,y_0)\in D$ and requested interval $[t_0,T]$, where $t_0\le T$ and $d\ge1$; an initial proposal $0<h_{\rm init}\le h_{\max}$; an embedded pair with low order $p\ge1$ as in [[def-embedded-runge-kutta-pair-and-error-estimator]]; tolerances $\mathrm{atol}>0$ and $\mathrm{rtol}\ge0$; safety $0<\sigma<1$; scale bounds $0<\gamma_{\min}\le1\le\gamma_{\max}$; step bounds $0<h_{\min}\le h_{\max}$; and a positive integer attempt budget $N$.

**Output.** Return a record consisting of one of `success`, `failure`, `minimum-step-rejected`, or `attempt-budget-exhausted`, together with the accepted mesh $\mathcal A=((t_0,y_0),\ldots,(t_m,y_m))$. The mesh always contains the initial pair and every accepted endpoint; on `success`, $t_m=T$ and $y_m$ is the returned endpoint approximation. On any other status, $\mathcal A$ is the accepted prefix and $y_m$ is the last accepted approximation.

**Procedure.** Initialize $t:=t_0$, $y:=y_0$, $\mathcal A:=((t_0,y_0))$, and proposal $h_{\rm prop}:=h_{\rm init}$. If $t_0=T$, return `success` with $\mathcal A$. For each attempt index $k=1,\ldots,N$, perform exactly the following steps:

1. Set $h:=\min(h_{\rm prop},h_{\max},T-t)$. The last term permits a final clipped step shorter than $h_{\min}$. If $h\le0$ before reaching $T$, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$.
2. Evaluate the shared stages in tableau order, checking before each evaluation that its time-state input lies in $D$. If a stage input is outside $D$, its evaluation is undefined, or its value is nonfinite, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$. Compute both pair outputs; if either output or any arithmetic needed to compute them is undefined, fails, or is nonfinite in the rounded realization, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$.
3. Define $s_i:=\mathrm{atol}+\mathrm{rtol}\max(|(y)_i|,|(Y)_i|)$ and $Q:=\max_i |(\widehat Y-Y)_i|/s_i$, where $Y$ is the high-order value and $\widehat Y$ the low-order value. If any scale or $Q$ operation fails or is nonfinite in the rounded realization, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$. If $Q\le1$, first check $(t+h,Y)\in D$; if not, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$. Otherwise accept: set $t:=t+h$, $y:=Y$, and append $(t,y)$ to $\mathcal A$. If $Q>1$, reject and retain $t,y,\mathcal A$.
4. If the attempt was accepted and $t=T$, return `success` with $\mathcal A$. Otherwise, if it was rejected and $h\le h_{\min}$, return `minimum-step-rejected` with $\mathcal A$. These terminal checks precede the budget check, so a final accepted step that reaches $T$ succeeds and a rejection at the minimum step reports that safeguard.
5. If $k=N$, return `attempt-budget-exhausted` with $\mathcal A$. Otherwise compute
$$g=\begin{cases}\gamma_{\max},&Q=0,\\ \min(\gamma_{\max},\max(\gamma_{\min},\sigma /\sqrt[p+1]{Q})),&Q>0.\end{cases}$$
Set $h_{\rm prop}:=\min(h_{\max},\max(h_{\min},gh))$ and continue to attempt $k+1$. A failed or nonfinite rounded computation of $g$ or $h_{\rm prop}$ returns `failure` with $\mathcal A$.

For $Q>0$, $\sqrt[p+1]{Q}$ is the unique positive $(p+1)$st root supplied by [[thm-nth-roots-exist]]. The exponent $1/(p+1)$ is a leading-error model for step selection; neither acceptance nor this controller is a global error certificate or a stiffness test.

A rounded implementation instead applies its fixed finite-format rounding rule to every stage, output, scale, and controller-factor arithmetic operation and uses the resulting stored high and low values in the displayed difference and acceptance test; nonfinite or failed operations return `failure`. The finite termination theorem applies to either realization when each attempt has finite work. The rounded realization has no a posteriori guarantee: a tolerance below its resolution can be accepted because both stored values coincide.

derivations.claim: Fix an attempt. Computing its trial size, its $s$ stages, its two weighted sums, and the finite-dimensional scaled maximum uses finitely many operations. Any stipulated undefined or nonfinite stage returns `failure`; an accepted step reaching $T$ returns `success`; and a rejection at the minimum step returns its stated status, in that order before the budget branch. A nonterminal attempt computes its next proposal and advances to the next loop index.

The loop visits only the finite indices $1,\ldots,N$, with exactly one trial per visited index. If no earlier terminal branch returns, the $N$th attempt returns `attempt-budget-exhausted`; in particular, an accepted step reaching $T$ on that attempt has already returned `success`. Thus termination occurs after at most $N$ attempts.

citations.quote:
Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and consider a first-order IVP and solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **one-step method** is a family of maps $\Psi_h(t,v)$, defined for admitted times $t$, positive step sizes $h$, and states $v$, whose value is the method's approximation at time $t+h$ from the single input state $v$ at time $t$. It does not use earlier numerical states.

If $y$ is an exact solution on an interval containing $[t,t+h]$, the **local defect** is

$$\delta_h(t;y):=\Psi_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h).$$

Let $K\subseteq D$ be a fixed compact time-state set. The method has **uniform local order $p$ on $K$ along $y$** if there are constants $C\ge0$ and $h_0>0$, independent of the admitted starting time $t$ and step $0<h\le h_0$, such that

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le C h^{p+1}$$

whenever the exact solution graph on $[t,t+h]$ and the associated method time-state inputs, stages, and outputs under consideration lie in $K$. Here $p$ is a positive integer and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

The method has **one-step Lipschitz stability on $K$** with constant $L\ge0$ if

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$

for every admitted step size $h$, admitted time $t$, and input states $u,v$ with $(t,u),(t,v)\in K$. This is a bound on the change in one step; it is separate from absolute or linear stability regions and does not itself assert a global error estimate.

Fix one initial value problem and initial state. Let $D_p(h):=\widehat Y(h)-y(t+h)$ be the low member's one-step defect and $D_{p+1}(h):=Y(h)-y(t+h)$ the high member's defect, using the same exact initial state and step start. Suppose, as $h\downarrow0$,
$$D_p(h)=a h^{p+1}+O(h^{p+2}),\qquad D_{p+1}(h)=O(h^{p+2})$$
for a fixed vector $a\in\mathbb R^d$. Here $O(h^r)$ for a vector means a remainder whose Euclidean norm is at most $C h^r$ for all sufficiently small positive $h$. Then $\widehat Y(h)-Y(h)=a h^{p+1}+O(h^{p+2})$. If $a\ne0$, the estimator satisfies $E(h)/\|D_p(h)\|_2\to1$. If $a=0$, these hypotheses do not imply that this ratio tends to one or that the estimator is nonzero; the Euler–Heun pair on $y\prime=t^2$, $y(0)=0$, has ratio $3/2$ as computed below.

derivations.claim: Define $F(s):=f(s,y(s))$. By [F3], $F'(t)=g$. Since $f$ is $C^2$ and $y'=f(t,y)$, another application of [F3] shows $F'$ is continuously differentiable with bounded derivative on the short segment. Hence $y''=F'$ and $y'''=F''$ are bounded there. Apply the $k=2$ Taylor formula [F4] to each component of $y$; the common derivative bounds and finite dimension give a uniform vector remainder. This gives $y(t+h)=y_0+hK_1+\frac12h^2g+O(h^3)$.

Apply the $k=1$ Taylor formula [F4] componentwise to $f$ at $(t,y_0)$ along the increment $(h,hK_1)$. Its linear term is $h\partial_t f+hD_yf K_1=hg$, and its second-derivative remainder is $O(h^2)$ uniformly by the boundedness assumption. Therefore $K_2=K_1+hg+O(h^2)$. Substitution into [F1] gives $Y_E=y_0+hK_1$ and $Y_H=y_0+hK_1+\frac12h^2g+O(h^3)$.

Subtract the exact expansion in step 1.1 to obtain the two defect formulas and subtract the Euler output from the Heun output to obtain the estimator expansion. These are uniform $O(h^2)$ and $O(h^3)$ defect bounds, so [F2] gives the stated local orders. For $p=1$, the Euler defect coefficient is $-g/2$ and the Heun defect is $O(h^3)$; if $g\ne0$, [F5] gives the ratio-one conclusion. If $g=0$, both leading coefficients vanish and [F5] supplies no such inference.

Fix a dimension $d\ge1$, rational times $a<T$, a rational initial vector $y_0$, and an ODE field $f$ represented by a finite acyclic expression DAG with rational constants, time/state inputs, and only $+,-,\times,\div$ nodes. Its domain consists of points where every division is defined. Write $D_yf$ for the matrix of partial derivatives with respect to the state coordinates. A **finite rational residual-tube certificate** consists of the following exact rational data:

1. A finite partition $a=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=T$. On each panel $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, a vector polynomial $U_j(t)$ with dyadic (hence rational) coefficients, whose neighboring endpoint values agree exactly. These stored coefficients define the actual reconstruction, including any endpoint correction or rounded stage value used by an implementation.
2. For each panel, a closed rational state box $X_j\subset\mathbb R^d$, rational bounds $L_j\ge0$, $\rho_j\ge0$, a rational $d_j\ge0$, and a polynomial radius $R_j(t)$ with rational coefficients. The radius polynomials agree at neighboring endpoints. For a panel's finite rational subdivision, the intended inequalities are $R_j(t)>0$, $R'_j(t)-L_jR_j(t)-\rho_j>0$, and $U_j(t)+[-R_j(t),R_j(t)]^d\subseteq X_j$.
3. A finite rational subdivision of every panel, with exact endpoint coverage, no gaps, and pairwise-disjoint interiors. It supplies cells on which each required range test below is performed. Rational cell endpoints and constants are enclosed by directed outward rounding to finite dyadic endpoints before interval evaluation; an unrepresentable or overflowing conversion cannot validate.
4. An initial check target $d_0\ge0$ with $\sum_i(U_0(a)_i-(y_0)_i)^2\le d_0^2$ and $d_0<R_0(a)$.

The certificate is **validated** only if outward-rounded real-interval evaluation on every supplied cell proves all three radius/tube inequalities, the range inclusion in $X_j$, that every division denominator in the field and its state derivatives excludes zero on the time-state box $[t_j,t_{j+1}]\times X_j$, and
$$\sum_{i=1}^d \sup|U'_{j,i}-f_i(t,U_j(t))|^2\le\rho_j^2,\qquad \sum_{i,k=1}^d \sup|\partial_{y_k}f_i(t,y)|^2\le L_j^2$$
there. Here each supremum is replaced in the check by the maximum absolute endpoint of a finite outward interval enclosure; the residual expression is evaluated at the actual polynomial $U_j$, so interpolation, stage, and storage errors already present in that reconstruction are included. Strict inequalities must have a certified positive interval lower endpoint; an inconclusive, nonfinite, unsupported, or failed test is not validation.

This format certifies only rational expression fields and polynomial reconstructions using the stated finite checks. It uses real intervals, not complex rectangles or balls, and does not claim an evaluator for transcendental functions or general library floating-point operations. The page proves the soundness of a validated certificate separately.

The finite DAG and real-interval conventions are those of [[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]] and [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

citations.quote:
Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

citations.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: Order the finite acyclic graph topologically. A constant node defines a constant smooth function with derivative zero; an input node is a coordinate projection with its coordinate derivative. Assume inductively that the parent nodes define $C^1$ functions with their assigned derivatives.

For an addition or subtraction node, [F2] gives the sum or difference of the parent derivatives. For a product node it gives $vDu+uDv$. For a division node, continuity of the denominator and its nonzero value give a neighborhood on which it remains nonzero; [F2] gives $(vDu-uDv)/v^2$. These rules produce continuous derivatives because the parent values and derivatives are continuous and division is taken away from zero.

Induction through the topological order proves that every node is $C^1$ with its recursively assigned derivative, so the root derivative is correct. Continuity and nonvanishing of the finitely many denominator functions give a ball around the input on which all denominators stay nonzero. Shrink it so every partial derivative of every root component is bounded in absolute value by a common finite $M$, using continuity at the center and the finite number of entries. For two points $u,v$ in this convex ball, apply [F4] to each scalar component along $v+s(u-v)$: its derivative has magnitude at most $M\sum_j|u_j-v_j|\le M\sqrt{d+1}\|u-v\|_2$ by [F5]. Combining the finitely many component bounds gives a Lipschitz constant for the root map. Thus the field is locally Lipschitz.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f$ be $C^2$ on an open neighborhood of a compact convex time-state set containing the initial point, the short exact solution segment, and the Euler stage points. Assume the first and second derivatives of $f$ are bounded there. For the exact solution $y'=f(t,y)$ starting from $y(t)=y_0$, put
$$g:=\partial_t f(t,y_0)+D_yf(t,y_0)f(t,y_0).$$
Here $\partial_t f$ is the time derivative and $D_yf$ is the Jacobian in the state variables. The notation $O(h^k)$ means a norm bounded by a constant times $h^k$ for sufficiently small positive $h$, uniformly over the compact starting set when stated. For all sufficiently small $h>0$, the Euler and Heun one-step values in [[def-heun-euler-embedded-runge-kutta-pair]] satisfy
$$Y_E-y(t+h)=-\tfrac12h^2g+O(h^3),\qquad Y_H-y(t+h)=O(h^3),\qquad Y_H-Y_E=\tfrac12h^2g+O(h^3).$$
For a family of starting points, assume one common $h_0>0$ for which all exact segments and stage points stay in the same neighborhood. Under this condition the estimates are uniform over the compact starting set because the derivative bounds are common. Thus Euler has local order one and Heun has local order at least two on that set. $$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$
citations.use_explanation: F4 supplies the exact stated interface used at 2.1.

derivations.claim: Substitute $K_2-K_1=hg+O(h^2)$ from [F2] and the identity $Y_H-Y_E=\frac h2(K_2-K_1)$ in [F1]. Since $0\le\theta^2\le1$, the stage remainder contributes at most a fixed constant times $h^3$, uniformly in $\theta$; hence $P_n(\theta)=y_n+\theta hK_1+\frac12\theta^2h^2g+O(h^3)$ uniformly.

Put $F(s)=f(s,y(s))$. By [F3], $F$ is differentiable and $F\prime(t_n)=g$; the $C^2$ hypothesis on $f$ and the chain rule show $F\prime\prime$ is bounded on the short segment. Apply [F4] to $y$ with increment $\theta h$: its first two Taylor terms are $y_n+\theta hK_1+\frac12\theta^2h^2g$, and its third-order remainder is bounded by a common constant times $|\theta h|^3\le h^3$. Subtracting this expansion from step 1.1 gives the asserted uniform estimate.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Fix a dimension $d\ge1$, rational times $a<T$, a rational initial vector $y_0$, and an ODE field $f$ represented by a finite acyclic expression DAG with rational constants, time/state inputs, and only $+,-,\times,\div$ nodes. Its domain consists of points where every division is defined. Write $D_yf$ for the matrix of partial derivatives with respect to the state coordinates. A **finite rational residual-tube certificate** consists of the following exact rational data:

1. A finite partition $a=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=T$. On each panel $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, a vector polynomial $U_j(t)$ with dyadic (hence rational) coefficients, whose neighboring endpoint values agree exactly. These stored coefficients define the actual reconstruction, including any endpoint correction or rounded stage value used by an implementation.
2. For each panel, a closed rational state box $X_j\subset\mathbb R^d$, rational bounds $L_j\ge0$, $\rho_j\ge0$, a rational $d_j\ge0$, and a polynomial radius $R_j(t)$ with rational coefficients. The radius polynomials agree at neighboring endpoints. For a panel's finite rational subdivision, the intended inequalities are $R_j(t)>0$, $R'_j(t)-L_jR_j(t)-\rho_j>0$, and $U_j(t)+[-R_j(t),R_j(t)]^d\subseteq X_j$.
3. A finite rational subdivision of every panel, with exact endpoint coverage, no gaps, and pairwise-disjoint interiors. It supplies cells on which each required range test below is performed. Rational cell endpoints and constants are enclosed by directed outward rounding to finite dyadic endpoints before interval evaluation; an unrepresentable or overflowing conversion cannot validate.
4. An initial check target $d_0\ge0$ with $\sum_i(U_0(a)_i-(y_0)_i)^2\le d_0^2$ and $d_0<R_0(a)$.

The certificate is **validated** only if outward-rounded real-interval evaluation on every supplied cell proves all three radius/tube inequalities, the range inclusion in $X_j$, that every division denominator in the field and its state derivatives excludes zero on the time-state box $[t_j,t_{j+1}]\times X_j$, and
$$\sum_{i=1}^d \sup|U'_{j,i}-f_i(t,U_j(t))|^2\le\rho_j^2,\qquad \sum_{i,k=1}^d \sup|\partial_{y_k}f_i(t,y)|^2\le L_j^2$$
there. Here each supremum is replaced in the check by the maximum absolute endpoint of a finite outward interval enclosure; the residual expression is evaluated at the actual polynomial $U_j$, so interpolation, stage, and storage errors already present in that reconstruction are included. Strict inequalities must have a certified positive interval lower endpoint; an inconclusive, nonfinite, unsupported, or failed test is not validation.

This format certifies only rational expression fields and polynomial reconstructions using the stated finite checks. It uses real intervals, not complex rectangles or balls, and does not claim an evaluator for transcendental functions or general library floating-point operations. The page proves the soundness of a validated certificate separately.

The finite DAG and real-interval conventions are those of [[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]] and [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]].

supplier_excerpts.quote:
For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$; the denominator interval is strictly positive because at
least one coordinate interval excludes zero. Division multiplies by this
reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
For a finite rational expression DAG of [[def-validated-residual-tube-certificate]], at every input point where each division denominator is nonzero, the DAG evaluates to a continuously differentiable function of time and state. The recursion assigning zero derivatives to constants, coordinate derivatives to inputs, sum/difference rules, the product rule, and
$$D(u/v)=\frac{vDu-uDv}{v^2}$$
for a division node computes its actual total derivative. On any open neighborhood where all denominators stay nonzero, the represented field is locally Lipschitz.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

citations.quote:
Let $d\ge1$ and $a<T$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuous, and let $y$ be an exact solution of $y'=f(t,y)$ on $[a,T]$. Let $U:[a,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuous and $C^1$ on each member of a finite partition (continuously differentiable on each closed panel, with one-sided endpoint derivatives), with graph in $D$. Let $\ell,\rho:[a,T]\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous on each partition interval, with one-sided endpoint values, and suppose on every open panel
$$\langle U-y,f(t,U)-f(t,y)\rangle\le\ell(t)\|U-y\|_2^2,\qquad \|U'(t)-f(t,U(t))\|_2\le\rho(t).$$
Then for every $t\in[a,T]$,
$$\|U(t)-y(t)\|_2\le e^{\int_a^t\ell(v)\,dv}\|U(a)-y(a)\|_2+\int_a^t e^{\int_s^t\ell(v)\,dv}\rho(s)\,ds.$$
The proof uses only finite-piece ordinary calculus and no choice axiom. The general absolutely continuous case is treated separately.

citations.quote: Let $d\ge1$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable. There is no maximal solution $x:I\to\mathbb R^d$ of $x'=f(t,x)$ whose interval has a finite right endpoint $b$ and for which some $t_0\in I$, $t_0<b$, and compact set $C\subseteq D$ satisfy $(t,x(t))\in C$ for every $t\in[t_0,b)$. The compact tube condition supplies boundedness of $f$ along the graph and a limit point inside the open domain.

citations.quote:
Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

citations.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

citations.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

citations.quote:
Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

citations.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular

derivations.claim: A `certified` return means each interval operation was finite and every listed inclusion and strict inequality passed. By [F2], all exact rational-DAG values and their derivative-DAG values lie in the checked intervals. Thus on each panel $f$ is defined on $[t_j,t_{j+1}]\times X_j$, the actual polynomial reconstruction has residual norm at most $\rho_j$, the state Jacobian entries have squared Frobenius sum at most $L_j^2$, and $U_j(t)+[-R_j(t),R_j(t)]^d\subseteq X_j$. Also $\|U_0(a)-y_0\|_2\le d_0<R_0(a)$ by the exact initial squared comparison.

Fix $w=u-v$ and define $\phi(s)=\langle w,f(t,v+sw)\rangle$ for $0\le s\le1$. The segment stays in $X_j$ by convexity. By [F3] and bilinearity in [F12], $\phi'(s)=\langle w,D_yf(t,v+sw)w\rangle$. The interval-verified Frobenius bound implies $\|D_yf\|_F\le L_j$ at every segment point; rowwise Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|D_yf\,w\|_2\le\|D_yf\|_F\|w\|_2$, and [F7] then gives $|\phi\prime(s)|\le L_j\|w\|_2^2$. [F6] on $[0,1]$ yields $\phi(1)-\phi(0)=\langle u-v,f(t,u)-f(t,v)\rangle\le L_j\|u-v\|_2^2$. Thus the one-sided Lipschitz hypothesis in [F4] holds with $\ell=L_j$ whenever the exact and reconstructed states lie in the certified box.

Picard–Lindelöf applies locally by [F3], and [F8] gives a unique maximal solution through $(a,y_0)$. On any interval where it exists and lies in the checked panel boxes, apply [F4] panel by panel. Write $\delta_j(t):=R_j'(t)-L_jR_j(t)-\rho_j$, which is strictly positive by the checker. Integrating the scalar identity $R_j'=L_jR_j+\rho_j+\delta_j$ with the same integrating factor shows that the radius dominates the error bound strictly: the initial gap is positive because $d_0<R_0(a)$, and each panel adds the positive integral of $e^{\int_s^t L_j}\delta_j(s)$, using positivity of the exponential [F11] and the fundamental theorem [F10]. Since the certified tube is inside $X_j$, the solution cannot first reach its radius boundary. At each panel endpoint the stored reconstructions and radii agree, so the strict inequality continues across the finite partition.

citations.quote:
For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$; the denominator interval is strictly positive because at
least one coordinate interval excludes zero. Division multiplies by this
reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

Inputs are an IVP in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], $y'=f(t,y)$ on an open domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ with initial data $(t_0,y_0)\in D$ and requested interval $[t_0,T]$, where $t_0\le T$ and $d\ge1$; an initial proposal $0<h_{\rm init}\le h_{\max}$; an embedded pair with low order $p\ge1$ as in [[def-embedded-runge-kutta-pair-and-error-estimator]]; tolerances $\mathrm{atol}>0$ and $\mathrm{rtol}\ge0$; safety $0<\sigma<1$; scale bounds $0<\gamma_{\min}\le1\le\gamma_{\max}$; step bounds $0<h_{\min}\le h_{\max}$; and a positive integer attempt budget $N$.

**Output.** Return a record consisting of one of `success`, `failure`, `minimum-step-rejected`, or `attempt-budget-exhausted`, together with the accepted mesh $\mathcal A=((t_0,y_0),\ldots,(t_m,y_m))$. The mesh always contains the initial pair and every accepted endpoint; on `success`, $t_m=T$ and $y_m$ is the returned endpoint approximation. On any other status, $\mathcal A$ is the accepted prefix and $y_m$ is the last accepted approximation.

**Procedure.** Initialize $t:=t_0$, $y:=y_0$, $\mathcal A:=((t_0,y_0))$, and proposal $h_{\rm prop}:=h_{\rm init}$. If $t_0=T$, return `success` with $\mathcal A$. For each attempt index $k=1,\ldots,N$, perform exactly the following steps:

1. Set $h:=\min(h_{\rm prop},h_{\max},T-t)$. The last term permits a final clipped step shorter than $h_{\min}$. If $h\le0$ before reaching $T$, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$.
2. Evaluate the shared stages in tableau order, checking before each evaluation that its time-state input lies in $D$. If a stage input is outside $D$, its evaluation is undefined, or its value is nonfinite, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$. Compute both pair outputs; if either output or any arithmetic needed to compute them is undefined, fails, or is nonfinite in the rounded realization, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$.
3. Define $s_i:=\mathrm{atol}+\mathrm{rtol}\max(|(y)_i|,|(Y)_i|)$ and $Q:=\max_i |(\widehat Y-Y)_i|/s_i$, where $Y$ is the high-order value and $\widehat Y$ the low-order value. If any scale or $Q$ operation fails or is nonfinite in the rounded realization, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$. If $Q\le1$, first check $(t+h,Y)\in D$; if not, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$. Otherwise accept: set $t:=t+h$, $y:=Y$, and append $(t,y)$ to $\mathcal A$. If $Q>1$, reject and retain $t,y,\mathcal A$.
4. If the attempt was accepted and $t=T$, return `success` with $\mathcal A$. Otherwise, if it was rejected and $h\le h_{\min}$, return `minimum-step-rejected` with $\mathcal A$. These terminal checks precede the budget check, so a final accepted step that reaches $T$ succeeds and a rejection at the minimum step reports that safeguard.
5. If $k=N$, return `attempt-budget-exhausted` with $\mathcal A$. Otherwise compute
$$g=\begin{cases}\gamma_{\max},&Q=0,\\ \min(\gamma_{\max},\max(\gamma_{\min},\sigma /\sqrt[p+1]{Q})),&Q>0.\end{cases}$$
Set $h_{\rm prop}:=\min(h_{\max},\max(h_{\min},gh))$ and continue to attempt $k+1$. A failed or nonfinite rounded computation of $g$ or $h_{\rm prop}$ returns `failure` with $\mathcal A$.

For $Q>0$, $\sqrt[p+1]{Q}$ is the unique positive $(p+1)$st root supplied by [[thm-nth-roots-exist]]. The exponent $1/(p+1)$ is a leading-error model for step selection; neither acceptance nor this controller is a global error certificate or a stiffness test.

The mathematical specification evaluates each displayed operation, including maximum, minimum, absolute value, and positive-root evaluation, exactly. A rounded implementation instead applies its fixed finite-format rounding rule to every stage, output, scale, and controller-factor arithmetic operation and uses the resulting stored high and low values in the displayed difference and acceptance test; nonfinite or failed operations return `failure`. The finite termination theorem applies to either realization when each attempt has finite work. The rounded realization has no a posteriori guarantee: a tolerance below its resolution can be accepted because both stored values coincide.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f$ be $C^2$ on an open neighborhood of a compact convex time-state set containing the initial point, the short exact solution segment, and the Euler stage points. Assume the first and second derivatives of $f$ are bounded there. For the exact solution $y'=f(t,y)$ starting from $y(t)=y_0$, put
$$g:=\partial_t f(t,y_0)+D_yf(t,y_0)f(t,y_0).$$
Here $\partial_t f$ is the time derivative and $D_yf$ is the Jacobian in the state variables. The notation $O(h^k)$ means a norm bounded by a constant times $h^k$ for sufficiently small positive $h$, uniformly over the compact starting set when stated. For all sufficiently small $h>0$, the Euler and Heun one-step values in [[def-heun-euler-embedded-runge-kutta-pair]] satisfy
$$Y_E-y(t+h)=-\tfrac12h^2g+O(h^3),\qquad Y_H-y(t+h)=O(h^3),\qquad Y_H-Y_E=\tfrac12h^2g+O(h^3).$$
For a family of starting points, assume one common $h_0>0$ for which all exact segments and stage points stay in the same neighborhood. Under this condition the estimates are uniform over the compact starting set because the derivative bounds are common. Thus Euler has local order one and Heun has local order at least two on that set. If $g\ne0$, the embedded norm estimates Euler's defect asymptotically with ratio one; when $g=0$, that ratio conclusion does not follow from these orders.

The exact solution is $y(t)=8+t$, so $y(1)=9$. The accepted stored endpoint is $8$, giving absolute error $|9-8|=1>1/4=\mathrm{atol}$. Thus the embedded difference can be zero while the actual error exceeds the requested tolerance.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f$ be $C^2$ on an open neighborhood of a compact convex time-state set containing the initial point, the short exact solution segment, and the Euler stage points. Assume the first and second derivatives of $f$ are bounded there. For the exact solution $y'=f(t,y)$ starting from $y(t)=y_0$, put
$$g:=\partial_t f(t,y_0)+D_yf(t,y_0)f(t,y_0).$$
Here $\partial_t f$ is the time derivative and $D_yf$ is the Jacobian in the state variables. The notation $O(h^k)$ means a norm bounded by a constant times $h^k$ for sufficiently small positive $h$, uniformly over the compact starting set when stated. For all sufficiently small $h>0$, the Euler and Heun one-step values in [[def-heun-euler-embedded-runge-kutta-pair]] satisfy
$$Y_E-y(t+h)=-\tfrac12h^2g+O(h^3),\qquad Y_H-y(t+h)=O(h^3),\qquad Y_H-Y_E=\tfrac12h^2g+O(h^3).$$
For a family of starting points, assume one common $h_0>0$ for which all exact segments and stage points stay in the same neighborhood. Under this condition the estimates are uniform over the compact starting set because the derivative bounds are common. Thus Euler has local order one and Heun has local order at least two on that set. If $g\ne0$, the embedded norm estimates Euler's defect asymptotically with ratio one; when $g=0$, that ratio conclusion does not follow from these orders.

Let $d\ge1$, let $U:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable, and let $M$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. Write $\nabla U$ for its Euclidean gradient, and let $\epsilon>0$.

For $a,b\in\mathbb R$, define the **force kick** and **drift shear**
$$K_a(q,p)=(q,p-a\nabla U(q)),\qquad D_b(q,p)=(q+bM^{-1}p,p).$$
The one-step leapfrog map is
$$\Phi_\epsilon=K_{\epsilon/2}\circ D_\epsilon\circ K_{\epsilon/2},$$
where composition is read right to left. For a finite integer $L\ge1$, its $L$-step map is $\Phi_\epsilon^L$. Define the momentum flip $R(q,p)=(q,-p)$ and the flipped proposal map $T_{\epsilon,L}=R\circ\Phi_\epsilon^L$.

Each kick and drift is a continuous bijection with inverse $K_{-a}$ or $D_{-b}$, respectively. These finite maps use only $\nabla U$ and do not require a solution of Hamilton's ODE. The classical derivative of a force kick is not part of this definition: for merely $U\in C^1$, $\nabla U$ need not be differentiable.

The local drift is the restriction of $D_b$ to
$$\{(q,p):q\in Q,\ q+bM^{-1}p\in Q\}.$$

For a signed step $h$, the local leapfrog map is the restriction of $K_{h/2}\circ D_h\circ K_{h/2}$ to the states for which all three intermediate configurations lie in $Q$. Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

$$D\varphi(x)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,\varphi(x)).$$

derivations.claim: Since $H\in C^2(U)$, the coordinate field $F$ is $C^1$. On the admitted closed ball, $T_z(W)=z+(h/2)F(W)$ maps the ball into itself because $\|T_z(W)-z\|\le |h|M/2\le\rho$. The mean-value estimate on this convex ball gives $\|T_z(W)-T_z(V)\|\le\theta\|W-V\|$ with $\theta=|h|L/2<1$. The ball is nonempty and complete, so [F1] gives a unique fixed point $Z$, keeps all iterates in the ball, and gives $\|Z_k-Z\|\le b_k=\theta^k\|Z_1-Z_0\|/(1-\theta)$. Multiplication by two gives $\|(2Z_k-z)-(2Z-z)\|=2\|Z_k-Z\|\le2b_k$, and $Z\in\overline B(z,\rho)$ gives $\|(2Z-z)-z\|\le2\rho$. The convention $\theta^0=1$ makes the bound valid at $k=0$. If $\theta=0$, $T_z$ is constant on the ball, hence $Z_1=T_z(z)=T_z(Z)=Z$ and every later iterate equals $Z$; thus $b_k=0$ for $k\ge1$. These assertions require only the $C^2$ hypotheses.

For the remaining claims, assume the additional $C^3$ and uniform branch hypotheses. Fix an admitted initial value $z$ and let $z_j\to z$ through admitted initial values with selected roots $Z_j$. Since $\|Z_j-z_j\|\le\rho$, the sequence is bounded; every convergent subsequence has a limit $Z_*\in\overline B(z,\rho)\subset U$, and continuity of $F$ in $Z_j=z_j+(h/2)F(Z_j)$ shows $Z_*=z+(h/2)F(Z_*)$. The contraction in step 1.1 gives uniqueness of this fixed point in $\overline B(z,\rho)$, so every convergent subsequence has limit $Z$ and therefore $Z_j\to Z$. Now put $G(z,Z)=Z-z-(h/2)F(Z)$. At the selected root, $D_ZG=I-(h/2)A$ with $A=DF(Z)$. Since $\|(h/2)A\|<1$, this matrix is invertible by the Neumann series, and [F2] supplies a local $C^1$ root branch. The continuity just proved and the IFT's local uniqueness identify the selected roots with this branch at every nearby admitted initial value. Differentiating $G=0$ gives $D_zZ=(I-(h/2)A)^{-1}$ and hence $S:=D\Psi_h=(I-B)^{-1}(I+B),\qquad B=(h/2)A.$

Put $m=2d$ and $\delta=Z-z$. The admitted fixed-point equation gives $\|\delta\|\le |h|\|F(Z)\|/2\le |h|M/2$, hence $\delta=O(|h|)$ uniformly. Since $H\in C^3$, $F\in C^2$. Apply the scalar theorem [F4] to each $F_i$ along $[z,Z]$: $F_i(z+\delta)=F_i(z)+DF_i(z)\delta+R_i$, where $R_i=\tfrac12D^2F_i(z+\vartheta_i\delta)[\delta,\delta]$ for some $\vartheta_i\in(0,1)$. These points may differ with $i$. Bounded second derivatives on the tube give $|R_i|\le C_i\|\delta\|^2$, hence $\|R\|_2\le(\sum_{i=1}^m C_i^2)^{1/2}\|\delta\|^2$. Substitution into $\delta=(h/2)F(z+\delta)$ first gives $\delta=(h/2)F(z)+O(h^2)$ and then $\delta=(h/2)F(z)+(h^2/4)DF(z)F(z)+O(|h|^3)$. Thus $2Z-z=z+hF(z)+(h^2/2)DF(z)F(z)+O(|h|^3)$. For the exact flow, write $g_i(t)=(\varphi_t(z))_i$. By [F3] and [F6], $g_i^{(1)}=F_i(\varphi_t(z))$, $g_i^{(2)}=DF_i(\varphi_t(z))F(\varphi_t(z))$, and $g_i^{(3)}=D^2F_i(\varphi_t(z))[F(\varphi_t(z)),F(\varphi_t(z))]+DF_i(\varphi_t(z))DF(\varphi_t(z))F(\varphi_t(z))$ are defined, with the third derivative uniformly bounded on the controlled trajectories. Scalar Taylor in time gives $g_i(h)=z_i+hF_i(z)+(h^2/2)(DF(z)F(z))_i+(h^3/6)g_i^{(3)}(\eta_i h)$ for $h\ne0$, with possibly distinct $\eta_i\in(0,1)$. Each last term is bounded by $C_i'|h|^3$; summing their squares gives a Euclidean remainder bound $(\sum_{i=1}^m(C_i')^2)^{1/2}|h|^3$. The case $h=0$ is immediate. The exact flow therefore has the same terms through degree two as $2Z-z$, giving the uniform one-step defect $C|h|^3$ for either sign of $h$. No common Lagrange intermediate point for the vector is used.
By [F5], $A=J\nabla^2H(Z)$ and $A^TJ+JA=0$; therefore $B^TJ+JB=0$. Expanding both products gives $(I+B)^TJ(I+B)-(I-B)^TJ(I-B)=2(B^TJ+JB)=0$. Thus $(I-B)^TJ(I-B)=(I+B)^TJ(I+B)$.

Differentiating the fixed-point relation shows $D\Psi_h=I+hDF(z)+O(h^2)$ uniformly on the tube; bounded derivatives make $\|D\Psi_h\|\le1+L_1|h|$ after decreasing $h_0$. The mean-value theorem on the stipulated convex comparison segments gives $e_{n+1}\le(1+L_1|h|)e_n+C|h|^3$. Iteration and $(1+L_1|h|)^n\le e^{L_1T}$ when $n|h|\le T$ give $e_n\le e^{L_1T}e_0+CTe^{L_1T}|h|^2$.

The matrices $I-B$ and $I+B$ commute. Multiplying the equality in step 3.1 on the left by $(I-B)^{-T}$ and on the right by $(I-B)^{-1}$ yields $J=(I-B)^{-T}(I+B)^TJ(I+B)(I-B)^{-1}=S^TJS$. This proves the exact branch is symplectic.

Step 1.1 proves existence, uniqueness, convergence, and the stage and output certificates under the $C^2$ hypotheses. Under the additional $C^3$ and tube hypotheses, step 2.1 proves the exact branch's stated regularity, step 4.1 proves symplecticity, and steps 2.2 and 3.2 prove local second order and the finite-time error.

derivations.claim: Fix $N$. Smoothness of the kick and drift formulas, and [F4] for the implicit midpoint branch, gives a Taylor expansion $\Phi_h(z)=z+\sum_{k=1}^{N+1}h^kd_k(z)+O(h^{N+2})$ on each compact subset where the maps are admitted. Its first coefficient is $d_1=X_H$ because the methods are consistent.

Seek $Y_h=X_H+\sum_{m=1}^Nh^mX_m$. The time-$h$ flow expansion is $z+\sum_{k=1}^{N+1}\frac{h^k}{k!}(Y_h\cdot\nabla)^{k-1}Y_h(z)+O(h^{N+2})$. At coefficient $h^{m+1}$, the first term $hY_h$ contributes $X_m$; every term with $k\ge2$ can involve only $X_1,\ldots,X_{m-1}$ at that degree. Thus set $X_m=d_{m+1}-P_m$, where $P_m$ is the already determined coefficient from those higher flow terms. This finite recursion matches coefficients through degree $N+1$. Since each method agrees with the exact $X_H$ flow through degree $r$, it gives $X_1=\cdots=X_{r-1}=0$.

For fixed parameter $h$, the pullback $Q_{h,t}$ of the time-$t$ flow of $Y_h$ obeys $\partial_t(Q_{h,t}f)=Q_{h,t}(\mathcal L_{Y_h}f)$ and $Q_{h,0}=I$. Coefficient recursion in $t$ therefore gives $Q_{h,t}=\sum_{k=0}^{N+1}t^k\mathcal L_{Y_h}^k/k!$ modulo terms of total order $N+2$; at $t=h$, this is $\exp(h\mathcal L_{Y_h})$. Step 1.2 gives $\Phi_h$ and its comparison flow equal Taylor coefficients through degree $N+1$, so [F6] makes their pullbacks equal modulo $h^{N+2}$. Since $P_h-I=O(h)$, the finite polynomial logarithm in the Statement is valid modulo $h^{N+2}$. The formal identity $\log(\exp A)=A$ in the truncated algebra then gives $\log_N(P_h)=h\mathcal L_{Y_h}$ modulo $h^{N+2}$.

Fix $m\in\{r,\ldots,N\}$ and assume $X_r,\ldots,X_{m-1}$ are Hamiltonian. The truncated field $Y_h^{[m-1]}=X_H+\sum_{j=r}^{m-1}h^jX_j$ is Hamiltonian, so by [F3] its time-$h$ flow $\psi_h$ is symplectic. Step 1.2 gives $\Phi_h-\psi_h=h^{m+1}X_m+O(h^{m+2})$ and, after differentiating the smooth expansions, $D\Phi_h-D\psi_h=h^{m+1}DX_m+O(h^{m+2})$.
The symplectic matrix identity for both maps and $D\psi_h=I+O(h)$ imply $0=h^{m+1}(DX_m^TJ+JDX_m)+O(h^{m+2})$. Divide by $h^{m+1}$ and take $h\to0$ to obtain $DX_m^TJ+JDX_m=0$.

Let $k,m,n\ge1$ and $p\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n+p}$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^k$. Suppose $F(a,b,\lambda_0)=0$ and $D_yF(a,b,\lambda_0)$ is invertible. Then there are neighbourhoods and a unique $C^k$ map $\varphi$ solving $F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)=0$. More precisely, on suitable open neighbourhoods $P$ of $(a,\lambda_0)$ and $Q$ of $b$,

$$F(x,y,\lambda)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x,\lambda),$$

and

$$D\varphi(x,\lambda)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)^{-1}D_{(x,\lambda)}F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda).$$

When no parameter block is present, this is the ordinary $C^k$ implicit function theorem.

Let $d\ge1$, let $U:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable, and let $M$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. Write $\nabla U$ for its Euclidean gradient, and let $\epsilon>0$.

For $a,b\in\mathbb R$, define the **force kick** and **drift shear**
$$K_a(q,p)=(q,p-a\nabla U(q)),\qquad D_b(q,p)=(q+bM^{-1}p,p).$$
The one-step leapfrog map is
$$\Phi_\epsilon=K_{\epsilon/2}\circ D_\epsilon\circ K_{\epsilon/2},$$
where composition is read right to left. For a finite integer $L\ge1$, its $L$-step map is $\Phi_\epsilon^L$. Define the momentum flip $R(q,p)=(q,-p)$ and the flipped proposal map $T_{\epsilon,L}=R\circ\Phi_\epsilon^L$.

Each kick and drift is a continuous bijection with inverse $K_{-a}$ or $D_{-b}$, respectively. These finite maps use only $\nabla U$ and do not require a solution of Hamilton's ODE. The classical derivative of a force kick is not part of this definition: for merely $U\in C^1$, $\nabla U$ need not be differentiable.

Direct multiplication gives $S_h^T\begin{pmatrix}s&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}S_h=\begin{pmatrix}s(a^2+h^2s)&0\\0&a^2+h^2s\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}s&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},$ because $a^2+h^2s=1$. For a finite interval $[0,L]$ with $a>0$, the inflow boundary is $x=0$. The upwind initial/boundary rows are $U_j^0=u_0(jh)$ for $j=0,\ldots,N$, $U_0^n=g(t_n)$ with $u_0(0)=g(0)$, and
$$ U_j^{n+1}=(1-
u)U_j^n+
u U_{j-1}^n,\qquad j=1,\ldots,N,\quad n\ge0. $$
The outflow node $j=N$ is computed by this row and receives no prescribed value. This item supplies no finite-interval boundary closure or stability statement for centered, Lax--Friedrichs, or Lax--Wendroff updates.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Write an arbitrary vector as $v=\sum_\ell c_\ell\psi_\ell$ in the orthonormal Fourier basis [F1]. The $m$-step update sends it to $\sum_\ell c_\ell g_\ell^m\psi_\ell$, so $\|T^mv\|_{2,h}^2=\sum_\ell|c_\ell|^2|g_\ell|^{2m}\le(\max_\ell|g_\ell|^m)^2\|v\|_{2,h}^2$. u$ by $|a|k/h$.
