citations.quote: Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)$ linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), and let $a:H\times H\to\mathbb K$ be sesquilinear in the sense of [[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]]: linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second. The form $a$ is **bounded** with bound $M\ge0$ when $$|a(u,v)|\le M\|u\|\,\|v\|\qquad\text{for all }u,v\in H,$$ and **coercive** with constant $\alpha>0$ when $$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2\qquad\text{for all }u\in H .$$ It is **symmetric** (Hermitian) when $a(u,v)=\overline{a(v,u)}$ for all $u,v$, over $\mathbb C$ this is equivalent to $a(u,u)\in\mathbb R$ for every $u$. Indeed, writing $q(u)=a(u,u)$, sesquilinearity gives $4a(u,v)=q(u+v)-q(u-v)+i q(u+iv)-i q(u-iv)$, and real diagonal values make this identity conjugate-symmetric. Over $\mathbb R$, symmetry means $a(u,v)=a(v,u)$; real diagonal values alone do not imply symmetry. The **adjoint form** is $a^*(u,v):=\overline{a(v,u)}$, and $(a^*)^*=a$. **Real bilinear convention.** When $H$ is a real Hilbert space the same definitions apply with $a$ bilinear and coercive in the form $a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2$; the conjugation in the second slot is then the identity. More generally, a real bilinear form may satisfy the boundedness and coercivity conditions without being symmetric; symmetry is an additional property, not part of either condition. When $H=\{0\}$ every form is bounded with bound $0$ and coercive with every $\alpha>0$; this degenerate case is kept but is never load-bearing. All constants below are named and never silently improved. No choice principle is used in this definition.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$. The metric used here is $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$, supplied over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]].

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be an infinite-dimensional
real or complex Hilbert space, let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space over
the same field, and let $J:V\to H$ be an injective, bounded, compact linear
map with dense range ([[def-compact-linear-operator]]). Let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ be bounded, Hermitian and coercive with constants
$M,\alpha>0$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]).
Then there is a sequence of eigenpairs $(\lambda_j,e_j)_{j\ge1}$ such that
$$0<\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\cdots,\qquad \lambda_j\longrightarrow+\infty,$$
where each eigenvalue is repeated according to multiplicity,
$e_j\in V$, $\|Je_j\|_H=1$, and
$$a(e_j,v)=\lambda_j(Je_j,Jv)_H\qquad(v\in V).$$
The vectors $Je_j$ form an orthonormal basis of $H$, and
$e_j/\sqrt{\lambda_j}$ form an orthonormal basis of $V$ for the energy inner
product $a$. In particular, for $v\in V$,
$$\|Jv\|_H^2=\sum_{j\ge1}|(Jv,Je_j)_H|^2,\qquad a(v,v)=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j|(Jv,Je_j)_H|^2,$$
and the Rayleigh quotient $R(v):=a(v,v)/\|Jv\|_H^2$ satisfies the attained
min–max identity
$$\lambda_m=\min_{\substack{S\subseteq V\\\dim S=m}} \max_{v\in S\setminus\{0\}}R(v)\qquad(m\ge1).$$
This is the abstract continuous spectral interface used below. The published
elliptic suppliers on the Dirichlet branch have their own stated domain and
axiom hypotheses; this theorem does not enlarge those imported interfaces.

Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space with a bounded, Hermitian,
coercive form $a$ as in [[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]].
Its energy norm is $\|v\|_a:=\sqrt{a(v,v)}$. Let $E\subseteq V$ be a
nonzero finite-dimensional subspace and let $V_h\subseteq V$ be a
finite-dimensional subspace. Define the directed energy distance and
best-approximation gap by
$$d_a(v,V_h):=\inf_{w_h\in V_h}\|v-w_h\|_a,\qquad \delta_a(E,V_h):=\sup_{\substack{v\in E\\\|v\|_a=1}}d_a(v,V_h).$$
When $E=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_m\}$ is the first $m$
continuous eigenspace directions and $V_h$ is the conforming Galerkin space,
write $\delta_h:=\delta_a(E,V_h)$. This is a directed gap from $E$ to $V_h$;
it does not by itself assert a two-sided gap between two eigenspaces.

The quantity is finite and satisfies $0\le\delta_a(E,V_h)\le1$, since
$0\in V_h$ gives $d_a(v,V_h)\le\|v\|_a$ on the unit sphere.

Assume Countable Choice and the compact coercive form setting of
[[thm-compact-coercive-form-spectrum-and-minmax]]. Suppose a continuous
eigenvalue $\lambda$ occupies the isolated cluster of indices
$r,\ldots,s$, so $\lambda_r=\cdots=\lambda_s=\lambda$ and
$\lambda_{s+1}>\lambda$, with $\lambda_{r-1}<\lambda$ when $r>1$. Let
$E:=\operatorname{span}\{e_r,\ldots,e_s\}$,
$E_s:=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_s\}$, and let
$V_h\subseteq V$ be conforming with $\dim V_h\ge s$. Put
$\delta_s:=\delta_a(E_s,V_h)$ using
[[def-eigenspace-best-approximation-gap]]. If $\delta_s$ is sufficiently
small that the eigenvalue theorem
[[thm-conforming-galerkin-eigenvalue-upper-bound-quadratic-gap-error]] applies
at index $s$ and, when $r>1$, at index $r-1$, and
$C_s\delta_s^2<\tfrac12(\lambda_{s+1}-\lambda)$ and, when $r>1$,
$C_{r-1}\delta_s^2<\tfrac12(\lambda-\lambda_{r-1})$, then
the discrete Ritz eigenspace $E_h$ associated with indices $r,\ldots,s$ has
dimension $s-r+1$ and
$$\delta_a(E,E_h)\le C_{r,s,\lambda}\,\delta_s.$$
This compares the invariant subspaces across the whole repeated eigenvalue;
it does not select individual eigenvectors inside the cluster.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $\varepsilon$ be a
real with $\varepsilon > 0$.

- A **finite $\varepsilon$-net** for $(X,d)$ is a finite subset $F \subseteq X$
  with
  $$X = \bigcup_{y \in F} B(y, \varepsilon) ,$$
  the balls being those of $(X,d)$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). *Finite* is the
  listing form fixed in [[def-metric-compactness]]: $F = \emptyset$, or
  $F = \{y_0, \dots, y_m\}$ for some $m \in \mathbb{N}$ and points
  $y_0, \dots, y_m \in X$.
- $(X,d)$ is **totally bounded** when it has a finite $\varepsilon$-net for every
  real $\varepsilon > 0$.
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is **totally bounded** when the metric subspace
  $(A,d_A)$ is ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]); its nets are then finite
  subsets of $A$ and its balls are the balls $B_A(a,\varepsilon)$ of the
  subspace.

**The empty space is totally bounded**, the empty net serving for every
$\varepsilon$, since a union over no indices is empty. Every space listed as
$\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is totally bounded too, itself being an $\varepsilon$-net
for every $\varepsilon$.

**The centres are required to lie in the space.** Writing the condition with
centres in $X$ and balls of $X$ is what makes total boundedness a property of the
metric space $(X,d)$ alone, matching the treatment of compactness in
[[def-metric-compactness]]. For a subset $A$ this matters: the nets of $(A,d_A)$
consist of points of $A$, not of nearby points of the ambient space.

**Total boundedness is stronger than boundedness and is not the same thing.**
A totally bounded space is bounded in the sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] — that is claim 1 of
[[lem-totally-bounded-basic]] — and the converse fails, as
[[fs-bounded-implies-totally-bounded]] records. Boundedness asks for one ball
containing the space; total boundedness asks for finitely many balls of *every*
prescribed radius, and it is the second condition that controls how spread out
the space is at small scales.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(X,d)$
be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) that is complete
([[def-complete-metric-space]]) and totally bounded ([[def-totally-bounded]]).
Then $(X,d)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]).

**Where the axiom is spent, and why the weaker principle suffices.**
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used exactly once, at step 3.1, to fix one finite
$1/(n+1)$-net **together with a listing of it** for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ at
once. The family of sets being chosen from is written down before any selection
is made and does not depend on the earlier selections, which is precisely the
situation countable choice covers and dependent choice
([[def-dependent-choice]]) is not needed for. Everything after step 3.1 is
canonical: at each stage the construction takes the **least** admissible index in
the listing already fixed.

As always on this page, the claim is an upper bound on the cost of the proof
given here, not an assertion that $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is necessary for the
theorem.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most

derivations.claim: The map $U:V\to\ell^2$ given by $(Uu)_j=\sqrt{\lambda_j}u_j$ is a surjective isometry, so $V$ is Hilbert and $a$ is its inner product. Since $\lambda_j\ge1$, $a(u,u)\ge\|Ju\|_H^2$, and $a(u,u)=\|u\|_V^2$; hence the form is coercive and bounded. Finite sequences lie in $V$ and are dense in $H$, so $J$ is injective with dense range.

Let $B_V:=\{u\in V:\|u\|_V\le1\}$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ so $1/\sqrt{\lambda_{N+1}}<\varepsilon/2$. If $x=Ju$ with $u\in B_V$, then $\sum_{j>N}|x_j|^2=\sum_{j>N}|u_j|^2\le\lambda_{N+1}^{-1}\sum_{j>N}\lambda_j|u_j|^2\le\lambda_{N+1}^{-1}$. The set $C_N:=\{(z_1,\ldots,z_N)\in\mathbb K^N:\sum_{j\le N}\lambda_j|z_j|^2\le1\}$ is closed and bounded in $\mathbb R^N$ (if $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$) or $\mathbb R^{2N}$ (if $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$), so it is compact by Heine--Borel and has a finite $\varepsilon/2$-net with centers in $C_N$. Each center $z$ lifts by zero padding to $\widetilde z=(z_1,\ldots,z_N,0,\ldots)\in J(B_V)$, because its weighted energy is at most one. For $x=Ju\in J(B_V)$, the prefix $(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$ belongs to $C_N$; the net and the tail bound therefore give $\|x-\widetilde z\|_{\ell^2}<\varepsilon$ for one of these finitely many lifts. Thus $J(B_V)$ is totally bounded with centers in itself. Its closure $C:=\overline{J(B_V)}$ is also totally bounded: a finite $\varepsilon/2$-net for $J(B_V)$ is an $\varepsilon$-net for $C$ by the triangle inequality and the definition of closure. The unit-ball criterion in [[def-compact-linear-operator]] now shows that $J$ is compact.

Each coordinate vector $e_j$ satisfies $a(e_j,v)=\lambda_j(Je_j,Jv)_H$. Their successive energy distances are $\|e_1-e_2\|_a=\sqrt2$, so $(u_h)$ is not Cauchy and cannot converge. ([[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]), let $x\in D$, and let
$p\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$. Define the open parameter set $S_{x,p}:=\{t\in\mathbb R:x+tp\in D\}$,
which contains $0$, the feasible ray $T_{x,p}:=S_{x,p}\cap[0,\infty)$,
and $\phi(t):=f(x+tp)$ for $t\in S_{x,p}$. At every $t\in S_{x,p}$,
including $0$, the chain rule gives $\phi'(t)=Df(x+tp)p$.
By [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],
the matrix of $Df$ is the Jacobian, whose scalar-field row is the transpose
of the gradient. Hence
$\phi'(t)=\langle\nabla f(x+tp),p\rangle$, using the gradient convention
of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the Euclidean inner product of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A direction is a **descent direction** at
$x$ when $\phi'(0)=\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle<0$.

Assume for the line-search conditions below that $p$ is a descent direction
at $x$.
Fix constants $0<c_1<c_2<1/2$. A feasible step $t>0$ is a **Wolfe step**
when
$$
\phi(t)\le\phi(0)+c_1t\phi'(0),\qquad \phi'(t)\ge c_2\phi'(0).
$$
It is a **strong Wolfe step** when it satisfies the first inequality and
$$
|\phi'(t)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|.
$$
The first inequality is the Armijo sufficient-decrease condition. The second
Wolfe inequality is the curvature condition. Every strong Wolfe step is a
Wolfe step, because $\phi'(0)<0$ and the strong curvature bound implies
$\phi'(t)\ge-c_2|\phi'(0)|=c_2\phi'(0)$.

For a descent direction define its **descent angle** $\theta\in[0,\pi/2)$ by
$$
\cos\theta:=-\frac{\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle}{\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\|p\|_2}.
$$
The denominator is nonzero for a descent direction. The Cauchy–Schwarz
inequality [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]] ensures $0<\cos\theta\le1$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

derivations.claim: The chain rule in [F1] makes $\phi$ continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of each finite point of $[0,\infty)$. Define $\psi(t):=\phi(t)-\phi(0)-c_1t\phi'(0)$. Then $\psi(0)=0$ and $d:=\psi'(0)=(1-c_1)\phi'(0)<0$. By [F3], $\psi(t)/t\to d$ as $t\to0$. Choose $\delta>0$ so that $\psi(t)/t<d/2<0$ for $0<t<\delta$; hence $\psi(t)<0$ there.

Since $\phi$ is bounded below and $-c_1\phi'(0)>0$, $\psi(t)\to+\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$. Thus $S:=\{t>0:\psi(t)\ge0\}$ is nonempty and bounded away from $0$. Let $t_*:=\inf S>0$. Continuity of $\psi$ implies $\psi(t_*)=0$: values below $t_*$ have $\psi<0$, while a sequence of points of $S$ converges to $t_*$.

Every $s\in(0,t_*)$ has $\psi(s)<0$, so Armijo holds strictly throughout that interval. Apply [F2] to $\phi$ on $[0,t_*]$ to get $\xi\in(0,t_*)$ with $\phi'(\xi)=(\phi(t_*)-\phi(0))/t_*=c_1\phi'(0)$. Hence $|\phi'(\xi)|=c_1|\phi'(0)|<c_2|\phi'(0)|$, so the strong curvature inequality holds strictly at $\xi$.

The strict Armijo inequality holds at every point of $(0,t_*)$, including $\xi$, and both $\phi$ and $\phi'$ are continuous there. Therefore both strict inequalities persist on some open interval about $\xi$ contained in $(0,t_*)$. Every point of that interval is a strong Wolfe step, proving the asserted nonemptiness.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$

2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  Suppose $A:=Df(a)$ is invertible and put
$B:=A^{-1}$.  Then there are $R>0$, $0\le q<1$, and $C>0$ such that
$\overline B(a,R)\subseteq U$, $\|Bv\|_2\le C\|v\|_2$, and, for every
$y\in\mathbb R^n$, the Newton map

$$T_y(x):=x+B(y-f(x))$$

satisfies

$$\|T_y(x)-T_y(z)\|_2\le q\|x-z\|_2\qquad(x,z\in\overline B(a,R)).$$

Moreover $Df(x)$ is invertible for every $x\in\overline B(a,R)$ and

$$\|Df(x)^{-1}v\|_2\le\frac C{1-q}\|v\|_2.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and write $J(x)=DF(x)$ as a matrix in the standard basis. The matrix
of $DF(x)$ agrees with the Jacobian matrix by
[[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For a
matrix $A$ let
$\|A\|_{\rm op}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Av\|_2$. Let $K\subseteq U$ be convex,
let $x_*,x\in K$, and suppose for some $L\ge0$ that
$$\|J(y)-J(z)\|_{\rm op}\le L\|y-z\|_2\qquad(y,z\in K).$$
Then
$$\|F(x)-F(x_*)-J(x)(x-x_*)\|_2\le\frac{L}{2}\|x-x_*\|_2^2.$$

Let $n\ge1$.  A linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$
([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) is **invertible** when there is a linear map
$B:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ such that

$$B(Au)=u\quad\hbox{and}\quad A(Bu)=u\qquad(u\in\mathbb R^n).$$

The map $B$ is unique: if $C$ has the same two properties, then
$C=C\circ(A\circ B)=(C\circ A)\circ B=B$.  It is denoted $A^{-1}$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: If $n=0$, the space $\mathbb R^0$ is a singleton. Its unique linear map is invertible, and $x=x_*=p=r=F(x)=0$ in this space. Take $r_0=R$, $C_F=1$, and $C=0$. Every claimed estimate is $0\le0$, so the assertion holds. For the remainder assume $n\ge1$, so the imported positive-dimensional Newton lemmas and operator-norm comparisons apply.

Put $K_*:=\|J_*^{-1}\|_{\rm op}$. The inverse identity gives $\|e\|_2=\|J_*^{-1}J_*e\|_2\le K_*\|e\|_*$, and the operator-norm definition gives $\|e\|_*\le\|J_*\|_{\rm op}\|e\|_2$. By [F3], choose a smaller radius $r_1\le R$ and $M>0$ such that every $J(x)$ on $\overline B_2(x_*,r_1)$ is invertible and $\|J(x)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}\le M$. Decrease $r_1$ if necessary so $r_1\le1$, and set $r_0:=r_1$.
The linear residual equation and steps 1.2–2.1 imply $\|p\|_2\le M\|J(x)p\|_2\le M(1+\eta)\|F(x)\|_2\le M(1+\bar\eta)C_F\|e\|_*$.

Put $e_+:=x+p-x_*$. From $J(x)p=-F(x)+r$, $J_*e_+=J_*e-F(x)+r+(J_*-J(x))p$. Step 1.2 and [F4] give $\|F(x)-J_*e\|_2\le(3L/2)\|e\|_2^2\le(3L/2)K_*^2\|e\|_*^2$, so $\|r\|_2\le\eta\|F(x)\|_2\le\eta\|e\|_*+(3\eta L K_*^2/2)\|e\|_*^2$. Also $\|J_*-J(x)\|_{\rm op}\le LK_*\|e\|_*$ and step 3.1 bounds $\|p\|_2\le M(1+\bar\eta)C_F\|e\|_*$. The triangle inequality and $\eta\le\bar\eta$ yield $\|e_+\|_*\le\eta\|e\|_*+\left(\frac{3(1+\bar\eta)LK_*^2}{2}+LK_*M(1+\bar\eta)C_F\right)\|e\|_*^2$. Set $C$ equal to this nonnegative coefficient; this is the claimed recurrence, and step 1.2 supplies invertibility.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, and
$x_*\in U$ satisfy $F(x_*)=0$ with $J_*:=DF(x_*)$ invertible. Suppose a
closed Euclidean ball $K=\overline B_2(x_*,R)\subseteq U$ with $R>0$ is convex and
$$
\|J(u)-J(v)\|_{\rm op}\le L\|u-v\|_2\qquad(u,v\in K),
$$
where $J(x):=DF(x)$ and
$\|A\|_{\rm op}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Av\|_2$ for $n\ge1$;
for $n=0$ set the norm of the unique linear map to $0$. Let
$\|v\|_*:=\|J_*v\|_2$ and fix $\bar\eta\in[0,1)$. There are constants
$r_0>0$, $C_F>0$, and $C\ge0$ such that, whenever
$\|x-x_*\|_2\le r_0$, $0\le\eta\le\bar\eta$, and $p,r\in\mathbb R^n$
satisfy
$$
J(x)p+F(x)=r,\qquad \|r\|_2\le\eta\|F(x)\|_2,
$$
then $J(x)$ is invertible,
$\|F(x)\|_2\le C_F\|x-x_*\|_*$, and
$$
\|x+p-x_*\|_*\le\bigl(\eta+C\|x-x_*\|_*\bigr)\|x-x_*\|_*.
$$

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a$, then $D_vf(a)$ exists for every $v\in\mathbb R^m$ and equals $Df(a)v$. In particular $\partial_jf(a)=Df(a)e_j$, and the matrix of $Df(a)$ is $Jf(a)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.
Let $k\ge2$. If $f\in C^k(U)$ for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, then every iterated derivative of $f$ of order $k$ is unchanged by any permutation of its coordinate differentiations.

derivations.claim: If $n=0$, every iterate, residual and correction is the unique zero vector and $x_k=x_*$ for all $k$. Choose any $\rho>0$ and $q=(1+\bar\eta)/2<1$; all error bounds are $0\le0$. The exact-root alternative applies from the start, including the quadratic zero-error bound. For the remainder assume $n\ge1$.
Let $C_F,C$ and a radius $r_0$ be supplied by [F1], and let $K_*:=\|J_*^{-1}\|_{\rm op}$. Set $q:=(1+\bar\eta)/2<1$. Choose $\rho>0$ with $K_*\rho\le r_0$ and, when $C>0$, $C\rho\le(1-\bar\eta)/2$.

Suppose $\|x_k-x_*\|_*\le\rho$. Then $\|x_k-x_*\|_2\le K_*\rho\le r_0$, so [F1] applies and gives $\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|_*\le(\eta_k+C\|x_k-x_*\|_*)\|x_k-x_*\|_*\le q\|x_k-x_*\|_*\le\rho$. Induction proves every iterate remains in the ball and the geometric bound.

By [F2] and step 2.1, $\|x_k-x_*\|_*\to0$. If $x_k\ne x_*$, divide the recurrence in [F1] by $\|x_k-x_*\|_*$ to get $\frac{\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|_*}{\|x_k-x_*\|_*}\le\eta_k+C\|x_k-x_*\|_*$. When $\eta_k\to0$, the right side tends to zero. If some $x_k=x_*$, then $F(x_k)=0$ and the residual bound gives $r_k=0$; local invertibility in [F1] forces $p_k=0$, so all later iterates remain there.
If $\eta_k\le C_\eta\|F(x_k)\|_2$, [F1] and step 2.1 yield $\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|_*\le\bigl(C_\eta C_F+C\bigr)\|x_k-x_*\|_*^2$, which is quadratic convergence in the $*$ norm.

In the specialization $F=\nabla f$ with $f\in C^2(U)$, each $F_i=\partial_i f$ has continuous first partials. By [F5] it is totally differentiable, and by [F4] the matrix of $DF$ has entries $J_{ij}=\partial_j(\partial_i f)$. By [F6] these equal $\partial_i(\partial_j f)$, the entries of the Hessian in [F3]. Thus $J(x)=\nabla^2f(x)$. Invertibility gives $K_*^{-1}\|e\|_2\le\|e\|_*\le\|J_*\|_{\rm op}\|e\|_2$ for every $e$. These fixed comparison constants transfer the linear, superlinear, and quadratic bounds from the $*$ norm to the Euclidean norm. The fixed-$\bar\eta$ geometric estimate of step 2.1 is linear convergence.

citations.quote:
If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be twice continuously differentiable, meaning that $f$ is $C^1$ and its
gradient is $C^1$.
Write $g(x):=\nabla f(x)$ and $H(x):=\nabla^2f(x)$ using
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and
[[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. The identity matrix $I_n$ and
matrix-vector products have the convention of
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. Use the matrix-free access
model of [[def-matrix-free-access-model-for-krylov-methods]] for products
$v\mapsto(H(x)+\lambda I_n)v$.

**Linear-solver input:** a fixed deterministic Krylov procedure $K$ which accepts a
matrix-free linear operator $A$, a right-hand side $b$, a tolerance $\tau\ge0$,
and a finite inner-iteration budget $M\in\mathbb N_0$. It returns either
`no-candidate` or `candidate` with a vector $p$ and an iteration count
$m\in\{0,1,\ldots,M\}$ satisfying $p\in K_m(A,b)$, where $K_m$ is as defined
by [[def-krylov-subspace-of-a-matrix-and-start-vector]]. A candidate's residual
status is never trusted: this algorithm recomputes
the requested residual using the supplied operator. **Other inputs:** $x_0\in U$, outer update budget
$N\in\mathbb N_0$, forcing values $\eta_k\in[0,\bar\eta]$ for a fixed
$0\le\bar\eta<1$, descent parameter $\sigma\in(0,1)$, regularization factor
$\gamma>1$, initial shift $\lambda_0>0$, shift cap $\lambda_{\max}\ge\lambda_0$,
regularized-attempt budget $J\in\mathbb N_0$, inner budget $M$, and the
parameters and finite expansion/zoom budgets of
[[alg-bracketing-zoom-strong-wolfe-search]]. **Output:** the last valid
iterate and one of `stationary`, `iteration-budget-exhausted`,
`no-descent-direction`, or `line-search-failure`; in the last case also
return the underlying line-search failure cause.

At iteration $k=0,1,\ldots,N$:

1. Compute $g_k:=g(x_k)$. If $g_k=0$, return $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$.
   If $k=N$, return $(x_k,\texttt{iteration-budget-exhausted})$.
2. Set $\lambda:=0$. For $j=0,1,\ldots,J$, call $K$ on
   $A_\lambda v:=H(x_k)v+\lambda I_nv$, right-hand side $-g_k$, tolerance
   $\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$, and budget $M$. A `no-candidate` result is a rejected
   attempt. If it returns a candidate $p$, compute
   $r:=(H(x_k)+\lambda I_n)p+g_k$. Accept this linear solve only when
   $\|r\|_2\le\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$ and
   $\langle g_k,p\rangle<-\sigma\|g_k\|_2\|p\|_2$; otherwise reject it.
   If the attempt is rejected and either $j=J$ or $\lambda=\lambda_{\max}$, stop the
   regularization loop. Otherwise set
   $\lambda:=\min\{\lambda_{\max},\lambda_0\}$ when $\lambda=0$, and
   $\lambda:=\min\{\lambda_{\max},\gamma\lambda\}$ when $\lambda>0$;
   then continue with the next $j$.
3. If no regularized attempt was accepted, set $p:=-g_k$ and check
   $\langle g_k,p\rangle<-\sigma\|g_k\|_2\|p\|_2$. If this check fails,
   return `no-descent-direction`. For the stated $\sigma$ and $g_k\ne0$ it
   passes, but the check remains part of the procedure.
4. Call [[alg-bracketing-zoom-strong-wolfe-search]] at $x_k$ in direction $p$.
   If it returns failure, return $(x_k,\texttt{line-search-failure},s)$, where $s$ is
   the returned line-search failure cause. Otherwise, for its returned strong Wolfe step $t_k$,
   set $x_{k+1}:=x_k+t_kp$ and continue.

The first unregularized system uses the forcing residual
$\|H(x_k)p+g_k\|_2\le\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$. A regularized attempt checks the
residual for the shifted system instead. Finite inner, regularization, and
line-search budgets can return failure; the procedure makes no global
convergence claim. The local rate theorem applies only to an unshifted
$\lambda=0$ sequence taking full steps $t_k=1$ and remaining in its stated
local tube. This algorithm does not assert that every run enters that branch.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:D\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$,
let $x\in D$, and let $p\in\mathbb R^n$ be arbitrary. Fix $0<c_1<c_2<1/2$ and finite
budgets $E,Z\in\mathbb N$ for expansion and zoom trials. After the direction check passes, use the functions
$\phi(t)=f(x+tp)$ and $\phi'(t)=\langle\nabla f(x+tp),p\rangle$ from
[[def-wolfe-and-strong-wolfe-conditions]]. **Output:** either a positive
strong Wolfe step, or one of `invalid-direction`, `domain-exit`, and
`evaluation-budget-exhausted`.

1. If $\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle\ge0$, return `invalid-direction`.
   Set $a:=0$ and $t:=1$. For at most $E$ expansion trials, in order:
   - If $x+tp\notin D$, return `domain-exit` without evaluating the trial.
   - Evaluate $\phi(t)$ and $\phi'(t)$. If
     $\phi(t)>\phi(0)+c_1t\phi'(0)$ or $\phi(t)\ge\phi(a)$, call the zoom
     procedure below with the ordered endpoint pair $(a,t)$ and return its
     output.
   - If $|\phi'(t)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|$, return $t$ as a strong Wolfe step.
   - If $\phi'(t)\ge0$, call zoom with the reversed endpoint pair $(t,a)$ and
     return its output.
   - Otherwise set $a:=t$ and $t:=2t$.
2. If the expansion budget is exhausted, return `evaluation-budget-exhausted`.

For `zoom(a,b)`, preserve the endpoint order even when $b<a$. For at most
$Z$ zoom trials, in order:

1. Set $m:=(a+b)/2$. If $x+mp\notin D$, return `domain-exit` without
   evaluating the trial.
2. Evaluate $\phi(m)$ and $\phi'(m)$. If
   $\phi(m)>\phi(0)+c_1m\phi'(0)$ or $\phi(m)\ge\phi(a)$, set $b:=m$.
   Otherwise, if $|\phi'(m)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|$, return $m$ as a strong Wolfe
   step. In the remaining branch, if $\phi'(m)(b-a)\ge0$, first set
   $b:=a$; then set $a:=m$.
3. If the zoom budget is exhausted, return `evaluation-budget-exhausted`.

The procedure returns a step only after both strong Wolfe inequalities have
been checked. Finite budgets and domain exits may return failure even when a
strong Wolfe step exists; no convergence claim follows from the procedure
alone.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:D\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$
([[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]), let $x\in D$, and let
$p\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$. Define the open parameter set $S_{x,p}:=\{t\in\mathbb R:x+tp\in D\}$,
which contains $0$, the feasible ray $T_{x,p}:=S_{x,p}\cap[0,\infty)$,
and $\phi(t):=f(x+tp)$ for $t\in S_{x,p}$. At every $t\in S_{x,p}$,
including $0$, the chain rule gives $\phi'(t)=Df(x+tp)p$.
By [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],
the matrix of $Df$ is the Jacobian, whose scalar-field row is the transpose
of the gradient. Hence
$\phi'(t)=\langle\nabla f(x+tp),p\rangle$, using the gradient convention
of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the Euclidean inner product of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A direction is a **descent direction** at
$x$ when $\phi'(0)=\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle<0$.

Assume for the line-search conditions below that $p$ is a descent direction
at $x$.
Fix constants $0<c_1<c_2<1/2$. A feasible step $t>0$ is a **Wolfe step**
when
$$
\phi(t)\le\phi(0)+c_1t\phi'(0),\qquad \phi'(t)\ge c_2\phi'(0).

be twice continuously differentiable, meaning that $f$ is $C^1$ and its
gradient is $C^1$.
Write $g(x):=\nabla f(x)$ and $H(x):=\nabla^2f(x)$ using
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and
[[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. The identity matrix $I_n$ and
matrix-vector products have the convention of
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. Use the matrix-free access
model of [[def-matrix-free-access-model-for-krylov-methods]] for products
$v\mapsto(H(x)+\lambda I_n)v$.

**Linear-solver input:** a fixed deterministic Krylov procedure $K$ which accepts a
matrix-free linear operator $A$, a right-hand side $b$, a tolerance $\tau\ge0$,
and a finite inner-iteration budget $M\in\mathbb N_0$. It returns either
`no-candidate` or `candidate` with a vector $p$ and an iteration count
$m\in\{0,1,\ldots,M\}$ satisfying $p\in K_m(A,b)$, where $K_m$ is as defined
by [[def-krylov-subspace-of-a-matrix-and-start-vector]]. A candidate's residual
status is never trusted: this algorithm recomputes
the requested residual using the supplied operator. **Other inputs:** $x_0\in U$, outer update budget
$N\in\mathbb N_0$, forcing values $\eta_k\in[0,\bar\eta]$ for a fixed
$0\le\bar\eta<1$, descent parameter $\sigma\in(0,1)$, regularization factor
$\gamma>1$, initial shift $\lambda_0>0$, shift cap $\lambda_{\max}\ge\lambda_0$,
regularized-attempt budget $J\in\mathbb N_0$, inner budget $M$, and the
parameters and finite expansion/zoom budgets of
[[alg-bracketing-zoom-strong-wolfe-search]]. **Output:** the last valid
iterate and one of `stationary`, `iteration-budget-exhausted`,
`no-descent-direction`, or `line-search-failure`; in the last case also
return the underlying line-search failure cause.

At iteration $k=0,1,\ldots,N$:

1. Compute $g_k:=g(x_k)$. If $g_k=0$, return $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$.
   If $k=N$, return $(x_k,\texttt{iteration-budget-exhausted})$.
2. Set $\lambda:=0$. For $j=0,1,\ldots,J$, call $K$ on
   $A_\lambda v:=H(x_k)v+\lambda I_nv$, right-hand side $-g_k$, tolerance
   $\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$, and budget $M$. A `no-candidate` result is a rejected

   $\langle g_k,p\rangle<-\sigma\|g_k\|_2\|p\|_2$. If this check fails,
   return `no-descent-direction`. For the stated $\sigma$ and $g_k\ne0$ it

$\bar\eta\in[0,1)$. For $n=0$ use the zero operator-norm convention
of [[lem-inexact-newton-error-recurrence-under-lipschitz-jacobian]]. Consider any sequence
$$x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k,\qquad J(x_k)p_k+F(x_k)=r_k,\qquad \|r_k\|_2\le\eta_k\|F(x_k)\|_2,$$
with $0\le\eta_k\le\bar\eta$. Define
$\|v\|_*:=\|J_*v\|_2$. There is $\rho>0$ such that, if
$\|x_0-x_*\|_*\le\rho$, every iterate remains in the ball and
$\|x_k-x_*\|_*\le q^k\|x_0-x_*\|_*$ for some $q<1$. Consequently:

1. If $\eta_k\to0$, the iterates converge superlinearly (unless an exact root
   is reached, in which case the exact recurrence remains there).
2. If $\eta_k\le C_\eta\|F(x_k)\|_2$ for a constant $C_\eta$, the iterates
   converge quadratically.

invertible, these rates in $\|\cdot\|_*$ are equivalent to the same local
rates in the Euclidean norm. For $F=\nabla f$ with $f\in C^2(U)$ (all ordered partial derivatives

residual is the inexact Newton residual

[[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. This theorem concerns the
unshifted full-step recurrence; it does not assert that a safeguarded
line-search algorithm eventually selects that branch.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].

$$K_m(A,b):=\operatorname{span}\{b,Ab,\dots,A^{m-1}b\}.$$

Thus $K_m(A,b)\subseteq K_{m+1}(A,b)$ for every $m\ge 0$.

derivations.claim: The exact scalar identities are $F(x)=x$, $J(x)=1$, and $g(x)=x$ by [F1]–[F2]. Induction on $j$ gives $p^{(j)}=-(1-\omega^j)x$, so the linear residual is $r_j=J(x)p^{(j)}+F(x)=\omega^j x$.

Since $0<\omega<1$, [F6] gives $\omega^j\to0$, so a least $j$ with $\omega^j\le\eta$ exists. As $\eta<1$, $j\ge1$ and minimality gives $\omega^j\le\eta<\omega^{j-1}$. If the requested tolerance is reduced, the set of eligible $j$ can only shrink, so the required inner iteration count cannot decrease. For any finite $N$, all $j_k$ on its first $N$ nonzero iterates are finite, so their finite maximum defines $M_N$. The specified solver therefore reaches its requested residual tolerance before its budget on that prefix, and [F7] verifies its scalar Krylov membership.
At this $j$, $|r_j|=\omega^j|x|\le\eta|x|$, while $g(x)p^{(j)}=-(1-\omega^j)x^2$ and $|g(x)|\,|p^{(j)}|=(1-\omega^j)x^2$. Because $0<\sigma<1$, the descent safeguard passes.

Let $q:=\omega^j\le\eta\le c_2$. The unit step gives $x_+=x+p^{(j)}=qx$. Its objective satisfies $f(x_+)=q^2x^2/2\le x^2(1-2c_1(1-q))/2=f(x)+c_1g(x)p^{(j)}$, because $1+q\ge1>2c_1$. Also $|\phi'(1)|=q(1-q)x^2\le c_2(1-q)x^2=c_2|\phi'(0)|$. Thus both strong Wolfe conditions hold, and [F4] accepts $t=1$.

For fixed $\eta$, $q=\omega^j$ is a constant in $(0,1)$ and $x_{k+1}=qx_k$, so the outer sequence is linearly convergent. If $0<|x_0|\le c_2$ and $\eta_k=|x_k|$, then $\eta_k\le c_2$ at every step and $|x_{k+1}|=\omega^{j_k}|x_k|\le|x_k|^2$. Here $\eta_k=|F(x_k)|$; the local tube in [F5] may contain $[-c_2,c_2]$ because $F(x)=x$ and $J(x)=1$ everywhere. Thus [F5] supplies the same local quadratic-rate conclusion.

2. If the expansion budget is exhausted, return `evaluation-budget-exhausted`.

1. Set $m:=(a+b)/2$. If $x+mp\notin D$, return `domain-exit` without

2. Evaluate $\phi(m)$ and $\phi'(m)$. If

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:D\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$
([[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]), let $x\in D$, and let
$p\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$. Define the open parameter set $S_{x,p}:=\{t\in\mathbb R:x+tp\in D\}$,
which contains $0$, the feasible ray $T_{x,p}:=S_{x,p}\cap[0,\infty)$,
and $\phi(t):=f(x+tp)$ for $t\in S_{x,p}$. At every $t\in S_{x,p}$,
including $0$, the chain rule gives $\phi'(t)=Df(x+tp)p$.
By [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],
the matrix of $Df$ is the Jacobian, whose scalar-field row is the transpose
of the gradient. Hence
$\phi'(t)=\langle\nabla f(x+tp),p\rangle$, using the gradient convention
of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the Euclidean inner product of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A direction is a **descent direction** at
$x$ when $\phi'(0)=\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle<0$.

Assume for the line-search conditions below that $p$ is a descent direction
at $x$.
Fix constants $0<c_1<c_2<1/2$. A feasible step $t>0$ is a **Wolfe step**
when
$$
\phi(t)\le\phi(0)+c_1t\phi'(0),\qquad \phi'(t)\ge c_2\phi'(0).
$$
It is a **strong Wolfe step** when it satisfies the first inequality and
$$
|\phi'(t)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|.
$$
The first inequality is the Armijo sufficient-decrease condition. The second
Wolfe inequality is the curvature condition. Every strong Wolfe step is a
Wolfe step, because $\phi'(0)<0$ and the strong curvature bound implies
$\phi'(t)\ge-c_2|\phi'(0)|=c_2\phi'(0)$.

For a descent direction define its **descent angle** $\theta\in[0,\pi/2)$ by
$$
\cos\theta:=-\frac{\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle}{\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\|p\|_2}.
$$
The denominator is nonzero for a descent direction. The Cauchy–Schwarz
inequality [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]] ensures $0<\cos\theta\le1$.

A midpoint of distinct nonnegative endpoints, at least one positive, is positive and strictly between them. Replacing $b$ by that midpoint preserves distinct nonnegative endpoints. In the other update, replacing $a$ by the midpoint, either retaining $b$ or first replacing $b$ by the old $a$, also preserves those properties. Before any trial evaluation the domain check either returns failure or verifies feasibility. In expansion, a return of a step occurs only after the Armijo-failure branch was bypassed and the strong curvature test passed. In zoom the same two tests precede every step return. Therefore [F2] and steps 1.1–2.1 prove every returned step has the asserted properties.

Each expansion pass either returns, calls zoom and returns its output, or consumes one of at most $E$ passes. Thus at most one zoom is called. Each zoom pass either returns or consumes one of at most $Z$ passes. All evaluations terminate by hypothesis; after exhaustion the specified failure is returned. There are at most $E+Z$ evaluated trial points, with the objective and directional derivative evaluated at each; domain exits consume no trial evaluation. Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be twice continuously differentiable, meaning that $f$ is $C^1$ and its
gradient is $C^1$.
Write $g(x):=\nabla f(x)$ and $H(x):=\nabla^2f(x)$ using
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and
[[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. The identity matrix $I_n$ and
matrix-vector products have the convention of
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. Use the matrix-free access
model of [[def-matrix-free-access-model-for-krylov-methods]] for products
$v\mapsto(H(x)+\lambda I_n)v$.

**Linear-solver input:** a fixed deterministic Krylov procedure $K$ which accepts a
matrix-free linear operator $A$, a right-hand side $b$, a tolerance $\tau\ge0$,
and a finite inner-iteration budget $M\in\mathbb N_0$. It returns either
`no-candidate` or `candidate` with a vector $p$ and an iteration count
$m\in\{0,1,\ldots,M\}$ satisfying $p\in K_m(A,b)$, where $K_m$ is as defined
by [[def-krylov-subspace-of-a-matrix-and-start-vector]]. A candidate's residual
status is never trusted: this algorithm recomputes
the requested residual using the supplied operator. **Other inputs:** $x_0\in U$, outer update budget
$N\in\mathbb N_0$, forcing values $\eta_k\in[0,\bar\eta]$ for a fixed
$0\le\bar\eta<1$, descent parameter $\sigma\in(0,1)$, regularization factor
$\gamma>1$, initial shift $\lambda_0>0$, shift cap $\lambda_{\max}\ge\lambda_0$,
regularized-attempt budget $J\in\mathbb N_0$, inner budget $M$, and the
parameters and finite expansion/zoom budgets of
[[alg-bracketing-zoom-strong-wolfe-search]]. **Output:** the last valid
iterate and one of `stationary`, `iteration-budget-exhausted`,
`no-descent-direction`, or `line-search-failure`; in the last case also
return the underlying line-search failure cause.

At iteration $k=0,1,\ldots,N$:

1. Compute $g_k:=g(x_k)$. If $g_k=0$, return $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$.
   If $k=N$, return $(x_k,\texttt{iteration-budget-exhausted})$.
2. Set $\lambda:=0$. For $j=0,1,\ldots,J$, call $K$ on
   $A_\lambda v:=H(x_k)v+\lambda I_nv$, right-hand side $-g_k$, tolerance
   $\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$, and budget $M$. A `no-candidate` result is a rejected
   attempt. If it returns a candidate $p$, compute
   $r:=(H(x_k)+\lambda I_n)p+g_k$. Accept this linear solve only when
   $\|r\|_2\le\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$ and
   $\langle g_k,p\rangle<-\sigma\|g_k\|_2\|p\|_2$; otherwise reject it.
   If the attempt is rejected and either $j=J$ or $\lambda=\lambda_{\max}$, stop the
   regularization loop. Otherwise set
   $\lambda:=\min\{\lambda_{\max},\lambda_0\}$ when $\lambda=0$, and
   $\lambda:=\min\{\lambda_{\max},\gamma\lambda\}$ when $\lambda>0$;
   then continue with the next $j$.
3. If no regularized attempt was accepted, set $p:=-g_k$ and check
   $\langle g_k,p\rangle<-\sigma\|g_k\|_2\|p\|_2$. If this check fails,
   return `no-descent-direction`. For the stated $\sigma$ and $g_k\ne0$ it
   passes, but the check remains part of the procedure.
4. Call [[alg-bracketing-zoom-strong-wolfe-search]] at $x_k$ in direction $p$.
   If it returns failure, return $(x_k,\texttt{line-search-failure},s)$, where $s$ is
   the returned line-search failure cause. Otherwise, for its returned strong Wolfe step $t_k$,
   set $x_{k+1}:=x_k+t_kp$ and continue.

The first unregularized system uses the forcing residual
$\|H(x_k)p+g_k\|_2\le\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$. A regularized attempt checks the
residual for the shifted system instead. Finite inner, regularization, and
line-search budgets can return failure; the procedure makes no global
convergence claim. The local rate theorem applies only to an unshifted
$\lambda=0$ sequence taking full steps $t_k=1$ and remaining in its stated
local tube. This algorithm does not assert that every run enters that branch.

Under the inputs of [[alg-bracketing-zoom-strong-wolfe-search]], assume all requested in-domain function and gradient evaluations terminate with real values and all prescribed comparisons are exact. The procedure terminates with its specified step or failure status. It makes at most $E$ expansion trial evaluations and at most one zoom call with at most $Z$ trial evaluations, hence at most $E+Z$ evaluated trial points. Each evaluates the objective and directional derivative at that point. Every returned step is positive, feasible, and satisfies both strong Wolfe inequalities. A domain-exit trial is not evaluated. The bound excludes the initial-point data and does not bound arithmetic work or guarantee success when a strong Wolfe step exists.

derivations.claim: Initially $x_0\in U$. At any nonstationary iteration the supplied solver calls and candidate residual evaluations terminate by assumption; the loop has at most $J+1$ attempts. Every accepted candidate satisfies $g_k^Tp<-\sigma\|g_k\|_2\|p\|_2<0$, since a candidate with $p=0$ cannot pass. If none passes, $p=-g_k$ gives $g_k^Tp=-\|g_k\|_2^2<-\sigma\|g_k\|_2^2$ because $g_k\ne0$ and $0<\sigma<1$. Thus a strict descent direction is always available and the fallback failure cannot occur in exact arithmetic.

By [F2] the ensuing search terminates. On failure the algorithm returns its last valid iterate, its line-search-failure status and the search cause. On success feasibility of the checked step gives $x_{k+1}\in U$. Induction proves feasibility of every iterate.

A solve or update can occur only for $k<N$. Thus at most $N$ updates and searches and $N(J+1)$ solver calls occur; each uses at most $M$ inner iterations. At most one candidate residual is recomputed per call, each by one Hessian action plus the displayed shift and vector arithmetic. By [F2] there are at most $N(E+Z)$ evaluated search trials. The outer loop computes its gradient once per visited index, at most $N+1$ times, separately from line-search gradient evaluations.

Every inner call and search terminates and every loop has its finite stated bound. Hence the algorithm reaches a specified return no later than its $k=N$ check. Steps 1.1–3.1 prove the asserted statuses, feasibility and counts; they do not specify the internal Hessian-action count of the arbitrary solver or a convergence theorem.

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let $D\subset E$ be open and convex, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R$ be $C^3$. Write $H_F(x)=D^2F(x)$ for its Hessian as a self-adjoint operator. A **self-concordant barrier** on $D$ is a strictly convex $F$ with positive-definite Hessian, with $F(x_k)\to+\infty$ whenever $x_k$ approaches a finite boundary point of $D$, and satisfying both conditions below.

For $x\in D$, define the local norm and its dual by
$$\|h\|_x=\sqrt{D^2F(x)[h,h]},\qquad \|\ell\|_{x,*}=\sup_{\|h\|_x\le1}|\ell[h]|.$$
The **Dikin inclusion** is $\{x+h:\|h\|_x<1\}\subset D$. The **self-concordance inequality** is
$$|D^3F(x)[u,v,v]|\le2\|u\|_x\|v\|_x^2\qquad(u,v\in E).$$
The Newton decrement is $\lambda_F(x)=\|DF(x)\|_{x,*}$.

If $K\subset E$ is a closed convex cone with nonempty interior and $D=\operatorname{int}K$, the barrier is **$\nu$-log-homogeneous** when $\nu>0$, $F(\alpha x)=F(x)-\nu\log\alpha$ for every $x\in D$ and $\alpha>0$, and $\lambda_F(x)\le\sqrt\nu$ for every $x\in D$. The number $\nu$ is its barrier parameter. When equality constraints $Ax=b$ are imposed, local norms and decrements are computed after restricting $D^2F$ and $DF$ to the tangent space $\ker A$.

derivations.claim: Fix $h\ne0$ and put $q(t)=\|h\|_{x+th}$. Differentiation gives $q'(t)=D^3F(x+th)[h,h,h]/(2q(t))$, so [F1] implies $|q'(t)|\le q(t)^2$. Therefore $|(1/q)'|\le1$. Integrating from $0$ to $t$ yields $1/r-t\le1/q(t)\le1/r+t$ whenever $tr<1$, and the lower inequality $1/q(t)\le1/r+t$ holds along every segment in $D$. Taking reciprocals gives the asserted two-sided metric bound for $tr<1$ and the lower bound for all $t\ge0$.

For a fixed $v\ne0$, put $p(t)=\sqrt{D^2F(x+th)[v,v]}$. By [F1], $|(\log p)'|=|D^3F[h,v,v]|/(2p^2)\le q(t)$. When $tr<1$, step 1.1 gives $q(t)\le r/(1-tr)$; integration gives $|\log(p(t)/p(0))|\le-\log(1-tr)$. Squaring this inequality for every $v$ proves the stated Hessian comparison.

For any $y\in D$, put $h=y-x$ and $r=\|h\|_x$. Taylor's formula with integral remainder and step 1.1 give $F(y)\ge F(x)+DF(x)[h]+r^2\int_0^1\frac{1-t}{(1+tr)^2}\,dt=F(x)+DF(x)[h]+r-\log(1+r)$. The dual-norm inequality $DF(x)[h]\ge-\lambda_F(x)r$ makes the right side at least $F(x)+(1-\lambda_F(x))r-\log(1+r)$, which tends to $+\infty$ as $r\to\infty$. Thus the sublevel set $\{y\in D:F(y)\le F(x)\}$ is bounded.

Since $\|d\|_x=\lambda$, the damped displacement $h=d/(1+\lambda)$ has local length $r=\lambda/(1+\lambda)<1$, so Dikin inclusion places $y$ in $D$. The gradient expansion is $
abla F(y)=
abla F(x)+H_xh+R$, where $R=\int_0^1(H_{x+th}-H_x)h\,dt$. The first two terms have $x$-dual norm $\lambda^2/(1+\lambda)$. By step 2.1, $\|R\|_{x,*}\le r\int_0^1((1-tr)^{-2}-1)\,dt=r^2/(1-r)=\lambda^2/(1+\lambda)$. Thus $\|
abla F(y)\|_{x,*}\le2\lambda^2/(1+\lambda)$. Since $H_y\succeq(1-r)^2H_x$, the dual norm at $y$ is at most $(1-r)^{-1}=1+\lambda$ times the $x$-dual norm, giving $\lambda_F(y)\le2\lambda^2$.

The sublevel set in step 2.2 cannot accumulate at a finite boundary point of $D$, because $F$ blows up there while its values on the sublevel are at most $F(x)$. It is closed in $E$ and bounded, hence compact. Continuity gives a minimizer on it, which is a global minimizer on $D$; positive-definite Hessian makes it unique.

Let $h=x_*-x$ and $r=\|h\|_x$. If $r=0$ the claim holds. Otherwise, stationarity at the minimizer from step 3.2 and the fundamental theorem of calculus give $-\nabla F(x)^Th=\int_0^1\|h\|_{x+th}^2\,dt$. By the global lower bound from step 1.1, this is at least $r^2\int_0^1(1+tr)^{-2}\,dt=r^2/(1+r)$. Cauchy–Schwarz in the local metric bounds it above by $\lambda_F(x)r$. Dividing by $r$ and rearranging gives $r\le\lambda_F(x)/(1-\lambda_F(x))$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

For a finite-dimensional real inner-product space $E$, a **cone** is a set closed under addition and multiplication by nonnegative scalars. A cone $K\subset E$ is **proper** when it is closed, convex, pointed ($K\cap(-K)=\{0\}$), and has nonempty interior. Its dual cone is
$$K^*=\{z\in E:\langle z,s\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }s\in K\}.$$

Let $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p$ and $G:\mathbb R^n\to E$ be linear, let $b\in\mathbb R^p$, $c\in\mathbb R^n$, and $h\in E$. A matrix $A$ has full row rank when its rows are linearly independent. The conic primal problem and its displayed dual pair are
$$\inf\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ h-Gx\in K\},\qquad \sup\{b^Ty-\langle h,z\rangle:A^Ty-G^*z=c,\ z\in K^*\},$$
where $G^*$ is the adjoint, defined by $\langle Gx,z\rangle=x^TG^*z$. For any feasible pair, its gap is
$$c^Tx-b^Ty+\langle h,z\rangle=\langle z,h-Gx\rangle\ge0.$$
The special case $\inf\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}$ has dual $\sup\{b^Ty:A^Ty+z=c,\ z\in K^*\}$ and gap $\langle z,x\rangle$.

For $K=\mathbb R_+^n$, the latter is the standard-form LP $\min c^Tx$ subject to $Ax=b$, $x\ge0$, with dual variables $y$ free and $s=c-A^Ty\ge0$. A convex QP in this convention has objective $f_0(x)=\tfrac12x^TQx+c^Tx$, with symmetric $Q\succeq0$, the same equality, and $x\ge0$. Its Lagrangian is $L(x,y,s)=f_0(x)+y^T(b-Ax)-s^Tx$; a feasible KKT tuple obeys $Qx+c-A^Ty-s=0$, and its dual value is $\inf_{w\in\mathbb R^n}L(w,y,s)$.

For a Lorentz cone $\mathcal L_{d+1}=\{(t,u)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d:t\ge\|u\|_2\}$, let $F_j\in\mathbb R^{d_j\times n}$, $f_j\in\mathbb R^{d_j}$, $g_j\in\mathbb R^n$, and $h_j\in\mathbb R$. Then $\|F_jx+f_j\|_2\le g_j^Tx+h_j$ is membership of $(g_j^Tx+h_j,F_jx+f_j)$ in $\mathcal L_{d_j+1}$. With no equality constraints, the SOCP $\min c^Tx$ under these constraints has dual
$$\max -\sum_j(f_j^Tu_j+h_j\tau_j)\quad\text{subject to }\sum_j(F_j^Tu_j+g_j\tau_j)=c,\quad(\tau_j,u_j)\in\mathcal L_{d_j+1}.$$
For symmetric matrices, $S\succeq0$ means $v^TSv\ge0$ for every $v$ and the pairing is $\langle X,S\rangle=X\bullet S:=\operatorname{tr}(XS)$. Thus $\min C\bullet X$ subject to $\mathcal A(X)=b$, $X\succeq0$ has dual $\max b^Ty$ subject to $\mathcal A^*y+S=C$, $S\succeq0$, with gap $X\bullet S$. The affine-matrix SDP $\min c^Tx$ subject to $F_0+\sum_i x_iF_i\succeq0$ has dual $\max -F_0\bullet Z$ subject to $F_i\bullet Z=c_i$ for every $i$ and $Z\succeq0$.

The smooth convex inequality convention is that of [[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]: inequalities are written $g_i(x)\le0$ and their multipliers are nonnegative. The Lagrangian dual-value convention is that of [[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]].

derivations.claim: Coordinatewise inequalities show that $K$ is closed, convex, and closed under addition and nonnegative scaling. If both $z$ and $-z$ lie in $K$, every coordinate is zero, so $K$ is pointed; because $m\ge1$, $D=\mathbb R_{++}^m$ is nonempty and is the interior of $K$. If $z\in K$, then $\langle z,y\rangle=\sum_i z_i y_i\ge0$ for every $y\in K$, so $z\in K^*$ by [F2]. Conversely, if $z\in K^*$, testing against each standard basis vector $e_i\in K$ gives $z_i=\langle z,e_i\rangle\ge0$. Hence $z\in K$ and $K^*=K$.

Direct differentiation gives $DF(x)[h]=-\sum_i h_i/x_i$, $D^2F(x)[h,k]=\sum_i h_i k_i/x_i^2$, and $D^3F(x)[u,v,v]=-2\sum_i u_i v_i^2/x_i^3$. The Hessian is positive definite because $D^2F(x)[h,h]=\sum_i(h_i/x_i)^2>0$ for $h\ne0$. If $\|h\|_x<1$, then each $|h_i|/x_i<1$, hence $x_i+h_i>0$ and the Dikin inclusion holds. If a sequence in $D$ approaches a finite boundary point, at least one coordinate tends to zero while all coordinates remain bounded above; each term $-\log x_i$ is bounded below and one tends to $+\infty$, so $F\to+\infty$.

Put $a_i=u_i/x_i$ and $b_i=v_i/x_i$. By [F1] and $\sum_i b_i^4\le(\sum_i b_i^2)^2$, $|D^3F(x)[u,v,v]|\le2\|a\|_2(\sum_i b_i^4)^{1/2}\le2\|u\|_x\|v\|_x^2$. Also $F(\alpha x)=F(x)-m\log\alpha$, and $\|DF(x)\|_{x,*}^2=\sum_i(1/x_i)^2x_i^2=m$. These are exactly the required self-concordance and parameter conditions.

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let $D\subset E$ be open and convex, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R$ be $C^3$. Write $H_F(x)=D^2F(x)$ for its Hessian as a self-adjoint operator. A **self-concordant barrier** on $D$ is a strictly convex $F$ with positive-definite Hessian, with $F(x_k)\to+\infty$ whenever $x_k$ approaches a finite boundary point of $D$, and satisfying both conditions below.

For $x\in D$, define the local norm and its dual by
$$\|h\|_x=\sqrt{D^2F(x)[h,h]},\qquad \|\ell\|_{x,*}=\sup_{\|h\|_x\le1}|\ell[h]|.$$
The **Dikin inclusion** is $\{x+h:\|h\|_x<1\}\subset D$. The **self-concordance inequality** is
$$|D^3F(x)[u,v,v]|\le2\|u\|_x\|v\|_x^2\qquad(u,v\in E).$$
The Newton decrement is $\lambda_F(x)=\|DF(x)\|_{x,*}$.

If $K\subset E$ is a closed convex cone with nonempty interior and $D=\operatorname{int}K$, the barrier is **$\nu$-log-homogeneous** when $\nu>0$, $F(\alpha x)=F(x)-\nu\log\alpha$ for every $x\in D$ and $\alpha>0$, and $\lambda_F(x)\le\sqrt\nu$ for every $x\in D$. The number $\nu$ is its barrier parameter. When equality constraints $Ax=b$ are imposed, local norms and decrements are computed after restricting $D^2F$ and $DF$ to the tangent space $\ker A$.

For a finite-dimensional real inner-product space $E$, a **cone** is a set closed under addition and multiplication by nonnegative scalars. A cone $K\subset E$ is **proper** when it is closed, convex, pointed ($K\cap(-K)=\{0\}$), and has nonempty interior. Its dual cone is
$$K^*=\{z\in E:\langle z,s\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }s\in K\}.$$

Let $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p$ and $G:\mathbb R^n\to E$ be linear, let $b\in\mathbb R^p$, $c\in\mathbb R^n$, and $h\in E$. A matrix $A$ has full row rank when its rows are linearly independent. The conic primal problem and its displayed dual pair are
$$\inf\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ h-Gx\in K\},\qquad \sup\{b^Ty-\langle h,z\rangle:A^Ty-G^*z=c,\ z\in K^*\},$$
where $G^*$ is the adjoint, defined by $\langle Gx,z\rangle=x^TG^*z$. For any feasible pair, its gap is
$$c^Tx-b^Ty+\langle h,z\rangle=\langle z,h-Gx\rangle\ge0.$$
The special case $\inf\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}$ has dual $\sup\{b^Ty:A^Ty+z=c,\ z\in K^*\}$ and gap $\langle z,x\rangle$.

For $K=\mathbb R_+^n$, the latter is the standard-form LP $\min c^Tx$ subject to $Ax=b$, $x\ge0$, with dual variables $y$ free and $s=c-A^Ty\ge0$. A convex QP in this convention has objective $f_0(x)=\tfrac12x^TQx+c^Tx$, with symmetric $Q\succeq0$, the same equality, and $x\ge0$. Its Lagrangian is $L(x,y,s)=f_0(x)+y^T(b-Ax)-s^Tx$; a feasible KKT tuple obeys $Qx+c-A^Ty-s=0$, and its dual value is $\inf_{w\in\mathbb R^n}L(w,y,s)$.

For a Lorentz cone $\mathcal L_{d+1}=\{(t,u)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d:t\ge\|u\|_2\}$, let $F_j\in\mathbb R^{d_j\times n}$, $f_j\in\mathbb R^{d_j}$, $g_j\in\mathbb R^n$, and $h_j\in\mathbb R$. Then $\|F_jx+f_j\|_2\le g_j^Tx+h_j$ is membership of $(g_j^Tx+h_j,F_jx+f_j)$ in $\mathcal L_{d_j+1}$. With no equality constraints, the SOCP $\min c^Tx$ under these constraints has dual
$$\max -\sum_j(f_j^Tu_j+h_j\tau_j)\quad\text{subject to }\sum_j(F_j^Tu_j+g_j\tau_j)=c,\quad(\tau_j,u_j)\in\mathcal L_{d_j+1}.$$
For symmetric matrices, $S\succeq0$ means $v^TSv\ge0$ for every $v$ and the pairing is $\langle X,S\rangle=X\bullet S:=\operatorname{tr}(XS)$. Thus $\min C\bullet X$ subject to $\mathcal A(X)=b$, $X\succeq0$ has dual $\max b^Ty$ subject to $\mathcal A^*y+S=C$, $S\succeq0$, with gap $X\bullet S$. The affine-matrix SDP $\min c^Tx$ subject to $F_0+\sum_i x_iF_i\succeq0$ has dual $\max -F_0\bullet Z$ subject to $F_i\bullet Z=c_i$ for every $i$ and $Z\succeq0$.

The smooth convex inequality convention is that of [[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]: inequalities are written $g_i(x)\le0$ and their multipliers are nonnegative. The Lagrangian dual-value convention is that of [[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]].

derivations.claim: Continuity of the Euclidean norm makes $K$ closed, and its triangle inequality makes $K$ convex and closed under addition and nonnegative scaling. If $(t,u)$ and its negative are both in $K$, then $t\ge\|u\|$ and $-t\ge\|u\|$, forcing $t=0,u=0$; hence $K$ is pointed. The point $(1,0)$ is interior, so $K$ is proper. If $(a,v)\in K$ and $(t,u)\in K$, then $at+v^Tu\ge at-\|v\|_2\|u\|_2\ge0$, so $K\subseteq K^*$ by [F2]. Conversely, suppose $(a,v)\in K^*$. If $v=0$ and $a<\|v\|_2=0$, then pairing with $(1,0)\in K$ gives $a<0$, a contradiction. If $v\ne0$ and $a<\|v\|_2$, pairing with $(1,-v/\|v\|_2)\in K$ gives $a-\|v\|_2<0$, also a contradiction. Thus $a\ge\|v\|_2$ and $K^*=K$.

Write $\rho=t^2-\|u\|_2^2>0$. An orthogonal change of spatial coordinates followed by the Lorentz boost $\rho^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}t&-\|u\|\\-\|u\|&t\end{pmatrix}$ on the time and first spatial coordinate preserves $\rho$ and maps $(t,u)$ to $(\sqrt\rho,0)$. Since $F$ is invariant under this invertible linear cone map, the chain rule transports its Hessian, third derivative, and local norms; the Newton decrement is invariant as well. At the canonical point $\nabla F=(-2/\sqrt\rho,0)$ and $D^2F=(2/\rho)I$. For directions $h=(a,p)$ and $k=(b,v)$, direct differentiation gives $D^3F[h,k,k]=-\frac{4\{a(b^2+\|v\|_2^2)+2b\,p^Tv\}}{\rho^{3/2}}$. These formulas also show the Hessian is positive definite.

By Cauchy–Schwarz and $2|b|\|v\|_2\le b^2+\|v\|_2^2$, the numerator in step 1.2 has absolute value at most $4\sqrt2\sqrt{a^2+\|p\|_2^2}(b^2+\|v\|_2^2)/\rho^{3/2}=2\|h\|_x\|k\|_x^2$. If $\|h\|_x<1$, set $A=|a|/\sqrt\rho$ and $B=\|p\|_2/\sqrt\rho$. Then $A^2+B^2<1/2$, so $1+a/\sqrt\rho\ge1-A>0$ and $(1+a/\sqrt\rho)^2-B^2\ge(1-A)^2-B^2>2(A-1/2)^2\ge0$. Thus $\sqrt\rho+a>\|p\|_2$ and the Dikin ball stays inside $D$. The Lorentz transformation carries this inclusion to every $x$. Approaching a finite boundary point makes $\rho\downarrow0$, hence $F\to+\infty$. Finally, $F(\alpha x)=F(x)-2\log\alpha$, and step 1.2 gives $\|DF(x)\|_{x,*}^2=2$.
