Let $A$ be a square matrix over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and let $b$ be a
vector of matching size. Define

$$K_0(A,b):=\{0\},$$

and for $m\ge 1$ define the $m$th **Krylov subspace**

$$K_m(A,b):=\operatorname{span}\{b,Ab,\dots,A^{m-1}b\}.$$

Thus $K_m(A,b)\subseteq K_{m+1}(A,b)$ for every $m\ge 0$.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, be symmetric with ordered eigenvalues
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n$. Let $r$ be the multiplicity of $\lambda_1$.
If $r<n$, assume $\lambda_1>\lambda_{r+1}$, and let $P$ be the orthogonal
projection onto the $\lambda_1$-eigenspace. Let $b\in\mathbb R^n$ be a unit
vector and, for $m\ge1$, define

$$K_m:=\operatorname{span}\{b,Ab,\ldots,A^{m-1}b\},\qquad \theta_m:=\max_{0\ne x\in K_m}\frac{x^{\mathsf T}Ax}{x^{\mathsf T}x}.$$

Thus $\theta_m$ is the largest Rayleigh–Ritz value on $K_m$; if Lanczos runs
through step $m$ without breakdown, it is the largest Ritz value of
$Q_m^{\mathsf T}AQ_m$. If $r=n$, then $A=\lambda_1I$ and $\theta_m=\lambda_1$
for every $m\ge1$. Suppose $r<n$.

1. If $Pb=0$, then $\theta_m\le\lambda_{r+1}$ for every $m$; no convergence
   to $\lambda_1$ is asserted.

2. If $Pb\ne0$, put
   $$\tau:=\frac{\|(I-P)b\|_2}{\|Pb\|_2}.$$
   If $\lambda_{r+1}>\lambda_n$, then for every $m\ge1$,
   $$0\le\lambda_1-\theta_m\le \frac{(\lambda_1-\lambda_n)\tau^2} {T_{m-1}\!\left(1+2\frac{\lambda_1-\lambda_{r+1}} {\lambda_{r+1}-\lambda_n}\right)^2}.$$
   For a simple top eigenvalue ($r=1$), $\tau$ is the tangent of the angle
   between $b$ and a unit top eigenvector, so the starting-angle denominator
   is explicit.

3. If $\lambda_{r+1}=\lambda_n$, then
   $$\lambda_1-\theta_1=(\lambda_1-\lambda_n) \frac{\|(I-P)b\|_2^2}{\|b\|_2^2},\qquad \theta_m=\lambda_1\quad(m\ge2).$$

When $r<n$, $Pb\ne0$, and exact Lanczos breakdown occurs at dimension $d$, then
$\theta_d=\lambda_1$ and $K_m=K_d$ for all $m\ge d$. These are exact-arithmetic
claims; they give no finite-precision grade-termination guarantee.

Let $X=\mathbb R^n$, $Y=\mathbb R^m$, let $f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ and
$g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper closed convex, and let $K:X\to Y$ be
linear. Its unique adjoint $K^*:Y\to X$ exists by
[[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]], including zero-dimensional
spaces. Identify $K$ with its matrix in the standard Euclidean bases when using
the induced matrix norm below. The primal problem is $\min_x f(x)+g(Kx)$, with saddle function
$$\Phi(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y),$$
where $g^*$ is defined by [[def-fenchel-conjugate-on-finite-dimensional-euclidean-space]].
The saddle function $\Phi$ is evaluated on
$\operatorname{dom}f\times\operatorname{dom}g^*$, where both function values
are finite; no undefined extended-real subtraction is used outside this domain.
Assume $\tau,\sigma>0$ and
$\tau\sigma\|K\|_2^2<1$, where $\|K\|_2$ is the induced Euclidean operator
norm of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]]. Starting from $x^0,y^0$ and
$\bar x^0=x^0$, the exact recurrence is
$$y^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma g^*}(y^k+\sigma K\bar x^k),\qquad x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}(x^k-\tau K^*y^{k+1}),\qquad \bar x^{k+1}=2x^{k+1}-x^k.$$
In positive-dimensional spaces the proximal maps are everywhere single-valued
by [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]]; in a
zero-dimensional space its sole input and output are the zero vector, so that
proximal call is single-valued directly. The proper closed convexity of $g^*$
follows from [[lem-fenchel-conjugate-is-proper-closed-convex]]. A finite implementation
uses finite call caps and advances an iterate only after both exact proximal
outputs are certified; otherwise it returns **prox-call-failed** or
**prox-cap-exhausted** and makes no convergence claim for that run.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

derivations.claim: Since $Kb=e_1=b$, every power $K^j b=b$. For $m=0$, the spanning list is empty and its span is $\{0\}$, with no nonzero vector on which to evaluate a Rayleigh quotient. For every $m\ge1$, the spanning set in [F1] consists of repetitions of the single nonzero vector $e_1$, and the Rayleigh quotient on this one-dimensional subspace is $e_1^TKe_1/(e_1^Te_1)=1$. Exact Lanczos terminates after one vector with Ritz value $1$.

For $x=(x_1,x_2)$, $\|Kx\|_2^2=x_1^2+4x_2^2\le4(x_1^2+x_2^2)$, with equality at $e_2$, so [F4] gives $\|K\|_2=2$. The top eigenspace is $\operatorname{span}\{e_2\}$ and $Pb=0$; [F2] identifies exactly this degenerate branch and supplies no top-eigenvalue convergence bound. Therefore the Ritz value $1$ is not the norm upper bound $2$ required by [F3].

Let $F$ be a field, and let $m,n,s\in\mathbb N$, where $\mathbb N$ includes
$0$. A **compressed sparse row (CSR) record** for an $m$ by $n$ matrix over
$F$ consists of integer arrays $r=(r_0,\ldots,r_m)$ and
$c=(c_0,\ldots,c_{s-1})$, and a value array $v=(v_0,\ldots,v_{s-1})\in F^s$,
satisfying

$$r_0=0,\qquad 0=r_0\le r_1\le\cdots\le r_m=s,\qquad 0\le c_t<n\quad(0\le t<s).$$

For each row $i<m$, its **stored entries** are the indices
$t$ with $r_i\le t<r_{i+1}$. The row is empty exactly when
$r_i=r_{i+1}$. Repeated column indices within one row and stored values
$v_t=0_F$ are permitted; each such entry remains a separate stored entry.

The represented matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ is defined entrywise by

$$A_{ij}:=\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}v_t\qquad(0\le i<m,\ 0\le j<n),$$

where $\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}$ is $1_F$ when $c_t=j$ and $0_F$ otherwise, and an
empty sum is $0_F$. Repeated entries in column $j$ are therefore added. The
number $s$ is the **stored-entry count**; it is not in general the number of
nonzero entries of $A$.

A CSR record is **canonical** when no row repeats a column and no stored value
is zero. In that case every nonzero matrix entry is stored exactly once and
$s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)$, where $\operatorname{nnz}(A)$ denotes the number of
nonzero entries of $A$. If $m=0$, the endpoint conditions force $s=0$ and the
row-pointer array has its single entry $r_0=0$. If $n=0$, the column-index
condition forces $s=0$ as well.

Fix a field $F$. The **validated CSR matrix-vector product** takes integer
dimension candidates $m,n$, integer arrays $r,c$, a value array $v$ of elements
of $F$, and a vector candidate $x$ of elements of $F$. All input arrays are
finite; write $s=\operatorname{length}(v)$.

1. If $m\notin\mathbb N$, $n\notin\mathbb N$,
   $\operatorname{length}(r)\ne m+1$,
   $\operatorname{length}(c)\ne s$, or
   $\operatorname{length}(x)\ne n$, return the status `invalid-dimension`.
2. For $i=0,\ldots,m$, check that $r_i\in\{0,\ldots,s\}$; return
   `invalid-index` if a check fails. Check $r_0=0$ and $r_m=s$, and for each
   $i=0,\ldots,m-1$ check $r_i\le r_{i+1}$; return `invalid-index` if any
   check fails. For each $t=0,\ldots,s-1$, check $0\le c_t<n$ and return
   `invalid-index` if a check fails.
3. Initialize $y_i=0_F$ for $0\le i<m$. For each row
   $i=0,\ldots,m-1$, and then each stored index
   $t=r_i,\ldots,r_{i+1}-1$, update
   $$y_i\gets y_i+v_t x_{c_t}.$$
4. Return the status `ok` together with $y\in F^m$.

For valid CSR data this uses exact field operations. Validation examines only
finite arrays, and the row intervals partition the $s$ stored entries, so the
specified loops are bounded. This procedure makes no floating-point rounding,
backward-stability, convergence, runtime, or memory-bandwidth claim.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n\in\mathbb N$, let a valid CSR record represent
$A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, and let $x=(x_j)_{j<n}\in F^n$. Define
$(Ax)_i:=\sum_{j<n}A_{ij}x_j$, the usual matrix-vector product from
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. Then the algorithm
[[alg-csr-matrix-vector-product-with-validation]] returns `ok` with output
$Ax$ in exact field arithmetic.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n\in\mathbb N$, and let a valid CSR record have
$s$ stored entries. Its input arrays use exactly $s$ field-value slots, $s$
integer column-index slots, and $m+1$ integer row-pointer slots, for a total of
$2s+m+1$ data slots. On valid input, the algorithm
[[alg-csr-matrix-vector-product-with-validation]] performs exactly $s$ field
multiplications, $s$ field additions, and $m$ zero initializations. Its index
validation and loop-control work is $O(m+s+1)$. Counting the CSR arrays and
returned output but excluding the supplied vector $x$ and constant-size
workspace, it uses exactly $2s+2m+1$ data slots, hence $O(m+s+1)$ slots; for
$m\ge1$ this is $O(m+s)$. Here $O(g)$ means bounded by $Cg$ for a constant $C$ independent of
the dimensions and input values.

For a square record of order $m\ge1$ with at least one stored entry in each
row, $s\ge m$, so the work and storage are $O(s)$. For a canonical record as defined in
[[def-csr-matrix-with-stored-entry-semantics]], $s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)$;
without that convention, the cost is in terms of stored entries, not
$\operatorname{nnz}(A)$. These are arithmetic, index, and storage counts, not
runtime, memory-bandwidth, convergence, or factorization-cost bounds.

$\Phi(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y)$ has a saddle point
$(x_*,y_*)$ in the sense of
[[def-saddle-point-for-convex-concave-lagrangian]]. For $N\ge1$ define
$$\bar x_N=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}x^{k+1},\qquad \bar y_N=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}y^{k+1}.$$

$$\Phi(\bar x_N,y)-\Phi(x,\bar y_N) \le\frac1N\left(\frac{\|x-x^0\|_2^2}{2\tau} +\frac{\|y-y^0\|_2^2}{2\sigma}\right).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. The endomorphism $T$ is **self-adjoint** when

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

$$TT^*=T^*T,$$

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]].

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

derivations.claim: Identify $z=x+iy\in\mathbb C^n$ with $(x,y)\in\mathbb R^{2n}$. Direct multiplication gives $\mathcal R(Z)(x,y)=(\Re(Zz),\Im(Zz))$; this identity shows that realification respects composition. Writing $Z=X+iY$ gives $\mathcal R(Z^*)=\begin{pmatrix}X^{\mathsf T}&Y^{\mathsf T}\\-Y^{\mathsf T}&X^{\mathsf T}\end{pmatrix}=\mathcal R(Z)^{\mathsf T}$.

The identification preserves Euclidean norms. Hence, by [F4], the suprema of $\|Ez\|_2$ over complex unit vectors and of $\|\mathcal R(E)u\|_2$ over real unit vectors agree, proving the operator-norm identity. If $Z$ is invertible, $\mathcal R(Z^{-1})$ is an inverse of $\mathcal R(Z)$ by step 1.1; conversely, if $\mathcal R(Z)$ is invertible, its kernel is zero, so $Zz=0$ implies $z=0$, and [F3] makes the square matrix $Z$ invertible.

Since $H$ is Hermitian it is normal, so [F1] gives $H=U\Lambda U^*$ with $U$ unitary and $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)$ real. By step 1.1, $\mathcal R(U)$ is real orthogonal and $\mathcal R(H)=\mathcal R(U)\mathcal R(\Lambda)\mathcal R(U)^{\mathsf T}$, where $\mathcal R(\Lambda)$ has each $\lambda_j$ twice on its diagonal. Thus $\mathcal R(H)$ is real symmetric with the asserted duplicated spectrum.

$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: Choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $u_1,\ldots,u_n$ with real eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$, and write $v=\sum_j c_j u_j$. Then, by [F2], $\|Av-\theta v\|_2^2=\sum_j|\lambda_j-\theta|^2|c_j|^2\ge d^2\sum_j|c_j|^2=d^2\|v\|_2^2$, where $d=\min_j|\lambda_j-\theta|$.
Since $v\ne0$, $d\le\|Av-\theta v\|_2/\|v\|_2\le\rho/\nu$. The finite minimum defining $d$ is attained by some $j$, and its eigenvalue obeys the required bound.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

For every $n\ge1$ and every real matrix $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$,
$$A\text{ is invertible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\det(A)\ne0.$$

$$
\mathcal R(Z)=\begin{pmatrix}X&-Y\\Y&X\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{2n\times2n}.
$$

For any complex matrix $E$, $\|\mathcal R(E)\|_2=\|E\|_2$.

Let $A,B$ be self-adjoint endomorphisms of an $n$-dimensional real inner
product space. Order the eigenvalues of $A$, $B$, and $A+B$ by

$$\alpha_1\ge\cdots\ge\alpha_n,\qquad \beta_1\ge\cdots\ge\beta_n,\qquad \gamma_1\ge\cdots\ge\gamma_n.$$

Then, for integers $1\le i,j\le n$:

1. If $i+j-1\le n$, then $\gamma_{i+j-1}\le \alpha_i+\beta_j$.
2. If $i+j-n\ge1$, then $\gamma_{i+j-n}\ge \alpha_i+\beta_j$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

Their eigenvalues in decreasing order repeat each complex eigenvalue twice, so the $2k$-th eigenvalue of $\mathcal R(A)$ is $\lambda_k(A)$ and similarly for $E$ and $A+E$. By [F2] with indices $i=2k,j=1$, the upper Weyl inequality gives $\lambda_{2k}(\mathcal R(A+E))\le\lambda_{2k}(\mathcal R(A))+\lambda_1(\mathcal R(E))$. With $i=2k,j=2n$, the lower inequality gives $\lambda_{2k}(\mathcal R(A+E))\ge\lambda_{2k}(\mathcal R(A))+\lambda_{2n}(\mathcal R(E))$.

The direct interval product $[-1,1]\cdot[-1,1]=[-1,1]$ encloses $t^2$, so the Leibniz interval expression $1-[-1,1]=[0,2]$ contains every determinant. At $t=1$, $A(1)(1,-1)^{\mathsf T}=0$ with a nonzero vector, so $A(1)$ is singular. The interval $[0,2]$ includes zero and is not $\{0\}$; [F1] therefore makes no uniform nonsingularity claim from this enclosure.

If uniform residual data with $q<1$ existed for this whole family and any nonempty right-hand-side set, [F2] would make $A(1)$ invertible. This contradicts the nonzero null vector just exhibited. Hence such a usable uniform residual certificate cannot hold for the family.

Interpret all interval endpoints and shifts exactly.

1. Outward-compute $M\ge\sup_{A}\|A\|_F$ by bounding each entry modulus and summing their squares. If a finite bound cannot be obtained, return `inconclusive` with no eigenvalue intervals. Otherwise initialize, for each increasing index $k=1,\ldots,n$, the bracket $I_k=[-M,M]$ and successful-query count $s_k=0$. The Frobenius eigenvalue bound guarantees that these brackets contain every eigenvalue of every family member.

2. Repeat while fewer than $B$ total queries have been used and there is an index whose bracket width exceeds $\varepsilon$ and which has not been marked blocked. Choose the least such index $k$. Query its exact midpoint $\tau$. Run [[alg-interval-hermitian-ldl-inertia-certifier]] on the shifted family $\{A-\tau I:A\in\mathcal A\}$ with the fixed plan. If the result is `pivot-inconclusive`, or its certified inertia has nonzero zero-count, mark this index blocked and leave $I_k$ unchanged. Otherwise set $\nu=n_-$, the certified number of negative eigenvalues. If $\nu\ge k$, replace the upper endpoint of $I_k$ by $\tau$; if $\nu<k$, replace the lower endpoint by $\tau$. Increase $s_k$ by one. A certified update halves the bracket width. Stop when the query budget is used or no such index exists.

3. Return every current bracket with status `enclosed` when its width is at most $\varepsilon$, `inconclusive` if its index was blocked, or `budget-exhausted` if the total budget ended first. Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $a\in R$, and $f\in R[x]$. Then $f(a)=0$ if and only if $x-a$ divides $f$ in $R[x]$.

More precisely, there is a unique $q\in R[x]$ such that $f=q(x-a)+f(a)$.

If $R$ is an integral domain and $f,g\in R[x]$ are nonzero, then $fg\ne0$ and

$$ \deg(fg)=\deg f+\deg g,\qquad \operatorname{lc}(fg)=\operatorname{lc}(f)\operatorname{lc}(g). $$

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Let $F$ be a field and let $f,g\in F[x]$ be not both zero. Since $F[x]$ is a principal ideal domain ([[cor-polynomial-ring-over-a-field-is-a-pid]]), the ideal $(f,g)$ generated by $f$ and $g$ ([[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]]) has a nonzero generator $d$. Multiplying $d$ by the inverse of its leading coefficient gives a monic generator, and any two monic generators of the same ideal are equal. The resulting polynomial is the **monic greatest common divisor** $\gcd(f,g)$.

Equivalently, $d=\gcd(f,g)$ is the unique monic polynomial such that $d$ divides both $f$ and $g$, and every common divisor of $f$ and $g$ divides $d$. The equivalence and the Bézout identity are proved in [[thm-bezout-identity-for-polynomials]]. The expression $\gcd(0,0)$ is left undefined.

Let $F$ be a field and let $f,g\in F[x]$ be not both zero. Repeated polynomial division terminates at a last nonzero remainder, whose monic associate is $d=\gcd(f,g)$. There are $A,B\in F[x]$ such that

$$ Af+Bg=d. $$

Moreover, $d$ divides both $f$ and $g$, and every common divisor of $f$ and $g$ divides $d$.
Let $F\subseteq E$ be a field extension and let $f,g\in F[x]$ be not both zero. The monic gcd of $f$ and $g$ computed in $F[x]$ is also their monic gcd in $E[x]$.

derivations.claim: By [F8], the monic gcd is constructed by Euclidean division over $\mathbb Q$, and the divisions terminate: each nonzero remainder has smaller nonnegative integer degree than the divisor by [F2]. The same argument defines $p_k$; if $\deg p_{k-1}>0$, then $p_{k-1}'\ne0$ and has smaller degree by [F3] and characteristic zero, so $\deg p_k<\deg p_{k-1}$. Thus $p_d=1$, and each $s_k=p_{k-1}/p_k$ is a polynomial.

By [F4], repeated application of [F5] factors $f$ over $\mathbb C$: $f(x)=\prod_{\alpha}(x-\alpha)^{m_\alpha}$, where the finite list contains each distinct root once and $m_\alpha\ge1$. The induction is finite because each division by $x-\alpha$ lowers degree by one by [F6].

Fix a current polynomial $p$ in the gcd chain and a root $\alpha$ of multiplicity $m>0$, so $p=(x-\alpha)^m u$ with $u(\alpha)\ne0$. The product rule [F3] gives $p'=(x-\alpha)^{m-1}\bigl(mu+(x-\alpha)u'\bigr)$, whose parenthesized factor is nonzero at $\alpha$ because the field has characteristic zero. Hence the gcd of $p$ and $p'$ has multiplicity exactly $m-1$ at $\alpha$; a root absent from $p$ is absent from their gcd. By [F9] for the field extension $\mathbb Q\subseteq\mathbb C$, the monic gcd computed over $\mathbb Q$ is exactly the monic gcd over $\mathbb C$. Thus this root-multiplicity computation applies to each $p_k$.

Induction on $k$ now shows that the multiplicity of $\alpha$ in $p_k$ is $\max(m_\alpha-k,0)$. Therefore $\alpha$ occurs once in $s_k=p_{k-1}/p_k$ exactly when $k\le m_\alpha$, and it occurs in $s_k/s_{k+1}$ exactly when $k=m_\alpha$. This root factorization proves $s_{k+1}$ divides $s_k$ over $\mathbb C[x]$; division over $\mathbb Q[x]$ has the same zero remainder, so $q_k=s_k/s_{k+1}$ lies in $\mathbb Q[x]$.

Each complex root of $f$ occurs in exactly one $q_k$, with exponent one there and exponent $k$ in $q_k^k$. The factorization in step 1.2 therefore gives $f=\prod_{k=1}^d q_k^k$; it also proves that each $q_k$ is squarefree and that distinct $q_k$ have no common root, hence are pairwise coprime. The degree-zero case has $f=1$ and an empty root list.

$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

Changing each Euclidean remainder by a minus sign changes neither common divisors nor termination. Thus [F6] and the stated gcd $1$ make the last nonzero remainder a nonzero constant $c$. Backward substitution in the division equations gives $A,B\in\mathbb Q[x]$ with $AP_0+BP_1=c$; dividing by $c$ gives a Bezout identity with right side $1$.

No two consecutive terms can vanish at the same real $c$. By step 1.1 there are $A,B\in\mathbb Q[x]$ with $AP_0+BP_1=1$; evaluating at $c$ rules out a common zero of $P_0,P_1$ even over $\mathbb C$. They have opposite signs. On either side of $c$, the signs of these neighbors are fixed; after zero entries are deleted, the adjacent nonzero neighbors of each internal zero contribute exactly one sign change. If several internal terms vanish at $c$, their indices are nonconsecutive, so these adjacent-pair contributions may share an endpoint but remain distinct terms in the total variation. The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$
Let $n\ge1$. If $A,B\in M_n(R)$ are similar over a commutative ring, then $\det(B)=\det(A)$.

If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

$$ f=qg+r,\qquad r=0\ \text{or}\ \deg r<\deg g. $$

The statement includes $f=0$ and nonzero constant divisors.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $a\in R$, and $f\in R[x]$. Then $f(a)=0$ if and only if $x-a$ divides $f$ in $R[x]$.

More precisely, there is a unique $q\in R[x]$ such that $f=q(x-a)+f(a)$.

The relation of [[def-rat-order]] is well defined and makes the field
$\mathbb{Q}$ ([[thm-rat-field]]) a totally ordered field: the order is total,
$x \le y$ implies $x + z \le y + z$, and $0 < x$, $0 < y$ imply
$0 < xy$.

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

If $R$ is an integral domain and $f,g\in R[x]$ are nonzero, then $fg\ne0$ and

$$ \deg(fg)=\deg f+\deg g,\qquad \operatorname{lc}(fg)=\operatorname{lc}(f)\operatorname{lc}(g). $$

derivations.claim: If $P(z)=0$ and $|z|>1+H$, then $|a_d||z|^d\le H\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}|z|^j < H|z|^d/(|z|-1)<|z|^d\le |a_d||z|^d$, because $|a_d|\ge1$ and $|z|-1>H$. This contradiction proves $|z|\le R$ for every root.

Let $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d$ be the distinct roots from [F1] and set $D=a_d^{2d-2}\prod_{i<j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2$. Form the coefficient map $\Phi(u,v)=uP+vP'$ from pairs with $\deg u\le d-2$, $\deg v\le d-1$ to polynomials of degree at most $2d-2$. Its square coefficient matrix $S$ has integer entries, so $\det S$ is an integer-coefficient polynomial in $a_d,\ldots,a_0$.

Divide each output polynomial by $P$ and record its quotient and remainder. In coefficient order from highest degree down, the map $(q,r)\mapsto qP+r$ has triangular diagonal consisting of $d-1$ copies of $a_d$ and $d$ copies of $1$, so the inverse coordinate change has determinant $\pm a_d^{-(d-1)}$. Under this change, $\Phi$ has block form $\begin{pmatrix}I&*\\0&M\end{pmatrix}$, where $M$ is multiplication by $P'$ on $\mathbb C[x]/(P)$. Hence $\det S=\pm a_d^{d-1}\det M$.

For each $i$ define $L_i(x)=\prod_{j\ne i}(x-\alpha_j)/(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)$. These degree-$(d-1)$ polynomials satisfy $L_i(\alpha_j)=1$ when $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise. For every degree-$<d$ representative $q$, the difference $q-\sum_iq(\alpha_i)L_i$ has degree $<d$ and vanishes at all $d$ distinct roots; [F7] and [F9] force this difference to be zero. Thus evaluation is an isomorphism $\mathbb C[x]/(P)\to\mathbb C^d$. It conjugates $M$ to the diagonal matrix with entries $P'(\alpha_i)$, so [F4] gives $\det M=\prod_iP'(\alpha_i)$. By [F2], $P'(\alpha_i)=a_d\prod_{j\ne i}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)$; pairing the two factors for each $i<j$ yields $\det S=\pm a_d^{2d-1}\prod_{i<j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2=\pm a_dD$.

Set the variable $a_d$ to zero in the integer-coefficient polynomial $\det S$. Then $\deg P\le d-1$ and $\deg P'\le d-2$, so every $uP+vP'$ has degree at most $2d-3$; the coefficient map misses the $x^{2d-2}$ coordinate and its determinant is zero. Therefore the constant term in $a_d$ of $\det S$ is zero, so $a_d$ divides $\det S$ as an integer-coefficient polynomial. At the given integer coefficients, $\det S/a_d$ is an integer, and [step 3.1] shows that $D$ is an integer up to sign.
Squarefreeness makes every root distinct, so every factor in $D$ is nonzero and $|D|\ge1$.

Let $\delta=\min_{i<j}|\alpha_i-\alpha_j|$ and choose a pair attaining it. Every other pairwise distance is at most $2R$ by [step 1.1] and the triangle inequality [F5]. Thus $1\le |D|\le H^{2d-2}\delta^2(2R)^{d(d-1)-2}$. Rearranging gives $\delta\ge H^{-(d-1)}(2R)^{-(d(d-1)-2)/2}=\sigma(P)$.

citations.quote:
Let $P\in\mathbb Q[x]$ be nonzero of degree $d$, and put $f=P/\operatorname{lc}(P)$, so $f$ is monic. Set $p_0=f$ and, recursively, let $p_k$ be the monic greatest common divisor of $p_{k-1}$ and $p_{k-1}'$ for $k\ge1$, with $\gcd(1,0)=1$. For $1\le k\le d$, put $s_k=p_{k-1}/p_k$ and put $s_{d+1}=1$. Then each $q_k=s_k/s_{k+1}$ is a monic polynomial in $\mathbb Q[x]$, the $q_k$ are squarefree and pairwise coprime, and
$$
f=\prod_{k=1}^{d}q_k^k.
$$
The complex roots of $q_k$ are exactly the roots of $P$ having multiplicity $k$. In particular, $\prod_{k=1}^{d}q_k$ is squarefree and has exactly the distinct roots of $P$. For $d=0$, the product is empty and $P$ has no roots.

Here a polynomial is called **squarefree** when each of its complex roots has multiplicity one.
---

Let $P\in\mathbb Q[x]$ be nonconstant with $\gcd(P,P')=1$. Define $P_0=P$, $P_1=P'$, and recursively
$$
P_{j+1}=-\operatorname{rem}(P_{j-1},P_j)
$$
until the final nonzero term $P_s$, which is constant. For a real $t$ that is not a root of $P$, let $V(t)$ be the number of sign changes in $P_0(t),\ldots,P_s(t)$ after zero entries are deleted. If $a<b$ and $P(a)P(b)\ne0$, then the number of distinct real roots of $P$ in $(a,b)$ is
$$
V(a)-V(b).
$$
---

Let $P(x)=a_dx^d+\cdots+a_0\in\mathbb Z[x]$ be primitive and squarefree, with $d\ge2$, $a_d\ne0$, and coefficient height $H=\max_j|a_j|\ge1$. Put $R=1+H$ and
$$
\sigma(P)=H^{-(d-1)}(2R)^{-(d(d-1)-2)/2}.
$$
Every complex root $\alpha$ of $P$ satisfies $|\alpha|\le R$, and any two distinct complex roots satisfy $|\alpha-\beta|\ge\sigma(P)$. For $d=1$, $P$ has at most one root, so no pairwise separation bound is needed.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].

Input a rational polynomial $p\in\mathbb Q[x]$. Arithmetic on coefficients and endpoints is exact.

1. If $p=0$, return status "identically zero"; it has no finite list of isolated roots. If $p$ is a nonzero constant, return status "complete" with an empty list.

2. Clear denominators and divide out the integer content, choosing the sign so the resulting primitive integer polynomial $P$ has positive leading coefficient. Apply [[lem-polynomial-squarefree-decomposition-and-multiplicity]] to the monic rational polynomial $P/\operatorname{lc}(P)$. For each nonconstant squarefree factor $q_k$ in that decomposition, let $Q_k$ be its primitive integer normalization with positive leading coefficient; take $Q_k=1$ when $q_k=1$. Then $P=c\prod_{k=1}^d Q_k^k$ for a nonzero rational $c$, and the factors label roots by multiplicity. Let $S$ be the primitive integer normalization with positive leading coefficient of $\prod_{k: \deg Q_k>0}Q_k$. Its roots are the distinct roots of $p$.

3. Put $B=H(S)+2$, where $H(S)$ is the maximum absolute coefficient of $S$. If $\deg S\ge2$, compute $\sigma(S)$ from [[lem-squarefree-integer-polynomial-root-separation-bound]]; if $\deg S=1$, no separation value is needed. Initialize a queue with the open interval $(-B,B)$ and retain the active squarefree factors $Q_k$.

4. Remove exact dyadic rational roots at a queue interval endpoint or bisection midpoint before counting on the adjacent intervals. If $r$ is such a root, test the factors $Q_k(r)$ exactly; the unique factor vanishing at $r$ gives its multiplicity $k$. Record the singleton $\{r\}$, divide that factor by $x-r$, and remove the same factor from the active product $S$. Immediately after any such removal, if $S$ is a nonzero constant, clear the remaining queue and return status "complete" with the records already obtained; every pending interval is then root-free. Do not form a Sturm sequence for a constant product.

5. For a queued open interval $(a,b)$ whose endpoints are not roots of the active $S$, form its Sturm sequence and set $N=V(a)-V(b)$ using [[thm-sturm-sign-variation-counts-distinct-roots]]. If $N=0$, discard the interval. If $N=1$, compute the Sturm count for each nonconstant active $Q_k$ (a constant factor has count $0$) and output $(a,b,k)$ for the unique factor whose count is $1$. If $N\ge2$, compare its width with $\sigma(S_0)/4$, where $S_0$ is the initial squarefree primitive polynomial. A count $N\ge2$ below that threshold is an internal inconsistency; otherwise bisect at $m=(a+b)/2$. If $S(m)=0$, record and remove that exact root as in step 4. Enqueue the open halves $(a,m)$ and $(m,b)$.

6. Return status "complete" when the queue is empty, with all singleton exact roots and open isolating intervals labelled by multiplicity. A nonzero constant active product has no remaining roots and requires no Sturm sequence.

The procedure uses no floating-point comparisons. Exact polynomial division, gcd, endpoint evaluation, sign variation, and width comparison are over rational numbers. Open intervals ensure that a root found exactly at a split point is represented only by its singleton record and not by either adjacent interval.

derivations.claim: Clearing denominators and dividing by the nonzero integer content preserves every root and its multiplicity. By [F1], the active squarefree product has exactly the distinct roots of $p$, and its factors assign each such root its unique multiplicity label.

If the initial squarefree polynomial has degree at least two, the coefficient-height bound in [F3] places every root strictly inside $(-B,B)$ because $B=H+2>H+1$. In degree one, write $S(x)=a_1x+a_0$ with nonzero integer $a_1$. Its unique root is $-a_0/a_1$, whose absolute value is at most $|a_0|\le H<B$ since $|a_1|\ge1$. Thus the initial endpoints are nonroots in either case. Bisection endpoints are midpoints tested exactly: a root midpoint is recorded and removed before its open halves are queued, while a nonroot midpoint leaves both endpoints nonroots for the active product.

In each queued interval with nonroot endpoints, [F2] makes the computed variation difference exactly its number of active roots. A zero count safely discards the interval. A count of one gives an isolating interval; the Sturm counts of the pairwise coprime $Q_k$ identify exactly one factor and hence the multiplicity label. If a midpoint is a root, exact division by $x-m$ removes it from that factor and the singleton record carries its multiplicity; otherwise the two open halves partition the parent interval. If removal leaves a nonzero constant active product, it has no remaining roots; the immediate complete-return branch safely clears the root-free queue without requesting another Sturm sequence.

Whenever an interval has at least two distinct active roots, their separation [F3] forces its width to be at least $\sigma$. At bisection depth $n$ the width is $2B(1/2)^n$. Since $(1/2)^n\to0$ by [F4], some finite depth has width below $\sigma/4$; such an interval cannot still contain two roots, so each branch stops with count zero or one. The branching factor is at most two and the depth is bounded, so the entire queue tree is finite. For degree one, the initial Sturm count is already zero or one. An earlier constant-active-product branch terminates immediately and cannot prolong the queue tree.

At each split, the roots in the parent are partitioned between the open children and, when the midpoint is a root, its exact singleton; a nonroot midpoint contributes no root. Every discarded interval is root-free, and every one-root interval is emitted once. The finite tree therefore accounts for every real root exactly once with the correct multiplicity.

citations.quote: Every continuous map $f:D^n\to D^n$ of the closed unit ball has a fixed point, for every integer $n\ge0$.

For an integer $n\ge1$, a **real box** is a nonempty product
$X=\prod_{j=1}^n[a_j,b_j]\subset\mathbb R^n$ of closed real intervals with finite dyadic endpoints $a_j\le b_j$, using the interval convention of [[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]]. Its interior is $\operatorname{int}X=\prod_{j=1}^n(a_j,b_j)$; it is empty if any side is degenerate.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex, let $X\subset U$ be a real box, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. An **interval Jacobian enclosure** on $X$ is an $n\times n$ matrix $J(X)=(J_{ij})$ of finite real intervals such that
$\partial_jF_i(X):=\{\partial_jF_i(x):x\in X\}\subseteq J_{ij}$ for every $i,j$, with partial derivatives and Jacobian entries as in [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. Write
$\mathcal J(X)=\{A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}:A_{ij}\in J_{ij}\}$ for the set of point matrices represented by this interval matrix.

derivations.claim: Let $J=\{j:a_j<b_j\}$ and $m=|J|$. If $m=0$, $X$ is a singleton, so its sole point is fixed. If $m>0$, deleting the fixed coordinates identifies $X$ with a box $X_J$ whose side lengths are positive. The coordinatewise affine map $T:[-1,1]^m\to X_J$, with $T(u)_j=(a_j+b_j)/2+(b_j-a_j)u_j/2$, is a homeomorphism. Reinserting the fixed coordinate values defines $\iota:X_J\to X$, and projection onto the free coordinates defines $\pi_J:X\to X_J$; since the fixed output coordinates of $f$ equal their singleton values, $f_J=\pi_J\circ f\circ\iota$ is a continuous self-map of $X_J$.

Define $\|u\|_2=(\sum_j|u_j|^2)^{1/2}$ and $\|u\|_\infty=\max_j|u_j|$, let $D^m=\{u:\|u\|_2\le1\}$, and put $C_m=[-1,1]^m$. For $u
e0$ set $h(u)=(\|u\|_2/\|u\|_\infty)u$, and set $h(0)=0$. Then $\|h(u)\|_\infty=\|u\|_2\le1$. For $y
e0$ in $C_m$, set $h^{-1}(y)=(\|y\|_\infty/\|y\|_2)y$, and set $h^{-1}(0)=0$. For $u
e0$, $\|h(u)\|_2=\|u\|_2^2/\|u\|_\infty$ and $\|h(u)\|_\infty=\|u\|_2$, so substituting in $h^{-1}$ gives $h^{-1}(h(u))=u$; the same norm calculation gives $h(h^{-1}(y))=y$ for $y
e0$. Both maps are continuous away from zero. For any vector $v$, one coordinate attains $\|v\|_\infty$, so $\|v\|_\infty^2\le\sum_j|v_j|^2$; each of the $m$ summands is at most $\|v\|_\infty^2$, so $\|v\|_2^2\le m\|v\|_\infty^2$. Taking nonnegative square roots gives $\|v\|_\infty\le\|v\|_2\le\sqrt m\,\|v\|_\infty$. Therefore for nonzero $u$, $\|h(u)\|_2=\|u\|_2^2/\|u\|_\infty\le\sqrt m\,\|u\|_2$, and for nonzero $y$, $\|h^{-1}(y)\|_2=\|y\|_\infty\le\|y\|_2$. These inequalities also hold at zero and show both maps are continuous there. Thus $h$ is a homeomorphism $D^m	o C_m$.

For $m>0$, $T\circ h$ is a homeomorphism from $D^m$ to $X_J$. The conjugate map $g=(T\circ h)^{-1}\circ f_J\circ(T\circ h):D^m\to D^m$ is continuous. By [F1], $g$ has a fixed point; mapping it back gives a fixed point of $f_J$, and applying $\iota$ gives a fixed point of $f$ in $X$.

citations.quote:
For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$; the denominator interval is strictly positive because at
least one coordinate interval excludes zero. Division multiplies by this
reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

For finite $x$ with $|x|\le N_{\max}$, the directed roundings defined in
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]] satisfy
$\operatorname{rd}(x)\le x\le\operatorname{ru}(x)$ and each endpoint error is
at most the stated $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)$ (with zero error when $x$ is
representable). For $x>N_{\max}$ the pair $(N_{\max},+\infty)$ encloses $x$;
for $x<-N_{\max}$ the pair $(-\infty,-N_{\max})$ encloses $x$. Overflow has
error bound $+\infty$ and cannot be reported as a finite-error result.

A **real interval** is a closed set $[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ with finite dyadic
endpoints $a\le b$. Its width is $b-a$, midpoint is $(a+b)/2$, and its
midpoint-radius form is $m+[-r,r]$ with $m=(a+b)/2$ and $r=(b-a)/2$. The empty
set is the status `empty`; the whole real line is `entire`. `overflow`,
`domain-error`, `split-domain`, and `inconclusive` are computation statuses,
not finite intervals.

A **complex rectangle** is $X+iY=\{x+iy:x\in X,\ y\in Y\}$ for real intervals
$X,Y$. Complex addition and multiplication use
$(x+iy)+(u+iv)=(x+u)+i(y+v)$ and
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$. For $z=x+iy$, its complex modulus is
$|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and for $z\ne0$ its reciprocal is
$1/z=(x-iy)/(x^2+y^2)$. A
**complex ball** $B(c,r)$ is
$\{z\in\mathbb C:|z-c|\le r\}$ with dyadic complex center $c$ and dyadic
$r\ge0$. For any two represented sets $S,T$, the inclusion order is
$S\sqsubseteq T$ iff $S\subseteq T$.

continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

For $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, continuity at $x\in[a,b]$ means that for every
$\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that
$|f(t)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $t\in[a,b]$ and $|t-x|<\delta$.
Differentiability at an interior point $c$ means that the two-sided limit
$$
f'(c)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h}
$$
exists in the real field; differentiability on $(a,b)$ means this holds at
every interior point. For higher derivatives, define recursively
$f^{(j+1)}=(f^{(j)})'$ on the points where the derivative exists. The class
$C^{n+1}$ on an open interval means that these derivatives through order
$n+1$ exist and are continuous there.

Input a $C^1$ function $f:U\to\mathbb R$ on an open interval $U$, a nonempty finite dyadic interval $X_0=[a,b]\subset U$, an integer update budget $N\ge0$, and interval evaluators $E_f(I)$ and $E_{f'}(I)$ for every queried subinterval $I\subseteq U$. Their admissibility condition is $f(I)\subseteq E_f(I)$ and $f'(I)\subseteq E_{f'}(I)$; a non-finite evaluator result is not an enclosure usable for certification.

Set $I=X_0$. At each of at most $N$ interval-Newton updates:

1. If a finite $E_f(I)$ excludes $0$, return "root-free" for $X_0$.
2. If $I=\{x\}$, return "unique-root" when $E_f(I)=\{0\}$, return "root-free" when $0\notin E_f(I)$, and otherwise return "inconclusive".
3. Obtain finite $D=E_{f'}(I)$. If the evaluation is non-finite or $0\in D$, return "inconclusive" with the original box.
4. Let $m$ be the midpoint of $I$ and obtain a finite enclosure $F_m=E_f(\{m\})$. If unavailable, return "inconclusive".
5. Compute the outward interval Newton image $N(I)=m-F_m/D$ and $Y=N(I)\cap I$. A non-finite operation returns "inconclusive". If $Y=\varnothing$, return "root-free". If $N(I)\subset\operatorname{int}I$, return "unique-root". If $Y$ is a strict nonempty subinterval of $I$, replace $I$ by $Y$ and continue; otherwise return "inconclusive".

If the update budget is exhausted, return "inconclusive" with the original box. A returned root-free or unique-root status applies to the original box. A failed derivative test, failed contraction, or exhausted budget proves no negative claim.

derivations.claim: If $r\in X$ is a root and $r=m$, then $0=f(m)\in F_m$, so $m\in N$. If $r\ne m$, the mean value theorem on the segment between $m$ and $r$ gives $\xi\in X$ with $f(m)=f'(\xi)(m-r)$. Since $f'(\xi)\in D$ and $f(m)\in F_m$, interval enclosure [F1] gives $r=m-f(m)/f'(\xi)\in N$. Hence every root in $X$ lies in $N\cap X$, and an empty intersection excludes all roots.
If $0\notin E_f(X)$ and the range enclosure is valid, no $x\in X$ can satisfy $f(x)=0$, because $f(X)\subseteq E_f(X)$.

Suppose $N\subset\operatorname{int}X$. Since $0\notin D$ and $D$ is an interval, every value of $f'$ on $X$ has one fixed strict sign. Let $\xi_a\in(a,m)$ and $\xi_b\in(m,b)$ be the mean-value points for $[a,m]$ and $[m,b]$, and put $d_a=f'(\xi_a)$ and $d_b=f'(\xi_b)$. The exact Newton points $n_a=m-f(m)/d_a$ and $n_b=m-f(m)/d_b$ lie in $N$, so $a<n_a$ and $n_b<b$.

At each strict interval update, every root of the current interval belongs to $N\cap I$ by step 1.1, so induction shows that no root of the original box is lost. If the current interval is a singleton $\{x\}$ and the algorithm returns "unique-root", then $E_f(\{x\})=\{0\}$ implies $f(x)=0$; root preservation shows this is the only root of the original box.

If $d_a,d_b>0$, the inequality $a<n_a$ gives $f(a)=f(m)-d_a(m-a)<0$, and $n_b<b$ gives $f(b)=f(m)+d_b(b-m)>0$. If $d_a,d_b<0$, multiplying the same inequalities by the negative derivatives reverses them and gives $f(a)>0>f(b)$. In either case [F3] supplies a root in $(a,b)$.

For any $x<y$ in $X$, [F2] gives $f(y)-f(x)=f'(\zeta)(y-x)$ for some $\zeta\in(x,y)$. The derivative has the same strict sign throughout $X$, so $f$ is strictly monotone there and has at most one root. Together with step 2.2, the root is unique.
If no exclusion or strict-inclusion test succeeds before the update budget ends, the algorithm's final branch returns "inconclusive" by [F5]; this branch supplies no root-absence conclusion.

Initialize a queue with $X_0$. While the queue is nonempty and fewer than $B$ boxes have been processed, remove its first interval $I$ and call [[alg-scalar-interval-newton-certification]] on $I$ with update budget $1$ and the supplied evaluators. If it returns "root-free", record $I$ as excluded. If it returns "unique-root", record $I$ as a certified box. Otherwise, if the width of $I$ exceeds $\eta$, bisect at its midpoint and append the two closed halves to the queue. If the width is at most $\eta$, record $I$ as unresolved. When the box budget is exhausted, append every remaining queued interval to the unresolved list.

Certified boxes may share a bisection endpoint. A strict interval-Newton inclusion places its root in the interior of the scalar call's box. The scalar procedure can also certify after contracting to an exact singleton; in that case the smooth isolator records the original processed interval, whose root may be at an endpoint. Let $f$ be $C^1$ on an open interval containing $X=[a,b]$, with $a<b$. derivations.claim: Initially the queue contains the initial interval. Each processed box is either certified root-free, certified to contain one root, recorded unresolved at the width threshold, or replaced by its two closed halves. Those halves cover their parent, so by induction every root not already certified remains in a queued or unresolved interval.

Each processing removes one queued box and adds at most two; after at most $B$ processed boxes the queue is finite with at most $B+1$ entries. The algorithm then records the entire remainder as unresolved, so it terminates for every finite budget.

By [F2], no root lies in an excluded box and each certified box has exactly one root. The queue-coverage invariant from step 1.1 places every other root in an unresolved box. Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ be a **closed** complex contour, that is a
rectifiable path with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$
([[def-complex-contours-reversal-concatenation-and-closedness]]), with trace
$\gamma^\ast$, and let $p\in\mathbb C$ with $p\notin\gamma^\ast$. The **winding
number**, or **index**, of $\gamma$ about $p$ is

$$n(\gamma,p):=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\gamma\frac{dz}{z-p},$$

the complex line integral of
[[def-complex-line-integral-over-a-rectifiable-path]].

The integral exists: $z\mapsto1/(z-p)$ is complex differentiable, hence
continuous, on $\mathbb C\setminus\{p\}$ by
[[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]] and
[[cor-complex-differentiability-implies-continuity]], the trace $\gamma^\ast$ is
contained in that set, and $\gamma$ is rectifiable, so
[[thm-existence-of-complex-line-integrals-on-rectifiable-paths]] applies.

Let $\gamma$ be a closed complex contour with trace $\gamma^\ast$ and length
$L(\gamma)$. Then $\mathbb C\setminus\gamma^\ast$ is open, and the index function
$p\mapsto n(\gamma,p)$ satisfies the quantitative estimate

$$|n(\gamma,p)-n(\gamma,p_0)|\ \le\ \frac{L(\gamma)\,|p-p_0|}{\pi\,d^2} \qquad\text{whenever }p_0\notin\gamma^\ast,\ d=\inf_{w\in\gamma^\ast}|w-p_0|,\ |p-p_0|<\tfrac d2 .$$

In particular $n(\gamma,\cdot)$ is continuous on $\mathbb C\setminus\gamma^\ast$;
it is constant on every connected component of that set; and since those
components are open, it is locally constant.

Let $\gamma$ be a closed complex contour with trace $\gamma^\ast$ and length
$L(\gamma)$. Then $\mathbb C\setminus\gamma^\ast$ has exactly one unbounded
connected component $U_\infty$, and

$$n(\gamma,p)=0\qquad\text{for every }p\in U_\infty.$$

More precisely, if $R>0$ satisfies $\gamma^\ast\subseteq\{z:|z|\le R\}$ and
$|p|>R+L(\gamma)/(2\pi)$, then $p\in U_\infty$ and $n(\gamma,p)=0$.

Expanding, dividing by $t>0$, and letting $t\downarrow0$ yields $\langle q-p,u-p\rangle\le0$. Hence the ray $q+s(q-p)$, $s\ge0$, remains strictly in the separating half-plane and avoids $P$. Each exterior point can therefore be joined outside $P$ to a circle containing $P$ in its interior; that circle is connected, so $\mathbb C\setminus P$ is connected and unbounded.

Its intersection with the convex polygon is a bounded interval starting at $z$, so the ray exits at the interior $p$ of a single edge with directed tangent $v\ne0$. The polygon interior lies locally to the left of this positively oriented edge. Apply the orientation-preserving similarity $\rho(w)=\overline v(w-p)/|v|$, which sends $p$ to $0$ and the edge tangent to the positive real direction. For every $a\notin\Gamma$, put $c=\overline v/|v|$. $$\dot Y(t)=D f(x_*(t))Y(t),\qquad Y(0)=I.$$

The matrix $Y(T)$ is the **monodromy matrix**; its eigenvalues, counted with algebraic multiplicity, are the **Floquet multipliers**. The multiplier $1$ in the direction $\dot x_*(0)$ is called the **phase multiplier**.

Then $s\mapsto\phi(t;s)$ is $C^1$ on $U$ for each $t\in[a,b]$. Its derivative matrix $S(t;s):=D_s\phi(t;s)$ is the unique solution of

$$S(t;s)=I_d+\int_a^t D_yf(r,\phi(r;s))S(r;s)\,dr,$$

and hence satisfies $\partial_tS=D_yf(t,\phi(t;s))S$, $S(a;s)=I_d$. The claim is local to the stated common compact tube; it does not assert differentiability beyond it.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $V:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a map. The
equation

$$x'(t)=V(x(t))$$

is an **autonomous ordinary differential equation**: its right-hand side depends
on the state alone and not explicitly on time. An initial value problem for this
equation consists of a time $t_0\in\mathbb R$ and a state $x_0\in U$, written
$x(t_0)=x_0$.

This is the special case of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]
obtained from the time-dependent field $F(t,x):=V(x)$ on
$\mathbb R\times U$. A solution on an interval $J$ is therefore a differentiable
curve $x:J\to U$ with $t_0\in J$ satisfying the equation at every $t\in J$ and
$x(t_0)=x_0$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $I=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a compact interval, let
$C:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be continuous, let $t_0\in I$, and let
$Y_0\in M_n(\mathbb R)$. Then the linear matrix initial value problem

$$Y'(t)=C(t)Y(t),\qquad Y(t_0)=Y_0,$$

has a unique solution on all of $I$.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: Fix a base state $x\in W$. By [F1], $\Phi$ is $C^1$ in $x$ and $S$ solves $S'=A S$, where $A(t)=Df(\Phi(t,x))$. The coefficient is bounded on $[0,T_+]$ by [F3]; integrating the variational equation by [F6] and applying [F5] bounds $S$ uniformly in $t$. The flow itself is jointly continuous in $(t,x)$ on the common tube by [F1] and the ODE relation [F2].

For a direction $h\in\mathbb R^n$, define a matrix $B_h(t)$ by $B_h(t)v=D^2f(\Phi(t,x))[S(t,x)h,S(t,x)v]$. It is continuous and has norm at most $C\|h\|_2$ for a finite constant $C$, by [F3] and the bound on $S$. Let $H_h$ solve $H_h'=AH_h+B_h$, $H_h(0)=0$. For each column, adjoining a constant coordinate turns its inhomogeneous linear IVP into a homogeneous linear system; applying [F4] to the augmented matrix gives a unique solution on $[0,T_+]$. Its integral equation from [F6] and [F5] give $\|H_h\|_\infty\le C'\|h\|_2$ for a finite constant $C'$.

For small $h$ with $x+h\in W$, put $\Delta(t)=\Phi(t,x+h)-\Phi(t,x)$, $S_h(t)=S(t,x+h)$, and $A_h(t)=Df(\Phi(t,x+h))$. The uniform remainder in [F1] gives $\Delta=S h+o(\|h\|_2)$ uniformly on $J$. On each segment between $\Phi(t,x)$ and $\Phi(t,x+h)$, the chain rule [F7] and [F6] applied coordinatewise to $Df$ give $ A_h-A=\int_0^1 D^2f(\Phi+s\Delta)[\Delta,\cdot] ds. $ Uniform continuity of $D^2f$ on $K$ [F3] and $\Delta=S h+o(\|h\|)$ therefore imply $A_h-A=D^2f(\Phi)[S h,\cdot]+o(\|h\|_2)$ uniformly in $t$.

The variational equations give $S_h'=A_hS_h$ and $S'=AS$. Subtract these and the equation for $H_h$ from step 2.1, setting $R_h=S_h-S-H_h$, to obtain $ R_h'=A_hR_h+(A_h-A)S+(A_h-A)H_h-B_h,\qquad R_h(0)=0. $ By step 2.2, $(A_h-A)S-B_h=o(\|h\|)$ uniformly; also $A_h-A=O(\|h\|)$ and $H_h=O(\|h\|)$ by steps 2.2 and 2.1. Thus the forcing after $A_hR_h$ is $o(\|h\|)$ uniformly. The coefficients $A_h$ are uniformly bounded on $K$, so [F5] applied to the integral equation for $R_h$ from [F6] gives $\|R_h\|_\infty=o(\|h\|_2)$. Therefore $D_xS(t,x)[h]=H_h(t)$, proving existence of the second state derivative.

If $x_j\to x$, [F1] gives uniform convergence of $\Phi(\cdot,x_j)$ and $S(\cdot,x_j)$ on $J$. Continuity of $D^2f$ on $K$ then gives uniform convergence of the coefficients and forcing in the linear equations for $H_h$; subtracting their integral equations and applying [F5] proves $H_h(\cdot,x_j)\to H_h(\cdot,x)$ uniformly. Thus the second state derivative is continuous in $(t,x)$.

By [F2], $\partial_t\Phi=f(\Phi)$. Differentiating this identity in $x$ and in $t$ using [F7] gives $\partial_{tx}\Phi=Df(\Phi)S$ and $\partial_{tt}\Phi=Df(\Phi)f(\Phi)$. These derivatives and $D_x^2\Phi=H$ are continuous by steps 1.1 and 4.1, so $\Phi$ is jointly $C^2$ on the stated tube.

Let $f:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be an autonomous $C^2$ vector field on an open set $U$, with the autonomous ODE convention of [[def-autonomous-ordinary-differential-equation]] and the $C^2$ map convention of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Let $\psi(x)=c^\top(x-x_{\rm ref})$ be an affine phase function with $c\ne0$. On the scaled interval $s\in[0,1]$, introduce the augmented state $u=(x,\theta)\in U\times(0,\infty)$ and vector field
$$
\widetilde f(x,\theta)=(\theta f(x),0).
$$
For endpoint states $u_0=(x_0,\theta_0)$ and $u_1=(x_1,\theta_1)$, define the boundary map
$$
B(u_0,u_1)=(x_1-x_0,\psi(x_0))\in\mathbb R^{d+1}.
$$
This is a square nonlinear BVP in the sense of [[def-nonlinear-two-point-bvp-and-boundary-residual]]: its state dimension and number of boundary equations are both $d+1$. The period coordinate is constant along solutions because its derivative is zero. The common-tube differentiability of the exact flow is given by [[lem-c1-ode-flow-on-common-tube]], and monodromy/Floquet terminology follows [[def-local-periodic-orbit-poincare-and-floquet-data]].

Whenever the exact autonomous flow $\phi_t$ exists on the required interval, the associated phase-bordered shooting residual is
$$
G(x,\theta)=\bigl(\phi_\theta(x)-x,\psi(x)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^{d+1},\qquad \theta>0.
$$
It is defined only for initial data whose flow exists through time $\theta$. Phase transversality at a nonstationary periodic point $x_*$ means $c^\top f(x_*)\ne0$. Neither existence of a zero nor invertibility of its Jacobian is part of this definition.

Fix $a<b$, an integer $d\ge1$, an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ containing $[a,b]\times$ the states under consideration, and a vector field $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$. Let $D_B\subseteq\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d$ be open and let $B:D_B\to\mathbb R^d$. A **square nonlinear two-point boundary-value problem (BVP)** is

$$y'(t)=f(t,y(t))\quad(a\le t\le b),\qquad B(y(a),y(b))=0,$$

where $y$ is a continuously differentiable curve whose graph lies in $\Omega$, whose endpoint pair lies in $D_B$, and where the $d$ scalar components of $B$ give exactly $d$ boundary equations. A **BVP solution** is such a curve satisfying both the differential equation and endpoint equation. No existence or uniqueness is part of this definition.

If the IVP from initial state $s\in\mathbb R^d$ has a unique solution $\phi(\cdot;s)$ on $[a,b]$, the **exact shooting residual** is $R(s):=B(s,\phi(b;s))$ whenever $(s,\phi(b;s))\in D_B$. For a mesh $a=t_0<\cdots<t_N=b$ and segment initial states $s_0,\ldots,s_N$, the **exact multiple-shooting residual** has rows $\phi_i(t_{i+1};s_i)-s_{i+1}$ for $0\le i<N$ and final row $B(s_0,s_N)$, where $\phi_i$ denotes the unique segment IVP solution when it exists. These residuals are defined only on their admissible IVP and boundary domains.

Let U⊂R^n be open and Y:U→R^n be C¹. There is a unique maximal flow Φ on an open domain
D⊂R×U containing {0}×U, and Φ is jointly C¹. Its time slices are local C¹
diffeomorphisms with inverse Φ_{−t}; $\partial_t\Phi=Y(\Phi)$ and $D_p\Phi$ is the
unique solution V of $V′=DY(\Phi)V$, V(0)=I. Each regular point has a C¹ flow box. If Y
is C², Φ and those flow boxes are C²; the second state variation W satisfies
$W′=DY(\Phi)W+D²Y(\Phi)[Ve_i,Ve_j]$, W(0)=0. Individual trajectories of a C¹ field are
C² in time. A trajectory remaining in a compact K⊂⊂U cannot have a finite maximal
endpoint. These Euclidean conclusions use no full AC or DC.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: Suppose $G(x,\theta)=0$. Set $u(s)=(\phi_{\theta s}(x),\theta)$. By [F3] and [F4], $u'(s)=(\theta f(\phi_{\theta s}(x)),0)=\widetilde f(u(s))$. Its endpoint state has the same $x$ component as its initial state, and its initial phase residual is $\psi(x)=0$, so [F1]–[F2] make it an augmented BVP solution.

Define $\gamma(t)=\phi_t(x)$ for $0\le t\le\theta$. By [F3] it solves $\gamma'=f(\gamma)$, and $G(x,\theta)=0$ gives $\gamma(\theta)=\gamma(0)$ and $\psi(\gamma(0))=0$. Since $f(x)\ne0$, it is nonconstant.

Conversely, let $\gamma$ be a nonconstant solution on $[0,\theta]$ with $\gamma(\theta)=\gamma(0)$ and $\psi(\gamma(0))=0$. Uniqueness in [F3] identifies $\gamma(t)=\phi_t(\gamma(0))$. Thus both components of $G(\gamma(0),\theta)$ vanish, and $u(s)=(\gamma(\theta s),\theta)$ satisfies the augmented BVP by the same chain-rule calculation as step 1.1.
