Fix an integer $d\ge1$, an open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^{d+d^2+1}$, and a continuously differentiable map $H:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{d+d^2+1}$. A rational box is a finite product of closed intervals with rational endpoints. A sound range provider on a compact convex rational box $K\subset\Omega$ is a procedure which, on each rational box $Q\subseteq K$, returns either a rational box $H^\#(Q)$ satisfying
$$
\{H(y):y\in Q\}\subseteq H^\#(Q),
$$
or the status inconclusive. It may not report a finite box without this inclusion. The provider also supplies rational bounds $L,M\ge0$ satisfying
$$
\|H(y)-H(z)\|_\infty\le L\|y-z\|_\infty,\qquad \|H(y)\|_\infty\le M\quad(y,z\in K).
$$
The function bounds are part of the input certificate and must hold on all of $K$. This interface says what a successful range computation means; it does not assert that a provider succeeds on every field or box.

Let $f:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^2$. Set $m=d+d^2+1$ and define the augmented autonomous field
$$
H(x,Z,\theta)=\bigl(\theta f(x),\ \theta Df(x)Z,\ 0\bigr)
$$
on an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$. The exact flow and its differentiability on a common compact tube use [[lem-c1-ode-flow-on-common-tube]]. Inputs are a rational initial-state box $X_0\subset U$, a rational period interval $\Theta=[\theta_-,\theta_+]\subset(0,\infty)$, an integer $N\ge1$, a compact convex rational tube $K\subset\Omega$, and a sound range oracle with rational bounds $L,M$ as in [[def-verified-flow-variational-range-oracle]]. Use the maximum norm and exact rational set arithmetic. Let $h=1/N$ and
$$
Y_0=X_0\times\{I_d\}\times\Theta.
$$
For $n=0,\ldots,N-1$, first set
$$
Q_n=Y_n+[-Mh,Mh]^m.
$$
If $Q_n\not\subseteq K$, return inconclusive. Then request $H^\#(Y_n)$. If it is inconclusive, return inconclusive. Otherwise form
$$
Y_{n+1}=Y_n+hH^\#(Y_n)+[-LMh^2/2,LMh^2/2]^m.
$$
If any required rational set operation is unavailable or the next box is not finite, return inconclusive; otherwise continue. On success return the tube boxes $Q_0,\ldots,Q_{N-1}$ and endpoint box $Y_N$. The first, second, and last coordinate blocks of $Y_N$ enclose the exact endpoint, the exact variational matrix, and the period, respectively. The procedure makes no success claim if the supplied range oracle or $L,M$ bounds are not sound on $K$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

Let $a<b$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^1$. Let $K\subseteq\Omega$ be compact and convex, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open. Assume that for every $s\in U$ the unique IVP solution $\phi(\cdot;s)$ from $\phi(a;s)=s$ exists on $[a,b]$ and $(t,\phi(t;s))\in K$ for every $t$. Then $s\mapsto\phi(t;s)$ is $C^1$ on $U$ for each $t\in[a,b]$. Its derivative matrix $S(t;s):=D_s\phi(t;s)$ is the unique solution of

$$S(t;s)=I_d+\int_a^t D_yf(r,\phi(r;s))S(r;s)\,dr,$$

and hence satisfies $\partial_tS=D_yf(t,\phi(t;s))S$, $S(a;s)=I_d$. The claim is local to the stated common compact tube; it does not assert differentiability beyond it.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim: Fix any exact state $y_n\in Y_n$ at time $nh$. While its solution remains in $K$, [F1] gives $\|H(y(t))\|_\infty\le M$, hence $\|y(t)-y_n\|_\infty\le M(t-nh)\le Mh$. If it first left $K$ before $nh+h$, continuity would place the exit point in $Q_n\subseteq K$, a contradiction. Thus the solution exists throughout this cell and stays in $Q_n$.

By [F5], the exact Euler defect on this cell is $\int_{nh}^{nh+h}(H(y(t))-H(y_n))\,dt$. By [F1], the integrand norm is at most $LM(t-nh)$, so its integral is at most $LMh^2/2$. Also $H(y_n)\in H^\#(Y_n)$; hence the exact next value lies in $Y_n+hH^\#(Y_n)+[-LMh^2/2,LMh^2/2]^m=Y_{n+1}$.

Initially the exact state lies in $Y_0$. Apply steps 1.1–1.2 successively for $n=0,\ldots,N-1$. Induction places each exact cell in $Q_n$ and its endpoint in $Y_{n+1}$, in particular the final endpoint in $Y_N$. The no-exit argument and maximal-solution property [F3] establish existence and uniqueness through all cells.

For $H(x,Z,\theta)=(\theta f(x),\theta Df(x)Z,0)$, the state block solves $x'=\theta f(x)$ and the matrix block solves $Z'=\theta Df(x)Z$ with $Z(0)=I_d$. Rescaling physical time $t=\theta s$ makes the state block $\phi_{\theta s}(x_0)$; [F4] identifies $Z(s)$ with its derivative in $x_0$. The terminal block inclusions from step 3.1 are therefore the claimed flow and monodromy enclosures.

For an autonomous vector field $\dot x=f(x)$, a nonconstant solution $x_*(t)$ with least positive period $T$ has periodic orbit $\Gamma=\{x_*(t):0\le t<T\}$. Its variational fundamental matrix $Y(t)$ solves

$$\dot Y(t)=D f(x_*(t))Y(t),\qquad Y(0)=I.$$

The matrix $Y(T)$ is the **monodromy matrix**; its eigenvalues, counted with algebraic multiplicity, are the **Floquet multipliers**. The multiplier $1$ in the direction $\dot x_*(0)$ is called the **phase multiplier**.

A **local Poincare section** at $x_*(0)$ is a smooth codimension-one surface through that point whose tangent space does not contain $f(x_*(0))$. The local return map sends a nearby point on the section to its next intersection after one turn around $\Gamma$. Its derivative at $x_*(0)$ is the Poincare derivative.

The orbit is **orbitally asymptotically stable** if it is Lyapunov stable as a set and the distance from every sufficiently nearby trajectory to $\Gamma$ tends to zero as time tends to $+\infty$. It is **orbitally unstable** if it is not Lyapunov stable as a set.

Let $f:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be an autonomous $C^2$ vector field on an open set $U$, with the autonomous ODE convention of [[def-autonomous-ordinary-differential-equation]] and the $C^2$ map convention of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Let $\psi(x)=c^\top(x-x_{\rm ref})$ be an affine phase function with $c\ne0$. On the scaled interval $s\in[0,1]$, introduce the augmented state $u=(x,\theta)\in U\times(0,\infty)$ and vector field
$$
\widetilde f(x,\theta)=(\theta f(x),0).
$$
For endpoint states $u_0=(x_0,\theta_0)$ and $u_1=(x_1,\theta_1)$, define the boundary map
$$
B(u_0,u_1)=(x_1-x_0,\psi(x_0))\in\mathbb R^{d+1}.
$$
This is a square nonlinear BVP in the sense of [[def-nonlinear-two-point-bvp-and-boundary-residual]]: its state dimension and number of boundary equations are both $d+1$. The period coordinate is constant along solutions because its derivative is zero. The common-tube differentiability of the exact flow is given by [[lem-c1-ode-flow-on-common-tube]], and monodromy/Floquet terminology follows [[def-local-periodic-orbit-poincare-and-floquet-data]].

Whenever the exact autonomous flow $\phi_t$ exists on the required interval, the associated phase-bordered shooting residual is
$$
G(x,\theta)=\bigl(\phi_\theta(x)-x,\psi(x)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^{d+1},\qquad \theta>0.
$$
It is defined only for initial data whose flow exists through time $\theta$. Phase transversality at a nonstationary periodic point $x_*$ means $c^\top f(x_*)\ne0$. Neither existence of a zero nor invertibility of its Jacobian is part of this definition.

Let $f$ be an autonomous $C^1$ vector field, let $\gamma(t)=\phi_t(x_*)$ be a nonconstant periodic solution of period $T>0$, and let $M=D_x\phi_T(x_*)$ be its monodromy matrix. Then
$$
M f(x_*)=f(x_*).
$$
In particular, $1$ is a Floquet multiplier.

Let $k,m,n\ge1$ and $p\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n+p}$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^k$. Suppose $F(a,b,\lambda_0)=0$ and $D_yF(a,b,\lambda_0)$ is invertible. Then there are neighbourhoods and a unique $C^k$ map $\varphi$ solving $F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)=0$. More precisely, on suitable open neighbourhoods $P$ of $(a,\lambda_0)$ and $Q$ of $b$,

$$F(x,y,\lambda)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x,\lambda),$$

and

$$D\varphi(x,\lambda)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)^{-1}D_{(x,\lambda)}F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda).$$

When no parameter block is present, this is the ordinary $C^k$ implicit function theorem.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is **totally differentiable at $a$** when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) such that

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

where the quotient is considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$. The map $L$, when it exists, is denoted $Df(a)$ and called the **total derivative**. Equivalently, $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with $\|r(h)\|_2/\|h\|_2\to0$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: Define $\Psi(t,x)=\psi(\phi_t(x))$. At $(T,x_*)$, $\Psi(T,x_*)=0$ and $\partial_t\Psi(T,x_*)=c^\top f(x_*)\ne0$. By [F4], there is a local return-time function $\tau(x)$ on the section with $\tau(x_*)=T$ and $\Psi(\tau(x),x)=0$. Differentiating this identity at $x_*$ in a tangent direction $v\in S:=\ker c^\top$ gives $D\tau(x_*)v=-c^\top Mv/(c^\top f(x_*))$.

The local return map is $P(x)=\phi_{\tau(x)}(x)$. The chain rule and step 1.1 give, for $v\in S$, $ DP(x_*)v=Mv-\frac{f(x_*)c^\top Mv}{c^\top f(x_*)}=\Pi Mv,\qquad \Pi=I-\frac{f(x_*)c^\top}{c^\top f(x_*)}. $ The map $\Pi$ identifies the quotient $\mathbb C^d/\operatorname{span}\{f(x_*)\}$ with $S$: it kills the phase direction and is the identity on $S$. Since $M f(x_*)=f(x_*)$ by [F3], it induces a linear map on this quotient, and $DP(x_*)$ is its conjugate under that identification.

In a basis whose first vector is $f(x_*)$, the matrix of $M$ is block upper triangular with first diagonal block $1$ and remaining block the induced quotient map. Its characteristic polynomial is therefore $(\lambda-1)$ times that of the quotient map. The eigenvalue $1$ is simple by hypothesis, so the quotient eigenvalues, with multiplicity, are exactly all the remaining eigenvalues of $M$. Step 2.1 identifies these with the Poincare derivative eigenvalues.

Let $f:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be an autonomous $C^2$ vector field on an open set $U$, with the autonomous ODE convention of [[def-autonomous-ordinary-differential-equation]] and the $C^2$ map convention of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Let $\psi(x)=c^\top(x-x_{\rm ref})$ be an affine phase function with $c\ne0$. On the scaled interval $s\in[0,1]$, introduce the augmented state $u=(x,\theta)\in U\times(0,\infty)$ and vector field
$$
\widetilde f(x,\theta)=(\theta f(x),0).
$$
For endpoint states $u_0=(x_0,\theta_0)$ and $u_1=(x_1,\theta_1)$, define the boundary map
$$
B(u_0,u_1)=(x_1-x_0,\psi(x_0))\in\mathbb R^{d+1}.
$$
This is a square nonlinear BVP in the sense of [[def-nonlinear-two-point-bvp-and-boundary-residual]]: its state dimension and number of boundary equations are both $d+1$. The period coordinate is constant along solutions because its derivative is zero. The common-tube differentiability of the exact flow is given by [[lem-c1-ode-flow-on-common-tube]], and monodromy/Floquet terminology follows [[def-local-periodic-orbit-poincare-and-floquet-data]].

Whenever the exact autonomous flow $\phi_t$ exists on the required interval, the associated phase-bordered shooting residual is
$$
G(x,\theta)=\bigl(\phi_\theta(x)-x,\psi(x)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^{d+1},\qquad \theta>0.
$$
It is defined only for initial data whose flow exists through time $\theta$. Phase transversality at a nonstationary periodic point $x_*$ means $c^\top f(x_*)\ne0$. Neither existence of a zero nor invertibility of its Jacobian is part of this definition.

Let $f$ be an autonomous $C^1$ vector field, let $\gamma(t)=\phi_t(x_*)$ be a nonconstant periodic solution of period $T>0$, and let $M=D_x\phi_T(x_*)$ be its monodromy matrix. Then
$$
M f(x_*)=f(x_*).
$$
In particular, $1$ is a Floquet multiplier.

Let $\lambda$ be a simple eigenvalue of $A$, and let $x,y\ne0$ be compatible
right and left eigenvectors. Then $y^\ast x\ne0$. Consequently, after rescaling
either vector, one may impose the normalization

$$y^\ast x=1.$$

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, equipped with the standard Hermitian inner
product, and let $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ be a simple eigenvalue of $A$. A nonzero vector
$x$ is a **right eigenvector** for $\lambda$ if

$$Ax=\lambda x.$$

A nonzero vector $y$ is a **left eigenvector** for $\lambda$ if

$$y^\ast A=\lambda y^\ast,$$

equivalently $A^\ast y=\overline{\lambda}\,y$.

Such $x$ and $y$ are called **compatible left and right eigenvectors** for the
simple eigenvalue $\lambda$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

Let $f \in \mathbb C[x]$ have degree $n \ge 1$. Then there exist distinct
complex numbers $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$ and positive integers
$m_1,\dots,m_r$ such that
$$ f(x)=c\prod_{j=1}^r (x-\alpha_j)^{m_j} $$
for some $c \in \mathbb C^\times$, with
$$ m_1+\cdots+m_r=n. $$
These exponents are uniquely determined by $f$. Equivalently, $f$ has exactly
$n$ roots counted with multiplicity.

An endomorphism of a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space has a Jordan canonical form over $F$ if and only if its characteristic polynomial splits into linear factors over $F$. This includes the zero space, where the characteristic polynomial is $1$ and the Jordan form is empty.

For an autonomous vector field $\dot x=f(x)$, a nonconstant solution $x_*(t)$ with least positive period $T$ has periodic orbit $\Gamma=\{x_*(t):0\le t<T\}$. Its variational fundamental matrix $Y(t)$ solves

$$\dot Y(t)=D f(x_*(t))Y(t),\qquad Y(0)=I.$$

The matrix $Y(T)$ is the **monodromy matrix**; its eigenvalues, counted with algebraic multiplicity, are the **Floquet multipliers**. The multiplier $1$ in the direction $\dot x_*(0)$ is called the **phase multiplier**.

A **local Poincare section** at $x_*(0)$ is a smooth codimension-one surface through that point whose tangent space does not contain $f(x_*(0))$. The local return map sends a nearby point on the section to its next intersection after one turn around $\Gamma$. Its derivative at $x_*(0)$ is the Poincare derivative.

The orbit is **orbitally asymptotically stable** if it is Lyapunov stable as a set and the distance from every sufficiently nearby trajectory to $\Gamma$ tends to zero as time tends to $+\infty$. It is **orbitally unstable** if it is not Lyapunov stable as a set.

Let U⊂R^n be open and Y:U→R^n be C¹. There is a unique maximal flow Φ on an open domain
D⊂R×U containing {0}×U, and Φ is jointly C¹. Its time slices are local C¹
diffeomorphisms with inverse Φ_{−t}; $\partial_t\Phi=Y(\Phi)$ and $D_p\Phi$ is the
unique solution V of $V′=DY(\Phi)V$, V(0)=I. Each regular point has a C¹ flow box. If Y
is C², Φ and those flow boxes are C²; the second state variation W satisfies
$W′=DY(\Phi)W+D²Y(\Phi)[Ve_i,Ve_j]$, W(0)=0. Individual trajectories of a C¹ field are
C² in time. A trajectory remaining in a compact K⊂⊂U cannot have a finite maximal
endpoint. These Euclidean conclusions use no full AC or DC.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F5], differentiating in $x$ gives $M-I_d$, differentiating in $T$ gives $f(\phi_T(x_*))=f_*$, and differentiating the phase row gives $(c^\top,0)$. This is the displayed matrix by [F6].

Suppose $1$ is algebraically simple. Then [F4] implies that the complex eigenspace for eigenvalue $1$ is one-dimensional. By [F2] its spanning eigenvector $f_*$ is real, so the real kernel is $\mathbb R f_*$ and rank-nullity gives $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M-I_d)=d-1$. Choose a real basis $v_1,\ldots,v_{d-1}$ of $\operatorname{range}(M-I_d)$. The $d-1$ real linear forms $w\mapsto v_j^\top w$ are independent: if a linear combination vanishes for every $w$, then the row $\bigl(\sum_j a_jv_j\bigr)^\top$ is zero, so $\sum_j a_jv_j=0$ and basis independence forces every coefficient $a_j$ to vanish. Rank-nullity therefore gives a nonzero real $w_0$ with $v_j^\top w_0=0$ for every $j$. Thus $w_0^\top(M-I_d)=0$. It is a compatible left eigenvector with the real right eigenvector $f_*$, so [F3], applied over $\mathbb C$, gives $w_0^\top f_*\ne0$. This pairing is real; normalize $w=w_0/(w_0^\top f_*)$, so $w$ is real, $w^\top M=w^\top$, and $w^\top f_*=1$. For $Q=I-f_*w^\top$ and $W=\ker w^\top$, one has $Qf_*=0$, $Q|_W=I_W$, and $QM=M-f_*w^\top M=M-f_*w^\top=M-Mf_*w^\top=MQ$. Hence $Q$ is the projection onto $W$, $M$ preserves $W$, and $M-I_d$ maps $W$ into $W$. Its restriction to $W$ is injective: a kernel vector there would be an eigenvector independent of $f_*$, contrary to simplicity. Since $W$ is finite dimensional, [F7] makes the restriction invertible. For $J(u,\tau)=(r,s)$, left multiplication of the first row by $w^\top$ gives $\tau=w^\top r$. Write $u=u_W+\alpha f_*$ with $u_W\in W$; applying $Q$ to the first row and using its commutation with $M$ gives $u_W=((M-I_d)|_W)^{-1}Qr$, and the phase row gives $\alpha=(s-c^\top u_W)/(c^\top f_*)$. Thus nonzero $c^\top f_*$ gives a unique solution for every right-hand side, so $J$ is invertible. Moreover, $|\tau|\le\|w\|_2\|r\|_2$, $\|u_W\|_2\le K_W\|Q\|_2\|r\|_2$, and $|\alpha|\le(|s|+\|c\|_2K_W\|Q\|_2\|r\|_2)/|c^\top f_*|$. By the triangle inequality and $\|r\|_2,|s|\le\|(r,s)\|_2$, these bounds yield the stated estimate.

If $c^\top f_*=0$, then $J(f_*,0)=0$, so $J$ is singular. Now suppose the algebraic multiplicity of $1$ exceeds one. If the complex eigenspace has dimension at least two, its real kernel also has dimension at least two: for the real matrix $M-I_d$, its complex kernel consists exactly of $u+iv$ with $u$ and $v$ in the real kernel. Choose a real $v\in\ker(M-I_d)$ independent of $f_*$. If $c^\top f_*=0$ the preceding argument applies; otherwise $u=v-(c^\top v)/(c^\top f_*)f_*$ is nonzero, lies in $\ker(M-I_d)$, and satisfies $c^\top u=0$, so $J(u,0)=0$. If instead the eigenspace is one-dimensional, Jordan form [F4] supplies a generalized vector which, after rescaling, satisfies $(M-I_d)v=f_*$ over $\mathbb C$. Since $M-I_d$ and $f_*$ are real, $\operatorname{Re}v$ is a real generalized vector satisfying the same equation; replace $v$ by this real vector. If $c^\top f_*=0$, $J(f_*,0)=0$; if not, put $u=v-(c^\top v)/(c^\top f_*)f_*$. Then $c^\top u=0$ and $(M-I_d)u=f_*$, so $J(u,-1)=0$. In every nonsimple case $J$ is singular.
Steps 2.1–2.2 prove both directions of the invertibility criterion.

Let $y^*\in C^1([a,b],\mathbb R^d)$ solve a square BVP, with $f$ and $B$ continuously differentiable on open neighborhoods of the trajectory and endpoint pair. Put $A(t)=D_yf(t,y^*(t))$, $B_1=D_1B(y^*(a),y^*(b))$, and $B_2=D_2B(y^*(a),y^*(b))$. Let

$$X=C^1([a,b],\mathbb R^d),\quad \|v\|_X=\|v\|_\infty+\|v'\|_\infty,$$

and

$$Z=C([a,b],\mathbb R^d)\times\mathbb R^d,\quad \|(g,q)\|_Z=\max\{\|g\|_\infty,\|q\|_2\}.$$

The **continuous linearized BVP operator** is the bounded linear map $\mathcal L:X\to Z$ given by

$$\mathcal L v=(v'-A v,\ B_1v(a)+B_2v(b)).$$

It is **boundedly invertible** when it is bijective and its inverse $\mathcal L^{-1}:Z\to X$ has finite operator norm. That norm is the conditioning constant for the linearized BVP used in the local discretization theorem.

At a phase-fixed periodic point $x_*$ with period $T$, let $M=D_x\phi_T(x_*)$, let $f_*=f(x_*)\ne0$, and let $c=D\psi(x_*)$ for the affine phase $\psi(x)=c^\top(x-x_{\rm ref})$. The derivative of the phase-bordered shooting residual is
$$ J=\begin{bmatrix}M-I_d&f_*\\c^\top&0\end{bmatrix}. $$
It is invertible if and only if $1$ is an algebraically simple eigenvalue of $M$ and $c^\top f_*\ne0$. In the simple case choose real left/right eigenvectors $w,f_*$ with $w^\top f_*=1$, put $Q=I-f_*w^\top$ and $W=\ker w^\top$, and let $K_W=\|((M-I_d)|_W)^{-1}\|_{2\to2}$. All vector and matrix norms below are Euclidean and induced Euclidean norms, and the product norm on $(u,\tau)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R$ is Euclidean. Then
$$ \|J^{-1}\|_{2\to2}\le K_W\|Q\|_2+\|w\|_2+ \frac{\|f_*\|_2\bigl(1+\|c\|_2K_W\|Q\|_2\bigr)}{|c^\top f_*|}. $$
The period column is the exact time-sensitivity $f_*$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $a<b$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^1$. Let $K\subseteq\Omega$ be compact and convex, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open. Assume that for every $s\in U$ the unique IVP solution $\phi(\cdot;s)$ from $\phi(a;s)=s$ exists on $[a,b]$ and $(t,\phi(t;s))\in K$ for every $t$. Then $s\mapsto\phi(t;s)$ is $C^1$ on $U$ for each $t\in[a,b]$. Its derivative matrix $S(t;s):=D_s\phi(t;s)$ is the unique solution of

$$S(t;s)=I_d+\int_a^t D_yf(r,\phi(r;s))S(r;s)\,dr,$$

and hence satisfies $\partial_tS=D_yf(t,\phi(t;s))S$, $S(a;s)=I_d$. The claim is local to the stated common compact tube; it does not assert differentiability beyond it.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: The coefficient $A$ is continuous on $[0,1]$. For $0\le s\le t\le1$, let $U(t,s)$ be the solution operator of $v'=A(t)v$. Local existence and uniqueness follow from [F3]. Gronwall gives $\|U(t,s)\|_2\le e^{a_0(t-s)}$, so the solution remains bounded and [F3] extends it through $t=1$. In particular $U$ exists on the full triangle $0\le s\le t\le1$.

The homogeneous solution with initial value $\xi$ is $U(t,0)\xi$. Its endpoint variation is the derivative of the augmented flow. The first $d$ endpoint coordinates differentiate to $Mv+f(\gamma(0))\tau$ in initial variation $(v,\tau)$: the $v$ column is monodromy, and the period column is $\partial_T\phi_T(\gamma(0))=f(\gamma(0))$ by [F5] and periodicity. Differentiating $B(u_0,u_1)=(x_1-x_0,\psi(x_0))$ by [F7] therefore gives $B_1+B_2U(1,0)=J$.

For data $(g,q)\in Z$, let $p$ be the unique solution of $p'=Ap+g$, $p(0)=0$. Local existence and uniqueness follow from [F3]; integrating this equation by [F6] gives $\|p(t)\|_2\le\|g\|_\infty+a_0\int_0^t\|p(s)\|_2ds$, hence $\|p\|_\infty\le E\|g\|_\infty$ by [F4]. This bound extends $p$ through the full interval by [F3]. Every solution with initial value $\xi$ equals $U(t,0)\xi+p(t)$, since their difference solves the homogeneous linear IVP with initial value $\xi$ and uniqueness [F3] applies.

The boundary condition for this solution is $J\xi+B_2p(1)=q$ by step 2.1. Thus its unique initial value is $\xi=J^{-1}(q-B_2p(1))$. Writing $D=\|(g,q)\|_Z=\max(\|g\|_\infty,\|q\|_2)$ gives $\|\xi\|_2\le K_J(1+\|B_2\|_2E)D$ and, by steps 1.1–2.1, $\|v\|_\infty\le[EK_J(1+\|B_2\|_2E)+E]D$.

Since $v'=Av+g$, $\|v'\|_\infty\le a_0\|v\|_\infty+D$. The definition of the $X$ norm now gives $\|v\|_X\le K_{\mathcal L}D$. Steps 2.2–2.2 construct a solution for every $(g,q)$; any solution is determined by $\xi$ and the invertible matrix $J$, so it is unique. Hence $\mathcal L$ is bijective with the stated inverse bound.

For a $d$-dimensional BVP on $[a,b]$, an integer $N\ge1$, uniform mesh width $h=(b-a)/N$, mesh nodes $t_i=a+ih$, and node vector $Y=(Y_0,\ldots,Y_N)\in(\mathbb R^d)^{N+1}$, let $D_h$ be the open set of node vectors for which every midpoint pair $(t_i+h/2,(Y_i+Y_{i+1})/2)$ lies in the vector-field domain and $(Y_0,Y_N)$ lies in the boundary-map domain. Define $G_h:D_h\to(\mathbb R^d)^{N+1}$ by

$$G_{h,i}(Y)=\frac{Y_{i+1}-Y_i}{h}-f\!\left(t_i+\frac h2,\frac{Y_i+Y_{i+1}}2\right)\quad(0\le i<N),\qquad G_{h,N}(Y)=B(Y_0,Y_N).$$

Use the maximum of the Euclidean block norms for both node and residual vectors. The interior rows are normalized by $h$; consequently an unscaled increment row has size $h$ times its normalized row.

Use the augmented state $u=(x,\theta)\in U\times(0,\infty)$, field $\widetilde f(u)=(\theta f(x),0)$, and boundary residual $B(u_0,u_N)=(x_N-x_0,\psi(x_0))$ from [[def-phase-bordered-periodic-orbit-bvp]]. On a mesh $0=s_0<\cdots<s_N=1$, write $u_i=(x_i,\theta_i)$.

The endpoint-pair boundary residual and square BVP convention are those of [[def-nonlinear-two-point-bvp-and-boundary-residual]]. The exact multiple-shooting residual has segment rows
$$
\Phi_{s_{i+1}-s_i}(u_i)-u_{i+1}\quad(0\le i<N)
$$
and final row $B(u_0,u_N)$, where $\Phi_h$ is the exact flow of $\widetilde f$. Its finite-budget candidate procedure is [[alg-multiple-shooting-for-nonlinear-bvps]] on this augmented BVP.

For uniform $h=1/N$, the normalized midpoint-collocation residual has rows
$$
\frac{u_{i+1}-u_i}{h}-\widetilde f\!\left(\frac{u_i+u_{i+1}}2\right)\quad(0\le i<N)
$$
and final row $B(u_0,u_N)$. This is [[def-midpoint-collocation-residual-for-bvps]] for the same augmented BVP; its finite-budget candidate procedure is [[alg-midpoint-collocation-for-nonlinear-bvps]]. Both systems are square: the state dimension is $d+1$, with $d+1$ boundary equations.

Let $u_*(s)=(\gamma(Ts),T)$, $0\le s\le1$, be the augmented solution from [[def-phase-bordered-periodic-orbit-bvp]] for a nonconstant $C^2$ autonomous periodic orbit of period $T>0$. Assume its phase multiplier $1$ is algebraically simple and its affine phase covector $c$ satisfies $c^\top f(\gamma(0))\ne0$. For the continuous linearized BVP operator $\mathcal L:X\to Z$ of [[def-linearized-two-point-bvp-operator-and-conditioning]], define
$$ A(s)=D\widetilde f(u_*(s)),\quad a_0=\sup_{0\le s\le1}\|A(s)\|_2, \quad B_2=D_2B(u_*(0),u_*(1)),\quad K_J\ge\|J^{-1}\|_{2\to2}, $$
where $J=\begin{bmatrix}M-I&f(\gamma(0))\\c^\top&0\end{bmatrix}$ and $M=D\phi_T(\gamma(0))$. Put $E=e^{a_0}$ and
$$ K_{\mathcal L}:=(1+a_0)\left[E K_J(1+\|B_2\|_2E)+E\right]+1. $$
Then $\mathcal L$ is bijective and $\|\mathcal L^{-1}\|_{Z\to X}\le K_{\mathcal L}$, with the spaces and norms defined in [[def-linearized-two-point-bvp-operator-and-conditioning]]. All constants are finite and explicit once the stated coefficient and shooting-inverse bounds are supplied.

Here $C^k$ means each coordinate has continuous total derivatives through order $k$. Let $f,B$ be $C^2$ near an exact solution $y^*\in C^3([a,b],\mathbb R^d)$ of a square BVP, and suppose the continuous linearized operator $\mathcal L$ in [[def-linearized-two-point-bvp-operator-and-conditioning]] is boundedly invertible. For uniform meshes with $h=(b-a)/N$, let $Y_i^*=y^*(t_i)$ and let $J_h=DG_h(Y^*)$ be the Jacobian of the normalized midpoint residual. There are $h_0>0$ and $C<\infty$ such that for every mesh width $0<h\le h_0$, $J_h$ is invertible and

$$\|J_h^{-1}\|_{\infty\to\infty}\le C,$$

where both finite-dimensional norms are the maximum of the Euclidean block norms. The bound is independent of $h$; this is a local linear inverse result, not a nonlinear convergence theorem.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

**Why this item is first.** The published definition of the integral does not
cover this page. [[def-darboux-integral]] is stated for reals $a < b$, because
the partitions it quantifies over are those of [[def-partition-and-refinement]],
whose standing hypothesis is $a < b$: with $a = b$ the chain
$a = t_0 < \dots < t_n = b$ is unsatisfiable. So $\int_a^b f$ is an undefined
symbol whenever $a \ge b$, and every additivity statement below would be
ill-formed as it is usually written. This item extends the notation, and nothing
else: the object it names is still the Darboux integral of
[[def-darboux-integral]].

Let $u, v \in \mathbb{R}$ and write

$$[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v] \;:=\; \text{the closed interval with endpoints } u \text{ and } v$$

([[def-interval]]). Let $f$ be a real-valued function whose domain contains that
interval. Say that **$f$ is integrable between $u$ and $v$** when either $u = v$,
or $u \ne v$ and the restriction of $f$ to $[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v]$ is bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux integrable there ([[def-darboux-integral]],
[[def-darboux-sums]]). For such $f$ define

$$\int_u^v f \;:=\; \begin{cases} \text{the Darboux integral of } f \text{ over } [u,v] & \text{if } u < v, \\[2pt] 0 & \text{if } u = v, \\[2pt] -\displaystyle\int_v^u f & \text{if } u > v. \end{cases}$$

**There is nothing to check for consistency.** The three clauses are indexed by
the three cases of trichotomy, $u < v$, $u = v$ and $u > v$, which are mutually
exclusive and exhaustive; no pair of them ever applies to the same $(u,v)$. In
particular the first clause is untouched, so on $u < v$ this is the published
integral verbatim and every published theorem about it applies unchanged.

**The middle clause is a stipulation, not a computation.** It is *not* claimed
that $0$ is a value forced by the $u < v$ definition in any limiting sense; that
definition simply says nothing at $u = v$, and $\int_u^u f := 0$ is what is
written there. It is also unconditional: no hypothesis on $f$ beyond being
defined at $u$ is asked for, since the case $u = v$ never refers to a partition.

### The two consequences used throughout the page

**Antisymmetry, for every pair.** For all reals $u, v$ with $f$ integrable
between them,

$$\int_u^v f \;=\; -\int_v^u f .$$

Indeed if $u < v$ then $v > u$ and the third clause reads
$\int_v^u f = -\int_u^v f$, which rearranges to the display; if $u = v$ both
sides are $0$; and if $u > v$ the third clause is the display itself.

**Absolute values agree.** Consequently
$\bigl|\int_u^v f\bigr| = \bigl|\int_v^u f\bigr|$ for every such pair.

**An obligation recorded here and discharged elsewhere.** With this convention
the additivity identity

$$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f$$

holds for **every** arrangement of $u, v, w$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable, not only for $u < v < w$. That is a theorem and not part of this
definition; it is proved as the last clause of
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], and nothing on this page uses it before it
is proved there.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be Banach spaces over the same scalar field
([[def-banach-space]]).

1. If $R\in\mathcal B(X)$ satisfies $\|R\|<1$
   ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]]), then $I-R$ is
   invertible with inverse the operator-norm limit of the partial sums
   $\sum_{n<N}R^n$, the norm limit being taken in
   $\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]), and
   $$\Bigl\|\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}R^n\Bigr\|\le\frac{1}{1-\|R\|}.$$
2. If $A\in\mathcal B(X,Y)$ is invertible with $A^{-1}\in\mathcal B(Y,X)$ and
   $E\in\mathcal B(X,Y)$ satisfies $\|A^{-1}E\|<1$, then $A+E$ is invertible
   with $(A+E)^{-1}=\bigl(I+A^{-1}E\bigr)^{-1}A^{-1}\in\mathcal B(Y,X)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

derivations.claim: On a mesh cell centered at $m_i$, repeated vector FTC gives $u_*'(m_i+s)=u_*'(m_i)+s u_*''(m_i)+r(s)$, where $r(s)=\int_0^s\int_0^v u_*'''(m_i+w)\,dw\,dv$. For negative limits reverse their orientation before applying the norm inequality. Thus $\|r(s)\|_2\le M_3|s|^2/2$. Averaging over $[-h/2,h/2]$ cancels the odd term and gives a difference-quotient defect at most $M_3h^2/24$. Applying the same integral argument to $u_*$ at $m_i\pm h/2$ bounds each first-order remainder by $M_2h^2/8$; their average therefore bounds the endpoint-average displacement from $u_*(m_i)$ by $M_2h^2/8$. Integrating $D\widetilde f$ on the connecting segment bounds the corresponding field difference by $L_fM_2h^2/8$. The affine boundary residual is zero. Taking the maximum of the cell bounds gives $\|G_h(Y^*)\|_\infty\le C_0h^2$.

Define $T_h(Y)=Y-J_h^{-1}G_h(Y)$. The Jacobian Lipschitz bound gives $\|T_h(Y)-T_h(Z)\|_\infty\le KL_Gr\|Y-Z\|_\infty\le\frac14\|Y-Z\|_\infty$ on the ball. Also $\|T_h(Y^*)-Y^*\|_\infty\le KC_0h^2\le r/2$, so $T_h$ maps the ball into itself. By [F3], it has a unique fixed point $Y_h$, and invertibility of $J_h$ makes fixed points exactly the zeros of $G_h$. The fixed-point equation also gives $\|Y_h-Y^*\|_\infty\le KC_0h^2/(1-1/4)\le2KC_0h^2$.

The perturbation bound $\|DG_h(Y_h)-J_h\|\le L_G\|Y_h-Y^*\|$ implies $\|J_h^{-1}(DG_h(Y_h)-J_h)\|\le2K^2L_GC_0h^2\le1/2$. The small-perturbation inverse bound [F5] therefore gives $DG_h(Y_h)^{-1}$ with norm at most $2K$.

Put $\delta=Y-Y_h$ and define $R(t)=G_h(Y_h+t\delta)-G_h(Y_h)-tDG_h(Y_h)\delta$ for $0\le t\le1$. The segment lies in the ball. By the chain rule [F6], $R\prime(t)=(DG_h(Y_h+t\delta)-DG_h(Y_h))\delta$, so the Lipschitz bound gives $\|R\prime(t)\|_\infty\le L_Gt\|\delta\|_\infty^2$. For each Euclidean block index $j$, [F7] gives $\|R_j(1)\|_2\le\int_0^1\|R_j\prime(t)\|_2dt\le\int_0^1\|R\prime(t)\|_\infty dt$; taking the finite maximum over $j$ gives $\|R(1)\|_\infty\le\int_0^1\|R\prime(t)\|_\infty dt\le(L_G/2)\|\delta\|_\infty^2$. Thus $G_h(Y)=DG_h(Y_h)(Y-Y_h)+R(1)$ with this remainder bound. Since both vectors lie in the radius-$r$ ball, $\|Y-Y_h\|_\infty\le2r$, and $2KL_Gr\le1/2$ yields $\|Y-Y_h\|_\infty\le2K\varepsilon+\frac12\|Y-Y_h\|_\infty$. Hence $\|Y-Y_h\|_\infty\le4K\varepsilon$.

Linear interpolation is a convex combination, so $\|P_h(Y-Y_h)\|_\infty\le\|Y-Y_h\|_\infty$. On a cell $[a,b]$ of length $h$, repeated FTC gives $u_*(t)-P_hY^*(t)=-\int_a^b K_t(s)u_*''(s)\,ds$, where $K_t(s)=(b-t)(s-a)/h$ for $s\le t$ and $K_t(s)=(t-a)(b-s)/h$ for $s\ge t$. This kernel is nonnegative and has integral $(t-a)(b-t)/2\le h^2/8$, so [F4] gives the interpolation bound $M_2h^2/8$. The sample error of $Y_h$ is at most $2KC_0h^2$ by step 2.1. Combining these bounds with step 4.1 proves the displayed estimate.

boundaries.reason: The statement requires its stated nonempty domain or admitted data and makes no claim for an empty input.

The claim is restricted to its stated nondegenerate hypotheses and asserts no degenerate extension.

Step 1.1 makes only the finite-dimensional or explicitly quantified selection stated there; no choice axiom is inferred.

citations.quote:
Let $f:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be an autonomous $C^2$ vector field on an open set $U$, with the autonomous ODE convention of [[def-autonomous-ordinary-differential-equation]] and the $C^2$ map convention of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Let $\psi(x)=c^\top(x-x_{\rm ref})$ be an affine phase function with $c\ne0$. On the scaled interval $s\in[0,1]$, introduce the augmented state $u=(x,\theta)\in U\times(0,\infty)$ and vector field
$$
\widetilde f(x,\theta)=(\theta f(x),0).
$$
For endpoint states $u_0=(x_0,\theta_0)$ and $u_1=(x_1,\theta_1)$, define the boundary map
$$
B(u_0,u_1)=(x_1-x_0,\psi(x_0))\in\mathbb R^{d+1}.
$$
This is a square nonlinear BVP in the sense of [[def-nonlinear-two-point-bvp-and-boundary-residual]]: its state dimension and number of boundary equations are both $d+1$. The period coordinate is constant along solutions because its derivative is zero. The common-tube differentiability of the exact flow is given by [[lem-c1-ode-flow-on-common-tube]], and monodromy/Floquet terminology follows [[def-local-periodic-orbit-poincare-and-floquet-data]].

Whenever the exact autonomous flow $\phi_t$ exists on the required interval, the associated phase-bordered shooting residual is
$$
G(x,\theta)=\bigl(\phi_\theta(x)-x,\psi(x)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^{d+1},\qquad \theta>0.
$$
It is defined only for initial data whose flow exists through time $\theta$. Phase transversality at a nonstationary periodic point $x_*$ means $c^\top f(x_*)\ne0$. Neither existence of a zero nor invertibility of its Jacobian is part of this definition.

At a phase-fixed periodic point $x_*$ with period $T$, let $M=D_x\phi_T(x_*)$, let $f_*=f(x_*)\ne0$, and let $c=D\psi(x_*)$ for the affine phase $\psi(x)=c^\top(x-x_{\rm ref})$. The derivative of the phase-bordered shooting residual is
$$ J=\begin{bmatrix}M-I_d&f_*\\c^\top&0\end{bmatrix}. $$
It is invertible if and only if $1$ is an algebraically simple eigenvalue of $M$ and $c^\top f_*\ne0$. In the simple case choose real left/right eigenvectors $w,f_*$ with $w^\top f_*=1$, put $Q=I-f_*w^\top$ and $W=\ker w^\top$, and let $K_W=\|((M-I_d)|_W)^{-1}\|_{2\to2}$. All vector and matrix norms below are Euclidean and induced Euclidean norms, and the product norm on $(u,\tau)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R$ is Euclidean. Then
$$ \|J^{-1}\|_{2\to2}\le K_W\|Q\|_2+\|w\|_2+ \frac{\|f_*\|_2\bigl(1+\|c\|_2K_W\|Q\|_2\bigr)}{|c^\top f_*|}. $$
The period column is the exact time-sensitivity $f_*$.

Let $f(x,\mu)$ be $C^2$ on an open set in $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^p$, let $q=(x,\mu)$, and set $g(q)=(f(x,\mu),0_p)$. Write $Pq=x$. For each fixed $\mu$, let $\Phi_\theta(q)$ be the time-$\theta$ flow of $q'=g(q)$, so its parameter coordinates remain constant. For an affine phase $\psi(x)=c^\top(x-x_{\rm ref})$, define
$$
G(q,\theta)=\begin{bmatrix}P\Phi_\theta(q)-Pq\\\psi(Pq)\end{bmatrix}.
$$
For $p=0$ this is the shooting residual in [[def-phase-bordered-periodic-orbit-bvp]]. Its Jacobian is
$$
DG(q,\theta)=\begin{bmatrix}P\mathcal M-P& f(P\Phi_\theta(q),\mu)\\ c^\top P&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathcal M=D_q\Phi_\theta(q).
$$

For a rational box $Q=X\times\Lambda\times\Theta$ with $\Theta\subset(0,\infty)$, a **validated shooting jet enclosure** consists of: (i) a box containing $P\Phi_\theta(q)$ for every $q,\theta$ in the input; (ii) a box containing the residual $G(Q)$; (iii) an interval matrix $J(Q)$ containing every $DG(q,\theta)$; and (iv) trajectory and monodromy boxes containing every scaled trajectory $P\Phi_{\theta s}(q)$, $0\le s\le1$, and the physical-state block of $\mathcal M$. The boxes use [[def-real-boxes-and-interval-jacobian-enclosures]] and [[lem-real-interval-arithmetic-preserves-enclosure]]. The exact derivative formula follows from [[prop-shooting-residual-derivative]], and its flow sensitivity is on the common tube of [[lem-c1-ode-flow-on-common-tube]]. A finite success record is admissible only when obtained by the range-oracle procedure of [[alg-validated-euler-flow-and-monodromy-enclosure]], whose exact flow and monodromy enclosure is guaranteed by [[thm-validated-euler-flow-and-monodromy-enclosure-soundness]], with all queries and interval operations successful and outward under [[def-verified-flow-variational-range-oracle]]. For this call instantiate that procedure and its soundness theorem with state dimension $n=d+p$, initial state box $X\times\Lambda$, field $g(q)=(f(x,\mu),0_p)$, and period interval $\Theta$. Its augmented field is $H_g(q,Z,\theta)=(\theta g(q),\theta Dg(q)Z,0)$ with $Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$; the supplied range provider is for this $H_g$ on its actual compact convex rational tube $K_g\subset\mathbb R^{n+n^2+1}$. Initialize $Y_0=(X\times\Lambda)\times\{I_n\}\times\Theta$ and require every Euler tube query and inclusion check in this same $K_g$ to succeed. Retain the full $n\times n$ endpoint variation enclosure for $\mathcal M=D_q\Phi_\theta(q)$ when forming $P\mathcal M-P$: its first $d$ rows include both the state and parameter sensitivity columns, while its lower parameter rows are $(0,I_p)$ because the parameters are constant. The physical monodromy is the first $d$ rows and first $d$ columns of $\mathcal M$.

To enclose the period column, let $X_T$ be the first $d$ coordinate projection of the successful endpoint enclosure $Y_N$. The exact augmented endpoint lies in $X_T\times\Lambda$: its parameter equals its initial value in $\Lambda$, even if a returned interval coordinate is wider. Form the rational query box $Q_T=(X_T\times\Lambda)\times\{I_n\}\times\Theta$ and check $Q_T\subseteq K_g$ before requesting $H_g^\#(Q_T)$ from that same supplied provider. If the inclusion or query fails, return inconclusive. The first $d$ entries of its vector-field block enclose every $\theta f(P\Phi_\theta(q),\mu)$; divide these entries outward by the positive interval $\Theta$ to enclose the entire period column. Thus the query includes every admitted parameter and the matching augmented identity. For $p=0$, $n=d$ and the parameter factor is the singleton empty tuple, giving the fixed-parameter construction. These residual/Jacobian boxes are in the named coordinate order $(q,\theta)=(x,\mu,\theta)$; a section callback whose variables are ordered $(x,\theta,\mu)$ applies that fixed column permutation before appending its affine section row. Any unavailable query or inclusion returns inconclusive. A finite Newton, multiple-shooting, or collocation residual alone is not a validated jet enclosure.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^2$ on an open set $U$. Let $T_+>0$, let $W\subset U$ be open, and suppose every solution from $x\in W$ exists on an open time interval containing $[0,T_+]$ and stays in one compact convex set $K\subset U$ for all $t\in[0,T_+]$. Write $\Phi(t,x)=\phi_t(x)$. Then $\Phi$ is $C^2$ jointly in $(t,x)$ on $(0,T_+)\times W$, locally on every common-tube neighborhood in $W$, and its derivatives extend continuously in time to $[0,T_+]$. Its first state derivative $S(t,x)=D_x\Phi(t,x)$ solves
$$
\partial_t S=Df(\Phi)S,\qquad S(0,x)=I_n,
$$
and its second state derivative is the bilinear map $H(t,x)$ determined by
$$
\partial_t H[u,v]=Df(\Phi)H[u,v]+D^2f(\Phi)[S u,S v],\qquad H(0,x)[u,v]=0.
$$
In particular $\partial_t\Phi=f(\Phi)$, $\partial_{tx}\Phi=Df(\Phi)S$, and $\partial_{tt}\Phi=Df(\Phi)f(\Phi)$. The assertion is local to the stated common tube.

derivations.claim: By [F6], $G$ is $C^2$ on the common validation tube. Put $\delta=z-z_*$. Since $G(z_*)=0$, Taylor's formula [F3] gives $G(z)=DG(z_*)\delta+R_2$ with $\|R_2\|_2\le(L_J/2)\|\delta\|_2^2$. The residual box inclusion [F2] implies $\|G(z)\|_2\le\epsilon$. Multiplying by $DG(z_*)^{-1}$ and using its norm bound yields $\|\delta\|_2\le K_J\epsilon+(K_JL_J/2)\|\delta\|_2^2$. The hypothesis $\|\delta\|_2\le r$ and $K_JL_Jr\le1$ make the quadratic term at most $\frac12\|\delta\|_2$; rearrangement proves $\|\delta\|_2\le2K_J\epsilon$.

Let $x(s)=\phi_{Ts}(x)$ and $x_*(s)=\phi_{T_*s}(x_*)$. The chain rule [F5] and the flow equation give their scaled equations and $ \|x'(s)-x_*'(s)\|_2\le T_+L_f\|x(s)-x_*(s)\|_2+M_f|T-T_*|. $ Integrating this inequality and applying [F4] gives $\|x(s)-x_*(s)\|_2\le e^{T_+L_f}(\|x-x_*\|_2+M_f|T-T_*|)$. Each initial-state or period difference is at most $\|\delta\|_2$, so step 1.1 proves the trajectory estimate.

citations.quote:
Let $\lambda$ be a simple eigenvalue of $A$, and let $x,y\ne0$ be compatible
right and left eigenvectors. Then $y^\ast x\ne0$. Consequently, after rescaling
either vector, one may impose the normalization

$$y^\ast x=1.$$

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, equipped with the standard Hermitian inner
product, and let $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ be a simple eigenvalue of $A$. A nonzero vector
$x$ is a **right eigenvector** for $\lambda$ if

$$Ax=\lambda x.$$

A nonzero vector $y$ is a **left eigenvector** for $\lambda$ if

$$y^\ast A=\lambda y^\ast,$$

equivalently $A^\ast y=\overline{\lambda}\,y$.

Such $x$ and $y$ are called **compatible left and right eigenvectors** for the
simple eigenvalue $\lambda$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

An endomorphism of a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space has a Jordan canonical form over $F$ if and only if its characteristic polynomial splits into linear factors over $F$. This includes the zero space, where the characteristic polynomial is $1$ and the Jordan form is empty.

Let $A(t)$ be differentiable, and let $\lambda(t)$ be a simple eigenvalue with
differentiable compatible eigenvectors $x(t),y(t)$ normalized by
$y(t)^\ast x(t)=1$. Then

$$\lambda'(t)=y(t)^\ast A'(t)x(t).$$

For an autonomous vector field $\dot x=f(x)$, a nonconstant solution $x_*(t)$ with least positive period $T$ has periodic orbit $\Gamma=\{x_*(t):0\le t<T\}$. Its variational fundamental matrix $Y(t)$ solves

$$\dot Y(t)=D f(x_*(t))Y(t),\qquad Y(0)=I.$$

The matrix $Y(T)$ is the **monodromy matrix**; its eigenvalues, counted with algebraic multiplicity, are the **Floquet multipliers**. The multiplier $1$ in the direction $\dot x_*(0)$ is called the **phase multiplier**.

A **local Poincare section** at $x_*(0)$ is a smooth codimension-one surface through that point whose tangent space does not contain $f(x_*(0))$. The local return map sends a nearby point on the section to its next intersection after one turn around $\Gamma$. Its derivative at $x_*(0)$ is the Poincare derivative.

The orbit is **orbitally asymptotically stable** if it is Lyapunov stable as a set and the distance from every sufficiently nearby trajectory to $\Gamma$ tends to zero as time tends to $+\infty$. It is **orbitally unstable** if it is not Lyapunov stable as a set.

Let $f(x,\mu)$ be $C^2$ on an open set in $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^p$, let $q=(x,\mu)$, and set $g(q)=(f(x,\mu),0_p)$. Write $Pq=x$. For each fixed $\mu$, let $\Phi_\theta(q)$ be the time-$\theta$ flow of $q'=g(q)$, so its parameter coordinates remain constant. For an affine phase $\psi(x)=c^\top(x-x_{\rm ref})$, define
$$
G(q,\theta)=\begin{bmatrix}P\Phi_\theta(q)-Pq\\\psi(Pq)\end{bmatrix}.
$$
For $p=0$ this is the shooting residual in [[def-phase-bordered-periodic-orbit-bvp]]. Its Jacobian is
$$
DG(q,\theta)=\begin{bmatrix}P\mathcal M-P& f(P\Phi_\theta(q),\mu)\\ c^\top P&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathcal M=D_q\Phi_\theta(q).
$$

For a rational box $Q=X\times\Lambda\times\Theta$ with $\Theta\subset(0,\infty)$, a **validated shooting jet enclosure** consists of: (i) a box containing $P\Phi_\theta(q)$ for every $q,\theta$ in the input; (ii) a box containing the residual $G(Q)$; (iii) an interval matrix $J(Q)$ containing every $DG(q,\theta)$; and (iv) trajectory and monodromy boxes containing every scaled trajectory $P\Phi_{\theta s}(q)$, $0\le s\le1$, and the physical-state block of $\mathcal M$. The boxes use [[def-real-boxes-and-interval-jacobian-enclosures]] and [[lem-real-interval-arithmetic-preserves-enclosure]]. The exact derivative formula follows from [[prop-shooting-residual-derivative]], and its flow sensitivity is on the common tube of [[lem-c1-ode-flow-on-common-tube]]. A finite success record is admissible only when obtained by the range-oracle procedure of [[alg-validated-euler-flow-and-monodromy-enclosure]], whose exact flow and monodromy enclosure is guaranteed by [[thm-validated-euler-flow-and-monodromy-enclosure-soundness]], with all queries and interval operations successful and outward under [[def-verified-flow-variational-range-oracle]]. For this call instantiate that procedure and its soundness theorem with state dimension $n=d+p$, initial state box $X\times\Lambda$, field $g(q)=(f(x,\mu),0_p)$, and period interval $\Theta$. Its augmented field is $H_g(q,Z,\theta)=(\theta g(q),\theta Dg(q)Z,0)$ with $Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$; the supplied range provider is for this $H_g$ on its actual compact convex rational tube $K_g\subset\mathbb R^{n+n^2+1}$. Initialize $Y_0=(X\times\Lambda)\times\{I_n\}\times\Theta$ and require every Euler tube query and inclusion check in this same $K_g$ to succeed. Retain the full $n\times n$ endpoint variation enclosure for $\mathcal M=D_q\Phi_\theta(q)$ when forming $P\mathcal M-P$: its first $d$ rows include both the state and parameter sensitivity columns, while its lower parameter rows are $(0,I_p)$ because the parameters are constant. The physical monodromy is the first $d$ rows and first $d$ columns of $\mathcal M$.

To enclose the period column, let $X_T$ be the first $d$ coordinate projection of the successful endpoint enclosure $Y_N$. The exact augmented endpoint lies in $X_T\times\Lambda$: its parameter equals its initial value in $\Lambda$, even if a returned interval coordinate is wider. Form the rational query box $Q_T=(X_T\times\Lambda)\times\{I_n\}\times\Theta$ and check $Q_T\subseteq K_g$ before requesting $H_g^\#(Q_T)$ from that same supplied provider. If the inclusion or query fails, return inconclusive. The first $d$ entries of its vector-field block enclose every $\theta f(P\Phi_\theta(q),\mu)$; divide these entries outward by the positive interval $\Theta$ to enclose the entire period column. Thus the query includes every admitted parameter and the matching augmented identity. For $p=0$, $n=d$ and the parameter factor is the singleton empty tuple, giving the fixed-parameter construction. These residual/Jacobian boxes are in the named coordinate order $(q,\theta)=(x,\mu,\theta)$; a section callback whose variables are ordered $(x,\theta,\mu)$ applies that fixed column permutation before appending its affine section row. Any unavailable query or inclusion returns inconclusive. A finite Newton, multiple-shooting, or collocation residual alone is not a validated jet enclosure.

derivations.claim: Since $w^*A=\lambda_0w^*$, $W$ is invariant; since $Av=\lambda_0v$ and $w^*v=1$, every vector splits uniquely as $\alpha v+y$ with $y\in W$. The restriction has no eigenvalue $\lambda_0$ by algebraic simplicity. Also $Q$ is the projection onto $W$. For $n\ge2$, its range is nonzero and $Q$ acts as the identity there, so $q\ge1$.

Let $\lambda\in D$ be an eigenvalue of $A+E$ with eigenvector $x=\alpha v+y$, $y\in W$. If $\alpha=0$, projection onto $W$ gives $y=(\lambda I_W-A_W)^{-1}QE y$. Thus $\|y\|_2\le Rq\delta\|y\|_2$, while $Rq\delta\le Rq^2\delta<1$, forcing $y=0$, contrary to $x\ne0$. Hence $\alpha\ne0$; rescale the eigenvector so $\alpha=1$.
Projecting $(A+E)(v+y)=\lambda(v+y)$ onto $W$ gives $y=(\lambda I_W-A_W)^{-1}QE(v+y)$. Therefore $\|y\|_2\le Rq\delta(1+\|y\|_2)$ and $\|y\|_2\le Rq\delta/(1-Rq\delta)$.

Applying $w^*$ to the same eigen-equation gives $\lambda-\lambda_0=w^*Ev+w^*Ey$. The first term is the first-order eigenvalue derivative [F3]; its modulus is at most $\kappa\delta$, while the second is at most $\kappa\delta\|y\|_2$. Substituting step 3.1 gives the stronger denominator $1-Rq\delta$. Since $q\ge1$, $1-Rq^2\delta\le1-Rq\delta$ and both are positive, so replacing by the smaller denominator yields the stated bound. If $A$ is monodromy, [F5] identifies $\lambda$ as a Floquet multiplier.

citations.quote: If the validator's input has $n\ge1$ and [[alg-complex-resolvent-cover-validator]] returns `certified-resolvent-cover` with bound $m$, then every $A$ in the input family and every $z$ on the supplied contour segments satisfy that $zI-A$ is invertible and $\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le m$. The result does not count eigenvalues inside the contour.

Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix and let $H$ be a direction matrix. Then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(A)H).$$

If $A$ is invertible, then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}H).$$

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $f$ be meromorphic on $\Omega$, and
let $\Gamma$ be admissible for the residue theorem in $\Omega$. Suppose in
addition that $f$ is not identically zero on any connected component of
$\Omega$ and that $f(z)\ne0$ for every $z\in\Gamma^\ast$. Then

$$\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma \frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\,dz=Z(f,\Gamma)-P(f,\Gamma),$$

where the weighted zero and pole counts are those of
[[def-weighted-zero-and-pole-counts-on-cycle]].

Only finitely many terms in those weighted counts are nonzero.

As in [[def-weighted-zero-and-pole-counts-on-cycle]], meromorphicity on the
possibly disconnected open set $\Omega$ is understood componentwise.

Let $v_0,\ldots,v_{m-1}\in\mathbb Q+i\mathbb Q$, $m\ge3$, be the cyclically ordered vertices of a simple strictly convex polygon whose edges are traversed counterclockwise. Let $P$ be its filled convex hull and let $\Gamma$ be the concatenation of its oriented edges. For every $z\notin\Gamma$, the winding number $n(\Gamma,z)$ is $1$ if $z\in\operatorname{int}P$ and $0$ if $z\notin P$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

Let $f \in \mathbb C[x]$ have degree $n \ge 1$. Then there exist distinct
complex numbers $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$ and positive integers
$m_1,\dots,m_r$ such that
$$ f(x)=c\prod_{j=1}^r (x-\alpha_j)^{m_j} $$
for some $c \in \mathbb C^\times$, with
$$ m_1+\cdots+m_r=n. $$
These exponents are uniquely determined by $f$. Equivalently, $f$ has exactly
$n$ roots counted with multiplicity.

For every $x\in\mathbb R$,

$$\frac{d}{dx}\arctan x=\frac1{1+x^2},\qquad \arctan x=\int_0^x\frac{dt}{1+t^2}.$$

For $|x|<1$,

$$\arctan x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n x^{2n+1}}{2n+1}.$$

At the endpoint, the ordinarily convergent alternating series satisfies

$$\frac\pi4=1-\frac13+\frac15-\frac17+\cdots.$$

Let $(\varepsilon_k)$ be the alternating sequence of [[lem-alternating-sequence]],
that is the unique sequence of reals with $\varepsilon_0 = 1$ and
$\varepsilon_{k+1} = -\varepsilon_k$, which is what is usually written
$\varepsilon_k = (-1)^k$; let $e$ and $o$ be its even and odd index maps, so that
$\varepsilon_{e_j} = 1$, $\varepsilon_{o_j} = -1$, and every natural number is
$e_j$ for exactly one $j$ or $o_j$ for exactly one $j$.

Let $(b_k)$ be a sequence of reals that is nonincreasing
([[def-monotone-sequence]]) and converges to $0$ ([[def-real-limit]]); then
$b_k \ge 0$ for every $k$. Write $t_n := \sum_{k<n} \varepsilon_k b_k$ for the
partial sums ([[def-series]]). Then:

1. the series $\sum \varepsilon_k b_k$ converges; write $L$ for its sum;
2. $t_{e_j} \le L \le t_{o_j}$ for every $j \in \mathbb{N}$, and for every
   $n \in \mathbb{N}$ the sum $L$ lies between the two consecutive partial sums
   $t_n$ and $t_{n+1}$;
3. $|L - t_n| \le b_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Claim 3 is the error bound: the partial sum $t_n$, which uses the $n$ terms
$\varepsilon_0 b_0, \dots, \varepsilon_{n-1}b_{n-1}$, differs from the sum by at
most the first term omitted.

**Only claim 1 is a corollary of [[thm-dirichlet-test]].** Claims 2 and 3 are not:
they come from the interlacing of the even-index and odd-index partial sums, and
that argument is carried out below rather than smuggled into the Dirichlet
estimate, which produces no bracketing at all.

Input a positive integer $n$, a nonempty complex matrix family $\mathcal M$ enclosed entrywise by finite dyadic real/imaginary rectangles, a dyadic center matrix $M_0$, a certified dyadic bound $\delta_A\ge\sup_{M\in\mathcal M}\|M-M_0\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}$, and a simple positively oriented strictly convex polygon $\Gamma$ with dyadic vertices and filled interior $P$. Supply the dyadic disk cover and point preconditioners required by [[alg-complex-resolvent-cover-validator]], a positive integer $N$ for midpoint subdivisions of each edge, a positive integer $K_\pi$ for the arctangent series, and a finite arithmetic budget. The family may be the monodromy block of a validated shooting jet; no correlation between matrix entries is required. A complex rectangle here is the product of one closed dyadic real interval and one closed dyadic imaginary interval for each matrix entry.

1. Verify the polygon orientation/strict convexity exactly, then run the resolvent-cover validator on every edge for the entire family. If any segment is uncovered, an outward inequality is not strict, or no finite upper bound $m$ on $\|(zI-M)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}$ is returned, output `inconclusive`.
2. Subdivide each oriented edge $e_j=b_j-a_j$ into $N$ equal parts, with rational midpoints $z_{jk}=a_j+(k+1/2)e_j/N$. By exact rational complex elimination, compute $R^0_{jk}=(z_{jk}I-M_0)^{-1}$; a singular center matrix or an incomplete operation returns `inconclusive`. For each rational complex entry $a+ib$ of $R^0_{jk}$, use rational square-root bisection to find an upper bound for $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, then sum row bounds to obtain $b_{jk}\ge\|R^0_{jk}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}$. Use the same bisection to obtain $s_j\ge|e_j|$. If the finite budget does not produce these rational bounds, return `inconclusive`.
3. Form the exact center midpoint sum
$$S_0=\sum_j\frac{e_j}{N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\operatorname{tr}R^0_{jk},$$
and the outward error allowance
$$E=\frac{n m^2}{2N}\sum_j|e_j|^2+\frac{n m\delta_A}{N}\sum_{j,k}s_jb_{jk}.$$
The first term uses the exact rational squared modulus of each rational edge; the second uses the rational upper edge length $s_j$. The first term bounds midpoint quadrature error; the second bounds replacing each family resolvent by the center resolvent. All sums and products are exact rationals; if a required rational square-root upper bound is unavailable, return `inconclusive`.
4. Enclose $\pi$ using $\pi=4\arctan(1)$ and the alternating partial sum $4\sum_{k=0}^{K_\pi-1}(-1)^k/(2k+1)$ with tail radius $4/(2K_\pi+1)$. Require a positive lower endpoint. Using exact rational endpoint arithmetic, enclose $S_0/(2\pi i)$ and inflate its real and imaginary intervals by $E/(2\pi_{\rm low})$; call the resulting rectangle $I$.
5. Choose an integer $c$ and return `certified-count(c)` only if $0\le c\le n$, $\operatorname{Re}I\subset(c-1/2,c+1/2)$, $\operatorname{Im}I\subset(-1/2,1/2)$, and $0\in\operatorname{Im}I$. Otherwise return `inconclusive`. This operation counts roots with algebraic multiplicity in $\operatorname{int}P$ for every matrix in the supplied family; it does not classify a cluster touching the unit circle as stable or unstable.

For a simple separated multiplier, an optional left/right-conditioned finite enclosure may also be reported using [[lem-separated-simple-floquet-multiplier-perturbation-bound]]. The contour count remains the required path for clusters or unresolved individual eigenvectors.

The matrix family may be taken from the monodromy block of [[def-validated-periodic-shooting-jet-enclosure]]. Resolvent bounds use the complex infinity norm [[def-complex-infinity-matrix-norm]] and its product inequality [[lem-complex-infinity-matrix-norm-submultiplicative]]; the boundary cover is interpreted by [[thm-complex-resolvent-cover-validator-soundness]]. Root counting uses [[thm-argument-principle-null-homologous-cycle]], the inside/outside polygon index [[lem-positive-convex-polygon-winding-index]], and the determinant derivative [[thm-determinant-differential-and-jacobis-formula]]. The root multiplicities are those of the characteristic polynomial by [[thm-complex-polynomial-has-exactly-degree-many-roots-counted-with-multiplicity]]. The rational $\pi$ enclosure uses [[thm-principal-inverse-tangent-calculus]] and [[thm-alternating-series-test]].

Use $\|A\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}$ and $\|x\|_\infty$ from [[def-complex-infinity-matrix-norm]]. For compatible complex matrices and vectors with every row and column dimension positive,
$$\|Ax\|_\infty\le\|A\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\|x\|_\infty,\qquad \|AB\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le\|A\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\|B\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}.$$

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$,
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]],
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-interval]]). Let
$M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $M \ge 0$ satisfy

$$\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } t \in (a,b).$$

Then

$$\lVert f(b) - f(a)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,(b-a).$$

**No integrability of $f'$ is assumed**, so the theorem applies to every
differentiable $f$; that is why it is proved from the scalar mean value theorem
rather than from
[[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]].
[[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]] records the comparison between the
two routes.

**The equality form is not asserted, and for $m \ge 2$ it is false.** There need
be **no** $\xi \in (a,b)$ with $f(b)-f(a) = f'(\xi)(b-a)$; the companion page
carries a differentiable witness on $[0,1]$. The $\xi$ produced in the proof
below depends on the fixed vector $u = f(b)-f(a)$ and is a mean value point of
the **real** function $t \mapsto \langle u, f(t)\rangle$, not of $f$.

derivations.claim: Fix $M\in\mathcal M$. Along an edge $z(t)=a+te$, put $R_M(t)=(z(t)I-M)^{-1}$. By [F1] this inverse exists and has norm at most $m$. For $h$ with $t,t+h\in[0,1]$, the resolvent identity gives $R_M(t+h)-R_M(t)=-heR_M(t+h)R_M(t)$. Thus [F1] and [F7] imply $\|R_M(t+h)-R_M(t)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le |h||e|m^2$, so $R_M$ is continuous; dividing the identity by $h$ and taking the limit gives $R_M\prime(t)=-eR_M(t)^2$ for interior $t$. Therefore $g(t)=e\operatorname{tr}R_M(t)$ has $g\prime(t)=-e^2\operatorname{tr}(R_M(t)^2)$. Since each diagonal entry is bounded by its row sum, $|\operatorname{tr}A|\le n\|A\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}$, so [F1] and [F7] give $|g\prime(t)|\le n|e|^2m^2$. By [F8], on each subinterval of length $1/N$, $|g(t)-g(t_{\rm mid})|\le n|e|^2m^2/(2N)$; hence the integral error on that cell is at most $n|e|^2m^2/(2N^2)$. Summing all $N$ cells and edges gives the first term of $E$.

At a sample point, the resolvent identity gives $R_M-R^0=R_M(M-M_0)R^0$. Therefore $|\operatorname{tr}(R_M-R^0)|\le nmb_{jk}\delta_A$. Multiplying by the edge weight and using $s_j\ge|e_j|$ yields the second term of $E$ after summing samples. Thus the exact contour integral $\int_\Gamma\operatorname{tr}(zI-M)^{-1}dz$ lies in the complex disk centered at $S_0$ with radius $E$, simultaneously for every $M\in\mathcal M$. Exact rational interval endpoint arithmetic and the valid $\pi$ interval [F5] make $I$ contain the normalized integral.

For each fixed $M$, put $p_M(z)=\det(zI-M)$. The boundary is in the resolvent by [F1], so $p_M$ is nonzero on $\Gamma$. By [F2] with $A=zI-M$ and direction $I$, $p_M'(z)/p_M(z)=\operatorname{tr}(zI-M)^{-1}$. Facts [F3]–[F4] therefore identify $(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\Gamma\operatorname{tr}(zI-M)^{-1}dz$ with the number of eigenvalues inside $P$, counted with algebraic multiplicity; it is an integer from $0$ to $n$.

The successful output places the real part of every such integer strictly inside the half-unit interval around $c$. There is only one integer in that interval, namely $c$. Its imaginary part is zero and is contained by the checked imaginary interval. Hence every $M$ has exactly $c$ interior eigenvalues and none on the resolvent-certified boundary. If a monodromy matrix lies in $\mathcal M$, the same universal statement applies to it.
