Report an invalid/nonpositive stored-vector norm as `breakdown`; every other invalid/out-of-range operation returns `range-failure` with its operation index and partial values.

The exact representative is $P(v)=I-2vv^*/(v^*v)$ for nonzero stored $v$. Store this product representation rather than identifying the rounded rank-one action with an exactly unitary dense matrix. For polynomial-vector initialization, form the reflector from that external vector and use its separate-block application on the entire active row panel; do not overwrite an unrelated matrix column. The proof-backed target and separate-block coefficients are supplied by [[lem-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-local-backward-error]].

Use the operationwise real/complex arithmetic model, with six-real-operation complex products and componentwise division by positive real scalars. A scaled norm of a nonzero complex vector first chooses the largest absolute real or imaginary component $s>0$, rounds every real component divided by $s$, sums their rounded squares sequentially, rounds the positive square root, and rounds multiplication by $s$. A norm of already scaled components omits the last multiplication. Zero input has exact norm zero. Reject every nonzero exact intermediate outside the normal range, nonfinite/invalid operation, and nonpositive required norm; return the first range-failure. All sign changes and conjugations are exact.

For a Householder active block $C=[x\;B]$, $x\in\mathbb C^r$, a zero $x$ copies the block with identity action. Otherwise compute $\widehat N$ by the scaled norm. If $x_1=0$ put $\widehat\phi=1$; otherwise compute its modulus $\widehat a$ by its own two-component scaled norm and divide its real and imaginary parts by $\widehat a$. Set $\widehat\alpha=-\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\phi\widehat N)$ using real-scalar component multiplication, and $v=\operatorname{fl}(x-\widehat\alpha e_1)$. Compute $w$ by sequential summation of all $2r$ rounded real component squares of $v$, and $\widehat\tau=\operatorname{fl}(2/w)$. Compute $d=\operatorname{fl}(v^*B)$, $p=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau v)$, $Z=\operatorname{fl}(pd)$, and $\widehat B=\operatorname{fl}(B-Z)$. Return $C_+=[\widehat\alpha e_1\;\widehat B]$, writing exact zeros below the target diagonal, and store $v,\widehat\tau$. Its theoretical representative is $H(v)=I-2vv^*/(v^*v)$. For a separate block application omit the column overwrite. For a right step apply these instructions to the conjugate-transposed block and transpose back.

For a Givens target pair $(a,b)$, use the identity when $b=0$, including $(0,0)$. Otherwise choose $\lambda$ as the largest absolute real/imaginary component of $(a,b)$, round $z=a/\lambda$ and $w=b/\lambda$ componentwise, and compute $h$ as the norm of their four already scaled components. If $z\ne0$, compute $n_z$ as the norm of its two components, $\widehat\phi=\operatorname{fl}(z/n_z)$, $c=\operatorname{fl}(n_z/h)$ and $s=\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\phi\overline w)/h)$. If $z=0$, set $c=0$ and $s=\operatorname{fl}(\overline w/h)$. Store $T=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-\overline s&c\end{pmatrix}$ and apply it to the chosen two rows using two complex products and one rounded componentwise addition for each output entry. For an actual target column, set its intended annihilated entry to exact zero after the update. The initial shift-vector rotation is formed from the shift vector but applied to the matrix without zeroing an unrelated matrix entry. Right applications use the conjugate-transposed form. Its exact unitary representative is $Q=T/\sqrt{c^2+|s|^2}$; this normalization defines a mathematical representative and is not an additional rounded operation.

These are arithmetic realizations of the canonical Householder and Givens methods. Returned dense transformation accumulators may be rounded; the exact unitary products used in backward-error statements are represented by the stored local data. 2. For each block, form the finite sum

All loops and matrix products have finite size. This is an exact-data evaluator;

Input a finite complex matrix $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ whose stored entries
are representable in the operationwise model, a Padé order $m\ge0$, an integer
scaling count $s\ge0$, finite nonnegative integer Householder-candidate and squaring-operation budgets,
finite scalar-series budgets, and an
error policy that is either candidate-only or certify. The procedure never
selects adaptive Higham parameters. Certification data, including contour
vertices and the radius, have exact dyadic or rational encodings.

1. Interpret the stored entries of $A$ as their exact real/imaginary values and

Continue only if the returned record contains a complete finite stored $n\times n$ matrix, with all entries marked complete, and status `verified-solution` or `candidate-unverified`. A partial candidate or any budget, range, representation or other failure is propagated with its original status and available partial record; do not square it. Retain a complete unverified candidate only in candidate-only mode; certification mode returns denominator-unverified. A complete matrix accompanying a failure status does not authorize continuation.

   Retain their exact stored real values and form

   matrix loops. Set
   $\delta_j=\max_i\sum_k(|\operatorname{Re}(D_j)_{ik}|
   +|\operatorname{Im}(D_j)_{ik}|)$; this exact nonnegative real number bounds
   $\|D_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}$.
4. In candidate-only mode, return the final candidate with status
   unevaluated-error-bound. Certification mode has these caller preconditions,
   which the procedure does not itself verify: (a) a supplied polygonal Cauchy
   cycle $\Gamma$ with dyadic vertices, trace in a disk $|z|\le\rho$ for
   dyadic $\rho>0$, $\sigma(B)\subset\{|z|<\rho\}$, disjointness from
   $\sigma(B)$, index one on $\sigma(B)$, and null-homology in that disk;
   (b) $d_m(\rho)>0$; (c) a supplied finite dyadic resolvent-cover input for
   the singleton family $\{B\}$; and (d) a finite term budget $K$.
   The contour-validator call
   [[alg-complex-resolvent-cover-validator]] must return
   certified-resolvent-cover with bound $M$, or the procedure returns
   inconclusive-resolvent. The validator checks resolvent inequalities and
   segment coverage only; it does not validate the caller's topological
   preconditions or count enclosed eigenvalues. Here $\sigma(B)$ denotes the
   eigenvalue set of $B$ from

5. For $x=\rho$ and for
   $\alpha=\max_i\sum_j(|\operatorname{Re}A_{ij}|+
   |\operatorname{Im}A_{ij}|)$, compute an upper bound $U(x)$ for $e^x$ as
   follows. If $x=0$, set $U(x)=1$. Otherwise, if $x\ge K+2$, return
   inconclusive-scalar-tail. If $x<K+2$, put
   $r=x/(K+2)$,
   $U(x)=\sum_{k=0}^Kx^k/k!+
   [x^{K+1}/(K+1)!]/(1-r)$.
   The scalar-tail inequality used by the error theorem is proved separately there; this step defines the finite expression, rather than treating a Definition sentence as its proof.
6. Write the supplied finite polygonal chain as $\Gamma=\sum_\nu m_\nu\gamma_\nu$, with integer coefficients. Let $\ell=\sum_\nu |m_\nu|\sum_{e\text{ in }\gamma_\nu}(|\Delta\operatorname{Re}e|+|\Delta\operatorname{Im}e|)$; then
   $\ell$ is an exact rational upper bound for the coefficient-weighted contour length $L_\Gamma=\sum_\nu|m_\nu|L(\gamma_\nu)$ (the supplied vertices have rational/dyadic encodings). Put
   $\epsilon=\rho^{2m+1}U(\rho)(m!)^2/
   ((2m)!(2m+1)!d_m(\rho))$. Since
   $\pi/4=\int_0^1(1+x^2)^{-1}\,dx$, the finite identity
   $1/(1+x^2)=\sum_{k=0}^7(-1)^kx^{2k}+x^{16}/(1+x^2)$ on $[0,1]$ gives
   $\pi/4>33976/45045>3/4$, hence $1/(2\pi)<1/6$. Set
   $E_0=\ell\epsilon M/6$.

   If every computed certification check succeeded, the denominator solve
   returned verified-solution, and the caller preconditions hold, return the
   final candidate with status conditional-error-bound and bound $E_s$.

For admitted inputs of [[alg-finite-budget-francis-schur-reduction]], including its terminating sign and outward-bound evaluators when supplied, the procedure terminates with one of its defined main statuses after finite initialization and at most $N$ sweeps. Its separate backward-certificate flag is `certified` only when every required local/evaluator bound is available, and otherwise is `inconclusive`. A `Schur-computed` return has the verified real or complex block pattern; its recorded exact reflector product is unitary. This asserts neither an exact Schur factorization of the original matrix nor convergence of any shift schedule, a forward spectral bound, or exact unitarity of a rounded dense product.

For admitted inputs of [[alg-bartels-stewart-sylvester-equation]], the procedure terminates with a declared status, using its finite Schur controls and bounded controller programs or the stated arbitrary-terminating controller mode. Every stored local solve is unique. On `success`, the full equation $AX+XB=C$ has exactly one solution, namely the returned $X$, without an additional spectral-disjointness assumption: successful exact local pivot checks themselves imply invertibility of the full block operator. Failure or a positive threshold rejection proves neither singularity nor nonexistence unless its exact tests explicitly do so.

Input a finite complex matrix $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, a
holomorphic function $f$ on a neighborhood of $\sigma(A)$ with the finite
derivative data required by the diagonal block evaluators, Schur controls, a
Sylvester separation threshold $\tau\ge0$, and a finite table of exact Jordan
certificates indexed by contiguous diagonal block intervals.

1. Call [[alg-finite-budget-francis-schur-reduction]] in its complex branch.
   Propagate any non-Schur status. Treat its returned $Q,T$ as candidates.
2. Verify by exact arithmetic that $Q^*Q=I$, $A=QTQ^*$, and $T$ is upper
   triangular. If any identity fails, return schur-certificate-failure. The
   computed Schur routine's residual diagnostic alone does not pass this test.
3. Start from the supplied contiguous block partition of $T$. For each block
   $T_{ii}$ call [[alg-exact-jordan-block-analytic-evaluation]] with its exact
   Jordan certificate and return value $F_{ii}$. If a certificate or required
   derivative is missing, return missing-jordan-data.
4. Visit block pairs by increasing distance $j-i$. Form
   $$C_{ij}=F_{ii}T_{ij}-T_{ij}F_{jj} +\sum_{i<k<j}(F_{ik}T_{kj}-T_{ik}F_{kj}).$$
   Call [[alg-bartels-stewart-sylvester-equation]] on
   $T_{ii}F_{ij}+F_{ij}(-T_{jj})=C_{ij}$ with threshold $\tau$. On an exact unique solve, store
   $F_{ij}$. If the solve reports a separation or pivot failure and the
   partition has multiple blocks, merge the contiguous blocks from $i$ through
   $j$, discard their old diagonal data, and restart step 3. Each merge reduces
   the block count, so there are at most $n-1$ merges. A different solve,
   range, or budget failure is returned as inconclusive-sylvester.

success branch requires exact Schur and local solve certificates.

Input a finite complex matrix $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ with $n\ge1$, a branch request selecting principal

Input $n\ge1$ and a nonempty finite union of complex line segments $\Gamma$, with each segment assigned to a proposed disk $D_j=B(z_j,r_j)$; a nonempty matrix family $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ enclosed by complex rectangles; a point center matrix $A_0\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$; and proposed point preconditioners $R_j\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$. 1. For each assigned segment verify that both endpoints lie in its disk by exact rational comparison of squared distances with $r_j^2$. Evaluate outward bounds
$$e_j\ge\|I-R_j(z_jI-A_0)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad \delta_A\ge\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}\|A-A_0\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad s_j\ge\|R_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}$$
using the complex rectangle operations and row sums of outward modulus bounds. If any check or operation cannot be completed, return `inconclusive`.

2. Outward-compute $q_j=e_j+s_j(r_j+\delta_A)$. Require $q_j<1$ for every disk and compute an outward upper bound $m\ge\max_j s_j/(1-q_j)$. If a strict inequality or division cannot be certified, return `inconclusive`; otherwise return `certified-resolvent-cover` with the disk assignments and $m$.

The validated endpoint cover covers each whole segment because disks are convex. Success certifies a resolvent bound on this supplied contour cover, but this procedure does not count enclosed eigenvalues or validate contour topology.

derivations.claim: Expand each candidate macro in [F1] into the actual [F2] scalar schedule. Induct over executed primitive requests: before a request the counter equals the number already executed. If the counter is $K_H$, no primitive is evaluated and the dispatcher returns exhaustion; otherwise it increments once and performs exactly the next prescribed rounded primitive. Thus it executes at most $K_H$ primitives and has the same intermediate values, branches and first arithmetic failure as the original schedule whenever the budget allows that prefix. Zero-column identity branches copy data and do not evaluate a zero-vector reflector denominator. Finite source index loops and finite exact control branches preclude a nonterminating primitive-free loop.

Each conversion, reflector, separate RHS application and triangular solve has finite dimensions. By step 1.1 their composition returns its defined result or a first budget/range/candidate failure in finite time. The completion mask is set only after each actual solution entry is computed; [F1] permits the exact row-major residual audit only after all $nr$ entries are set. That audit has $nr$ finite inner products and exact component tests, or the explicit finite-codebook adapter/failure, hence terminates. Neither partial values nor an unavailable representation are labeled a verified solution.

The Jordan routine checks finitely many exact identities and block entries and evaluates finitely many finite nilpotent sums using the supplied jets; missing data fail. Thus [F3] terminates. The Padé procedure forms finite polynomial matrices and calls the terminating solve of step 2.1 with $K_H$. Its complete-candidate gate excludes every partial or failure status from squaring. Each of its $s$ squares has finite scalar loops and a before-primitive squaring-budget check, proved bounded by the same counter argument as step 1.1. Exact defects, the finite series/tail expressions and the $s$ bound recurrences are finite; the finite cover validator in [F9] either succeeds or fails. Therefore every Padé path returns a declared status, and a failure/partial candidate cannot be interpreted as a conditional error-bound success.

Each polar/sign iteration makes one finite-budget denominator call and only continues on its complete verified solution; otherwise it returns the solve status and the last candidate. Its component update has finitely many operations and explicit range failures. At most $N$ such iterations occur by [F5], including no iteration at $N=0$, proving termination and the stated budget/status separation without asserting convergence of rounded iterates.

By [F6], each delegated Schur or Sylvester call terminates. A fixed Schur–Parlett partition has finitely many block pairs and Jordan calls, terminating by step 3.1 and [F6]. Each merge strictly lowers the initial block count, which is at most $n$, so at most $n-1$ restarts occur. Every other failure is returned. Thus [F7] terminates. The principal-function routine adds only finitely many exact branch/sign comparisons before that procedure, or an unavailable-comparison return, so [F8] also terminates. Its branch test supplies no claim beyond its original spectral/holomorphic-domain assumptions.

Steps 1.1–4.1 cover all seven procedures and their return branches. They bound only the explicitly counted rounded operations and finite loop counts; they neither bound the work of arbitrary-real exact arithmetic nor establish any separate analytic/error/iteration convergence premise. This is exactly the stated separation between termination, candidate generation and mathematical certificates.

derivations.claim: The matrix $C$ is symmetric because $K$ and $I$ are symmetric. For every nonzero $v$, $v^TCv=v^TKv+\sigma^2\|v\|_2^2$. If $\sigma^2>0$, the first term is nonnegative and the second is strictly positive, so $v^TCv>0$; hence $C$ is positive definite by [F1].

Let $x\in[l_x,u_x]$ and $y\in[l_y,u_y]$, where all four endpoints are finite and ordered, and let $w$ be an additional real variable representing the product $xy$. The **McCormick polytope** for this box is the set of $(x,y,w)$ satisfying the box bounds and
$$ w\ge l_xy+l_yx-l_xl_y,\qquad w\ge u_xy+u_yx-u_xu_y $$
$$ w\le u_xy+l_yx-u_xl_y,\qquad w\le l_xy+u_yx-l_xu_y $$
The term **McCormick envelope** will mean this polytope. Its exact relation to the convex hull of the product graph is established by the local bilinear-hull result.

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

derivations.claim: On the graph $w=xy$, subtracting the first lower plane from $xy$ gives $(x-l_x)(y-l_y)\ge0$, and subtracting the second lower plane gives $(u_x-x)(u_y-y)\ge0$. Subtracting $xy$ from the first upper plane gives $(u_x-x)(y-l_y)\ge0$, and subtracting it from the second upper plane gives $(x-l_x)(u_y-y)\ge0$. Thus every graph point satisfies all four inequalities.

If both widths are positive, put $s=u_x-l_x>0$, $t=u_y-l_y>0$, $X=(x-l_x)/s$, $Y=(y-l_y)/t$, and $W=(w-l_xy-l_yx+l_xl_y)/(st)$. The inequalities become $0\le X,Y\le1$, $W\ge0$, $W\ge X+Y-1$, $W\le X$, and $W\le Y$.

Every defining bound and McCormick inequality is affine in $(x,y,w)$. If two points satisfy one such affine inequality, their line segment also satisfies it by linearity, so the polytope is convex by [F2]. By step 1.1 every graph point lies in this polytope, and therefore each finite convex combination of graph points lies there by repeated segment closure [L1].

If $u_x=l_x$, the first lower and first upper inequalities force $w=l_xy$; all graph points satisfy the other inequalities by step 1.1. For any $y,y'\in[l_y,u_y]$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$, the segment between $(l_x,y,l_xy)$ and $(l_x,y',l_xy')$ is $(l_x,\theta y+(1-\theta)y',l_x(\theta y+(1-\theta)y'))$, again on the graph. If $u_y=l_y$, the first lower and second upper inequalities force $w=x l_y$, and the same calculation with $x,x'\in[l_x,u_x]$ proves convexity. Thus either degenerate case gives the product graph itself.

In the nondegenerate case of step 1.2, set $\lambda_{11}=W$, $\lambda_{10}=X-W$, $\lambda_{01}=Y-W$, and $\lambda_{00}=1-X-Y+W$. Step 1.2 makes each coefficient nonnegative; their sum is $1$, and $(X,Y,W)=\lambda_{00}(0,0,0)+\lambda_{10}(1,0,0)+\lambda_{01}(0,1,0)+\lambda_{11}(1,1,1)$. Each vertex lies on $W=XY$, so every normalized polytope point is a convex combination of graph points.

If either width is zero, step 2.2 gives equality directly. If both are positive, the affine map in step 1.2 is invertible, and steps 2.1 and 2.3 prove both inclusions after normalization. These cases exhaust the ordered endpoint choices, proving equality of the original polytope and graph convex hull.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Assume AC and let $f=(f_t)_{t\in T}$ be a real Gaussian process with mean
$m$ and covariance kernel $k$; when $m$ and $k$ are specified as a prior,
the canonical cylinder-space process exists by
[[thm-gaussian-process-exists-from-mean-and-positive-semidefinite-covariance-kernel]].
Let $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in T^n$ and $X_*=(x_1^*,\ldots,x_p^*)\in T^p$,
where $n,p\ge1$ and repeated indices are allowed. Write
$f_X=(f_{x_i})_{i=1}^n$, $f_{X_*}=(f_{x_j^*})_{j=1}^p$,
$m_X=(m(x_i))_{i=1}^n$, and $m_*=(m(x_j^*))_{j=1}^p$. For finite lists
$A=(a_i)$ and $B=(b_j)$, define
$K_{AB}=(k(a_i,b_j))_{i,j}$.

Let $\epsilon\sim N_n(0,R)$ be independent of the process, where $R$ is
symmetric positive semidefinite, and set $Y=f_X+\epsilon$. Assume the
observed covariance $C=K_{XX}+R$ is positive definite. Then a version of the
conditional law of $f_{X_*}$ given $Y=y$ is, for every $y\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$N_p\!\left(m_*+K_{*X}C^{-1}(y-m_X),\;K_{**}-K_{*X}C^{-1}K_{X*}\right).$$
The displayed conditional covariance is positive semidefinite and may be
singular; $K_{XX}$ and $K_{**}$ may also be singular. If a prediction-noise
vector $\eta_*\sim N_p(0,R_*)$ jointly independent of the process and
$\epsilon$ is added to $f_{X_*}$, with $R_*$ symmetric positive semidefinite,
the conditional mean is unchanged and
$R_*$ is added to the conditional covariance. The displayed kernel is a
version defined at every $y$; conditional-law versions are determined only
$P_Y$-almost surely.

For computation, the occurrences of $C^{-1}v$ mean solving $Cu=v$. Since
$C$ is positive definite, its Cholesky factorization and forward/back
substitution evaluate these solves without forming $C^{-1}$.

the canonical cylinder-space process exists by

Input a candidate list $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_M)$, a horizon parameter $N$, an initial-list length $s$, a real-mean candidate $m$, a kernel candidate $k$, an observation-variance candidate $\sigma^2$, acquisition-coefficient candidates $b_t$, an initial data list $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^s$, an observation oracle $O$, and a deterministic candidate-selection routine. First validate that $X$ is nonempty, finite and ordered, $N$ and $s$ are integers with $N\ge0$ and $0\le s\le N$, every initial site lies in $X$, all mean, kernel, noise, coefficient and observation values are finite reals, the kernel matrix on $X$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, $\sigma^2\ge0$, and every $b_t\ge0$. If any validation fails, return inadmissible-model before computing a posterior. The observation oracle must finish each call in finite time and return either a finite real observation or observation-unavailable. For a true-posterior interpretation, the initial sites are fixed before their observations and each observation is $f(x_i)+\xi_i$ under this model, with errors independent centered Gaussian variables of variance $\sigma^2$ and independent of the entire process. Otherwise the procedure computes only the all-data-vector posterior kernel for the specified surrogate and makes no claim that it is the conditional law of an externally supplied data-generating process. The Axiom of Choice is included as required by [[thm-finite-gaussian-process-posterior-and-predictive-laws]].

Write $X_t=(x_1,\ldots,x_t)$, $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_t)$, $m_{X_t}=(m(x_i))_{i\le t}$, and $k_t(x)=(k(x_i,x))_{i\le t}$. The initial data list has length $s$, so the current history length starts at $t=s$ and the procedure selects at stages $t=s,\ldots,N-1$, stopping when the total history length reaches $N$. The output is the finite selected-site/observation trace, its current posterior state, and every verified acquisition error $\delta_t$. For $t=0$, use prior mean $\mu_0(x)=m(x)$ and variance $v_0(x)=k(x,x)$, with no matrix inverse. For $t\ge1$, form $K_t=(k(x_i,x_j))_{i,j\le t}$ and $C_t=K_t+\sigma^2 I$. If $C_t$ is not certified positive definite, return posterior-solve-unavailable with the last valid state and no posterior or acquisition at stage $t$. If $C_t$ is positive definite, compute the required solves by a Cholesky factorization $C_t=L_tL_t^T$ and forward/back substitution as in [[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]] and [[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]]. If a factorization or solve is unavailable, return the same status; never use a pseudoinverse or clip a negative variance.

For each candidate, compute
$$\mu_t(x)=m(x)+k_t(x)^T C_t^{-1}(y-m_{X_t})$$
$$v_t(x)=k(x,x)-k_t(x)^T C_t^{-1}k_t(x),\qquad s_t(x)=\sqrt{v_t(x)}$$
where the observed covariance and solves satisfy the hypotheses of [[thm-finite-gaussian-process-posterior-and-predictive-laws]]. Its conditional covariance is positive semidefinite, so $v_t(x)\ge0$; [[thm-of-square-roots]] supplies the unique nonnegative square root used here. If nonnegativity of a computed $v_t(x)$ cannot be verified, return posterior-solve-unavailable. Form the acquisition value $a_t(x)=\mu_t(x)+b_t s_t(x)$ and inspect all $M$ candidates. The default routine returns the exact least-index maximizer with $\delta_t=0$. An optional approximate routine must be a deterministic measurable function of the finite observation history and return a candidate $x_{j_t}$ with a verified $\delta_t\ge0$ satisfying $a_t(x_{j_t})\ge\max_{x\in X}a_t(x)-\delta_t$. If no such comparison certificate is available, return acquisition-inconclusive. Record every $\delta_t$.

Call $O$ at the selected candidate. If it returns observation-unavailable, return that status with the current trace and last valid posterior state, without appending a value. Otherwise append the returned observation and repeat until the finite horizon is reached. A finite budget exhaustion returns the current trace and no unearned posterior status. For a deterministic simulator or a misspecified prior, these formulas describe only the chosen surrogate model; the algorithm asserts no generic regret, global-optimality, or model-truth result.

derivations.claim: At the initial history, no adaptive observations have yet been added; if the supplied fixed initial list is empty, the conditional law is the given GP prior, and otherwise [F1] gives its posterior whenever its observed covariance is positive definite. The all-data-vector posterior version in [F1] fixes the kernel for every possible observed value.

Assume as the induction hypothesis that the posterior formula is valid after a finite history $H_t$. By [F3], the next candidate index is a measurable function of $H_t$; the finite tie rule (and any measurable deterministic certified $\delta_t$ routine) therefore adds no information beyond $H_t$. Conditional on $H_t$, this site is fixed. The fresh observation error is independent of the process and previous errors by [A2]. Hence the conditional joint law of the candidate process values and new noisy observation is exactly the fixed-list Gaussian model in [F1], using the augmented selected-site list and its positive-definite observed covariance.

Applying [F1] to that augmented list yields the stated posterior after the new observation for every observed value. This proves the induction step, including repeated selected sites whenever the augmented covariance remains positive definite. If the solve is unavailable, the algorithm returns before asserting this step.

Induction over the finite successful history proves the sequential posterior formula at every history before a failure status. The argument uses only conditional Gaussian updating and the history-measurable finite selection rule, so it gives no regret or global-optimality conclusion.

Input a candidate list $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_M)$, a horizon parameter $N$, an initial-list length $s$, a real-mean candidate $m$, a kernel candidate $k$, an observation-variance candidate $\sigma^2$, acquisition-coefficient candidates $b_t$, an initial data list $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^s$, an observation oracle $O$, and a deterministic candidate-selection routine. First validate that $X$ is nonempty, finite and ordered, $N$ and $s$ are integers with $N\ge0$ and $0\le s\le N$, every initial site lies in $X$, all mean, kernel, noise, coefficient and observation values are finite reals, the kernel matrix on $X$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, $\sigma^2\ge0$, and every $b_t\ge0$. If any validation fails, return inadmissible-model before computing a posterior. The observation oracle must finish each call in finite time and return either a finite real observation or observation-unavailable. For a true-posterior interpretation, the initial sites are fixed before their observations and each observation is $f(x_i)+\xi_i$ under this model, with errors independent centered Gaussian variables of variance $\sigma^2$ and independent of the entire process. Otherwise the procedure computes only the all-data-vector posterior kernel for the specified surrogate and makes no claim that it is the conditional law of an externally supplied data-generating process. The Axiom of Choice is included as required by [[thm-finite-gaussian-process-posterior-and-predictive-laws]].

Write $X_t=(x_1,\ldots,x_t)$, $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_t)$, $m_{X_t}=(m(x_i))_{i\le t}$, and $k_t(x)=(k(x_i,x))_{i\le t}$. The initial data list has length $s$, so the current history length starts at $t=s$ and the procedure selects at stages $t=s,\ldots,N-1$, stopping when the total history length reaches $N$. The output is the finite selected-site/observation trace, its current posterior state, and every verified acquisition error $\delta_t$. For $t=0$, use prior mean $\mu_0(x)=m(x)$ and variance $v_0(x)=k(x,x)$, with no matrix inverse. For $t\ge1$, form $K_t=(k(x_i,x_j))_{i,j\le t}$ and $C_t=K_t+\sigma^2 I$. If $C_t$ is not certified positive definite, return posterior-solve-unavailable with the last valid state and no posterior or acquisition at stage $t$. If $C_t$ is positive definite, compute the required solves by a Cholesky factorization $C_t=L_tL_t^T$ and forward/back substitution as in [[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]] and [[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]]. If a factorization or solve is unavailable, return the same status; never use a pseudoinverse or clip a negative variance.

For each candidate, compute
$$\mu_t(x)=m(x)+k_t(x)^T C_t^{-1}(y-m_{X_t})$$
$$v_t(x)=k(x,x)-k_t(x)^T C_t^{-1}k_t(x),\qquad s_t(x)=\sqrt{v_t(x)}$$
where the observed covariance and solves satisfy the hypotheses of [[thm-finite-gaussian-process-posterior-and-predictive-laws]]. Its conditional covariance is positive semidefinite, so $v_t(x)\ge0$; [[thm-of-square-roots]] supplies the unique nonnegative square root used here. If nonnegativity of a computed $v_t(x)$ cannot be verified, return posterior-solve-unavailable. Form the acquisition value $a_t(x)=\mu_t(x)+b_t s_t(x)$ and inspect all $M$ candidates. The default routine returns the exact least-index maximizer with $\delta_t=0$. An optional approximate routine must be a deterministic measurable function of the finite observation history and return a candidate $x_{j_t}$ with a verified $\delta_t\ge0$ satisfying $a_t(x_{j_t})\ge\max_{x\in X}a_t(x)-\delta_t$. If no such comparison certificate is available, return acquisition-inconclusive. Record every $\delta_t$.

Call $O$ at the selected candidate. If it returns observation-unavailable, return that status with the current trace and last valid posterior state, without appending a value. Otherwise append the returned observation and repeat until the finite horizon is reached. A finite budget exhaustion returns the current trace and no unearned posterior status. For a deterministic simulator or a misspecified prior, these formulas describe only the chosen surrogate model; the algorithm asserts no generic regret, global-optimality, or model-truth result.

Each successful stage appends one observation, so at most $N$ horizon stages occur; after the last stage the method returns its trace. If validation fails or any solve, comparison, or observation reports unavailable, the algorithm returns immediately. Thus all branches terminate after finitely many operations.

Input a compact-box instance $(D_0,C,f)$ from [[def-spatial-global-optimization-problem]], a tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, a positive integer node budget $N$, and a deterministic box-report oracle implementing [[def-spatial-box-bound-certificate]]. Every oracle call must finish in finite time or return an unavailable status. The budget counts each oracle call, including the root and both children after every split. The oracle may request higher precision on a repeated box; each such refinement is another counted call.

Initialize a leaf ledger with the root box $D_0$, no incumbent, and zero calls. Before every oracle call, if the call counter is already $N$, return the complete current ledger with budget-exhausted; otherwise call the oracle and increment the counter by one. Store every returned field. A feasible witness $(x,U_x)$ updates the incumbent upper bound to $U=\min U_x$. An empty-box proof marks that leaf empty. For constraints $g_i(x)\le0$, a sound interval lower bound $\underline g_i(B)>0$ is an empty-box proof. Store every valid lower bound $\ell_B$ even if the leaf is later closed. A missing or non-finite required field returns inconclusive; it never becomes a bound.

Whenever all current leaves have been evaluated, first return infeasible if they are all certified empty. Otherwise put $L=\min\{\ell_B:B\text{ is not certified empty}\}$ if every nonempty leaf has a lower bound. If $U<+\infty$, $L$ is finite, and $U-L\le\varepsilon$, return a feasible witness and the epsilon-global certificate $(L,U)$. Mark any leaf with $\ell_B\ge U-\varepsilon$ closed while retaining its lower bound.

If no certificate is returned and no pending child awaits evaluation, split the nonclosed leaf with least lower bound; ties use creation order. In a box with positive widths, bisect a longest coordinate at its exact midpoint, using the least coordinate index among ties. The two closed children cover their parent. In the unconstrained mode, the oracle returns the exact midpoint as a feasible witness and exact objective value; the termination theorem uses this mode. For a zero-width singleton that has not been certified, request a deterministic higher-precision report for that same point; each refinement consumes one call. If refinement is unavailable, return inconclusive. When no certificate or infeasibility result has been established and another oracle call is needed after $N$ calls, the pre-call guard returns the complete current ledger with no optimality claim. This finite-budget procedure is global-search bookkeeping: a local stationary point or a solver tolerance is not a lower-bound certificate.

Fix an instance $(D_0,C,f)$ from [[def-spatial-global-optimization-problem]] and a closed subbox $B\subseteq D_0$. A **certified box report** may contain any combination of the following fields:

- A **feasible witness** $(x_B,U_B)$, with $x_B\in B\cap C$ and a verified upper bound $f(x_B)\le U_B$.
- A **lower bound** $\ell_B\in\mathbb R$ satisfying $\ell_B\le f(x)$ for every $x\in B\cap C$. This pointwise condition is vacuous when $B\cap C=\emptyset$; when $B\cap C\ne\emptyset$, it is equivalent to $\ell_B\le\inf_{x\in B\cap C}f(x)$.
- An **empty-box proof** establishing $B\cap C=\emptyset$.
- A non-finite or unavailable status, which makes no feasibility, lower-bound, or optimality claim.

A box is **closed** for a requested tolerance $\varepsilon>0$ only when it has a lower bound and $\ell_B\ge U-\varepsilon$, where $U$ is the best currently verified feasible upper bound. Closing a box stops further subdivision but retains its lower bound in the global ledger. A report lacking a required field is not repaired by a numerical guess.

derivations.claim: At the start of a call, if the counter is $N$ the algorithm returns by [F1]. Otherwise it consumes exactly one unit for that call; every branch either schedules a finite two-child list or reaches a stated return condition.

After at most $N$ evaluations, either a certificate, infeasibility result, or oracle status has already returned, or another call is required and the pre-call guard returns budget-exhausted. Each oracle call terminates by the Given condition, and each unavailable report has the explicit no-claim meaning in [F2], so the procedure terminates within at most $N$ calls.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

No choice principle is used: both covers below are given by a rule, and the
indexed form of [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] returns indices rather than
sets.

**The converse is false in general.** A closed and bounded subset of an arbitrary
metric space need not be compact
([[fs-closed-and-bounded-implies-compact-in-every-metric-space]]); it is exactly
in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that the converse holds ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below. Then $S$ has a
greatest lower bound in $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-infimum]]), and it is given by

$$\inf S = -\sup(-S), \qquad \text{where } -S = \{-s : s \in S\}.$$

In particular the complete ordered field $\mathbb{R}$ has the
greatest-lower-bound property, which is therefore not an extra axiom: it is a
consequence of the least-upper-bound property.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below, and let $\ell$ be a
lower bound of $S$ ([[def-bounded-set]]). Then

$$\ell = \inf S \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \text{for every } \varepsilon > 0 \text{ there exists } s \in S \text{ with } s < \ell + \varepsilon.$$

In words: among the lower bounds of $S$, the infimum is exactly the one that
cannot be raised by any positive amount and still bound $S$ from below.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $A \subseteq X$,
with closure, derived set and limit points as in
[[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]. Then:

1. If $A \ne \emptyset$, then $\overline{A} = \{\, x \in X : d(x,A) = 0 \,\}$,
   where $d(x,A)$ is the distance from a point to a nonempty set
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
2. $\overline{A} = A \cup A'$.
3. $\overline{A}$ is closed, contains $A$, and is contained in every closed
   $F \subseteq X$ with $A \subseteq F$. So $\overline{A}$ is the smallest closed
   superset of $A$, and $A$ is closed if and only if $A = \overline{A}$.

Claims 2 and 3 hold for every $A$, the empty set included: $\overline{\emptyset}$
is empty because no ball meets $\emptyset$, and $\emptyset$ is closed because $X$
is open ([[def-metric-topology]]). Claim 1 carries the hypothesis $A \ne \emptyset$
because $d(x,A)$ is defined only for nonempty $A$
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

Define $d_{\mathbb{R}} : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) := |x - y|$ ([[def-abs-value]]). Then:

1. $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-metric-space]]); it is
   called the **usual metric** of $\mathbb{R}$.
2. For $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $r > 0$ the open ball is the bounded open interval
   ([[def-interval]], [[def-metric-ball]])
   $$B(x,r) = (x-r,\ x+r),$$
   and the closed ball is $\bar B(x,r) = [x-r,\ x+r]$.
3. Consequently $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is open in the metric topology of
   $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ ([[def-metric-topology]]) exactly when for every $x \in U$
   there is $r > 0$ with $(x-r, x+r) \subseteq U$. This topology is called the
   **usual topology** of $\mathbb{R}$.
4. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ is not a bounded metric space
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]): no ball contains $\mathbb{R}$, so
   $\operatorname{diam}(\mathbb{R})$ is not defined.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$A, B \subseteq X$.

**Bounded subset.** $A$ is **bounded** if $A = \emptyset$ or there are $x_0 \in X$
and a real $r > 0$ with $A \subseteq B(x_0, r)$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). The space
$(X,d)$ is a **bounded metric space** if $X$ is a bounded subset of itself.

**Diameter, for nonempty bounded $A$ only.** Suppose $A$ is nonempty and
bounded, and put

$$D(A) := \{\, d(a,b) : a, b \in A \,\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}.$$

Then $D(A)$ is nonempty, since $A$ is, and it is bounded above: fixing $x_0$ and
$r$ with $A \subseteq B(x_0,r)$, every $a, b \in A$ satisfy
$d(a,b) \le d(a,x_0) + d(x_0,b) < r + r$ by the triangle inequality, symmetry
([[def-metric-space]]) and addition of inequalities ([[lem-of-add-order]],
[[def-ordered-field]]), so $r + r$ is an upper bound of $D(A)$
([[def-bounded-set]]). Hence $D(A)$ has a least upper bound in $\mathbb{R}$ by
the least-upper-bound property ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), and that bound
is unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]). Define

$$\operatorname{diam}(A) := \sup D(A).$$

**Distance from a point to a set, for nonempty $A$ only.** Let $x \in X$ and let
$A$ be nonempty, and put $E(x,A) := \{\, d(x,a) : a \in A \,\}$. Then $E(x,A)$ is
nonempty and bounded below by $0$, since a metric is nonnegative
([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]], [[def-bounded-set]]), so it has a greatest lower
bound ([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]), unique by [[lem-sup-unique]].
Define

$$d(x,A) := \inf E(x,A).$$

**Distance between two sets, for nonempty $A$ and $B$ only.** Put
$E(A,B) := \{\, d(a,b) : a \in A,\ b \in B \,\}$, again nonempty and bounded
below by $0$, and define

$$d(A,B) := \inf E(A,B).$$

**Every one of the three scope restrictions is load bearing.** In this library
$\sup$ and $\inf$ denote real numbers and are written only after existence has
been established; the least-upper-bound property of [[def-complete-ordered-field]] and the
greatest-lower-bound property of [[thm-infimum-property]] apply to nonempty
real sets with the respective bounds. Empty or unbounded sets acquire no
real supremum or infimum by convention. Accordingly:

- $\operatorname{diam}(A)$ is defined exactly when $A$ is nonempty **and**
  bounded. It is not defined for $A = \emptyset$, and it is not defined, not even
  as an infinite value, for an unbounded $A$.
- $d(x,A)$ is defined exactly when $A \ne \emptyset$, and $d(A,B)$ exactly when
  both $A$ and $B$ are nonempty. No boundedness is needed for these two, because
  $0$ is always a lower bound.

For each $k \in \mathbb{N}$ let $I_k = [a_k, b_k]$ be a closed bounded interval
with $a_k \le b_k$ ([[def-interval]]), and suppose the family is **nested**:

$$I_{k+1} \subseteq I_k \qquad (k \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $\ell_k = b_k - a_k \ge 0$ for the length of $I_k$. Then:

1. $\displaystyle\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k$ is **nonempty**. More precisely,
   with $a = \sup\{a_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ and
   $b = \inf\{b_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$, both of which exist, one has $a \le b$
   and $$\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k = [a, b].$$
2. $\displaystyle\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k$ is a **single point** if and only
   if $\ell_k \to 0$ ([[def-real-limit]]).

Every hypothesis is load bearing. Dropping closedness makes the intersection
empty; dropping boundedness does the same; and dropping nonemptiness of the
individual intervals is vacuously fatal.

derivations.claim: The box $D_0$ is nonempty (its left-endpoint vector belongs to it) and compact by [F1]. Therefore $f[D_0]$ is nonempty and compact by [F2], hence closed and bounded. By the boundedness definition and [F5], there are $c\in\mathbb R$ and $r>0$ such that $f[D_0]\subseteq(c-r,c+r)$, so $c-r$ is a lower bound. Let $f^*=\inf f[D_0]$, which exists by [F3]. For every $\eta>0$, [F3] gives $y\in f[D_0]$ with $f^*\le y<f^*+\eta$; by [F5] every open ball around $f^*$ meets $f[D_0]$. Thus $f^*\in\overline{f[D_0]}$ by [F4], and closedness gives $f^*\in f[D_0]$. So $f$ attains its minimum on $D_0$, and every feasible objective value is at least $f^*$.

The incumbent upper bounds $U_k$ are nonincreasing, and each is at least the attained minimum $f^*$ by step 1.1 and [A2]. If the unlimited continuation did not terminate, it would expand infinitely many boxes. The expansion tree is binary, so there is an infinite nested branch: recursively take the left child if it has infinitely many expanded descendants and otherwise take the right child. This rule is deterministic and requires no choice principle.

Along this branch, longest-side bisection makes every side length tend to zero. Fix $\eta>0$. Each coordinate can be halved only finitely many times while its side length is at least $\eta$, because each halving divides a finite initial length by two and never increases it. There are finitely many coordinates, and every split whose box has a side of length at least $\eta$ halves one such longest side, so only finitely many such splits occur. Thus the maximum side length tends to zero. The nested closed coordinate intervals have a unique common point in each coordinate by [F7], giving $x\in D_0$.

Each expanded box on the branch was nonclosed, so [F6] gives $\ell(B_k)<U_k-\varepsilon$. Consistency [A1] implies $\ell(B_k)\to f(x)$. Its midpoint $m_k$ tends to $x$, and [A2] gives the exact midpoint upper $U(B_k)=f(m_k)$, which tends to $f(x)$ by continuity. Since $U_{k+1}\le U(B_k)$, the limit $U_\infty=\lim_k U_k$ satisfies $U_\infty\le f(x)$. Taking limits in the strict lower-bound inequalities yields $f(x)\le U_\infty-\varepsilon$, contradicting $\varepsilon>0$.

Thus the unlimited continuation cannot expand infinitely many boxes without meeting $U-L\le\varepsilon$. It reaches that certificate after finitely many calls, so any larger finite call budget returns it.

Input a compact-box instance $(D_0,C,f)$ from [[def-spatial-global-optimization-problem]], a tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, a positive integer node budget $N$, and a deterministic box-report oracle implementing [[def-spatial-box-bound-certificate]]. Every oracle call must finish in finite time or return an unavailable status. The budget counts each oracle call, including the root and both children after every split. The oracle may request higher precision on a repeated box; each such refinement is another counted call.

Initialize a leaf ledger with the root box $D_0$, no incumbent, and zero calls. Before every oracle call, if the call counter is already $N$, return the complete current ledger with budget-exhausted; otherwise call the oracle and increment the counter by one. Store every returned field. A feasible witness $(x,U_x)$ updates the incumbent upper bound to $U=\min U_x$. An empty-box proof marks that leaf empty. For constraints $g_i(x)\le0$, a sound interval lower bound $\underline g_i(B)>0$ is an empty-box proof. Store every valid lower bound $\ell_B$ even if the leaf is later closed. A missing or non-finite required field returns inconclusive; it never becomes a bound.

Whenever all current leaves have been evaluated, first return infeasible if they are all certified empty. Otherwise put $L=\min\{\ell_B:B\text{ is not certified empty}\}$ if every nonempty leaf has a lower bound. If $U<+\infty$, $L$ is finite, and $U-L\le\varepsilon$, return a feasible witness and the epsilon-global certificate $(L,U)$. Mark any leaf with $\ell_B\ge U-\varepsilon$ closed while retaining its lower bound.

If no certificate is returned and no pending child awaits evaluation, split the nonclosed leaf with least lower bound; ties use creation order. In a box with positive widths, bisect a longest coordinate at its exact midpoint, using the least coordinate index among ties. The two closed children cover their parent. In the unconstrained mode, the oracle returns the exact midpoint as a feasible witness and exact objective value; the termination theorem uses this mode. For a zero-width singleton that has not been certified, request a deterministic higher-precision report for that same point; each refinement consumes one call. If refinement is unavailable, return inconclusive. When no certificate or infeasibility result has been established and another oracle call is needed after $N$ calls, the pre-call guard returns the complete current ledger with no optimality claim. This finite-budget procedure is global-search bookkeeping: a local stationary point or a solver tolerance is not a lower-bound certificate.

Fix an instance $(D_0,C,f)$ from [[def-spatial-global-optimization-problem]] and a closed subbox $B\subseteq D_0$. A **certified box report** may contain any combination of the following fields:

- A **feasible witness** $(x_B,U_B)$, with $x_B\in B\cap C$ and a verified upper bound $f(x_B)\le U_B$.
- A **lower bound** $\ell_B\in\mathbb R$ satisfying $\ell_B\le f(x)$ for every $x\in B\cap C$. This pointwise condition is vacuous when $B\cap C=\emptyset$; when $B\cap C\ne\emptyset$, it is equivalent to $\ell_B\le\inf_{x\in B\cap C}f(x)$.
- An **empty-box proof** establishing $B\cap C=\emptyset$.
- A non-finite or unavailable status, which makes no feasibility, lower-bound, or optimality claim.

A box is **closed** for a requested tolerance $\varepsilon>0$ only when it has a lower bound and $\ell_B\ge U-\varepsilon$, where $U$ is the best currently verified feasible upper bound. Closing a box stops further subdivision but retains its lower bound in the global ledger. A report lacking a required field is not repaired by a numerical guess.

derivations.claim: By induction on the finite number of splits, the union of terminal leaves is $D_0$: it holds at initialization, and each split replaces one leaf by two children whose union is the parent by [F1]. Every feasible point is therefore in a terminal leaf that is not certified empty.

For any $x\in C$, choose a terminal leaf $B$ containing $x$ using step 1.1. Its lower-bound report is valid by [F2], so $L\le\ell_B\le f(x)$. Since this holds for every feasible $x$, $L\le\inf_{x\in C}f(x)$.

The witness bound [F3] and $U-L\le\varepsilon$ give $f(\hat x)\le U\le L+\varepsilon\le\inf_{x\in C}f(x)+\varepsilon$, proving the global gap claim. If every leaf is certified empty, step 1.1 covers $D_0$ by leaves disjoint from $C$, so $C=\emptyset$.

A finite **factorable expression DAG** on a box $B$ has input variables, certified constants, affine nodes, product nodes, and optional unary nonlinear nodes. A **certified convex relaxation** of its constrained minimization problem consists of a convex-program representation in the form of [[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]], with feasible set $R_B$ in lifted variables and convex objective $\phi_B$ on $R_B$, and an exact-value embedding $\iota_B$ with these properties:

1. For every original feasible point $x\in B\cap C$, the exact value of each DAG node defines $\iota_B(x)\in R_B$.
2. The relaxed objective underestimates the original: $\phi_B(\iota_B(x))\le f(x)$.
3. Every product node $w=uv$ is represented by a McCormick polytope from [[def-mccormick-bilinear-box-envelope]] using operand bounds that enclose their exact ranges. Every other nonlinear node must use supplied convex and concave graph enclosures with verified domain hypotheses. If no such enclosure is supplied, no relaxation is defined.
4. Every interval bound and coefficient affected by finite precision carries an outward-rounded enclosure from [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]. A non-finite status or unverified coefficient makes the relaxation unavailable.

For a convex program represented in [[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]], a dual certificate is a dual-feasible pair $(\lambda,\nu)$ together with a verified real lower bound $\ell$ for its Lagrangian dual value $q(\lambda,\nu)$. The definition records a certificate interface only; it does not assert that a solver finds one.

For every finite box $[l_x,u_x]\times[l_y,u_y]$, the McCormick polytope from [[def-mccormick-bilinear-box-envelope]] is exactly the convex hull in $\mathbb R^3$ of the graph $\{(x,y,xy):x\in[l_x,u_x],y\in[l_y,u_y]\}$.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

For the convex program and Lagrangian dual of
[[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]], every primal feasible
$x$ and every dual feasible $(\lambda,\nu)$ satisfy
$$q(\lambda,\nu)\le f_0(x).$$
Consequently, when the primal feasible set is nonempty, $d^*\le p^*$.

derivations.claim: Fix $x\in B\cap C$. Traverse its finite expression DAG in topological order and assign each lifted variable its exact node value. Affine equalities hold by construction. At each product node the exact operands lie within their certified ranges by [F3], and the exact product graph lies in its McCormick polytope by [F2]. Every other nonlinear relation is included only with a verified outer graph enclosure by the algorithm definition. Thus the constructed lifted point $\iota_B(x)$ lies in $R_B$, and the relaxed objective satisfies $\phi_B(\iota_B(x))\le f(x)$ by [F1].

Weak duality [F4], applied to the relaxed primal point $\iota_B(x)$ from step 1.1, gives $q(\lambda,\nu)\le\phi_B(\iota_B(x))$. Since the verified certificate satisfies $\ell\le q(\lambda,\nu)$, we obtain $\ell\le\phi_B(\iota_B(x))\le f(x)$.
The inequality in step 2.1 holds for every $x\in B\cap C$, so taking the infimum over that set yields $\ell\le\inf_{x\in B\cap C}f(x)$.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

For finite $x$ with $|x|\le N_{\max}$, the directed roundings defined in
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]] satisfy
$\operatorname{rd}(x)\le x\le\operatorname{ru}(x)$ and each endpoint error is
at most the stated $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)$ (with zero error when $x$ is
representable). For $x>N_{\max}$ the pair $(N_{\max},+\infty)$ encloses $x$;
for $x<-N_{\max}$ the pair $(-\infty,-N_{\max})$ encloses $x$. Overflow has
error bound $+\infty$ and cannot be reported as a finite-error result.

An exact dyadic rational is a number $m2^q$ with integers $m,q$.
Fix integers $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$. Put
$\eta=2^{e_{\min}-p+1}$ and
$N_{\max}=(2^p-1)2^{e_{\max}-p+1}$. The finite representable set $\mathbb F$
consists of zero, both signs of every normal number $k2^{e-p+1}$ with
$e_{\min}\le e\le e_{\max}$ and $2^{p-1}\le k<2^p$, and both signs of every
subnormal number $k\eta$ with $1\le k<2^{p-1}$. The smallest positive
subnormal is $\eta$, the smallest positive normal is $2^{e_{\min}}$, and the
largest finite magnitude is $N_{\max}$. The extended endpoint set also contains
$-\infty$ and $+\infty$ as enclosure sentinels; they are not finite machine
numbers.

For a real $x$ with $|x|\le N_{\max}$, define $\operatorname{rd}(x)$ as the
greatest member of $\mathbb F$ not exceeding $x$, and $\operatorname{ru}(x)$ as
the least member of $\mathbb F$ not less than $x$. Define
$\rho(x)=\operatorname{ru}(x)-\operatorname{rd}(x)$. For nonzero $x$ in the
subnormal range, define the absolute-error bound $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=\eta$;
for $2^e\le |x|<2^{e+1}$ in the normal range, define
$\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=2^{e-p+2}$. At finite overflow, a directed result is
the corresponding infinite sentinel and its error bound is $+\infty$; the
status is `overflow`. The rounding procedure reports `finite`, `subnormal`, or
`overflow`, so no relative-error assumption is implicit.

An exact rational intermediate may be converted by comparing integer
numerators and denominators after clearing powers of two. A directed interval
endpoint is the resulting greatest lower or least upper member of $\mathbb F$.

Input a box $B=\prod_j[a_j,b_j]\subseteq D_0$ with arbitrary finite ordered real endpoints, a finite real expression DAG from [[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]] using addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, a precision $p\ge2$, and a dyadic format with fixed exponent bounds. Round each input endpoint outward at precision $p$, replacing $[a_j,b_j]$ by $[\operatorname{rd}_p(a_j),\operatorname{ru}_p(b_j)]$; if an endpoint rounding overflows, return overflow. Thus every interval passed to an interval operation has dyadic endpoints and contains the original box coordinate interval. The same rule applies to a singleton input, including a midpoint point-evaluation path. The DAG must define a real-valued function at every point of $B$; for each division node its denominator range on $B$ must exclude zero. Each constant is either an exact dyadic, enclosed by $[\operatorname{rd}_p(c),\operatorname{ru}_p(c)]$, or is accompanied by a precision-indexed certified interval containing it whose width tends to zero as $p\to\infty$. If any constant enclosure overflows or is unavailable, return that status with no finite bound claim. Traverse the finite DAG in topological order. Enclose each input by its outward-rounded interval, each constant by its certified interval at precision $p$, and apply the corresponding outward-rounded operation from [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] at precision $p$. Return the root enclosure $I_p(B)=[a_-,a_+]$, its lower and upper endpoints, and the exact midpoint of $B$ as a candidate point. If any operation returns overflow, split-domain, domain-error, entire, or inconclusive, return that status with no finite bound claim.

For a continuous objective on an unconstrained box, the midpoint is feasible and $a_+$ is a verified upper bound for its objective value. On a constrained box, the midpoint is only a candidate: a separate feasibility witness is required. To refine arithmetic error, callers increase $p$ along any sequence of shrinking boxes. Fixed exponent bounds must be chosen so no exact intermediate on the certified domain overflows; otherwise the procedure returns an explicit failure status.

A **real interval** is a closed set $[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ with finite dyadic
endpoints $a\le b$. Its width is $b-a$, midpoint is $(a+b)/2$, and its
midpoint-radius form is $m+[-r,r]$ with $m=(a+b)/2$ and $r=(b-a)/2$. The empty
set is the status `empty`; the whole real line is `entire`. `overflow`,
`domain-error`, `split-domain`, and `inconclusive` are computation statuses,
not finite intervals.

A **complex rectangle** is $X+iY=\{x+iy:x\in X,\ y\in Y\}$ for real intervals
$X,Y$. Complex addition and multiplication use
$(x+iy)+(u+iv)=(x+u)+i(y+v)$ and
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$. For $z=x+iy$, its complex modulus is
$|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and for $z\ne0$ its reciprocal is
$1/z=(x-iy)/(x^2+y^2)$. A
**complex ball** $B(c,r)$ is
$\{z\in\mathbb C:|z-c|\le r\}$ with dyadic complex center $c$ and dyadic
$r\ge0$. For any two represented sets $S,T$, the inclusion order is
$S\sqsubseteq T$ iff $S\subseteq T$.

The width of a complex rectangle with coordinate widths $w_X,w_Y$ is its
Euclidean diameter $\sqrt{w_X^2+w_Y^2}$; the width of a ball $B(c,r)$ is its
diameter $2r$. Width comparisons against a dyadic tolerance can be decided by
exact rational comparisons after squaring the nonnegative quantities.

The **range** of a real or complex function $f$ on a set $S$ is
$f(S)=\{f(x):x\in S\cap\operatorname{dom}(f)\}$. A finite expression DAG is a
finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes, constant nodes, and operation
nodes; constants are exact dyadics or are supplied with certified enclosing
intervals. Sharing a node means the exact same intermediate value is reused.

For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$; the denominator interval is strictly positive because at
least one coordinate interval excludes zero. Division multiplies by this
reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

Input a compact-box instance $(D_0,C,f)$, a finite arithmetic expression DAG representing $f$, a closed box $B=\prod_{j=1}^n[a_j,b_j]\subseteq D_0$, a nonnegative certified constant $L$, a precision $p\ge2$, a dyadic interval format with fixed exponent bounds, a certificate that the midpoint $m$ is in $C$ (automatic when $C=D_0$), and a validated inequality
$$|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\max_j|x_j-y_j|\qquad(x,y\in B).$$
Let $m_j=(a_j+b_j)/2$ and $r=\max_j(b_j-a_j)/2$. Apply [[alg-interval-dag-box-enclosure-and-bound]] to the supplied DAG at the singleton $\{m\}$ with the supplied precision and format to obtain $I_p(\{m\})=[q_-,q_+]$; its endpoint-rounding rule encloses a possibly non-dyadic midpoint. Compute a directed-rounding upper bound $r^+\ge r$ and a downward-rounded lower endpoint $\ell_B\le q_- - Lr^+$. Return the pointwise lower-bound report $\ell_B$ and the feasible midpoint candidate $(m,q_+)$. If the feasibility certificate or either interval or arithmetic calculation is unavailable or non-finite, return inconclusive without a feasible-witness claim.

derivations.claim: By the endpoint-rounding rule and [F2], the dyadic input intervals used by the algorithm contain the original box $B$. The DAG enclosure statement [F1] therefore implies $a_-\le f(x)\le a_+$ for every $x\in B$. Thus $a_-$ and $a_+$ are valid lower and upper bounds on the entire box, not estimates from a sample point.

For a nested shrinking sequence $B_k\to\{x\}$ with precision $p_k\to\infty$, outward-rounded input endpoints tend to their exact endpoint values by [F2], and each certified constant enclosure tends to its exact constant by the hypothesis. Induct in topological order through the finite DAG. At each addition, subtraction, or multiplication node the exact endpoint formulas are continuous in the input endpoints; at a division node the denominator is bounded away from zero, so the reciprocal endpoint formulas are continuous for all sufficiently large $k$. The directed-rounding error tends to zero by [F2]. Therefore each node enclosure converges to its exact node value at $x$, and in particular the root endpoints converge to $f(x)$.
For the Lipschitz procedure, every $x\in B$ satisfies $\max_j|x_j-m_j|\le r\le r^+$. By [F4], $f(x)\ge f(m)-Lr\ge q_- - Lr^+\ge\ell_B$, so $\ell_B$ is valid on $B$.

Along a shrinking sequence, $m_k\to x$, $r_k^+\to0$, and the singleton enclosure endpoints $q_{k,-},q_{k,+}$ tend to $f(x)$ by step 1.2. Hence $q_{k,-}-Lr_k^+\to f(x)$, and the extra directed-rounding error also tends to zero by [F2]; therefore $\ell_{B_k}\to f(x)$.
