Let $d,N\ge1$, let $X=\mathbb R^d$, and fix macro times $t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N$. A **fine/coarse propagator pair** is a pair of deterministic maps $F_n:D_n^F\to X$ and $G_n:D_n^G\to X$, for each $0\le n<N$, where $D_n^F,D_n^G\subseteq X$ are their admitted input sets. Both maps advance a state across the same interval $[t_n,t_{n+1}]$. The labels fine and coarse identify the two roles chosen by the user; they assert no accuracy, stability, cost, or convergence property.

For an initial state $x_0\in X$, whenever every call succeeds, the **sequential fine trajectory** is the finite sequence $x_{n+1}=F_n(x_n)$, and the **sequential coarse trajectory** is defined by replacing each $F_n$ with $G_n$. A partially defined map is unavailable outside its admitted set; a failed stage evaluation or an unavailable implicit branch is a propagation failure, not a numerical value.

A canonical ODE instantiation uses the explicit Runge–Kutta stage map of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]] for $r\ge1$ fine substeps of size $(t_{n+1}-t_n)/r$, composed in order to form $F_n$. A coarse backward Euler value is an endpoint $z$ satisfying the equation in [[def-backward-euler-step-equation]] over the full macro interval. Its branch selector is part of the input and must select exactly one admissible root for each admitted start state; if no such selected root exists, the coarse map is unavailable. The backward Euler definition alone asserts neither root existence nor uniqueness.

This definition distinguishes the sequential fine trajectory from samples of an exact ODE solution. Any estimate of the fine method's error relative to that exact solution is a separate obligation.

Input: an admissible propagator pair from [[def-parareal-propagator-pair]], initial state $x_0$, number of macro intervals $N$, sweep budget $K\ge0$, and optionally a wall-clock budget $\tau\ge0$ and a user-supplied convergence certificate. Each map call either returns one state or a declared failure status. The output is every fully completed row of the table $U_n^k$ for $0\le k\le K$, the last completed endpoint, and a status.

Initialize $U_0^0=x_0$ and, in increasing order of $n$, set $U_{n+1}^0=G_n(U_n^0)$. Store the values $G_n(U_n^0)$. For each $k=0,\ldots,K-1$, set $U_0^{k+1}=x_0$. Evaluate $F_n(U_n^k)$ independently for all $n$; the stored $G_n(U_n^k)$ values are reused from the preceding row. Then, in increasing order of $n$, compute $G_n(U_n^{k+1})$ and set
$$U_{n+1}^{k+1}=G_n(U_n^{k+1})+F_n(U_n^k)-G_n(U_n^k).$$
The fine calls in a sweep can run in parallel, while the corrected row is computed sequentially.

If a map call fails, return the last fully completed row and status propagation-failure; a prefix of the failed row may be reported separately but is not a completed iterate. If the time budget expires at a call boundary, return the last fully completed row and status budget-exhausted. Return status converged only if the supplied convergence certificate is verified for the returned iterate. Otherwise return status budget-exhausted when the requested initialization and $K$ sweeps finish; the procedure does not infer convergence from completion of its finite budget.

For the exact-arithmetic recurrence, an update computed with inexact fine/coarse values or an inexact correction solve can be written as the displayed right-hand side plus a combined defect $\eta_n^{k+1}$. A residual tolerance alone does not bound that defect in forward error.

**Work model.** For nonnegative call costs $c_F,c_G,\tau_{\rm sync}$ and a positive integer processor count $P$, if one fine call costs $c_F$, one coarse call costs $c_G$, and $P$ processors can evaluate independent fine calls concurrently, the initial coarse pass uses $N$ serial calls. Each completed sweep uses $N$ fine calls, with ideal fine-call span $\lceil N/P\rceil c_F$, and $N$ new coarse calls in serial order, with span $Nc_G$, plus its measured communication and synchronization cost $\tau_{\rm sync}$. The resulting idealized span is
$$Nc_G+K\bigl(\lceil N/P\rceil c_F+Nc_G+\tau_{\rm sync}\bigr).$$
This is a cost model, not a speedup guarantee; actual work, communication, processor placement, and iteration budget determine realized performance.

derivations.claim: At sweep $k=0$, the only claimed node is $n=0$, and $U_0^0=x_0=x_0$ by initialization and the definition of the fine trajectory [F1].

Suppose the claim holds at sweep $k$. At sweep $k+1$, $U_0^{k+1}=x_0$ by [F2]. Induct on $n$ from $0$ to $\min\{k,N-1\}$; if $U_n^{k+1}=x_n$, then $n\le k$ also gives $U_n^k=x_n$, so [F2] yields $U_{n+1}^{k+1}=G_n(x_n)+F_n(x_n)-G_n(x_n)=F_n(x_n)=x_{n+1}$ by [F1]. Thus the claim holds through node $\min\{k+1,N\}$.
Induction on $k$ proves the first assertion, and taking $k=K\ge N$ includes every node $0\le n\le N$.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

Subtract $x_{n+1}=F_n(x_n)$ from the recurrence in [F2] and add and subtract $G_n(x_n)$; this gives $e_{n+1}^{k+1}=G_n(U_n^{k+1})-G_n(x_n)+(F_n-G_n)(U_n^k)-(F_n-G_n)(x_n)$. By [A1] and the triangle inequality in [F3], $E_{n+1}^{k+1}\le aE_n^{k+1}+bE_n^k$, where $E_n^k=\|e_n^k\|$.
At node $0$, $E_0^k=0$ for every $k$ by [F2]. At sweep $k=0$, [A1] gives $E_n^0\le M\le MA^n$. These are the initial cases for induction on the node, simultaneously over all completed sweeps.

Assume the bound holds at node $n$. For the level-zero row at node $n+1$, [A1] gives $E_{n+1}^0\le M\le MA^{n+1}$. For each $k\ge0$, [step 1.1] gives $E_{n+1}^{k+1}\le MA^n b^{k+1}\left(a\binom n{k+1}+\binom nk\right)\le MA^{n+1}b^{k+1}\left(\binom n{k+1}+\binom nk\right)$. The last inequality uses $a\le A$ and $1\le A$. Partitioning the $(k+1)$-element subsets of an $(n+1)$-element set according to whether they contain its final element gives $\binom n{k+1}+\binom nk=\binom{n+1}{k+1}$, including the zero convention. Thus the bound holds at node $n+1$, and induction proves the first estimate.

In the fixed-horizon branch, $A\le1+C_aH\le\exp(C_aH)$ by [A2], [F4], and the definition of $\exp$ in [F6]. Repeated use of [F5] gives $A^N\le\exp(C_aNH)=\exp(C_aT)$. Each $k$-element subset of an $N$-element set has a unique increasing $k$-tuple, so $\binom Nk\le N^k$. Substituting these bounds and $b\le C_bH^{q+1}$ into the first estimate gives $\|U_N^k-x_N\|\le M N^k\exp(C_aT)(C_bH^{q+1})^k=M(C_bT)^k\exp(C_aT)H^{qk}$. For fixed $T,k$ and uniform $M$, this is $O(H^{qk})$.

Let $d,N\ge1$, let $\Phi_i\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ for $1\le i\le N$, and let $u_0\in\mathbb R^d$ be fixed. The linear part of a fine propagator in [[def-parareal-propagator-pair]] is represented by $\Phi_i$. For forcing vectors $g_i\in\mathbb R^d$, write the fine recurrence as $u_i=\Phi_i u_{i-1}+g_i$. On the unknown vector $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_N)\in(\mathbb R^d)^N$, define $A_t$ by $(A_tv)_1=v_1$ and $(A_tv)_i=v_i-\Phi_i v_{i-1}$ for $2\le i\le N$. With $b_1=\Phi_1u_0+g_1$ and $b_i=g_i$ for $i\ge2$, the recurrence is exactly $A_tv=b$.

For a coarsening factor $m\ge2$ dividing $N$, the coarse indices are $0,m,2m,\ldots,N$. Among unknowns, let $C=\{m,2m,\ldots,N\}$ and $F=\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus C$. Reordering the unknown vector as $(v_F,v_C)$ gives
$$A_t=\begin{pmatrix}A_{FF}&A_{FC}\\ A_{CF}&A_{CC}\end{pmatrix}.$$
A practical coarse propagator $\Psi_j$ on each interval is the linear subcase of the coarse maps $G_n$ in [[def-parareal-propagator-pair]]; the exact coarse operator is determined by eliminating F-points and is not generally the same as this practical choice. This definition asserts no stability or convergence property.

derivations.claim: For any right-hand side, solve the fine equations in increasing index: the first unknown is determined by its identity diagonal block, and each later unknown is uniquely $u_i=r_i+\Phi_i u_{i-1}$. This proves $A_t$ is invertible. Holding all C-values fixed, the F-equations in each interval between consecutive C-points have the same forward-substitution form with identity diagonal blocks, so they uniquely determine the F-values; hence $A_{FF}$ is invertible.

In the reordered block system, the F rows give $u_F=A_{FF}^{-1}(b_F-A_{FC}u_C)$. Substituting this expression in the C rows gives $(A_{CC}-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}A_{FC})u_C=b_C-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}b_F$. Conversely, any solution $u_C$ of this coarse system, together with the displayed formula for $u_F$, satisfies both the F and C rows. Thus elimination preserves exactly the solution set.

Repeated substitution in $u_i=\Phi_i u_{i-1}+g_i$, for $i=(j-1)m+1,\ldots,jm$, gives $u_{jm}=(\Phi_{jm}\cdots\Phi_{(j-1)m+1})u_{(j-1)m}+\sum_{s=1}^{m}(\Phi_{jm}\cdots\Phi_{(j-1)m+s+1})g_{(j-1)m+s}$. For $s=m$ the product is empty and equals $I$. This is exactly the coarse recurrence in the Statement; the coefficient product reduces to $\Phi^m$ when every $\Phi_i=\Phi$.

Let $x_{n+1}=F_n(x_n)$ be the sequential fine trajectory and let $U_n^k$ be the exact-arithmetic table from [[alg-parareal-correction-sweeps]]. Let $D\subseteq X$ contain every $x_n$ and every iterate used in the requested sweeps. Suppose constants $a,b,M\ge0$ satisfy, for every $0\le n<N$ and $u,v\in D$,
$$\|G_n(u)-G_n(v)\|\le a\|u-v\|,\qquad
\|(F_n-G_n)(u)-(F_n-G_n)(v)\|\le b\|u-v\|,$$
and $\|U_n^0-x_n\|\le M$ for all $0\le n\le N$. Use $\binom nk$ for the number of $k$-element subsets of an $n$-element set, set it to $0$ for $k>n$, and put $A=\max\{1,a\}$. Then for every node $0\le n\le N$ and completed sweep $k\ge0$,
$$\|U_n^k-x_n\|\le M\binom nk A^n b^k,$$
with $b^0=1$. The hypotheses include all comparison points; invariance of $D$ under $F_n,G_n$ alone does not ensure that corrected iterates stay in $D$.

For a fixed horizon $T=NH$, suppose $a\le1+C_aH$, $b\le C_bH^{q+1}$ for constants $C_a,C_b\ge0$ and integer $q\ge1$, and one $M$ works uniformly as $N$ varies. Then, for each fixed $k\le N$,
$$\|U_N^k-x_N\|\le M(C_bT)^k\exp(C_aT)H^{qk}.$$
Thus the exact-solve error is $O(H^{qk})$ at each fixed iteration $k$ under these uniform assumptions. Neither estimate includes finite-solver error; that effect requires a separate update-defect analysis.

derivations.claim: Set $e_n^k=\|V_n^k-x_n\|$. Subtracting $x_{n+1}=F_n(x_n)$ from the computed recurrence, splitting off the update defect, and applying the two Lipschitz inequalities gives $e_{n+1}^{k+1}\le a e_n^{k+1}+b e_n^k+\eta\le A e_n^{k+1}+b e_n^k+\eta$.
At node $0$, $e_0^k=0$, $P_0^k=0$ for $k>0$, and $R_0^k=0$; at $k=0$, the base coarse-error assumption gives $e_n^0\le M\le P_n^0+R_n^0$.

Assume $e_n^k\le P_n^k+R_n^k$ at node $n$ for every completed sweep. For $k\ge0$, step 1.1 gives $e_{n+1}^{k+1}\le A(P_n^{k+1}+R_n^{k+1})+b(P_n^k+R_n^k)+\eta$. The $P$ terms satisfy $A P_n^{k+1}+bP_n^k=MA^n b^{k+1}\left(A\binom n{k+1}+\binom nk\right)\le MA^{n+1}b^{k+1}\left(\binom n{k+1}+\binom nk\right)=P_{n+1}^{k+1}$ because $A\ge1$ and Pascal's identity holds. The remaining terms equal $R_{n+1}^{k+1}$ by definition. Therefore the bound holds at node $n+1$; induction proves it for all nodes and sweeps.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $d,N\ge1$, let $X=\mathbb R^d$, and fix macro times $t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N$. A **fine/coarse propagator pair** is a pair of deterministic maps $F_n:D_n^F\to X$ and $G_n:D_n^G\to X$, for each $0\le n<N$, where $D_n^F,D_n^G\subseteq X$ are their admitted input sets. Both maps advance a state across the same interval $[t_n,t_{n+1}]$. The labels fine and coarse identify the two roles chosen by the user; they assert no accuracy, stability, cost, or convergence property.

For an initial state $x_0\in X$, whenever every call succeeds, the **sequential fine trajectory** is the finite sequence $x_{n+1}=F_n(x_n)$, and the **sequential coarse trajectory** is defined by replacing each $F_n$ with $G_n$. A partially defined map is unavailable outside its admitted set; a failed stage evaluation or an unavailable implicit branch is a propagation failure, not a numerical value.

A canonical ODE instantiation uses the explicit Runge–Kutta stage map of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]] for $r\ge1$ fine substeps of size $(t_{n+1}-t_n)/r$, composed in order to form $F_n$. A coarse backward Euler value is an endpoint $z$ satisfying the equation in [[def-backward-euler-step-equation]] over the full macro interval. Its branch selector is part of the input and must select exactly one admissible root for each admitted start state; if no such selected root exists, the coarse map is unavailable. The backward Euler definition alone asserts neither root existence nor uniqueness.

This definition distinguishes the sequential fine trajectory from samples of an exact ODE solution. Any estimate of the fine method's error relative to that exact solution is a separate obligation.

Use the notation and Lipschitz hypotheses of [[thm-parareal-binomial-error-bound]], with $A=\max\{1,a\}$. Let computed iterates $V_n^k$ satisfy $V_0^k=x_0$, $\|V_n^0-x_n\|\le M$, and, for each requested correction,
$$\left\|V_{n+1}^{k+1}-\left[G_n(V_n^{k+1})+(F_n-G_n)(V_n^k)\right]\right\|\le\eta$$
for a constant $\eta\ge0$. Define $P_n^k=M\binom nk A^n b^k$ and a nonnegative forcing array by $R_0^k=0$, $R_n^0=0$, and
$$R_{n+1}^{k+1}=A R_n^{k+1}+bR_n^k+\eta.$$
Then $\|V_n^k-x_n\|\le P_n^k+R_n^k$ for every completed node and sweep.

The base envelope $M$ includes coarse-initialization error relative to the fine trajectory. The per-update defect $\eta$ must bound the actual combined effect of fine/coarse evaluation errors and correction-solve error; a residual tolerance alone supplies no forward-error bound.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $x_n$ is the sequential fine node; since $t_n\in[0,T]$, [F1] gives the solution value $y(t_n)$. Insert and subtract $x_n$ and apply the norm triangle inequality: $\|V_n^K-y(t_n)\|\le\|V_n^K-x_n\|+\|x_n-y(t_n)\|$.
Substitute the two given bounds from [A1] and [F3]. This gives the displayed conclusion, while leaving $\delta_F$ as a separate fine-method obligation.

Input: a linear fine-grid system $A_tu=b$ with $N\ge1$ fine intervals as in [[def-linear-all-at-once-time-operator]], a coarsening factor $m\ge2$ dividing $N$ and its C/F partition as in [[lem-mgrit-exact-coarse-elimination]], practical coarse propagators $\Psi_j\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ for $1\le j\le N_c:=N/m$, an initial fine-grid iterate $u_{\rm in}$, pre- and post-relaxation choices from $\{F,FCF\}$, a real-valued norm on the fine-grid residual space as in [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], a nonnegative integer cycle budget $J_{\rm cyc}$, and a residual tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$. The symbol $J_{\rm cyc}$ is the number of permitted cycles; the coarse-interval count is $N_c$ (the letter $J$ in [[lem-mgrit-exact-coarse-elimination]] denotes that lemma's coarse-interval count). The output is the last iterate, its residual norm, the number of completed cycles, and status `converged` or `budget-exhausted`.

In F/C ordering define ideal interpolation $P$ and restriction $R$ by
$$P=\begin{bmatrix}-A_{FF}^{-1}A_{FC}\\ I_C\end{bmatrix},
\qquad R=\begin{bmatrix}-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}&I_C\end{bmatrix}.$$

The exact coarse operator is the Schur complement $RA_tP=A_{CC}-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}A_{FC}$ from [[lem-mgrit-exact-coarse-elimination]]. The practical correction matrix $A_c$ has identity diagonal blocks and subdiagonal blocks $-\Psi_j$ for $2\le j\le N_c$; its first row corresponds to the fixed zero initial correction $z_0=0$. For any right-hand side $\rho$, forward substitution uniquely solves $A_cz=\rho$ by setting $z_0=0$ and, in increasing order for $j=1,\ldots,N_c$, setting $z_j=\rho_j+\Psi_jz_{j-1}$. Thus $A_c$ is invertible even when an individual $\Psi_j$ is singular.

Define the relaxations on $A_tu=b$ as follows. An F-relaxation holds every C-value fixed and, for each coarse interval $j=1,\ldots,N_c$, updates its F-indices $i=(j-1)m+1,\ldots,jm-1$ in increasing order: set $u_1=b_1$ if $i=1$, and otherwise set $u_i=b_i+\Phi_i u_{i-1}$. Different coarse intervals have independent F-updates and may be processed in parallel. A C-relaxation holds every F-value fixed and, for $j=1,\ldots,N_c$ in increasing order, sets $u_{jm}=b_{jm}+\Phi_{jm}u_{jm-1}$; these C-updates are independent because $m\ge2$ and each predecessor is an F-index. An FCF-relaxation applies F-relaxation, then C-relaxation, then F-relaxation. Each relaxation is a finite linear update; write $S_{\rm pre}$ and $S_{\rm post}$ for the error maps of the selected pre- and post-relaxations.

For one cycle from a current iterate $u$, apply the selected pre-relaxation; form $r=b-A_tu$ and $\rho=Rr$; solve $A_cz=\rho$ by the forward substitution above; correct $u\leftarrow u+Pz$; then apply the selected post-relaxation. The exact error-propagation matrix of this fixed cycle is
$$E=S_{\rm post}(I-PA_c^{-1}RA_t)S_{\rm pre}.$$

Initialize $u^{(0)}=u_{\rm in}$ and compute $\|b-A_tu^{(0)}\|$. If this is at most $\varepsilon$, return $u^{(0)}$, zero completed cycles, and status `converged`. Otherwise, for $j_{\rm cyc}=1,\ldots,J_{\rm cyc}$, perform one cycle, call the resulting iterate $u^{(j_{\rm cyc})}$, and compute $\|b-A_tu^{(j_{\rm cyc})}\|$. If this norm is at most $\varepsilon$, return that iterate, $j_{\rm cyc}$ completed cycles, and status `converged`; if not, continue. If all $J_{\rm cyc}$ cycles finish without this condition (including when $J_{\rm cyc}=0$), return the last iterate, its residual norm, and status `budget-exhausted`. The matrix $E$ describes exact arithmetic and exact coarse solves; inexact solves contribute an update defect that needs its own bound.

**Work model.** Let $N_f=N$ and $N_c=N/m$. One F-relaxation updates $N_f-N_c$ F-points, but its boundary assignment $u_1=b_1$ uses the supplied right-hand side and makes no fine-propagator call; thus it uses $N_f-N_c-1$ fine-propagator calls; one C-relaxation uses $N_c$ fine-propagator calls, one for each C equation; one FCF-relaxation uses $2(N_f-N_c-1)+N_c$ fine-propagator calls. Residual formation and ideal interpolation add their actual fine-propagator applications and communication when recomputed rather than cached. The specified coarse forward substitution uses $N_c$ practical coarse-propagator applications, including $\Psi_1z_0$ with $z_0=0$. If a fine call costs $c_\Phi$, a coarse call costs $c_\Psi$, and $p_{\rm proc}$ processors share independent F-intervals (the interpolation matrix remains $P$), work is the sum of these calls and communication, while span includes the sequential dependence within each F-interval, the coarse forward solve, and synchronization. A multilevel cycle adds the work and span on every visited level. This model gives no speedup guarantee.

Use [[def-linear-all-at-once-time-operator]] with $N=Jm$, $m\ge2$, and its F/C partition. Both $A_t$ and $A_{FF}$ are invertible. Eliminating the F unknowns from $A_tv=b$ gives the coarse system with Schur complement
$$S=A_{CC}-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}A_{FC}.$$
On coarse interval $j$, its recurrence is
$$u_{jm}-(\Phi_{jm}\Phi_{jm-1}\cdots\Phi_{(j-1)m+1})u_{(j-1)m}=\bar g_j,$$
where
$$\bar g_j=\sum_{s=1}^{m}(\Phi_{jm}\Phi_{jm-1}\cdots\Phi_{(j-1)m+s+1})g_{(j-1)m+s},$$
with an empty product defined to be the identity. If $\Phi_i=\Phi$ for every fine step, the exact coarse propagator is $\Phi^m$.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

The following are the explicit Runge–Kutta tableaus in the convention of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]].

Forward Euler has $s=1$, $A=(0)$, $b=(1)$, and $c=(0)$.

Explicit midpoint has $s=2$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\[2pt]1/2&0\end{pmatrix}$, $b=(0,1)$, and $c=(0,1/2)$.

The classical four-stage Runge–Kutta method has $s=4$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0&0\\[2pt]1/2&0&0&0\\[2pt]0&1/2&0&0\\[2pt]0&0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $b=(1/6,1/3,1/3,1/6)$, and $c=(0,1/2,1/2,1)$.

Each displayed $c_i$ is the row sum required in the definition of an explicit tableau. These tableaus specify the stage equations; their order and scalar stability functions are proved separately.

Let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ define a first-order initial-value problem on an open time-state domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$. Given a time $t_n$, step $h_n>0$, and state $y_n$ with $(t_n,y_n)\in D$, an admissible endpoint $y_{n+1}$ must satisfy $(t_n+h_n,y_{n+1})\in D$. The backward Euler endpoint is any such $y_{n+1}$ satisfying

$$y_{n+1}=y_n+h_n f(t_n+h_n,y_{n+1}).$$

Its update residual at an approximate endpoint $z$ with $(t_n+h_n,z)\in D$ is

$$G_n^{\rm BE}(z)=z-y_n-h_n f(t_n+h_n,z).$$

When $f$ is defined at the endpoint, the derivative residual is $G_n^{\rm BE}(z)/h_n$. The equation can have no, one, or several roots on a restricted admissible branch set; this definition by itself asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

Input: an admissible propagator pair from [[def-parareal-propagator-pair]], initial state $x_0$, number of macro intervals $N$, sweep budget $K\ge0$, and optionally a wall-clock budget $\tau\ge0$ and a user-supplied convergence certificate. Each map call either returns one state or a declared failure status. The output is every fully completed row of the table $U_n^k$ for $0\le k\le K$, the last completed endpoint, and a status.

Initialize $U_0^0=x_0$ and, in increasing order of $n$, set $U_{n+1}^0=G_n(U_n^0)$. Store the values $G_n(U_n^0)$. For each $k=0,\ldots,K-1$, set $U_0^{k+1}=x_0$. Evaluate $F_n(U_n^k)$ independently for all $n$; the stored $G_n(U_n^k)$ values are reused from the preceding row. Then, in increasing order of $n$, compute $G_n(U_n^{k+1})$ and set
$$U_{n+1}^{k+1}=G_n(U_n^{k+1})+F_n(U_n^k)-G_n(U_n^k).$$
The fine calls in a sweep can run in parallel, while the corrected row is computed sequentially.

If a map call fails, return the last fully completed row and status propagation-failure; a prefix of the failed row may be reported separately but is not a completed iterate. If the time budget expires at a call boundary, return the last fully completed row and status budget-exhausted. Return status converged only if the supplied convergence certificate is verified for the returned iterate. Otherwise return status budget-exhausted when the requested initialization and $K$ sweeps finish; the procedure does not infer convergence from completion of its finite budget.

For the exact-arithmetic recurrence, an update computed with inexact fine/coarse values or an inexact correction solve can be written as the displayed right-hand side plus a combined defect $\eta_n^{k+1}$. A residual tolerance alone does not bound that defect in forward error.

**Work model.** For nonnegative call costs $c_F,c_G,\tau_{\rm sync}$ and a positive integer processor count $P$, if one fine call costs $c_F$, one coarse call costs $c_G$, and $P$ processors can evaluate independent fine calls concurrently, the initial coarse pass uses $N$ serial calls. Each completed sweep uses $N$ fine calls, with ideal fine-call span $\lceil N/P\rceil c_F$, and $N$ new coarse calls in serial order, with span $Nc_G$, plus its measured communication and synchronization cost $\tau_{\rm sync}$. The resulting idealized span is
$$Nc_G+K\bigl(\lceil N/P\rceil c_F+Nc_G+\tau_{\rm sync}\bigr).$$
This is a cost model, not a speedup guarantee; actual work, communication, processor placement, and iteration budget determine realized performance.

The exact coarse operator is the Schur complement $RA_tP=A_{CC}-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}A_{FC}$ from [[lem-mgrit-exact-coarse-elimination]]. The practical correction matrix $A_c$ has identity diagonal blocks and subdiagonal blocks $-\Psi_j$ for $2\le j\le N_c$; its first row corresponds to the fixed zero initial correction $z_0=0$. For any right-hand side $\rho$, forward substitution uniquely solves $A_cz=\rho$ by setting $z_0=0$ and, in increasing order for $j=1,\ldots,N_c$, setting $z_j=\rho_j+\Psi_jz_{j-1}$. Thus $A_c$ is invertible even when an individual $\Psi_j$ is singular.

Define the relaxations on $A_tu=b$ as follows. An F-relaxation holds every C-value fixed and, for each coarse interval $j=1,\ldots,N_c$, updates its F-indices $i=(j-1)m+1,\ldots,jm-1$ in increasing order: set $u_1=b_1$ if $i=1$, and otherwise set $u_i=b_i+\Phi_i u_{i-1}$. Different coarse intervals have independent F-updates and may be processed in parallel. A C-relaxation holds every F-value fixed and, for $j=1,\ldots,N_c$ in increasing order, sets $u_{jm}=b_{jm}+\Phi_{jm}u_{jm-1}$; these C-updates are independent because $m\ge2$ and each predecessor is an F-index. An FCF-relaxation applies F-relaxation, then C-relaxation, then F-relaxation. Each relaxation is a finite linear update; write $S_{\rm pre}$ and $S_{\rm post}$ for the error maps of the selected pre- and post-relaxations.

For one cycle from a current iterate $u$, apply the selected pre-relaxation; form $r=b-A_tu$ and $\rho=Rr$; solve $A_cz=\rho$ by the forward substitution above; correct $u\leftarrow u+Pz$; then apply the selected post-relaxation. The exact error-propagation matrix of this fixed cycle is
$$E=S_{\rm post}(I-PA_c^{-1}RA_t)S_{\rm pre}.$$

Initialize $u^{(0)}=u_{\rm in}$ and compute $\|b-A_tu^{(0)}\|$. If this is at most $\varepsilon$, return $u^{(0)}$, zero completed cycles, and status `converged`. Otherwise, for $j_{\rm cyc}=1,\ldots,J_{\rm cyc}$, perform one cycle, call the resulting iterate $u^{(j_{\rm cyc})}$, and compute $\|b-A_tu^{(j_{\rm cyc})}\|$. If this norm is at most $\varepsilon$, return that iterate, $j_{\rm cyc}$ completed cycles, and status `converged`; if not, continue. If all $J_{\rm cyc}$ cycles finish without this condition (including when $J_{\rm cyc}=0$), return the last iterate, its residual norm, and status `budget-exhausted`. The matrix $E$ describes exact arithmetic and exact coarse solves; inexact solves contribute an update defect that needs its own bound.

**Work model.** Let $N_f=N$ and $N_c=N/m$. One F-relaxation updates $N_f-N_c$ F-points, but its boundary assignment $u_1=b_1$ uses the supplied right-hand side and makes no fine-propagator call; thus it uses $N_f-N_c-1$ fine-propagator calls; one C-relaxation uses $N_c$ fine-propagator calls, one for each C equation; one FCF-relaxation uses $2(N_f-N_c-1)+N_c$ fine-propagator calls. Residual formation and ideal interpolation add their actual fine-propagator applications and communication when recomputed rather than cached. The specified coarse forward substitution uses $N_c$ practical coarse-propagator applications, including $\Psi_1z_0$ with $z_0=0$. If a fine call costs $c_\Phi$, a coarse call costs $c_\Psi$, and $p_{\rm proc}$ processors share independent F-intervals (the interpolation matrix remains $P$), work is the sum of these calls and communication, while span includes the sequential dependence within each F-interval, the coarse forward solve, and synchronization. A multilevel cycle adds the work and span on every visited level. This model gives no speedup guarantee.

Let $A_tu_*=b$ be the fine-grid system from [[def-linear-all-at-once-time-operator]]. By [[lem-mgrit-exact-coarse-elimination]], $A_t$ is invertible. Let $E$ be the exact error matrix for one fixed two-level cycle in [[alg-mgrit-two-level-cycle]]. Choose a real-valued norm $\|\cdot\|$ on $(\mathbb R^d)^N$ and define its induced operator norm by $\|T\|=\sup_{v\ne0}\|Tv\|/\|v\|$. Assume $\|A_t\|$ and $\|A_t^{-1}\|$ are finite for this norm. If a direct calculation or other proof establishes $\|E\|\le q<1$, then after $r\ge0$ cycles the error satisfies $\|e^{(r)}\|\le q^r\|e^{(0)}\|$, with the convention $q^0=1$. The residual $s^{(r)}=b-A_tu^{(r)}=A_te^{(r)}$ obeys $\|s^{(r)}\|\le\|A_t\|q^r\|e^{(0)}\|$, and for every error/residual pair,
$$\|s\|\le\|A_t\|\|e\|,\qquad \|e\|\le\|A_t^{-1}\|\|s\|.$$

The contraction hypothesis is a property to prove for the declared operators, norm, and cycle. The MGRIT name alone supplies no such bound, and this theorem makes no multilevel convergence claim.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

derivations.claim: By [F1], each fine Euler step for $\dot y=-y$ multiplies by $\alpha=1-h=3/4$. By [F2], a backward-Euler macro step solves $z=x-\frac12z$, so its multiplier is $\psi=2/3$.

In fine order the error operator is $A_t=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&0\\-\alpha&1&0&0\\0&-\alpha&1&0\\0&0&-\alpha&1\end{pmatrix}$. In F/C order $F=(1,3)$, $C=(2,4)$, its blocks are $A_{FF}=I$, $A_{FC}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\-\alpha&0\end{pmatrix}$, $A_{CF}=\begin{pmatrix}-\alpha&0\\0&-\alpha\end{pmatrix}$, and $A_{CC}=I$. Hence [F4] gives $S=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-\alpha^2&1\end{pmatrix}$.

F-relaxation maps an error $(e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4)$ to $(0,e_2,\alpha e_2,e_4)$, so the F-row residuals vanish and the ideal restriction in [F5] reduces to the C residual $(e_2,e_4-\alpha^2e_2)$. Solving the practical coarse system $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-\psi&1\end{pmatrix}z=(e_2,e_4-\alpha^2e_2)$ gives $z_1=e_2$, $z_2=e_4+(\psi-\alpha^2)e_2$. Subtracting the ideal interpolation [F5] leaves $(0,0,0,(\alpha^2-\psi)e_2)$; post-F-relaxation leaves this vector unchanged.

Therefore $E$ has its only nonzero entry in row $4$, column $2$, equal to $\alpha^2-\psi=\frac9{16}-\frac23=-\frac5{48}$. For the norm in [A1], $\|Ee\|_\infty=\frac5{48}|e_2|\le\frac5{48}\|e\|_\infty$, with equality when $e=(0,1,0,0)$. Thus $\|E\|_\infty=5/48<1$.

For every $e\in\mathbb R^4$, $\|e\|_\infty=\max_i|e_i|$ is nonnegative and vanishes only when every coordinate is zero; $\|\lambda e\|_\infty=|\lambda|\|e\|_\infty$; and $\|e+f\|_\infty\le\|e\|_\infty+\|f\|_\infty$. Thus the norm in [A1] satisfies [F7]. For any matrix $B$, $\|Bv\|_\infty\le(\max_i\sum_j|B_{ij}|)\|v\|_\infty$ by applying the finite triangle inequality to each row. The row sums of $A_t$ are at most $1+\alpha=7/4$. If $A_tu=w$, forward substitution gives $u_1=w_1$ and $u_i=w_i+\alpha u_{i-1}$, hence by induction $u_i=\sum_{j=1}^{i}\alpha^{i-j}w_j$. Therefore $A_t^{-1}$ has entries $\alpha^{i-j}$ for $i\ge j$ and zero otherwise, with row sums at most $1+\alpha+\alpha^2+\alpha^3=175/64$. Thus $\|A_t\|_\infty\le7/4$ and $\|A_t^{-1}\|_\infty\le175/64$. All hypotheses of [F6] hold with $q=5/48$, so the error after $r$ cycles is at most $(5/48)^r$ times its initial value.

derivations.claim: Let $D=\operatorname{diag}(m_{11},\ldots,m_{mm})$ and $C=I-MD^{-1}$. Then $D$ is invertible, $C\ge0$, and for each column $j$, $r_j:=\sum_i C_{ij}=\sum_{i\ne j}|m_{ij}|/m_{jj}<1$. Since there are finitely many columns, $r:=\max_j r_j<1$.

For every $k\ge0$, $C^k\ge0$ and $\sum_i(C^k)_{ij}\le r^k$ for every column $j$: it holds at $k=0$, and multiplying by $C$ gives $\sum_i(C^{k+1})_{ij}=\sum_\ell(\sum_iC_{i\ell})(C^k)_{\ell j}\le r\sum_\ell(C^k)_{\ell j}$. Thus each entry series in $S:=\sum_{k=0}^\infty C^k$ converges and is nonnegative.

The finite geometric identity $(I-C)\sum_{k=0}^N C^k=\sum_{k=0}^N C^k(I-C)=I-C^{N+1}$ holds by cancellation of adjacent powers. Step 2.1 gives $C^{N+1}\to0$ entrywise, so $(I-C)S=S(I-C)=I$. Since $M=(I-C)D$, $M^{-1}=D^{-1}S\ge0$, proving invertibility and inverse nonnegativity.
If $b\ge0$, then $M^{-1}b\ge0$ by step 3.1. If $b>0$, then $S\ge I$ entrywise, so $D^{-1}Sb\ge D^{-1}b>0$ coordinatewise. This proves both vector conclusions.

Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and a domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$; its admissible nonnegative states are $\Omega_+:=\Omega\cap[0,\infty)^m$. For every ordered pair $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $p_{ij},d_{ij}:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be production and destruction transfer rates that are nonnegative on $\Omega_+$. A **finite conservative production destruction system** (finite conservative PDS) is the autonomous ODE

$$y_i'=F_i(y):=\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(p_{ij}(y)-d_{ij}(y)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,$$

with internal-transfer identities

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

The index $j$ is the donor/source of $p_{ij}$ and the index $i$ is its recipient/destination; $d_{ji}$ is the same transfer viewed as destruction from $j$. The total mass is $M(y):=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i$. The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. No existence, positivity, or regularity assertion about solutions is part of this definition.

Let $m\ge1$, let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with state domain $\Omega$, and take an input state $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$, a step size $h$, and declared denominators $\sigma_i$. If $y^n\notin\Omega_+$, $h\le0$, or any $\sigma_i\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating any rate. Otherwise the **modified Patankar Euler step** returns the unique solution $y^{n+1}$ of

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(p_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_j^{n+1}}{\sigma_j}-d_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_i^{n+1}}{\sigma_i}\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.$$

Equivalently, form $M\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ by

$$M_{ii}=1+h\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{d_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_i},\qquad M_{ij}=-h\frac{p_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_j}\quad(i\ne j),$$

and solve $My^{n+1}=y^n$. The rates in the solve are evaluated only at the admissible state $y^n\in\Omega_+$. For every input passing the branch, return the unique exact solution of the stated linear system. The standard first-order choice is $\sigma_i=y_i^n$, which is admissible only when every $y_i^n>0$. A separately defined rate-factor form extends a first-order step to zero donor coordinates under an additional source-factorization hypothesis.

Let $M=(m_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for a finite $m\ge1$. Suppose $m_{jj}>0$, $m_{ij}\le0$ for $i\ne j$, and

$$m_{jj}>\sum_{i\ne j}|m_{ij}|\qquad(j=1,\ldots,m).$$

Then $M$ is invertible and every entry of $M^{-1}$ is nonnegative. If $b\in\mathbb R^m$ has nonnegative coordinates, then $M^{-1}b\ge0$; if every coordinate of $b$ is positive, then every coordinate of $M^{-1}b$ is positive.

Let $m\ge1$, let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with state domain $\Omega$, and take an input state $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$, a step size $h$, and declared denominators $\sigma_i$. If $y^n\notin\Omega_+$, $h\le0$, or any $\sigma_i\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating any rate. Otherwise the **modified Patankar Euler step** returns the unique solution $y^{n+1}$ of

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(p_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_j^{n+1}}{\sigma_j}-d_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_i^{n+1}}{\sigma_i}\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.$$

Equivalently, form $M\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ by

$$M_{ii}=1+h\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{d_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_i},\qquad M_{ij}=-h\frac{p_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_j}\quad(i\ne j),$$

and solve $My^{n+1}=y^n$. The rates in the solve are evaluated only at the admissible state $y^n\in\Omega_+$. For every input passing the branch, return the unique exact solution of the stated linear system. The standard first-order choice is $\sigma_i=y_i^n$, which is admissible only when every $y_i^n>0$. A separately defined rate-factor form extends a first-order step to zero donor coordinates under an additional source-factorization hypothesis.

Let $M=(m_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for a finite $m\ge1$. Suppose $m_{jj}>0$, $m_{ij}\le0$ for $i\ne j$, and

$$m_{jj}>\sum_{i\ne j}|m_{ij}|\qquad(j=1,\ldots,m).$$

Then $M$ is invertible and every entry of $M^{-1}$ is nonnegative. If $b\in\mathbb R^m$ has nonnegative coordinates, then $M^{-1}b\ge0$; if every coordinate of $b$ is positive, then every coordinate of $M^{-1}b$ is positive.

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and consider a first-order IVP and solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **one-step method** is a family of maps $\Psi_h(t,v)$, defined for admitted times $t$, positive step sizes $h$, and states $v$, whose value is the method's approximation at time $t+h$ from the single input state $v$ at time $t$. It does not use earlier numerical states.

If $y$ is an exact solution on an interval containing $[t,t+h]$, the **local defect** is

$$\delta_h(t;y):=\Psi_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h).$$

Let $K\subseteq D$ be a fixed compact time-state set. The method has **uniform local order $p$ on $K$ along $y$** if there are constants $C\ge0$ and $h_0>0$, independent of the admitted starting time $t$ and step $0<h\le h_0$, such that

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le C h^{p+1}$$

whenever the exact solution graph on $[t,t+h]$ and the associated method time-state inputs, stages, and outputs under consideration lie in $K$. Here $p$ is a positive integer and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

The method has **one-step Lipschitz stability on $K$** with constant $L\ge0$ if

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$

for every admitted step size $h$, admitted time $t$, and input states $u,v$ with $(t,u),(t,v)\in K$. This is a bound on the change in one step; it is separate from absolute or linear stability regions and does not itself assert a global error estimate.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,
   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$
   where $I_n$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]];
   at $n=0$ the unique empty matrix $I_0\in M_0(\mathbb{R})$ has
   $\lVert I_0\rVert_p=0$, the convention of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

derivations.claim:
Since $U\subset\mathbb R_{>0}^m$, each coordinate $y_j$ stays bounded away from zero on $\overline U$. On $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ the reciprocal $s\mapsto s^{-1}$ has derivatives $-s^{-2}$ and $2s^{-3}$, obtained from the difference quotients $-1/(s(s+t))$ and $(2s+t)/(s^2(s+t)^2)$; composing with the coordinate projection gives continuous first and second partials for $y\mapsto y_j^{-1}$. Applying the product rule [F7] twice shows every entry $A_{ij}(y)=p_{ij}(y)y_j^{-1}$ ($i
e j$), and hence every diagonal sum, is $C^2$ on $U$; [F6] applied to these entries and their first partials supplies continuous total derivatives through order two. The row equations give $A(y)y=F(y)$: the off-diagonal terms contribute $\sum_{j
e i}p_{ij}$, and the diagonal term is $-\sum_{j
e i}d_{ij}$. For column $j$, $\sum_i A_{ij}=0$ because $A_{jj}=-\sum_{i
e j}A_{ij}$.

The off-diagonal entries of $A$ are nonnegative and its diagonal entries are nonpositive. Thus $I-hA(y)$ has positive diagonal, nonpositive off-diagonal entries, and strict column diagonal-dominance margin $1$; [F3] makes it invertible. On $[0,h_0]\times\overline U$, the entries of $I-hA(y)$ and its determinant are $C^2$; the determinant is nonzero by [F3]. Its cofactors and determinant are finite sums of products of entries, and the scalar reciprocal of the determinant is $C^2$ by the same reciprocal calculation as in step 1.1. The adjugate formula therefore makes the inverse a $C^2$ matrix-valued function there; compactness gives uniform bounds for the inverse and its first derivatives.

The matrix identity $(I-hA)^{-1}=I+hA+h^2A^2(I-hA)^{-1}$ yields $\Phi_h(y)=y+hF(y)+h^2G(h,y)$ with $G(h,y):=A(y)^2(I-hA(y))^{-1}y$. Step 1.2 and compactness bound $G$ uniformly. Along the exact solution, [F5]–[F7] give $y''(t)=DF(y(t))F(y(t))$, which is uniformly bounded on the compact tube. Taylor's formula [F11] gives $y(t+h)=y(t)+hF(y(t))+O(h^2)$ uniformly. Subtracting the expansions proves the local-defect estimate in [F4].

The function $G$ in step 2.1 is continuously differentiable in $y$ with uniformly bounded derivative on $\overline U$ by [F5]–[F7] and step 1.2. Differentiating that identity gives $D_y\Phi_h(y)=I+hDF(y)+h^2D_yG(h,y)$. Compactness bounds $\|DF(y)\|_2$ by $L_0$ and $\|D_yG(h,y)\|_2$ by $G_0$. The matrix-norm triangle inequality from [F8] and $\|I\|_2=1$ from [F9] yield $\|D_y\Phi_h(y)\|_2\le1+hL_0+h^2G_0\le1+(L_0+h_0G_0)h$ for $0<h\le h_0$.

Apply [F10] to $\Phi_h$ on the convex open set $U$ using the uniform derivative bound from step 3.1. This gives $\|\Phi_h(u)-\Phi_h(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$ for every $u,v\in U$, exactly the one-step stability assertion of [F4].

Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and a domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$; its admissible nonnegative states are $\Omega_+:=\Omega\cap[0,\infty)^m$. For every ordered pair $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $p_{ij},d_{ij}:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be production and destruction transfer rates that are nonnegative on $\Omega_+$. A **finite conservative production destruction system** (finite conservative PDS) is the autonomous ODE

$$y_i'=F_i(y):=\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(p_{ij}(y)-d_{ij}(y)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,$$

with internal-transfer identities

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

The index $j$ is the donor/source of $p_{ij}$ and the index $i$ is its recipient/destination; $d_{ji}$ is the same transfer viewed as destruction from $j$. The total mass is $M(y):=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i$. The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. No existence, positivity, or regularity assertion about solutions is part of this definition.

Let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]]. A **source-factored transfer representation** on an open set $U\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ containing a compact set $K\subseteq[0,\infty)^m$ consists of functions $a_{ij}:U\to\mathbb R$, $i\ne j$, such that each $a_{ij}$ is $C^2$ on the open subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ in the multivariable sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], is nonnegative on $U\cap[0,\infty)^m$, and, for every $y\in U\cap[0,\infty)^m$,

$$p_{ij}(y)=y_j a_{ij}(y),\qquad d_{ij}(y)=y_i a_{ji}(y),\qquad a_{ii}:=0.$$

Here $a_{ij}$ is the transfer rate from donor $j$ to recipient $i$ per unit of donor quantity. Nonnegativity is required on admissible nonnegative states; the $C^2$ extension to the open neighborhood is used for local analysis and need not be nonnegative at inadmissible states with negative coordinates. The factorization is an additional hypothesis, not a consequence of nonnegative rates and the identity $p_{ij}=d_{ji}$. On strictly positive states the ratio $p_{ij}(y)/y_j$ equals $a_{ij}(y)$; at a zero donor coordinate the factorized coefficient remains defined and avoids the indeterminate expression $0/0$.

Let $K$ be a compact nonnegative state set with a source-factored transfer representation [[def-source-factored-production-destruction-rates]]. Given $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$ and a step size $h$, if $y^n\notin K$ or $h\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating any factor. Otherwise form $B(y^n)\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ by

$$B_{ij}(y^n)=a_{ij}(y^n)\ (i\ne j),\qquad B_{jj}(y^n)=-\sum_{i\ne j}a_{ij}(y^n).$$

Return the unique solution $y^{n+1}$ of

$$\bigl(I-hB(y^n)\bigr)y^{n+1}=y^n.$$

Equivalently, component $i$ satisfies

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(a_{ij}(y^n)y_j^{n+1}-a_{ji}(y^n)y_i^{n+1}\right).$$

This procedure uses no denominator $y_j^n$ and is defined when some donor coordinates vanish. It is the factorized extension of the first-order Patankar Euler formula to the zero-state boundary. In exact arithmetic its linear system is uniquely solvable by [[lem-strict-column-dominance-implies-nonnegative-inverse]].

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and a domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$; its admissible nonnegative states are $\Omega_+:=\Omega\cap[0,\infty)^m$. For every ordered pair $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $p_{ij},d_{ij}:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be production and destruction transfer rates that are nonnegative on $\Omega_+$. A **finite conservative production destruction system** (finite conservative PDS) is the autonomous ODE

$$y_i'=F_i(y):=\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(p_{ij}(y)-d_{ij}(y)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,$$

with internal-transfer identities

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

The index $j$ is the donor/source of $p_{ij}$ and the index $i$ is its recipient/destination; $d_{ji}$ is the same transfer viewed as destruction from $j$. The total mass is $M(y):=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i$. The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. No existence, positivity, or regularity assertion about solutions is part of this definition.

Let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with state domain $\Omega$. Given $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$ and $h$, if $y^n\notin\Omega_+$, any coordinate of $y^n$ is nonpositive, or $h\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating rates or solving a system. First compute the stage $z$ by invoking [[alg-modified-patankar-euler]] with denominators $\sigma_i=y_i^n$:

$$z_i=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(p_{ij}(y^n)\frac{z_j}{y_j^n}-d_{ij}(y^n)\frac{z_i}{y_i^n}\right).$$

If the stage solve does not return a unique vector, return stage-failure. If its output $z\notin\Omega_+$, return rate-domain-failure before evaluating rates at $z$. Otherwise form $B(y^n,z)$ with, for $i\ne j$,

$$B_{ij}(y^n,z):=\frac{p_{ij}(y^n)+p_{ij}(z)}{2z_j},\qquad B_{jj}(y^n,z):=-\sum_{i\ne j}B_{ij}(y^n,z),$$

and solve

$$\bigl(I-hB(y^n,z)\bigr)y^{n+1}=y^n.$$

Equivalently,

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+\frac h2\sum_{j\ne i}\left((p_{ij}(y^n)+p_{ij}(z))\frac{y_j^{n+1}}{z_j}-(d_{ij}(y^n)+d_{ij}(z))\frac{y_i^{n+1}}{z_i}\right).$$

If the final solve is not uniquely solvable, return update-failure; otherwise return its unique solution $y^{n+1}$. The stage solve is uniquely solvable and its output is positive under the finite conservative PDS and positive-input hypotheses; when the rate-domain check passes, [[lem-strict-column-dominance-implies-nonnegative-inverse]] also guarantees a unique final solve. No zero-stage or denominator-regularized second-order variant is defined here.

Let $M=(m_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for a finite $m\ge1$. Suppose $m_{jj}>0$, $m_{ij}\le0$ for $i\ne j$, and

$$m_{jj}>\sum_{i\ne j}|m_{ij}|\qquad(j=1,\ldots,m).$$

Then $M$ is invertible and every entry of $M^{-1}$ is nonnegative. If $b\in\mathbb R^m$ has nonnegative coordinates, then $M^{-1}b\ge0$; if every coordinate of $b$ is positive, then every coordinate of $M^{-1}b$ is positive.

derivations.claim: For the stage, $M^{(1)}:=I-hA(y^n)$ has off-diagonal entries $-hp_{ij}(y^n)/y_j^n\le0$ and diagonal entries $1+h\sum_{i\ne j}p_{ij}(y^n)/y_j^n>0$ in column $j$. Also $\sum_i M^{(1)}_{ij}=1$ for every column, hence $\sum_i z_i=\sum_i y_i^n$.

Since $z>0$, every denominator in $B(y^n,z)$ is positive. Its off-diagonal entries are nonnegative, its diagonal entries are nonpositive, and its columns sum to zero by [F2]. Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

derivations.claim: Define $A(y)$ as in [F2]. On $U$, the coordinate reciprocals $y_j^{-1}$ have continuous partials $\partial_k(y_j^{-1})=-\delta_{jk}y_j^{-2}$ and $\partial_\ell\partial_k(y_j^{-1})=2\delta_{jk}\delta_{\ell j}y_j^{-3}$, as follows from the scalar reciprocal difference quotients on $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$; the product rule [F7] then makes every entry of $A$ $C^2$ from the rate data [F6]. By the continuous-partials theorem [F6], these entries have continuous total derivatives through order two. Direct multiplication gives $A(y)y=F(y)$. The matrix $I-hA(y)$ is invertible for $h>0$ by [F4] and equals $I$ at $h=0$; its determinant and cofactors are $C^2$ finite sums of products, and its determinant is nonzero, so the adjugate formula and the scalar reciprocal calculation make its inverse $C^2$ on the compact set of admitted $(h,y)$. It is uniformly bounded there for small $h$. Since $y>0$, [F4] gives $z=(I-hA(y))^{-1}y>0$. The identity $(I-hA)^{-1}=I+hA+h^2A^2(I-hA)^{-1}$ now gives $z=y+hF(y)+O(h^2)$ uniformly; in particular $z-y=O(h)$, so after decreasing $h_0$ we have $z\in V\subset\Omega$ uniformly for $y\in U$. Thus all stage denominators and the final rate evaluations are valid.

Write $B=B(y,z)$ for the final coefficient matrix in [F3]. Its entries are $C^2$ on the compact region of pairs produced inside $V$ by step 1.1: the rates are $C^2$, the stage map is $C^2$, and each reciprocal $z_j^{-1}$ has the same coordinate derivative formulas as in step 1.1. Its columns sum to zero, and direct multiplication using $p_{ij}=d_{ji}$ gives $B(y,z)z=\tfrac12(F(y)+F(z))$. For small $h$, step 1.1 keeps every $z_j$ bounded away from zero, so $B$ and its first derivatives are uniformly bounded. Also $B(y,y)=A(y)$; the mean-value theorem on the compact tube and $z-y=O(h)$ give $B(y,z)=A(y)+O(h)$. The final matrix $I-hB$ is invertible by [F4] and its inverse is uniformly bounded by the adjugate formula. Expanding its inverse yields $\Psi_h(y)=y+hB(y,z)y+O(h^2)=y+hF(y)+O(h^2)$. Comparing with step 1.1 gives $\Psi_h(y)-z=O(h^2)$.

The stage and final maps are $C^1$ in $y$ near the compact positive tube: their rates are $C^2$, their denominators stay bounded away from zero, and their matrix inverses are $C^2$ by the adjugate formula and the reciprocal calculation in steps 1.1–2.1. For any direction $v$, differentiating $z=y+hA(y)z$ gives $(I-hA)D_yz[v]=v+h(DA(y)[v])z$; boundedness from step 1.1 therefore gives $D_yz[v]=v+O(h)$ uniformly for $\|v\|_2\le1$.

Using $\Psi_h-y=hB\Psi_h$, substitute $z$ and use step 2.1 to obtain $\Psi_h-y=hBz+hB(\Psi_h-z)=\tfrac h2(F(y)+F(z))+O(h^3)$. Taylor expansion of $F$ at $y$, together with $z-y=hF(y)+O(h^2)$ from step 1.1, gives $F(z)=F(y)+hDF(y)F(y)+O(h^2)$. Thus $\Psi_h(y)=y+hF(y)+\tfrac{h^2}{2}DF(y)F(y)+O(h^3)$. By [F5]–[F7], the exact solution has the same expansion: $y''=DF(y)F(y)$ and its third derivative is bounded, so the one-variable Taylor remainder applied coordinatewise is $O(h^3)$. Their difference is the asserted uniform exact-start defect in [F9].
Differentiating $\Psi_h=y+hB(y,z)\Psi_h$ in direction $v$ gives $D_y\Psi_h[v]=(I-hB(y,z))^{-1}(v+h(D_1B(y,z)[v]+D_2B(y,z)[D_yz[v]])\Psi_h)$, with the inverse defined by step 2.1.

Steps 1.1–2.2 give $z=y+O(h)$, $\Psi_h=y+O(h)$, $B(y,z)=A(y)+O(h)$, and $(I-hB)^{-1}=I+hB+O(h^2)$ uniformly. Substitution yields $D_y\Psi_h[v]=v+h(A(y)v+(D_1B(y,y)[v]+D_2B(y,y)[v])y)+o(h)$. Differentiating $B(y,y)y=F(y)$ with the chain and product rules identifies the coefficient as $DF(y)v$; compactness makes the remainder uniform, so $D_y\Psi_h(y)=I+hDF(y)+hE(h,y)$ with $\sup_{y\in U}\|E(h,y)\|_2\to0$.

Compactness bounds $\|DF(y)\|_2$ uniformly, and step 4.1 makes the $E$ contribution at most $h$ for sufficiently small $h$. The norm properties in [F10] then give $\|D_y\Psi_h(y)\|_2\le1+Lh$ after decreasing $h_0$ and increasing $L$. Applying [F11] on convex $U$ proves $\|\Psi_h(u)-\Psi_h(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$.
