Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and a domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$; its admissible nonnegative states are $\Omega_+:=\Omega\cap[0,\infty)^m$. For every ordered pair $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $p_{ij},d_{ij}:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be production and destruction transfer rates that are nonnegative on $\Omega_+$. A **finite conservative production destruction system** (finite conservative PDS) is the autonomous ODE

$$y_i'=F_i(y):=\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(p_{ij}(y)-d_{ij}(y)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,$$

with internal-transfer identities

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

The index $j$ is the donor/source of $p_{ij}$ and the index $i$ is its recipient/destination; $d_{ji}$ is the same transfer viewed as destruction from $j$. The total mass is $M(y):=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i$. The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. No existence, positivity, or regularity assertion about solutions is part of this definition.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $m\ge1$, let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with state domain $\Omega$, and take an input state $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$, a step size $h$, and declared denominators $\sigma_i$. If $y^n\notin\Omega_+$, $h\le0$, or any $\sigma_i\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating any rate. Otherwise the **modified Patankar Euler step** returns the unique solution $y^{n+1}$ of

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(p_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_j^{n+1}}{\sigma_j}-d_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_i^{n+1}}{\sigma_i}\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.$$

Equivalently, form $M\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ by

$$M_{ii}=1+h\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{d_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_i},\qquad M_{ij}=-h\frac{p_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_j}\quad(i\ne j),$$

and solve $My^{n+1}=y^n$. The rates in the solve are evaluated only at the admissible state $y^n\in\Omega_+$. For every input passing the branch, return the unique exact solution of the stated linear system. The standard first-order choice is $\sigma_i=y_i^n$, which is admissible only when every $y_i^n>0$. A separately defined rate-factor form extends a first-order step to zero donor coordinates under an additional source-factorization hypothesis.

Let $F$ be the vector field of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] on a bounded open convex set $U\subset\Omega\cap\mathbb R_{>0}^m$ with $\overline U\subset\mathbb R_{>0}^m$. Suppose there is an open set $V$ with $\overline U\subset V\subset\Omega\cap\mathbb R_{>0}^m$ on which the transfer rates are multivariable $C^2$ and their derivatives through order two are bounded. For $y\in U$, let $\Phi_h(y)$ be [[alg-modified-patankar-euler]] with the standard denominators $\sigma_i=y_i$. Then there are constants $C,L,h_0>0$ such that, for $0<h\le h_0$:

1. for every exact solution $y(t)$ whose segment and the method states under consideration remain in a compact subset of $U$, the exact-start local defect satisfies $\|\Phi_h(y(t))-y(t+h)\|_2\le Ch^2$; and
2. for all $u,v\in U$, $\|\Phi_h(u)-\Phi_h(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$.

The defect is the method output minus the exact next state and the second inequality is one-step Lipschitz stability in the convention of [[def-one-step-ode-method-local-defect-order-and-stability]]. This result is restricted to a compact positive tube; it does not define the standard ratio formula at zero compartments.

Let $d,N,p\ge1$, $T>0$, $h=T/N$, and $t_n=nh$. Let $y:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ solve an initial-value problem in an open time-state domain $D$. Use the Euclidean norm $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], whose triangle inequality is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]. Let $\mathcal T\subset D$ be a common compact time-state tube with positive margin in $D$, and write $\mathcal T_t:=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:(t,v)\in\mathcal T\}$. Suppose a one-step map $\Psi_{h,n}$ is defined on $\mathcal T_{t_n}$, produces $y_{n+1}=\Psi_{h,n}(y_n)$, and the entire exact path, all numerical grid states, and every method stage lie in $\mathcal T$. If constants $C,C_0,L\ge0$, independent of $N$ and $n$, satisfy
$$\|y_0-y(0)\|_2\le C_0h^p,\qquad \|\Psi_{h,n}(y(t_n))-y(t_{n+1})\|_2\le Ch^{p+1},$$
and
$$\|\Psi_{h,n}(u)-\Psi_{h,n}(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$
for every $u,v\in\mathcal T_{t_n}$ and $0\le n<N$, then, for $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, for $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

derivations.claim: The assumption $y_n\in K\subset(0,\infty)^m$ makes every standard denominator $\sigma_i=(y_n)_i$ positive, so [F3] is admissible at every step. By [F4] the local defect is bounded by $Ch^2$ and the one-step map has factor $1+Lh$, with constants independent of $n$ and $N$. The initial error is zero, and the tube hypothesis supplies the common-tube condition of [F5].
Apply [F5] with $p=1$ and $C_0=0$. If $L>0$, its bound is $C(\exp(LT)-1)h/L$; if $L=0$, it is $CTh$. Both are $C_T h$ for a constant independent of $N$.

Let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with state domain $\Omega$. Given $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$ and $h$, if $y^n\notin\Omega_+$, any coordinate of $y^n$ is nonpositive, or $h\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating rates or solving a system. First compute the stage $z$ by invoking [[alg-modified-patankar-euler]] with denominators $\sigma_i=y_i^n$:

$$z_i=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(p_{ij}(y^n)\frac{z_j}{y_j^n}-d_{ij}(y^n)\frac{z_i}{y_i^n}\right).$$

If the stage solve does not return a unique vector, return stage-failure. If its output $z\notin\Omega_+$, return rate-domain-failure before evaluating rates at $z$. Otherwise form $B(y^n,z)$ with, for $i\ne j$,

$$B_{ij}(y^n,z):=\frac{p_{ij}(y^n)+p_{ij}(z)}{2z_j},\qquad B_{jj}(y^n,z):=-\sum_{i\ne j}B_{ij}(y^n,z),$$

and solve

$$\bigl(I-hB(y^n,z)\bigr)y^{n+1}=y^n.$$

Equivalently,

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+\frac h2\sum_{j\ne i}\left((p_{ij}(y^n)+p_{ij}(z))\frac{y_j^{n+1}}{z_j}-(d_{ij}(y^n)+d_{ij}(z))\frac{y_i^{n+1}}{z_i}\right).$$

If the final solve is not uniquely solvable, return update-failure; otherwise return its unique solution $y^{n+1}$. The stage solve is uniquely solvable and its output is positive under the finite conservative PDS and positive-input hypotheses; when the rate-domain check passes, [[lem-strict-column-dominance-implies-nonnegative-inverse]] also guarantees a unique final solve. Let $M=(m_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for a finite $m\ge1$. Suppose $m_{jj}>0$, $m_{ij}\le0$ for $i\ne j$, and

$$m_{jj}>\sum_{i\ne j}|m_{ij}|\qquad(j=1,\ldots,m).$$

Then $M$ is invertible and every entry of $M^{-1}$ is nonnegative. If $b\in\mathbb R^m$ has nonnegative coordinates, then $M^{-1}b\ge0$; if every coordinate of $b$ is positive, then every coordinate of $M^{-1}b$ is positive.

Let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be as in [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]]. Here fl is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, on each real exact result that is zero or normal; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range x, fl(sqrt(x)) is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression ab+c; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $x\in\mathbb F^n$, $y\in\mathbb F^m$ have stored real or complex entries, with $m,n\ge1$. Use the operationwise arithmetic model, successful sequential dot products, and $0<u<1$ with $(\max(m,n)-1)u<1$. Define
$$g_k=\frac{1+6u}{1-(k-1)u}-1,\qquad F=\|A\|_F,\quad X=\|x\|_2,\quad Y=\|y\|_2.$$
For $\widehat v=\operatorname{fl}(Ax)$ and $\widehat w=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-y)$, put $V=g_nFX$ and $W=V+u(\|\widehat v\|_2+Y)$. Then
$$\|\widehat w-(Ax-y)\|_2\le W.$$
For a stored real $\lambda>0$, also compute $\widehat z=\operatorname{fl}(A^*\widehat w)$, $\widehat l=\operatorname{fl}(\lambda x)$ and $\widehat r=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat z+\widehat l)$, rounding scalar multiplication componentwise. The exact intended normal residual $r=A^*(Ax-y)+\lambda x$ satisfies
$$\|\widehat r-r\|_2\le\rho:=FW+g_mF\|\widehat w\|_2+u\lambda X+u(\|\widehat z\|_2+\|\widehat l\|_2).$$
Norms in these certificates mean exact norms or certified upper bounds. Uncontrolled rounding of the certificate itself is not authorized. The linear bound applies columnwise to certify $\|I-AB\|_2\le\|I-AB\|_F$ from stored basis-solve columns $B$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and a domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$; its admissible nonnegative states are $\Omega_+:=\Omega\cap[0,\infty)^m$. For every ordered pair $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $p_{ij},d_{ij}:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be production and destruction transfer rates that are nonnegative on $\Omega_+$. A **finite conservative production destruction system** (finite conservative PDS) is the autonomous ODE

$$y_i'=F_i(y):=\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(p_{ij}(y)-d_{ij}(y)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,$$

with internal-transfer identities

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

The index $j$ is the donor/source of $p_{ij}$ and the index $i$ is its recipient/destination; $d_{ji}$ is the same transfer viewed as destruction from $j$. The total mass is $M(y):=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i$. The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. No existence, positivity, or regularity assertion about solutions is part of this definition.

Let $m\ge1$, let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with state domain $\Omega$, and take an input state $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$, a step size $h$, and declared denominators $\sigma_i$. If $y^n\notin\Omega_+$, $h\le0$, or any $\sigma_i\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating any rate. Otherwise the **modified Patankar Euler step** returns the unique solution $y^{n+1}$ of

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(p_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_j^{n+1}}{\sigma_j}-d_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_i^{n+1}}{\sigma_i}\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.$$

Equivalently, form $M\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ by

$$M_{ii}=1+h\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{d_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_i},\qquad M_{ij}=-h\frac{p_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_j}\quad(i\ne j),$$

and solve $My^{n+1}=y^n$. The rates in the solve are evaluated only at the admissible state $y^n\in\Omega_+$. For every input passing the branch, return the unique exact solution of the stated linear system. The standard first-order choice is $\sigma_i=y_i^n$, which is admissible only when every $y_i^n>0$. A separately defined rate-factor form extends a first-order step to zero donor coordinates under an additional source-factorization hypothesis.

Let $M\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be an exact linear-system matrix from a successfully completed [[alg-modified-patankar-euler]] step with admissible positive denominators, or from a completed stage/final solve of [[alg-mprk22-1]], for a finite conservative PDS. Let $b\ge0$ be its exact right-hand side. For either scheme, the PDS transfer identity gives $\mathbf 1^TM=\mathbf 1^T$ and strict column diagonal dominance, so $M^{-1}\ge0$. Let $\widehat y$ be a stored candidate and compute $\widehat v=\operatorname{fl}(M\widehat y)$ and $\widehat w=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-b)$ in the operationwise model of [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]], with $0<u<1$, $(m-1)u<1$, every nonzero exact intermediate normal, zero operations exact, successful sequential dot products and subtraction, and exact or certified upper bounds for the norms used by the supplier. Let $W$ be the certified allowance from [[lem-rounded-linear-and-normal-residual-certificates]], using exact norms or certified upper bounds, and set $\rho:=\|\widehat w\|_2+W$. Then

$$\|M\widehat y-b\|_2\le\rho,\qquad \left|\mathbf1^T\widehat y-\mathbf1^Tb\right|\le\sqrt m\,\rho.$$

If $y^*:=M^{-1}b$ is the exact solution of the stored linear system, then

$$\|\widehat y-y^*\|_1\le\sqrt m\,\rho.$$

The absolute stability region of a listed method is $\{z\in\mathbb C:|R(z)|\le1\}$. On the negative real axis, the Euler and midpoint regions are exactly $[-2,0]$. No maximal real interval is asserted here for RK4.

$$\{z\in\mathbb C:|z+1|\le1\}.$$

On the negative real axis, for $y'=-\rho y$ with $\rho>0$, the method is absolutely stable exactly when $0<h\rho\le2$.

Fix a finite horizon $T>0$. Let mortality and fertility be bounded Lipschitz functions $\mu,\beta:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, and let $n_0\in L^1(0,\infty)$ be nonnegative. The **linear age-structured renewal transport problem** is

$$n_t(t,a)+n_a(t,a)=-\mu(a)n(t,a),\qquad a>0,\quad 0<t\le T,$$

with initial density $n(0,a)=n_0(a)$ and inflow condition

$$n(t,0)=B(t),\qquad B(t):=\int_0^\infty \beta(a)n(t,a)\,da.$$

Here $a$ is age, $B$ is the birth rate, and the characteristic age path solves the first-order initial value problem $a'(s)=1$ in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], hence $a(s)=a(0)+s$. Define survival from age $a$ over duration $s\ge0$ by

$$S(a,s):=\exp\!\left(-\int_a^{a+s}\mu(r)\,dr\right).$$

A **weak solution** on $[0,T]$ is a nonnegative $n\in C([0,T];L^1(0,\infty))$ with continuous $B:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying $B(t)=\int_0^\infty\beta(a)n(t,a)\,da$ and, for every $\phi\in C_c^1([0,T]\times[0,\infty))$ with $\phi(T,a)=0$,

$$-\int_0^T\!\int_0^\infty n(t,a)(\phi_t+\phi_a-\mu(a)\phi)\,da\,dt=\int_0^\infty n_0(a)\phi(0,a)\,da+\int_0^T B(t)\phi(t,0)\,dt.$$

A **mild solution** is a weak solution that also satisfies, for almost every $a\ge0$,

$$n(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0(a-t)S(a-t,t),&a\ge t,\\B(t-a)S(0,a),&0\le a<t,\end{cases}$$

The formula follows the age characteristics $a'(s)=1$ and their mortality survival. No delay equation or finite-age cutoff is identified with this model by definition.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

derivations.claim: The characteristic path through age $x$ at time $0$ is $a(s)=x+s$ by [F1] and [F2]. Along it the PDE gives $\frac{d}{ds}n(s,x+s)=-\mu(x+s)n(s,x+s)$, so integrating the scalar equation yields $n(t,x+t)=n_0(x)\exp(-\int_x^{x+t}\mu)$. A characteristic entering at age $0$ at time $t-a$ instead starts with value $B(t-a)$ and is multiplied by $e^{-M(a)}$, giving the two branches in the Statement.
Substitute the two branches into $B(t)=\int_0^\infty\beta(a)n(t,a)\,da$ and split at $a=t$. In the old-cohort part set $x=a-t$; the result is exactly $G(t)+\int_0^t\beta(a)e^{-M(a)}B(t-a)\,da$.

The functions $K$ and $G$ are continuous. Indeed, $K$ is a product of Lipschitz functions; for $s,t\in[0,T]$, the integrand multiplier in $G$ changes by at most $(\operatorname{Lip}(\beta)+\|\beta\|_\infty\|\mu\|_\infty)|t-s|$, since $|e^{-u}-e^{-v}|\le|u-v|$ for $u,v\ge0$. Multiplication by $n_0\in L^1$ and integration gives continuity of $G$.

On any interval of length $\tau$ with $\tau\|K\|_\infty<1$, the right side of the Volterra equation is a contraction in the sup norm on continuous birth-rate functions: the difference of two outputs is bounded by $\tau\|K\|_\infty$ times the input difference. If $\|K\|_\infty=0$, the equation is simply $B=G$. Starting at time zero and then treating the already determined history as a fixed forcing term, finitely many such intervals cover $[0,T]$; each interval therefore has one continuous solution and the solutions agree at their shared endpoints.

When $n_0\ge0$, $G,K\ge0$. Picard iteration from the zero function on the first interval preserves nonnegativity and converges to its unique fixed point; the same argument applies on each continuation interval because its known-history forcing is nonnegative. Thus $B\ge0$, and the characteristic formula gives $n\ge0$.

The formula has finite $L^1$ norm because its old-cohort contribution is at most $\|n_0\|_1$ and its newborn contribution is at most $\int_0^t B(s)\,ds$. On the old branch, continuity in time follows from translation continuity of $n_0$ in $L^1$ and dominated convergence for the survival multiplier. On the newborn branch, continuity follows from continuity and boundedness of $B$ and $S$, with the interval of newly entering cohorts having length tending to zero. Thus $n\in C([0,T];L^1)$.

Let $\phi\in C_c^1([0,T]\times[0,\infty))$ satisfy $\phi(T,a)=0$. On an initial cohort with coordinate $x=a-t\ge0$, the chain rule gives $\frac{d}{dt}[n_0(x)S(x,t)\phi(t,x+t)]=n(t,x+t)(\phi_t+\phi_a-\mu\phi)(t,x+t)$ for almost every $t$. Integrating from $0$ to $T$ makes the terminal term zero and leaves $-n_0(x)\phi(0,x)$; integration over $x\ge0$ gives the initial-data contribution to the weak identity.

For a newborn cohort with birth time $s=t-a\ge0$, the chain rule gives $\frac{d}{da}[B(s)S(0,a)\phi(s+a,a)]=n(s+a,a)(\phi_t+\phi_a-\mu\phi)(s+a,a)$. Integrating from $a=0$ to $T-s$ gives $-B(s)\phi(s,0)$ because $\phi(T,T-s)=0$; integrating over $s\in[0,T]$ gives the renewal-boundary contribution.

The old-cohort region $a\ge t$ and newborn region $a<t$ partition the time-age domain up to a measure-zero diagonal. Adding their integrals from steps 4.1 and 4.2, then multiplying by $-1$, gives exactly the weak identity in [F1] with initial term $\int n_0(x)\phi(0,x)dx$ and boundary term $\int_0^T B(s)\phi(s,0)ds$. Step 1.2 gives $B(t)=\int_0^\infty\beta(a)n(t,a)da$, and step 3.2 gives $n\in C([0,T];L^1)$ and nonnegativity. Thus the characteristic formula is a weak, hence mild, solution.

Any mild solution has a birth rate satisfying the Volterra equation in step 1.2. Uniqueness from step 2.2 forces that same birth rate, and the characteristic formula in step 1.1 then forces the same density.

$$-\int_0^T\!\int_0^\infty n(t,a)(\phi_t+\phi_a-\mu(a)\phi)\,da\,dt=\int_0^\infty n_0(a)\phi(0,a)\,da+\int_0^T B(t)\phi(t,0)\,dt.$$

A **mild solution** is a weak solution that also satisfies, for almost every $a\ge0$,

$$n(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0(a-t)S(a-t,t),&a\ge t,\\B(t-a)S(0,a),&0\le a<t,\end{cases}$$

The formula follows the age characteristics $a'(s)=1$ and their mortality survival. No delay equation or finite-age cutoff is identified with this model by definition.

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]], put $M(a)=\int_0^a\mu(r)\,dr$, $K(a)=\beta(a)e^{-M(a)}$, and

$$G(t)=\int_0^\infty \beta(x+t)\exp\!\left(-\int_x^{x+t}\mu(r)\,dr\right)n_0(x)\,dx.$$

There is a unique mild solution. Its birth rate is the unique continuous solution of

$$B(t)=G(t)+\int_0^t K(a)B(t-a)\,da,$$

and its density, for almost every $a\ge0$, is

$$n(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0(a-t)\exp\!\left(-\int_{a-t}^{a}\mu(r)\,dr\right),&a\ge t,\\ B(t-a)e^{-M(a)},&0\le a<t.\end{cases}$$

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

derivations.claim: The formula in [F2] is linear in $n_0$, and uniqueness in [F2] implies that the solution for a sum of two initial data is the sum of their solutions and that scalar multiples are preserved. Nonnegative $n_0$ gives nonnegative $G$, Volterra kernel and density by [F1]–[F2], so the solution operator is positive.

Integrating the two characteristic branches in [F2] gives $N(t)=\int_0^\infty n_0(x)S(x,t)\,dx+\int_0^t B(t-a)S(0,a)\,da$. Bounded $\mu$ and continuous $B$ permit differentiation under these integrals; using $\partial_tS(x,t)=-\mu(x+t)S(x,t)$ and $\partial_aS(0,a)=-\mu(a)S(0,a)$ yields $N'(t)=B(t)-\int_0^\infty\mu(a)n(t,a)\,da$ for almost every $t$. Since $0\le B(t)\le\beta_\infty N(t)$ and $\mu n\ge0$, we have $N'(t)\le\beta_\infty N(t)$.

Integrating the differential inequality in step 1.2 gives $N(t)\le N(0)+\int_0^t\beta_\infty N(s)\,ds$. Apply [F3] with $a(t)=N(0)$ and $b=\beta_\infty$ to obtain the asserted positive-semigroup bound.

Subtract the two transport equations and write $w=n-\widetilde n$. Along characteristics, its interior forcing is $(\widetilde\mu-\mu)\widetilde n$ and its inflow forcing is $\int\beta w+\int(\beta-\widetilde\beta)\widetilde n$. Taking absolute values in the characteristic integral formula, integrating over age, and using nonnegative survival factors gives $E(t)\le E(0)+\int_0^t[\beta_\infty E(s)+\delta\widetilde N(s)]\,ds$, where $E=\|w\|_1$ and $\widetilde N=\|\widetilde n\|_1$.

By step 1.3 applied to $\widetilde n$, $\widetilde N(s)\le e^{\widetilde\beta_\infty s}\|\widetilde n_0\|_1$. Thus the nondecreasing function $a(t)=E(0)+\delta t e^{\widetilde\beta_\infty t}\|\widetilde n_0\|_1$ bounds the forcing integral in step 2.1, and [F3] yields the claimed coefficient-and-initial-data stability estimate.

Fix a finite horizon $T>0$ and a nondegenerate fixed size interval $[0,X]$ with $X>0$. Let $g,\mu,\gamma:[0,X]\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded Lipschitz functions, with $g(x)\ge g_{\min}>0$. Here $g$ is size growth, $\mu$ is ordinary mortality, and $\gamma$ is the rate at which a dividing parent is removed. For each parent size $y$, let $K_y$ be a finite nonnegative Borel measure of daughter sizes, supported on $[0,y]$. Assume $y\mapsto K_y(E)$ is measurable for every Borel set $E\subseteq[0,X]$, and that the number moment $k_0(y):=K_y([0,y])$ is uniformly bounded; the size moment $k_1(y):=\int_{[0,y]}x\,K_y(dx)$ is then finite. The **size-structured transport and division model** is

$$\partial_t n+\partial_x(gn)=-(\mu+\gamma)n+\int_{[0,X]}K_y(dx)n(t,y)\,dy,\qquad 0<x<X,$$

with zero incoming flux at $x=0$ and absorbing outflow $g(X)n(t,X)$ at $x=X$. Let $\Pi_{[0,X]}(x):=\min\{X,\max\{0,x\}\}$ and extend the growth field to $\widetilde g(x):=g(\Pi_{[0,X]}(x))$ on $\mathbb R$. This is a bounded Lipschitz vector field. By [[thm-size-structured-positivity-number-and-weighted-moment-identities]], its IVP has a unique solution on the finite time horizon; a model characteristic is this solution restricted to the interval from its initial size until its first hitting of $X$, including that hitting time when it occurs by $T$. On this restricted interval, $\widetilde g=g$. The characteristic is understood as a first-order IVP solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. The weak equation is obtained by testing against $\phi\in C^1([0,X])$: transport contributes $\int_0^Xg\phi'n$, mortality and parent removal contribute $-\int_0^X(\mu+\gamma)\phi n$, division contributes $\int_0^X\int\phi(x)K_y(dx)n(t,y)\,dy$, and the upper boundary contributes $-\phi(X)g(X)n(t,X)$. The interval is fixed; moving boundaries, zero growth and discontinuous coefficients are outside this definition.

Input a partition $0=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_J=X$ with $J\ge1$, a time step $\Delta t>0$, a nonnegative current mass vector $M^k=(M_j^k)_{j=1}^J$, and the coefficients and kernel from [[def-size-structured-transport-and-division-kernel]]. Partition $[0,X]$ into disjoint cells $C_j=[x_{j-1},x_j)$ for $j<J$ and $C_J=[x_{J-1},X]$, with widths $h_j=x_j-x_{j-1}>0$ and centers $x_j^c=(x_{j-1}+x_j)/2$. Set $u_j^k=M_j^k/h_j$, the incoming flux $F_0^k=0$, the internal and outgoing upwind fluxes $F_j^k=g(x_j)u_j^k$ for $1\le j\le J$, and $d_j=\mu(x_j^c)+\gamma(x_j^c)$.

For each parent cell $C_\ell$, form nonnegative daughter coefficients

$$A_{j\ell}=\frac{1}{h_\ell}\,Q_M\bigl(y\mapsto K_y(C_j);x_{\ell-1},x_\ell,1\bigr),$$

using [[alg-composite-midpoint-rule]] on the parent-size interval. Since the one-panel midpoint rule is $Q_M(f;x_{\ell-1},x_\ell,1)=h_\ell f(x_\ell^c)$, this gives $A_{j\ell}=K_{x_\ell^c}(C_j)\ge0$. If $\Delta t(g(x_j)/h_j+d_j)>1$ for any cell, return `invalid-cfl` without an update. Otherwise the finite-volume update is

$$M_j^{k+1}=M_j^k-\Delta t(F_j^k-F_{j-1}^k)-\Delta t\,d_jM_j^k+\Delta t\sum_{\ell=1}^JA_{j\ell}M_\ell^k.$$

The flux $F_J^k$ is absorbing outflow. The admissible variable-width CFL is $\Delta t(g(x_j)/h_j+d_j)\le1$ for every cell. If a grid or any required coefficient/kernel evaluation fails, return failure without a partial update. Otherwise return $M^{k+1}$ together with the fluxes and daughter coefficients used in the step.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

derivations.claim: In [F2], the coefficient of $M_j^k$ outside the division source is $1-\Delta t(g(x_j)/h_j+d_j)$, which is nonnegative by the CFL. For $j\ge2$ the incoming transport term has coefficient $\Delta t g(x_{j-1})/h_{j-1}\ge0$; for $j=1$ the incoming flux is $F_0=0$. Every division term has coefficient $\Delta t A_{j\ell}\ge0$. Hence each new mass is a sum of nonnegative terms when [A1] holds. Induction on $k$ proves $M_j^k\ge0$.

Sum [F2] over $j$. The finite flux sum telescopes to $F_J-F_0=F_J$ because $F_0=0$. Interchanging the finite sums in the kernel source gives $\sum_\ell(\sum_jA_{j\ell})M_\ell=\sum_\ell k_{0,\ell}^hM_\ell$. Subtracting $N_h^k$ yields the number identity.

Multiply [F2] by $x_j^c$ and sum over $j$. For the flux term, finite summation by parts gives $\sum_jx_j^c(F_j-F_{j-1})=x_J^cF_J-\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}(x_{j+1}^c-x_j^c)F_j$ since $F_0=0$. The loss term is $-\sum_jx_j^cd_jM_j$, and the source term is $\sum_\ell(\sum_jx_j^cA_{j\ell})M_\ell=\sum_\ell k_{1,\ell}^hM_\ell$. Rearranging proves the weighted-moment identity and the stated condition for cancellation.

Let $M=\|g\|_\infty$ and let $L$ be a Lipschitz constant for $g$ on $[0,X]$. The projection $\Pi_{[0,X]}$ is $1$-Lipschitz, so the extension $\widetilde g=g\circ\Pi_{[0,X]}$ is globally bounded by $M$ and globally Lipschitz with constant $L$ on the open domain $\mathbb R$. Since $g\ge g_{\min}>0$, choose $h_0>0$ with $h_0M\le1$ and $Lh_0<1$. For every starting time $t_0\in\mathbb R$ and state $z\in\mathbb R$, the cylinder $[t_0-h_0,t_0+h_0]\times[z-1,z+1]$ lies in $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$, and [F3] gives a unique solution through $(t_0,z)$ on that interval; the same bounds apply after every restart. Restricting and concatenating at most $\lceil T/h_0\rceil$ such forward segments gives a solution on $[0,T]$, and the uniqueness clause of [F3] makes it unique there. Along this solution $\chi_y'(s)=\widetilde g(\chi_y(s))\ge g_{\min}$, so it is strictly increasing. Starting from $y\in[0,X]$, it stays in $[0,X]$ through its first hitting of $X$, where $\widetilde g=g$; that restricted segment is the model characteristic.

citations.quote: Fix $0<T<A$, bounded nonnegative Lipschitz rates $\mu,\beta:[0,A]\to[0,\infty)$, and initial density $n_0^A\in L^1_+(0,A)$. The **finite-age renewal model with absorbing outflow** is the age transport problem on $0<a<A$ with the same renewal inflow $B_A(t)=\int_0^A\beta(a)n^A(t,a)\,da$ as in [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]]. A cohort follows age speed $1$, retains its mortality survival $S(a,s)$ until it reaches $A$, and is then removed; no cohort enters from ages above $A$. The initial density is $n_0^A$ on $[0,A]$. A mild solution is the characteristic formula on $0<a<A$, with an initial-cohort branch for $a\ge t$, a newborn branch for $a<t$, and zero extension to $a\ge A$. Since $A>T$, no cohort born during $[0,T]$ reaches the outflow boundary.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

derivations.claim: The kernel $K$ is continuous on $[0,T]$. The moving-limit forcing $G_A$ is also continuous: on the common part of the integration intervals its integrand changes uniformly continuously with $t$, and the integral over the symmetric difference tends to zero by absolute continuity of the integral of $n_0^A$. It is nonnegative.

On any interval of length $\delta$ with $\delta\|K\|_\infty<1$, the map $b\mapsto G_A(t)+\int_0^tK(a)b(t-a)da$ is a contraction on the unknown continuous birth-rate segment, with contraction factor at most $\delta\|K\|_\infty$ after the already determined history is placed in the forcing. If $K=0$, the equation reduces to $B_A=G_A$. Finitely many such intervals cover $[0,T]$, and at each endpoint the defining equation fixes the same value from either adjacent interval; this constructs a unique continuous solution. Picard iteration from zero on each interval preserves nonnegativity because $G_A,K\ge0$, so $B_A\ge0$.

Substitute the displayed density formula into $\int_0^A\beta(a)n^A(t,a)da$. On the initial-cohort part $t\le a<A$, use $x=a-t$ to obtain $G_A(t)$. On the newborn part $0\le a<t$, the integral is $\int_0^t\beta(a)S(0,a)B_A(t-a)da=\int_0^tK(a)B_A(t-a)da$. The Volterra equation therefore gives exactly the renewal boundary relation. Both parts are nonnegative and have finite $L^1$ mass, bounded by $\|n_0^A\|_1+\int_0^tB_A(s)ds$.

Integrating the two characteristic branches gives $N_A(t)=\int_0^{A-t}n_0^A(x)S(x,t)dx+\int_0^tB_A(t-a)S(0,a)da$. This mass function is absolutely continuous; the moving-limit rule and $\partial_tS(x,t)=-\mu(x+t)S(x,t)$ show for almost every $t$ that $N_A'(t)=B_A(t)-\int_0^A\mu(a)n^A(t,a)da-n_0^A(A-t)S(A-t,t)$. The final term is nonnegative outflow, so $N_A'(t)\le B_A(t)\le\beta_\infty N_A(t)$. Integrating and applying [F2] yields $N_A(t)\le e^{\beta_\infty t}N_A(0)$.

For $t\le T<A$, newborn cohorts have age at most $T$ and cannot reach $A$. An initial cohort with age $x$ exits by time $t$ precisely when $A-t\le x<A$; it survives until exit by $S(x,A-x)$. Integrating its initial density over those ages gives the stated $O_A(t)$. Any mild solution must follow these same characteristics and its birth rate must solve the Volterra equation from step 2.1, whose solution is unique by step 1.2. Thus the density and outflow are unique. Translation continuity in $L^1$, continuity of $B_A$ and of $S$, and the vanishing measure of the newly entering cohort region give continuity of $n^A$ in time with values in $L^1(0,A)$.

Fix a finite horizon $T>0$. Let mortality and fertility be bounded Lipschitz functions $\mu,\beta:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, and let $n_0\in L^1(0,\infty)$ be nonnegative. The **linear age-structured renewal transport problem** is

$$n_t(t,a)+n_a(t,a)=-\mu(a)n(t,a),\qquad a>0,\quad 0<t\le T,$$

with initial density $n(0,a)=n_0(a)$ and inflow condition

$$n(t,0)=B(t),\qquad B(t):=\int_0^\infty \beta(a)n(t,a)\,da.$$

Here $a$ is age, $B$ is the birth rate, and the characteristic age path solves the first-order initial value problem $a'(s)=1$ in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], hence $a(s)=a(0)+s$. Define survival from age $a$ over duration $s\ge0$ by

$$S(a,s):=\exp\!\left(-\int_a^{a+s}\mu(r)\,dr\right).$$

A **weak solution** on $[0,T]$ is a nonnegative $n\in C([0,T];L^1(0,\infty))$ with continuous $B:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying $B(t)=\int_0^\infty\beta(a)n(t,a)\,da$ and, for every $\phi\in C_c^1([0,T]\times[0,\infty))$ with $\phi(T,a)=0$,

$$-\int_0^T\!\int_0^\infty n(t,a)(\phi_t+\phi_a-\mu(a)\phi)\,da\,dt=\int_0^\infty n_0(a)\phi(0,a)\,da+\int_0^T B(t)\phi(t,0)\,dt.$$

A **mild solution** is a weak solution that also satisfies, for almost every $a\ge0$,

$$n(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0(a-t)S(a-t,t),&a\ge t,\\B(t-a)S(0,a),&0\le a<t,\end{cases}$$

The formula follows the age characteristics $a'(s)=1$ and their mortality survival. No delay equation or finite-age cutoff is identified with this model by definition.

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]], put $M(a)=\int_0^a\mu(r)\,dr$, $K(a)=\beta(a)e^{-M(a)}$, and

$$G(t)=\int_0^\infty \beta(x+t)\exp\!\left(-\int_x^{x+t}\mu(r)\,dr\right)n_0(x)\,dx.$$

There is a unique mild solution. Its birth rate is the unique continuous solution of

$$B(t)=G(t)+\int_0^t K(a)B(t-a)\,da,$$

and its density, for almost every $a\ge0$, is

$$n(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0(a-t)\exp\!\left(-\int_{a-t}^{a}\mu(r)\,dr\right),&a\ge t,\\ B(t-a)e^{-M(a)},&0\le a<t.\end{cases}$$

Input a finite horizon $T>0$, a time step $\Delta t>0$, an age cutoff $A>0$, bounded nonnegative rates $\mu,\beta$ on $[0,A]$, and a finite positive initial quadrature $(a_i,m_i^0)_{i=1}^I$ supported in $[0,A)$ for the initial age measure on that interval. Set $N=\lfloor T/\Delta t\rfloor$; the procedure returns levels at $t_k=k\Delta t$ for $0\le k\le N$, with final time $N\Delta t\le T$. One option is the composite midpoint rule on a partition of $[0,A]$: for each panel midpoint $a_i$, set $m_i^0=\Delta a\,n_0(a_i)$. A cohort at age $a_i^k$ and mass $m_i^k$ follows the exact age characteristic

$$a_i^{k+1}=a_i^k+\Delta t$$

and updates its survival mass by forward Euler,

$$m_i^{k+1}=(1-\Delta t\,\mu(a_i^k))m_i^k.$$

If $\Delta t\|\mu\|_\infty>1$, return status invalid-step with no updates. Otherwise initialize the birth and outflow records as empty and set $\nu_h^0=\sum_i m_i^0\delta_{a_i^0}$. For each $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, first calculate $B_h^k=\sum_i\beta(a_i^k)m_i^k$. Advance every existing cohort by $a_i^{k+1}=a_i^k+\Delta t$ and update its survival mass by $m_i^{k+1}=(1-\Delta t\mu(a_i^k))m_i^k$. If an updated age is at least $A$, record that updated mass as discrete outflow and discard the cohort; otherwise retain it. Then insert a newborn cohort of age $0$ and mass $\Delta t B_h^k$ at time $t_{k+1}$. Record $B_h^k$ and the step's outflow, and form $\nu_h^{k+1}$ from the retained cohorts and this newborn. A failed rate evaluation returns failure with no partial update. The procedure returns the finite sequence $(\nu_h^k)_{k=0}^N$ and its birth/outflow records. The bounded-Lipschitz quadrature defect of the initial measure and the Euler survival error are separate inputs to any consistency claim.

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $V\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be an open time-state domain whose fibers $V_t:=\{z:(t,z)\in V\}$ are open and convex. Let $K\subset V$ be compact. Let $f:V\to\mathbb R^d$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and suppose $y$ is a solution of $y'=f(t,y)$, $y(0)=y_0$, on an open interval containing $[0,T]$, with graph on $[0,T]$ contained in $K$. For each local defect under consideration, require the Euler input and output time-state pairs to lie in $K$; the exact solution segment already lies in $K$.

For $1\le i,j\le d$, assume finite constants $F_j,M_{t,i},M_{ij},L\ge0$ satisfy throughout $V$

$$|f_j(t,z)|\le F_j,\qquad |\partial_t f_i(t,z)|\le M_{t,i},\qquad |\partial_{z_j}f_i(t,z)|\le M_{ij},\qquad \|D_yf(t,z)w\|_2\le L\|w\|_2\quad(w\in\mathbb R^d).$$

Here $D_yf$ is the matrix with entries $\partial_{z_j}f_i$, and the last inequality defines the operator bound used below. The forward Euler map is $\Psi_h(t,v)=v+h f(t,v)$. Then, with $B_i:=M_{t,i}+\sum_{j=1}^dM_{ij}F_j$, for every $t\in[0,T)$ and $h>0$ with $t+h\le T$ whose Euler input and output pairs lie in $K$, its local defect satisfies

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le \frac{h^2}{2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^d B_i^2\right)^{1/2},$$

so it has uniform local order one on $K$ along $y|_{[0,T]}$, with $h_0=T$. For every $t\in[0,T]$, every admitted $h>0$, and every $u,v\in V_t$,

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2.$$

This is a local defect and one-step stability result. It does not assert a global error estimate or an order for any other named method.

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]], let $\beta_\infty=\|\beta\|_\infty$. The solution map $S_{\mu,\beta}(t):n_0\mapsto n(t,\cdot)$ is linear and positive, and

$$\|S_{\mu,\beta}(t)n_0\|_1\le e^{\beta_\infty t}\|n_0\|_1.$$

If $n,\widetilde n$ use possibly different nonnegative bounded coefficients $(\mu,\beta)$ and $(\widetilde\mu,\widetilde\beta)$ and initial data $n_0,\widetilde n_0$, put $\delta=\|\mu-\widetilde\mu\|_\infty+\|\beta-\widetilde\beta\|_\infty$ and $\widetilde\beta_\infty=\|\widetilde\beta\|_\infty$. Then

$$\|n(t)-\widetilde n(t)\|_1\le e^{\beta_\infty t}\left(\|n_0-\widetilde n_0\|_1+\delta t e^{\widetilde\beta_\infty t}\|\widetilde n_0\|_1\right).$$

Let $T>0$, $N\ge1$, $h=T/N$, $p\ge1$, and $C_0,C,L\ge0$. If nonnegative real numbers $e_0,\ldots,e_N$ satisfy
$$e_0\le C_0h^p,\qquad e_{n+1}\le(1+Lh)e_n+Ch^{p+1}\quad(0\le n<N),$$
then, when $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}e_n\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, when $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}e_n\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

derivations.claim: Let $\widehat n$ be the exact solution with initial density $\widehat n_0$. Applying the characteristic formula [F2] and changing variables from age $a$ to birth time $s=t-a$ gives, for every bounded Lipschitz $\phi$, $\int\phi(a)\widehat n(t,a)da=\int_0^{A-T}\phi(x+t)S(x,t)n_0(x)dx+\int_0^t\phi(t-s)S(0,t-s)\widehat B(s)ds$. The birth kernel $K(s)=\beta(s)S(0,s)$ is bounded and Lipschitz, and $\widehat G(t)=\int_0^{A-T}\beta(x+t)S(x,t)n_0(x)dx$ is bounded and Lipschitz because $\beta,\mu$ have bounded first derivatives and $n_0$ is integrable. The mass estimate [F5] bounds $\widehat B$ by $\beta_\infty e^{\beta_\infty T}\|n_0\|_1$. Subtracting its Volterra equation at $t$ and $t+h$, the old-history kernel difference is at most $\operatorname{Lip}(K)h\int_0^T|\widehat B|$ and the new interval at most $h\|K\|_\infty\|\widehat B\|_\infty$. Thus $\widehat B$ is Lipschitz on $[0,T]$.

If $N=0$, there are no time steps and the survival-error claim is zero. Suppose $N\ge1$, and put $T_h=N\Delta t>0$. A cohort born with mass $m_0$ and initial age $a_0$ has exact survival mass solving $m'(s)=-\mu(a_0+s)m(s)$; let $q=m_0$ be its reference mass. To apply [F4] at $a_0=0$, define the extension $\bar\mu(r)=\mu(r)$ for $r\ge0$ and $\bar\mu(r)=\mu(0)+\mu'_+(0)r e^r$ for $r<0$. The one-sided derivative $\mu'_+(0)$ exists; the two formulas and their first derivatives match at zero, and $\bar\mu$ and $\bar\mu'$ are bounded on $\mathbb R$. For a cohort whose reference mass is $q>0$, the vector field $f(s,m)=-\bar\mu(a_0+s)m$ is $C^1$ on the open tube $V=(-1,T_h+1)\times(-q,2q)$, where $T_h=N\Delta t$, with all bounds required by [F4] uniform in $a_0$ and proportional to $q$ except for the state-Lipschitz constant, which is bounded by $\|\bar\mu\|_\infty$. The exact continuation $m(s)=m_{\mathrm{start}}\exp(-\int_0^s\bar\mu(a_0+r)\,dr)$ exists on an open interval containing $[0,T_h]$; after shrinking that interval at the endpoints its graph lies in $V$. Its exact forward solution from any $m\in[0,q]$ and its Euler input/output states lie in $K=[0,T_h]\times[0,q]$: mortality is nonnegative for ages $a_0+s\ge0$, and $\Delta t\|\mu\|_\infty\le1$. Thus [F4] gives one-step defect at most $C\Delta t^2q$ and a stability factor $1+L\Delta t$, with constants independent of $a_0$ and proportional to $q$. Applying [L1] on the aligned horizon $T_h=N\Delta t$ gives survival-weight error at most $C_T\Delta t q$ over the full run; the zero-mass case is exact. For the discrete total cohort mass $N_h^k$, positivity and $B_h^k\le\beta_\infty N_h^k$ give $N_h^{k+1}\le(1+\Delta t\beta_\infty)N_h^k$, hence $N_h^k\le e^{\beta_\infty T}N_h^0$. Since $N_h^0\le\|n_0\|_1+\epsilon_0$ (test the initial BL defect with $\phi\equiv1$), the sum of the initial cohort masses and all inserted newborn masses $\sum_{j<k}\Delta t B_h^j$ is at most $C_T(\|n_0\|_1+\epsilon_0)$. Thus the sum of all cohort survival-weight errors is at most $C_T\Delta t(\|n_0\|_1+\epsilon_0)$.

Write $e_k=|B_h^k-\widehat B(t_k)|$. The initial-cohort contribution is at most $C_T(\epsilon_0+\Delta t)$: the test $x\mapsto\beta(x+t_k)S(x,t_k)$ has bounded-Lipschitz norm at most $C_T$, and step 2.1 bounds the accumulated Euler survival error. Each cohort born during $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$ is inserted at $t_{j+1}$ with mass $\Delta t B_h^j$, so at $t_k$ its age is $(k-j-1)\Delta t$. The exact renewal convolution is the integral of $K(t_k-s)\widehat B(s)$ over $s\in[0,t_k]$. Since $K$ and $\widehat B$ are Lipschitz, replacing this integral by the left-endpoint sum with age $(k-j-1)\Delta t$ costs at most $C_T\Delta t$ (the age sample differs from $t_k-t_j$ by one step). Replacing $\widehat B(t_j)$ by $B_h^j$ contributes at most $\|K\|_\infty\Delta t\sum_{j<k}e_j$, and replacing exact newborn survival by its Euler product contributes at most $C_T\Delta t$ by step 2.1. Therefore $e_k\le C_T(\epsilon_0+\Delta t)+\|K\|_\infty\Delta t\sum_{j<k}e_j$. Set $r_k=C_T(\epsilon_0+\Delta t)+\|K\|_\infty\Delta t\sum_{j<k}e_j$. Then $e_k\le r_k$ and $r_{k+1}=r_k+\|K\|_\infty\Delta t e_k\le(1+\|K\|_\infty\Delta t)r_k$, so $e_k\le e^{\|K\|_\infty T}C_T(\epsilon_0+\Delta t)$.

For any test function with $\|\phi\|_\infty+\operatorname{Lip}(\phi)\le1$, the initial cohort pushforward differs from the first integral for $\widehat n$ in step 1.1 by at most $C_T(\epsilon_0+\Delta t)$, using step 2.1 and the bounded-Lipschitz norm of $x\mapsto\phi(x+t)S(x,t)$. The newborn cohort sum differs from the second integral by its left-Riemann error $C_T\Delta t$ plus $\Delta t\sum_{j<k}e_j\le C_T(\epsilon_0+\Delta t)$ by step 2.2. Thus $\|\nu_h^k-\widehat n(t_k,a)da\|_{BL^*}\le C_T(\epsilon_0+\Delta t)$. The initial data difference is $\|n_0-\widehat n_0\|_1=\tau_A$, so [F5] gives $\|n(t_k)-\widehat n(t_k)\|_1\le e^{\beta_\infty T}\tau_A$. The inequality $\|f(a)da\|_{BL^*}\le\|f\|_1$ and the triangle inequality prove the stated bound.

Input a uniform age partition $0=a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_J=A$ with $\Delta a=a_j-a_{j-1}$, nonnegative cell masses $M_j$, and a bounded nonnegative fertility function $\beta:[0,A]\to[0,\beta_\infty]$. In each cell $C_j=[a_{j-1},a_j]$, let $u_j=M_j/\Delta a$ and approximate $\int_{C_j}\beta(a)u_j\,da$ by one of these positive rules:

1. **Midpoint mode:** choose an integer $q_j\ge1$ and use $u_j Q_M(\beta; a_{j-1},a_j,q_j)$ from [[alg-composite-midpoint-rule]].
2. **Capped adaptive mode:** call [[alg-adaptive-simpson-with-finite-depth-and-panel-cap]] on $\beta$ over $C_j$ with the requested finite depth, panel budget and indicator tolerance, then multiply its estimate by $u_j$.

If an evaluation fails, return `failure` and no birth rate. Otherwise return

$$B_h=\sum_{j=1}^J u_jQ_j(\beta),$$

the per-cell statuses, and the sum of any reported adaptive indicators. Both rules have nonnegative quadrature weights summing to $\Delta a$, so $0\le B_h\le\beta_\infty\sum_jM_j$. An adaptive `accepted` status means only that its indicators meet the requested budget; neither that indicator nor a `cap-reached` estimate bounds the true quadrature error. Any convergence theorem using this procedure must separately assume or prove a true quadrature-defect bound.

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]], input a finite horizon $T>0$, a cutoff $A>T$, integers $J,N\ge1$, and use the uniform grid $a_j=j\Delta a$ with $\Delta a=A/J$ and cells $C_j=[a_{j-1},a_j]$. Set $\Delta t=T/N$ and $t_k=k\Delta t$ for $0\le k\le N$. Input nonnegative initial cell masses $M_j^0$ and evaluate $\mu_j=\mu((a_{j-1}+a_j)/2)$. Require the transport-plus-loss CFL

$$\lambda+\Delta t\,\mu_\infty\le1,\qquad \lambda=\Delta t/\Delta a,\quad\mu_\infty=\|\mu\|_\infty.$$

If the CFL inequality fails, return status `invalid-cfl` without an update.

Initialize birth, quadrature-status, and outflow records as empty, and set cumulative outflow $O_h^0=0$. For each $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, put $u_j^k=M_j^k/\Delta a$, compute $B_h^k$ with [[alg-age-structured-positive-birth-quadrature]], and set the upwind fluxes $F_0^k=B_h^k$ and $F_j^k=u_j^k$ for $1\le j\le J$. Update, for $1\le j\le J$,

$$M_j^{k+1}=M_j^k-\Delta t(F_j^k-F_{j-1}^k)-\Delta t\,\mu_jM_j^k.$$

The right flux $F_J^k$ is absorbing outflow: record and discard the step mass $\Delta t F_J^k$, set $O_h^{k+1}=O_h^k+\Delta t F_J^k$, and allow no inflow from ages above $A$. Append $B_h^k$, the quadrature status, and the step outflow record, then proceed to step $k+1$. Return $(M^k)_{k=0}^N$ with the birth, quadrature-status, step-outflow, and cumulative-outflow records. An invalid grid or failed rate/quadrature evaluation returns failure with no partial current step. A `cap-reached` adaptive quadrature estimate may be used for a finite step, but its status is retained and carries no accuracy claim.

derivations.claim: In midpoint mode, each of the $q_j$ samples has weight $\Delta a/q_j>0$, so the weights sum to the cell width. In capped-adaptive mode, every returned estimate is a finite sum of Simpson panel estimates on its leaf intervals; a two-panel Simpson block has weights proportional to $(1,4,1)$, all positive, and their sum is the block width. The leaf intervals partition the cell, so the combined weights are nonnegative and sum to its width, including when a cap is reached. Hence the cell contribution lies between $0$ and $u_j\beta_\infty\Delta a=\beta_\infty M_j$, and summing over cells gives the stated birth bound. A failure returns no estimate.

Substituting $F_j^k=M_j^k/\Delta a$ in [F2] gives $M_1^{k+1}=(1-\lambda-\Delta t\mu_1)M_1^k+\Delta t B_h^k$ and, for $j\ge2$, $M_j^{k+1}=(1-\lambda-\Delta t\mu_j)M_j^k+\lambda M_{j-1}^k$. The CFL makes every displayed coefficient nonnegative, while [F1] makes $B_h^k\ge0$; induction in $k$ proves nonnegativity.

Summing [F2] over cells telescopes the fluxes to $F_J^k-F_0^k$, hence $N_h^{k+1}=N_h^k-\Delta t F_J^k+\Delta t B_h^k-\Delta t\sum_j\mu_jM_j^k$. Since $F_J^k,\mu_j,M_j^k\ge0$ and step 1.1 gives $B_h^k\le\beta_\infty N_h^k$, the asserted mass-growth inequality follows.

The update is a linear matrix with nonnegative entries by step 1.2. In each column, transport and mortality leave total coefficient at most $1$, because outflow or mortality removes mass; the birth quadrature adds at most $\Delta t\beta_\infty$ to that column by step 1.1. Thus its induced $\ell^1$ norm is at most $1+\Delta t\beta_\infty$. Applying this matrix to $M^k-\widetilde M^k$ proves the difference estimate.

citations.quote: Fix $0<T<A$, bounded nonnegative Lipschitz rates $\mu,\beta:[0,A]\to[0,\infty)$, and initial density $n_0^A\in L^1_+(0,A)$. The **finite-age renewal model with absorbing outflow** is the age transport problem on $0<a<A$ with the same renewal inflow $B_A(t)=\int_0^A\beta(a)n^A(t,a)\,da$ as in [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]]. A cohort follows age speed $1$, retains its mortality survival $S(a,s)$ until it reaches $A$, and is then removed; no cohort enters from ages above $A$. The initial density is $n_0^A$ on $[0,A]$. A mild solution is the characteristic formula on $0<a<A$, with an initial-cohort branch for $a\ge t$, a newborn branch for $a<t$, and zero extension to $a\ge A$. Since $A>T$, no cohort born during $[0,T]$ reaches the outflow boundary.

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-finite-cutoff-model]], define $K(a)=\beta(a)S(0,a)$ and

$$G_A(t)=\int_0^{A-t}\beta(x+t)S(x,t)n_0^A(x)\,dx,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$

There is a unique continuous nonnegative birth rate satisfying

$$B_A(t)=G_A(t)+\int_0^tK(a)B_A(t-a)\,da,$$

and the finite-age density is, for almost every $0<a<A$,

$$n^A(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0^A(a-t)S(a-t,t),&t\le a<A,\\B_A(t-a)S(0,a),&0\le a<t.\end{cases}$$

It is the unique mild solution, has $B_A(t)=\int_0^A\beta(a)n^A(t,a)\,da$, and obeys

$$\|n^A(t,\cdot)\|_1\le e^{\beta_\infty t}\|n_0^A\|_1,\qquad \beta_\infty=\|\beta\|_\infty.$$

For $t\le T<A$, its exact cumulative number outflow is

$$O_A(t)=\int_{A-t}^{A}n_0^A(x)S(x,A-x)\,dx.$$

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]], input a finite horizon $T>0$, a cutoff $A>T$, integers $J,N\ge1$, and use the uniform grid $a_j=j\Delta a$ with $\Delta a=A/J$ and cells $C_j=[a_{j-1},a_j]$. Set $\Delta t=T/N$ and $t_k=k\Delta t$ for $0\le k\le N$. Input nonnegative initial cell masses $M_j^0$ and evaluate $\mu_j=\mu((a_{j-1}+a_j)/2)$. Require the transport-plus-loss CFL

$$\lambda+\Delta t\,\mu_\infty\le1,\qquad \lambda=\Delta t/\Delta a,\quad\mu_\infty=\|\mu\|_\infty.$$

If the CFL inequality fails, return status `invalid-cfl` without an update.

Initialize birth, quadrature-status, and outflow records as empty, and set cumulative outflow $O_h^0=0$. For each $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, put $u_j^k=M_j^k/\Delta a$, compute $B_h^k$ with [[alg-age-structured-positive-birth-quadrature]], and set the upwind fluxes $F_0^k=B_h^k$ and $F_j^k=u_j^k$ for $1\le j\le J$. Update, for $1\le j\le J$,

$$M_j^{k+1}=M_j^k-\Delta t(F_j^k-F_{j-1}^k)-\Delta t\,\mu_jM_j^k.$$

The right flux $F_J^k$ is absorbing outflow: record and discard the step mass $\Delta t F_J^k$, set $O_h^{k+1}=O_h^k+\Delta t F_J^k$, and allow no inflow from ages above $A$. Append $B_h^k$, the quadrature status, and the step outflow record, then proceed to step $k+1$. Return $(M^k)_{k=0}^N$ with the birth, quadrature-status, step-outflow, and cumulative-outflow records. An invalid grid or failed rate/quadrature evaluation returns failure with no partial current step. A `cap-reached` adaptive quadrature estimate may be used for a finite step, but its status is retained and carries no accuracy claim.

For the bounded fertility rate in the age model, write $\beta_\infty:=\|\beta\|_\infty$. Whenever [[alg-age-structured-positive-birth-quadrature]] returns an estimate for nonnegative cell masses and a bounded nonnegative fertility rate with upper bound $\beta_\infty$, its birth value satisfies $0\le B_h\le\beta_\infty\sum_jM_j$.

In the update of [[alg-age-structured-renewal-upwind-finite-volume]], suppose the initial masses are nonnegative, the CFL holds, and each cell quadrature has nonnegative weights summing to $\Delta a$. Then all updated masses remain nonnegative and, with $N_h^k=\sum_{j=1}^J M_j^k$,

$$N_h^{k+1}\le(1+\Delta t\,\beta_\infty)N_h^k.$$

For two runs with the same grid, rates and quadrature rule but different nonnegative initial mass vectors $M^0,\widetilde M^0$, the one-step difference satisfies

$$\|M^{k+1}-\widetilde M^{k+1}\|_{\ell^1}\le(1+\Delta t\,\beta_\infty)\|M^k-\widetilde M^k\|_{\ell^1}.$$

Let $a<b$, let $n\ge1$ be an integer, and put $h=(b-a)/n$. If
$f\in C^2([a,b])$, define $M_2=\max_{x\in[a,b]}|f''(x)|$. The composite
midpoint value $Q_M(f;a,b,n)$ of [[alg-composite-midpoint-rule]] satisfies

$$\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-Q_M(f;a,b,n)\right|\le\frac{(b-a)h^2}{24}M_2.$$

The integral is the Riemann integral. This is an exact-arithmetic quadrature
bound; evaluation and summation roundoff are not included.

Let $T>0$, $N\ge1$, $h=T/N$, $p\ge1$, and $C_0,C,L\ge0$. If nonnegative real numbers $e_0,\ldots,e_N$ satisfy
$$e_0\le C_0h^p,\qquad e_{n+1}\le(1+Lh)e_n+Ch^{p+1}\quad(0\le n<N),$$
then, when $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}e_n\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, when $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}e_n\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

derivations.claim: Let $\overline M_j(t)=\int_{C_j}n^A(t,a)\,da$ and $\overline u_j(t)=\overline M_j(t)/\Delta a$. The smooth finite-age characteristic solution [F2] satisfies the transport equation and renewal boundary in [F1]. Integrating [F1] over one cell and one time step gives $\overline M_j(t_{k+1})=\overline M_j(t_k)-\int_{t_k}^{t_{k+1}}[n^A(s,a_j)-n^A(s,a_{j-1})]ds-\int_{t_k}^{t_{k+1}}\int_{C_j}\mu(a)n^A(s,a)\,da\,ds$, with $n^A(s,a_0)=B_A(s)$ and the outgoing trace at $a_J=A$.

Taylor's formula in age gives $\overline u_j(t)-n^A(t,a_j)=-\frac{\Delta a}{2}(n^A)_a(t,a_j)+O(\Delta a^2)$ uniformly. For interior cells, subtracting adjacent face-flux errors cancels the leading term and leaves $O((\Delta a)^2)$ per cell because $(n^A)_{aa}$ is bounded. In the first and last cells there is only one uncancelled endpoint face error, of size $O(\Delta a)$; these two cells contribute $O(\Delta t\Delta a)$ in total. Taylor's formula in time gives a face-integral remainder $O(\Delta t^2\Delta a)$ per cell after adjacent differences, using bounded $(n^A)_{ta}$, hence $O(\Delta t^2)$ after summing. At the inlet, the smooth trace gives $(n^A)_t(t,a_0)=B_A'(t)$, so the time derivative of $n^A(t,a_1)-B_A(t)$ is also bounded by $\Delta a\|(n^A)_{ta}\|_\infty$; thus the boundary birth flux has no additional O(\Delta t^2) term beyond this face remainder and $\Delta t\epsilon_Q$. For the reaction term, first note that $\overline u_j(t)=n^A(t,a_j^c)+O((\Delta a)^2)$ by the symmetric cell average. Thus replacing $\mu(a)n^A(t,a)$ by $\mu(a_j^c)\overline u_j(t)$ has per-cell error $O((\Delta a)^3)$: the midpoint formula [F5] bounds the error for $\mu n^A$, and the cell-average replacement changes the midpoint value by $O((\Delta a)^2)$ times the cell width. Summing and multiplying by $\Delta t$ gives $O(\Delta t(\Delta a)^2)$. Freezing the reaction term at $t_k$ instead of integrating in time contributes $O(\Delta t^2)$ after summing cells, since $(\mu n^A)_t$ is bounded. Therefore $\|\rho^k\|_{\ell^1}\le C\Delta t(\Delta a+\Delta t+\epsilon_Q)$ for sufficiently fine meshes with $\Delta a\le1$.

Set $e_k=\sum_j|M_j^k-\overline M_j(t_k)|$. Apply the one-step stability [F4] to the numerical and exact cell-average states and add the local defect from step 1.2; this yields $e_{k+1}\le(1+\beta_\infty\Delta t)e_k+C\Delta t(\Delta a+\Delta t+\epsilon_Q)$, with $e_0=0$.

Put $D=\Delta a+\Delta t+\epsilon_Q$. Iterating the recurrence in step 2.1 gives $e_k\le C\Delta tD\sum_{r=0}^{k-1}(1+\beta_\infty\Delta t)^r\le C_TD$, where the bound also holds when $\beta_\infty=0$, in which case the sum is $k\le T/\Delta t$. For the midpoint birth rule, split each cell defect into $\overline u_j[Q_M(\beta;C_j,1)-\int_{C_j}\beta]$ and $\int_{C_j}\beta(a)(\overline u_j-n^A(t_k,a))\,da$. The first term is $O((\Delta a)^3)$ per cell by [F5] and bounded $n^A$; in the second, subtract $\beta$ at the cell midpoint because $\int_{C_j}(\overline u_j-n^A)=0$, then use $|\beta(a)-\beta(a_j^c)|\le\operatorname{Lip}(\beta)\Delta a$ and $\int_{C_j}|\overline u_j-n^A|=O((\Delta a)^2)$ from bounded $(n^A)_a$. Summing gives $\epsilon_Q=O((\Delta a)^2)$, hence in particular $O(\Delta a)$. With the two-sided mesh ratio, $D=O(\Delta t)$; the recurrence then has additive term $C'\Delta t^2$, and [F6] gives the stated first-order estimate. Finally, on each cell $\int_{C_j}|n^A(t_k,a)-\overline u_j(t_k)|da\le (\Delta a)^2\|(n^A)_a\|_\infty$; summing over $A/\Delta a$ cells adds only $O(\Delta a)$ to the cell-mass error, proving the reconstruction claim.

Fix a finite horizon $T>0$. Let mortality and fertility be bounded Lipschitz functions $\mu,\beta:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, and let $n_0\in L^1(0,\infty)$ be nonnegative. The **linear age-structured renewal transport problem** is

$$n_t(t,a)+n_a(t,a)=-\mu(a)n(t,a),\qquad a>0,\quad 0<t\le T,$$

with initial density $n(0,a)=n_0(a)$ and inflow condition

$$n(t,0)=B(t),\qquad B(t):=\int_0^\infty \beta(a)n(t,a)\,da.$$

Here $a$ is age, $B$ is the birth rate, and the characteristic age path solves the first-order initial value problem $a'(s)=1$ in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], hence $a(s)=a(0)+s$. Define survival from age $a$ over duration $s\ge0$ by

$$S(a,s):=\exp\!\left(-\int_a^{a+s}\mu(r)\,dr\right).$$

A **weak solution** on $[0,T]$ is a nonnegative $n\in C([0,T];L^1(0,\infty))$ with continuous $B:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying $B(t)=\int_0^\infty\beta(a)n(t,a)\,da$ and, for every $\phi\in C_c^1([0,T]\times[0,\infty))$ with $\phi(T,a)=0$,

$$-\int_0^T\!\int_0^\infty n(t,a)(\phi_t+\phi_a-\mu(a)\phi)\,da\,dt=\int_0^\infty n_0(a)\phi(0,a)\,da+\int_0^T B(t)\phi(t,0)\,dt.$$

A **mild solution** is a weak solution that also satisfies, for almost every $a\ge0$,

$$n(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0(a-t)S(a-t,t),&a\ge t,\\B(t-a)S(0,a),&0\le a<t,\end{cases}$$

The formula follows the age characteristics $a'(s)=1$ and their mortality survival. No delay equation or finite-age cutoff is identified with this model by definition.

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]], put $M(a)=\int_0^a\mu(r)\,dr$, $K(a)=\beta(a)e^{-M(a)}$, and

$$G(t)=\int_0^\infty \beta(x+t)\exp\!\left(-\int_x^{x+t}\mu(r)\,dr\right)n_0(x)\,dx.$$

There is a unique mild solution. Its birth rate is the unique continuous solution of

$$B(t)=G(t)+\int_0^t K(a)B(t-a)\,da,$$

and its density, for almost every $a\ge0$, is

$$n(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0(a-t)\exp\!\left(-\int_{a-t}^{a}\mu(r)\,dr\right),&a\ge t,\\ B(t-a)e^{-M(a)},&0\le a<t.\end{cases}$$

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]], input a finite horizon $T>0$, a cutoff $A>T$, integers $J,N\ge1$, and use the uniform grid $a_j=j\Delta a$ with $\Delta a=A/J$ and cells $C_j=[a_{j-1},a_j]$. Set $\Delta t=T/N$ and $t_k=k\Delta t$ for $0\le k\le N$. Input nonnegative initial cell masses $M_j^0$ and evaluate $\mu_j=\mu((a_{j-1}+a_j)/2)$. Require the transport-plus-loss CFL

$$\lambda+\Delta t\,\mu_\infty\le1,\qquad \lambda=\Delta t/\Delta a,\quad\mu_\infty=\|\mu\|_\infty.$$

If the CFL inequality fails, return status `invalid-cfl` without an update.

Initialize birth, quadrature-status, and outflow records as empty, and set cumulative outflow $O_h^0=0$. For each $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, put $u_j^k=M_j^k/\Delta a$, compute $B_h^k$ with [[alg-age-structured-positive-birth-quadrature]], and set the upwind fluxes $F_0^k=B_h^k$ and $F_j^k=u_j^k$ for $1\le j\le J$. Update, for $1\le j\le J$,

$$M_j^{k+1}=M_j^k-\Delta t(F_j^k-F_{j-1}^k)-\Delta t\,\mu_jM_j^k.$$

The right flux $F_J^k$ is absorbing outflow: record and discard the step mass $\Delta t F_J^k$, set $O_h^{k+1}=O_h^k+\Delta t F_J^k$, and allow no inflow from ages above $A$. Append $B_h^k$, the quadrature status, and the step outflow record, then proceed to step $k+1$. Return $(M^k)_{k=0}^N$ with the birth, quadrature-status, step-outflow, and cumulative-outflow records. An invalid grid or failed rate/quadrature evaluation returns failure with no partial current step. A `cap-reached` adaptive quadrature estimate may be used for a finite step, but its status is retained and carries no accuracy claim.

For the bounded fertility rate in the age model, write $\beta_\infty:=\|\beta\|_\infty$. Whenever [[alg-age-structured-positive-birth-quadrature]] returns an estimate for nonnegative cell masses and a bounded nonnegative fertility rate with upper bound $\beta_\infty$, its birth value satisfies $0\le B_h\le\beta_\infty\sum_jM_j$.

In the update of [[alg-age-structured-renewal-upwind-finite-volume]], suppose the initial masses are nonnegative, the CFL holds, and each cell quadrature has nonnegative weights summing to $\Delta a$. Then all updated masses remain nonnegative and, with $N_h^k=\sum_{j=1}^J M_j^k$,

$$N_h^{k+1}\le(1+\Delta t\,\beta_\infty)N_h^k.$$

For two runs with the same grid, rates and quadrature rule but different nonnegative initial mass vectors $M^0,\widetilde M^0$, the one-step difference satisfies

$$\|M^{k+1}-\widetilde M^{k+1}\|_{\ell^1}\le(1+\Delta t\,\beta_\infty)\|M^k-\widetilde M^k\|_{\ell^1}.$$

derivations.claim: Write $u_j^k=M_j^k/\Delta a$, $B_k=B_h^k$, $\lambda=\Delta t/\Delta a$, and $V_k=|u_1^k-B_k|+\sum_{j=2}^{J}|u_j^k-u_{j-1}^k|$. The initial cell averages satisfy $V_0\le\operatorname{TV}(n_0)+\|n_0\|_\infty+\beta_\infty\|n_0\|_1$, which is finite because an integrable function of finite total variation on the half-line has finite essential supremum; the first term bounds differences of adjacent cell averages by averaging the variation measure.

Put $d_1^k=u_1^k-B_k$ and $d_j^k=u_j^k-u_{j-1}^k$ for $2\le j\le J$. For $j\ge2$, subtract adjacent updates from [F3] to obtain $u_j^{k+1}-u_{j-1}^{k+1}=(1-\lambda-\Delta t\mu_j)(u_j^k-u_{j-1}^k)+\lambda(u_{j-1}^k-u_{j-2}^k)+\Delta t(\mu_{j-1}-\mu_j)u_{j-1}^k$. The CFL makes the first two coefficients nonnegative, and $|\mu_j-\mu_{j-1}|\le\operatorname{Lip}(\mu)\Delta a$. Summing their absolute-value bounds for $j=2,\dots,J$ gives at most $\sum_{j=2}^{J-1}|d_j^k|+(1-\lambda)|d_J^k|+\lambda|d_1^k|+\Delta t\operatorname{Lip}(\mu)N_k$: for $2\le j<J$ the two transport coefficients add to at most $1$, the last-cell coefficient is at most $1-\lambda$, and the boundary difference contributes $\lambda|d_1^k|$. The first-cell jump is $d_1^{k+1}=(1-\lambda-\Delta t\mu_1)d_1^k+(1-\Delta t\mu_1)B_k-B_{k+1}$. The quadrature weights are fixed and nonnegative, so $|B_{k+1}-B_k|\le\beta_\infty\sum_j|M_j^{k+1}-M_j^k|$. The update and the definition of $V_k$ give $\sum_j|M_j^{k+1}-M_j^k|\le\Delta t(V_k+\mu_\infty N_k)$. Also $|(1-\Delta t\mu_1)B_k-B_{k+1}|\le |B_k-B_{k+1}|+\Delta t\mu_\infty B_k$ and $B_k\le\beta_\infty N_k$. Adding the first-cell bound to the preceding sum combines the $d_1^k$ coefficients as $(1-\lambda-\Delta t\mu_1)+\lambda\le1$; all other variation coefficients are at most $1$. Therefore $V_{k+1}\le(1+C\Delta t)V_k+C\Delta t N_k$, with $C$ depending only on the rate bounds and Lipschitz constants.

Iterating [F4] gives $N_k\le(1+\Delta t\beta_\infty)^kN_0\le e^{k\Delta t\beta_\infty}N_0\le e^{\beta_\infty T}N_0$. Iterating the recurrence in step 1.2 gives $V_k\le(1+C\Delta t)^kV_0+C\Delta t\sum_{r=0}^{k-1}(1+C\Delta t)^{k-1-r}N_r\le e^{CT}(V_0+CTe^{\beta_\infty T}N_0)$. The same update gives $\sum_j\Delta a|u_j^{k+1}-u_j^k|\le\Delta t(V_k+\mu_\infty N_k)$; hence the linear time interpolation is uniformly Lipschitz into $L^1$.

On any fixed interval $[0,R]$, the uniform $L^1$ and variation bounds make the time slices precompact in $L^1$: replacing each slice by averages on blocks of width $\rho$ changes its $L^1$ norm by at most $\rho V_k$, while those block averages lie in a bounded finite-dimensional set. A diagonal extraction at rational times and the uniform time-Lipschitz bound from step 1.3 give a subsequence converging uniformly in time in $L^1$ on every bounded age interval. A newborn cohort has age at most $T$; under the upwind update it can move at most one cell per step, so all newborn mass lies below age $T/c_-+\Delta a$. For $R>T/c_-+\Delta a$, births therefore contribute nothing above $R$. An initial cell moves by at most $k$ cells, so any initial mass reconstructed above $R$ came from initial cells whose lower endpoint exceeds $R-k\Delta a-\Delta a\ge R-T/c_- -\Delta a$. Its mass is at most $\int_{R-T/c_- -2\Delta a}^\infty n_0$ (extend $n_0$ by zero to negative ages); mortality and outflow only decrease that inherited mass. This tail tends to zero uniformly as $R\to\infty$. For the exact solution, [F2] shows that newborns have age at most $T$, while mass above $R>T$ comes only from initial ages above $R-T$ and is at most $\int_{R-T}^\infty n_0$. Hence the subsequence converges in $C([0,T];L^1(0,\infty))$.

Let $\phi_j^k=\phi(t_k,(a_{j-1}+a_j)/2)$ for a compactly supported $C^1$ test function with terminal value zero. Multiplying [F3] by $\phi_j^{k+1}$ and summing by parts gives the exact discrete weak identity $-\sum_{k,j}M_j^k(\phi_j^{k+1}-\phi_j^k)-\Delta t\sum_{k,j<J}F_j^k(\phi_{j+1}^{k+1}-\phi_j^{k+1})+\Delta t\sum_{k,j}\mu_jM_j^k\phi_j^{k+1}=\sum_jM_j^0\phi_j^0+\Delta t\sum_kB_k\phi_1^{k+1}$; the outflow term vanishes because the test is supported below the cutoff. Uniform $L^1$ convergence, Lipschitz continuity of $\mu,\beta$, and mesh refinement make the sums converge to the weak transport/loss terms. Since each positive birth rule is supported in its cell and its weights sum to $\Delta a$, $|B_k-\int\beta(a)u_h(t_k,a)da|\le2\operatorname{Lip}(\beta)\Delta a\,N_k$, so the birth sum converges to the boundary term. The limit therefore satisfies [F1] with the given initial trace.

In characteristic coordinates $x=a-t$ on $a>t$, the weak identity [F1] becomes $\partial_t v(t,x)=-\mu(x+t)v(t,x)$ in distributions; multiplication by $\exp(\int_x^{x+t}\mu)$ makes its distributional $t$-derivative zero, and the initial trace gives $v(t,x)=n_0(x)S(x,t)$. On $0<a<t$, use $s=t-a$ and obtain $\partial_a w(s,a)=-\mu(a)w(s,a)$ with trace $w(s,0)=B(s)$; the same integrating-factor argument gives $w(s,a)=B(s)S(0,a)$. Substitution into the renewal relation in [F1] yields the Volterra equation of [F2], whose solution is unique. Thus every subsequential limit equals the mild solution. Since every subsequence has a further subsequence with this same limit, the entire sequence converges.

If $n,\widetilde n$ use possibly different nonnegative bounded coefficients $(\mu,\beta)$ and $(\widetilde\mu,\widetilde\beta)$ and initial data $n_0,\widetilde n_0$, put $\delta=\|\mu-\widetilde\mu\|_\infty+\|\beta-\widetilde\beta\|_\infty$ and $\widetilde\beta_\infty=\|\widetilde\beta\|_\infty$. $$\|n(t)-\widetilde n(t)\|_1\le e^{\beta_\infty t}\left(\|n_0-\widetilde n_0\|_1+\delta t e^{\widetilde\beta_\infty t}\|\widetilde n_0\|_1\right).$$

Fix $T>0$ and a cutoff $A>T$. Let $n^A$ be the finite-age solution from [[thm-age-structured-renewal-finite-cutoff-characteristic-solution]] with initial density $n_0^A\in C^2([0,A])$ and assume $\mu,\beta\in C^2([0,A])$ are nonnegative and bounded. Assume $n^A$ extends to $C^2([0,T]\times[0,A])$. Its smoothness at the renewal corner includes $n_0^A(0)=B_A(0)$ and $-(n_0^A)'(0)-\mu(0)n_0^A(0)=B_A'(0)$; no boundary value is imposed at the absorbing outflow. Take integers $J,N\ge1$, set $\Delta a=A/J$ and $\Delta t=T/N$, and use the corresponding uniform age and time grids. Initialize with exact cell masses and use the one-panel midpoint rule in each cell from [[alg-age-structured-positive-birth-quadrature]]. Assume $\Delta t/\Delta a\in[c_-,c_+]$ for fixed $0<c_-\le c_+<\infty$ and the transport-plus-loss CFL. Define

$$\epsilon_Q:=\max_{0\le k<N}\left|B_h(\overline M(t_k))-\int_0^A\beta(a)n^A(t_k,a)\,da\right|,$$

where $B_h(\overline M(t_k))$ is the birth-rate quadrature applied to the exact cell-average masses $\overline M_j(t_k)=\int_{C_j}n^A(t_k,a)\,da$. Then the cell-mass error $E_k=\sum_j|M_j^k-\int_{C_j}n^A(t_k,a)\,da|$ obeys

$$\max_{0\le k\le N}E_k\le C_T(\Delta a+\Delta t+\epsilon_Q).$$

The piecewise-constant reconstruction $u_h^k=M_j^k/\Delta a$ on cell $C_j$ and zero above $A$ satisfies the same $L^1$ error order. For the midpoint rule, $\epsilon_Q\le C_T\Delta a$ under the stated regularity, so the method is first order in age mesh and time step. If the capped adaptive rule is used instead, the estimate requires an independently established true $\epsilon_Q$; its reported indicator is not substituted for that hypothesis.

derivations.claim: For an initial cohort at age $a$, the survival factor is the exponential of minus the integrated mortality along $a(s)=a+s$ by [F1]. Since $\mu_*\le\mu(r)\le\|\mu\|_\infty$ almost everywhere, integrating these inequalities over $[a,a+s]$ and exponentiating proves the two survival bounds.

A newborn has age at most $t\le T<A$ by time $t$, so it cannot contribute to outflow at $A$. An initial individual of age $a$ exits by time $t$ exactly when $A-t\le a\le A$, and its survival to the exit age is $S(a,A-a)$. Integrating over those initial ages gives the formula for $O_A(t)$; using $S\le1$ and $A-t\ge A-T$ gives the stated upper bound.

Split $n_0=n_0\mathbf 1_{[0,A-T]}+n_0\mathbf 1_{(A-T,\infty)}$. By linearity of the Volterra equations in [F2] and [F3], it suffices to compare the evolutions of these two parts. Every initial cohort in the first part remains below age $A$ through time $T$, and its newborn descendants have age at most $T<A$; the characteristic formulas therefore make the infinite-age and finite-age evolutions identical for this part. The infinite-age evolution of the second part has mass at most $e^{\beta_\infty T}\int_{A-T}^\infty n_0$ by [F4]. The finite-age model starts this part only with its restriction to $[0,A]$, whose mass is no larger than the same tail; its mass is at most that same exponential factor by [F3]. The triangle inequality gives the factor-two bound in the Statement.

Under the smooth hypotheses of [F5], the piecewise-constant reconstruction differs in $L^1$ from the finite-age solution by at most $C_T(\Delta a+\Delta t+\epsilon_Q)$ at each time level. Add this to the infinite-versus-cutoff error from step 2.1 by the triangle inequality. This is the displayed fully discrete bound, with the mesh/time/quadrature and age-tail contributions separate.

derivations.claim: Direct integration gives $\int\rho_\varepsilon(a)\,da=1$ and symmetry about $a_*$ gives $\int a\rho_\varepsilon(a)\,da=a_*$. Its second centered moment is $\int(a-a_*)^2\rho_\varepsilon(a)\,da=\varepsilon^2/6$.

Let $b$ be Lipschitz on $[0,T]$ and take $t\ge a_*+\varepsilon$. The support of $\rho_\varepsilon$ is contained in $[0,t]$, so the convolution in [F2] is $H_\varepsilon(t)=R\int\rho_\varepsilon(a)e^{-ma}b(t-a)\,da$. For each supported $a$, $|e^{-ma}b(t-a)-e^{-ma_*}b(t-a_*)|\le(\operatorname{Lip}(b)+m\|b\|_\infty)|a-a_*|$. Since $|a-a_*|\le\varepsilon$ and the kernel has unit mass, $|H_\varepsilon(t)-Re^{-ma_*}b(t-a_*)|\le R\varepsilon(\operatorname{Lip}(b)+m\|b\|_\infty)$.

A finite-width fertility is not an exact delay: set $m=0$ and $b(s)=s^2$ on the relevant nonnegative interval. By step 1.1, $H_\varepsilon(t)=R((t-a_*)^2+\varepsilon^2/6)$, while the point-delay term is $Rb(t-a_*)=R(t-a_*)^2$; their difference is $R\varepsilon^2/6>0$.

Fix a finite horizon $T>0$ and a nondegenerate fixed size interval $[0,X]$ with $X>0$. Let $g,\mu,\gamma:[0,X]\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded Lipschitz functions, with $g(x)\ge g_{\min}>0$. Here $g$ is size growth, $\mu$ is ordinary mortality, and $\gamma$ is the rate at which a dividing parent is removed. For each parent size $y$, let $K_y$ be a finite nonnegative Borel measure of daughter sizes, supported on $[0,y]$. Assume $y\mapsto K_y(E)$ is measurable for every Borel set $E\subseteq[0,X]$, and that the number moment $k_0(y):=K_y([0,y])$ is uniformly bounded; the size moment $k_1(y):=\int_{[0,y]}x\,K_y(dx)$ is then finite. The **size-structured transport and division model** is

$$\partial_t n+\partial_x(gn)=-(\mu+\gamma)n+\int_{[0,X]}K_y(dx)n(t,y)\,dy,\qquad 0<x<X,$$

with zero incoming flux at $x=0$ and absorbing outflow $g(X)n(t,X)$ at $x=X$. Let $\Pi_{[0,X]}(x):=\min\{X,\max\{0,x\}\}$ and extend the growth field to $\widetilde g(x):=g(\Pi_{[0,X]}(x))$ on $\mathbb R$. This is a bounded Lipschitz vector field. By [[thm-size-structured-positivity-number-and-weighted-moment-identities]], its IVP has a unique solution on the finite time horizon; a model characteristic is this solution restricted to the interval from its initial size until its first hitting of $X$, including that hitting time when it occurs by $T$. On this restricted interval, $\widetilde g=g$. The characteristic is understood as a first-order IVP solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. The weak equation is obtained by testing against $\phi\in C^1([0,X])$: transport contributes $\int_0^Xg\phi'n$, mortality and parent removal contribute $-\int_0^X(\mu+\gamma)\phi n$, division contributes $\int_0^X\int\phi(x)K_y(dx)n(t,y)\,dy$, and the upper boundary contributes $-\phi(X)g(X)n(t,X)$. The interval is fixed; moving boundaries, zero growth and discontinuous coefficients are outside this definition.

Input a partition $0=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_J=X$ with $J\ge1$, a time step $\Delta t>0$, a nonnegative current mass vector $M^k=(M_j^k)_{j=1}^J$, and the coefficients and kernel from [[def-size-structured-transport-and-division-kernel]]. Partition $[0,X]$ into disjoint cells $C_j=[x_{j-1},x_j)$ for $j<J$ and $C_J=[x_{J-1},X]$, with widths $h_j=x_j-x_{j-1}>0$ and centers $x_j^c=(x_{j-1}+x_j)/2$. Set $u_j^k=M_j^k/h_j$, the incoming flux $F_0^k=0$, the internal and outgoing upwind fluxes $F_j^k=g(x_j)u_j^k$ for $1\le j\le J$, and $d_j=\mu(x_j^c)+\gamma(x_j^c)$.

For each parent cell $C_\ell$, form nonnegative daughter coefficients

$$A_{j\ell}=\frac{1}{h_\ell}\,Q_M\bigl(y\mapsto K_y(C_j);x_{\ell-1},x_\ell,1\bigr),$$

using [[alg-composite-midpoint-rule]] on the parent-size interval. Since the one-panel midpoint rule is $Q_M(f;x_{\ell-1},x_\ell,1)=h_\ell f(x_\ell^c)$, this gives $A_{j\ell}=K_{x_\ell^c}(C_j)\ge0$. If $\Delta t(g(x_j)/h_j+d_j)>1$ for any cell, return `invalid-cfl` without an update. Otherwise the finite-volume update is

$$M_j^{k+1}=M_j^k-\Delta t(F_j^k-F_{j-1}^k)-\Delta t\,d_jM_j^k+\Delta t\sum_{\ell=1}^JA_{j\ell}M_\ell^k.$$

The flux $F_J^k$ is absorbing outflow. The admissible variable-width CFL is $\Delta t(g(x_j)/h_j+d_j)\le1$ for every cell. If a grid or any required coefficient/kernel evaluation fails, return failure without a partial update. Otherwise return $M^{k+1}$ together with the fluxes and daughter coefficients used in the step.

Under [[def-size-structured-transport-and-division-kernel]], for every initial size $y\in[0,X]$ the extended IVP specified there has a unique solution $\chi_y$ on $[0,T]$. The solution is strictly increasing and agrees with the original growth field until it first reaches $X$, so its restriction through that first hit is the model characteristic.

For [[alg-size-structured-finite-volume-flux-and-kernel-quadrature]], assume nonnegative initial masses, nonnegative quadrature coefficients $A_{j\ell}$, and the stated CFL. Then all $M_j^k$ remain nonnegative. Define the cell number and center-weighted size moment by $N_h^k=\sum_jM_j^k$ and $W_h^k=\sum_jx_j^cM_j^k$. With $k_{0,\ell}^h=\sum_jA_{j\ell}$ and $k_{1,\ell}^h=\sum_jx_j^cA_{j\ell}$, the exact balances are

$$N_h^{k+1}-N_h^k=\Delta t\left(-F_J^k-\sum_jd_jM_j^k+\sum_\ell k_{0,\ell}^hM_\ell^k\right),$$

$$W_h^{k+1}-W_h^k=\Delta t\left(\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}(x_{j+1}^c-x_j^c)F_j^k-x_J^cF_J^k-\sum_jx_j^cd_jM_j^k+\sum_\ell k_{1,\ell}^hM_\ell^k\right).$$

Thus a division kernel preserves the discrete size moment only when its first-moment production cancels the parent-removal term; this identity is not automatic for an arbitrary kernel.

derivations.claim: The parent center $2$ lies in the third cell and its daughters have size $1$, exactly the second cell center. Thus the positive midpoint kernel quadrature gives $A_{2,3}=2$ and all other daughter coefficients for the occupied parent column vanish. The CFL number is $0.1(0.1/0.5+1)=0.12$ in cell 1 and $0.1(0.1/1+1)=0.11$ in each of cells 2–4, so the global maximum is $0.12\le1$.

The rightward internal flux from cell $C_3$ into $C_4$ is $F_3=gM_3/h_3=0.3$; the absorbing boundary flux is $F_4=0$. The daughter source is $\Delta t A_{2,3}M_3=0.6$, and parent removal is $\Delta t\gamma M_3=0.3$. Therefore the updated cell masses are $M_2'=0.6$, $M_3'=3-0.03-0.3=2.67$, and $M_4'=0.03$, with $M_1'=0$; they are all nonnegative.

The discrete number changes from $3$ to $0.6+2.67+0.03=3.3$, an increase $0.3$ equal to $\Delta t(2-1)\gamma M_3$. The weighted-size total changes from $2\cdot3=6$ to $1\cdot0.6+2\cdot2.67+3\cdot0.03=6.03$. Formula [F3] gives the same $0.03$ increase from transport, while division contributes $\Delta t(2\cdot1-2\cdot1)M_3=0$. Thus the first moment is conserved by division and changes only by the size-growth flux in this step.
