Let $d\ge1$ and, for each coordinate $j=1,\ldots,d$, let
$Q_j(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{m_j}w_i^{(j)}f(x_i^{(j)})$ be a well-defined Gaussian rule
as in [[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]] and
[[lem-gauss-quadrature-rule-data-well-defined]]. Its **tensor-product
quadrature rule** is
$$ Q_{\otimes}(f):= \sum_{i_1=1}^{m_1}\cdots\sum_{i_d=1}^{m_d} \left(\prod_{j=1}^{d}w_{i_j}^{(j)}\right) f\left(x_{i_1}^{(1)},\ldots,x_{i_d}^{(d)}\right). $$
Its node set is the Cartesian product of the one-dimensional node sets; the
displayed finite sum is its value on any function defined on that node set.

For $d\ge1$, let $(a_j,b_j,m_j,2m_j-1,\mu_j)$ be Gaussian moment data for
each coordinate $j=1,\ldots,d$, and write
$M^{(j)}_k:=\int x^k\,d\mu_j(x)$. A **coordinatewise tensor polynomial** is a
finite family $(c_\alpha)$, with $c_\alpha\in\mathbb R$ for every index, indexed by multi-indices
$\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)$ with
$0\le\alpha_j\le2m_j-1$, evaluated by
$$ P(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{d}x_j^{\alpha_j}. $$
Define its **coordinatewise product-moment value** by
$$ I_\otimes(P):=\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{d}M^{(j)}_{\alpha_j}. $$
In both sums, list the finite multi-index box in increasing lexicographic
order (coordinate $1$ first, then coordinate $2$, and so on), and take the
ordinary finite-list sum in that order. The products use increasing coordinate
order $j=1,\ldots,d$. The real coefficient family is part of the formal
polynomial data, so these formulas specify finite real sums. This definition specifies the product-moment functional
used for coordinatewise exactness without requiring a measure-product
construction.

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], and let $Q_m$ and $w_i$ be the rule and weights of
[[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]. For every real polynomial $f$ of degree at most
$2m-1$,
$$ \int_{[a,b]} f(x)\,d\mu(x)=Q_m(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_if(x_i). $$
Moreover, $w_i>0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_iw_i=\mu([a,b])$.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, let $d$ be the
unique natural number satisfying $m+d=n+1$. Existence is the definition of
natural order ([[def-nat-order]]); if $m+d=m+e$, commutativity
([[lem-nat-add-commutative]]) gives $d+m=e+m$, so cancellation
([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]) gives $d=e$. On these admissible bounds only,
we may write this unique additive gap as $d=n+1-m$; no total natural subtraction
operation is presupposed. With $d$ thus fixed, define

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Equivalently, for naturals $m \le r$, the half-open endpoint notation
$\sum_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ and $\prod_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ means
$\sum_{j<d}a_{m+j}$ and $\prod_{j<d}a_{m+j}$, respectively, where $d$ is the
unique natural with $m+d=r$. Here $r-1$ is an endpoint label for the terms
before $r$, so this notation needs no total subtraction operation. For $m=r$,
the unique gap is $0$ because $m+0=m$, giving the empty sum and product; the
case $m=r=0$ is the $-1$ endpoint convention just stipulated.

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $(M,\cdot,e)$ be a monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]) and let
$g : \mathbb{N} \to M$ be a family of elements of $M$, written $g_i := g(i)$.
There is exactly one function $P_g : \mathbb{N} \to M$ satisfying

$$P_g(0) = e, \qquad P_g(\sigma(n)) = P_g(n) \cdot g_n \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}),$$

and we write

$$\prod_{i<n} g_i \;:=\; P_g(n), \qquad \text{also written } g_0 g_1 \cdots g_{n-1}.$$

In particular the **empty product** is $\prod_{i<0} g_i = e$, and
$\prod_{i<1} g_i = e \cdot g_0 = g_0$.

**Why the recursion is legitimate.** The clause $P_g(\sigma(n)) = P_g(n) \cdot g_n$
consults $n$ as well as $P_g(n)$, so [[thm-recursion]] does not apply to it
directly. Apply that theorem instead with the set $A = \mathbb{N} \times M$, the
element $a = (0,e)$, and the function $F : A \to A$ given by
$F(n,x) = (\sigma(n),\, x \cdot g_n)$: it yields a unique
$H : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times M$ with $H(0) = (0,e)$ and
$H(\sigma(n)) = F(H(n))$. Writing $H(n) = (H_1(n), H_2(n))$, induction
([[thm-induction-principle]]) gives $H_1(n) = n$ for every $n$, since $H_1(0) = 0$
and $H_1(\sigma(n)) = \sigma(H_1(n))$. Hence
$H(\sigma(n)) = (\sigma(n),\, H_2(n) \cdot g_n)$, so $P_g := H_2$ satisfies the two
displayed equations. It is the only such function: if $Q$ satisfies them too, then
$\{ n : P_g(n) = Q(n) \}$ contains $0$ and is closed under $\sigma$, hence is all
of $\mathbb{N}$ by induction.

**The value depends only on $g_0,\dots,g_{n-1}$.** If $g, g' : \mathbb{N} \to M$
satisfy $g_i = g'_i$ for every $i < n$, then $P_g(n) = P_{g'}(n)$. Indeed the set
of $n$ for which this implication holds contains $0$, both products then being
$e$; and if it holds at $n$, and $g, g'$ agree at every $i < \sigma(n)$, then they
agree at every $i < n$ and also at $n$ itself, because $i < \sigma(n)$ is
equivalent to $i \le n$ ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so
$P_g(\sigma(n)) = P_g(n) \cdot g_n = P_{g'}(n) \cdot g'_n = P_{g'}(\sigma(n))$.
Induction finishes it. This is what makes the notation $g_0 g_1 \cdots g_{n-1}$
unambiguous: it names a value determined by the first $n$ terms alone, and a
finite list $u$ of length $n$, that is a function $u : n \to M$ on the von Neumann
natural $n = \{0,\dots,n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), determines the product
$\prod_{i<n} u_i := P_{\tilde u}(n)$ computed from any extension
$\tilde u : \mathbb{N} \to M$ of $u$.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.
$\mathbb{R} = \mathcal{C}/\mathcal{N}$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is a field.

derivations.claim: For a coordinate monomial $P_\alpha(x)=\prod_{j=1}^{d}x_j^{\alpha_j}$, substitute the rule definition [F1] and distribute the finite sums: $Q_\otimes(P_\alpha) =\prod_{j=1}^{d}\left(\sum_{i_j=1}^{m_j}w_{i_j}^{(j)}(x_{i_j}^{(j)})^{\alpha_j}\right).$
Since $0\le\alpha_j\le2m_j-1$, [F3] makes the $j$th factor in step 1.1 equal to $M_{\alpha_j}^{(j)}$. Their product is exactly $I_\otimes(P_\alpha)$ by [F2].

A coordinatewise tensor polynomial is a finite linear combination of these monomials. Both $Q_\otimes$ and $I_\otimes$ are linear finite sums, so step 2.1 extends term by term and proves $Q_\otimes(P)=I_\otimes(P)$.

Each one-dimensional node list has $m_j$ distinct entries by [[thm-gauss-orthogonal-polynomial-has-simple-interior-zeros]]. Two different tuples differ in at least one coordinate, whose node entries are distinct, so they give different points. The nested index loops in [F1] enumerate $m_1$ tuples for $d=1$; appending coordinate $d+1$ replaces each prior tuple by exactly $m_{d+1}$ distinct extensions. Iterating this finite recurrence gives exactly $\prod_jm_j$ nodes, hence $m^d$ when every $m_j=m\ge2$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $a<b$ be real numbers, let $m\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$r\in\{2m-1,2m\}$. A **Gaussian quadrature moment datum of order $r$** is a
finite positive measure $\mu$ on the relative Borel sigma-algebra
$\mathcal B([a,b])$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-measure-space]],
[[def-measure]], [[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) such that
$\mu([a,b])>0$, and whose **relative support**
$$ S_\mu:=\{x\in[a,b]:\mu(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open }U\subseteq[a,b]\text{ with }x\in U\} $$
contains at least $m+1$ distinct points. For every integer $0\le k\le r$,
require $x\mapsto |x|^k$ to be integrable with respect to $\mu$
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]) and put
$M_k:=\int_{[a,b]}x^k\,d\mu(x)$. Powers use the natural-exponent
recursion of [[def-integer-power]], with $x^0=1$ for every real $x$, including
$x=0$; thus $M_0$ is the integral of the constant function $1$.

The branch $r=2m-1$ supplies all moments used to construct the monic
degree-$m$ orthogonal polynomial and prove rule exactness. The stronger branch
$r=2m$ also defines its squared norm and is used for the remainder formula.
Because $[a,b]$ is bounded and $\mu$ is finite, these absolute-moment
integrability conditions follow from finiteness; they are stated to make the
two moment interfaces explicit.

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data and let $Q_m$ have nodes $x_i$ and
weights $w_i$ as in [[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]. Let $J_m$ be the Jacobi
matrix of [[thm-jacobi-matrix-spectrum-equals-gauss-nodes]], and let $v_i$ be
any unit eigenvector of $J_m$ for eigenvalue $x_i$. Then
$$ w_i=\mu([a,b])\,|v_{i,1}|^2. $$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: Normalize $\widehat v:=v/\|v\|_2$. Then $\|J\widehat v-\theta\widehat v\|_2=\|Jv-\theta v\|_2/\|v\|_2\le\rho/s$. Expand $\widehat v=\sum_{k=1}^m c_ku_k$ in the orthonormal basis [F1]. Then $\|J\widehat v-\theta\widehat v\|_2^2=\sum_{k=1}^{m}c_k^2(\lambda_k-\theta)^2 \ge g^2\sum_{k\ne i}c_k^2.$ Thus $\sum_{k\ne i}c_k^2\le\rho^2/(s^2g^2)$.

Put $\varepsilon=1$ if $c_i\ge0$ and $\varepsilon=-1$ otherwise. Since $\widehat v$ and $u_i$ are unit vectors, $\|\widehat v-\varepsilon u_i\|_2^2=2(1-|c_i|)\le2(1-c_i^2)=2\sum_{k\ne i}c_k^2\le2\rho^2/(s^2g^2)$.

By [F4], $\widehat v_1^2\le\sum_{k=1}^m\widehat v_k^2=1$ and $(u_i)_1^2\le\sum_{k=1}^m(u_i)_k^2=1$, since all coordinate squares are nonnegative. Hence $|\widehat v_1|,|(u_i)_1|\le1$. Therefore $|\widehat v_1^2-(u_i)_1^2| =|\widehat v_1-\varepsilon(u_i)_1|\,|\widehat v_1+\varepsilon(u_i)_1| \le2\|\widehat v-\varepsilon u_i\|_2 \le2\sqrt2\,\rho/(sg).$
Since $\widehat v_1^2=v_1^2/\|v\|_2^2$, multiply step 3.1 by $\mu_0>0$ from [F2] and use [F3]. The result is the claimed Gaussian weight bound.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

Let $(a,b,m,r,\mu)$ be moment data from
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], with $r\ge2m-1$, and let $p_m$ be the monic
orthogonal polynomial from
[[thm-monic-gauss-orthogonal-polynomials-exist-uniquely]]. Then $p_m$ has
exactly $m$ distinct roots $a<x_1<\cdots<x_m<b$, each simple, and
$$ p_m(X)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}(X-x_i). $$

Let $(a,b,m,r,\mu)$ be moment data from [[def-gauss-moment-data]] with
$r\ge2m-1$. For $0\le j<m$, let $h_j,\alpha_j$ be as in
[[lem-gauss-monic-three-term-recurrence]], and for $1\le j<m$ let
$\beta_j=h_j/h_{j-1}$. Put $\beta_0=0$ and define the real symmetric
tridiagonal **Jacobi matrix**
$$ J_m= \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_0&\sqrt{\beta_1}\\ \sqrt{\beta_1}&\alpha_1&\ddots\\ &\ddots&\ddots&\sqrt{\beta_{m-1}}\\ &&\sqrt{\beta_{m-1}}&\alpha_{m-1} \end{pmatrix}, $$
with the evident one-by-one interpretation for $m=1$. If
$a<x_1<\cdots<x_m<b$ are the roots of $p_m$, then
$\operatorname{spec}(J_m)=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$, where spectrum denotes the set
of eigenvalues as in [[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]];
every eigenvalue is simple. If $q_j:=p_j/\sqrt{h_j}$ for $0\le j<m$, then
$(q_0(x_i),\ldots,q_{m-1}(x_i))^{\mathsf T}$ is a nonzero eigenvector of $J_m$
for $x_i$.

Input $n\ge1$, a nonempty family of Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices enclosed by complex rectangles, a point matrix $V\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, a real diagonal matrix $\Theta\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, and proposed nonnegative bounds $\delta,\rho,M_A,M_\Theta,\tau$. Treat point data as exact dyadics and the family as any subset of its enclosure.

1. With outward interval evaluation, enclose $V^*V-I$ and every $AV-V\Theta$ for the full family. Form Frobenius upper bounds $d,r$ for these two matrices. Also form Frobenius upper bounds $m_A$ for every $A$ in the family and $m_\Theta$ for $\Theta$. If any enclosure or square-root operation is non-finite, return `inconclusive`.

2. Verify by outward scalar comparisons that $d\le\delta<1$, $r\le\rho$, $m_A\le M_A$, $m_\Theta\le M_\Theta$, and that $1-\sqrt{1-\delta}\le\tau$. If any comparison is undecided or false, return `inconclusive` with the failed check. Otherwise outward-compute a finite upper bound $\bar\eta\ge\rho+(M_A+M_\Theta)\tau$. For each increasingly sorted diagonal entry $\theta_{(k)}$, outward-compute finite endpoints $\ell_k\le\theta_{(k)}-\bar\eta$ and $u_k\ge\theta_{(k)}+\bar\eta$, and set $I_k=[\ell_k,u_k]$. If the radius bound or any final endpoint cannot be enclosed finitely, return `inconclusive`; otherwise return `certified` with radius bound $\bar\eta$ and intervals $I_1,\ldots,I_n$.

The checks use the Frobenius norm as an upper bound for the operator 2-norm. An inconclusive check makes no statement about the true spectrum.

If [[alg-near-orthonormal-hermitian-eigenvalue-certifier]] returns `certified` with outward radius bound $\bar\eta$ and intervals $I_k$, then for every admitted Hermitian $A$ its $k$-th increasing eigenvalue lies in $I_k$. Each $I_k$ contains the symmetric interval $[\theta_{(k)}-\bar\eta,\theta_{(k)}+\bar\eta]$. Inconclusive output makes no spectral claim.

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data and let $Q_m$ have nodes $x_i$ and
weights $w_i$ as in [[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]. Let $J_m$ be the Jacobi
matrix of [[thm-jacobi-matrix-spectrum-equals-gauss-nodes]], and let $v_i$ be
any unit eigenvector of $J_m$ for eigenvalue $x_i$. Then
$$ w_i=\mu([a,b])\,|v_{i,1}|^2. $$

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data. Put $\mu_0:=\mu([a,b])>0$.
Let $J$ be the $m\times m$ real symmetric Jacobi matrix of
[[thm-jacobi-matrix-spectrum-equals-gauss-nodes]], with distinct eigenvalues
$\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_m$ and Gaussian weights $w_i$ of
[[thm-gauss-weights-equal-mu0-times-first-eigenvector-coordinate-squared]].
Fix $i$, a nonzero vector $v\in\mathbb R^m$, a real number $\theta$, and
$\rho\ge0$. Suppose $\|v\|_2\ge s>0$ and
$$ \|Jv-\theta v\|_2\le\rho,\qquad g:=\min_{k\ne i}|\lambda_k-\theta|>0. $$
For $m\ge2$,
$$ \left|w_i-\mu_0\frac{v_1^2}{\|v\|_2^2}\right| \le \frac{2\sqrt2\,\mu_0\rho}{sg}. $$

derivations.claim: Each coefficient solve in step 1 uses the full moment rectangle families, which contain the actual Hankel matrix and right-hand side by the moment promise. By [F1], successful uniform residual certification encloses the unique actual coefficient vector. The true Hankel matrices are positive definite by the support hypothesis and [[thm-gauss-polynomial-moment-pairing-is-an-inner-product]]; thus these solutions are the coefficients of the monic orthogonal polynomials. By [F2], the arithmetic in step 2 encloses every true $h_j,\alpha_j,\beta_j$ and hence the true Jacobi matrix.

If $m=1$, the true Jacobi matrix is the one-by-one matrix $[\alpha_0]$. By [F3] its sole eigenvalue is the sole Gaussian node $x_1$, so $x_1=\alpha_0$. Its unit eigenvector is $(1)$, and [F5] gives $w_1=\mu_0$. The outward interval $\alpha_0$ and moment interval $I_0$ in step 3 of the algorithm contain these exact values by [F2].

Assume $m\ge2$. By [F3], the eigenvalues of the true Jacobi matrix are precisely the Gaussian nodes. The matrix family in step 5 contains this matrix by step 1.1, and successful near-orthonormal certification gives $x_i\in N_i$ by [F4].

For column $v_i$ of $V$, the accepted checks in step 5 and [F4] certify $\|Jv_i-\theta_i v_i\|_2\le\rho$ and $\|V^*V-I\|_2\le d<1$. Therefore $\|v_i\|_2^2\ge1-d$, so the positive lower endpoint $s$ of the outward enclosure of $\sqrt{1-d}$ is a lower bound on its norm. The disjoint ordered intervals in step 5 make $g_i$ in step 6 a positive lower bound for the distance from $\theta_i$ to every other true node.

Apply [F6] to $(v_i,\theta_i)$ and the bounds of step 3.1. The interval $C_i$ contains $\mu_0(v_i)_1^2/\|v_i\|_2^2$ and $R_i$ is at least the resulting error bound, because $\sup(I_0)\ge\mu_0$. Thus the exact Gaussian weight $w_i$ belongs to $C_i+[-R_i,R_i]=W_i$ by [F5].
The $m=1$ case is step 2.1; for $m\ge2$, steps 2.2 and 4.1 give every node and weight enclosure. These cases exhaust $m\ge1$, proving the claim.

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]]. Let $p_m$ be its monic degree-$m$ orthogonal
polynomial and write its ordered roots as
$a<x_1<\cdots<x_m<b$, as established in
[[thm-gauss-orthogonal-polynomial-has-simple-interior-zeros]]. For
$i=1,\ldots,m$, define the Lagrange cardinal polynomial
$$ \ell_i(X):=\prod_{\substack{1\le j\le m\\j\ne i}}\frac{X-x_j}{x_i-x_j} $$
using the convention of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
the **Gaussian quadrature weights** and the **m-node Gaussian rule** by
$$ w_i:=\int_{[a,b]}\ell_i(x)\,d\mu(x),\qquad Q_m(f):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i f(x_i) $$
for any real-valued function $f$ defined at the nodes. This definition
asserts no accuracy; well-definedness of the nodes, cardinal polynomials,
weights, and finite sum is proved in
[[lem-gauss-quadrature-rule-data-well-defined]].

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], and let $Q_m$ and $w_i$ be the rule and weights of
[[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]. For every real polynomial $f$ of degree at most
$2m-1$,
$$ \int_{[a,b]} f(x)\,d\mu(x)=Q_m(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_if(x_i). $$
Moreover, $w_i>0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_iw_i=\mu([a,b])$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Define the node polynomial and barycentric weights by
$$\omega_n(X)=\prod_{k=0}^{n}(X-x_k),\qquad w_j=\left(\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}(x_j-x_k)\right)^{-1}\quad(0\le j\le n).$$
An empty product is $1$, so $w_0=1$ when $n=0$.

In these formulas, $X$ is a real argument, and for real $a$ and nonzero real $b$, $a/b$ denotes $ab^{-1}$ in the field $\mathbb R$ ([[def-field]]).

For each $j$, the cardinal function is
$$\ell_j(X)=\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}\frac{X-x_k}{x_j-x_k}.$$
The interpolation function for the data $y=(y_0,\ldots,y_n)$ is
$$I_n y(X)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}y_j\ell_j(X).$$
For a real function $f$ defined at the nodes, write $I_n f:=I_n(f(x_0),\ldots,f(x_n))$.

For products indexed by $k\ne j$, use the length-$n$ list $\widehat x_{j,k}$ ($0\le k<n$), where $\widehat x_{j,k}=x_k$ for $k<j$ and $\widehat x_{j,k}=x_{k+1}$ for $k\ge j$; the product is in this order and is empty when $n=0$. Strict ordering gives $x_j-\widehat x_{j,k}\ne0$ for every factor, so [[lem-finite-product-of-nonzero-reals-is-nonzero]] and the field inverse law make each $w_j$ well defined.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Each cardinal function $\ell_j$ of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] is the evaluation of a formal polynomial of degree $n$. The node function $\omega_n$ is the evaluation of a monic formal polynomial of degree $n+1$, and $\omega_n(x)\ne0$ whenever $x$ differs from every node. The function $I_n y$ is the evaluation of a formal polynomial of degree at most $n$. At every pair $i,j\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, $\ell_j(x_i)=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise.

Let $a<b$ be real numbers, let $m\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$r\in\{2m-1,2m\}$. A **Gaussian quadrature moment datum of order $r$** is a
finite positive measure $\mu$ on the relative Borel sigma-algebra
$\mathcal B([a,b])$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-measure-space]],
[[def-measure]], [[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) such that
$\mu([a,b])>0$, and whose **relative support**
$$ S_\mu:=\{x\in[a,b]:\mu(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open }U\subseteq[a,b]\text{ with }x\in U\} $$
contains at least $m+1$ distinct points. For every integer $0\le k\le r$,
require $x\mapsto |x|^k$ to be integrable with respect to $\mu$
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]) and put
$M_k:=\int_{[a,b]}x^k\,d\mu(x)$. Powers use the natural-exponent
recursion of [[def-integer-power]], with $x^0=1$ for every real $x$, including
$x=0$; thus $M_0$ is the integral of the constant function $1$.

The branch $r=2m-1$ supplies all moments used to construct the monic
degree-$m$ orthogonal polynomial and prove rule exactness. The stronger branch
$r=2m$ also defines its squared norm and is used for the remainder formula.
Because $[a,b]$ is bounded and $\mu$ is finite, these absolute-moment
integrability conditions follow from finiteness; they are stated to make the
two moment interfaces explicit.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: Since $\deg(\ell_i^2)=2$, exactness [F2] gives $Q_2(\ell_i^2)=\int\ell_i^2\,d\mu=w_i$. Expanding the finite rule sum and using the cardinal values [F3] gives $Q_2(\ell_i^2)=w_i$.

The formula for $\ell_1$ gives $\ell_1(x)^2=(x^2-2x_2x+x_2^2)/(x_1-x_2)^2$. Integrating term by term using [F4] proves the displayed expression for $w_1$. Replacing the omitted node $x_2$ by $x_1$ gives the displayed expression for $w_2$. Their strict positivity is [F2].

Let $d\ge1$ and, for each coordinate $j=1,\ldots,d$, let
$Q_j(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{m_j}w_i^{(j)}f(x_i^{(j)})$ be a well-defined Gaussian rule
as in [[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]] and
[[lem-gauss-quadrature-rule-data-well-defined]]. Its **tensor-product
quadrature rule** is
$$ Q_{\otimes}(f):= \sum_{i_1=1}^{m_1}\cdots\sum_{i_d=1}^{m_d} \left(\prod_{j=1}^{d}w_{i_j}^{(j)}\right) f\left(x_{i_1}^{(1)},\ldots,x_{i_d}^{(d)}\right). $$
Its node set is the Cartesian product of the one-dimensional node sets; the
displayed finite sum is its value on any function defined on that node set.

For $d\ge1$, let $(a_j,b_j,m_j,2m_j-1,\mu_j)$ be Gaussian moment data for
each coordinate $j=1,\ldots,d$, and write
$M^{(j)}_k:=\int x^k\,d\mu_j(x)$. A **coordinatewise tensor polynomial** is a
finite family $(c_\alpha)$, with $c_\alpha\in\mathbb R$ for every index, indexed by multi-indices
$\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)$ with
$0\le\alpha_j\le2m_j-1$, evaluated by
$$ P(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{d}x_j^{\alpha_j}. $$
Define its **coordinatewise product-moment value** by
$$ I_\otimes(P):=\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{d}M^{(j)}_{\alpha_j}. $$
In both sums, list the finite multi-index box in increasing lexicographic
order (coordinate $1$ first, then coordinate $2$, and so on), and take the
ordinary finite-list sum in that order. The products use increasing coordinate
order $j=1,\ldots,d$. The real coefficient family is part of the formal
polynomial data, so these formulas specify finite real sums. This definition specifies the product-moment functional
used for coordinatewise exactness without requiring a measure-product
construction.

For $d\ge1$, take one-dimensional Gaussian rules $Q_j$ with orders $m_j$ and
moment data $(a_j,b_j,m_j,2m_j-1,\mu_j)$, and form their tensor rule
$Q_\otimes$ as in [[def-tensor-product-gauss-rule]]. For every coordinatewise
tensor polynomial $P$ of [[def-coordinatewise-product-moment-functional]],
$$ Q_\otimes(P)=I_\otimes(P). $$
The tensor rule has exactly $\prod_{j=1}^{d}m_j$ distinct nodes. In particular,
using the same $m\ge2$ nodes in each coordinate requires $m^d$ node
evaluations, exponential growth in $d$.

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], and let $Q_m$ and $w_i$ be the rule and weights of
[[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]. For every real polynomial $f$ of degree at most
$2m-1$,
$$ \int_{[a,b]} f(x)\,d\mu(x)=Q_m(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_if(x_i). $$
Moreover, $w_i>0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_iw_i=\mu([a,b])$.

Let $(a,b,m,r,\mu)$ be moment data from
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], with $r\ge2m-1$, and let $p_m$ be the monic
orthogonal polynomial from
[[thm-monic-gauss-orthogonal-polynomials-exist-uniquely]]. Then $p_m$ has
exactly $m$ distinct roots $a<x_1<\cdots<x_m<b$, each simple, and
$$ p_m(X)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}(X-x_i). $$

derivations.claim: Since each coordinate has two distinct nodes by [F5], the sixteen coordinate tuples are distinct: two different tuples differ in a coordinate whose node entries are distinct.

The node-count statement of [F3] gives $2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2=16$. For each coordinate degree $\alpha_j\le3$, [F4] evaluates the corresponding one-dimensional sum as its moment. Distributing the finite sums in [F1] therefore gives the product of those four moments, which is [F2]. Taking the specified exponents proves the displayed calculation and the general coordinatewise exactness claim.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

Let $(a,b,m,r,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], with $m\ge1$ and $r\ge2m-1$. For each
$j=0,\ldots,m$ there is a unique monic real polynomial $p_j$ of degree $j$
such that
$$ \int_{[a,b]}p_j(x)q(x)\,d\mu(x)=0 $$
for every real polynomial $q$ of degree less than $j$. For $j=0$, this means
$p_0=1$ and the orthogonality condition is vacuous. The $j=m$ polynomial uses
moments only through degree $2m-1$; its squared norm is asserted only when the
moment datum has order $2m$.

Let $(a,b,m,r,\mu)$ be moment data from [[def-gauss-moment-data]] with
$r\ge2m-1$, and let $p_0,\ldots,p_m$ be the monic orthogonal polynomials of
[[thm-monic-gauss-orthogonal-polynomials-exist-uniquely]]. For $0\le j<m$ put
$$ h_j:=\int_{[a,b]}p_j(x)^2\,d\mu(x),\qquad \alpha_j:=\frac{\int_{[a,b]}x\,p_j(x)^2\,d\mu(x)}{h_j}. $$
For $1\le j<m$ put $\beta_j:=h_j/h_{j-1}$. These numbers are defined,
$h_j>0$, and $\beta_j>0$. The recurrence is
$$ xp_0=p_1+\alpha_0p_0 $$
and, for $1\le j<m$,
$$ xp_j=p_{j+1}+\alpha_jp_j+\beta_jp_{j-1}. $$
Only moments through degree $2m-1$ are used.

Let $(a,b,m,r,\mu)$ be moment data from [[def-gauss-moment-data]] with
$r\ge2m-1$. For $0\le j<m$, let $h_j,\alpha_j$ be as in
[[lem-gauss-monic-three-term-recurrence]], and for $1\le j<m$ let
$\beta_j=h_j/h_{j-1}$. Put $\beta_0=0$ and define the real symmetric
tridiagonal **Jacobi matrix**
$$ J_m= \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_0&\sqrt{\beta_1}\\ \sqrt{\beta_1}&\alpha_1&\ddots\\ &\ddots&\ddots&\sqrt{\beta_{m-1}}\\ &&\sqrt{\beta_{m-1}}&\alpha_{m-1} \end{pmatrix}, $$
with the evident one-by-one interpretation for $m=1$. If
$a<x_1<\cdots<x_m<b$ are the roots of $p_m$, then
$\operatorname{spec}(J_m)=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$, where spectrum denotes the set
of eigenvalues as in [[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]];
every eigenvalue is simple. If $q_j:=p_j/\sqrt{h_j}$ for $0\le j<m$, then
$(q_0(x_i),\ldots,q_{m-1}(x_i))^{\mathsf T}$ is a nonzero eigenvector of $J_m$
for $x_i$.

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data and let $Q_m$ have nodes $x_i$ and
weights $w_i$ as in [[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]. Let $J_m$ be the Jacobi
matrix of [[thm-jacobi-matrix-spectrum-equals-gauss-nodes]], and let $v_i$ be
any unit eigenvector of $J_m$ for eigenvalue $x_i$. Then
$$ w_i=\mu([a,b])\,|v_{i,1}|^2. $$

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], and let $Q_m$ and $w_i$ be the rule and weights of
[[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]. For every real polynomial $f$ of degree at most
$2m-1$,
$$ \int_{[a,b]} f(x)\,d\mu(x)=Q_m(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_if(x_i). $$
Moreover, $w_i>0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_iw_i=\mu([a,b])$.

Define $d_{\mathbb{R}} : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) := |x - y|$ ([[def-abs-value]]). Then:

1. $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-metric-space]]); it is
   called the **usual metric** of $\mathbb{R}$.
2. For $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $r > 0$ the open ball is the bounded open interval
   ([[def-interval]], [[def-metric-ball]])
   $$B(x,r) = (x-r,\ x+r),$$
   and the closed ball is $\bar B(x,r) = [x-r,\ x+r]$.
3. Consequently $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is open in the metric topology of
   $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ ([[def-metric-topology]]) exactly when for every $x \in U$
   there is $r > 0$ with $(x-r, x+r) \subseteq U$. This topology is called the
   **usual topology** of $\mathbb{R}$.
4. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ is not a bounded metric space
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]): no ball contains $\mathbb{R}$, so
   $\operatorname{diam}(\mathbb{R})$ is not defined.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq X$. The **subspace topology** (also *relative topology*) on $S$ is

$$\mathcal{T}_S := \{\, U \cap S : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\},$$

the family of **traces** on $S$ of the open sets of $X$. The pair
$(S, \mathcal{T}_S)$ is a **subspace** of $X$. A subset of $S$ that lies in
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is said to be **open in $S$**, and *relatively open* where the
ambient space needs emphasis.

**$\mathcal{T}_S$ is a topology, and this is discharged here.** (T1):
$\varnothing = \varnothing \cap S$ and $S = X \cap S$ are traces. (T2): if
$\mathcal{S}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}_S$, choose for each member a set of
$\mathcal{T}$ tracing to it — no choice principle is needed, since
$U' := \bigcup \{\, U \in \mathcal{T} : U \cap S \subseteq W \,\}$ is a canonical
such set for $W \in \mathcal{T}_S$, being open by (T2) in $X$ and satisfying
$U' \cap S = W$ — and then
$\bigcup_i (U_i \cap S) = (\bigcup_i U_i) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by (T2) in
$X$. (T3): $(U \cap S) \cap (V \cap S) = (U \cap V) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by
(T3) in $X$.

**Closed sets of a subspace are the traces of the closed sets.** A set
$C \subseteq S$ is closed in $S$ if and only if $C = F \cap S$ for some closed
$F \subseteq X$. Indeed $S \setminus (U \cap S) = (X \setminus U) \cap S$ and
$S \setminus (F \cap S) = (X \setminus F) \cap S$, so complementation inside $S$
matches complementation inside $X$ under tracing.

**Bases and subbases trace as well.** If $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]) then
$\mathcal{B}_S := \{\, B \cap S : B \in \mathcal{B} \,\}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$: its members are open in $S$, and for $W = U \cap S$ open in $S$
and $x \in W$ there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U$, whence
$x \in B \cap S \subseteq W$. The same computation with a subbasis $\mathcal{S}$
shows that $\{\, S_0 \cap S : S_0 \in \mathcal{S} \,\}$ is a subbasis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$, since tracing commutes with finite intersections and with
unions.

**The inclusion is continuous.** The inclusion map $\iota : S \to X$,
$\iota(s) = s$, satisfies $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$,
so preimages of open sets are open and $\iota$ is continuous
([[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]], clause (b)). Moreover
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is the **coarsest** topology on $S$ making $\iota$ continuous: any
topology on $S$ for which $\iota$ is continuous must contain every
$\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$, hence contain $\mathcal{T}_S$.

**Characteristic property of a map into a subspace.** Let $(Z, \mathcal{T}_Z)$ be
a topological space and let $g : Z \to S$ be a function. Then

$$g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (S,\mathcal{T}_S) \iff \iota \circ g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (X,\mathcal{T}) .$$

*Proof.* For $U \in \mathcal{T}$ one has
$(\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U] = g^{-1}[\iota^{-1}[U]] = g^{-1}[U \cap S]$. If $g$ is
continuous then each $g^{-1}[U \cap S]$ is open, so $\iota \circ g$ is continuous;
conversely if $\iota \circ g$ is continuous then for any $W = U \cap S$ open in
$S$ the set $g^{-1}[W] = (\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U]$ is open, so $g$ is continuous.
Both directions use only clause (b) of [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]].

**Restriction of a continuous map.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous and
$S \subseteq X$, then $f|_S : S \to Y$ is continuous, since
$(f|_S)^{-1}[V] = f^{-1}[V] \cap S$ is open in $S$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]).

**When relative and ambient agree.** If $S$ is open in $X$ then a subset of $S$
is open in $S$ if and only if it is open in $X$: a trace $U \cap S$ is then an
intersection of two open sets of $X$, and conversely an open subset of $X$
contained in $S$ is its own trace. The same statement with "closed" throughout
holds when $S$ is closed in $X$. Both are used in the pasting lemma of the next
item, and both fail without the hypothesis: $S$ itself is always open and closed
in $S$, and need be neither in $X$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Let $Y$ be a subspace of a topological space $X$. Then

$$\mathcal B(Y)=\mathcal B(X)|_Y.$$

In a Dedekind-complete ordered field, every $x\ge0$ has a unique $y\ge0$ with
$y^2=x$.

derivations.claim: By [F10], every relative Borel set is $B\cap[-1,1]$ for ambient Borel $B$. The interval is closed, hence ambient Borel, so this intersection is ambient Borel and is Lebesgue measurable by [F1]. Restricting Lebesgue measure to this sigma-algebra therefore defines the asserted positive measure; disjoint relative Borel unions are the same ambient measurable unions, so countable additivity is inherited. For $x\in[-1,1]$, [F9] gives an $\varepsilon>0$ such that $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\cap[-1,1]$ lies in any chosen relative open neighborhood $U$ of $x$. Choose a closed interval $I$ of positive length inside that intersection, using a one-sided interval when $x$ is an endpoint. Then $I$ is relative Borel and [F2] gives $\mu(I)>0$. Since $U=I\sqcup(U\setminus I)$ and both sets are relative Borel, countable additivity and nonnegativity from [F1] imply $\mu(U)\ge\mu(I)>0$. Thus every $x$ lies in the relative support, which has at least three points.

The functions $1,x,x^2,x^3$ are continuous, hence Riemann integrable by [F3]. Their primitives $x,x^2/2,x^3/3,x^4/4$, evaluated at $-1$ and $1$, give respectively $2,0,2/3,0$. The Riemann–Lebesgue equality in [F3] gives the stated moment values.

The monic polynomials $1$ and $X$ are orthogonal in the required degrees: $\int x\,d\mu=0$. The monic polynomial $X^2-1/3$ is orthogonal to $1$ because $\mu_2-(1/3)\mu_0=0$, and to $X$ because $\mu_3-(1/3)\mu_1=0$. Uniqueness [F4] identifies $p_0,p_1,p_2$ as stated. By [F11], $\sqrt3>0$ exists uniquely. The identity $X^2-1/3=(X-1/\sqrt3)(X+1/\sqrt3)$ gives exactly the two roots $\pm1/\sqrt3$.

Here $h_0=\mu_0=2$, $h_1=\int x^2\,d\mu=2/3$, and both recurrence diagonal entries are zero by the odd moments. Hence $\beta_1=h_1/h_0=1/3$, and [F5] gives the displayed $J_2$. Direct multiplication shows its two displayed unit eigenvectors have eigenvalues $-1/\sqrt3$ and $1/\sqrt3$; [F6] identifies those as the Gaussian nodes.
For either unit eigenvector, the first-coordinate square is $1/2$. Applying [F7] with $\mu_0=2$ gives each weight as $1$. Exactness through degree three is [F8], proving the stated rule.

Let $a<b$ be real numbers, let $m\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$r\in\{2m-1,2m\}$. A **Gaussian quadrature moment datum of order $r$** is a
finite positive measure $\mu$ on the relative Borel sigma-algebra
$\mathcal B([a,b])$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-measure-space]],
[[def-measure]], [[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) such that
$\mu([a,b])>0$, and whose **relative support**
$$ S_\mu:=\{x\in[a,b]:\mu(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open }U\subseteq[a,b]\text{ with }x\in U\} $$
contains at least $m+1$ distinct points. For every integer $0\le k\le r$,
require $x\mapsto |x|^k$ to be integrable with respect to $\mu$
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]) and put
$M_k:=\int_{[a,b]}x^k\,d\mu(x)$. Powers use the natural-exponent
recursion of [[def-integer-power]], with $x^0=1$ for every real $x$, including
$x=0$; thus $M_0$ is the integral of the constant function $1$.

The branch $r=2m-1$ supplies all moments used to construct the monic
degree-$m$ orthogonal polynomial and prove rule exactness. The stronger branch
$r=2m$ also defines its squared norm and is used for the remainder formula.
Because $[a,b]$ is bounded and $\mu$ is finite, these absolute-moment
integrability conditions follow from finiteness; they are stated to make the
two moment interfaces explicit.

For $d\ge1$, let $(a_j,b_j,m_j,2m_j-1,\mu_j)$ be Gaussian moment data for
each coordinate $j=1,\ldots,d$, and write
$M^{(j)}_k:=\int x^k\,d\mu_j(x)$. A **coordinatewise tensor polynomial** is a
finite family $(c_\alpha)$, with $c_\alpha\in\mathbb R$ for every index, indexed by multi-indices
$\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)$ with
$0\le\alpha_j\le2m_j-1$, evaluated by
$$ P(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{d}x_j^{\alpha_j}. $$
Define its **coordinatewise product-moment value** by
$$ I_\otimes(P):=\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{d}M^{(j)}_{\alpha_j}. $$
In both sums, list the finite multi-index box in increasing lexicographic
order (coordinate $1$ first, then coordinate $2$, and so on), and take the
ordinary finite-list sum in that order. The products use increasing coordinate
order $j=1,\ldots,d$. The real coefficient family is part of the formal
polynomial data, so these formulas specify finite real sums. This definition specifies the product-moment functional
used for coordinatewise exactness without requiring a measure-product
construction.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

Let $Y$ be a subspace of a topological space $X$. Then

$$\mathcal B(Y)=\mathcal B(X)|_Y.$$

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

derivations.claim: Each factor measure is finite, hence sigma-finite. Iterating [F2] constructs the finite product and makes it finite, with total mass equal to the product of the finite factor masses. For the product of intervals, the product sigma-algebra is the trace of the Euclidean Borel sigma-algebra: [F5] gives the binary Euclidean equality, and tracing its rectangle generators to the interval factors gives the corresponding trace equality; finite induction gives the $d$-factor case. Hence each coordinate monomial and its absolute value are product-measurable by [F5].

Fix an allowed multi-index $\alpha$. Apply [F3] successively to the nonnegative function $\prod_{j=1}^d|x_j|^{\alpha_j}$. At each step the inner one-variable integral is the finite absolute moment of the last coordinate, and it factors out as a nonnegative finite scalar. Induction therefore gives $\int\prod_j|x_j|^{\alpha_j}\,d\mu=\prod_j\int|x_j|^{\alpha_j}\,d\mu_j<\infty$. Thus the signed real monomial is integrable.

Apply [F4] to that integrable monomial, integrating the last coordinate first. Its one-variable signed moment is $M^{(d)}_{\alpha_d}$; repeat for the preceding coordinates. Each use is legitimate by the absolute integrability in step 2.1, and finite induction yields $\int\prod_jx_j^{\alpha_j}\,d\mu=\prod_jM^{(j)}_{\alpha_j}$. At $d=1$ this is the moment definition itself.

A finite real linear combination of these integrable monomials is integrable by [F4]. Integrating that combination term by term in the fixed coefficient order from [F1] and substituting step 3.1 gives $\int P\,d\mu=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha\prod_jM^{(j)}_{\alpha_j}=I_\otimes(P)$. No probability normalization or new choice assumption was used.

Statement uses measures on closed intervals, including endpoint atoms; Tonelli/Fubini in steps 2.1 and 3.1 do not omit them.

([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $I \subseteq A$ be order-convex

extreme value theorem supplies the endpoints.

Let $(a,b,m,r,\mu)$ be moment data from [[def-gauss-moment-data]] with
$r\ge2m-1$. For $0\le j<m$, let $h_j,\alpha_j$ be as in
[[lem-gauss-monic-three-term-recurrence]], and for $1\le j<m$ let
$\beta_j=h_j/h_{j-1}$. Put $\beta_0=0$ and define the real symmetric
tridiagonal **Jacobi matrix**
$$ J_m= \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_0&\sqrt{\beta_1}\\ \sqrt{\beta_1}&\alpha_1&\ddots\\ &\ddots&\ddots&\sqrt{\beta_{m-1}}\\ &&\sqrt{\beta_{m-1}}&\alpha_{m-1} \end{pmatrix}, $$
with the evident one-by-one interpretation for $m=1$. If
$a<x_1<\cdots<x_m<b$ are the roots of $p_m$, then
$\operatorname{spec}(J_m)=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$, where spectrum denotes the set
of eigenvalues as in [[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]];
every eigenvalue is simple. If $q_j:=p_j/\sqrt{h_j}$ for $0\le j<m$, then

Let $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let $0\leq n\leq N$.
The **Stiefel space**

$$V_n(\mathbb F^N)=\{(v_1,\ldots,v_n):\langle v_i,v_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}\}$$

has the subspace topology from $(\mathbb F^N)^n$. The group
$K_n=\operatorname O(n)$ in the real case and
$K_n=\operatorname U(n)$ in the complex case acts freely on the right by
change of orthonormal frame. The **Grassmannian**
$\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N)=V_n(\mathbb F^N)/K_n$ is the space of
$n$-planes with this quotient topology.

Graph charts about a plane identify nearby planes with linear maps to its
orthogonal complement. They locally trivialize
$V_n(\mathbb F^N)\to\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N)$ as a principal
$K_n$-bundle. Its associated standard vector bundle, in the convention of
[[def-frame-bundle-and-associated-vector-bundle]], is the **tautological
bundle**

$$\gamma_n^N=\{(W,v)\in\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N)\times\mathbb F^N:v\in W\}.$$

Equivalently, its graph-chart transition matrices glue it by
[[thm-vector-bundles-glued-from-transition-cocycles]].

The coordinate inclusions $\mathbb F^N\subseteq\mathbb F^{N+1}$ define
compatible inclusions of Stiefel spaces, Grassmannians, and tautological
bundles. Write

$$V_n(\mathbb F^\infty)=\bigcup_{N\geq n}V_n(\mathbb F^N),\qquad \operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^\infty)=\bigcup_{N\geq n}\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N),$$

with the weak direct-limit topology: a set is closed exactly when its
intersection with every finite stage is closed. The later Schubert theorem
identifies this with the weak topology in
[[def-cw-complex-with-closure-finiteness-and-weak-topology]]. For $n=0$,
the Stiefel spaces, Grassmannians, and their stable colimits are points, and
$\gamma_0$ is the zero bundle.

A **Riemannian metric** on a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $g$ such that $g_p(v,v)>0$ for every point $p$ and every nonzero $v\in T_pM$. A **Riemannian manifold** is the pair $(M,g)$.

This is a [[def-smooth-tensor-field]] giving a [[def-smooth-bundle-metric]] on $TM$. Dimension zero is allowed: its zero bilinear form is positive definite because there are no nonzero vectors. The empty manifold has its unique empty metric. Boundaries are allowed where stated, with smoothness understood up to the boundary.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $V$ be an $n$-dimensional vector space over $k$. For $0\le r\le n$, $\operatorname{Gr}(r,V)$ denotes the parameter set of $r$-dimensional linear subspaces of $V$. Thus $\operatorname{Gr}(0,V)=\{0\}$ and $\operatorname{Gr}(n,V)=\{V\}$. For $r<0$ or $r>n$ we set $\operatorname{Gr}(r,V)=\varnothing$.

routine_steps.claim: For any real matrix $U$, $\langle U,U\rangle_F=\sum_{i,j}U_{ij}^2$, so this pairing is symmetric bilinear and positive for every nonzero $U$ by [F3]. Its restriction to each tangent or horizontal subspace is therefore a positive-definite inner product, as required by [F2].

By [F4], each frame represents an $r$-dimensional subspace, and [F1] identifies frames representing the same subspace by the right orthogonal action. For $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_r$, cyclicity of trace gives $\langle UQ,VQ\rangle_F=\operatorname{tr}(Q^{\mathsf T}U^{\mathsf T}VQ)=\operatorname{tr}(U^{\mathsf T}V)$. Thus the action is isometric and the horizontal pairing is independent of the chosen orthonormal frame.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

derivations.claim: The equations $X^{\mathsf T}X=I_r$ are polynomial equations in the entries, so their common zero set is closed. Also $\|X\|_F^2=\operatorname{tr}(X^{\mathsf T}X)=r$, so the set is bounded. The matrix with columns $e_1,\ldots,e_r$ belongs to it, so it is nonempty.

Let $\mathcal U$ be any open cover of $\operatorname{Gr}(r,n)$. By [F2], the sets $q^{-1}(U)$ for $U\in\mathcal U$ are open in $\operatorname{St}(n,r)$ and cover it. Compactness from step 1.1 gives $U_1,\ldots,U_k\in\mathcal U$ whose preimages cover $\operatorname{St}(n,r)$. Since $q$ is surjective, $U_1,\ldots,U_k$ cover $\operatorname{Gr}(r,n)$. Thus the quotient is compact directly from the open-cover definition.
Step 1.1 proves compactness of $\operatorname{St}(n,r)$ and step 2.1 proves compactness of $\operatorname{Gr}(r,n)$, as claimed.

citations.quote:
Let $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let $0\leq n\leq N$.
The **Stiefel space**

$$V_n(\mathbb F^N)=\{(v_1,\ldots,v_n):\langle v_i,v_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}\}$$

has the subspace topology from $(\mathbb F^N)^n$. The group
$K_n=\operatorname O(n)$ in the real case and
$K_n=\operatorname U(n)$ in the complex case acts freely on the right by
change of orthonormal frame. The **Grassmannian**
$\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N)=V_n(\mathbb F^N)/K_n$ is the space of
$n$-planes with this quotient topology.

Graph charts about a plane identify nearby planes with linear maps to its
orthogonal complement. They locally trivialize
$V_n(\mathbb F^N)\to\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N)$ as a principal
$K_n$-bundle. Its associated standard vector bundle, in the convention of
[[def-frame-bundle-and-associated-vector-bundle]], is the **tautological
bundle**

$$\gamma_n^N=\{(W,v)\in\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N)\times\mathbb F^N:v\in W\}.$$

Equivalently, its graph-chart transition matrices glue it by
[[thm-vector-bundles-glued-from-transition-cocycles]].

The coordinate inclusions $\mathbb F^N\subseteq\mathbb F^{N+1}$ define
compatible inclusions of Stiefel spaces, Grassmannians, and tautological
bundles. Write

$$V_n(\mathbb F^\infty)=\bigcup_{N\geq n}V_n(\mathbb F^N),\qquad \operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^\infty)=\bigcup_{N\geq n}\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N),$$

with the weak direct-limit topology: a set is closed exactly when its
intersection with every finite stage is closed. The later Schubert theorem
identifies this with the weak topology in
[[def-cw-complex-with-closure-finiteness-and-weak-topology]]. For $n=0$,
the Stiefel spaces, Grassmannians, and their stable colimits are points, and
$\gamma_0$ is the zero bundle.

Let $F:M\to N$ be smooth, let $q$ be a regular value, and let $p\in F^{-1}(q)$.
Then

$$T_p\bigl(F^{-1}(q)\bigr)=\ker dF_p.$$

derivations.claim: The derivative of $F$ at $X$ is $DF_X[Z]=X^{\mathsf T}Z+Z^{\mathsf T}X$. It is onto the symmetric matrices because for any symmetric $H$, the choice $Z=XH/2$ gives $DF_X[Z]=H$. Thus $0$ is a regular value; [F2] identifies the tangent space with the displayed kernel.

Write $S=\operatorname{sym}(X^{\mathsf T}G)$. Then $X^{\mathsf T}(G-XS)+(G-XS)^{\mathsf T}X=0$, so $G-XS$ is tangent. For every symmetric $H$ and tangent $Z$, $\langle XH,Z\rangle_F=\operatorname{tr}(H X^{\mathsf T}Z)=0$ because $X^{\mathsf T}Z$ is skew-symmetric. Hence $XS$ is normal and $G-XS$ is the orthogonal projection.

The vertical tangent to the right action is $X\Omega$ with $\Omega^{\mathsf T}=-\Omega$. Every Stiefel tangent $Z$ decomposes as $Z=X\Omega+(I-XX^{\mathsf T})Z$, where $\Omega=X^{\mathsf T}Z$ is skew and the second term is horizontal. These summands are orthogonal, so the quotient tangent is represented uniquely by the horizontal summand.

The matrix $(I-XX^{\mathsf T})G$ is horizontal. For every horizontal $Z$, $\langle G-(I-XX^{\mathsf T})G,Z\rangle_F=\langle XX^{\mathsf T}G,Z\rangle_F=0$, since $X^{\mathsf T}Z=0$. Therefore it is the quotient-metric projection. Under $X\mapsto XQ$ and $G\mapsto GQ$ it becomes $(I-XX^{\mathsf T})GQ$, the same tangent vector in the changed representative.

For $1\le r\le n$, set $\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)=\{X\in\mathbb C^{n\times r}:X^*X=I_r\}$ and $\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(r,n)=\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)/\operatorname U(r)$.
The class $[X]$ represents the complex column space of $X$; two orthonormal
frames represent the same space exactly when they differ by right multiplication
by a unitary $r\times r$ matrix. Regard each complex matrix space as a real
vector space and use the real Frobenius inner product
$$\langle U,V\rangle_{\mathbb R}:=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(U^*V).$$
Give the complex Stiefel manifold its induced metric. On the complex Grassmann
quotient, represent tangent vectors horizontally by matrices $Z$ with $X^*Z=0$
and pair these representatives by $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathbb R}$.
For $A=A_0+iA_1\in\mathbb C^{n\times r}$, write
$$\rho(A):=\begin{pmatrix}A_0&-A_1\\A_1&A_0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{2n\times2r}$$
for its realification, the real matrix acting on real/imaginary coordinates as
$A$ acts on complex coordinates. Write $\operatorname{Herm}(A)=(A+A^*)/2$.

derivations.claim: Regard the Hermitian $r\times r$ matrices as a real vector space. The derivative of $F(X)=X^*X-I_r$ is $DF_X[Z]=X^*Z+Z^*X$. It is onto that space: for any Hermitian $H$, $Z=XH/2$ gives $DF_X[Z]=H$. Hence the level is regular, and [F2] gives the displayed tangent kernel.

Set $S=\operatorname{Herm}(X^*G)$. Then $X^*(G-XS)+(G-XS)^*X=0$, so $G-XS$ is tangent. For tangent $Z$, put $K=X^*Z$, which is skew-Hermitian. For Hermitian $S$, $\overline{\operatorname{tr}(SK)}=-\operatorname{tr}(SK)$ by adjoint and cyclic-trace identities; thus $\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(SK)=0$. Therefore $XS$ is normal in the real Frobenius metric, and the stated formula is the Stiefel orthogonal projection.

By the graph-chart quotient in [F3], vertical tangents are derivatives of the right unitary action, hence are $X\Omega$ with $\Omega^*=-\Omega$. Every Stiefel tangent decomposes as $Z=X\Omega+(I-XX^*)Z$ with $\Omega=X^*Z$. The second summand is horizontal. For any vertical $X\Omega$ and horizontal $W$, $\langle X\Omega,W\rangle_{\mathbb R}=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(\Omega^*X^*W)=0$, so the summands are orthogonal. The decomposition is unique, and the graph-chart quotient identifies its horizontal component with the quotient tangent.

The matrix $(I-XX^*)G$ is horizontal. For every horizontal $Z$, $\langle G-(I-XX^*)G,Z\rangle_{\mathbb R}=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(XX^*G)^*Z=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(G^*XZ)=0$ since $X^*Z=0$. Thus it is the horizontal orthogonal projection. Under $(X,G)\mapsto(XQ,GQ)$ for unitary $Q$, it transforms to $(I-XX^*)GQ$, the same tangent vector in the changed frame.

citations.quote:
For $X\in\operatorname{St}(n,r)$, the tangent space and its Frobenius
orthogonal projection are
$$T_X\operatorname{St}(n,r)=\{Z:X^{\mathsf T}Z+Z^{\mathsf T}X=0\},\qquad \Pi_X^{\rm St}(G)=G-X\operatorname{sym}(X^{\mathsf T}G).$$
For $[X]\in\operatorname{Gr}(r,n)$, its tangent vectors have unique horizontal
representatives $Z$ with $X^{\mathsf T}Z=0$, and the quotient-metric projection
of an ambient $G$ to this horizontal space is
$$\Pi_X^{\rm Gr}(G)=(I-XX^{\mathsf T})G.$$

Let $g$ be a Riemannian metric on a smooth manifold $M$ and let
$f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth.  The **Riemannian gradient** of $f$ is the
smooth vector field $\operatorname{grad}_g f$ characterized by

$$ g_x\bigl((\operatorname{grad}_g f)_x,v\bigr)=df_x(v) \quad\text{for every }x\in M\text{ and }v\in T_xM. $$

Pointwise, it is the inverse metric-dual of $df_x$.  In a local frame with
metric matrix $(g_{ij})$ and inverse $(g^{ij})$, it is

$$ \operatorname{grad}_g f=\sum_{i,j}g^{ij}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}\partial_{x^i}; $$

the displayed coefficients are smooth, so this pointwise definition is a
smooth vector field.
