If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For a Riemannian metric $g$, a smooth $f:M\to\mathbb R$, and $x\in M$,
$\operatorname{grad}_g f(x)=0$ if and only if $x$ is a critical point of $f$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: Let $E_{ij}$ be the coordinate-basis matrices. Smoothness of $F$ makes $dF_X$ linear, and by the definition in [F4], $dF_X[E_{ij}]=\partial_{ij}F(X)=G_{ij}$. Expanding $Z=\sum_{i,j}Z_{ij}E_{ij}$ therefore gives $dF_X[Z]=\sum_{i,j}G_{ij}Z_{ij}=\langle G,Z\rangle_F$. Restriction to Stiefel has this same differential on tangent vectors. By [F1], $\Pi_X^{\rm St}G$ is tangent and $G-\Pi_X^{\rm St}G$ is normal, hence $\langle\Pi_X^{\rm St}G,Z\rangle_F=\langle G,Z\rangle_F$. The metric-dual characterization [F2] proves the Stiefel formula.

Invariance and [F3] make $f([X])=F(X)$ well-defined. The graph charts for the quotient in [F3] provide smooth local frame sections; in each chart, $f$ is the composition of $F$ with such a section and is therefore smooth. The derivative along each vertical vector $X\Omega$, $\Omega^{\mathsf T}=-\Omega$, vanishes because $F(X\exp(t\Omega))$ is constant in $t$. Thus the differential descends to horizontal representatives.

For a horizontal $Z$, the descended differential is $\langle G,Z\rangle_F$ by [F4] and [F6]. By [F1], $(I-XX^{\mathsf T})G$ is horizontal and its difference from $G$ is orthogonal to every horizontal $Z$, so it is the metric dual on the quotient. [F5] gives the asserted equivalence between a zero gradient and criticality on each manifold.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $(X+\eta)^*(X+\eta)=I+\eta^*\eta$. For every nonzero $v\in\mathbb C^r$, $v^*(I+\eta^*\eta)v=\|v\|_2^2+\|\eta v\|_2^2>0$, so the Gram matrix is Hermitian positive definite. Apply [F2] on $\mathbb C^r$: its unique nonnegative Hermitian square root has strictly positive eigenvalues and is invertible, which defines the inverse root in the formula.

Write $C=(X+\eta)^*(X+\eta)$ and $Y=(X+\eta)C^{-1/2}$. Since $C^{-1/2}$ is Hermitian and $C^{-1/2}CC^{-1/2}=I_r$, we have $Y^*Y=I_r$. Thus $Y$ is a complex orthonormal frame and its range is a point of the stated Grassmannian.

By the quotient convention [F3], frames related by a unitary matrix represent the same point. For unitary $Q$, the Gram matrix of $(XQ,\eta Q)$ is $Q^*CQ$. Uniqueness of the positive square root gives $(Q^*CQ)^{-1/2}=Q^*C^{-1/2}Q$. Hence the resulting frame is $YQ$, with the same column space as $Y$.

For $X\in\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)$ and horizontal $\eta\in T_{[X]}\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(r,n)$, so $X^*\eta=0$, define $R_X^{\rm pol}(\eta)=(X+\eta)\bigl((X+\eta)^*(X+\eta)\bigr)^{-1/2}$ and $R_{[X]}^{\rm pol}(\eta)=\operatorname{range}(R_X^{\rm pol}(\eta))$.
The inverse square root is the inverse of the unique positive-definite
Hermitian square root. The horizontal condition gives
$(X+\eta)^*(X+\eta)=I+\eta^*\eta\succ0$, so this map is defined for every
horizontal tangent vector, and its frame representative is unchanged as a
Grassmann point when $(X,\eta)$ is replaced by $(XQ,\eta Q)$ with unitary $Q$.

Let $E\to M$ be a finite-rank real vector bundle with a smooth bundle metric,
and let $T\in\Gamma(\operatorname{End}E)$ be smooth, self-adjoint, and positive
definite in every fibre. There is a unique smooth self-adjoint positive-definite
bundle endomorphism $S$ with $S^2=T$.

For $X\in\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)$, as a real manifold, $T_X\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)=\{Z:X^*Z+Z^*X=0\}$ and $\Pi_X^{\rm St}(G)=G-X\operatorname{Herm}(X^*G)$. The complex Grassmann tangent has the unique horizontal representative $X^*Z=0$, and its quotient-metric projection is $\Pi_X^{\rm Gr}(G)=(I-XX^*)G$.

Let $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let $0\leq n\leq N$.
The **Stiefel space**

$$V_n(\mathbb F^N)=\{(v_1,\ldots,v_n):\langle v_i,v_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}\}$$

has the subspace topology from $(\mathbb F^N)^n$. The group
$K_n=\operatorname O(n)$ in the real case and
$K_n=\operatorname U(n)$ in the complex case acts freely on the right by
change of orthonormal frame. The **Grassmannian**
$\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N)=V_n(\mathbb F^N)/K_n$ is the space of
$n$-planes with this quotient topology.

Graph charts about a plane identify nearby planes with linear maps to its
orthogonal complement. They locally trivialize
$V_n(\mathbb F^N)\to\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N)$ as a principal
$K_n$-bundle. Its associated standard vector bundle, in the convention of
[[def-frame-bundle-and-associated-vector-bundle]], is the **tautological
bundle**

$$\gamma_n^N=\{(W,v)\in\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N)\times\mathbb F^N:v\in W\}.$$

Equivalently, its graph-chart transition matrices glue it by
[[thm-vector-bundles-glued-from-transition-cocycles]].

The coordinate inclusions $\mathbb F^N\subseteq\mathbb F^{N+1}$ define
compatible inclusions of Stiefel spaces, Grassmannians, and tautological
bundles. Write

$$V_n(\mathbb F^\infty)=\bigcup_{N\geq n}V_n(\mathbb F^N),\qquad \operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^\infty)=\bigcup_{N\geq n}\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N),$$

with the weak direct-limit topology: a set is closed exactly when its
intersection with every finite stage is closed. The later Schubert theorem
identifies this with the weak topology in
[[def-cw-complex-with-closure-finiteness-and-weak-topology]]. For $n=0$,
the Stiefel spaces, Grassmannians, and their stable colimits are points, and
$\gamma_0$ is the zero bundle.

For $1\le r\le n$, set $\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)=\{X\in\mathbb C^{n\times r}:X^*X=I_r\}$ and $\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(r,n)=\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)/\operatorname U(r)$.
The class $[X]$ represents the complex column space of $X$; two orthonormal
frames represent the same space exactly when they differ by right multiplication
by a unitary $r\times r$ matrix. Regard each complex matrix space as a real
vector space and use the real Frobenius inner product
$$\langle U,V\rangle_{\mathbb R}:=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(U^*V).$$
Give the complex Stiefel manifold its induced metric. On the complex Grassmann
quotient, represent tangent vectors horizontally by matrices $Z$ with $X^*Z=0$
and pair these representatives by $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathbb R}$.
For $A=A_0+iA_1\in\mathbb C^{n\times r}$, write
$$\rho(A):=\begin{pmatrix}A_0&-A_1\\A_1&A_0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{2n\times2r}$$
for its realification, the real matrix acting on real/imaginary coordinates as
$A$ acts on complex coordinates. Write $\operatorname{Herm}(A)=(A+A^*)/2$.
Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $r\in\mathbb N$. If the entries of $A:U\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ are $C^r$ and $\det A$ never vanishes, then the entries of $A^{-1}$ are $C^r$.

derivations.claim: The Gram matrix $C(X,\eta)=I+\eta^*\eta$ is Hermitian positive definite by [F1]. Its realification $\rho(C)$ is real symmetric because $\rho(C)^\mathsf T=\rho(C^*)=\rho(C)$, and positive definite because, for $z=x+iy$, $(x,y)^{\mathsf T}\rho(C)(x,y)=z^*Cz>0$. The matrix $\rho(C^{1/2})$ is real symmetric by the same transpose identity, squares to $\rho(C)$ by [F5], and is positive definite by the same quadratic-form identity. Uniqueness of the positive square root and [F2] therefore make $C^{1/2}$ smooth in real coordinates. It stays invertible, so [F5] applied to its realification makes its inverse smooth for every finite $k$, and that inverse is the realification of $C^{-1/2}$. The frame formula and its range are smooth.

Fix horizontal $\eta$ and set $Y(t)=(X+t\eta)(I+t^2\eta^*\eta)^{-1/2}$. The Gram factor has value $I$ at zero and derivative zero there because its argument is $I+t^2\eta^*\eta$ and the inverse-root map is smooth by [F2] and [F5]. The product rule gives $Y(0)=X$ and $Y'(0)=\eta$. By [F3], this is precisely identity on the quotient tangent.

By [F4], the unitary-equivariant frame formula descends through the smooth Grassmann quotient. The definition's computation shows that replacing $(X,\eta)$ by $(XQ,\eta Q)$ changes $Y$ to $YQ$, leaving its range unchanged. Its identity differential from step 1.2 is therefore representative-independent.

Let $g$ be a Riemannian metric on a smooth manifold $M$ and let
$f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth.  The **Riemannian gradient** of $f$ is the
smooth vector field $\operatorname{grad}_g f$ characterized by

$$ g_x\bigl((\operatorname{grad}_g f)_x,v\bigr)=df_x(v) \quad\text{for every }x\in M\text{ and }v\in T_xM. $$

Pointwise, it is the inverse metric-dual of $df_x$.  In a local frame with
metric matrix $(g_{ij})$ and inverse $(g^{ij})$, it is

$$ \operatorname{grad}_g f=\sum_{i,j}g^{ij}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}\partial_{x^i}; $$

the displayed coefficients are smooth, so this pointwise definition is a
smooth vector field.

The frame formula of [[def-complex-grassmann-polar-retraction]] is smooth on the

derivations.claim: For unitary $Q$, $(XQ)(XQ)^*=XX^*$, so $E(XX^*)$ is independent of the representative. In the local graph charts [F4], it therefore defines a differentiable function $f$ on the quotient. Let $Y(t)=R_X^{\rm pol}(tZ)$ and $P(t)=Y(t)Y(t)^*$. By [F5], $Y(0)=X$ and $Y'(0)=Z$, so differentiating gives $P(0)=P$ and $P'(0)=ZX^*+XZ^*$. Since $E$ is defined on an open neighborhood of $P$, the chain rule gives the differential of $f$ along this Grassmann curve.

Using $K=K^*$, cyclicity of trace, and [F1], $df_{[X]}[Z]=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(K(ZX^*+XZ^*))=2\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}((KX)^*Z)=\langle 2KX,Z\rangle_{\mathbb R}$. The horizontal metric dual is the projection of $2KX$. By [F2] it equals $2(I-XX^*)KX$, which is the claimed gradient by [F3].

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $E\to M$ be a finite-rank real vector bundle with a smooth bundle metric,
and let $T\in\Gamma(\operatorname{End}E)$ be smooth, self-adjoint, and positive
definite in every fibre. There is a unique smooth self-adjoint positive-definite
bundle endomorphism $S$ with $S^2=T$.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ with $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$
and $m\ge n$.

A **full QR factorisation** of $A$ is a factorisation

$$A=QR,$$where $Q\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ is orthogonal or unitary and $R\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ is upper trapezoidal. A **reduced QR factorisation** is a factorisation$$A=\widehat Q\widehat R,$$where $\widehat Q\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ has orthonormal columns ($\widehat Q^*\widehat Q=I_n$) and $\widehat R\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ is upper triangular. A **column-pivoted QR factorisation** is a factorisation$$A\Pi=\widehat Q R,$$

where $\Pi$ is a permutation matrix acting on columns, $\widehat Q$ has
orthonormal columns, and $R$ is upper trapezoidal or upper triangular according
to whether the full or reduced form is used. Computationally, one obtains these
factorisations by successive Householder reflectors or Givens transformations
that zero entries below the diagonal, with the pivoted version choosing the next
column after a permutation.

For $X\in\operatorname{St}(n,r)$, the tangent space and its Frobenius
orthogonal projection are
$$T_X\operatorname{St}(n,r)=\{Z:X^{\mathsf T}Z+Z^{\mathsf T}X=0\},\qquad \Pi_X^{\rm St}(G)=G-X\operatorname{sym}(X^{\mathsf T}G).$$
For $[X]\in\operatorname{Gr}(r,n)$, its tangent vectors have unique horizontal
representatives $Z$ with $X^{\mathsf T}Z=0$, and the quotient-metric projection
of an ambient $G$ to this horizontal space is
$$\Pi_X^{\rm Gr}(G)=(I-XX^{\mathsf T})G.$$

routine_steps.claim: By [F5], tangency gives $X^{\mathsf T}\eta+\eta^{\mathsf T}X=0$. Therefore for $v\ne0$, $$\|(X+\eta)v\|_2^2=\|v\|_2^2+v^{\mathsf T}(X^{\mathsf T}\eta+\eta^{\mathsf T}X)v+\|\eta v\|_2^2=\|v\|_2^2+\|\eta v\|_2^2>0.$$ Thus $X+\eta$ has full column rank. More generally, the definitions apply to every full-rank $Y$; [F1] supplies the QR factor and [F2] makes $Y^{\mathsf T}Y$ positive definite with the inverse root in [F3].

For full-column-rank $Y=[y_1\ \cdots\ y_r]$, its columns are linearly independent. Apply Gram–Schmidt [F1], writing $u_j=y_j-\sum_{i<j}(q_i^{\mathsf T}y_j)q_i$ and $q_j=u_j/\|u_j\|_2$. The residuals are nonzero, so $Q=[q_1\ \cdots\ q_r]$ has orthonormal columns. Set $R=Q^{\mathsf T}Y$. For $i>j$, $q_i$ is orthogonal to $\operatorname{span}(y_1,\ldots,y_j)$, so $R_{ij}=0$; and $R_{jj}=q_j^{\mathsf T}y_j=\|u_j\|_2>0$. Since each $y_j$ lies in $\operatorname{span}(q_1,\ldots,q_j)$, $QR=Y$. This constructs a reduced QR factorization with positive diagonal. To check uniqueness, if $Y=Q_1R_1=Q_2R_2$ are two such factorizations, then $Q_2^{\mathsf T}Q_1=R_2R_1^{-1}$ is orthogonal and upper triangular with positive diagonal. Its first column has only its first entry, which must be $1$ by unit norm and positivity; orthogonality zeros the rest of its first row. Induction on the remaining block makes it $I_r$, so $Q_1=Q_2$ and $R_1=R_2$. For the polar factor $U=Y(Y^{\mathsf T}Y)^{-1/2}$, symmetry of the root and its defining square give $U^{\mathsf T}U=(Y^{\mathsf T}Y)^{-1/2}(Y^{\mathsf T}Y)(Y^{\mathsf T}Y)^{-1/2}=I_r$. Hence both outputs have orthonormal columns. If $Y$ is replaced by $YQ_0$ for $Q_0\in\operatorname O(r)$, the column space is unchanged; uniqueness of the positive root gives $(Q_0^{\mathsf T}Y^{\mathsf T}YQ_0)^{-1/2}=Q_0^{\mathsf T}(Y^{\mathsf T}Y)^{-1/2}Q_0$, so the polar output is multiplied by $Q_0$. Thus the Grassmann outputs are well-defined.

$\operatorname{qf}(Y)$ be the $Q$ factor in the unique reduced QR factorization
$Y=QR$ with $R$ upper triangular and positive diagonal. Define the **QR map**
by $R_X^{\rm QR}(\eta)=\operatorname{qf}(X+\eta)$. Define the **polar map**
by
$$R_X^{\rm pol}(\eta)=(X+\eta)\bigl((X+\eta)^{\mathsf T}(X+\eta)\bigr)^{-1/2},$$
where the exponent denotes the inverse of the unique positive-definite square
root. Both Stiefel maps induce Grassmann maps by taking the output column space.
The polar formula is right-equivariant:
$R_{XQ}^{\rm pol}(\eta Q)=R_X^{\rm pol}(\eta)Q$ for every $Q\in\operatorname O(r)$.

These are defined only where the displayed input is full rank. In fact, for a
Stiefel tangent $\eta$, $X+\eta$ always has full column rank, since
$\|(X+\eta)v\|_2^2=\|v\|_2^2+\|\eta v\|_2^2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^r$.

derivations.claim: On the full-rank set, the Gram–Schmidt recurrences divide only by positive residual norms, so [F3] expresses the QR factors by smooth additions, products, divisions by nonzero functions, and positive square roots. The polar formula is smooth there by [F4], [F5] applied to its positive-definite Gram matrix, and smooth matrix multiplication. Both maps land in Stiefel by [F1]. At $\eta=0$, the factorizations are $X=X I_r$, so each map returns $X$.

For the polar map, $Y(t)^{\mathsf T}Y(t)=I_r+t^2\eta^{\mathsf T}\eta$ by [F2]. Its inverse square root equals $I_r+O(t^2)$ by smoothness in [F4] and [F5] and its value $I_r$ at $I_r$. Consequently $R_X^{\rm pol}(t\eta)=X+t\eta+O(t^2)$, so its derivative at zero is $\eta$.

Set $Y(t)=X+t\eta$ and write its positive-diagonal QR factorization as $Y(t)=Q(t)R(t)$. By step 1.1, $Q,R$ are differentiable near zero; $Q(0)=X$, $R(0)=I_r$. Put $W=Q'(0)$ and $U=R'(0)$, so $\eta=W+XU$ and $U$ is upper triangular. Differentiating $Q(t)^{\mathsf T}Q(t)=I_r$ shows $X^{\mathsf T}W$ is skew-symmetric. By [F2], $X^{\mathsf T}\eta$ is skew-symmetric; hence $U=X^{\mathsf T}\eta-X^{\mathsf T}W$ is skew-symmetric as well. A real matrix both upper triangular and skew-symmetric is zero, so $U=0$ and $W=\eta$.

Under $(X,\eta)\mapsto(XQ_0,\eta Q_0)$, the inputs $X+\eta$ and $(X+\eta)Q_0$ have the same column space. Their QR outputs may differ as frames, but induce the same Grassmann point; the polar output transforms by $Q_0$. Differentiating the induced maps therefore gives the same horizontal class of $\eta$, which is the identity on the quotient tangent space.

For $X\in\operatorname{St}(n,r)$, the tangent space and its Frobenius
orthogonal projection are
$$T_X\operatorname{St}(n,r)=\{Z:X^{\mathsf T}Z+Z^{\mathsf T}X=0\},\qquad \Pi_X^{\rm St}(G)=G-X\operatorname{sym}(X^{\mathsf T}G).$$
For $[X]\in\operatorname{Gr}(r,n)$, its tangent vectors have unique horizontal
representatives $Z$ with $X^{\mathsf T}Z=0$, and the quotient-metric projection
of an ambient $G$ to this horizontal space is
$$\Pi_X^{\rm Gr}(G)=(I-XX^{\mathsf T})G.$$

For $X\in\operatorname{St}(n,r)$ and $\eta\in T_X\operatorname{St}(n,r)$,
put $Y=X+\eta$. On the domain where $Y$ has full column rank, let
$\operatorname{qf}(Y)$ be the $Q$ factor in the unique reduced QR factorization
$Y=QR$ with $R$ upper triangular and positive diagonal. Define the **QR map**
by $R_X^{\rm QR}(\eta)=\operatorname{qf}(X+\eta)$. Define the **polar map**
by
$$R_X^{\rm pol}(\eta)=(X+\eta)\bigl((X+\eta)^{\mathsf T}(X+\eta)\bigr)^{-1/2},$$
where the exponent denotes the inverse of the unique positive-definite square
root. Both Stiefel maps induce Grassmann maps by taking the output column space.
The polar formula is right-equivariant:
$R_{XQ}^{\rm pol}(\eta Q)=R_X^{\rm pol}(\eta)Q$ for every $Q\in\operatorname O(r)$.

These are defined only where the displayed input is full rank. In fact, for a
Stiefel tangent $\eta$, $X+\eta$ always has full column rank, since
$\|(X+\eta)v\|_2^2=\|v\|_2^2+\|\eta v\|_2^2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^r$.

On the full-column-rank domains of [[def-stiefel-qr-polar-retractions]], the
positive-diagonal QR and polar maps are smooth, take values in
$\operatorname{St}(n,r)$, fix $\eta=0$, and have differential
$D R_X(0)[\eta]=\eta$. Their induced Grassmann maps are independent of the
representative and have identity differential under the horizontal tangent
identification. Thus they are first-order retractions. This theorem makes no
second-order claim; in particular, the QR map need not be second order.

routine_steps.claim: The first displayed map is exactly the Stiefel tangent projection from [F1], and the second is exactly the horizontal Grassmann projection from [F1]. By [F2], the endpoint is a valid frame; each formula is linear in $Z$ and takes values in the stated destination tangent space.

Under a change $(X,\eta,Z)\mapsto(XQ,\eta Q,ZQ)$, [F2] gives the polar endpoint $YQ$; hence $I-(YQ)(YQ)^{\mathsf T}=I-YY^{\mathsf T}$ and the output changes to $VQ$. This is exactly the changed horizontal representative, so the Grassmann tangent vector is independent of the frame. At $\eta=0$, [F3] gives $Y=X$; a Stiefel tangent has $\operatorname{sym}(X^{\mathsf T}Z)=0$, and a Grassmann horizontal representative has $X^{\mathsf T}Z=0$, so both transports return $Z$.

On the full-column-rank domains of [[def-stiefel-qr-polar-retractions]], the
positive-diagonal QR and polar maps are smooth, take values in
$\operatorname{St}(n,r)$, fix $\eta=0$, and have differential
$D R_X(0)[\eta]=\eta$. Their induced Grassmann maps are independent of the
representative and have identity differential under the horizontal tangent
identification. Thus they are first-order retractions. This theorem makes no
second-order claim; in particular, the QR map need not be second order.

The frame formula of [[def-complex-grassmann-polar-retraction]] is smooth on the
horizontal tangent bundle, maps into $\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)$,
fixes zero, and has frame differential $D R_X^{\rm pol}(0)[\eta]=\eta$ for
horizontal $\eta$. It is right-unitary equivariant, so its range map is
representative-independent and has identity differential under the horizontal
tangent identification. Thus it is a first-order retraction on
$\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(r,n)$.

Let $1\le r\le n$. Let $M$ be a real Stiefel manifold
$\operatorname{St}(n,r)$, a real Grassmannian $\operatorname{Gr}(r,n)$, or a
complex Grassmannian $\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(r,n)$, with each tangent
space regarded as a real inner-product space under the corresponding
Frobenius metric. On a real Stiefel manifold or real Grassmannian choose the
induced map of either the real QR or real polar formula from
[[def-stiefel-qr-polar-retractions]]; on a complex Grassmannian choose the
complex polar map from [[def-complex-grassmann-polar-retraction]]. Denote the
chosen map by $R$. Let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$ and take an initial point
$x_0\in M$. For this regularity, $\operatorname{grad}f(x)$ denotes the
pointwise metric dual of $df_x$: in any orthonormal real basis $e_i$ of
$T_xM$, it is $\sum_i df_x(e_i)e_i$ (the empty sum is zero). This
convention agrees with [[def-riemannian-gradient-of-a-smooth-function]]
when $f$ is smooth; no infinitely differentiable gradient field is required.

Fix $0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$, $0<\gamma_{\rm dec}<1<\gamma_{\rm inc}$,
$0<\theta_C\le1$, a declared model-operator bound $M_B\ge0$, a maximum
radius $\Delta_{\max}>0$, an initial radius $0<\Delta_0\le\Delta_{\max}$,
target $\varepsilon\ge0$, and finite outer cap $N\in\mathbb N_0$. Each
self-adjoint real-linear model operator $B_x$ on the Stiefel tangent or
Grassmann horizontal space must satisfy $\|B_x\|_{\rm op}\le M_B$, where
$$\|B_x\|_{\rm op}:=\sup_{s\ne0}\frac{\|B_xs\|}{\|s\|},$$
with $\|B_x\|_{\rm op}=0$ when the tangent space is $\{0\}$. The subproblem
routine $S$ has a finite budget and returns a candidate tangent vector or
failure.

Starting with $x_0$ and $\Delta_0$, process $k=0,\ldots,N$ in order:

1. Set $g_k=\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)$. Return $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$ if
   $g_k=0$, $(x_k,\texttt{target-achieved})$ if $\|g_k\|\le\varepsilon$, and
   $(x_k,\texttt{outer-budget-exhausted})$ if $k=N$.
2. Form the real pullback quadratic model
   $$m_k(s)=f(x_k)+\langle g_k,s\rangle+\tfrac12\langle s,B_{x_k}s\rangle.$$
   With $c_k=\langle g_k,B_{x_k}g_k\rangle$, set
   $$\tau_k=\begin{cases}\Delta_k/\|g_k\|,&c_k\le0,\\
   \min\{\|g_k\|^2/c_k,\Delta_k/\|g_k\|\},&c_k>0,\end{cases}
   \qquad p_C=-\tau_k g_k,$$
   and set $P_C=m_k(0)-m_k(p_C)$.
3. Query $S$. If it returned a vector $q$ with $\|q\|\le\Delta_k$ and
   $m_k(0)-m_k(q)\ge\theta_C P_C$, set $p_k=q$; otherwise set $p_k=p_C$. If
   $\Delta_k\le\|g_k\|/(2M_B)$, replace the candidate by $p_k=p_C$, interpreting
   that threshold as $+\infty$ when $M_B=0$. Set
   $P_k=m_k(0)-m_k(p_k)$.
4. If $P_k\le0$, return $(x_k,\texttt{model-evaluation-failure})$. Otherwise
   evaluate $y_k=R_{x_k}(p_k)$; if the selected retraction is unavailable,
   return $(x_k,\texttt{model-evaluation-failure})$. If $f(y_k)$ cannot be
   evaluated, return the same status. Otherwise set
   $\rho_k=(f(x_k)-f(y_k))/P_k$.
5. If $\rho_k<\eta_1$, reject and set
   $(x_{k+1},\Delta_{k+1})=(x_k,\gamma_{\rm dec}\Delta_k)$. Otherwise accept
   and set $x_{k+1}=y_k$. If also $\rho_k\ge\eta_2$ and $\|p_k\|=\Delta_k$,
   set $\Delta_{k+1}=\min\{\gamma_{\rm inc}\Delta_k,\Delta_{\max}\}$; in every
   other accepted case set $\Delta_{k+1}=\Delta_k$.

Return the last accepted point with the corresponding stop status. A failed
finite subproblem call, infeasible candidate, or candidate that misses the
fraction-of-Cauchy test uses $p_C$.

Input a model of [[def-trust-region-quadratic-model-and-ratio]] with gradient
$g$, symmetric model matrix $B$, and
radius $\Delta>0$. If $g=0$, return $p_C=0$ with status `stationary`. If
$g\ne0$, set $c:=g^TBg$ and define
$$\tau:=\begin{cases}
\Delta/\|g\|_2,&c\le0,\\
\min\{\|g\|_2^2/c,\ \Delta/\|g\|_2\},&c>0.
\end{cases}$$
Return $p_C:=-\tau g$ with status `step`.

In the quadratic model of [[def-trust-region-quadratic-model-and-ratio]],
let $g\ne0$, let $B$ be symmetric, and let $\Delta>0$. Write
$M:=\|B\|_2$ for the induced Euclidean matrix norm, with the convention
$\min\{\Delta,\|g\|_2/M\}=\Delta$ when $M=0$. The Cauchy step
$p_C$ of [[alg-trust-region-cauchy-step]] minimizes the model on the
negative-gradient segment $\{-tg:0\le t\le\Delta/\|g\|_2\}$ and satisfies
$$m(0)-m(p_C)\ge\tfrac12\|g\|_2
\min\{\Delta,\|g\|_2/M\}.$$

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,
   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$
   where $I_n$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]];
   at $n=0$ the unique empty matrix $I_0\in M_0(\mathbb{R})$ has
   $\lVert I_0\rVert_p=0$, the convention of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Write $a=\|g\|>0$ and $c=\langle g,B_xg\rangle$. The operator norm bound and Cauchy–Schwarz in [F5] give $c\le |c|\le a\|B_xg\|\le M_Ba^2$. If $c\le0$, [F3] gives a boundary Cauchy step. If $c>0$, then $M_B>0$, the unconstrained segment minimizer has length $a^3/c\ge a/M_B$, and $\Delta\le a/(2M_B)$ forces the constrained minimizer to the boundary. Thus $\|p_C\|=\Delta$ in both branches, including $M_B=0$.

Choose orthonormal real coordinates on the finite-dimensional tangent or horizontal space. In these coordinates [F4] applies, and $\|B_x\|_2=\|B_x\|_{\rm op}$. Since $\|B_x\|_{\rm op}\le M_B$ and step 1.1 gives $\|p_C\|=\Delta$, the Cauchy decrease is at least $\tfrac12a\Delta$. The trial condition and [F2] therefore give $P=m_x(0)-m_x(p)\ge\tfrac12\theta_Ca\Delta>0$. This verifies that $\rho$ is defined.

Put $\phi(t)=\widehat f_x(tp)$ and $h(t)=\phi(t)-\phi(0)-t\phi'(0)$. By [F1], $\phi'(0)=\langle g,p\rangle$. Lipschitz continuity and [F5] give $|h'(t)|\le L_Rt\|p\|^2\le L_R\|p\|^2$ for $0\le t\le1$. Apply [F6] on $[0,1]$ to obtain $|h(1)|\le L_R\|p\|^2$. The quadratic model contributes at most $\tfrac12M_B\|p\|^2$ beyond the linear term, so $$|f(x)-f(R_x(p))-P|\le(L_R+M_B)\|p\|^2.$$ Since $\|p\|\le\Delta$, step 2.1 gives $$|\rho-1|\le\frac{(L_R+M_B)\Delta^2}{\theta_Ca\Delta/2} =\frac{2(L_R+M_B)\Delta}{\theta_Ca}.$$ If $L_R+M_B=0$, the numerator error is zero and $\rho=1$. Otherwise the stated radius threshold makes $|\rho-1|\le1-\eta_2$, hence $\rho\ge\eta_2$.

$$\mathcal T_Y^{\rm Gr}(Z):=(I-YY^{\mathsf T})Z.$$

By [F2], $W$ is a Stiefel tangent. The projection formulas are linear in $Z$ and smooth in $Y$; [F3] makes their composition with the retraction smooth in $\eta$.

The Grassmann output $V=(I-YY^{\mathsf T})Z$ satisfies $Y^{\mathsf T}V=0$, so it is horizontal by [F2], and it depends linearly on $Z$. citations.quote:
On the full-column-rank domains of [[def-stiefel-qr-polar-retractions]], the
positive-diagonal QR and polar maps are smooth, take values in
$\operatorname{St}(n,r)$, fix $\eta=0$, and have differential
$D R_X(0)[\eta]=\eta$. Their induced Grassmann maps are independent of the
representative and have identity differential under the horizontal tangent
identification. Thus they are first-order retractions. This theorem makes no
second-order claim; in particular, the QR map need not be second order.

Let $g$ be a Riemannian metric on a smooth manifold $M$ and let
$f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth.  The **Riemannian gradient** of $f$ is the
smooth vector field $\operatorname{grad}_g f$ characterized by

$$ g_x\bigl((\operatorname{grad}_g f)_x,v\bigr)=df_x(v) \quad\text{for every }x\in M\text{ and }v\in T_xM. $$

Pointwise, it is the inverse metric-dual of $df_x$.  In a local frame with
metric matrix $(g_{ij})$ and inverse $(g^{ij})$, it is

$$ \operatorname{grad}_g f=\sum_{i,j}g^{ij}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}\partial_{x^i}; $$

the displayed coefficients are smooth, so this pointwise definition is a
smooth vector field.

Let $M$ be $\operatorname{St}(n,r)$ or $\operatorname{Gr}(r,n)$, let $f:M\to\mathbb R$
be smooth, and choose one retraction $R$ from
[[def-stiefel-qr-polar-retractions]]. At $x\in M$, let $g=\operatorname{grad}f(x)$.
Fix $a\in(0,1)$, $\beta\in(0,1)$ and an integer budget $J\ge0$.

If $g=0$, return `(x, stationary)`. Otherwise test, in order,
$t_j=\beta^j$ for $j=0,\ldots,J$. At each trial form $y_j=R_x(-t_jg)$;
if the chosen retraction's full-rank condition fails, reject that trial without
evaluating $f(y_j)$. Otherwise accept and return $(y_j,t_j)$ at the first index
with
$$f(y_j)\le f(x)-a t_j\|g\|^2.$$
If no trial passes, return `(x, budget-exhausted)`.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: Since $g\ne0$ and $\|g\|\le G$, we have $G>0$. For $0<t\le\delta$, $\eta=-tg$ has norm $t\|g\|\le tG\le1/2$, so the entire segment $s\eta$, $0\le s\le1$, lies in the unit ball.

By [F1] and [F2], $D\widehat f_x(0)[\eta]=\langle g,\eta\rangle=-t\|g\|^2$. The fundamental theorem of calculus along $s\mapsto s\eta$ and the assumed Lipschitz bound give $$\widehat f_x(\eta)\le f(x)-t\|g\|^2+\int_0^1 L_R s\|\eta\|^2\,ds =f(x)-t\|g\|^2+\tfrac12L_Rt^2\|g\|^2.$$ The integral bound uses [F4] to estimate the inner product of the gradient difference with $\eta$. If $L_R=0$ the last error is zero; otherwise $t\le2(1-a)/L_R$ makes the right side at most $f(x)-a t\|g\|^2$. Thus every tested $t\le\delta$ satisfies the Armijo test in [F3].

Let $j$ be the first tested index with $\beta^j\le\delta$. By step 2.1 this trial passes, so the algorithm stops no later than $j$. If $j=0$, then $t=1\ge\beta\delta$ because $\delta\le1$. If $j>0$, minimality gives $\beta^{j-1}>\delta$, hence $\beta^j>\beta\delta$. Any earlier accepted grid point is larger still.

citations.quote:
Let $M=\operatorname{St}(n,r)$ or $\operatorname{Gr}(r,n)$ be compact, let
$f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth, and let $R$ be a QR or polar retraction with the
first-order property of [[thm-stiefel-retractions-are-first-order]]. Write
$\widehat f_x(\eta)=f(R_x(\eta))$. Assume a uniform bound
$\|\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|\le G$ and a constant $L_R\ge0$ such that, for
every $x$ and $\|\eta\|\le1$,
$$\|\operatorname{grad}\widehat f_x(\eta)-\operatorname{grad}\widehat f_x(0)\|\le L_R\|\eta\|.$$
For $a\in(0,1)$ and a nonstationary iterate, set
$$\delta=\min\{1,(2G)^{-1},2(1-a)/L_R\},$$
where a reciprocal of zero is interpreted as $+\infty$. If the finite
backtracking budget tests some $t_j=\beta^j\le\delta$, then it accepts a step;
the first accepted step obeys $t\ge\beta\delta$. The bound
$t\|\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|\le1/2$ keeps the pullback argument inside its
assumed unit tangent ball.

Let $M$ be $\operatorname{St}(n,r)$ or $\operatorname{Gr}(r,n)$, let $f:M\to\mathbb R$
be smooth, and choose one retraction $R$ from
[[def-stiefel-qr-polar-retractions]]. At $x\in M$, let $g=\operatorname{grad}f(x)$.
Fix $a\in(0,1)$, $\beta\in(0,1)$ and an integer budget $J\ge0$.

If $g=0$, return `(x, stationary)`. Otherwise test, in order,
$t_j=\beta^j$ for $j=0,\ldots,J$. At each trial form $y_j=R_x(-t_jg)$;
if the chosen retraction's full-rank condition fails, reject that trial without
evaluating $f(y_j)$. Otherwise accept and return $(y_j,t_j)$ at the first index
with
$$f(y_j)\le f(x)-a t_j\|g\|^2.$$
If no trial passes, return `(x, budget-exhausted)`.

derivations.claim: For every accepted update, [F1] and [F2] imply $f(x_k)-f(x_{k+1})\ge a\beta\delta\|\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\|^2$. Summing for $k=0,\ldots,N-1$ telescopes to $$a\beta\delta\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\|\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\|^2\le f(x_0)-f(x_N)\le f(x_0)-f_{\inf}.$$ At least one of the $N$ nonnegative terms is no greater than their average, giving the stated bound.

If every pre-update gradient norm were greater than $\epsilon$, the sum in step 1.1 would exceed $N\epsilon^2$. This contradicts its upper bound whenever $N>(f(x_0)-f_{\inf})/(a\beta\delta\epsilon^2)$, proving the finite accepted-update claim.

citations.quote:
Let $1\le r\le n$. Let $M$ be a real Stiefel manifold
$\operatorname{St}(n,r)$, a real Grassmannian $\operatorname{Gr}(r,n)$, or a
complex Grassmannian $\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(r,n)$, with each tangent
space regarded as a real inner-product space under the corresponding
Frobenius metric. On a real Stiefel manifold or real Grassmannian choose the
induced map of either the real QR or real polar formula from
[[def-stiefel-qr-polar-retractions]]; on a complex Grassmannian choose the
complex polar map from [[def-complex-grassmann-polar-retraction]]. Denote the
chosen map by $R$. Let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$ and take an initial point
$x_0\in M$. For this regularity, $\operatorname{grad}f(x)$ denotes the
pointwise metric dual of $df_x$: in any orthonormal real basis $e_i$ of
$T_xM$, it is $\sum_i df_x(e_i)e_i$ (the empty sum is zero). This
convention agrees with [[def-riemannian-gradient-of-a-smooth-function]]
when $f$ is smooth; no infinitely differentiable gradient field is required.

Fix $0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$, $0<\gamma_{\rm dec}<1<\gamma_{\rm inc}$,
$0<\theta_C\le1$, a declared model-operator bound $M_B\ge0$, a maximum
radius $\Delta_{\max}>0$, an initial radius $0<\Delta_0\le\Delta_{\max}$,
target $\varepsilon\ge0$, and finite outer cap $N\in\mathbb N_0$. Each
self-adjoint real-linear model operator $B_x$ on the Stiefel tangent or
Grassmann horizontal space must satisfy $\|B_x\|_{\rm op}\le M_B$, where
$$\|B_x\|_{\rm op}:=\sup_{s\ne0}\frac{\|B_xs\|}{\|s\|},$$
with $\|B_x\|_{\rm op}=0$ when the tangent space is $\{0\}$. The subproblem
routine $S$ has a finite budget and returns a candidate tangent vector or
failure.

Starting with $x_0$ and $\Delta_0$, process $k=0,\ldots,N$ in order:

1. Set $g_k=\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)$. Return $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$ if
   $g_k=0$, $(x_k,\texttt{target-achieved})$ if $\|g_k\|\le\varepsilon$, and
   $(x_k,\texttt{outer-budget-exhausted})$ if $k=N$.
2. Form the real pullback quadratic model
   $$m_k(s)=f(x_k)+\langle g_k,s\rangle+\tfrac12\langle s,B_{x_k}s\rangle.$$
   With $c_k=\langle g_k,B_{x_k}g_k\rangle$, set
   $$\tau_k=\begin{cases}\Delta_k/\|g_k\|,&c_k\le0,\\
   \min\{\|g_k\|^2/c_k,\Delta_k/\|g_k\|\},&c_k>0,\end{cases}
   \qquad p_C=-\tau_k g_k,$$
   and set $P_C=m_k(0)-m_k(p_C)$.
3. Query $S$. If it returned a vector $q$ with $\|q\|\le\Delta_k$ and
   $m_k(0)-m_k(q)\ge\theta_C P_C$, set $p_k=q$; otherwise set $p_k=p_C$. If
   $\Delta_k\le\|g_k\|/(2M_B)$, replace the candidate by $p_k=p_C$, interpreting
   that threshold as $+\infty$ when $M_B=0$. Set
   $P_k=m_k(0)-m_k(p_k)$.
4. If $P_k\le0$, return $(x_k,\texttt{model-evaluation-failure})$. Otherwise
   evaluate $y_k=R_{x_k}(p_k)$; if the selected retraction is unavailable,
   return $(x_k,\texttt{model-evaluation-failure})$. If $f(y_k)$ cannot be
   evaluated, return the same status. Otherwise set
   $\rho_k=(f(x_k)-f(y_k))/P_k$.
5. If $\rho_k<\eta_1$, reject and set
   $(x_{k+1},\Delta_{k+1})=(x_k,\gamma_{\rm dec}\Delta_k)$. Otherwise accept
   and set $x_{k+1}=y_k$. If also $\rho_k\ge\eta_2$ and $\|p_k\|=\Delta_k$,
   set $\Delta_{k+1}=\min\{\gamma_{\rm inc}\Delta_k,\Delta_{\max}\}$; in every
   other accepted case set $\Delta_{k+1}=\Delta_k$.

Return the last accepted point with the corresponding stop status. A failed
finite subproblem call, infeasible candidate, or candidate that misses the
fraction-of-Cauchy test uses $p_C$.

Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional real Stiefel or Grassmann manifold, or a
complex Grassmannian, with its real Frobenius metric. Regard every tangent
space as real, let $x\in M$, and let $g=\operatorname{grad}f(x)\ne0$.
Choose a first-order retraction $R$ and write
$\widehat f_x(s)=f(R_x(s))$ on the tangent (or horizontal) space, equipped
with its real Frobenius inner product. Suppose $\nabla\widehat f_x$ is
$L_R$-Lipschitz on the ball $\|s\|\le\Delta$, and let
$m_x(s)=f(x)+\langle g,s\rangle+\tfrac12\langle s,B_xs\rangle$ with
$B_x$ self-adjoint and real-linear. Define its induced operator norm by
$$\|B_x\|_{\rm op}:=\sup_{s\ne0}\frac{\|B_xs\|}{\|s\|},$$
and assume $\|B_x\|_{\rm op}\le M_B$. Let $p_C$ be the negative-gradient
Cauchy step, and let a feasible trial $p$ satisfy
$m_x(0)-m_x(p)\ge\theta_C[m_x(0)-m_x(p_C)]$ for $0<\theta_C\le1$.
With a zero denominator interpreted as $+\infty$, if
$\Delta\le\|g\|/(2M_B)$, then its predicted decrease $P$ is positive and
$$|\rho-1|\le\frac{2(L_R+M_B)\Delta}{\theta_C\|g\|},\qquad \rho=\frac{f(x)-f(R_x(p))}{P}.$$
Consequently, for $0<\eta_2<1$, if
$$\Delta\le \min\left\{\frac{\|g\|}{2M_B}, \frac{\theta_C(1-\eta_2)\|g\|}{2(L_R+M_B)}\right\},$$
then $\rho\ge\eta_2$. If $L_R+M_B=0$, the ratio equals $1$.

In the quadratic model of [[def-trust-region-quadratic-model-and-ratio]],
let $g\ne0$, let $B$ be symmetric, and let $\Delta>0$. Write
$M:=\|B\|_2$ for the induced Euclidean matrix norm, with the convention
$\min\{\Delta,\|g\|_2/M\}=\Delta$ when $M=0$. The Cauchy step
$p_C$ of [[alg-trust-region-cauchy-step]] minimizes the model on the
negative-gradient segment $\{-tg:0\le t\le\Delta/\|g\|_2\}$ and satisfies
$$m(0)-m(p_C)\ge\tfrac12\|g\|_2
\min\{\Delta,\|g\|_2/M\}.$$

For $1\le r\le n$, $\operatorname{St}(n,r)$ is a nonempty closed bounded
subset of $\mathbb R^{n\times r}$, and $\operatorname{Gr}(r,n)$ is compact as
its continuous quotient image. Hence both spaces are compact.

For $1\le r\le n$, $\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)$ is a nonempty closed
bounded subset of the real coordinate space $\mathbb R^{2nr}$, and
$\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(r,n)$ is its continuous quotient image. Both
spaces are compact.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For every real $x\ge1$, the natural logarithm of
[[def-natural-logarithm]] satisfies
$$0\le\log x\le x-1\le x.$$

Every complete ordered field $F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].

derivations.claim: If $M=\operatorname{St}(n,r)$, the real-coordinate Stiefel set is a nonempty compact metric space by [F4], so [F4] gives an attained minimum of $f$. If $M$ is either Grassmannian, let $q$ be its continuous surjective quotient map from the corresponding real or complex Stiefel set. Then $f\circ q$ is continuous on that nonempty compact metric frame set and attains its minimum by [F4]. Surjectivity makes this the minimum of $f$ on $M$. Thus $f_{\inf}$ is finite and attained in every case.

Fix $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and write $\bar\delta_\varepsilon=\min\{c_\delta\varepsilon,\Delta_{\max}\}$. Whenever $\|g_k\|>\varepsilon$ and $\Delta_k\le\bar\delta_\varepsilon$, the hypotheses of [F2] hold because $\Delta_k\le c_\delta\|g_k\|$. Thus $\rho_k\ge\eta_2>\eta_1$, and [F1] forbids rejection. Therefore every radius before target is at least $$r_\varepsilon=\min\{\Delta_0,\gamma_{\rm dec}\bar\delta_\varepsilon\}>0.$$ Indeed the initial radius has this bound; an accepted update does not shrink it, and a rejected update starts above $\bar\delta_\varepsilon$ and leaves a radius above $\gamma_{\rm dec}\bar\delta_\varepsilon$. Induction proves the claim.

The pointwise gradient convention requires only differentiability. In an orthonormal real tangent basis $e_i$, write $v=\sum_i v_i e_i$ and $G=\sum_i df_x(e_i)e_i$. Then $\langle G,v\rangle=\sum_i df_x(e_i)v_i=df_x(v)$ by linearity, and if $H$ has the same pairing with every $v$, taking $v=G-H$ gives $\|G-H\|^2=0$, hence $G=H$. The zero tangent space has $G=0$. Thus the gradient is well-defined for a $C^2$ objective. First-order retraction differentiation identifies it with the pullback gradient at zero, as in [F2]; all subsequent estimates require only the stated pullback Lipschitz bound and the continuity used in step 1.1.

Choose orthonormal real coordinates on each finite-dimensional tangent or horizontal space. In those coordinates [F3] applies and the matrix norm of $B_x$ is $\|B_x\|_{\rm op}$. If $\|g_k\|>\varepsilon$, then $$r_\varepsilon\ge c_R\varepsilon,\qquad \min\{\Delta_k,\|g_k\|/\|B_{x_k}\|_{\rm op}\}\ge c_P\varepsilon,$$ with the stated infinite-ratio convention when $M_B=0$. The first inequality follows from $\varepsilon\le1$ and the definitions of $r_\varepsilon,c_R$; the second follows from $\Delta_k\ge r_\varepsilon$, $\|g_k\|>\varepsilon$, and $\|B_{x_k}\|_{\rm op}\le M_B$. By [F1] and [F3], the selected step has predicted decrease at least the Cauchy fraction, hence at least $\tfrac12\theta_Cc_P\varepsilon^2$. Every accepted step has $\rho_k\ge\eta_1$, so its actual decrease is at least $c_S\varepsilon^2$. Run the update rule without applying the outer cap. If the target were never reached and only finitely many steps were accepted, the resulting infinite block of rejections would keep the point fixed and force its radius to zero by [F8], contradicting the radius floor in step 1.2. Thus the uncapped process must have infinitely many accepted steps unless it reaches the target. By [F7], choose an integer $m>(f(x_0)-f_{\inf})/(c_S\varepsilon^2)$. After $m$ accepted steps the objective would be below $f_{\inf}$, a contradiction. Thus the target is reached after finitely many accepted steps. Summing their decreases and using step 1.1 gives $$N_s\le\frac{f(x_0)-f_{\inf}}{c_S\varepsilon^2}.$$

If the initial point already meets the target, then $N_s=N_u=0$ and the bounds hold. Otherwise let $\Delta_T$ be the radius after the accepted step that first reaches the target. Each rejected trial multiplies the radius by $\gamma_{\rm dec}$, and each accepted update multiplies it by a factor $q_j\in[1,\gamma_{\rm inc}]$. Hence $$\Delta_T=\Delta_0\gamma_{\rm dec}^{N_u}\prod_{j=1}^{N_s}q_j, \qquad \Delta_T\ge r_\varepsilon$$ by step 1.2. Taking logarithms using [F5], then rearranging and using $\log q_j\le\log\gamma_{\rm inc}$, gives $$N_u|\log\gamma_{\rm dec}| =\log(\Delta_0/\Delta_T)+\sum_{j=1}^{N_s}\log q_j \le\log(\Delta_0/r_\varepsilon)+N_s\log\gamma_{\rm inc}.$$ This is the asserted rejected-trial bound.

By step 1.1, $f_{\inf}$ is finite. The definitions give $r_\varepsilon\ge c_R\varepsilon$, so [F5] gives $$\log(\Delta_0/r_\varepsilon) \le \log(\Delta_0/(c_R\varepsilon)) =\log(\Delta_0/c_R)+\log(1/\varepsilon).$$ By [F6], $\log(1/\varepsilon)\le1/\varepsilon\le1/\varepsilon^2$ for $0<\varepsilon\le1$. Thus this radius term is $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$; step 2.2 gives the same order for $N_s$, and step 2.3 gives it for $N_u$. A finite integer outer cap at least the resulting trial bound therefore suffices to return stationary or target-achieved. The algorithm tests zero gradient first, so stationary is possible; either return has gradient norm at most $\varepsilon$.

citations.quote:
Let $F$ be smooth on an open neighborhood of $\operatorname{St}(n,r)$, and
write $G=\nabla F(X)$ for its Euclidean gradient. Its restriction to Stiefel
has Riemannian gradient $G-X\operatorname{sym}(X^{\mathsf T}G)$. If
$F(XQ)=F(X)$ for every $Q\in\operatorname O(r)$, it descends to a smooth
Grassmann objective and its gradient has horizontal representative
$(I-XX^{\mathsf T})G$. In either metric, gradient zero is equivalent to a
critical point of the restricted objective.

For $X\in\operatorname{St}(n,r)$, the tangent space and its Frobenius
orthogonal projection are
$$T_X\operatorname{St}(n,r)=\{Z:X^{\mathsf T}Z+Z^{\mathsf T}X=0\},\qquad \Pi_X^{\rm St}(G)=G-X\operatorname{sym}(X^{\mathsf T}G).$$
For $[X]\in\operatorname{Gr}(r,n)$, its tangent vectors have unique horizontal
representatives $Z$ with $X^{\mathsf T}Z=0$, and the quotient-metric projection
of an ambient $G$ to this horizontal space is
$$\Pi_X^{\rm Gr}(G)=(I-XX^{\mathsf T})G.$$

derivations.claim: For $q=\pm1\in\operatorname O(1)$, $(xq)^{\mathsf T}A(xq)=x^{\mathsf T}Ax$, so the objective is well-defined on lines by [F1]. Since $A$ is positive semidefinite, $f([x])\ge0$ for every unit $x$. If $x\in\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2)$, then $Ax=0$ and $f([x])=0$, so every such line is a global minimizer.

The vectors $x=(\cos\theta)e_1+(\sin\theta)e_2$ for $0\le\theta<\pi$ are unit and give distinct lines: two such vectors span the same line only when their angles differ by a multiple of $\pi$, which cannot occur for distinct parameters in this half-open interval. Thus they parametrize continuum many distinct lines. At each such $x$, $Ax=0$, so the ambient gradient $2Ax$ and its horizontal projection vanish. The family is a continuum of Grassmann critical minimizers.

derivations.claim: The ambient gradient is $\nabla f(x)=2Ax$, so $\nabla f(e_2)=2e_2$. Its Stiefel projection is $2e_2-e_2(e_2^{\mathsf T}2e_2)=0$ by [F1]; hence $e_2$ is critical.

Both $e_1$ and $e_3$ are tangent at $e_2$ by [F2]. The curves $x_-(t)=\cos(t)e_2+\sin(t)e_1$ and $x_+(t)=\cos(t)e_2+\sin(t)e_3$ stay on the unit sphere and have initial velocities $e_1,e_3$. Their objective values are $f(x_-(t))=\cos^2t<1$ and $f(x_+(t))=\cos^2t+2\sin^2t=1+\sin^2t>1$ for all sufficiently small nonzero $t$. Thus arbitrarily nearby feasible points have smaller and larger values, proving strict saddle behavior.

citations.quote:
Let $F$ be smooth on an open neighborhood of $\operatorname{St}(n,r)$, and
write $G=\nabla F(X)$ for its Euclidean gradient. Its restriction to Stiefel
has Riemannian gradient $G-X\operatorname{sym}(X^{\mathsf T}G)$. If
$F(XQ)=F(X)$ for every $Q\in\operatorname O(r)$, it descends to a smooth
Grassmann objective and its gradient has horizontal representative
$(I-XX^{\mathsf T})G$. In either metric, gradient zero is equivalent to a
critical point of the restricted objective.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, be symmetric with ordered eigenvalues
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n$. Let $r$ be the multiplicity of $\lambda_1$.
If $r<n$, assume $\lambda_1>\lambda_{r+1}$, and let $P$ be the orthogonal
projection onto the $\lambda_1$-eigenspace. Let $b\in\mathbb R^n$ be a unit
vector and, for $m\ge1$, define

$$K_m:=\operatorname{span}\{b,Ab,\ldots,A^{m-1}b\},\qquad \theta_m:=\max_{0\ne x\in K_m}\frac{x^{\mathsf T}Ax}{x^{\mathsf T}x}.$$

Thus $\theta_m$ is the largest Rayleigh–Ritz value on $K_m$; if Lanczos runs
through step $m$ without breakdown, it is the largest Ritz value of
$Q_m^{\mathsf T}AQ_m$. If $r=n$, then $A=\lambda_1I$ and $\theta_m=\lambda_1$
for every $m\ge1$. Suppose $r<n$.

1. If $Pb=0$, then $\theta_m\le\lambda_{r+1}$ for every $m$; no convergence
   to $\lambda_1$ is asserted.

2. If $Pb\ne0$, put
   $$\tau:=\frac{\|(I-P)b\|_2}{\|Pb\|_2}.$$
   If $\lambda_{r+1}>\lambda_n$, then for every $m\ge1$,
   $$0\le\lambda_1-\theta_m\le \frac{(\lambda_1-\lambda_n)\tau^2} {T_{m-1}\!\left(1+2\frac{\lambda_1-\lambda_{r+1}} {\lambda_{r+1}-\lambda_n}\right)^2}.$$
   For a simple top eigenvalue ($r=1$), $\tau$ is the tangent of the angle
   between $b$ and a unit top eigenvector, so the starting-angle denominator
   is explicit.

3. If $\lambda_{r+1}=\lambda_n$, then
   $$\lambda_1-\theta_1=(\lambda_1-\lambda_n) \frac{\|(I-P)b\|_2^2}{\|b\|_2^2},\qquad \theta_m=\lambda_1\quad(m\ge2).$$

When $r<n$, $Pb\ne0$, and exact Lanczos breakdown occurs at dimension $d$, then
$\theta_d=\lambda_1$ and $K_m=K_d$ for all $m\ge d$. These are exact-arithmetic
claims; they give no finite-precision grade-termination guarantee.

derivations.claim: The ambient gradient of $f$ is $-2Ax$. At $x=e_2$, the Stiefel projection in [F1] is zero, so the eigendirection is stationary; at the global minimizer $e_1$, $f(e_1)=-5$. For the displayed start, $p(A)b=(1,1/4,-1/4)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt3$ is nonzero and belongs to $K_2(A,b)=\operatorname{span}\{b,Ab\}$.
The squared norm of this vector is $(1+1/16+1/16)/3=3/8$, and its $A$-quadratic form is $(5+2/16)/3=41/24$. Dividing gives Rayleigh quotient $41/9$, hence objective $-41/9$ and gap $5-41/9=4/9$.

Here $\lambda_1=5$, $\lambda_2=2$, $\lambda_3=0$, the top multiplicity is one, and $\tau=\|(I-P)b\|/\|Pb\|=\sqrt2$. Since step 1.1 places the candidate in $K_2$, its quotient shows $\theta_2\ge41/9$. For Krylov dimension $m=2$, the theorem [F2] gives $$\lambda_1-\theta_2\le\frac{(5-0)(\sqrt2)^2}{T_1(1+2(5-2)/(2-0))^2}=\frac{10}{4^2}=\frac58.$$ Since $\theta_2\ge41/9$, its Ritz gap obeys $0\le\lambda_1-\theta_2\le4/9\le5/8$, so the candidate comparison and source bound agree. Also $b$ and $Ab$ are independent because the third coordinate of $Ab$ is zero while that of $b$ is nonzero, so the two-dimensional Krylov space is attained without breakdown.

citations.quote:
Let $S=S^*\succ0$ be an $n\times n$ finite-basis overlap matrix and supply its
Cholesky factor $L$ with $S=LL^*$, $L$ invertible
([[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]],
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]).
If $h_0=h_0^*$ is the coefficient-basis one-body matrix, set
$h=L^{-1}h_0L^{-*}$, where $L^{-*}=(L^*)^{-1}$; this is the Cholesky
whitening whose generalized Ritz quotient is preserved by
[[prop-positive-definite-overlap-whitening-preserves-generalized-ritz-pencil]].
For coefficient vectors use $y=L^*c$; the interaction map and chosen
exchange-correlation functional below are supplied in these orthonormal
coordinates. Fix $1\le r<n$ and the
projector domain $\mathcal P_r$ of [[def-rank-r-orthogonal-projector-domain]].

Supply a Hermitian matrix $h$, a real-linear self-adjoint map
$G:\mathbb H_n\to\mathbb H_n$ for the Frobenius inner product, and a real-valued
$C^2$ functional $E_{xc}$ on an open neighborhood of $\mathcal P_r$. Define
$$E(P):=\operatorname{tr}(hP)+\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(P G(P))+E_{xc}(P),\qquad F(P):=h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P).$$
Here $F(P)$ is the Hermitian Frobenius-gradient formula justified by
[[prop-finite-projector-energy-reality-and-gradient]].

The finite-basis Hartree–Fock model is the special case $E_{xc}=0$ with a
supplied symmetry-compatible Coulomb/exchange tensor defining $G$. A
Kohn–Sham-like model supplies its density map and chosen differentiable
exchange-correlation functional. These are finite-dimensional mathematical
models; this definition makes no assertion that the selected functional is an
exact continuum physical energy.

For the data of [[def-finite-basis-projector-energy-model]], $E(P)$ is real
and $C^2$ on its stated neighborhood. For every Hermitian $P$ in that
neighborhood and every Hermitian direction $H$,
$$DE(P)[H]=\operatorname{tr}\big((h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P))H\big)=\langle F(P),H\rangle_F.$$
Thus $F(P)$ is the Hermitian Frobenius gradient of $E$.

For $X\in\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)$, as a real manifold, $T_X\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)=\{Z:X^*Z+Z^*X=0\}$ and $\Pi_X^{\rm St}(G)=G-X\operatorname{Herm}(X^*G)$. The complex Grassmann tangent has the unique horizontal representative $X^*Z=0$, and its quotient-metric projection is $\Pi_X^{\rm Gr}(G)=(I-XX^*)G$.

Let $1\le r\le n$, and let $E$ be real-valued and continuously differentiable on an open set of
Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices containing the rank-$r$ orthogonal projectors.
Suppose its real Frobenius gradient $K(P)=K(P)^*$ satisfies
$$DE(P)[H]=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(K(P)^*H)$$
for every Hermitian direction $H$. Then $f([X])=E(XX^*)$ is well-defined on
$\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(r,n)$ and has horizontal gradient
$$\operatorname{grad}f([X])=2(I-XX^*)K(XX^*)X.$$

For $1\le r\le n$, $\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)$ is a nonempty closed
bounded subset of the real coordinate space $\mathbb R^{2nr}$, and
$\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(r,n)$ is its continuous quotient image. Both
spaces are compact.

For $X\in\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)$ and horizontal $\eta\in T_{[X]}\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(r,n)$, so $X^*\eta=0$, define $R_X^{\rm pol}(\eta)=(X+\eta)\bigl((X+\eta)^*(X+\eta)\bigr)^{-1/2}$ and $R_{[X]}^{\rm pol}(\eta)=\operatorname{range}(R_X^{\rm pol}(\eta))$.
The inverse square root is the inverse of the unique positive-definite
Hermitian square root. The horizontal condition gives
$(X+\eta)^*(X+\eta)=I+\eta^*\eta\succ0$, so this map is defined for every
horizontal tangent vector, and its frame representative is unchanged as a
Grassmann point when $(X,\eta)$ is replaced by $(XQ,\eta Q)$ with unitary $Q$.

The frame formula of [[def-complex-grassmann-polar-retraction]] is smooth on the
horizontal tangent bundle, maps into $\operatorname{St}_{\mathbb C}(n,r)$,
fixes zero, and has frame differential $D R_X^{\rm pol}(0)[\eta]=\eta$ for
horizontal $\eta$. It is right-unitary equivariant, so its range map is
representative-independent and has identity differential under the horizontal
tangent identification. Thus it is a first-order retraction on
$\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(r,n)$.

Let $1\le r\le n$. Let $M$ be a real Stiefel manifold
$\operatorname{St}(n,r)$, a real Grassmannian $\operatorname{Gr}(r,n)$, or a
complex Grassmannian $\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(r,n)$, with each tangent
space regarded as a real inner-product space under the corresponding
Frobenius metric. On a real Stiefel manifold or real Grassmannian choose the
induced map of either the real QR or real polar formula from
[[def-stiefel-qr-polar-retractions]]; on a complex Grassmannian choose the
complex polar map from [[def-complex-grassmann-polar-retraction]]. Denote the
chosen map by $R$. Let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$ and take an initial point
$x_0\in M$. For this regularity, $\operatorname{grad}f(x)$ denotes the
pointwise metric dual of $df_x$: in any orthonormal real basis $e_i$ of
$T_xM$, it is $\sum_i df_x(e_i)e_i$ (the empty sum is zero). This
convention agrees with [[def-riemannian-gradient-of-a-smooth-function]]
when $f$ is smooth; no infinitely differentiable gradient field is required.

Fix $0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$, $0<\gamma_{\rm dec}<1<\gamma_{\rm inc}$,
$0<\theta_C\le1$, a declared model-operator bound $M_B\ge0$, a maximum
radius $\Delta_{\max}>0$, an initial radius $0<\Delta_0\le\Delta_{\max}$,
target $\varepsilon\ge0$, and finite outer cap $N\in\mathbb N_0$. Each
self-adjoint real-linear model operator $B_x$ on the Stiefel tangent or
Grassmann horizontal space must satisfy $\|B_x\|_{\rm op}\le M_B$, where
$$\|B_x\|_{\rm op}:=\sup_{s\ne0}\frac{\|B_xs\|}{\|s\|},$$
with $\|B_x\|_{\rm op}=0$ when the tangent space is $\{0\}$. The subproblem
routine $S$ has a finite budget and returns a candidate tangent vector or
failure.

Starting with $x_0$ and $\Delta_0$, process $k=0,\ldots,N$ in order:

1. Set $g_k=\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)$. Return $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$ if
   $g_k=0$, $(x_k,\texttt{target-achieved})$ if $\|g_k\|\le\varepsilon$, and
   $(x_k,\texttt{outer-budget-exhausted})$ if $k=N$.
2. Form the real pullback quadratic model
   $$m_k(s)=f(x_k)+\langle g_k,s\rangle+\tfrac12\langle s,B_{x_k}s\rangle.$$
   With $c_k=\langle g_k,B_{x_k}g_k\rangle$, set
   $$\tau_k=\begin{cases}\Delta_k/\|g_k\|,&c_k\le0,\\
   \min\{\|g_k\|^2/c_k,\Delta_k/\|g_k\|\},&c_k>0,\end{cases}
   \qquad p_C=-\tau_k g_k,$$
   and set $P_C=m_k(0)-m_k(p_C)$.
3. Query $S$. If it returned a vector $q$ with $\|q\|\le\Delta_k$ and
   $m_k(0)-m_k(q)\ge\theta_C P_C$, set $p_k=q$; otherwise set $p_k=p_C$. If
   $\Delta_k\le\|g_k\|/(2M_B)$, replace the candidate by $p_k=p_C$, interpreting
   that threshold as $+\infty$ when $M_B=0$. Set
   $P_k=m_k(0)-m_k(p_k)$.
4. If $P_k\le0$, return $(x_k,\texttt{model-evaluation-failure})$. Otherwise
   evaluate $y_k=R_{x_k}(p_k)$; if the selected retraction is unavailable,
   return $(x_k,\texttt{model-evaluation-failure})$. If $f(y_k)$ cannot be
   evaluated, return the same status. Otherwise set
   $\rho_k=(f(x_k)-f(y_k))/P_k$.
5. If $\rho_k<\eta_1$, reject and set
   $(x_{k+1},\Delta_{k+1})=(x_k,\gamma_{\rm dec}\Delta_k)$. Otherwise accept
   and set $x_{k+1}=y_k$. If also $\rho_k\ge\eta_2$ and $\|p_k\|=\Delta_k$,
   set $\Delta_{k+1}=\min\{\gamma_{\rm inc}\Delta_k,\Delta_{\max}\}$; in every
   other accepted case set $\Delta_{k+1}=\Delta_k$.

Return the last accepted point with the corresponding stop status. A failed
finite subproblem call, infeasible candidate, or candidate that misses the
fraction-of-Cauchy test uses $p_C$.

Let $1\le r\le n$, and let $M$ be a compact real Stiefel manifold
$\operatorname{St}(n,r)$, a compact real Grassmannian $\operatorname{Gr}(r,n)$,
or a compact complex Grassmannian $\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(r,n)$. Let
$f:M\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$ and take $x_0\in M$; set
$f_{\inf}=\min_M f$, whose existence is proved below. Equip each tangent or
horizontal space with its real Frobenius inner product. For each self-adjoint
real-linear model operator $B_x$, define
$$\|B_x\|_{\rm op}:=\sup_{s\ne0}\frac{\|B_xs\|}{\|s\|},$$
with value $0$ on a zero tangent space, and assume $\|B_x\|_{\rm op}\le M_B$
for some $M_B\ge0$. Assume the pullback gradients of the chosen first-order
retraction are uniformly $L_R$-Lipschitz on every trial ball of radius at most
$\Delta_{\max}$, for some $L_R\ge0$. Run
[[alg-riemannian-trust-region]] with fixed
$0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$, $0<\gamma_{\rm dec}<1<\gamma_{\rm inc}$,
$0<\theta_C\le1$, $0<\Delta_0\le\Delta_{\max}$, and target
$0<\varepsilon\le1$. Assume every model and objective evaluation on a valid
trial is available. The counts concern the uncapped trial sequence up to its
first target iterate; for the finite-cap implementation, choose an outer cap
at least the resulting total-trial bound.

Using $+\infty$ for reciprocals of zero, define
$$c_\delta=\min\left\{\frac1{2M_B}, \frac{\theta_C(1-\eta_2)}{2(L_R+M_B)}\right\},\qquad c_R=\min\{\Delta_0,\gamma_{\rm dec}\min\{c_\delta,\Delta_{\max}\}\},$$
$$c_P=\min\{c_R,1/M_B\},\qquad c_S=\tfrac12\eta_1\theta_Cc_P>0,\qquad r_\varepsilon=\min\{\Delta_0,\gamma_{\rm dec}\min\{c_\delta\varepsilon,\Delta_{\max}\}\}.$$
Then the number $N_s$ of accepted steps and $N_u$ of rejected trials before
the first iterate with $\|\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\|\le\varepsilon$ obey
$$N_s\le\frac{f(x_0)-f_{\inf}}{c_S\varepsilon^2},\qquad N_u\le \frac{\log(\Delta_0/r_\varepsilon)+N_s\log\gamma_{\rm inc}} {|\log\gamma_{\rm dec}|}.$$
Consequently accepted steps and total trials $N_s+N_u$ are
$O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, with all displayed
constants fixed. Such a finite cap suffices to return either stationary or target-achieved
status, in both cases with gradient norm at most $\varepsilon$; a smaller cap may return outer-budget-exhausted first. The constants
and proof count accepted and rejected outer trials; they do not bound inner subproblem
operations.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

derivations.claim: If $X^*X=I_r$, then $P=XX^*$ is Hermitian and $P^2=X(X^*X)X^*=P$, with range equal to the column space of $X$ and therefore rank $r$. For unitary $Q$, $(XQ)(XQ)^*=XQQ^*X^*=P$. Thus $E(XX^*)$ is unitary-invariant and descends to complex Grassmann by [F1].

For every horizontal $Z$, [F2] and [F4] yield the complex Grassmann gradient $2(I-P)F(P)X$. This formula uses the real derivative of the Hermitian-matrix energy, as required for a real-valued objective on complex coordinates.

Conversely, let $P$ be any rank-$r$ orthogonal projector. Choose an orthonormal basis of its $r$-dimensional range by [F7] and collect its vectors as the columns of $X$. Then $X^*X=I_r$ and $XX^*=P$, so the parameterization covers exactly the model's projector domain. By [F5], the polar-retracted trial remains a complex orthonormal frame, so its projector remains Hermitian, idempotent, and rank $r$; rejection leaves the old projector unchanged by [F6].

Fix any finite $\Delta_{\max}>0$. The set of pairs $(X,\eta)$ with $X^*X=I_r$, $X^*\eta=0$, and $\|\eta\|_F\le\Delta_{\max}$ is closed and bounded in a finite-dimensional real coordinate space, hence compact by [F8]. The polar retraction is smooth on it, and [F1]–[F2] make the pullback energy $C^2$ along the horizontal tangent bundle. Its fiber Hessian is continuous on this compact set, so its operator norm has a finite maximum by [F9]. Integrating this Hessian along each fiber segment gives a uniform Lipschitz bound for the pullback gradient. Choose the model operator $B_x=0$, which is self-adjoint and uniformly bounded by $M_B=0$. Hence all regularity and model hypotheses in [F6] hold, and a finite cap at least the theorem's trial bound suffices.
