Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

derivations.claim: For each parameter multi-index $\beta$, differentiate the identities $\partial_h^j f(0,\alpha)=0$ in $\alpha$ using [F2]; thus every $\partial_\alpha^\beta f$ also vanishes to order $r$ in $h$ at zero.

For each parameter multi-index $\beta$ with $|\beta|\le k$, put $k_\beta=k-|\beta|$, $N=r+k_\beta$, and $g_\beta(h)=\partial_\alpha^\beta f(h,\alpha)$. For every $s\le k_\beta$, put $m=N-s$. If $m\ge2$, apply [F1] componentwise to $g_\beta^{(s)}$ through degree $m-1$; continuity of its highest derivative lets us replace the Lagrange coefficient at $\theta h$ by its value at zero plus $o(1)$. If $m=1$, subtract the linear Taylor polynomial: the derivative of the remainder is $o(1)$ by continuity, so [F3] gives a remainder $o(|h|)$. Thus in every case $g_\beta^{(s)}(h)$ equals its Taylor polynomial through degree $m$ plus $o(|h|^m)$. By step 1.1 all coefficients of degrees below $r$ vanish. For $h\ne0$, the quotient rule expresses the $\ell$th derivative of $g_\beta/h^r$ as a finite linear combination of $h^{-r-\ell+s}g_\beta^{(s)}(h)$, $0\le s\le\ell$. Substituting the expansions shows that the remainder terms are $o(|h|^{k_\beta-\ell})$; the polynomial part has a continuous extension whose $\ell$th derivative at zero is $\ell!\partial_h^{r+\ell}\partial_\alpha^\beta f(0,\alpha)/(r+\ell)!$. Continuity of the derivatives on compact parameter neighborhoods makes these limits locally uniform in $\alpha$.

Define the value at $h=0$ by the displayed limit formula. For each $|\beta|+\ell\le k$, step 2.1 gives a locally uniform limit for the corresponding derivative as $h\to0$; at $h=0$ these formulas are differentiable in $\alpha$ because $f$ is $C^{k+r}$, and their $h$-derivatives agree with the next displayed coefficient. Induction on total derivative order therefore shows that all mixed partial derivatives through order $k$ exist and are continuous across $h=0$. The extension is $C^k$ with the asserted formula.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $c:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be smooth (that is, $C^\infty$) with $1\le m<d$, let $M$ be a constant symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix, and let $V:U\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. A **holonomic constraint** is the position condition $c(q)=0$. Write $J(q)=Dc(q)$, let $Q=\{q\in U:c(q)=0\}$, and define its regular part by $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$. For $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A(q)=J(q)M^{-1}J(q)^T$ is positive definite. On a compact regular chart $K\subset Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A^{-1}$ is uniformly bounded: $\sup_{q\in K}\|A(q)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty$.

A position-momentum pair $(q,p)$ is **consistent** when $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$. The **regular constrained phase manifold** is
$$\mathcal M=\{(q,p)\in U\times\mathbb R^d:c(q)=0,\ J(q)M^{-1}p=0,\ q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}\}.$$
The ambient canonical two-form is $\omega_0=\sum_{i=1}^d dq_i\wedge dp_i$; its restriction to $\mathcal M$ is denoted $\omega_{\mathcal M}$.

For $v=M^{-1}p$, the constrained Hamilton equations are
$$\dot q=v,\qquad \dot p=-\nabla V(q)-J(q)^T\lambda,$$
with multiplier
$$\lambda=A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr).$$
Here $D^2c(q)[v,v]\in\mathbb R^m$ has components $v^TD^2c_j(q)v$. This multiplier is the one that keeps both $c(q)=0$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$ satisfied.

Let $k,m,n\ge1$ and $p\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n+p}$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^k$. Suppose $F(a,b,\lambda_0)=0$ and $D_yF(a,b,\lambda_0)$ is invertible. Then there are neighbourhoods and a unique $C^k$ map $\varphi$ solving $F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)=0$. More precisely, on suitable open neighbourhoods $P$ of $(a,\lambda_0)$ and $Q$ of $b$,

$$F(x,y,\lambda)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x,\lambda),$$

and

$$D\varphi(x,\lambda)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)^{-1}D_{(x,\lambda)}F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda).$$

When no parameter block is present, this is the ordinary $C^k$ implicit function theorem.

A **symplectic form** on a smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth two-form $\omega$
such that

1. $d\omega=0$, and
2. $(T_pM,\omega_p)$ is a [[def-symplectic-vector-space|symplectic vector
   space]] for every $p\in M$.

The pair $(M,\omega)$ is a **symplectic manifold**. Thus both closedness and
pointwise nondegeneracy are required. A zero-dimensional manifold with its
zero two-form satisfies the definition.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: At any $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, full row rank of $J(q)$ gives a permutation of coordinates $q=(x,y)$ for which the $m\times m$ block $D_yc(q)$ is invertible. Apply [F2] to the smooth map $c$ for each finite $k\ge1$. The resulting local graphs agree with the unique $C^1$ graph on overlaps, so that graph is $C^k$ locally for every $k$ and hence smooth. Thus locally $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is $y=\psi(x)$; $\phi(x)=(x,\psi(x))$ parametrizes it, and $D\phi$ has rank $d-m$ with image $\ker J$.

Define $G(x)=D\phi(x)^TMD\phi(x)$. For every nonzero $\xi$, $D\phi\,\xi\ne0$ and $\xi^TG(x)\xi=(D\phi\,\xi)^TM(D\phi\,\xi)>0$, so $G$ is invertible. Its entries are smooth, and $G^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(G)/\det G$ is smooth because $\det G>0$. For a cotangent coordinate $\pi\in\mathbb R^{d-m}$, put $p=MD\phi\,G^{-1}\pi$. Then $JM^{-1}p=JD\phi\,G^{-1}\pi=0$ and $D\phi^Tp=G G^{-1}\pi=\pi$. Conversely, if $JM^{-1}p=0$, then $M^{-1}p=D\phi\,\xi$ for a unique $\xi$, and $D\phi^Tp=G\xi$; hence the displayed formula gives the unique ambient $p$ representing $\pi$. Both this map and its inverse $(q,p)\mapsto(x,D\phi(x)^Tp)$ are smooth, so $(x,\pi)\mapsto(\phi(x),p)$ is a local diffeomorphism from $T^*Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ onto the part of $\mathcal M$ over this chart.

Let $\theta_0=p^Tdq$ be the ambient canonical one-form. Under the chart just constructed, $dq=D\phi\,dx$ and $D\phi^Tp=\pi$, so its pullback is $\pi^Tdx$. Therefore the pullback of $\omega_0=-d\theta_0$ is $\sum_{j=1}^{d-m}dx_j\wedge d\pi_j$, which is closed and nondegenerate.
Every point of $\mathcal M$ has a chart of this form; the local calculation proves the restricted two-form is closed and nondegenerate everywhere. By [F3] it is symplectic, as claimed.

derivations.claim: At a point of the compact regular chart $K\subset Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, permute coordinates as $q=(x,y)$ so $D_yc$ is an invertible $m\times m$ block. Apply [F2] for each finite regularity order; uniqueness makes these graphs agree locally, so the graph $y=\psi(x)$ is smooth. Write $\phi(x)=(x,\psi(x))$ and $T(x)=D\phi(x)$. Since $J(\phi(x))T(x)=0$ and both kernels have dimension $d-m$, $\operatorname{im}T=\ker J$.

After shrinking to a convex coordinate neighborhood, $B(x)=D_yc(x,\psi(x))$ remains invertible and $\|B(x)^{-1}(D_yc(x,y)-B(x))\|\le\frac12$. Set $R_x(y)=c(x,y)-B(x)(y-\psi(x))$. Then $R_x(\psi(x))=0$ and the derivative of $B(x)^{-1}R_x$ has norm at most $\frac12$. The mean-value inequality [F4] gives $\|B(x)^{-1}R_x(y)\|\le\frac12\|y-\psi(x)\|$. Since $B^{-1}c=(y-\psi)+B^{-1}R_x(y)$, it follows that $\|q-\phi(x)\|=\|y-\psi(x)\|\le 2\|B(x)^{-1}\|\,\|c(q)\|$. Compactness makes the constant uniform on a finite chart cover.

For $\bar q=\phi(x)$, put $G=T^TMT$ and define $\bar p=MTG^{-1}T^Tp$. Positive definiteness of $M$ and injectivity of $T$ make $G$ invertible; its smooth entries and positive determinant give a smooth inverse by $G^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(G)/\det G$. Then $J(\bar q)M^{-1}\bar p=0$ and $T^T(p-\bar p)=0$. Since $\ker T^T$ and $\operatorname{im}J(\bar q)^T$ both have dimension $m$ and the latter is contained in the former, $p-\bar p=J(\bar q)^T\eta$ for a unique $\eta$.

The identity $J(\bar q)M^{-1}(p-\bar p)=A(\bar q)\eta$ and [F1] imply $\|p-\bar p\|\le C\|A(\bar q)^{-1}\|\bigl(\|J(q)M^{-1}p\|+\|J(\bar q)-J(q)\|\,\|M^{-1}p\|\bigr)$. The momentum set is bounded and $J$ is locally Lipschitz, so step 2.1 bounds the right side by $C(\|J(q)M^{-1}p\|+\|c(q)\|)$. Thus $\Pi(q,p)=(\bar q,\bar p)$ has the asserted distance bound and lies in $\mathcal M$. If $(q,p)\in\mathcal M$, then $\bar q=q$ and the formula for $\bar p$ returns $p$, so $\Pi$ is the identity there. By [F3] the coordinate formula is smooth, and it is the identity on the consistent phase set in this neighborhood. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $c:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be smooth (that is, $C^\infty$) with $1\le m<d$, let $M$ be a constant symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix, and let $V:U\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. A **holonomic constraint** is the position condition $c(q)=0$. Write $J(q)=Dc(q)$, let $Q=\{q\in U:c(q)=0\}$, and define its regular part by $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$. For $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A(q)=J(q)M^{-1}J(q)^T$ is positive definite. On a compact regular chart $K\subset Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A^{-1}$ is uniformly bounded: $\sup_{q\in K}\|A(q)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty$.

A position-momentum pair $(q,p)$ is **consistent** when $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$. The **regular constrained phase manifold** is
$$\mathcal M=\{(q,p)\in U\times\mathbb R^d:c(q)=0,\ J(q)M^{-1}p=0,\ q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}\}.$$
The ambient canonical two-form is $\omega_0=\sum_{i=1}^d dq_i\wedge dp_i$; its restriction to $\mathcal M$ is denoted $\omega_{\mathcal M}$.

For $v=M^{-1}p$, the constrained Hamilton equations are
$$\dot q=v,\qquad \dot p=-\nabla V(q)-J(q)^T\lambda,$$
with multiplier
$$\lambda=A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr).$$
Here $D^2c(q)[v,v]\in\mathbb R^m$ has components $v^TD^2c_j(q)v$. This multiplier is the one that keeps both $c(q)=0$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$ satisfied.

Under the hypotheses of [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]], let $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$. It is a smooth manifold of dimension $d-m$. Choose a local configuration chart $\phi:O\subseteq\mathbb R^{d-m}\to Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and write $T=D\phi$, $G=T^TMT$. The cotangent coordinates $\pi=T^Tp$ identify the part of $\mathcal M$ over this chart locally with $T^*Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$: the unique consistent ambient momentum representing $\pi$ is $p=MTG^{-1}\pi$. In these coordinates the restricted canonical one-form $p^Tdq$ is $\pi^Tdx$, so the restricted two-form is $\omega_{\mathcal M}=\sum_{j=1}^{d-m}dx_j\wedge d\pi_j$. It is closed and nondegenerate, hence is symplectic on the regular phase manifold.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

derivations.claim: Since $J(q)$ has full row rank and $M^{-1}$ is SPD, for every nonzero $\eta\in\mathbb R^m$ we have $\eta^TA(q)\eta=(J(q)^T\eta)^TM^{-1}(J(q)^T\eta)>0$. Thus $A(q)$ is invertible; its entries are smooth and $A^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(A)/\det A$, so its inverse and the displayed multiplier are smooth on a neighborhood of the chart.

Extend the formula in [F1] to an open neighborhood of $q_0$ on which $A$ remains invertible and define the ambient vector field $(q,p)\mapsto(M^{-1}p,-\nabla V(q)-J(q)^T\lambda(q,p))$. It is smooth, hence locally Lipschitz, so [F3] gives a unique local solution through $(q_0,p_0)$. Shrink its time interval so $q(t)$ stays in that neighborhood.

Along this solution, the chain rule gives $\frac d{dt}c(q)=J(q)M^{-1}p$ and $\frac d{dt}(J(q)M^{-1}p)=D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)-A(q)\lambda(q,p)=0$, where $v=M^{-1}p$. Since the second constraint starts at zero, it remains zero; the first derivative is therefore zero and $c(q)$ also remains zero. The chosen neighborhood is regular, and [F2] identifies its consistent constraint set as a smooth phase manifold, so the trajectory stays in $\mathcal M$.
The local uniqueness from [F3] applies to every solution of the same ambient extension, so in particular the constrained solution is unique.

$$\lambda_* =\mu_* =\frac12A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr).$$
For nonzero signed $h$, form the sequential scaled residual equations
$$F_q(\lambda)=h^{-2}c\!\left(q+hM^{-1}\left(p-\frac h2\nabla V(q)-hJ(q)^T\lambda\right)\right)=0,$$
$$F_p(\mu;\lambda)=h^{-1}J(q_1)M^{-1}p_1=0,$$
where $q_1,p_{1/2},p_1$ are given by the updates below. The selected multiplier pair, when it exists uniquely, is the local root branch whose limits as $h\to0$ are $\lambda_*$ and $\mu_*$. This defines a partial exact step map; no root-existence assertion is part of this definition.

For such a selected pair $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R^m$, define
$$p_{1/2}=p-\frac h2\nabla V(q)-hJ(q)^T\lambda,\qquad q_1=q+hM^{-1}p_{1/2},$$

Let $P\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $r\in\{1,2\}$ and $k\ge1$, and let $f:(-\delta,\delta)\times P\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^{k+r}$. Suppose $\partial_h^j f(0,\alpha)=0$ for every $\alpha\in P$ and $0\le j<r$. Then $f(h,\alpha)/h^r$, initially defined for $h\ne0$, has a $C^k$ extension $F$ to $(-\delta,\delta)\times P$. Its mixed derivatives at zero satisfy
$$\partial_h^\ell\partial_\alpha^\beta F(0,\alpha)=\frac{\ell!}{(r+\ell)!}\partial_h^{r+\ell}\partial_\alpha^\beta f(0,\alpha)\qquad(\ell+|\beta|\le k).$$

Let $k,m,n\ge1$ and $p\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n+p}$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^k$. Suppose $F(a,b,\lambda_0)=0$ and $D_yF(a,b,\lambda_0)$ is invertible. Then there are neighbourhoods and a unique $C^k$ map $\varphi$ solving $F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)=0$. More precisely, on suitable open neighbourhoods $P$ of $(a,\lambda_0)$ and $Q$ of $b$,

$$F(x,y,\lambda)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x,\lambda),$$

and

$$D\varphi(x,\lambda)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)^{-1}D_{(x,\lambda)}F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda).$$

When no parameter block is present, this is the ordinary $C^k$ implicit function theorem.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: Put $v=M^{-1}p$ and $w(\lambda)=-M^{-1}(\frac12\nabla V(q)+J(q)^T\lambda)$. Then $q_1=q+hv+h^2w(\lambda)$. Since $c(q)=0$ and $J(q)v=0$, [F3] extends $h^{-2}c(q_1)$ smoothly, with value $F_q(0,q,p,\lambda)=\frac12D^2c(q)[v,v]-\frac12J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)-A(q)\lambda$. Its $\lambda$ derivative is $-A(q)$, which is invertible. Since $A$ is smooth and invertible, $A^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(A)/\det A$ is smooth locally, so the center $\lambda_0$ varies smoothly with the phase input. Thus [F4] gives the unique local position multiplier branch at that center.

Let $G(h,q,p,\lambda,\mu)=J(q_1)M^{-1}p_1$. Consistency gives $G(0,q,p,\lambda,\mu)=0$, and [F3] extends $h^{-1}G$ smoothly. By [F5], its value at zero is $F_p(0,q,p,\lambda,\mu)=D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)-A(q)(\lambda+\mu)$. Its $\mu$ derivative is $-A(q)$. At $\lambda=\lambda_0$, the unique zero is $\mu=\lambda_0$, so [F4] gives a unique local momentum branch.

The branch equations are smooth in local phase coordinates, and $A^{-1}$ is uniformly bounded on the compact configuration projection of $C$. Since $J$ has full row rank on that compact projection, continuity gives an ambient neighborhood where it remains full row rank. Around each point of $C$, shrink the phase and multiplier neighborhoods so both roots remain in common IFT uniqueness neighborhoods on overlaps and exact $q_1$ remains in this regular neighborhood. These neighborhoods cover $C$; compactness gives a finite subcover and the minimum of their positive step radii is a common $h_0(C)$. The smooth branch derivatives are bounded on smaller compact neighborhoods covering $C$ for $|h|\le h_0(C)$, and continuity of the multiplier Jacobians preserves uniform invertibility after a further shrink.

derivations.claim: The exact first constraint equation gives $c(q_1)=0$, the exact final projection equation gives $J(q_1)M^{-1}p_1=0$, and [F3] keeps $q_1$ in $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$. By [F1], this is exactly $(q_1,p_1)\in\mathcal M$.

Starting from the forward equations, use the reverse step size $-h$ and choose its first multiplier to be the forward $\mu$. Its first half-momentum is then $p_1+\frac h2\nabla V(q_1)+hJ(q_1)^T\mu=p_{1/2}$, so its next position is $q_1-hM^{-1}p_{1/2}=q$.

Choose the reverse step's final multiplier to be the forward $\lambda$. Its final momentum is then $p_{1/2}+\frac h2\nabla V(q)+hJ(q)^T\lambda=p$. The reverse constraint equations hold because the endpoints are the forward consistent states. As $h\to0$, the swapped multipliers and the reverse input converge to the same regular-chart branch centers; after shrinking $h_0$, both multipliers lie in the reverse IFT neighborhoods. By uniqueness of the selected branches [F3], this reverse solve is the defined $-h$ step. Thus $\Psi_{-h}\Psi_h=\mathrm{id}$; interchanging the endpoints and the multipliers proves $\Psi_h\Psi_{-h}=\mathrm{id}$.

A **symplectic form** on a smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth two-form $\omega$
such that

1. $d\omega=0$, and
2. $(T_pM,\omega_p)$ is a [[def-symplectic-vector-space|symplectic vector
   space]] for every $p\in M$.

The pair $(M,\omega)$ is a **symplectic manifold**. Thus both closedness and
pointwise nondegeneracy are required. A zero-dimensional manifold with its
zero two-form satisfies the definition.

On the local branch of [[def-regular-classical-rattle-step-map]], an exact solve sends every consistent $(q,p)\in\mathcal M$ to a consistent $(q_1,p_1)\in\mathcal M$. The signed-step maps satisfy $\Psi_{-h}\circ\Psi_h=\mathrm{id}$ and $\Psi_h\circ\Psi_{-h}=\mathrm{id}$ whenever both branch steps remain in the regular chart.

The input state is consistent, $(q,p)\in\mathcal M$. For $h=0$, return $(q,p)$ with status `exact-identity`. For nonzero $h$, fix a compact phase subset $C\subset\mathcal M$ over a compact regular configuration chart with $(q,p)\in C$ and $0<|h|<h_0(C)$, using branch balls $U_q,U_p$ supplied by [[lem-rattle-scaled-position-and-momentum-branches]]. The admissible inputs also include initial guesses $\lambda_{\mathrm{init}}\in U_q$, $\mu_{\mathrm{init}}\in U_p$, tolerances $\varepsilon_q,\varepsilon_p\ge0$, finite correction budgets $N_q,N_p\in\mathbb N_0$, and terminating exact factorization/solve backends $\mathcal B_q,\mathcal B_p$ for the two chord calls. Each backend accepts a square $m\times m$ Jacobian, returns a singularity report exactly when it is singular, and otherwise returns a retained factor object. For every right-hand side, solving on this object terminates with the exact unique solution for that matrix; factorization and retained-factor solves are separate operations, as in [[alg-newton-chord-implicit-residual-with-factorization-reuse]]. All evaluations of $c,J,\nabla V$ and the displayed matrix operations in the updates, residual and exact residual-Jacobian evaluations, arithmetic, Euclidean norm evaluation/comparison, and domain-membership tests are returning primitives; no bound on their internal cost is specified. The multiplier domains $U_q,U_p\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ are open balls within the regular branch neighborhoods. Choose the balls so that $F_q$ is $C^1$ on $U_q$ and, for every $\lambda\in U_q$, the corresponding $F_p$ is $C^1$ on $U_p$ and all evaluations in the updates are defined and the corresponding positions remain in the ambient full-row-rank configuration region of the branch lemma. Inconsistent input, missing branch balls, or maps not defined on these domains are outside the algorithm's admissible inputs. On success the routine returns the approximate state, both multipliers, and both scaled residual norms; on failure it returns the residual solver's status, last valid multiplier iterate, and actual scaled residual norm, together with any position-stage values already computed.

1. Form
$$F_q(\lambda)=h^{-2}c\!\left(q+hM^{-1}\left(p-\frac h2\nabla V(q)-hJ(q)^T\lambda\right)\right).$$
Run [[alg-newton-chord-implicit-residual-with-factorization-reuse]] on $F_q$ in chord mode with refresh period $1$, domain $U_q$, initial value $\lambda_{\mathrm{init}}$, tolerance $\varepsilon_q$, budget $N_q$, and backend $\mathcal B_q$. If it returns anything other than `root`, return its exact status (`iteration-budget-exhausted`, `singular-jacobian`, or `invalid-trial`), last valid multiplier iterate, and actual scaled residual norm; do not continue.

2. For its returned $\widetilde\lambda$, compute $\widetilde p_{1/2}=p-\frac h2\nabla V(q)-hJ(q)^T\widetilde\lambda$ and $\widetilde q_1=q+hM^{-1}\widetilde p_{1/2}$. Form
$$F_p(\mu)=h^{-1}J(\widetilde q_1)M^{-1}\left(\widetilde p_{1/2}-\frac h2\nabla V(\widetilde q_1)-hJ(\widetilde q_1)^T\mu\right).$$
Run the same supplier procedure on $F_p$ in chord mode with refresh period $1$, domain $U_p$, initial value $\mu_{\mathrm{init}}$, tolerance $\varepsilon_p$, budget $N_p$, and backend $\mathcal B_p$. If it returns anything other than `root`, return its exact status (`iteration-budget-exhausted`, `singular-jacobian`, or `invalid-trial`), last valid multiplier iterate, actual scaled tangency residual norm, and the successful position-stage values; do not continue.

3. If both calls meet their residual tolerances, set
$$\widetilde p_1=\widetilde p_{1/2}-\frac h2\nabla V(\widetilde q_1)-hJ(\widetilde q_1)^T\widetilde\mu$$
and return $(\widetilde q_1,\widetilde p_1,\widetilde\lambda,\widetilde\mu)$, the norms $\|F_q(\widetilde\lambda)\|_2$, $\|F_p(\widetilde\mu)\|_2$, and status “residual tolerances met”.

For nonzero $h$, leaving a branch ball returns `invalid-trial`, a singular factorization returns `singular-jacobian`, and exhausting either correction budget returns `iteration-budget-exhausted`; the supplier supplies the last valid iterate and its evaluated residual norm in each case. No undefined-evaluation status is needed because the admissible domains require all evaluations to be defined. A successful output with nonzero residuals need not lie in $\mathcal M$; applying the routine again requires a consistent input, for example one restored by [[lem-regular-holonomic-phase-residuals-control-distance-to-phase-manifold]]. The supplier status `root` means only that its stated residual tolerance was met; it does not certify an exact root or a forward-error bound. No finite budget is claimed to succeed on every admissible input.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $G:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$, $z_0\in U$, residual tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$, correction budget $N\in\mathbb N_0$, and refresh period $q\in\mathbb N$, $q\ge1$. Use the coordinate Jacobian convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. Since $G$ is $C^1$, [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] identifies this Jacobian with the matrix of $DG(z)$; write it as $J(z)$. Residual and Jacobian evaluations, norm comparisons and domain tests are returning primitives; no bound on their internal cost is specified. In chord mode also supply a terminating exact linear-system backend: on each square Jacobian it reports singularity if the matrix is singular, and otherwise returns a retained factor object, and each solve on that object terminates with the exact unique solution for its right-hand side. Factorization and solve work are charged individually. The output is a last valid iterate $z\in U$, a status, and the actual residual norm $\|G(z)\|_2$.

In **updated-Newton mode**, invoke [[alg-finite-budget-newton-for-vector-residuals]] with $G,z_0,\varepsilon,N$. It recomputes the Jacobian at every correction and returns its stated residual/budget/failure status. Re-evaluate $G$ at the returned iterate to provide the output residual norm. Count each Jacobian assembly, factorization attempt, and linear solve actually performed.

In **chord mode**, for $k=0,1,\ldots,N$, first evaluate $G(z_k)$ and put $r_k=\|G(z_k)\|_2$. If $r_k\le\varepsilon$, return $(z_k,\texttt{root},r_k)$; this status means only that the residual tolerance was met. If $k=N$, return $(z_k,\texttt{iteration-budget-exhausted},r_k)$. Otherwise, at $k=0,q,2q,\ldots$, refresh by forming $J_k=DG(z_k)$, attempting to factor it, and retaining the factorization until the next scheduled refresh. The factorization backend must either report singularity or return a factor object whose solve operation gives the exact unique solution of $J_k s=-G(z_k)$. If it reports singularity, return $(z_k,\texttt{singular-jacobian},r_k)$. At each correction obtain $s_k$ by calling the solve operation on that retained factor object with right-hand side $-G(z_k)$; do not refactor or invoke a fresh matrix-only solve. The exact-solve backend contract makes this the mathematical correction in [[alg-newton-correction-for-vector-residuals]]. If the correction $s_k$ has $z_k+s_k\notin U$, return $(z_k,\texttt{invalid-trial},r_k)$; otherwise set $z_{k+1}=z_k+s_k$ and continue. A refresh period $q=1$ updates the Jacobian every correction; $q>1$ is a chord iteration.

Both modes make no claim that a finite budget reaches an exact root or that a small residual is a forward-error bound. Record the number of Jacobian assemblies, factorization attempts, and linear solves actually performed; a dense LU correction uses one forward and one backward triangular solve. Sparse cost depends on the actual stage matrix and factorization backend and is not bounded here.

derivations.claim: If $h=0$, [F1] returns `exact-identity` immediately. For nonzero $h$, consider either chord call with budget $N$ and refresh period $1$. Its initial iterate lies in its open domain. At index $k$, its residual evaluation and norm comparison terminate by the admitted primitive contract. The tolerance and budget branches return the current valid iterate and its actual residual norm. If neither branch returns, then $k<N$; one terminating Jacobian evaluation and factorization attempt either return `singular-jacobian` with this same data or supply a retained factor. Its terminating exact solve produces the correction. The returning domain test either returns `invalid-trial` with the old valid iterate and evaluated residual or admits the new iterate and increments the index. Thus induction preserves domain membership and validity of all returned residual data.

Every continuing pass strictly increments $k$, and an entered pass $k=N$ returns before a factorization or correction. Consequently there are at most $N+1$ residual checks and at most $N$ correction attempts, Jacobian assemblies, factorization attempts, and retained-factor solves. Each pass consists of finitely many returning operations by step 1.1, so the call terminates, including when $N=0$. These are counts of loop operations, not a uniform bound on the internal cost of a supplied evaluation or backend.

Apply step 2.1 first with $N=N_q$. A non-root position status is returned immediately with its last valid multiplier and actual residual, without a momentum call. On position success the finite assignments in [F1] form the momentum residual. The all-$\lambda\in U_q$ admissibility condition ensures that even this approximate returned position multiplier supplies a $C^1$ momentum residual on the whole open $U_p$ with returning evaluations. Apply step 2.1 with $N=N_p$ to the second call. Any failure returns the last valid momentum multiplier and actual tangency residual together with the successful position-stage values. If it succeeds, the remaining assignments and output norms terminate and return the prescribed state, both multipliers, residual norms, and success status. There are at most two calls, at most $N_q+N_p+2$ loop residual checks, and at most $N_q+N_p$ correction/factorization/solve attempts in total. No branch or count asserts success for every finite budget, an exact zero from a positive tolerance, or a forward-error certificate.

Assume the hypotheses of [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]] on a compact regular chart $K$. For every consistent initial pair $(q_0,p_0)\in\mathcal M$ with $q_0\in K$ there is a unique local solution of
$$\dot q=M^{-1}p,\qquad \dot p=-\nabla V(q)-J(q)^T\lambda(q,p),$$
with $\lambda$ as defined there. The solution remains in $\mathcal M$ throughout its local interval.

Let $C$ be a compact subset of the regular phase manifold whose configuration projection lies in a compact regular chart. For each $(q,p)\in C$, the two scaled RATTLE equations in [[def-regular-classical-rattle-step-map]] have unique local roots in neighborhoods of
$$\lambda_0=\mu_0=\frac12A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr),\qquad v=M^{-1}p.$$
In local phase coordinates the position root depends smoothly on $(h,q,p)$, and the momentum root depends smoothly on $(h,q,p,\lambda)$ when the position multiplier is treated as a parameter near its selected root. The local branches agree on overlaps after shrinking their neighborhoods. A finite cover of $C$ therefore gives a common $h_0(C)>0$ for $|h|<h_0(C)$; the derivatives of each fixed finite order are uniformly bounded on this cover, and the two multiplier Jacobians remain uniformly invertible there. The exact position roots can also be kept in an ambient neighborhood of the compact regular configuration projection where $J$ has full row rank, so their constrained positions remain in $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$. At $h=0$ both Jacobians equal $-A(q)$.

On the local branch of [[def-regular-classical-rattle-step-map]], an exact solve sends every consistent $(q,p)\in\mathcal M$ to a consistent $(q_1,p_1)\in\mathcal M$. The signed-step maps satisfy $\Psi_{-h}\circ\Psi_h=\mathrm{id}$ and $\Psi_h\circ\Psi_{-h}=\mathrm{id}$ whenever both branch steps remain in the regular chart.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], differentiating the RATTLE equations at $h=0$ gives $D_h\Psi_0(z)=X(z)$: the position derivative is $M^{-1}p$, and the momentum derivative is $-\nabla V-J^T(\Lambda/2+\Lambda/2)$. The selected map is $C^3$ in $(h,z)$ by [F2].

In chart coordinates choose a slightly larger compact phase neighborhood around the exact path. The revised compact-subset conclusion of [F2] gives one step range and uniform $C^3$ bounds there. Write $\Psi_h(z)=z+hX(z)+h^2a(z)+O(h^3)$ uniformly on this neighborhood. Substitution into the inverse equation gives $\Psi_h^{-1}(z)=z-hX(z)+h^2(DX(z)X(z)-a(z))+O(h^3)$. By [F3], this equals $\Psi_{-h}(z)=z-hX(z)+h^2a(z)+O(h^3)$. Comparing quadratic coefficients yields $a(z)=\frac12DX(z)X(z)$.

Since $\Psi_0$ is the identity and $\Psi_h$ is $C^3$, its state derivative is $D_z\Psi_h=I+O(h)$ uniformly on the larger compact chart. Thus $\|D_z\Psi_h\|\le1+Lh$ for some $L\ge0$ and small $h>0$. Applying [F5] in the convex chart gives $\|\Psi_h(x)-\Psi_h(y)\|\le(1+Lh)\|x-y\|$ there.

The exact flow satisfies $\dot z=X(z)$ and hence $\ddot z=DX(z)X(z)$. Its third time derivative is bounded on the compact tube. Taylor's theorem [F4] therefore gives $z(t+h)=z(t)+hX(z(t))+\frac12h^2DX(z(t))X(z(t))+O(h^3)$. Comparing with step 1.2 proves the local defect $\|\Psi_h(z(t))-z(t+h)\|\le C h^3$ uniformly in $t$.

Until a numerical state leaves the larger chart, steps 2.1 and 1.3 give $e_{n+1}\le(1+Lh)e_n+C h^3$, where $e_n=\|z_n^h-z(t_n)\|$. Induction yields $e_n\le(1+Lh)^ne_0+C h^3\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(1+Lh)^j\le e^{LT}(C_0+CT)h^2$. For sufficiently small $h$, this bound is less than the positive distance from the exact compact path to the boundary of the larger chart, so a first-exit index cannot exist. The estimate therefore holds for every $n\le N$.

Let $G:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be the residual map of an implicit equation, where $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is the admissible set for the unknown vector. An exact solution is a point $z^*\in U$ with $G(z^*)=0$.

The **update residual** at an approximate solution $\widetilde z\in U$ is the vector $G(\widetilde z)$, measured in the same units as $z$. If the original equation was divided by a positive step scale $\sigma$, then the **derivative residual** is $G(\widetilde z)/\sigma$, and the corresponding update residual is $\sigma$ times that derivative residual. A residual norm is not a forward-error bound unless a separate inverse or stability estimate converts it to $\|\widetilde z-z^*\|$.

For a first-order vector field $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ on an open time-state domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]), take a time $t$, input $y\in\mathbb R^d$, and step $h>0$ with $(t,y)\in D$. For backward Euler, an endpoint $z$ is admissible only when $(t+h,z)\in D$, and its update residual is

$$G_{\rm BE}(z)=z-y-hf(t+h,z),$$

so the derivative residual is $G_{\rm BE}(z)/h$.

For an $s$-stage implicit Runge–Kutta tableau $(A,b,c)$, a stage vector $Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_s)$ is admissible only when $(t+c_jh,Y_j)\in D$ for every $j$. On that admissible set, its stage update residual has blocks

$$G_i(Y)=Y_i-y-h\sum_{j=1}^s a_{ij}f(t+c_jh,Y_j),\qquad i=1,\ldots,s.$$

The stage derivative residual is $G(Y)/h$. These conventions distinguish an equation residual from the distance to its exact root.

with multiplier

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Let $G:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be the residual map of an implicit equation, where $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is the admissible set for the unknown vector. An exact solution is a point $z^*\in U$ with $G(z^*)=0$.

The **update residual** at an approximate solution $\widetilde z\in U$ is the vector $G(\widetilde z)$, measured in the same units as $z$. If the original equation was divided by a positive step scale $\sigma$, then the **derivative residual** is $G(\widetilde z)/\sigma$, and the corresponding update residual is $\sigma$ times that derivative residual. A residual norm is not a forward-error bound unless a separate inverse or stability estimate converts it to $\|\widetilde z-z^*\|$.

For a first-order vector field $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ on an open time-state domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]), take a time $t$, input $y\in\mathbb R^d$, and step $h>0$ with $(t,y)\in D$. $$G_{\rm BE}(z)=z-y-hf(t+h,z),$$

so the derivative residual is $G_{\rm BE}(z)/h$.

$$G_i(Y)=Y_i-y-h\sum_{j=1}^s a_{ij}f(t+c_jh,Y_j),\qquad i=1,\ldots,s.$$

The stage derivative residual is $G(Y)/h$. These conventions distinguish an equation residual from the distance to its exact root.

$$d_{BL}(\mu,\nu)=\sup_{\|\varphi\|_\infty\le1,\ \operatorname{Lip}(\varphi)\le1}\left|\int_E\varphi\,d(\mu-\nu)\right|,$$

Fix a basic mass $a>0$ and an integer $N\ge2$. Species $i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ has mass $m_i=ia$ and number concentration $n_i\ge0$. A symmetric nonnegative array $K_{ij}=K_{ji}$ specifies binary aggregation. In the ordered-pair convention, the event rate for $(i,j)$ is $K_{ij}n_in_j/2$; summing over ordered pairs counts an unequal pair twice and an equal pair once with its required factor $1/2$.

If $i+j\le N$, an aggregation event has stoichiometric increment $e_{i+j}-e_i-e_j$, where $e_i$ is the $i$th coordinate vector. If $i+j>N$, it removes the two parents from the retained bins and adds mass $m_i+m_j$ to a scalar overflow reservoir $L$; the reservoir has no return dynamics. Thus this branch is a truncation model and is not a physical state law for particles that later fragment.

For fragmentation, species $i$ has event rate $\beta_i n_i$, where $\beta_i\ge0$ and $\beta_1=0$. Its expected daughter counts are $b_i(k)\ge0$ for $1\le k<i$, with $\sum_{k<i}k b_i(k)=i$. One event has increment $-e_i+\sum_{k<i}b_i(k)e_k$. The mean equations are the finite sums of these event rates times their increments, together with the stated overflow-reservoir equation. When $b_i$ is specified as an actual random daughter law, these equations describe its expected event increment.

derivations.claim: For $i+j\le N$, summing the coordinates of $e_{i+j}-e_i-e_j$ gives $1-1-1=-1$, and pairing it with the mass vector $(m_k)$ gives $(i+j)a-ia-ja=0$.
For $i+j>N$, the two parent removals give number change $-2$ and retained-mass change $-(m_i+m_j)$; the reservoir increment is exactly $m_i+m_j$, so augmented mass change is zero.
Fragmentation changes number by $-1+\sum_{k<i}b_i(k)$. Its mass change is $-ia+\sum_{k<i}ka b_i(k)=a(-i+i)=0$ by the daughter normalization.

Let $x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_M=R$ be a finite grid of positive pivot masses with integer $M\ge1$, and let $\Delta=\max_{0\le i<M}(x_{i+1}-x_i)$. For $z\in[x_i,x_{i+1}]$, define the fixed-pivot probability measure

$$P_\Delta(z)=\frac{x_{i+1}-z}{x_{i+1}-x_i}\,\delta_{x_i}+\frac{z-x_i}{x_{i+1}-x_i}\,\delta_{x_{i+1}}.$$

At a grid node this rule returns the single Dirac mass at that node, including at both endpoints. For $z>R$, the rule returns an overflow record of mass $z$ and no last-bin particle. For $z<x_0$ it returns an invalid-grid status. The domain convention is therefore part of the method: every retained aggregation product and every daughter size must be at least $x_0$, and a product above $R$ is handled by the overflow rule.

For error analysis, the same barycentric formula is also used on a semi-infinite grid $x_0<x_1<\cdots$ with $x_i\to\infty$ and $\sup_i(x_{i+1}-x_i)\le\Delta$. On that grid it is defined for every $z\ge x_0$ and never overflows; this is an auxiliary unbounded-pivot dynamics, distinct from the finite-cutoff method above.

derivations.claim: Since $x_i\le z\le x_{i+1}$ and $x_{i+1}-x_i>0$, both fractions in [F1] are nonnegative. Their sum is $((x_{i+1}-z)+(z-x_i))/(x_{i+1}-x_i)=1$.
Their weighted mass is $\frac{(x_{i+1}-z)x_i+(z-x_i)x_{i+1}}{x_{i+1}-x_i}=z$ after expanding and cancelling terms.

Writing $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i$, the weighted second moment is $\frac{x_{i+1}-z}{h_i}x_i^2+\frac{z-x_i}{h_i}x_{i+1}^2$. Subtracting $z^2$ and factoring gives $(z-x_i)(x_{i+1}-z)$, which is nonnegative and at most $h_i^2/4\le\Delta^2/4$ because $(z-x_i)+(x_{i+1}-z)=h_i$.
At a grid endpoint the single pivot has mass $z$ and second moment $z^2$, so the excess is zero; this proves the endpoint clauses too.

In an interior cell, the expected absolute displacement is
$$\frac{x_{i+1}-z}{h_i}(z-x_i)+\frac{z-x_i}{h_i}(x_{i+1}-z)=\frac{2(z-x_i)(x_{i+1}-z)}{h_i}\le\frac{h_i}{2}\le\frac\Delta2,$$
by step 2.1. At a node the displacement is zero by [F1].

$$[x^n]H(w)=\frac1n[u^{n-1}]H'(u)\phi(u)^n.$$

In particular, for $1\le k\le n$,

$$[x^n]w^k=\frac{k}{n}[u^{n-k}]\phi(u)^n,$$

and this coefficient is $0$ when $k>n$.

For formal series over a commutative ring,

$$D(f+g)=Df+Dg,\quad D(rf)=rDf,\quad D(fg)=(Df)g+fDg,$$

and, for $m\in\mathbb N$,

$$D(f^m)=mf^{m-1}Df$$

when $m\ge1$, while $D(f^0)=D(1)=0$. If $f$ is a unit, then

$$D(f^{-1})=-f^{-2}Df.$$

Consequently, if $g$ is a unit, then

$$D(f/g)=\frac{(Df)g-fDg}{g^2}.$$

Whenever $f\circ g$ is admissible and the resulting termwise differentiated family is summable,

$$D(f\circ g)=(Df\circ g)Dg.$$

If $R$ is a commutative $\mathbb Q$-algebra, then $[x^n]f=(D^nf)(0)/n!$. Over any commutative ring the Hasse derivative

$$D^{[n]}f:=\sum_{m\ge n}\binom mn[x^m]f\,x^{m-n}$$

satisfies $(D^{[n]}f)(0)=[x^n]f$. Finally, if $f(0)=g(0)=0$ and $g'(0)$ is a unit, then $f/g$ is a well-defined formal series and

$$[x^0](f/g)=f'(0)g'(0)^{-1}.$$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $f=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n\in R\llbracket x\rrbracket$. Then $f$ is a unit in $R\llbracket x\rrbracket$ if and only if $a_0$ is a unit in $R$.

$$b_0=a_0^{-1},\qquad b_n=-a_0^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_{n-i}\quad(n\ge1).$$

The criterion also holds in the zero ring.

For every real $x$,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{x}{\iota(n)}\right)^n=\exp(x),$$
with the sequence started after $n>|x|$, so the base is positive.

$$F'(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}na_nx^{n-1}.$$

For each Borel set $A$, the series $\eta_{n_1}(A)+\sum_{j\ge1}(\eta_{n_{j+1}}-\eta_{n_j})(A)$ converges absolutely, uniformly in $A$, because each summand is bounded by its total-variation norm. Define $\eta(A)$ by that sum. When $b_i$ is specified as an actual random daughter law, these equations describe its expected event increment.

An overflow event changes retained number by $-2$, retained mass by $-(m_i+m_j)$, and reservoir mass by $m_i+m_j$. A fragmentation event of species $i$ changes number by $\sum_{k<i}b_i(k)-1$ and mass by $0$.

Let $x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_M=R$ be a finite grid of positive pivot masses with integer $M\ge1$, and let $\Delta=\max_{0\le i<M}(x_{i+1}-x_i)$. For $z\in[x_i,x_{i+1}]$, define the fixed-pivot probability measure

$$P_\Delta(z)=\frac{x_{i+1}-z}{x_{i+1}-x_i}\,\delta_{x_i}+\frac{z-x_i}{x_{i+1}-x_i}\,\delta_{x_{i+1}}.$$

At a grid node this rule returns the single Dirac mass at that node, including at both endpoints. For $z>R$, the rule returns an overflow record of mass $z$ and no last-bin particle. For $z<x_0$ it returns an invalid-grid status. The domain convention is therefore part of the method: every retained aggregation product and every daughter size must be at least $x_0$, and a product above $R$ is handled by the overflow rule.

For error analysis, the same barycentric formula is also used on a semi-infinite grid $x_0<x_1<\cdots$ with $x_i\to\infty$ and $\sup_i(x_{i+1}-x_i)\le\Delta$. On that grid it is defined for every $z\ge x_0$ and never overflows; this is an auxiliary unbounded-pivot dynamics, distinct from the finite-cutoff method above.

For every $z\in[x_i,x_{i+1}]$, the two weights in [[def-conservative-fixed-pivot-redistribution]] are nonnegative, sum to $1$, and have weighted pivot mass $z$. Their expected absolute displacement is at most $\Delta/2$, and their weighted second moment satisfies

$$\int u^2\,P_\Delta(z)(du)-z^2=(z-x_i)(x_{i+1}-z)\le\frac{\Delta^2}{4}.$$

At a grid endpoint the same conclusions hold for the single-pivot endpoint rule, with zero second-moment excess.

derivations.claim: Substituting $x_i=2$, $x_{i+1}=4$, and $z=3$ in [F1] gives both weights equal to $(4-3)/(4-2)=1/2$. Thus the replacement is exactly $\tfrac12\delta_2+\tfrac12\delta_4$.

The weights sum to $1$, their weighted mass is $(2+4)/2=3$, and their weighted second moment is $(2^2+4^2)/2=10$. Hence the number and mass statements agree with [F2], and the second-moment excess is $10-3^2=1$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the cited integral and semigroup suppliers.

Let $Y$ be a Banach space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval, let $n\ge0$ be an integer, and let
$u:I\to Y$. For a nondegenerate interval, $u\in C^{n+1}(I;Y)$ means that
$u$ is continuous on $I$, its restriction to $\operatorname{int}I$ has
norm-continuous derivatives through order $n+1$, and each derivative extends
continuously to $I$. Derivatives on the interior are taken with respect to
the real parameter, using the underlying real Banach space when $Y$ is complex
([[def-frechet-derivative-between-banach-spaces]]), and $u^{(k)}$ denotes the
continuous extension at any included endpoint; set $u^{(0)}=u$.
Assume this regularity. Then for all $t\in I$ and $h\in\mathbb R$ with
$[\min\{t,t+h\},\max\{t,t+h\}]\subseteq I$,
$$u(t+h)=\sum_{k=0}^nu^{(k)}(t)\frac{h^k}{k!}+\frac{1}{n!}\int_t^{t+h}(t+h-s)^n\,u^{(n+1)}(s)\,ds,$$
the integral being a Bochner integral
([[def-bochner-integrable-function]]); for $h<0$ the symbol
$\int_t^{t+h}$ denotes the oriented Bochner interval integral
$-\int_{t+h}^{t}$. For $n=0$ the formula is the fundamental theorem of
calculus. For $h=0$ the formula is understood as $u(t)=u(t)$; this also
covers singleton intervals without assigning higher derivatives there.
No choice principle beyond Countable Choice is used.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, and let $f,g:\Omega\to X$ be Bochner integrable ([[def-bochner-integrable-function]]) with $\alpha,\beta$ scalars. Then $\alpha f+\beta g$ is Bochner integrable and $\int_\Omega(\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int_\Omega f\,d\mu+\beta\int_\Omega g\,d\mu$; for a measurable set $E$ the same identity holds with $f,g$ replaced by $f\mathbf 1_E,g\mathbf 1_E$. The integral is therefore additive and homogeneous, and in particular well defined on differences.

If $f:\Omega\to X$ is Bochner integrable, then for every measurable $E$,

$$\left\|\int_E f\,d\mu\right\|\leq\int_E\|f\|\,d\mu.$$

On this page the scalar field is the field $\mathbb R$ of real numbers: $X$, $Y$
and $Z$ always denote real Banach spaces ([[def-banach-space]]) and $U
\subseteq X$ always denotes an open subset of $X$, in the metric topology of the
norm ([[def-metric-topology]]).

Let $f : U \to Y$ be a map and let $x \in U$. For a bounded linear operator
$T \in \mathcal B(X,Y)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
[[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]) write

$$r(h) := f(x+h) - f(x) - Th \qquad (h \in X,\ x+h \in U).$$

Then $f$ is **Fréchet differentiable at $x$** when there is
$T \in \mathcal B(X,Y)$ with

$$\lim_{\substack{h \to 0 \\ h \ne 0}} \frac{\|f(x+h)-f(x)-Th\|}{\|h\|} = 0 ,$$

the limit being taken over those $h$ with $x + h \in U$. Such an operator $T$ is
a **Fréchet derivative of $f$ at $x$**, written $T = Df(x)$, and $\|T\|$ is its
operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). When $f$ is Fréchet differentiable at
every point of $U$, $f$ is **differentiable on $U$** and the **derivative** is
the map $Df : U \to \mathcal B(X,Y)$, $x \mapsto Df(x)$.

Convexity gives $z+th\in K\subseteq U$ for $0\le t\le1$. If $h\ne0$ and $0<t<1$, put $u=z+th$. For real $s\to0$ with $t+s\in[0,1]$, Fréchet differentiability at $u$ gives
$$\left\|\frac{F(u+sh)-F(u)}s-F'(u)h\right\|
=\frac{\|F(u+sh)-F(u)-F'(u)(sh)\|}{|s|}\longrightarrow0,$$
because $F'(u)$ is linear over the common field and hence over real scalars.
Thus $\gamma'(t)=F'(z+th)h$. If $h=0$, $\gamma$ is constant and the same
formula holds. Differentiability at every point of $U$ also makes $F$ and hence
$\gamma$ continuous on the segment, directly from the Fréchet remainder
definition. In either case this derivative is continuous in $t$ and extends
to the endpoints, since $F'$ is Lipschitz on $K$. The Banach-valued fundamental
theorem [F1] therefore gives
$F(x)-F(z)=\int_0^1F'(z+th)h\,dt$. The constant vector function
$t\mapsto F'(z)h$ has integral $F'(z)h$ by [F2]. Subtracting that integral and
using linearity gives
$F(x)-F(z)-F'(z)h=\int_0^1(F'(z+th)-F'(z))h\,dt$.

For each $t\in[0,1]$, the Lipschitz hypothesis and bounded linearity give $\|(F'(z+th)-F'(z))h\|\le Lt\|h\|^2$. Therefore [F3] and scalar integration give $\|F(x)-F(z)-F'(z)h\|\le\int_0^1Lt\|h\|^2\,dt=(L/2)\|h\|^2$.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $b\in\mathbb R^m$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$,
$\delta\ge0$, $\tau>1$, and a budget $N\in\mathbb N$ be given. All
operations are exact. Put $r_0=b-Ax_0$. If $\|r_0\|_2=0$, return
$(x_0,0,\text{zero-residual})$. If $\|r_0\|_2\le\tau\delta$, return
$(x_0,0,\text{discrepancy})$. If $N=0$, return
$(x_0,0,\text{budget-exhausted})$. Otherwise initialize
$\beta_1=\|r_0\|_2$, $u_1=r_0/\beta_1$, and
$\alpha_1=\|A^Tu_1\|_2$. If $\alpha_1=0$, return
$(x_0,0,\text{stationary-nonzero-residual})$. Otherwise set
$v_1=A^Tu_1/\alpha_1$.

Initialize the current best iterate and index to $(x_{\rm best},j_{\rm best})
=(x_0,0)$. If a Givens rotation is undefined, return
$(x_{\rm best},j_{\rm best},\text{small-QR-breakdown})$.

For $j=1,\ldots,N$, perform these steps.

1. Compute $p_j=Av_j-\alpha_j u_j$ and $\beta_{j+1}=\|p_j\|_2$. If
   $\beta_{j+1}>0$, set $u_{j+1}=p_j/\beta_{j+1}$.
2. If $\beta_{j+1}>0$, compute
   $q_j=A^Tu_{j+1}-\beta_{j+1}v_j$ and $\alpha_{j+1}=\|q_j\|_2$. If
   $\alpha_{j+1}>0$, set $v_{j+1}=q_j/\alpha_{j+1}$. A zero
   $\beta_{j+1}$ or $\alpha_{j+1}$ marks bidiagonalization breakdown.
3. Form the $(j+1)\times j$ lower-bidiagonal matrix $B_j$ with diagonal
   $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_j$ and subdiagonal
   $\beta_2,\ldots,\beta_{j+1}$, using $\beta_{j+1}=0$ if step 1 broke down.
   Let $e_1=(1,0,\ldots,0)^T\in\mathbb R^{j+1}$ and $c=\beta_1e_1$.
   For $i=1,\ldots,j$, let $a,b$ be the current entries at positions
   $(i,i),(i+1,i)$ of the rotated matrix and put $\rho=(a^2+b^2)^{1/2}$.
   If $\rho=0$, return the current best output with status
   `small-QR-breakdown`. Otherwise put $c_i=a/\rho$, $s_i=b/\rho$ and
   apply $\begin{pmatrix}c_i&s_i\\-s_i&c_i\end{pmatrix}$ to rows
   $i,i+1$ of the full matrix and right-hand side. After these $j$ rotations,
   let $R_j$ be the first $j$ rows of the rotated matrix and $d_j$ the first
   $j$ entries of the rotated right-hand side. Solve $R_jz_j=d_j$ by back
   substitution. Update $(x_{\rm best},j_{\rm best})=(x_0+V_jz_j,j)$.
4. Put $V_j=[v_1,\ldots,v_j]$ and $x_j=x_0+V_jz_j$. Compute the physical
   residual $\|Ax_j-b\|_2$. If it is at most $\tau\delta$, return
   $(x_j,j,\text{discrepancy})$. If bidiagonalization broke down, return
   $(x_j,j,\text{bidiagonalization-breakdown})$. If $j=N$, return
   $(x_j,j,\text{budget-exhausted})$; otherwise continue.

The procedure makes no claim that a finite-budget status is a successful
regularized approximation. Its exact-arithmetic residual-minimization property
is a separate theorem.

Let $A$ be a square matrix over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and let $b$ be a
vector of matching size. Define

$$K_0(A,b):=\{0\},$$

and for $m\ge 1$ define the $m$th **Krylov subspace**

$$K_m(A,b):=\operatorname{span}\{b,Ab,\dots,A^{m-1}b\}.$$

Thus $K_m(A,b)\subseteq K_{m+1}(A,b)$ for every $m\ge 0$.

Let $A$ be a square matrix over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $b$ be a vector
of matching size, and let $m\ge 1$. Then

$$K_m(A,b)=\{p(A)b:p=0\text{ or }\deg p<m\}.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces and let $b\in W$. A vector $x\in V$ minimises $\lVert Tx-b\rVert$ if and only if

$$T^*(Tx-b)=0,$$

equivalently $T^*Tx=T^*b$. Minimisers exist, and if $x_0$ is one minimiser, then the full set of minimisers is $x_0+\ker T$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

For $A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, the **transpose** of $A$ is the matrix
$A^{\mathsf T}\in M_{n\times m}(F)$ defined by

$$(A^{\mathsf T})_{ji}:=a_{ij}.$$

Thus transposition interchanges rows and columns. The transpose of a zero-sized
matrix is the unique matrix of the transposed zero-sized shape.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice, as required for the Hilbert-space adjoint in the
iteration.

Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces, let $A:X\to Y$ be a nonzero
compact linear operator, and let $\omega$ satisfy
$0<\omega<2/\|A\|^2$. The input consists of data $y_\delta\in Y$, a noise
bound $\delta\ge0$, a discrepancy factor $\tau>1$, and a finite iteration
budget $N\in\mathbb N$. Define the associated infinite mathematical path by
$x_0=0$ and
$$x_{k+1}=x_k+\omega A^*(y_\delta-Ax_k),\qquad k\ge0.$$
For the finite procedure, evaluate only the prefix through index $N$, in
increasing order, and return at its first stopping condition. Values of the
mathematical path after an earlier return remain defined by the recurrence but
need not be computed by an implementation.

For $k=0,\ldots,N$ in increasing order, compute
$r_k=y_\delta-Ax_k$. If $\|r_k\|\le\tau\delta$, return
$(x_k,k,\texttt{discrepancy})$. If $k=N$, return
$(x_k,k,\texttt{budget-exhausted})$. Otherwise set
$$x_{k+1}=x_k+\omega A^*(y_\delta-Ax_k).$$

The procedure uses exact Hilbert-space operations. It reports a finite-budget
failure to cross as inconclusive; that status is not a convergence conclusion.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:X\to Y$ be compact and bounded, with adjoint $A^*:Y\to X$. Then both
$A^*A:X\to X$ and $AA^*:Y\to Y$ are compact, self-adjoint and positive, and
$$\ker(A^*A)=\ker A,\qquad \ker(AA^*)=\ker A^*.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
$H$ be an $\mathbb F$-Hilbert space, and let $S:H\to H$ be compact and
self-adjoint. Let $\Sigma$ be its set of nonzero
eigenvalues, $E_t=\ker(S-tI)$, $P_t$ the orthogonal projection onto $E_t$,
and $P_0$ the orthogonal projection onto $\ker S$. If
$q:\{0\}\cup\Sigma\to\mathbb F$ is bounded, then for every $x\in H$ the
finite-subset net
$$q(0)P_0x+\sum_{t\in F}q(t)P_tx,\qquad F\subseteq\Sigma\text{ finite},$$
converges in norm to a vector $Q_qx$. The map $Q_q:H\to H$ is bounded and
linear, with $\|Q_q\|\le\sup_{t\in\{0\}\cup\Sigma}|q(t)|$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:X\to Y$ be compact and bounded. Put $S=A^*A$. By
[[lem-compact-gram-operator-is-positive-and-has-kernel]], $S$ is compact,
positive, and self-adjoint, with $\ker S=\ker A$. Let $\Sigma$ be the set of
nonzero eigenvalues of $S$ and $P_t$ the orthogonal projection onto the
eigenspace of $t\in\Sigma$; let $P_0$ be the orthogonal projection onto
$\ker S$. The compact spectral multiplier of a bounded scalar function
$q:\{0\}\cup\Sigma\to\mathbb F$ is
$$q(S)x:=q(0)P_0x+\sum_{t\in\Sigma}q(t)P_tx,$$
where the finite-subset net converges in norm by
[[lem-compact-spectral-multiplier-is-well-defined]]. For $\nu>0$, define
$S^\nu$ by the multiplier $q_\nu(0)=0$ and $q_\nu(t)=t^\nu$ for $t>0$.

For $\lambda>0$, the Tikhonov filter and residual filter are
$$g_\lambda(t)=\frac1{t+\lambda},\qquad r_\lambda(t)=1-tg_\lambda(t)=\frac{\lambda}{t+\lambda}.$$
The Tikhonov solution for data $y_\delta\in Y$ is
$$x_\lambda^\delta=g_\lambda(S)A^*y_\delta =(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*y_\delta.$$
The source condition of order $\nu>0$ and radius $R\ge0$ means that
$x^\dagger=S^\nu w$ for some $w\in X$ with $\|w\|\le R$. A family of
filters $g_\alpha$ with residual filters $r_\alpha(t)=1-tg_\alpha(t)$ has
qualification at least $p>0$ when, for each $0<\nu\le p$, some finite
constant $C_\nu$ satisfies
$$\sup_{t\in\Sigma}t^\nu|r_\alpha(t)|\le C_\nu\alpha^\nu \quad\text{for every }\alpha>0.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

derivations.claim: The adjoint identity [F5] gives $A^*A=T$. Thus [F1] rewrites each update before stopping as $x_{j+1}=(I-\omega T)x_j+\omega A^*y_\delta$. The scalar geometric identity $1-(1-\omega t)^k=\omega t\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(1-\omega t)^j$ also identifies the vector expression from step 1.1 with $g_k(T)A^*y_\delta$.

If $y_\delta=Ax^\dagger$, then [step 1.1] and $A^*y_\delta=Tx^\dagger$ give $x_k=\omega\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(I-\omega T)^jTx^\dagger=[I-(I-\omega T)^k]x^\dagger$ by the same polynomial identity. > For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Assume Countable Choice, as required for the Hilbert-space adjoints in the
normal equation.

Let $X,Y$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
let $U\subseteq X$ be open, and let $F:U\to Y$ be continuously Fréchet
differentiable over $\mathbb F$. In the complex case, each $F'(x)$ is a bounded
complex-linear operator and the Fréchet remainder is measured over complex
increments, so
$$\lim_{\substack{h\to0,\ h\ne0\\x+h\in U}}
\frac{\|F(x+h)-F(x)-F'(x)h\|}{\|h\|}=0.$$
Inputs are
$x_0\in U$, noisy data $y_\delta\in Y$, a bound $\delta\ge0$, a discrepancy
factor $\tau>1$, a finite budget $N\in\mathbb N$, and parameters
$\alpha_0>0$ and $q\in(0,1)$. At iteration $k$, if $x_k\notin U$ return
$(x_k,k,\text{domain-failure})$. Otherwise put $A_k=F'(x_k)$ and
$\alpha_k=\alpha_0q^k$. Before computing an update, if
$\|F(x_k)-y_\delta\|\le\tau\delta$, return
$(x_k,k,\text{discrepancy})$. If $k=N$, return
$(x_k,k,\text{budget-exhausted})$.

For $k<N$, solve the unique Hilbert-space Tikhonov normal equation
$$\bigl(A_k^*A_k+\alpha_k I_X\bigr)s_k=A_k^*(y_\delta-F(x_k))$$
and set $x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k$. The shifted normal operator is invertible by
[[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]]. If the returned iterate
leaves $U$, the next call returns domain-failure. The procedure asserts no
convergence theorem; its prescribed step is the unanchored Levenberg–Marquardt
form used in the assigned contract.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real or complex
Hilbert spaces and let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded, with Hilbert adjoint $A^*$. For
$\lambda>0$, define

$$B_\lambda:=A^*A+\lambda I_X.$$

Then $B_\lambda:X\to X$ is bijective and

$$\|B_\lambda^{-1}\|\le\frac1\lambda.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:X\to Y$ be bounded, with Hilbert adjoint $A^*$. For $\lambda>0$, put
$R_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*$, which is well-defined by
[[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]]. Then for every $g\in Y$,

$$\|R_\lambda g\|\le\frac{\|g\|}{2\sqrt\lambda},\qquad \|R_\lambda\|\le\frac1{2\sqrt\lambda}.$$

The proof uses the normal equation and the Hilbert-space inner product; it
does not use a compact-operator convergence rate or a source condition.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let
$X,Y$ be Banach spaces over the same field $\mathbb F$. Let $U\subseteq X$ be
open and let $F:U\to Y$ be continuously Fréchet differentiable over
$\mathbb F$. Thus $F'(u)$ is bounded $\mathbb F$-linear for each $u\in U$ and
$$\lim_{\substack{h\to0,\ h\ne0\\u+h\in U}}
\frac{\|F(u+h)-F(u)-F'(u)h\|}{\|h\|}=0.$$

ranges over complex increments. Let $K\subseteq U$ be convex and let
$x,z\in K$. If
$\|F'(u)-F'(v)\|\le L\|u-v\|$ for all $u,v\in K$, where $L\ge0$, then
$$\|F(x)-F(z)-F'(z)(x-z)\|\le\frac L2\|x-z\|^2.$$

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space. Vectors $x,y\in V$ are
**orthogonal**, written $x\perp y$, when

$$\langle x,y\rangle=0 .$$

For a subset $S\subseteq V$ the **orthogonal complement** of $S$ is

$$S^\perp:=\{\,v\in V : \langle v,s\rangle=0 \text{ for every } s\in S\,\}.$$

**Orthogonality is symmetric.** If $\langle x,y\rangle=0$, then
$\langle y,x\rangle=\overline{\langle x,y\rangle}=0$, so $x\perp y$ exactly
when $y\perp x$; in particular the condition defining $S^\perp$ is symmetric in

$\langle 0,s\rangle=0$, and if $u,v\in S^\perp$ then
$\langle au+bv,s\rangle=a\langle u,s\rangle+b\langle v,s\rangle=0$ by linearity
in the first argument, so $au+bv\in S^\perp$. Thus $S^\perp$ is a linear
subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]) for every subset $S$, whether or not
$S$ is a subspace. Moreover $0\in S^\perp$ always, and $v\in V$ lies in
$\{0\}^\perp$ for every $v$, so $\{0\}^\perp=V$.

**Monotonicity.** If $S\subseteq T\subseteq V$, then every vector orthogonal to
all of $T$ is orthogonal to all of $S$, so $T^\perp\subseteq S^\perp$.

**Nontriviality of orthogonality.** By positive definiteness
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2=0$ exactly for $v=0$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]),
so a vector orthogonal to itself is zero, and $\{0\}^\perp=V$, $V^\perp=\{0\}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
$H$ be an $\mathbb F$-Hilbert space, and let $S:H\to H$ be compact and
self-adjoint. Let $\Sigma$ be its set of nonzero
eigenvalues, $E_t=\ker(S-tI)$, $P_t$ the orthogonal projection onto $E_t$,
and $P_0$ the orthogonal projection onto $\ker S$. If
$q:\{0\}\cup\Sigma\to\mathbb F$ is bounded, then for every $x\in H$ the
finite-subset net
$$q(0)P_0x+\sum_{t\in F}q(t)P_tx,\qquad F\subseteq\Sigma\text{ finite},$$
converges in norm to a vector $Q_qx$. The map $Q_q:H\to H$ is bounded and
linear, with $\|Q_q\|\le\sup_{t\in\{0\}\cup\Sigma}|q(t)|$.

derivations.claim: For every nonzero eigenvalue $t$ of $T$, [F3]–[F4] give $0<t\le M$, so $0<\omega t<2$ and $|1-\omega t|<1$. Therefore $|r_k(t)|$ decreases with $k$ and tends to $0$. Since $x^\dagger\perp\ker T$ by [F3] and [F5], [F6] expands it using only positive-eigenvalue components. By [F1], each component of $x_k-x^\dagger$ is multiplied by $-r_k(t)$; its magnitude decreases to zero and is bounded by the corresponding component of $x^\dagger$. Given $\epsilon>0$, choose a finite set of eigenvalues whose omitted squared components of $x^\dagger$ sum to less than $\epsilon$; on the chosen finite set every component tends to zero. The squared error sum therefore tends to at most $\epsilon$, and arbitrariness of $\epsilon$ proves norm convergence. The componentwise decrease also proves monotonicity of the norm.

Choose an integer $m>s$. For $v\ge0$ and an integer $n\ge0$,
$(1+v)^n\ge1+nv$: induction proves this, since multiplying the bound at
$n$ by $1+v$ gives $1+(n+1)v+nv^2\ge1+(n+1)v$. For $k\ge2m$, let
$n=\lfloor k/m\rfloor$, so $mn\le k$ and $n\ge k/(2m)$.
If $0<t\le\min\{M,\omega^{-1}\}$, put $u=\omega t\in(0,1]$. At $u=1$
the filter is zero. If $0<u\le1/k$, then $u^s(1-u)^k\le k^{-s}$. If
$k\ge2m$ and $1/k<u<1$, the identity $(1-u)(1+u)=1-u^2\le1$ gives
$(1-u)^{-k}\ge(1+u)^k\ge(1+u)^{mn}=((1+u)^n)^m\ge(nu)^m$.
Consequently
$$u^s(1-u)^k\le n^{-m}u^{s-m}\le n^{-m}k^{m-s}
\le(2m)^m k^{-s}.$$
For $k<2m$ the same product is at most $1\le(2m)^s k^{-s}$. Thus on this
range $t^s|r_k(t)|=\omega^{-s}u^s(1-u)^k\le C_{s,\omega}k^{-s}$.
If $\omega^{-1}<t\le M$, a range that exists only when $\omega M>1$, then
$|1-\omega t|=\omega t-1\le\omega M-1=:q\in(0,1)$. Put
$a=q^{-1}-1>0$. For $k\ge2m$ and the same $n$,
$$q^{-k}=(1+a)^k\ge(1+a)^{mn}=((1+a)^n)^m\ge(na)^m,$$
so $k^s q^k\le(2m)^m a^{-m}k^{s-m}\le(2m)^m a^{-m}$. For $k<2m$,
$k^s q^k\le(2m)^s$. Hence $\sup_{k\ge1}k^s q^k<\infty$ and
$t^s|r_k(t)|\le M^s q^k\le C_{s,M,\omega}k^{-s}$. Combining the two
ranges proves $\sup_{t\in\sigma(T)\setminus\{0\}}t^s|r_k(t)|\le
C_{s,A,\omega}k^{-s}$.

For $k\ge1$, the scalar geometric identity gives $g_k(t)=[1-(1-\omega t)^k]/t$ for $t>0$. Since $|1-\omega t|\le1$, both the bound by $2$ and the finite-sum bound by $k\omega t$ hold for its numerator. Hence $$\sqrt t\,|g_k(t)|\le\min\{2/\sqrt t,\omega k\sqrt t\}\le\sqrt{2\omega k}.$$ The last inequality follows by splitting at $t=2/(\omega k)$. For $Q_k=g_k(T)A^*$, adjoint multiplication gives $Q_kQ_k^*=g_k(T)Tg_k(T)^*$, the compact spectral multiplier with scalar values $t|g_k(t)|^2$ and value zero on $\ker T$. [F7] bounds its norm by the supremum of these values; [F4] and $\|Q_k\|^2=\|Q_kQ_k^*\|$ then give $\|Q_k\|\le\sqrt{2\omega k}$. Applying [F1] to $y_\delta-y$ gives $\|x_k^\delta-x_k\|=\|Q_k(y_\delta-y)\|\le\sqrt{2\omega k}\,\delta$.

Under $x^\dagger=T^sw$, [F1] gives $x_k-x^\dagger=-r_k(T)T^sw$. On every eigenspace the product multiplier is $t^sr_k(t)$, bounded by [step 1.2]; [F7] therefore yields $\|x_k-x^\dagger\|\le\sup_{t>0}t^s|r_k(t)|\,\|w\|$. Substituting the bound in [step 1.2] proves the source-bias estimate.
The triangle inequality gives $\|x_k^\delta-x^\dagger\|\le\|x_k^\delta-x_k\|+\|x_k-x^\dagger\|$; substituting the bounds from [step 2.1] and [step 1.3] proves the final estimate.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $A:X\to Y$ be a nonzero compact operator between
real or complex Hilbert spaces, set $T=A^*A$, choose
$0<\omega<2/\|A\|^2$, and let $y=Ax^\dagger$ with
$x^\dagger\in(\ker A)^\perp$. Let $x_k$ be the exact-data Landweber iterates
in the infinite recurrence-defined path of
[[alg-landweber-iteration-with-discrepancy-stopping]] for datum $y$; this path
depends on $A,\omega,y$ and not on a finite cap or stopping test. Put
$r_k(t)=(1-\omega t)^k$. Then $\|x_k-x^\dagger\|$ is nonincreasing and
$x_k\to x^\dagger$ in norm. For every $s>0$, if $x^\dagger=T^s w$ with
$w\in X$, then for $k\ge1$,
$$\|x_k-x^\dagger\|\le C_{s,A,\omega}\|w\|k^{-s}.$$
The scalar filter also satisfies
$$\sup_{t\in\Sigma}t^s|r_k(t)|\le C_{s,A,\omega}k^{-s},$$
where $\Sigma$ is the set of nonzero eigenvalues of $T$.
For noisy data $y_\delta$ with $\|y_\delta-y\|\le\delta$, let
$x_k^\delta$ be the infinite recurrence-defined path for datum $y_\delta$.
It satisfies
$$\|x_k^\delta-x_k\|\le\sqrt{2\omega k}\,\delta.$$
Consequently, under the source condition $x^\dagger=T^\nu w$,
$0<\nu\le1$, the total error obeys
$$\|x_k^\delta-x^\dagger\|\le C_{\nu,A,\omega}\|w\|k^{-\nu} +\sqrt{2\omega k}\,\delta.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $A:X\to Y$ and $\omega$ satisfy the
hypotheses of [[alg-landweber-iteration-with-discrepancy-stopping]] and put
$T=A^*A$. For each integer $k\ge0$, define
$g_0(t)=0$ and
$g_k(t)=\omega\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(1-\omega t)^j$ for $k\ge1$, with
$r_k(t)=(1-\omega t)^k$. For the associated infinite mathematical path,
$$x_k=g_k(T)A^*y_\delta,\qquad y_\delta-Ax_k=r_k(AA^*)y_\delta.$$
If $y_\delta=Ax^\dagger$, then
$$x^\dagger-x_k=r_k(T)x^\dagger.$$
Here $g_k(T)$ and $r_k(T)$ are the compact spectral multipliers defined in
[[def-compact-spectral-filter-and-qualification]]; $r_k(AA^*)$ is the
multiplier with scalar function $t\mapsto(1-\omega t)^k$ on the compact
self-adjoint operator $AA^*$, as supplied by
[[lem-compact-spectral-multiplier-is-well-defined]].

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:X\to Y$ be compact and bounded. Put $S=A^*A$. By
[[lem-compact-gram-operator-is-positive-and-has-kernel]], $S$ is compact,
positive, and self-adjoint, with $\ker S=\ker A$. Let $\Sigma$ be the set of
nonzero eigenvalues of $S$ and $P_t$ the orthogonal projection onto the
eigenspace of $t\in\Sigma$; let $P_0$ be the orthogonal projection onto
$\ker S$. The compact spectral multiplier of a bounded scalar function
$q:\{0\}\cup\Sigma\to\mathbb F$ is
$$q(S)x:=q(0)P_0x+\sum_{t\in\Sigma}q(t)P_tx,$$
where the finite-subset net converges in norm by
[[lem-compact-spectral-multiplier-is-well-defined]]. For $\nu>0$, define
$S^\nu$ by the multiplier $q_\nu(0)=0$ and $q_\nu(t)=t^\nu$ for $t>0$.

For $\lambda>0$, the Tikhonov filter and residual filter are
$$g_\lambda(t)=\frac1{t+\lambda},\qquad r_\lambda(t)=1-tg_\lambda(t)=\frac{\lambda}{t+\lambda}.$$
The Tikhonov solution for data $y_\delta\in Y$ is
$$x_\lambda^\delta=g_\lambda(S)A^*y_\delta =(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*y_\delta.$$
The source condition of order $\nu>0$ and radius $R\ge0$ means that
$x^\dagger=S^\nu w$ for some $w\in X$ with $\|w\|\le R$. A family of
filters $g_\alpha$ with residual filters $r_\alpha(t)=1-tg_\alpha(t)$ has
qualification at least $p>0$ when, for each $0<\nu\le p$, some finite
constant $C_\nu$ satisfies
$$\sup_{t\in\Sigma}t^\nu|r_\alpha(t)|\le C_\nu\alpha^\nu \quad\text{for every }\alpha>0.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
$H$ be an $\mathbb F$-Hilbert space, and let $S:H\to H$ be compact and
self-adjoint. Let $\Sigma$ be its set of nonzero
eigenvalues, $E_t=\ker(S-tI)$, $P_t$ the orthogonal projection onto $E_t$,
and $P_0$ the orthogonal projection onto $\ker S$. If
$q:\{0\}\cup\Sigma\to\mathbb F$ is bounded, then for every $x\in H$ the
finite-subset net
$$q(0)P_0x+\sum_{t\in F}q(t)P_tx,\qquad F\subseteq\Sigma\text{ finite},$$
converges in norm to a vector $Q_qx$. The map $Q_q:H\to H$ is bounded and
linear, with $\|Q_q\|\le\sup_{t\in\{0\}\cup\Sigma}|q(t)|$.

real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:X\to Y$ be compact and bounded, with adjoint $A^*:Y\to X$. Then both
$A^*A:X\to X$ and $AA^*:Y\to Y$ are compact, self-adjoint and positive, and
$$\ker(A^*A)=\ker A,\qquad \ker(AA^*)=\ker A^*.$$
