For $s\ge0$, define $H_C^s$ to be the completion of finite real Chebyshev sums $p=\sum_{n=0}^{M}c_nT_n$ in the norm
$$
\|p\|_{H_C^s}^2=\pi|c_0|^2+\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{M}(1+n^2)^s|c_n|^2.
$$
By [[lem-chebyshev-polynomials-orthogonal-in-arcsine-weight]], the coefficients of a finite sum are unique and this is a norm. At $s=0$, this norm on finite sums is the arcsine-weighted norm from [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]]. This is the spectral Sobolev scale for the named weight and domain; it is defined by Chebyshev coefficients, and no equivalence with an unweighted derivative-based Sobolev norm is asserted.

Identify the completion isometrically with the weighted coefficient sequence space
$$
\left\{(c_n)_{n\ge0}:\ c_n\in\mathbb R\text{ for every }n,\ \pi|c_0|^2+\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{n\ge1}(1+n^2)^s|c_n|^2<\infty\right\},
$$
so $u=\sum_{n\ge0}c_nT_n$ denotes its coefficient representation in the completion; it does not assert pointwise convergence of the series. The norm of a completion element is the completion norm, given by the displayed weighted coefficient sum.

At $s=0$, denote this completion by $L_C^2:=H_C^0$ and define
$$
\|u\|_C^2:=\|u\|_{H_C^0}^2=\pi|c_0|^2+\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{n\ge1}|c_n|^2.
$$
By the orthogonality lemma, this is the unique norm extension from finite sums of the arcsine-weighted norm of [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]]. Since $(1+n^2)^s\ge1$ for $s\ge0$, every $H_C^s$ embeds continuously in $L_C^2$, so $\|u\|_C$ is defined for every $u\in H_C^s$, including when $s=0$.

If an element has a continuous representative given by a uniformly convergent Chebyshev series, its arcsine integral norm agrees with this completion norm: for continuous $h$, the defining pairing gives $\|h\|_C\le\sqrt\pi\|h\|_\infty$, so uniform convergence implies convergence in the arcsine norm as well.

For $u=\sum_{n\ge0}c_nT_n$ in this coefficient completion, define the degree-$N$ orthogonal projection by
$$
\Pi_Nu=\sum_{n=0}^{N}c_nT_n.
$$
The projection is well-defined by coefficient truncation and the positive coefficient norm above.

Under the pairing of [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]],
$$
\langle T_m,T_n\rangle_C=
\begin{cases}
\pi,&m=n=0,\\
\pi/2,&m=n\ge1,\\
0,&m\ne n.
\end{cases}
$$
The polynomials $T_0,T_1,\ldots$ form a basis of the real polynomial space, and the pairing is positive definite on continuous real functions on $[-1,1]$. If a continuous real function $h$ satisfies $\langle h,T_n\rangle_C=0$ for every $n\ge0$, then $h=0$ on $[-1,1]$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $u-\Pi_Nu=\sum_{n>N}c_nT_n$. Orthogonality from [F2] gives $\|u-\Pi_Nu\|_C^2=\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{n>N}|c_n|^2.$ Since $n>N$ implies $(1+n^2)^s\ge(1+(N+1)^2)^s$, this is at most $(1+(N+1)^2)^{-s}\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{n>N}(1+n^2)^s|c_n|^2 \le(1+(N+1)^2)^{-s}\|u\|_{H_C^s}^2.$ Taking square roots proves the result for finite sums.

Finite sums are dense in the completion defining $H_C^s$. The truncation $\Pi_N$ is a contraction in the coefficient norm and in the $C$-norm, so both sides of the finite-sum inequality pass to the limit along any Cauchy sequence of finite sums. This yields the stated estimate for every $u\in H_C^s$.

For either Chebyshev node family, every $n\geq0$, and every
$f\in C[-1,1]$,
$$\|f-I_n^\sigma f\|_\infty \leq (1+\Lambda_n^\sigma)E_n(f).$$
Here $E_n$ is the best degree-$n$ uniform error and $\Lambda_n^\sigma$
is the operator norm defined in
[[def-best-uniform-polynomial-approximation-error-and-chebyshev-interpolants]].

For continuous real functions $f,g$ on $[-1,1]$, define
$$
\langle f,g\rangle_C:=\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)g(\cos\theta)\,d\theta,\qquad \|f\|_C^2:=\langle f,f\rangle_C.
$$
This is the arcsine-weighted pairing on the compact Chebyshev interval: in the variable $x=\cos\theta$ its weight is $\omega_C(x)=(1-x^2)^{-1/2}$ for $-1<x<1$. The angular integral is the endpoint convention, so no endpoint value of the singular density is required.

derivations.claim: For every $\theta\in[0,\pi]$, $|h(\cos\theta)|\le\|h\|_\infty$. Integrating its square in [F2] gives $\|h\|_C^2\le\pi\|h\|_\infty^2$ and hence $\|h\|_C\le\sqrt{\pi}\|h\|_\infty$.
Apply step 1.1 to $h=f-I_N^Lf$, then use the uniform near-best bound [F1]. The result is $\|f-I_N^Lf\|_C\le\sqrt{\pi}(1+\Lambda_N^L)E_N(f)$.

Let $N\ge1$, let $x_j=\cos(j\pi/N)$, and let $I_N^L$ denote degree-at-most-$N$ interpolation on these nodes. For every integer $n\ge0$, let $\rho_N(n)$ be the unique integer $r\in\{0,\ldots,N\}$ congruent to either $n$ or $-n$ modulo $2N$. Then
$$
I_N^L T_n=T_{\rho_N(n)}.
$$
In particular, sampling a Chebyshev series on the Lobatto grid can fold every degree $n>N$ to a degree at most $N$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Define the node polynomial and barycentric weights by
$$\omega_n(X)=\prod_{k=0}^{n}(X-x_k),\qquad w_j=\left(\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}(x_j-x_k)\right)^{-1}\quad(0\le j\le n).$$
An empty product is $1$, so $w_0=1$ when $n=0$.

In these formulas, $X$ is a real argument, and for real $a$ and nonzero real $b$, $a/b$ denotes $ab^{-1}$ in the field $\mathbb R$ ([[def-field]]).

For each $j$, the cardinal function is
$$\ell_j(X)=\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}\frac{X-x_k}{x_j-x_k}.$$
The interpolation function for the data $y=(y_0,\ldots,y_n)$ is
$$I_n y(X)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}y_j\ell_j(X).$$
For a real function $f$ defined at the nodes, write $I_n f:=I_n(f(x_0),\ldots,f(x_n))$.

For products indexed by $k\ne j$, use the length-$n$ list $\widehat x_{j,k}$ ($0\le k<n$), where $\widehat x_{j,k}=x_k$ for $k<j$ and $\widehat x_{j,k}=x_{k+1}$ for $k\ge j$; the product is in this order and is empty when $n=0$. Strict ordering gives $x_j-\widehat x_{j,k}\ne0$ for every factor, so [[lem-finite-product-of-nonzero-reals-is-nonzero]] and the field inverse law make each $w_j$ well defined.

Under the pairing of [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]],
$$
\langle T_m,T_n\rangle_C=
\begin{cases}
\pi,&m=n=0,\\
\pi/2,&m=n\ge1,\\
0,&m\ne n.
\end{cases}
$$
The polynomials $T_0,T_1,\ldots$ form a basis of the real polynomial space, and the pairing is positive definite on continuous real functions on $[-1,1]$. If a continuous real function $h$ satisfies $\langle h,T_n\rangle_C=0$ for every $n\ge0$, then $h=0$ on $[-1,1]$.

For every $n\in\mathbb N$ and real $\theta$,
$$T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos(n\theta),\qquad U_n(\cos\theta)\sin\theta=\sin((n+1)\theta).$$ In particular, for $n\ge1$ and $0\le j\le n$, $T_n(\cos(j\pi/n))=(-1)^j$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-induction-principle]].

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.
Let $s>1/2$. If a sequence $(a_k)$ satisfies $\sum_k(1+|k|)^{2s}|a_k|^2<\infty$, then $(a_k)\in\ell^1(\mathbb Z)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ and $b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}$ be
reals, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then

$$\Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big)^{2} \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}\Big),$$

and, in root form ([[thm-of-square-roots]]),

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big| \;\le\; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}} \; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}}.$$

Equality holds in the first display if and only if the two lists are
proportional, in the symmetric sense that there is a pair
$(\lambda, \mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda a_k = \mu b_k$ for every
$k < n$.

**No root is used in the proof of the squared form.** That form is an identity
plus a sign argument in the ordered field, and the root form is only a
restatement of it through the monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives
([[lem-of-square-monotone]]); the root enters nowhere but the last step, where
that restatement is made and [[thm-of-square-roots]] is what supplies the
square-root symbol. This matters here, because it makes the squared
inequality independent of the existence theorem for roots.

derivations.claim: Put $a_n=c_n$ for $n\ge0$ and $a_n=0$ for negative $n$. By [F1], $\sum_{n\ge0}(1+n^2)^s|c_n|^2<\infty$; since $(1+n)^{2s}\le2^s(1+n^2)^s$, [F6] gives $\sum_{n\ge0}|c_n|<\infty$. By [F5], $|T_n(x)|\le1$ on $[-1,1]$, so the series converges uniformly and its nodal values are defined.

Write $u=S_N+R_N$, where $S_N=\sum_{n=0}^Nc_nT_n$ and $R_N=\sum_{n>N}c_nT_n$. The Lagrange operator [F3] reproduces $S_N$ and is continuous in the uniform norm; therefore $u-I_N^Lu=R_N-I_N^LR_N$. By [F2], uniform convergence and the finite cardinal sum give $I_N^LR_N=\sum_{r=0}^Nb_rT_r$, where $b_r=\sum_{n>N:\rho_N(n)=r}c_n$.

Fix $r\in\{0,\ldots,N\}$. Since $n\equiv r$ or $-r\pmod{2N}$, every index in its alias class has form $2qN+r$ or $2qN-r$. When $n>N$ the corresponding integer $q$ is positive. For each $q$ there are at most two candidates; the plus candidate is at least $qN$, and the minus candidate is at least $(2q-1)N\ge qN$. Hence $\sum_{n>N:\rho_N(n)=r}(1+n^2)^{-s}\le2N^{-2s}\sum_{q\ge1}q^{-2s}\le2\left(1+\frac1{2s-1}\right)N^{-2s}.$ The last inequality separates the $q=1$ term and bounds the decreasing tail by $\int_1^\infty x^{-2s}\,dx$.

Let $A_s=1+1/(2s-1)$. Apply [F7] to finite partial sums over an alias class, use step 3.1, and pass to the limit; the coefficient sums converge absolutely by step 1.1. This gives $|b_r|^2\le2A_sN^{-2s}\sum_{n>N:\rho_N(n)=r}(1+n^2)^s|c_n|^2.$ The alias classes partition $n>N$. By [F4], $\|I_N^LR_N\|_C^2\le\pi\sum_{r=0}^N|b_r|^2\le2\pi A_sN^{-2s}\sum_{n>N}(1+n^2)^s|c_n|^2\le4A_sN^{-2s}\|u\|_{H_C^s}^2,$ where the last inequality uses [F1]. Also [F1] and [F4] give $\|R_N\|_C^2=\frac\pi2\sum_{n>N}|c_n|^2\le(N+1)^{-2s}\|u\|_{H_C^s}^2.$ Thus $\|R_N\|_C\le(N+1)^{-s}\|u\|_{H_C^s}$.
By step 2.1 and the triangle inequality, $\|u-I_N^Lu\|_C\le\|R_N\|_C+\|I_N^LR_N\|_C\le(1+2\sqrt{A_s})N^{-s}\|u\|_{H_C^s}$ because $(N+1)^{-s}\le N^{-s}$. This is the claimed estimate.

Let $N\ge1$ be an integer and put $x_j=\cos(j\pi/N)$ for $j=0,\ldots,N$. The ordering is decreasing: $x_0=1$ and $x_N=-1$. These are the Chebyshev–Gauss–Lobatto nodes; [[thm-chebyshev-multiple-angle-identities]] gives $T_N(x_j)=(-1)^j$. They are distinct because cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ by [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]].

For interpolation using [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]], use the increasing reindexing $z_k=x_{N-k}$, $k=0,\ldots,N$. For descending-grid data $U_j$, the corresponding increasing data are $Y_k=U_{N-k}$.

For nodal data $U_0,\ldots,U_N$, define $I_N^LU$ to be the cardinal interpolant of $(Y_k)_{k=0}^N$ at $(z_k)_{k=0}^N$. For a function $f$ defined on the interval, write $I_N^Lf$ for the interpolant of its nodal values. The increasing-node interpolation theorem [[thm-cardinal-polynomial-interpolant-exists-uniquely]] makes this polynomial unique.

Let $\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ be the set of formal real polynomials of
[[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]]. Associate to every
$P\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ an eventually zero coefficient sequence $(p_k)$:
use its displayed finite coefficient list and extend it by zeros when $P\ne0$,
and put $p_k=0$ for every $k$ when $P=0$. Do the same for $Q$, with coefficients
$(q_k)$. Define $P+Q$ coefficientwise and define $PQ$ by the convolution
coefficients
$$ (P+Q)_k=p_k+q_k,\qquad (PQ)_k=\sum_{j=0}^{k}p_jq_{k-j}. $$
using the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. In either construction, discard
trailing zero coefficients; if every coefficient is zero, the result is the zero
polynomial. Scalar multiplication and subtraction are the corresponding
coefficientwise operations. Thus these formulas define operations on the formal
coefficient-list objects, independently of evaluation.

Write $1=(1)$ and $X=(0,1)$, and define
$$ \Phi(P,Q):=(Q,2XQ-P)\qquad(P,Q\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}). $$
Apply [[thm-recursion]] to the set
$\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}\times\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$, first with initial value
$(1,X)$ and then with initial value $(1,2X)$, always using the function $\Phi$.
This gives unique pair sequences $H^T,H^U$. Define $T_n$ and $U_n$ to be the
first coordinates of $H^T_n$ and $H^U_n$, respectively. Since the first
coordinate of $\Phi(P,Q)$ is $Q$, the second coordinate of $H^T_n$ is
$T_{n+1}$ and the second coordinate of $H^U_n$ is $U_{n+1}$. Consequently
$$ T_0=1,\quad T_1=X,\quad T_{n+2}=2XT_{n+1}-T_n, $$
$$ U_0=1,\quad U_1=2X,\quad U_{n+2}=2XU_{n+1}-U_n $$
for every $n\in\mathbb N$. These unique sequences are the **Chebyshev
polynomials of the first and second kinds**.

For $n\ge1$, $T_n$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $2^{n-1}$, while $U_n$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $2^n$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]], [[thm-induction-principle]], [[def-integer-power]].

For every $n\in\mathbb N$ and real $\theta$,
$$T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos(n\theta),\qquad U_n(\cos\theta)\sin\theta=\sin((n+1)\theta).$$ In particular, for $n\ge1$ and $0\le j\le n$, $T_n(\cos(j\pi/n))=(-1)^j$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-induction-principle]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Define the node polynomial and barycentric weights by
$$\omega_n(X)=\prod_{k=0}^{n}(X-x_k),\qquad w_j=\left(\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}(x_j-x_k)\right)^{-1}\quad(0\le j\le n).$$
An empty product is $1$, so $w_0=1$ when $n=0$.

In these formulas, $X$ is a real argument, and for real $a$ and nonzero real $b$, $a/b$ denotes $ab^{-1}$ in the field $\mathbb R$ ([[def-field]]).

For each $j$, the cardinal function is
$$\ell_j(X)=\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}\frac{X-x_k}{x_j-x_k}.$$
The interpolation function for the data $y=(y_0,\ldots,y_n)$ is
$$I_n y(X)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}y_j\ell_j(X).$$
For a real function $f$ defined at the nodes, write $I_n f:=I_n(f(x_0),\ldots,f(x_n))$.

For products indexed by $k\ne j$, use the length-$n$ list $\widehat x_{j,k}$ ($0\le k<n$), where $\widehat x_{j,k}=x_k$ for $k<j$ and $\widehat x_{j,k}=x_{k+1}$ for $k\ge j$; the product is in this order and is empty when $n=0$. Strict ordering gives $x_j-\widehat x_{j,k}\ne0$ for every factor, so [[lem-finite-product-of-nonzero-reals-is-nonzero]] and the field inverse law make each $w_j$ well defined.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, $n\ge0$, let $a<b$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ lie in $[a,b]$, and let $f\in C^{n+1}([a,b],\mathbb R)$ with the convention of [[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]]. Put $p=I_n f$ and $\omega_n(X)=\prod_{j=0}^n(X-x_j)$ as in [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. If $x=x_j$ for a node, then $f(x)-p(x)=0$. If $x\in[a,b]$ is not a node, there is
$$\xi\in\bigl(\min\{x,x_0\},\max\{x,x_n\}\bigr)$$
such that
$$f(x)-p(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!_{\mathbb R}}\,\omega_n(x),$$
where $(n+1)!_{\mathbb R}:=\prod_{j=1}^{n+1}j$, with each natural factor read as its canonical real image under [[def-canonical-natural]].

For continuous real functions $f,g$ on $[-1,1]$, define
$$
\langle f,g\rangle_C:=\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)g(\cos\theta)\,d\theta,\qquad \|f\|_C^2:=\langle f,f\rangle_C.
$$
This is the arcsine-weighted pairing on the compact Chebyshev interval: in the variable $x=\cos\theta$ its weight is $\omega_C(x)=(1-x^2)^{-1/2}$ for $-1<x<1$. The angular integral is the endpoint convention, so no endpoint value of the singular density is required.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$. Then the closed bounded interval
$[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]]) is compact ([[def-open-cover-r]]): every family of
open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ whose union contains $[a,b]$ has a finite subfamily
whose union already contains $[a,b]$.

The proof is by repeated bisection. Supposing some open cover admits no finite
subcover, one halves the interval, keeps a half that still admits none, and
iterates; the halves shrink to a point, which the cover does reach, and a single
member of the cover then swallows a whole late-stage half. **The halving rule is
canonical**, taking the left half whenever the left half works, so the recursion
uses [[thm-recursion]] and no choice principle.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be **nonempty** and compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $\sup f[K]$ and $\inf f[K]$ exist and are
**attained**: there are $p, q \in K$ with

$$f(q) \;=\; \inf f[K] \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; \sup f[K] \;=\; f(p) \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, the set $f[K]$ has a maximum and a minimum
([[def-max-min]]), namely $\max f[K] = f(p)$ and $\min f[K] = f(q)$.

**Nonemptiness of $K$ is a hypothesis, not an oversight.** For $K = \varnothing$
the set $f[K]$ is empty, and neither a supremum nor a maximum of the empty set
exists in this library ([[def-complete-ordered-field]] supplies suprema of
nonempty sets bounded above only).

**This theorem is stated twice in this library, on purpose.** Its metric-space
twin is [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], proved from the cover machinery of metric
spaces; the proof below is $\mathbb{R}$-native, running through Heine-Borel for
$\mathbb{R}$ and the order-completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, and it uses no cover
argument beyond the one already spent in
[[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-set-r]]. That the two statements are the
same statement in two vocabularies is proved in
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]], later on this page.

A nonzero real polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n$ distinct real roots. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]], [[lem-real-polynomial-factor-at-a-root]], [[thm-induction-principle]].

At nodes the interpolation error is zero; off the nodes apply [F7] and step 2.1. Since the maximum in [F9] is finite, this gives $\|f-I_N^Lf\|_\infty\le \frac{2^{1-N}}{(N+1)!}\max_{[-1,1]}|f^{(N+1)}|.$
Apply the weighted-norm estimate [F8] to the uniform error in step 3.1. This proves the stated inequality.

$$\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz=0.$$

The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-induction-principle]].

$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $N\ge1$, let $x_j=\cos(j\pi/N)$, and let $I_N^L$ denote degree-at-most-$N$ interpolation on these nodes. For every integer $n\ge0$, let $\rho_N(n)$ be the unique integer $r\in\{0,\ldots,N\}$ congruent to either $n$ or $-n$ modulo $2N$. Then
$$
I_N^L T_n=T_{\rho_N(n)}.
$$
In particular, sampling a Chebyshev series on the Lobatto grid can fold every degree $n>N$ to a degree at most $N$.

Under the pairing of [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]],
$$
\langle T_m,T_n\rangle_C=
\begin{cases}
\pi,&m=n=0,\\
\pi/2,&m=n\ge1,\\
0,&m\ne n.
\end{cases}
$$
The polynomials $T_0,T_1,\ldots$ form a basis of the real polynomial space, and the pairing is positive definite on continuous real functions on $[-1,1]$. If a continuous real function $h$ satisfies $\langle h,T_n\rangle_C=0$ for every $n\ge0$, then $h=0$ on $[-1,1]$.

For continuous real functions $f,g$ on $[-1,1]$, define
$$
\langle f,g\rangle_C:=\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)g(\cos\theta)\,d\theta,\qquad \|f\|_C^2:=\langle f,f\rangle_C.

This is the arcsine-weighted pairing on the compact Chebyshev interval: in the variable $x=\cos\theta$ its weight is $\omega_C(x)=(1-x^2)^{-1/2}$ for $-1<x<1$. The angular integral is the endpoint convention, so no endpoint value of the singular density is required.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

derivations.claim: For $z=\theta-it$ with $0\le t\le\log\rho$, $\cos z=\cos\theta\cosh t+i\sin\theta\sinh t.$ For fixed $t>0$, its real and imaginary parts satisfy $x^2/\cosh^2t+y^2/\sinh^2t=1$, so the image is the Bernstein ellipse with parameter $e^t$; these ellipses are nested. Since $f$ is holomorphic on a neighborhood of $E_\rho$, $g(z):=f(\cos z)$ is holomorphic on an open strip containing the rectangle $-\pi\le\Re z\le\pi$, $-\log\rho\le\Im z\le0$. On its lower edge $|g(\theta-i\log\rho)|\le M$.

For $n\ge1$, set $H_n(z)=g(z)e^{-inz}$. It is holomorphic on that strip and $2\pi$-periodic. Apply [F1] to the boundary of the rectangle with vertices $-\pi,\pi,\pi-i\log\rho,-\pi-i\log\rho$. The vertical integrals cancel by periodicity, so the top and lower horizontal integrals, both oriented from left to right, are equal. By [F2] and evenness, the coefficient in [F4] is $c_n=\frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}g(\theta)e^{-in\theta}\,d\theta.$ On the lower edge, $|e^{-in(\theta-i\log\rho)}|=\rho^{-n}$, so the shifted integral gives $|c_n|\le2M\rho^{-n}$. Also [F4] and $|f|\le M$ give $|c_0|\le M$.

The coefficient bounds in step 2.1 make $\sum_{n\ge0}c_nT_n$ uniformly convergent, since [F2] and [F6] give $|T_n(x)|\le1$. Uniform convergence permits termwise integration against each bounded $T_k$; orthogonality [F4] shows that this series and $f$ have the same Chebyshev coefficients. Their continuous difference therefore has every coefficient zero, so [F4] gives $f=\sum_{n\ge0}c_nT_n$ on $[-1,1]$.

By [F3], every mode $T_n$ with $n>N$ interpolates to a Chebyshev mode. Each such mode has sup norm at most one by [F2] and [F6]. Thus the series tail and its interpolant each have sup norm at most $\sum_{n>N}|c_n|$, and $\|f-I_N^Lf\|_\infty\le2\sum_{n>N}|c_n|\le4M\sum_{n>N}\rho^{-n}=\frac{4M}{\rho-1}\rho^{-N},$ where [F7] evaluates the geometric tail.
Apply [F5] to the uniform error in step 4.1. This yields $\|f-I_N^Lf\|_C\le4\sqrt\pi M(\rho-1)^{-1}\rho^{-N}$, as claimed.

Input a polynomial degree $N\ge0$ and an even integer $M\ge2$ specifying the number of uniform subintervals of $[0,\pi]$. For $0\le i,j\le N$, form
$$
g_{ij}(\theta)=T_i(\cos\theta)T_j(\cos\theta)
$$
and return
$$
M^{S}_{ij}:=Q_S(g_{ij};0,\pi,M),
$$
where $Q_S$ is the composite Simpson procedure from [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]]. By the Chebyshev multiple-angle identity, $g_{ij}(\theta)=\cos(i\theta)\cos(j\theta)$, so this is the composite-Simpson approximation of the corresponding arcsine-weighted mass entry. The procedure uses exact real arithmetic and asserts no quadrature or floating-point accuracy beyond a separately proved bound.

Let $a<b$, let $n\ge2$ be an even integer, and put $h=(b-a)/n$. If
$f\in C^4([a,b])$, set $M_4=\max_{x\in[a,b]}|f^{(4)}(x)|$. Then the value
$Q_S(f;a,b,n)$ of [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]] satisfies

$$\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-Q_S(f;a,b,n)\right|\le\frac{(b-a)h^4}{180}M_4.$$

The integral is the Riemann integral. This is an exact-arithmetic quadrature
bound; evaluation and summation roundoff are not included.

Let $\mu$ be a finite positive Borel measure on a compact interval $[a,b]$ with infinite relative support. For each integer $N\ge0$, the moment data $(a,b,m=N+1,r=2N+1,\mu)$ satisfy the hypotheses of [[def-gauss-moment-data]]. Let $p_0,\ldots,p_N$ be the monic orthogonal polynomials supplied by [[thm-monic-gauss-orthogonal-polynomials-exist-uniquely]], and write
$$
h_n=\int_{[a,b]}p_n(x)^2\,d\mu(x)>0.
$$
The finite-dimensional weighted Galerkin space is
$$
V_N(\mu)=\operatorname{span}\{p_0,\ldots,p_N\}\subset L^2(\mu).
$$
Here $L^2(\mu)$ means measurable functions with finite integral of the squared absolute value, modulo equality $\mu$-almost everywhere.

For a coefficient sequence $(c_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $\sum_{n\ge0}(1+n^2)^s|c_n|^2h_n<\infty$, define its weighted spectral Sobolev norm by
$$
\left\|\sum_{n\ge0}c_np_n\right\|_{H^s_\mu}^2
=\sum_{n\ge0}(1+n^2)^s|c_n|^2h_n,\qquad s\ge0.
$$
The associated orthogonal Galerkin projection is $\Pi_N(\sum_{n\ge0}c_np_n)=\sum_{n=0}^Nc_np_n$. This coefficient-defined scale is specific to the weight $\mu$ and the selected orthogonal-polynomial family; no equivalence with a derivative-based Sobolev norm is asserted here.

Let $(a,b,m,r,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]]. For $0\le k\le m$ with $2k\le r$, the pairing
[[def-gauss-polynomial-moment-inner-product]] is a well-defined real inner
product on $\mathbb R^{k+1}$.

derivations.claim: Each numerator is finite by [F3], and each denominator $h_j$ is finite and strictly positive by [F1]–[F2]. Thus every coefficient in the displayed finite sum is a defined real number.

Orthogonality of the $p_j$ gives, for each $i\le N$, $\int (u-\Pi_Nu)p_i\,d\mu =\int u p_i\,d\mu-\sum_{j=0}^{N}\frac{\int u p_j\,d\mu}{h_j}\int p_jp_i\,d\mu =0,$ because all terms with $j\ne i$ vanish and the $j=i$ term equals $\int u p_i\,d\mu$. Thus $\Pi_Nu\in V_N(\mu)$ has the required residual orthogonality.

If $v\in V_N(\mu)$ has the same residual property, then $w=v-\Pi_Nu$ lies in $V_N(\mu)$ and is orthogonal to every basis vector, hence to itself. Positive definiteness in [F2] gives $\int w^2\,d\mu=0$, so $w=0$ in $L^2(\mu)$ and $v=\Pi_Nu$. This proves uniqueness.

The finite-dimensional weighted Galerkin space is
$$
V_N(\mu)=\operatorname{span}\{p_0,\ldots,p_N\}\subset L^2(\mu).
$$
Here $L^2(\mu)$ means measurable functions with finite integral of the squared absolute value, modulo equality $\mu$-almost everywhere.

For a coefficient sequence $(c_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $\sum_{n\ge0}(1+n^2)^s|c_n|^2h_n<\infty$, define its weighted spectral Sobolev norm by
$$
\left\|\sum_{n\ge0}c_np_n\right\|_{H^s_\mu}^2
=\sum_{n\ge0}(1+n^2)^s|c_n|^2h_n,\qquad s\ge0.
$$
The associated orthogonal Galerkin projection is $\Pi_N(\sum_{n\ge0}c_np_n)=\sum_{n=0}^Nc_np_n$. This coefficient-defined scale is specific to the weight $\mu$ and the selected orthogonal-polynomial family; no equivalence with a derivative-based Sobolev norm is asserted here.

Input a degree $N\ge0$, the monic orthogonal basis $p_0,\ldots,p_N$ and the $(N+1)$-node Gaussian rule for the same positive measure $\mu$ from [[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]. With Gaussian nodes $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{N+1}$ and weights $w_1,\ldots,w_{N+1}$, output the matrix
$$
M_{ij}^{G}:=\sum_{r=1}^{N+1}w_r p_i(\xi_r)p_j(\xi_r),\qquad 0\le i,j\le N.
$$
The inputs are admissible only when the moment data have order at least $2N+1$ and the rule nodes, weights, and basis all use the same measure. The algorithm performs the displayed finite exact-arithmetic sums; no floating-point conditioning claim is made.

derivations.claim: The product $p_i p_j$ has degree $i+j\le2N<2N+1=2(N+1)-1$. Thus [F1] applies with $m=N+1$ and gives $M_{ij}^{G}=\sum_{r=1}^{N+1}w_rp_i(\xi_r)p_j(\xi_r)=\int p_i(x)p_j(x)\,d\mu(x)$ by [F3].

If $i\ne j$, the higher-degree polynomial is orthogonal to the lower-degree one by [F2], so the integral in step 1.1 is zero. If $i=j$, it is $h_i$ by [F2]. This is the displayed diagonal matrix identity.

For each integer $n\ge0$, define the Legendre polynomial
$$
P_n(x):=\frac{1}{2^n n!}\frac{d^n}{dx^n}(x^2-1)^n,
$$
with $n!$ as in [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]] and repeated derivatives as in [[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]]. Define the unweighted pairing of real polynomials by
$$
\langle p,q\rangle_L:=\int_{-1}^1p(x)q(x)\,dx,\qquad \|p\|_L^2:=\langle p,p\rangle_L.
$$
The integral is the ordinary integral of a continuous function. The normalization and all polynomial identities needed for the orthogonal Galerkin scale are proved in [[lem-legendre-weighted-derivative-orthogonality-and-norm]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

derivations.claim: Write $(x^2-1)^n=(x-1)^n(x+1)^n$. For every $j<n$, its $j$th derivative vanishes at both endpoints: by the product rule, every term differentiates each factor at most $j<n$ times and retains a positive power of the factor that vanishes at that endpoint. Thus $n$ integrations by parts in [F2] give, for every polynomial $q$ of degree less than $n$, $\int_{-1}^1P_nq=\frac{(-1)^n}{2^nn!}\int_{-1}^1(x^2-1)^nq^{(n)}=0,$ because $q^{(n)}=0$ by [F3]. Hence $P_n$ is orthogonal to every lower-degree polynomial.

The leading term of $(x^2-1)^n$ is $x^{2n}$; differentiating it $n$ times gives $(2n)!/n!$ times $x^n$ by [F3]. All other terms have lower degree after differentiation. Therefore $P_n$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $\kappa_n=(2n)!/(2^n(n!)^2)>0$. The distinct degrees imply the family $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ is linearly independent and spans every polynomial of degree at most $N$, by successive elimination of leading terms.

Since $P_n-\kappa_nx^n$ has degree less than $n$, step 1.1 gives $\int_{-1}^1P_n^2=\kappa_n\int_{-1}^1P_nx^n.$ Apply [F2] $n$ times to the Rodrigues formula against $x^n$. The endpoint terms vanish as in step 1.1 and $(x^n)^{(n)}=n!$, so $\int_{-1}^1P_nx^n=\frac1{2^n}\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)^n\,dx.$

Put $J_n=\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)^n dx$. Then $J_0=2$. For $n\ge1$, the endpoint values of $x(1-x^2)^n$ are zero, so integrating its derivative gives $0=J_n-2n(J_{n-1}-J_n),\qquad J_n=\frac{2n}{2n+1}J_{n-1}.$ Induction yields $J_n=2^{2n+1}(n!)^2/(2n+1)!$. Substituting this and $\kappa_n$ from step 2.1 into step 3.1 gives $\int P_n^2=2/(2n+1)$. Together with step 1.1 this proves the first orthogonality formula, including $n=0$.

When $n=0$, $P_0=1$ and $Q_0=-((1-x^2)P_0')'=0$, so $Q_0=0\cdot P_0$. Now take $n\ge1$ and define $Q_n=-((1-x^2)P_n')'$. Its leading term is $n(n+1)\kappa_nx^n$, so $Q_n-n(n+1)P_n$ has degree less than $n$. For any polynomial $q$ of degree less than $n$, two integrations by parts give $\int_{-1}^1Q_nq=\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'q'=-\int_{-1}^1P_n((1-x^2)q')'=0,$ where both boundary terms vanish because of the factor $1-x^2$, and the last polynomial paired with $P_n$ has degree less than $n$, so step 1.1 applies. Therefore $Q_n-n(n+1)P_n$ is a lower-degree polynomial orthogonal to every lower-degree polynomial. Expand it in the basis from step 2.1; the first formula and the positive norms in step 4.1 force every coefficient to be zero. Thus $Q_n=n(n+1)P_n$.

One integration by parts and step 5.1 give $\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'P_m'=\int_{-1}^1Q_nP_m=n(n+1)\int_{-1}^1P_nP_m.$ The first formula, already proved in step 4.1 and step 1.1, yields the displayed weighted derivative identity for every $m,n\ge0$.

For $s\ge0$, define $H_L^s$ as the completion of finite Legendre sums $p=\sum_{n=0}^Mc_nP_n$ in the coefficient norm
$$
\|p\|_{H_L^s}^2=\sum_{n=0}^M(1+n(n+1))^s\frac{2}{2n+1}|c_n|^2.
$$
The coefficients are unique because the polynomials have distinct degrees by [[lem-legendre-weighted-derivative-orthogonality-and-norm]]. At $s=0$ this norm is exactly the unweighted $L^2([-1,1])$ norm on finite sums, by the same lemma; its completion is denoted $L_L^2$. Define the degree-$N$ orthogonal projection on finite sums by
$$
\Pi_Nu=\sum_{n=0}^Nc_nP_n.
$$
It extends to the coefficient completion by truncation. This explicitly coefficient-defined scale uses the Legendre weight $1$ on $[-1,1]$; no equivalence with an unweighted derivative-based Sobolev norm is asserted here.

For $m,n\ge0$, the polynomials of [[def-legendre-polynomial-family-and-l2-pairing]] satisfy
$$
\int_{-1}^1P_n(x)P_m(x)\,dx=\frac{2}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn},
\qquad
\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'(x)P_m'(x)\,dx=\frac{2n(n+1)}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn},
$$
where $\delta_{mn}=1$ if $m=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Each $P_n$ has degree $n$ and nonzero leading coefficient, so $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ form a basis of polynomials of degree at most $N$.

derivations.claim: For a finite Legendre sum, [F1] gives $u-\Pi_Nu=\sum_{n>N}c_nP_n$. Orthogonality [F2] therefore gives $\|u-\Pi_Nu\|_{L_L^2}^2=\sum_{n>N}\frac{2}{2n+1}|c_n|^2.$ For every $n>N$, $1+n(n+1)\ge1+(N+1)(N+2)$; multiplying each term by the inverse weight gives the stated squared bound for finite sums.

Finite sums are dense in the completion defining $H_L^s$. The truncation $\Pi_N$ is contractive in both the coefficient norm and the $s=0$ norm, so the finite-sum inequality passes to the limit along any Cauchy sequence of finite sums. Taking square roots proves the claimed estimate for every $u\in H_L^s$.

Let $N\ge2$ be an integer, let $x_j=2\pi j/N$ for $j=0,\ldots,N-1$, and identify $x_N$ with $x_0$ periodically. The real trigonometric interpolation space is
$$
\mathcal T_N=
\begin{cases}
\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{1,\cos(kx),\sin(kx):1\le k\le (N-1)/2\},&N\text{ odd},\\
\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{1,\cos(kx),\sin(kx):1\le k<N/2\}\oplus\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{\cos(Nx/2)\},&N\text{ even}.
\end{cases}
$$
For real nodal data $U=(U_0,\ldots,U_{N-1})$, define its periodic Fourier interpolant by
$$
I_NU(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}U_jL_j(x),
$$
where, for $N=2K+1$,
$$
L_j(x)=\frac1N\left(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{K}\cos(k(x-x_j))\right),
$$
and, for $N=2K$,
$$
L_j(x)=\frac1N\left(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{K-1}\cos(k(x-x_j))+\cos(K(x-x_j))\right).
$$
Thus the even-grid Nyquist component is the real cosine $\cos(Nx/2)$ only. Its sampled derivative is defined by differentiating this interpolant; the resulting Nyquist derivative values are zero at every grid point.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $N\ge2$, let $U=(U_j)_{j=0}^{N-1}\in\mathbb R^N$, and let $p=I_NU\in\mathcal T_N$ be the interpolant defined in [[def-periodic-fourier-collocation-grid]]. The matrix [[alg-periodic-fourier-collocation-differentiation-matrix]] satisfies
$$
(D_NU)_i=p'(x_i),\qquad 0\le i<N.
$$
For even $N$, this statement includes the Nyquist cosine mode, whose derivative vanishes at the grid nodes.

derivations.claim: Substitution of $x_0=0,x_1=\pi/2,x_2=\pi,x_3=3\pi/2$ into $p$ using [F2] gives respectively $-1,8,-5,2$. The frequencies $0,1,2$ lie in [F1]'s interpolation space, so $p$ is the interpolant of these samples.
By [F3], $p'(x)=-2\sin x+3\cos x+8\sin(2x)$. At the four nodes, the final term is zero and the first two terms give $3,-2,-3,2$.
Exactness [F4] therefore gives $D_4U=(3,-2,-3,2)$, including the vanishing nodal derivative of the Nyquist mode.

Let $N\ge1$ be an integer and put $x_j=\cos(j\pi/N)$ for $j=0,\ldots,N$. The ordering is decreasing: $x_0=1$ and $x_N=-1$. These are the Chebyshev–Gauss–Lobatto nodes; [[thm-chebyshev-multiple-angle-identities]] gives $T_N(x_j)=(-1)^j$. They are distinct because cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ by [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]].

For interpolation using [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]], use the increasing reindexing $z_k=x_{N-k}$, $k=0,\ldots,N$. For descending-grid data $U_j$, the corresponding increasing data are $Y_k=U_{N-k}$.

For nodal data $U_0,\ldots,U_N$, define $I_N^LU$ to be the cardinal interpolant of $(Y_k)_{k=0}^N$ at $(z_k)_{k=0}^N$. For a function $f$ defined on the interval, write $I_N^Lf$ for the interpolant of its nodal values. The increasing-node interpolation theorem [[thm-cardinal-polynomial-interpolant-exists-uniquely]] makes this polynomial unique.

For all real $u,v$,
$$\sin(u-v)=\sin u\cos v-\cos u\sin v,\qquad \cos(u-v)=\cos u\cos v+\sin u\sin v.$$ The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]].

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For $0\leq u\leq\pi/2$,
$$\sin u\geq \frac{2u}{\pi}.$$
For all real $u,v$,
$$|\sin u-\sin v|\leq |u-v|.$$

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

derivations.claim: The subtraction and addition identities [F2] give $x_j-x_{j+1}=2\sin\left(\frac{(2j+1)\pi}{2N}\right)\sin\left(\frac\pi{2N}\right),\qquad x_0-x_1=2\sin^2\left(\frac\pi{2N}\right).$ By [F3], $\sin(\pi/(2N))\le\pi/(2N)$, hence $x_0-x_1\le\pi^2/(2N^2)$.

If $N$ is odd, choose $j=(N-1)/2$; then $(2j+1)\pi/(2N)=\pi/2$ and [F4] gives sine equal to $1$, so the gap formula in step 1.1 and [F3] give a central gap at least $2/N\ge\sqrt2/N$. If $N$ is even, choose $j=N/2-1$ and write $t=\pi/2-\pi/(2N)\ge\pi/4$. The addition and subtraction formulas [F2] give $\sin(\pi/4)=\cos(\pi/4)$ and $2\sin(\pi/4)\cos(\pi/4)=\sin(\pi/2)=1$. The chord bound [F3] gives $\sin(\pi/4)\ge1/2>0$, hence $\sin(\pi/4)=\sqrt2/2$; monotonicity [F4] now gives $\sin t\ge\sqrt2/2$. In either parity, [F3] also gives $\sin(\pi/(2N))\ge1/N$, so the selected central gap in step 1.1 is at least $\sqrt2/N$.
The ratio of the endpoint gap to this central gap is at most $\pi^2/(2N)$, which tends to zero as $N\to\infty$. This proves the stated endpoint clustering and nonuniformity.

Let $\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ be the set of formal real polynomials of
[[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]]. Associate to every
$P\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ an eventually zero coefficient sequence $(p_k)$:
use its displayed finite coefficient list and extend it by zeros when $P\ne0$,
and put $p_k=0$ for every $k$ when $P=0$. Do the same for $Q$, with coefficients
$(q_k)$. Define $P+Q$ coefficientwise and define $PQ$ by the convolution
coefficients
$$ (P+Q)_k=p_k+q_k,\qquad (PQ)_k=\sum_{j=0}^{k}p_jq_{k-j}. $$
using the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. In either construction, discard
trailing zero coefficients; if every coefficient is zero, the result is the zero
polynomial. Scalar multiplication and subtraction are the corresponding
coefficientwise operations. Thus these formulas define operations on the formal
coefficient-list objects, independently of evaluation.

Write $1=(1)$ and $X=(0,1)$, and define
$$ \Phi(P,Q):=(Q,2XQ-P)\qquad(P,Q\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}). $$
Apply [[thm-recursion]] to the set
$\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}\times\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$, first with initial value
$(1,X)$ and then with initial value $(1,2X)$, always using the function $\Phi$.
This gives unique pair sequences $H^T,H^U$. Define $T_n$ and $U_n$ to be the
first coordinates of $H^T_n$ and $H^U_n$, respectively. Since the first
coordinate of $\Phi(P,Q)$ is $Q$, the second coordinate of $H^T_n$ is
$T_{n+1}$ and the second coordinate of $H^U_n$ is $U_{n+1}$. Consequently
$$ T_0=1,\quad T_1=X,\quad T_{n+2}=2XT_{n+1}-T_n, $$
$$ U_0=1,\quad U_1=2X,\quad U_{n+2}=2XU_{n+1}-U_n $$
for every $n\in\mathbb N$. These unique sequences are the **Chebyshev
polynomials of the first and second kinds**.

For every $n\in\mathbb N$ and real $\theta$,
$$T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos(n\theta),\qquad U_n(\cos\theta)\sin\theta=\sin((n+1)\theta).$$ In particular, for $n\ge1$ and $0\le j\le n$, $T_n(\cos(j\pi/n))=(-1)^j$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-induction-principle]].

For continuous real functions $f,g$ on $[-1,1]$, define
$$
\langle f,g\rangle_C:=\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)g(\cos\theta)\,d\theta,\qquad \|f\|_C^2:=\langle f,f\rangle_C.
$$
This is the arcsine-weighted pairing on the compact Chebyshev interval: in the variable $x=\cos\theta$ its weight is $\omega_C(x)=(1-x^2)^{-1/2}$ for $-1<x<1$. The angular integral is the endpoint convention, so no endpoint value of the singular density is required.

Under the pairing of [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]],
$$
\langle T_m,T_n\rangle_C=
\begin{cases}
\pi,&m=n=0,\\
\pi/2,&m=n\ge1,\\
0,&m\ne n.
\end{cases}
$$
The polynomials $T_0,T_1,\ldots$ form a basis of the real polynomial space, and the pairing is positive definite on continuous real functions on $[-1,1]$. If a continuous real function $h$ satisfies $\langle h,T_n\rangle_C=0$ for every $n\ge0$, then $h=0$ on $[-1,1]$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb C$. The function $f$ is **complex differentiable at $a$** if the limit

$$ \lim_{\substack{h\to0\\ h\ne0,\ a+h\in U}}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} $$

exists in the metric of [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. Its value is the **complex derivative** of $f$ at $a$, denoted $f'(a)$. The increments are nonzero and remain in the domain; because $U$ is open, all sufficiently small increments are allowed.

The function $f$ is **holomorphic on $U$** when it is complex differentiable at every point of $U$. A function holomorphic on all of $\mathbb C$ is **entire**. The word analytic is reserved for the local power-series notion.

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For all real $u,v$,
$$\sin(u-v)=\sin u\cos v-\cos u\sin v,\qquad \cos(u-v)=\cos u\cos v+\sin u\sin v.$$ The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $u,v\in\mathbb{R}$, and let $f$ and $g$ be integrable between $u$ and $v$.
If $\eta\ge0$ and

$$|f(x)-g(x)|\le\eta$$

throughout the closed interval with endpoints $u$ and $v$, then

$$\left|\int_u^v f-\int_u^v g\right|\le \eta\,|v-u|.$$

derivations.claim: The set $\Omega=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<3/2\}$ is an open neighborhood of $[-1,1]$ and omits $2$. For $z,z_0\in\Omega$ with $z\ne z_0$, $\frac{f_a(z)-f_a(z_0)}{z-z_0}=\frac1{(2-z)(2-z_0)}\longrightarrow\frac1{(2-z_0)^2}\quad(z\to z_0).$ Thus [F4] makes $f_a$ holomorphic on a neighborhood of the interval.

The function $f_s(x)=|x|$ is not differentiable at $0$: for $h>0$ its difference quotient is $1$, while for $h<0$ it is $-1$, so the two-sided limit in [F11] does not exist. By [F7], $|\cos\theta|=\cos\theta$ on $[0,\pi/2]$ and $|\cos\theta|=-\cos\theta$ on $[\pi/2,\pi]$. The subtraction identity [F9] gives $\cos(n(\pi-\theta))=(-1)^n\cos(n\theta)$, so reflection makes each odd coefficient integral its own negative. Therefore $a_0(f_s)=\frac1\pi\int_0^\pi|\cos\theta|\,d\theta=\frac2\pi.$ For odd $n$, that reflection makes $a_n(f_s)=0$.

Put $q=2-\sqrt3$. Then $0<q<1$, $q^{-1}=2+\sqrt3$, $q+q^{-1}=4$, and $1-q^2=2\sqrt3q$. By [F8], $z=qe^{i\theta}$ has modulus $q$. For $m\ge1$, put $S_m(z)=\sum_{n=1}^m z^n$. Multiplying the finite sum by $1-z$ cancels consecutive terms and gives $(1-z)S_m=z-z^{m+1}$. The triangle inequality in [F3] gives $|1-z|\ge1-q>0$, so $$\left|S_m(z)-\frac z{1-z}\right|=\frac{|z|^{m+1}}{|1-z|}\le\frac{q^{m+1}}{1-q}.$$ Induction using the addition formulas in [F5] and Euler's identity in [F8] gives $z^n=q^n(\cos(n\theta)+i\sin(n\theta))$. Thus $C_m(\theta):=1+2\sum_{n=1}^m q^n\cos(n\theta)$ differs from $1+2\operatorname{Re}(z/(1-z))$ by at most $2q^{m+1}/(1-q)$, uniformly for $\theta\in[0,\pi]$.

Multiplying numerator and denominator by $1-q\cos\theta+iq\sin\theta$ and using [F10] gives $$\operatorname{Re}\frac z{1-z}=\frac{q\cos\theta-q^2}{1-2q\cos\theta+q^2}.$$ Hence $$1+2\operatorname{Re}\frac z{1-z}=\frac{1-q^2}{1-2q\cos\theta+q^2}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2-\cos\theta},$$ because the denominator equals $2q(2-\cos\theta)$. By step 1.3, the continuous functions $C_m/\sqrt3$ satisfy $$\sup_{0\le\theta\le\pi}\left|\frac{C_m(\theta)}{\sqrt3}-f_a(\cos\theta)\right|\le\eta_m:=\frac{2q^{m+1}}{\sqrt3(1-q)}\longrightarrow0$$ by [F3]. This also establishes the claimed convergent Chebyshev expansion through [F1].

Fix a coefficient index $n\ge0$. By [F12], $f_a(\cos\theta)$, $C_m/\sqrt3$, and their products with $\cos(n\theta)$ are integrable. Since $|\cos(n\theta)|\le1$ by [F7], [F13] bounds the corresponding coefficient differences by $\eta_m$ for index zero and by $2\eta_m$ for positive indices. For every $m\ge n$, finite integration and orthogonality [F2] give the coefficients of $C_m/\sqrt3$ as $1/\sqrt3$ at zero and $2q^n/\sqrt3$ at each $1\le n\le m$. Letting $m\to\infty$ therefore yields exactly the asserted coefficients of $f_a$; no interchange of an unbounded infinite sum and integral is assumed.

For $m\ge1$, symmetry about $\pi/2$ and [F5] give $\int_0^\pi|\cos\theta|\cos(2m\theta)\,d\theta=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos\theta\cos(2m\theta)\,d\theta=\frac{2(-1)^{m-1}}{4m^2-1},$ where the last equality follows by integrating $\frac12[\cos((2m+1)\theta)+\cos((2m-1)\theta)]$ using [F6]–[F7]. Multiplying by $2/\pi$ gives $a_{2m}(f_s)=4(-1)^{m-1}/(\pi(4m^2-1))$. This coefficient magnitude is asymptotic to $1/(\pi m^2)$.

Let $N\ge2$ be an integer, let $x_j=2\pi j/N$ for $j=0,\ldots,N-1$, and identify $x_N$ with $x_0$ periodically. The real trigonometric interpolation space is
$$
\mathcal T_N=
\begin{cases}
\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{1,\cos(kx),\sin(kx):1\le k\le (N-1)/2\},&N\text{ odd},\\
\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{1,\cos(kx),\sin(kx):1\le k<N/2\}\oplus\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{\cos(Nx/2)\},&N\text{ even}.
\end{cases}
$$
For real nodal data $U=(U_0,\ldots,U_{N-1})$, define its periodic Fourier interpolant by
$$
I_NU(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}U_jL_j(x),
$$
where, for $N=2K+1$,
$$
L_j(x)=\frac1N\left(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{K}\cos(k(x-x_j))\right),
$$
and, for $N=2K$,
$$
L_j(x)=\frac1N\left(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{K-1}\cos(k(x-x_j))+\cos(K(x-x_j))\right).
$$
Thus the even-grid Nyquist component is the real cosine $\cos(Nx/2)$ only. Its sampled derivative is defined by differentiating this interpolant; the resulting Nyquist derivative values are zero at every grid point.

Let $N\ge2$ and $x_j=2\pi j/N$. If integers $k,r$ satisfy $k\equiv r\pmod N$, then
$$
e^{ikx_j}=e^{irx_j}\qquad(0\le j<N).
$$
Consequently, sampling a product of Fourier modes with frequencies $k_1,\ldots,k_s$ gives the same nodal data as the single mode whose frequency is the sum $\sum_{\ell=1}^s k_\ell$ reduced modulo $N$.

The frequency space in [[def-periodic-fourier-collocation-grid]] is real-valued. For complex data, let $\mathcal T_N^{\mathbb C}$ be the space obtained by allowing complex coefficients in that same real basis, and extend its cardinal formula by
$$
I_N^{\mathbb C}V(x):=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}V_jL_j(x),\qquad V\in\mathbb C^N.
$$
Then $I_N^{\mathbb C}V$ is the unique member of $\mathcal T_N^{\mathbb C}$ with nodal data $V$. On real data this formula agrees with $I_N$; in the even case the complex Nyquist samples are interpolated by the real basis function $\cos(Nx/2)$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

derivations.claim: By [F3], $p(x)^2=\cos^2x+2\cos x\cos(2x)+\cos^2(2x)=1+\cos x+\frac12\cos(2x)+\cos(3x)+\frac12\cos(4x).$
At every grid node [F4] turns this into $p(x_j)^2=\frac32+2\cos(x_j)+\frac12\cos(2x_j)$. The right side belongs to [F1]'s interpolation space.

The modes at frequencies $3$ and $4$ in step 1.1 are identified on the grid by the congruences $3\equiv-1\pmod4$ and $4\equiv0\pmod4$, exactly as [F2] states. Thus the displayed interpolant has the same samples as $p^2$, with the two alias contributions combined.
