citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $a<b$ be real numbers, let $m\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$r\in\{2m-1,2m\}$. A **Gaussian quadrature moment datum of order $r$** is a
finite positive measure $\mu$ on the relative Borel sigma-algebra
$\mathcal B([a,b])$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-measure-space]],
[[def-measure]], [[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) such that
$\mu([a,b])>0$, and whose **relative support**
$$ S_\mu:=\{x\in[a,b]:\mu(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open }U\subseteq[a,b]\text{ with }x\in U\} $$
contains at least $m+1$ distinct points. For every integer $0\le k\le r$,
require $x\mapsto |x|^k$ to be integrable with respect to $\mu$
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]) and put
$M_k:=\int_{[a,b]}x^k\,d\mu(x)$. Powers use the natural-exponent
recursion of [[def-integer-power]], with $x^0=1$ for every real $x$, including
$x=0$; thus $M_0$ is the integral of the constant function $1$.

The branch $r=2m-1$ supplies all moments used to construct the monic
degree-$m$ orthogonal polynomial and prove rule exactness. The stronger branch
$r=2m$ also defines its squared norm and is used for the remainder formula.
Because $[a,b]$ is bounded and $\mu$ is finite, these absolute-moment
integrability conditions follow from finiteness; they are stated to make the
two moment interfaces explicit.

Let $(a,b,m,r,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], with $m\ge1$ and $r\ge2m-1$. For each
$j=0,\ldots,m$ there is a unique monic real polynomial $p_j$ of degree $j$
such that
$$ \int_{[a,b]}p_j(x)q(x)\,d\mu(x)=0 $$
for every real polynomial $q$ of degree less than $j$. For $j=0$, this means
$p_0=1$ and the orthogonality condition is vacuous. The $j=m$ polynomial uses
moments only through degree $2m-1$; its squared norm is asserted only when the
moment datum has order $2m$.

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]]. Let $p_m$ be its monic degree-$m$ orthogonal
polynomial and write its ordered roots as
$a<x_1<\cdots<x_m<b$, as established in
[[thm-gauss-orthogonal-polynomial-has-simple-interior-zeros]]. For
$i=1,\ldots,m$, define the Lagrange cardinal polynomial
$$ \ell_i(X):=\prod_{\substack{1\le j\le m\\j\ne i}}\frac{X-x_j}{x_i-x_j} $$
using the convention of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
the **Gaussian quadrature weights** and the **m-node Gaussian rule** by
$$ w_i:=\int_{[a,b]}\ell_i(x)\,d\mu(x),\qquad Q_m(f):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i f(x_i) $$
for any real-valued function $f$ defined at the nodes. This definition
asserts no accuracy; well-definedness of the nodes, cardinal polynomials,
weights, and finite sum is proved in
[[lem-gauss-quadrature-rule-data-well-defined]].

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], and let $Q_m$ and $w_i$ be the rule and weights of
[[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]. For every real polynomial $f$ of degree at most
$2m-1$,
$$ \int_{[a,b]} f(x)\,d\mu(x)=Q_m(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_if(x_i). $$
Moreover, $w_i>0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_iw_i=\mu([a,b])$.

For $m,n\ge0$, the polynomials of [[def-legendre-polynomial-family-and-l2-pairing]] satisfy
$$
\int_{-1}^1P_n(x)P_m(x)\,dx=\frac{2}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn},
\qquad
\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'(x)P_m'(x)\,dx=\frac{2n(n+1)}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn},
$$
where $\delta_{mn}=1$ if $m=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Each $P_n$ has degree $n$ and nonzero leading coefficient, so $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ form a basis of polynomials of degree at most $N$.

Input a degree $N\ge0$, the monic orthogonal basis $p_0,\ldots,p_N$ and the $(N+1)$-node Gaussian rule for the same positive measure $\mu$ from [[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]. With Gaussian nodes $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{N+1}$ and weights $w_1,\ldots,w_{N+1}$, output the matrix
$$
M_{ij}^{G}:=\sum_{r=1}^{N+1}w_r p_i(\xi_r)p_j(\xi_r),\qquad 0\le i,j\le N.
$$
The inputs are admissible only when the moment data have order at least $2N+1$ and the rule nodes, weights, and basis all use the same measure. The algorithm performs the displayed finite exact-arithmetic sums; no floating-point conditioning claim is made.

Let $N\ge0$, take moment data of order $2N+1$ for a finite positive measure $\mu$ with support containing at least $N+2$ points, and use its $(N+1)$-node Gaussian rule and orthogonal polynomials $p_0,\ldots,p_N$. The matrix from [[alg-gaussian-orthogonal-polynomial-galerkin-mass-matrix]] has entries
$$
M_{ij}^{G}=\int p_i(x)p_j(x)\,d\mu(x)=
\begin{cases}
0,&i\ne j,\\
h_i,&i=j.
\end{cases}
$$

For continuous real functions $f,g$ on $[-1,1]$, define
$$
\langle f,g\rangle_C:=\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)g(\cos\theta)\,d\theta,\qquad \|f\|_C^2:=\langle f,f\rangle_C.
$$
This is the arcsine-weighted pairing on the compact Chebyshev interval: in the variable $x=\cos\theta$ its weight is $\omega_C(x)=(1-x^2)^{-1/2}$ for $-1<x<1$. The angular integral is the endpoint convention, so no endpoint value of the singular density is required.

Input a polynomial degree $N\ge0$ and an even integer $M\ge2$ specifying the number of uniform subintervals of $[0,\pi]$. For $0\le i,j\le N$, form
$$
g_{ij}(\theta)=T_i(\cos\theta)T_j(\cos\theta)
$$
and return
$$
M^{S}_{ij}:=Q_S(g_{ij};0,\pi,M),
$$
where $Q_S$ is the composite Simpson procedure from [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]]. By the Chebyshev multiple-angle identity, $g_{ij}(\theta)=\cos(i\theta)\cos(j\theta)$, so this is the composite-Simpson approximation of the corresponding arcsine-weighted mass entry. The procedure uses exact real arithmetic and asserts no quadrature or floating-point accuracy beyond a separately proved bound.

Let $N\ge0$, let $M\ge2$ be even, put $h=\pi/M$, and let $G_{ij}=\langle T_i,T_j\rangle_C$ be the exact weighted mass entry from [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]]. The approximation $M^S_{ij}$ from [[alg-chebyshev-composite-simpson-weighted-mass-matrix]] satisfies
$$
|G_{ij}-M^S_{ij}|\le \frac{\pi h^4}{180}(i+j)^4,\qquad 0\le i,j\le N.
$$

Under the pairing of [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]],
$$
\langle T_m,T_n\rangle_C=
\begin{cases}
\pi,&m=n=0,\\
\pi/2,&m=n\ge1,\\
0,&m\ne n.
\end{cases}
$$
The polynomials $T_0,T_1,\ldots$ form a basis of the real polynomial space, and the pairing is positive definite on continuous real functions on $[-1,1]$. If a continuous real function $h$ satisfies $\langle h,T_n\rangle_C=0$ for every $n\ge0$, then $h=0$ on $[-1,1]$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

For every $n\in\mathbb N$ and real $\theta$,
$$T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos(n\theta),\qquad U_n(\cos\theta)\sin\theta=\sin((n+1)\theta).$$ In particular, for $n\ge1$ and $0\le j\le n$, $T_n(\cos(j\pi/n))=(-1)^j$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-induction-principle]].

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq X$. The **subspace topology** (also *relative topology*) on $S$ is

$$\mathcal{T}_S := \{\, U \cap S : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\},$$

the family of **traces** on $S$ of the open sets of $X$. The pair
$(S, \mathcal{T}_S)$ is a **subspace** of $X$. A subset of $S$ that lies in
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is said to be **open in $S$**, and *relatively open* where the
ambient space needs emphasis.

**$\mathcal{T}_S$ is a topology, and this is discharged here.** (T1):
$\varnothing = \varnothing \cap S$ and $S = X \cap S$ are traces. (T2): if
$\mathcal{S}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}_S$, choose for each member a set of
$\mathcal{T}$ tracing to it — no choice principle is needed, since
$U' := \bigcup \{\, U \in \mathcal{T} : U \cap S \subseteq W \,\}$ is a canonical
such set for $W \in \mathcal{T}_S$, being open by (T2) in $X$ and satisfying
$U' \cap S = W$ — and then
$\bigcup_i (U_i \cap S) = (\bigcup_i U_i) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by (T2) in
$X$. (T3): $(U \cap S) \cap (V \cap S) = (U \cap V) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by
(T3) in $X$.

**Closed sets of a subspace are the traces of the closed sets.** A set
$C \subseteq S$ is closed in $S$ if and only if $C = F \cap S$ for some closed
$F \subseteq X$. Indeed $S \setminus (U \cap S) = (X \setminus U) \cap S$ and
$S \setminus (F \cap S) = (X \setminus F) \cap S$, so complementation inside $S$
matches complementation inside $X$ under tracing.

**Bases and subbases trace as well.** If $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]) then
$\mathcal{B}_S := \{\, B \cap S : B \in \mathcal{B} \,\}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$: its members are open in $S$, and for $W = U \cap S$ open in $S$
and $x \in W$ there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U$, whence
$x \in B \cap S \subseteq W$. The same computation with a subbasis $\mathcal{S}$
shows that $\{\, S_0 \cap S : S_0 \in \mathcal{S} \,\}$ is a subbasis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$, since tracing commutes with finite intersections and with
unions.

**The inclusion is continuous.** The inclusion map $\iota : S \to X$,
$\iota(s) = s$, satisfies $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$,
so preimages of open sets are open and $\iota$ is continuous
([[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]], clause (b)). Moreover
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is the **coarsest** topology on $S$ making $\iota$ continuous: any
topology on $S$ for which $\iota$ is continuous must contain every
$\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$, hence contain $\mathcal{T}_S$.

**Characteristic property of a map into a subspace.** Let $(Z, \mathcal{T}_Z)$ be
a topological space and let $g : Z \to S$ be a function. Then

$$g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (S,\mathcal{T}_S) \iff \iota \circ g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (X,\mathcal{T}) .$$

*Proof.* For $U \in \mathcal{T}$ one has
$(\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U] = g^{-1}[\iota^{-1}[U]] = g^{-1}[U \cap S]$. If $g$ is
continuous then each $g^{-1}[U \cap S]$ is open, so $\iota \circ g$ is continuous;
conversely if $\iota \circ g$ is continuous then for any $W = U \cap S$ open in
$S$ the set $g^{-1}[W] = (\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U]$ is open, so $g$ is continuous.
Both directions use only clause (b) of [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]].

**Restriction of a continuous map.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous and
$S \subseteq X$, then $f|_S : S \to Y$ is continuous, since
$(f|_S)^{-1}[V] = f^{-1}[V] \cap S$ is open in $S$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]).

**When relative and ambient agree.** If $S$ is open in $X$ then a subset of $S$
is open in $S$ if and only if it is open in $X$: a trace $U \cap S$ is then an
intersection of two open sets of $X$, and conversely an open subset of $X$
contained in $S$ is its own trace. The same statement with "closed" throughout
holds when $S$ is closed in $X$. Both are used in the pasting lemma of the next
item, and both fail without the hypothesis: $S$ itself is always open and closed
in $S$, and need be neither in $X$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: Under [A1], let $\mu$ be Lebesgue measure restricted to the relative Borel sets of $[-1,1]$. It is a positive measure with total mass $2$ by [F10]. Every relative open neighborhood of a point of $[-1,1]$ contains a positive-length interval, including a one-sided interval at either endpoint, so [F10] and measure monotonicity give that neighborhood positive measure. Thus the relative support is all of $[-1,1]$, containing at least three points. Every $|x|^k$ for $0\le k\le3$ is continuous and bounded on $[-1,1]$, so [F11] gives its integrability. These are exactly the order-three, $m=2$ moment-data conditions in [F1]. The primitives $x,x^2/2,x^3/3,x^4/4$ give moments $\mu_0=2,\mu_1=0,\mu_2=2/3,\mu_3=0$ by [F11].

By [F9], $g_{00}=1$, $g_{01}=\cos\theta$, and $g_{11}=\cos^2\theta$. Substitution of the quarter-turn values [F8] into [F5] gives $M^S_{00}=\pi$, $M^S_{01}=0$, and $M^S_{11}=\pi/3$. The exact mass matrix is $G=\operatorname{diag}(\pi,\pi/2)$ by [F7].

The monic polynomial $p_2(x)=x^2-1/3$ is orthogonal to $1$ and $x$, since $\mu_2-\mu_0/3=0$ and $\mu_3-\mu_1/3=0$ by step 1.1 and [F12]. Finite linearity extends this to every polynomial of degree below two, so uniqueness in [F1] identifies $p_2$ with the Gaussian orthogonal polynomial. Its nodes are $x_1=-1/\sqrt3$ and $x_2=1/\sqrt3$. Their cardinal polynomials are $\ell_1(x)=(1-\sqrt3x)/2$ and $\ell_2(x)=(1+\sqrt3x)/2$, so [F12] and the first two moments give $w_1=w_2=1$. The rule Definition and exactness theorem in [F1] therefore give $Q_2(f)=f(-1/\sqrt3)+f(1/\sqrt3)$, exact for degrees through three.

The Gaussian sum for the basis $1,x$ is $\begin{pmatrix}1&-1/\sqrt3\\1&1/\sqrt3\end{pmatrix}^{\!T} \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}1&-1/\sqrt3\\1&1/\sqrt3\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2/3\end{pmatrix}.$ The entries agree with exact integrals by [F2], as also asserted by [F3].

The only nonzero entry error is $|G_{11}-M^S_{11}|=\pi/6$. The Simpson theorem [F6] applies with $M=2$, $h=\pi/2$, and $i=j=1$, and gives its bound $\pi^5/180$. Therefore the displayed finite calculation matches the general entrywise estimate.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a$, then $D_vf(a)$ exists for every $v\in\mathbb R^m$ and equals $Df(a)v$. In particular $\partial_jf(a)=Df(a)e_j$, and the matrix of $Df(a)$ is $Jf(a)$.
For a $C^2$ scalar field $f$, $H_f(a)^T=H_f(a)$ at every point $a$.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

derivations.claim: Let $I$ be the open interval component of $\{t\in\mathbb R:x+tv\in U\}$ containing $[-\epsilon,\epsilon]$; it exists because that line segment lies in the open set $U$. Each $g_j(t):=\partial_jV(x+tv)$ is $C^3$ on the open, convex interval $I$. Apply [F2] to $g_j$ at $0$ with displacements $\pm\epsilon$. The linear terms are $\pm\epsilon(Hv)_j$ by [F1], the quadratic terms agree, and the coordinate remainders satisfy $|(r_\pm)_j|\le M_4\epsilon^3/6$ by [A1]. Thus $\|r_\pm\|_2\le\sqrt d\,M_4\epsilon^3/6$. Subtracting and dividing by $2\epsilon$ cancels the constant and quadratic terms and gives $\|D_\epsilon(x,v)-\nabla^2V(x)v\|_2\le\sqrt d\,M_4\epsilon^2/6$.

Write $e_\pm=\widehat g_\pm-g(x\pm\epsilon v)$. Then $\|e_+-e_-\|_2\le\|e_+\|_2+\|e_-\|_2\le2\eta$, so their contribution after division by $2\epsilon$ is at most $\eta/\epsilon$. Adding this to step 1.1 proves the inequality. A bound on this single direction alone supplies no bound on an operator acting on all directions.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is
**continuously differentiable**, or of class $C^1$, when it is totally
differentiable at every point of $U$ and the entries of its derivative matrix
are continuous functions on $U$.

For an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $a\in U$, a **local inverse of $f$ at
$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

Let $n\ge1$.  A linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$
([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) is **invertible** when there is a linear map
$B:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ such that

$$B(Au)=u\quad\hbox{and}\quad A(Bu)=u\qquad(u\in\mathbb R^n).$$

The map $B$ is unique: if $C$ has the same two properties, then
$C=C\circ(A\circ B)=(C\circ A)\circ B=B$.  It is denoted $A^{-1}$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open and closed sets
as in [[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]]. Then:

1. **Balls are open.** $B(x,r)$ is open, for every $x \in X$ and every $r > 0$.
2. **Arbitrary unions.** If $\mathcal{U}$ is any collection of open subsets of
   $X$, then $\bigcup \mathcal{U}$ is open.
3. **Finite intersections.** If $n \ge 1$ and $U_0, \dots, U_{n-1}$ are open,
   then $U_0 \cap \dots \cap U_{n-1}$ is open.
4. **Closed balls are closed.** $\bar B(x,r)$ is closed, for every $x \in X$ and
   every $r > 0$.

Together with the fact that $\emptyset$ and $X$ are open, recorded already in
[[def-metric-topology]], claims 2 and 3 say that $\mathcal{T}_d$ has exactly the
closure properties that the word *topology* names.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $A \subseteq X$
carry the subspace metric $d_A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]). Then:

1. **Under countable choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]),
   if $(A,d_A)$ is complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]), then $A$ is closed
   in $(X,d)$ ([[def-metric-topology]]). No completeness hypothesis on $X$ is needed.
2. **In ZF, without a choice axiom**, if $(X,d)$ is complete and $A$ is closed
   in $(X,d)$, then $(A,d_A)$ is complete.

Consequently, under countable choice, a subspace of a complete metric space is
complete if and only if it is closed.

The following form of the first direction is also choice-free: a complete
subspace contains the ambient limit of every convergent sequence of its
points. Hence it is closed whenever every point of its ambient closure is
already known to be the limit of a sequence from that subspace. This last
condition is pointwise existence, not a chosen family of sequences.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

derivations.claim: Since $\beta>0$ and $\epsilon>0$, $r=2\beta\epsilon>0$. On $B_2(x_0,2r)$ define $\Phi(y):=y-A^{-1}F(y)$. By [F1] and the chain rule, $D\Phi(y)=I-A^{-1}J(y)=A^{-1}(A-J(y))$. Since $A=J(x_0)$, the Lipschitz hypothesis gives $\|D\Phi(y)\|_{\rm op}\le\beta L\|y-x_0\|_2\le\beta Lr\le\tfrac12$ for $y\in\overline B_2(x_0,r)$.

On the open convex ball $B_2(x_0,r)$, step 1.1 gives $\|D\Phi(y)\|_{\rm op}\le\beta L\|y-x_0\|_2\le\beta Lr\le\tfrac12$. Applying [F3] on this open ball shows that $\Phi$ is $1/2$-Lipschitz there. Since $\Phi$ is continuous on $B_2(x_0,2r)$ by [F1], approximation by interior points extends the same inequality to every pair in $\overline B_2(x_0,r)$.

At the center, $\|\Phi(x_0)-x_0\|_2=\|A^{-1}F(x_0)\|_2\le\beta\epsilon=r/2$. For every $y\in\overline B_2(x_0,r)$, step 2.1 therefore gives $\|\Phi(y)-x_0\|_2\le\|\Phi(y)-\Phi(x_0)\|_2+\|\Phi(x_0)-x_0\|_2\le r/2+r/2=r$. Thus $\Phi$ maps the closed ball into itself.

The ball is nonempty and complete by [F4], so [F5] gives a unique fixed point $x_*\in\overline B_2(x_0,r)$. The fixed-point equation is $A^{-1}F(x_*)=0$; invertibility in [F2] yields $F(x_*)=0$. The ball membership gives the stated distance, and any zero in the ball is a fixed point of $\Phi$, so it equals $x_*$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is
**continuously differentiable**, or of class $C^1$, when it is totally
differentiable at every point of $U$ and the entries of its derivative matrix
are continuous functions on $U$.

For an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $a\in U$, a **local inverse of $f$ at
$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

Let $n\ge1$.  A linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$
([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) is **invertible** when there is a linear map
$B:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ such that

$$B(Au)=u\quad\hbox{and}\quad A(Bu)=u\qquad(u\in\mathbb R^n).$$

The map $B$ is unique: if $C$ has the same two properties, then
$C=C\circ(A\circ B)=(C\circ A)\circ B=B$.  It is denoted $A^{-1}$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be the function space of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], with $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$.

### The $p$-norm, for a rational exponent $p \ge 1$

Let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_p \;:=\; \Bigl(\sum_{k<n} |x_k|^{p}\Bigr)^{1/p},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]), the sum is the finite
sum of [[def-finite-sum]], and both powers are the **rational** powers of
[[def-rational-power]].

**Every power written here is defined.** Each base $|x_k|$ is a nonnegative real
and $p > 0$, so $|x_k|^{p}$ is given by [[def-rational-power]] for $|x_k| > 0$
and by its supplementary clause $0^{p} = 0$ for $|x_k| = 0$; the sum of these
nonnegative terms is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), and
$1/p$ is a positive rational, so the outer power is defined for the same two
reasons. The value does not depend on which representative of $p$ or of $1/p$ is
used ([[lem-rational-power-well-defined]]).

**The exponent is rational in this definition.**
[[def-rational-power]] supplies the nonnegative-base powers used here, and
[[thm-minkowski-finite]] supplies the corresponding triangle inequality for
rational $p \ge 1$. This item makes no claim with $p$ ranging over a real
interval; its rational domain is unchanged.

### The maximum norm

For $n \ge 1$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_\infty \;:=\; \max\{\, |x_k| \;:\; k < n \,\},$$

the maximum of a nonempty finite set of reals, which exists and is one of its
elements ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is required and propagates.** At $n = 0$ the set
$\{|x_k| : k<n\}$ is empty and has no maximum ([[def-max-min]]). This is the same
restriction the published [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] carries, for the same reason, and
**every statement on this page that mentions $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ inherits
it**. The $p$-norms for rational $p \ge 1$ carry no such restriction: at $n = 0$
each is the empty sum raised to a positive rational power, hence $0$.

### The three cases the rest of the page uses

- $\lVert x\rVert_1 = \sum_{k<n}|x_k|$, since $t^{1} = t$ for $t \ge 0$
  ([[lem-rational-power-laws]], and $0^{1} = 0$ by the supplementary clause).
- $\lVert x\rVert_2 = \bigl(\sum_{k<n}|x_k|^{2}\bigr)^{1/2} = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}x_k^{2}}$,
  which is exactly the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: the
  exponent $2$ agrees with the integer power, so $|x_k|^{2} = x_k^{2}$
  ([[lem-of-abs-value]]), and $t^{1/2}$ is the unique nonnegative square root of
  $t$, which is $\sqrt{t}$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[thm-of-square-roots]]).
  **The two notations denote the same function and no second Euclidean norm is
  introduced.**
- $\lVert x\rVert_\infty$ as above, for $n \ge 1$.

That each of these is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], and
that the metrics they induce are exactly the published $d_1$, $d_2$ and
$d_\infty$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], is
[[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]; it is proved there
and is not assumed here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. A von Neumann natural is the set of its
predecessors, $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so it can be
used directly as an index set. Define

$$\mathbb{R}^n := \{\, x : x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\},$$

and write $x_k$ for $x(k)$, $k < n$. Two elements of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are equal
exactly when they agree at every $k < n$, functions being equal when they have
the same values. For $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ put

$$d_1(x,y) := \sum_{k<n} |x_k - y_k|, \qquad d_2(x,y) := \sqrt{\ \sum_{k<n} (x_k - y_k)^2\ }, \qquad d_\infty(x,y) := \max\{\, |x_k - y_k| : k < n \,\}.$$

All three are well defined: the finite sums are those of [[def-finite-sum]]; the
sum of squares is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[lem-of-square-positive]])
so it has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); and
$\{|x_k - y_k| : k < n\}$ is a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$, because
$n \ge 1$, so it has a maximum ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**Then $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$ are metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$**
([[def-metric-space]]).

**Why $n \ge 1$.** For $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^0$ has exactly one element,
the empty function, and $d_1$ and $d_2$ are the empty sum $0$ and its root; but
$d_\infty$ would be the maximum of the empty set, which does not exist. The
hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is therefore not decoration, and it is carried by every
statement about $d_\infty$ in this library.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open and closed sets
as in [[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]]. Then:

1. **Balls are open.** $B(x,r)$ is open, for every $x \in X$ and every $r > 0$.
2. **Arbitrary unions.** If $\mathcal{U}$ is any collection of open subsets of
   $X$, then $\bigcup \mathcal{U}$ is open.
3. **Finite intersections.** If $n \ge 1$ and $U_0, \dots, U_{n-1}$ are open,
   then $U_0 \cap \dots \cap U_{n-1}$ is open.
4. **Closed balls are closed.** $\bar B(x,r)$ is closed, for every $x \in X$ and
   every $r > 0$.

Together with the fact that $\emptyset$ and $X$ are open, recorded already in
[[def-metric-topology]], claims 2 and 3 say that $\mathcal{T}_d$ has exactly the
closure properties that the word *topology* names.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $A \subseteq X$
carry the subspace metric $d_A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]). Then:

1. **Under countable choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]),
   if $(A,d_A)$ is complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]), then $A$ is closed
   in $(X,d)$ ([[def-metric-topology]]). No completeness hypothesis on $X$ is needed.
2. **In ZF, without a choice axiom**, if $(X,d)$ is complete and $A$ is closed
   in $(X,d)$, then $(A,d_A)$ is complete.

Consequently, under countable choice, a subspace of a complete metric space is
complete if and only if it is closed.

The following form of the first direction is also choice-free: a complete
subspace contains the ambient limit of every convergent sequence of its
points. Hence it is closed whenever every point of its ambient closure is
already known to be the limit of a sequence from that subspace. This last
condition is pointwise existence, not a chosen family of sequences.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

derivations.claim: Define $\Phi(y):=y-A^{-1}F(y)$ on $B_\infty(x_0,2r)$. By [F1] and the chain rule, $D\Phi(y)=I-A^{-1}DF(y)=A^{-1}(A-DF(y))$. The induced maximum norm is submultiplicative directly from its definition, so for $y\in\overline B_\infty(x_0,r)$ the Lipschitz hypothesis gives $\|D\Phi(y)\|_\infty\le\beta L\|y-x_0\|_\infty\le\beta Lr\le\tfrac12$.

For any $y,z$ in the closed radius-$r$ ball, their joining segment lies in the open radius-$2r$ ball. For each coordinate $j$, the scalar function $t\mapsto\Phi_j(z+t(y-z))$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ and differentiable on $(0,1)$ by [F1] and the chain rule. Its derivative has absolute value at most $\|D\Phi(z+t(y-z))\|_\infty\|y-z\|_\infty\le\tfrac12\|y-z\|_\infty$. Applying [F3] coordinatewise and taking the maximum gives $\|\Phi(y)-\Phi(z)\|_\infty\le\tfrac12\|y-z\|_\infty$.

At the center, $\|\Phi(x_0)-x_0\|_\infty=\|A^{-1}F(x_0)\|_\infty\le\beta\epsilon\le r/2$. Thus for $y$ in the closed ball, step 2.1 gives $\|\Phi(y)-x_0\|_\infty\le\|\Phi(y)-\Phi(x_0)\|_\infty+\|\Phi(x_0)-x_0\|_\infty\le r/2+r/2=r$, so $\Phi$ maps the ball into itself.

Let $(x^{(m)})$ be Cauchy in $d_\infty$. For every $j<n$, $|x^{(m)}_j-x^{(l)}_j|\le d_\infty(x^{(m)},x^{(l)})$, so the $j$th coordinate sequence is Cauchy in $\mathbb R$ and converges to some $y_j$ by [F4]. The finitely many unique limits define $y\in\mathbb R^n$. Given $\delta>0$, choose for each $j<n$ an index $K_j$ such that $|x^{(m)}_j-y_j|<\delta$ for $m\ge K_j$; since $n\ge1$, [F7] gives $K=\max_{j<n}K_j$. Then $d_\infty(x^{(m)},y)<\delta$ for $m\ge K$. Thus $(\mathbb R^n,d_\infty)$ is complete.

The closed ball is nonempty and complete by step 3.2 and [F5]. Hence [F6] gives a unique fixed point $x_*\in\overline B_\infty(x_0,r)$. Its fixed-point equation gives $A^{-1}F(x_*)=0$, and invertibility in [F2] yields $F(x_*)=0$.

By step 2.1, $\|\Phi(x_*)-\Phi(x_0)\|_\infty\le\tfrac12\|x_*-x_0\|_\infty$. The fixed-point identity $\Phi(x_*)=x_*$ and the center estimate in step 3.1 therefore give $\|x_*-x_0\|_\infty\le\tfrac12\|x_*-x_0\|_\infty+\beta\epsilon$, hence $\|x_*-x_0\|_\infty\le2\beta\epsilon$. Any zero in the ball is a fixed point of $\Phi$, hence equals $x_*$.

Let $d\ge2$, let $C_{\rm bad}\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the model's prescribed set of forbidden configurations, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d\setminus C_{\rm bad}$ be open. Call $U$ a **declared collision-free tube** when it is the supplied open domain on which the potential is defined; no physical interpretation of the choice of $U$ is implied. Let $V\in C^4(U,\mathbb R)$, using the $C^k$ convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], and let $a,b\in U$. A **regular path with fixed endpoints** is $R\in C^1([0,1],U;\mathbb R^d)$ such that $R(0)=a$, $R(1)=b$, and $R'(s)\ne0$ for every $s\in[0,1]$ (with one-sided derivatives at the endpoints). Its unit tangent and normal projector are

$$t(s):=\frac{R'(s)}{\|R'(s)\|_2},\qquad P_{t(s)}^\perp:=I-t(s)t(s)^T.$$

The path is a **regular minimum-energy path (MEP)** when

$$P_{t(s)}^\perp\nabla V(R(s))=0\qquad(0\le s\le1),$$

where $\nabla V$ is the gradient in [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. Thus the gradient is tangent to the path; at points where it vanishes the equation still holds. The endpoints are fixed data and need not be local minima unless that is added as a hypothesis. This is a conditional mathematical definition and makes no claim about reaction rates, physical mechanisms, or uniqueness.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

derivations.claim: Taylor's formula [F2] at $s+h$ and $s-h$ gives $R(s\pm h)=R(s)\pm hR'(s)+\frac{h^2}{2}R''(s)+r_\pm$ with $\|r_\pm\|_2\le M_3h^3/6$ by [A1]. Subtracting cancels the second-derivative terms, so $d_h=R'(s)+(r_+-r_-)/(2h)$ and $\|d_h-R'(s)\|_2\le M_3h^2/6=\delta_h$.

For unequal steps, write $R(s)-R(s-h_-)=h_-R'-\frac{h_-^2}{2}R''+r_-$ and $R(s+h_+)-R(s)=h_+R'+\frac{h_+^2}{2}R''+r_+$ with $\|r_\pm\|_2\le M_3h_\pm^3/6$ by [A1, F2]. Substitution into $d_{h_-,h_+}$ gives coefficient $1$ on $R'(s)$ and $0$ on $R''(s)$; the two remainder coefficients yield $\|d_{h_-,h_+}-R'(s)\|_2\le M_3h_-h_+/6=\delta_{h_-,h_+}$.

Since $\|R'(s)\|_2=1$, step 1.1 gives $\|d_h\|_2\ge1-\delta_h\ge1/2$, so $d_h\ne0$. Moreover, $|\|d_h\|_2-1|\le\delta_h$, and therefore $\|d_h/\|d_h\|_2-R'(s)\|_2\le\|d_h-R'(s)\|_2/\|d_h\|_2+|1-\|d_h\|_2|/\|d_h\|_2\le4\delta_h$.

The same normalization argument as in step 2.1, using $\delta_{h_-,h_+}\le1/2$, gives nonzero $d_{h_-,h_+}$ and normalized error at most $4\delta_{h_-,h_+}$. Setting $h_-=h_+=h$ recovers the centered formula, and if both steps are bounded by a fixed multiple of their maximum mesh size, their product is $O(h^2)$.

The path is a **regular minimum-energy path (MEP)** when

$$P_{t(s)}^\perp\nabla V(R(s))=0\qquad(0\le s\le1),$$

where $\nabla V$ is the gradient in [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. Thus the gradient is tangent to the path; at points where it vanishes the equation still holds. The endpoints are fixed data and need not be local minima unless that is added as a hypothesis. This is a conditional mathematical definition and makes no claim about reaction rates, physical mechanisms, or uniqueness.

Let $R:J\to\mathbb R^d$ be a unit-speed $C^3$ curve on an open interval $J$ containing $[0,1]$, and suppose $\max_j\sup_{s\in J_0}|R_j'''(s)|\le M_3/\sqrt d$ on the stencil interval $J_0$. For $s-h,s+h\in J_0$, define

$$d_h:=\frac{R(s+h)-R(s-h)}{2h},\qquad \widehat t_h:=\frac{d_h}{\|d_h\|_2}.$$

If $\delta_h:=M_3h^2/6\le1/2$, then $d_h\ne0$ and

$$\|d_h-R'(s)\|_2\le\delta_h,\qquad \|\widehat t_h-R'(s)\|_2\le4\delta_h.$$

For unequal positive steps $h_-,h_+$ with $s-h_-,s+h_+\in J_0$, define

$$d_{h_-,h_+}:=\frac{h_+}{h_-(h_-+h_+)}(R(s)-R(s-h_-))+\frac{h_-}{h_+(h_-+h_+)}(R(s+h_+)-R(s)).$$

If $\delta_{h_-,h_+}:=M_3h_-h_+/6\le1/2$, then it is nonzero and its unit normalization differs from $R'(s)$ by at most $4\delta_{h_-,h_+}$. In particular, equal steps give an $O(h^2)$ unit-tangent error; quasiuniform unequal steps give an $O(h_-h_+)$ error. No second-order claim is made for a one-sided tangent branch.

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-taylor-schlomilch-roche-remainder]], there are points $\xi_L,\xi_C$ between $a$ and $x$ such that
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_L)}{\iota((n+1)!)}(x-a)^{n+1}$$
and
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_C)}{\iota(n!)}(x-\xi_C)^n(x-a).$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

derivations.claim: On each mesh interval $[s,s+h]$, apply the one-dimensional degree-two formula [F3] to each coordinate of the extended curve at $s$; the endpoint convention supplies the required derivative continuity, and [A1, F2] gives a remainder vector $r$ with $\|r\|_2\le M_3h^3/6$. Thus $R(s+h)-R(s)=hT+\frac{h^2}{2}K+r$ with $T=R'(s)$, $K=R''(s)$, and $\|K\|_2\le K_2$. Differentiating $\|R'(s)\|_2^2=1$ gives $T^TK=0$ by the chain rule [F4]. Hence $|\|R(s+h)-R(s)\|_2^2-h^2|\le C h^4$ for a constant depending only on $K_2,M_3$; for sufficiently small $h$ the chord is at least $h/2$, so division by its sum with $h$ yields $|\ell_i-h|\le C_1h^3$.

For $s=ih+\theta h$ with $0\le\theta\le1$, apply the one-dimensional degree-one formula [F3] on $[ih,s]$ and $[ih,(i+1)h]$. The remainder bound in [F3] and $\|R''\|_2\le K_2$ give $R(s)=R(ih)+\theta hR'(ih)+O(K_2h^2)$ and $R((i+1)h)=R(ih)+hR'(ih)+O(K_2h^2)$. Subtracting the linear interpolant cancels the first-order term, so the pointwise interpolation error is bounded by $C_2h^2$, uniformly over all intervals.

Let $p_i=\sum_{m=1}^{i}\ell_m$ and $L_h=p_M$. Step 1.1 gives $|p_i-ih|\le iC_1h^3\le C_1Lh^2$ and $|L_h-L|\le C_1Lh^2$. Thus the redistributed target $q_j=jL_h/M$ satisfies $|q_j-jh|\le C_1Lh^2$. Each segment has length at least $h/2$ for small $h$. If target $q_j$ lies on segment $i$ at fraction $\theta$, then $p_{i-1}+\theta\ell_i=q_j$; combining $|p_{i-1}-(i-1)h|\le C_1Lh^2$, $|q_j-jh|\le C_1Lh^2$, and $|\ell_i-h|\le C_1h^3$ gives $|(i-1)h+\theta h-jh|\le C h^2$.

The point on the true curve at parameter $(i-1)h+\theta h$ is within $C_2h^2$ of the redistributed polygon point by step 1.2, and it is within $C h^2$ of $R(jh)$ by unit speed and step 2.1. The triangle inequality gives the claimed $C_3h^2$ bound, including endpoints where redistribution fixes the endpoints.

Let $V$ and $U$ be as in [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]], let $x\in U$, and let $H=\nabla^2V(x)$ use the convention of [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. Since $V\in C^4(U)$, it is $C^2$; [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]] gives $H^T=H$. In the standard Euclidean inner product this makes the endomorphism represented by $H$ self-adjoint. Therefore the real spectral theorem [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] applies, and $H$ has ordered eigenvalues $\lambda_1(H)\le\cdots\le\lambda_d(H)$.

A **validated ordered eigenvalue enclosure** is a list of intervals $I_j=[\ell_j,u_j]$ together with an independently checked certificate proving $\lambda_j(H)\in I_j$ for every $j$ and preserving the stated ordering. The exact Hessian $H$, interval arithmetic or another validated spectral method, and all rounding assumptions used by the certificate are part of that external certificate; a Ritz value or residual alone is not, by definition, such a certificate.

For $d\ge2$ and $\gamma>0$, the enclosure certifies **index one with gap $\gamma$** when $u_1\le-\gamma$ and $\ell_j\ge\gamma$ for every $j\ge2$. For $d=1$, the condition is $u_1\le-\gamma$, with no positive-eigenvalue clauses. A validated enclosure records the input evidence; this definition does not assert that any particular eigensolver produces it.
For a $C^2$ scalar field $f$, $H_f(a)^T=H_f(a)$ at every point $a$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a$, then $D_vf(a)$ exists for every $v\in\mathbb R^m$ and equals $Df(a)v$. In particular $\partial_jf(a)=Df(a)e_j$, and the matrix of $Df(a)$ is $Jf(a)$.
For a $C^2$ scalar field $f$, $H_f(a)^T=H_f(a)$ at every point $a$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ with Jacobian $J=DF$. Take $x_0\in U$ such that $A:=J(x_0)$ is invertible, and let $\beta>0$ be any bound with $\|A^{-1}\|_{\rm op}\le\beta$. Suppose $\epsilon:=\|F(x_0)\|_2>0$, set $r:=2\beta\epsilon$, and assume the open ball $B_2(x_0,2r)$ lies in $U$ and

$$\|J(x)-J(y)\|_{\rm op}\le L\|x-y\|_2\qquad(x,y\in B_2(x_0,2r))$$

for some $L\ge0$ with $\beta Lr\le\tfrac12$. Then $F$ has exactly one zero $x_*$ in the closed ball $\overline B_2(x_0,r)$, and

$$\|x_*-x_0\|_2\le2\beta\|F(x_0)\|_2.$$

If $F(x_0)=0$, then $x_0$ itself is a zero; this separate case makes no local uniqueness assertion.

Let $T:V\to V$ be self-adjoint on an $n$-dimensional real inner product space,
and list its eigenvalues in weakly decreasing order:

$$\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n.$$

Then for every $1\le k\le n$,

$$\lambda_k=\min_{\dim W=n-k+1}\ \max_{0\ne v\in W} R_T(v)=\max_{\dim U=k}\ \min_{0\ne v\in U} R_T(v).$$

derivations.claim: By [F1], the eigenvalues of $H$ are all at least distance $\gamma$ from zero. Using the orthonormal eigenbasis in [F2], $H$ is invertible and $\|H^{-1}\|_{\rm op}\le1/\gamma$.

If $\epsilon_g=0$, [F3] says $x$ is critical, and [F1] says its Hessian has exactly one negative eigenvalue. Suppose henceforth $\epsilon_g>0$ and use the inverse bound $\beta=1/\gamma$ from step 1.1. The radius in [F4] is then exactly $2\beta\epsilon_g=\rho$, and its Lipschitz condition is $\beta L\rho=L\rho/\gamma\le1/2$. Since $B_2(x,2\rho)\subset U$, every hypothesis of [F4] holds on the stated ball, so there is exactly one zero $x_*$ of $\nabla V$ in $\overline B_2(x,\rho)$ and $\|x_*-x\|_2\le\rho$.

Set $A=-H(x)$ and $E=-(H(x_*)-H(x))$. Then $A$ is symmetric with largest eigenvalue at least $\gamma$ and second-largest at most $-\gamma$. The Lipschitz hypothesis and $\|x_*-x\|_2\le\rho$ from step 2.1 give $\|E\|_{\rm op}\le L\rho\le\gamma/2$.

Let $q_1$ be a unit leading eigenvector of $A$. The maximum Rayleigh formula in [F5] yields $\lambda_1(A+E)\ge q_1^T(A+E)q_1\ge\lambda_1(A)-\|E\|_{\rm op}\ge\gamma/2>0$. The second-eigenvalue min-max formula in [F5], applied to $q_1^\perp$, yields $\lambda_2(A+E)\le\lambda_2(A)+\|E\|_{\rm op}\le-\gamma/2<0$. Every later eigenvalue is at most the second, so $A+E=-H(x_*)$ has exactly one positive eigenvalue and no zero eigenvalue. Thus $H(x_*)$ has exactly one negative eigenvalue and no zero eigenvalues. Together with step 2.1 this proves the stated local certificate; if $\epsilon_g=0$, step 2.1 already proved it.

Let $d\ge2$, let $C_{\rm bad}\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the model's prescribed set of forbidden configurations, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d\setminus C_{\rm bad}$ be open. Call $U$ a **declared collision-free tube** when it is the supplied open domain on which the potential is defined; no physical interpretation of the choice of $U$ is implied. Let $V\in C^4(U,\mathbb R)$, using the $C^k$ convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], and let $a,b\in U$. A **regular path with fixed endpoints** is $R\in C^1([0,1],U;\mathbb R^d)$ such that $R(0)=a$, $R(1)=b$, and $R'(s)\ne0$ for every $s\in[0,1]$ (with one-sided derivatives at the endpoints). Its unit tangent and normal projector are

$$t(s):=\frac{R'(s)}{\|R'(s)\|_2},\qquad P_{t(s)}^\perp:=I-t(s)t(s)^T.$$

The path is a **regular minimum-energy path (MEP)** when

$$P_{t(s)}^\perp\nabla V(R(s))=0\qquad(0\le s\le1),$$

where $\nabla V$ is the gradient in [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. Thus the gradient is tangent to the path; at points where it vanishes the equation still holds. The endpoints are fixed data and need not be local minima unless that is added as a hypothesis. This is a conditional mathematical definition and makes no claim about reaction rates, physical mechanisms, or uniqueness.

Let $R:J\to\mathbb R^d$ be a unit-speed $C^3$ curve on an open interval $J$ containing $[0,1]$, and suppose $\max_j\sup_{s\in J_0}|R_j'''(s)|\le M_3/\sqrt d$ on the stencil interval $J_0$. For $s-h,s+h\in J_0$, define

$$d_h:=\frac{R(s+h)-R(s-h)}{2h},\qquad \widehat t_h:=\frac{d_h}{\|d_h\|_2}.$$

If $\delta_h:=M_3h^2/6\le1/2$, then $d_h\ne0$ and

$$\|d_h-R'(s)\|_2\le\delta_h,\qquad \|\widehat t_h-R'(s)\|_2\le4\delta_h.$$

For unequal positive steps $h_-,h_+$ with $s-h_-,s+h_+\in J_0$, define

$$d_{h_-,h_+}:=\frac{h_+}{h_-(h_-+h_+)}(R(s)-R(s-h_-))+\frac{h_-}{h_+(h_-+h_+)}(R(s+h_+)-R(s)).$$

If $\delta_{h_-,h_+}:=M_3h_-h_+/6\le1/2$, then it is nonzero and its unit normalization differs from $R'(s)$ by at most $4\delta_{h_-,h_+}$. In particular, equal steps give an $O(h^2)$ unit-tangent error; quasiuniform unequal steps give an $O(h_-h_+)$ error. No second-order claim is made for a one-sided tangent branch.

Let $L>0$, let $M\ge1$ be an integer, and let $R:[0,L]\to\mathbb R^d$ be a unit-speed $C^3$ curve with $M$ equal arc-length intervals of length $h=L/M$. Suppose $\|R''\|_2\le K_2$ and the coordinate third derivatives satisfy the bound in [[lem-centered-chord-and-unequal-step-tangent-error]] with constant $M_3$. For sufficiently small $h$, each chord length $\ell_i=\|R(ih)-R((i-1)h)\|_2$ satisfies $|\ell_i-h|\le C_1h^3$, where $C_1$ depends only on $K_2,M_3$. The piecewise-linear interpolant through the samples differs from $R$ in supremum norm by at most $C_2h^2$. If this polygon is redistributed by linear interpolation at equally spaced cumulative-length targets, the $j$th redistributed image is within $C_3h^2$ of $R(jh)$, for every $j=0,\ldots,M$.

Here $C^3$ on $[0,L]$ means that $R$ is the restriction of a $C^3$ curve on an open interval containing $[0,L]$; derivatives at the endpoints are the continuous one-sided values, and the unit-speed and derivative bounds are required on $[0,L]$.

Let $U,V,a,b$ satisfy [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]]. **Inputs:** an integer $M\ge2$, images $R_0=a,R_1,\ldots,R_{M-1},R_M=b$ in $U$, a step size $\eta>0$, force and spacing tolerances $\tau_F,\tau_s\ge0$, and a finite update budget $N\in\mathbb N_0$. **Output:** the last image chain and one of `tolerances-met`, `geometry-failure`, `nonfinite-evaluation`, or `budget-exhausted`. A stop status is an algorithmic report, not a continuum-error certificate.

At iteration $k=0,\ldots,N$, perform the following in order.

1. For each interior $i=1,\ldots,M-1$, form the centered chord $c_i=R_{i+1}-R_{i-1}$. If $c_i=0$, return `geometry-failure`. Otherwise put $t_i=c_i/\|c_i\|_2$ and $F_i^\perp=-(I-t_it_i^T)\nabla V(R_i)$. If any force is nonfinite, return `nonfinite-evaluation`.
2. For the current chain set $\ell_i=\|R_i-R_{i-1}\|_2$ for $1\le i\le M$, $\bar\ell=M^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^M\ell_i$, $r_F=\max_{1\le i<M}\|F_i^\perp\|_2$, and $r_s=\max_{1\le i\le M}|\ell_i-\bar\ell|$. If $r_F\le\tau_F$ and $r_s\le\tau_s$, return `tolerances-met`.
3. If $k=N$, return `budget-exhausted`. Otherwise set $Y_0=a$, $Y_M=b$, and $Y_i=R_i+\eta F_i^\perp$ for interior images. Reject any nonfinite $Y_i$ with `nonfinite-evaluation`; if any $Y_i\notin U$, return `geometry-failure`.
4. Compute cumulative lengths $s_0=0$, $s_j=\sum_{i=1}^j\|Y_i-Y_{i-1}\|_2$, and total length $S=s_M$. If $S=0$ or any segment length is zero, return `geometry-failure`. For $j=1,\ldots,M-1$, place the new image at the unique point of the piecewise-linear polygon $Y_0,\ldots,Y_M$ whose cumulative length is $jS/M$; if that target is a vertex, use that vertex, and otherwise use linear interpolation on its unique containing segment. If any redistributed image lies outside $U$, return `geometry-failure`. Set $R_0^{k+1}=a,R_M^{k+1}=b$ and use the checked redistributed points as the new interior images.

This is the specified projected-force string variant. No convergence from arbitrary initial images, no automatic endpoint minimization, and no error estimate follow from the procedure alone.

derivations.claim: For unit vectors $u,v$, $uu^T-vv^T=(u-v)u^T+v(u-v)^T$, so $\|uu^T-vv^T\|_{\rm op}\le2\|u-v\|_2$. Apply this with $u=\widehat t_i$ and $v=t(ih)$. Since $P_v^\perp\nabla V(R_i)=0$ by [F1], we obtain $\|P_{\widehat t_i}^\perp\nabla V(R_i)\|_2\le2G\|\widehat t_i-t(ih)\|_2\le2GC_th^2$.

By [F3], write each neighboring chord length as $\ell_i^\pm=h+e_i^\pm$ with $|e_i^\pm|\le C_1h^3$. Hence $k|\ell_i^+-\ell_i^-|\le2kC_1h^3$, because the triangle inequality bounds the difference by $|e_i^+|+|e_i^-|$.

The spring term is tangent and has the bound in step 1.2; the normal component has the bound in step 1.1. Since $h\le1$, $h^3\le h^2$, so their sum is bounded by $(2GC_t+2kC_1)h^2$. The string redistribution error is the last assertion of [F3]. These statements concern the centered-tangent string discretization specified by [F4]; the improved NEB tangent is a different branch and is treated separately.

Let $U,V$ be as in [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]]. **Inputs:** an initial point $x_0\in U$, a unit initial mode reference $v_{\rm ref}\in\mathbb R^d$, a local-ball center $x_{\rm ref}\in U$, radius $r_{\rm loc}>0$, gradient tolerance $\tau_g\ge0$, eigenvalue margin $\gamma>0$, eigenpair residual tolerance $\tau_{\rm eig}\ge0$, mode-overlap threshold $0\le\tau_{\rm mode}<1$, and update budget $N\in\mathbb N_0$. Return the last point, aligned lowest-mode reference and one of `geometry-failure`, `outside-local-basin`, `gradient-residual-tolerance`, `budget-exhausted`, `eigensolve-tolerance-failure`, `index-one-branch-failure`, `mode-tracking-failure`, or a status returned by the vector Newton correction. At each iterate $x_k$, the eigensolver supplies an orthogonal matrix $Q=[q_1,\ldots,q_d]$, ordered approximate eigenvalues $\widehat\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\widehat\lambda_d$, and validated intervals $I_j=[\ell_j,u_j]$ in the sense of [[def-validated-eigenvalue-enclosures-for-an-index-one-hessian]]. Require every residual $\|H(x_k)q_j-\widehat\lambda_jq_j\|_2\le\tau_{\rm eig}$, $\sqrt d\,\tau_{\rm eig}\le\gamma/2$, and $\widehat\lambda_j\in I_j$. The Hessian $H=\nabla^2V$ is symmetric by [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]].

For $k=0,\ldots,N$, in order:

1. If $x_k\notin U$, return `geometry-failure`. If $x_k\notin B_2(x_{\rm ref},r_{\rm loc})$, return `outside-local-basin`. Compute $g_k=\nabla V(x_k)$. If $\|g_k\|_2\le\tau_g$, return `gradient-residual-tolerance`; if $k=N$, return `budget-exhausted`.
2. If an eigenpair residual exceeds $\tau_{\rm eig}$, $\sqrt d\tau_{\rm eig}>\gamma/2$, or some $\widehat\lambda_j\notin I_j$, return `eigensolve-tolerance-failure`. If the validated intervals do not satisfy $u_1\le-\gamma$ and $\ell_j\ge\gamma$ for all $j\ge2$ (with the dimension-one convention in the definition), return `index-one-branch-failure`. If $|q_1^Tv_{\rm ref}|<\tau_{\rm mode}$, return `mode-tracking-failure`; otherwise replace $q_1$ by its sign-aligned representative with $q_1^Tv_{\rm ref}\ge0$ and use this as the next mode reference. This overlap check detects a mode-branch change but does not alter the Newton correction.
3. Call [[alg-newton-correction-for-vector-residuals]] with $A=H(x_k)$ and $r=g_k$. If its Jacobian is singular, return `singular-hessian`. Its correction $p_k$ is the exact Newton solution of $H(x_k)p_k=-g_k$ in the mathematical model; the eigenpair data certifies the index-one branch but does not replace this linear solve.
4. If $x_k+p_k\notin U$ or lies outside $B_2(x_{\rm ref},r_{\rm loc})$, return `outside-local-basin`. Otherwise set $x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k$ and continue.

An approximate eigensolve has a finite residual-tolerance branch and an explicit failure status. The definition makes no global-convergence claim. Local quadratic behavior is stated separately and requires the hypotheses of [[thm-updated-jacobian-newton-local-quadratic-convergence]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be a linear map, and let
$r\in\mathbb R^n$ be a residual vector. If $A$ is not invertible in the sense
of [[def-invertible-euclidean-linear-map]], return
$(\texttt{singular-jacobian},\varnothing)$. If $A$ is invertible, return
$(\texttt{correction},s)$, where $s$ is the unique vector solving
$$As=-r.$$

The output is a linear correction, not a claim that $r$ came from a nonlinear
function or that applying the correction decreases a residual.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let
$F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^2$, meaning $F$ is $C^1$ and its first derivative
is itself continuously differentiable. Write $J(x)=DF(x)$ as a matrix in the
standard basis. Let $x_*\in U$ satisfy $F(x_*)=0$ and suppose $J(x_*)$ is
invertible. Suppose there are $R>0$ and $L\ge0$ such that the closed Euclidean
ball
$$\overline B_2(x_*,R):=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x-x_*\|_2\le R\}$$
lies in $U$ and
$$\|J(x)-J(y)\|_{\rm op}\le L\|x-y\|_2\qquad(x,y\in\overline B_2(x_*,R)),$$
where $\|A\|_{\rm op}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Av\|_2$. Then there are
$r\in(0,R]$ and $K>0$ such that every $J(x)$ on $\overline B_2(x_*,r)$ is
invertible with $\|J(x)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}\le K$. Put $C:=KL/2$ and choose
$\rho\in(0,r]$ with $C\rho\le1/2$ (if $L=0$, any $\rho\le r$ works).

For every $x_0\in\overline B_2(x_*,\rho)$, each update attempted by
[[alg-finite-budget-newton-for-vector-residuals]] is defined, remains in this
ball, and satisfies
$$\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|_2\le C\|x_k-x_*\|_2^2.$$
If the ordinary exact-Jacobian Newton recurrence is continued indefinitely,
these estimates imply $x_k\to x_*$ with a quadratic error bound. A finite
budget may stop before the residual tolerance is met; `root` status records
only that tolerance, not an exact-zero certificate. This result gives no
arbitrary-start or global-convergence guarantee.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a$, then $D_vf(a)$ exists for every $v\in\mathbb R^m$ and equals $Df(a)v$. In particular $\partial_jf(a)=Df(a)e_j$, and the matrix of $Df(a)$ is $Jf(a)$.
For a $C^2$ scalar field $f$, $H_f(a)^T=H_f(a)$ at every point $a$.

derivations.claim: At an accepted update, [F1] supplies the exact Hessian Jacobian and gradient residual to the Newton-correction procedure, and its validated ordered enclosures put every Hessian eigenvalue at distance at least $\gamma$ from zero. Thus the Hessian is invertible; [F2] makes the returned correction the unique solution of $\nabla^2V(x)p=-\nabla V(x)$, so the selected step is exactly the vector Newton step.

Let $x_*$ be the critical point. By [F4], $F(x_*)=0$ and $DF(x_*)=\nabla^2V(x_*)$ is invertible by [A1]. Since $V\in C^4$, $F$ is $C^2$; the assumed local Hessian-Lipschitz bound is a local Lipschitz bound on $DF$. Thus the hypotheses of [F3] hold.

The algorithm's update, whenever it is attempted, is the exact correction from step 1.1. Applying [F3] to this recurrence gives the asserted local quadratic bound and invariant neighborhood for every attempted update; if the algorithm stops on a residual or certification branch, there is no later point to which that update claim applies. No conclusion outside the local hypotheses follows.
