Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

For $\phi(x)=x\log x+(1-x)\log(1-x)$ with $0\log0=0$, the map
$D\mapsto\operatorname{tr}\phi(D)$ is continuous on the full domain
$\mathcal D_r$, including matrices with eigenvalues $0$ or $1$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Diagonalize $D$ by [F2], with eigenvalues $d_j\in[0,1]$ and $\sum_jd_j=r$. If $d_i=0$, then $r>0$ gives an index $j$ with $d_j>0$. For small $t>0$, $D_t=D+t(e_ie_i^*-e_je_j^*)$ remains in $\mathcal D_r$. If $d_j\in(0,1)$, $\phi'$ is bounded near $d_j$, so [F4] gives $\phi(d_j-t)-\phi(d_j)=O(t)$. Also $(1-t)\log(1-t)=O(t)$ because this scalar function is differentiable at $0$. Thus the entropy change is $\phi(t)+\phi(d_j-t)-\phi(0)-\phi(d_j)=t\log t+O(t)$ by [F3]. If $d_j=1$, it is $\phi(t)+\phi(1-t)=2t\log t+O(t)$ by $\phi(1-t)=\phi(t)$. The energy change is $O(t)$ by Fréchet differentiability of $\mathcal E$ at $D$ along the fixed direction $e_ie_i^*-e_je_j^*$. Dividing the total free-energy change by $t$ gives $\beta^{-1}\log t+O(1)$ (or $2\beta^{-1}\log t+O(1)$), which is negative for sufficiently small $t$. This contradicts minimality.

If $d_i=1$, then $r<n$ gives $j$ with $d_j<1$. Transfer $t$ from the $i$th eigendirection to the $j$th: $D_t=D+t(e_je_j^*-e_ie_i^*)$. If $d_j\in(0,1)$, the term that leaves the endpoint $1$ is $\phi(1-t)=\phi(t)=t\log t+O(t)$ and the interior term changes by $O(t)$ by [F4]. If $d_j=0$, the two endpoint terms change by $2\phi(t)=2t\log t+O(t)$. The energy change is $O(t)$ by differentiability as in step 1.1. Dividing by $t$ again gives a negative free-energy change for small $t$, contradicting minimality. No eigenvalue can equal $0$ or $1$, proving the claim.

Let $n\ge2$ and let $r$ be an integer with $1\le r<n$. Use Hermitian
adjoints and matrices as in [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], trace as in
[[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]], and the Frobenius norm as in
[[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]. Write
$$\mathbb H_n:=\{A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}:A=A^*\}$$
for the real vector space of Hermitian matrices, with Frobenius inner product
$$\langle A,B\rangle_F:=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(A^*B)=\operatorname{tr}(AB).$$
The **rank-$r$ orthogonal projector domain** is
$$\mathcal P_r:=\{P\in\mathbb H_n:P^2=P,\ \operatorname{tr}P=r\}.$$
An element of $\mathcal P_r$ is an orthogonal projector; its range is the occupied
subspace. The statement that its range has dimension $r$ is justified by
[[lem-hermitian-idempotent-trace-equals-rank]]. A frame $Y\in\mathbb C^{n\times r}$
with $Y^*Y=I_r$ represents $P=YY^*$; replacing $Y$ by $YQ$ for a unitary
$Q\in\mathbb C^{r\times r}$ leaves $P$ unchanged.

Fix $P_0\in\mathcal P_r$, put $U=\operatorname{range}P_0$ (range as in
[[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]), and use the orthogonal decomposition
$\mathbb C^n=U\oplus U^\perp$. Write $P_V$ for the orthogonal projector onto an
$r$-dimensional subspace $V$. Such a subspace $V$ for which the orthogonal projection
$\pi_U|_V:V\to U$ is invertible is uniquely a
graph $V_X=\{u+Xu:u\in U\}$ of a linear map $X:U\to U^\perp$. Its projector is
$$P(X)=J_X(I_U+X^*X)^{-1}J_X^*,\qquad J_Xu=u+Xu.$$
These graph coordinates form an open neighborhood of $P_0$ in the projector
Grassmannian. In the block decomposition at $P_0$, its tangent space is
$$T_{P_0}\mathcal P_r=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}0&B^*\\B&0\end{pmatrix}:B:U\to U^\perp\right\}.$$
The projector representation also removes orbital-frame gauge: two orthonormal
frames represent the same projector exactly when they differ by right
multiplication by a unitary matrix.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map whose domain $V$ is finite-dimensional over
$F$. Its **nullity** and **rank** are

$$\operatorname{nullity}T:=\dim_F(\ker T),\qquad \operatorname{rank}T:=\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Both dimensions are defined. The kernel is a linear subspace of the
finite-dimensional space $V$, so it is finite-dimensional by
[[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]] and
[[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]]. The image is finite-dimensional because
[[lem-kernel-basis-extension-gives-image-basis]] constructs a finite basis of
it from a basis of $V$. Thus rank and nullity are natural numbers, including
when $V$ is the zero space.

Let $A$ be invertible. Then the inversion map is real Fr\'echet differentiable
at $A$, and for every direction $H$,

$$D\operatorname{inv}(A)[H]=-A^{-1}HA^{-1}.$$

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

derivations.claim: Put $M_t=I-tK/2$. If $t\ne0$ and $M_tx=0$ for a nonzero $x$, then $Kx=(2/t)x$. By [F3], $\operatorname{Re}\langle Kx,x\rangle=0$, while this equation gives $\langle Kx,x\rangle=(2/t)\|x\|^2$, a nonzero real number. This contradiction shows $\ker M_t=\{0\}$; $M_0=I$ is also injective. By [F4], $M_t$ is invertible for every real $t$.

Put $N_t=I+tK/2$, so $M_t^*=N_t$. Since $M_t$ and $N_t$ are polynomials in $K$, they commute, and the same holds for $M_t^{-1}$. For $Q_K(t)=N_tM_t^{-1}$, the adjoint rules in [F5] give $Q_K(t)^*=N_t^{-1}M_t$. Thus $Q_K(t)^*Q_K(t)=N_t^{-1}M_tN_tM_t^{-1}=I$. In finite dimension this makes $Q_K(t)$ unitary.

We have $Q_K(0)=I$. From $M'_0=-K/2$ and [F5], $(M_t^{-1})'|_{t=0}=K/2$, hence the product rule gives $Q'_K(0)=K$. The curve $P_K(t)=Q_K(t)P Q_K(t)^*$ lies in $\mathcal P_r$: unitarity preserves self-adjointness and idempotence, and $\operatorname{tr}(Q_K(t)P Q_K(t)^*)=\operatorname{tr}(P Q_K(t)^*Q_K(t))=\operatorname{tr}P$ by the finite trace identity $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$. Its derivative at zero is $P'_K(0)=KP-PK=[K,P]$, so every such commutator is tangent.

Conversely, by [F2] any tangent at $P$ has block form $H_X=\begin{pmatrix}0&X^*\\X&0\end{pmatrix}$ in $\operatorname{range}P\oplus(\operatorname{range}P)^\perp$. Set $K_X=\begin{pmatrix}0&-X^*\\X&0\end{pmatrix}$, which satisfies $K_X^*=-K_X$. With $P=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, block multiplication gives $[K_X,P]=H_X$. Thus every tangent is a skew-Hermitian commutator direction, proving the equality.

For the data of [[def-finite-basis-projector-energy-model]], $E(P)$ is real
and $C^2$ on its stated neighborhood. For every Hermitian $P$ in that
neighborhood and every Hermitian direction $H$,
$$DE(P)[H]=\operatorname{tr}\big((h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P))H\big)=\langle F(P),H\rangle_F.$$
Thus $F(P)$ is the Hermitian Frobenius gradient of $E$.

Let $P\in\mathcal P_r$ and define the tangent space by velocities of differentiable curves in $\mathcal P_r$. Then
$$T_P\mathcal P_r=\{[K,P]:K^*=-K\},\qquad [K,P]:=KP-PK.$$
For each skew-Hermitian $K$, the curve can be realized near $t=0$ as
$P_K(t)=Q_K(t)P Q_K(t)^*$, where
$$Q_K(t):=(I+tK/2)(I-tK/2)^{-1}.$$

derivations.claim: Let $K^*=-K$. By [F2], $H_K=[K,P]$ is the velocity at zero of a feasible curve through $P$. The gradient formula [F1] gives $DE(P)[H_K]=\operatorname{tr}(F(P)(KP-PK))$. Cyclicity of trace, which follows from $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ji}=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$, rewrites this as $-\operatorname{tr}([F(P),P]K)$.

Put $C=[F(P),P]$. Since $F(P)$ and $P$ are Hermitian, $C^*=-C$. If $P$ is stationary, step 1.1 vanishes for every skew-Hermitian $K$; choosing $K=C$ gives $0=-\operatorname{tr}(C^2)=\operatorname{tr}(C^*C)=\|C\|_F^2$, so $C=0$. Conversely, if $C=0$, step 1.1 vanishes for every $K$, and [F2] says these are all tangent directions, so $P$ is stationary.

Let $n\ge2$, $r\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}$, and $\beta>0$. The fixed-particle
density-matrix domain is
$$\mathcal D_r:=\{D\in\mathbb H_n:0\preceq D\preceq I,\ \operatorname{tr}D=r\},$$
where $0\preceq D\preceq I$ means that both $D$ and $I-D$ are positive
semidefinite in the operator order ([[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]).
Define the continuous scalar entropy integrand on $[0,1]$ by
$$\phi(x):=x\log x+(1-x)\log(1-x),\qquad 0\log0:=0.$$
For $D\in\mathcal D_r$, $\phi(D)$ is defined by the spectral functional
calculus ([[def-functional-calculus-for-a-normal-endomorphism]],
[[prop-functional-calculus-for-normal-endomorphisms]]). The logarithm is the
natural logarithm on $(0,\infty)$ ([[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]).
Supply a real $C^1$ energy $\mathcal E$ on an open neighborhood of
$\mathcal D_r$ and its Hermitian Frobenius gradient $F_{\mathcal E}(D)$,
defined by $D\mathcal E(D)[H]=\langle F_{\mathcal E}(D),H\rangle_F$ for every
Hermitian direction $H$. Define
$$\mathcal F_\beta(D):=\mathcal E(D)+\beta^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\phi(D).$$
The fixed-Hermitian-field case is $\mathcal E(D)=\operatorname{tr}(FD)$ for a
fixed Hermitian $F$. For nonlinear self-consistent models, $\mathcal E$ and its
gradient may depend on $D$; the definition alone asserts no uniqueness of a
minimizing density.

Assume $\mathcal E$ in the model of
[[def-finite-temperature-density-matrix-free-energy]] is $C^1$ on an open
neighborhood of $\mathcal D_r$, with $0<r<n$ and $\beta>0$. Every global
minimizer $D$ of $\mathcal F_\beta$ satisfies $0\prec D\prec I$; equivalently,
each eigenvalue of $D$ lies strictly between $0$ and $1$.

For $0\prec D\prec I$ and every Hermitian direction $H$, let
$\mathcal S(D)=\operatorname{tr}(D\log D+(I-D)\log(I-D))$. Then
$$D\mathcal S(D)[H]=\operatorname{tr}\big(H(\log D-\log(I-D))\big).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space, let $T:V\to V$ be
normal, and let $f,g:\sigma(T)\to\mathbb C$.

1. $(f+g)(T)=f(T)+g(T)$.
2. $(fg)(T)=f(T)g(T)$.
3. If $\overline f(\lambda)=\overline{f(\lambda)}$, then $\overline f(T)=f(T)^*$.
4. If $h:f(\sigma(T))\to\mathbb C$, then $(h\circ f)(T)=h(f(T))$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

$$\exp(x)\to+\infty\quad(x\to+\infty),\qquad \exp(x)\to0\quad(x\to-\infty),$$
and the range of $\exp$ is contained in $(0,\infty)$ and is unbounded above with infimum $0$.

derivations.claim:
Let $H$ be any traceless Hermitian matrix. Since $D$ and $I-D$ are positive definite, their least eigenvalues have a positive minimum $\delta$. For $|t|\|H\|_2<\delta$, both $D+tH$ and $I-D-tH$ remain positive definite, and the trace remains $r$. Thus $D+tH$ is feasible for both signs of small $t$. At a minimizer its directional derivative is zero; [F3] gives
$$\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\left[F_{\mathcal E}(D)+\beta^{-1}(\log D-\log(I-D))\right]H\right)=0.$$

Put $A=F_{\mathcal E}(D)+\beta^{-1}(\log D-\log(I-D))$. This is Hermitian. Choose $H=A-(\operatorname{tr}A/n)I$, which is Hermitian and traceless. Step 1.1 gives $0=\operatorname{tr}(AH)=\operatorname{tr}(H^2)=\|H\|_F^2$, hence $H=0$ and $A=\mu I$ with real $\mu=\operatorname{tr}A/n$.

Rearranging step 2.1 gives $F_{\mathcal E}(D)=\mu I-\beta^{-1}(\log D-\log(I-D))$, so $F_{\mathcal E}(D)$ is a scalar function of $D$. In the spectral basis of $D$, for each eigenvalue $d\in(0,1)$ the scalar equation is $\lambda=\mu-\beta^{-1}\log(d/(1-d))$, whose unique solution is $d=(1+\exp(\beta(\lambda-\mu)))^{-1}$. Applying this scalar identity to the spectral functional calculus [F4] proves the matrix formula.

For a fixed Hermitian $F$, diagonalize it by [F4] with real eigenvalues $\lambda_j(F)$, and define $g(\mu):=\sum_{j=1}^n(1+\exp(\beta(\lambda_j(F)-\mu)))^{-1}$. By [F6] and $\beta>0$, each summand is continuous and strictly increasing in $\mu$. Its limits are $0$ as $\mu\to-\infty$ and $1$ as $\mu\to+\infty$, so $g$ is continuous and strictly increasing with limits $0$ and $n$. Since $0<r<n$, these limits give finite real numbers $\mu_-$ and $\mu_+$ with $g(\mu_-)<r<g(\mu_+)$. Strict increase implies $\mu_-<\mu_+$. Applying [F5] to $g$ on the closed interval $[\mu_-,\mu_+]$ gives a solution with $g(\mu)=r$, and strict increase makes it unique. This scalar argument proves uniqueness of the multiplier for the fixed field only.

Let $E$ and $F(P)=\nabla E(P)$ be the finite-basis model and gradient of
[[def-finite-basis-projector-energy-model]]. A projector $P\in\mathcal P_r$
is stationary for $E$ restricted to $\mathcal P_r$ if and only if
$$[F(P),P]:=F(P)P-PF(P)=0.$$
Stationarity is only a first-order condition; it does not assert that $P$ is a
minimum.

Fix $P_0\in\mathcal P_r$, put $U=\operatorname{range}P_0$ (range as in
[[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]), and use the orthogonal decomposition
$\mathbb C^n=U\oplus U^\perp$. Write $P_V$ for the orthogonal projector onto an
$r$-dimensional subspace $V$. Such a subspace $V$ for which the orthogonal projection
$\pi_U|_V:V\to U$ is invertible is uniquely a
graph $V_X=\{u+Xu:u\in U\}$ of a linear map $X:U\to U^\perp$. Its projector is
$$P(X)=J_X(I_U+X^*X)^{-1}J_X^*,\qquad J_Xu=u+Xu.$$
These graph coordinates form an open neighborhood of $P_0$ in the projector
Grassmannian. In the block decomposition at $P_0$, its tangent space is
$$T_{P_0}\mathcal P_r=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}0&B^*\\B&0\end{pmatrix}:B:U\to U^\perp\right\}.$$
The projector representation also removes orbital-frame gauge: two orthonormal
frames represent the same projector exactly when they differ by right
multiplication by a unitary matrix.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

derivations.claim: The derivative of $\psi$ at $0$ is $D\psi(0)[X]=DE(P_0)[DP(0)[X]]$. The chart differential is tangent by [F2], so stationarity [F1] makes this derivative zero for every $X$.

For $X$ in this neighborhood, the one-variable fundamental theorem of calculus [F3] applied twice to $t\mapsto\psi(tX)$ gives $\psi(X)-\psi(0)-D\psi(0)[X]=\int_0^1(1-t)D^2\psi(tX)[X,X]dt\ge\frac c4\|X\|_F^2$. The graph chart is one-to-one and maps an open neighborhood of $0$ onto a neighborhood of $P_0$ in projector space by [F2]. Projectors represent unitary-equivalence classes of occupied frames, so the same statement is strict local minimality modulo orbital gauge.

Let $K_1\subseteq K_2\subseteq\cdots$ be nonempty compact feasible sets in a
common finite-basis or continuum feasible set $K$, and let $E:K\to\mathbb R$
be continuous. Put $m_j=\min_{P\in K_j}E(P)$. Then $m_j$ is nonincreasing and
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}m_j=\inf_{P\in\bigcup_jK_j}E(P),$$
where the limit is allowed to be $-\infty$. If additionally every $P\in K$ has
a sequence $P_j\in\bigcup_jK_j$ with $P_j\to P$ in the chosen energy topology
and $E(P_j)\to E(P)$, then this limit equals $\inf_{P\in K}E(P)$. In
particular, equality with a continuum infimum requires a proved energy-recovery
property for the specified functional; nestedness alone does not imply it.

In this statement, infima are taken in the extended real line
$\overline{\mathbb R}:=\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}$: for a nonempty
set of real values, the infimum is its real greatest lower bound when it is
bounded below, and is $-\infty$ when it is unbounded below. In the bounded-below
case this agrees with [[def-infimum]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric

image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $A$ be a Hermitian operator on a nonzero
finite-dimensional real or complex Hilbert space. Let $u$ be a unit vector,
$\mu:=(Au,u)$ its Rayleigh quotient, and
$\rho:=\|(A-\mu I)u\|$. Let $\Sigma(A)$ be the finite set of eigenvalues of
$A$ and, for a nonempty finite set $S\subseteq\mathbb R$, define
$\operatorname{dist}(x,S):=\min_{\nu\in S}|x-\nu|$. Then
$$\operatorname{dist}(\mu,\Sigma(A))\le\rho.$$
If a specified target eigenvalue $\lambda\in\Sigma(A)$ is simple, let $e$ be
any unit eigenvector for it. If $\Sigma(A)\setminus\{\lambda\}$ is nonempty,
assume the certified separation
$$\Delta:=\min_{\nu\in\Sigma(A)\setminus\{\lambda\}}|\mu-\nu|>0.$$
Then the phase-invariant angle satisfies
$$\sin\angle(u,e):=\sqrt{1-| (u,e) |^2}\le\rho/\Delta.$$
If the target is the only eigenvalue, simplicity implies the Hilbert space is
one-dimensional and the angle is zero.
The residual alone does not identify which eigenvalue is nearby, in particular
it does not certify that the target is the lowest eigenvalue.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis

derivations.claim: By [F2], the eigenvalues of $A$ are $-1$ and $1$, so its ground eigenvalue is $-1$. The vector $u=e_2$ is a unit eigenvector for $1$, whence $\mu=u^*Au=1$ and $(A-\mu I)u=0$. Thus $\rho=0$.

Let $H=H^*\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ be a finite Hermitian stiffness matrix and
let $S=S^*>0$ be a positive-definite overlap or mass matrix. By Cholesky
factorization ([[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]),
write $S=LL^*$ with $L$ invertible lower triangular and positive diagonal.
Define the whitened Hermitian matrix
$$\widetilde H:=L^{-1}HL^{-*},\qquad L^{-*}:=(L^*)^{-1}.$$
The generalized Ritz equation $Hc=\lambda Sc$ is equivalent under the
invertible change of coordinates $y=L^*c$ to
$\widetilde H y=\lambda y$. The Rayleigh quotients agree:
$$\frac{c^*Hc}{c^*Sc}=\frac{y^*\widetilde H y}{y^*y}\qquad(c\ne0).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

derivations.claim: The vectors $q_+=(1,1)/\sqrt2$ and $q_-=(1,-1)/\sqrt2$ are orthonormal and satisfy $S_\varepsilon q_+=(2-\varepsilon)q_+$ and $S_\varepsilon q_-=\varepsilon q_-$. Both eigenvalues are positive, and their ratio is $(2-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon$.

Let $S_\varepsilon=LL^*$ be its Cholesky factorization. By [F1], $y=L^*c$ preserves the exact generalized eigenvalues and Rayleigh quotient. Also $(L^{-1})^*L^{-1}=L^{-*}L^{-1}=S_\varepsilon^{-1}$, so [F2] gives $\|L^{-1}\|_2=\varepsilon^{-1/2}$; the inverse coordinate map $c=L^{-*}y$ has the same operator norm. A unit perturbation in a maximizing singular direction can therefore be amplified by this factor when converted back to coefficient coordinates.

As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, the condition number and coordinate amplification diverge, although the exact whitening identities in [F1] continue to hold for each $\varepsilon>0$. $$\mathcal P_r:=\{P\in\mathbb H_n:P^2=P,\ \operatorname{tr}P=r\}.$$

subspace. The statement that its range has dimension $r$ is justified by

Let $Q:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be a finite quadrature functional of the form
$$Q(g)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i g(x_i),$$
where $m\ge1$, the nodes $x_i\in[0,1]$ are distinct, and $w_i\in\mathbb R$.
A one-dimensional **nested level hierarchy** is a sequence
$(Q_\ell)_{\ell\in\mathbb N_0}$ of such functionals, with node sets
$X_\ell=\{x_{\ell,i}:1\le i\le m_\ell\}$ satisfying
$X_{\ell-1}\subseteq X_\ell$ for every $\ell\ge1$.
Set $Q_{-1}:=0$, the zero functional, and define the **detail functional**
$$\Delta_0:=Q_0,\qquad \Delta_\ell:=Q_\ell-Q_{\ell-1}\quad(\ell\ge1).$$
Finite sums are as in [[def-finite-sum]]. For each $d\ge1$, the integration
functional used below is $I_d(f):=\int_{[0,1]^d}f$, with the multiple Riemann
integral convention of [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]].

The convergence and rate results in this pair use the **dyadic composite-
Simpson hierarchy**
$$Q_\ell(g):=Q_S(g;0,1,2^{\ell+1}),\qquad X_\ell=\{k/2^{\ell+1}:0\le k\le2^{\ell+1}\},$$
where $Q_S$ is the even-panel rule of [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]]. The
number of panels is even and at least two. The sets are nested because
$k/2^{\ell}=2k/2^{\ell+1}$, and their weights are nonnegative with total
weight one: each two-panel block has nonnegative weights $H(1,4,1)/6$
summing to its length $H$, and the blocks partition an interval of length one.
Level zero has nodes $0,1/2,1$ and weights $1/6,4/6,1/6$.

For a multi-index $\ell=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$, any tensor
product $R_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes R_{\ell_d}^{(d)}$ of these
finite functionals means the finite weighted functional obtained by multiplying
the coordinate weights and evaluating on the corresponding node tuples. In
particular, $\Delta_\ell:=\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes
\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)}$. No exactness or error property is implied by the
notation alone.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

A bounded $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle is Riemann
integrable if and only if, for every $\varepsilon>0$, some grid $P$ satisfies
$U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\varepsilon$.

A **grid partition** $P$ of a nondegenerate rectangle $Q=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is a family, one for each $j<m$, of one-dimensional partitions $a_j=t_{j,0}<\cdots<t_{j,n_j}=b_j$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]). For a multi-index $i=(i_0,\ldots,i_{m-1})$ with $i_j<n_j$, its cell is
$$Q_i:=\prod_{j<m}[t_{j,i_j},t_{j,i_j+1}].$$
A sum over cells means the iterated recursive sum $\sum_{i_0<n_0}\cdots\sum_{i_{m-1}<n_{m-1}}$ of [[def-finite-sum]]. The **mesh** is $\max_{j<m,i_j<n_j}(t_{j,i_j+1}-t_{j,i_j})$, which exists by [[lem-finite-set-has-max]] and is the largest $d_\infty$-diameter ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]], [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]).

Refinement is coordinatewise. Coordinatewise union gives a common refinement. The cells cover $Q$ and have pairwise disjoint interiors. Repeated splitting of finite sums and induction on $m$ give
$$\sum_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)=\operatorname{vol}(Q).$$
These statements include boundary overlaps: boundaries may meet, but interiors do not, and volume splitting is algebraic.

Let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded on a nondegenerate rectangle and let $P$ be a grid. For each cell $Q_i$, put
$$m_i:=\inf f[Q_i],\quad M_i:=\sup f[Q_i],\quad L(f,P):=\sum_i m_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),\quad U(f,P):=\sum_i M_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i).$$
The extrema exist as finite reals because each nonempty image is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]), and the sums use the iterated convention of [[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]].

Since $m_i\le M_i$ and cell volumes are nonnegative, $L(f,P)\le U(f,P)$. Moreover
$$U(f,P)-L(f,P)=\sum_i(M_i-m_i)\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),$$
the sum of cell oscillations weighted by volume ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.

Input real endpoints $a,b$, an integer $n$, and an evaluation function $f$.
If $a\ge b$ or $n<2$, return invalid-grid without evaluating $f$. For the
remaining inputs require $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ to be evaluable at every
point of $[a,b]$. If $n$ is odd, the procedure returns
invalid-Simpson-panel-count. If $n$ is even, put
$h=(b-a)/n$ and $x_j=a+jh$ for $0\le j\le n$; return

$$Q_S(f;a,b,n):=\frac h3\sum_{j<n/2}\bigl(f(x_{2j})+4f(x_{2j+1})+f(x_{2j+2})\bigr).$$

The sum is a finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Each two-panel block
$[x_{2j},x_{2j+2}]$ uses its endpoints and midpoint. Expanding the block sum
gives weights $1,4,2,\ldots,4,1$. The even condition
$n\ge2$ makes the number of blocks a positive integer. The formula is an exact-real
procedure; floating point evaluation and summation error are separate from
its quadrature error.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].

A sequence $(x_k)$ of reals **converges** to $x \in \mathbb{R}$ when for
every rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K$ with
$|x_k - x| < \hat\varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$. It is **Cauchy** when for
every rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K$ with
$|x_k - x_l| < \hat\varepsilon$ for all $k, l \ge K$.

Let $a, b$ be elements of a field ([[def-field]]) and let integer powers be as in
[[def-integer-power]].

1. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$: $a^{m+n} = a^m a^n$, $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$ and $(ab)^n = a^n b^n$.
2. If $a \ne 0$ then $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $a^{-m} = (a^m)^{-1}$ for every $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ ([[def-int-operations]]).
3. If $a \ne 0$ and $b \ne 0$ then all three identities of claim 1 hold for all $m, n \in \mathbb{Z}$.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in [[def-field]], and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ then $ab > 0$.
2. If $a > 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab < 0$.
3. If $a < 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab > 0$.
4. If $c > 0$ then $a < b \iff ac < bc$.
5. If $c < 0$ then $a < b \iff bc < ac$ (multiplication by a negative reverses order).

derivations.claim: Fix $\varepsilon>0$. By [F2] and [F3], $f$ is uniformly continuous on $[0,1]^d$. Choose $\delta>0$ such that $\|x-y\|_2<\delta$ implies $|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon$. By [F12], $\delta/\sqrt d>0$; use [F11] to choose a positive rational $\rho<\delta/\sqrt d$, then [F10] to choose $L$ with $H=2^{-L}<\rho$. Thus $\sqrt d\,H<\delta$, and every cell of the uniform $d$-dimensional grid has diameter $\sqrt d\,H$.

For the $L$ chosen in step 1.1, the tensor Simpson rule is the sum over grid cells of their tensor two-panel block rules: each cell contributes $H^d$ times a weighted average of its $3^d$ endpoint/midpoint tensor nodes, with coefficients $\prod_{j=1}^d(1,4,1)_{i_j}/6^d$. These coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one by [F7]. Each closed cell is compact and nonempty, so [F9] gives finite infimum and supremum of $f$ there. Every node lies in its cell and its value lies between those extrema. Regrouping finite sums by [F8] gives $L(f,P_L)\le Q_L^{\otimes d}(f)\le U(f,P_L)$, with the factors $H^d$ equal to cell volumes.

By step 1.1, the oscillation of $f$ on each cell is at most $\varepsilon$. Thus [F5]–[F6] give $U(f,P_L)-L(f,P_L)\le\varepsilon\sum_C\operatorname{vol}(C)=\varepsilon$. By [F4], $I_d(f)$ lies between these Darboux sums; step 2.1 places the tensor-Simpson value between them as well. Therefore $|Q_L^{\otimes d}(f)-I_d(f)|\le\varepsilon$. This holds for sufficiently large $L$ for each $\varepsilon>0$, proving convergence.

Let $Q:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be a finite quadrature functional of the form
$$Q(g)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i g(x_i),$$
where $m\ge1$, the nodes $x_i\in[0,1]$ are distinct, and $w_i\in\mathbb R$.
A one-dimensional **nested level hierarchy** is a sequence
$(Q_\ell)_{\ell\in\mathbb N_0}$ of such functionals, with node sets
$X_\ell=\{x_{\ell,i}:1\le i\le m_\ell\}$ satisfying
$X_{\ell-1}\subseteq X_\ell$ for every $\ell\ge1$.
Set $Q_{-1}:=0$, the zero functional, and define the **detail functional**
$$\Delta_0:=Q_0,\qquad \Delta_\ell:=Q_\ell-Q_{\ell-1}\quad(\ell\ge1).$$
Finite sums are as in [[def-finite-sum]]. For each $d\ge1$, the integration
functional used below is $I_d(f):=\int_{[0,1]^d}f$, with the multiple Riemann
integral convention of [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]].

The convergence and rate results in this pair use the **dyadic composite-
Simpson hierarchy**
$$Q_\ell(g):=Q_S(g;0,1,2^{\ell+1}),\qquad X_\ell=\{k/2^{\ell+1}:0\le k\le2^{\ell+1}\},$$
where $Q_S$ is the even-panel rule of [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]]. The
number of panels is even and at least two. The sets are nested because
$k/2^{\ell}=2k/2^{\ell+1}$, and their weights are nonnegative with total
weight one: each two-panel block has nonnegative weights $H(1,4,1)/6$
summing to its length $H$, and the blocks partition an interval of length one.
Level zero has nodes $0,1/2,1$ and weights $1/6,4/6,1/6$.

For a multi-index $\ell=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$, any tensor
product $R_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes R_{\ell_d}^{(d)}$ of these
finite functionals means the finite weighted functional obtained by multiplying
the coordinate weights and evaluating on the corresponding node tuples. In
particular, $\Delta_\ell:=\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes
\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)}$. No exactness or error property is implied by the
notation alone.

Let $a<b$, let $n\ge2$ be an even integer, and put $h=(b-a)/n$. If
$f\in C^4([a,b])$, set $M_4=\max_{x\in[a,b]}|f^{(4)}(x)|$. Then the value
$Q_S(f;a,b,n)$ of [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]] satisfies

$$\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-Q_S(f;a,b,n)\right|\le\frac{(b-a)h^4}{180}M_4.$$

The integral is the Riemann integral. This is an exact-arithmetic quadrature
bound; evaluation and summation roundoff are not included.

Input real endpoints $a,b$, an integer $n$, and an evaluation function $f$.
If $a\ge b$ or $n<2$, return invalid-grid without evaluating $f$. For the
remaining inputs require $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ to be evaluable at every
point of $[a,b]$. If $n$ is odd, the procedure returns
invalid-Simpson-panel-count. If $n$ is even, put
$h=(b-a)/n$ and $x_j=a+jh$ for $0\le j\le n$; return

$$Q_S(f;a,b,n):=\frac h3\sum_{j<n/2}\bigl(f(x_{2j})+4f(x_{2j+1})+f(x_{2j+2})\bigr).$$

The sum is a finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Each two-panel block
$[x_{2j},x_{2j+2}]$ uses its endpoints and midpoint. Expanding the block sum
gives weights $1,4,2,\ldots,4,1$. The even condition
$n\ge2$ makes the number of blocks a positive integer. The formula is an exact-real
procedure; floating point evaluation and summation error are separate from
its quadrature error.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals and $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the absolute value as in
[[def-abs-value]]. Then

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k\Big| \le \sum_{k<n} |a_k|.$$

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $a, b$ be elements of a field ([[def-field]]) and let integer powers be as in
[[def-integer-power]].

1. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$: $a^{m+n} = a^m a^n$, $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$ and $(ab)^n = a^n b^n$.
2. If $a \ne 0$ then $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $a^{-m} = (a^m)^{-1}$ for every $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ ([[def-int-operations]]).
3. If $a \ne 0$ and $b \ne 0$ then all three identities of claim 1 hold for all $m, n \in \mathbb{Z}$.

derivations.claim: For $\ell\ge1$, use [F2] on levels $\ell$ and $\ell-1$, inserting the exact integral between their values. With panel counts $2^{\ell+1}$ and $2^\ell$, [F5] gives $|\Delta_\ell g|\le(2^{-4(\ell+1)}/180+2^{-4\ell}/180)\|g^{(4)}\|_\infty=(17/2880)16^{-\ell}\|g^{(4)}\|_\infty$. For $\ell=0$, [F3] gives $|\Delta_0g|=|Q_0g|\le\|g\|_\infty$.

Apply the one-dimensional bounds successively in the coordinates. A finite quadrature functional commutes with derivatives in any other coordinate because it is a finite weighted sum. In each active coordinate $j$, apply step 1.1 to the section after the earlier-coordinate derivatives have been taken; the needed fourth derivative is the corresponding sequential mixed derivative. In each inactive coordinate use the level-zero supremum bound. Multiplying the bounds gives $M_{S(\ell)}(17/2880)^{|S(\ell)|}16^{-\sum_{j\in S(\ell)}\ell_j}$. The stated continuous mixed derivatives justify each section estimate, and [F6] justifies the finite tensor expansions.

Fix finite $F$ and group indices by $S=S(\ell)$. For a fixed nonempty $S$, enlarge its levels to the finite box $1\le\ell_j\le R_j$ where $R_j$ is the largest such coordinate level in that group. By step 2.1 and [F6], the sum over that box is at most $M_S\prod_{j\in S}((17/2880)\sum_{r=1}^{R_j}16^{-r})\le M_S(17/43200)^{|S|}$, using [F7]. For $S=\varnothing$, the only possible index is $0$ and its term is at most $M_\varnothing$. Summing over all subsets proves the finite-subsum claim; the right side is finite.

Let $Q:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be a finite quadrature functional of the form
$$Q(g)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i g(x_i),$$
where $m\ge1$, the nodes $x_i\in[0,1]$ are distinct, and $w_i\in\mathbb R$.
A one-dimensional **nested level hierarchy** is a sequence
$(Q_\ell)_{\ell\in\mathbb N_0}$ of such functionals, with node sets
$X_\ell=\{x_{\ell,i}:1\le i\le m_\ell\}$ satisfying
$X_{\ell-1}\subseteq X_\ell$ for every $\ell\ge1$.
Set $Q_{-1}:=0$, the zero functional, and define the **detail functional**
$$\Delta_0:=Q_0,\qquad \Delta_\ell:=Q_\ell-Q_{\ell-1}\quad(\ell\ge1).$$
Finite sums are as in [[def-finite-sum]]. For each $d\ge1$, the integration
functional used below is $I_d(f):=\int_{[0,1]^d}f$, with the multiple Riemann
integral convention of [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]].

The convergence and rate results in this pair use the **dyadic composite-
Simpson hierarchy**
$$Q_\ell(g):=Q_S(g;0,1,2^{\ell+1}),\qquad X_\ell=\{k/2^{\ell+1}:0\le k\le2^{\ell+1}\},$$
where $Q_S$ is the even-panel rule of [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]]. The
number of panels is even and at least two. The sets are nested because
$k/2^{\ell}=2k/2^{\ell+1}$, and their weights are nonnegative with total
weight one: each two-panel block has nonnegative weights $H(1,4,1)/6$
summing to its length $H$, and the blocks partition an interval of length one.
Level zero has nodes $0,1/2,1$ and weights $1/6,4/6,1/6$.

For a multi-index $\ell=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$, any tensor
product $R_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes R_{\ell_d}^{(d)}$ of these
finite functionals means the finite weighted functional obtained by multiplying
the coordinate weights and evaluating on the corresponding node tuples. In
particular, $\Delta_\ell:=\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes
\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)}$. No exactness or error property is implied by the
notation alone.

Fix a dimension $d\ge1$. A finite set $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$ is
**downward closed** if, whenever $\ell\in\Lambda$ and $\ell_j>0$, the index
$\ell-e_j$ also belongs to $\Lambda$; here $e_j$ is the $j$th coordinate unit
vector. In this pair an admissible Smolyak set is a nonempty finite downward-
closed $\Lambda$ that contains $0$.

For a level hierarchy from [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]], define
the **Smolyak cubature functional**
$$Q_\Lambda(f):=\sum_{\ell\in\Lambda}(\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)})(f).$$
Each summand is a finite signed weighted sum. Expanding all differences and
adding coefficients at equal points gives one finite signed weight for each
distinct node in
$$\mathcal N_\Lambda:=\bigcup_{\ell\in\Lambda}X_{\ell_1}\times\cdots\times X_{\ell_d}.$$
The **node-union work count** for this direct evaluation convention is
$W(\Lambda):=|\mathcal N_\Lambda|$, so shared nodes are counted once. A
combined weight may be negative or zero; no positivity claim follows from the
definition.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $(M,\cdot,e)$ be a monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]) and let
$g : \mathbb{N} \to M$ be a family of elements of $M$, written $g_i := g(i)$.
There is exactly one function $P_g : \mathbb{N} \to M$ satisfying

$$P_g(0) = e, \qquad P_g(\sigma(n)) = P_g(n) \cdot g_n \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}),$$

and we write

$$\prod_{i<n} g_i \;:=\; P_g(n), \qquad \text{also written } g_0 g_1 \cdots g_{n-1}.$$

In particular the **empty product** is $\prod_{i<0} g_i = e$, and
$\prod_{i<1} g_i = e \cdot g_0 = g_0$.

**Why the recursion is legitimate.** The clause $P_g(\sigma(n)) = P_g(n) \cdot g_n$
consults $n$ as well as $P_g(n)$, so [[thm-recursion]] does not apply to it
directly. Apply that theorem instead with the set $A = \mathbb{N} \times M$, the
element $a = (0,e)$, and the function $F : A \to A$ given by
$F(n,x) = (\sigma(n),\, x \cdot g_n)$: it yields a unique
$H : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times M$ with $H(0) = (0,e)$ and
$H(\sigma(n)) = F(H(n))$. Writing $H(n) = (H_1(n), H_2(n))$, induction
([[thm-induction-principle]]) gives $H_1(n) = n$ for every $n$, since $H_1(0) = 0$
and $H_1(\sigma(n)) = \sigma(H_1(n))$. Hence
$H(\sigma(n)) = (\sigma(n),\, H_2(n) \cdot g_n)$, so $P_g := H_2$ satisfies the two
displayed equations. It is the only such function: if $Q$ satisfies them too, then
$\{ n : P_g(n) = Q(n) \}$ contains $0$ and is closed under $\sigma$, hence is all
of $\mathbb{N}$ by induction.

**The value depends only on $g_0,\dots,g_{n-1}$.** If $g, g' : \mathbb{N} \to M$
satisfy $g_i = g'_i$ for every $i < n$, then $P_g(n) = P_{g'}(n)$. Indeed the set
of $n$ for which this implication holds contains $0$, both products then being
$e$; and if it holds at $n$, and $g, g'$ agree at every $i < \sigma(n)$, then they
agree at every $i < n$ and also at $n$ itself, because $i < \sigma(n)$ is
equivalent to $i \le n$ ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so
$P_g(\sigma(n)) = P_g(n) \cdot g_n = P_{g'}(n) \cdot g'_n = P_{g'}(\sigma(n))$.
Induction finishes it. This is what makes the notation $g_0 g_1 \cdots g_{n-1}$
unambiguous: it names a value determined by the first $n$ terms alone, and a
finite list $u$ of length $n$, that is a function $u : n \to M$ on the von Neumann
natural $n = \{0,\dots,n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), determines the product
$\prod_{i<n} u_i := P_{\tilde u}(n)$ computed from any extension
$\tilde u : \mathbb{N} \to M$ of $u$.

derivations.claim: Fix any one-dimensional input $g$ and coordinate $j$, and put $c_r:=Q_r(g)$. By [F3], $\sum_{r=1}^{m_j}(c_r-c_{r-1})=c_{m_j}-c_0$; for $m_j=0$ this is the empty-sum identity. Adding $Q_0(g)$ and using [F1] yields $\sum_{r=0}^{m_j}\Delta_r(g)=Q_{m_j}(g)$. Since $g$ was arbitrary, this is equality of functionals.

Expand $\bigotimes_{j=1}^d\left(\sum_{r=0}^{m_j}\Delta_r^{(j)}\right)$ by distributing each finite coordinate sum. By [F3]–[F4] the resulting terms are exactly the tensor details indexed once by $R_m$, which is the Smolyak sum $Q_{R_m}$ by [F2]. Applying step 1.1 in every coordinate identifies this expansion with $Q_{m_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes Q_{m_d}^{(d)}$, as claimed.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$ and let $a_\ell\ge0$ for $\ell\in A$. The
nonnegative sum $\sum_{\ell\in A}a_\ell$ is defined when the set
$$\left\{\sum_{\ell\in F}a_\ell:F\subseteq A\text{ finite}\right\}$$
is bounded above; its value is the supremum of that set in the complete ordered
field $\mathbb R$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). The empty finite sum is $0$.
This definition does not require an enumeration of $A$.

For the Smolyak details $\delta_\ell(f)$ of [[def-smolyak-cubature]],
**absolute detail summability** means that $\sum_{\ell\in A}|\delta_\ell(f)|$
is defined for $A=\mathbb N_0^d$. For an omitted set
$A=\mathbb N_0^d\setminus\Lambda$, the same definition gives the omitted
absolute-detail tail.

Let $d\ge1$ and $m=(m_1,\ldots,m_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$. For
$R_m:=\{\ell\in\mathbb N_0^d:0\le\ell_j\le m_j\text{ for every }j\}$ and
the details of [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]],
$$\sum_{\ell\in R_m}\Delta_\ell=Q_{m_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes Q_{m_d}^{(d)}.$$

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. For the dyadic
composite-Simpson hierarchy of [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]],
the tensor product $Q_L^{\otimes d}$ converges to the multiple Riemann
integral:
$$\lim_{L\to\infty} Q_L^{\otimes d}(f)=I_d(f).$$

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals and $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the absolute value as in
[[def-abs-value]]. Then

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k\Big| \le \sum_{k<n} |a_k|.$$

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

A sequence $(x_k)$ of reals **converges** to $x \in \mathbb{R}$ when for
every rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K$ with
$|x_k - x| < \hat\varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$. It is **Cauchy** when for
every rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K$ with
$|x_k - x_l| < \hat\varepsilon$ for all $k, l \ge K$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

Use the dyadic composite-Simpson hierarchy of
[[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]]. Let $d\ge1$. For
$S=\{j_1<\cdots<j_k\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$, define
$$D_Sf:=\partial_{x_{j_k}}^4\cdots\partial_{x_{j_1}}^4f,$$
so these derivatives are applied in increasing coordinate order; set
$D_\varnothing f=f$. Assume every $D_Sf$ is continuous on the closed cube,
with the one-sided endpoint convention of
[[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]], and choose finite bounds $M_S\ge0$
such that $|D_Sf(x)|\le M_S$ on $[0,1]^d$. For
$\ell\in\mathbb N_0^d$, put $S(\ell):=\{j:\ell_j\ge1\}$ and
$$\delta_\ell(f):=(\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)})(f).$$
Then
$$|\delta_\ell(f)|\le M_{S(\ell)}\left(\frac{17}{2880}\right)^{|S(\ell)|}16^{-\sum_{j\in S(\ell)}\ell_j}.$$
Moreover, for every finite $F\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$,
$$\sum_{\ell\in F}|\delta_\ell(f)|\le\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}M_S\left(\frac{17}{43200}\right)^{|S|}<\infty.$$

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

derivations.claim: Choose $L$ large enough that $\Lambda\subseteq R_L$. By [F1], [F3], and [F6], $Q_L^{\otimes d}(f)-Q_\Lambda(f)=\sum_{\ell\in R_L\setminus\Lambda}\delta_\ell(f)$. The index set on the right is finite and is contained in $\mathbb N_0^d\setminus\Lambda$.

By [F5] and [F2], the absolute value of the right side in step 1.1 is at most the omitted-detail tail $T_\Lambda:=\sum_{\ell\notin\Lambda}|\delta_\ell(f)|$ for every sufficiently large $L$. Put $x_L:=Q_L^{\otimes d}(f)-Q_\Lambda(f)$ and $z:=I_d(f)-Q_\Lambda(f)$; the convergence hypothesis in **Given** says $|x_L-z|=|Q_L^{\otimes d}(f)-I_d(f)|$ is eventually below every positive rational tolerance. If $|z|>T_\Lambda$, [F10] supplies a positive rational $\varepsilon$ with $2\varepsilon<|z|-T_\Lambda$. For sufficiently large $L$, both $\Lambda\subseteq R_L$ and $|x_L-z|<\varepsilon$ hold by finiteness of $\Lambda$ and [F7]. The triangle inequality [F8] then gives $|x_L|\ge |z|-|x_L-z|>|z|-\varepsilon>T_\Lambda$, contradicting the preceding tail bound. Hence the displayed omitted-tail inequality holds.

For the dyadic composite-Simpson hierarchy, [F4] supplies the convergence hypothesis in **Given**. If the mixed-derivative hypotheses of [F9] hold, its common bound makes the finite subsums of $\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb N_0^d}|\delta_\ell(f)|$ bounded above. By the definition [F2], the full absolute-detail sum is therefore defined and finite, so step 2.1 applies and proves the stated particular error case.

$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $a<b$, let $n\ge2$ be an even integer, and let
$p(x)=c_0+c_1x+c_2x^2+c_3x^3$ with real coefficients. Then

$$\int_a^b p(x)\,dx=Q_S(p;a,b,n),$$

where $Q_S$ is the composite Simpson value of
[[alg-composite-simpson-rule]].

derivations.claim: Fix a tensor polynomial $p(x)=\prod_{j=1}^dp_j(x_j)$. If some $\ell_j>q_j$, then $\ell_j-1\ge q_j$, so [A1] makes both $Q_{\ell_j}$ and $Q_{\ell_j-1}$ exact on $p_j$; hence $\Delta_{\ell_j}(p_j)=0$. Therefore every tensor detail with $\ell\notin R_q$ vanishes on $p$.

Since $R_q\subseteq\Lambda$, [F2] and step 1.1 reduce $Q_\Lambda(p)$ to the rectangular detail sum. By [F3] this is $\prod_{j=1}^d Q_{q_j}(p_j)$, which equals $\prod_j\int_0^1p_j$ by [A1]. Repeated application of [F4] identifies this product with $I_d(p)$.

Every stated tensor polynomial is a finite linear combination of products handled in step 2.1. The finite rule and the multiple integral are linear by [F5]–[F6], so exactness extends term by term. If $\sum_jq_j\le n$, every $\ell\in R_q$ has $|\ell|_1\le n$, hence $R_q\subseteq\Lambda_n$, proving the isotropic-simplex claim.

For the hierarchy of [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]], each level has panel count $2^{\ell+1}$, which is even and at least two. Thus [F7] makes every $Q_\ell$ exact through degree three. Set $r_\ell=3$ for all $\ell$; for coordinate degrees $s_j\le3$ the least levels are $q_j=0$, so $R_q=\{0\}\subseteq\Lambda$. Step 3.1 gives the stated exactness for these tensor polynomials.

citations.quote:
**Input:** dimension $d\ge1$; a finite downward-closed cap
$\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$ containing $0$; for each coordinate, the
one-dimensional quadrature rules from a hierarchy as in
[[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]] through every level used by
$\Gamma$, with canonical node keys that agree exactly if and only if the real
nodes agree and are totally ordered; a function $f$ evaluable at the nodes; and
an integer evaluation budget $B\ge0$. Admissible inputs supply all these rules
and keys at every level required by $\Gamma$.

**Output:** a current downward-closed index set $\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma$, its
Smolyak value when the initial rule fits the budget, the computed detail
surpluses, the distinct nodes actually sampled, and one status:
`budget-too-small`, `budget-exhausted`, or `frontier-exhausted`.

1. An index $\ell\in\Gamma\setminus\Lambda$ is **admissible** when every
   immediate predecessor $\ell-e_j$ with $\ell_j>0$ already belongs to
   $\Lambda$. Its **surplus** is the exact detail value $\delta_\ell(f)$ and
   its selection indicator is $|\delta_\ell(f)|$.
2. Form the baseline node set $X_0^d$. If its cardinality exceeds $B$, return
   `budget-too-small`, an empty $\Lambda$, no cubature value, and no sampled
   nodes. Otherwise set $\Lambda:=\{0\}$, initialize the active candidate set
   as empty, evaluate $f$ once at every baseline node, and set the current
   value to $Q_{\{0\}}(f)$. Then process every initially admissible index in
   $\Gamma\setminus\Lambda$ in lexicographic order using step 3.
3. Visit newly admissible indices in lexicographic order, skipping any index
   already recorded as active, accepted, or `uncomputed-budget`. To compute one
   surplus, form its finite tensor-detail node set and the new keys not already
   sampled. If adding them would exceed $B$, record this candidate as
   `uncomputed-budget` without evaluating those nodes. Otherwise evaluate each
   new key once, store the values, compute $\delta_\ell(f)$ from the finite
   signed weights, and add the index to the active candidate set.
4. If the active set is empty and an admissible `uncomputed-budget` candidate
   remains, return `budget-exhausted`. Otherwise, if the active set is empty,
   return `frontier-exhausted`.
5. Otherwise select the active index with largest absolute surplus, breaking
   ties lexicographically. Remove it from the active set, mark it accepted, add
   it to $\Lambda$, update the cubature value by adding its signed surplus, and
   inspect its finite forward neighbors for newly admissible indices; process
   them by step 3. Repeat from step 4.

The evaluation budget counts the union of distinct keys sampled while computing
both accepted and candidate surpluses. The indicator $|\delta_\ell(f)|$ is a
refinement heuristic only. A threshold on this indicator, or exhaustion of the
finite candidate cap, is not an error certificate unless a separate omitted-tail
bound applies.

Fix a dimension $d\ge1$. A finite set $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$ is
**downward closed** if, whenever $\ell\in\Lambda$ and $\ell_j>0$, the index
$\ell-e_j$ also belongs to $\Lambda$; here $e_j$ is the $j$th coordinate unit
vector. In this pair an admissible Smolyak set is a nonempty finite downward-
closed $\Lambda$ that contains $0$.

For a level hierarchy from [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]], define
the **Smolyak cubature functional**
$$Q_\Lambda(f):=\sum_{\ell\in\Lambda}(\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)})(f).$$
Each summand is a finite signed weighted sum. Expanding all differences and
adding coefficients at equal points gives one finite signed weight for each
distinct node in
$$\mathcal N_\Lambda:=\bigcup_{\ell\in\Lambda}X_{\ell_1}\times\cdots\times X_{\ell_d}.$$
The **node-union work count** for this direct evaluation convention is
$W(\Lambda):=|\mathcal N_\Lambda|$, so shared nodes are counted once. A
combined weight may be negative or zero; no positivity claim follows from the
definition.

derivations.claim: The initial set $\{0\}$ is downward closed. Assume the current $\Lambda$ is downward closed and the algorithm admits $\ell$. For any $\mu\le\ell$ coordinatewise with $\mu\ne\ell$, choose $j$ with $\mu_j<\ell_j$. Then $\ell_j>0$, so admissibility gives $\ell-e_j\in\Lambda$, and $\mu\le\ell-e_j$; downward closure gives $\mu\in\Lambda$. Thus $\Lambda\cup\{\ell\}$ is downward closed, and induction over additions preserves the invariant.

Every accepted addition is a previously unaccepted element of finite $\Gamma$, and the procedure records each computed or budget-uncomputed candidate so it cannot be processed repeatedly. Each candidate's node set and detail expansion are finite. Hence there are at most $|\Gamma|$ additions and finitely many candidate inspections; when none remains computable the algorithm returns `budget-exhausted` or `frontier-exhausted`, while the undersized initial budget returns `budget-too-small`.
