derivations.claim: By [F1], $U'(t)=AU(t)$. The coordinate identification [F7] makes entrywise real differentiation legitimate; taking conjugate transposes and using [F2], [F3], and $A^*=-A$ gives $(U(t)^*)'=U(t)^*A^*=-U(t)^*A$.
Apply the product rule [F3] to $U(t)^*U(t)$; its derivative is $-U(t)^*AU(t)+U(t)^*AU(t)=0$.

Each real and imaginary coordinate of $U(t)^*U(t)$ has zero derivative, so [F4] makes every coordinate constant. Evaluating at $t=0$ with [F1] and [F6] gives $U(t)^*U(t)=I_d$ for all $t$. By [F5] and matrix multiplication, $\|U(t)v\|_2^2=(U(t)v)^*U(t)v=v^*U(t)^*U(t)v=v^*v=\|v\|_2^2$.

citations.quote:
Use the first-variable-linear standard inner product on $\mathbb C^n$ and its norm $\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\sum_{i<n}|x_i|^2}$ from [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]] and [[def-inner-product-norm]]. The matrix norm $\|X\|_2$ is the operator norm of the linear map $x\mapsto Xx$ in [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]. On $\mathbb C^0=\{0\}$ this operator norm is $0$, as specified in that definition.

For each integer $k\ge0$, define the scalar phi function and its finite-matrix action by

$$\varphi_k(z):=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^j}{(j+k)!},\qquad \varphi_k(X):=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{X^j}{(j+k)!}.$$

Here $z\in\mathbb C$, $X\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $n\ge0$, $X^0=I_n$, and factorials are the usual positive integer factorials. [[lem-phi-series-converges-absolutely]] establishes that both series converge absolutely for every such input, so these expressions define values on their full stated domains. By the published power-series definition [[def-complex-exponential]], $\varphi_0(z)=\exp z$; for matrices, $\varphi_0(X)$ is the bounded-operator exponential series of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]].

At zero, the series gives $\varphi_k(0)=1/k!$ and $\varphi_k(0_{n\times n})=I_n/k!$ for every $n\ge0$. For $n\ge1$, only the $j=0$ matrix term can be nonzero. For $n=0$, [[def-matrix-space]] and [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] identify $I_0$ with the unique empty matrix $0_{0\times0}$; every power $X^j$ and every partial sum is that matrix. Thus $\varphi_k(0_{0\times0})=I_0/k!=0_{0\times0}$, including $k=0$.

The recurrence is always interpreted as a series identity, including at zero; division by $z$ is not part of this definition.

For every integer $k\ge0$, the scalar series defining $\varphi_k(z)$ converges absolutely for every $z\in\mathbb C$, and the matrix series defining $\varphi_k(X)$ converges absolutely in operator $2$-norm for every $X\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $n\ge0$. At zero, $\varphi_k(0)=1/k!$ and $\varphi_k(0_{n\times n})=I_n/k!$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);

of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;

each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

The map
$$\Phi:\mathbb C\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad \Phi(a+bi)=(a,b),$$
is a bijection. Under it,
$$\Phi((a+bi)+(u+vi))=(a+u,b+v)$$
and

Substituting $u=1-\theta$ gives $\int_0^1\theta(1-\theta)^j\,d\theta=\int_0^1(1-u)u^j\,du=1/(j+1)-1/(j+2)=1/((j+1)(j+2))$.

$$a_h(t,y):=e^{hA}y+h\varphi_1(hA)g(t,y),$$

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound

member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and $S \subseteq F$.

**least-upper-bound property**, or is **Dedekind complete**) if every nonempty

derivations.claim: By [F6], the defining sets are nonempty and bounded, so $K_+$ and $K_-$ are finite. Substituting $e^{tA}z$ into the exponential Euler formula and using [F2]–[F3] gives $\Theta^E_h(t,z)=z+\int_0^h e^{-(t+s)A}g(t,e^{tA}z)\,ds$. For every integer $k\ge0$, scalar $z\in\mathbb C$, and square matrix $X\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ with $n\ge0$, the series-defined functions of [[def-phi-functions-by-everywhere-convergent-series]] satisfy

$$\varphi_k(z)=\frac1{k!}+z\varphi_{k+1}(z),\qquad \varphi_k(X)=\frac1{k!}I_n+X\varphi_{k+1}(X).$$

For $k\ge1$ and $w\in\mathbb C^n$, let $J_k\in M_k(\mathbb C)$ have ones on the superdiagonal and zeros elsewhere, and let $e_1,e_k\in\mathbb C^k$ be the first and last coordinate vectors. Define $B_k(X,w):=\begin{bmatrix}X&we_1^*\\0&J_k\end{bmatrix}$. Then the first $n$ entries of $e^{B_k(X,w)}\begin{bmatrix}0\\e_k\end{bmatrix}$ equal $\varphi_k(X)w$. The identity is valid at $X=0$ and requires no division by $X$ or by a scalar argument.

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $n\ge1$, $v\in\mathbb C^n$, $\beta\ge0$, $V\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb C)$, $H\in M_m(\mathbb C)$, and $1\le m\le n$. For exact Arnoldi, $\beta=\|v\|_2$; in a certified finite-precision run, $\beta$ may be the backend's returned nonnegative scalar, with its effect included in the initial mismatch. Put $c(s):=e^{sH}\beta e_1$ and $u(s):=Vc(s)$. For every real $t$, the exact defect identity is

$$e^{tA}v-u(t)=e^{tA}(v-\beta Ve_1)+\int_0^t e^{(t-s)A}(AV-VH)c(s)\,ds,$$

where the integral is oriented. Let $I_t=[0,t]$ for $t\ge0$ and $I_t=[t,0]$ for $t<0$; let $\sigma_t=1$ for $t\ge0$ and $\sigma_t=-1$ for $t<0$. If $t=0$ the integral is zero. Suppose the Arnoldi relation is

$$AV=VH+h v_{m+1}e_m^*+D+\Omega,$$

where $h\ge0$, $\|v_{m+1}\|_2=1$ when $h>0$, $D=[d_1,\ldots,d_m]$, $\eta_j\ge0$, $\|d_j\|_2\le\eta_j$, $\eta_{\rm orth}\ge0$, and $\|\Omega\|_2\le\eta_{\rm orth}$. In exact happy breakdown, interpret the rank-one term as zero and set $D=\Omega=0$. If a reduced computation returns $\widehat c(t)$ with $\|\widehat c(t)-c(t)\|_2\le\epsilon_{\rm red}(t)$ for $\epsilon_{\rm red}(t)\ge0$ and its final projection returns $\widehat x$ with $\|\widehat x-V\widehat c(t)\|_2\le\eta_{\rm proj}$ for $\eta_{\rm proj}\ge0$, then

$$\|e^{tA}v-\widehat x\|_2\le e^{|t|\mu_2(\sigma_t A)}\|v-\beta Ve_1\|_2+\int_{I_t}e^{|t-s|\mu_2(\sigma_t A)}\left(h|e_m^*c(s)|+\left(\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^m\eta_j^2}+\eta_{\rm orth}\right)\|c(s)\|_2\right)ds+\|V\|_2\epsilon_{\rm red}(t)+\eta_{\rm proj}.$$

For exact Arnoldi from a nonzero start with no breakdown through $m$, $D=\Omega=0$, $V$ has orthonormal columns, and $v=\beta Ve_1$, recovering the standard residual integral. Whenever $AV=VH$ and $v=\beta Ve_1$, the invariant-subspace relation gives $\varphi_k(tA)v=\beta V\varphi_k(tH)e_1$ for every $k\ge0$ and every real $t$; exact happy breakdown of Arnoldi from a nonzero start is a sufficient case.

**Inputs:** $T>0$, $d\ge1$, $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, a state $y\in U\subseteq\mathbb C^d$, a step $(t,h)$ with $0\le t<t+h\le T$, a method choice $E$ or $2$, a field $g:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb C^d$, a nonnegative state-Lipschitz bound $L$ on an admitted tube containing the input and, when method $2$ is selected, the exact and computed ETD2 predictor stages, a certified semigroup bound $\|e^{sA}\|_2\le M e^{\omega s}$ for $0\le s\le h$ with $M\ge1$ and $\omega\in\mathbb R$, finite Arnoldi budgets $1\le m_0\le d$, $1\le m_1\le d+1$, $1\le m_2\le d+2$, certified field-evaluation, membership, scalar-enclosure, and vector-arithmetic providers, and a finite integer cap $C_{\max}\ge0$ for all nested backend/provider calls in this step. Each service call must terminate for the supplied finite budgets, supply a finite pre-call upper bound for its total nested call count, and return its actual call count and work counters. The step is admissible only when the initial state and every evaluated stage have certified membership in $U$ and, for method $2$, the exact ETD2 predictor also has certified membership in $U$; every needed service-call bound must fit within the remaining $C_{\max}$.

For each nonzero Arnoldi action request with matrix $B$, positive time $\tau$, and input $u$, the backend must certify a relation $BV_j=V_jH_j+\gamma v_{j+1}e_j^*+D+\Omega$ with $\beta,\gamma,\eta_i,\eta_{\rm orth},\eta_{\rm init},\nu_V,\epsilon_{\rm red},\eta_{\rm proj}\ge0$, $\|v_{j+1}\|_2=1$ when $\gamma>0$, $\|d_i\|_2\le\eta_i$, $\|\Omega\|_2\le\eta_{\rm orth}$, $\|u-\beta V_je_1\|_2\le\eta_{\rm init}$, $\|V_j\|_2\le\nu_V$, $\mu_2(B)\le\rho_B$ with $\rho_B\ge0$, and $\|H_j\|_2\le\rho_H$ with $\rho_H\ge0$. Its reduced-action certificate $\epsilon_{\rm red}$ may be used only when the reduced scaled-Taylor call has `success`: [[thm-scaled-taylor-exponential-action-error-and-work]] then bounds that call's error, and any subsequent scaling error is included. The backend also returns a final-projection error $\eta_{\rm proj}$, an actual work record, and its total nested-call count. Missing or uncertified bounds, work counters, or call counts make that request inconclusive. In exact Arnoldi, the exact relation, initial representation, and orthonormal basis supply the corresponding relation bounds.

For each positive-time request, compute the full action-error bound from [[thm-arnoldi-exponential-action-error-bound]] using
$$\epsilon_{\rm act}:=e^{\rho_B\tau}\eta_{\rm init}+\beta\tau e^{\tau\max(\rho_B,\rho_H)}\left(\gamma+\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^j\eta_i^2}+\eta_{\rm orth}\right)+\nu_V\epsilon_{\rm red}+\eta_{\rm proj}.$$
If any required quantity or its upward-rounded arithmetic enclosure is missing, return inconclusive. Define an action request $\operatorname{Act}(k,v)$ for $k=0,1,2$ as follows. If $v=0$, return the exact zero vector with bound zero and zero action work before constructing any augmented matrix. For $k=0$ and $v\ne0$, call [[alg-arnoldi-exponential-and-phi-actions]] with matrix $A$, time $h$, input $v$, index $0$, and budget $m_0$. For $k=1,2$ and $v\ne0$, use [[thm-phi-recurrence-and-augmented-matrix-actions]]: let $J_k$ have ones on its superdiagonal, let $e_1,e_k$ be the first and last coordinate vectors in $\mathbb C^k$, set
$$B_k(hA,v):=\begin{bmatrix}hA&ve_1^*\\0&J_k\end{bmatrix},\qquad w_k:=\begin{bmatrix}0\\e_k\end{bmatrix},$$
and call [[alg-arnoldi-exponential-and-phi-actions]] with matrix $B_k(hA,v)$, time $1$, input $w_k$, index $0$, and budget $m_k$. Here $w_k\ne0$; the zero-phi-input shortcut was applied to $v$ before forming this augmented request. By [[thm-phi-recurrence-and-augmented-matrix-actions]], the top $d$ coordinates of $e^{B_k(hA,v)}w_k$ equal $\varphi_k(hA)v$. In either nonzero case compute the full action-error bound using its certified Arnoldi relation and successful reduced-action certificate, then project to the requested vector; coordinate projection cannot increase the Euclidean error. Here $\varphi_0(hA)=e^{hA}$.

The calling implementation instruments each [[alg-arnoldi-exponential-and-phi-actions]] request and its nested providers, then returns the actual work counters and total nested-call count with that action result. The work record is $W=(N_A,N_{\rm other},W_{\rm dense})$: $N_A$ counts actual products with $A$, including the upper-left $hA$ multiplication inside each augmented $B_k$ product; $N_{\rm other}$ counts products with every other matrix, including augmented and reduced matrices and final projection matrices; $W_{\rm dense}$ records the backend's declared matrix-function work for dense implementations. These are type-specific counters rather than a sum. The algorithm sums each field across every service call and returns the totals. Each backend/provider call contributes its actual nested-call count to $C$; a call may begin only when its certified pre-call upper count fits in $C_{\max}-C$. If a count is missing, inconsistent, or exceeds its pre-call bound, return inconclusive with the accrued counters. Set
$$B_h:=M e^{\max(\omega,0)h};$$
Use $B_h$ and $B_h/2$ as the respective operator-norm bounds for $\varphi_1(hA)$ and $\varphi_2(hA)$. Their validity, and termination and work-counter accounting under the stated service contracts, are proved separately in [[lem-certified-exponential-step-action-error]].

**Outputs:** a candidate next state when available, a nonnegative one-step action-error bound $\delta_n$ only with certified status, the actual work counters described above, total nested-call count $C$, and status `certified`, `inconclusive`, or `invalid-input`.

**Procedure:**

1. Initialize all work counters and $C$ to zero. Reject malformed dimensions, budgets, method choice, time step, semigroup/evaluation/arithmetic configuration, or a certified-false membership check for the input state or, when method $2$ is selected, the exact ETD2 predictor with `invalid-input`. If any needed membership check or service-call upper bound cannot be certified, or the global call budget cannot fit a required service call, return `inconclusive`. A failed provider response with no sound bound is `inconclusive`.
2. Evaluate $g(t,y)$ as $\widetilde q_0$ with a certified error $\eta_0$, reserving its pre-call upper count first and then adding its actual count to $C$. Request $\operatorname{Act}(0,y)$ and $\operatorname{Act}(1,\widetilde q_0)$, reserving and accumulating their call/work counters. A zero phi input is handled by $\operatorname{Act}$ before any Arnoldi call. If a request is inconclusive, return inconclusive without accepting a step. Denote the candidates by $\widehat E y$ and $\widehat P_1$ and their bounds by $\epsilon_0,\epsilon_1$.
3. For method $E$, form $\widetilde y^+=\widehat E y+h\widehat P_1$. If $\alpha_E$ bounds the scalar/vector arithmetic error in this combination and its provider call fits the remaining call cap, accumulate its counters and set
$$\delta_n=\epsilon_0+h(\epsilon_1+B_h\eta_0)+\alpha_E.$$
4. For method $2$, first form the predictor candidate $\widetilde a=\widehat E y+h\widehat P_1$ using a certified arithmetic provider and accumulate its work/call counters. Check $(t+h,\widetilde a)$ for certified membership in the domain and admitted tube before evaluating $g(t+h,\widetilde a)$. A certified-false membership result returns `invalid-input`; an inconclusive membership result returns `inconclusive`. If $\alpha_a$ bounds the predictor arithmetic error, set $\eta_a:=\epsilon_0+h(\epsilon_1+B_h\eta_0)+\alpha_a$. Evaluate $g(t+h,\widetilde a)$ as $\widetilde q_a$ with a certified error $\eta_a^g$, reserving and accumulating its service counters. Request $\operatorname{Act}(2,\widetilde q_0)$ and $\operatorname{Act}(2,\widetilde q_a)$; if either request is inconclusive, return inconclusive without accepting a step. With their action-error bounds $\epsilon_{20},\epsilon_{2a}$, form
$$\widetilde y^+=\widehat E y+h(\widehat P_1-\widehat P_{20}+\widehat P_{2a}),$$
where $\widehat P_{20}$ and $\widehat P_{2a}$ are the two $\varphi_2$ candidates. If $\alpha_2$ bounds the final combination arithmetic error and its provider call fits the remaining call cap, accumulate its counters and set
$$\delta_n=\epsilon_0+h\left(\epsilon_1+B_h\eta_0+\epsilon_{20}+\frac{B_h}{2}\eta_0+\epsilon_{2a}+\frac{B_h}{2}(L\eta_a+\eta_a^g)\right)+\alpha_2.$$
5. Before returning `certified`, verify all action calls have certified Arnoldi relations, reduced-action status `success`, and certified final projections; all field-evaluation and arithmetic bounds are finite; all returned work/call counters are present and within their pre-call bounds; and the displayed scalar calculations have certified upward enclosures. If any check fails, return `inconclusive` and do not accept the step. Return the accrued work record and $C$ with every status.

Every scalar bound computation, including $\epsilon_{\rm act}$, $B_h$, and $\delta_n$, is rounded upward with a certified enclosure; if its enclosure is missing or fails to dominate the exact expression, return inconclusive. The returned work record is the sum of the actual counts supplied by the services for the action requests and arithmetic/evaluation operations. The finite call cap and each finite nested-action budget are checked before calls; the exact mathematical map is not a zero-cost oracle.

Let $n\ge1$ and $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$. In the standard complex inner product from [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]], the adjoint matrix is the conjugate transpose $A^*$ by [[thm-matrix-of-the-adjoint-is-the-conjugate-transpose]]. The Hermitian part is $H_A:=(A+A^*)/2$. It is self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]].

Define the Euclidean logarithmic norm by $\mu_2(A):=\lambda_{\max}(H_A)$, where $\lambda_{\max}$ denotes the largest eigenvalue of the Hermitian matrix $H_A$. The item [[lem-logarithmic-norm-is-real-and-variational]] establishes that this eigenvalue exists, is real, and equals $\max_{\|x\|_2=1}\operatorname{Re}\langle Ax,x\rangle$. This is a real growth bound, not a matrix norm.

Let $d\ge1$, $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, $g:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb C^d$, and $t\ge0$, $h>0$ with $t+h\le T$. The inputs $y$ and all displayed stages must lie in $U$. The functions $\varphi_k(hA)$ are the finite-matrix series of [[def-phi-functions-by-everywhere-convergent-series]], whose convergence is supplied by [[lem-phi-series-converges-absolutely]].

The **exponential Euler map** is
$$\Psi^{E}_h(t,y):=e^{hA}y+h\varphi_1(hA)g(t,y).$$

For the two-stage **exponential time-differencing Runge–Kutta map ETD2**, first form the exponential Euler predictor
$$a_h(t,y):=e^{hA}y+h\varphi_1(hA)g(t,y),$$
and then set
$$\Psi^{2}_h(t,y):=e^{hA}y+h\bigl(\varphi_1(hA)-\varphi_2(hA)\bigr)g(t,y)+h\varphi_2(hA)g(t+h,a_h(t,y)).$$
These are exact mathematical step maps; an implementation must separately account for every approximate matrix-function action and arithmetic error.

For every $d\ge1$ and $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, the series-defined functions [[def-phi-functions-by-everywhere-convergent-series]] satisfy
$$\varphi_1(X)=\int_0^1 e^{(1-\theta)X}\,d\theta,\qquad \varphi_2(X)=\int_0^1 \theta e^{(1-\theta)X}\,d\theta.$$
The integrals are componentwise. These formulas define the values at $X=0$ directly and do not use division by $X$.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $n\ge1$, $v\in\mathbb C^n$, $t\in\mathbb R$, and choose $s\ge1$, $p\ge0$, and rational $R\in[0,1]$ with $|t|\|A\|_2/s\le R$. Put $\delta=t/s$, $P:=\sum_{j=0}^p(\delta A)^j/j!$, and

$$Q_p(R):=\frac{R^{p+1}}{(p+1)!\left(1-R/(p+2)\right)}.$$

Suppose each computed substep $\widehat w_\ell$ has local term and summation certificates $\alpha_{\ell j},\zeta_{\ell j}\ge0$ as in [[alg-scaled-taylor-exponential-action]], and define $d_{\ell0}:=0$, $d_{\ell j}:=(R/j)d_{\ell,j-1}+\alpha_{\ell j}$, and $\epsilon_\ell:=\sum_{j=1}^p(d_{\ell j}+\zeta_{\ell j})$ (empty sums are zero). Then

$$\|e^{tA}v-\widehat w_s\|_2\le s\,3^{s-1}Q_p(R)\|v\|_2+\sum_{\ell=1}^s3^{s-\ell}\epsilon_\ell.$$

If the algorithm has rational upper bound $\rho_v\ge\|v\|_2$ and returns `success`, its reported certificate is valid and at most the requested tolerance. It uses exactly $sp$ calls to $A$ outside the exact zero-input or zero-action branches.

**Inputs:** $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ with $n\ge1$, $v\in\mathbb C^n$, time $t\in\mathbb R$, integer $k\ge0$, Krylov budget $1\le m\le n$, nonnegative threshold $\tau$, an exact-arithmetic Arnoldi run or a finite-precision Arnoldi backend, and a reduced-action configuration. In finite precision, the backend returns a length $j$ with $1\le j\le m$, $\beta>0$ for $v\ne0$, $V_j\in\mathbb C^{n\times j}$, $H_j\in M_j(\mathbb C)$, and a computed subdiagonal; it may supply the relation certificate in Step 2 and an exact happy-breakdown certificate verifying the full Arnoldi recurrence from $v$ through $j$ steps with zero terminal residual. The reduced-action configuration supplies, for each Taylor call, rational operator-norm and input-vector norm upper bounds, a positive tolerance, finite scaling/order budgets, and a provider satisfying [[def-certified-matvec-and-vector-arithmetic]] for Taylor calls, scalar scaling, and final projection. Missing or invalid bounds produce an inconclusive status.

**Outputs:** a vector candidate when data are available, reduced-coefficient error bound $\epsilon_{\rm red}\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\cup\{+\infty\}$, final-projection error bound $\eta_{\rm proj}\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\cup\{+\infty\}$, Arnoldi data, any relation-error certificates, `arnoldi_status` (`zero-start`, `happy-breakdown`, `projected`, `numerical-breakdown`, `inconclusive-arnoldi`, or `invalid-input`), `relation_status` (`exact`, `certified`, `inconclusive`, or `not-run`), `reduced_action_status` (`success`, `inconclusive`, or `not-run`), and `projection_status` (`exact`, `certified`, `inconclusive`, or `not-run`). An invalid input may return no candidate.

**Procedure:**

1. Reject invalid dimensions, $m$, $k$, or threshold by returning no candidate, both error bounds $+\infty$, no Arnoldi data or relation certificates, `arnoldi_status=invalid-input`, and `relation_status=reduced_action_status=projection_status=not-run`. If $v=0$, return the zero vector with both error bounds zero, `arnoldi_status=zero-start`, and `relation_status=reduced_action_status=projection_status=not-run`, without division.
2. In exact-arithmetic mode, run [[def-arnoldi-process]] for at most $m$ steps and retain $\beta:=\|v\|_2$, $V_j=[v_1,\ldots,v_j]$, and the leading square Hessenberg matrix $H_j$; set `relation_status=exact`. Stop when the Arnoldi residual norm is exactly zero and set `arnoldi_status=happy-breakdown`; otherwise continue until $m$ steps and leave the Arnoldi status pending. In finite-precision mode, if the backend data have invalid dimensions or fail $\beta>0$ for $v\ne0$, return the zero candidate, both bounds $+\infty$, `arnoldi_status=inconclusive-arnoldi`, `relation_status=inconclusive`, and `reduced_action_status=projection_status=not-run`. Otherwise use the backend's $V_j,H_j,\beta$ and computed subdiagonal. When available, it supplies a relation certificate $AV_j=V_jH_j+h_{j+1,j}v_{j+1}e_j^*+D+\Omega$, with $\|v_{j+1}\|_2=1$, column bounds $\|d_i\|_2\le\eta_i$ for $D=[d_1,\ldots,d_j]$, and a norm bound for $\Omega$. Set `relation_status=certified` if this relation is supplied and verified, and `relation_status=inconclusive` otherwise. A verified exact happy-breakdown certificate sets `relation_status=certified` and `arnoldi_status=happy-breakdown`; it verifies the exact Arnoldi recurrence, including $AV_j=V_jH_j$ and $v=\beta V_je_1$. Without that full certificate, a computed subdiagonal at most $\tau$ sets `arnoldi_status=numerical-breakdown`; continue to the reduced evaluation but never label it happy breakdown. Otherwise leave the Arnoldi status pending until Step 5.
3. For $k=0$, request a reduced configuration for $(H_j,\beta e_1,t)$ and call [[alg-scaled-taylor-exponential-action]] to approximate $e^{tH_j}\beta e_1$. If the Taylor call returns no candidate, set $\epsilon_{\rm red}=\eta_{\rm proj}=+\infty$, set `reduced_action_status=inconclusive` and `projection_status=not-run`, set a pending `arnoldi_status` to `inconclusive-arnoldi` when `relation_status=inconclusive` and to `projected` otherwise, and return no candidate. Otherwise set $\widehat c$ and $\epsilon_{\rm red}$ to its candidate and bound. Set `reduced_action_status=success` only when the Taylor status is `success`; otherwise set it to `inconclusive`. Continue to Step 5 with the returned candidate in either case.
4. For $k\ge1$, form $B_k(tH_j,e_1)$ from [[thm-phi-recurrence-and-augmented-matrix-actions]], request a reduced configuration for $(B_k(tH_j,e_1),e_{j+k},1)$, and call [[alg-scaled-taylor-exponential-action]]. If the Taylor call returns no candidate, set $\epsilon_{\rm red}=\eta_{\rm proj}=+\infty$, set `reduced_action_status=inconclusive` and `projection_status=not-run`, set a pending `arnoldi_status` to `inconclusive-arnoldi` when `relation_status=inconclusive` and to `projected` otherwise, and return no candidate. Otherwise let $q$ be the first $j$ entries of its candidate and use the certified vector-scaling provider with scalar $\beta$ to obtain $\widehat c$ and local bound $\xi_\beta$. Set $\epsilon_{\rm red}:=\beta\epsilon_{\rm aug}+\xi_\beta$, where $\epsilon_{\rm aug}$ is the augmented Taylor bound; if either certificate is missing set $\epsilon_{\rm red}=+\infty$ and `reduced_action_status=inconclusive`. Set `reduced_action_status=success` only when the Taylor status and scaling certificate both succeed. Continue to Step 5 in either case.
5. In exact-arithmetic mode set $x:=V_j\widehat c$, $\eta_{\rm proj}=0$, and `projection_status=exact`. In finite precision, use the certified matrix-vector provider with matrix $V_j$, scalar $1$, and vector $\widehat c$ to return $x$ and bound $\eta_{\rm proj}$; missing certification sets $\eta_{\rm proj}=+\infty$ and `projection_status=inconclusive`. Return $x$. If `arnoldi_status` is still pending, set it to `inconclusive-arnoldi` when `relation_status=inconclusive` and `projected` otherwise.

In exact arithmetic the projected formula is $\beta V_j\varphi_k(tH_j)e_1$. Exact happy breakdown means the generated Krylov subspace is invariant and this projected formula equals $\varphi_k(tA)v$; a finite Taylor evaluation still has its separately reported reduced-action error. A numerical-breakdown status asserts no exact invariance.

The map
$$\Phi:\mathbb C\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad \Phi(a+bi)=(a,b),$$
is a bijection. Under it,
$$\Phi((a+bi)+(u+vi))=(a+u,b+v)$$
and
$$\Phi((a+bi)(u+vi))=(au-bv,av+bu).$$

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

**Inputs:** $T>0$, $d\ge1$, $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, a state $y\in U\subseteq\mathbb C^d$, a step $(t,h)$ with $0\le t<t+h\le T$, a method choice $E$ or $2$, a field $g:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb C^d$, a nonnegative state-Lipschitz bound $L$ on an admitted tube containing the input and, when method $2$ is selected, the exact and computed ETD2 predictor stages, a certified semigroup bound $\|e^{sA}\|_2\le M e^{\omega s}$ for $0\le s\le h$ with $M\ge1$ and $\omega\in\mathbb R$, finite Arnoldi budgets $1\le m_0\le d$, $1\le m_1\le d+1$, $1\le m_2\le d+2$, certified field-evaluation, membership, scalar-enclosure, and vector-arithmetic providers, and a finite integer cap $C_{\max}\ge0$ for all nested backend/provider calls in this step. Each service call must terminate for the supplied finite budgets, supply a finite pre-call upper bound for its total nested call count, and return its actual call count and work counters. The step is admissible only when the initial state and every evaluated stage have certified membership in $U$ and, for method $2$, the exact ETD2 predictor also has certified membership in $U$; every needed service-call bound must fit within the remaining $C_{\max}$.

For each nonzero Arnoldi action request with matrix $B$, positive time $\tau$, and input $u$, the backend must certify a relation $BV_j=V_jH_j+\gamma v_{j+1}e_j^*+D+\Omega$ with $\beta,\gamma,\eta_i,\eta_{\rm orth},\eta_{\rm init},\nu_V,\epsilon_{\rm red},\eta_{\rm proj}\ge0$, $\|v_{j+1}\|_2=1$ when $\gamma>0$, $\|d_i\|_2\le\eta_i$, $\|\Omega\|_2\le\eta_{\rm orth}$, $\|u-\beta V_je_1\|_2\le\eta_{\rm init}$, $\|V_j\|_2\le\nu_V$, $\mu_2(B)\le\rho_B$ with $\rho_B\ge0$, and $\|H_j\|_2\le\rho_H$ with $\rho_H\ge0$. Its reduced-action certificate $\epsilon_{\rm red}$ may be used only when the reduced scaled-Taylor call has `success`: [[thm-scaled-taylor-exponential-action-error-and-work]] then bounds that call's error, and any subsequent scaling error is included. The backend also returns a final-projection error $\eta_{\rm proj}$, an actual work record, and its total nested-call count. Missing or uncertified bounds, work counters, or call counts make that request inconclusive. In exact Arnoldi, the exact relation, initial representation, and orthonormal basis supply the corresponding relation bounds.

For each positive-time request, compute the full action-error bound from [[thm-arnoldi-exponential-action-error-bound]] using
$$\epsilon_{\rm act}:=e^{\rho_B\tau}\eta_{\rm init}+\beta\tau e^{\tau\max(\rho_B,\rho_H)}\left(\gamma+\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^j\eta_i^2}+\eta_{\rm orth}\right)+\nu_V\epsilon_{\rm red}+\eta_{\rm proj}.$$
If any required quantity or its upward-rounded arithmetic enclosure is missing, return inconclusive. Define an action request $\operatorname{Act}(k,v)$ for $k=0,1,2$ as follows. If $v=0$, return the exact zero vector with bound zero and zero action work before constructing any augmented matrix. For $k=0$ and $v\ne0$, call [[alg-arnoldi-exponential-and-phi-actions]] with matrix $A$, time $h$, input $v$, index $0$, and budget $m_0$. For $k=1,2$ and $v\ne0$, use [[thm-phi-recurrence-and-augmented-matrix-actions]]: let $J_k$ have ones on its superdiagonal, let $e_1,e_k$ be the first and last coordinate vectors in $\mathbb C^k$, set
$$B_k(hA,v):=\begin{bmatrix}hA&ve_1^*\\0&J_k\end{bmatrix},\qquad w_k:=\begin{bmatrix}0\\e_k\end{bmatrix},$$
and call [[alg-arnoldi-exponential-and-phi-actions]] with matrix $B_k(hA,v)$, time $1$, input $w_k$, index $0$, and budget $m_k$. Here $w_k\ne0$; the zero-phi-input shortcut was applied to $v$ before forming this augmented request. By [[thm-phi-recurrence-and-augmented-matrix-actions]], the top $d$ coordinates of $e^{B_k(hA,v)}w_k$ equal $\varphi_k(hA)v$. In either nonzero case compute the full action-error bound using its certified Arnoldi relation and successful reduced-action certificate, then project to the requested vector; coordinate projection cannot increase the Euclidean error. Here $\varphi_0(hA)=e^{hA}$.

The calling implementation instruments each [[alg-arnoldi-exponential-and-phi-actions]] request and its nested providers, then returns the actual work counters and total nested-call count with that action result. The work record is $W=(N_A,N_{\rm other},W_{\rm dense})$: $N_A$ counts actual products with $A$, including the upper-left $hA$ multiplication inside each augmented $B_k$ product; $N_{\rm other}$ counts products with every other matrix, including augmented and reduced matrices and final projection matrices; $W_{\rm dense}$ records the backend's declared matrix-function work for dense implementations. These are type-specific counters rather than a sum. The algorithm sums each field across every service call and returns the totals. Each backend/provider call contributes its actual nested-call count to $C$; a call may begin only when its certified pre-call upper count fits in $C_{\max}-C$. If a count is missing, inconsistent, or exceeds its pre-call bound, return inconclusive with the accrued counters. Set
$$B_h:=M e^{\max(\omega,0)h};$$
Use $B_h$ and $B_h/2$ as the respective operator-norm bounds for $\varphi_1(hA)$ and $\varphi_2(hA)$. Their validity, and termination and work-counter accounting under the stated service contracts, are proved separately in [[lem-certified-exponential-step-action-error]].

**Outputs:** a candidate next state when available, a nonnegative one-step action-error bound $\delta_n$ only with certified status, the actual work counters described above, total nested-call count $C$, and status `certified`, `inconclusive`, or `invalid-input`.

**Procedure:**

1. Initialize all work counters and $C$ to zero. Reject malformed dimensions, budgets, method choice, time step, semigroup/evaluation/arithmetic configuration, or a certified-false membership check for the input state or, when method $2$ is selected, the exact ETD2 predictor with `invalid-input`. If any needed membership check or service-call upper bound cannot be certified, or the global call budget cannot fit a required service call, return `inconclusive`. A failed provider response with no sound bound is `inconclusive`.
2. Evaluate $g(t,y)$ as $\widetilde q_0$ with a certified error $\eta_0$, reserving its pre-call upper count first and then adding its actual count to $C$. Request $\operatorname{Act}(0,y)$ and $\operatorname{Act}(1,\widetilde q_0)$, reserving and accumulating their call/work counters. A zero phi input is handled by $\operatorname{Act}$ before any Arnoldi call. If a request is inconclusive, return inconclusive without accepting a step. Denote the candidates by $\widehat E y$ and $\widehat P_1$ and their bounds by $\epsilon_0,\epsilon_1$.
3. For method $E$, form $\widetilde y^+=\widehat E y+h\widehat P_1$. If $\alpha_E$ bounds the scalar/vector arithmetic error in this combination and its provider call fits the remaining call cap, accumulate its counters and set
$$\delta_n=\epsilon_0+h(\epsilon_1+B_h\eta_0)+\alpha_E.$$
4. For method $2$, first form the predictor candidate $\widetilde a=\widehat E y+h\widehat P_1$ using a certified arithmetic provider and accumulate its work/call counters. Check $(t+h,\widetilde a)$ for certified membership in the domain and admitted tube before evaluating $g(t+h,\widetilde a)$. A certified-false membership result returns `invalid-input`; an inconclusive membership result returns `inconclusive`. If $\alpha_a$ bounds the predictor arithmetic error, set $\eta_a:=\epsilon_0+h(\epsilon_1+B_h\eta_0)+\alpha_a$. Evaluate $g(t+h,\widetilde a)$ as $\widetilde q_a$ with a certified error $\eta_a^g$, reserving and accumulating its service counters. Request $\operatorname{Act}(2,\widetilde q_0)$ and $\operatorname{Act}(2,\widetilde q_a)$; if either request is inconclusive, return inconclusive without accepting a step. With their action-error bounds $\epsilon_{20},\epsilon_{2a}$, form
$$\widetilde y^+=\widehat E y+h(\widehat P_1-\widehat P_{20}+\widehat P_{2a}),$$
where $\widehat P_{20}$ and $\widehat P_{2a}$ are the two $\varphi_2$ candidates. If $\alpha_2$ bounds the final combination arithmetic error and its provider call fits the remaining call cap, accumulate its counters and set
$$\delta_n=\epsilon_0+h\left(\epsilon_1+B_h\eta_0+\epsilon_{20}+\frac{B_h}{2}\eta_0+\epsilon_{2a}+\frac{B_h}{2}(L\eta_a+\eta_a^g)\right)+\alpha_2.$$
5. Before returning `certified`, verify all action calls have certified Arnoldi relations, reduced-action status `success`, and certified final projections; all field-evaluation and arithmetic bounds are finite; all returned work/call counters are present and within their pre-call bounds; and the displayed scalar calculations have certified upward enclosures. If any check fails, return `inconclusive` and do not accept the step. Return the accrued work record and $C$ with every status.

Every scalar bound computation, including $\epsilon_{\rm act}$, $B_h$, and $\delta_n$, is rounded upward with a certified enclosure; if its enclosure is missing or fails to dominate the exact expression, return inconclusive. The returned work record is the sum of the actual counts supplied by the services for the action requests and arithmetic/evaluation operations. The finite call cap and each finite nested-action budget are checked before calls; the exact mathematical map is not a zero-cost oracle.

derivations.claim: For a nonzero action request, [F11] makes the scaled-Taylor output certificate a valid $\epsilon_{\rm red}$; put $c(s)=e^{sH}\beta e_1$ in [F2]. By [F8] and $\rho_H\ge\|H\|_2$, $\|c(s)\|_2\le\beta e^{s\rho_H}$; [F10] gives $|e_j^*c(s)|\le\|c(s)\|_2$. Since $\rho_B\ge\mu_2(B)$, [F9] bounds the initial term in [F2] by $e^{\rho_B\tau}\eta_{\rm init}$ and its integral by $\beta\tau e^{\tau\max(\rho_B,\rho_H)}(\gamma+\sqrt{\sum_i\eta_i^2}+\eta_{\rm orth})$. The reduced and final projection terms are at most $\nu_V\epsilon_{\rm red}+\eta_{\rm proj}$ by [F7]. Thus [F3]'s $\epsilon_{\rm act}$ bounds the full exponential-action error. For a zero input, the algorithm returns the exact zero action with bound zero.

For $0\le\theta\le1$, put $s=(1-\theta)h$. Then $0\le s\le h$ and $\omega s\le\max(\omega,0)h$: for $\omega\ge0$ this follows from $s\le h$, and for $\omega<0$ it follows from $s\ge0$. The semigroup bound in [A1] and scalar monotonicity [F9] therefore give $\|e^{(1-\theta)hA}\|_2\le M e^{\omega s}\le B_h$. For each unit vector $v\in\mathbb C^d$, [F5] and componentwise linearity in [F12] yield $\varphi_1(hA)v=\int_0^1e^{(1-\theta)hA}v\,d\theta$ and the analogous identity with weight $\theta$ for $\varphi_2$. These curves are continuous by [F12]. Apply the norm inequality in [F12] and the matrix-action inequality in [F7]: the two norms are at most $B_h\int_0^1d\theta=B_h$ and $B_h\int_0^1\theta d\theta=B_h/2$. Taking the operator-norm maximum over unit vectors in [F7], valid since $d\ge1$ is an input condition, proves both asserted phi bounds.

For exponential Euler, the exact formula [F4] applies $e^{hA}$ to $y$ and $h\varphi_1(hA)$ to $g(t,y)$. [F3] supplies action-error bounds for $e^{hA}y$ and the full augmented action whose top block is $\varphi_1(hA)\widetilde q_0$ by [F1]; coordinate projection cannot increase its error. Replacing $g(t,y)$ by $\widetilde q_0$ changes the phi action by at most $B_h\eta_0$ by step 1.2 and [A1]. Multiplication by $h$ and the certified combination error $\alpha_E$ give the exponential-Euler $\delta_n$.

For ETD2, the predictor's difference from the exact predictor $a_h(t,y)$ is at most $\epsilon_0+h(\epsilon_1+B_h\eta_0)+\alpha_a=\eta_a$ by the triangle inequality, using the exponential-Euler estimate from step 2.1. Therefore the exact stage forcing differs from the evaluated $\widetilde q_a$ by at most $L\eta_a+\eta_a^g$, using [A1].

Using the phi bounds proved in step 1.2, in the final ETD2 update, the $\varphi_1$ action at $g(t,y)$ contributes at most $\epsilon_1+B_h\eta_0$; the $\varphi_2$ action at $g(t,y)$ contributes at most $\epsilon_{20}+(B_h/2)\eta_0$; and the stage $\varphi_2$ action contributes at most $\epsilon_{2a}+(B_h/2)(L\eta_a+\eta_a^g)$. Each phi action certificate follows from [F1] and step 1.1. The exponential action contributes $\epsilon_0$. Multiplying the three phi terms by $h$, adding the certified final arithmetic error $\alpha_2$, and applying the triangle inequality gives exactly the ETD2 $\delta_n$ in [F3].

Under the stated service contracts, each started backend/provider call terminates, including every call nested inside an Arnoldi or reduced-action request. Outside these services the procedure has a fixed finite sequence of branches: at most two action requests for method $E$ and four for method $2$, together with finitely many field, membership, enclosure, and vector-arithmetic requests. A missing certificate or insufficient pre-call allowance returns immediately, and every started service returns in finite time by its contract, so the entire algorithm terminates. For the counters, begin with $C=0$ and $W=0$. Before a service starts, its certified upper count $b$ satisfies $b\le C_{\max}-C$; its valid returned actual count $c$ obeys $0\le c\le b$, so the update gives $0\le C+c\le C_{\max}$. Induction over the finitely many completed top-level services proves the count bound, with their nested work already included in their returned records. At each such update, the algorithm also adds the actual service work record componentwise to $W$. The same finite induction makes each component exactly the sum of its accrued actual counters; an early return retains these accrued totals. Zero-input action shortcuts contribute zero action work. This proves termination and the advertised accounting without adding calls or presuming that a missing mathematical certificate succeeds.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $y$ solve $y'=Ay+g(t,y(t))$ on $[t,t+h]$, with $0<h\le T$, and put $q(r):=g(r,y(r))$. Suppose $q$ is continuously differentiable with $\sup_{t\le r\le t+h}\|q'(r)\|_2\le Q_1$, and let $K_+:=\sup_{0\le s\le T}\|e^{sA}\|_2$. Then the exact-start local defect of the exponential Euler map satisfies
$$\|\Psi^E_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h)\|_2\le \frac{K_+Q_1}{2}h^2.$$

Let $y'=Ay+g(t,y(t))$ on $[t,t+h]$, $0<h\le T$, and let $q(r):=g(r,y(r))$. Suppose $q\in C^2$, $\sup\|q'(r)\|_2\le Q_1$, $\sup\|q''(r)\|_2\le Q_2$, $g$ is $L$-Lipschitz in its state variable on a tube containing the exact path and predictor, and $K_+:=\sup_{0\le s\le T}\|e^{sA}\|_2$. Set $C_E:=K_+Q_1/2$. Then the exact-start defect of $\Psi^2_h$ satisfies
$$\|\Psi^2_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h)\|_2\le K_+\left(Q_2+\frac{LC_E}{2}\right)h^3.$$

Fix $T>0$, $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, and define
$$K_+:=\sup_{0\le r\le T}\|e^{rA}\|_2,\qquad K_-:=\sup_{0\le r\le T}\|e^{-rA}\|_2,\qquad \kappa:=LK_+K_-.$$
These constants are finite by continuity of the finite-matrix exponential. Let $g$ be $L$-Lipschitz in its state variable on a common tube containing all states and stages below. For $0<h\le T$ and an admissible $t$, define the transformed maps
$$\Theta^E_h(t,z):=e^{-(t+h)A}\Psi^E_h(t,e^{tA}z),\qquad \Theta^2_h(t,z):=e^{-(t+h)A}\Psi^2_h(t,e^{tA}z).$$
Then
$$\|\Theta^E_h(t,z)-\Theta^E_h(t,w)\|_2\le(1+\kappa h)\|z-w\|_2,$$
and
$$\|\Theta^2_h(t,z)-\Theta^2_h(t,w)\|_2\le\left(1+h\left(\kappa+\frac{T\kappa^2}{2}\right)\right)\|z-w\|_2.$$

Suppose [[alg-certified-exponential-euler-etd2-step]] returns certified status with per-action, field-evaluation, arithmetic, and semigroup bounds as in its Definition. Let $\Psi_h^E$ or $\Psi_h^2$ be the corresponding exact map of [[def-exponential-euler-and-etd2-step-maps]], and let $\widetilde\Psi_h$ be the returned candidate map. Then the algorithm's reported value satisfies
$$\|\widetilde\Psi_h(y)-\Psi_h(y)\|_2\le\delta_n.$$

For the algorithm's semigroup data, $B_h:=M e^{\max(\omega,0)h}$ satisfies
$$\|\varphi_1(hA)\|_2\le B_h,\qquad \|\varphi_2(hA)\|_2\le B_h/2.$$
For every admissible input whose services obey the declared finite-termination, pre-call upper-count, and valid returned-count/work-record contracts, the algorithm terminates with one of its stated statuses. It returns a total nested-call count $0\le C\le C_{\max}$, and each component of its work record is the sum of the actual corresponding service counters accrued before return. These are counts of the declared work, without a wall-clock bound.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $X$ be a real or complex normed space. If $K\subseteq X$ is nonempty compact, $C\subseteq X$ is nonempty closed, and $K\cap C=\varnothing$, then there is $\delta>0$ with
$$\|k-c\|\ge\delta\qquad(k\in K,\ c\in C).$$
No convexity, completeness, HB, or infinite choice principle is required.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function, with images and preimages written $f[\,\cdot\,]$
and $f^{-1}[\,\cdot\,]$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). Conditions
(a), (b), (c), and (e) below are equivalent without choice, and each implies
(d). Assuming Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), all five are
equivalent. The authorized Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) suffices;
only its countable instance is used for the converse from (d).

- **(a)** $f$ is continuous at every point of $X$ in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$
  sense ([[def-metric-continuity]]).
- **(b)** $f^{-1}[V]$ is open in $X$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
  ([[def-metric-topology]]).
- **(c)** $f^{-1}[G]$ is closed in $X$ for every closed $G \subseteq Y$.
- **(d)** $f$ is **sequentially continuous**: whenever $x_k \to x$ in $(X,d_X)$,
  also $f(x_k) \to f(x)$ in $(Y,d_Y)$ ([[def-metric-convergence]]).
- **(e)** $f[\overline{A}] \subseteq \overline{f[A]}$ for every $A \subseteq X$
  ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

**Where choice is used.** Only the implication (d) $\Rightarrow$ (e) uses a
choice principle, and it uses it only through
[[thm-metric-sequential-closure]], whose forward direction spends the Axiom of
Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The cycle
(a) $\Rightarrow$ (b) $\Rightarrow$ (c) $\Rightarrow$ (e) $\Rightarrow$ (a) and
the implication (a) $\Rightarrow$ (d) are choice free.

The map
$$\Phi:\mathbb C\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad \Phi(a+bi)=(a,b),$$
is a bijection. Under it,
$$\Phi((a+bi)+(u+vi))=(a+u,b+v)$$
and
$$\Phi((a+bi)(u+vi))=(au-bv,av+bu).$$

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and $S \subseteq F$.

- $u \in F$ is an **upper bound** of $S$ if $s \le u$ for all $s \in S$; $S$ is
  **bounded above** if it has an upper bound.
- $u \in F$ is a **least upper bound** (or **supremum**, $\sup S$) of $S$ if $u$
  is an upper bound of $S$ and $u \le u'$ for every upper bound $u'$ of $S$.

$F$ is a **complete ordered field** (equivalently, $F$ has the
**least-upper-bound property**, or is **Dedekind complete**) if every nonempty
$S \subseteq F$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $F$.

Let $d,N,p\ge1$, $T>0$, $h=T/N$, and $t_n=nh$. Let $y:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ solve an initial-value problem in an open time-state domain $D$. Use the Euclidean norm $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], whose triangle inequality is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]. Let $\mathcal T\subset D$ be a common compact time-state tube with positive margin in $D$, and write $\mathcal T_t:=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:(t,v)\in\mathcal T\}$. Suppose a one-step map $\Psi_{h,n}$ is defined on $\mathcal T_{t_n}$, produces $y_{n+1}=\Psi_{h,n}(y_n)$, and the entire exact path, all numerical grid states, and every method stage lie in $\mathcal T$. If constants $C,C_0,L\ge0$, independent of $N$ and $n$, satisfy
$$\|y_0-y(0)\|_2\le C_0h^p,\qquad \|\Psi_{h,n}(y(t_n))-y(t_{n+1})\|_2\le Ch^{p+1},$$
and
$$\|\Psi_{h,n}(u)-\Psi_{h,n}(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$
for every $u,v\in\mathcal T_{t_n}$ and $0\le n<N$, then, for $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, for $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

derivations.claim: By [F13], the complex state equation and the transformed equation are real finite-dimensional systems with the same Euclidean error norm. Set $z(t):=e^{-tA}y(t)$. The product rule and [F1], [F6] give $z'(t)=e^{-tA}g(t,y(t))=e^{-tA}g(t,e^{tA}z(t))$. Conjugating the exact numerical map and exact endpoint by $e^{-(t+h)A}$ cancels their common $e^{hA}$ linear term and multiplies their difference by $e^{-(t+h)A}$. Hence [F2], [F3], and [F9] give transformed exact-start defects at most $K_-C_Eh^2$ and $K_-C_2h^3$.

By [F14], both amplification suprema used here are finite. Set $D_z:=\{(t,z):(t,e^{tA}z)\in D\}$, open as the preimage of $D$ under the continuous map $(t,z)\mapsto(t,e^{tA}z)$ by [F6], [F9], [F10], and [F12]. The map $(t,u)\mapsto(t,e^{-tA}u)$ continuously sends $\mathcal T$ to a compact tube in $D_z$ containing the transformed exact path, states, and stages; [F10]–[F11] give positive margin. Its stability is $1+L_ph$ by [F4], and its local constant is $K_-C_p$ by step 1.1. Thus [L1] applies with exact initial data.

For certified actions, put $\widetilde z_n:=e^{-t_nA}\widetilde y_n$ and $r_n:=\|\widetilde z_n-z(t_n)\|_2$. Stability [F4], local defect [F2] or [F3] transformed by [F6] and step 1.1, and perturbation bound [F5] transformed using [F9] by $e^{-(t_{n+1})A}$ give by the triangle inequality $r_{n+1}\le(1+L_ph)r_n+K_-C_ph^{p+1}+K_-\delta_n$, with $r_0=0$.

Applying [L1] as in step 2.1 yields $\max_n\|z_n-z(t_n)\|_2\le K_-C_p\Gamma(L_p,T)h^p$. Since $y(t_n)=e^{t_nA}z(t_n)$ and [F9] with the definition of $K_+$ bounds multiplication by $e^{t_nA}$, this gives the first displayed bound.

Induction in step 2.2 gives $r_n\le K_-\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(1+L_ph)^{n-1-j}(C_ph^{p+1}+\delta_j)$: the base case is the empty sum, and multiplying the bound for $r_n$ by $1+L_ph$ and adding the $j=n$ defect and action terms gives the formula for $r_{n+1}$.

Since $1+L_ph\le e^{L_ph}$ by [F7], each power in step 3.2 is at most $e^{L_pT}$ by [F8] and $nh\le T$. Also $Nh=T$, so $NC_ph^{p+1}=C_pT h^p$. Thus $r_n\le K_-e^{L_pT}(C_pT h^p+\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\delta_j)$. Multiplication by $e^{t_nA}$ and [F9] with the bound $K_+$ give the certified-action estimate for every $n$, hence for their maximum.
