$$Q_{ij}:=\int_0^{c_i}\ell_j(s)\,ds,\qquad b_j:=\int_0^1\ell_j(s)\,ds.$$
The matrix $Q\in\mathbb R^{M\times M}$ and vector $b\in\mathbb R^M$ are the collocation tableau coefficients. For an IVP $y'=f(t,y)$ on the open domain of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], write
$$F_j(U):=f(t+c_jh,U_j),\qquad QF(U):=\left(\sum_{j=1}^M Q_{ij}F_j(U)\right)_{i=1}^M.$$
All displayed integrals use the oriented Riemann convention of [[def-oriented-integral]]. In particular $Q_{ij}=0$ when $c_i=0$, and the integral in $u_h$ vanishes at $\tau=0$. The collocation stages and endpoint are the implicit Runge–Kutta equations of [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]] with $A=Q$, nodes $c$, and weights $b$:
$$U=\mathbf1u+hQF(U),\qquad \Psi_h(t,u)=u+h\sum_{j=1}^M b_jF_j(U).$$
The associated collocation polynomial on normalized time $\tau\in[0,1]$ is
$$u_h(\tau):=u+h\int_0^\tau\sum_{j=1}^M\ell_j(s)F_j(U)\,ds.$$
Thus $u_h(c_i)=U_i$, $u_h'(c_i)=hF_i(U)$, and $u_h(1)=\Psi_h(t,u)$ whenever $U$ is an admissible solution. This definition alone asserts no branch existence or uniqueness.

For interpolation estimates define the **Lebesgue constant** of this fixed node set by
$$\Lambda_M:=\max_{0\le s\le1}\sum_{j=1}^M|\ell_j(s)|.$$
For a real matrix $A$, write $\|A\|_\infty:=\max_i\sum_j|a_{ij}|$. These constants depend on the nodes and on $M$; no uniform-in-$M$ bound is part of the definition.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be the open time-state domain of an IVP $y'=f(t,y)$, with $d\ge1$. The inputs are a time $t\in\mathbb R$, an initial state $u\in\mathbb R^d$ with $(t,u)\in D$, a step $h>0$, an integer $M\ge1$, distinct ordered nodes $0\le c_1<\cdots<c_M\le1$, a predictor (default $U^0=\mathbf1u$), a Lipschitz bound $L\ge0$, a tolerance $\mathrm{tol}>0$, an integer sweep budget $K\ge0$, and a supplied stage set $\mathcal C$. A stage vector $U$ is admissible only when $(t+c_jh,U_j)\in D$ for every $j$.

After validating the node data, form the collocation tableau $Q,b$ of [[def-collocation-quadrature-tableau]]. Let $c_0=0$, $\Delta c_j=c_j-c_{j-1}$, and define the left-Euler node-subinterval preconditioner by its initial column $a_i=c_1$ and stage block
$$ (Q_\Delta)_{ij}=\begin{cases}\Delta c_{j+1},&j<i,\\0,&j\ge i.\end{cases} $$
The stage block is strictly lower triangular. In augmented notation, set $\widehat Q=(0\mid Q)$, $\widehat Q_\Delta=(a\mid Q_\Delta)$, and $\widehat F(U)=(f(t,u),F(U))$. One sweep is
$$U^{k+1}=\mathbf1u+h\widehat Q_\Delta\widehat F(U^{k+1})+h(\widehat Q-\widehat Q_\Delta)\widehat F(U^k).$$
The fixed initial-column contributions cancel, so the procedure below does not evaluate $F_0=f(t,u)$. For a stage vector $U$, write $F_j(U)=f(t+c_jh,U_j)$. Since $Q_\Delta$ is strictly lower triangular, for fixed previous stages $U^k$ the unique new stages are computed in increasing $i$ by the forward recursion
$$U_i^{k+1}=u+h\sum_{j<i}(Q_\Delta)_{ij}F_j(U^{k+1})+h\sum_{j=1}^M(Q_{ij}-(Q_\Delta)_{ij})F_j(U^k),\quad i=1,\ldots,M.$$

Use $\|V\|_{\infty,2}=\max_i\|V_i\|_2$ and $\|A\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_j|A_{ij}|$. After forming $Q_\Delta$, compute $a=hL\|Q_\Delta\|_\infty$. If $a\ge1$, return `contraction-not-certified` with no accepted endpoint. For $a<1$, compute $q=hL\|Q-Q_\Delta\|_\infty/(1-a)$; if $q\ge1$ or invariance is not certified, return `contraction-not-certified` with no accepted endpoint. The exact procedure is:

1. Reject repeated, unordered, or out-of-range nodes as `invalid-node-data` before forming the tableau.
2. Form $Q,b,Q_\Delta$ from the valid nodes and apply the contraction and invariance checks described above.
3. If the predictor is outside $\mathcal C$ or any required stage evaluation $(t+c_jh,U_j)$ lies outside $D$, return `inadmissible-stage` and no accepted endpoint.
4. Evaluate and store all $M$ values $F_j(U^0)$ once.
5. If $K=0$, return `iteration-budget-exhausted` and no accepted endpoint; no residual test has been performed.
6. For $k=0,1,\ldots,K-1$, compute $U^{k+1}$ in increasing stage order using the displayed recursion, reusing the stored $F(U^k)$ and evaluating each new $F_j(U^{k+1})$ once. If a new stage is outside $D$, return `inadmissible-stage` and no accepted endpoint. Then compute $r_k=\|U^{k+1}-U^k\|_{\infty,2}$. If $r_k\le(1-q)\,\mathrm{tol}$, return status `residual-tolerance-met`, the stage vector $U^k$, and endpoint $u+h\sum_{j=1}^M b_jF_j(U^k)$. If this is the $K$th sweep and the test failed, return `iteration-budget-exhausted` and no accepted endpoint; otherwise use $U^{k+1}$ and its stored field values as the next iterate.

These statuses report only the stated branch outcome; they do not assert convergence when a check fails.

Form $Q,b,Q_\Delta$ once per invocation and retain their coefficients through the sweep loop. Retain the old and current stage vectors and their field values while computing a sweep and testing its residual. On continuation, reuse these buffers for the next sweep; on acceptance, use the retained $U^k$ and $F(U^k)$ for the returned stage vector and endpoint in step 6. Perform the displayed operations in exact real arithmetic.

$$Z\longmapsto \mathbf1u+hQ_\Delta F(Z)+h(Q-Q_\Delta)F(V)$$
maps $\mathcal C$ into itself, and assume the stage field $F(U)=(f(t+c_i h,U_i))_{i=1}^M$ is $L$-Lipschitz there for some $L\ge0$. Put
$$a=hL\|Q_\Delta\|_\infty,\qquad q=\frac{hL\|Q-Q_\Delta\|_\infty}{1-a}.$$

Let $a<b$ be real numbers, let $m\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$r\in\{2m-1,2m\}$. A **Gaussian quadrature moment datum of order $r$** is a
finite positive measure $\mu$ on the relative Borel sigma-algebra
$\mathcal B([a,b])$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-measure-space]],
[[def-measure]], [[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) such that
$\mu([a,b])>0$, and whose **relative support**
$$ S_\mu:=\{x\in[a,b]:\mu(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open }U\subseteq[a,b]\text{ with }x\in U\} $$
contains at least $m+1$ distinct points. For every integer $0\le k\le r$,
require $x\mapsto |x|^k$ to be integrable with respect to $\mu$
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]) and put
$M_k:=\int_{[a,b]}x^k\,d\mu(x)$. Powers use the natural-exponent
recursion of [[def-integer-power]], with $x^0=1$ for every real $x$, including
$x=0$; thus $M_0$ is the integral of the constant function $1$.

The branch $r=2m-1$ supplies all moments used to construct the monic
degree-$m$ orthogonal polynomial and prove rule exactness. The stronger branch
$r=2m$ also defines its squared norm and is used for the remainder formula.
Because $[a,b]$ is bounded and $\mu$ is finite, these absolute-moment
integrability conditions follow from finiteness; they are stated to make the
two moment interfaces explicit.

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]]. Let $p_m$ be its monic degree-$m$ orthogonal
polynomial and write its ordered roots as
$a<x_1<\cdots<x_m<b$, as established in
[[thm-gauss-orthogonal-polynomial-has-simple-interior-zeros]]. For
$i=1,\ldots,m$, define the Lagrange cardinal polynomial
$$ \ell_i(X):=\prod_{\substack{1\le j\le m\\j\ne i}}\frac{X-x_j}{x_i-x_j} $$
using the convention of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
the **Gaussian quadrature weights** and the **m-node Gaussian rule** by
$$ w_i:=\int_{[a,b]}\ell_i(x)\,d\mu(x),\qquad Q_m(f):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i f(x_i) $$
for any real-valued function $f$ defined at the nodes. This definition
asserts no accuracy; well-definedness of the nodes, cardinal polynomials,
weights, and finite sum is proved in
[[lem-gauss-quadrature-rule-data-well-defined]].
Assume Countable Choice. Let $g:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Its Riemann integral and its Lebesgue integral with respect to Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$ both exist and are equal.

Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue interval-measure formula. Fix $M\ge1$, the $M$-node Gauss rule for Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$, a time $t$, and an exact IVP solution $y$ on an interval containing $[t,t+h_0]$ for some $h_0>0$, with initial state $u=y(t)$. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be an IVP vector field on a neighborhood of a common compact convex tube, let $u_h$ be its Gauss collocation polynomial for this exact start, and put $g_h(s)=f(t+hs,u_h(s))$. Assume each scalar coordinate of $f$ has continuous partial derivatives through total order $2M+1$, all bounded on the tube; vector smoothness and derivatives below are understood componentwise, with scalar Taylor and quadrature results applied coordinatewise. The tube contains the exact path, $u_h$, and every segment joining them, and the collocation branch and tube are uniform for sufficiently small $h\le h_0$. Use the induced Euclidean operator norm $\|A\|_{op}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Av\|_2$, and assume $\|D_yf\|_{op}\le L$ on the tube. Then its endpoint defect satisfies
$$\|y(t+h)-u_h(1)\|_2\le C h^{2M+1},$$
where $C$ may depend on the fixed nodes and on $M$.

Let $M,d\ge1$, let $0\le c_1<\cdots<c_M\le1$ be distinct collocation nodes, and let $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_M$ be their cardinal polynomials from [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
$$Q_{ij}:=\int_0^{c_i}\ell_j(s)\,ds,\qquad b_j:=\int_0^1\ell_j(s)\,ds.$$
The matrix $Q\in\mathbb R^{M\times M}$ and vector $b\in\mathbb R^M$ are the collocation tableau coefficients. For an IVP $y'=f(t,y)$ on the open domain of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], write
$$F_j(U):=f(t+c_jh,U_j),\qquad QF(U):=\left(\sum_{j=1}^M Q_{ij}F_j(U)\right)_{i=1}^M.$$
All displayed integrals use the oriented Riemann convention of [[def-oriented-integral]]. In particular $Q_{ij}=0$ when $c_i=0$, and the integral in $u_h$ vanishes at $\tau=0$. The collocation stages and endpoint are the implicit Runge–Kutta equations of [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]] with $A=Q$, nodes $c$, and weights $b$:
$$U=\mathbf1u+hQF(U),\qquad \Psi_h(t,u)=u+h\sum_{j=1}^M b_jF_j(U).$$
The associated collocation polynomial on normalized time $\tau\in[0,1]$ is
$$u_h(\tau):=u+h\int_0^\tau\sum_{j=1}^M\ell_j(s)F_j(U)\,ds.$$
Thus $u_h(c_i)=U_i$, $u_h'(c_i)=hF_i(U)$, and $u_h(1)=\Psi_h(t,u)$ whenever $U$ is an admissible solution. This definition alone asserts no branch existence or uniqueness.

For interpolation estimates define the **Lebesgue constant** of this fixed node set by
$$\Lambda_M:=\max_{0\le s\le1}\sum_{j=1}^M|\ell_j(s)|.$$
For a real matrix $A$, write $\|A\|_\infty:=\max_i\sum_j|a_{ij}|$. These constants depend on the nodes and on $M$; no uniform-in-$M$ bound is part of the definition.
For the distinct nodes and cardinal polynomials in [[def-collocation-quadrature-tableau]], every entry of $Q$, every component of $b$, and the Lebesgue constant $\Lambda_M$ is a finite real number.
Assume Countable Choice. For every integer $M\ge1$, Lebesgue measure on the relative Borel space $[0,1]$ is Gaussian quadrature moment data of order $2M$ in the sense of [[def-gauss-moment-data]].

derivations.claim: By [F5] under [A1] the chosen Gaussian rule has admissible Lebesgue moment data. Fact [F1] gives its nodes and cardinal-integral weights, and [F4] makes the matching collocation tableau finite and defined.

The smoothness, common-tube, and branch hypotheses of [F3] are precisely those in the Statement and [A2]. The lemma therefore gives $\|y(t+h)-\Psi_h(y(t))\|_2\le Ch^{2M+1}$, which is the claimed exact-start local defect estimate. Agreement of the integral conventions is [F2].

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be the open time-state domain of an IVP $y'=f(t,y)$, with $d\ge1$. The inputs are a time $t\in\mathbb R$, an initial state $u\in\mathbb R^d$ with $(t,u)\in D$, a step $h>0$, an integer $M\ge1$, distinct ordered nodes $0\le c_1<\cdots<c_M\le1$, a predictor (default $U^0=\mathbf1u$), a Lipschitz bound $L\ge0$, a tolerance $\mathrm{tol}>0$, an integer sweep budget $K\ge0$, and a supplied stage set $\mathcal C$. A stage vector $U$ is admissible only when $(t+c_jh,U_j)\in D$ for every $j$.

After validating the node data, form the collocation tableau $Q,b$ of [[def-collocation-quadrature-tableau]]. Let $c_0=0$, $\Delta c_j=c_j-c_{j-1}$, and define the left-Euler node-subinterval preconditioner by its initial column $a_i=c_1$ and stage block
$$ (Q_\Delta)_{ij}=\begin{cases}\Delta c_{j+1},&j<i,\\0,&j\ge i.\end{cases} $$
The stage block is strictly lower triangular. In augmented notation, set $\widehat Q=(0\mid Q)$, $\widehat Q_\Delta=(a\mid Q_\Delta)$, and $\widehat F(U)=(f(t,u),F(U))$. One sweep is
$$U^{k+1}=\mathbf1u+h\widehat Q_\Delta\widehat F(U^{k+1})+h(\widehat Q-\widehat Q_\Delta)\widehat F(U^k).$$
The fixed initial-column contributions cancel, so the procedure below does not evaluate $F_0=f(t,u)$. For a stage vector $U$, write $F_j(U)=f(t+c_jh,U_j)$. Since $Q_\Delta$ is strictly lower triangular, for fixed previous stages $U^k$ the unique new stages are computed in increasing $i$ by the forward recursion
$$U_i^{k+1}=u+h\sum_{j<i}(Q_\Delta)_{ij}F_j(U^{k+1})+h\sum_{j=1}^M(Q_{ij}-(Q_\Delta)_{ij})F_j(U^k),\quad i=1,\ldots,M.$$

Use $\|V\|_{\infty,2}=\max_i\|V_i\|_2$ and $\|A\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_j|A_{ij}|$. The supplied set $\mathcal C$ must be a nonempty closed product ball of admissible stage vectors, contain the predictor, be invariant under each inner stage map and outer sweep, and have an $L$-Lipschitz stage field $F(U)=(F_j(U))_{j=1}^M$ in this norm. After forming $Q_\Delta$, compute $a=hL\|Q_\Delta\|_\infty$. If $a\ge1$, return `contraction-not-certified` with no accepted endpoint. For $a<1$, compute $q=hL\|Q-Q_\Delta\|_\infty/(1-a)$; if $q\ge1$ or invariance is not certified, return `contraction-not-certified` with no accepted endpoint. The exact procedure is:

1. Reject repeated, unordered, or out-of-range nodes as `invalid-node-data` before forming the tableau.
2. Form $Q,b,Q_\Delta$ from the valid nodes and apply the contraction and invariance checks described above.
3. If the predictor is outside $\mathcal C$ or any required stage evaluation $(t+c_jh,U_j)$ lies outside $D$, return `inadmissible-stage` and no accepted endpoint.
4. Evaluate and store all $M$ values $F_j(U^0)$ once.
5. If $K=0$, return `iteration-budget-exhausted` and no accepted endpoint; no residual test has been performed.
6. For $k=0,1,\ldots,K-1$, compute $U^{k+1}$ in increasing stage order using the displayed recursion, reusing the stored $F(U^k)$ and evaluating each new $F_j(U^{k+1})$ once. If a new stage is outside $D$, return `inadmissible-stage` and no accepted endpoint. Then compute $r_k=\|U^{k+1}-U^k\|_{\infty,2}$. If $r_k\le(1-q)\,\mathrm{tol}$, return status `residual-tolerance-met`, the stage vector $U^k$, and endpoint $u+h\sum_{j=1}^M b_jF_j(U^k)$. If this is the $K$th sweep and the test failed, return `iteration-budget-exhausted` and no accepted endpoint; otherwise use $U^{k+1}$ and its stored field values as the next iterate.

These statuses report only the stated branch outcome; they do not assert convergence when a check fails.

Form $Q,b,Q_\Delta$ once per invocation and retain their coefficients through the sweep loop. Retain the old and current stage vectors and their field values while computing a sweep and testing its residual. On continuation, reuse these buffers for the next sweep; on acceptance, use the retained $U^k$ and $F(U^k)$ for the returned stage vector and endpoint in step 6. Perform the displayed operations in exact real arithmetic.

Consider the procedure of [[alg-explicit-left-euler-sdc-sweep]] with $M,d\ge1$ and budget $K\ge0$. Count one **stage call** for each instructed evaluation of $F_j(U)=f(t+c_jh,U_j)$, even when different calls happen to have equal arguments. Generating the supplied predictor and constructing or checking external admissibility, set-membership or invariance certificates are outside this call count. Assume each invoked evaluation and check returns. The following counts apply to any supplied predictor, including the default constant predictor.

- An exit at the node, contraction, invariance or predictor-admissibility checks before step 4 uses zero instructed stage calls. A run completing step 4 uses $M$ predictor calls. If $K=0$, it then returns `iteration-budget-exhausted`, with no residual test and no accepted endpoint.
- If predictor evaluation and exactly $s$ full sweeps complete, with no incomplete sweep, the run uses exactly $M(s+1)$ stage calls, where $0\le s\le K$. If the next sweep instead exits at an inadmissible stage after evaluating a prefix of $p$ new stages, where $0\le p<M$ and $s<K$, the count is exactly $M(s+1)+p$.
- Hence every execution uses at most $M(K+1)$ instructed stage calls. Equality holds for a run completing predictor evaluation and all $K$ sweeps, including the $K=0$ case after predictor evaluation. Acceptance after $s\ge1$ completed sweeps returns $U^{s-1}$; forming its endpoint uses the cached $F(U^{s-1})$ and adds no stage call. No $F_0=f(t,u)$ call is required.

For direct dense evaluation of the prescribed finite sums, the stored tableau and preconditioner use $O(M^2)$ real coefficients, and old/current stage and derivative buffers use $O(Md)$ real scalars. A complete sweep uses $O(M^2d)$ scalar arithmetic in addition to its $M$ stage calls. Its residual requires $O(Md)$ scalar arithmetic, at most $M$ square roots and $O(M)$ comparisons; the accepted endpoint requires $O(Md)$ further arithmetic and no stage calls. These bounds also bound any evaluated prefix of a failed sweep. After the quadrature data are supplied, forming the preconditioner, coefficient differences and contraction row norms uses $O(M^2)$ scalar arithmetic and absolute-value operations. Including default constant-predictor initialization, all direct algebraic work through any exit is bounded by $O(M^2+(K+1)M^2d)$, with at most $KM$ square roots for residuals; scalar absolute values and loop/comparison work obey the same asymptotic bound. The storage bound is independent of $K$ when buffers are reused as instructed.

These bounds exclude the work and internal storage of evaluating $f$, constructing the polynomial quadrature data, generating a supplied nondefault predictor, and performing the external domain/set/certificate checks. They do not bound those unspecified tasks or assert that a failed execution completed $K$ sweeps. All counts concern exact real arithmetic and give no floating-point roundoff guarantee.

If the run stops after $s>0$ completed sweeps with no incomplete sweep, each adds exactly $M$ evaluations because its $M$ new stage states are evaluated once and the previous $F(U^j)$ values are reused. Thus the total is $M+sM=M(s+1)$, and for $s\le K$ this is at most $M(K+1)$, attained if all $K$ sweeps complete. A failed run with a partially evaluated sweep is counted by its actual prefix as in [F2], and still obeys that bound. Acceptance after $s\ge1$ sweeps returns $U^{s-1}$ and uses its cached endpoint derivatives with no additional calls.

The stored dense matrices $Q,Q_\Delta$ each have $M^2$ real entries, so their storage is $O(M^2)$; retaining old/current stage vectors and their derivative values takes $O(Md)$ additional scalar storage. Each forward-recursion stage has two sums with at most $2M$ vector terms in total, for at most $O(M^2d)$ scalar arithmetic per sweep. Residual formation adds $O(Md)$ scalar arithmetic and at most $M$ square roots; an accepted endpoint adds $O(Md)$ arithmetic and no new field evaluations. These are the proved counts in [F2]. They omit the cost of evaluating $f$, constructing the polynomial quadrature data (which depends on their representation), supplied predictor generation, and external admissibility/invariance certification and their internal storage. The model uses exact real arithmetic and gives no floating-point roundoff guarantee.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be the open time-state domain of an IVP $y'=f(t,y)$, with $d\ge1$. The inputs are a time $t\in\mathbb R$, an initial state $u\in\mathbb R^d$ with $(t,u)\in D$, a step $h>0$, an integer $M\ge1$, distinct ordered nodes $0\le c_1<\cdots<c_M\le1$, a predictor (default $U^0=\mathbf1u$), a Lipschitz bound $L\ge0$, a tolerance $\mathrm{tol}>0$, an integer sweep budget $K\ge0$, and a supplied stage set $\mathcal C$. A stage vector $U$ is admissible only when $(t+c_jh,U_j)\in D$ for every $j$.

After validating the node data, form the collocation tableau $Q,b$ of [[def-collocation-quadrature-tableau]]. Let $c_0=0$, $\Delta c_j=c_j-c_{j-1}$, and define the left-Euler node-subinterval preconditioner by its initial column $a_i=c_1$ and stage block
$$ (Q_\Delta)_{ij}=\begin{cases}\Delta c_{j+1},&j<i,\\0,&j\ge i.\end{cases} $$
The stage block is strictly lower triangular. In augmented notation, set $\widehat Q=(0\mid Q)$, $\widehat Q_\Delta=(a\mid Q_\Delta)$, and $\widehat F(U)=(f(t,u),F(U))$. One sweep is
$$U^{k+1}=\mathbf1u+h\widehat Q_\Delta\widehat F(U^{k+1})+h(\widehat Q-\widehat Q_\Delta)\widehat F(U^k).$$
The fixed initial-column contributions cancel, so the procedure below does not evaluate $F_0=f(t,u)$. For a stage vector $U$, write $F_j(U)=f(t+c_jh,U_j)$. Since $Q_\Delta$ is strictly lower triangular, for fixed previous stages $U^k$ the unique new stages are computed in increasing $i$ by the forward recursion
$$U_i^{k+1}=u+h\sum_{j<i}(Q_\Delta)_{ij}F_j(U^{k+1})+h\sum_{j=1}^M(Q_{ij}-(Q_\Delta)_{ij})F_j(U^k),\quad i=1,\ldots,M.$$

Use $\|V\|_{\infty,2}=\max_i\|V_i\|_2$ and $\|A\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_j|A_{ij}|$. The supplied set $\mathcal C$ must be a nonempty closed product ball of admissible stage vectors, contain the predictor, be invariant under each inner stage map and outer sweep, and have an $L$-Lipschitz stage field $F(U)=(F_j(U))_{j=1}^M$ in this norm. After forming $Q_\Delta$, compute $a=hL\|Q_\Delta\|_\infty$. If $a\ge1$, return `contraction-not-certified` with no accepted endpoint. For $a<1$, compute $q=hL\|Q-Q_\Delta\|_\infty/(1-a)$; if $q\ge1$ or invariance is not certified, return `contraction-not-certified` with no accepted endpoint. The exact procedure is:

1. Reject repeated, unordered, or out-of-range nodes as `invalid-node-data` before forming the tableau.
2. Form $Q,b,Q_\Delta$ from the valid nodes and apply the contraction and invariance checks described above.
3. If the predictor is outside $\mathcal C$ or any required stage evaluation $(t+c_jh,U_j)$ lies outside $D$, return `inadmissible-stage` and no accepted endpoint.
4. Evaluate and store all $M$ values $F_j(U^0)$ once.
5. If $K=0$, return `iteration-budget-exhausted` and no accepted endpoint; no residual test has been performed.
6. For $k=0,1,\ldots,K-1$, compute $U^{k+1}$ in increasing stage order using the displayed recursion, reusing the stored $F(U^k)$ and evaluating each new $F_j(U^{k+1})$ once. If a new stage is outside $D$, return `inadmissible-stage` and no accepted endpoint. Then compute $r_k=\|U^{k+1}-U^k\|_{\infty,2}$. If $r_k\le(1-q)\,\mathrm{tol}$, return status `residual-tolerance-met`, the stage vector $U^k$, and endpoint $u+h\sum_{j=1}^M b_jF_j(U^k)$. If this is the $K$th sweep and the test failed, return `iteration-budget-exhausted` and no accepted endpoint; otherwise use $U^{k+1}$ and its stored field values as the next iterate.

These statuses report only the stated branch outcome; they do not assert convergence when a check fails.

Form $Q,b,Q_\Delta$ once per invocation and retain their coefficients through the sweep loop. Retain the old and current stage vectors and their field values while computing a sweep and testing its residual. On continuation, reuse these buffers for the next sweep; on acceptance, use the retained $U^k$ and $F(U^k)$ for the returned stage vector and endpoint in step 6. Perform the displayed operations in exact real arithmetic.

Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue interval-measure formula. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be an IVP vector field on a neighborhood of a common compact convex tube; consider an exact solution $y$ of $y'=f(t,y)$ on a fixed interval $[0,T]$ in this tube. Assume each scalar coordinate has continuous partial derivatives through total order two and is Lipschitz in $y$ there. Smoothness and Taylor expansions for vector-valued functions are interpreted componentwise, by applying scalar results to each coordinate. Assume the small-step one-stage collocation branch exists uniquely in this tube and its stages, the exact path, and the segments used in the estimates remain there. For the one-node Gaussian tableau of [[lem-one-node-gauss-data-is-midpoint]], the method is the implicit midpoint rule and has global order two on any fixed interval for which these hypotheses hold uniformly.

Fix $M\ge1$ collocation nodes and a nonnegative integer $k$ independent of $h$. Use the explicit-left-Euler SDC sweep in [[alg-explicit-left-euler-sdc-sweep]] with constant predictor $U^0=\mathbf1u$ and form the candidate endpoint from $U^k$, after $k$ completed sweeps. Assume each coordinate of $f$ has continuous partial derivatives through total order $M$ on an open neighborhood of a common compact tube $\mathcal T$; assume $f$ is state-Lipschitz with constant $L$ and bounded by $B$ on $\mathcal T$, which contains the exact path, all iterates, and the comparison segments. Also assume the exact-path integrand has the derivative bound required by [[thm-collocation-local-defect-order-m]]. At each mesh time $t_n$, let $\mathcal U_n\subseteq\mathcal T_{t_n}:=\{u:(t_n,u)\in\mathcal T\}$ be a set of starting states containing the exact and numerical grid states used in the global-error comparison. For every $u\in\mathcal U_n$, assume the constant predictor $U^0=\mathbf1u$ belongs to a nonempty closed product ball $\mathcal C_{n,u}$ used in [[thm-sdc-sweep-contraction-and-error-bound]], and each inner stage map and sweep preserves $\mathcal C_{n,u}$. Assume the contraction theorem holds uniformly with $a=hL\|Q_\Delta\|_\infty\le1/2$ and $q\le C_qh<1$. For fixed $k$, the $U^k$ endpoint map has exact-start defect $O(h^{p+1})$ and global order $p=\min(M,k+1)$ on any fixed interval, provided all grid states stay in $\mathcal T$. The claim is local-step and fixed-$k$; it asserts no uniform constants as $M$ or $k$ grows.

Fix $M$ nodes and an integer $1\le p\le M$. On a fixed interval use exact collocation stages $U_n^*$ and the collocation endpoint map $\Psi_{h,n}$ of [[def-collocation-quadrature-tableau]]. Assume the hypotheses of [[thm-sdc-sweep-contraction-and-error-bound]] hold uniformly, with contraction constants $q_n\le q_0<1$, the common field Lipschitz constant is $L$, and all exact and approximate stages and grid states stay in one compact tube. Suppose the SDC stage vector $V_n$ used for the endpoint satisfies
$$\|S_n(V_n)-V_n\|_{\infty,2}\le(1-q_n)C_\tau h^{p+1}.$$
Starting from the exact initial value and setting $y_{n+1}=y_n+h\sum_jb_jf(t_n+c_jh,(V_n)_j)$, the inexact method has global error $O(h^p)$. Thus a fixed residual constant and a stage target $O(h^{p+1})$ preserve any collocation order $p\le M$; the bound is conditional on the stated local contraction and tube assumptions.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

For all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$(x+y)^{n} \;=\; \sum_{k<n+1} \iota\binom{n}{k}\, x^{k}\, y^{\,n-k},$$

where the powers are the integer powers of [[def-integer-power]], the sum is the
real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] over $k = 0, 1, \dots, n$, the difference
$n-k$ is a genuine one because $k \le n$ throughout the range, and $\iota$ is the
canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]].

**The coefficient is $\iota\binom{n}{k}$ and not $\binom{n}{k}$.** A binomial
coefficient is a natural number, that is a von Neumann natural, that is a set; it
is not an element of $\mathbb{R}$, and it enters the field through $\iota$.

**The identity is stated in $\mathbb{R}$ and only in $\mathbb{R}$.** The same
proof uses nothing but commutativity, associativity, distributivity and
natural-number multiples of a ring element, so a commutative-ring version is
available wherever rings are; rings are not available at this point in the
reading order, and the ring statement is a separate statement, to be made where
they are. See the Remarks below.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue interval-measure formula. For Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$, the one-node Gaussian quadrature rule has node $c_1=1/2$ and weight $b_1=1$. Its one-stage collocation tableau therefore has $Q_{11}=1/2$ and endpoint weight $b_1=1$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be the open time-state domain of an IVP $y'=f(t,y)$, with $d\ge1$. The inputs are a time $t\in\mathbb R$, an initial state $u\in\mathbb R^d$ with $(t,u)\in D$, a step $h>0$, an integer $M\ge1$, distinct ordered nodes $0\le c_1<\cdots<c_M\le1$, a predictor (default $U^0=\mathbf1u$), a Lipschitz bound $L\ge0$, a tolerance $\mathrm{tol}>0$, an integer sweep budget $K\ge0$, and a supplied stage set $\mathcal C$. A stage vector $U$ is admissible only when $(t+c_jh,U_j)\in D$ for every $j$.

After validating the node data, form the collocation tableau $Q,b$ of [[def-collocation-quadrature-tableau]]. Let $c_0=0$, $\Delta c_j=c_j-c_{j-1}$, and define the left-Euler node-subinterval preconditioner by its initial column $a_i=c_1$ and stage block
$$ (Q_\Delta)_{ij}=\begin{cases}\Delta c_{j+1},&j<i,\\0,&j\ge i.\end{cases} $$
The stage block is strictly lower triangular. In augmented notation, set $\widehat Q=(0\mid Q)$, $\widehat Q_\Delta=(a\mid Q_\Delta)$, and $\widehat F(U)=(f(t,u),F(U))$. One sweep is
$$U^{k+1}=\mathbf1u+h\widehat Q_\Delta\widehat F(U^{k+1})+h(\widehat Q-\widehat Q_\Delta)\widehat F(U^k).$$
The fixed initial-column contributions cancel, so the procedure below does not evaluate $F_0=f(t,u)$. For a stage vector $U$, write $F_j(U)=f(t+c_jh,U_j)$. Since $Q_\Delta$ is strictly lower triangular, for fixed previous stages $U^k$ the unique new stages are computed in increasing $i$ by the forward recursion
$$U_i^{k+1}=u+h\sum_{j<i}(Q_\Delta)_{ij}F_j(U^{k+1})+h\sum_{j=1}^M(Q_{ij}-(Q_\Delta)_{ij})F_j(U^k),\quad i=1,\ldots,M.$$

Use $\|V\|_{\infty,2}=\max_i\|V_i\|_2$ and $\|A\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_j|A_{ij}|$. The supplied set $\mathcal C$ must be a nonempty closed product ball of admissible stage vectors, contain the predictor, be invariant under each inner stage map and outer sweep, and have an $L$-Lipschitz stage field $F(U)=(F_j(U))_{j=1}^M$ in this norm. After forming $Q_\Delta$, compute $a=hL\|Q_\Delta\|_\infty$. If $a\ge1$, return `contraction-not-certified` with no accepted endpoint. For $a<1$, compute $q=hL\|Q-Q_\Delta\|_\infty/(1-a)$; if $q\ge1$ or invariance is not certified, return `contraction-not-certified` with no accepted endpoint. The exact procedure is:

1. Reject repeated, unordered, or out-of-range nodes as `invalid-node-data` before forming the tableau.
2. Form $Q,b,Q_\Delta$ from the valid nodes and apply the contraction and invariance checks described above.
3. If the predictor is outside $\mathcal C$ or any required stage evaluation $(t+c_jh,U_j)$ lies outside $D$, return `inadmissible-stage` and no accepted endpoint.
4. Evaluate and store all $M$ values $F_j(U^0)$ once.
5. If $K=0$, return `iteration-budget-exhausted` and no accepted endpoint; no residual test has been performed.
6. For $k=0,1,\ldots,K-1$, compute $U^{k+1}$ in increasing stage order using the displayed recursion, reusing the stored $F(U^k)$ and evaluating each new $F_j(U^{k+1})$ once. If a new stage is outside $D$, return `inadmissible-stage` and no accepted endpoint. Then compute $r_k=\|U^{k+1}-U^k\|_{\infty,2}$. If $r_k\le(1-q)\,\mathrm{tol}$, return status `residual-tolerance-met`, the stage vector $U^k$, and endpoint $u+h\sum_{j=1}^M b_jF_j(U^k)$. If this is the $K$th sweep and the test failed, return `iteration-budget-exhausted` and no accepted endpoint; otherwise use $U^{k+1}$ and its stored field values as the next iterate.

These statuses report only the stated branch outcome; they do not assert convergence when a check fails.

Form $Q,b,Q_\Delta$ once per invocation and retain their coefficients through the sweep loop. Retain the old and current stage vectors and their field values while computing a sweep and testing its residual. On continuation, reuse these buffers for the next sweep; on acceptance, use the retained $U^k$ and $F(U^k)$ for the returned stage vector and endpoint in step 6. Perform the displayed operations in exact real arithmetic.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a nonempty closed product ball of admissible stage vectors in $(\mathbb R^d)^M$, with metric $\|U-V\|_{\infty,2}=\max_i\|U_i-V_i\|_2$. For each $V\in\mathcal C$, assume the inner stage map
$$Z\longmapsto \mathbf1u+hQ_\Delta F(Z)+h(Q-Q_\Delta)F(V)$$
maps $\mathcal C$ into itself, and assume the stage field $F(U)=(f(t+c_i h,U_i))_{i=1}^M$ is $L$-Lipschitz there for some $L\ge0$. Put
$$a=hL\|Q_\Delta\|_\infty,\qquad q=\frac{hL\|Q-Q_\Delta\|_\infty}{1-a}.$$
If $a<1$ and $q<1$, then every sweep is uniquely defined in $\mathcal C$, the sweep map $S:U^k\mapsto U^{k+1}$ is a contraction with constant $q$, and its unique fixed point $U^*$ is the unique collocation stage vector in $\mathcal C$. For every $V\in\mathcal C$,
$$\|V-U^*\|_{\infty,2}\le\frac{\|S(V)-V\|_{\infty,2}}{1-q}.$$
If the initial iterate satisfies $U^0\in\mathcal C$, then the iterates $U^{k+1}=S(U^k)$ obey $\|U^k-U^*\|_{\infty,2}\le q^k\|U^0-U^*\|_{\infty,2}$. In particular, a residual-certified predictor used with [[alg-explicit-left-euler-sdc-sweep]] must lie in $\mathcal C$. These are local stage-iteration claims; they assert no convergence when either contraction inequality fails.

Let $M\ge1$, let $0\le c_1<\cdots<c_M\le1$ be fixed distinct nodes, and fix an exact IVP solution $y$ on an interval containing $[t,t+h_0]$ for some $h_0>0$, with initial state $u=y(t)$. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open with $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ an IVP vector field on a neighborhood of a fixed compact convex tube. Assume each scalar coordinate of $f$ has continuous partial derivatives through total order $M$, bounded on the tube, and is $L$-Lipschitz in state there. Smoothness and derivative statements for vector-valued functions are componentwise; scalar Taylor is applied to each coordinate. Assume the exact path, stages, collocation polynomial, and comparison segments stay in the tube. In particular, the composite $g_h(s)=f(t+hs,y(t+hs))$ satisfies $\|g_h^{(M)}\|_\infty\le C_Fh^M$ uniformly; the stated componentwise smoothness and bounded exact-path derivatives imply this bound. Assume directly that for every sufficiently small $h>0$ the collocation stage equation has a unique solution in the tube. Then its endpoint map has uniform exact-start local defect $O(h^{M+1})$ as $h\downarrow0$. The constant depends on the fixed nodes, including their Lebesgue constant $\Lambda_M$; no uniform-in-$M$ estimate is asserted.

derivations.claim: Let the common state tube be $[0,2e]$ and take the time-fiber start sets $\mathcal U_n=[1,e]$; the field $f(t,y)=y$ is bounded there by $B=2e$ and is $1$-Lipschitz. For every start $u\in\mathcal U_n$, use the one-stage closed product ball $\mathcal C_u=[0,2u]$, which contains the constant predictor $U^0=u$. By [F12], for $V\in\mathcal C_u$ the inner/outer sweep map is $S_u(V)=u+(h/2)V$, whose values lie in $[u,u+hu]\subseteq[u,2u]\subseteq\mathcal C_u$ when $0<h\le1$. The contraction constants are $a=0$ and $q=h/2\le1/2$, with $q=(1/2)h$. Thus [F13] supplies the unique local collocation branch in $\mathcal C_u$, uniformly for the start states used in the stability comparison. Now induct on the mesh index. If all earlier checks passed, then $y_n=(1+h)^n>0$; for $nh\le1$, [F6] gives $(1+h)^n\le\exp(nh)$ and [F11] gives $\exp(nh)\le e$, so $y_n\in\mathcal U_n$ and the stage set hypotheses just verified apply. The first sweep value is $U^1=y_n+(h/2)y_n$, with update residual $r_0=h|y_n|/2\le eh/2$. For sufficiently small $h$, $eh/2\le1-h/2=(1-q)\mathrm{tol}$, so [F1] returns $U^0$ after the first check and the endpoint is $y_{n+1}=(1+h)y_n$. This closes the induction for every step.

Let $y$ be any exact IVP solution. By [F8]–[F9], $z(t)=\exp(-t)y(t)$ has derivative $z'(t)=-\exp(-t)y(t)+\exp(-t)y'(t)=0$. [F10] on each interval $[0,t]$ gives $z(t)=z(0)=1$; the addition formula [F9] then gives $y(t)=\exp(t)$ and in particular $y(1)=e$. Thus the exact grid states also lie in $\mathcal U_n=[1,e]$. On a step starting at $t_n$, the exact-path integrand is $g_h(s)=e^{t_n+hs}$, so $g_h'(s)=he^{t_n+hs}$ and $\|g_h'\|_\infty\le eh$ for $0\le t_n+hs\le1$. This verifies the $M=1$ exact-path derivative premise in [F14].

The computed final value is $(1+1/N)^N$. For $N\ge2$, [F7] gives its $j$th coefficient as $\binom NjN^{-j}=\frac1{j!}\prod_{r=0}^{j-1}(1-r/N)$ for $j\le N$, which is at most $1/j!$; omitted terms for $j>N$ are positive in [F5]. The $j=2$ coefficient alone differs from $1/2!$ by $1/(2N)$, so $e-(1+1/N)^N\ge1/(2N)=h/2$. Therefore this accepted finite-tolerance method is not order two; [F3] predicts only order $\min(1,0+1)=1$ from the uncorrected stage, while [F2] gives order two for the fully solved collocation method. More explicitly, step 1.1 gives $y_n=(1+h)^n\ge1$, hence the accepted first residual obeys $r_0=hy_n/2\ge h/2$. For any fixed residual constant $C_\tau$, $r_0/h^3\ge1/(2h^2)\to\infty$, so this residual cannot satisfy the $O(h^3)$ target required by [F4] to preserve order two.

$$\|S_n(V_n)-V_n\|_{\infty,2}\le(1-q_n)C_\tau h^{p+1}.$$

Thus a fixed residual constant and a stage target $O(h^{p+1})$ preserve any collocation order $p\le M$; the bound is conditional on the stated local contraction and tube assumptions.

Let $m,d\ge1$, $h>0$, $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$, and centers $c=(c_1,\ldots,c_m)\in(\mathbb R^d)^m$. On block vectors define

$$\|Y\|_{\infty,2}:=\max_{1\le i\le m}\|Y_i\|_2,\qquad \|A\|_\infty:=\max_i\sum_{j=1}^m|a_{ij}|.$$

Let $F:\mathcal B\to(\mathbb R^d)^m$, with components $F_i:\mathcal B\to\mathbb R^d$, be defined on the closed product ball $\mathcal B=\{Y:\|Y-c\|_{\infty,2}\le R\}$, where $R>0$. Suppose constants $M,L\ge0$ satisfy, for all $Y,Z\in\mathcal B$,

$$\|F(Y)\|_{\infty,2}\le M,\qquad \|F(Y)-F(Z)\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|Y-Z\|_{\infty,2},$$

$$\|\widetilde Y-Y^*\|_{\infty,2}\le\frac{\|G(\widetilde Y)\|_{\infty,2}}{1-q}.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $I=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a compact interval, let
$C:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be continuous, let $t_0\in I$, and let
$Y_0\in M_n(\mathbb R)$. Then the linear matrix initial value problem

$$Y'(t)=C(t)Y(t),\qquad Y(t_0)=Y_0,$$

has a unique solution on all of $I$.

derivations.claim: Let $\delta_h(t)=u_{\theta_0+h}(t)-u_{\theta_0}(t)$. Differentiability of $u_0$ gives $\|u_0(\theta_0+h)-u_0(\theta_0)\|_2\le C_0\|h\|_2$ for small $h$. Subtract the Volterra equations [F1] and apply [F2] on the segment between $(u_{\theta_0+h}(t),\theta_0+h)$ and $(u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$. Boundedness of $D f$ on $O$ gives $$\|\delta_h(t)\|_2\le C_0\|h\|_2+L\int_0^t(\|\delta_h(s)\|_2+\|h\|_2)\,ds.$$ Since $t\le T$, [F3] yields $\sup_t\|\delta_h(t)\|_2\le(C_0+LT)e^{LT}\|h\|_2$.

Put $A(t)=D_u f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$ and let $B_j(t)$ be column $j$ of $D_\theta f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$. For each parameter coordinate $j$, the augmented vector $Z_j=(S_{\cdot j},1)$ solves the homogeneous linear system $$Z_j'(t)=\begin{pmatrix}A(t)&B_j(t)\\0&0\end{pmatrix}Z_j(t),\qquad Z_j(0)=\begin{pmatrix}D u_0(\theta_0)_{\cdot j}\\1\end{pmatrix}.$$ Embed $Z_j(0)$ as one column of a square $(d+1)\times(d+1)$ initial matrix, with all other columns zero. The unique linear matrix solution supplied by [F5] has that vector solution as the selected column. Thus the tangent equation has a unique solution for each of the finitely many columns.

Put $A(t)=D_u f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$ and $B(t)=D_\theta f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$, and define $\rho_h(t)=f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t)+\delta_h(t),\theta_0+h)-f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)-A(t)\delta_h(t)-B(t)h$. Uniform continuity of $D f$ on $\overline O$ and the integral remainder along the secant give $\sup_t\|\rho_h(t)\|_2=o(\|h\|_2)$, since step 1.1 gives $\sup_t(\|\delta_h(t)\|_2+\|h\|_2)=O(\|h\|_2)$. Also $u_0(\theta_0+h)-u_0(\theta_0)=D u_0(\theta_0)h+o(\|h\|_2)$.

Let $E_h(t)=\delta_h(t)-S(t)h$, and let $r_0(h)=u_0(\theta_0+h)-u_0(\theta_0)-D u_0(\theta_0)h$. The Volterra equations and the field remainder $\rho_h$ from step 2.1 give $E_h(t)=r_0(h)+\int_0^t\bigl(A(s)E_h(s)+\rho_h(s)\bigr)ds$, where $A(s)=D_u f(s,u_{\theta_0}(s),\theta_0)$. By [F4], $\|E_h(t)\|_2\le\|r_0(h)\|_2+T\sup_s\|\rho_h(s)\|_2+L\int_0^t\|E_h(s)\|_2ds$. Both first terms are $o(\|h\|_2)$ by step 2.1 and differentiability of $u_0$. Applying [F3] yields $\sup_t\|E_h(t)\|_2=o(\|h\|_2)$. Thus the Fréchet derivative at $\theta_0$ exists and equals $S$.

For any sequence $\theta_j\to\theta_0$ in $V_\theta$, step 1.1 gives $u_{\theta_j}\to u_{\theta_0}$ uniformly, and uniform continuity of $D f$ on $\overline O$ makes the tangent coefficients $A_j,B_j$ converge uniformly to $A,B$. Subtracting the tangent integral equations gives $S_j(t)-S(t)=D u_0(\theta_j)-D u_0(\theta_0)+\int_0^t\bigl(A_j(s)(S_j(s)-S(s))+(A_j(s)-A(s))S(s)+B_j(s)-B(s)\bigr)ds$. The initial and coefficient differences tend to zero, while $A_j$ are uniformly bounded; [F3] then gives $\|S_j-S\|_{C([0,T])}\to0$. Since $\theta_0$ is arbitrary in $V_\theta$, the derivative is continuous throughout that set, so the flow map is $C^1$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim: Write $p^T S=\sum_{i=1}^d p_i S_{i,\cdot}$. By [F2] coordinatewise, $(p^TS)'=(p')^TS+p^TS'$. Substituting the two equations yields $(-A^Tp-g)^TS+p^T(AS+B)=-g^TS+p^TB$, because $(A^Tp)^TS=p^TAS$.
The right-hand side in step 1.1 is continuous and hence integrable. Apply [F3] to the scalar function $p^TS$ and integrate step 1.1 over $[0,T]$. This gives the stated endpoint identity.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $N\ge1$, and for $0\le n\le N$ let $U_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_n}$ be open. A finite parameterized state-step graph consists of a $C^1$ initial map $x_0:\Theta\to U_0$ and $C^1$ step maps $\Psi_n:U_n\times\Theta\to U_{n+1}$ for $0\le n<N$, such that the recursion $x_{n+1}(\theta)=\Psi_n(x_n(\theta),\theta)$ is defined for every $\theta$ in the chosen parameter neighborhood. A $C^1$ running objective consists of maps $\ell_n:U_n\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ and a terminal objective $\phi:U_N\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$, all $C^1$. Its reduced objective is
$$J(\theta)=\phi(x_N(\theta),\theta)+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\ell_n(x_n(\theta),\theta).$$
The maps and objective define one finite real-arithmetic graph. A gradient of this graph is the derivative of this finite composition; it is not the derivative of an exact implicit solution unless the step map itself is that solution map.

Input a graph from [[def-finite-straight-line-computational-program]] and an admissible point $x$. Evaluate and store all primal values in topological order. Initialize every operation cotangent and every input cotangent to zero. Seed the scalar output by setting its cotangent to $1$: if $o$ is an operation, set $\bar z_o=1$; if $o$ is input coordinate $i$, set $\bar x_i=1$. For $j=T,T-1,\ldots,1$, and for every parent slot $k=1,\ldots,r_j$, compute the contribution
$$c_{j,k}=D_k\phi_j(z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,z_{p_{j,r_j}})^T\bar z_j$$
and add it to the cotangent accumulator of that parent: use $\bar x_i$ if the parent is input coordinate $i$, and $\bar z_\ell$ if it is operation node $\ell$. If the same parent node occurs in multiple slots, add every slot contribution. Return the scalar output $f(x)$ and the input cotangents $(\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_n)$ as the Euclidean gradient. A point outside the admissible domain returns DOMAIN_ERROR; a branch boundary or ambiguous active branch returns NONDIFFERENTIABLE and no gradient. The procedure differentiates the real-arithmetic graph; it makes no floating-point error claim.

For a finite $C^1$ program with one scalar output $f$, on a fixed strict branch and at every admissible $x$, the reverse-mode algorithm returns $Df(x)^T1$, the gradient of $f$. More precisely, at any operation node $i$, if its value is temporarily treated as an independent variable and all later operations are recomputed from it, then the accumulated cotangent at $i$ is the derivative of the scalar output with respect to that independent node value.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: By the chain rule [F4] applied to $x_{n+1}(\theta)=\Psi_n(x_n(\theta),\theta)$, $S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n$; differentiating the initial map gives $S_0=Dx_0(\theta)$. These are the forward tangent equations for this finite composition.

Apply the reverse accumulation rule [F2] to the finite graph of states and objective summands in [F1]. The terminal contribution seeds $p_N=D_x\phi^T$; at each state node $x_n$, its local running-cost edge contributes $D_x\ell_n^T$, while its state-transition edge contributes $A_n^Tp_{n+1}$. Thus the accumulated state cotangent is exactly $p_n$ as defined in the Statement, and the direct parameter edges contribute $D_\theta\phi^T$ and $D_\theta\ell_n^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}$. By [F3], reverse mode returns the exact derivative of this finite C1 graph.

Differentiate the objective in [F1] using the forward sensitivities in step 1.1. The chain rule gives $$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi^T+S_N^TD_x\phi^T+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}(D_\theta\ell_n^T+S_n^TD_x\ell_n^T).$$ This is the direct tangent expression, with all derivatives evaluated along the trajectory.

The adjoint equation gives $p_n^TS_n=D_x\ell_nS_n+p_{n+1}^TA_nS_n$. Since $S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n$, rearranging yields $$D_x\ell_nS_n=p_n^TS_n-p_{n+1}^TS_{n+1}+p_{n+1}^TB_n.$$ Summing over $n$ telescopes; $p_N=D_x\phi^T$ cancels the terminal tangent term in step 2.1 and leaves $S_0^Tp_0+\sum_n B_n^Tp_{n+1}$. Adding the direct parameter derivatives from step 2.1 gives the displayed adjoint formula.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta$ be open, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuously differentiable. Let $V_\theta\subseteq\Theta$ be open and $u_0:V_\theta\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^1$. Assume there is a bounded convex open set $O\subset D$ with compact closure in $D$ such that for every $\theta\in V_\theta$ the unique solution of $u'=f(t,u,\theta)$, $u(0)=u_0(\theta)$, exists on $[0,T]$, and all triples $(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)$ lie in $O$. Then $\theta\mapsto u_\theta$ is $C^1$ as a map to $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$. For any $\theta_0\in V_\theta$, its tangent matrix $S(t)=D_\theta u_\theta(t)|_{\theta=\theta_0}$ is the unique solution of
$$S'(t)=D_u f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)S(t)+D_\theta f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0),\qquad S(0)=D u_0(\theta_0).$$
The result is local to the stated common compact tube and claims no differentiability outside it.

Let $S\in C^1([0,T];\mathbb R^{d\times m})$ and $p\in C^1([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $S'=A S+B$ and $p'=-A^T p-g$, where $A,B,g$ are continuous and have compatible dimensions. Then
$$p(T)^T S(T)-p(0)^T S(0)=\int_0^T\bigl(-g(t)^T S(t)+p(t)^T B(t)\bigr)\,dt.$$

Let $I=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a compact interval, let
$C:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be continuous, let $t_0\in I$, and let
$Y_0\in M_n(\mathbb R)$. Then the linear matrix initial value problem

$$Y'(t)=C(t)Y(t),\qquad Y(t_0)=Y_0,$$

has a unique solution on all of $I$.

derivations.claim: By [F3], the terminal linear adjoint equation has a unique $C^1$ solution on $[0,T]$.

By [F1], the state depends $C^1$ on the parameter and has sensitivity $S$. The chain rule gives the column gradient of the running integrand as $D_\theta\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T+S(t)^TD_u\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T$. The mean-value integral formula, boundedness and uniform continuity of the objective derivatives on the common compact tube, and the uniform first-order state remainder from [F1] make the running first-order remainder $o(\|h\|)$ uniformly in $t$ for a parameter increment $h$. Integration therefore gives its derivative by integrating that column gradient. The terminal chain rule gives $D_\theta\phi^T+S(T)^TD_u\phi^T$. Consequently $\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi^T+S(T)^TD_u\phi^T+\int_0^T(D_\theta\ell^T+S^TD_u\ell^T)\,dt$.

In [F2], set $A=D_uf$, $B=D_\theta f$, and $g=D_u\ell^T$. The adjoint equation in the Statement and tangent equation in [F1] satisfy its hypotheses. Transposing that row pairing identity and using $p(T)=D_u\phi^T$ gives $$S(T)^TD_u\phi^T-D_\theta u_0^Tp(0)=\int_0^T(-S^TD_u\ell^T+D_\theta f^Tp)\,dt.$$
Substitute step 1.3 into step 1.2; the terms involving $S^TD_u\ell^T$ cancel, leaving the asserted continuous adjoint gradient formula.

Let $u_\theta$ solve the parameter-dependent ODE of [[lem-parameter-ode-flow-tangent-on-common-tube]] on $[0,T]$. Let
$$J(\theta)=\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)+\int_0^T\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)\,dt,$$
where $\phi$ and $\ell$ are $C^1$ on a neighborhood of the trajectory tube and their first derivatives are bounded and uniformly continuous there. Let $S=D_\theta u_\theta$ be the tangent from that lemma. Let $p$ solve the terminal adjoint problem
$$-p'(t)=D_u f(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^Tp(t)+D_u\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^T,\qquad p(T)=D_u\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T.$$
Then
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T+D_\theta u_0(\theta)^Tp(0)+\int_0^T\bigl(D_\theta\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T+D_\theta f(t,u_\theta,\theta)^Tp(t)\bigr)\,dt.$$
This formula separates initial, terminal, running-cost and vector-field parameter terms. It applies only while the common-tube and differentiability hypotheses hold.

Use the setting of [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]]. Write $A_n=D_x\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, $B_n=D_\theta\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, and let $S_n=D_\theta x_n$. Then
$$S_0=D x_0(\theta),\qquad S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n.$$
Define $p_N=D_x\phi(x_N,\theta)^T$ and, backward for $n=N-1,\ldots,0$,
$$p_n=D_x\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+A_n^Tp_{n+1}.$$
The exact gradient of the finite objective is
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(x_N,\theta)^T+S_0^Tp_0+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\bigl(D_\theta\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}\bigr).$$
The recursion is the reverse derivative of the finite graph in exact real arithmetic; it makes no convergence claim about an iteration used to choose $\theta$.

Let $d,N,p\ge1$, $T>0$, $h=T/N$, and $t_n=nh$. Let $y:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ solve an initial-value problem in an open time-state domain $D$. Use the Euclidean norm $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], whose triangle inequality is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]. Let $\mathcal T\subset D$ be a common compact time-state tube with positive margin in $D$, and write $\mathcal T_t:=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:(t,v)\in\mathcal T\}$. Suppose a one-step map $\Psi_{h,n}$ is defined on $\mathcal T_{t_n}$, produces $y_{n+1}=\Psi_{h,n}(y_n)$, and the entire exact path, all numerical grid states, and every method stage lie in $\mathcal T$. If constants $C,C_0,L\ge0$, independent of $N$ and $n$, satisfy
$$\|y_0-y(0)\|_2\le C_0h^p,\qquad \|\Psi_{h,n}(y(t_n))-y(t_{n+1})\|_2\le Ch^{p+1},$$
and
$$\|\Psi_{h,n}(u)-\Psi_{h,n}(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$
for every $u,v\in\mathcal T_{t_n}$ and $0\le n<N$, then, for $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, for $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

Let $p\ge1$ be an integer, $T>0$, $h=T/N\le h_0\le1$, and $t_n=nh$. The state dimension $d$ and parameter dimension $m$ are fixed. All vector norms are Euclidean and all matrix norms are their induced operator norms; gradients are columns.

Consider the continuous objective
$$J(\theta)=\phi(u(T,\theta),\theta)+\int_0^T\ell(t,u(t,\theta),\theta)\,dt,$$
and the actual finite graph
$$x_{n+1}=\Psi_n(x_n,\theta),\qquad J_h(\theta)=\phi_h(x_N,\theta)+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}L_n(x_n,\theta).$$
Assume the hypotheses of the continuous flow-tangent and adjoint-gradient results hold on a common tube. Write $\Phi_n(x,\theta)$ for the exact flow from $t_n$ to $t_{n+1}$ and
$$K_n(x,\theta)=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}\ell(t,u(t;t_n,x,\theta),\theta)\,dt.$$
These exact maps and the actual numerical maps are $C^1$ on open neighborhoods of the admitted state and parameter sets. For every relevant $n$, all states $x_n,u(t_n)$ and the segment joining them belong to a convex admitted state set. All estimates below hold uniformly on those sets and a fixed parameter neighborhood, independently of $N,n$.

For $r=e,h$, define
$$A_n^e=D_x\Phi_n,\quad B_n^e=D_\theta\Phi_n,\quad c_n^e=D_xK_n^T,\quad d_n^e=D_\theta K_n^T,$$
$$A_n^h=D_x\Psi_n,\quad B_n^h=D_\theta\Psi_n,\quad c_n^h=D_xL_n^T,\quad d_n^h=D_\theta L_n^T.$$
Suppose constants $c_v,c_1,L,M,H\ge0$ satisfy, at each admitted $(x,\theta)$,
$$\|\Psi_n-\Phi_n\|\le c_vh^{p+1},$$
$$\|A_n^h-A_n^e\|,\ \|B_n^h-B_n^e\|,\ \|c_n^h-c_n^e\|,\ \|d_n^h-d_n^e\|\le c_1h^{p+1},$$
$$\|A_n^r\|\le1+Lh,\qquad \|B_n^r\|,\ \|c_n^r\|,\ \|d_n^r\|\le Mh.$$
Each of $A_n^e,B_n^e,c_n^e,d_n^e$ is Lipschitz in $x$, with constant at most $Hh$.

Let $S_0=D_\theta u(0,\theta)$ and $S_0^h=D_\theta x_0(\theta)$. Assume
$$\|x_0-u(0)\|\le c_0h^p,\qquad \|S_0^h-S_0\|\le c_{s0}h^p,\qquad \|S_0\|\le M_0.$$
The terminal costs are $C^1$. The exact columns $D_x\phi^T,D_\theta\phi^T$ have norm at most $M_\phi$ and are Lipschitz in $x$ with constant $H_\phi$; at the same admitted $(x,\theta)$,
$$\|D_x\phi_h^T-D_x\phi^T\|,\ \|D_\theta\phi_h^T-D_\theta\phi^T\|\le C_\phi h^p.$$
No terminal value-error hypothesis is needed for the gradient conclusion.

Let $S_n^h=D_\theta x_n$, and let $p_n^h$ be the exact discrete adjoint of this numerical graph. Let $S(t)=D_\theta u(t)$ and let $p(t)$ be the continuous adjoint with terminal value $D_x\phi(u(T),\theta)^T$. Define
$$E=e^{LT},\quad X=E(c_0+Tc_v),\quad \overline S=E(M_0+TM),\quad \overline P=E(M_\phi+TM),$$
$$R=c_1+HX,\quad C_S=E\{c_{s0}+TR(\overline S+1)\},\quad D=C_\phi+H_\phi X,$$
$$C_P=E\{D+TR(\overline P+1)\},$$
$$C_G=D+c_{s0}\overline P+(M_0+c_{s0})C_P+T\{R(1+\overline P)+MC_P\}.$$
Then
$$\max_n\|x_n-u(t_n)\|\le Xh^p,\qquad \max_n\|S_n^h-S(t_n)\|\le C_Sh^p,$$
$$\max_n\|p_n^h-p(t_n)\|\le C_Ph^p,\qquad \|\nabla J_h-\nabla J\|\le C_Gh^p.$$
These conclusions assume local value and first-derivative consistency, rather than a global adjoint-error estimate. They require no representation by nonnegative quadrature weights.

Use the dimensions, exact interval maps $\Phi_n,K_n$, terminal and initial data, and Euclidean conventions of [[lem-local-c1-step-consistency-implies-tangent-adjoint-gradient-order]]. Let $(A,b,c)$ be a fixed explicit $s$-stage tableau with $c_i=\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}$ and $\sum_i b_i=1$. Its weights may be negative or zero. The actual numerical state and cost maps are
$$Y_i=x+h\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}f(t_n+c_jh,Y_j,\theta),$$
$$\Psi_n=x+h\sum_i b_if(t_n+c_ih,Y_i,\theta),\qquad L_n=h\sum_i b_i\ell(t_n+c_ih,Y_i,\theta).$$
These are exact finite-stage maps, not outputs of a stopped implicit solver.

Assume $f:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^d$ and $\ell:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R$ are $C^2$ on an open convex time-state-parameter domain. On a common compact convex subset with positive margin in $\mathcal D$, their derivatives through order two are uniformly bounded. All admitted local exact trajectories, all numerical trajectories and stages, and all needed joining segments lie in this domain and common tube, uniformly over the fixed parameter neighborhood and $h\le h_0$. Stage times outside $[t_n,t_{n+1}]$ are included when the tableau has such abscissae. Unique admitted local flows are assumed as in the flow-tangent supplier.

Put $r=d+m$, $E=[I_d\ 0]\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}$ and $E_\theta=[0\ I_m]\in\mathbb R^{m\times r}$. Consider the autonomous augmented system, with components $t,u,\vartheta,C,V,g$,
$$t'=1,\quad \vartheta'=0,\quad u'=f(t,u,\vartheta),\quad C'=\ell(t,u,\vartheta),$$
$$V'=f_u(t,u,\vartheta)V+f_\theta(t,u,\vartheta)E_\theta,$$
$$g'=V^T\ell_u(t,u,\vartheta)^T+E_\theta^T\ell_\theta(t,u,\vartheta)^T.$$
For every admitted local start use $(t_n,x,\theta,0,E,0)$. Suppose application of the same tableau to this augmented system has uniform exact-start defect at most $C_a h^{p+1}$, for an integer $p\ge1$, on a common compact convex augmented tube with positive margin. This is a local augmented-order hypothesis, not a global tangent, adjoint or gradient-error assumption.

Then the actual maps $\Psi_n,L_n$ satisfy all local value, first-derivative, $1+Lh$ derivative-stability, $Mh$ derivative-size, and $Hh$ exact-derivative Lipschitz hypotheses of [[lem-local-c1-step-consistency-implies-tangent-adjoint-gradient-order]], with constants independent of $n,N$. Subject to that lemma's initial and terminal hypotheses, their actual differentiated graph tangents, exact reverse adjoints, and reduced gradients consequently have order-$p$ global error.

A concrete sufficient instantiation for $1\le p\le4$ is that this augmented vector field is $C^4$ with bounded derivatives through order four on its admitted compact convex tube and the tableau satisfies the coefficient equations through order $p$ in [[prop-explicit-rk-order-conditions-through-four]]. Jointly $C^5$ base data $f,\ell$ with bounded derivatives through order five on the base tube are sufficient for this augmented $C^4$ condition. The classical RK4 tableau
$$a_{21}=a_{32}=\tfrac12,\quad a_{43}=1,\quad b=(\tfrac16,\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac16),\quad c=(0,\tfrac12,\tfrac12,1),$$
with all other $a_{ij}=0$, therefore gives the claimed order-four tangent, nodal-adjoint and gradient approximation under these hypotheses. For general $p$, retain the explicit local augmented-defect hypothesis above; no higher-order coefficient theorem is being asserted.

derivations.claim: If the stated explicit Runge--Kutta conditions are used for the state field, [F4] supplies the exact-start defect required by [F3]. Under the stated stability, common-tube and initial-error hypotheses, [F3] gives the state part of the asserted $C_xh^p$ bound; the adjoint part in the weighted conclusion remains the separately assumed bound.

Independently assume [A2]. Apply [F5] to the actual maps defining $J_h$ and the exact interval flow and running-cost maps defining $J$. Its forward recurrences give state and tangent errors, its backward recurrence gives the nodal-adjoint error, and its graph-gradient comparison gives the stated $C_Gh^p$ bound. This argument uses no weighted decomposition.

By [F1], [F2], and the explicit weighted representation in the Statement, the two gradients are their respective endpoint terms plus, respectively, the weighted sum of $\widehat q_n$ and the integral of $q$. At each node, insert and subtract $q(t_n,u_n,p_n)$. The derivative-data assumption and Lipschitz bound give $\|\widehat q_n-q(t_n)\|_2\le(C_d+L_qC_x)h^p$.

Since $w_n\ge0$ and $\sum_nw_n=T$, the node-data perturbation contributes at most $T(C_d+L_qC_x)h^p$. The exact-integrand quadrature error contributes at most $C_Qh^p$, and the endpoint difference at most $C_bh^p$. The Euclidean triangle inequality gives the displayed weighted bound.

For the RK specialization, [F6] differentiates the actual finite stages, proves the local derivative-size and Lipschitz bounds, and obtains the needed local $C^1$ consistency from augmented local order. Its application of [F4] to the augmented field verifies this order for $p\le4$ under the actual augmented smoothness and tube assumptions. Its RK4 coefficient calculation supplies the concrete fourth-order instance. Therefore step 1.2 applies.

Let $d,s\ge1$, $A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{s\times s}$, $b,c\in\mathbb R^s$, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be a vector field on an open time-state domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]). For an initial state $y\in\mathbb R^d$ and time $t$ with $(t,y)\in D$, and a step $h>0$, a stage vector $Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_s)\in(\mathbb R^d)^s$ is admissible only when $(t+c_jh,Y_j)\in D$ for every $j$. An admissible vector solves

$$Y_i=y+h\sum_{j=1}^s a_{ij}f(t+c_jh,Y_j),\qquad i=1,\ldots,s.$$

When a solution $Y$ is selected, the method update is

$$\Psi_h(t,y)=y+h\sum_{i=1}^s b_i f(t+c_ih,Y_i).$$

On the admissible stage set, the **stage update residual** is the vector with blocks

$$G_i(Y)=Y_i-y-h\sum_{j=1}^s a_{ij}f(t+c_jh,Y_j).$$

The associated stage derivative residual is $G(Y)/h$. The tableau is **stiffly accurate** when $b_j=a_{sj}$ for all $j$ and $c_s=1$; in that case the last stage $Y_s$ equals the method update. The equations may have no, one, or several solutions in a proposed branch set; this definition alone asserts no solvability.

Let $m,d\ge1$, $h>0$, $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$, and centers $c=(c_1,\ldots,c_m)\in(\mathbb R^d)^m$. On block vectors define

$$\|Y\|_{\infty,2}:=\max_{1\le i\le m}\|Y_i\|_2,\qquad \|A\|_\infty:=\max_i\sum_{j=1}^m|a_{ij}|.$$

Let $F:\mathcal B\to(\mathbb R^d)^m$, with components $F_i:\mathcal B\to\mathbb R^d$, be defined on the closed product ball $\mathcal B=\{Y:\|Y-c\|_{\infty,2}\le R\}$, where $R>0$. Suppose constants $M,L\ge0$ satisfy, for all $Y,Z\in\mathcal B$,

$$\|F(Y)\|_{\infty,2}\le M,\qquad \|F(Y)-F(Z)\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|Y-Z\|_{\infty,2},$$

and $h\|A\|_\infty M\le R$, $q:=h\|A\|_\infty L<1$. Define $\Phi(Y)=c+h(A\otimes I_d)F(Y)$ and $G(Y)=Y-\Phi(Y)$. Then $\Phi$ has a unique fixed point $Y^*\in\mathcal B$, equivalently $G(Y^*)=0$. Every approximate stage vector $\widetilde Y\in\mathcal B$ satisfies

$$\|\widetilde Y-Y^*\|_{\infty,2}\le\frac{\|G(\widetilde Y)\|_{\infty,2}}{1-q}.$$

If the derivative-scaled stage residual is $r=G(\widetilde Y)/h$, the right side is $h\|r\|_{\infty,2}/(1-q)$. The hypotheses $h\|A\|_\infty L<1$ and the invariant-ball bound are local solvability conditions; this result gives no global branch outside $\mathcal B$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$,
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]],
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-interval]]). Let
$M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $M \ge 0$ satisfy

$$\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } t \in (a,b).$$

Then

$$\lVert f(b) - f(a)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,(b-a).$$

**No integrability of $f'$ is assumed**, so the theorem applies to every
differentiable $f$; that is why it is proved from the scalar mean value theorem
rather than from
[[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]].
[[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]] records the comparison between the
two routes.

**The equality form is not asserted, and for $m \ge 2$ it is false.** There need
be **no** $\xi \in (a,b)$ with $f(b)-f(a) = f'(\xi)(b-a)$; the companion page
carries a differentiable witness on $[0,1]$. The $\xi$ produced in the proof
below depends on the fixed vector $u = f(b)-f(a)$ and is a mean value point of
the **real** function $t \mapsto \langle u, f(t)\rangle$, not of $f$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

derivations.claim: Let $Y,W$ belong to the invariant ball. Its convexity puts $Y+t(W-Y)$ in the ball for $0\le t\le1$. For each block $i$, the curve $\gamma_i(t)=F_i(Y+t(W-Y))$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ and differentiable inside because $F$ is $C^1$ on an open neighborhood. Its derivative obeys $$\|\gamma_i'(t)\|_2\le\|D_YF(Y+t(W-Y))(W-Y)\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|W-Y\|_{\infty,2}.$$ Apply [F3] to each block and take the maximum. This gives $\|F(W)-F(Y)\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|W-Y\|_{\infty,2}$ using only the derivative bound on the ball. Hence [F2] applies with its invariant-ball hypotheses and the selected root exists uniquely.

Differentiating [F1] with respect to $Y$ gives $D_YG=I-h(A\otimes I_d)D_YF$. If $D_YG\,Z=0$, the block row-sum norm and the derivative bound imply $$\|Z\|_{\infty,2}\le h\|A\|_\infty L\|Z\|_{\infty,2}=q\|Z\|_{\infty,2}.$$ Since $q<1$, this forces $Z=0$; thus the square finite-dimensional map $D_YG$ has trivial kernel.

By [F4], a linear map on the stage space has rank equal to its dimension when its kernel has dimension zero. Therefore $D_YG$ is onto as well as one-to-one, hence invertible. This holds at every point of the prescribed branch ball.

Let $R:\Theta\times Z\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$, where $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $Z\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ are open. Suppose $R(\theta_0,z_0)=0$ and the state Jacobian $R_z(\theta_0,z_0)$ is invertible. The Euclidean implicit function theorem gives a local $C^1$ solution branch $z=\phi(\theta)$, and
$$D\phi(\theta_0)=-R_z(\theta_0,z_0)^{-1}R_\theta(\theta_0,z_0).$$
For a scalar $C^1$ objective $J(\theta,z)$, its derivative along that branch is
$$D(J(\theta,\phi(\theta)))|_{\theta_0}=J_\theta-J_zR_z^{-1}R_\theta.$$
Equivalently, if $\lambda$ solves $R_z^T\lambda=J_z^T$, this derivative is $J_\theta-\lambda^TR_\theta$. These formulas concern the exact local solution branch; differentiating a stopped iteration is a separate finite-map derivative.

Use the implicit Runge–Kutta residual $G(Y)=Y-\mathbf1\otimes u-h(A\otimes I_d)F(Y)$ from [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]] on a convex open neighborhood of an invariant stage ball. Suppose $F$ is $C^1$ there and $\|D_YF(Y)Z\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|Z\|_{\infty,2}$ for every $Y$ in the ball and every block vector $Z$. If $q=h\|A\|_\infty L<1$, then $D_YG(Y)$ is invertible at every point of the selected stage branch. The contraction hypotheses of [[lem-small-step-implicit-rk-branch-and-residual-error]] provide existence and uniqueness of the root in that ball; this lemma supplies nonsingularity for implicit differentiation.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and
