derivations.claim: By [F2], the stated root exists on the selected ball, and [F4] makes $G_Y$ invertible there. Regard $R(\theta,Y)=G(Y,u(\theta),\theta)$. Its parameter derivative is $R_\theta=G_uD_\theta u+G_\theta$. Apply [F3] to obtain the local branch and the displayed formula for $D_\theta Y$.

The update is the finite composition of $u(\theta)$, $Y(\theta)$ and the $C^1$ stage evaluation map in [F1]. Apply [F5] and the product rule for the linear output map $h(\mathbf1_b^T\otimes I_d)$ to get the displayed derivative.

The calculation differentiates the exact equation $G(Y,u(\theta),\theta)=0$ on its selected branch. It contains no update of a finite stage solver, so no derivative of a stopped iteration is asserted.

citations.quote: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $V$ be a real Hilbert space, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and write $V^*$ for the continuous real dual. A parameter-dependent coercive elliptic variational problem is a family of bounded bilinear forms $a_\theta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ and bounded linear functionals $\ell_\theta\in V^*$ such that, on each parameter neighborhood under discussion, $\|a_\theta\|\le M$ and $a_\theta(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2$ for fixed $M<\infty$ and $\alpha>0$. Operator-norm $C^1$ data means that the maps $\theta\mapsto A_\theta\in\mathcal L(V,V^*)$, $A_\theta u:=a_\theta(u,\cdot)$, and $\theta\mapsto\ell_\theta\in V^*$ are continuously Fréchet differentiable. A state at $\theta$ is a vector $u_\theta\in V$ satisfying $a_\theta(u_\theta,v)=\ell_\theta(v)$ for every $v\in V$. When a state is specified, a $C^1$ objective $J:V\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ defines the reduced objective $j(\theta)=J(u_\theta,\theta)$. This definition alone asserts neither state existence nor uniqueness of an optimizer.

derivations.claim: For each $\theta\in\Theta_0$, apply [F1] to $a_\theta$ and $\ell_\theta$; this gives a unique $u_\theta$ and the bound $\|u_\theta\|_V\le\alpha^{-1}\|\ell_\theta\|_{V^*}$. Since $\ell_\theta$ is continuous, these state norms are locally bounded in $\theta$.

For sufficiently small $h$ with $\theta+h\in\Theta_0$, put $\delta u=u_{\theta+h}-u_\theta$, $\delta A=A_{\theta+h}-A_\theta$, and $\delta\ell=\ell_{\theta+h}-\ell_\theta$. Subtract the two variational equations to get $a_\theta(\delta u,v)=\delta\ell(v)-(\delta A\,u_{\theta+h})(v)$. Taking $v=\delta u$, using coercivity and the dual norm, and dividing by $\|\delta u\|_V$ when it is nonzero gives $\|\delta u\|_V\le\alpha^{-1}\bigl(\|\delta\ell\|_{V^*}+\|\delta A\|\,\|u_{\theta+h}\|_V\bigr)=O(\|h\|_2)$. The same bound is immediate when $\delta u=0$. Thus the state map is locally Lipschitz.

For each direction $h\in\mathbb R^m$, define $w_h$ by $a_\theta(w_h,v)=D\ell_\theta[h](v)-\bigl(DA_\theta[h]u_\theta\bigr)(v)$. The right side is a bounded linear functional, so [F1] gives a unique $w_h$. Uniqueness and linearity of the right side in $h$ show $h\mapsto w_h$ is linear.

Write $\delta\ell=D\ell_\theta[h]+r_\ell$ and $\delta A=DA_\theta[h]+r_A$, where $\|r_\ell\|+\|r_A\|=o(\|h\|_2)$ by [F2]. Subtract the equation for $w_h$ in step 2.2 from the state-difference equation in step 2.1. With $e_h=\delta u-w_h$, this gives $a_\theta(e_h,v)=r_\ell(v)-(r_Au_\theta)(v)-(DA_\theta[h]\delta u)(v)-(r_A\delta u)(v)$. The first two terms have dual norm $o(\|h\|_2)$; the last two have that order because $\|DA_\theta[h]\|=O(\|h\|_2)$, $\|r_A\|=o(\|h\|_2)$, and $\|\delta u\|_V=O(\|h\|_2)$ by step 2.1. Coercivity yields $\|e_h\|_V=o(\|h\|_2)$, proving Fréchet differentiability and the stated derivative equation.

The solution operator $A_\theta^{-1}:V^*\to V$ has norm at most $\alpha^{-1}$. For nearby $\theta,\widetilde\theta$, the identity $A_{\widetilde\theta}^{-1}-A_\theta^{-1} =A_{\widetilde\theta}^{-1}(A_\theta-A_{\widetilde\theta})A_\theta^{-1}$ shows its operator-norm continuity. The formula in step 2.2, together with continuity of $u_\theta$, $D A_\theta$, and $D\ell_\theta$, then shows $D_\theta u_\theta$ is continuous. Hence the state map is $C^1$.

On an open neighborhood $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, suppose the same constants $M<\infty$ and $\alpha>0$ give boundedness and coercivity for every $a_\theta$, and $\theta\mapsto A_\theta$ and $\theta\mapsto\ell_\theta$ are operator-norm $C^1$. $$a_\theta(w_\eta,v)=D_\theta\ell_\theta[\eta](v)-D_\theta a_\theta[\eta](u_\theta,v)\qquad(v\in V).$$
Uniform coercivity is required on the parameter neighborhood; no differentiability conclusion is asserted at a loss of coercivity.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ be linear in the first slot, conjugate-linear in
the second, bounded by $M$, and coercive with constant $\alpha>0$:
$$|a(u,v)|\le M\|u\|_V\|v\|_V.$$
$$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|_V^2.$$
For every bounded linear functional $G:V\to\mathbb K$, there is a unique
$z\in V$ such that
$$a(v,z)=G(v)\qquad(v\in V),$$
and $\alpha\|z\|_V\le\|G\|_{V^*}$. In the real case conjugation is the
identity and both forms and functionals are linear over $\mathbb R$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

$$a_\theta(v,p_\theta)=D_uJ(u_\theta,\theta)[v]\qquad(v\in V).$$
Then the reduced objective $j(\theta)=J(u_\theta,\theta)$ is $C^1$ and
$$D_\theta j(\theta)[\eta]=D_\theta J(u_\theta,\theta)[\eta]+D_\theta\ell_\theta[\eta](p_\theta)-D_\theta a_\theta[\eta](u_\theta,p_\theta).$$
No symmetry of $a_\theta$ is required; the adjoint uses the transposed variational form displayed above.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ be linear in its first argument, conjugate-linear
in its second, bounded by $M$, and coercive with constant $\alpha>0$:
$$|a(v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad \operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2.$$
Let $F:V\to\mathbb K$ be bounded and conjugate-linear, and let $V_h\subseteq V$
be finite-dimensional. Then there are unique $u\in V$ and $u_h\in V_h$ with
$$a(u,v)=F(v)\quad(v\in V).$$
$$a(u_h,v_h)=F(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h).$$
The solutions satisfy
$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac M\alpha\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.$$
The real bilinear case uses linear functionals and reads $\operatorname{Re}$ as
the identity.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, $a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded coercive form with boundedness constant $M$ and coercivity constant $\alpha>0$, and $F:V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded functional linear in the real case and conjugate-linear in the complex test argument. Let $V_h\subseteq V$ be finite-dimensional, and let $a_h:V_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ and $F_h:V_h\to\mathbb K$ be bounded, with $F_h$ having the same test-linearity as $F$, and $a_h$ coercive with constant $\alpha_h>0$ in the inherited norm. There are unique exact and discrete solutions $u$ and $u_h$, and

$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\left((1+M/\alpha_h)\|u-v_h\|_V+\frac{\delta_{a,h}(v_h)+\delta_{F,h}}{\alpha_h}\right),$$

where the defects are those of [[def-variational-crime-error-framework]]. For a family of meshes this is a uniform estimate whenever $\inf_h\alpha_h>0$ and the displayed approximation and defect terms are uniformly controlled. The term $\delta_{F,h}$ retains source approximation and data oscillation.

Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. In the **exact variational problem**, $V$ is a Hilbert space, $a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ is a bounded coercive sesquilinear form (bilinear when $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$), linear in its first argument and conjugate-linear in its second when $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$, and $F:V\to\mathbb K$ is bounded and has the same linearity in its test argument as the second argument of $a$. Exact solutions satisfy $a(u,v)=F(v)$ for every $v\in V$. Boundedness and coercivity have the meanings in [[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]].

For a **conforming perturbed Galerkin problem**, $V_h\subseteq V$ is a finite-dimensional subspace, $a_h:V_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ and $F_h:V_h\to\mathbb K$ are the discrete form and load, and $u_h\in V_h$ solves $a_h(u_h,w_h)=F_h(w_h)$. Its discrete coercivity constant is any $\alpha_h>0$ such that $\operatorname{Re}a_h(w_h,w_h)\ge\alpha_h\|w_h\|_V^2$ for every $w_h\in V_h$. For $v_h\in V_h$, define

$$\delta_{a,h}(v_h):=\sup_{w_h\in V_h\setminus\{0\}}\frac{|a(v_h,w_h)-a_h(v_h,w_h)|}{\|w_h\|_V},\qquad \delta_{F,h}:=\sup_{w_h\in V_h\setminus\{0\}}\frac{|F(w_h)-F_h(w_h)|}{\|w_h\|_V}.$$

If $V_h=\{0\}$, both defects are defined to be zero. The load defect $\delta_{F,h}$ includes any source approximation or data oscillation; it is not assumed small or zero without a separate bound.

For a **nonconforming problem**, the exact space $V$ and finite-dimensional trial space $V_h$ need not satisfy $V_h\subseteq V$. Put $X_h:=V+V_h$ and equip it with a norm $\|\cdot\|_h$ whose restrictions to $V$ and $V_h$ are norms. The discrete form $a_h$ is defined on $V_h\times V_h$, and a bounded extension $\widetilde a_h:X_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ means $\widetilde a_h=a_h$ on $V_h\times V_h$ and $|\widetilde a_h(z,w_h)|\le M_h\|z\|_h\|w_h\|_h$. For an exact solution $u\in V$, define the nonconforming consistency defect

$$\delta^{\mathrm{nc}}_h(u):=\sup_{w_h\in V_h\setminus\{0\}}\frac{|F_h(w_h)-\widetilde a_h(u,w_h)|}{\|w_h\|_h},$$

with value zero if $V_h=\{0\}$. This residual need not vanish: the exact weak equation is only asserted for tests in $V$.

Geometry and quadrature defects are components of the appropriate form defect when the implemented form is compared with the pulled-back exact form. No exact Galerkin orthogonality is asserted after replacing the form or test space.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

derivations.claim: Apply [F2] to an exact conforming Galerkin state and its adjoint, or [F3] to each conforming perturbed equation, using the transposed form $a^\dagger(v,w)=a(w,v)$ for the adjoint. Transposition preserves boundedness and coercivity constants. Under [A1], the resulting two bounds are $E_u,E_p$, with all applicable form and load defects, including geometry and quadrature contributions, retained as specified by [F3].

Choose a basis of $V_h$. Coercivity makes the discrete state matrix $K_h(\theta)$ invertible, and its entries and the load coordinates are $C^1$. The identity $K_h(\theta+z)^{-1}-K_h(\theta)^{-1}=-K_h(\theta+z)^{-1}(K_h(\theta+z)-K_h(\theta))K_h(\theta)^{-1}$ shows that its inverse, and hence $u_h(\theta)$, is $C^1$. Differentiating the state equation gives $a_{\theta,h}(w_h,v_h)=\ell_{\theta,h}'[\eta](v_h)-a_{\theta,h}'[\eta](u_h,v_h)$. By [F4], $D j_h[\eta]=J_{\theta,h}'[\eta]+D_uJ_h[w_h]$; use the discrete adjoint equation with $v_h=w_h$, then the differentiated state equation with $v_h=p_h$, to obtain the formula for $g_h$ in the Statement. The continuous formula is supplied by [F1].

Fix $\eta$ with $\|\eta\|_2\le1$. Subtract the continuous and discrete formulas. The direct-objective term is bounded by $\varepsilon_J$. Add and subtract $\ell_{\theta,h}'[\eta](p_h)$; the load-derivative difference is at most $\varepsilon_\ell P_*+M_\ell E_p$.

Add and subtract $a_\theta'[\eta](u_h,p_h)$. The derivative-form data defect contributes at most $\varepsilon_a U_*P_*$. The remaining state/adjoint perturbation is $$|a_\theta'[\eta](u_h-u,p_h)+a_\theta'[\eta](u,p_h-p)|\le M_a(E_uP_*+U_*E_p).$$ Thus for every unit $\eta$, $|g_h[\eta]-g[\eta]|$ is bounded by the displayed constant.
Taking the supremum over all $\|\eta\|_2\le1$ gives the asserted dual norm bound. The separate $\varepsilon$ terms show why state error alone does not certify a reduced-gradient error.

Assume Countable Choice. Assume the real scalar finite-element setting of
[[cor-shape-regular-affine-fe-primal-energy-approximation]], and set
$V:=H^1_0(\Omega)$ with its usual $H^1$ norm. Let $V_h\subseteq V$ be the
stated conforming discrete space, let $a:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be the same
bounded coercive form as in
[[thm-cea-quasi-optimality-for-conforming-galerkin-approximations]], and let
$u\in W^{r+1,2}(\Omega)\cap V$ and $u_h\in V_h$ solve the continuous and
discrete equations for the same bounded linear datum $F:V\to\mathbb R$;
assume also that $V_h$ is finite-dimensional. The natural inclusion
$J:V\to L^2(\Omega)$ obeys $\|Jv\|_{L^2}\le\|v\|_{H^1}$. For
$e:=J(u-u_h)$, let $z_e$ be the adjoint solution from
[[thm-aubin-nitsche-l2-error-estimate-under-adjoint-regularity]]. Suppose
there are $s\in(0,1]$, a normed regularity space $R_s\subseteq V$ for $z_e$,
and constants $C_D,C_R$ independent of $h$ and $e$ such that
$$\|z_e\|_{R_s}\le C_R\|e\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
$$\inf_{w_h\in V_h}\|z_e-w_h\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C_D h^s\|z_e\|_{R_s}.$$
Then
$$\|u-u_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le \frac{M^2}{\alpha}C_{\rm FE}C_DC_R h^{r+s}|u|_{W^{r+1,2}(\Omega)}.$$
Here $C_{\rm FE}$ is the primal interpolation constant and $M,\alpha$ are
the boundedness and coercivity constants of $a$. In a full-adjoint Poisson
branch, one may take $R_1=H^2(\Omega)\cap H^1_0(\Omega)$ with the $H^2$ norm,
provided both displayed dual bounds hold. The $h^{r+1}$ rate is conditional
on those bounds and the primal approximation bound; no full-adjoint
regularity is asserted on an arbitrary Lipschitz domain.

Assume Countable Choice and the elliptic state/adjoint setting of [[thm-elliptic-adjoint-reduced-gradient]]. Let $V_h\subseteq V$ be a finite-dimensional conforming space. Let $a_{\theta,h}$ and $\ell_{\theta,h}$ be operator-norm $C^1$ in $\theta$, uniformly coercive on $V_h$, and define the discrete state by $a_{\theta,h}(u_h,v_h)=\ell_{\theta,h}(v_h)$. Let $J_h:V_h\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$, and let $p_h\in V_h$ solve $a_{\theta,h}(v_h,p_h)=D_uJ_h(u_h,\theta)[v_h]$. Suppose the parameter derivatives of the discrete forms and loads have specified bounded extensions to $V$ that agree with their values on $V_h$. Let $u,p$ be the exact state and adjoint, and let $u_h,p_h\in V_h$ be their discrete counterparts, with certified energy bounds
$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le E_u,\qquad \|p-p_h\|_V\le E_p.$$
For an exact conforming Galerkin solve these bounds may be supplied by [[thm-cea-quasi-optimality-for-conforming-galerkin-approximations]]; for a conforming perturbed solve they may be supplied by [[thm-first-strang-lemma-for-conforming-perturbed-galerkin]], with all load, form, geometry and quadrature defects retained as in [[def-variational-crime-error-framework]]. Define exact and discrete reduced gradients by
$$g[\eta]=D_\theta J(u,\theta)[\eta]+\ell_\theta'[\eta](p)-a_\theta'[\eta](u,p),\qquad g_h[\eta]=D_\theta J_h(u_h,\theta)[\eta]+\ell_{\theta,h}'[\eta](p_h)-a_{\theta,h}'[\eta](u_h,p_h).$$
Assume for $\|\eta\|_2\le1$ that $\|\ell_\theta'[\eta]\|_{V^*}\le M_\ell$, $\|a_\theta'[\eta]\|_{\mathcal L(V,V^*)}\le M_a$, the direct-objective defect satisfies $|D_\theta J_h(u_h,\theta)[\eta]-D_\theta J(u,\theta)[\eta]|\le\varepsilon_J$, and the derivative-data defects obey
$$\|\ell_{\theta,h}'[\eta]-\ell_\theta'[\eta]\|_{V^*}\le\varepsilon_\ell,\qquad \|a_{\theta,h}'[\eta]-a_\theta'[\eta]\|_{\mathcal L(V,V^*)}\le\varepsilon_a.$$
Put $U_*=\max(\|u\|_V,\|u_h\|_V)$ and $P_*=\max(\|p\|_V,\|p_h\|_V)$. Then
$$\|g_h-g\|_{\Theta^*}\le\varepsilon_J+M_\ell E_p+\varepsilon_\ell P_*+M_a(E_uP_*+U_*E_p)+\varepsilon_aU_*P_*.$$

Apply the exact gradient subtraction in [F2]. Let $(V,H,V^*)$ be the real evolution triple and let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open. A parameter-dependent parabolic variational problem specifies, for each $\theta\in\Theta$, a bilinear form $a_\theta(t;\cdot,\cdot)$ and data $f_\theta\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$, $u_{0,\theta}\in H$. A state is a function $u_\theta\in W(0,T;V)$ with continuous $H$ trace, $u_\theta(0)=u_{0,\theta}$, and
$$\langle u_\theta'(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}+a_\theta(t;u_\theta(t),v)=\langle f_\theta(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}$$
for every $v\in V$ and almost every $t$. When a state is specified, a differentiable terminal and running objective $\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)+\int_0^T L(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)\,dt$ defines its reduced objective. This definition does not assert existence, parameter differentiability, or optimality.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(V,H,V^*)$ be the real evolution triple of
[[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]], and let
$u,v\in W(0,T;V)$. Each has a unique representative in $C([0,T];H)$, and
for all $0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$\|u(t)\|_H^2-\|u(s)\|_H^2 =2\int_s^t\langle u'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\,dr,$$
$$(u(t),v(t))_H-(u(s),v(s))_H =\int_s^t\bigl(\langle u'(r),v(r)\rangle_{V^*,V} +\langle v'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\bigr)\,dr.$$
Writing $c_i=\|i:V\to H\|$, the trace obeys
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)\|_H^2 \le \frac{c_i^2}{T}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2 +2\|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}.$$

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if

   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

about one $x$ at a time.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(V,H,V^*)$ be the real evolution triple of
[[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]], and let
$u,v\in W(0,T;V)$. Each has a unique representative in $C([0,T];H)$, and
for all $0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$\|u(t)\|_H^2-\|u(s)\|_H^2 =2\int_s^t\langle u'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\,dr,$$
$$(u(t),v(t))_H-(u(s),v(s))_H =\int_s^t\bigl(\langle u'(r),v(r)\rangle_{V^*,V} +\langle v'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\bigr)\,dr.$$

$$-\langle p'(t),v\rangle+a_\theta(t;v,p(t))=D_uL(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)[v],\qquad p(T)=\nabla_H\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta).$$
Then for $j(\theta)=\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)+\int_0^T L(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)\,dt$,
$$D j(\theta)[\eta]=D_\theta\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)[\eta]+(p(0),u_{0,\theta}'[\eta])_H+\int_0^T\left(D_\theta L(t,u_\theta,\theta)[\eta]+\langle f_\theta'[\eta](t),p(t)\rangle-a_\theta'[\eta](t;u_\theta(t),p(t))\right)dt.$$

derivations.claim: For the forward state, the product rule [F3] gives $\rho_u'=P_{u,h}'u+P_{u,h}u'-u'$, so the residual in [F2] is exactly the one displayed in the Statement. Apply the energy estimate in [F2] to $\vartheta_u$; it gives $\|\vartheta_u\|_{L^2(V)}\le\alpha^{-1/2}(\|\vartheta_u(0)\|_H^2+\alpha^{-1}\|\mathcal R_u\|_{L^2(V_h^*)}^2)^{1/2}$. Since $u-u_h=-\rho_u-\vartheta_u$, the triangle inequality proves the stated $E_u$ bound.

Set $s=T-t$ and $q(s)=p(T-s)$. The backward adjoint equation becomes a forward parabolic variational equation with transposed form $a_\theta(T-s;v,w)$, which has the same boundedness and coercivity constants. The comparison $\widetilde P_{p,h}(s)=P_{p,h}(T-s)$ is operator-norm $C^1$ and $\widetilde P_{p,h}'(s)=-P_{p,h}'(T-s)$. By [F3], its residual contains $\widetilde P_{p,h}'q+\widetilde P_{p,h}q'-q'$; apply the energy estimate in [F2] and the splitting $p-p_h=-\rho_p-\vartheta_p$ to get the stated $E_p$ bound by the same triangle inequality as step 1.1.

Subtract the two gradient formulas [F1]. The direct term contributes $\varepsilon_J$. For the initial pairing, add and subtract $(p_h(0),D_\theta u_0)$; Cauchy--Schwarz bounds the difference by $U_0'E_{p,0}+P_{0,*}\varepsilon_0$. In the forcing term, add and subtract $D_\theta f[p_h]$; the derivative-data defect is at most $\varepsilon_fP_*$, and the exact derivative contributes at most $M_fE_p$ by step 2.1. Thus the direct, initial, and forcing contributions are bounded by the first four terms in the stated gradient estimate.

For the form term, add and subtract $D_\theta a[u_h,p_h]$. Its derivative-data defect is at most $\varepsilon_aU_*P_*$. Split the exact derivative difference as $D_\theta a[u_h-u,p_h]+D_\theta a[u,p_h-p]$; Cauchy--Schwarz in time, the bound $\|D_\theta a[\eta]\|\le M_a$, and steps 1.1 and 2.1 give $M_a(E_uP_*+U_*E_p)$. Combine this with step 3.1 and take the supremum over $\|\eta\|_2\le1$ to obtain the displayed dual norm bound.

Every invertible matrix $A\in M_n(\mathbb F)$, where $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, has a unique factorisation

$$A=QR,$$

where $Q^*Q=I$ and $R$ is upper triangular with positive real diagonal entries. Thus $Q$ is orthogonal over $\mathbb R$ and unitary over $\mathbb C$. The assertion includes the unique $0\times0$ factorisation.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$

The orthogonal operators on a finite-dimensional real inner product space form a group under composition, as do the unitary operators on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space. Every such operator $T$ satisfies

$$|\det T|=1.$$

Over $\mathbb R$, this says $\det T\in\{-1,1\}$. In dimension zero, the unique determinant is $1$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

derivations.claim: Induction on $k$ using $A_kQ_{k-1}=Q_kR_k$ gives $$P_kQ_0=Q_kR_kR_{k-1}\cdots R_1,\qquad P_k:=A_k\cdots A_1.$$ For $k=1$ this is the defining factorization; multiplying the identity at $k$ on the left by $A_{k+1}$ and substituting $A_{k+1}Q_k=Q_{k+1}R_{k+1}$ proves the next case.

Orthogonal factors preserve Euclidean norms, so $\sigma_{\min}(R_k)=\sigma_{\min}(Q_kR_k)=\sigma_{\min}(A_kQ_{k-1})=\sigma_{\min}(A_k)\ge\sigma$. For a fixed $i$, the leading $(i-1)\times(i-1)$ block of $R_k$ is invertible. Choose $x\in\mathbb R^{i-1}$ solving $R_{1:i-1,1:i-1}x=-R_{1:i-1,i}$ and set $z=(x,1,0,\ldots,0)^T$. Upper triangularity gives $R_kz=r_{k,ii}e_i$ and $\|z\|_2\ge1$, so $\sigma_{\min}(R_k)\le\|R_kz\|_2/\|z\|_2\le r_{k,ii}$. For $i=1$, take $z=e_1$. Hence $r_{k,ii}\ge\sigma$.

Take determinants in step 1.1. By [F2], $\det(P_N)\det(Q_0)=\det(Q_N)\prod_{k=1}^N\det(R_k)$. By [F3] each $\det(R_k)=\prod_i r_{k,ii}>0$, and by [F4] $|\det(Q_0)|=|\det(Q_N)|=1$. Thus $|\det(P_N)|=\prod_{k,i}r_{k,ii}$. Taking logarithms of positive numbers proves the exact identity.

Both $r_{k,ii}$ and $\widetilde r_{k,ii}$ are at least $\sigma/2$. By [F5], $|\log\widetilde r_{k,ii}-\log r_{k,ii}|\le(2/\sigma)|\widetilde r_{k,ii}-r_{k,ii}|$. Adding the computation error $\delta_{k,i}$ and summing the scalar bounds by the triangle inequality proves the stated numerical log bound. The lower singular-value bound is essential to keep the log derivative bounded; if any factor is singular its determinant is zero and its log-volume is undefined.

Use the setting of [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]]. Write $A_n=D_x\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, $B_n=D_\theta\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, and let $S_n=D_\theta x_n$. Then
$$S_0=D x_0(\theta),\qquad S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n.$$
Define $p_N=D_x\phi(x_N,\theta)^T$ and, backward for $n=N-1,\ldots,0$,
$$p_n=D_x\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+A_n^Tp_{n+1}.$$
The exact gradient of the finite objective is
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(x_N,\theta)^T+S_0^Tp_0+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\bigl(D_\theta\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}\bigr).$$
The recursion is the reverse derivative of the finite graph in exact real arithmetic; it makes no convergence claim about an iteration used to choose $\theta$.

Fix $T\ge1$, positive dimensions $d_0,\ldots,d_T$ and $p_1,\ldots,p_T$, open sets $U_t\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_t}$, and continuously differentiable maps $\Psi_{t-1}:U_{t-1}\to U_t$ and $G_t:U_t\to\mathbb R^{p_t}$. Let $m_b\in\mathbb R^{d_0}$, $B\in\mathbb R^{d_0\times d_0}$ be symmetric positive definite, $y_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t}$, and $\Gamma_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times p_t}$ be symmetric positive definite. In weak-constraint mode also require symmetric positive-definite $Q_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_t}$. The strong-constraint decision domain is $U_0$; the weak-constraint decision domain is $U_0\times\cdots\times U_T$. Both objectives are continuously differentiable on their stated open decision domains. For a positive-definite covariance $M$, write $\|v\|_{M^{-1}}^2=v^TM^{-1}v$.

In **strong-constraint 4DVAR**, choose the initial state $u_0$ and generate $u_t=\Psi_{t-1}(u_{t-1})$ for $1\le t\le T$. Minimize the trajectory objective
$$J_s(u_0)=\tfrac12\|u_0-m_b\|_{B^{-1}}^2+\tfrac12\sum_{t=1}^T\|y_t-G_t(u_t)\|_{\Gamma_t^{-1}}^2.$$

In **weak-constraint 4DVAR**, the decision variable is the full path $(u_0,\ldots,u_T)$. Given model-error covariances $Q_t\succ0$, minimize
$$J_w(u_0,\ldots,u_T)=\tfrac12\|u_0-m_b\|_{B^{-1}}^2+\tfrac12\sum_{t=1}^T\|y_t-G_t(u_t)\|_{\Gamma_t^{-1}}^2+\tfrac12\sum_{t=1}^T\|u_t-\Psi_{t-1}(u_{t-1})\|_{Q_t^{-1}}^2.$$

Select one objective, an initial decision vector in its stated decision domain, a finite iteration limit $M\ge0$, and either positive fixed steps or the backtracking parameters required by [[alg-gradient-descent]]. Run that algorithm on the selected objective for at most $M$ updates and return its last iterate (or report its domain failure). In strong mode return the trajectory generated from the last initial-state iterate; in weak mode return the last path iterate. This is a finite numerical procedure, not a guarantee that a global or local minimizer is reached. The page's BCS-20 hypotheses for gradient descent supply no general guarantee for these objectives.

Let $m,d\ge1$, $h>0$, $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$, and centers $c=(c_1,\ldots,c_m)\in(\mathbb R^d)^m$. On block vectors define

$$\|Y\|_{\infty,2}:=\max_{1\le i\le m}\|Y_i\|_2,\qquad \|A\|_\infty:=\max_i\sum_{j=1}^m|a_{ij}|.$$

Let $F:\mathcal B\to(\mathbb R^d)^m$, with components $F_i:\mathcal B\to\mathbb R^d$, be defined on the closed product ball $\mathcal B=\{Y:\|Y-c\|_{\infty,2}\le R\}$, where $R>0$. Suppose constants $M,L\ge0$ satisfy, for all $Y,Z\in\mathcal B$,

$$\|F(Y)\|_{\infty,2}\le M,\qquad \|F(Y)-F(Z)\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|Y-Z\|_{\infty,2},$$

and $h\|A\|_\infty M\le R$, $q:=h\|A\|_\infty L<1$. Define $\Phi(Y)=c+h(A\otimes I_d)F(Y)$ and $G(Y)=Y-\Phi(Y)$. Then $\Phi$ has a unique fixed point $Y^*\in\mathcal B$, equivalently $G(Y^*)=0$. Every approximate stage vector $\widetilde Y\in\mathcal B$ satisfies

$$\|\widetilde Y-Y^*\|_{\infty,2}\le\frac{\|G(\widetilde Y)\|_{\infty,2}}{1-q}.$$

If the derivative-scaled stage residual is $r=G(\widetilde Y)/h$, the right side is $h\|r\|_{\infty,2}/(1-q)$. The hypotheses $h\|A\|_\infty L<1$ and the invariant-ball bound are local solvability conditions; this result gives no global branch outside $\mathcal B$.

Let $u=u(\theta)$ be $C^1$ and consider a selected $s$-stage Runge–Kutta branch for a $C^1$ parameter-dependent vector field $f(t,y,\theta)$. Let $F(Y,u,\theta)$ be the stack of its stage evaluations and
$$G(Y,u,\theta)=Y-\mathbf1\otimes u-h(A\otimes I_d)F(Y,u,\theta).$$
Assume the branch is the unique root in the invariant ball of [[lem-small-step-implicit-rk-branch-and-residual-error]], and its stage derivative $G_Y$ obeys the hypotheses of [[lem-implicit-rk-stage-jacobian-nonsingular-on-branch]]. Then the branch $Y(\theta)$ is locally $C^1$ and
$$D_\theta Y=-G_Y^{-1}\bigl(G_uD_\theta u+G_\theta\bigr).$$
For the update $\Psi_h(u,\theta)=u+h(\mathbf1^T_b\otimes I_d)F(Y(\theta),u(\theta),\theta)$,
$$D_\theta\Psi_h=D_\theta u+h(b^T\otimes I_d)\bigl(F_YD_\theta Y+F_uD_\theta u+F_\theta\bigr).$$
These are exact derivatives of the selected algebraic stage branch. A finite-budget stage iteration is a different map and is not covered by this formula.

Let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ define a first-order initial-value problem on an open time-state domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$. Given a time $t_n$, step $h_n>0$, and state $y_n$ with $(t_n,y_n)\in D$, an admissible endpoint $y_{n+1}$ must satisfy $(t_n+h_n,y_{n+1})\in D$. The backward Euler endpoint is any such $y_{n+1}$ satisfying

$$y_{n+1}=y_n+h_n f(t_n+h_n,y_{n+1}).$$

Its update residual at an approximate endpoint $z$ with $(t_n+h_n,z)\in D$ is

$$G_n^{\rm BE}(z)=z-y_n-h_n f(t_n+h_n,z).$$

When $f$ is defined at the endpoint, the derivative residual is $G_n^{\rm BE}(z)/h_n$. The equation can have no, one, or several roots on a restricted admissible branch set; this definition by itself asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

derivations.claim: Solving the scalar residual gives $(1+hk)Y=u_0$, hence $Y=u_0/(1+hk)$. Since $1+hk>0$, this is the unique root in the stated interval and agrees with the branch in [F1].
Differentiate the residual $(1+hk)Y-u_0=0$: $(1+hk)Y_k+hY=0$, so [F2] gives $Y_k=-hu_0/(1+hk)^2$. Therefore $J_k=YY_k=-hu_0^2/(1+hk)^3$.

Assume Countable Choice and the elliptic state setting of [[def-parameterized-elliptic-variational-problem]] and [[lem-elliptic-state-map-c1-under-uniform-coercivity]]. Let $J:V\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. For a parameter $\theta$, let $p_\theta\in V$ solve the adjoint variational problem
$$a_\theta(v,p_\theta)=D_uJ(u_\theta,\theta)[v]\qquad(v\in V).$$
Then the reduced objective $j(\theta)=J(u_\theta,\theta)$ is $C^1$ and
$$D_\theta j(\theta)[\eta]=D_\theta J(u_\theta,\theta)[\eta]+D_\theta\ell_\theta[\eta](p_\theta)-D_\theta a_\theta[\eta](u_\theta,p_\theta).$$
No symmetry of $a_\theta$ is required; the adjoint uses the transposed variational form displayed above.

Let $V$ be a real Hilbert space, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and write $V^*$ for the continuous real dual. A parameter-dependent coercive elliptic variational problem is a family of bounded bilinear forms $a_\theta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ and bounded linear functionals $\ell_\theta\in V^*$ such that, on each parameter neighborhood under discussion, $\|a_\theta\|\le M$ and $a_\theta(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2$ for fixed $M<\infty$ and $\alpha>0$. Operator-norm $C^1$ data means that the maps $\theta\mapsto A_\theta\in\mathcal L(V,V^*)$, $A_\theta u:=a_\theta(u,\cdot)$, and $\theta\mapsto\ell_\theta\in V^*$ are continuously Fréchet differentiable. A state at $\theta$ is a vector $u_\theta\in V$ satisfying $a_\theta(u_\theta,v)=\ell_\theta(v)$ for every $v\in V$. When a state is specified, a $C^1$ objective $J:V\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ defines the reduced objective $j(\theta)=J(u_\theta,\theta)$. This definition alone asserts neither state existence nor uniqueness of an optimizer.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $I=(0,1)$ and define
$$\phi(x)=\begin{cases}2x,&0\le x\le\frac12,\\2(1-x),&\frac12\le x\le1,\end{cases} \qquad p(x)=\frac12x(1-x).$$
Then $\phi|_I,p|_I\in H^1_0(I)=W^{1,2}_0(I)$, the closure of
$C_c^\infty(I)$ in $W^{1,2}(I)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

Assume Countable Choice. For every real $v\in H^1_0(0,1)$,

$$\|v\|_{L^2(0,1)}\le\|v'\|_{L^2(0,1)}.$$

Consequently $\|v\|_{H^1(0,1)}\le\sqrt2\,\|v'\|_{L^2(0,1)}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Put $w(x)=x(1-x)/2$. Direct differentiation gives $w''=-1$, $w(0)=w(1)=0$, and [F3] gives $w\in V$. For each $v\in V$ and $\varepsilon>0$, [F5] supplies $v_\varepsilon\in C_c^\infty(0,1)$ with $\|v-v_\varepsilon\|_{H^1}<\varepsilon$. By the product rule [F7], $(w'v_\varepsilon)'=w''v_\varepsilon+w'v_\varepsilon'$; since $v_\varepsilon$ vanishes at both endpoints, [F6] gives $\int_0^1w'v_\varepsilon'=\int_0^1v_\varepsilon$. By [F8], the difference between the two sides with $v$ in place of $v_\varepsilon$ is at most $(\|w'\|_{L^2}+1)\varepsilon$, so the weak identity $\int_0^1w'v'=\int_0^1v$ follows as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Also, [F4] gives $a_\theta(v,v)\ge(1+\theta)\|v\|_{H^1}^2/2$; on a neighborhood of each $\theta>-1$ this is a uniform coercivity bound. Hence $u_\theta=w/(1+\theta)$ solves the state equation and is unique. Finally $\int_0^1w=1/12$, so $j(\theta)=1/(12(1+\theta))$.

The adjoint equation is $a_\theta(v,p)=D_uJ[v]=\int_0^1v$ for all $v\in V$, so symmetry of $a_\theta$ and uniqueness give $p=u_\theta$. The direct parameter derivatives of $J$ and $\ell$ vanish. For the scalar parameter direction $1$, $D_\theta a[1](u,p)=\int_0^1u'p'\,dx=(1+\theta)^{-2}\int_0^1(w')^2dx$. Direct integration gives $\int_0^1(w')^2dx=\frac14\int_0^1(1-2x)^2dx=1/12$, hence $D_\theta a[1](u,p)=1/(12(1+\theta)^2)$.
Formula [F1] therefore gives $j'(\theta)=-1/(12(1+\theta)^2)$, equal to the derivative of the explicit reduced objective in step 1.1.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta$ be open, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuously differentiable. Let $V_\theta\subseteq\Theta$ be open and $u_0:V_\theta\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^1$. Assume there is a bounded convex open set $O\subset D$ with compact closure in $D$ such that for every $\theta\in V_\theta$ the unique solution of $u'=f(t,u,\theta)$, $u(0)=u_0(\theta)$, exists on $[0,T]$, and all triples $(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)$ lie in $O$. Then $\theta\mapsto u_\theta$ is $C^1$ as a map to $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$. For any $\theta_0\in V_\theta$, its tangent matrix $S(t)=D_\theta u_\theta(t)|_{\theta=\theta_0}$ is the unique solution of
$$S'(t)=D_u f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)S(t)+D_\theta f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0),\qquad S(0)=D u_0(\theta_0).$$
The result is local to the stated common compact tube and claims no differentiability outside it.

Use the setting of [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]]. Write $A_n=D_x\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, $B_n=D_\theta\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, and let $S_n=D_\theta x_n$. Then
$$S_0=D x_0(\theta),\qquad S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n.$$
Define $p_N=D_x\phi(x_N,\theta)^T$ and, backward for $n=N-1,\ldots,0$,
$$p_n=D_x\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+A_n^Tp_{n+1}.$$
The exact gradient of the finite objective is
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(x_N,\theta)^T+S_0^Tp_0+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\bigl(D_\theta\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}\bigr).$$
The recursion is the reverse derivative of the finite graph in exact real arithmetic; it makes no convergence claim about an iteration used to choose $\theta$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

derivations.claim: The function $u(t)=e^{\theta t}s$ satisfies $u'=\theta u$ and $u(0)=s$. Conversely, for any solution $v$ with this initial value, the product and chain rules give $(e^{-\theta t}v(t))'=0$. By [F4] this product is constantly $s$ on its solution interval, and positivity and the reciprocal identity in [F3] imply $v(t)=e^{\theta t}s$. Thus the displayed solution exists globally and is unique.

Verify the actual common-tube hypotheses locally at any $(s_*,\theta_*)$. Fix $\varepsilon,\delta,\eta>0$ and restrict the parameters to $|s-s_*|<\varepsilon$, $|\theta-\theta_*|<\delta$. For $-\eta\le t\le\tau+\eta$, $$|e^{\theta t}s|\le B:=(|s_*|+\varepsilon)\exp((|\theta_*|+\delta)(\tau+\eta)).$$ Treat $(s,\theta)$ as the flow parameter, with initial map $(s,\theta)\mapsto s$ and field $(t,u,s,\theta)\mapsto\theta u$ on $\mathbb R^4$. The bounded convex open set $$(-\eta,\tau+\eta)\times(-B-1,B+1)\times(s_*-2\varepsilon,s_*+2\varepsilon)\times(\theta_*-2\delta,\theta_*+2\delta)$$ has compact closure inside that field's domain and contains all these trajectories for $0\le t\le\tau$ and the restricted parameters. The field and initial map are $C^1$. Step 1.1 supplies existence and uniqueness, so [F1] applies. Each shooting interval uses this same argument with its own initial node; since there are two intervals, a common finite bound may also be taken.

The exact interval map is therefore $\Phi_\tau(s,\theta)=e^{\tau\theta}s$. Differentiate the residuals with respect to $(z_0,z_1,z_2)$ and $\theta$, writing $E=e^{\tau\theta}$: $$D_zR=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\-E&1&0\\0&-E&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad D_\theta R=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-\tau E z_0\\-\tau E z_1\end{pmatrix}.$$ The state Jacobian is lower bidiagonal, and the parameter column contains the two local flow sensitivities.

Solving $R=0$ gives $z_0=a$, $z_1=Ea$, and $z_2=E^2a$. Direct differentiation yields $D_\theta z_2=2\tau E^2a$. The discrete adjoint for the two flow steps seeds $p_2=1$, then gives $p_1=E$ and $p_0=E^2$; its parameter sum is $\tau E z_0p_1+\tau E z_1p_2=2\tau E^2a$. Thus the reverse gradient agrees with the differentiated shooting solution.

Let $A_1,\ldots,A_N\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be invertible, with $n,N\ge1$, and let $Q_0$ be orthogonal. For $1\le k\le N$, form the unique positive-diagonal QR factorization
$$A_kQ_{k-1}=Q_kR_k,$$
where $Q_k$ is orthogonal and $R_k$ is upper triangular with positive diagonal $r_{k,ii}$. Put $P_N=A_N\cdots A_1$ and define the exact finite-time log-volume change by $\log|\det P_N|$. Then
$$\log|\det P_N|=\sum_{k=1}^N\sum_{i=1}^n\log r_{k,ii}.$$
No infinite-time Lyapunov exponent or shadowing conclusion follows.

For a numerical log record, define $\sigma_{\min}(A):=\inf_{\|x\|_2=1}\|Ax\|_2$. If $\sigma_{\min}(A_k)\ge\sigma>0$, each exact $r_{k,ii}\ge\sigma$. If positive computed diagonals $\widetilde r_{k,ii}$ satisfy $|\widetilde r_{k,ii}-r_{k,ii}|\le\varepsilon_{k,i}\le\sigma/2$, and each computed logarithm $\widehat l_{k,i}$ satisfies $|\widehat l_{k,i}-\log\widetilde r_{k,ii}|\le\delta_{k,i}$, then
$$\left|\sum_{k,i}\widehat l_{k,i}-\log|\det P_N|\right|\le\sum_{k,i}\left(\frac{2\varepsilon_{k,i}}{\sigma}+\delta_{k,i}\right).$$
If any factor loses rank, this log-volume branch returns failure.

Let $J$ and $J_h$ be the continuous and finite state-step objectives of [[thm-continuous-ode-adjoint-gradient-formula]] and [[thm-discrete-adjoint-gradient-recursion]], respectively, and put $h=T/N$. Let $q(t,u,p)=D_\theta\ell(t,u,\theta)^T+D_\theta f(t,u,\theta)^Tp$ be the continuous running-gradient vector, evaluated on its exact state and adjoint as $q(t):=q(t,u(t),p(t))$. Suppose the exact and numerical state/adjoint pairs lie in a common tube and
$$\max_n\bigl(\|u_n-u(t_n)\|_2+\|p_n-p(t_n)\|_2\bigr)\le C_xh^p.$$
For the state part of this bound, it is sufficient that the hypotheses of [[thm-global-error-from-one-step-defect-and-stability]] hold with a uniform $O(h^{p+1})$ exact-start defect; the coefficient conditions of [[prop-explicit-rk-order-conditions-through-four]] supply that defect for an explicit Runge--Kutta method of order $p\le4$ under that item's $C^4$ and common-tube assumptions. No cited state-error result supplies the adjoint part, which is an independent hypothesis here. Write $b$ and $b_h$ for the column initial/terminal contribution vectors in the continuous and discrete gradient formulas. Assume the discrete running-gradient terms admit vectors $\widehat q_n$ and nonnegative weights $w_n$, $0\le n\le N$, with
$$\nabla J_h=b_h+\sum_{n=0}^N w_n\widehat q_n,\qquad \nabla J=b+\int_0^Tq(t)\,dt,\qquad \sum_{n=0}^Nw_n=T.$$
The weighted discrete representation is an explicit premise; it is not implied by the generic finite state-step adjoint recursion. Suppose
$$\|\widehat q_n-q(t_n,u_n,p_n)\|_2\le C_dh^p,\qquad \|b_h-b\|_2\le C_bh^p,$$
and that the same weights give the quadrature $Q_h(q)=\sum_{n=0}^Nw_nq(t_n)$ satisfying
$$\left\|Q_h(q)-\int_0^Tq(t)\,dt\right\|_2\le C_Qh^p.$$
If $q$ is Lipschitz in $(u,p)$ on the common tube with constant $L_q$ in the sum norm, then
$$\|\nabla J_h-\nabla J\|_2\le\bigl(C_b+T(C_d+L_qC_x)+C_Q\bigr)h^p.$$
The adjoint, derivative-data and quadrature hypotheses are separate from state accuracy; without them the state estimate alone gives no gradient error conclusion.

There is also the following independent method-consistency conclusion. Under the local $C^1$ step-and-cost consistency, derivative stability, derivative Lipschitz, initial-data, terminal-derivative and tube hypotheses of [[lem-local-c1-step-consistency-implies-tangent-adjoint-gradient-order]], the actual numerical graph satisfies
$$\max_n\|D_\theta u_n-D_\theta u(t_n)\|_2\le C_Sh^p,\qquad \max_n\|p_n-p(t_n)\|_2\le C_Ph^p,$$
$$\|\nabla J_h-\nabla J\|_2\le C_Gh^p,$$
with that lemma's explicit constants, together with its state bound. These conclusions derive the global tangent and adjoint errors from local map errors. They do not assume the preceding global state/adjoint bound or weighted representation.

In particular, [[lem-explicit-rk-differentiated-stages-give-local-c1-order]] supplies these local hypotheses for the actual explicit RK state map and the cost using the same tableau, under its common-tube, base $C^2$, and local augmented-order hypotheses. For $p\le4$, its augmented $C^4$ hypothesis and the existing coefficient conditions suffice; jointly $C^5$ base data are an explicit sufficient smoothness condition, and its displayed classical RK4 tableau gives a concrete order-four instance. Generic $p$ is retained through its genuine local augmented-order hypothesis. This branch permits negative or zero RK weights and makes no internal-stage adjoint accuracy claim.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta$ be open, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuously differentiable. Let $V_\theta\subseteq\Theta$ be open and $u_0:V_\theta\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^1$. Assume there is a bounded convex open set $O\subset D$ with compact closure in $D$ such that for every $\theta\in V_\theta$ the unique solution of $u'=f(t,u,\theta)$, $u(0)=u_0(\theta)$, exists on $[0,T]$, and all triples $(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)$ lie in $O$. Then $\theta\mapsto u_\theta$ is $C^1$ as a map to $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$. For any $\theta_0\in V_\theta$, its tangent matrix $S(t)=D_\theta u_\theta(t)|_{\theta=\theta_0}$ is the unique solution of
$$S'(t)=D_u f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)S(t)+D_\theta f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0),\qquad S(0)=D u_0(\theta_0).$$
The result is local to the stated common compact tube and claims no differentiability outside it.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$,
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]],
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-interval]]). Let
$M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $M \ge 0$ satisfy

$$\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } t \in (a,b).$$

Then

$$\lVert f(b) - f(a)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,(b-a).$$

**No integrability of $f'$ is assumed**, so the theorem applies to every
differentiable $f$; that is why it is proved from the scalar mean value theorem
rather than from
[[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]].
[[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]] records the comparison between the
two routes.

**The equality form is not asserted, and for $m \ge 2$ it is false.** There need
be **no** $\xi \in (a,b)$ with $f(b)-f(a) = f'(\xi)(b-a)$; the companion page
carries a differentiable witness on $[0,1]$. The $\xi$ produced in the proof
below depends on the fixed vector $u = f(b)-f(a)$ and is a mean value point of
the **real** function $t \mapsto \langle u, f(t)\rangle$, not of $f$.

Let $S\in C^1([0,T];\mathbb R^{d\times m})$ and $p\in C^1([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $S'=A S+B$ and $p'=-A^T p-g$, where $A,B,g$ are continuous and have compatible dimensions. Then
$$p(T)^T S(T)-p(0)^T S(0)=\int_0^T\bigl(-g(t)^T S(t)+p(t)^T B(t)\bigr)\,dt.$$

Let $u_\theta$ solve the parameter-dependent ODE of [[lem-parameter-ode-flow-tangent-on-common-tube]] on $[0,T]$. Let
$$J(\theta)=\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)+\int_0^T\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)\,dt,$$
where $\phi$ and $\ell$ are $C^1$ on a neighborhood of the trajectory tube and their first derivatives are bounded and uniformly continuous there. Let $S=D_\theta u_\theta$ be the tangent from that lemma. Let $p$ solve the terminal adjoint problem
$$-p'(t)=D_u f(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^Tp(t)+D_u\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^T,\qquad p(T)=D_u\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T.$$
Then
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T+D_\theta u_0(\theta)^Tp(0)+\int_0^T\bigl(D_\theta\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T+D_\theta f(t,u_\theta,\theta)^Tp(t)\bigr)\,dt.$$
This formula separates initial, terminal, running-cost and vector-field parameter terms. It applies only while the common-tube and differentiability hypotheses hold.

Use the setting of [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]]. Write $A_n=D_x\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, $B_n=D_\theta\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, and let $S_n=D_\theta x_n$. Then
$$S_0=D x_0(\theta),\qquad S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n.$$
Define $p_N=D_x\phi(x_N,\theta)^T$ and, backward for $n=N-1,\ldots,0$,
$$p_n=D_x\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+A_n^Tp_{n+1}.$$
The exact gradient of the finite objective is
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(x_N,\theta)^T+S_0^Tp_0+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\bigl(D_\theta\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}\bigr).$$
The recursion is the reverse derivative of the finite graph in exact real arithmetic; it makes no convergence claim about an iteration used to choose $\theta$.

Let $T>0$, $N\ge1$, $h=T/N$, $p\ge1$, and $C_0,C,L\ge0$. If nonnegative real numbers $e_0,\ldots,e_N$ satisfy
$$e_0\le C_0h^p,\qquad e_{n+1}\le(1+Lh)e_n+Ch^{p+1}\quad(0\le n<N),$$
then, when $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}e_n\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, when $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}e_n\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

derivations.claim: The exact objective is also the finite graph with maps $\Phi_n$, costs $K_n$, initial state $u(0)$ and terminal cost $\phi$: the intervals partition the integral. Differentiability of $K_n$ follows by differentiating its integral using the common-tube flow derivative and the uniform continuous derivative bounds. In particular the initial-state variational matrix $V$ on interval $n$ has $V(t_n)=I$, $V'=f_uV$, and $$c_n^e=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}V(t)^T\ell_u(t)^T\,dt.$$ The pairing identity gives $$p(t_n)=c_n^e(u(t_n),\theta)+A_n^e(u(t_n),\theta)^Tp(t_{n+1}).$$ Thus the exact-flow graph adjoint equals the continuous adjoint at every node. Its tangent and gradient are also those of the exact continuous objective.

Write $u_n=u(t_n)$ and $e_n=\|x_n-u_n\|$. For $d\ge1$, parameterize the admitted segment by $s\mapsto u_n+s(x_n-u_n)$, $0\le s\le1$. The chain rule and the derivative bound for $\Psi_n$ bound the derivative of its composition with this segment by $(1+Lh)\|x_n-u_n\|$; the vector mean value inequality [F1] therefore gives its endpoint Lipschitz bound with constant $1+Lh$. For $d=0$, the state difference and both endpoint values lie in the zero vector space, so the same bound is immediate. Consequently $$e_{n+1}\le(1+Lh)e_n+c_vh^{p+1}.$$ By [F3], $e_n\le Xh^p$.

The exact tangent and adjoint recurrences give $$\|S_{n+1}\|\le(1+Lh)\|S_n\|+Mh,\qquad \|p(t_n)\|\le(1+Lh)\|p(t_{n+1})\|+Mh.$$ Expanding these finite recurrences and using $(1+Lh)^k\le e^{LT}$ shows $\|S_n\|\le\overline S$ and $\|p(t_n)\|\le\overline P$. These bounds include $L=0$. For any one of the four derivative maps, comparison at numerical and exact nodes gives $$\|F_n^h(x_n,\theta)-F_n^e(u_n,\theta)\|\le c_1h^{p+1}+Hh e_n\le Rh^{p+1}.$$

The actual differentiated numerical graph satisfies $S_{n+1}^h=A_n^h(x_n)S_n^h+B_n^h(x_n)$. Subtract the exact recurrence and split the matrix product using $A_n^h(S_n^h-S_n)+(A_n^h-A_n^e)S_n$. Hence $$\|S_{n+1}^h-S_{n+1}\|\le(1+Lh)\|S_n^h-S_n\|+R(\overline S+1)h^{p+1}.$$ The initial derivative bound and [F3] yield $C_Sh^p$.

At the terminal node, the difference of adjoint seeds is at most $Dh^p$. Subtract the two backward recurrences, splitting $A_h^Tp_h-A_e^Tp_e=A_h^T(p_h-p_e)+(A_h-A_e)^Tp_e$. The Euclidean operator norm of a transpose equals that of the matrix. For every finite-dimensional Euclidean vector $v$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|v\|=\sup_{\|w\|\le1}|w^Tv|$: if $v\ne0$, equality is attained at $w=v/\|v\|$, while for $v=0$ both sides vanish, including in dimension zero. Applying this closed-unit-ball formula to both sides of the pairing gives the transpose identity in all finite dimensions. Therefore $$\|p_n^h-p(t_n)\|\le(1+Lh)\|p_{n+1}^h-p(t_{n+1})\|+R(\overline P+1)h^{p+1}.$$ Reverse the indices and apply [F3]. This gives $C_Ph^p$.

Apply the finite-graph gradient formula to both graphs: $$\nabla J_h=D_\theta\phi_h(x_N)^T+(S_0^h)^Tp_0^h+\sum_{n<N}\{d_n^h(x_n)+(B_n^h(x_n))^Tp_{n+1}^h\},$$ $$\nabla J=D_\theta\phi(u_N)^T+S_0^Tp(0)+\sum_{n<N}\{d_n^e(u_n)+(B_n^e(u_n))^Tp(t_{n+1})\}.$$ The terminal direct-derivative difference is at most $Dh^p$. The initial contribution is bounded by $$\{c_{s0}\overline P+(M_0+c_{s0})C_P\}h^p,$$ since $h\le1$ implies $\|S_0^h\|\le M_0+c_{s0}$. Each running difference is bounded by $$\{R+R\overline P+MC_P\}h^{p+1},$$ using $B_h^T(p_h-p)+(B_h-B_e)^Tp$. Summing $N$ terms and using $Nh=T$ proves the stated $C_G$ bound.

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be an open time-state domain, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be the right-hand side of a first-order initial-value problem in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. An explicit $s$-stage Runge–Kutta tableau consists of a positive integer $s$, real coefficients $a_{ij}$, $b_i$, and $c_i$ with $a_{ij}=0$ whenever $j\ge i$, and
$$c_i=\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}\qquad(1\le i\le s).$$
The finite row sum is empty, hence $c_1=0$.

For a step size $h>0$ from an admitted base pair $(t,y)\in D$, compute in order
$$Y_i=y+h\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}K_j,\qquad t_i=t+c_i h,\qquad K_i=f(t_i,Y_i)\quad(i=1,\ldots,s).$$
The strict lower-triangular condition makes each stage depend only on already computed slopes; no implicit stage equation is solved. If every stage is defined, the candidate output is
$$y^+=y+h\sum_{i=1}^s b_iK_i.$$

The procedure accepts an exact right-hand-side evaluation oracle that returns either the value $f(t_i,Y_i)$ or an evaluation-failure status. Before each query it checks $(t_i,Y_i)\in D$. It returns domain-failure with the first failing stage if that check fails, evaluation-failure with the stage index if the oracle fails, and domain-failure at output if $(t+h,y^+)\notin D$. Otherwise it returns success with $(t+h,y^+)$. In the exact mathematical model the oracle returns $f$ at every point of $D$; the failure branch records only an unavailable numerical evaluation. On success this is a one-step map in the sense of [[def-one-step-ode-method-local-defect-order-and-stability]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta$ be open, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuously differentiable. Let $V_\theta\subseteq\Theta$ be open and $u_0:V_\theta\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^1$. Assume there is a bounded convex open set $O\subset D$ with compact closure in $D$ such that for every $\theta\in V_\theta$ the unique solution of $u'=f(t,u,\theta)$, $u(0)=u_0(\theta)$, exists on $[0,T]$, and all triples $(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)$ lie in $O$. Then $\theta\mapsto u_\theta$ is $C^1$ as a map to $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$. For any $\theta_0\in V_\theta$, its tangent matrix $S(t)=D_\theta u_\theta(t)|_{\theta=\theta_0}$ is the unique solution of
$$S'(t)=D_u f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)S(t)+D_\theta f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0),\qquad S(0)=D u_0(\theta_0).$$
The result is local to the stated common compact tube and claims no differentiability outside it.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $d,N,p\ge1$, $T>0$, $h=T/N$, and $t_n=nh$. Let $y:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ solve an initial-value problem in an open time-state domain $D$. Use the Euclidean norm $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], whose triangle inequality is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]. Let $\mathcal T\subset D$ be a common compact time-state tube with positive margin in $D$, and write $\mathcal T_t:=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:(t,v)\in\mathcal T\}$. Suppose a one-step map $\Psi_{h,n}$ is defined on $\mathcal T_{t_n}$, produces $y_{n+1}=\Psi_{h,n}(y_n)$, and the entire exact path, all numerical grid states, and every method stage lie in $\mathcal T$. If constants $C,C_0,L\ge0$, independent of $N$ and $n$, satisfy
$$\|y_0-y(0)\|_2\le C_0h^p,\qquad \|\Psi_{h,n}(y(t_n))-y(t_{n+1})\|_2\le Ch^{p+1},$$
and
$$\|\Psi_{h,n}(u)-\Psi_{h,n}(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$
for every $u,v\in\mathcal T_{t_n}$ and $0\le n<N$, then, for $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, for $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

Let $p\ge1$ be an integer, $T>0$, $h=T/N\le h_0\le1$, and $t_n=nh$. The state dimension $d$ and parameter dimension $m$ are fixed. All vector norms are Euclidean and all matrix norms are their induced operator norms; gradients are columns.

Consider the continuous objective
$$J(\theta)=\phi(u(T,\theta),\theta)+\int_0^T\ell(t,u(t,\theta),\theta)\,dt,$$
and the actual finite graph
$$x_{n+1}=\Psi_n(x_n,\theta),\qquad J_h(\theta)=\phi_h(x_N,\theta)+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}L_n(x_n,\theta).$$
Assume the hypotheses of the continuous flow-tangent and adjoint-gradient results hold on a common tube. Write $\Phi_n(x,\theta)$ for the exact flow from $t_n$ to $t_{n+1}$ and
$$K_n(x,\theta)=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}\ell(t,u(t;t_n,x,\theta),\theta)\,dt.$$
These exact maps and the actual numerical maps are $C^1$ on open neighborhoods of the admitted state and parameter sets. For every relevant $n$, all states $x_n,u(t_n)$ and the segment joining them belong to a convex admitted state set. All estimates below hold uniformly on those sets and a fixed parameter neighborhood, independently of $N,n$.

For $r=e,h$, define
$$A_n^e=D_x\Phi_n,\quad B_n^e=D_\theta\Phi_n,\quad c_n^e=D_xK_n^T,\quad d_n^e=D_\theta K_n^T,$$
$$A_n^h=D_x\Psi_n,\quad B_n^h=D_\theta\Psi_n,\quad c_n^h=D_xL_n^T,\quad d_n^h=D_\theta L_n^T.$$
Suppose constants $c_v,c_1,L,M,H\ge0$ satisfy, at each admitted $(x,\theta)$,
$$\|\Psi_n-\Phi_n\|\le c_vh^{p+1},$$
$$\|A_n^h-A_n^e\|,\ \|B_n^h-B_n^e\|,\ \|c_n^h-c_n^e\|,\ \|d_n^h-d_n^e\|\le c_1h^{p+1},$$
$$\|A_n^r\|\le1+Lh,\qquad \|B_n^r\|,\ \|c_n^r\|,\ \|d_n^r\|\le Mh.$$
Each of $A_n^e,B_n^e,c_n^e,d_n^e$ is Lipschitz in $x$, with constant at most $Hh$.

Let $S_0=D_\theta u(0,\theta)$ and $S_0^h=D_\theta x_0(\theta)$. Assume
$$\|x_0-u(0)\|\le c_0h^p,\qquad \|S_0^h-S_0\|\le c_{s0}h^p,\qquad \|S_0\|\le M_0.$$
The terminal costs are $C^1$. The exact columns $D_x\phi^T,D_\theta\phi^T$ have norm at most $M_\phi$ and are Lipschitz in $x$ with constant $H_\phi$; at the same admitted $(x,\theta)$,
$$\|D_x\phi_h^T-D_x\phi^T\|,\ \|D_\theta\phi_h^T-D_\theta\phi^T\|\le C_\phi h^p.$$
No terminal value-error hypothesis is needed for the gradient conclusion.

Let $S_n^h=D_\theta x_n$, and let $p_n^h$ be the exact discrete adjoint of this numerical graph. Let $S(t)=D_\theta u(t)$ and let $p(t)$ be the continuous adjoint with terminal value $D_x\phi(u(T),\theta)^T$. Define
$$E=e^{LT},\quad X=E(c_0+Tc_v),\quad \overline S=E(M_0+TM),\quad \overline P=E(M_\phi+TM),$$
$$R=c_1+HX,\quad C_S=E\{c_{s0}+TR(\overline S+1)\},\quad D=C_\phi+H_\phi X,$$
$$C_P=E\{D+TR(\overline P+1)\},$$
$$C_G=D+c_{s0}\overline P+(M_0+c_{s0})C_P+T\{R(1+\overline P)+MC_P\}.$$
Then
$$\max_n\|x_n-u(t_n)\|\le Xh^p,\qquad \max_n\|S_n^h-S(t_n)\|\le C_Sh^p,$$
$$\max_n\|p_n^h-p(t_n)\|\le C_Ph^p,\qquad \|\nabla J_h-\nabla J\|\le C_Gh^p.$$
These conclusions assume local value and first-derivative consistency, rather than a global adjoint-error estimate. They require no representation by nonnegative quadrature weights.

derivations.claim: Set $\xi=(x,\theta)$. The exact local solution has $V(t)=D_\xi u(t)$ because $V(t_n)=E$ and its displayed equation is the variational equation, with $D_\xi\theta=E_\theta$. Differentiating the cost integral gives $g(t)=D_\xi C(t)^T$. Thus at the local endpoint, $$V^+=[D_x\Phi_n\ D_\theta\Phi_n],\qquad g^+=\begin{pmatrix}D_xK_n^T\\D_\theta K_n^T\end{pmatrix}.$$ The flow result and bounded continuous derivatives justify these differentiations uniformly.

Differentiate each actual stage, in its explicit order. If $V_i=D_\xi Y_i$, then $$V_i=E+h\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}(f_{u,j}V_j+f_{\theta,j}E_\theta),$$ $$D_\xi\Psi_n=E+h\sum_i b_i(f_{u,i}V_i+f_{\theta,i}E_\theta),$$ $$D_\xi L_n^T=h\sum_i b_i(V_i^T\ell_{u,i}^T+E_\theta^T\ell_{\theta,i}^T).$$ These are exactly the $V$ and $g$ outputs obtained by applying the same RK tableau to the augmented system. Its $C$ output is $L_n$ and its $u$ output is $\Psi_n$. Consequently the assumed augmented local defect bounds $\Psi_n-\Phi_n$, $L_n-K_n$, and all four first-derivative differences by constants times $h^{p+1}$. Projection to a component does not increase the Euclidean norm; a matrix Frobenius bound also bounds its operator norm.

For a fixed finite tableau, the stage derivative recurrences in step 2.1 give uniform bounds on $D_xY_i,D_\theta Y_i$ by induction, using $h\le h_0$ and the bounded first derivatives of $f$. Here $D_xY_i=I+O(h)$ and $D_\theta Y_i=O(h)$. Substitution into the output derivatives gives $$D_x\Psi_n=I+O(h),\quad D_\theta\Psi_n=O(h),\quad D_xL_n^T=O(h),\quad D_\theta L_n^T=O(h),$$ uniformly. In particular $\|D_x\Psi_n\|\le1+L_hh$ for a fixed constant $L_h$. The exact variational integral equation gives the same bounds for the exact maps, with $\|D_x\Phi_n\|\le e^{Kh}\le1+Ke^{Kh_0}h$. Enlarging the constants gives the common $L,M$ required by the preceding lemma.

For $p\le4$, apply [F3] to the displayed autonomous augmented field itself. Its derivatives through order four exist and are uniformly bounded under the asserted augmented $C^4$ hypothesis. Joint base $C^5$ regularity is sufficient because its variational components use first derivatives of the base fields. All its exact paths and stages are admitted by [A1]. The source proposition therefore supplies the exact local augmented-defect premise used in step 2.1. This application concerns the differentiated augmented method, rather than just its state projection.

The exact maps have the required second-derivative bounds of size $O(h)$. To justify differentiating their variational equations, apply the common-tube $C^1$ flow result to the first variational system: its field is $C^1$ since $f$ is $C^2$, its initial derivative seed is constant, and its variational components remain bounded by [F2]. For coordinate directions $a,b$ of $\xi$, put $W_{ab}=D_{\xi_a}D_{\xi_b}u$. Then $$W_{ab}'=f_uW_{ab}+D^2_{(u,\theta)}f[(V_a,E_{\theta,a}),(V_b,E_{\theta,b})],\qquad W_{ab}(t_n)=0.$$ The forcing is uniformly bounded, so Grönwall on an interval of length $h$ gives $\|W_{ab}\|\le C h$. Differentiating the cost integral twice produces the integrand $$D^2_{(u,\theta)}\ell[(V_a,E_{\theta,a}),(V_b,E_{\theta,b})]+\ell_uW_{ab},$$ which is uniformly bounded, and hence $D_\xi^2K_n=O(h)$. Thus $D_\xi^2\Phi_n=O(h)$ and $D_\xi^2K_n=O(h)$. Applying the one-dimensional mean value inequality along each admitted state segment gives Lipschitz constants $Hh$ for $A_n^e,B_n^e,c_n^e,d_n^e$.

There is also a direct augmented global-error interpretation. Along a full trajectory append $C'=\ell$ and the column $G'=S^T\ell_u^T+\ell_\theta^T$, with $C(0)=0,G(0)=0$ and $S'=f_uS+f_\theta$. Differentiating the actual stages shows that its numerical step is exactly $$S^+=A_n^hS+B_n^h,\quad C^+=C+L_n,\quad G^+=G+S^Tc_n^h+d_n^h.$$ The analogous exact step uses the exact maps. On bounded $S$ sets, step 2.1 therefore supplies a uniform $O(h^{p+1})$ local defect for $(u,S,C,G)$. Exact $S$ is bounded by Grönwall; numerical $S$ is bounded by the $1+Lh,Mh$ recurrence from step 3.1. The sums defining $C,G$ then bound them uniformly as well. Their stage values are bounded by the same finite-stage induction.

Steps 2.1–4.1 establish precisely the local hypotheses of the preceding lemma. That lemma now proves the global state, actual graph-tangent, backward nodal-adjoint and gradient bounds. In particular the adjoint conclusion is derived; it is not inserted as an additional hypothesis.

On a common compact convex augmented tube containing these values and joining stage segments, the $C^1$ augmented field has a derivative bound $K$. For two starting augmented states with difference $\delta$, explicit stage differences obey $\delta_i\le\delta+hK\sum_{j<i}|a_{ij}|\delta_j$. Induction gives $\delta_i\le D_i\delta$, where $D_1=1$ and $D_i=1+h_0K\sum_{j<i}|a_{ij}|D_j$. The output difference is at most $(1+hK\sum_i|b_i|D_i)\delta$. Thus the actual augmented method has one-step stability $1+\Lambda h$. The global-error supplier applies, giving order-$p$ error in the actual tangent and accumulated cost derivative as well. This independently exhibits the augmented local-to-global route; step 5.1 additionally supplies the nodal adjoint.

For the displayed RK4 tableau the eight coefficient sums, in the order stated in the source proposition, are $1,1/2,1/3,1/6,1/4,1/12,1/8,1/24$. For example $Ac=(0,0,1/4,1/2)$, $Ac^{[2]}=(0,0,1/8,1/4)$, and $A^2c=(0,0,0,1/4)$, which verify the mixed sums directly. Hence step 3.2 applies with $p=4$. No division by an individual $b_i$ or internal-stage adjoint order condition occurs in this argument.
