Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

derivations.claim: The vector $e_1=(1,0,\ldots,0)$ belongs to $\mathcal C_{s,C}$ because its entries sum to $1$ and its $\ell^1$ norm is $1\le C$. Thus the coefficient set is nonempty. It is closed: the sum constraint is the inverse image of the closed singleton $\{1\}$ under a continuous linear map, and the $\ell^1$ bound is the inverse image of the closed interval $(-\infty,C]$ under the continuous function $c\mapsto\sum_i|c_i|$. It is bounded because $\|c\|_1^2=\sum_i c_i^2+2\sum_{i<j}|c_i||c_j|\ge\|c\|_2^2$ and $\|c\|_1\le C$. Therefore [F2] makes $\mathcal C_{s,C}$ compact.

The map $c\mapsto\sum_i c_iR_i$ is linear and continuous in finite dimensions, and its squared Frobenius norm is continuous by [F1]. The extreme-value theorem gives a minimum; its minimizer set is closed as the inverse image of the singleton containing that minimum, hence compact as a closed subset of $\mathcal C_{s,C}$. Thus [F2] gives a nonempty compact set $M=\operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in\mathcal C_{s,C}}J(c)$.

For $c,d\in\mathcal C_{s,C}$ and $0\le t\le1$, the coefficients $e=(1-t)c+td$ satisfy $\sum_i e_i=(1-t)\sum_i c_i+t\sum_i d_i=1$. By [F3], $\sum_i|e_i|\le(1-t)\sum_i|c_i|+t\sum_i|d_i|\le C$, so $\mathcal C_{s,C}$ is convex. The set $M$ is also convex: for matrices $A,B$ the identity $\|(1-t)A+tB\|_F^2=(1-t)\|A\|_F^2+t\|B\|_F^2-t(1-t)\|A-B\|_F^2$ proves convexity of the squared norm. Applying it to $A=\sum_i c_iR_i$ and $B=\sum_i d_iR_i$ shows $J((1-t)c+td)\le(1-t)J(c)+tJ(d)=\min J$, so the convex combination also minimizes. Since $M$ is compact, the continuous function $c\mapsto\|c\|_2^2$ has a minimizer $c_*\in M$.

If distinct $c,d\in M$ both had minimum Euclidean norm, their midpoint would lie in $M$ and satisfy $\left\|\frac{c+d}{2}\right\|_2^2=\frac{\|c\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2}{2}-\frac{\|c-d\|_2^2}{4}<\frac{\|c\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2}{2},$ contradicting minimality. Thus $c_*$ is the unique minimum-norm least-squares minimizer. No nonsingularity of the Gram matrix is needed for existence or tie-breaking.

For Hermitian $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, write their eigenvalues in
descending order with multiplicity as $\lambda_1(A)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n(A)$
and $\lambda_1(B)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n(B)$. Then, for every $j$,
$$|\lambda_j(A)-\lambda_j(B)|\le\|A-B\|_2.$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

derivations.claim: Since $\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)=\lambda_r(H_0)+g$, we have $R=\lambda_r(H_0)-\lambda_1(H_0)+g/2\ge g/2>0$. Reversing the descending-index convention in [F1] gives the same perturbation bound for the ascending eigenvalues used here. Thus if $\|H-H_0\|_{op}\le g/4$, then $\lambda_1(H)\ge c-g/4$ and $\lambda_r(H)\le c+R-g/4$. Since $R-g/4\ge g/4$, every first-$r$ eigenvalue therefore satisfies $|\lambda_j(H)-c|\le R-g/4$, so it lies at least $g/4$ inside the circle centered at $c$.

The same eigenvalue estimate gives $\lambda_{r+1}(H)\ge c+R+g/4$, so all remaining eigenvalues satisfy $|\lambda_j(H)-c|\ge R+g/4$ and lie at least $g/4$ outside the circle. Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $n\ge2$, $1\le r<n$, and use the real Hermitian matrix space $\mathbb H_n$
and projector set $\mathcal P_r$ of
[[def-rank-r-orthogonal-projector-domain]]. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb H_n$ be open
and let $F:U\to\mathbb H_n$ be a specified map. For a Hermitian matrix $H$,
write its eigenvalues with multiplicity in ascending order as
$$\lambda_1(H)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(H).$$
Write $\sigma(H):=\{\lambda_j(H):1\le j\le n\}$ for its finite spectrum,
with multiplicity omitted in this set notation.
For any Hermitian $H$ with $\lambda_r(H)<\lambda_{r+1}(H)$, write $\Pi_r(H)$
for the orthogonal projector onto the sum of eigenspaces belonging to its $r$
lowest eigenvalues. At a point $X\in U$ where
$$\lambda_r(F(X))<\lambda_{r+1}(F(X)),$$
define $\Phi(X):=\Pi_r(F(X))$. The strict gap separates the occupied cluster
from the unoccupied cluster; eigenvalue multiplicities within either cluster
are allowed. The construction's well-definedness as a unique member of
$\mathcal P_r$ is proved in [[lem-gapped-projector-map-well-defined]].

A set $K\subseteq U$ has a **uniform occupied/unoccupied gap** $g>0$ when the
displayed gap is at least $g$ for every $X\in K$. A self-consistent fixed point
is a point $X_*$ with $\Phi(X_*)=X_*$. Its fixed-point residual is
$\rho(X):=\|X-\Phi(X)\|_F$ whenever $\Phi(X)$ is defined. The map is not
asserted to be contractive merely because its gap is positive.

Let $n\ge2$ and let $r$ be an integer with $1\le r<n$. Use Hermitian
adjoints and matrices as in [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], trace as in
[[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]], and the Frobenius norm as in
[[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]. Write
$$\mathbb H_n:=\{A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}:A=A^*\}$$
for the real vector space of Hermitian matrices, with Frobenius inner product
$$\langle A,B\rangle_F:=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(A^*B)=\operatorname{tr}(AB).$$
The **rank-$r$ orthogonal projector domain** is
$$\mathcal P_r:=\{P\in\mathbb H_n:P^2=P,\ \operatorname{tr}P=r\}.$$
An element of $\mathcal P_r$ is an orthogonal projector; its range is the occupied
subspace. The statement that its range has dimension $r$ is justified by
[[lem-hermitian-idempotent-trace-equals-rank]]. A frame $Y\in\mathbb C^{n\times r}$
with $Y^*Y=I_r$ represents $P=YY^*$; replacing $Y$ by $YQ$ for a unitary
$Q\in\mathbb C^{r\times r}$ leaves $P$ unchanged.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$ of $F(X)$ with the eigenvalues in the given order. The strict gap prevents an eigenspace for one eigenvalue from straddling positions $r$ and $r+1$, so the sum of the first $r$ eigenspaces is the span of exactly the first $r$ basis vectors.

Changing the orthonormal basis within a repeated eigenspace below the gap leaves that entire eigenspace in the sum; changing one within a repeated eigenspace above the gap leaves that entire eigenspace out. Thus the selected subspace does not depend on the eigenbasis chosen in step 1.1. Its orthogonal projector is $P=\sum_{j=1}^r u_ju_j^*$, which satisfies $P=P^*$ and $P^2=P$ by orthonormality. By [F3], $\operatorname{tr}P=\sum_{a=1}^n P_{aa}=\sum_{a=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^r (u_j)_a\overline{(u_j)_a}=\sum_{j=1}^r\sum_{a=1}^n|(u_j)_a|^2=\sum_{j=1}^r1=r$, since each $u_j$ is a unit vector.

The operator in step 2.1 is independent of all allowed basis choices, lies in $\mathcal P_r$ by [L1], and is exactly the map specified by [F2]. Hence it is the unique rank-$r$ occupied spectral projector.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the

derivations.claim: The diagonal matrix $D_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,1,0,\ldots,0)$ with $r$ ones is Hermitian, satisfies $0\preceq D_0\preceq I_n$, and has trace $r$. Thus $D_0\in\mathcal D_r$, so the domain is nonempty.

Let $(D_k)$ be a Frobenius-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal D_r$. Each real and imaginary matrix entry is Cauchy because $| (D_k-D_\ell)_{ij}|\le\|D_k-D_\ell\|_F$. By [F2] the finitely many coordinates converge, defining a matrix $D$; conjugate symmetry passes to coordinate limits, so $D=D^*$.

For every fixed $x\in\mathbb C^n$, entrywise convergence gives $x^*D_kx\to x^*Dx$ and $x^*(I_n-D_k)x\to x^*(I_n-D)x$. Since both sequences are nonnegative, their limits are nonnegative, so $0\preceq D\preceq I_n$. Finite sums commute with coordinate limits, hence $\operatorname{tr}D=\lim_k\operatorname{tr}D_k=r$. Therefore $D\in\mathcal D_r$.

The finitely many entries converge, so the sum of their squared absolute errors tends to zero; thus $\|D_k-D\|_F\to0$. Every Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal D_r$ therefore converges there, proving completeness. Any ambient-convergent sequence in $\mathcal D_r$ is Cauchy, so the same limit argument shows its limit belongs to $\mathcal D_r$; this proves closedness.

If $D_1,D_2\in\mathcal D_r$ and $t\in[0,1]$, then $tD_1+(1-t)D_2$ is Hermitian; its quadratic form and that of $I_n-tD_1-(1-t)D_2$ are convex combinations of nonnegative quadratic forms, and its trace is $t\operatorname{tr}D_1+(1-t)\operatorname{tr}D_2=tr+(1-t)r=r$. Hence it lies in $\mathcal D_r$, proving convexity.

Let $H_0\in\mathbb H_n$ have eigenvalues with multiplicity
$\lambda_1(H_0)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(H_0)$ and gap
$g=\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)-\lambda_r(H_0)>0$. Put
$$c=\lambda_1(H_0),\qquad R=\frac{\lambda_r(H_0)+\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)}2-c,$$
and let $\Gamma=\{c+Re^{it}:0\le t\le2\pi\}$ be positively oriented.
For Hermitian $H$, write $\sigma(H)=\{\lambda_j(H):1\le j\le n\}$.
Then
$R\ge g/2$. For every Hermitian $H$ with $\|H-H_0\|_{op}\le g/4$, exactly
the $r$ lowest eigenvalues of $H$, counted with multiplicity, lie inside $\Gamma$;
the gap is at least $g/2$, and
$$\operatorname{dist}(\Gamma,\sigma(H))\ge g/4,\qquad \|(zI-H)^{-1}\|_{op}\le4/g\quad(z\in\Gamma).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $a\in\mathbb C$, let $R>0$, and let $f$ be holomorphic on the disc

$$D(a,R)=\{\zeta\in\mathbb C:|\zeta-a|<R\}.$$

If $0<r<R$, $|z-a|<r$, and $\gamma(t)=a+r\exp(it)$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$, then

$$f(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\gamma\frac{f(\zeta)}{\zeta-z}\,d\zeta.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open and star-shaped, let $p\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb C$ be continuous and holomorphic on $U\setminus\{p\}$. Then $f$ has a primitive on $U$, and for every closed rectifiable contour $\gamma$ in $U$,

$$\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz=0.$$

Let $\gamma=x+iy:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ be a rectifiable contour in the sense of [[def-complex-contours-reversal-concatenation-and-closedness]] and let $f=u+iv$ be continuous on its trace, with real and imaginary parts from [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. Define
$$\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz:=\int_a^b u(\gamma(t))\,dx(t)-\int_a^b v(\gamma(t))\,dy(t)+i\left(\int_a^b v(\gamma(t))\,dx(t)+\int_a^b u(\gamma(t))\,dy(t)\right),$$
where the four integrals are the real Riemann–Stieltjes integrals of [[def-riemann-stieltjes-sum-and-integral]]. Their existence is proved in [[thm-existence-of-complex-line-integrals-on-rectifiable-paths]]. On a singleton parameter interval the integral is $0$.

For continuous $f,g$ on the trace of a rectifiable contour $\gamma$ and $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$,
$$\int_\gamma(\alpha f+\beta g)\,dz=\alpha\int_\gamma f\,dz+\beta\int_\gamma g\,dz.$$

Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ be rectifiable and let $f$ be continuous on its trace. Then the complex line integral [[def-complex-line-integral-over-a-rectifiable-path]] and the absolute line integral [[def-absolute-line-integral-over-a-rectifiable-path]] both exist.

Let $U$ be an open subset of a real matrix space $\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ or of
a complex matrix space $\mathbb C^{m\times n}$ viewed as a real vector space,
and let $F:U\to W$ take values in a finite-dimensional real normed vector
space $(W,\|\,\cdot\,\|_W)$.
We say that $F$ is **real Fr\'echet differentiable** at $A\in U$ if there is a
real-linear map $L$ such that

$$\frac{\|F(A+H)-F(A)-L[H]\|_W}{\|H\|_F}\longrightarrow0\qquad(H\to0,\ H\ne0).$$

That map $L$ is the **real Fr\'echet derivative** of $F$ at $A$ and is denoted
$DF(A)$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

derivations.claim: Diagonalize $H=U\operatorname{diag}(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n)U^*$ with $\mu_1\le\cdots\le\mu_n$ by [F2]. Since [F1] places exactly $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r$ inside $\Gamma$, the resolvent is $U\operatorname{diag}((z-\mu_j)^{-1})U^*$ on the contour.

For a sufficiently small Hermitian perturbation $E$ with $H+E$ still in the ball, the inverse identity gives $R_{H+E}=R_H+R_HE R_{H+E}$. Subtracting $R_H+R_HE R_H$ yields $R_{H+E}-R_H-R_HE R_H=R_HE R_HE R_{H+E}.$ The identity follows by multiplying the two inverse equations for $zI-H$ and $zI-H-E$; all inverses exist by [F1].

Integrating each diagonal entry and using [F3], linearity in [F4], and the finite spectral expansion gives $\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma R_H(z)\,dz=U\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,1,0,\ldots,0)U^*=\Pi_r(H).$ Thus the contour expression represents the full occupied cluster projector, including repeated eigenvalues within that cluster.

For any matrix $A$ and matrix $X$ with columns $x_j$, the operator-norm definition gives $\|AX\|_F^2=\sum_j\|Ax_j\|_2^2\le\|A\|_{op}^2\|X\|_F^2$. Applying this also to adjoints gives the right-multiplication bound $\|XB\|_F\le\|X\|_F\|B\|_{op}$. Iterating these inequalities, then using [F1] and [F6], bounds the Frobenius norm of the right side by $(4/g)^3\|E\|_F^2$, uniformly for $z\in\Gamma$. The Riemann-sum triangle inequality in [F4] then bounds the integrated remainder by $\ell(\Gamma)(4/g)^3\|E\|_F^2/(2\pi)$. Dividing by $\|E\|_F$ makes this tend to zero, so the contour formula in step 2.1 is Frechet differentiable in the sense of [F5] and its derivative is the stated integral of $R_HE R_H$. Each difference quotient of the Hermitian-valued projector is Hermitian for real nonzero increments; since $\mathbb H_n$ is closed, the derivative is Hermitian-valued as well.

The same left/right multiplication inequalities give $\|R_H(z)ER_H(z)\|_F\le(4/g)^2\|E\|_F$ by [F1] and [F6]. Integrating over length $2\pi R$ yields $\|D\Pi_r(H)[E]\|_F\le R(4/g)^2\|E\|_F=16R\|E\|_F/g^2$. For nearby $H'$ in the ball, the resolvent identity and [F1] give uniformly on $\Gamma$ $\|R_{H'}-R_H\|_{op}\le(4/g)^2\|H'-H\|_{op}$. Subtracting the two derivative integrands gives $R_{H'}E(R_{H'}-R_H)+(R_{H'}-R_H)ER_H$. Each summand has Frobenius norm at most $(4/g)^3\|H'-H\|_F\|E\|_F$ by the left/right multiplication bounds and [F6], so their sum is at most twice this quantity. Integrating over length $2\pi R$ and dividing by $2\pi$ bounds the difference of derivative values by $2R(4/g)^3\|H'-H\|_F\|E\|_F$. The same estimate in operator norm for the derivative maps shows the derivative varies continuously in $H$. By the definition of a real Frechet $C^1$ map, this proves the claimed regularity and bound.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function. Recall that a metric takes nonnegative real values
([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]).

- $f$ is **Lipschitz** with **constant** $L$, where $L \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $L \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; L \, d_X(x,x') \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X .$$
  $f$ is *Lipschitz* if it is Lipschitz with some such constant.
- Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $0 < \alpha \le 1$ ([[def-rat-order]]). $f$ is
  **$\alpha$-Hölder** with **constant** $C$, where $C \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $C \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; C \, d_X(x,x')^{\alpha} \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X ,$$
  the power being the rational power of a nonnegative base
  ([[def-rational-power]]). $f$ is *$\alpha$-Hölder* if it is so with some such
  constant, and *Hölder* if it is $\alpha$-Hölder for some rational
  $\alpha \in (0,1]$.
- $f$ is a **contraction** with constant $q$ if it is Lipschitz with constant $q$
  and $0 \le q < 1$. The number $q$ is then called a **contraction constant** for
  $f$.

**The power $d_X(x,x')^{\alpha}$ is defined at every pair, including $x = x'$.**
The base $d_X(x,x')$ is a nonnegative real, and [[def-rational-power]] defines
$a^{\alpha}$ for every $a > 0$ and, by its supplementary clause, sets
$0^{\alpha} = 0$ for every rational $\alpha > 0$. Since $\alpha > 0$ is required
here, the displayed inequality at $x = x'$ reads $0 \le C \cdot 0$, which holds;
so no separate clause and no restriction to $x \ne x'$ is needed. Note that this
does not by itself explain the strict inequality $\alpha>0$: if one extended the
formula to $\alpha=0$ using the convention $0^0=1$ of [[def-integer-power]], the
equal-point inequality would still be the automatic $0\le C$. Globally, however,
that extension would reduce to the bounded-diameter condition
$d_Y(f(x),f(x'))\le C$, outside the standard Hölder range adopted here.

**Why the exponent is rational on this page and why it is at most $1$.** At this
point in the reading order only rational powers are available
([[def-rational-power]]), so $\alpha$ ranges over the rationals. The upper
bound $\alpha \le 1$ is the standard convention, and it is where the notion is
useful: the classical theory reserves the name for $\alpha \in (0,1]$, and
nothing in this library uses an exponent outside that range. No claim is made
here about what an exponent $\alpha > 1$ would do.

**Constants are not unique and are not part of the data.** If $f$ is Lipschitz
with constant $L$ it is Lipschitz with every constant $L' \ge L$, and likewise
for Hölder constants; the adjectives above are existential statements. A
*contraction*, by contrast, requires a constant strictly below $1$, and that is a
real restriction: exhibiting the constant is part of exhibiting a contraction, and
a map that shrinks every distance without admitting one uniform constant is not a
contraction here.

derivations.claim: By [F1], there is a unique $X_*$ with $\Phi(X_*)=X_*$. In the projector application, [L1] supplies the stated map wherever the strict gap hypothesis holds.

derivations.claim: Assume $PF=FP$. Then both $\operatorname{ran}P$ and $\operatorname{ran}(I-P)$ are invariant under $F$: if $x=Px$, then $P(Fx)=F(Px)=Fx$, and the analogous identity holds when $Px=0$. Relative to their orthogonal direct sum, $F$ is block diagonal and $F_s$ leaves the occupied block unchanged while adding $sI$ on the virtual block.

By [F2], the eigenvalues of $F_s$ are exactly those of $F_{occ}$ together with those of $F_{vir}$ shifted by $s$. If $\max\sigma(F_{occ})<\min\sigma(F_{vir})+s$, the lowest $r$ eigenvalues are precisely the occupied block and the gap is strict; [L1] gives $\Pi_r(F_s)=P$.

Conversely, if $\Pi_r(F_s)=P$, the isolated lowest-$r$ spectral projector commutes with $F_s$ by [F2]. Since $[s(I-P),P]=0$, this gives $[F,P]=0$, so the two restrictions in the statement are defined. The map's strict-gap domain in [F2] and uniqueness in [L1] require the largest occupied eigenvalue to be strictly smaller than the smallest shifted virtual eigenvalue; equality closes the $r$th gap, while reverse ordering selects a different spectral block. Hence the displayed ordering holds.

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

By [F1] and [F3], the common-contour formula and inverse identity give, pointwise on $\Gamma$, $R_{H_X}(z)-R_{H_Y}(z)=R_{H_X}(z)(H_X-H_Y)R_{H_Y}(z).$ Integrating entrywise and using [F5] yields $\Phi(X)-\Phi(Y)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma R_{H_X}(z)(H_X-H_Y)R_{H_Y}(z)\,dz.$

Each resolvent in step 1.1 has operator norm at most $4/g$ by [F2]. For matrices $A,X$, writing $X$ by columns gives $\|AX\|_F^2\le\|A\|_{op}^2\|X\|_F^2$; applying this to adjoints and using [F4] gives $\|AXB\|_F\le\|A\|_{op}\|X\|_F\|B\|_{op}$. Thus the Frobenius norm of the integrand in step 1.1 is at most $(4/g)^2\|F(X)-F(Y)\|_F$. The contour has length $2\pi R$, so [F5]'s line-integral triangle inequality gives $\|\Phi(X)-\Phi(Y)\|_F\le R(4/g)^2\|F(X)-F(Y)\|_F.$
Substituting $\|F(X)-F(Y)\|_F\le L_F\|X-Y\|_F$ into step 2.1 gives the stated factor $q=16RL_F/g^2$. If $q<1$ and $\Phi(K)\subseteq K$, this is exactly the contraction condition on $K$.

Let $S=S^*\succ0$ be an $n\times n$ finite-basis overlap matrix and supply its
Cholesky factor $L$ with $S=LL^*$, $L$ invertible
([[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]],
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]).
If $h_0=h_0^*$ is the coefficient-basis one-body matrix, set
$h=L^{-1}h_0L^{-*}$, where $L^{-*}=(L^*)^{-1}$; this is the Cholesky
whitening whose generalized Ritz quotient is preserved by
[[prop-positive-definite-overlap-whitening-preserves-generalized-ritz-pencil]].
For coefficient vectors use $y=L^*c$; the interaction map and chosen
exchange-correlation functional below are supplied in these orthonormal
coordinates. Fix $1\le r<n$ and the
projector domain $\mathcal P_r$ of [[def-rank-r-orthogonal-projector-domain]].

Supply a Hermitian matrix $h$, a real-linear self-adjoint map
$G:\mathbb H_n\to\mathbb H_n$ for the Frobenius inner product, and a real-valued
$C^2$ functional $E_{xc}$ on an open neighborhood of $\mathcal P_r$. Define
$$E(P):=\operatorname{tr}(hP)+\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(P G(P))+E_{xc}(P),\qquad F(P):=h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P).$$
Here $F(P)$ is the Hermitian Frobenius-gradient formula justified by
[[prop-finite-projector-energy-reality-and-gradient]].

The finite-basis Hartree–Fock model is the special case $E_{xc}=0$ with a
supplied symmetry-compatible Coulomb/exchange tensor defining $G$. A
Kohn–Sham-like model supplies its density map and chosen differentiable
exchange-correlation functional. These are finite-dimensional mathematical
models; this definition makes no assertion that the selected functional is an
exact continuum physical energy.

Let $U$ be an open subset of a real matrix space $\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ or of
a complex matrix space $\mathbb C^{m\times n}$ viewed as a real vector space,
and let $F:U\to W$ take values in a finite-dimensional real normed vector
space $(W,\|\,\cdot\,\|_W)$.
We say that $F$ is **real Fr\'echet differentiable** at $A\in U$ if there is a
real-linear map $L$ such that

$$\frac{\|F(A+H)-F(A)-L[H]\|_W}{\|H\|_F}\longrightarrow0\qquad(H\to0,\ H\ne0).$$

That map $L$ is the **real Fr\'echet derivative** of $F$ at $A$ and is denoted
$DF(A)$.

Let $H_0\in\mathbb H_n$ have an occupied/unoccupied gap
$g=\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)-\lambda_r(H_0)>0$, and let $c,R,\Gamma$ be the circle
from [[lem-spectral-gap-persistence-and-uniform-resolvent-bound]]. For Hermitian
$H$ in the open operator-norm ball $\|H-H_0\|_{op}<g/4$, let $\Pi_r(H)$ be its
projector onto the $r$ lowest eigenvalues. Then $H\mapsto\Pi_r(H)$ is real
Frechet $C^1$ in the Frobenius norm and
$$D\Pi_r(H)[E]=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma (zI-H)^{-1}E(zI-H)^{-1}\,dz$$
for each Hermitian direction $E$. With $\ell(\Gamma)=2\pi R$,
$$\|D\Pi_r(H)[E]\|_F\le\frac{16R}{g^2}\|E\|_F.$$
This is a block/cluster statement: no gap between eigenvalues inside either
cluster is required.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $H_0\in\mathbb H_n$ have eigenvalues with multiplicity
$\lambda_1(H_0)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(H_0)$ and gap
$g=\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)-\lambda_r(H_0)>0$. Put
$$c=\lambda_1(H_0),\qquad R=\frac{\lambda_r(H_0)+\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)}2-c,$$
and let $\Gamma=\{c+Re^{it}:0\le t\le2\pi\}$ be positively oriented.
For Hermitian $H$, write $\sigma(H)=\{\lambda_j(H):1\le j\le n\}$.
Then
$R\ge g/2$. For every Hermitian $H$ with $\|H-H_0\|_{op}\le g/4$, exactly
the $r$ lowest eigenvalues of $H$, counted with multiplicity, lie inside $\Gamma$;
the gap is at least $g/2$, and
$$\operatorname{dist}(\Gamma,\sigma(H))\ge g/4,\qquad \|(zI-H)^{-1}\|_{op}\le4/g\quad(z\in\Gamma).$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

For every $X\in U$ at which the response map of
[[def-self-consistent-projector-response-map]] has a strict $r$th gap,
$\Phi(X)$ is a uniquely defined member of $\mathcal P_r$. Degeneracies among
the first $r$ eigenvalues or among the remaining eigenvalues do not affect it.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

For every linear $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ there is a unique matrix $A=(a_{ij})_{i<n,j<m}$ such that $(Lh)_i=\sum_{j<m}a_{ij}h_j$. Moreover there is $K\ge0$ with $\|Lh\|_2\le K\|h\|_2$ for every $h$.

derivations.claim: Identify the real Hermitian space with its finite coordinate space. The constant map $P\mapsto h$ has derivative zero. The real-linear map $G$ is continuous by [F9] and has derivative $G$ at every point because $G(P+H)-G(P)-G(H)=0$. By [F7] the first partials of $E_{xc}$ are $C^1$: each has first partials given by the continuous second partials of $E_{xc}$, and [F8] makes each component of $\nabla E_{xc}$ total differentiable with continuous derivative. Thus all three summands in [F1] are $C^1$, so $F$ is $C^1$ and Hermitian-valued on the model's open domain.

Continuity of $F$ gives a neighborhood $V$ of $P_0$ on which $\|F(P)-F(P_0)\|_F<g/4$, where $g$ is the gap at $P_0$. By [F6], the operator-norm difference is also less than $g/4$. By [F5] this image lies in a common gap-preserving ball; [F3] makes its block projector $C^1$ there and [L1] identifies it with the defined occupied projector. By [F4], $\Phi=\Pi_r\circ F$ is $C^1$ on $V$.

Let $n\ge2$, $1\le r<n$, and use the real Hermitian matrix space $\mathbb H_n$
and projector set $\mathcal P_r$ of
[[def-rank-r-orthogonal-projector-domain]]. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb H_n$ be open
and let $F:U\to\mathbb H_n$ be a specified map. For a Hermitian matrix $H$,
write its eigenvalues with multiplicity in ascending order as
$$\lambda_1(H)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(H).$$
Write $\sigma(H):=\{\lambda_j(H):1\le j\le n\}$ for its finite spectrum,
with multiplicity omitted in this set notation.
For any Hermitian $H$ with $\lambda_r(H)<\lambda_{r+1}(H)$, write $\Pi_r(H)$
for the orthogonal projector onto the sum of eigenspaces belonging to its $r$
lowest eigenvalues. At a point $X\in U$ where
$$\lambda_r(F(X))<\lambda_{r+1}(F(X)),$$
define $\Phi(X):=\Pi_r(F(X))$. The strict gap separates the occupied cluster
from the unoccupied cluster; eigenvalue multiplicities within either cluster
are allowed. The construction's well-definedness as a unique member of
$\mathcal P_r$ is proved in [[lem-gapped-projector-map-well-defined]].

A set $K\subseteq U$ has a **uniform occupied/unoccupied gap** $g>0$ when the
displayed gap is at least $g$ for every $X\in K$. A self-consistent fixed point
is a point $X_*$ with $\Phi(X_*)=X_*$. Its fixed-point residual is
$\rho(X):=\|X-\Phi(X)\|_F$ whenever $\Phi(X)$ is defined. The map is not
asserted to be contractive merely because its gap is positive.

For every $X\in U$ at which the response map of
[[def-self-consistent-projector-response-map]] has a strict $r$th gap,
$\Phi(X)$ is a uniquely defined member of $\mathcal P_r$. Degeneracies among
the first $r$ eigenvalues or among the remaining eigenvalues do not affect it.

Let $H_0\in\mathbb H_n$ have an occupied/unoccupied gap
$g=\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)-\lambda_r(H_0)>0$, and let $c,R,\Gamma$ be the circle
from [[lem-spectral-gap-persistence-and-uniform-resolvent-bound]]. For Hermitian
$H$ in the open operator-norm ball $\|H-H_0\|_{op}<g/4$, let $\Pi_r(H)$ be its
projector onto the $r$ lowest eigenvalues. Then $H\mapsto\Pi_r(H)$ is real
Frechet $C^1$ in the Frobenius norm and
$$D\Pi_r(H)[E]=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma (zI-H)^{-1}E(zI-H)^{-1}\,dz$$
for each Hermitian direction $E$. With $\ell(\Gamma)=2\pi R$,
$$\|D\Pi_r(H)[E]\|_F\le\frac{16R}{g^2}\|E\|_F.$$
This is a block/cluster statement: no gap between eigenvalues inside either
cluster is required.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is
**continuously differentiable**, or of class $C^1$, when it is totally
differentiable at every point of $U$ and the entries of its derivative matrix
are continuous functions on $U$.

For an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $a\in U$, a **local inverse of $f$ at
$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

For $n\ge2$ and $1\le r<n$, the set $\mathcal D_r$ of
[[def-admissible-hermitian-density-domain]] is nonempty, closed, and convex in
$\mathbb H_n$, and complete in the Frobenius metric.

derivations.claim: For $D,E\in K$, convexity puts the segment $Z(t)=E+t(D-E)$ in $K$ for $t\in[0,1]$. By [F1] and [L1], $\Phi$ is defined along this segment; [F2] gives its local $C^1$ regularity. For an increment $H$, $T_\alpha(D+H)-T_\alpha(D)=(1-\alpha)H+\alpha(\Phi(D+H)-\Phi(D))$, so Frechet differentiability of $\Phi$ gives $DT_\alpha(D)=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha D\Phi(D)$. The chain rule [F5] on the segment gives $\frac d{dt}T_\alpha(Z(t))=DT_\alpha(Z(t))[D-E]$. Its norm is at most $q\|D-E\|_F$ by the assumed induced-norm bound; continuity follows from [F2] and [F6].
Apply [F3] on $[0,1]$ to this path. It yields $\|T_\alpha(D)-T_\alpha(E)\|_F\le q\|D-E\|_F$, so $T_\alpha$ is a contraction on $K$.

Any Frobenius-Cauchy sequence in $K$ is Cauchy in $\mathcal D_r$, so [F7] gives a limit in $\mathcal D_r$; closedness of $K$ places that limit in $K$. Thus $K$ is complete. Invariance and step 2.1 allow [F4] to give a unique fixed point and convergence of all iterates from $K$.

Let $(K,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space and let $\Phi:K\to K$ be a
contraction with constant $0\le q<1$. In the SCF application, $K$ is a
complete invariant subset of the response-map domain from
[[def-self-consistent-projector-response-map]], with $d(X,Y)=\|X-Y\|_F$.
Then $\Phi$ has a unique fixed point $X_*$ and exact iterates
$X_{k+1}=\Phi(X_k)$ satisfy
$$d(X_k,X_*)\le q^k d(X_0,X_*).$$
For every $X\in K$,
$$d(X,X_*)\le\frac{d(X,\Phi(X))}{1-q}.$$
If computed updates $X_{k+1}\in K$ obey
$d(X_{k+1},\Phi(X_k))\le\eta_k$, then
$$e_{k+1}\le q e_k+\eta_k,\qquad e_k\le q^k e_0+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}q^{k-1-j}\eta_j,$$
where $e_k=d(X_k,X_*)$ and $X_0$ is the supplied initial point.
Use the convention $q^0=1$, including when $q=0$.

Input: a complete invariant set $K$ and a gapped response map $\Phi:K\to K$
with a certified contraction factor $q<1$; an initial projector $P_0\in K$;
a certified initial error bound $E_0\ge\|P_0-P_*\|_F$ for the unique fixed
point $P_*$; residual tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$; finite update budget
$N\in\mathbb N_0$; memory $m\ge1$; coefficient cap $C\ge1$; and an eigensolver
which, on success at $X$, returns $\widetilde\Phi(X)\in K$ and a certified
$\eta(X)\ge0$ with $\|\widetilde\Phi(X)-\Phi(X)\|_F\le\eta(X)$. The solver
returns a separate failure status if it cannot certify the gap or this error.

For $k=0,\ldots,N$:

1. If no certified response evaluation is cached for $P_k$, evaluate the finite-basis matrix $F(P_k)$ and its occupied projector solver. If the gap fails, return $\texttt{gap-loss}$; if the eigensolver cannot certify its output/error, return $\texttt{eigensolve-failure}$. Cache the certified evaluation $(F(P_k),\widetilde\Phi(P_k),\eta(P_k))$ at exactly $P_k$. Whether this evaluation is newly obtained or already cached, use that current evaluation, check the certified baseline output belongs to $K$ (return $\texttt{invariance-certificate-failure}$ if not), and retain the current pair $(P_k,F(P_k))$ for this proposal step. Set $\bar\rho_k=\|P_k-\widetilde\Phi(P_k)\|_F+\eta(P_k)$. If $\bar\rho_k\le\varepsilon$, return $\texttt{residual-tolerance-met}$ with error bound $\bar\rho_k/(1-q)$.
2. If $k=N$, return $\texttt{iteration-budget-exhausted}$ with current bound $E_k$.
3. Call [[alg-capped-diis-projector-proposal]] with the up-to-$m-1$ preceding stored pairs and the current pair $(P_k,F(P_k))$. For a candidate $Y$, certify $Y\in K$, the gap at $Y$, and one eigensolver evaluation $\widetilde\Phi(Y)$ with error $\eta(Y)$. Accept $Y$ only if all certificates succeed and
$$\frac{\|Y-\widetilde\Phi(Y)\|_F+\eta(Y)}{1-q}\le qE_k.$$
If accepted, set $P_{k+1}=Y$ and $E_{k+1}=qE_k$.
4. If step 3 does not accept a candidate for any reason, use the certified baseline update from step 1. In particular this includes a singular/uncertified least-squares solve, coefficient-cap or affine-constraint failure, failed candidate $K$-membership, failed candidate gap, failed candidate eigensolver output/error certificate, or failed candidate fixed-point residual test. In this fallback branch, set $P_{k+1}=\widetilde\Phi(P_k)$ and $E_{k+1}=qE_k+\eta(P_k)$. If the baseline certificate or $K$-membership check fails, return its distinct gap, eigensolver, or invariance-certificate failure status.
5. Append the current pair $(P_k,F(P_k))$ to the preceding-iterate history, retaining at most the newest $m-1$ preceding pairs. If step 3 accepted $Y$, cache its certified evaluation $(F(Y),\widetilde\Phi(Y),\eta(Y))$ as the next iteration's current evaluation; if the baseline branch was used, evaluate its new iterate when the next loop begins. Input: $n,r$, a response map $F:U\to\mathbb H_n$ and its occupied projector
map $\Phi$ from [[def-self-consistent-projector-response-map]], an initial
projector $P_0\in\mathcal P_r$, a required gap $g_{min}>0$, residual tolerance
$\varepsilon\ge0$, and update budget $N\in\mathbb N_0$. Assume each iterate
belongs to a declared invariant input set $K\subseteq U$. Use the Frobenius
metric and the fixed-point interface of [[alg-fixed-point-iteration]].

For $k=0,1,\ldots,N$:

1. Compute the ordered eigenvalues of $F(P_k)$. If the eigensolver fails with no certified ordered spectrum, return $(P_k,\texttt{eigensolve-failure},\varnothing,k)$. If $\lambda_{r+1}(F(P_k))-\lambda_r(F(P_k))<g_{min}$, return $(P_k,\texttt{gap-loss},\varnothing,k)$.

3. If $k=N$, return $(P_k,\texttt{iteration-budget-exhausted},\rho_k,k)$. Otherwise set $P_{k+1}=P_{k+1}^{raw}$ and continue.

Input: $D_0\in\mathcal D_r$ from
[[def-admissible-hermitian-density-domain]], a response map $\Phi$ defined at
each required iterate, a fixed mixing parameter $\alpha\in[0,1]$, a fixed-point
residual tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$, and a finite update budget
$N\in\mathbb N_0$. For $k=0,\ldots,N$, first certify that the occupied gap at
$D_k$ is positive. If the eigensolver fails, return
$(D_k,\texttt{eigensolve-failure},\varnothing,k)$; if the gap is absent, return
$(D_k,\texttt{gap-loss},\varnothing,k)$. Otherwise evaluate $\Phi(D_k)$ and
$$r_k=\|D_k-((1-\alpha)D_k+\alpha\Phi(D_k))\|_F.$$
If $r_k\le\varepsilon$, return
$(D_k,\texttt{residual-tolerance-met},r_k,k)$. If $k=N$, return
$(D_k,\texttt{iteration-budget-exhausted},r_k,k)$. Otherwise update
$$D_{k+1}=(1-\alpha)D_k+\alpha\Phi(D_k)$$
and continue.

By [[lem-density-mixing-preserves-domain-but-not-projectors]], each successful
update stays in $\mathcal D_r$; it need not be idempotent. This algorithm is the
fixed-point iteration of [[alg-fixed-point-iteration]] applied to the relaxed
map. It makes no convergence claim unless the derivative-bound and invariance
hypotheses in [[thm-density-mixing-contracts-under-jacobian-certificate]] are
verified. If $\alpha=0$, then the relaxed residual is identically zero and the
update does not move; that stop status alone says nothing about the unmixed
response residual.

Let $\mathcal H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, with square-summability as in [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Define the diagonal operator $A$ by
$$D(A)=\left\{u\in\mathcal H:\sum_{k\ge1} k^4|u_k|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad (Au)_k=-k^2u_k.$$
Let $g\in\mathcal H$ be the fixed sequence $g_k=1/k$ for odd $k$ and $g_k=0$ for even $k$; membership follows from [[thm-p-series-real-exponents]] with exponent $2$. The split evolution is $u'=Au+g$. For $t\ge0$, define the exact diagonal subflow $E_tu=(e^{-k^2t}u_k)_{k\ge1}$ and the exact translation subflow $B_tu=u+tg$. By [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]] and [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $0<e^{-k^2t}\le1$, so each $E_t$ maps $\mathcal H$ to itself; each $B_t$ does so because $g\in\mathcal H$. The associated Strang modal step is
$$S_h=E_{h/2}\circ B_h\circ E_{h/2},\qquad h>0,$$
where the rightmost map is applied first. Each coordinate of $E_t$ solves $u_k'=-k^2u_k$, and each coordinate of $B_t$ solves $u_k'=g_k$. This is a precisely defined sequence-space model; it records one Dirichlet sine-mode boundary mismatch and makes no general convergence assertion for unbounded PDE operators.

Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Coordinatewise, [F2] gives $e^{-k^2(t+s)}=e^{-k^2t}e^{-k^2s}$ and $E_0u=u$, so $E_{t+s}=E_tE_s$. If $t\ge0$, [F3] gives $0<e^{-k^2t}\le1$; hence $\sum_k|(E_tu)_k|^2\le\sum_k|u_k|^2$, proving that $E_t$ maps $\mathcal H$ to itself and is a contraction.

For every $x\ge0$, [F4] applied to $s\mapsto e^{-s}$ on $[0,x]$ gives $0\le1-e^{-x}\le x$: the difference is $xe^{-\xi}$ for some $\xi\in[0,x]$, and [F3] bounds $e^{-\xi}$ by $1$. For $u\in D(A)$, the $k$th coordinate of $(E_tu-u)/t$ tends to $-k^2u_k$ by the chain rule and exponential derivative in [F4]. Its difference from that limit has absolute value at most $2k^2|u_k|$, by the same bound. The squared tail of these differences is therefore at most $4\sum_{k>K}k^4|u_k|^2$, which tends to zero; on every finite head the coordinate limits give norm convergence. Hence the right limit exists in $\mathcal H$ and equals $Au$.

Fix $u\in\mathcal H$ and $\varepsilon>0$. By convergence of its square sum, choose $K$ so that $\sum_{k>K}|u_k|^2<\varepsilon^2/4$. The squared norm of the tail of $E_tu-u$ is at most this tail because $|e^{-k^2t}-1|\le1$ by [F3]; for the finitely many indices $k\le K$, continuity of the exponential at zero from [F4] makes their squared sum less than $\varepsilon^2/4$ for all sufficiently small $t>0$. Thus $\|E_tu-u\|_2<\varepsilon$, proving strong continuity at zero.

Conversely, suppose $(E_tu-u)/t$ converges in $\mathcal H$ to $v$. For each $k$, coordinate evaluation is continuous since $|w_k|\le\|w\|_2$; therefore its limit is $v_k=-k^2u_k$, using [F4]. Since $v\in\mathcal H$, $\sum_k k^4|u_k|^2=\sum_k|v_k|^2<\infty$, so $u\in D(A)$. Together with step 1.2 this identifies the generator domain and its value.

For the additive ODE partition [[def-additive-ode-and-partition]], take a current state $y\in U$, a step $h>0$, a closed ball $\overline B(c,R)\subset U$ centered at $c:=y+h a(y)$, bounds $M_b,L_b\ge0$ for $\|b\|_2$ and its Lipschitz constant on that ball, a tolerance $\tau\ge0$, and a solve routine that returns either a candidate $z\in\overline B(c,R)$ or a failure status. The procedure is:

1. If the solve routine is unavailable, return `solver-unavailable`.
2. If $hM_b>R$ or $hL_b\ge1$, return `branch-not-certified` without claiming a root.
3. Call the solve routine on $z=c+h b(z)$.
4. If it returns failure, return that failure status. If it returns $z\notin\overline B(c,R)$, return `out-of-branch-ball`.
5. Compute the update residual $r:=z-c-hb(z)$ in the state units of [[def-implicit-residual-and-algebraic-error-units]]. If $\|r\|_2>\tau$, return `residual-too-large` with $z$ and $r$; otherwise return `success` with $z$ and $r$.

When the routine returns an exact root, $r=0$ and $z$ is the IMEX Euler step $Y=y+h a(y)+h b(Y)$. A success status records only the requested residual check; the forward error conclusion is supplied separately by the residual theorem. This procedure uses one explicit evaluation of $a$ and one implicit solve.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

$(X,d)$ is **complete** if every Cauchy sequence in $(X,d)$
([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]) converges to a point of $X$
([[def-metric-convergence]]).

A subset $A \subseteq X$ is called **complete** when the metric subspace
$(A, d_A)$ is complete ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]); as always, the
metric is part of the data, and $d_A$ is the restriction of $d$ to $A \times A$.

**The limit is unique when it exists**, since limits in a metric space are unique
([[lem-metric-limits-unique]]), so a complete space assigns to each of its Cauchy
sequences one point and not a set of points.

**Completeness is a property of the pair $(X,d)$, not of $X$ and not of the
topology of $d$.** Both quantifiers in the definition are about the metric: the
Cauchy condition is stated with distances, and so is convergence. Two metrics on
the same set can have the same open sets while exactly one of them is complete,
which is the content of [[fs-completeness-is-a-topological-property]] and its
witness. Read the word *complete* as an abbreviation for *complete with respect
to this metric*, always.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function. Recall that a metric takes nonnegative real values
([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]).

- $f$ is **Lipschitz** with **constant** $L$, where $L \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $L \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; L \, d_X(x,x') \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X .$$
  $f$ is *Lipschitz* if it is Lipschitz with some such constant.
- Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $0 < \alpha \le 1$ ([[def-rat-order]]). $f$ is
  **$\alpha$-Hölder** with **constant** $C$, where $C \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $C \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; C \, d_X(x,x')^{\alpha} \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X ,$$
  the power being the rational power of a nonnegative base
  ([[def-rational-power]]). $f$ is *$\alpha$-Hölder* if it is so with some such
  constant, and *Hölder* if it is $\alpha$-Hölder for some rational
  $\alpha \in (0,1]$.
- $f$ is a **contraction** with constant $q$ if it is Lipschitz with constant $q$
  and $0 \le q < 1$. The number $q$ is then called a **contraction constant** for
  $f$.

**The power $d_X(x,x')^{\alpha}$ is defined at every pair, including $x = x'$.**
The base $d_X(x,x')$ is a nonnegative real, and [[def-rational-power]] defines
$a^{\alpha}$ for every $a > 0$ and, by its supplementary clause, sets
$0^{\alpha} = 0$ for every rational $\alpha > 0$. Since $\alpha > 0$ is required
here, the displayed inequality at $x = x'$ reads $0 \le C \cdot 0$, which holds;
so no separate clause and no restriction to $x \ne x'$ is needed. Note that this
does not by itself explain the strict inequality $\alpha>0$: if one extended the
formula to $\alpha=0$ using the convention $0^0=1$ of [[def-integer-power]], the
equal-point inequality would still be the automatic $0\le C$. Globally, however,
that extension would reduce to the bounded-diameter condition
$d_Y(f(x),f(x'))\le C$, outside the standard Hölder range adopted here.

**Why the exponent is rational on this page and why it is at most $1$.** At this
point in the reading order only rational powers are available
([[def-rational-power]]), so $\alpha$ ranges over the rationals. The upper
bound $\alpha \le 1$ is the standard convention, and it is where the notion is
useful: the classical theory reserves the name for $\alpha \in (0,1]$, and
nothing in this library uses an exponent outside that range. No claim is made
here about what an exponent $\alpha > 1$ would do.

**Constants are not unique and are not part of the data.** If $f$ is Lipschitz
with constant $L$ it is Lipschitz with every constant $L' \ge L$, and likewise
for Hölder constants; the adjectives above are existential statements. A
*contraction*, by contrast, requires a constant strictly below $1$, and that is a
real restriction: exhibiting the constant is part of exhibiting a contraction, and
a map that shrinks every distance without admitting one uniform constant is not a
contraction here.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

derivations.claim: The ball is nonempty because it contains $c$. If $(z_n)$ is Cauchy in the ball, it is Cauchy in $\mathbb R^d$, so [F2] gives a limit $z\in\mathbb R^d$. By [F4], $\|z-c\|_2\le\|z-z_n\|_2+\|z_n-c\|_2\le\|z-z_n\|_2+R$; letting $n\to\infty$ gives $\|z-c\|_2\le R$, so $z$ remains in the ball. Thus the ball is a nonempty complete metric space by [F3].

Define $T(z):=c+h b(z)$. For every $z$ in the ball, $\|T(z)-c\|_2=h\|b(z)\|_2\le hM\le R$, so $T$ maps the ball into itself; for $z,w$ in the ball, $\|T(z)-T(w)\|_2\le hL\|z-w\|_2$, and $hL<1$ makes $T$ a contraction as in [F5].
Applying [F6] to the complete ball and the contraction from step 1.2 gives a unique fixed point $Y$, which is exactly the unique solution of $Y=c+hb(Y)$ in the ball.

For any $\widetilde Y$ in the ball, [F4] and step 2.1 give $\|\widetilde Y-Y\|_2\le\|\widetilde Y-T(\widetilde Y)\|_2+\|T(\widetilde Y)-T(Y)\|_2\le\|\widetilde Y-c-hb(\widetilde Y)\|_2+hL\|\widetilde Y-Y\|_2$. Since $1-hL>0$, rearranging proves the residual bound.
