Let $a,b:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^3$ fields on an open set, and restrict attention to points and time intervals for which the unique local solutions of $x'=a(x)$ and $x'=b(x)$ remain in $U$. Denote their exact solution maps by $\Phi_a^t$ and $\Phi_b^t$. The **Lie split map** applies $a$ and then $b$:
$$L_h:=\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^h.$$
The **Strang split map** applies half of $a$, then $b$, then half of $a$:
$$S_h:=\Phi_a^{h/2}\circ\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^{h/2}.$$
Define the vector-field Lie bracket convention
$$[a,b](y):=Db(y)a(y)-Da(y)b(y).$$
This definition is finite-dimensional. It asserts neither that an unbounded operator has a common invariant domain nor that its commutators are bounded.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.
Let $k\ge2$. If $f\in C^k(U)$ for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, then every iterated derivative of $f$ of order $k$ is unchanged by any permutation of its coordinate differentiations.

derivations.claim: For a $C^3$ field $c$ and a smooth scalar coordinate function $q(y)=y_j$, define $L_cq:=Dq\,c$. By [F2], differentiating $q(\Phi_c^t(y))$ successively in $t$ gives $L_cq$, $L_c^2q$, and $L_c^3q$, evaluated along the flow. Three uses of [F3] give the expansion through degree two with integral remainder $\frac12\int_0^h(h-s)^2(L_c^3q)(\Phi_c^s(y))\,ds$; [A1] bounds this remainder uniformly by $C h^3$ and continuity at $s=0$ gives cubic coefficient $\frac16L_c^3q(y)$ with pointwise remainder $o(h^3)$. The same reasoning applies successively to the finite flow compositions.

For a map $M$, define its pullback by $M^*q:=q\circ M$, and for a vector field $c$ put $L_cq:=Dq\,c$. Set $X=L_a$ and $Y=L_b$. The pullback of a composition reverses composition order, so [F1] and step 1.1 give, through degree two, $L_h^*q=q+h(X+Y)q+h^2\left(\frac12X^2+XY+\frac12Y^2\right)q+O(h^3).$ The exact total-flow pullback is $q+h(X+Y)q+\frac12h^2(X+Y)^2q+O(h^3)$. Subtracting leaves $\frac12h^2(XY-YX)q+O(h^3)$.

For any $C^2$ scalar $q$, the chain rule gives $[L_a,L_b]q=D^2q(a,b)+Dq\,Db\,a-D^2q(b,a)-Dq\,Da\,b=Dq\,(Db\,a-Da\,b),$ where [F4] cancels the Hessian terms. Thus $[X,Y]q=L_{[a,b]}q$. Applying this to each coordinate function in step 2.1 gives the stated Lie map expansion.

Pullback reversal and [F1] give $S_h^*=\Phi_a^{h/2*}\Phi_b^{h*}\Phi_a^{h/2*}$. Expanding its three factors by step 1.1 gives the cubic part $\frac16X^3+\frac16Y^3+\frac18X^2Y+\frac14XYX+\frac18YX^2+\frac14XY^2+\frac14Y^2X.$ Multiplying the three degree-three Taylor polynomials gives these coefficients: the $X^3$ term is $1/48+1/48+1/16+1/16=1/6$, and the $Y^3$ term is $1/6$. The mixed coefficients are $X^2Y:(1/8)(1)=1/8$, $XYX:(1/2)(1)(1/2)=1/4$, $YX^2:(1)(1/8)=1/8$, $XY^2:(1/2)(1/2)=1/4$, and $Y^2X:(1/2)(1/2)=1/4$; $YXY$ is absent because neither outer factor contains $Y$. The exact total-flow cubic part is $\frac16(X+Y)^3$, whose eight words each have coefficient $1/6$. Degrees zero through two agree, so subtraction gives $-\frac1{24}(X^2Y-2XYX+YX^2)-\frac1{12}(2YXY-Y^2X-XY^2)+o(h^3).$

Step 3.1 also applies with the second field equal to $[a,b]$, which is $C^2$ under the $C^3$ hypotheses. Hence $[X,[X,Y]]=L_{[a,[a,b]]}$ and $[Y,[X,Y]]=L_{[b,[a,b]]}$. Applying step 3.2 to each coordinate yields the stated Strang coefficient and pointwise $o(h^3)$ remainder. The uniform $O(h^3)$ defect follows already from the uniform degree-two remainder in step 1.1 and the equality of all coefficients through degree two.

Let $\mathcal H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, with square-summability as in [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Define the diagonal operator $A$ by
$$D(A)=\left\{u\in\mathcal H:\sum_{k\ge1} k^4|u_k|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad (Au)_k=-k^2u_k.$$
Let $g\in\mathcal H$ be the fixed sequence $g_k=1/k$ for odd $k$ and $g_k=0$ for even $k$; membership follows from [[thm-p-series-real-exponents]] with exponent $2$. The split evolution is $u'=Au+g$. For $t\ge0$, define the exact diagonal subflow $E_tu=(e^{-k^2t}u_k)_{k\ge1}$ and the exact translation subflow $B_tu=u+tg$. By [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]] and [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $0<e^{-k^2t}\le1$, so each $E_t$ maps $\mathcal H$ to itself; each $B_t$ does so because $g\in\mathcal H$. The associated Strang modal step is
$$S_h=E_{h/2}\circ B_h\circ E_{h/2},\qquad h>0,$$
where the rightmost map is applied first. Each coordinate of $E_t$ solves $u_k'=-k^2u_k$, and each coordinate of $B_t$ solves $u_k'=g_k$. This is a precisely defined sequence-space model; it records one Dirichlet sine-mode boundary mismatch and makes no general convergence assertion for unbounded PDE operators.

Let $\mathcal H$, $A$, and $E_t$ be as in [[def-dirichlet-sine-mode-heat-splitting-model]]. The maps $E_t$ for $t\ge0$ satisfy $E_0=I$ and $E_{t+s}=E_tE_s$, are contractions in $\ell^2$, and are strongly continuous at $t=0$. Define the generator domain to consist of those $u\in\mathcal H$ for which the right limit
$$\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{E_tu-u}{t}$$
exists in $\mathcal H$. This domain is exactly $D(A)=\{u:\sum_{k\ge1}k^4|u_k|^2<\infty\}$, and the limit equals $Au=(-k^2u_k)_{k\ge1}$.

For every real $p$,
$$\sum_{k\ge1}\frac1{k^p}\text{ converges}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p>1.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $\gamma$ be the unique smallest positive zero of cosine supplied by [[thm-cosine-has-a-smallest-positive-zero]]. Define
$$\pi:=2\gamma.$$

Thus $\pi>0$ and $\pi/2=\gamma$.

derivations.claim: By [F4], an antiderivative of $\sin(kx)$ is $-\cos(kx)/k$; applying [F3] and [F5] gives $\widehat f_k=\frac2\pi\cdot\frac\pi4\cdot\frac{1-(-1)^k}{k}=\frac{1-(-1)^k}{2k}.$ This is $1/k$ for odd $k$ and $0$ for even $k$, exactly the sequence in [F1].
The squared coefficients sum to $\sum_{j\ge0}(2j+1)^{-2}\le\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-2}<\infty$ by [F2], so $g\in\mathcal H$.
The generator-domain sum is $\sum_{k\ge1}k^4|g_k|^2=\sum_{j\ge0}(2j+1)^2$, whose partial sums are at least the number of terms and hence unbounded. Therefore $g\notin D(A)$ by [F1].

By [F6], the constant forcing $f=\pi/4$ is nonzero. By [F5], every sine mode $\sin(kx)$ vanishes at both $x=0$ and $x=\pi$. Hence the forcing is incompatible with the homogeneous Dirichlet endpoint values. This modal observation supplies no general PDE error theorem.

For the additive ODE partition [[def-additive-ode-and-partition]], take a current state $y\in U$, a step $h>0$, a closed ball $\overline B(c,R)\subset U$ centered at $c:=y+h a(y)$, bounds $M_b,L_b\ge0$ for $\|b\|_2$ and its Lipschitz constant on that ball, a tolerance $\tau\ge0$, and a solve routine that returns either a candidate $z\in\overline B(c,R)$ or a failure status. The procedure is:

1. If the solve routine is unavailable, return `solver-unavailable`.
2. If $hM_b>R$ or $hL_b\ge1$, return `branch-not-certified` without claiming a root.
3. Call the solve routine on $z=c+h b(z)$.
4. If it returns failure, return that failure status. If it returns $z\notin\overline B(c,R)$, return `out-of-branch-ball`.
5. Compute the update residual $r:=z-c-hb(z)$ in the state units of [[def-implicit-residual-and-algebraic-error-units]]. If $\|r\|_2>\tau$, return `residual-too-large` with $z$ and $r$; otherwise return `success` with $z$ and $r$.

When the routine returns an exact root, $r=0$ and $z$ is the IMEX Euler step $Y=y+h a(y)+h b(Y)$. A success status records only the requested residual check; the forward error conclusion is supplied separately by the residual theorem. This procedure uses one explicit evaluation of $a$ and one implicit solve.

Let $c\in\mathbb R^d$, $R>0$, $h>0$, and let $b$ be defined on the closed Euclidean ball $\overline B(c,R)$. Suppose $\|b(z)\|_2\le M$ and $\|b(z)-b(w)\|_2\le L\|z-w\|_2$ there, with $hM\le R$ and $hL<1$. Then the IMEX Euler equation $Y=c+h b(Y)$ has exactly one solution in $\overline B(c,R)$. Every $\widetilde Y$ in that ball satisfies
$$\|\widetilde Y-Y\|_2\le\frac{\|\widetilde Y-c-hb(\widetilde Y)\|_2}{1-hL}.$$
In the algorithm [[alg-imex-euler-step]], $c=y+h a(y)$; this is a local branch result and gives no root outside the selected ball.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

derivations.claim: By [F3], for $0\le s\le h$, $\phi_s-y=\int_0^sF(\phi_r)\,dr$, so [F4] and [A1] give $\|\phi_s-y\|_2\le M_Fs$. Subtracting $hF(y)$ from the integral at $h$ and applying [F4] again yields $\|\phi_h-y-hF(y)\|_2\le\int_0^hL_F\|\phi_s-y\|_2ds\le\frac12L_FM_Fh^2$.

Set $c=y+ha(y)$ and evaluate the implicit residual of the exact endpoint: $r_\phi:=\phi_h-c-hb(\phi_h)=(\phi_h-y-hF(y))-h(b(\phi_h)-b(y))$. By [A1] and step 1.1, $\|r_\phi\|_2\le M_F(\frac12L_F+L_b)h^2$. The exact endpoint and the branch root lie in the same admitted branch ball, so [F2] gives $\|\Psi_h(y)-\phi_h\|_2\le2M_F(\frac12L_F+L_b)h^2$.

For two inputs $u,v$ with selected roots $Y_u,Y_v$, subtracting their equations in [F1] and using the Lipschitz bounds gives $(1-hL_b)\|Y_u-Y_v\|_2\le(1+hL_a)\|u-v\|_2$. Since $hL_b\le1/2$, $(1+hL_a)/(1-hL_b)=1+h(L_a+L_b)/(1-hL_b)\le1+2(L_a+L_b)h$. This is the stated one-step stability bound.

For the autonomous split problem $y'=a(y)+b(y)$ of [[def-additive-ode-and-partition]], set
$$\gamma:=1-\frac1{\sqrt2},\qquad \delta:=-\frac1{\sqrt2}.$$
The explicit tableau and the lower-triangular implicit tableau, using the separate stage conventions of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]] and [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]], are
$$\widetilde A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\\gamma&0&0\\\delta&1-\delta&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \widetilde b=(\delta,1-\delta,0),\quad \widetilde c=(0,\gamma,1),$$
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&\gamma&0\\0&1-\gamma&\gamma\end{pmatrix},\quad b=(0,1-\gamma,\gamma),\quad c=(0,\gamma,1).$$
For a step $h>0$ from $y$, the method is defined by
$$Y_1=y,\qquad Y_2=y+\gamma h a(Y_1)+\gamma h b(Y_2),$$
$$Y_3=y+h\bigl[\delta a(Y_1)+(1-\delta)a(Y_2)\bigr]+h\bigl[(1-\gamma)b(Y_2)+\gamma b(Y_3)\bigr],\qquad y^+=Y_3.$$
Thus there are two implicit solves per step, one for each nonzero diagonal implicit stage. The unscaled stage-equation residual uses the update-residual convention of [[def-implicit-residual-and-algebraic-error-units]]. The tableaus and stages alone assert neither branch existence nor stability.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

derivations.claim: Let $r=\sqrt2$. If $r\le1$, then $0\le r\le1$ and [F3] gives $r^2\le1$, contradicting $r^2=2$ from [F2]; hence $r>1$. Applying [F4] to $0<1<r$ gives $0<1/r<1$, so $\gamma=1-1/r>0$.
By [F1] and $\gamma=(r-1)/r$ from step 1.1, $1-1/(2\gamma)=1-r/(2(r-1))=(r-2)/(2(r-1))$. Since $r^2=2$, $r(r-2)=2-2r=-2(r-1)$; dividing by the nonzero $2r(r-1)$ gives $(r-2)/(2(r-1))=-1/r=\delta$.
The identity in step 2.1 gives $\gamma(1-\gamma-\delta)=\gamma(1/(2\gamma)-\gamma)=1/2-\gamma^2$. This proves all coefficient identities.

Let $m,d\ge1$, $h>0$, $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$, and centers $c=(c_1,\ldots,c_m)\in(\mathbb R^d)^m$. On block vectors define

$$\|Y\|_{\infty,2}:=\max_{1\le i\le m}\|Y_i\|_2,\qquad \|A\|_\infty:=\max_i\sum_{j=1}^m|a_{ij}|.$$

Let $F:\mathcal B\to(\mathbb R^d)^m$, with components $F_i:\mathcal B\to\mathbb R^d$, be defined on the closed product ball $\mathcal B=\{Y:\|Y-c\|_{\infty,2}\le R\}$, where $R>0$. Suppose constants $M,L\ge0$ satisfy, for all $Y,Z\in\mathcal B$,

$$\|F(Y)\|_{\infty,2}\le M,\qquad \|F(Y)-F(Z)\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|Y-Z\|_{\infty,2},$$

and $h\|A\|_\infty M\le R$, $q:=h\|A\|_\infty L<1$. Define $\Phi(Y)=c+h(A\otimes I_d)F(Y)$ and $G(Y)=Y-\Phi(Y)$. Then $\Phi$ has a unique fixed point $Y^*\in\mathcal B$, equivalently $G(Y^*)=0$. Every approximate stage vector $\widetilde Y\in\mathcal B$ satisfies

$$\|\widetilde Y-Y^*\|_{\infty,2}\le\frac{\|G(\widetilde Y)\|_{\infty,2}}{1-q}.$$

If the derivative-scaled stage residual is $r=G(\widetilde Y)/h$, the right side is $h\|r\|_{\infty,2}/(1-q)$. The hypotheses $h\|A\|_\infty L<1$ and the invariant-ball bound are local solvability conditions; this result gives no global branch outside $\mathcal B$.

derivations.claim: For stage two in [F1], apply [F2] to the one-stage matrix $A=[\gamma]$, the one-block function $F_1=b$, and center $c_2$; its matrix row norm is $\|A\|_\infty=|\gamma|$, so [A1] gives the invariant-ball and contraction hypotheses. Hence the second stage root exists uniquely, and its residual bound is the one in [F2], with contraction factor $|\gamma|hL$.

With that selected $Y_2$, the third-stage center $c_3$ in [F1] is fixed. Apply [F2] again to the one-stage matrix $[\gamma]$, function $b$, and ball centered at $c_3$; [A1] verifies the same hypotheses, giving a unique $Y_3$ and its residual bound with contraction factor $|\gamma|hL$.

The stages are solved in order, so step 1.1 determines the center used in step 2.1. Both roots are unique in their selected balls, and the residual estimates hold for every candidate in those balls; no statement is made outside them.

Let $a,b\in C^3(U,\mathbb R^d)$ on an open set and let $K_0\subset K\subset U$, where $K_0$ is compact and $K$ is compact and convex. Assume the exact subflows and their compositions from $K_0$ remain in $K$ for all sufficiently small $h>0$, and the fields and derivatives through order three are bounded on $K$. Uniformly for $y\in K_0$,
$$L_h(y)-\Phi_{a+b}^h(y)=\frac{h^2}{2}[a,b](y)+O(h^3),$$
and the Strang expansion, pointwise in $y$, is
$$S_h(y)-\Phi_{a+b}^h(y)=-\frac{h^3}{24}[a,[a,b]](y)-\frac{h^3}{12}[b,[a,b]](y)+o(h^3).$$
The Strang defect is also uniformly $O(h^3)$ on $K_0$. The maps and bracket use [[def-exact-split-flows-lie-strang-and-bracket]]; the claim is finite-dimensional.

Let $a,b:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^3$ fields on an open set, and restrict attention to points and time intervals for which the unique local solutions of $x'=a(x)$ and $x'=b(x)$ remain in $U$. Denote their exact solution maps by $\Phi_a^t$ and $\Phi_b^t$. The **Lie split map** applies $a$ and then $b$:
$$L_h:=\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^h.$$
The **Strang split map** applies half of $a$, then $b$, then half of $a$:
$$S_h:=\Phi_a^{h/2}\circ\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^{h/2}.$$
Define the vector-field Lie bracket convention
$$[a,b](y):=Db(y)a(y)-Da(y)b(y).$$
This definition is finite-dimensional. It asserts neither that an unbounded operator has a common invariant domain nor that its commutators are bounded.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $d,N,p\ge1$, $T>0$, $h=T/N$, and $t_n=nh$. Let $y:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ solve an initial-value problem in an open time-state domain $D$. Use the Euclidean norm $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], whose triangle inequality is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]. Let $\mathcal T\subset D$ be a common compact time-state tube with positive margin in $D$, and write $\mathcal T_t:=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:(t,v)\in\mathcal T\}$. Suppose a one-step map $\Psi_{h,n}$ is defined on $\mathcal T_{t_n}$, produces $y_{n+1}=\Psi_{h,n}(y_n)$, and the entire exact path, all numerical grid states, and every method stage lie in $\mathcal T$. If constants $C,C_0,L\ge0$, independent of $N$ and $n$, satisfy
$$\|y_0-y(0)\|_2\le C_0h^p,\qquad \|\Psi_{h,n}(y(t_n))-y(t_{n+1})\|_2\le Ch^{p+1},$$
and
$$\|\Psi_{h,n}(u)-\Psi_{h,n}(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$
for every $u,v\in\mathcal T_{t_n}$ and $0\le n<N$, then, for $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, for $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

derivations.claim: Let $K=L_a+L_b$. For either field $c\in\{a,b\}$, let $x(t)$ and $z(t)$ start at $u$ and $v$. By [F3] and [F4], $\|x(t)-z(t)\|_2\le\|u-v\|_2+L_c\int_0^t\|x(s)-z(s)\|_2\,ds.$ The constant case of [F5] yields $\|\Phi_c^t(u)-\Phi_c^t(v)\|_2\le e^{L_ct}\|u-v\|_2$. Composing these bounds according to [F2] shows both exact split maps are Lipschitz with factor $e^{Kh}$.

Fix $h_0>0$ within the admitted step range. For $0\le h\le h_0$, [F6] and the mean value theorem give $e^{Kh}-1=Kh e^\xi\le K h e^{Kh_0}$ for some $\xi\in[0,Kh]$, using monotonicity from [F7]. Thus both exact split maps satisfy a one-step bound $1+Lh$, with $L=K e^{Kh_0}$ (and $L=0$ when $K=0$).

Fix a starting state $u$ in the tube. For Lie, insert the exact $b$ flow between the two compositions and use its Lipschitz bound from step 1.1: $\|\widehat\Phi_b^h(\widehat\Phi_a^h(u))-\Phi_b^h(\Phi_a^h(u))\|_2\le\epsilon_b(h)+e^{L_bh}\epsilon_a(h).$ For Strang, inserting the exact outer $a$ and middle $b$ maps in sequence gives $\|\widehat\Phi_a^{h/2}(\widehat\Phi_b^h(\widehat\Phi_a^{h/2}(u)))-\Phi_a^{h/2}(\Phi_b^h(\Phi_a^{h/2}(u)))\|_2\le\epsilon_a(h/2)+e^{L_ah/2}\epsilon_b(h)+e^{(L_a/2+L_b)h}\epsilon_a(h/2).$ The inequalities hold uniformly over all starting states in the tube.

Let $F=a+b$ on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. On a common compact convex tube suppose $a,b$ are bounded and Lipschitz with constants $M_a,M_b,L_a,L_b$, the exact IVP solution and its endpoint stay in the tube, and the IMEX branch balls of [[lem-imex-euler-local-branch]] contain the exact endpoint and selected root. For sufficiently small $h>0$ with $hL_b\le1/2$, let $\Psi_h(y)$ be the exact root map $Y=y+ha(y)+hb(Y)$. Then, uniformly on the tube,
$$\|\Psi_h(y(t))-y(t+h)\|_2\le C h^2,\qquad \|\Psi_h(u)-\Psi_h(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2,$$
where one may take $L=2(L_a+L_b)$ and $C$ depends only on the stated tube bounds and branch margins. The local defect is therefore $O(h^2)$, and the exact-root method is first order locally.

Let $d,N,p\ge1$, $T>0$, $h=T/N$, and $t_n=nh$. Let $y:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ solve an initial-value problem in an open time-state domain $D$. Use the Euclidean norm $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], whose triangle inequality is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]. Let $\mathcal T\subset D$ be a common compact time-state tube with positive margin in $D$, and write $\mathcal T_t:=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:(t,v)\in\mathcal T\}$. Suppose a one-step map $\Psi_{h,n}$ is defined on $\mathcal T_{t_n}$, produces $y_{n+1}=\Psi_{h,n}(y_n)$, and the entire exact path, all numerical grid states, and every method stage lie in $\mathcal T$. If constants $C,C_0,L\ge0$, independent of $N$ and $n$, satisfy
$$\|y_0-y(0)\|_2\le C_0h^p,\qquad \|\Psi_{h,n}(y(t_n))-y(t_{n+1})\|_2\le Ch^{p+1},$$
and
$$\|\Psi_{h,n}(u)-\Psi_{h,n}(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$
for every $u,v\in\mathcal T_{t_n}$ and $0\le n<N$, then, for $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, for $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [A1], for each $n<N$ the exact-start local defect satisfies $\|\Psi_h(y(t_n))-y(t_{n+1})\|_2\le Ch^2$, and for all compared states in the tube $\|\Psi_h(u)-\Psi_h(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$. The exact initial value gives zero initial error, which is at most $0\cdot h$.

Apply [F2] with $p=1$, $C_0=0$, and the constants from step 1.1. All hypotheses are satisfied by [A1], so its fixed-time estimate gives $\max_{n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le C_T h$ for a constant independent of $h$ and $n$.

Let $c\in\mathbb R^d$, $R>0$, $h>0$, and let $b$ be defined on the closed Euclidean ball $\overline B(c,R)$. Suppose $\|b(z)\|_2\le M$ and $\|b(z)-b(w)\|_2\le L\|z-w\|_2$ there, with $hM\le R$ and $hL<1$. Then the IMEX Euler equation $Y=c+h b(Y)$ has exactly one solution in $\overline B(c,R)$. Every $\widetilde Y$ in that ball satisfies
$$\|\widetilde Y-Y\|_2\le\frac{\|\widetilde Y-c-hb(\widetilde Y)\|_2}{1-hL}.$$
In the algorithm [[alg-imex-euler-step]], $c=y+h a(y)$; this is a local branch result and gives no root outside the selected ball.

Let $T>0$, $N\ge1$, $h=T/N$, $p\ge1$, and $C_0,C,L\ge0$. If nonnegative real numbers $e_0,\ldots,e_N$ satisfy
$$e_0\le C_0h^p,\qquad e_{n+1}\le(1+Lh)e_n+Ch^{p+1}\quad(0\le n<N),$$
then, when $L>0$,

Let $G:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be the residual map of an implicit equation, where $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is the admissible set for the unknown vector. An exact solution is a point $z^*\in U$ with $G(z^*)=0$.

The **update residual** at an approximate solution $\widetilde z\in U$ is the vector $G(\widetilde z)$, measured in the same units as $z$. If the original equation was divided by a positive step scale $\sigma$, then the **derivative residual** is $G(\widetilde z)/\sigma$, and the corresponding update residual is $\sigma$ times that derivative residual. A residual norm is not a forward-error bound unless a separate inverse or stability estimate converts it to $\|\widetilde z-z^*\|$.

For a first-order vector field $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ on an open time-state domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]), take a time $t$, input $y\in\mathbb R^d$, and step $h>0$ with $(t,y)\in D$. For backward Euler, an endpoint $z$ is admissible only when $(t+h,z)\in D$, and its update residual is

$$G_{\rm BE}(z)=z-y-hf(t+h,z),$$

so the derivative residual is $G_{\rm BE}(z)/h$.

For an $s$-stage implicit Runge–Kutta tableau $(A,b,c)$, a stage vector $Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_s)$ is admissible only when $(t+c_jh,Y_j)\in D$ for every $j$. On that admissible set, its stage update residual has blocks

$$G_i(Y)=Y_i-y-h\sum_{j=1}^s a_{ij}f(t+c_jh,Y_j),\qquad i=1,\ldots,s.$$

The stage derivative residual is $G(Y)/h$. These conventions distinguish an equation residual from the distance to its exact root.

derivations.claim: Since $hL_b\le1/2$, [F2] gives $\|\widetilde y_{n+1}-\Psi_h(y_n)\|_2\le2C_rh^2$, where $\Psi_h(y_n)=y_{n+1}^*$ is the exact-root update from the current numerical state. The bound is valid at every step by [A1].

By the triangle inequality, [F1], and step 1.1, $e_{n+1}:=\|\widetilde y_{n+1}-y(t_{n+1})\|_2\le(1+Lh)e_n+(C_\ell+2C_r)h^2.$ Here the first term compares the exact-root map at $\widetilde y_n$ with that map at $y(t_n)$; the local-defect term compares the latter output with the exact next state.

Apply [F3] to this recurrence with $p=1$, $C=C_\ell+2C_r$, and the initial error from the Statement. This proves the displayed $O(h)$ global bound. By [F4], if a solver instead reports the derivative-scaled residual $r_n/h$, the assumed update-residual budget is obtained by multiplying that bound by $h$.

For the autonomous split problem $y'=a(y)+b(y)$ of [[def-additive-ode-and-partition]], set
$$\gamma:=1-\frac1{\sqrt2},\qquad \delta:=-\frac1{\sqrt2}.$$
The explicit tableau and the lower-triangular implicit tableau, using the separate stage conventions of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]] and [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]], are
$$\widetilde A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\\gamma&0&0\\\delta&1-\delta&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \widetilde b=(\delta,1-\delta,0),\quad \widetilde c=(0,\gamma,1),$$
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&\gamma&0\\0&1-\gamma&\gamma\end{pmatrix},\quad b=(0,1-\gamma,\gamma),\quad c=(0,\gamma,1).$$
For a step $h>0$ from $y$, the method is defined by
$$Y_1=y,\qquad Y_2=y+\gamma h a(Y_1)+\gamma h b(Y_2),$$
$$Y_3=y+h\bigl[\delta a(Y_1)+(1-\delta)a(Y_2)\bigr]+h\bigl[(1-\gamma)b(Y_2)+\gamma b(Y_3)\bigr],\qquad y^+=Y_3.$$
Thus there are two implicit solves per step, one for each nonzero diagonal implicit stage. The unscaled stage-equation residual uses the update-residual convention of [[def-implicit-residual-and-algebraic-error-units]]. The tableaus and stages alone assert neither branch existence nor stability.

Let $\gamma=1-1/\sqrt2$ as in [[def-ars222-additive-tableau-and-stages]]. For each of the two implicit stages, let $c_j$ be its center after the previous stages have been selected. Suppose $b$ is bounded by $M$ and $L$-Lipschitz on a closed ball $\overline B(c_j,R_j)\subset U$, and $|\gamma|hM\le R_j$, $|\gamma|hL<1$. Then stage $Y_j=c_j+\gamma h b(Y_j)$ has a unique root in that ball. Every candidate $\widetilde Y_j$ in the same ball with unscaled stage-equation residual $r_j$ satisfies
$$\|\widetilde Y_j-Y_j\|_2\le\frac{\|r_j\|_2}{1-|\gamma|hL}.$$
The claim is local to these stage balls; it asserts no remote-root or large-step branch.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

For $\gamma=1-1/\sqrt2$ and $\delta=-1/\sqrt2$ in [[def-ars222-additive-tableau-and-stages]], one has $\gamma>0$ and
$$\delta=1-\frac1{2\gamma},\qquad \gamma(1-\delta)=\frac12,\qquad \gamma(2-\gamma)=\frac12,\qquad \gamma(1-\gamma-\delta)=\frac12-\gamma^2.$$

Let $T>0$, $N\ge1$, $h=T/N$, $p\ge1$, and $C_0,C,L\ge0$. If nonnegative real numbers $e_0,\ldots,e_N$ satisfy
$$e_0\le C_0h^p,\qquad e_{n+1}\le(1+Lh)e_n+Ch^{p+1}\quad(0\le n<N),$$
then, when $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}e_n\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, when $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}e_n\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

derivations.claim: Let $\phi_s$ be the exact solution starting at $y$. By [F4], $\phi_s-y=\int_0^sF(\phi_r)\,dr$. Boundedness gives $\|\phi_r-y\|=O(r)$, and Lipschitz continuity then gives $\|\phi_s-y-sF(y)\|\le\int_0^sL_F\|\phi_r-y\|dr=O(s^2)$, where $L_F=L_a+L_b$. Taylor's formula [F5] gives $F(\phi_s)=F(y)+DF(y)(\phi_s-y)+O(s^2)$, hence $F(\phi_s)=F(y)+sDF(y)F(y)+O(s^2)$. Integrating this identity from $0$ to $h$ yields $\phi_h=y+hF(y)+\frac12h^2DF(y)F(y)+O(h^3).$

For two inputs $u,v$ with exact selected second stages $Y_2(u),Y_2(v)$, subtract the first equation in [F1] and use the Lipschitz bounds. Since $\gamma>0$ from [F6] and $\gamma hL_b\le1/2$, this gives $\|Y_2(u)-Y_2(v)\|_2\le\frac{1+\gamma hL_a}{1-\gamma hL_b}\|u-v\|_2\le(1+2\gamma(L_a+L_b)h)\|u-v\|_2.$

Let $e_2=\|\widetilde Y_2-Y_2\|_2$. By $\gamma>0$ from [F6] and $|\gamma|hL_b\le1/2$ from [A1], subtracting the second-stage equations and using its residual gives $(1-\gamma hL_b)e_2\le\|r_2\|_2$, hence $e_2\le2\|r_2\|_2$. For the final stage, subtract the equations with the same initial input; the terms depending on $Y_2$ are bounded by $hK_s e_2$, where $K_s=|1-\delta|L_a+|1-\gamma|L_b$. The final-stage residual therefore gives $\|\widetilde Y_3-Y_3\|_2\le2\|r_3\|_2+4K_s h\|r_2\|_2.$ This is at most $C_{\rm alg}h^3$ under the two stated residual budgets.

By [F2] and [A1], the selected second-stage root exists in its branch ball. Its equation in [F1] and boundedness first give $Y_2-y=O(h)$. Lipschitz continuity gives $b(Y_2)=b(y)+O(h)$, so the same equation gives $Y_2-y=\gamma hF(y)+O(h^2)$. Applying [F5] to $b(Y_2)$ then gives $b(Y_2)=b(y)+\gamma h\,Db(y)F(y)+O(h^2)$, and substitution into [F1] yields $Y_2=y+\gamma hF(y)+\gamma^2h^2Db(y)F(y)+O(h^3).$

Let $K_2=2\gamma(L_a+L_b)$ and $K_3=|\delta|L_a+(|1-\delta|L_a+|1-\gamma|L_b)(1+K_2h_0)$ for $h\le h_0$, where $h_0$ is any fixed upper bound on the small steps. The third-stage centers in [F1] then differ by at most $(1+K_3h)\|u-v\|_2$. Applying the same subtraction to the third-stage equation and using $(1-\gamma hL_b)^{-1}\le1+2\gamma hL_b$ gives $\|\Psi_h(u)-\Psi_h(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$ for $L:=K_3+2\gamma L_b+2\gamma L_bK_3h_0$, which is independent of $h$ and the step index.

By [F2] and [A1], the selected third-stage root exists after $Y_2$ is selected. Since $Y_2-y=O(h)$ and the stage equations give $Y_3-y=O(h)$, Lipschitz continuity and the weight sums $\delta+(1-\delta)=1$ and $(1-\gamma)+\gamma=1$ imply $Y_3-y=hF(y)+O(h^2)$. Taylor's formula applied to the last-stage terms gives $a(Y_2)=a(y)+\gamma h\,Da(y)F(y)+O(h^2),\quad b(Y_2)=b(y)+\gamma h\,Db(y)F(y)+O(h^2),\quad b(Y_3)=b(y)+h\,Db(y)F(y)+O(h^2).$ Substituting these expansions into [F1] and collecting the coefficients gives $Y_3=y+hF(y)+h^2\{\gamma(1-\delta)Da(y)F(y)+\gamma(2-\gamma)Db(y)F(y)\}+O(h^3).$

The identities [F6] make both second-order coefficients in step 3.1 equal to $1/2$, so its expansion agrees with the exact expansion in step 1.1. Thus $\|\Psi_h(y)-\phi_h\|_2\le C h^3$ uniformly on the tube.

Put $e_n=\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2$. Compare the computed output first with the exact-root ARS output at $y_n$, then with that map at $y(t_n)$, then with the exact next state. Steps 4.1, 2.2, and 4.1 give $e_{n+1}\le(1+Lh)e_n+(C+C_{\rm alg})h^3.$ Apply [F7] with $p=2$ and the initial error from the Statement to obtain the claimed fixed-time $O(h^2)$ bound. By [F3], a derivative-scaled residual must be multiplied by $h$ before it is tested against either stage budget.

For the autonomous split problem $y'=a(y)+b(y)$ of [[def-additive-ode-and-partition]], set
$$\gamma:=1-\frac1{\sqrt2},\qquad \delta:=-\frac1{\sqrt2}.$$
The explicit tableau and the lower-triangular implicit tableau, using the separate stage conventions of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]] and [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]], are
$$\widetilde A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\\gamma&0&0\\\delta&1-\delta&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \widetilde b=(\delta,1-\delta,0),\quad \widetilde c=(0,\gamma,1),$$
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&\gamma&0\\0&1-\gamma&\gamma\end{pmatrix},\quad b=(0,1-\gamma,\gamma),\quad c=(0,\gamma,1).$$
For a step $h>0$ from $y$, the method is defined by
$$Y_1=y,\qquad Y_2=y+\gamma h a(Y_1)+\gamma h b(Y_2),$$
$$Y_3=y+h\bigl[\delta a(Y_1)+(1-\delta)a(Y_2)\bigr]+h\bigl[(1-\gamma)b(Y_2)+\gamma b(Y_3)\bigr],\qquad y^+=Y_3.$$
Thus there are two implicit solves per step, one for each nonzero diagonal implicit stage. The unscaled stage-equation residual uses the update-residual convention of [[def-implicit-residual-and-algebraic-error-units]]. The tableaus and stages alone assert neither branch existence nor stability.

For $\gamma=1-1/\sqrt2$ and $\delta=-1/\sqrt2$ in [[def-ars222-additive-tableau-and-stages]], one has $\gamma>0$ and
$$\delta=1-\frac1{2\gamma},\qquad \gamma(1-\delta)=\frac12,\qquad \gamma(2-\gamma)=\frac12,\qquad \gamma(1-\gamma-\delta)=\frac12-\gamma^2.$$

Form the polynomial ring $\mathbb R[x]$
([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and define the **complex
numbers** by the quotient ring
$$\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$$
([[def-quotient-ring]]). Write $a$ for the constant class $a+(x^2+1)$ and set
$$i:=x+(x^2+1).$$
Thus $i^2=-1$ in the quotient. The constant-class map
$\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ is the specified real map; its injectivity and the
field structure are proved in [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], after which
$\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ is a field extension in the sense of
[[def-field-extension-generated-subfields-and-simple-extension]].

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

derivations.claim: Substituting $a(y)=\lambda_a y$ and $b(y)=\lambda_b y$ into [F1] gives $Y_2/y=(1+\gamma z_a)/(1-\gamma z_b)$ whenever the denominator is nonzero. The third stage then satisfies $\frac{Y_3}{y}=\frac{1+\delta z_a+[(1-\delta)z_a+(1-\gamma)z_b](Y_2/y)}{1-\gamma z_b}.$ These formulas are linear coefficient identities, so they also define the amplification when $y=0$.

Substituting the stage-two ratio from step 1.1 gives numerator $(1+\delta z_a)(1-\gamma z_b)+[(1-\delta)z_a+(1-\gamma)z_b](1+\gamma z_a)$ over denominator $(1-\gamma z_b)^2$. Collecting terms yields $1+z_a+(1-2\gamma)z_b+\gamma(1-\delta)z_a^2+\gamma(1-\gamma-\delta)z_az_b$.
The identities in [F2] simplify the $z_a^2$ and $z_az_b$ coefficients in step 2.1; the remaining $z_b$ coefficient is $1-2\gamma$. Substitution gives the displayed $R(z_a,z_b)$.

Repeated application to the scalar test equation multiplies its state by $R$ at each step, so nonincrease of the absolute value is exactly $|R|\le1$. Since $| (1-\gamma z_b)^2|=|1-\gamma z_b|^2$, this is precisely the displayed set $\mathcal S$, with the pole excluded because the implicit stage equation is singular there. Setting either variable to zero gives the stated axis sections by substitution.

For the additive ODE partition [[def-additive-ode-and-partition]], take a current state $y\in U$, a step $h>0$, a closed ball $\overline B(c,R)\subset U$ centered at $c:=y+h a(y)$, bounds $M_b,L_b\ge0$ for $\|b\|_2$ and its Lipschitz constant on that ball, a tolerance $\tau\ge0$, and a solve routine that returns either a candidate $z\in\overline B(c,R)$ or a failure status. The procedure is:

1. If the solve routine is unavailable, return `solver-unavailable`.
2. If $hM_b>R$ or $hL_b\ge1$, return `branch-not-certified` without claiming a root.
3. Call the solve routine on $z=c+h b(z)$.
4. If it returns failure, return that failure status. If it returns $z\notin\overline B(c,R)$, return `out-of-branch-ball`.
5. Compute the update residual $r:=z-c-hb(z)$ in the state units of [[def-implicit-residual-and-algebraic-error-units]]. If $\|r\|_2>\tau$, return `residual-too-large` with $z$ and $r$; otherwise return `success` with $z$ and $r$.

When the routine returns an exact root, $r=0$ and $z$ is the IMEX Euler step $Y=y+h a(y)+h b(Y)$. A success status records only the requested residual check; the forward error conclusion is supplied separately by the residual theorem. This procedure uses one explicit evaluation of $a$ and one implicit solve.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

derivations.claim: With $a(y)=-\kappa y$ and $b=0$, [F1] gives $Y=(1-h\kappa)y$, so after $N$ steps the numerical value is $(1-h\kappa)^N$. If $h\kappa>2$, then $1-h\kappa<-1$ and $|1-h\kappa|^N>1$ for every $N\ge1$. By [F2], $y(t)=e^{-\kappa t}$ is the exact solution, and [F3] gives $|y(Nh)|=e^{-\kappa Nh}<1$.

With $a=0$ and $b(y)=-\kappa y$, the equation in [F1] becomes $(1+h\kappa)Y=y$. Since $0<1<1+h\kappa$, [F4] gives $0<(1+h\kappa)^{-1}<1$. Thus the implicit treatment damps every such scalar step, while the explicit treatment grows whenever $h\kappa>2$.

At the boundary $h\kappa=2$, the explicit amplification is $-1$, whose magnitude is exactly one. Thus the strict instability condition is $h\kappa>2$; equality is neutral for this scalar test equation.

Let $a,b:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^3$ fields on an open set, and restrict attention to points and time intervals for which the unique local solutions of $x'=a(x)$ and $x'=b(x)$ remain in $U$. Denote their exact solution maps by $\Phi_a^t$ and $\Phi_b^t$. The **Lie split map** applies $a$ and then $b$:
$$L_h:=\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^h.$$
The **Strang split map** applies half of $a$, then $b$, then half of $a$:
$$S_h:=\Phi_a^{h/2}\circ\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^{h/2}.$$
Define the vector-field Lie bracket convention
$$[a,b](y):=Db(y)a(y)-Da(y)b(y).$$
This definition is finite-dimensional. It asserts neither that an unbounded operator has a common invariant domain nor that its commutators are bounded.

Let $a,b\in C^3(U,\mathbb R^d)$ on an open set and let $K_0\subset K\subset U$, where $K_0$ is compact and $K$ is compact and convex. Assume the exact subflows and their compositions from $K_0$ remain in $K$ for all sufficiently small $h>0$, and the fields and derivatives through order three are bounded on $K$. Uniformly for $y\in K_0$,
$$L_h(y)-\Phi_{a+b}^h(y)=\frac{h^2}{2}[a,b](y)+O(h^3),$$
and the Strang expansion, pointwise in $y$, is
$$S_h(y)-\Phi_{a+b}^h(y)=-\frac{h^3}{24}[a,[a,b]](y)-\frac{h^3}{12}[b,[a,b]](y)+o(h^3).$$
The Strang defect is also uniformly $O(h^3)$ on $K_0$. The maps and bracket use [[def-exact-split-flows-lie-strang-and-bracket]]; the claim is finite-dimensional.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

derivations.claim: By [F4], the linear fields have global exact flows. Direct multiplication gives $BA=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad AB=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad C:=BA-AB=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$ By [F1], $[a,b](x)=Cx$.

Multiplying once more gives $CA-AC=\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad CB-BC=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\2&0\end{pmatrix}.$ These are the matrices of $[a,[a,b]]$ and $[b,[a,b]]$ under the same convention.
At $e_1$, $Ce_1=-e_1\ne0$, so [F2] gives Lie local defect $-\frac12h^2e_1+O(h^3)$, whose leading coefficient is nonzero. Thus its local error has exact order two.

The Strang leading matrix from step 2.1 is $-\frac1{24}(CA-AC)-\frac1{12}(CB-BC)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/12\\-1/6&0\end{pmatrix}.$ It sends $e_1$ to $(0,-1/6)^T\ne0$, so [F2] gives a nonzero cubic leading local defect and exact local order three.

The **Strang split map** applies half of $a$, then $b$, then half of $a$:
$$S_h:=\Phi_a^{h/2}\circ\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^{h/2}.$$
Define the vector-field Lie bracket convention
$$[a,b](y):=Db(y)a(y)-Da(y)b(y).$$
This definition is finite-dimensional. It asserts neither that an unbounded operator has a common invariant domain nor that its commutators are bounded.

Let $a,b\in C^3(U,\mathbb R^d)$ on an open set and let $K_0\subset K\subset U$, where $K_0$ is compact and $K$ is compact and convex. Assume the exact subflows and their compositions from $K_0$ remain in $K$ for all sufficiently small $h>0$, and the fields and derivatives through order three are bounded on $K$. Uniformly for $y\in K_0$,
$$L_h(y)-\Phi_{a+b}^h(y)=\frac{h^2}{2}[a,b](y)+O(h^3),$$
and the Strang expansion, pointwise in $y$, is

The Strang defect is also uniformly $O(h^3)$ on $K_0$. The maps and bracket use [[def-exact-split-flows-lie-strang-and-bracket]]; the claim is finite-dimensional.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces. In orthonormal bases $\mathcal E=(e_j)$ of $V$ and $\mathcal F=(f_i)$ of $W$,

$$[T^*]_{\mathcal E\leftarrow\mathcal F}=\overline{[T]_{\mathcal F\leftarrow\mathcal E}}^{\mathsf T}.$$

Over $\mathbb R$ this is the transpose. The statement includes zero-sized bases.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

derivations.claim: Let $H$ be any of $H_K$, $V$, or $H_K+V$. Its exact flow exists for all real time by [F7], and every solution obeys $\psi'=-iH\psi$. By [F3]–[F6], differentiating the real function $\psi^*\psi$ gives $\frac{d}{dt}(\psi^*\psi)=(\psi')^*\psi+\psi^*\psi'=i\psi^*H^*\psi-i\psi^*H\psi=0,$ where [A1] supplies $H^*=H$. Therefore [F6] makes $\|\psi(t)\|_2^2$ constant on every admitted interval, and each exact subflow and the total flow preserve norm.

Direct multiplication gives $C:=BA-AB=H_KV-VH_K=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\ne0.$ This is the linear matrix of $[a,b]$ by [F1]. Also $CA-AC=i\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad CB-BC=2i\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$
By [F1], a Lie or Strang step is a composition of exact component flows. Each factor preserves norm by step 1.1, so the composition preserves norm by repeated application of the same equality.

For $\psi=e_1$, the Lie coefficient $\frac12C\psi$ is nonzero. The Strang coefficient $-\frac1{24}(CA-AC)\psi-\frac1{12}(CB-BC)\psi$ is also nonzero, since its first coordinate is $-i/6$. Applying [F2] shows the exact subflows retain norm while the Lie and Strang maps have their respective nonzero local splitting defects.

Let $\mathcal H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, with square-summability as in [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Define the diagonal operator $A$ by
$$D(A)=\left\{u\in\mathcal H:\sum_{k\ge1} k^4|u_k|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad (Au)_k=-k^2u_k.$$
Let $g\in\mathcal H$ be the fixed sequence $g_k=1/k$ for odd $k$ and $g_k=0$ for even $k$; membership follows from [[thm-p-series-real-exponents]] with exponent $2$. The split evolution is $u'=Au+g$. For $t\ge0$, define the exact diagonal subflow $E_tu=(e^{-k^2t}u_k)_{k\ge1}$ and the exact translation subflow $B_tu=u+tg$. By [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]] and [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $0<e^{-k^2t}\le1$, so each $E_t$ maps $\mathcal H$ to itself; each $B_t$ does so because $g\in\mathcal H$. The associated Strang modal step is
$$S_h=E_{h/2}\circ B_h\circ E_{h/2},\qquad h>0,$$
where the rightmost map is applied first. Each coordinate of $E_t$ solves $u_k'=-k^2u_k$, and each coordinate of $B_t$ solves $u_k'=g_k$. This is a precisely defined sequence-space model; it records one Dirichlet sine-mode boundary mismatch and makes no general convergence assertion for unbounded PDE operators.

Let $\mathcal H$, $A$, and $E_t$ be as in [[def-dirichlet-sine-mode-heat-splitting-model]]. The maps $E_t$ for $t\ge0$ satisfy $E_0=I$ and $E_{t+s}=E_tE_s$, are contractions in $\ell^2$, and are strongly continuous at $t=0$. Define the generator domain to consist of those $u\in\mathcal H$ for which the right limit
$$\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{E_tu-u}{t}$$
exists in $\mathcal H$. This domain is exactly $D(A)=\{u:\sum_{k\ge1}k^4|u_k|^2<\infty\}$, and the limit equals $Au=(-k^2u_k)_{k\ge1}$.

For the constant forcing $f(x):=\pi/4$ on $(0,\pi)$, define its Fourier sine coefficient by
$$\widehat f_k:=\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi f(x)\sin(kx)\,dx.$$
Then $\widehat f_k=g_k$ from [[def-dirichlet-sine-mode-heat-splitting-model]]. Thus $g\in\mathcal H$ but $g$ is outside the generator domain of $A$. The constant forcing has nonzero endpoint value, while every Dirichlet sine mode vanishes at both endpoints.

For every real $p$,
$$\sum_{k\ge1}\frac1{k^p}\text{ converges}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p>1.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

derivations.claim: For each mode, solving $u_k'=-k^2u_k+g_k$, $u_k(0)=0$, gives $u_k(t)=\frac{g_k}{k^2}(1-e^{-k^2t}).$ Differentiating verifies the equation and initial value. Also $|u_k(t)|\le |g_k|/k^2\le k^{-3}$, so [F4] shows the reference state belongs to $\ell^2$ for every $t\ge0$.

Put $x=k^2h$. By [F1], each Strang coordinate obeys $\widetilde u_{n+1,k}=e^{-x}\widetilde u_{n,k}+h e^{-x/2}g_k.$ Starting from zero and summing this scalar recurrence gives $\widetilde u_{N,k}=h e^{-x/2}\frac{1-e^{-Nx}}{1-e^{-x}}g_k,$ where the finite geometric identity follows by multiplying the sum by $1-e^{-x}$; the denominator is positive because $x>0$ and the exponential is strictly increasing.

For $x>0$, $\sigma'(x)=\tfrac12(e^{x/2}+e^{-x/2})>1$, because $e^{x/2}+e^{-x/2}-2=(e^{x/4}-e^{-x/4})^2>0.$ Thus [F6] gives $\sigma(x)>x$, so $0<q(x)<1$. Direct differentiation gives $\sigma(0)=0$, $\sigma'(0)=1$, and $\sigma''(0)=0$; [F7] therefore gives $\sigma(x)=x+O(x^3)$ on $0<x\le1$. Hence $q(x)=(\sigma(x)-x)/\sigma(x)\le Cx^2$ there.

By [F2] and [F3], this constant Dirichlet forcing is outside the generator domain and has nonzero boundary value while the sine modes vanish at both endpoints. The modal comparison below therefore concerns the boundary-incompatible data identified in the Statement.

Since $Nx=k^2T$, the identity $\frac{h e^{-x/2}}{1-e^{-x}}=\frac{1}{k^2}\frac{x}{e^{x/2}-e^{-x/2}}$ turns the numerical value into the exact modal value times $x/\sigma(x)$, where $\sigma(x):=e^{x/2}-e^{-x/2}$. Therefore for odd $k$, $|\widetilde u_{N,k}-u_k(T)|=k^{-3}(1-e^{-k^2T})q(k^2h),\qquad q(x):=1-\frac{x}{\sigma(x)},$ and the error is zero for even $k$.

The quotient $\sigma(x)/x$ is increasing for $x>0$: its derivative has numerator $p(x)=x\sigma'(x)-\sigma(x)$, with $p(0)=0$ and $p'(x)=x\sigma''(x)=x\sigma(x)/4>0$. Therefore $x/\sigma(x)$ decreases and $q$ increases. In particular $q(x)\ge q(1)>0$ on $1\le x\le4$.

Let $H=h^{-1/2}\ge1$. For odd $k\le H$, steps 2.2 and 1.3 give $|\widetilde u_{N,k}-u_k(T)|\le C h^2 k$. The sum of their squared errors is at most $C h^4H^3=C h^{5/2}$. For $k>H$, use $q<1$ and $1-e^{-k^2T}<1$; dyadic blocks $[2^jH,2^{j+1}H)$ contain at most $2^{j+1}H$ integers and contribute at most $2^{j+1}H(2^jH)^{-6}$. Summing the geometric series gives a tail at most $C H^{-5}=C h^{5/2}$. Thus the squared $\ell^2$ error is at most $C_T h^{5/2}$.

For sufficiently small $h$, $H\ge8$ and $h\le T$. The interval $[H,2H]$ contains at least $H-1$ integers, and among any $m$ consecutive integers at least $(m-1)/2$ are odd; hence it contains at least $H/4$ odd integers. For each such $k$, $1\le k^2h\le4$, $k^{-6}\ge(2H)^{-6}$, $q(k^2h)\ge q(1)$ by step 2.3, and $1-e^{-k^2T}\ge1-e^{-T/h}>1/2$ since $T/h\ge1$ and $e=1+1+\sum_{n\ge2}1/n!>2$. Therefore the sum of squared errors over these modes is at least $\frac H4\,(2H)^{-6}\,\frac{q(1)^2}{4}=cH^{-5}=c h^{5/2}$ for a constant $c>0$. Taking square roots of the upper bound in step 3.1 and this lower bound proves the claimed two-sided $h^{5/4}$ error rate.

For the autonomous split problem $y'=a(y)+b(y)$ of [[def-additive-ode-and-partition]], set
$$\gamma:=1-\frac1{\sqrt2},\qquad \delta:=-\frac1{\sqrt2}.$$
The explicit tableau and the lower-triangular implicit tableau, using the separate stage conventions of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]] and [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]], are
$$\widetilde A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\\gamma&0&0\\\delta&1-\delta&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \widetilde b=(\delta,1-\delta,0),\quad \widetilde c=(0,\gamma,1),$$
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&\gamma&0\\0&1-\gamma&\gamma\end{pmatrix},\quad b=(0,1-\gamma,\gamma),\quad c=(0,\gamma,1).$$
For a step $h>0$ from $y$, the method is defined by
$$Y_1=y,\qquad Y_2=y+\gamma h a(Y_1)+\gamma h b(Y_2),$$
$$Y_3=y+h\bigl[\delta a(Y_1)+(1-\delta)a(Y_2)\bigr]+h\bigl[(1-\gamma)b(Y_2)+\gamma b(Y_3)\bigr],\qquad y^+=Y_3.$$
Thus there are two implicit solves per step, one for each nonzero diagonal implicit stage. The unscaled stage-equation residual uses the update-residual convention of [[def-implicit-residual-and-algebraic-error-units]]. The tableaus and stages alone assert neither branch existence nor stability.

Apply [[def-ars222-additive-tableau-and-stages]] to the scalar split test equation $y'=\lambda_a y+\lambda_b y$, with $z_a=h\lambda_a$ and $z_b=h\lambda_b$ in $\mathbb C$. If $1-\gamma z_b\ne0$, the one-step amplification factor is
$$R(z_a,z_b)=\frac{1+z_a+(1-2\gamma)z_b+\frac12z_a^2+(\frac12-\gamma^2)z_az_b}{(1-\gamma z_b)^2}.$$
The exact scalar absolute-stability region for this tableau is
$$\mathcal S=\left\{(z_a,z_b)\in\mathbb C^2:1-\gamma z_b\ne0,\ \left|1+z_a+(1-2\gamma)z_b+\frac12z_a^2+(\frac12-\gamma^2)z_az_b\right|\le|1-\gamma z_b|^2\right\}.$$
On $z_b=0$ this reduces to $|1+z_a+z_a^2/2|\le1$; on $z_a=0$ it reduces to $|1+(1-2\gamma)z_b|\le|1-\gamma z_b|^2$. This is a scalar, two-variable region; it makes no matrix-nonnormality or PDE stability claim.

For $\gamma=1-1/\sqrt2$ and $\delta=-1/\sqrt2$ in [[def-ars222-additive-tableau-and-stages]], one has $\gamma>0$ and
$$\delta=1-\frac1{2\gamma},\qquad \gamma(1-\delta)=\frac12,\qquad \gamma(2-\gamma)=\frac12,\qquad \gamma(1-\gamma-\delta)=\frac12-\gamma^2.$$

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

derivations.claim: Direct multiplication gives $Lv_0=0$ for $v_0=(1,1)^T$ and $Lv_1=-2v_1$ for $v_1=(1,-1)^T$. These vectors are linearly independent, so they form a basis of $\mathbb R^2$ and diagonalize both $a(y)=y$ and $b(y)=10Ly$.

On each span $\mathbb Rv_j$, every stage equation in [F1] remains in that span. The implicit denominators are $1$ on $v_0$ and $1+20\gamma h>0$ on $v_1$, so the stage solves are unique there. Hence [F2] applies with $z_a=h$ and $z_b=0$ or $z_b=-20h$, respectively.
For $v_0$ and $h=1/10$, $z_b=0$, so [F2] gives $R(1/10,0)=1+\frac1{10}+\frac1{200}=\frac{221}{200}>1.$ This mode grows under the positive reaction term.

For $v_1$, $z_b=-2$. Substituting [F3] into [F2] gives the displayed fraction, with denominator $(1+2\gamma)^2=(3-\sqrt2)^2=11-6\sqrt2$. By [F5], $7/5<\sqrt2<3/2$: squaring the positive endpoints gives $49/25<2<9/4$. Thus the numerator is greater than $1/200$ and less than $9/40$, while the denominator is greater than $2$. Consequently $0<R(1/10,-2)<9/80<1$.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, independent real random variables
$Y_1,\ldots,Y_d$ with marginal Borel probability laws $\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_d$,
and a degree cutoff vector $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$. Their joint
law is $\rho=\rho_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_d$, as in
[[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]. Write
$\Gamma=\prod_{j=1}^d\operatorname{supp}(\rho_j)$, with the product Borel
sigma-algebra. The cutoff vector $p$ is **admissible** when, for every
$j=1,\ldots,d$,
$$\int |y|^{2p_j}\,d\rho_j(y)<\infty$$
and the monomial Gram matrix
$$G_j=(\int y^{r+s}\,d\rho_j(y))_{0\le r,s\le p_j}$$
is positive definite, meaning $c^T G_jc>0$ for each nonzero
$c\in\mathbb R^{p_j+1}$. Throughout the pair, assume the selected cutoff
vector is admissible. The admissible degree box is
$\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d:0\le\alpha_j\le p_j\text{ for every }j\}$.
Admissibility gives a finite inner product on each stated polynomial space.
It is only a finite-degree condition; it does not assert that polynomials are
dense in any $L^2(\rho_j)$.

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

derivations.claim: Let $\mathcal P_{p_j}$ be the real vector space spanned by the formal monomials $1,y,\ldots,y^{p_j}$. For $q,r\in\mathcal P_{p_j}$ define $\langle q,r\rangle_{\rho_j}:=\int q(y)r(y)\,d\rho_j(y)$. Every product $qr$ has degree at most $2p_j$ and is integrable by [F2], so the pairing is finite; linearity of the integral makes it bilinear and symmetric. If $q(y)=\sum_{r=0}^{p_j}c_ry^r$, then $\langle q,q\rangle_{\rho_j}=c^TG_jc$, which is positive for each nonzero formal polynomial by [F1]. Thus this is an inner product on $\mathcal P_{p_j}$.

Every $q\in\mathcal P_{p_j}$ has finite squared integral by [F2], so it defines an $L^2(\rho_j)$ class. If that class is zero, then $q=0$ almost everywhere and $\int q^2\,d\rho_j=0$; by [F1] its coefficient vector must be zero. Thus the class map is injective and the monomial classes are linearly independent. The formal monomials are also independent by uniqueness of their coefficient lists, so [F3] applies to this list in $\mathcal P_{p_j}$. Its residual at stage $k$ is $y^k$ minus a polynomial of degree at most $k-1$, so it has degree $k$ and leading coefficient $1$.

Each residual is nonzero in $\mathcal P_{p_j}$ by its degree and leading coefficient, so [F4] makes its norm strictly positive. The normalized residual is orthogonal to the preceding polynomials and has positive leading coefficient. At $k=0$, the residual is $1$ and its norm is $\sqrt{\int1\,d\rho_j}=1$ because $\rho_j$ is a probability law; hence $\phi_{j,0}=1$. This proves the stated finite orthonormal family.

$p=(p_1,\ldots,p_d)$ from [[def-finite-product-chaos-input]], the cutoff
total-degree set of order $s\ge0$ and cutoff hyperbolic-cross set of
threshold $N\ge1$ are
$$\Lambda^{\mathrm{TD}}_{s,p}=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d:0\le\alpha_j\le p_j,\ \sum_{j=1}^d\alpha_j\le s\},\qquad
\Lambda^{\mathrm{HC}}_{N,p}=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d:0\le\alpha_j\le p_j,\ \prod_{j=1}^d(\alpha_j+1)\le N\},$$
The cutoff vector prevents either set from requesting
polynomials above the moment degree declared in

downward-closed set is required, this means $\alpha\in\Lambda$ and

derivations.claim: If $\alpha\in\Lambda^{\mathrm{TD}}_{s,p}$, then every coordinate satisfies $0\le\alpha_j\le p_j$ by the cutoff condition in [F1]. Hence this set is a subset of the finite box $\prod_j\{0,\ldots,p_j\}$.

Let $(\Gamma,\mathcal B(\Gamma),\rho)$ be the finite product-law probability
space of [[def-finite-product-chaos-input]], and let $V$ be a separable real
Hilbert space. Define $L^2_\rho(V)$ to be the space of strongly measurable
maps $U:\Gamma\to V$ for which
$\int_\Gamma\|U(y)\|_V^2\,d\rho(y)<\infty$, modulo equality
$\rho$-almost everywhere. Its inner product is
$$ (U,W)_{L^2_\rho(V)}=\int_\Gamma (U(y),W(y))_V\,d\rho(y). $$

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, let $B$ be a separable
Banach space, and let $f:\Omega\to B$ be Borel-measurable. Then $f$ is strongly
measurable: outside a $P$-null set it is the pointwise limit of finite-valued
measurable simple functions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For $U,W\in L^2_\rho(V)$, pointwise Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|(U(y),W(y))_V|\le\|U(y)\|_V\|W(y)\|_V$. Integrating and applying [F3] shows that the product is integrable and the pairing is finite. Changing either representative on a null set does not change the integral. The pairing is bilinear and symmetric. If its value on $(U,U)$ is zero, then for each integer $n\ge1$ the set $E_n=\{y:\|U(y)\|_V\ge1/n\}$ has measure zero, since $0=\int\|U\|^2\ge\rho(E_n)/n^2$; their countable union contains every point where $U\ne0$. Thus the class of $U$ is zero, proving positive definiteness.

Let $(U_n)$ be Cauchy in the displayed norm. By [A1] select a subsequence $(U_{n_k})$ with $\|U_{n_{k+1}}-U_{n_k}\|_{L^2_\rho(V)}\le2^{-k}$. By [A2], choose strongly measurable representatives for these countably many classes and simple-approximation witnesses for each representative; replace each representative by zero on its measurable null exceptional set, obtaining Borel versions of the same classes. Put $d_k(y)=\|U_{n_{k+1}}(y)-U_{n_k}(y)\|_V$ and $s_m=\sum_{k=1}^m d_k$. Minkowski [F4] gives $\|s_m\|_2\le\sum_{k=1}^m2^{-k}\le1$. The functions $s_m^2$ increase, so monotone convergence [F4] yields $\int(\lim_m s_m)^2\,d\rho\le1$. Therefore $\sum_kd_k(y)<\infty$ outside a measurable null set; otherwise its square integral would be infinite on a set of positive measure.

Let $E=\{y:\sum_kd_k(y)<\infty\}$, a Borel set of full measure by step 1.2. On $E$, $(U_{n_k}(y))$ is Cauchy in $V$ and hence has a limit by [F2]. Define $U(y)$ to be this limit on $E$ and zero on $E^c$. The Borel maps equal to $U_{n_k}$ on $E$ and zero on $E^c$ converge pointwise everywhere to $U$; their pointwise limit is Borel measurable (equivalently, distances to a countable dense subset of $V$ are Borel limits). By [F5], $U$ is strongly measurable. If $g_m=\sum_{k\ge m}d_k$, then $g_m\downarrow0$ almost everywhere, $g_m\le\lim_k s_k$, and the latter is in $L^2$ by step 1.2. Dominated convergence [F6] gives $\|g_m\|_2\to0$, while $\|U-U_{n_m}\|_V\le g_m$ almost everywhere on $E$. Thus $U_{n_m}\to U$ in $L^2_\rho(V)$.

Since $(U_n)$ is Cauchy and its subsequence converges to $U$, the full sequence converges to $U$: for $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ so $\|U_n-U_m\|<\varepsilon/2$ for $m,n\ge N$, then choose $n_k\ge N$ with $\|U_{n_k}-U\|<\varepsilon/2$; the triangle inequality gives $\|U_n-U\|<\varepsilon$ for $n\ge N$. This proves completeness.

Let $U\in L^2_\rho(V)$ and choose a strongly measurable representative with simple approximants and measurable null exceptional set as in the definition. Change the representative and approximants to zero on that set; the resulting representative is measurable and the finite-valued simple approximants converge to it everywhere. Truncate each approximant to zero where its norm exceeds $2\|U(y)\|_V$. The truncation set is measurable; the truncated functions remain finite-valued simple functions, converge to $U$ almost everywhere, and their squared errors are bounded by $9\|U(y)\|_V^2$. Dominated convergence [F6] gives convergence in $L^2_\rho(V)$, proving density.
