Let $D\subset\mathbb R^m$ be a bounded polyhedral open set and
$V=H_0^1(D;\mathbb R)$ with norm $\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}$.
[[lem-parabolic-zero-boundary-sobolev-space-is-separable]] supplies the
separable Hilbert structure under Countable Choice; the gradient norm is
equivalent to its Sobolev norm there.

Let $Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_d)$ have the product law $\rho$ of
[[def-finite-product-chaos-input]], and assume its support $\Gamma$ is bounded,
so $|y_j|\le R_j<\infty$ for every $y\in\Gamma$.
For real coefficient functions $a_0,\ldots,a_d\in L^\infty(D)$ define
$$a(x,y)=a_0(x)+\sum_{j=1}^d y_j a_j(x).$$
Assume constants $0<a_*\le a^*<\infty$ satisfy, for every $y\in\Gamma$,
$a_*\le a(x,y)\le a^*$ for almost every $x\in D$. This explicit
all-parameter condition ensures the pointwise variational problem is
well-posed for every stated parameter, not merely almost every one. Let
$F(y)=f_0+\sum_{j=1}^d y_j f_j$ with $f_j\in V^*$.

The pointwise weak form is
$$a_y(u,v)=\int_Da(x,y)\nabla u(x)\cdot\nabla v(x)\,dx=F(y)(v),\qquad v\in V.$$
The Bochner weak form uses the bilinear form
$$\mathcal A(U,W)=\int_\Gamma a_y(U(y),W(y))\,d\rho(y)$$
and the functional $\mathcal F(W)=\int_\Gamma F(y)(W(y))\,d\rho(y)$ on
$L^2_\rho(V)$ from [[def-finite-input-bochner-l2-space]].

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $(\Gamma,\mathcal B(\Gamma),\rho)$ be the finite product-law probability
space of [[def-finite-product-chaos-input]], and let $V$ be a separable real
Hilbert space. Define $L^2_\rho(V)$ to be the space of strongly measurable
maps $U:\Gamma\to V$ for which
$\int_\Gamma\|U(y)\|_V^2\,d\rho(y)<\infty$, modulo equality
$\rho$-almost everywhere. Its inner product is
$$ (U,W)_{L^2_\rho(V)}=\int_\Gamma (U(y),W(y))_V\,d\rho(y). $$

derivations.claim: Choose finite-valued measurable simple maps $U_n,W_n$ converging respectively to $U,W$ almost everywhere, using [F2]. On every intersection of their finite partition sets, $y\mapsto a_y(U_n(y),W_n(y))$ is an affine continuous scalar function of $y$ by the displayed coefficient formula in [F1]. It is therefore measurable. On the common full-measure set where both approximations converge, continuity of the bounded bilinear form gives convergence to $a_y(U(y),W(y))$. Defining the scalar function arbitrarily on the measurable exceptional null set gives a measurable representative.

For a finite-valued simple $W_n$ converging almost everywhere to $W$, the scalar function $F(y)(W_n(y))$ is measurable on each partition piece because $F(y)$ is affine continuous into the finite-dimensional span of $f_0,\ldots,f_d$. Its pointwise limit on the full-measure convergence set is $F(y)(W(y))$, so the latter has a measurable representative. Since $|y_j|\le R_j$, $\|F(y)\|_{V^*}\le\|f_0\|_{V^*}+\sum_jR_j\|f_j\|_{V^*}$; hence $F\in L^2_\rho(V^*)$.

The pointwise bound [F1] gives $|a_y(U(y),W(y))|\le a^*\|U(y)\|_V\|W(y)\|_V$. Both norm functions are square-integrable, so [F3] makes this majorant integrable. The form integral is finite and depends only on the almost-everywhere classes by [F4].
Pointwise duality gives $|F(y)(W(y))|\le\|F(y)\|_{V^*}\|W(y)\|_V$. Apply [F3] to obtain the stated integrability and functional bound.

Integrating the pointwise coercivity bound [F1] gives $\mathcal A(U,U)\ge a_*\int\|U(y)\|_V^2\,d\rho=a_*\|U\|_{\mathcal H}^2$. Integrating the pointwise continuity bound and applying [F3] as in step 2.1 gives $|\mathcal A(U,W)|\le a^*\|U\|_{\mathcal H}\|W\|_{\mathcal H}$. These estimates prove the remaining assertions.

Let $\rho_j$ be one factor law with admissible degree $p_j$ as in
[[def-finite-product-chaos-input]]. The monomial classes
$1,y,\ldots,y^{p_j}$ are linearly independent in $L^2(\rho_j)$. Applying the
finite Gram–Schmidt recursion to this ordered list gives real orthonormal
polynomials $\phi_{j,0},\ldots,\phi_{j,p_j}$, where $\phi_{j,k}$ has degree
$k$, positive leading coefficient, and $\phi_{j,0}=1$.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: For $\alpha,\beta$ in the admissible box set $g_j(y_j)=\phi_{j,\alpha_j}(y_j)\phi_{j,\beta_j}(y_j)$. Each $g_j$ is integrable because it is a polynomial of degree at most $2p_j$ and the $2p_j$ moment is finite. Repeated Tonelli [F3] first gives $\int_\Gamma\prod_j|g_j(y_j)|\,d\rho=\prod_{j=1}^d\int|g_j|\,d\rho_j<\infty$; repeated Fubini [F3] then gives $\int_\Gamma\prod_jg_j(y_j)\,d\rho=\prod_{j=1}^d\int g_j\,d\rho_j$. The product-law statement [F2] identifies this finite product measure with the joint law.

The factorization in step 1.1 and univariate orthonormality [F1] give $\int_\Gamma\psi_\alpha\psi_\beta\,d\rho=\prod_{j=1}^d\delta_{\alpha_j\beta_j}$. This product is one exactly when every coordinate agrees, and zero otherwise; with $\beta=\alpha$ it also shows $\psi_\alpha\in L^2(\rho)$. Multiplying $\phi_{j,0}=1$ over the finitely many coordinates gives $\psi_0=1$, so whenever $0\in\Lambda$ the finite family includes this constant mode.

Let $\Lambda$ be finite, contain $0$, and let
$\psi=(\psi_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Lambda}$ be the real orthonormal basis of
[[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]]. Set $N=|\Lambda|$ and
$$K_\Lambda(y)=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}|\psi_\alpha(y)|^2.$$
The algorithm takes an evaluable real function $u$, a positive integer sample
count $M$, and independent samples $X_1,\ldots,X_M$ from the probability law
$d\nu=(K_\Lambda/N)\,d\rho$. It forms
$$G=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M\frac{N}{K_\Lambda(X_i)}\psi(X_i)\psi(X_i)^T,\qquad
b=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M\frac{N}{K_\Lambda(X_i)}u(X_i)\psi(X_i).$$
If every eigenvalue of $G$ lies in $[1/2,3/2]$, return the unique coefficient
vector $c=G^{-1}b$ and polynomial $\hat u=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha\psi_\alpha$.
Otherwise return `unstable-sample` and no coefficients. The weighted empirical
objective minimized on the accepted branch is
$$\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M\frac{N}{K_\Lambda(X_i)}|u(X_i)-p(X_i)|^2,$$
over $p\in\mathcal P_\Lambda$.

Let $\rho=\otimes_{j=1}^d\rho_j$ and form $\psi_\alpha$ from
[[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]] for indices in the admissible degree
box. Then each $\psi_\alpha$ belongs to
$L^2(\rho)$ and
$$\int_\Gamma\psi_\alpha(y)\psi_\beta(y)\,d\rho(y)=\begin{cases}1,&\alpha=\beta,\\0,&\alpha\ne\beta.\end{cases}$$
In particular, the family indexed by any finite subset $\Lambda$ of the box is
orthonormal; when $0\in\Lambda$, it includes the constant mode $\psi_0=1$.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

derivations.claim: Since $0\in\Lambda$ and $\psi_0=1$, $K_\Lambda(y)\ge1$. By [F2]–[F3], $\int K_\Lambda\,d\rho=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}\int|\psi_\alpha|^2\,d\rho=N$. Therefore $d\nu=(K_\Lambda/N)d\rho$ is a probability measure and the denominator in [F1] is positive everywhere.

For each pair $\alpha, eta$, [F4] and $\int|\psi_\alpha\psi_ eta|\,dho\le1$ show $\int|A_{\alpha eta}|\,d
u=\int|\psi_\alpha\psi_ eta|\,dho\le1$, so the entry is integrable under $
u$. Using the signed density identity in [F4], its expectation is $\int_\Gamma \psi_\alpha(y)\psi_ eta(y)\,dho(y)=\delta_{\alpha eta}$ by [F2], hence $\mathbb E_
u A=I_N$. The rank-one outer product is positive semidefinite and has operator norm $N\|\psi(y)\|_2^2/K_\Lambda(y)=N$, proving the remaining assertions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded
polyhedral open set with $d\ge1$. Put
$$H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R),\qquad V=W^{1,2}_0(\Omega;\mathbb R),\qquad \|v\|_V=\|v\|_{W^{1,2}(\Omega)}.$$
Then $V$ is a separable real Hilbert space, and the inclusion
$V\hookrightarrow H$ is continuous, injective and dense. Consequently
$(V,H,V^*)$ is a real evolution triple in the sense of
[[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]]. The gradient norm
$\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$ is equivalent to this norm on $V$ by Poincare's
inequality.

Let $D\subset\mathbb R^m$ be a bounded polyhedral open set and
$V=H_0^1(D;\mathbb R)$ with norm $\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}$.
[[lem-parabolic-zero-boundary-sobolev-space-is-separable]] supplies the
separable Hilbert structure under Countable Choice; the gradient norm is
equivalent to its Sobolev norm there.

Let $Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_d)$ have the product law $\rho$ of
[[def-finite-product-chaos-input]], and assume its support $\Gamma$ is bounded,
so $|y_j|\le R_j<\infty$ for every $y\in\Gamma$.
For real coefficient functions $a_0,\ldots,a_d\in L^\infty(D)$ define
$$a(x,y)=a_0(x)+\sum_{j=1}^d y_j a_j(x).$$
Assume constants $0<a_*\le a^*<\infty$ satisfy, for every $y\in\Gamma$,
$a_*\le a(x,y)\le a^*$ for almost every $x\in D$. This explicit
all-parameter condition ensures the pointwise variational problem is
well-posed for every stated parameter, not merely almost every one. Let
$F(y)=f_0+\sum_{j=1}^d y_j f_j$ with $f_j\in V^*$.

The pointwise weak form is
$$a_y(u,v)=\int_Da(x,y)\nabla u(x)\cdot\nabla v(x)\,dx=F(y)(v),\qquad v\in V.$$
The Bochner weak form uses the bilinear form
$$\mathcal A(U,W)=\int_\Gamma a_y(U(y),W(y))\,d\rho(y)$$
and the functional $\mathcal F(W)=\int_\Gamma F(y)(W(y))\,d\rho(y)$ on
$L^2_\rho(V)$ from [[def-finite-input-bochner-l2-space]].

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, let $B$ be a separable
Banach space, and let $f:\Omega\to B$ be Borel-measurable. Then $f$ is strongly
measurable: outside a $P$-null set it is the pointwise limit of finite-valued
measurable simple functions.

For the model of [[def-uniformly-elliptic-affine-random-diffusion]], let
$\mathcal H=L^2_\rho(V)$. For $U,W\in\mathcal H$, the scalar functions
$y\mapsto a_y(U(y),W(y))$ and $y\mapsto F(y)(W(y))$ are measurable and
integrable, so $\mathcal A(U,W)$ and $\mathcal F(W)$ are well-defined on
equivalence classes. They satisfy
$$|\mathcal A(U,W)|\le a^*\|U\|_{\mathcal H}\|W\|_{\mathcal H},\qquad
\mathcal A(U,U)\ge a_*\|U\|_{\mathcal H}^2,$$
and
$$|\mathcal F(W)|\le \|F\|_{L^2_\rho(V^*)}\|W\|_{\mathcal H}<\infty.$$

Assume Countable Choice. For the space $L^2_\rho(V)$ of
[[def-finite-input-bochner-l2-space]], the displayed integral pairing is a
well-defined real inner product, its norm is
$$\|U\|_{L^2_\rho(V)}=\left(\int_\Gamma\|U(y)\|_V^2\,d\rho(y)\right)^{1/2},$$
and this norm is complete. Moreover, finite-valued strongly measurable
functions are dense in this space.

derivations.claim: For each $y\in\Gamma$, [F2] verifies the boundedness and coercivity hypotheses of [F3], while $F(y)=f_0+\sum_j y_j f_j$ is a bounded functional. Lax–Milgram gives a unique $u(y)\in V$ and $\|u(y)\|_V\le F_{\max}/a_*$, where $F_{\max}:=\sup_{y\in\Gamma}\|F(y)\|_{V^*}<\infty$ because $\Gamma$ is bounded.

For $y,z\in\Gamma$, put $d=u(y)-u(z)$ and subtract the weak equations: $a_y(d,v)=(F(y)-F(z))(v)+(a_z-a_y)(u(z),v).$ The affine formulas give $\|F(y)-F(z)\|_{V^*}\le C_F\|y-z\|_1$ and $|a_z(v,w)-a_y(v,w)|\le C_a\|y-z\|_1\|v\|_V\|w\|_V$, where $C_F=\sum_j\|f_j\|_{V^*}$ and $C_a=\sum_j\|a_j\|_{L^\infty(D)}$. Set $v=d$ and use [F2] and the bound $\|u(z)\|_V\le F_{\max}/a_*$ from step 1.1. If $d\ne0$, divide the resulting coercive inequality by $\|d\|_V$; if $d=0$ the conclusion is immediate. This proves $\|u(y)-u(z)\|_V\le a_*^{-1}(C_F+C_aF_{\max}/a_*)\|y-z\|_1$. Thus $u$ is Lipschitz and Borel measurable.

Since $V$ is separable, [F4] makes $u$ strongly measurable. The uniform bound in step 1.1 and $\rho(\Gamma)=1$ give $\int_\Gamma\|u(y)\|_V^2\,d\rho(y)\le(F_{\max}/a_*)^2<\infty$, so $u\in L^2_\rho(V)$.

For a finite-valued simple test $W(y)=\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1_{E_i}(y)v_i$, integrate the pointwise weak identity for each $v_i$ over $E_i$ and sum; [F5] ensures the scalar integrands are measurable and integrable. This gives $\mathcal A(u,W)=\mathcal F(W)$.

The bounds in [F5] make both sides continuous on $L^2_\rho(V)$. Finite-valued simple tests are dense by [F6], so step 3.1 extends to every $W$. If two Bochner solutions existed, testing their difference against itself and using the coercivity bound in [F5] would force their difference to be zero.

For real $u\in L^2(\rho)$ and finite $\Lambda$, define
$$c_\alpha=\langle u,\psi_\alpha\rangle_{L^2(\rho)}=\int u(y)\psi_\alpha(y)\,d\rho(y),\qquad P_\Lambda u=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha\psi_\alpha.$$
The scalar integral pairing is choice-free: for representatives $f,g$ of
classes in $L^2(\rho)$, Cauchy–Schwarz makes $fg$ integrable, and the integral
is unchanged when either representative is changed on a null set. Its
bilinearity follows from linearity of the integral and its symmetry from
commutativity of multiplication; moreover
$\int f^2\,d\rho=\|[f]\|_2^2$, so it is positive definite on the quotient.
These facts use only the integral pairing, not completeness of $L^2(\rho)$.
The displayed finite sum is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal P_\Lambda$
of [[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]].

Let $\rho=\otimes_{j=1}^d\rho_j$ and form $\psi_\alpha$ from
[[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]] for indices in the admissible degree

$L^2(\rho)$ and

In particular, the family indexed by any finite subset $\Lambda$ of the box is
orthonormal; when $0\in\Lambda$, it includes the constant mode $\psi_0=1$.

For real $u\in L^2(\rho)$ and finite $\Lambda$, define
$$c_\alpha=\langle u,\psi_\alpha\rangle_{L^2(\rho)}=\int u(y)\psi_\alpha(y)\,d\rho(y),\qquad P_\Lambda u=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha\psi_\alpha.$$
The scalar integral pairing is choice-free: for representatives $f,g$ of
classes in $L^2(\rho)$, Cauchy–Schwarz makes $fg$ integrable, and the integral
is unchanged when either representative is changed on a null set. Its
bilinearity follows from linearity of the integral and its symmetry from
commutativity of multiplication; moreover
$\int f^2\,d\rho=\|[f]\|_2^2$, so it is positive definite on the quotient.
These facts use only the integral pairing, not completeness of $L^2(\rho)$.
The displayed finite sum is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal P_\Lambda$
of [[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]].

derivations.claim: For each $\beta\in\Lambda$, bilinearity and [F2] give $\langle u-P_\Lambda u,\psi_\beta\rangle =c_\beta-\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha\delta_{\alpha\beta}=0$. Thus the residual is orthogonal to every basis vector and hence to their finite span.

Write $u=P_\Lambda u+(u-P_\Lambda u)$. By step 1.1 the two terms are orthogonal, so bilinearity and symmetry from [F3] give $\|u\|_2^2=\|P_\Lambda u\|_2^2+\|u-P_\Lambda u\|_2^2$. Expanding the finite sum with [F2] gives $\|P_\Lambda u\|_2^2=\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in\Lambda}c_\alpha c_\beta\delta_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha^2$. This proves the norm identity directly from the integral pairing.

Since $\psi_0=1$, $c_0=\langle u,1\rangle=\mathbb E[u]$. The centered variable decomposes as $u-\mathbb E[u]=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}}c_\alpha\psi_\alpha+(u-P_\Lambda u)$. The two summands are orthogonal by step 1.1, and expansion of the integral norm square as in step 2.1, followed by [F2], gives the displayed variance identity.

Let $(\Gamma,\mathcal B(\Gamma),\rho)$ be the finite product-law probability
space of [[def-finite-product-chaos-input]], and let $V$ be a separable real
Hilbert space. Define $L^2_\rho(V)$ to be the space of strongly measurable
maps $U:\Gamma\to V$ for which
$\int_\Gamma\|U(y)\|_V^2\,d\rho(y)<\infty$, modulo equality
$\rho$-almost everywhere. Its inner product is
$$ (U,W)_{L^2_\rho(V)}=\int_\Gamma (U(y),W(y))_V\,d\rho(y). $$

Assume Countable Choice. For the space $L^2_\rho(V)$ of
[[def-finite-input-bochner-l2-space]], the displayed integral pairing is a
well-defined real inner product, its norm is
$$\|U\|_{L^2_\rho(V)}=\left(\int_\Gamma\|U(y)\|_V^2\,d\rho(y)\right)^{1/2},$$
and this norm is complete. Moreover, finite-valued strongly measurable
functions are dense in this space.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

derivations.claim: Fix $U\in L^2_\rho(V)$ and $\varepsilon>0$. By [F2], choose a finite-valued simple map $S=\sum_{k=1}^m\mathbf1_{E_k}v_k$ with $\|U-S\|_{L^2_\rho(V)}<\varepsilon/2$. Because there are finitely many values, it is enough to approximate each term $\mathbf1_{E_k}v_k$ so that the sum of its errors is less than $\varepsilon/2$.

For each $k$, use [F3] and [F4] to choose $s_k\in\mathcal S$ and $w_k\in V_0$ with $\|\mathbf1_{E_k}-s_k\|_{L^2(\rho)}\|v_k\|_V+ \|s_k\|_{L^2(\rho)}\|v_k-w_k\|_V<\varepsilon/(2m)$. Such choices are possible by first making the scalar error arbitrarily small, which bounds $\|s_k\|_2\le\|\mathbf1_{E_k}\|_2+\|\mathbf1_{E_k}-s_k\|_2$, and then making the vector error small. The product norm estimate $\|\mathbf1_{E_k}v_k-s_kw_k\|_{L^2_\rho(V)} \le\|\mathbf1_{E_k}-s_k\|_2\|v_k\|_V+\|s_k\|_2\|v_k-w_k\|_V$ follows pointwise from the triangle inequality and then from scalar square-integral estimation. Each product is strongly measurable by [F5], so these are legitimate Bochner-space norms.

The finite sum $\sum_{k=1}^m s_kw_k$ belongs to the displayed algebraic tensor span, and the triangle inequality with step 2.1 gives distance less than $\varepsilon/2$ from $S$. Together with step 1.1 its distance from $U$ is less than $\varepsilon$. Since $U$ and $\varepsilon$ were arbitrary, the span is dense.

Let $\Lambda$ be a finite index set and let $Q$ be any declared finite
cubature functional
$Q(g)=\sum_{q=1}^Jw_qg(y^{(q)})$ whose nodes lie in the domain of evaluation
of $g$. For an evaluable real function $u$, define the quadrature coefficient
and the resulting polynomial by
$$\widehat c_\alpha:=Q(u\psi_\alpha),\qquad
\widehat P_\Lambda u:=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}\widehat c_\alpha\psi_\alpha.$$
The exact coefficients $c_\alpha$ and projection $P_\Lambda u$ are those of
[[def-finite-chaos-orthogonal-projection]]. This definition gives no
accuracy claim for a general cubature rule.

Let $\Lambda$ be finite, contain $0$, and let the real basis
$(\psi_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Lambda}$ be as in
[[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]]. For real $u\in L^2(\rho)$ set
$c_\alpha=\langle u,\psi_\alpha\rangle$ and
$P_\Lambda u=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha\psi_\alpha$ as in
[[def-finite-chaos-orthogonal-projection]]. Then
$$\|u\|_{L^2(\rho)}^2=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha^2+
\|u-P_\Lambda u\|_{L^2(\rho)}^2.$$
The residual is orthogonal to $\mathcal P_\Lambda$,
$\mathbb E[u]=c_0$, and
$$\operatorname{Var}(u)=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}}c_\alpha^2+
\|u-P_\Lambda u\|_{L^2(\rho)}^2.$$
Here $\operatorname{Var}(u)=\mathbb E[(u-\mathbb E u)^2]$; no completeness of
the polynomial family is assumed.

Let $\rho=\otimes_{j=1}^d\rho_j$ and form $\psi_\alpha$ from
[[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]] for indices in the admissible degree
box. Then each $\psi_\alpha$ belongs to
$L^2(\rho)$ and
$$\int_\Gamma\psi_\alpha(y)\psi_\beta(y)\,d\rho(y)=\begin{cases}1,&\alpha=\beta,\\0,&\alpha\ne\beta.\end{cases}$$
In particular, the family indexed by any finite subset $\Lambda$ of the box is
orthonormal; when $0\in\Lambda$, it includes the constant mode $\psi_0=1$.

For real $u\in L^2(\rho)$ and finite $\Lambda$, define
$$c_\alpha=\langle u,\psi_\alpha\rangle_{L^2(\rho)}=\int u(y)\psi_\alpha(y)\,d\rho(y),\qquad P_\Lambda u=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha\psi_\alpha.$$
The scalar integral pairing is choice-free: for representatives $f,g$ of
classes in $L^2(\rho)$, Cauchy–Schwarz makes $fg$ integrable, and the integral
is unchanged when either representative is changed on a null set. Its
bilinearity follows from linearity of the integral and its symmetry from
commutativity of multiplication; moreover
$\int f^2\,d\rho=\|[f]\|_2^2$, so it is positive definite on the quotient.
These facts use only the integral pairing, not completeness of $L^2(\rho)$.
The displayed finite sum is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal P_\Lambda$
of [[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]].

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Subtract the two finite expansions to obtain $\widehat P_\Lambda u-P_\Lambda u=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}(\widehat c_\alpha-c_\alpha)\psi_\alpha\in\mathcal P_\Lambda$. By [F2], this difference is orthogonal to $u-P_\Lambda u$.

The identity $u-\widehat P_\Lambda u=(u-P_\Lambda u)-(\widehat P_\Lambda u-P_\Lambda u)$ is an orthogonal sum by step 1.1. Expanding its squared norm using [F4] gives $\|u-\widehat P_\Lambda u\|^2 =\|u-P_\Lambda u\|^2+\|\widehat P_\Lambda u-P_\Lambda u\|^2$; orthonormality [F3] identifies the second term with $\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}|\widehat c_\alpha-c_\alpha|^2$. To obtain the final inequality, use [F5] to expand $\|v+w\|_2^2$ and deduce $\|v+w\|_2\le\|v\|_2+\|w\|_2$ for $v=u-P_\Lambda u$ and $w=P_\Lambda u-\widehat P_\Lambda u$.

Let $\Lambda$ and $K_\Lambda$ be as in
[[alg-christoffel-weighted-least-squares-collocation]], with
$N=|\Lambda|\ge1$. Then $K_\Lambda\ge1$ pointwise, the measure
$d\nu=(K_\Lambda/N)d\rho$ is a probability measure, and the random matrix
$$A(X)=\frac{N}{K_\Lambda(X)}\psi(X)\psi(X)^T,\qquad X\sim\nu,$$
satisfies $A\succeq0$, $\mathbb E_\nu A=I_N$, and
$\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le N$ almost surely.

Let $\Lambda$ be finite, contain $0$, and let
$\psi=(\psi_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Lambda}$ be the real orthonormal basis of
[[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]]. Set $N=|\Lambda|$ and
$$K_\Lambda(y)=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}|\psi_\alpha(y)|^2.$$
The algorithm takes an evaluable real function $u$, a positive integer sample
count $M$, and independent samples $X_1,\ldots,X_M$ from the probability law
$d\nu=(K_\Lambda/N)\,d\rho$. It forms
$$G=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M\frac{N}{K_\Lambda(X_i)}\psi(X_i)\psi(X_i)^T,\qquad
b=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M\frac{N}{K_\Lambda(X_i)}u(X_i)\psi(X_i).$$
If every eigenvalue of $G$ lies in $[1/2,3/2]$, return the unique coefficient
vector $c=G^{-1}b$ and polynomial $\hat u=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha\psi_\alpha$.
Otherwise return `unstable-sample` and no coefficients. The weighted empirical
objective minimized on the accepted branch is
$$\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M\frac{N}{K_\Lambda(X_i)}|u(X_i)-p(X_i)|^2,$$
over $p\in\mathcal P_\Lambda$.

Let $B_1,\ldots,B_m$ be independent centered random Hermitian $q\times q$ matrices, $q,m\ge1$. Suppose $R>0$, $v\ge0$, and
$$\|B_i\|_{\rm op}\le R\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad\|\mathbb E B_i^2\|_{\rm op}\le v\quad(1\le i\le m).$$
Writing $Y=\sum_{i=1}^m B_i$, for $0<s<3/R$ one has
$$\mathbb E\operatorname{tr}\exp(sY)\le q\exp\left(\frac{ms^2v}{2(1-sR/3)}\right).$$
Consequently, for $u>0$ when $v>0$,
$$\mathbb P\{\lambda_{\max}(Y)\ge u\}\le q\exp\left(-\frac{u^2}{2(mv+Ru/3)}\right).$$
For every $b>0$, the following convenient forms also hold:
$$\mathbb P\left\{\lambda_{\max}(Y)>\sqrt{2mvb}+\frac{2Rb}{3}\right\}\le qe^{-b},\qquad\mathbb P\left\{\|Y\|_{\rm op}>\sqrt{2mvb}+\frac{2Rb}{3}\right\}\le2qe^{-b}.$$
If $v=0$, all $B_i$ and $Y$ vanish almost surely, so the displayed positive-threshold conclusions remain valid.

Let $\Lambda$ be finite, contain $0$, and let
$\psi=(\psi_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Lambda}$ be the real orthonormal basis of
[[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]]. Set $N=|\Lambda|$ and
$$K_\Lambda(y)=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}|\psi_\alpha(y)|^2.$$
The algorithm takes an evaluable real function $u$, a positive integer sample
count $M$, and independent samples $X_1,\ldots,X_M$ from the probability law
$d\nu=(K_\Lambda/N)\,d\rho$. It forms
$$G=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M\frac{N}{K_\Lambda(X_i)}\psi(X_i)\psi(X_i)^T,\qquad
b=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M\frac{N}{K_\Lambda(X_i)}u(X_i)\psi(X_i).$$
If every eigenvalue of $G$ lies in $[1/2,3/2]$, return the unique coefficient
vector $c=G^{-1}b$ and polynomial $\hat u=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha\psi_\alpha$.
Otherwise return `unstable-sample` and no coefficients. The weighted empirical
objective minimized on the accepted branch is
$$\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M\frac{N}{K_\Lambda(X_i)}|u(X_i)-p(X_i)|^2,$$
over $p\in\mathcal P_\Lambda$.

derivations.claim: Put $B_i=A_i-I_N$. Then $\mathbb EB_i=0$. Since $0\preceq A_i\preceq NI_N$, spectral calculus gives $A_i^2\preceq NA_i$, and hence $0\preceq\mathbb EB_i^2=\mathbb EA_i^2-I_N\preceq(N-1)I_N\preceq NI_N$. Also every eigenvalue of $A_i$ lies in $[0,N]$, so $\|B_i\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le N$. These are the hypotheses of [F2] with $R=v=N$.

Apply [F3] to $Y=\sum_{i=1}^M B_i$ with $t=M/2$. Direct substitution gives $\mathbb P\{\|G-I_N\|_{\mathrm{op}}>1/2\}\le 2N\exp(-3M/(28N))$, because $G-I_N=Y/M$ and $(M/2)^2/[2(MN+N(M/2)/3)]=3M/(28N)$.

The sample-size condition makes the last bound at most $2N\exp[-(9/7)\log(2N/\delta)] =\delta(\delta/(2N))^{2/7}\le\delta$, since $0<\delta/(2N)<1$. On the complementary event, for every unit vector $x$, $|x^T(G-I_N)x|\le\|G-I_N\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1/2$; the Rayleigh quotient characterization therefore puts every eigenvalue of $G$ in $[1/2,3/2]$.

For the model of [[def-uniformly-elliptic-affine-random-diffusion]], let
$\mathcal H=L^2_\rho(V)$. For $U,W\in\mathcal H$, the scalar functions
$y\mapsto a_y(U(y),W(y))$ and $y\mapsto F(y)(W(y))$ are measurable and
integrable, so $\mathcal A(U,W)$ and $\mathcal F(W)$ are well-defined on
equivalence classes. They satisfy
$$|\mathcal A(U,W)|\le a^*\|U\|_{\mathcal H}\|W\|_{\mathcal H},\qquad
\mathcal A(U,U)\ge a_*\|U\|_{\mathcal H}^2,$$
and
$$|\mathcal F(W)|\le \|F\|_{L^2_\rho(V^*)}\|W\|_{\mathcal H}<\infty.$$

Under the hypotheses of [[def-uniformly-elliptic-affine-random-diffusion]],
for each $y\in\Gamma$ there is a unique $u(y)\in V$ satisfying the pointwise
weak problem. The map $y\mapsto u(y)$ is Lipschitz on the bounded parameter
set, strongly measurable, and belongs to $L^2_\rho(V)$. It is also the unique
solution of the Bochner weak equation
$$\mathcal A(u,W)=\mathcal F(W)\qquad(W\in L^2_\rho(V)).$$

Assume Countable Choice. For the space $L^2_\rho(V)$ of
[[def-finite-input-bochner-l2-space]], the displayed integral pairing is a
well-defined real inner product, its norm is
$$\|U\|_{L^2_\rho(V)}=\left(\int_\Gamma\|U(y)\|_V^2\,d\rho(y)\right)^{1/2},$$
and this norm is complete. Moreover, finite-valued strongly measurable
functions are dense in this space.

Let $\rho=\otimes_{j=1}^d\rho_j$ and form $\psi_\alpha$ from
[[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]] for indices in the admissible degree
box. Then each $\psi_\alpha$ belongs to
$L^2(\rho)$ and
$$\int_\Gamma\psi_\alpha(y)\psi_\beta(y)\,d\rho(y)=\begin{cases}1,&\alpha=\beta,\\0,&\alpha\ne\beta.\end{cases}$$
In particular, the family indexed by any finite subset $\Lambda$ of the box is
orthonormal; when $0\in\Lambda$, it includes the constant mode $\psi_0=1$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ be linear in its first argument, conjugate-linear
in its second, bounded by $M$, and coercive with constant $\alpha>0$:
$$|a(v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad \operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2.$$
Let $F:V\to\mathbb K$ be bounded and conjugate-linear, and let $V_h\subseteq V$
be finite-dimensional. Then there are unique $u\in V$ and $u_h\in V_h$ with
$$a(u,v)=F(v)\quad(v\in V).$$
$$a(u_h,v_h)=F(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h).$$
The solutions satisfy
$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac M\alpha\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.$$
The real bilinear case uses linear functionals and reads $\operatorname{Re}$ as
the identity.

derivations.claim: Each $\psi_\alpha$ is a continuous scalar polynomial. Approximate it pointwise by finite-valued measurable simple real functions; multiplying those functions by a fixed $v\in V$ gives simple $V$-valued maps converging to $\psi_\alpha v$. Thus $\psi_\alpha v$ is strongly measurable by [F5] and has Bochner norm $\|\psi_\alpha\|_{L^2(\rho)}\|v\|_V=\|v\|_V$ by [F4]. A finite basis of $V_h$ and finite $\Lambda$ therefore generate $\mathcal V_{\Lambda,h}$ from finitely many members of $L^2_\rho(V)$, making it finite-dimensional and conforming.

The model form and load satisfy the boundedness and coercivity hypotheses in [F6] by [F1], and the ambient space is Hilbert by [F3]. The finite-dimensional subspace condition is step 1.1. Apply [F6] with $M=a^*$ and $\alpha=a_*$; it gives the unique discrete solution and $\|u-U_{\Lambda,h}\|\le(a^*/a_*)\inf_{W_h\in\mathcal V_{\Lambda,h}}\|u-W_h\|$. This is the claimed estimate.

Use the dyadic composite-Simpson hierarchy of
[[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]]. Let $d\ge1$, $n\ge2d$, and let
$f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$ satisfy the
continuous mixed fourth-derivative hypotheses and bounds $M_S$ of
[[lem-smolyak-mixed-simpson-detail-decay]]. Define the isotropic index set
$$\Lambda_n:=\{\ell\in\mathbb N_0^d:|\ell|_1\le n\},$$
and let $W_{n,d}:=|\mathcal N_{\Lambda_n}|$ be the distinct-node work count
of [[def-smolyak-cubature]] and [[alg-smolyak-node-deduplication]]. For a
dyadic node $x$, let $t(x)=0$ for $x=0,1,1/2$; if $x=p/2^{r+1}$ is interior
and reduced with odd numerator $p$, let $t(x)=r\ge1$. Put
$$a_0:=3,\qquad a_r:=2^r\ (r\ge1),$$
$$\|f\|_{\mathrm{mix},d}:=\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}\left(\frac{17}{2880}\right)^{|S|}M_S,\quad T_d:=\sup_{N\ge1}\sum_{r=1}^{N}r^{d-1}16^{-r},$$
$$D_d:=2\cdot3^d d^{d-1},\qquad C_d:=D_d^4T_d\left(\frac3{\log 2}\right)^{5(d-1)},$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm of [[def-natural-logarithm]]. Then
$T_d<\infty$, and the actual node-union count and error satisfy
$$W_{n,d}=\sum_{\substack{t\in\mathbb N_0^d\\|t|_1\le n}}\prod_{j=1}^d a_{t_j},\qquad 2^n\binom{n-1}{d-1}\le W_{n,d}\le D_d2^n(n+1)^{d-1},$$
$$|I_d(f)-Q_{\Lambda_n}(f)|\le T_d\|f\|_{\mathrm{mix},d}16^{-n}(n+1)^{d-1}\le C_d\|f\|_{\mathrm{mix},d}W_{n,d}^{-4}\bigl(\log(2+W_{n,d})\bigr)^{5(d-1)}.$$
All constants and the mixed-derivative quantity display their dimension
dependence; no weighted-anisotropic tractability claim is made.

Use the dyadic composite-Simpson hierarchy of
[[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]]. Let $d\ge1$. For
$S=\{j_1<\cdots<j_k\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$, define
$$D_Sf:=\partial_{x_{j_k}}^4\cdots\partial_{x_{j_1}}^4f,$$
so these derivatives are applied in increasing coordinate order; set
$D_\varnothing f=f$. Assume every $D_Sf$ is continuous on the closed cube,
with the one-sided endpoint convention of
[[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]], and choose finite bounds $M_S\ge0$
such that $|D_Sf(x)|\le M_S$ on $[0,1]^d$. For
$\ell\in\mathbb N_0^d$, put $S(\ell):=\{j:\ell_j\ge1\}$ and
$$\delta_\ell(f):=(\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)})(f).$$
Then
$$|\delta_\ell(f)|\le M_{S(\ell)}\left(\frac{17}{2880}\right)^{|S(\ell)|}16^{-\sum_{j\in S(\ell)}\ell_j}.$$
Moreover, for every finite $F\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$,
$$\sum_{\ell\in F}|\delta_\ell(f)|\le\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}M_S\left(\frac{17}{43200}\right)^{|S|}<\infty.$$

Fix a dimension $d\ge1$. A finite set $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$ is
**downward closed** if, whenever $\ell\in\Lambda$ and $\ell_j>0$, the index
$\ell-e_j$ also belongs to $\Lambda$; here $e_j$ is the $j$th coordinate unit
vector. In this pair an admissible Smolyak set is a nonempty finite downward-
closed $\Lambda$ that contains $0$.

For a level hierarchy from [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]], define
the **Smolyak cubature functional**
$$Q_\Lambda(f):=\sum_{\ell\in\Lambda}(\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)})(f).$$
Each summand is a finite signed weighted sum. Expanding all differences and
adding coefficients at equal points gives one finite signed weight for each
distinct node in
$$\mathcal N_\Lambda:=\bigcup_{\ell\in\Lambda}X_{\ell_1}\times\cdots\times X_{\ell_d}.$$
The **node-union work count** for this direct evaluation convention is
$W(\Lambda):=|\mathcal N_\Lambda|$, so shared nodes are counted once. A
combined weight may be negative or zero; no positivity claim follows from the
definition.

Let $u\in L^2(\rho)$ be real, choose a representative $\widetilde u$ defined
at every node of the finite cubature rule used below, let $\Lambda$ be finite,
and use the exact and quadrature coefficients from
[[def-finite-chaos-orthogonal-projection]] and
[[def-chaos-quadrature-coefficient-estimator]], with $\widetilde u$ as the
evaluable input to that estimator. Then
$$\|u-\widehat P_\Lambda u\|_{L^2(\rho)}^2
=\|u-P_\Lambda u\|_{L^2(\rho)}^2+
\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}|\widehat c_\alpha-c_\alpha|^2.$$
Since the finite sum equals
$\|\widehat P_\Lambda u-P_\Lambda u\|_{L^2(\rho)}^2$, the triangle inequality
also gives
$$\|u-\widehat P_\Lambda u\|_{L^2(\rho)}
\le\|u-P_\Lambda u\|_{L^2(\rho)}
+\|\widehat P_\Lambda u-P_\Lambda u\|_{L^2(\rho)}.$$
Thus coefficient quadrature error and finite-space projection error remain
separate even when no completeness statement is available.

derivations.claim: For each $\alpha$, apply [F1] to $g_\alpha=\widetilde u\psi_\alpha$. Its assumptions are exactly the mixed-derivative bounds and cube domain in **Given**, with [F2] supplying the theorem's specified mixed norm. Thus $|Q_{\Lambda_n}(g_\alpha)-\int g_\alpha\,d\rho|\le E_{\alpha,n}$. Since $\widetilde u$ represents $u$, the integral equals $\langle u,\psi_\alpha\rangle$ by the uniform product law.
Square the finitely many nonnegative inequalities from step 1.1, sum over $\alpha$, and take square roots; monotonicity of the square root gives the stated Euclidean bound.

Apply [F4] with these coefficient errors. Its exact orthogonal error decomposition leaves the projection residual unchanged and adds the bounded Euclidean coefficient term, which proves the final assertion.

Assume Countable Choice and the affine diffusion hypotheses of
[[def-uniformly-elliptic-affine-random-diffusion]]. Let $p$ be the selected
admissible cutoff vector of the finite product-law input, and let
$\Lambda\subseteq\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d:0\le\alpha_j\le p_j\text{ for all }j\}$
be finite. Let $V_h\subset V$ be any
finite-dimensional conforming spatial subspace. Define the stochastic
Galerkin space
$$\mathcal V_{\Lambda,h}:=
\operatorname{span}\{\,\psi_\alpha(\cdot)v:
\alpha\in\Lambda,\ v\in V_h\,\}\subset L^2_\rho(V).$$
The Bochner form is continuous with constant $a^*$ and coercive with constant
$a_*$. There is a unique $U_{\Lambda,h}\in\mathcal V_{\Lambda,h}$ satisfying
$$\mathcal A(U_{\Lambda,h},W_h)=\mathcal F(W_h)
\qquad(W_h\in\mathcal V_{\Lambda,h}),$$

Let $\Lambda$ be finite, contain $0$, and let
$\psi=(\psi_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Lambda}$ be the real orthonormal basis of
[[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]]. Set $N=|\Lambda|$ and
$$K_\Lambda(y)=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}|\psi_\alpha(y)|^2.$$
The algorithm takes an evaluable real function $u$, a positive integer sample
count $M$, and independent samples $X_1,\ldots,X_M$ from the probability law
$d\nu=(K_\Lambda/N)\,d\rho$. It forms
$$G=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M\frac{N}{K_\Lambda(X_i)}\psi(X_i)\psi(X_i)^T,\qquad
b=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M\frac{N}{K_\Lambda(X_i)}u(X_i)\psi(X_i).$$
If every eigenvalue of $G$ lies in $[1/2,3/2]$, return the unique coefficient
vector $c=G^{-1}b$ and polynomial $\hat u=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha\psi_\alpha$.
Otherwise return `unstable-sample` and no coefficients. The weighted empirical
objective minimized on the accepted branch is
$$\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M\frac{N}{K_\Lambda(X_i)}|u(X_i)-p(X_i)|^2,$$
over $p\in\mathcal P_\Lambda$.

Let $\Lambda$, $N=|\Lambda|\ge1$, and the independent Christoffel samples
$X_1,\ldots,X_M$ be as in
[[alg-christoffel-weighted-least-squares-collocation]]. Let $G$ be its
weighted empirical Gram matrix. For $0<\delta<1$, if
$$M\ge12N\log(2N/\delta),$$
then
$$\mathbb P\{\,\operatorname{spec}(G)\subseteq[1/2,3/2]\,\}\ge1-\delta.$$

For real $u\in L^2(\rho)$ and finite $\Lambda$, define
$$c_\alpha=\langle u,\psi_\alpha\rangle_{L^2(\rho)}=\int u(y)\psi_\alpha(y)\,d\rho(y),\qquad P_\Lambda u=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha\psi_\alpha.$$
The scalar integral pairing is choice-free: for representatives $f,g$ of
classes in $L^2(\rho)$, Cauchy–Schwarz makes $fg$ integrable, and the integral
is unchanged when either representative is changed on a null set. Its
bilinearity follows from linearity of the integral and its symmetry from
commutativity of multiplication; moreover
$\int f^2\,d\rho=\|[f]\|_2^2$, so it is positive definite on the quotient.
These facts use only the integral pairing, not completeness of $L^2(\rho)$.
The displayed finite sum is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal P_\Lambda$
of [[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]].

Let $\Lambda$ be finite, contain $0$, and let the real basis
$(\psi_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Lambda}$ be as in
[[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]]. For real $u\in L^2(\rho)$ set
$c_\alpha=\langle u,\psi_\alpha\rangle$ and
$P_\Lambda u=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha\psi_\alpha$ as in
[[def-finite-chaos-orthogonal-projection]]. Then
$$\|u\|_{L^2(\rho)}^2=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha^2+
\|u-P_\Lambda u\|_{L^2(\rho)}^2.$$
The residual is orthogonal to $\mathcal P_\Lambda$,
$\mathbb E[u]=c_0$, and
$$\operatorname{Var}(u)=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}}c_\alpha^2+
\|u-P_\Lambda u\|_{L^2(\rho)}^2.$$
Here $\operatorname{Var}(u)=\mathbb E[(u-\mathbb E u)^2]$; no completeness of
the polynomial family is assumed.

Let $\rho=\otimes_{j=1}^d\rho_j$ and form $\psi_\alpha$ from
[[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]] for indices in the admissible degree
box. Then each $\psi_\alpha$ belongs to
$L^2(\rho)$ and
$$\int_\Gamma\psi_\alpha(y)\psi_\beta(y)\,d\rho(y)=\begin{cases}1,&\alpha=\beta,\\0,&\alpha\ne\beta.\end{cases}$$
In particular, the family indexed by any finite subset $\Lambda$ of the box is
orthonormal; when $0\in\Lambda$, it includes the constant mode $\psi_0=1$.

derivations.claim: Put $w_i=N/K_\Lambda(X_i)>0$, and let the $i$th row of the design matrix $A$ be $\sqrt{w_i/M}\,\psi(X_i)^T$. Then $A^TA=G$. On the good event, $G$ is positive definite, so the normal equations have the unique solution $\widehat c=G^{-1}A^Tz$, where $z_i=\sqrt{w_i/M}\,u(X_i)$.

Let $c$ be the exact coefficient vector of $P_\Lambda u$ and let $r_i=u(X_i)-P_\Lambda u(X_i)$. Then $z-Ac$ has entries $\sqrt{w_i/M}\,r_i$, and the normal equations give $\widehat c-c=G^{-1}A^T(z-Ac)$. Moreover, $(G^{-1}A^T)(G^{-1}A^T)^T=G^{-1}A^TAG^{-1}=G^{-1}$. Thus $\|G^{-1}A^T\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2=\lambda_{\max}(G^{-1})=1/\lambda_{\min}(G)\le2$, yielding the first bound.

Orthonormality [F5] gives $\|\widehat u-P_\Lambda u\|_{L^2(\rho)}=\|\widehat c-c\|_2$. By [F4], $u-P_\Lambda u$ is orthogonal to this polynomial difference, so Pythagoras gives $\|u-\widehat u\|^2=\|u-P_\Lambda u\|^2+\|\widehat u-P_\Lambda u\|^2$. Substitute the first bound and square it to obtain the second inequality.
The probability assertion is exactly [F2] under its stated independent sampling and budget hypotheses; no probability is asserted outside that good-event regime.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, independent real random variables
$Y_1,\ldots,Y_d$ with marginal Borel probability laws $\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_d$,
and a degree cutoff vector $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$. Their joint
law is $\rho=\rho_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_d$, as in
[[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]. Write
$\Gamma=\prod_{j=1}^d\operatorname{supp}(\rho_j)$, with the product Borel
sigma-algebra. The cutoff vector $p$ is **admissible** when, for every
$j=1,\ldots,d$,
$$\int |y|^{2p_j}\,d\rho_j(y)<\infty$$
and the monomial Gram matrix
$$G_j=(\int y^{r+s}\,d\rho_j(y))_{0\le r,s\le p_j}$$
is positive definite, meaning $c^T G_jc>0$ for each nonzero
$c\in\mathbb R^{p_j+1}$. Throughout the pair, assume the selected cutoff
vector is admissible. The admissible degree box is
$\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d:0\le\alpha_j\le p_j\text{ for every }j\}$.
Admissibility gives a finite inner product on each stated polynomial space.
It is only a finite-degree condition; it does not assert that polynomials are
dense in any $L^2(\rho_j)$.

Let $\phi_{j,k}$ be the Gram–Schmidt polynomials from
[[lem-positive-moment-gram-produces-univariate-chaos-polynomials]], and let
$\Lambda$ be a finite subset of the admissible degree box in
[[def-finite-product-chaos-input]]. For $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)\in\Lambda$,
define
$$\psi_\alpha(y_1,\ldots,y_d)=\prod_{j=1}^d\phi_{j,\alpha_j}(y_j).$$
The **finite polynomial-chaos space** is
$\mathcal P_\Lambda=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_\alpha:\alpha\in\Lambda\}$
inside $L^2(\rho)$. Whenever $0\in\Lambda$ (in particular, for the stated
total-degree and hyperbolic-cross sets), the family contains the constant mode
$\psi_0=1$. No density of $\mathcal P_\Lambda$ in $L^2(\rho)$ is part of this
definition.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

For $d\ge1$, let $(a_j,b_j,m_j,2m_j-1,\mu_j)$ be Gaussian moment data for
each coordinate $j=1,\ldots,d$, and write
$M^{(j)}_k:=\int x^k\,d\mu_j(x)$. A **coordinatewise tensor polynomial** is a
finite family $(c_\alpha)$, with $c_\alpha\in\mathbb R$ for every index, indexed by multi-indices
$\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)$ with
$0\le\alpha_j\le2m_j-1$, evaluated by
$$ P(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{d}x_j^{\alpha_j}. $$
Define its **coordinatewise product-moment value** by
$$ I_\otimes(P):=\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{d}M^{(j)}_{\alpha_j}. $$
In both sums, list the finite multi-index box in increasing lexicographic
order (coordinate $1$ first, then coordinate $2$, and so on), and take the
ordinary finite-list sum in that order. The products use increasing coordinate
order $j=1,\ldots,d$. The real coefficient family is part of the formal
polynomial data, so these formulas specify finite real sums. This definition specifies the product-moment functional
used for coordinatewise exactness without requiring a measure-product
construction.

For the Gaussian coordinate data of [[def-coordinatewise-product-moment-functional]], let $\mu=\mu_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\mu_d$ on the finite product of the relative Borel interval spaces, with binary products iterated from left to right. Every real coordinatewise tensor polynomial $P$ in that definition is integrable and
$$\int P\,d\mu=I_\otimes(P).$$
This supplies a measure interpretation of the algebraic functional without redefining it. The conclusion also applies when each marginal measure is a probability law.

For $d\ge1$, take one-dimensional Gaussian rules $Q_j$ with orders $m_j$ and
moment data $(a_j,b_j,m_j,2m_j-1,\mu_j)$, and form their tensor rule
$Q_\otimes$ as in [[def-tensor-product-gauss-rule]]. For every coordinatewise
tensor polynomial $P$ of [[def-coordinatewise-product-moment-functional]],
$$ Q_\otimes(P)=I_\otimes(P). $$
The tensor rule has exactly $\prod_{j=1}^{d}m_j$ distinct nodes. In particular,
using the same $m\ge2$ nodes in each coordinate requires $m^d$ node
evaluations, exponential growth in $d$.

Let $\rho=\otimes_{j=1}^d\rho_j$ and form $\psi_\alpha$ from
[[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]] for indices in the admissible degree
box. Then each $\psi_\alpha$ belongs to
$L^2(\rho)$ and
$$\int_\Gamma\psi_\alpha(y)\psi_\beta(y)\,d\rho(y)=\begin{cases}1,&\alpha=\beta,\\0,&\alpha\ne\beta.\end{cases}$$
In particular, the family indexed by any finite subset $\Lambda$ of the box is
orthonormal; when $0\in\Lambda$, it includes the constant mode $\psi_0=1$.

Let $\Lambda$ be a finite index set and let $Q$ be any declared finite
cubature functional
$Q(g)=\sum_{q=1}^Jw_qg(y^{(q)})$ whose nodes lie in the domain of evaluation
of $g$. For an evaluable real function $u$, define the quadrature coefficient
and the resulting polynomial by
$$\widehat c_\alpha:=Q(u\psi_\alpha),\qquad
\widehat P_\Lambda u:=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}\widehat c_\alpha\psi_\alpha.$$
The exact coefficients $c_\alpha$ and projection $P_\Lambda u$ are those of
[[def-finite-chaos-orthogonal-projection]]. This definition gives no
accuracy claim for a general cubature rule.

derivations.claim: Expand $u=\sum_{\beta\in\Lambda}c_\beta\psi_\beta$. By [F1] and [F2], each $\psi_\beta$ has coordinate degree $\beta_j\le p_j$, so each product $\psi_\beta\psi_\alpha$ has degree at most $2p_j\le2m_j-2\le2m_j-1$ in coordinate $j$.

By [F3] and [F4], the product-law integral of this finite polynomial equals its coordinatewise product-moment functional. Its degrees satisfy the limits checked in step 1.1, so [F5] gives $Q_\otimes(\psi_\beta\psi_\alpha)=\int\psi_\beta\psi_\alpha\,d\rho=\delta_{\alpha\beta}$ by [F6]. Finite linearity then gives $Q_\otimes(u\psi_\alpha)=c_\alpha=\langle u,\psi_\alpha\rangle$.

The equality in step 2.1 holds for every $\alpha\in\Lambda$, so all coefficient differences vanish and the finite sums defining $\widehat P_\Lambda u$ and $P_\Lambda u$ coincide. The quadrature contribution in the error split is therefore zero.

derivations.claim: Take the standard Cauchy law, whose density is $\rho(x)=1/(\pi(1+x^2))$ on $\mathbb R$. Its second moment integral is $\int x^2\,d\rho(x)=\pi^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R}x^2/(1+x^2)\,dx.$ For $|x|\ge1$, $x^2/(1+x^2)\ge1/2$, so the integral over $[-R,-1]\cup[1,R]$ is at least $(R-1)/\pi$.

Letting $R\to\infty$ shows the second moment is infinite. Hence $x\notin L^2(\rho)$, the degree-one monomial Gram entry is not finite, and [F1] fails; the finite Gram--Schmidt construction cannot supply a degree-one chaos basis for this law.

separable Hilbert structure under Countable Choice; the gradient norm is
equivalent to its Sobolev norm there.

Let $Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_d)$ have the product law $\rho$ of
[[def-finite-product-chaos-input]], and assume its support $\Gamma$ is bounded,
so $|y_j|\le R_j<\infty$ for every $y\in\Gamma$.
For real coefficient functions $a_0,\ldots,a_d\in L^\infty(D)$ define
$$a(x,y)=a_0(x)+\sum_{j=1}^d y_j a_j(x).$$
Assume constants $0<a_*\le a^*<\infty$ satisfy, for every $y\in\Gamma$,
$a_*\le a(x,y)\le a^*$ for almost every $x\in D$. This explicit
all-parameter condition ensures the pointwise variational problem is
well-posed for every stated parameter, not merely almost every one. Let
$F(y)=f_0+\sum_{j=1}^d y_j f_j$ with $f_j\in V^*$.

The pointwise weak form is
$$a_y(u,v)=\int_Da(x,y)\nabla u(x)\cdot\nabla v(x)\,dx=F(y)(v),\qquad v\in V.$$
The Bochner weak form uses the bilinear form
$$\mathcal A(U,W)=\int_\Gamma a_y(U(y),W(y))\,d\rho(y)$$
and the functional $\mathcal F(W)=\int_\Gamma F(y)(W(y))\,d\rho(y)$ on
$L^2_\rho(V)$ from [[def-finite-input-bochner-l2-space]].

Under the hypotheses of [[def-uniformly-elliptic-affine-random-diffusion]],
for each $y\in\Gamma$ there is a unique $u(y)\in V$ satisfying the pointwise
weak problem. The map $y\mapsto u(y)$ is Lipschitz on the bounded parameter
set, strongly measurable, and belongs to $L^2_\rho(V)$. It is also the unique
solution of the Bochner weak equation
$$\mathcal A(u,W)=\mathcal F(W)\qquad(W\in L^2_\rho(V)).$$

derivations.claim: At cutoff $p_1=0$, the only moment-Gram matrix is $[1]$, so the uniform probability law is admissible by [F1]. Its support is $\Gamma=[-1,1]$, and for every $y\in\Gamma$, $1\le2+y\le3$. Thus the diffusion definition applies with $a_*=1$ and $a^*=3$, and $F=0$ is a bounded affine forcing.

The pointwise weak equation is $\int_0^1(2+y)u'(x)v'(x)\,dx=0$ for every $v\in H_0^1(0,1)$. Taking $v=u$ and using $2+y\ge1$ gives $\|u\|_{H_0^1}^2\le0$, so $u=0$ for every $y$. This solution is a strongly measurable square-integrable zero function and satisfies the Bochner equation; uniqueness also follows from [F3].

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, independent real random variables
$Y_1,\ldots,Y_d$ with marginal Borel probability laws $\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_d$,
and a degree cutoff vector $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$. Their joint
law is $\rho=\rho_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_d$, as in
[[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]. Write
$\Gamma=\prod_{j=1}^d\operatorname{supp}(\rho_j)$, with the product Borel
sigma-algebra. The cutoff vector $p$ is **admissible** when, for every
$j=1,\ldots,d$,
$$\int |y|^{2p_j}\,d\rho_j(y)<\infty$$
and the monomial Gram matrix
$$G_j=(\int y^{r+s}\,d\rho_j(y))_{0\le r,s\le p_j}$$
is positive definite, meaning $c^T G_jc>0$ for each nonzero
$c\in\mathbb R^{p_j+1}$. Throughout the pair, assume the selected cutoff
vector is admissible. The admissible degree box is
$\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d:0\le\alpha_j\le p_j\text{ for every }j\}$.
Admissibility gives a finite inner product on each stated polynomial space.
It is only a finite-degree condition; it does not assert that polynomials are
dense in any $L^2(\rho_j)$.

Let $\rho_j$ be one factor law with admissible degree $p_j$ as in
[[def-finite-product-chaos-input]]. The monomial classes
$1,y,\ldots,y^{p_j}$ are linearly independent in $L^2(\rho_j)$. Applying the
finite Gram–Schmidt recursion to this ordered list gives real orthonormal
polynomials $\phi_{j,0},\ldots,\phi_{j,p_j}$, where $\phi_{j,k}$ has degree
$k$, positive leading coefficient, and $\phi_{j,0}=1$.

Let $\Lambda$ be finite, contain $0$, and let the real basis
$(\psi_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Lambda}$ be as in
[[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]]. For real $u\in L^2(\rho)$ set
$c_\alpha=\langle u,\psi_\alpha\rangle$ and
$P_\Lambda u=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha\psi_\alpha$ as in
[[def-finite-chaos-orthogonal-projection]]. Then
$$\|u\|_{L^2(\rho)}^2=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha^2+
\|u-P_\Lambda u\|_{L^2(\rho)}^2.$$
The residual is orthogonal to $\mathcal P_\Lambda$,
$\mathbb E[u]=c_0$, and
$$\operatorname{Var}(u)=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}}c_\alpha^2+
\|u-P_\Lambda u\|_{L^2(\rho)}^2.$$
Here $\operatorname{Var}(u)=\mathbb E[(u-\mathbb E u)^2]$; no completeness of
the polynomial family is assumed.

derivations.claim: The first two moments are $\mathbb E[Y]=0$ and $\mathbb E[Y^2]=1$, so the degree-one Gram matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, positive definite. Thus [F1] applies. Gram--Schmidt gives $\psi_0=1$ and $\psi_1=Y$, since $Y$ already has mean zero and unit norm and its leading coefficient is positive.

Substitution gives $k(Y)=\kappa\psi_0+\kappa\eta\psi_1$ at both support points, so the degree-one projection residual is identically zero. Its coefficients are $c_0=\mathbb E[k(Y)]=\kappa$ and $c_1=\mathbb E[k(Y)Y]=\kappa\eta$. By [F3], the mean is $c_0$ and variance is $c_1^2=\kappa^2\eta^2$.

The condition $|\eta|<1$ implies $1+\eta Y\ge1-|\eta|>0$ at both states, so the reaction rate is positive on its whole support. Every function on this support also has the exact form $g(Y)=\frac{g(1)+g(-1)}2+\frac{g(1)-g(-1)}2Y$; hence this two-dimensional finite basis spans $L^2(\rho)$ for this particular law.

For $d$ inputs with admissible cutoff vector
$p=(p_1,\ldots,p_d)$ from [[def-finite-product-chaos-input]], the cutoff
total-degree set of order $s\ge0$ and cutoff hyperbolic-cross set of
threshold $N\ge1$ are
$$\Lambda^{\mathrm{TD}}_{s,p}=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d:0\le\alpha_j\le p_j,\ \sum_{j=1}^d\alpha_j\le s\},\qquad
\Lambda^{\mathrm{HC}}_{N,p}=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d:0\le\alpha_j\le p_j,\ \prod_{j=1}^d(\alpha_j+1)\le N\},$$
The cutoff vector prevents either set from requesting
polynomials above the moment degree declared in
[[def-finite-product-chaos-input]]. Both are finite and contain zero.
An arbitrary finite index set used below is denoted by $\Lambda$; whenever a
downward-closed set is required, this means $\alpha\in\Lambda$ and
$0\le\beta_j\le\alpha_j$ for every $j$ imply $\beta\in\Lambda$.

For every admissible cutoff vector $p\in\mathbb N_0^d$, order $s\ge0$, and
threshold $N\ge1$, the sets $\Lambda^{\mathrm{TD}}_{s,p}$ and
$\Lambda^{\mathrm{HC}}_{N,p}$ of
[[def-chaos-total-degree-and-hyperbolic-cross-index-sets]] are finite and
contain $0$.

For $d\ge1$, take one-dimensional Gaussian rules $Q_j$ with orders $m_j$ and
moment data $(a_j,b_j,m_j,2m_j-1,\mu_j)$, and form their tensor rule
$Q_\otimes$ as in [[def-tensor-product-gauss-rule]]. For every coordinatewise
tensor polynomial $P$ of [[def-coordinatewise-product-moment-functional]],
$$ Q_\otimes(P)=I_\otimes(P). $$
The tensor rule has exactly $\prod_{j=1}^{d}m_j$ distinct nodes. In particular,
using the same $m\ge2$ nodes in each coordinate requires $m^d$ node
evaluations, exponential growth in $d$.

derivations.claim: For one uniform marginal, the moment Gram matrix through degree two is $\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1/3\\0&1/3&0\\1/3&0&1/5\end{pmatrix}$. Its quadratic form at $(c_0,c_1,c_2)$ is $(c_0+c_2/3)^2+c_1^2/3+4c_2^2/45$, which is positive for every nonzero vector; all required moments are finite on $[-1,1]$. Thus the cutoff is admissible. In three coordinates, the total-degree set has one zero multi-index, three degree-one indices, three indices $2e_j$, and three indices $e_i+e_j$ with $i<j$. These are disjoint and exhaust the nonnegative triples with sum at most two, so its cardinality is $1+3+3+3=10$.

The full degree-two tensor box has $3$ choices in each of three coordinates, hence $3^3=27$ multi-indices. The three-node Gaussian rules are defined for the positive uniform measures on $[-1,1]$; their tensor rule with $m_1=m_2=m_3=3$ has $3^3=27$ distinct nodes by [F3]. Thus in this example the total-degree basis uses ten modes compared with twenty-seven tensor modes and node evaluations.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.
For $f\in L^1[a,b]$, the function $I_f(x)=\int_a^x f$ is absolutely continuous.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then $F$ is differentiable for almost every $x\in(a,b)$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)$$
at every such point.

Let $(K,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space. Every member of
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is bounded, so the supremum metric

$$d_\infty(f,g):=\sup_{x\in K}|f(x)-g(x)|$$

is defined on $C(K,\mathbb{R})$. With this metric,
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is complete.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For any Lebesgue-integrable vector function $h$ with $\int\|h\|_2<\infty$, write $I=\int h$. If $I=0$, the norm inequality is immediate. Otherwise put $q=I/\|I\|_2$. Then $\|I\|_2=\int q^Th\le\int|q^Th|\le\int\|h\|_2$, by [F1], linearity componentwise, and $\|q\|_2=1$. Thus the vector integral estimate needed below holds for these Lebesgue integrands. Now put $g=Bu\in L^1(0,T;\mathbb R^n)$; this follows from $B\in L^\infty$, $u\in L^2$, and [F5]. Choose a finite partition $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$ with $\|A\|_\infty(t_{j+1}-t_j)<1$ on each subinterval when $\|A\|_\infty>0$; if $\|A\|_\infty=0$, use $N=1$. Given the already constructed value $x(t_j)$, define $\mathcal T z(t)=x(t_j)+\int_{t_j}^t(A(s)z(s)+g(s))ds$ on $C([t_j,t_{j+1}];\mathbb R^n)$. By [F2], $\mathcal T$ maps continuous functions to continuous functions, and the vector-integral estimate just proved gives $\|\mathcal T z-\mathcal T w\|_\infty\le q_j\|z-w\|_\infty$ with $q_j=\|A\|_\infty(t_{j+1}-t_j)<1$.

Starting from the constant function $z_0=x(t_j)$, let $z_{k+1}=\mathcal T z_k$. Then $\|z_{k+1}-z_k\|_\infty\le q_j^k\|z_1-z_0\|_\infty$, so the successive differences have summable norms. Each coordinate converges uniformly by [F3], and the finite coordinate limit is a continuous vector function $z$. The integral estimate in step 1.1 makes $\mathcal T$ continuous in the supremum norm, hence $z=\mathcal Tz$. If $z,w$ are two fixed points, $\|z-w\|_\infty\le q_j\|z-w\|_\infty$, so $z=w$. Solving the finitely many subintervals in order gives one continuous solution on $[0,T]$, and the same uniqueness on each subinterval proves global uniqueness.

The integrand $Ax+Bu$ lies in $L^1$. Its indefinite integral is absolutely continuous by [F2], as required in the Statement. Under [A1], the $L^1$ fundamental theorem in [F2] differentiates the integral equation almost everywhere and yields $\dot x=Ax+Bu$. The same equation is independent of the chosen representatives of $A,B,u$ by [F6].

From the integral equation and step 1.1, $\|x(t)\|_2\le \|x_0\|_2+\|B\|_\infty\|u\|_{L^1}+\|A\|_\infty\int_0^t\|x(s)\|_2ds$. Apply [F4] with $c=\|x_0\|_2+\|B\|_\infty\|u\|_{L^1}$ and then [F5]; this gives the displayed supremum bound.

Linearity of the integral [F6] shows that a linear combination of two zero-initial-state solutions is the solution for the same linear combination of controls; uniqueness from step 2.1 makes the zero-initial-state map linear. Step 3.2 with $x_0=0$ bounds this linear map in the $L^2$ and supremum norms, while the fixed initial-state contribution is independent of $u$. Hence the full map is affine and bounded as claimed.

Fix a finite horizon $T>0$, state and control dimensions $n,m\ge1$, and the real quotient space $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$ of measurable controls modulo equality almost everywhere ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Let $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$ be equivalence classes, let $x_0,x_T\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $x_d\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^n)$. Let $U_c\subset\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty, compact and convex. The pointwise control set is
$$
\mathcal U_c:=\{u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m):u(t)\in U_c\text{ for almost every }t\}.
$$
Let $Q\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $R\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{m\times m})$ be symmetric almost everywhere, with $Q(t)\succeq0$ and $rI\preceq R(t)\preceq MI$ almost everywhere for constants $0<r\le M<\infty$. Let $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite. For each $u\in\mathcal U_c$, its state is the unique continuous solution of the Volterra equation
$$
x_u(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x_u(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
The same state equation is defined for every $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and the running and terminal cost on that ambient space is
$$
J(u)=\frac12\int_0^T\!\left((x_u(t)-x_d(t))^TQ(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t))+u(t)^TR(t)u(t)\right)dt+\frac12(x_u(T)-x_T)^TP(x_u(T)-x_T).
$$
The constrained problem minimizes this ambient functional over $\mathcal F$, where additional path or terminal constraints are represented by a nonempty convex weakly sequentially closed set $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal U_c$; with no additional state constraints, $\mathcal F=\mathcal U_c$. “Weakly sequentially closed” means that every weakly convergent sequence in $\mathcal F$ has its weak limit in $\mathcal F$ ([[def-weak-convergence-of-nets-and-sequences]]). Write $\|A\|_\infty$ and $\|B\|_\infty$ for the essential suprema of their Euclidean operator norms. There is a unique absolutely continuous $x:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^n$ satisfying
$$
x(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
Under Countable Choice it satisfies $\dot x=A x+B u$ almost everywhere, and it always satisfies
$$
\|x\|_\infty\le e^{\|A\|_\infty T}\left(\|x_0\|_2+\|B\|_\infty\sqrt T\,\|u\|_2\right).
$$
For fixed $A,B,x_0$, the map $u\mapsto x_u$ is affine into $C([0,T];\mathbb R^n)$, and its zero-initial-state linear part is bounded from $L^2$ to the supremum norm.

Let $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite. For each $u\in\mathcal U_c$, its state is the unique continuous solution of the Volterra equation
$$
x_u(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x_u(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
The same state equation is defined for every $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and the running and terminal cost on that ambient space is
$$
J(u)=\frac12\int_0^T\!\left((x_u(t)-x_d(t))^TQ(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t))+u(t)^TR(t)u(t)\right)dt+\frac12(x_u(T)-x_T)^TP(x_u(T)-x_T).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], the states have a common bound $M_x$ in supremum norm. For $s,t\in[0,T]$, the integral equation and [F4] give $\|x_{u_k}(t)-x_{u_k}(s)\|_2\le L|t-s|$, where $L:=\|A\|_\infty M_x+\|B\|_\infty M_c$. The same bound holds for $x_u$.
For each fixed $t$, evaluation at $t$ composed with the bounded linear zero-initial-state map in [F1] is a bounded linear functional on $L^2$. Thus [F3] gives $x_{u_k}(t)\to x_u(t)$ coordinatewise.

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: On each interval $I_j=[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, let $m_j=h^{-1}\int_{I_j}u(s)ds$. If $m_j\notin U_c$, compactness and [F3] give a nearest point $y\in U_c$. For every $c\in U_c$, the segment $y+\theta(c-y)$ belongs to $U_c$ for $0\le\theta\le1$; minimality of $y$ gives $\|m_j-y-\theta(c-y)\|_2^2\ge\|m_j-y\|_2^2$. Divide by $\theta>0$ and let $\theta\downarrow0$ to get $(m_j-y)^T(c-y)\le0$. With $q_0=m_j-y\ne0$, this implies $q_0^Tm_j>\sup_{c\in U_c}q_0^Tc$. But $q_0^Tu(s)\le\sup_{c\in U_c}q_0^Tc$ almost everywhere, so integration contradicts the strict inequality. Thus every cell average lies in $U_c$ and $P_Nu$ is pointwise admissible.

For any $w\in L^2$, [F2] on a cell $I_j$ gives $h\|h^{-1}\int_{I_j}w\|_2^2\le\int_{I_j}\|w(s)\|_2^2ds$; summing proves $\|P_Nw\|_2\le\|w\|_2$. For an interval indicator, $P_N$ agrees with it on cells not meeting an endpoint, and at most two endpoint cells contribute to the squared error, at most $2h$. By linearity, $P_Ns\to s$ for every finite linear combination $s$ of interval indicators.

Fix $u\in L^2$ and $\varepsilon>0$. By [F1] choose such an interval step function $s$ with $\|u-s\|_2<\varepsilon$. The contraction bound in step 1.2 gives $\|P_Nu-u\|_2\le2\varepsilon+\|P_Ns-s\|_2$. Taking $N\to\infty$ yields $\limsup_N\|P_Nu-u\|_2\le2\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, $P_Nu\to u$ strongly in $L^2$.

Let $U_c\subset\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty, compact and convex, and let $\mathcal U_c$ be the pointwise admissible set in [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]]. If $u_k\in\mathcal U_c$ and $u_k\rightharpoonup u$ weakly in real $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, then $u\in\mathcal U_c$. Thus $\mathcal U_c$ is weakly sequentially closed.

derivations.claim: By [F4], the weak limit $u$ belongs to $\mathcal U_c$, so [F2] applies. Put $e_k=x_{u_k}-x_d$ and $e=x_u-x_d$; their difference $e_k-e=x_{u_k}-x_u$ tends to zero uniformly. Since $Q$ is essentially bounded, the estimate $|a^TQ(t)a-b^TQ(t)b|\le\|Q(t)\|_2(\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2)\|a-b\|_2$ shows that $\int_0^T e_k^TQe_k\,dt\to\int_0^T e^TQe\,dt$. The terminal terms converge by the same estimate with $P$ and $x_{u_k}(T)\to x_u(T)$.

Let $\mathscr Rv=R(\cdot)v(\cdot)$. The bounds on $R$ imply $\|\mathscr Rv\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ and $\langle\mathscr Rv,v\rangle\ge0$; symmetry gives $\langle\mathscr Rv,w\rangle=\langle v,\mathscr Rw\rangle$. For every fixed $w\in L^2$, $\langle\mathscr Ru_k,u_k\rangle\ge2\langle\mathscr Ru_k,w\rangle-\langle\mathscr Rw,w\rangle$, because the difference is $\langle\mathscr R(u_k-w),u_k-w\rangle\ge0$. The right-hand side converges to $2\langle\mathscr Ru,w\rangle-\langle\mathscr Rw,w\rangle$ by weak convergence, as [F3] makes $v\mapsto\langle\mathscr Rv,w\rangle=\langle v,\mathscr Rw\rangle$ bounded. Taking the supremum over $w$ gives $\liminf_k\langle\mathscr Ru_k,u_k\rangle\ge\langle\mathscr Ru,u\rangle$, with equality in the supremum at $w=u$.

The state and terminal cost terms converge by step 1.1, while the control quadratic term is lower semicontinuous by step 1.2. Multiplying by $1/2$ and adding these three terms gives $J(u)\le\liminf_k J(u_k)$.

Let $T>0$, $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$, $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$, $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$. Write $\|A\|_\infty$ and $\|B\|_\infty$ for the essential suprema of their Euclidean operator norms. There is a unique absolutely continuous $x:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^n$ satisfying
$$
x(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
Under Countable Choice it satisfies $\dot x=A x+B u$ almost everywhere, and it always satisfies
$$
\|x\|_\infty\le e^{\|A\|_\infty T}\left(\|x_0\|_2+\|B\|_\infty\sqrt T\,\|u\|_2\right).
$$
For fixed $A,B,x_0$, the map $u\mapsto x_u$ is affine into $C([0,T];\mathbb R^n)$, and its zero-initial-state linear part is bounded from $L^2$ to the supremum norm.

The almost-everywhere derivative assertion uses Countable Choice, as required by the cited $L^1$ fundamental theorem. The integral-equation existence, uniqueness, bound, and affine-map claims do not require that axiom.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For the data of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]] and an admissible control $u$ with state $x_u$, a **continuous LQR adjoint** is an absolutely continuous curve $p:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^n$ satisfying, almost everywhere,
$$
-\dot p(t)=A(t)^Tp(t)+Q(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t)),\qquad p(T)=P(x_u(T)-x_T).
$$
The equation defines the adjoint notion without asserting existence. Existence and uniqueness for each admissible control are established under Countable Choice by [[lem-ctrl1-lqr-adjoint-exists-uniquely]]. This sign convention is the one for the minimization Hamiltonian $H(t,x,p,u)=L(t,x,u)+p^T(A(t)x+B(t)u)$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $a\le b$.

1. If $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is absolutely continuous and $F'=0$ almost everywhere on $(a,b)$, then $F$ is constant.
2. Let $n\ge1$, let $y:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ have absolutely continuous coordinates, and let $h\in L^1([a,b];\mathbb R^n)$. If $y'_j=h_j$ almost everywhere for each coordinate $j$, then, for every $t\in[a,b]$,
$$y(t)=y(a)+\int_a^t h(s)\,ds.$$
Here $h\in L^1([a,b];\mathbb R^n)$ means that each coordinate $h_j$ is Lebesgue integrable, and the integral is the componentwise Lebesgue integral. For $a=b$ it is zero.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$.

1. If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f'$ extends
   continuously to $[a,b]$, then $f$ is Lipschitz.
2. Every Lipschitz $f$ is absolutely continuous.
3. Every absolutely continuous $f$ is continuous and has bounded variation.

Thus, with $C^1$ understood in the endpoint-extension sense of claim 1,
$C^1\subseteq\mathrm{Lipschitz}\subseteq AC\subseteq C\cap BV$ on a compact
interval.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $f$ is **bounded on $K$**: there is a real
$M \ge 0$ with

$$|f(x)| \le M \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, $f[K]$ is a bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-bounded-set]]).

**The hypothesis is compactness of $K$, not of $A$**, and it cannot be relaxed
to boundedness of $K$ or to closedness of $K$ alone: the identity is unbounded
on the closed set $[0,\infty)$, and $x \mapsto 1/x$ is unbounded on the bounded
set $(0,1)$. The general statement of that is
[[thm-compactness-is-necessary-for-evt-and-uniform-continuity]], later on this
page.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

derivations.claim: The forcing $g(s):=Q(T-s)(x_u(T-s)-x_d(T-s))$ lies in $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^n)$: $Q$ is essentially bounded, $x_u$ is continuous on a compact interval and hence bounded, and $x_d\in L^2$. Also $C(s):=A(T-s)^T\in L^\infty$. Apply [F1] with $D(s)=I$ and initial value $q(0)=P(x_u(T)-x_T)$ to obtain an absolutely continuous $q$ satisfying the forward Volterra integral equation and $\dot q=Cq+g$ almost everywhere.

Set $p(t)=q(T-t)$. Time reversal preserves absolute continuity, and differentiating almost everywhere gives $-\dot p(t)=A(t)^Tp(t)+Q(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t))$ with $p(T)=q(0)=P(x_u(T)-x_T)$. Thus $p$ satisfies [F2].

If $\widetilde p$ is another adjoint solution, time reversal gives an absolutely continuous $\widetilde q(s)=\widetilde p(T-s)$ with $\widetilde q(0)=q(0)$ and $\dot{\widetilde q}=C\widetilde q+g$ almost everywhere. By [F4], $\widetilde q$ is continuous and bounded componentwise. Since $C\in L^\infty$, $g\in L^2$ and [F5] gives $g\in L^1$, the function $h=C\widetilde q+g$ belongs to $L^1$ componentwise. Apply [F3] to obtain $\widetilde q(s)=q(0)+\int_0^s(C(r)\widetilde q(r)+g(r))\,dr$ for every $s$. This is exactly the forward Volterra equation used to construct $q$ in step 1.1. Its actual integral-equation uniqueness in [F1] gives $\widetilde q=q$, hence $\widetilde p=p$.
