citations.quote:
Fix a finite horizon $T>0$, state and control dimensions $n,m\ge1$, and the real quotient space $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$ of measurable controls modulo equality almost everywhere ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Let $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$ be equivalence classes, let $x_0,x_T\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $x_d\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^n)$. Let $U_c\subset\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty, compact and convex. The pointwise control set is
$$
\mathcal U_c:=\{u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m):u(t)\in U_c\text{ for almost every }t\}.
$$
Let $Q\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $R\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{m\times m})$ be symmetric almost everywhere, with $Q(t)\succeq0$ and $rI\preceq R(t)\preceq MI$ almost everywhere for constants $0<r\le M<\infty$. Let $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite. For each $u\in\mathcal U_c$, its state is the unique continuous solution of the Volterra equation
$$
x_u(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x_u(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
The same state equation is defined for every $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and the running and terminal cost on that ambient space is
$$
J(u)=\frac12\int_0^T\!\left((x_u(t)-x_d(t))^TQ(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t))+u(t)^TR(t)u(t)\right)dt+\frac12(x_u(T)-x_T)^TP(x_u(T)-x_T).
$$
The constrained problem minimizes this ambient functional over $\mathcal F$, where additional path or terminal constraints are represented by a nonempty convex weakly sequentially closed set $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal U_c$; with no additional state constraints, $\mathcal F=\mathcal U_c$. “Weakly sequentially closed” means that every weakly convergent sequence in $\mathcal F$ has its weak limit in $\mathcal F$ ([[def-weak-convergence-of-nets-and-sequences]]). The definition asserts no optimizer or adjoint existence; the state-map well-definedness is supplied by [[lem-ctrl1-measurable-linear-ode-state-map]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

For every LQR data set in [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]] and every admissible control $u$, the adjoint in [[def-ctrl1-lqr-adjoint-equation]] exists and is unique.

For the data of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]] and an admissible control $u$ with state $x_u$, a **continuous LQR adjoint** is an absolutely continuous curve $p:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^n$ satisfying, almost everywhere,
$$
-\dot p(t)=A(t)^Tp(t)+Q(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t)),\qquad p(T)=P(x_u(T)-x_T).
$$
The equation defines the adjoint notion without asserting existence. Existence and uniqueness for each admissible control are established under Countable Choice by [[lem-ctrl1-lqr-adjoint-exists-uniquely]]. This sign convention is the one for the minimization Hamiltonian $H(t,x,p,u)=L(t,x,u)+p^T(A(t)x+B(t)u)$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice.

For the LQR problem of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]], let $u\in\mathcal U_c$, let $x=x_u$, and let $p$ be its adjoint from [[def-ctrl1-lqr-adjoint-equation]]. Define the bounded linear map $DJ(u):L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)\to\mathbb R$ by
$$DJ(u)[w]=\int_0^T\big(B(t)^Tp(t)+R(t)u(t)\big)^Tw(t)\,dt.$$
It is the first-order norm derivative of $J$ at $u$ in the precise sense that $J(u+w)-J(u)-DJ(u)[w]=O(\|w\|_2^2)$ as $\|w\|_2\to0$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Put $m=\int_0^1u(t)dt$. Since $\int_0^1(u-m)^2dt=\int_0^1u^2dt-m^2$, direct expansion gives $J(u)=\frac12\|u-m\|_2^2+\frac12[m^2+(m-1)^2]=\frac12\|u-m\|_2^2+(m-\frac12)^2+\frac14$.

Both squared terms are nonnegative, so $J(u)\ge\frac14$. Equality holds exactly when $u=m$ almost everywhere and $m=\frac12$, hence exactly for $u^*(t)=\frac12$ almost everywhere. This control satisfies $[-1,1]$ and direct substitution gives $J(u^*)=\frac14$. Therefore it is the unique minimizer.

The state is $x(t)=t/2$. By [F2], the adjoint equation is $-\dot p=0$ with terminal value $p(1)=x(1)-1=-1/2$. The constant curve $p(t)=-1/2$ solves it, and uniqueness in [F2] makes this the adjoint. Under [A1], [F3] gives the reduced gradient $g=p+u^*=0$. Thus $g(t)(c-u^*(t))=0$ for every $c\in[-1,1]$, so the control-only pointwise variational inequality holds with equality for this example. The optimizer and objective calculation in steps 1.1–2.1 used no choice axiom.

citations.quote:
Let $T>0$, $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$, $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$, $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$. Write $\|A\|_\infty$ and $\|B\|_\infty$ for the essential suprema of their Euclidean operator norms. There is a unique absolutely continuous $x:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^n$ satisfying
$$
x(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
Under Countable Choice it satisfies $\dot x=A x+B u$ almost everywhere, and it always satisfies
$$
\|x\|_\infty\le e^{\|A\|_\infty T}\left(\|x_0\|_2+\|B\|_\infty\sqrt T\,\|u\|_2\right).
$$
For fixed $A,B,x_0$, the map $u\mapsto x_u$ is affine into $C([0,T];\mathbb R^n)$, and its zero-initial-state linear part is bounded from $L^2$ to the supremum norm.

The almost-everywhere derivative assertion uses Countable Choice, as required by the cited $L^1$ fundamental theorem. The integral-equation existence, uniqueness, bound, and affine-map claims do not require that axiom.

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be an open time-state domain, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be the right-hand side of a first-order initial-value problem in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. An explicit $s$-stage Runge–Kutta tableau consists of a positive integer $s$, real coefficients $a_{ij}$, $b_i$, and $c_i$ with $a_{ij}=0$ whenever $j\ge i$, and
$$c_i=\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}\qquad(1\le i\le s).$$
The finite row sum is empty, hence $c_1=0$.

For a step size $h>0$ from an admitted base pair $(t,y)\in D$, compute in order
$$Y_i=y+h\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}K_j,\qquad t_i=t+c_i h,\qquad K_i=f(t_i,Y_i)\quad(i=1,\ldots,s).$$
The strict lower-triangular condition makes each stage depend only on already computed slopes; no implicit stage equation is solved. If every stage is defined, the candidate output is
$$y^+=y+h\sum_{i=1}^s b_iK_i.$$

The procedure accepts an exact right-hand-side evaluation oracle that returns either the value $f(t_i,Y_i)$ or an evaluation-failure status. Before each query it checks $(t_i,Y_i)\in D$. It returns domain-failure with the first failing stage if that check fails, evaluation-failure with the stage index if the oracle fails, and domain-failure at output if $(t+h,y^+)\notin D$. Otherwise it returns success with $(t+h,y^+)$. In the exact mathematical model the oracle returns $f$ at every point of $D$; the failure branch records only an unavailable numerical evaluation. On success this is a one-step map in the sense of [[def-one-step-ode-method-local-defect-order-and-stability]].

For the horizon $[0,T]$ of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]], a time mesh is a finite partition $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N=T$ with $N\ge1$. Its cell widths are $h_j=t_{j+1}-t_j>0$ and its mesh size is $|\Delta|=\max_{0\le j<N}h_j$. A piecewise-constant control vector is $(u_0,\ldots,u_{N-1})$ and represents the measurable control $u^\Delta(t)=u_j$ for $t\in[t_j,t_{j+1})$; its value at $T$ is immaterial in $L^2$. If $u_j\in U_c$ for every $j$, then $u^\Delta\in\mathcal U_c$. A mesh family is refining when its mesh sizes tend to zero.

Inputs are an IVP in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], $y'=f(t,y)$ on an open domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ with initial data $(t_0,y_0)\in D$ and requested interval $[t_0,T]$, where $t_0\le T$ and $d\ge1$; an initial proposal $0<h_{\rm init}\le h_{\max}$; an embedded pair with low order $p\ge1$ as in [[def-embedded-runge-kutta-pair-and-error-estimator]]; tolerances $\mathrm{atol}>0$ and $\mathrm{rtol}\ge0$; safety $0<\sigma<1$; scale bounds $0<\gamma_{\min}\le1\le\gamma_{\max}$; step bounds $0<h_{\min}\le h_{\max}$; and a positive integer attempt budget $N$.

**Output.** Return a record consisting of one of `success`, `failure`, `minimum-step-rejected`, or `attempt-budget-exhausted`, together with the accepted mesh $\mathcal A=((t_0,y_0),\ldots,(t_m,y_m))$. The mesh always contains the initial pair and every accepted endpoint; on `success`, $t_m=T$ and $y_m$ is the returned endpoint approximation. On any other status, $\mathcal A$ is the accepted prefix and $y_m$ is the last accepted approximation.

**Procedure.** Initialize $t:=t_0$, $y:=y_0$, $\mathcal A:=((t_0,y_0))$, and proposal $h_{\rm prop}:=h_{\rm init}$. If $t_0=T$, return `success` with $\mathcal A$. For each attempt index $k=1,\ldots,N$, perform exactly the following steps:

1. Set $h:=\min(h_{\rm prop},h_{\max},T-t)$. The last term permits a final clipped step shorter than $h_{\min}$. If $h\le0$ before reaching $T$, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$.
2. Evaluate the shared stages in tableau order, checking before each evaluation that its time-state input lies in $D$. If a stage input is outside $D$, its evaluation is undefined, or its value is nonfinite, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$. Compute both pair outputs; if either output or any arithmetic needed to compute them is undefined, fails, or is nonfinite in the rounded realization, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$.
3. Define $s_i:=\mathrm{atol}+\mathrm{rtol}\max(|(y)_i|,|(Y)_i|)$ and $Q:=\max_i |(\widehat Y-Y)_i|/s_i$, where $Y$ is the high-order value and $\widehat Y$ the low-order value. If any scale or $Q$ operation fails or is nonfinite in the rounded realization, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$. If $Q\le1$, first check $(t+h,Y)\in D$; if not, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$. Otherwise accept: set $t:=t+h$, $y:=Y$, and append $(t,y)$ to $\mathcal A$. If $Q>1$, reject and retain $t,y,\mathcal A$.
4. If the attempt was accepted and $t=T$, return `success` with $\mathcal A$. Otherwise, if it was rejected and $h\le h_{\min}$, return `minimum-step-rejected` with $\mathcal A$. These terminal checks precede the budget check, so a final accepted step that reaches $T$ succeeds and a rejection at the minimum step reports that safeguard.
5. If $k=N$, return `attempt-budget-exhausted` with $\mathcal A$. Otherwise compute
$$g=\begin{cases}\gamma_{\max},&Q=0,\\ \min(\gamma_{\max},\max(\gamma_{\min},\sigma /\sqrt[p+1]{Q})),&Q>0.\end{cases}$$
Set $h_{\rm prop}:=\min(h_{\max},\max(h_{\min},gh))$ and continue to attempt $k+1$. A failed or nonfinite rounded computation of $g$ or $h_{\rm prop}$ returns `failure` with $\mathcal A$.

For $Q>0$, $\sqrt[p+1]{Q}$ is the unique positive $(p+1)$st root supplied by [[thm-nth-roots-exist]]. The exponent $1/(p+1)$ is a leading-error model for step selection; neither acceptance nor this controller is a global error certificate or a stiffness test.

The mathematical specification evaluates each displayed operation, including maximum, minimum, absolute value, and positive-root evaluation, exactly. A rounded implementation instead applies its fixed finite-format rounding rule to every stage, output, scale, and controller-factor arithmetic operation and uses the resulting stored high and low values in the displayed difference and acceptance test; nonfinite or failed operations return `failure`. The finite termination theorem applies to either realization when each attempt has finite work. The rounded realization has no a posteriori guarantee: a tolerance below its resolution can be accepted because both stored values coincide.

For finite-dimensional states and the finite-budget procedure in [[alg-bounded-adaptive-runge-kutta-controller]], the controller returns one of `success`, `failure`, `minimum-step-rejected`, or `attempt-budget-exhausted` after at most $N$ trial attempts. Each individual attempt uses finitely many stage evaluations and arithmetic operations.

derivations.claim: The exact integral equation is $x(t)=\int_0^t(-x(s)+1)ds$. The function $x(t)=1-e^{-t}$ has $x(0)=0$ and derivative $e^{-t}=-(1-e^{-t})+1$, so it solves the equation; uniqueness follows from [F1].

On the one-cell mesh, the explicit midpoint first slope is $K_1=-x_0+u=1$. The second stage is $X_2=x_0+\frac12K_1=\frac12$, so $K_2=-X_2+u=\frac12$. The output is $x_1=x_0+K_2=\frac12$ by [F2]; the exact endpoint is $1-e^{-1}$ by step 1.1.

The exponential series gives $e=1+1+\sum_{k\ge2}1/k!>2$, so $1-e^{-1}>1/2$ and the midpoint endpoint differs from the exact endpoint. The procedure returns the stated value, not a bound on the true error, by [F4].

**Inputs.** Supply pointwise smooth data on $[0,T]$ from [[def-ctrl1-smooth-transcription-data]], an original mesh, a piecewise-constant control parameterization, an explicit tableau from [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]] or a possibly implicit tableau from [[def-ctrl1-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-collocation]], one of `single-shooting`, `multiple-shooting`, or `collocation` mode, a finite smooth representation of the control constraints when a solver-ready NLP is requested, finite sets of declared path-constraint times, endpoint constraints, the tableau quadrature rule, an initial decision vector $z_0$ and multiplier vector $\mu_0$, a stage residual tolerance $\tau_s\ge0$, a quadrature error tolerance $\tau_q\ge0$, a stage Newton correction cap $M_s\in\mathbb N_0$, and a maximum number of mesh nodes. Supply a deterministic derivative evaluator for the actual returned stage maps and resulting finite NLP on an open neighborhood of the queried candidate. On a locally fixed strict stopping branch of the finite stage-iteration procedure, differentiate that finite graph, including when the residual happens to be exactly zero at the queried point. Implicit differentiation as in [[thm-implicit-differentiation-forward-and-adjoint-formulas]] is permitted only when the selected returned stage map is certified to agree on that neighborhood with the exact local solution branch and its residual Jacobian is nonsingular there; an exact residual at the queried point alone does not establish this agreement. Return `derivative-failure` when no derivative of the actual returned map is available. Supply a quadrature error evaluator which returns a certified upper bound for the objective quadrature discrepancy or `unavailable`. Each supplied evaluator returns a value or failure in finite time. An optional trajectory-estimation request supplies the inputs of [[alg-bounded-adaptive-runge-kutta-controller]].
$$X_{j,i}=X_{j,0}+h_j\sum_{k<i}a_{ik}F_{j,k},\quad t_{j,i}=t_j+c_ih_j,\quad F_{j,i}=f(t_{j,i},X_{j,i},u_j),\quad \Phi_j(X_{j,0},u_j)=X_{j,0}+h_j\sum_i b_iF_{j,i}.$$

**Mesh and constraints.** Check $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$, all declared constraint and quadrature times in $[0,T]$, and all stage times $t_j+c_i h_j$ in $[0,T]$ before querying $f$ or $L$. An invalid time returns `mesh-domain-failure` with no evaluation. Insert every declared path-constraint time not already a node into the mesh, unless this exceeds the supplied node cap, in which case return `mesh-budget-exhausted`. Tie each inserted subcell's control to its original containing cell, so the parameterization is unchanged. A path constraint is evaluated at its declared times, now mesh nodes; an endpoint constraint is evaluated at its declared endpoint. This is finite sampling and does not assert continuous-path feasibility.

**Stage evaluation.** On each cell write $h_j=t_{j+1}-t_j$ and $u_j$ for its tied constant control. For an explicit tableau, form the stages recursively by the displayed equations. Before each query of $f$ or $L$, check that the time is in $[0,T]$, the state lies in $\Omega_x$, and the control lies in $\Omega_u$; a failed membership check returns `stage-domain-failure`, and an unavailable function value returns `stage-evaluation-failure` with the cell and stage index. Apply the same checks to every declared path-constraint evaluation.

For an implicit tableau, do not leave the collocation stages as outer NLP decision variables. Form the coupled slope residual
$$R_j(K;X_{j,0},u_j)_i=K_i-f\!\left(t_j+c_ih_j,X_{j,0}+h_j\sum_k a_{ik}K_k,u_j\right),\quad i=1,\ldots,s.$$
Its open domain consists of stage vectors for which every state-control input is in the smooth-data tube. In the sampled linear-quadratic branch, form the finite matrix $M_j$ with blocks $(M_j)_{ik}=\delta_{ik}I-h_ja_{ik}A(t_{j,i})$ and right-hand side $r_i=A(t_{j,i})X_{j,0}+B(t_{j,i})u_j$. Use exact Gaussian elimination on the stored sample coefficients: scan columns left to right, pivot on the first nonzero entry at or below the current row, swap, eliminate below, and back-substitute. If no pivot is available, return `singular-stage-matrix`; otherwise the exact solution of $M_jK=r$ is the stage vector and the nonlinear-solve status is `exact-linear-stage-solve`. In all other smooth cases, form the deterministic initial guess $K_i^{(0)}=f(t_j,X_{j,0},u_j)$ after checking that this query is defined. Before calling Newton, check that the entire seed $K^{(0)}$ belongs to the declared open domain of $R_j$, equivalently that every induced stage state lies in $\Omega_x$ and every required control lies in $\Omega_u$. If this check fails, return `stage-domain-failure` with the failing cell and stage index, the partial result record, and no objective candidate. Otherwise call [[alg-finite-budget-newton-for-vector-residuals]] on $R_j$ with that open evaluation domain, tolerance $\tau_s$ and cap $M_s$. Record its iterate, residual vector, and exact status for each cell. Only `root` supplies a stage candidate; it means $\|R_j\|_2\le\tau_s$, not an exact root unless $\tau_s=0$. Any other status returns the partial result record with `nlp_status=stage-solve-failure`, the failing cell, and no objective candidate. On a returned stage vector use $X_{j,i}=X_{j,0}+h_j\sum_k a_{ik}K_k$ and $\Phi_j=X_{j,0}+h_j\sum_i b_iK_i$. A singular stage Jacobian or failed stage query is reported, not interpreted as lack of an exact solution.

**Transcription modes.** In single shooting, the decision variables are the original-cell controls; set $X_{0,0}=x_0$ and recursively compute $X_{j+1,0}=\Phi_j(X_{j,0},u_j)$. In multiple shooting, the decision variables are node states and controls; fix $X_{0,0}=x_0$ and define defects $d_j=X_{j+1,0}-\Phi_j(X_{j,0},u_j)$. In collocation mode, use the same node/control variables and solved internal stage states; the collocation equations are solved internally by the implicit-stage procedure above. Explicit stages are likewise internal deterministic evaluations. In every mode the finite feasible set includes $u_j\in U_c$ for each original cell. The finite objective is $\sum_j h_j\sum_i b_iL(t_{j,i},X_{j,i},u_j)+\phi(X_{N,0})$, and the finite constraints are exactly the declared node/time constraints, the represented control constraints, and endpoint constraints. If $U_c$ is available only as a compact set-membership constraint and has no finite smooth representation, return the finite set-constrained model with `nlp_status=not-smooth-nlp`; the dispatcher must not treat it as an SQP-ready NLP. A QP solver route additionally requires the sampled control constraints to be affine.

**Output.** Evaluate the supplied initial candidate and return a record containing its ordered decision variables, defect residuals, per-cell implicit-stage residuals, path/endpoint constraint residuals, KKT residuals, and objective value, when available. For equality residual $h$, inequality residual $g\le0$, and multiplier pair $(\nu,\lambda)$, report $r_p=(h,[g]_+)$, $r_d=\nabla J_N+Dh^T\nu+Dg^T\lambda$, $r_\lambda=[-\lambda]_+$, and $r_c=\lambda\odot g$. Include a model that can reevaluate these quantities at a later solver candidate. Return separate `nlp_status`, per-cell `implicit_stage_status`, optional `ivp_status`, `quadrature_status`, `mesh_status`, and `budget_status` fields. A quadrature bound at most $\tau_q$ is `bound-met`; a larger bound is `bound-not-met`; an unavailable bound is `unavailable`. The build-stage budget field is `not-run`; the solver dispatcher fills its final value. A failed derivative evaluation leaves KKT residuals unavailable with its exact status. An unevaluated optional IVP estimate is `not-requested`; if requested, report the adaptive controller's exact finite status, not an error certificate.

This direct transcription samples pointwise data; an $L^\infty$ equivalence class without a chosen representative and sampling rule is not stage-evaluable. For a single-shooting reduced objective represented as the finite state-step graph of [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]], its exact real-arithmetic reduced gradient is given by [[thm-discrete-adjoint-gradient-recursion]]. Agreement with the continuous ODE adjoint gradient is only conditional on the weighted discrete-gradient representation and the separate state, adjoint, derivative-data, endpoint, and quadrature estimates in [[thm-discrete-continuous-gradient-error-order-p]]. The optional adaptive RK estimate is separate from the fixed NLP and its embedded difference is not a certified global error bound. The algorithm makes no continuous-path feasibility, convergence-rate, global-optimality, or unconditioned discrete-adjoint accuracy claim.

Fix a mesh, controls $u_0,\ldots,u_{N-1}$, and a successful deterministic Runge–Kutta interval map $\Phi_j$ from [[alg-ctrl1-runge-kutta-shooting-and-collocation-transcription]]. In the single-shooting NLP, define states recursively from $X_{0,0}=x_0$ and $X_{j+1,0}=\Phi_j(X_{j,0},u_j)$. In the multiple-shooting NLP, impose the same initial state and continuity equations. Then projection from the multiple-shooting feasible set onto its control coordinates is a bijection onto the single-shooting feasible controls. Any objective and node constraints that use the same recursively determined states have identical reduced values and feasibility. This is an algebraic equivalence of the discrete NLPs; it is not an equivalence to the continuous ODE problem.

derivations.claim: On the first cell every stage slope equals $v_0$, so its endpoint increment is $\frac12v_0\sum_i b_i=\frac12v_0$. The second cell adds $\frac12v_1\sum_i b_i=\frac12v_1$. Thus single shooting gives the stated $x_1$ and $x_2$.

The multiple-shooting continuity equations uniquely impose $x_1=\frac12v_0$ and $x_2=x_1+\frac12v_1=\frac12(v_0+v_1)$. Substitution into its objective gives exactly the single-shooting objective. This is the concrete bijection and reduced-objective identity stated in [F3].

citations.quote:
Let $a\le b$ and $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]). The function $f$ is
**absolutely continuous** on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$\delta>0$ such that every finite family of subintervals
$[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, indexed by $j<m$, whose open interiors are pairwise
disjoint and which satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}(v_j-u_j)<\delta$$

also satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}|f(v_j)-f(u_j)|<\varepsilon.$$

Finite sums and the empty sum are those of [[def-finite-sum]] and
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. For $m=0$ both sums are $0$, so the condition is
automatic. On $[a,a]$ every permitted interval is a singleton and every endpoint
increment is $0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), so every function on that singleton is
absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity implies ordinary continuity
([[def-continuity-real]]); that implication is proved next rather than built into
the definition.

For $a\le b$, every gauge on a compact interval admits a fine tagged partition.

Equivalently, every gauge admits a fine tagged partition, and every gauge admits at least one fine tagged partition. In particular, every gauge on each complementary compact interval admits a fine tagged partition.

Let $a\le b$. A **gauge** on $[a,b]$ is a function $\delta:[a,b]\to(0,\infty)$. A tagged partition is written

$$P=\{([x_{i-1},x_i],\xi_i):1\le i\le m\},$$

where $a=x_0<\cdots<x_m=b$ and $\xi_i\in[x_{i-1},x_i]$. It is **$\delta$-fine** when

$$[x_{i-1},x_i]\subset(\xi_i-\delta(\xi_i),\xi_i+\delta(\xi_i))$$

for every $i$. Its Riemann sum is $S(f,P)=\sum_{i=1}^m f(\xi_i)(x_i-x_{i-1})$.

When $a=b$, the single degenerate tagged cell $([a,a],a)$ is declared a fine tagged partition for every gauge, and its Riemann sum is $0$. A **fine partial tagged partition** is any finite pairwise interior-disjoint family of cells $([u_j,v_j],\xi_j)$ with $[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, $u_j\le v_j$, and $\xi_j\in[u_j,v_j]$, each satisfying the same gauge-containment condition. The empty family is allowed and has sum $0$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). For **every** subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$,
measurable or not,

$$\lambda_n^*(E) \;=\; \inf\,\{\, \lambda_n(U) \;:\; U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \text{ open and } E \subseteq U \,\},$$

the infimum being taken in $[0,+\infty]$ over a family that is nonempty because
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is open.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$. **Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then Lebesgue outer measure $\lambda_n^*$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]) is an outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-outer-measure]]): it vanishes at $\varnothing$, is monotone, and is
countably subadditive.

**The agreement clause is a theorem of ZF and needs no choice principle:**
$\lambda_n^*(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every elementary set $A$
([[def-elementary-set-in-rn]]), where $\mu_0$ is elementary volume. In
particular $\lambda_n^*(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
and $\lambda_n^*(\varnothing) = 0$.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].
For $f\in L^1[a,b]$, the function $I_f(x)=\int_a^x f$ is absolutely continuous.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then $F$ is differentiable for almost every $x\in(a,b)$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)$$
at every such point.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

derivations.claim: If $a=b$, both conclusions hold directly. Otherwise fix $a\le s<t\le b$ and $\varepsilon>0$ for claim 1. Let $E$ be a null exceptional set for $F'=0$ on $[s,t]$, enlarged by $s,t$; it is null by [F4]. Restricting [F1] to $[s,t]$, choose $d>0$ so that total interval length below $d$ implies total absolute increment below $\varepsilon/2$. Put $\eta=\varepsilon/(2(t-s+1))$. By [F3], choose one open $U\supseteq E$ with $\lambda(U)<d$.

For $x\notin E$, define $k(x)$ as the least $k\in\mathbb N_0$ such that $|F(y)-F(x)|\le\eta|y-x|$ whenever $y\in[s,t]$ and $|y-x|<2^{-k}$. This set is nonempty by $F'(x)=0$, [F7] and [F5], including $y=x$ by equality. For $x\in E$, instead take the least $k$ with $(x-2^{-k},x+2^{-k})\subseteq U$; openness and [F5] give existence. Set $\gamma(x)=2^{-k(x)}$. These uniquely specified least integers define one positive gauge; no arbitrary pointwise radius selections are needed. Obtain one finite $\gamma$-fine partition $\{([x_{i-1},x_i],\xi_i)\}_{i=1}^m$ from [F2].

Cells tagged in $E$ lie in $U$. Their interiors are disjoint, and their total length is the measure of their finite union, since shared endpoints form a finite null set. By [F4] this sum is at most $\lambda(U)<d$, so [F1] bounds their total absolute $F$-increment by $\varepsilon/2$; for an empty family the sum is zero.

For every other cell, strict fineness and step 2.1 give $|F(x_i)-F(x_{i-1})|\le|F(x_i)-F(\xi_i)|+|F(\xi_i)-F(x_{i-1})|\le\eta(x_i-x_{i-1})$, because the tag lies in the cell. The sum over these cells is at most $\eta(t-s)<\varepsilon/2$. Telescoping all cells and applying step 3.1 yields $|F(t)-F(s)|<\varepsilon$. Arbitrary positive $\varepsilon$ gives equality, and arbitrary $s,t$ prove claim 1.

For claim 2 with $a<b$, fix a coordinate $j$ and put $I_j(t)=\int_a^t h_j(s)\,ds$. By [F6], $I_j$ is absolutely continuous and $I'_j=h_j$ almost everywhere. The function $H_j=y_j-y_j(a)-I_j$ is absolutely continuous: for each positive tolerance use the [F1] moduli for $y_j,I_j$ at half that tolerance and take their minimum. Outside the union of the two exceptional null sets, [F7] gives $H'_j=0$. Claim 1 makes $H_j$ constant, and $H_j(a)=0$, so $y_j(t)=y_j(a)+I_j(t)$ for all $t$. Applying this argument to the finitely many coordinates proves the displayed vector identity.

boundaries.reason: Statement assumes a compact interval [a,b]; the equal-endpoint case is treated separately, not an empty interval.

boundaries.evidence: Statement permits a=b; proof 1.1 treats both conclusions directly. Zero derivative is the explicit hypothesis of its scalar claim.
Statement includes n=1 and proof 5.1 applies scalar reconstruction separately to each of finitely many coordinates.
Statement imposes no nonzero derivative or function requirement; proof 2.1 uses least natural gauge indices and proof 3.1 treats the empty exceptional-tag family as sum zero.

Let $E\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set. Let $U=L^2(E;\mathbb R)$ with inner product
$$
(q,r)_U=\int_E q(x)r(x)\,dx
$$
and the corresponding norm. This is a real Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] under Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]].

For bounds $q_a,q_b\in U$ with $q_a\le q_b$ almost everywhere, define the **admissible box**
$$
Q_{ad}(q_a,q_b)=\{q\in U:q_a(x)\le q(x)\le q_b(x)\text{ for almost every }x\in E\}.
$$
Equalities and inequalities between controls are understood as almost-everywhere statements about their $L^2$ classes. The box is nonempty because it contains $q_a$. When a finite-element control space is used, its cellwise-constant admissible set is the intersection of this box with the stated piecewise-constant subspace; cellwise averaging preserves the box when both bounds are constant on each control cell.

derivations.claim: The control $q_a$ belongs to $Q_{ad}$ because $q_a\le q_a\le q_b$ almost everywhere, so $Q_{ad}$ is nonempty. If $q,r\in Q_{ad}$ and $0\le t\le1$, then $q_a\le tq+(1-t)r\le q_b$ almost everywhere; hence the convex combination is in $Q_{ad}$. The pointwise inequality also gives $|q|\le |q_a|+|q_b|$ almost everywhere for each $q\in Q_{ad}$, so $\|q\|_{L^2}\le\|q_a\|_{L^2}+\|q_b\|_{L^2}$ and the box is bounded.

Suppose $q_n\in Q_{ad}$ and $q_n\to q$ in $L^2(E)$. For almost every $x$, $q_n(x)\ge q_a(x)$, so $(q_a-q)^+\le |q_n-q|$ almost everywhere, where $s^+=\max\{s,0\}$. Therefore $\|(q_a-q)^+\|_2\le\|q_n-q\|_2\to0$ and $q\ge q_a$ almost everywhere. Similarly $(q-q_b)^+\le|q-q_n|$ gives $q\le q_b$ almost everywhere. Thus $q\in Q_{ad}$ and the box is norm closed.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. The finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
half-open boxes with rational endpoints and rational coefficients form a
countable dense subset of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Define $Z:L^2(E)\to L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ by zero extension and $R:L^2(\mathbb R^d)\to L^2(E)$ by restriction. The maps are well-defined on almost-everywhere classes, $RZ$ is the identity on $L^2(E)$, and $\|R f\|_{L^2(E)}\le\|f\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}$.

Let $\mathcal S$ be the countable dense rational box-step family from [F1]. The set $R(\mathcal S)$ is countable. For $q\in L^2(E)$, choose any $\varepsilon>0$ and extend it by $Zq$. By density there is $s\in\mathcal S$ with $\|Zq-s\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}<\varepsilon$; then $\|q-Rs\|_{L^2(E)}=\|R(Zq-s)\|_2\le\|Zq-s\|_2<\varepsilon$. Thus $R(\mathcal S)$ is dense in $L^2(E)$, proving separability.
The integral pairing makes $L^2(E)$ a real Hilbert space by [F3], so it is both separable and Hilbert. Countable Choice is the only stated choice principle in [F1] and [F3].

For each $k \in \mathbb{N}$ let $I_k = [a_k, b_k]$ be a closed bounded interval
with $a_k \le b_k$ ([[def-interval]]), and suppose the family is **nested**:

$$I_{k+1} \subseteq I_k \qquad (k \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $\ell_k = b_k - a_k \ge 0$ for the length of $I_k$. Then:

1. $\displaystyle\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k$ is **nonempty**. More precisely,
   with $a = \sup\{a_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ and
   $b = \inf\{b_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$, both of which exist, one has $a \le b$
   and $$\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k = [a, b].$$
2. $\displaystyle\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k$ is a **single point** if and only
   if $\ell_k \to 0$ ([[def-real-limit]]).

Every hypothesis is load bearing. Dropping closedness makes the intersection
empty; dropping boundedness does the same; and dropping nonemptiness of the
individual intervals is vacuously fatal.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Recall that a natural number is a von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$ and $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, so
that

$$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$$

is itself the set of its predecessors. Here $<$ is the order of
[[def-nat-order]], which is defined additively, so the displayed identity is a
theorem and not a convention: it is [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]], proved
immediately above. Let $A$ be a set, and let $\approx$ be equinumerosity
([[def-equinumerous]]).

- $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite.
- $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.

derivations.claim: By separability choose a dense subset $D\subseteq H$ that is at most countable. It is nonempty because $H$ contains $0$. If $D$ is finite, a finite listing from its bijection with a natural number, repeated periodically, gives a sequence; if $D$ is countably infinite, a bijection with $\mathbb N$ gives a sequence. Thus [F4] supplies a dense sequence $(v_j)_{j\ge1}$ without any choice principle beyond the witnesses in the definition of countability.

For any bounded real sequence $(a_k)$ in $[-R,R]$, start with $I_0=[-R,R]$. At each stage split the current interval into its two closed halves and choose the left half if it contains infinitely many terms of the current sequence, and otherwise choose the right half. At least one half contains infinitely many terms. Choose the least index later than the preceding selected index whose term lies in the chosen half. The resulting nested intervals have lengths tending to zero, so [F1] gives a common point, and the selected subsequence converges to it. Every choice in this construction is the least natural index or the leftmost of two alternatives, so the extraction is determined by its input sequence.

For each $j$, the scalar sequence $\langle x_n,v_j\rangle_H$ is bounded by $C\|v_j\|_H$ by [F3]. Apply the deterministic extraction in step 1.2 successively to these coordinate sequences, each time inside the previously obtained subsequence. This recursive rule produces nested infinite subsequences $N_1\supseteq N_2\supseteq\cdots$ on which the first, first two, and then first $j$ pairings converge, respectively. Let $n_k$ be the $k$th index of $N_k$. Nestedness makes $(n_k)$ strictly increasing, and for each fixed $j$ the sequence $\langle x_{n_k},v_j\rangle_H$ converges because its tail is a subsequence of $N_j$.

For any $v\in H$, choose $v_j$ arbitrarily close to $v$. For indices $k,\ell$, [F3] gives $|\langle x_{n_k}-x_{n_\ell},v\rangle_H| \le |\langle x_{n_k}-x_{n_\ell},v_j\rangle_H|+2C\|v-v_j\|_H.$ The first term tends to zero as $k,\ell\to\infty$ for fixed $j$, and the second can be made arbitrarily small by density. Thus $\langle x_{n_k},v\rangle_H$ converges for every $v$. Its limit $L(v)$ is linear and satisfies $|L(v)|\le C\|v\|_H$, so $L$ is a bounded linear functional. By [F2] there is a unique $x\in H$ with $L(v)=\langle x,v\rangle_H$ for all $v$. Therefore $x_{n_k}\rightharpoonup x$.

derivations.claim: Let $A=\{x\in E:q(x)<q_a(x)\}$. If $A$ had positive measure, then for some integer $m\ge1$ the measurable set $A_m=\{x:q(x)\le q_a(x)-1/m\}$ would have positive measure, because $A=\bigcup_{m\ge1}A_m$. Since $E$ has finite measure, $\mathbf1_{A_m}\in L^2(E)$. Weak convergence and $q_n\ge q_a$ give $\int_{A_m}(q-q_a)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{A_m}(q_n-q_a)\ge0,$ whereas the definition of $A_m$ makes the left side at most $-\mu(A_m)/m<0$. This contradiction proves $q\ge q_a$ almost everywhere.

Apply the same argument to $B=\{x:q(x)>q_b(x)\}$ and $B_m=\{x:q(x)\ge q_b(x)+1/m\}$. Weak convergence gives $\int_{B_m}(q-q_b)=\lim_n\int_{B_m}(q_n-q_b)\le0$, while the defining inequality on $B_m$ makes this integral at least $\mu(B_m)/m>0$ if $B_m$ has positive measure. Thus $q\le q_b$ almost everywhere, and [F1] gives $q\in Q_{ad}$.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, $V=H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and $H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Use the real integral pairing on $H$. Equip $V$ with the standard full Sobolev inner product and norm
$$
(v,w)_V=(v,w)_H+\sum_{i=1}^d(D_i v,D_i w)_H,\qquad
\|v\|_V^2=\|v\|_H^2+\sum_{i=1}^d\|D_i v\|_H^2.
$$
Here $H^1_0=W^{1,2}_0$ is the closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ in the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]. Under Countable Choice, $H$ and $V$ are real Hilbert spaces; the local proof of completeness of $V$ is included in [[thm-linear-elliptic-control-state-and-adjoint-wellposedness]]. The inclusion $J:V\to H$ is continuous with $\|J\|\le1$.

Let $E\subseteq\Omega$ be bounded and measurable, $U=L^2(E;\mathbb R)$ with its real integral inner product, and let $Q_{ad}\subset U$ be the pointwise box of [[def-pde-box-control-set]]. Under Countable Choice, $U$ is a real Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Let $a:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be bilinear, bounded with constant $M$, and coercive with constant $\beta>0$ in the stated $V$ norm; symmetry is not assumed. Let $B:U\to V^*$ be bounded and linear, and fix $f\in V^*$, $u_d\in H$, and $\alpha>0$.

For every $q\in U$, the **state** $u(q)\in V$ is required to satisfy
$$
a(u(q),v)=\langle f+Bq,v\rangle_{V^*,V}\qquad(v\in V).
$$
The reduced objective, defined on all of $U$ and minimized over $Q_{ad}$, is
$$
\widehat J(q)=\frac12\|Ju(q)-u_d\|_H^2+\frac\alpha2\|q\|_U^2.
$$
A spatially varying coefficient, boundary control, variational crimes, finite-element control discretization, and parabolic evolution are separate hypotheses or branches; none is implicit in this definition. The state well-definedness is supplied by [[thm-linear-elliptic-control-state-and-adjoint-wellposedness]].

Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)$ linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), and let $a:H\times H\to\mathbb K$ be sesquilinear in the sense of [[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]]: linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second. The form $a$ is **bounded** with bound $M\ge0$ when $$|a(u,v)|\le M\|u\|\,\|v\|\qquad\text{for all }u,v\in H,$$ and **coercive** with constant $\alpha>0$ when $$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2\qquad\text{for all }u\in H .$$ It is **symmetric** (Hermitian) when $a(u,v)=\overline{a(v,u)}$ for all $u,v$, over $\mathbb C$ this is equivalent to $a(u,u)\in\mathbb R$ for every $u$. Indeed, writing $q(u)=a(u,u)$, sesquilinearity gives $4a(u,v)=q(u+v)-q(u-v)+i q(u+iv)-i q(u-iv)$, and real diagonal values make this identity conjugate-symmetric. Over $\mathbb R$, symmetry means $a(u,v)=a(v,u)$; real diagonal values alone do not imply symmetry. The **adjoint form** is $a^*(u,v):=\overline{a(v,u)}$, and $(a^*)^*=a$. **Real bilinear convention.** When $H$ is a real Hilbert space the same definitions apply with $a$ bilinear and coercive in the form $a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2$; the conjugation in the second slot is then the identity. More generally, a real bilinear form may satisfy the boundedness and coercivity conditions without being symmetric; symmetry is an additional property, not part of either condition. When $H=\{0\}$ every form is bounded with bound $0$ and coercive with every $\alpha>0$; this degenerate case is kept but is never load-bearing. All constants below are named and never silently improved. No choice principle is used in this definition.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$,
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, and $u,v,w\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$. If both
$v$ and $w$ are weak $\alpha$-derivatives of $u$, then
$$v=w\quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Omega.$$
Thus a weak derivative, when it exists, is unique as an almost-everywhere
class. No connectedness assumption is needed.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the assertion holds because there is only the zero
class and no nonzero tests.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: The weak-derivative test identities are linear, and [F4] makes each derivative coordinate intrinsic, so $W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ is a vector space with the inner product induced from $L^2(\Omega)^{d+1}$; it induces the displayed full Sobolev norm and is definite because its zeroth coordinate is $v$. Let $(v_n)$ be Cauchy in this norm. Its function coordinates and each of its finitely many weak-derivative coordinates are Cauchy in $L^2(\Omega)$ because each coordinate norm is bounded by the full $W^{1,2}$ norm. By [F3], there are $v,g_1,\ldots,g_d\in L^2(\Omega)$ with $v_n\to v$ and $D_i v_n\to g_i$ in $L^2$ for each $i$.

For every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and $i$, the weak-derivative identity for $v_n$ is $\int_\Omega v_nD_i\varphi=-\int_\Omega (D_i v_n)\varphi$. By [F5], both test functions are in $L^2$; Cauchy–Schwarz lets both integrals pass to the limits in [F3], giving $\int_\Omega vD_i\varphi=-\int_\Omega g_i\varphi$. Thus each $g_i$ is a weak derivative of $v$. By uniqueness in [F4], $D_i v=g_i$ as an $L^2$ class, and the component convergences from step 1.1 give $v_n\to v$ in the full $W^{1,2}$ norm. Hence $W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ is complete.

By [F4], $V=H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ is the closure of the linear space $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ in $W^{1,2}$. It is therefore a closed linear subspace of that complete space, and the inherited inner product is exactly the one in [[def-linear-elliptic-pde-constrained-control-problem]]. Thus $V$ is a real Hilbert space under Countable Choice.

For fixed $q$, the functional $F_q(v)=\langle f+Bq,v\rangle$ is bounded and linear, with $\|F_q\|_{V^*}\le\|f+Bq\|_{V^*}$. Applying [F2] to $a$ and $F_q$ now gives the unique state and the stated bound.

Define the adjoint form $a^*(p,v):=a(v,p)$. It is bounded with the same constant $M$, and $a^*(p,p)=a(p,p)\ge\beta\|p\|_V^2$, so it is coercive with the same $\beta$. The functional $G_q(v)=(Ju(q)-u_d,Jv)_H$ is bounded by $\|J\|\|Ju(q)-u_d\|_H\|v\|_V$. Apply [F2] to $a^*$ and $G_q$; the result is the unique $p(q)$ with $a(v,p(q))=G_q(v)$ and the stated bound. No symmetry of $a$ is used.

Steps 1.1–1.3 establish the real Hilbert structure required by [F2] using Countable Choice through the real $L^2$ completeness result [F3]. Steps 2.1–2.2 give the state, adjoint, uniqueness, and both estimates.

derivations.claim: For $h\in U$, let $w_h=u(q+h)-u(q)$. Subtracting the two state equations gives $a(w_h,v)=\langle Bh,v\rangle$ for all $v$, so $w_h$ depends linearly and boundedly on $h$ by the state estimate in [F1]. Thus $Sh=Jw_h$ is a bounded linear map from $U$ to $H$. The functional $h\mapsto\langle Bh,p(q)\rangle$ is bounded, so [F2] gives the unique $B^*p(q)\in U$ in the displayed definition.

Expanding the two squared norms in $\widehat J(q+h)$ yields $\widehat J(q+h)-\widehat J(q) =(Ju(q)-u_d,Jw_h)_H+\alpha(q,h)_U+\frac12\|Sh\|_H^2+\frac\alpha2\|h\|_U^2.$ The adjoint equation with $v=w_h$ and the state variation equation with test $p(q)$ give $(Ju(q)-u_d,Jw_h)_H=a(w_h,p(q))=\langle Bh,p(q)\rangle=(B^*p(q),h)_U$. The last two terms are bounded by a constant times $\|h\|_U^2$, so the Fréchet derivative is $B^*p(q)+\alpha q$.

Since the state map is affine with linear part $S$, the same exact expansion at any $q$ shows the second derivative is $D^2\widehat J[h,k]=(Sh,Sk)_H+\alpha(h,k)_U$, represented by $S^*S+\alpha I$. Hence $((S^*S+\alpha I)h,h)=\|Sh\|_H^2+\alpha\|h\|_U^2\ge\alpha\|h\|_U^2$ and $\|S^*S+\alpha I\|\le\|S\|^2+\alpha$. The constant Hessian gives the stated Lipschitz-gradient bound; the exact quadratic expansion gives strong convexity.

derivations.claim: The box is nonempty by [F1], so $m:=\inf_{q\in Q_{ad}}\widehat J(q)$ is finite: $\widehat J\ge0$ and $\widehat J(q_a)<\infty$. By Countable Choice choose $q_n\in Q_{ad}$ with $\widehat J(q_n)<m+1/n$. Since $\widehat J(q_n)\ge\alpha\|q_n\|_U^2/2$, the sequence is bounded. By [F2], a subsequence converges weakly to some $q\in U$, and [F1] gives $q\in Q_{ad}$.

If $q_*$ minimizes, fix $v\in Q_{ad}$. Convexity gives $q_*+t(v-q_*)\in Q_{ad}$ for $0\le t\le1$. Minimality makes the right directional quotient nonnegative for every $t>0$; letting $t\downarrow0$ and using [F4] proves the variational inequality.

Write $Ju(q_n)-u_d=J u(0)-u_d+S q_n$. Bounded linear maps preserve weak convergence, so along the subsequence this state residual converges weakly in $H$ to $Ju(q)-u_d$; the controls converge weakly in $U$. The Hilbert norm is weakly lower semicontinuous: if $z\ne0$, then $\|z_n\|\ge |(z_n,z/\|z\|)|\to\|z\|$, while the case $z=0$ is immediate. Applying this to both squared norms in $\widehat J$ gives $\widehat J(q)\le\liminf_n\widehat J(q_n)=m$. Thus $q$ attains the infimum.

The exact expansion in [F3] shows strict convexity: for distinct $q,r\in U$ and $0<t<1$, $\widehat J(tq+(1-t)r)=t\widehat J(q)+(1-t)\widehat J(r)-\frac{t(1-t)}2\bigl(\|S(q-r)\|_H^2+\alpha\|q-r\|_U^2\bigr).$ The last subtracted term is positive, so two different minimizers in the convex box cannot exist.

Conversely, if $q$ satisfies the variational inequality, then for every $v\in Q_{ad}$ the exact expansion [F3] gives $\widehat J(v)-\widehat J(q)=(B^*p(q)+\alpha q,v-q)_U+\frac12\|S(v-q)\|_H^2+\frac\alpha2\|v-q\|_U^2\ge0.$ Thus $q$ is a minimizer; step 3.1 gives uniqueness.

Let $E\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set. Let $U=L^2(E;\mathbb R)$ with inner product
$$
(q,r)_U=\int_E q(x)r(x)\,dx
$$
and the corresponding norm. This is a real Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] under Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]].

For bounds $q_a,q_b\in U$ with $q_a\le q_b$ almost everywhere, define the **admissible box**
$$
Q_{ad}(q_a,q_b)=\{q\in U:q_a(x)\le q(x)\le q_b(x)\text{ for almost every }x\in E\}.
$$
Equalities and inequalities between controls are understood as almost-everywhere statements about their $L^2$ classes. The box is nonempty because it contains $q_a$. When a finite-element control space is used, its cellwise-constant admissible set is the intersection of this box with the stated piecewise-constant subspace; cellwise averaging preserves the box when both bounds are constant on each control cell.

derivations.claim: Put $q(x)=\min\{q_b(x),\max\{q_a(x),r(x)\}\}$. This function is measurable and lies between $q_a$ and $q_b$; therefore $q\in Q_{ad}$ and $q\in L^2(E)$. For real numbers $a\le b$, the clipped value $c=\min\{b,\max\{a,s\}\}$ satisfies $(c-s)(t-c)\ge0$ for every $t\in[a,b]$: if $s<a$, then $c=a$ and both factors are nonnegative; if $a\le s\le b$, then $c=s$ and the product is zero; if $s>b$, then $c=b$ and both factors are nonpositive. Applying this pointwise with $s=r(x)$ and $t=v(x)$ and integrating gives $(q-r,v-q)_{L^2}\ge0$ for every $v\in Q_{ad}$.

For any $v\in Q_{ad}$, $\|v-r\|_2^2-\|q-r\|_2^2 =\|v-q\|_2^2+2(q-r,v-q)_2\ge\|v-q\|_2^2.$ Thus $q$ minimizes the distance and equality can hold only when $v=q$ in $L^2$. Conversely, if $q$ is a distance minimizer, then for any $v\in Q_{ad}$ and $0<t\le1$, $q+t(v-q)\in Q_{ad}$. Expanding $\|q+t(v-q)-r\|_2^2\ge\|q-r\|_2^2$, dividing by $2t$, and letting $t\downarrow0$ gives $(q-r,v-q)_2\ge0$.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ be an affine bijection from a bounded open
set $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ to $K$, where $A$ is invertible, and let
$1\le p\le\infty$. For every integer $r\ge0$ and scalar
$v\in W^{r,p}(K)$, the pullback $\widehat v:=v\circ F$ belongs to
$W^{r,p}(\widehat K)$. For $r\ge1$ its first weak derivatives satisfy
$$D_{\widehat x_j}\widehat v=\sum_{i=1}^d A_{ij}(D_{x_i}v)\circ F,$$
and higher derivatives are obtained by applying this constant-matrix rule
repeatedly. In particular, for each $0\le m\le r$,
$$|\widehat v|_{W^{m,p}(\widehat K)}\le C(d,m)\|A\|^m|\det A|^{-1/p}|v|_{W^{m,p}(K)},$$
where $|\det A|^{-1/p}:=1$ for $p=\infty$. The reverse estimate holds
with $A^{-1}$ and $|\det A|^{1/p}$ in place of $A$ and
$|\det A|^{-1/p}$.

Assume Countable Choice. For every $1\le p<\infty$ there is
$C_{d,p}<\infty$ such that for all
$u\in W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)$,
$$\|u-u_{\widehat S_d}\|_{L^p(\widehat S_d)} \le C_{d,p}|u|_{W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d)},\qquad u_{\widehat S_d}:=|\widehat S_d|^{-1}\int_{\widehat S_d}u\,dx.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

$$
(v,w)_V=(v,w)_H+\sum_{i=1}^d(D_i v,D_i w)_H,\qquad
\|v\|_V^2=\|v\|_H^2+\sum_{i=1}^d\|D_i v\|_H^2.
$$
Here $H^1_0=W^{1,2}_0$ is the closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ in the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]. Under Countable Choice, $H$ and $V$ are real Hilbert spaces; the local proof of completeness of $V$ is included in [[thm-linear-elliptic-control-state-and-adjoint-wellposedness]]. The inclusion $J:V\to H$ is continuous with $\|J\|\le1$.

Let $E\subseteq\Omega$ be bounded and measurable, $U=L^2(E;\mathbb R)$ with its real integral inner product, and let $Q_{ad}\subset U$ be the pointwise box of [[def-pde-box-control-set]]. Under Countable Choice, $U$ is a real Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Let $a:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be bilinear, bounded with constant $M$, and coercive with constant $\beta>0$ in the stated $V$ norm; symmetry is not assumed. Let $B:U\to V^*$ be bounded and linear, and fix $f\in V^*$, $u_d\in H$, and $\alpha>0$.

For every $q\in U$, the **state** $u(q)\in V$ is required to satisfy
$$
a(u(q),v)=\langle f+Bq,v\rangle_{V^*,V}\qquad(v\in V).
$$
The reduced objective, defined on all of $U$ and minimized over $Q_{ad}$, is
$$
\widehat J(q)=\frac12\|Ju(q)-u_d\|_H^2+\frac\alpha2\|q\|_U^2.
$$
A spatially varying coefficient, boundary control, variational crimes, finite-element control discretization, and parabolic evolution are separate hypotheses or branches; none is implicit in this definition. The state well-definedness is supplied by [[thm-linear-elliptic-control-state-and-adjoint-wellposedness]].

Assume Countable Choice and the setting of [[def-linear-elliptic-pde-constrained-control-problem]]. For every $q\in U$, there is a unique state $u(q)\in V$ satisfying
$$
a(u(q),v)=\langle f+Bq,v\rangle\qquad(v\in V),
$$
and
$$
\|u(q)\|_V\le \beta^{-1}\|f+Bq\|_{V^*}.
$$
For every $q\in U$, there is also a unique adjoint $p(q)\in V$ satisfying
$$
a(v,p(q))=(Ju(q)-u_d,Jv)_H\qquad(v\in V),
$$
with
$$
\|p(q)\|_V\le \beta^{-1}\|J\|\,\|Ju(q)-u_d\|_H.
$$

Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, $a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded coercive form with boundedness constant $M$ and coercivity constant $\alpha>0$, and $F:V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded functional linear in the real case and conjugate-linear in the complex test argument. Let $V_h\subseteq V$ be finite-dimensional, and let $a_h:V_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ and $F_h:V_h\to\mathbb K$ be bounded, with $F_h$ having the same test-linearity as $F$, and $a_h$ coercive with constant $\alpha_h>0$ in the inherited norm. There are unique exact and discrete solutions $u$ and $u_h$, and

$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\left((1+M/\alpha_h)\|u-v_h\|_V+\frac{\delta_{a,h}(v_h)+\delta_{F,h}}{\alpha_h}\right),$$

where the defects are those of [[def-variational-crime-error-framework]]. For a family of meshes this is a uniform estimate whenever $\inf_h\alpha_h>0$ and the displayed approximation and defect terms are uniformly controlled. The term $\delta_{F,h}$ retains source approximation and data oscillation.

Assume the setting of [[def-linear-elliptic-pde-constrained-control-problem]] and Countable Choice. Let $S:U\to H$ be the linear part of the state map, so $Ju(q)=Ju(0)+Sq$. Then $\widehat J$ is Fréchet differentiable on $U$, with
$$
\nabla\widehat J(q)=B^*p(q)+\alpha q,
$$
where $p(q)$ is the adjoint from [[thm-linear-elliptic-control-state-and-adjoint-wellposedness]] and $B^*:V\to U$ is defined by
$$
(B^*p,h)_U=\langle Bh,p\rangle_{V^*,V}.
$$
Its Hessian is the bounded self-adjoint operator $S^*S+\alpha I$, and for every $h\in U$,
$$
\alpha\|h\|_U^2\le ((S^*S+\alpha I)h,h)_U\le(\|S\|^2+\alpha)\|h\|_U^2.

Consequently $\nabla\widehat J$ is Lipschitz with constant $L=\|S\|^2+\alpha$, and $\widehat J$ is $\alpha$-strongly convex.

derivations.claim: Apply [F2] to the exact state equation and the computed state equation. By the definition of $\varepsilon_u$, this gives $\|u-\tilde u\|_V\le\varepsilon_u$. The adjoint load formed with $\tilde u$ differs from the exact adjoint load by the functional $v\longmapsto (J(\tilde u-u),Jv)_H,$ whose norm is at most $\|J\|^2\|\tilde u-u\|_V\le\|J\|^2\varepsilon_u$. Including this term in the adjoint load defect and applying [F2] to the transposed form gives $\|p-\tilde p\|_V\le\varepsilon_p$.

The exact reduced gradient is $B^*p+\alpha q$ by [F3], and the computed one is $B^*\tilde p+\alpha q$. Therefore $\|\nabla\widehat J(q)-(B^*\tilde p+\alpha q)\|_U =\|B^*(p-\tilde p)\|_U \le\|B\|\,\|p-\tilde p\|_V \le\|B\|\,\varepsilon_p.$ The displayed certificate includes every Strang approximation and consistency term used to form $\varepsilon_p$.

Assume Countable Choice and the setting of [[def-linear-elliptic-pde-constrained-control-problem]]. Then $\widehat J$ has a unique minimizer $q_*\in Q_{ad}$. It is characterized by
$$
(B^*p(q_*)+\alpha q_*,v-q_*)_U\ge0\qquad(v\in Q_{ad}),

where $p(q_*)$ is the adjoint from [[thm-linear-elliptic-control-state-and-adjoint-wellposedness]]. Conversely, every $q\in Q_{ad}$ satisfying this variational inequality is the unique minimizer.

Let $\{\mathcal T_h\}$ be a family of matching affine simplicial meshes of a bounded control domain $E\subset\mathbb R^d$, and let $h=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\operatorname{diam}(K)$. Define $\Pi_h q$ on each cell by
$$

$$
If the box bounds $q_a,q_b$ are constant on each cell and $q\in Q_{ad}\cap H^1(E)$, then $\Pi_hq\in Q_{ad}$, $\Pi_h$ is the $L^2$ orthogonal projection onto the cellwise-constant space, and

Assume the continuous problem of [[def-linear-elliptic-pde-constrained-control-problem]], Countable Choice, and a finite-dimensional conforming subspace $V_h\subset V$. Let $u=u(q)$ and $p=p(q)$ be the exact state and adjoint. Let $\tilde u,\tilde p\in V_h$ be computed state and adjoint, where $\tilde p$ uses $\tilde u$ in its right-hand side. Let $\varepsilon_u$ be the first-Strang right-hand side for the primal problem, and let $\varepsilon_p$ be that right-hand side for the adjoint problem when its load defect includes the additional term $\|J\|^2\varepsilon_u$. Then
$$
\|u-\tilde u\|_V\le\varepsilon_u,\qquad \|p-\tilde p\|_V\le\varepsilon_p,\qquad \|\nabla\widehat J(q)-(B^*\tilde p+\alpha q)\|_U\le\|B\|\,\varepsilon_p.
$$
The Strang terms retain best-approximation, quadrature/geometry form defects, and load defects; no defect is silently set to zero.
