derivations.claim: Put $e=q_h-q_*$. By [F1], $\alpha\|e\|_U^2\le(g(q_h)-g(q_*),e)_U.$ Replace $g(q_h)$ by $g_h(q_h)$ at a cost at most $C_g h\|e\|_U$ by [F4]. The continuous variational inequality in [F2] gives $-(g(q_*),e)_U\le0$. The discrete variational inequality with the feasible test $\Pi_hq_*$ gives $(g_h(q_h),e)_U\le(g_h(q_h),\Pi_hq_*-q_*)_U.$ Since $g_h(q_h)=B^*p_h(q_h)+\alpha q_h$ and $q_h\in Q_h$, orthogonality in [F3] cancels the regularization term. Orthogonality also lets us subtract $\Pi_h(B^*p_h(q_h))$ from the remaining factor. Hence $\alpha\|e\|_U^2 \le C_\Pi^2 C_p\|q_*\|_{H^1}h^2+C_g h\|e\|_U.$

Since every mesh cell is a nondegenerate simplex, $h>0$. Let $t=\|e\|_U/h$ and divide the inequality in step 1.1 by $h^2$ to obtain $\alpha t^2-C_g t-C_\Pi^2 C_p\|q_*\|_{H^1}\le0.$ Thus $t$ is at most the positive root $\frac{C_g+\sqrt{C_g^2+4\alpha C_\Pi^2C_p\|q_*\|_{H^1}}}{2\alpha},$ which is independent of $h$. The resulting upper bound for $t$ is independent of $h$, proving the $O(h)$ estimate.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T>0$, let $V$ be a separable real Hilbert
space, and let $(V,H,V^*)$ be its real evolution triple. Suppose
$a(t;\cdot,\cdot):V\times V\to\mathbb R$ is bilinear and scalar measurable
for each fixed pair $v,w\in V$, and there is one null set outside which
$$|a(t;v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad a(t;v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2$$
for all $v,w\in V$, with constants $M>0$ and $\alpha>0$. Let
$f\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$ and $u_0\in H$. Then there is a unique
$u\in W(0,T;V)$ with $u(0)=u_0$ and, for almost every $t$,
$$\langle u'(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}+a(t;u(t),v) =\langle f(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\qquad(v\in V).$$
For every $t\in[0,T]$ it satisfies
$$\|u(t)\|_H^2+\alpha\int_0^t\|u(s)\|_V^2\,ds \le\|u_0\|_H^2+\alpha^{-1}\int_0^t\|f(s)\|_{V^*}^2\,ds.$$
The proof applies BNB to the space-time form. Scalar measurability suffices
because $V$ is separable and the measurable inverse action is proved locally.

Let $V$ and $H$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective,
continuous linear map with dense range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real linear
dual of $V$. Identify $H$ with its Hilbert dual by its inner product and embed
$H$ into $V^*$ by
$$h\longmapsto\bigl(v\longmapsto (h,i v)_H\bigr).$$
The resulting dense continuous embeddings are written
$$V\hookrightarrow H\cong H^*\hookrightarrow V^*$$
and $(V,H,V^*)$ is called an **evolution triple**. The pairing between $V^*$
and $V$ is denoted $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$.

For a Hilbert space $X$, $L^2(0,T;X)$ is the space of equivalence classes of
strongly measurable $X$-valued functions $w$ with
$$\int_0^T\|w(t)\|_X^2\,dt<\infty.$$
Strong measurability means being an almost-everywhere pointwise limit of
measurable simple functions. For $u\in L^2(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$,
say that $g$ is the **weak time derivative** of $u$ when
$$\int_0^T (i u(t),i v)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. The derivative is
unique up to equality almost everywhere. The **parabolic energy space** is
$$W(0,T;V):=\{u\in L^2(0,T;V):u'\in L^2(0,T;V^*)\},$$
with norm
$$\|u\|_{W(0,T;V)}:=\bigl(\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2+ \|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}^2\bigr)^{1/2}.$$
No endpoint values are part of this definition; they are assigned only after
a continuous $H$ trace representative has been proved. Separability is an
additional hypothesis when it is needed by a later result.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(V,H,V^*)$ be the real evolution triple of
[[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]], and let
$u,v\in W(0,T;V)$. Each has a unique representative in $C([0,T];H)$, and
for all $0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$\|u(t)\|_H^2-\|u(s)\|_H^2 =2\int_s^t\langle u'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\,dr,$$
$$(u(t),v(t))_H-(u(s),v(s))_H =\int_s^t\bigl(\langle u'(r),v(r)\rangle_{V^*,V} +\langle v'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\bigr)\,dr.$$
Writing $c_i=\|i:V\to H\|$, the trace obeys
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)\|_H^2 \le \frac{c_i^2}{T}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2 +2\|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}.$$

Let $E\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set. Let $U=L^2(E;\mathbb R)$ with inner product
$$
(q,r)_U=\int_E q(x)r(x)\,dx
$$
and the corresponding norm. This is a real Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] under Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]].

For bounds $q_a,q_b\in U$ with $q_a\le q_b$ almost everywhere, define the **admissible box**
$$
Q_{ad}(q_a,q_b)=\{q\in U:q_a(x)\le q(x)\le q_b(x)\text{ for almost every }x\in E\}.
$$
Equalities and inequalities between controls are understood as almost-everywhere statements about their $L^2$ classes. The box is nonempty because it contains $q_a$. When a finite-element control space is used, its cellwise-constant admissible set is the intersection of this box with the stated piecewise-constant subspace; cellwise averaging preserves the box when both bounds are constant on each control cell.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a separable real Hilbert space and $Y$ a real Hilbert space, and
let $u\in H^1(0,T;X)$ (meaning
$u,u'\in L^2(0,T;X)$ with distribution derivative). It has a unique
continuous representative on $[0,T]$. Let
$P\in\mathcal L(X,Y)$ be a fixed bounded linear map. Then
$Pu\in H^1(0,T;Y)$ and $(Pu)'=Pu'$.

If instead $P:[0,T]\to\mathcal L(X,Y)$ is continuously differentiable in
operator norm, then $P(t)u(t)\in H^1(0,T;Y)$ and
$$\frac{d}{dt}(P(t)u(t))=P'(t)u(t)+P(t)u'(t)\quad\text{a.e.}$$
In particular, a differentiable time-dependent Ritz comparison contributes
the term $P'(t)u(t)$ to its residual derivative.

Assume Countable Choice and the bounded polyhedral mesh setting, spaces,
form and data of [[thm-parabolic-fem-semidiscrete-existence-energy]]. Let $u$
be the continuous solution supplied by
[[thm-parabolic-variational-wellposedness-and-energy-stability]] on the same
evolution triple and let $u_h$ be the corresponding semidiscrete solution.
For this error identity, assume the additional regularity $u\in H^1(0,T;V)$,
meaning $u,u'\in L^2(0,T;V)$ with the unique continuous representative
supplied by [[lem-parabolic-projection-time-product-rule]]. Let
$P_h:V\to V_h$ be a fixed bounded linear
comparison map, define
$$\rho(t)=P_hu(t)-u(t),\qquad\theta(t)=u_h(t)-P_hu(t),$$
and let $\mathcal R_h(t)\in V_h^*$ be the full residual
$$\mathcal R_h(t)(v_h)=(\rho'(t),v_h)_H+a(t;\rho(t),v_h).$$
Then for almost every $t$ and every $v_h\in V_h$,
$$(\theta'(t),v_h)_H+a(t;\theta(t),v_h)=-\mathcal R_h(t)(v_h),$$
and for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|\theta(t)\|_H^2+\alpha\int_0^t\|\theta(s)\|_V^2ds \le\|\theta(0)\|_H^2+ \alpha^{-1}\int_0^t\|\mathcal R_h(s)\|_{V_h^*}^2ds.$$

The same identity and energy bound hold for an operator-norm $C^1$
time-dependent comparison map $P_h(t):V\to V_h$, with its time derivative
included in $\rho'$ as stated below. For a time-independent form and the
Ritz projection $P_h=R_h$ from
[[def-parabolic-ritz-projection]], Galerkin orthogonality makes
$a(\rho(t),v_h)=0$, so the residual is exactly
$(R_hu'(t)-u'(t),v_h)_H$. If a time-dependent comparison $P_h(t)$ is used,
it must be operator-norm $C^1$; then
$\rho'=P_h'(t)u+P_h(t)u'-u'$, including the projection-derivative term.
For a measurable time-dependent form with a fixed comparison map, no
orthogonality is inferred and the full displayed residual remains.

derivations.claim: For a direction $r\in U$, the state difference $z=u(q+r)-u(q)$ satisfies $z'+A(t)z=Br$ and $z(0)=0$. By [A1, F1] and linearity, $z=S r$ for a bounded linear solution map $S:U\to L^2(0,T;H)$. Expanding the two squared norms gives $\widehat J(q+r)-\widehat J(q)=(u-u_d,z)_{L^2(0,T;H)}+\alpha(q,r)_U+\tfrac12\|z\|_{L^2(0,T;H)}^2+\tfrac\alpha2\|r\|_U^2.$ The last two terms are quadratic in $r$, so the first two terms give the Fr\'echet derivative once the observation residual is paired with $z$.

Set $g=u-u_d$ and reverse time: with $s=T-t$, $\tilde p(s)=p(T-s)$, $\tilde g(s)=g(T-s)$, and $\tilde a^*(s;x,y)=a(T-s;y,x)$, the backward equation becomes the forward equation $\langle\tilde p',v\rangle+\tilde a^*(s;\tilde p,v)=(\tilde g,v)_H$ with initial value $\tilde p(0)=0$. The transposed reversed form is measurable, bounded, and coercive with the same constants, so [A1, F1] supplies its unique energy solution; reflecting back proves [F3] and gives $p\in W$. Its weak equation is $\langle-p',v\rangle+a(t;v,p)=(g,v)_H$. By the energy integration-by-parts identity [F2], testing with the state variation $z$ and using $z(0)=0$ and $p(T)=0$ gives $\int_0^T(g,z)_Hdt=\int_0^T\bigl(\langle z',p\rangle+a(t;z,p)\bigr)dt=\int_0^T\langle Br,p\rangle dt=(B^*p,r)_U.$ Therefore the linear term in step 1.1 is $(B^*p,r)_U$, and the derivative is $B^*p+\alpha q$.

Boundedness of $S$ makes the remainder in step 1.1 bounded by $\tfrac12\|S\|^2\|r\|_U^2+\tfrac\alpha2\|r\|_U^2$, which is $o(\|r\|_U)$. Therefore the derivative is Fr\'echet; Riesz representation in [A1] gives the stated gradient.

In the additional finite-element setting of [F5], differentiate $\rho(t)=P_h(t)u(t)-u(t)$ in the weak time sense. The product rule gives $\rho'=P_h'(t)u(t)+P_h(t)u'(t)-u'(t)$. Thus the comparison residual contains the full displayed derivative, including $P_h'u$; the reduced-gradient formula does not authorize dropping it.

Then
$$
\|u-\tilde u\|_V\le\varepsilon_u,\qquad \|p-\tilde p\|_V\le\varepsilon_p,\qquad \|\nabla\widehat J(q)-(B^*\tilde p+\alpha q)\|_U\le\|B\|\,\varepsilon_p.
$$
The Strang terms retain best-approximation, quadrature/geometry form defects, and load defects; no defect is silently set to zero.

Let $\mathcal T_h$ be a finite simplicial partition of a bounded control domain $E$, and let $U_h\subset L^2(E)$ be the subspace of functions constant on each cell. $$

where $\operatorname{clip}_{[a,b]}(s)=\min\{b,\max\{a,s\}\}$. Then $P_{Q_h}r$ is the unique $L^2(E)$-nearest point in $Q_h$ to $r$, and $P_{Q_h}$ is nonexpansive: $\|P_{Q_h}r-P_{Q_h}s\|_{L^2(E)}\le\|r-s\|_{L^2(E)}$.

Its Hessian is the bounded self-adjoint operator $S^*S+\alpha I$, and for every $h\in U$,
$$

$$
Consequently $\nabla\widehat J$ is Lipschitz with constant $L=\|S\|^2+\alpha$, and $\widehat J$ is $\alpha$-strongly convex.

self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $U_h\subset U=L^2(E)$ be the finite-dimensional space of cellwise-constant controls on a finite affine mesh, and let $Q_h=U_h\cap Q_{ad}$ be nonempty with bounds constant on each control cell. The target is the **exact continuous reduced objective** $\widehat J$ of [[def-linear-elliptic-pde-constrained-control-problem]], restricted to $Q_h$; write $Ju(q)=c+Sq$ and $g(q)=\nabla\widehat J(q)=B^*p(q)+\alpha q$. Choose a certified $L_h\ge\|S|_{U_h}\|^2+\alpha>0$. Given a finite budget $N\ge1$, tolerance $\tau\ge0$, and initial $q_0\in Q_h$, repeat for $k=0,\ldots,N-1$:

An additional input is a residual-evaluation routine $\mathcal C$. For every queried $q_k$, it must return in finite time either a valid tuple $(\tilde u_k,\tilde p_k,\varepsilon_{u,k},\varepsilon_{p,k})$ or `failure`. A valid tuple has $\tilde u_k,\tilde p_k\in V_h$, nonnegative finite bounds that dominate the complete primal and adjoint first-Strang right-hand sides, and an adjoint load defect that includes the state-error contribution $\|J\|^2\varepsilon_{u,k}$. The finite-return condition is part of the algorithm's admissible input contract.

A second input is a projection-evaluation routine $\mathcal P$. Write $q_{k,K}:=q_k|_K$. For every queried $(q_k,\tilde p_k,L_h)$ it must return in finite time either `failure` or finite real cell values $z_{k,K}$ and a finite real $r_k\ge0$ satisfying
$$z_{k,K}=\operatorname{clip}_{[q_a|_K,q_b|_K]}\left(q_{k,K}-\frac{\alpha q_{k,K}+|K|^{-1}\int_K B^*\tilde p_k}{L_h}\right),\qquad r_k^2=\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}|K|\,|q_{k,K}-z_{k,K}|^2.$$
Thus the returned cellwise function is exactly $P_{Q_h}(q_k-\tilde g_k/L_h)$ and $r_k$ is its exact step norm by [[lem-p0-box-projection-is-clipped-cell-average]]. Computing the required cell averages, clipped values and norm is part of this finite-return backend contract; it is not inferred from boundedness of $B$, and no finite representation of the entire function $B^*\tilde p_k$ is assumed. Unavailable exact values must be reported as `failure`, not left pending.

1. Call $\mathcal C(q_k)$. If it returns `failure` or no valid bounds, return $(q_k,\texttt{inconclusive},+\infty)$. Otherwise use its conforming finite-element state and adjoint approximations $\tilde u_k,\tilde p_k$ and complete Strang bounds $\varepsilon_{u,k},\varepsilon_{p,k}$, including form, geometry, quadrature, and load defects. Set $\delta_k=\|B\|\varepsilon_{p,k}$ and $\tilde g_k=B^*\tilde p_k+\alpha q_k$.
2. Call $\mathcal P(q_k,\tilde p_k,L_h)$. If it returns `failure` or no valid cell values and norm, return $(q_k,\texttt{inconclusive},+\infty)$. Otherwise set $\tilde q_{k+1}|_K=z_{k,K}$ and $\tilde\rho_k=r_k$ from its valid return.
3. If $\tilde\rho_k+\delta_k/L_h\le\tau$, return $(q_k,\texttt{certified},\tilde\rho_k+\delta_k/L_h)$.
4. Otherwise set $q_{k+1}=\tilde q_{k+1}$ and continue.

If all $N$ iterations finish without that test, return the last evaluated iterate $(q_{N-1},\texttt{budget-exhausted},\tilde\rho_{N-1}+\delta_{N-1}/L_h)$. Both routines' finite-return contracts ensure that an unavailable state/adjoint bound or projection/residual value is reported as `failure` rather than left pending. The reported number certifies a projected-gradient residual for the exact continuous PDE objective restricted to $Q_h$; it is not a continuous-control discretization error bound.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Put $g=\nabla\widehat J$, $T(q)=P_{Q_h}(q-g(q)/L_h)$, and $\widetilde T_k=P_{Q_h}(q_k-\tilde g_k/L_h)$. By [F1] and nonexpansiveness [F2], $\|T(q_k)-\widetilde T_k\|_U\le\delta_k/L_h$. Since $\tilde\rho_k=\|q_k-\widetilde T_k\|_U$, the triangle inequality gives $\|q_k-T(q_k)\|_U\le\tilde\rho_k+\delta_k/L_h=\rho_k$.

Let $P_{U_h}$ be the orthogonal projection onto cellwise constants. The clipped-cell-average formula [F2] gives $P_{Q_h}(w)=P_{Q_h}(P_{U_h}w)$. For $x,y\in U_h$, [F3] yields $g(x)-g(y)=(S^*S+\alpha I)(x-y)$, so applying $P_{U_h}$ gives $H_h(x-y)$, where $H_h=P_{U_h}(S^*S+\alpha I)|_{U_h}$. Its Rayleigh quotients lie in $[\alpha,L_h]$; [F6] therefore implies $\|I-H_h/L_h\|\le1-\alpha/L_h$. Nonexpansiveness now gives $\|T(x)-T(y)\|_U\le(1-\alpha/L_h)\|x-y\|_U$.

Since $Q_h$ is a nonempty compact box in finite-dimensional $U_h$, [F5] gives a minimizer, and $\alpha$-strong convexity [F4] makes it unique. For any $v\in Q_h$, the feasible segment from $q_h^*$ to $v$ and differentiability imply $(g(q_h^*),v-q_h^*)_U\ge0$. Set $w=q_h^*-g(q_h^*)/L_h$. Then $\|w-v\|_U^2-\|w-q_h^*\|_U^2=\|v-q_h^*\|_U^2+(2/L_h)(g(q_h^*),v-q_h^*)_U\ge0$. Thus $q_h^*$ is the unique nearest point in $Q_h$ to $w$, so $T(q_h^*)=q_h^*$.

By [F7], a \texttt{certified} return is issued only when $\rho_k\le\tau$, so step 1.1 proves the reported bound for the exact mapping residual. By [F8], each residual and projection call returns in finite time, and each is called at most $N$ times; the projection routine supplies the exact cell values and step norm used in step 1.1, and all remaining steps are finite scalar arithmetic and comparisons, so the algorithm terminates with one of its stated statuses.
For $r=\|q-T(q)\|_U$, steps 1.2–1.3 and the triangle inequality imply $\|q-q_h^*\|_U\le r+\|T(q)-T(q_h^*)\|_U\le r+(1-\alpha/L_h)\|q-q_h^*\|_U$. Rearranging yields $\|q-q_h^*\|_U\le(L_h/\alpha)r$.
On a \texttt{certified} return, step 1.1 gives $r\le\rho=\tilde\rho+\delta/L_h$; substituting into step 2.2 proves both displayed distance bounds.

Let $H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive definite, $c\in\mathbb R^n$, and $\ell,u\in\mathbb R^n$ with $\ell_i\le u_i$. For $\phi(x)=\frac12x^THx+c^Tx$, enumerate the finite set of status vectors $\sigma\in\{L,F,U\}^n$ in lexicographic order. For each status, set $x_i=\ell_i$ if $\sigma_i=L$, set $x_i=u_i$ if $\sigma_i=U$, and for the free indices $F$ solve
$$
H_{FF}x_F=-c_F-H_{FA}x_A,
$$
where $A=L\cup U$. Skip a singular solve. Retain a candidate only if $\ell_i<x_i<u_i$ for $i\in F$, and the gradient $g=Hx+c$ satisfies $g_i\ge0$ on $L$, $g_i=0$ on $F$, and $g_i\le0$ on $U$. Return the first retained candidate; if none is retained, return `no-candidate`. Computations in this definition are exact real arithmetic. If $\ell_i=u_i$, that coordinate may be assigned status $L$ or $U$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and compact. Every lower semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded below and attains a minimum. Dually, every upper semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded above and attains a maximum.

derivations.claim: The box is compact and $\phi$ is continuous, so [F2] supplies a minimizer $x_*$. If $\ell_i<u_i$ and $x_{*,i}=\ell_i$, the feasible right derivative is $g_i\ge0$; if $x_{*,i}=u_i$, the feasible left derivative gives $g_i\le0$; and if $\ell_i<x_{*,i}<u_i$, both signs of perturbation are feasible, so $g_i=0$. For a fixed coordinate with $\ell_i=u_i$, assign lower status if $g_i\ge0$ and upper status if $g_i\le0$ (either if $g_i=0$).

The resulting status has its fixed coordinates equal to the bounds and zero gradient on its free coordinates, so its free subsystem is the one solved by the algorithm. The checked gradient signs hold by step 1.1, hence this candidate is retained by [F1]. The algorithm terminates within $3^n$ checks.

Let $x$ be a retained candidate and $g=Hx+c$. For any feasible $y$, the checked coordinate signs give $g_i(y_i-x_i)\ge0$ on lower-active coordinates, the same inequality on upper-active coordinates, and zero on free coordinates; hence $g^T(y-x)\ge0$. The exact expansion $\phi(y)-\phi(x)=g^T(y-x)+\tfrac12(y-x)^TH(y-x)$ is nonnegative, and is strictly positive when $y\ne x$ because $H$ is positive definite. Thus every retained candidate is the unique minimizer, so the first one returned by the algorithm is.

Let $F_A(z)=0$ be the active KKT system of a finite-dimensional reduced FE control problem, where $z=(x,\mu)$ stacks the control and active multipliers. Given $z_0$, an ordered finite list of proposed active sets $A_0,\ldots,A_{m-1}$, maximum budget $N\ge1$, residual tolerance $\tau\ge0$, a terminating exact-storage routine satisfying the input contract of [[alg-sqp-finite-precision-kkt-qr-solve-and-residual-check]], and the floating-point hypotheses of [[alg-sqp-finite-precision-kkt-qr-solve-and-residual-check]], process at most $\min(m,N)$ candidates:

1. For candidate $A_j$, form $F_{A_j}(z_j)$ and its exact-Hessian active KKT Jacobian $K_j=DF_{A_j}(z_j)$.
2. Use the active KKT-map/Jacobian convention and rank/reduced-curvature applicability conditions of [[alg-sqp-exact-hessian-newton-step]]. Do not invoke its exact linear solve. Set $b_j=-F_{A_j}(z_j)$ and call [[alg-sqp-finite-precision-kkt-qr-solve-and-residual-check]] exactly once on the intended system $K_js=b_j$, supplying the terminating exact-storage routine. Before numerical factorization or residual evaluation, that call must verify stored entries equal to the intended $K_j,b_j$; unavailable or unverified admission is a failed QR solve with no residual certificate. A failed applicability check or QR solve records `numerical-failure`, sets $z_{j+1}=z_j$, and proceeds.
3. On a successful QR return, let $(\widehat s_j,\eta_j)$ be its step vector and residual bound. Set $z_j^+=z_j+\widehat s_j$ and $z_{j+1}=z_j^+$. The QR vector $\widehat s_j$ is the only step used by this wrapper. If $\eta_j\le\tau$, return $(z_j^+,A_j,\texttt{active-kkt-residual-certified},\eta_j)$; otherwise proceed.

If the finite list or budget is exhausted, return `budget-exhausted` with the smallest successfully computed residual bound, or `inconclusive` if no solve succeeded. This status concerns the active KKT equation residual only. Box feasibility, multiplier signs, global optimality, and forward accuracy require separate validated checks; none follows from a small linear-system residual alone.

Suppose [[alg-sqp-finite-precision-kkt-qr-solve-and-residual-check]]
successfully returns $\widehat z$ and a certified $\eta$ for a nonsingular
square matrix $K$ and vector $b$. Then
$$\|K\widehat z-b\|_2\le\eta.$$
If $z_*=K^{-1}b$, then also
$$\|\widehat z-z_*\|_2\le\|K^{-1}\|_2\eta.$$
The certificate may be large; the theorem makes no accuracy claim without
an additional bound on $\|K^{-1}\|_2$ and a small certified $\eta$.

Let $x_*$ be a KKT point of a $C^2$ nonlinear program, with multiplier
$\mu_*=(\nu_*,\lambda_{*,I})$ and active set $I=I(x_*)$. Assume LICQ,
strict complementarity $\lambda_{*,i}>0$ for every $i\in I$, and the
second-order sufficient condition
$$d^T\nabla^2_{xx}L(x_*,\mu_*)d>0 \quad\text{for every nonzero critical direction }d.$$
Assume also that the active KKT map $F_A$ has a locally Lipschitz
Jacobian: on some ball, $\|DF_A(z)-DF_A(z\prime)\|_2\le L\|z-z\prime\|_2$.
Once the correct active set is used, exact arithmetic full steps of
[[alg-sqp-exact-hessian-newton-step]], started sufficiently close to
$(x_*,\mu_*)$, are well-defined and converge quadratically to that pair.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.

ball differ by a factor of two.

quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;

Among real $z_K\in[q_a|_K,q_b|_K]$, the square $|z_K-\bar r_K|^2$ is uniquely minimized by the clipped value: if $\bar r_K$ is below the interval the nearest endpoint is the lower bound; if it is inside, it is itself; if it is above, the nearest endpoint is the upper bound. Thus the displayed cell value uniquely minimizes the cell integral, and it lies in the required interval by [F1].

The cell choices are independent, so summing the cellwise minima from step 2.1 proves that $P_{Q_h}r$ is the unique global minimizer. For $v\in Q_h$, convexity makes $p+t(v-p)$ feasible, where $p=P_{Q_h}r$ and $0<t\le1$. Let $p=P_{Q_h}r$ and $q=P_{Q_h}s$. Apply the variational inequality from step 3.1 with $v=q$ and $v=p$, respectively. Adding gives $\|p-q\|_2^2\le(r-s,p-q)_2$. Cauchy–Schwarz then yields $\|p-q\|_2\le\|r-s\|_2$ when $p\ne q$; if $p=q$ the inequality is immediate.

$$
a(v,p(q))=(Ju(q)-u_d,Jv)_H\qquad(v\in V),

with

q_*(x)=\min\left\{q_b(x),\max\left\{q_a(x),-\frac{B^*p(q_*)(x)}{\alpha}\right\}\right\} \quad\text{for almost every }x\in E.

diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

**operator norm** of $T$ by

inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of

differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,

Let $p\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be open, and let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set of experimental conditions. For each $x\in\mathcal X$, let $q_x\ge1$, let $F_x:\Theta\to\mathbb R^{q_x}$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]], and let $W_x\in\mathbb R^{q_x\times q_x}$ be a symmetric positive-definite weight matrix, meaning $z^T W_x z>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^{q_x}$.

An **approximate design** is a function $\xi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x=1$, as in [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. Its support is $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)=\{x\in\mathcal X:\xi_x>0\}$. Define the joint observation map by
$$F_\xi(\theta)=(F_x(\theta))_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)},$$
where the finite product is ordered by any fixed listing of $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. Its **stacked sensitivity Jacobian** at $\theta$ is the vertical concatenation $J_\xi(\theta)$ of the matrices $J_x(\theta)=DF_x(\theta)$ for $x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. The associated **weighted information matrix** is
$$M_\theta(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x J_x(\theta)^T W_x J_x(\theta).$$
The matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because each summand has nonnegative quadratic form.

For a fixed design $\xi$, the observation map is **locally identifiable at $\theta_0\in\Theta$** if it is injective on some open neighborhood of $\theta_0$ in $\Theta$. It is **globally identifiable on $\Theta$** if it is injective on all of $\Theta$. A matrix $J:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^m$ has full column rank when $Jv=0$ implies $v=0$. Its smallest singular value is $\sigma_{\min}(J)=\inf_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Jv\|_2$; thus $\sigma_{\min}(J)\ge\mu$ means $\|Jv\|_2\ge\mu\|v\|_2$ for every $v$.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,
   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$
   where $I_n$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]];
   at $n=0$ the unique empty matrix $I_0\in M_0(\mathbb{R})$ has
   $\lVert I_0\rVert_p=0$, the convention of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces.

If $V=0$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=0.$$

If $V\ne0$ and $s_1$ is the largest singular value of $T$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=s_1.$$

In the nonzero case, the maximum in
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] is attained at
a right-singular vector for $s_1$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: Put $E_x=J_{h,x}-J_x$. By [F4], $J_{h,x}^TW_xJ_{h,x}-J_x^TW_xJ_x=J_x^TW_xE_x+E_x^TW_xJ_x+E_x^TW_xE_x$. By [F2] and [F3], the Euclidean operator norm of the right side is at most $\|J_x\|_2\|W_x\|_2\|E_x\|_2+\|E_x\|_2\|W_x\|_2\|J_x\|_2+\|E_x\|_2\|W_x\|_2\|E_x\|_2\le w(2K\eta+\eta^2)=\delta$.
Taking the design-weighted sum and using the triangle inequality gives $\|M_h(\xi)-M(\xi)\|_2\le\sum_x\xi_x\delta=\delta$, since the weights are nonnegative and sum to one.

Let $v\in\mathbb R^p$. By step 2.1, the operator norm bound and Cauchy–Schwarz [F5], $|v^T(M_h-M)v|\le\|v\|_2\|(M_h-M)v\|_2\le\delta\|v\|_2^2$. Therefore $v^TM_hv\ge v^TMv-|v^T(M_h-M)v|\ge(\alpha-\delta)\|v\|_2^2$. Since $\alpha>\delta$, this is positive for every nonzero $v$, proving positive definiteness.

$$F_\xi(\theta)=(F_x(\theta))_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)},$$
where the finite product is ordered by any fixed listing of $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. Its **stacked sensitivity Jacobian** at $\theta$ is the vertical concatenation $J_\xi(\theta)$ of the matrices $J_x(\theta)=DF_x(\theta)$ for $x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. The associated **weighted information matrix** is
$$M_\theta(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x J_x(\theta)^T W_x J_x(\theta).$$
The matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because each summand has nonnegative quadratic form.

For a fixed design $\xi$, the observation map is **locally identifiable at $\theta_0\in\Theta$** if it is injective on some open neighborhood of $\theta_0$ in $\Theta$. It is **globally identifiable on $\Theta$** if it is injective on all of $\Theta$. A matrix $J:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^m$ has full column rank when $Jv=0$ implies $v=0$. Its smallest singular value is $\sigma_{\min}(J)=\inf_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Jv\|_2$; thus $\sigma_{\min}(J)\ge\mu$ means $\|Jv\|_2\ge\mu\|v\|_2$ for every $v$.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$. Its **row space** $\operatorname{Row}(A)\subseteq F^n$ is the span of its rows, its **column space** $\operatorname{Col}(A)\subseteq F^m$ is the span of its columns, and its **nullspace** is
$$N(A):=\{x\in F^n:Ax=0\}.$$

The **row rank** and **column rank** are
$$\operatorname{rrank}(A):=\dim_F\operatorname{Row}(A),\qquad \operatorname{crank}(A):=\dim_F\operatorname{Col}(A).$$
These dimensions are defined because each space is spanned by a finite list.
Starting with the empty list, inspect the spanning vectors in order and retain a
vector exactly when it is not in the span of those already retained. Induction
shows that the retained list is independent and has the same span as the
original finite list, so it is a finite basis. The **rank** of $A$ is its row
rank; [[thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank]] proves that it also equals the column
rank.

For every finite matrix over a field,
$$\operatorname{rrank}(A)=\operatorname{crank}(A).$$
Both dimensions equal the number of pivots in any echelon form of $A$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) that is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F V = n$ ([[def-dimension]]), and let $U$ be a
linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Then

1. $U$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ and $\dim_F U \le n$;
2. $\dim_F U = n$ **if and only if** $U = V$;
3. **Extension, with no choice principle.** Every linearly independent
   $A_0 \subseteq U$ is contained in a basis of $U$: there is a basis $B$ of $U$
   with $A_0 \subseteq B \subseteq U$. Claim 1 is the case $A_0 = \varnothing$.
   Since $V$ is itself a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), claim 3
   applies with $V$ in place of $U$, and hence to **any** finite-dimensional
   vector space over $F$ in place of the pair $(V, U)$.

**Nothing above uses a choice principle**, and claim 3 in particular is the
finite-dimensional substitute for the Zorn-based extension theorem stated earlier
on this page. In finite dimension the extension terminates on its own, because
[[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]] bounds the size
of an independent set and [[thm-well-ordering-principle]] then supplies a largest
one; no selection is made anywhere.

**Finiteness is essential in claim 2.** Without it the equality case fails: the
companion page exhibits a
proper linear subspace of an infinite-dimensional space whose basis is
equinumerous with a basis of the whole space.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb R)$ and let $1\le r\le\min\{m,n\}$. Then $\operatorname{rank}A\ge r$ if and only if some $r$-rowed minor of $A$ is nonzero ([[def-submatrix-minors-of-a-rectangular-matrix]]). Equivalently, the rank of $A$ is the largest positive size of a nonzero minor when $A\ne0$, and it is $0$ when every entry is zero ([[cor-matrix-rank-equals-the-rank-of-its-linear-map]]).

For every $n\ge1$ and every real matrix $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$,
$$A\text{ is invertible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\det(A)\ne0.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

derivations.claim: Full column rank means the $p$ columns of $J_\xi(\theta_0)$ are independent. They lie in $\mathbb R^m$, so [F3] gives $p\le m$. By [F2] the matrix rank is $p$, and [F4] supplies a set $I$ of $p$ rows whose square submatrix $B=J_\xi(\theta_0)[I,:]$ has nonzero determinant.

By [F5], $B$ is invertible. Let $P_I:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p$ be the coordinate projection onto the rows in $I$, and set $G=P_I\circ F_\xi$. The map $P_I$ is linear, so [F6] gives $DG(\theta_0)=P_IJ_\xi(\theta_0)=B$.

Apply [F7] to $G$: there is an open neighborhood $V\subseteq\Theta$ of $\theta_0$ on which $G$ is injective. If $\theta,\theta'\in V$ satisfy $F_\xi(\theta)=F_\xi(\theta')$, then applying $P_I$ gives $G(\theta)=G(\theta')$, hence $\theta=\theta'$. Thus $F_\xi$ is injective on $V$, which is local identifiability by [F1]. The argument selects one of finitely many row minors and uses no choice axiom.

Its **stacked sensitivity Jacobian** at $\theta$ is the vertical concatenation $J_\xi(\theta)$ of the matrices $J_x(\theta)=DF_x(\theta)$ for $x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. The associated **weighted information matrix** is

The matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because each summand has nonnegative quadratic form.

For a fixed design $\xi$, the observation map is **locally identifiable at $\theta_0\in\Theta$** if it is injective on some open neighborhood of $\theta_0$ in $\Theta$. It is **globally identifiable on $\Theta$** if it is injective on all of $\Theta$. A matrix $J:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^m$ has full column rank when $Jv=0$ implies $v=0$. Its smallest singular value is $\sigma_{\min}(J)=\inf_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Jv\|_2$; thus $\sigma_{\min}(J)\ge\mu$ means $\|Jv\|_2\ge\mu\|v\|_2$ for every $v$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: For any $v\in\mathbb R^p$, [F1] and [F2] give $v^TM_\theta(\xi)v=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)}\xi_x(J_x(\theta)v)^TW_x(J_x(\theta)v)$. Every term is nonnegative by [F3], and a term is strictly positive exactly when $J_x(\theta)v\ne0$, since $\xi_x>0$ on the support and $W_x$ is positive definite.

If $J_\xi(\theta)v=0$, every support component $J_x(\theta)v$ is zero, so step 1.1 gives $v^TM_\theta(\xi)v=0$. Conversely, if $v^TM_\theta(\xi)v=0$, the finite sum of nonnegative terms in step 1.1 can vanish only if every support component $J_x(\theta)v=0$, hence $J_\xi(\theta)v=0$. Thus the quadratic form is positive on every nonzero $v$ exactly when $\ker J_\xi(\theta)=\{0\}$, as claimed.

Let $p\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be open, and let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set of experimental conditions. For each $x\in\mathcal X$, let $q_x\ge1$, let $F_x:\Theta\to\mathbb R^{q_x}$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]], and let $W_x\in\mathbb R^{q_x\times q_x}$ be a symmetric positive-definite weight matrix, meaning $z^T W_x z>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^{q_x}$.

An **approximate design** is a function $\xi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x=1$, as in [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. Its support is $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)=\{x\in\mathcal X:\xi_x>0\}$. Define the joint observation map by
$$F_\xi(\theta)=(F_x(\theta))_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)},$$
where the finite product is ordered by any fixed listing of $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. Its **stacked sensitivity Jacobian** at $\theta$ is the vertical concatenation $J_\xi(\theta)$ of the matrices $J_x(\theta)=DF_x(\theta)$ for $x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. The associated **weighted information matrix** is
$$M_\theta(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x J_x(\theta)^T W_x J_x(\theta).$$
The matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because each summand has nonnegative quadratic form.

For a fixed design $\xi$, the observation map is **locally identifiable at $\theta_0\in\Theta$** if it is injective on some open neighborhood of $\theta_0$ in $\Theta$. It is **globally identifiable on $\Theta$** if it is injective on all of $\Theta$. A matrix $J:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^m$ has full column rank when $Jv=0$ implies $v=0$. Its smallest singular value is $\sigma_{\min}(J)=\inf_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Jv\|_2$; thus $\sigma_{\min}(J)\ge\mu$ means $\|Jv\|_2\ge\mu\|v\|_2$ for every $v$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function. Recall that a metric takes nonnegative real values
([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]).

- $f$ is **Lipschitz** with **constant** $L$, where $L \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $L \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; L \, d_X(x,x') \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X .$$
  $f$ is *Lipschitz* if it is Lipschitz with some such constant.
- Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $0 < \alpha \le 1$ ([[def-rat-order]]). $f$ is
  **$\alpha$-Hölder** with **constant** $C$, where $C \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $C \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; C \, d_X(x,x')^{\alpha} \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X ,$$
  the power being the rational power of a nonnegative base
  ([[def-rational-power]]). $f$ is *$\alpha$-Hölder* if it is so with some such
  constant, and *Hölder* if it is $\alpha$-Hölder for some rational
  $\alpha \in (0,1]$.
- $f$ is a **contraction** with constant $q$ if it is Lipschitz with constant $q$
  and $0 \le q < 1$. The number $q$ is then called a **contraction constant** for
  $f$.

**The power $d_X(x,x')^{\alpha}$ is defined at every pair, including $x = x'$.**
The base $d_X(x,x')$ is a nonnegative real, and [[def-rational-power]] defines
$a^{\alpha}$ for every $a > 0$ and, by its supplementary clause, sets
$0^{\alpha} = 0$ for every rational $\alpha > 0$. Since $\alpha > 0$ is required
here, the displayed inequality at $x = x'$ reads $0 \le C \cdot 0$, which holds;
so no separate clause and no restriction to $x \ne x'$ is needed. Note that this
does not by itself explain the strict inequality $\alpha>0$: if one extended the
formula to $\alpha=0$ using the convention $0^0=1$ of [[def-integer-power]], the
equal-point inequality would still be the automatic $0\le C$. Globally, however,
that extension would reduce to the bounded-diameter condition
$d_Y(f(x),f(x'))\le C$, outside the standard Hölder range adopted here.

**Why the exponent is rational on this page and why it is at most $1$.** At this
point in the reading order only rational powers are available
([[def-rational-power]]), so $\alpha$ ranges over the rationals. The upper
bound $\alpha \le 1$ is the standard convention, and it is where the notion is
useful: the classical theory reserves the name for $\alpha \in (0,1]$, and
nothing in this library uses an exponent outside that range. No claim is made
here about what an exponent $\alpha > 1$ would do.

**Constants are not unique and are not part of the data.** If $f$ is Lipschitz
with constant $L$ it is Lipschitz with every constant $L' \ge L$, and likewise
for Hölder constants; the adjectives above are existential statements. A
*contraction*, by contrast, requires a constant strictly below $1$, and that is a
real restriction: exhibiting the constant is part of exhibiting a contraction, and
a map that shrinks every distance without admitting one uniform constant is not a
contraction here.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: Put $h=\widehat\theta-\theta_0$ and define $R(t)=F(\theta_0+th)-F(\theta_0)-tDF(\theta_0)h$ for $0\le t\le1$. The segment stays in the convex ball. By [F2], $R'(t)=(DF(\theta_0+th)-DF(\theta_0))h$.

By [F4] and [F3], $\|R'(t)\|_2\le Lt\|h\|_2^2\le L\|h\|_2^2$ for $0<t<1$. Since $R$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ and differentiable on $(0,1)$, [F5] gives $\|R(1)-R(0)\|_2\le L\|h\|_2^2$. As $R(0)=0$, this is the first-order remainder bound $\|F(\theta_0+h)-F(\theta_0)-DF(\theta_0)h\|_2\le L\|h\|_2^2$.

If $L>0$, then $\|h\|_2\le r\le\mu/(2L)$, so [F1], step 2.1, and the reverse-triangle inequality [F6] yield $\|F(\widehat\theta)-F(\theta_0)\|_2\ge\mu\|h\|_2-L\|h\|_2^2\ge(\mu/2)\|h\|_2$. If $L=0$, step 2.1 gives zero remainder, and the same lower bound follows from [F1].

The fit condition and $y=F(\theta_0)+e$ give $\|F(\widehat\theta)-F(\theta_0)\|_2\le\|F(\widehat\theta)-y\|_2+\|e\|_2\le\varepsilon+\delta$. Combining with step 3.1 gives $(\mu/2)\|h\|_2\le\varepsilon+\delta$, and division by $\mu/2>0$ proves the asserted bound.

Let $p\ge1$, let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty candidate set, and let $f_x\in\mathbb R^p$ be the feature vector for each $x\in\mathcal X$. An approximate design $\xi$ and information matrix $M(\xi)=\sum_x\xi_xf_xf_x^T$ use the convention of [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. The same vectors may be scalar-observation sensitivities at a fixed parameter, as in [[def-nonlinear-experimental-design-and-local-identifiability]], with a scalar precision absorbed into $f_x$. The procedure uses exact arithmetic.

**Input:** A finite nonempty $\mathcal X$, $p\ge1$, its feature vectors $(f_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$, an approximate initial design $\xi^{(0)}$, and a finite nonnegative integer budget $N$ counting weight updates.

**Procedure:** Form $M_0=M(\xi^{(0)})$. If $M_0$ is not positive definite, return $(\xi^{(0)},\text{undefined violation},\text{invalid initial design})$. Otherwise, for $k=0,1,\ldots,N$, with current $\xi^{(k)}$ and $M_k=M(\xi^{(k)})$, compute
$$s_x^{(k)}=f_x^TM_k^{-1}f_x\quad(x\in\mathcal X),\qquad v_k=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}s_x^{(k)}-p.$$
If $v_k=0$, return $(\xi^{(k)},v_k,\text{equivalence-certified})$. If $k=N$, return $(\xi^{(k)},v_k,\text{budget-exhausted})$. Otherwise set
$$\xi_x^{(k+1)}=\xi_x^{(k)}\frac{s_x^{(k)}}p\quad(x\in\mathcal X),$$
form $M_{k+1}=\sum_x\xi_x^{(k+1)}f_xf_x^T$, and continue. The proved update invariant keeps every later $M_k$ positive definite.

The budget guarantees at most $N$ updates and $N+1$ sensitivity scans. A nonzero returned violation is reported as-is; it is not an exact D-optimality certificate. The exact integer allocation problem remains separate from this approximate-weight procedure.

Let $p\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be open, and let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set of experimental conditions. For each $x\in\mathcal X$, let $q_x\ge1$, let $F_x:\Theta\to\mathbb R^{q_x}$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]], and let $W_x\in\mathbb R^{q_x\times q_x}$ be a symmetric positive-definite weight matrix, meaning $z^T W_x z>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^{q_x}$.

An **approximate design** is a function $\xi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x=1$, as in [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. Its support is $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)=\{x\in\mathcal X:\xi_x>0\}$. Define the joint observation map by
$$F_\xi(\theta)=(F_x(\theta))_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)},$$
where the finite product is ordered by any fixed listing of $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. Its **stacked sensitivity Jacobian** at $\theta$ is the vertical concatenation $J_\xi(\theta)$ of the matrices $J_x(\theta)=DF_x(\theta)$ for $x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. The associated **weighted information matrix** is
$$M_\theta(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x J_x(\theta)^T W_x J_x(\theta).$$
The matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because each summand has nonnegative quadratic form.

For a fixed design $\xi$, the observation map is **locally identifiable at $\theta_0\in\Theta$** if it is injective on some open neighborhood of $\theta_0$ in $\Theta$. It is **globally identifiable on $\Theta$** if it is injective on all of $\Theta$. A matrix $J:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^m$ has full column rank when $Jv=0$ implies $v=0$. Its smallest singular value is $\sigma_{\min}(J)=\inf_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Jv\|_2$; thus $\sigma_{\min}(J)\ge\mu$ means $\|Jv\|_2\ge\mu\|v\|_2$ for every $v$.

For the finite nonlinear observation design of [[def-nonlinear-experimental-design-and-local-identifiability]], fix $\theta\in\Theta$ and an approximate design $\xi$. The matrix $M_\theta(\xi)$ is positive definite, meaning symmetric with $v^TM_\theta(\xi)v>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$, if and only if the stacked support sensitivity Jacobian $J_\xi(\theta)$ has trivial kernel, equivalently full column rank.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty candidate set, let $p\ge1$, and let $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^p$ be the declared regression-vector map. Work under the stated linear mean model $Y=f(x)^{\mathsf T}\beta+\epsilon$, with mean-zero independent run errors of common variance $\sigma^2>0$. These are modeling assumptions, not claims about an experiment's empirical adequacy.

An **approximate design** is a weight function $\xi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x=1$. Its support is $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)=\{x:\xi_x>0\}$ and its information matrix is
$$M(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x f(x)f(x)^{\mathsf T}.$$
This matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite. A design is **nonsingular** when $M(\xi)$ is positive definite. For a singular design, the page's estimability convention is that a specified coefficient contrast $c^{\mathsf T}\beta$ is estimable exactly when $c\in\operatorname{span}\{f(x):x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)\}$; the inverse-matrix criteria below are defined only for nonsingular designs.

For nonsingular designs on this fixed $f$ and $\mathcal X$, **D-optimality** maximizes $\log\det M(\xi)$, **A-optimality** minimizes $\operatorname{tr}(M(\xi)^{-1})$, **E-optimality** maximizes $\lambda_{\min}(M(\xi))$, and **$c$-optimality** for a fixed $c\in\mathbb R^p$ minimizes $c^{\mathsf T}M(\xi)^{-1}c$; $c=0$ gives a trivial tie. The smallest eigenvalue is real because $M(\xi)$ is real symmetric ([[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]). These are different model- and candidate-dependent objectives; none is a universal design ranking.

An **exact $n$-run design**, for an integer $n\ge1$, has weights $\xi_x=n_x/n$ with nonnegative integer counts $n_x$ summing to $n$; optimizing over those integer allocations is a separate finite problem.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

derivations.claim: Fix an update at a current approximate design with positive-definite $M=\sum_x\xi_xf_xf_x^T$. For each $x$, put $s_x=f_x^TM^{-1}f_x$. Since $M$ is symmetric positive definite, $s_x\ge0$, and $s_x>0$ whenever $f_x\ne0$: writing $u=M^{-1}f_x$, one has $f_x^TM^{-1}f_x=u^TMu>0$ for $f_x\ne0$. By [F4] and [F5], $\sum_x\xi_xs_x=\sum_x\xi_x\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}f_xf_x^T)=\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}M)=\operatorname{tr}(I_p)=p$. Therefore $\xi_x^+=\xi_xs_x/p$ is nonnegative and $\sum_x\xi_x^+=1$, so it is again an approximate design.

For every feature $f_x$, a positive old weight remains positive after the update exactly when $f_x\ne0$: step 1.1 gives $s_x>0$ for nonzero $f_x$, and $s_x=0$ for $f_x=0$; zero weights remain zero. Thus the stacked scalar sensitivity matrix loses at most zero rows, so its kernel is unchanged. The current matrix is positive definite, so [F2] gives this kernel is trivial; applying [F2] to the new weights gives positive definiteness of the updated matrix. Induction applies this argument at every update, so no later inverse is undefined.

The loop checks one finite candidate set at each index $k=0,\ldots,N$, returns immediately on zero violation, and otherwise makes an update only when $k<N$. Thus it makes at most $N$ updates and at most $N+1$ sensitivity scans, and at $k=N$ returns the current design and its finite violation. The invariant argument above ensures every scan and update is well-defined.

Use the finite observation designs of [[def-nonlinear-experimental-design-and-local-identifiability]]. Suppose uniformly over $x\in\mathcal X$ that $\|J_x\|_2\le K$, $\|J_{h,x}-J_x\|_2\le\eta$, and $\|W_x\|_2\le w$, where $K,\eta,w\ge0$. For every approximate design $\xi$,
$$\|M_h(\xi)-M(\xi)\|_2\le\delta:=w(2K\eta+\eta^2),$$
where $M_h(\xi)=\sum_x\xi_xJ_{h,x}^TW_xJ_{h,x}$. If $M(\xi)$ satisfies $v^TM(\xi)v\ge\alpha\|v\|_2^2$ for every $v$ with some $\alpha>\delta$, then
$$v^TM_h(\xi)v\ge(\alpha-\delta)\|v\|_2^2$$
for every $v$, so the computed information matrix remains positive definite.

Let $p\ge1$ and let $A,B\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric. Put $E=B-A$ and $A_t=(1-t)A+tB$ for $0\le t\le1$. Suppose there is $\alpha>0$ such that $v^T A_t v\ge\alpha\|v\|_2^2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^p$ and every $t\in[0,1]$. Then $A_t$ is positive definite and
$$|\log\det B-\log\det A|\le\frac{p\|E\|_2}{\alpha}.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

derivations.claim: For each $\xi\in\Xi$, [F1] defines the two information matrices and [F2] gives $\|M_h(\xi)-M(\xi)\|_2\le\delta$. Applying [F3] on their segment gives the uniform bound $|\Phi_h(\xi)-\Phi(\xi)|\le e:=p\delta/\alpha$. By [F4], both maxima are attained; write $\xi_h$ for a computed maximizer.

The $\tau$-approximate maximality of $\widehat\xi$ gives $\Phi_h(\xi_h)-\Phi_h(\widehat\xi)\le\tau$. Write $\Phi(\xi^*)-\Phi(\widehat\xi)=[\Phi(\xi^*)-\Phi_h(\xi^*)]+[\Phi_h(\xi^*)-\Phi_h(\widehat\xi)]+[\Phi_h(\widehat\xi)-\Phi(\widehat\xi)]$. The middle term is at most $\tau$ because $\xi_h$ maximizes $\Phi_h$, and the first and last terms are at most $e$ by step 1.1. Let $p\ge1$, let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty candidate set, and let $f_x\in\mathbb R^p$ be the feature vector for each $x\in\mathcal X$. An approximate design $\xi$ and information matrix $M(\xi)=\sum_x\xi_xf_xf_x^T$ use the convention of [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. The same vectors may be scalar-observation sensitivities at a fixed parameter, as in [[def-nonlinear-experimental-design-and-local-identifiability]], with a scalar precision absorbed into $f_x$. The procedure uses exact arithmetic.

**Input:** A finite nonempty $\mathcal X$, $p\ge1$, its feature vectors $(f_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$, an approximate initial design $\xi^{(0)}$, and a finite nonnegative integer budget $N$ counting weight updates.

**Procedure:** Form $M_0=M(\xi^{(0)})$. If $M_0$ is not positive definite, return $(\xi^{(0)},\text{undefined violation},\text{invalid initial design})$. Otherwise, for $k=0,1,\ldots,N$, with current $\xi^{(k)}$ and $M_k=M(\xi^{(k)})$, compute
$$s_x^{(k)}=f_x^TM_k^{-1}f_x\quad(x\in\mathcal X),\qquad v_k=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}s_x^{(k)}-p.$$
If $v_k=0$, return $(\xi^{(k)},v_k,\text{equivalence-certified})$. If $k=N$, return $(\xi^{(k)},v_k,\text{budget-exhausted})$. Otherwise set
$$\xi_x^{(k+1)}=\xi_x^{(k)}\frac{s_x^{(k)}}p\quad(x\in\mathcal X),$$
form $M_{k+1}=\sum_x\xi_x^{(k+1)}f_xf_x^T$, and continue. The proved update invariant keeps every later $M_k$ positive definite.

The budget guarantees at most $N$ updates and $N+1$ sensitivity scans. A nonzero returned violation is reported as-is; it is not an exact D-optimality certificate. The exact integer allocation problem remains separate from this approximate-weight procedure.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty candidate set, let $p\ge1$, and let $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^p$ be the declared regression-vector map. Work under the stated linear mean model $Y=f(x)^{\mathsf T}\beta+\epsilon$, with mean-zero independent run errors of common variance $\sigma^2>0$. These are modeling assumptions, not claims about an experiment's empirical adequacy.

An **approximate design** is a weight function $\xi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x=1$. Its support is $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)=\{x:\xi_x>0\}$ and its information matrix is
$$M(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x f(x)f(x)^{\mathsf T}.$$
This matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite. A design is **nonsingular** when $M(\xi)$ is positive definite. For a singular design, the page's estimability convention is that a specified coefficient contrast $c^{\mathsf T}\beta$ is estimable exactly when $c\in\operatorname{span}\{f(x):x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)\}$; the inverse-matrix criteria below are defined only for nonsingular designs.

For nonsingular designs on this fixed $f$ and $\mathcal X$, **D-optimality** maximizes $\log\det M(\xi)$, **A-optimality** minimizes $\operatorname{tr}(M(\xi)^{-1})$, **E-optimality** maximizes $\lambda_{\min}(M(\xi))$, and **$c$-optimality** for a fixed $c\in\mathbb R^p$ minimizes $c^{\mathsf T}M(\xi)^{-1}c$; $c=0$ gives a trivial tie. The smallest eigenvalue is real because $M(\xi)$ is real symmetric ([[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]). These are different model- and candidate-dependent objectives; none is a universal design ranking.

An **exact $n$-run design**, for an integer $n\ge1$, has weights $\xi_x=n_x/n$ with nonnegative integer counts $n_x$ summing to $n$; optimizing over those integer allocations is a separate finite problem.

For $p\ge1$, if $A_0,A_1\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ are symmetric and $v^{\mathsf T}A_i v>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$ and $i\in\{0,1\}$, then for every $t\in[0,1]$,
$$\log\det((1-t)A_0+tA_1)\ge(1-t)\log\det A_0+t\log\det A_1.$$

Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix and let $H$ be a direction matrix. Then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(A)H).$$

If $A$ is invertible, then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}H).$$

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty candidate set, $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^p$, and let $\xi^*$ be a nonsingular approximate design as in [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. Write $M^*=M(\xi^*)$ and $u^*(x)=f(x)^{\mathsf T}(M^*)^{-1}f(x)$. Then $\xi^*$ is D-optimal among nonsingular approximate designs if and only if $u^*(x)\le p$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$. Whenever this holds, $u^*(x)=p$ for every $x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi^*)$. No existence of a nonsingular optimum is asserted.

derivations.claim:
By [F1] and [F5],
$$\sum_x\xi_xs_x=\sum_x\xi_x\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}f_xf_x^T)=\operatorname{tr}\!\left(M^{-1}\sum_x\xi_xf_xf_x^T\right)=\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}M)=\operatorname{tr}(I_p)=p.$$
The first rank-one trace identity follows by expanding the diagonal sum: $\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}f_xf_x^T)=\sum_{i,j}(M^{-1})_{ij}(f_x)_j(f_x)_i=f_x^TM^{-1}f_x$. Since the $\xi_x$ are nonnegative and sum to one, their weighted average of the $s_x$ is at most their maximum. The displayed equality therefore gives $\max_xs_x\ge p$ and $v\ge0$.

Let $\eta$ be any nonsingular approximate competitor and put $N=M(\eta)$ and $M_t=(1-t)M+tN$. The segment is positive definite because for each nonzero $u$, $u^TM_tu=(1-t)u^TMu+t u^TNu>0$. Define $g(t)=\log\det M_t$. By [F3], $g$ is concave, and [F4] gives $g'(0)=\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}(N-M))$. For $0<s<1$, concavity gives $g(s)\ge(1-s)g(0)+sg(1)$, hence $g(1)-g(0)\le(g(s)-g(0))/s$. Letting $s\downarrow0$ and using the right derivative $g'(0)$ proves $\log\det N-\log\det M\le\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}(N-M))$.

Expand $N=\sum_x\eta_x f_xf_x^T$ and $M=\sum_x\xi_xf_xf_x^T$. By the rank-one trace identity proved in step 1.1, $\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}N)=\sum_x\eta_xs_x$ and $\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}M)=p$. Since $\eta$ is an approximate design, $\sum_x\eta_xs_x\le\max_xs_x=p+v$. Thus step 1.2 yields $\log\det M(\eta)-\log\det M(\xi)\le v$.

If $v=0$, then $s_x\le p$ for every $x$, so [F6] makes $\xi$ D-optimal. Conversely, if $\xi$ is D-optimal, [F6] gives $s_x\le p$ for every $x$; step 1.1 says their $\xi$-weighted average equals $p$, so their maximum is exactly $p$ and $v=0$. This proves both directions.

Let $p\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be open, and let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set of experimental conditions. For each $x\in\mathcal X$, let $q_x\ge1$, let $F_x:\Theta\to\mathbb R^{q_x}$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]], and let $W_x\in\mathbb R^{q_x\times q_x}$ be a symmetric positive-definite weight matrix, meaning $z^T W_x z>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^{q_x}$.

An **approximate design** is a function $\xi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x=1$, as in [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. Its support is $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)=\{x\in\mathcal X:\xi_x>0\}$. Define the joint observation map by
$$F_\xi(\theta)=(F_x(\theta))_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)},$$
where the finite product is ordered by any fixed listing of $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. Its **stacked sensitivity Jacobian** at $\theta$ is the vertical concatenation $J_\xi(\theta)$ of the matrices $J_x(\theta)=DF_x(\theta)$ for $x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. The associated **weighted information matrix** is
$$M_\theta(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x J_x(\theta)^T W_x J_x(\theta).$$
The matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because each summand has nonnegative quadratic form.

For a fixed design $\xi$, the observation map is **locally identifiable at $\theta_0\in\Theta$** if it is injective on some open neighborhood of $\theta_0$ in $\Theta$. It is **globally identifiable on $\Theta$** if it is injective on all of $\Theta$. A matrix $J:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^m$ has full column rank when $Jv=0$ implies $v=0$. Its smallest singular value is $\sigma_{\min}(J)=\inf_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Jv\|_2$; thus $\sigma_{\min}(J)\ge\mu$ means $\|Jv\|_2\ge\mu\|v\|_2$ for every $v$.

derivations.claim: Differentiation gives $F'(\theta)=3\theta^2$, so $F'(0)=0$ and the Jacobian has rank $0<1$.

If $u^3=v^3$, then $(u-v)(u^2+uv+v^2)=0$. The second factor is $(u+v/2)^2+3v^2/4$, which is nonnegative and vanishes only when $u=v=0$. Hence either $u=v$ directly or the second factor vanishes and again $u=v=0$. Thus $F$ is injective on $\mathbb R$, in particular on a neighborhood of $0$, so local identifiability holds despite the rank-deficient Jacobian.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Put $\lambda=k_1+k_2$. The function $A(t)=A_0e^{-\lambda t}$ satisfies the rate equation and initial value. If $\widetilde A$ is any other differentiable solution, then $(e^{\lambda t}\widetilde A(t))'=0$; applying [F3] on every compact time interval shows this product is constant, and its value at $0$ is $A_0$. Thus the observation map is $F(k_1,k_2)=(A_0e^{-(k_1+k_2)t})_{t\in\mathcal T}$. Now fix any neighborhood $U$ of $(k_1,k_2)$ inside $(0,\infty)^2$. Since $U$ is open, it contains a ball of some radius $r>0$. Choose $0<\varepsilon<\min\{k_2,r/2\}$. Then $(k_1+\varepsilon,k_2-\varepsilon)$ is positive, distinct from $(k_1,k_2)$, and lies in that ball. The sums of the rates agree, so these two parameters have identical observations. Every neighborhood therefore contains a distinct parameter with identical observations; the model is not locally identifiable by [F1], and hence is not globally identifiable.

For each $t\in\mathcal T$, differentiating the observation gives the row $-A_0t e^{-(k_1+k_2)t}(1,1)$. Every row is a scalar multiple of $(1,1)$, so the stacked Jacobian has rank at most one and has the nonzero kernel vector $(1,-1)$. By [F2], every supported design's information matrix is singular. This rank failure agrees with, but is weaker than, the exact aliases proved in step 1.1.
