Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Put $S=\sqrt{2\gamma\beta^{-1}}M^{1/2}$. Multiplying the O equation by the deterministic integrating factor $e^{\gamma t}$ and applying [F3] componentwise gives $d(e^{\gamma t}P_t)=e^{\gamma t}S\,dW_t$. Integrating from $0$ to $h$ and multiplying by $e^{-\gamma h}$ yields [F1, F2, F3, A1, given, algebra]
$$P_h=e^{-\gamma h}P_0+\int_0^h e^{-\gamma(h-s)}S\,dW_s.$$
The integrand is deterministic and square-integrable. By [F2] the integral is centered Gaussian, independent of the starting sigma algebra, with covariance
$$\int_0^h e^{-2\gamma(h-s)}SS^T\,ds=2\gamma\beta^{-1}M\int_0^h e^{-2\gamma(h-s)}ds=\beta^{-1}(1-e^{-2\gamma h})M.$$

By [F4], the displayed covariance has square root $\sqrt{\beta^{-1}(1-e^{-2\gamma h})}M^{1/2}$. A centered Gaussian vector with this covariance has the same law as that matrix times $\xi\sim N_d(0,I_d)$; [F2] gives independence from the starting sigma algebra. This proves the exact transition and conditional moments.

derivations.claim: The power bound gives $\|A^jGG^T(A^T)^j\|\le C^2\theta^{2j}\|G\|^2$. The geometric series therefore converges entrywise and in matrix norm. Each summand is symmetric positive semidefinite because $x^TA^jGG^T(A^T)^jx=|G^T(A^T)^jx|^2\ge0$, so $P$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Shifting the summation index gives $APA^T+GG^T=P$.

Let $Z\sim N_d(0,P)$ and $\xi\sim N_m(0,I_m)$ be independent; [F3] supplies their finite product probability space. By [F1]–[F2], $AZ+G\xi$ has characteristic function $u\mapsto\exp[-\tfrac12u^T(APA^T+GG^T)u]=\exp[-\tfrac12u^TPu]$. The covariance identity in step 1.1 and [F4] show that $AZ+G\xi$ has the same law as $Z$. Thus $N_d(0,P)$ is invariant.

Let $\nu$ be any invariant probability law and let $\varphi(u)=\int e^{iu\cdot x}\,\nu(dx)$. Invariance and independence of a fresh innovation imply [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, given, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]
$$\varphi(u)=\varphi(A^Tu)\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12u^TGG^Tu\right).$$
Iterating $n$ times gives
$$\varphi(u)=\varphi((A^T)^nu)\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12u^T\left[\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}A^jGG^T(A^T)^j\right]u\right).$$
The power bound gives $(A^T)^nu\to0$, so the dominated convergence theorem [F5] in the integral defining $\varphi$ gives $\varphi((A^T)^nu)\to1$. Step 1.1 makes the matrix sum converge to $P$, whence $\varphi(u)=e^{-u^TPu/2}$, the characteristic function of the invariant Gaussian from step 2.1. By [F4], $\nu=N_d(0,P)$. If $P'$ is another finite matrix solution of the Lyapunov equation, $D=P'-P$ satisfies $D=ADA^T$, hence $D=A^nD(A^T)^n\to0$ by the power bound; therefore $P'=P$. This proves uniqueness of the invariant law and covariance solution.

Assume the data and hypotheses of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] on $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$, finite
dimensions $d,m\ge1$, Lipschitz constant $L$, and linear-growth constant
$K$. There is a strong solution $X$ on the given filtered probability space.
It is unique up to indistinguishability among strong solutions with the same
initial value and Brownian driver, and it satisfies
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t|^2\le(1+3E|X_0|^2)e^{C_TT},\qquad C_T:=6K^2T+24mK^2.$$
The bound is independent of any later numerical mesh.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

citations.quote: Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer and $p_\theta(x)=\theta\cdot x$ for $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R^d$ are determined by all the laws $(p_\theta)_*\mu$. Moreover, if $(p_\theta)_*\mu_n\Rightarrow(p_\theta)_*\mu$ for every $\theta$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$, then $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

the square-matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]],
be symmetric positive definite in the sense of
[[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]]. Let $\lambda_d$ denote
the Lebesgue measure of
[[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]. Interpret the
displayed integral as the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\exp\!\left(-\frac12 u^{\mathsf T}Hu\right)\,d\lambda_d(u) =\frac{(2\pi)^{d/2}}{\sqrt{\det H}}.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$ be finite, let $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be symmetric positive definite (that is, $x^TMx>0$ for every nonzero $x$), and let $\beta,\gamma>0$. Then $M$ is invertible, and $M^{1/2}$ denotes its unique symmetric positive square root. Let $W_t$ be standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to a complete usual filtration, and let $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. The **underdamped Langevin equation** is the It\^o SDE on phase space $\mathbb R^d_q\times\mathbb R^d_p$
$$dQ_t=M^{-1}P_t\,dt,\qquad dP_t=-\nabla V(Q_t)\,dt-\gamma P_t\,dt+\sqrt{2\gamma\beta^{-1}}\,M^{1/2}dW_t.$$
Its Hamiltonian is $H(q,p)=\tfrac12p^TM^{-1}p+V(q)$. If $Z=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}e^{-\beta H(q,p)}\,dq\,dp$ is finite and positive, the **canonical Gibbs probability** is the probability measure with density $\rho(q,p)=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H(q,p)}$ with respect to $2d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. This definition alone asserts no stationarity or ergodicity.

For the finite-time order results below, $D^jV$ denotes the $j$th derivative as a multilinear map. The notation $C_b^k$ means that a function and each of its derivatives through order $k$ are continuous and bounded. The notation $C_P^k$ means that a function and each of its derivatives through order $k$ are continuous and bounded by $C(1+|z|^r)$ for some finite constants $C,r$ that may depend on the derivative. These growth conventions are used only where stated.

Use the equation and conventions of [[def-underdamped-langevin-equation-and-canonical-gibbs-density]]. Given a valid state $(q_n,p_n)\in\mathbb R^{2d}$, a step $h>0$, and a fresh independent vector $\xi_n\sim N_d(0,I_d)$, put $a=e^{-\gamma h}$ and execute exactly these five substeps in order:

1. **B half kick:** $p^{(1)}=p_n-\tfrac h2\nabla V(q_n)$.
2. **A half drift:** $q^{(1)}=q_n+\tfrac h2M^{-1}p^{(1)}$.
3. **O full thermostat:** $p^{(2)}=a p^{(1)}+\sqrt{\beta^{-1}(1-a^2)}M^{1/2}\xi_n$.
4. **A half drift:** $q_{n+1}=q^{(1)}+\tfrac h2M^{-1}p^{(2)}$.
5. **B half kick:** $p_{n+1}=p^{(2)}-\tfrac h2\nabla V(q_{n+1})$.

The output is $(q_{n+1},p_{n+1})$. If any required gradient is undefined or any input violates $h>0$, $\beta>0$, $\gamma>0$, or positive definiteness of $M$, return `failure` without an updated state. For a differentiable $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ and finite valid state, both gradient calls are defined; reusing the stored value $\nabla V(q_{n+1})$ as the next step's first force means one new force evaluation per subsequent step. The random-vector cost is one fresh $d$-dimensional standard normal per step.
citations.use_explanation: [F2] records the exact local interface used here: : one step is the ordered B/2, A/2, O, A/2, B/2 sequence, with the exact OU momentum update.

$$P_h=e^{-\gamma h}P_0+\sqrt{\beta^{-1}(1-e^{-2\gamma h})}\,M^{1/2}\xi,$$

Assume AC. Let $A\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ and $G\in\mathbb R^{d\times m}$, with finite $d,m\ge1$. Suppose there are $C<\infty$ and $0<\theta<1$ such that $\|A^n\|\le C\theta^n$ for every integer $n\ge0$. A probability law $\nu$ is **invariant** for this recursion if, whenever $Z_0\sim\nu$ is independent of a fresh $\xi_1\sim N_m(0,I_m)$, the updated state $AZ_0+G\xi_1$ also has law $\nu$. Consider the Markov chain
$$Z_{n+1}=AZ_n+G\xi_{n+1},$$
where each $\xi_{n+1}\sim N_m(0,I_m)$ is independent of the current state and of the earlier innovations. Then the chain has a unique invariant probability law. It is $N_d(0,P)$, where the convergent positive-semidefinite series
$$P=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}A^jGG^T(A^T)^j$$
satisfies $P=APA^T+GG^T$. This is the unique finite matrix solution of that discrete Lyapunov equation.
citations.use_explanation: [L1] records the exact local interface used here: : if a linear Gaussian recursion has exponentially decaying matrix powers, it has a unique invariant Gaussian whose covariance is the convergent discrete Lyapunov series.

The canonical density factorizes over $q$ and $p$. By [F4] its normalizer is the product of the two one-dimensional Gaussian integrals, and [F5] gives $Z_q=\sqrt{2\pi/(\beta k)}$ and $Z_p=\sqrt{2\pi m/\beta}$. The normalized factors are centered. For $c>0$, [F6] on $[-R,R]$ gives
$$\int_{-R}^R x^2e^{-cx^2/2}dx=\frac1c\left(\int_{-R}^R e^{-cx^2/2}dx-2Re^{-cR^2/2}\right).$$
Letting $R\to\infty$ and using $Re^{-cR^2/2}\to0$ gives $\int_{\mathbb R}x^2e^{-cx^2/2}dx=c^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-cx^2/2}dx$; oddness gives zero mean. Therefore the canonical variances are $1/(\beta k)$ and $m/\beta$, with zero cross-covariance. These are the canonical values used below.

Set $v=p/m$, $s=h/2$, and $\sigma^2=\beta^{-1}(1-a^2)/m$. Applying [F2] in sequence and using $F(q)=-kq$ gives [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]
$$q'=(1-r(1+a))q+s(1+a)v+s\sigma\xi,$$
$$v'=-s\omega^2(1+a)(1-r)q+(a-r(1+a))v+(1-r)\sigma\xi,$$
where $\xi\sim N(0,1)$. Thus $z'=(q',v')^T=Az+g\xi$, with
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}1-r(1+a)&s(1+a)\\-s\omega^2(1+a)(1-r)&a-r(1+a)\end{pmatrix},\qquad g=\sigma\begin{pmatrix}s\\1-r\end{pmatrix}.$$

Direct expansion gives $\det A=a$ and $\operatorname{tr}A=(1+a)(1-2r)$. The characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2-(1+a)(1-2r)\lambda+a$. Since $0<a<1$, for $0<r<1$ its values at $1$ and $-1$ satisfy [F1, step 1.2, algebra]
$$1-\operatorname{tr}A+\det A=2r(1+a)>0,\qquad 1+\operatorname{tr}A+\det A=2(1+a)(1-r)>0.$$
If its roots are nonreal, they are conjugate with modulus $\sqrt a<1$. If they are real, their product $a>0$ makes them have the same sign. For two positive roots, the first displayed product is positive and their product is below one, so neither can be at least one. For two negative roots, the second displayed product is positive and their product is below one, so neither can be at most $-1$. Hence both roots have modulus less than one. At $r=1$, the polynomial has root $-1$. At $r>1$, its value at $-1$ is negative while it tends to positive infinity as $\lambda\to-\infty$, so it has a root $\lambda_u<-1$; its other root is $a/\lambda_u$ and has modulus less than one. Therefore $\rho(A)<1$ exactly when $0<r<1$.

For $0<r<1$, the characteristic roots have modulus less than one by step 2.1. If they differ, Cayley–Hamilton writes $A^n$ as a linear combination of their $n$th powers. If they coincide at $\lambda$, Cayley–Hamilton gives $(A-\lambda I)^2=0$, so $A^n=\lambda^nI+n\lambda^{n-1}(A-\lambda I)$; for $|\lambda|<1$ this is bounded by $C\theta^n$ for any fixed $|\lambda|<\theta<1$. Thus the power-decay hypothesis of [L1] holds. Its discrete Lyapunov covariance in $(q,v)$ coordinates is [F1, F3, L1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]
$$P=\frac1{\beta m}\begin{pmatrix}\omega^{-2}&0\\0&1-r\end{pmatrix}.$$
Indeed, substituting $A,g$ from step 1.2 gives $APA^T+gg^T=P$: the off-diagonal identity reduces to $s(1-r)[(1+a)(a-1)+(1-a^2)]=0$; the first diagonal identity reduces, after multiplication by $\beta m\omega^2$, to
$$[1-r(1+a)]^2+r(1+a)[2-r(1+a)]=1;$$
and the second diagonal identity, after division by $1-r$ and multiplication by $\beta m$, reduces to
$$[a-r(1+a)]^2+r(1+a)^2(1-r)+(1-a^2)(1-r)=1.$$
Both displayed scalar identities follow by expansion and $r=s^2\omega^2$. Thus [L1] gives the unique invariant Gaussian with this covariance. Transforming back by $p=mv$ gives $\operatorname{Var}(Q)=1/(\beta k)$, $\operatorname{Var}(P)=m(1-r)/\beta$, and zero covariance.

For $r>1$, step 2.1 gives a real left eigenvector $\ell$ for $\lambda_u<-1$. The innovation vector excites that mode: direct multiplication gives $\det[g,Ag]=-2\sigma^2s(1-r)
e0$, so $\ell^Tg
e0$ (otherwise $g$ would lie in the other right eigenspace and $g,Ag$ would be dependent). If an invariant probability existed, its projection $X=\ell^Tz$ would satisfy $X'=\lambda_uX+\zeta$ with independent nondegenerate centered normal $\zeta=\ell^Tg\xi$. Its characteristic function would obey $\varphi(t)=\varphi(\lambda_ut)e^{-\operatorname{Var}(\zeta)t^2/2}$. Iterating and using $|\varphi|\le1$ forces $\varphi(t)=0$ for every $t
e0$. For any probability law of a finite real random variable $X$, [F7] and dominated convergence applied to $e^{itX}	o1$ with majorant $1$ give $\varphi(t)	o1$ as $t	o0$, contradicting this forced vanishing. Hence no invariant probability exists for $r>1$. Since $r=h^2k/(4m)$, the threshold is $h=2\sqrt{m/k}$. The boundary $r=1$ has an eigenvalue $-1$, so [L1] does not give a unique invariant law there. This proves the stated stable, boundary, and unstable cases without making any nonharmonic invariant-law claim.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$ be finite, let $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be symmetric positive definite (that is, $x^TMx>0$ for every nonzero $x$), and let $\beta,\gamma>0$. Then $M$ is invertible, and $M^{1/2}$ denotes its unique symmetric positive square root. Let $W_t$ be standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to a complete usual filtration, and let $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. The **underdamped Langevin equation** is the It\^o SDE on phase space $\mathbb R^d_q\times\mathbb R^d_p$
$$dQ_t=M^{-1}P_t\,dt,\qquad dP_t=-\nabla V(Q_t)\,dt-\gamma P_t\,dt+\sqrt{2\gamma\beta^{-1}}\,M^{1/2}dW_t.$$
Its Hamiltonian is $H(q,p)=\tfrac12p^TM^{-1}p+V(q)$. If $Z=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}e^{-\beta H(q,p)}\,dq\,dp$ is finite and positive, the **canonical Gibbs probability** is the probability measure with density $\rho(q,p)=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H(q,p)}$ with respect to $2d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. This definition alone asserts no stationarity or ergodicity.

For the finite-time order results below, $D^jV$ denotes the $j$th derivative as a multilinear map. The notation $C_b^k$ means that a function and each of its derivatives through order $k$ are continuous and bounded. The notation $C_P^k$ means that a function and each of its derivatives through order $k$ are continuous and bounded by $C(1+|z|^r)$ for some finite constants $C,r$ that may depend on the derivative. These growth conventions are used only where stated.
citations.use_explanation: [F1] records the exact local interface used here: and : $b(q,p)=(M^{-1}p,F(q)-\gamma p)$, the diffusion matrix is the constant $G$, and the solution has the usual adapted It\^o integral representation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the stochastic-integral interfaces
below. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ and finite integers $d,m\ge1$. Work on
a complete filtered probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$ whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$ (the usual conditions).

Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] adapted to this filtration, with
$W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ for $0\le s<t\le T$. Let
$X_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, satisfy
$E|X_0|^2<\infty$, and be independent of the future Brownian increments.
Explicitly, $X_0$ is independent of the sigma-algebra
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.

Continuity of a process means continuity on one measurable event of
probability one. We use an everywhere-continuous adapted representative: if
the chosen process is continuous only on such an event $A$, replace it off $A$
by its initial value. Since $A^c$ is a null set and the filtration is complete,
$A^c\in\mathcal F_0$; the replacement preserves adaptedness and changes the
SDE identity only on a null event, hence preserves it up to
indistinguishability.

The drift and diffusion coefficients are jointly Borel maps
$$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad \sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}.$$
For nonnegative finite constants $L,K$, assume for every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ that
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|).$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and
$\|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{k=1}^m|A^{ik}|^2$ is the Frobenius norm.

For an adapted continuous candidate $X:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$,
the vector Itô equation
$$X_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(s,X_s)\,ds+\left(\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}(s,X_s)\,dW_s^k\right)_{i=1}^d,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
uses a pathwise Lebesgue integral for the drift and, in each coordinate, the
localized Itô integral from
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], clause 2. Require
$\int_0^T|b(s,X_s)|ds<\infty$ and
$\int_0^T\|\sigma(s,X_s)\|_F^2ds<\infty$ almost surely; these are the local
coefficient-integrability conditions in that definition. When a coordinate
integrand has finite expected energy, its integral is the square-integrable
Itô integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]];
the Picard estimates below establish that stronger condition for every input
in $\mathcal H_T$. Equality of processes means
equality for every $t$ on one measurable event of probability one, that is,
indistinguishability
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. A **strong
solution on $[0,T]$** is an adapted continuous process satisfying this
integral equation indistinguishably. No moment bound is included in the
definition; the existence theorem proves its $L^2$ path-sup bound.
The usual-filtration, continuity, and finite-coordinate conventions agree
with the multidimensional class of continuous Brownian Itô processes
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. This definition makes no ellipticity,
transition-density, forward-equation, or time-reversal assertion.

Brownian motion here means the finite-horizon version of the cited definition:
$W_0=0$ almost surely, with continuous paths and the stated increments on
$[0,T]$. All cited stochastic-calculus interfaces are used on this interval.
Their constructions require no extension of $W$ beyond $T$: elementary
integrals use only increments between partition points in $[0,T]$, and their
$L^2$ limits and continuous versions are constructed on that same interval.
For a predictable scalar integrand $H$ with finite pathwise energy, localize
at $\rho_n=\inf\{t\in[0,T]:\int_0^t H_s^2ds\ge n\}\wedge T$.
Here $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$.
The stopped integrands have expected energy at most $n$; their continuous
integrals agree up to the smaller stop by the finite-energy stopping identity.
On the full event of finite energy, $\rho_n=T$ for all sufficiently large
$n$, so these integrals paste uniquely on the whole closed interval $[0,T]$,
exactly as in the localized construction of
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. At $T=0$ every integral is zero.

Use the equation and conventions of [[def-underdamped-langevin-equation-and-canonical-gibbs-density]]. Given a valid state $(q_n,p_n)\in\mathbb R^{2d}$, a step $h>0$, and a fresh independent vector $\xi_n\sim N_d(0,I_d)$, put $a=e^{-\gamma h}$ and execute exactly these five substeps in order:

1. **B half kick:** $p^{(1)}=p_n-\tfrac h2\nabla V(q_n)$.
2. **A half drift:** $q^{(1)}=q_n+\tfrac h2M^{-1}p^{(1)}$.
3. **O full thermostat:** $p^{(2)}=a p^{(1)}+\sqrt{\beta^{-1}(1-a^2)}M^{1/2}\xi_n$.
4. **A half drift:** $q_{n+1}=q^{(1)}+\tfrac h2M^{-1}p^{(2)}$.
5. **B half kick:** $p_{n+1}=p^{(2)}-\tfrac h2\nabla V(q_{n+1})$.

The output is $(q_{n+1},p_{n+1})$. If any required gradient is undefined or any input violates $h>0$, $\beta>0$, $\gamma>0$, or positive definiteness of $M$, return `failure` without an updated state. For a differentiable $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ and finite valid state, both gradient calls are defined; reusing the stored value $\nabla V(q_{n+1})$ as the next step's first force means one new force evaluation per subsequent step. The random-vector cost is one fresh $d$-dimensional standard normal per step.
citations.use_explanation: [F2] records the exact local interface used here: : the B/A/O/A/B step consists of two force kicks, two linear drifts, and the exact OU update.

For the O subproblem $dP_t=-\gamma P_t\,dt+\sqrt{2\gamma\beta^{-1}}M^{1/2}dW_t$ over a step $h>0$, with $P_0$ measurable at the start of the step and Brownian increments independent of the starting sigma algebra,
$$P_h=e^{-\gamma h}P_0+\sqrt{\beta^{-1}(1-e^{-2\gamma h})}\,M^{1/2}\xi,$$
where $\xi\sim N_d(0,I_d)$ is independent of the starting sigma algebra. In particular, conditionally on $P_0$, the transition is Gaussian with mean $e^{-\gamma h}P_0$ and covariance $\beta^{-1}(1-e^{-2\gamma h})M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$ and let
$h\in L^2[0,T]$ be deterministic, choose a Borel representative of its
Lebesgue-equivalence class, and set $h(s,\omega):=h(s)$. This process is
predictable with finite energy. Then the Ito integral
$\int_0^Th_s\,dB_s$
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] is centered
normal with variance $\int_0^Th^2ds$: its law is $N(0,\int_0^Th^2ds)$ in the
convention of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], where $N(0,0)$ is the
Dirac law at $0$. More generally, for deterministic $h_1,\dots,h_d\in L^2[0,T]$
the vector of integrals is jointly Gaussian in the sense of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: its law is $N_d(0,\Sigma)$ with
$$\Sigma_{jk}=\int_0^Th_j(s)h_k(s)\,ds .$$
In particular the covariance of the pair is
$\operatorname{Cov}(\int h_jdB,\int h_kdB)=\int h_jh_k$, the integrals are
uncorrelated exactly when $\int h_jh_k=0$, and integrals of deterministic
integrands with disjoint supports are independent.
citations.use_explanation: [F4] records the exact local interface used here: : deterministic It\^o integrals are centered Gaussian with covariance equal to the integral of the product of their integrands; in particular $\eta-S\Delta W=\int_0^h(e^{-\gamma(h-s)}-1)S\,dW_{t+s}$ has mean zero and second moment at most $Ch^3$.

Assume the data and hypotheses of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] on $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$, finite
dimensions $d,m\ge1$, Lipschitz constant $L$, and linear-growth constant
$K$. There is a strong solution $X$ on the given filtered probability space.
It is unique up to indistinguishability among strong solutions with the same
initial value and Brownian driver, and it satisfies
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t|^2\le(1+3E|X_0|^2)e^{C_TT},\qquad C_T:=6K^2T+24mK^2.$$
The bound is independent of any later numerical mesh.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.
citations.use_explanation: [F6] records the exact local interface used here: : It\^o's formula applies componentwise to the $C^2$ drift $b$; its generator applied to $b$ has linear growth under the stated derivative bounds.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim:
Set $s=h/2$, $a=e^{-\gamma h}$, $\Delta W=W_{t+h}-W_t$, and $\eta=\int_0^h e^{-\gamma(h-r)}S\,dW_{t+r}$. Writing the BAOAB stages from [F2] gives [F1, F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]
$$q'=q+s(1+a)M^{-1}p+s^2(1+a)M^{-1}F(q)+sM^{-1}\eta,\qquad p'=ap+asF(q)+\eta+sF(q').$$
Subtracting $z+h b(z)+G\Delta W$ yields
$$R_q^B=s(a-1)M^{-1}p+s^2(1+a)M^{-1}F(q)+sM^{-1}\eta,$$
$$R_p^B=(a-1+\gamma h)p+s\bigl((a-1)F(q)+F(q')-F(q)\bigr)+\eta-S\Delta W.$$
Since $|a-1|\le Ch$ and $|a-1+\gamma h|\le Ch^2$, the deterministic terms have size at most $Ch^2(1+|z|)$. The displayed formula and linear growth give $\mathbb E[|q'-q|\mid\mathcal F_t]\le Ch(1+|z|)$ and $\mathbb E[|q'-q|^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\le Ch^2(1+|z|^2)$. Lipschitz continuity of $F$ and [F4] therefore give $|\mathbb E[R^B\mid\mathcal F_t]|\le Ch^2(1+|z|)$ and $\mathbb E[|R^B|^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\le Ch^3(1+|z|^2)$.

For two starting states driven by the same $\eta$, subtract the expression for $q'$ in step 1.1. The result and the Lipschitz bound on $F$ give $|q'(z)-q'(\tilde z)|\le C|z-\tilde z|$. Subtracting the two $R_q^B$ formulas then gives $|R_q^B(z)-R_q^B(\tilde z)|\le Ch^2|z-\tilde z|$. The $R_p^B$ formula gives the same bound for its linear and $(a-1)F$ terms; its last force difference is bounded by $sL(|q'(z)-q'(\tilde z)|+|q-\tilde q|)\le Ch|z-\tilde z|$. Combining components proves $|R^B(z)-R^B(\tilde z)|\le Ch|z-\tilde z|$.

With $b,G$ from step 1.1, the exact residual is $R^E=\int_t^{t+h}(b(Z_r)-b(Z_t))dr$. For $0\le u\le h$, the integral equation, linear growth of $b$, Cauchy–Schwarz in time, and [F4] give, with $m(u)=\mathbb E[1+|Z_{t+u}|^2\mid\mathcal F_t]$, [A1, F1, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1]
$$m(u)\le C(1+|Z_t|^2)+C\int_0^u m(v)dv.$$
Set $M(u)=C(1+|Z_t|^2)+C\int_0^u m(v)dv$ with the constant enlarged so $m\le M$. Then $M'(u)=Cm(u)\le CM(u)$ almost everywhere, so $(e^{-Cu}M(u))'\le0$ and $m(u)\le C(1+|Z_t|^2)$ for $u\le1$. Substitution in the integral equation gives $\mathbb E[|Z_{t+u}-Z_t|^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\le Cu(1+|Z_t|^2)$, and Cauchy–Schwarz in time gives $\mathbb E[|R^E|^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\le Ch^3(1+|Z_t|^2)$. For its mean, [F6] gives $Lb=Db\,b+\tfrac12(GG^T):D^2b$, which has linear growth because $Db,D^2b$ are bounded and $b$ has linear growth. Conditional expectation removes the martingale integral, so $|\mathbb E[b(Z_{t+u})-b(Z_t)\mid\mathcal F_t]|\le Cu(1+|Z_t|)$; integration yields $|\mathbb E[R^E\mid\mathcal F_t]|\le Ch^2(1+|Z_t|)$.

Steps 1.1 and 2.2 establish both residual decompositions and their conditional bounds, and step 2.1 gives the same-noise Lipschitz estimate. Time homogeneity makes the constants uniform in $t$; they depend only on the fixed coefficient bounds.

Assume the data and hypotheses of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] on $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$, finite
dimensions $d,m\ge1$, Lipschitz constant $L$, and linear-growth constant
$K$. There is a strong solution $X$ on the given filtered probability space.
It is unique up to indistinguishability among strong solutions with the same

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by

derivations.claim: The exact solution has $\sup_{t\le T}\mathbb E|Z_t|^2<\infty$ by [F1]. Each B or A half-step changes the state by a quantity bounded by $Ch(1+|z|)$, because $F$ has linear growth and $M^{-1}$ is fixed. For the O step, $p\mapsto ap+\eta$ with $0<a<1$, $\mathbb E[\eta\mid\mathcal F_n]=0$, and $\mathbb E|\eta|^2\le Ch$ by [L1], so $\mathbb E[|ap+\eta|^2\mid\mathcal F_n]\le |p|^2+Ch$. Expanding the squares of the finitely many B/A/O stage updates and using $2|x||y|\le h|x|^2+h^{-1}|y|^2$ shows $\mathbb E[1+|Z_{n+1}^B|^2\mid\mathcal F_n]\le(1+Ch)(1+|Z_n^B|^2)+Ch$. Iterating this scalar inequality for $Nh=T$ yields $\max_{n\le N}\mathbb E|Z_n^B|^2\le C_T(1+\mathbb E|Z_0|^2)$.

Write $e_n=Z_n^B-Z_{t_n}$. Apply [L1] at the common state $Z_{t_n}$ and at the two actual states, and subtract the two one-step expansions. The result is [F1, L1, given, algebra]
$$e_{n+1}=e_n+h(b(Z_n^B)-b(Z_{t_n}))+\Delta_n+\delta_n,$$
where $\Delta_n=R^B(Z_n^B)-R^B(Z_{t_n})$ and $\delta_n=R^B(Z_{t_n})-R^E(Z_{t_n})$. Let $d_n=\mathbb E[\Delta_n\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]$ and $M_{n+1}=\Delta_n-d_n$. The residual Lipschitz bound in [L1] gives $|d_n|\le Ch|e_n|$ and $\mathbb E|M_{n+1}|^2\le Ch^2\mathbb E|e_n|^2$. Put $r_n=\mathbb E[\delta_n\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]$ and $Q_{n+1}=\delta_n-r_n$. Conditional Jensen and [L1], together with the exact-state moment bound from [F1], give $\mathbb E|r_n|^2\le Ch^4$ and $\mathbb E|Q_{n+1}|^2\le Ch^3$. Both $M_{n+1}$ and $Q_{n+1}$ have conditional mean zero. Hence, with $u_n=b(Z_n^B)-b(Z_{t_n})+d_n/h$, the error recurrence is $e_{n+1}=e_n+hu_n+r_n+M_{n+1}+Q_{n+1}$, where $|u_n|\le C|e_n|$ by global Lipschitz continuity of $b$ and the bound on $d_n$.

Since $e_n+hu_n+r_n$ is $\mathcal F_{t_n}$-measurable, its cross expectation with the centered sum $M_{n+1}+Q_{n+1}$ is zero. Young's inequality and the bounds in step 1.2 give [F1, L1, A1, step 1.2, algebra]
$$\mathbb E|e_n+hu_n+r_n|^2\le(1+Ch)\mathbb E|e_n|^2+Ch^3,$$
$$\mathbb E|M_{n+1}+Q_{n+1}|^2\le2Ch^2\mathbb E|e_n|^2+2Ch^3\le Ch\mathbb E|e_n|^2+Ch^3.$$
Therefore $\mathbb E|e_{n+1}|^2\le(1+Ch)\mathbb E|e_n|^2+Ch^3$. Starting from $e_0=0$ and iterating gives
$$\mathbb E|e_n|^2\le Ch^3\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(1+Ch)^j\le C_T h^3N e^{CT}\le C_T h^2$$
for each $n\le N$, because $Nh=T$. Taking the maximum over the finitely many grid indices proves the statement. AC enters only through [A1].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$ be finite, let $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be symmetric positive definite (that is, $x^TMx>0$ for every nonzero $x$), and let $\beta,\gamma>0$. Then $M$ is invertible, and $M^{1/2}$ denotes its unique symmetric positive square root. Let $W_t$ be standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to a complete usual filtration, and let $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. The **underdamped Langevin equation** is the It\^o SDE on phase space $\mathbb R^d_q\times\mathbb R^d_p$
$$dQ_t=M^{-1}P_t\,dt,\qquad dP_t=-\nabla V(Q_t)\,dt-\gamma P_t\,dt+\sqrt{2\gamma\beta^{-1}}\,M^{1/2}dW_t.$$
Its Hamiltonian is $H(q,p)=\tfrac12p^TM^{-1}p+V(q)$. If $Z=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}e^{-\beta H(q,p)}\,dq\,dp$ is finite and positive, the **canonical Gibbs probability** is the probability measure with density $\rho(q,p)=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H(q,p)}$ with respect to $2d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. This definition alone asserts no stationarity or ergodicity.

For the finite-time order results below, $D^jV$ denotes the $j$th derivative as a multilinear map. The notation $C_b^k$ means that a function and each of its derivatives through order $k$ are continuous and bounded. The notation $C_P^k$ means that a function and each of its derivatives through order $k$ are continuous and bounded by $C(1+|z|^r)$ for some finite constants $C,r$ that may depend on the derivative. These growth conventions are used only where stated.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

Use the equation and conventions of [[def-underdamped-langevin-equation-and-canonical-gibbs-density]]. Given a valid state $(q_n,p_n)\in\mathbb R^{2d}$, a step $h>0$, and a fresh independent vector $\xi_n\sim N_d(0,I_d)$, put $a=e^{-\gamma h}$ and execute exactly these five substeps in order:

1. **B half kick:** $p^{(1)}=p_n-\tfrac h2\nabla V(q_n)$.
2. **A half drift:** $q^{(1)}=q_n+\tfrac h2M^{-1}p^{(1)}$.
3. **O full thermostat:** $p^{(2)}=a p^{(1)}+\sqrt{\beta^{-1}(1-a^2)}M^{1/2}\xi_n$.
4. **A half drift:** $q_{n+1}=q^{(1)}+\tfrac h2M^{-1}p^{(2)}$.
5. **B half kick:** $p_{n+1}=p^{(2)}-\tfrac h2\nabla V(q_{n+1})$.

The output is $(q_{n+1},p_{n+1})$. If any required gradient is undefined or any input violates $h>0$, $\beta>0$, $\gamma>0$, or positive definiteness of $M$, return `failure` without an updated state. For a differentiable $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ and finite valid state, both gradient calls are defined; reusing the stored value $\nabla V(q_{n+1})$ as the next step's first force means one new force evaluation per subsequent step. The random-vector cost is one fresh $d$-dimensional standard normal per step.

derivations.claim: Choose an integer $p\ge0$ and $K<\infty$ such that $|D^j\phi(z)|\le K(1+|z|^p)$ for $0\le j\le6$, and put $W_r(z)=(1+|z|^2)^{r/2}$. For a bounded $C_b^6$ family choose $p=0$ and a common $K$. The explicit A and B maps are $(q,p_0)\mapsto(q+sM^{-1}p_0,p_0)$ and $(q,p_0)\mapsto(q,p_0+sF(q))$, where $F=-\nabla V$. They have linear growth and uniformly bounded spatial derivatives of orders one through six for $0\le s\le1$, because $D^jF$ is bounded for $1\le j\le6$. The O map is affine with centered Gaussian noise of uniformly bounded moments of every fixed order by [F2]. Differentiating these explicit maps and taking Gaussian expectations therefore shows that each $P_s^C$, $C\in\{A,B,O\}$, preserves bounds $|D^j\psi(z)|\le K_0W_r(z)$ through any stated order $k\le6$, uniformly for $s\le1$. Each generator maps such bounds through order $k$ to bounds through order $k-2$ with weight $W_{r+1}$: its drift coefficients grow at most linearly, their positive-order derivatives are bounded, and its second-order coefficients are constant. Thus a composition with at most three generator applications, even with subflow semigroups between them, uses at most six test derivatives and is bounded by $CW_{p+3}(z)$.

For any $r\ge0$, direct differentiation of $W_r$ and the linear-growth drift and constant diffusion give $|LW_r|\le C_rW_r$. Itô's formula [F3] stopped on a ball, the integral Gronwall estimate, and Fatou [F5] as the stopping radius increases give $P_uW_r(z)\le C_rW_r(z)$ for $0\le u\le1$. These are estimates from a fixed deterministic starting point; higher weights can be used to justify the localization limits. In particular, $|L^3\phi(z)|\le CW_{p+3}(z)$ by the same coefficient and derivative count as in step 1.1, and $|P_uL^3\phi(z)|\le CW_{p+3}(z)$. For the bounded-test branch this is the cubic weight $W_3$, using the same Lyapunov function with exponent $3/2$, not a higher initial-moment assumption.

Applying the localized Itô integral identity successively to $\phi$, $L\phi$ and $L^2\phi$ in which the three test functions have respectively six, four and two continuous spatial derivatives, gives the following identity. [A1, F3, F4, F5, given, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]
$$P_h\phi=\phi+hL\phi+\tfrac12h^2L^2\phi+\tfrac12\int_0^h(h-u)^2P_uL^3\phi\,du.$$
The polynomial bounds from steps 1.1 and 2.1 justify taking expectations and removing the stopping times in these three identities. Step 2.1 bounds the remainder by $Ch^3W_{p+3}(z)$.

Subtracting steps 2.2 and 3.1 cancels all terms through order two and gives $|K_h\phi(z)-P_h\phi(z)|\le Ch^3W_{p+3}(z)\le C'h^3(1+|z|^{p+3})$. This proves the original polynomial-growth claim with some finite exponent. When the test family has a common $C_b^6$ bound, $p=0$ in every preceding estimate, so the same argument proves the uniform cubic-growth bound $Ch^3(1+|z|^3)$. Neither conclusion is an invariant-measure statement.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Put $W_s(z)=(1+|z|^2)^s$ for integer $s\ge1$. The drift $b$ has linear growth and bounded derivatives of positive order, and $G$ is constant, so $|LW_s(z)|\le C_sW_s(z)$. Applying [F4] to the solution stopped on radius $R$, taking expectations and applying Gronwall gives $\mathbb EW_s(Z_{t\wedge\tau_R})\le e^{C_st}\mathbb EW_s(Z_0)$; Fatou’s lemma [F6] as $R\to\infty$ gives uniformly bounded exact moments through order six on $[0,T]$. Each B or A stage has the form $z+h\delta(z)$ with $|\delta(z)|\le C(1+|z|)$, hence the mean-value formula and Young’s inequality give $W_s(z+h\delta(z))\le(1+Ch)W_s(z)+Ch$. In the O stage $p$ becomes $ap+\eta$; conditional terms linear in $\eta$ vanish and terms of degree $j\ge2$ have moments at most $C_jh^{j/2}$, so Young’s inequality gives the same stage bound. Composing five stages and iterating over $Nh=T$ yields $\max_{n\le N}\mathbb EW_s(Z_n^B)\le C_T$ for $s\le3$.

For $0\le t\le T$, the solution flow is differentiable through order six in its initial state. The first derivative solves $\dot J=Db(Z_t)J$; each higher derivative solves the same linear equation with forcing a finite sum of products of lower flow derivatives and bounded derivatives of $b$. Induction and Gronwall bound these derivatives uniformly. Differentiating $P_t\phi(z)=\mathbb E\phi(Z_t^z)$ under expectation is justified by bounded derivatives of $\phi$ and the flow bounds, so $P_t\phi$ has bounded derivatives through order six uniformly. Together with the Markov bound $\|P_t\phi\|_\infty\le\|\phi\|_\infty$, these derivative estimates give a common $C_b^6$ bound for $\psi_n=P_{T-t_{n+1}}\phi$. Apply precisely the bounded-test branch of [F2], whose cubic weight is uniform in $n,N$; no generic polynomial-growth exponent is substituted.

Let $K_h$ be the BAOAB transition and $P_h$ the exact transition. Inserting one exact transition at a time and using the Markov property gives [A1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]
$$\mathbb E\phi(Z_N^B)-\mathbb E\phi(Z_T)=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mathbb E\bigl[(K_h-P_h)P_{T-t_{n+1}}\phi(Z_n^B)\bigr].$$
By [F2] and step 2.1, each summand has absolute value at most $Ch^3\mathbb E(1+|Z_n^B|^3)\le C_T h^3$ using the $s=2$ moment bound in step 1.1. Summing $N=T/h$ terms gives $C_TNh^3=C_TTh^2$. The result is finite-time weak order two and says nothing about invariant bias.

Let $d=1$, $M=m>0$, $V(q)=kq^2/2$ with $k>0$, and $\beta,\gamma,h>0$. Put
$$\omega^2=\frac{k}{m},\qquad r=\frac{h^2\omega^2}{4}=\frac{h^2k}{4m},\qquad a=e^{-\gamma h}.$$
For $0<h<2\sqrt{m/k}$, the BAOAB chain of [[alg-baoab-underdamped-langevin-splitting]] has the unique invariant law
$$\begin{pmatrix}Q\\P\end{pmatrix}\sim N_2\!\left(0,\begin{pmatrix}(\beta k)^{-1}&0\\0&(m/\beta)(1-r)\end{pmatrix}\right).$$
Thus the position variance is exactly the canonical Gibbs variance $1/(\beta k)$, while the momentum variance has bias $-h^2k/(4\beta)$ relative to the canonical value $m/\beta$. The linear transition matrix $A$ in proof step 1.2 has spectral radius $\rho(A):=\max\{|\lambda|:\lambda\text{ is a complex eigenvalue of }A\}$ less than one exactly for $0<h<2\sqrt{m/k}$; at equality its spectral radius is one, and for $h>2\sqrt{m/k}$ the chain has no invariant probability law. No conclusion about nonquadratic potentials or general BAOAB superconvergence follows from this harmonic calculation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$ be finite, let $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be symmetric positive definite (that is, $x^TMx>0$ for every nonzero $x$), and let $\beta,\gamma>0$. Then $M$ is invertible, and $M^{1/2}$ denotes its unique symmetric positive square root. Let $W_t$ be standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to a complete usual filtration, and let $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. The **underdamped Langevin equation** is the It\^o SDE on phase space $\mathbb R^d_q\times\mathbb R^d_p$
$$dQ_t=M^{-1}P_t\,dt,\qquad dP_t=-\nabla V(Q_t)\,dt-\gamma P_t\,dt+\sqrt{2\gamma\beta^{-1}}\,M^{1/2}dW_t.$$
Its Hamiltonian is $H(q,p)=\tfrac12p^TM^{-1}p+V(q)$. If $Z=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}e^{-\beta H(q,p)}\,dq\,dp$ is finite and positive, the **canonical Gibbs probability** is the probability measure with density $\rho(q,p)=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H(q,p)}$ with respect to $2d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. This definition alone asserts no stationarity or ergodicity.

For the finite-time order results below, $D^jV$ denotes the $j$th derivative as a multilinear map. The notation $C_b^k$ means that a function and each of its derivatives through order $k$ are continuous and bounded. The notation $C_P^k$ means that a function and each of its derivatives through order $k$ are continuous and bounded by $C(1+|z|^r)$ for some finite constants $C,r$ that may depend on the derivative. These growth conventions are used only where stated.
citations.use_explanation: [F1] records the exact local interface used here: : a canonical Gibbs probability requires a finite positive normalizing integral $Z=\int e^{-\beta H(q,p)}dq\,dp$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $a\le b$ and $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]). The function $f$ is
**absolutely continuous** on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$\delta>0$ such that every finite family of subintervals
$[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, indexed by $j<m$, whose open interiors are pairwise
disjoint and which satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}(v_j-u_j)<\delta$$

also satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}|f(v_j)-f(u_j)|<\varepsilon.$$

Finite sums and the empty sum are those of [[def-finite-sum]] and
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. For $m=0$ both sums are $0$, so the condition is
automatic. On $[a,a]$ every permitted interval is a singleton and every endpoint
increment is $0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), so every function on that singleton is
absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity implies ordinary continuity
([[def-continuity-real]]); that implication is proved next rather than built into
the definition.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F,G\in AC[a,b]$,
$$\int_a^bFG'+\int_a^bF'G=F(b)G(b)-F(a)G(a).$$

Throughout, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$ is written
$\lambda_n$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]), and
$\mathbb Z\subseteq\mathbb R$ is the copy of the integers
([[def-integers]]).

**The torus.** Let $q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the
canonical projection of the quotient of the additive group $\mathbb R$ by its
subgroup $\mathbb Z$, carrying the quotient topology
([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-topological-space]]); we write
$[t]:=q(t)=t+\mathbb Z$. Thus $[s]=[t]$ exactly when $s-t\in\mathbb Z$. The map
$q$ is continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and $\mathbb T$ is a compact
Hausdorff space homeomorphic to the Euclidean unit circle.

**Fundamental domain.** Every class has exactly one representative in $[0,1)$:
for $t\in\mathbb R$ the integer part $n=\lfloor t\rfloor$ satisfies
$n\le t<n+1$, so $t-n\in[0,1)$ represents $[t]$ ([[lem-integer-part]]); and if
$s,t\in[0,1)$ satisfy $s-t\in\mathbb Z$, then $|s-t|<1$ forces $s=t$.
Consequently the map $[0,1)\to\mathbb T$, $t\mapsto[t]$, is a bijection.

**Topological checks.** The closed interval $[0,1]$ is compact by [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and maps onto $\mathbb T$, so the quotient is compact by [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. The map $t\mapsto(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)$ is continuous by [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], and is constant on quotient fibres by [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]. It induces a continuous map $\varphi:\mathbb T\to S^1$ by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]]. The bijection of $[0,2\pi)$ with the circle in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]], together with the unique representatives in $[0,1)$, makes $\varphi$ bijective. The Euclidean circle is Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]], so the compact-to-Hausdorff clause of [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]] makes $\varphi$ a homeomorphism. In particular $\mathbb T$ is Hausdorff.

The map $q$ is open: for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R$, its saturation $q^{-1}[q[U]]=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}(U+k)$ is open. The images under $q$ of rational-endpoint open intervals form a countable base: if $q(t)\in V$ with $V$ open, choose such an interval containing $t$ and contained in $q^{-1}[V]$. Its image is an open neighbourhood contained in $V$.

**The measure.** For a Borel set $E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) the preimage $q^{-1}[E]$ is a Borel subset of
$\mathbb R$, because $q$ is continuous
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]), hence Lebesgue
measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). Define

$$m_{\mathbb T}(E):=\lambda_1\bigl(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)\bigr) ,$$

the value at $q^{-1}[E]$ of the same-ambient restriction of $\lambda_1$ to $[0,1)$
([[def-restriction-of-a-measure]]).

This is a measure on $\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$ by [[prop-restriction-is-a-measure]]:
the assignment $E\mapsto\lambda_1(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1))$ is the composition of the
restriction measure with the inverse image along $q$, and inverse images preserve
the empty set, complements and countable unions, while countable additivity is
that of $\lambda_1$. It is a **probability measure**:
$m_{\mathbb T}(\mathbb T)=\lambda_1([0,1))=1$
([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]). Thus
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T})$ is a probability measure space
([[def-measure-space]], [[def-measure]]).

**The integral.** For a Borel measurable $F:\mathbb T\to[0,+\infty]$, define

$$\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}:=\int_{[0,1)}F\circ q\,d\lambda_1 .$$

The defining integral is meaningful because $F\circ q$ is Borel
([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]],
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]). The assignment agrees with
$E\mapsto m_{\mathbb T}(E)$ on indicators, and it is additive and homogeneous on
finite nonnegative simple functions; for a sequence $0\le F_0\le F_1\le\cdots$
with $F_n\uparrow F$ pointwise the identity passes to the limit because
$F_n\circ q\uparrow F\circ q$ and monotone convergence holds for $\lambda_1$
([[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]],
[[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]). For real or complex integrable
$F$ the integral is defined by decomposition into nonnegative parts or into real
and imaginary parts, and it is linear
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]],
[[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]). In particular
$\int_{\mathbb T}1\,dm_{\mathbb T}=1$, and the same formula holds with $[0,1)$
replaced by any half-open interval $[a,a+1)$ or $(a,a+1]$, by the periodicity of
$q^{-1}[E]$ and the translation invariance of $\lambda_1$
([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]).

**Translation invariance.** For $y\in\mathbb R$ the map
$\tau_y:\mathbb T\to\mathbb T$, $\tau_y([t]):=[t+y]$, is well defined (if
$s-t\in\mathbb Z$ then $(s+y)-(t+y)\in\mathbb Z$) and continuous, because it is
induced by the continuous map $t\mapsto q(t+y)$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb T$. This composite is constant on the fibres of $q$, since $q(t)=q(s)$ implies $q(t+y)=q(s+y)$ ([[thm-quotient-universal-property]]). It preserves
$m_{\mathbb T}$: write $y=n+r$ with $n=\lfloor y\rfloor$ and $r\in[0,1)$, put
$A:=q^{-1}[E]$ and use that $A-n=A$ and that
$A\cap[0,1)=\bigl(A\cap[0,r)\bigr)\cup\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)$ while
$A\cap[r,r+1)=\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)\cup\bigl((A\cap[0,r))+1\bigr)$, so that

$$m_{\mathbb T}(\tau_y^{-1}E)=\lambda_1\bigl((A-y)\cap[0,1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[r,r+1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[0,1)\bigr)=m_{\mathbb T}(E),$$

the middle equality by translation invariance of $\lambda_1$. Hence
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T},\tau_y)$ is a measure-preserving
system for every $y$, and the published integral-invariance theorem gives
$\int_{\mathbb T}F\circ\tau_y\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}$
for every measurable $F\ge0$ and every integrable $F$
([[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]],
[[thm-integrals-are-invariant-under-measure-preserving-maps]]). This is the
**normalized Haar integral** of $\mathbb T$; abstract Haar theory is not
invoked.

**The finite torus.** For a natural $n\ge1$ put
$\mathbb T^n:=\mathbb R^n/\mathbb Z^n$ with the quotient topology of the
canonical projection $q_n$, and define

$$m_{\mathbb T^n}(E):=\lambda_n\bigl(q_n^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)^n\bigr),\qquad \int_{\mathbb T^n}F\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}:=\int_{[0,1)^n}F\circ q_n\,d\lambda_n .$$

Coordinatewise integer parts give unique representatives in $[0,1)^n$, and the continuous quotient map sends the compact cube $[0,1]^n$ onto $\mathbb T^n$. Compactness of the cube follows from [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], and compactness of its image follows from [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. Preimages of Borel sets are Borel; disjoint preimages and countable additivity make the displayed set function a measure, and the box formula gives total mass one. The integral identity follows from indicators, increasing simple approximation and decomposition exactly as in one dimension. For translation invariance, discard the integer parts of the translation vector, split each coordinate of $[0,1)^n$ at its fractional part, and translate the resulting $2^n$ disjoint half-open boxes by integer vectors to partition the translated cube. The periodic preimage set is unchanged by these integer vectors; finite additivity and Lebesgue translation invariance give the same measure. Applying the indicator identity, simple approximation and decomposition gives the integral formula on any translated cube. The coordinate projections induce a continuous bijection
$\Phi:\mathbb T^n\to(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^n$ by the universal property. Its
domain is compact by the preceding check, while its codomain is a finite
product of Hausdorff spaces and hence Hausdorff ([[lem-products-preserve-t0-t1-and-hausdorff]]); the continuous-bijection
theorem therefore makes $\Phi$ a homeomorphism. Thus $\mathbb T^n$ carries the
finite product topology ([[def-product-topology]],
[[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]],
[[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), and its characters
$x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, are defined on this compact
Hausdorff space: replacing representatives by integer vectors leaves the exponential unchanged by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and the trigonometric period. Finite products of the countable base above form a countable rectangular base. Hence every product-open set is a countable union of Borel rectangles. Conversely coordinate projections are continuous, so Borel rectangles are Borel in the product. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb T^n$. On a product $A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1}$ of Borel subsets
of the factors, the defining fundamental-domain formula and repeated application of [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] give
$m_{\mathbb T^n}(A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1})=\prod_jm_{\mathbb T}(A_j)$, so
$m_{\mathbb T^n}$ agrees on every measurable rectangle with the product measure
$m_{\mathbb T}\times\cdots\times m_{\mathbb T}$
([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]); both are probability measures,
and uniqueness of the product measure on sigma-finite spaces identifies them
on the entire Borel sigma-algebra
([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
Fubini's theorem then computes iterated integrals of $L^1$ functions on
$\mathbb T^n$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: Let $m=\mathbb E[g(U)]$ and $h(x)=g(a+Lx)-m$ for $0\le x\le1$. Define $H(t)=h(2t)$ for $0\le t\le1/2$ and $H(t)=h(2-2t)$ for $1/2\le t\le1$, then extend $H$ periodically to $\mathbb T$. The two absolutely continuous pieces match at $t=1/2$, and $H(0)=H(1)$. A finite paste of absolutely continuous pieces with matching endpoint values is absolutely continuous: split every interval crossing the junction into its at most two pieces and apply [F1] on each piece with half the error tolerance. Thus $H$ is absolutely continuous on the period interval. Its mean is zero, $\|H\|_{L^2(\mathbb T)}^2=\operatorname{Var}(g(U))$, and affine changes of variables give $\|H'\|_{L^2(\mathbb T)}^2=4L^2\mathbb E|g'(U)|^2$.

For each integer $n$, apply integration by parts [F2] to $H(t)e^{-2\pi int}$ on $[0,1]$, taking real and imaginary parts. The boundary term vanishes since $H(0)=H(1)$ and $e^{-2\pi in}=1$, giving $\widehat{H'}(n)=2\pi in\widehat H(n)$. Parseval [F4] and the zero mean in step 1.1 yield $$\|H'\|_2^2=\sum_{n\ne0}4\pi^2n^2|\widehat H(n)|^2\ge4\pi^2\sum_{n\ne0}|\widehat H(n)|^2=4\pi^2\|H\|_2^2.$$ Substituting the two norm identities from step 1.1 and dividing by $4\pi^2$ proves the claimed bound. Equality holds for $g(x)=\cos(\pi(x-a)/L)$: its mean is zero, its variance is $1/2$, and its derivative second moment is $\pi^2/(2L^2)$. Hence the constant $L^2/\pi^2$ is sharp.

Let $d\ge1$ be finite, let $(E_j,\mathcal E_j,\mu_j)$ be probability spaces,
and let $(E,\mathcal E,\mu)=\prod_{j=1}^d(E_j,\mathcal E_j,\mu_j)$ be their
finite product with product sigma-algebra and product probability. Write
$[d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}$. For $J\subseteq[d]$, let $E_J$ and $\mu_J$ denote the
corresponding coordinate product; the empty product is a one-point probability
space. For real $f\in L^2(\mu)$, define the coordinate average
$$P_Jf(x_J)=\int_{E_{[d]\setminus J}}f(x_J,z_{[d]\setminus J})\,d\mu_{[d]\setminus J}(z_{[d]\setminus J})$$
for almost every $x_J$ for which the section is integrable, and assign zero on
the exceptional null set. Regard $P_Jf$ also as a function on the full product
that is constant in the coordinates outside $J$. The conventions are
$P_{[d]}f=f$ as an $L^2$ class and $P_\varnothing f=\int f\,d\mu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

derivations.claim: Let $f\in L^2(\mu)$. Tonelli applied to $|f|^2$ shows that for almost every $x_J$, the section $z\mapsto f(x_J,z)$ is square-integrable on the complementary probability space. Cauchy–Schwarz with the constant function $1$ makes that section integrable, so [F1] defines its average there. If representatives $f$ and $\tilde f$ agree almost everywhere, Tonelli applied to $|f-\tilde f|^2$ shows their sections agree almost everywhere for almost every $x_J$; their averages therefore define the same almost-sure class. Fubini gives measurability of the section-average function.

On almost every section, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|P_Jf(x_J)|^2\le\int|f(x_J,z)|^2\,d\mu_{-J}(z)$ because $\mu_{-J}$ has mass one. Integrating in $x_J$ and using Tonelli yields $\|P_Jf\|_2^2\le\|f\|_2^2$, so $P_J$ is a contraction. Averaging a function already independent of $z_{-J}$ leaves it unchanged, hence $P_J^2=P_J$.

For $f,g\in L^2$, Cauchy–Schwarz makes $fg$ integrable. Fubini in the two groups of coordinates gives $\langle P_Jf,g\rangle=\int_{E_J}(P_Jf)(P_Jg)\,d\mu_J=\langle f,P_Jg\rangle$. Thus $P_J$ is self-adjoint.

Applying $P_K$ and then $P_J$ integrates over the coordinates outside $K$, then over the coordinates in $K\setminus J$. Repeated finite-product Fubini permits this order and identifies the iterated integral with integration over the complement of $J\cap K$. The equality holds almost everywhere by [F3], including when either set is empty or full, so $P_JP_Kf=P_{J\cap K}f$ in $L^2$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

$d\ge1$ be finite and let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_d)$ be any jointly distributed
finite family of random elements. Let $Y=f(X)\in L^2(\mathbb P)$, and put
$V=\operatorname{Var}(Y)$. For $S\subseteq[d]$, set
$\mathcal G_S=\sigma(X_j:j\in S)$, with $\mathcal G_\varnothing=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$, and
$$v(S)=\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal G_S]).$$
If $V>0$, let $\mathfrak S_d$ be the set of all $d!$ permutations of $[d]$,
and let $P_i^\pi$ contain the indices occurring before $i$ in $\pi$. The
**Shapley effect** of coordinate $i$ under this convention is
$$\phi_i=\frac{1}{d!\,V}\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak S_d}\bigl(v(P_i^\pi\cup\{i\})-v(P_i^\pi)\bigr).$$
If $V=0$, the normalized effects are undefined. This definition is for
dependent inputs as well as independent ones; the independent Sobol ANOVA

variance game of [[def-dependent-input-shapley-effects]].

1. Initialize $A_i=0$ for every $i\in[d]$.
2. For each of the $d!$ permutations $\pi$, traverse its entries in order. Start
